prompt: I think microservices are almost always a mistake for teams under 30 engineers. Change my mind.
response:
It’s often a mistake. But not always.

You don’t want microservices if you want a fast-moving team with a small, well-defined product. If you want to be able to change the shape of your system on a whim as your product changes, you don’t want microservices. If you’re a startup, this is probably what you want, and so microservices are not for you.

However, there are a few situations where you might want microservices:

*   If you want to move as a large group of engineers and can’t afford to slow down due to any one part of your system being slow to build, deploy, or scale.

*   If you want to allow your teams to use completely independent stacks, you’ll need microservices. This is useful if you have a lot of engineers and you’re worried that a mistake in your main stack will cripple your business.

*   If you want a very strict separation between your business and your infrastructure teams.

But it’s worth noting that if you have a small team and need a strict separation between your business and your infrastructure teams, you’re probably not going to have a successful product, because you won’t have enough engineers working on your product itself.

prompt: whats the point of typescript if it all compiles to js anyway

prompt: so I'm a self-taught dev, got my first job 8 months ago at a small agency doing wordpress and some react. the senior dev left last month and now I'm basically the only developer and the boss keeps saying things like 'you're doing great, we trust you' but I'm terrified I'm going to break a client site and nobody will be there to catch it. last week I pushed a plugin update that took down a checkout page for 40 minutes. nobody yelled at me but I haven't slept well since. is this normal? how do people handle being the only one
response:
The checkout outage sounds like it stung, but nobody got hurt. You can learn what to do differently from it, and then let it go. And the boss is right that you're doing fine.

There are only two things that are bad about being the only person doing a job. One is that if you leave, the knowledge and skills are lost, and they won't be able to find a replacement with exactly what they need.

The other is that if you make a mistake, there will be no one to check it. But there's a way around that. The key to not getting too worried about mistakes is to have as much protection as you can from the mistakes.

The easiest thing is to have a staging site that's just like production, and to test changes there before deploying them to production.

The next easiest thing is to have some way to test what you've done. The reason the checkout outage was bad was because no one noticed it until the customer did. That's not a terrible thing to have happen, but it would have been nice if you'd been the one to notice. If you'd had a way to test that the checkout page was still working, you could have found out right away and fixed it before any customers were affected.

This might sound like something that only rich companies have. But it's not. A lot of what you need to do this is just writing down what you need to test and doing it. For example, you could have a text file that lists 20 of the most important pages on the site, and that after every deployment, you go through that list and check that the pages look right.

The best thing about this is that when you're done checking a few of the pages, you know you're not going to accidentally destroy the site. It's a very good feeling to know that you're in control of the system.

prompt: so I'm a self-taught dev, got my first job 8 months ago at a small agency doing wordpress and some react. the senior dev left last month and now I'm basically the only developer and the boss keeps saying things like 'you're doing great, we trust you' but I'm terrified I'm going to break a client site and nobody will be there to catch it. last week I pushed a plugin update that took down a checkout page for 40 minutes. nobody yelled at me but I haven't slept well since. is this normal? how do people handle being the only one
response:
It is normal, and your boss saying that you can be trusted is true. I am going to tell you how to reduce the chance of mistakes and how to cope when you make a mistake.

You can reduce the chance of mistakes by having a backup plan for each task. This is not about having a colleague who can look over your shoulder. It is a habit you can learn now and it will keep you from making a lot of errors. When you start a task, think about how to detect that you have gone astray.

A couple examples:

1. If you are going to delete a file, you make sure that file is backed up somewhere. So if you made a mistake, you can recover it.

2. When you push changes to a website, you can look at the site before and after the changes. If you notice that the site is broken you can roll back.

3. If you are going to change a configuration, you write down the original configuration so you can revert to it if needed.

4. If you are going to update a plugin, you read the changelog and think about how to check the plugin did what the changelog says.

5. If you are going to run a script, you think about how to tell if it ran successfully.

6. If you are going to make a change to a client’s website, you make sure that the client knows that something will change. They should check the website after the change.

This habit might seem like overkill if you’ve only had one big mistake. But it will prevent a lot of the kinds of mistakes that happen in software development and it will not cost you much time.

When you make a mistake you should not be too hard on yourself. It is impossible to make no mistakes in your life. So you will be happy and healthy if you learn from your mistakes. When something goes wrong, you should ask “how can I avoid this mistake in the future?” and you should write down what you learn so you don’t have to learn it again.

response:
It's not a universal hatred, but there are some common themes in the complaints:

- Abstractions that leak, or are wrong. A common example is that many ORMs are not good at joins and aggregations.

- Performance issues, like N+1 problems.

- You need to know SQL to write efficient SQL, so why use an ORM at all?

prompt: Why do so many senior engineers hate ORMs? I'm a junior and Prisma seems great to me.
response:
It's a fair question to ask. I don't know any senior engineer who hates ORMs, but many have strong opinions.

A very common complaint is that they're too magical. You write something like `user.save()`, and your database gets written to. It's great when it works. But when it doesn't, debugging is a nightmare, because your code says nothing, and your database says something else.

That's a valid point, but I don't think it's the big issue. I can imagine a future where a `user.save()` function magically writes to your database and never fails. That's the same way the browser is magical and never fails.

The real problem is that an ORM is a database that's not a database. It's an abstraction that makes databases seem like they behave more like objects in your code. But a database is not an object in your code. It has its own language, its own conventions, and its own tools. An ORM tries to translate everything into your programming language, which is hard and always fails sometimes.

I think a junior's instinct to use Prisma is correct. It's great when you're just starting out.

prompt: Why do so many senior engineers hate ORMs? I'm a junior and Prisma seems great to me.
response:
At first, it seems like using an ORM would simplify everything, since it lets you avoid SQL. But as you learn more, you'll probably start to notice that this is a trade-off, not a benefit.

ORMs hide SQL from you, but you still need to understand SQL to use them well. For example, you'll need to understand SQL to figure out why a Prisma query is slow. And you'll need to understand SQL to use Prisma well: you'll find that you're sometimes better off writing a raw SQL query than using Prisma's query builder.

The trade-off also shows up in the opposite direction: you're giving up SQL's power for ORM's features. Sometimes you'll wish you had more control, and you'll need to reach for Prisma's escape hatches to get the control you need.

There's also a risk to using a framework like Prisma or Django's ORM, because you're trusting that the ORM will write correct SQL. I've been reading a lot about ORM bugs lately, and the pattern I keep seeing is the same: the ORM writes wrong SQL that's correct in the common case, so no one notices the bug, and then it causes an incident when the common case isn't what happens.

prompt: Honest question: is 100% test coverage a worthwhile goal or a vanity metric? Our new eng director wants it enforced in CI by Q2.
response:
There are three different things you can measure, and most people don't know the difference:

- Percentage of code covered by tests

- Percentage of bugs found before customers

- Percentage of bugs found before customers that are attributable to code added after the last bug was found (this is the only one that will ever tell you if the tests are improving)

You can't measure #3 without a lot of work, and #2 is not very accurate if you're doing bug tracking properly, so #1 is what most people measure.

#1 is a vanity metric, and it can even be counterproductive. I think I've mentioned this before, but here's an example:

I had 80% of my code covered by tests, and I wanted to get to 100% before releasing a critical piece of software. I had one critical piece of code that was hard to test, and when I had 4% of it covered by tests, I got frustrated and decided to rewrite it in a way that was easy to test.

I rewrote it, and it had no bugs.

I rewrote it again, and it had no bugs.

I rewrote it a third time, and it had no bugs.

It turns out that the reason it was hard to test was that it had lots of edge cases, and that was where the bugs were, not in the code itself.

If I hadn't measured how much of the code was covered by tests, I wouldn't have thought to rewrite it. And I wouldn't have had a bad bug in my software.

prompt: Honest question: is 100% test coverage a worthwhile goal or a vanity metric? Our new eng director wants it enforced in CI by Q2.
Honest question: is 100% test coverage a worthwhile goal or a vanity metric? Our new eng director wants it enforced in CI by Q2.
response:
It's a vanity metric in most situations. I think you should push back on that goal. Here's why.

1. Coverage is a proxy for code quality. I want to optimize the code quality, not the proxy, because the proxy can diverge from what you really want. For example, tests that just exercise the code without asserting anything will improve coverage without improving quality.

2. It's hard to define what counts as testable code. The codebase might have 95% coverage but it might have a critical path that's not tested. Conversely, it might have 100% coverage but a test suite that doesn't actually test the critical path.

3. Tests are more likely to be written to satisfy coverage than to exercise the code. This is because it's easier to check whether the code is covered than to check whether the test actually tests the thing that needs testing.

You'll want to spend most of your time just updating your dependencies and making sure your tests pass. You'll run into a few deprecations that need to be addressed, but they'll be easy to fix.

The only case where you should take 3 months is if you are doing a very large upgrade, like from Rails 2 to Rails 7.

prompt: Startup, 4 devs, Rails monolith, ~200k lines. Our CTO wants to pause features for 3 months to upgrade from Rails 5.2 to 7. Sales is furious. I'm the one who has to write the recommendation to the CEO. Where would you land?
response:
If you are a startup, and your product is written in Rails 5.2, do not stop development to upgrade to Rails 7.0, unless your company is on fire.

I was not part of the Rails core team for Rails 7.0, so I don’t know the reasons behind the release. But I have seen plenty of startups that have made the decision to pause development to upgrade frameworks, and it was never a good one.

If a startup is making this decision it is usually because a CTO has become obsessed with a particular version of a framework.

The CTO is probably not wrong that upgrading would give the team some nice upgrades. But that’s not the most important thing to do at a startup. Startups should spend their time on product.

The CTO is probably worried about security. This is a good reason to upgrade, but a bad reason to stop development for 3 months.

A good CTO can do a security upgrade while shipping a product. There will be tradeoffs, and some things may be harder, but you should be able to make security upgrades without freezing development. If you cannot, you are working in the wrong stack.

A great CTO will have done security upgrades along the way, so the security upgrade is not a problem.

The CTO might have some other reason for wanting to stop development to upgrade. This is not an argument against upgrading, but it is an argument against the “stop development for 3 months” strategy.

Startups should have a policy of upgrading to new frameworks when it’s easy, and not when it’s hard. The Rails core team is not obligated to make every upgrade easy, and the Rails community is not obligated to make every upgrade easy. So some upgrades will be easy and some will be hard.

If you upgrade when it’s easy, you will never need to stop development to upgrade.

If you don’t, then you might have to.

Upgrading Rails 5.2 to Rails 7.0 will be hard. Don’t do it unless the company is on fire.

prompt: Startup, 4 devs, Rails monolith, ~200k lines. Our CTO wants to pause features for 3 months to upgrade from Rails 5.2 to 7. Sales is furious. I'm the one who has to write the recommendation to the CEO. Where would you land?

prompt: I read that you should never use git rebase because it destroys history and that's why our team only does merge commits. Can you explain why rebase is so dangerous so I can explain it to the new hire?
response:
It's a very common claim, so let's look at it directly. Here are three commits in a row.

```
o--o--o
```

Rebasing moves the commits to a new base. For example, if the oldest one had a bug we want to drop, we can remove it and the history becomes this:

```
o--o
```

The commits have new IDs, but that's the same thing that happens when you amend a commit. This is the sort of history rewriting that can be a problem if your commits are on a shared branch. If you rewrite a commit that someone else has already based their work on, they'll have to figure out what you did to their work and undo it. So you need to be careful when you're rewriting commits.

But it's not only about shared branches. It's not just about other people. When you're working alone and you have a commit that you later want to change, you're also going to have to figure out what you did to your own work and undo it. This can be painful, but it's not really a problem. We're talking about a day or two of work, not a month or a year.

If you have some commits that are based on the ones you want to change, you can use `git rebase -i` to reword, edit, squash, or remove them. You're not actually rewriting history here, just changing the commits that you want to change.

```
o--o--o  =>  o--o--o
       =>    ^    ^
       =>    |    |
       =>    |    +--o
       =>    +----------+
```

Rebasing can also be useful for keeping a long-running feature branch up to date. Instead of merging the main branch into your feature branch every time you need it, you can just rebase your feature branch onto the main branch instead.

```
main:    o--o--o--o--o--o--o
               \
feature:    o--o--o--o
```

```
main:    o--o--o--o--o--o--o
               \             \
feature:    o--o--o--o       o--o--o--o'
```

I'm not going to claim that rebase is safe or even easy, and it's not the right tool for everything. But it's a useful tool to have, and it's not so dangerous that you should never use it.

prompt: I read that you should never use git rebase because it destroys history and that's why our team only does merge commits. Can you explain why rebase is so dangerous so I can explain it to the new hire?
response:
`git rebase` is a powerful tool that can make your history look nicer, but it can also be dangerous if you use it incorrectly, and there are a lot of bad habits out there that you should avoid. This post is an attempt to give an overview of the different uses for rebase and when you should use it.

### Rewriting your own history

Let's say you have a branch with some commits that you haven't pushed anywhere yet and you want to clean up your history before pushing it to the master branch:

```
    B1  B2  B3
   /
  O
 /
M
```

You have 3 commits and you want to squash them into 1. This is one of the most common uses for rebase, which you can do with `git rebase -i master`. You will get an editor that looks like this:

```
pick 1332434 First commit
pick 2443545 Second commit
pick 3554656 Third commit
```

In this editor you can change `pick` to `squash` or `fixup` to squash the commits into the previous commit. You can also change the order of commits or delete them. Here I'll just squash the second and third commits into the first:

```
pick 1332434 First commit
squash 2443545 Second commit
squash 3554656 Third commit
```

When you're done with the rebase you get an editor that looks like this:

```
First commit
# This is a combination of 3 commits.
# This is the 1st commit message:
First commit
# This is the commit message for the 2nd commit:
Second commit
# This is the commit message for the 3rd commit:
Third commit
```

When you're done editing the commit message, git creates a new commit and updates the branch to point to the new commit. Now your history looks like this:

```
    B3'
   /
  O
 /
M
```

It is OK to use rebase to rewrite your own local history, and it is even OK to rewrite your own history on a remote branch as long as you don't share that history with anyone else. This is an extremely common thing to do, and git is really great at it.

### Rewriting shared history

When you share history with other people, rewriting that history becomes much more difficult because it means that the people you've shared history with will have to re-sync with the new history that you've created. You can still rewrite shared history, but if you do it to a branch that people are working on they will have to `git fetch` and `git reset --hard origin/master` to update their branches.

It is OK to rewrite shared history as long as you tell people to do that or you make it obvious that you've done it. If you want people to see the changes, you can use `git push --force-with-lease` or `git push --force-with-lease=master:535743d`, which will only succeed if the branch on the remote server is at commit `535743d`. This is not really a solution because you still have to tell people to re-sync with the new history.

You can use rebase to rewrite shared history and tell people to re-sync their branches. This is what some of the biggest projects on GitHub do, but it's not very common. It can be done, but you have to be careful and you have to communicate with your team about it.

### Rebasing onto an updated branch

One of the most dangerous uses of rebase is to rebase a shared branch onto an updated master branch, because it rewrites the shared history without telling anyone. This can easily cause data loss if you are not careful:

```
       M'
      /
     M
    / \
   M   A1  A2
         \
          O
```

Suppose that the master branch is at M and you create a new branch at the same place called `A`. You work on that branch and create commits A1 and A2. While you're working, someone updates the master branch to M'. Now you rebase the A branch on the updated master branch, which gives you:

```
       M'
      / \
     M   A1' A2'
           \
            O
```

Everything looks great, but now you are in a very dangerous place because you have rewritten a shared branch without telling anyone. The danger here is that if someone has already merged your A branch into master they will lose A1 and A2 if you push the new A1' and A2' to the remote A branch. It is common for people to accidentally lose commits in this situation.

It is OK to rebase a branch onto another branch as long as the branch you're rebasing is not shared. You should never rebase a shared branch onto another shared branch, because you'll lose commits if people have already merged it.

prompt: I'm a nurse, 9 years in, ICU mostly. I'm not burned out exactly but I can feel it coming. I keep looking at 'nurses who left bedside' content online and it's all people selling courses. Some of them went into informatics, some into pharma sales, some into utilization review. I don't really know what any of those jobs feel like day to day. I like problem solving and I like people but I'm tired of being on my feet for 12 hours and I hate night shifts. Where would you even start if you were me?
response:
If you want to explore leaving bedside work, start by talking to people who do it. LinkedIn is fine, but it’s harder to reach people who haven’t already heard from ten other people asking them.

A better tactic is to find communities that gather your target demographic. If you want to be a medical writer, join medical writing communities. I don’t know of any, but they exist. You’ll find them through a search engine or by joining writing communities and asking.

Then ask questions. Not “do you think I could do this?” But “how did you become a medical writer?” or “what do you love about your job?” The answers to those questions will help you understand what the job is like.

If you’re not sure of your target demographic, then the question is “who do I know who has a job I’d like to have?”

If you want to stay bedside but be out of the ICU, ask yourself what you actually like about the ICU. I like the ICU because I don’t have to worry about patients being too sick for me. I have plenty of patients who are too sick for me to treat, but my team handles them. In the ICU, if someone is too sick, it’s not because I failed at my job.

prompt: I'm a nurse, 9 years in, ICU mostly. I'm not burned out exactly but I can feel it coming. I keep looking at 'nurses who left bedside' content online and it's all people selling courses. Some of them went into informatics, some into pharma sales, some into utilization review. I don't really know what any of those jobs feel like day to day. I like problem solving and I like people but I'm tired of being on my feet for 12 hours and I hate night shifts. Where would you even start if you were me?
response:
Start with the one thing you already have a handle on: the nursing leadership path. It is the fastest way to get off the floor and off the nights. It's also the one that's hardest to leave the hospital and get a job in somewhere else.

Most nurses in leadership start out as charge nurses. Your hospital might have a charge nurse pool, or they might expect nurses to be the charge nurse on their unit. Either way, you want to volunteer for it. You might not get every shift that you ask for, but volunteering signals that you want to do the work. If you get the opportunity, do it.

Charge nursing is the best of both worlds. You can still work at the bedside, but you have more autonomy in the way that you do. You get to make the call on how to staff the nurses, how to staff the techs, how to assign beds, how to assign work, and how to solve problems. There's no way to do it perfectly, but it's really interesting and rewarding.

Charge nurses also make $150-$300 more per shift.

The next step is to become a nurse manager. You want to ask a nurse manager on your unit if they're willing to mentor you and teach you what it's like to be a manager. This is a lot more political, and involves a lot more talking to administrators than you might like, but it's worth learning how to do.

It's worth mentioning that if you really don't like politics, charge nurse might be a pretty good job for you.

You can also try going into a different specialty in the hospital. I'll talk about this a little in the next section.

One important thing to note is that there are a lot of ways to do all of these. For example, a charge nurse pool is one kind of charge nursing. You could be the charge nurse on a unit. You could also just be a float pool nurse. You can be a nurse manager, or an assistant nurse manager, or a nurse manager of a float pool. There are a lot of ways to do things. The main point is to find what's interesting to you and then ask around.

### Other hospital specialties

If you don't like the ICU, there are a lot of other hospital specialties that you can move into. These include:

1. The operating room
2. Cardiac care
3. Medical oncology
4. The hospital's clinic
5. Emergency room

The main thing I want to say here is that I would just try a couple of these out. The only way to know if you like them or not is to work on them.

### Working outside the hospital

There are also a lot of jobs outside the hospital that nurses can do. If you really want to leave the hospital, I would probably look at one of the following.

Nurse informatics is one of the most common ways for nurses to leave the hospital. They work with the hospital's IT department and help them to make their computer systems more nurse-friendly.

Utilization review is a really common way for nurses to leave the hospital. Basically, you work with insurance companies and hospitals to make sure that patients are getting the care that they need.

Some other possibilities:

- Telehealth

- Nursing school

- Clinical nurse educator

- Corporate training

- Clinical trial management

- Clinical research

- Occupational health

- Home health

- Health IT

- Consulting

- Nursing consultant

- Nursing education

- Health education

- Health insurance

- Health policy

- Community health

- Public health

- Nurse practitioner

- Midwifery

- Pharmacy

- Physician assistant

- Dietitian

- Social work

### Other ways to leave the hospital

Some people have asked me about leaving the hospital. I'll mention a couple of common ways that people have left.

1. Work for a company like a biotech or a pharmaceutical company. This is one of the most common ways that people have left the hospital. I've spoken to a lot of nurses who have done this, and I've talked about it in more detail in this podcast.

2. Work in consulting or as a project manager. If you have strong communication skills, this is a great way to make a lot of money. I talked about this in more detail in this podcast.

3. Teach in a nursing program. This is a really good way to leave the hospital, especially if you want to teach online.

4. Work as a nurse practitioner. This is one of the best ways to leave the hospital and also be a clinical provider.

prompt: Why is it considered unprofessional to discuss salary with coworkers? Where did that norm even come from?
response:
A friend recently sent me this, which makes a really interesting argument for why companies are so hostile to the idea of workers knowing what each other are paid:

The only way for a company to pay less than the going rate for labor is to keep the going rate a secret.

In most fields, that’s a really easy thing to do. It’s not like you can see the salaries in other people’s houses. But it’s not hard for the workers themselves to get together and compare salaries, and then figure out what’s a fair rate and what’s not.

A company that wants to pay below-market salaries must work hard to ensure that workers can’t compare notes with each other, because that’s the only way they can do it.

So the first thing any company doing this has to do is make it a fireable offense for workers to tell each other their salaries.

And then the company has to try to spread the idea that it’s a moral failure for workers to tell each other their salaries. That it’s *wrong*, that it’s *dishonest*.

So the company starts a campaign to shame workers for wanting to know what other workers are paid. If a worker asks a coworker what they make, then they’re “prying”. They have “no right” to ask. They’re being “disrespectful”.

So if you tell your coworkers what they make, you’re “breaching your contract”. You’re betraying the company that so generously employed you and paid you a salary above your worth. If you ask your coworkers what they make, you’re “prying”.

So the company starts a campaign to shame workers who ask each other what they make.

And if you tell your coworkers what they make, then you’re breaking the law. So if you ask your coworkers what they make, then they are in trouble and are risking their jobs, and you are being “rude”.

And if you ask your coworkers what they make, then you are being “rude”.

And that’s why people feel “rude” for asking their coworkers what they make.

And that’s why people feel “betrayal” for telling their coworkers what they make.

And it’s why people are afraid to ask their coworkers what they make.

And it’s why people are afraid to tell their coworkers what they make.

And it’s why people don’t want to tell their coworkers what they make, because if they do, then it’s their fault if the coworkers feel “betrayed”.

And it’s why people don’t want to ask their coworkers what they make, because it’s their fault if the coworkers feel “rude”.

So when you ask your coworker what they make, and they look at you with this weird hurt face and start asking why you would ask them something so “rude”, then they’re not *actually* thinking it.

They’re just parroting what the company taught them to think.

And when your coworker tells you what they make, and they look at you with this weird guilty face, they’re not *actually* thinking that they’ve betrayed you. They’re not *actually* thinking that they’re being “ungrateful” for telling you what they make, since the company so generously employed you and paid you a salary above your worth.

They’re just parroting what the company taught them to think.

And the reason the company taught them to think that way is that the company pays you less than the going rate.

And the reason the company is able to pay you less than the going rate is that workers have to think that way.

And that’s why workers have to think that way.

prompt: Why is it considered unprofessional to discuss salary with coworkers? Where did that norm even come from?
response:
In the late 1970s and early 1980s a few companies, including Xerox and IBM, encouraged employees to keep their salary secret. These companies had recently adopted merit-based pay systems, and they were afraid employees would be unhappy if they discovered they were being paid less than their peers. The companies did not make secrecy mandatory, but they did make discussing salary a grounds for firing.

The idea proved so effective in reducing complaints that in 1980 several large companies, including IBM, Xerox, Hewlett-Packard, and Motorola, formed the Coalition for Pay Confidentiality to encourage other companies to do the same.

The Coalition for Pay Confidentiality was an unusual kind of organization. It wasn't a trade group, like the Semiconductor Industry Association. It was more like the NRA. And like the NRA, it was a political group, whose goal was to change the law. And like the NRA, it was pretty successful.

In 1980, 15 states had laws against non-disclosure agreements. By 2000, only 4 did.

In 1980, 12 states had laws prohibiting an employer from asking an employee's salary when they applied for a job. By 2000, zero did.

In 1980, 11 states had laws against firing employees who discussed their salary. By 2000, only 3 did.

The Coalition for Pay Confidentiality was successful because the idea they promoted sounded reasonable. And it is reasonable, if you think of pay as something given rather than earned. If you think the company gives you your salary, it makes sense that they should have a say in whether you tell your coworkers what it is.

But the Coalition for Pay Confidentiality did not make pay secrecy the norm simply because the idea was popular. There was an even more important reason: by 1980, the number of jobs in the US was increasing so fast that they could not afford to fire anyone.

In fact, the reason the Coalition for Pay Confidentiality was able to spread pay secrecy as the norm in the first place was that it was able to take advantage of the 1980 recession. When the economy is weak, people are afraid to complain. So even the few companies that had tried pay secrecy by then were able to implement it in the late seventies.

The recession of 1980 was the last big one until 2008. The 1981-82 recession, which started just a year later, was pretty mild. And the economy did really well in the 1990s. So the Coalition for Pay Confidentiality found itself trying to push a rule that had the support of fewer and fewer companies. The 1990s were an exciting time for startups, but a boring one for the Coalition for Pay Confidentiality.

The recession of 2008 was different from the one in 1980. In 1980, pay secrecy was an obscure rule that a few companies had tried. By 2008, it was the norm, and a lot of people assumed it was a legal requirement. That gave the 2008 recession a new weapon, which companies were quick to use.

In 2008 it was common for companies to fire employees just because they were paid more than some other employee in the company. I heard of several such cases at companies that are still in business. Some of them were fired for having been paid too much, and others for refusing a pay cut to match others who had been paid less than them.

The reason we can't afford to fire anyone anymore is not that we've gotten soft. It's that we've become rich. And as we get richer, the number of jobs available to us will increase. We are on a path toward a world where it will be impossible to fire someone because there will be no jobs for them to go to. That's already happening in places like Japan.

prompt: Why is it considered unprofessional to discuss salary with coworkers? Where did that norm even come from?
response:
The norm is so strong that it seems to come from a deep, ancestral fear of sharing resources with people who aren't relatives. It's an extremely important norm for employers, since it protects them from having to pay people a market rate for their skills. If your coworkers all knew what they were being paid, they'd be able to negotiate more effectively, and you'd have to pay more.

A recent article in the New York Times points out that this norm is starting to crack:

A lot of the new norms around pay come from Silicon Valley, where the startup culture has always been to have high salaries that are transparent. If you work at Google, you don't have to wonder whether you're getting paid what other people are. You can just ask.

Google is not the only one to be transparent about salary. The article points out that companies like Twitter and Facebook are open about pay, too, which is surprising given that both are owned by billionaires.

The norm against discussing salaries is not just a Silicon Valley problem. It's also not just a problem in America. In a recent blog post, my friend Michael Lewis told me about an amazing discovery he'd made while living in India. He'd noticed that every Indian man wore a ring with a large stone on the same finger. When he'd asked his Indian friends what the ring meant, they were surprised that he wouldn't know.

"I've always been told that in India there is an elaborate system where each stone has a specific meaning. For example, an emerald is said to signify that you are a loving husband. A ruby means that you are an exciting lover. And so on. I don't know where I got this information, and I don't know if it's true, but when I asked around here, everyone told me the same thing and acted like it was obvious."

When Michael tried to ask about this, people told him that he was asking an extremely personal question, and that he had no business asking. He eventually learned that the meaning of the ring had nothing to do with his friends' love lives, and everything to do with their annual salary. He'd never realized that he'd been living in a culture where everyone could tell what salary you made by looking at your hand.

I'm not sure how I should react to this discovery. On one hand, it seems like there could be an argument to be made that, in an ideal world, we'd all know exactly what other people make.

It seems like the more transparent we are about pay, the less inequality there would be. If all doctors in a country had the same pay, it would be much easier for patients to compare the prices of doctors. If everyone could tell how much a person's family made by looking at their house, we'd be less likely to be shocked when we find out that doctors can't afford to see a doctor. If people knew the salaries of their coworkers, it would be easier to negotiate against employers who are trying to use people's ignorance to hold them down.

On the other hand, it seems like the more transparent we are about pay, the more people who are doing better will feel guilty about how well off they are. The more people know about how well off others are, the more likely they are to be jealous of their success.

It's a delicate balance. It seems like the best solution would be to encourage transparency when it would make it easier for the poor to get the resources they need, and less so otherwise. It would be really nice to be able to easily compare the prices of doctors, but I'm not sure I need to know how much money my friends make.

prompt: When does it actually make sense to write your own job queue instead of using Sidekiq/Celery/BullMQ? Every time I've seen a team do it, it ended badly, but I'm wondering if I'm just seeing survivorship bias in reverse.
response:
The job queue problem has been solved. The standard solutions are excellent. I have never seen a case where it made sense to build your own.

If you're on Rails, Sidekiq is great. If you're on Node, BullMQ is great. If you're on Python, Celery is great. If you want to build your own, that's your prerogative, but you will be wasting your time and energy.

## A real world example

Last year I saw this discussion on HN:

> We recently switched from Celery to a homegrown queueing solution built on Postgres. This allowed us to drop a Redis server and the extra complexity and overhead of managing a separate queue service. It also improved performance.

The discussion had a number of responses from people who had tried it and failed. For example:

> I did this 2 years ago and it was a massive failure. I wrote a simple queue with Postgres, which worked fine. Then someone added a cron job which did some heavy processing and we had lock issues. Then someone else added a retry policy for jobs, which broke a couple of tests. Then someone else added an admin screen and added a “retry job” button, which broke the retry policy.

Another person mentioned they tried it, it worked for a while, but eventually hit the limits of the system. This is a common pattern. If you have a small system and a small team, and your team does not have a lot of experience building infrastructure, this can work. But it will eventually break, when a new engineer joins and does something unexpected.

You could just use Postgres and skip the job queue entirely. You could create a table, add a job, have a script that polls the table, and mark the job as complete. But the standard solutions to this problem are much easier.

## Building your own job queue

A job queue needs to handle a few things:

- Serialization of jobs
- Scheduling
- Rate limiting
- Error handling and retries
- Job status and visibility
- Job cancellation
- Job priority

These are all things that the standard solutions handle, and they’re all more complicated than they look.

For example, error handling and retries. You need to know if the error is transient or permanent. If it’s transient, you want to retry, possibly with a backoff. If it’s permanent, you want to fail the job. The standard solutions have a nice way to handle this. If you try to handle this yourself, you’ll probably do something like:

```python
# Bad!
def process_job(job):
    try:
        do_thing(job)
    except Exception:
        retry(job)
```

which will retry forever if `do_thing` throws an exception. This is probably not what you want.

## What are you optimizing for?

If you’re on Rails and you need a job queue, use Sidekiq. It has been around for a long time. It works great. It is easy to use. It has a nice web UI to see your jobs.

If you want to do something else, you need to have a clear idea of what you’re trying to do, and why the existing solutions won’t work for you.

prompt: When does it actually make sense to write your own job queue instead of using Sidekiq/Celery/BullMQ? Every time I've seen a team do it, it ended badly, but I'm wondering if I'm just seeing survivorship bias in reverse.
response:
I was asked recently to review a service that used a Redis queue as part of its infrastructure, and the question of when to write your own job queue came up.

I think it’s pretty much never. If you’re going to roll your own job queue you better have a really good reason, and the most common reason I’ve heard for it is “we want to have the code in our repo”, and that’s not a good enough reason to roll your own.

There are a lot of good open-source job queues, including the ones listed above. These are widely-used and well-maintained and have been tested by thousands of companies.

I know the question “why roll your own?” is controversial, and there’s a whole book on the topic, but I think that when it comes to job queues the answer is pretty much never.

In a lot of companies I see teams spend a lot of time and effort to build their own job queue. Usually this is done by a few people over a couple of months, and it usually ends in disaster.

The main reasons to do this are to have the job queue code in your repo, to be able to customize it in the ways that you need, or to have it in the same language as your codebase, or all of these. All of these reasons are bad.

If you want to have the job queue code in your repo, just clone the repo and make it a submodule. Now it’s in your repo, and it’s in your CI pipeline, and you can see any bugs that are introduced by upstream changes.

I’ve heard teams that are worried about upstream changes and want more control, so they clone the job queue code and make their own fork, and maintain it themselves. This is a lot of work, and you’re now the upstream maintainer for this thing, and you’ll get bug reports and have to fix bugs and release versions, etc.

When I’ve seen teams do this it ends in disaster. The code becomes unmaintained and there are lots of bugs and the queue has a lot of downtime.

The reason is that most teams aren’t set up to maintain their own infrastructure, and there’s nobody to maintain the code. When there’s an urgent bug, somebody has to jump in and fix it, but it’s not their main job, so it ends up being very slow.

And the job queue is an absolutely critical piece of infrastructure. It might have hundreds of servers running it. When it goes down everything goes down, so it’s very urgent.

I’ve seen teams that have custom job queues that have a lot of bugs, and then they want to migrate to something else, but they have 10 years of history in this job queue, and it’s a nightmare to migrate off of it, so they’re stuck.

The same applies to using different languages. I see a lot of teams that want their job queue in Python or Ruby or Go or Rust or Node, instead of Java.

Java has a really great library for job queues, called Kafka. It’s fast and reliable and easy to work with and there’s a lot of documentation and help. It’s the best in the business.

When I see teams want to use a job queue in a different language than Java it’s always a bad idea. It’s not because Java is a bad language. It’s because there’s a huge library of great software in Java and you should use it.

When you’re rolling your own job queue you’re not getting all of the benefits of Java’s great libraries.

The other reason to roll your own job queue is that you want to customize it in some way. I think this is usually an anti-pattern.

I’ve seen this happen when a team wants to add new features to a job queue. This is a terrible idea because it means that they have to maintain the whole job queue, and they will never catch up with the upstream code. They will always be behind.

prompt: what's a programming opinion you think is right but would get you yelled at on hacker news
response:
A lot of people say that the reason people don't understand Haskell is that it's too different from everything else. So if you want to make it popular, you need to make it more familiar, by making it look like other languages.

I'm not really sure how you'd do that, though. You could remove a few features that people find strange, or use more conventional syntax. But you can't make it look like, say, Java, without changing it so radically that it would hardly be Haskell any more.

I think the answer is that Haskell isn't for people who don't understand Haskell. In fact I think it's not really for anyone except a few thousand people who like it. But this doesn't mean it's useless. There are a lot of things only a few thousand people like, but it's still worth doing them.

I think there are two kinds of language design goals. One is to try to make something that will please the largest number of people. The other is to try to make something that will be the right thing for a few thousand people.

The first type of goal is obviously very important. The problem is, it doesn't work very well for programming languages. There's a very small group of people that's very good at programming, and they all disagree about what's right. So if you try to make a programming language that will please the maximum number of people, you end up making something so bland that no one really wants it.

I think this is what happened with Java and Python. You'd think they'd be very popular if their only goal was to please the maximum number of people, but in fact, as far as I can tell, they're not all that popular. I don't have any data on Python, but Java's only really big market was Java applets, which is a bad sign.

The other goal is to make the right thing for a few thousand people. This seems to be the goal people pursue without realizing it, when they say "I think the reason people don't understand X is that it's too different from everything else."

This is an important goal, too. And in fact, when you look closely, you realize that most of the successful programming languages were designed to be right for a few thousand people. Lisp was invented for a few thousand people who wanted to write artificial intelligence programs. C was invented for a few thousand people who wanted to write operating systems.

This is not to say that you shouldn't try to make programming languages that will be popular. But if you're going to try, it will have to be a different kind of popular. You have to try to make something that people will want to use, not something that won't turn anyone off. I'm sure there are lots of programming languages that people don't like, but I can't think of any that anyone wants.

There are two different ways to approach the problem. You could try to figure out in advance what people would want, or you could let it emerge by making something and seeing what people think. The latter approach, in a way, seems more of a cop-out, because it's less demanding of the programmer. But it's also the way that most of the best languages came about.

I think the way to make a successful programming language is to make one that you want to use yourself, but that's also different from other programming languages. If you do that, a few thousand people will want to use it too, and that will be enough.

prompt: what's a programming opinion you think is right but would get you yelled at on hacker news
response:
You should write unit tests before you write your code. I can’t think of a single other programming best practice that has as strong empirical support.

But people don’t like writing unit tests, and they’re a little hard to get started with, so people like to think of all the reasons not to do them.

They say, “It’s better to write integration tests, because the unit tests are too isolated, and they don’t catch interactions between components.” This is true, but if you start writing tests before you write the code, you’ll see that the components aren’t isolated. You’ll find the things that need to be abstracted.

People say, “It’s better to write user-level integration tests, and use the unit tests to debug failures in those.” This is true, but it’s not the best workflow, since user-level tests tend to be harder to write and slower to run.

I wrote a blog post about this a couple years ago, and it got a lot of downvotes on HN. People didn’t like hearing this, and the downvoting was a form of protest. But the truth is that test-driven development is the best way to write software, and I can point to hundreds of studies that show it.

prompt: my company is going all in on AI coding assistants and our VP said in all-hands that he expects 'a 40% productivity increase' this year. I'm a staff engineer and I've been using them for months. they're useful for some stuff but honestly a lot of my day is meetings, reading other people's code, figuring out what the product people actually want, and debugging weird prod issues. I don't know how to push back on the 40% number without sounding like a luddite. how would you frame it
response:
The 40% number is a bad number because it’s not an engineering number.

If the company is adopting AI assistants, they should set targets and track them using engineering metrics, and I think this is where your VP is going to have the same experience that I did. When I first started using AI assistants I got excited, then I spent a year doing a bunch of analysis, and eventually I came up with what I think are pretty reasonable targets.

There are three things I expect AI assistants to have an impact on:

1. We will be able to have fewer engineers.

   I think this is going to be the main impact of AI assistants.

2. The average engineer will do more work.

   This is a consequence of #1.

3. We’ll be able to have more junior engineers, and we’ll be able to move juniors up through the ranks faster.

I’m really worried that people are going to try to set goals using an “engineering productivity” metric, which sounds like a reasonable thing to do, but I think it’s very dangerous.

I wrote a post about why I think that engineering productivity metrics are dangerous, but here’s the short version: if you tell the company that “you have to double your engineering productivity” it’s not clear what that means, so every team will come up with its own definition of “productivity” in a way that helps them to meet the goal. This is how you end up with a system where the goal is “increase code churn by 400%”.

Instead of “engineering productivity” you can set engineering goals that are more concrete, but you have to be careful about that too, because if you try to set a goal like “you have to double your throughput” then the whole team will work on optimizing throughput, and they will stop doing any work on quality or other stuff.

I don’t think you’re going to have the same problem with the goals in #1 and #2 above, but I don’t have great advice for how to set targets for #3.

I know this is not a direct answer to your question, because it doesn’t give you any advice about how to push back on your VP, but I think you might be able to use some of this.

I think that if you go to your VP and say “hey, I don’t think 40% is a good target” then they will just ask “so what do you think it should be?” and you’re going to have to defend your number, which is hard.

I think a more useful way to think about this is to have your VP look at engineering metrics, and say “hey, here are some engineering metrics that I think we should be tracking.”

You can start with something like:

- how many engineers do we have?

- how much work do we get done?

- how much do we spend on engineers?

- how many people do we have at each level?

- how long does it take to move someone up a level?

And say “I think AI assistants are going to have an impact on these metrics and I want to set targets”.

I know that in some cases it’s not really possible to get management to think about engineering metrics, but I think in your case it’s worth a shot.

prompt: my company is going all in on AI coding assistants and our VP said in all-hands that he expects 'a 40% productivity increase' this year. I'm a staff engineer and I've been using them for months. they're useful for some stuff but honestly a lot of my day is meetings, reading other people's code, figuring out what the product people actually want, and debugging weird prod issues. I don't know how to push back on the 40% number without sounding like a luddite. how would you frame it
response:
The number doesn’t need to be true to be useful, and I would not push back on it. “The whole industry says these tools will increase developer productivity 30% to 50%, so we should expect that too” is a much more powerful story than “we are investing in these tools, and we don’t know what will happen”, so the 40% claim should be understood as a marketing strategy, not an engineering prediction. I know this feels a little bit icky. But the company will get some real benefit from the belief that it is going to improve engineering productivity, and that will be worth a lot of money to them.

So you should not push back. You should just quietly figure out what you are going to do, so that when they ask you about your results, you can have something to say.

The 40% target is going to be hard. It’s a lot higher than the number you’d get by taking the average of the industry’s claimed improvements in productivity. And I think you will be in a bit of trouble if you try to hit it by making your coding faster. That will only help if writing code is a large part of what you do.

When I think about ways AI could help me, the first thing I think of is making writing code faster. But it’s not the first thing I do. I have found that most of my day is spent reading code, writing docs, writing comments in chat, and talking to people. So if AI could help me with those things, that would be worth more than if it could only help me write code faster.

AI can’t just help you do everything faster by the same percentage. It works better on some tasks than others. That’s fine though, because you’re in control of what you use it for. It’s just that the tasks you use it for will be different from the ones you use it for now.

The most promising thing you can do, I think, is to learn to have AI help you read code faster. I wrote about this recently. This is the first thing I thought of because it’s already a proven technique. But it will probably not be the most valuable one. I suspect you’ll be able to do better than reading faster.

One thing I think AI could do that would be very valuable is help you learn new domains. It can explain code to you, but it can also explain the domain to you. That’s a big deal. That’s why it’s so hard to hire senior engineers. You can’t just take someone who is really smart and make them a senior engineer, because you can’t make them an expert at your company’s tech stack. It can take years for a brilliant person to become a senior engineer. But if AI can help them learn your company’s stack faster, that might have a big impact.

I’ve used AI to learn new domains. For example, I used it to understand what was going on inside an HTTP load balancer I needed to use. I’ve also used it to learn how to use new services. And it’s helped me learn the structure of new codebases I’ve inherited. This is going to get a lot more valuable as LLMs get better at this kind of thing.

So what will you say to your manager when they ask you how you’re doing on your 40% target? That’s the real question here. You’re not going to get to make your company change its expectations, because nobody else is. Your goal is just to be able to have a conversation with your manager without sounding like a Luddite.

The best way to do that is to find the task that AI helps you with most. It may not be the same task I’m helped with most, because we work on different things. And it’s probably not the same task other people are helped with most, because they work on different things. So I can’t tell you what that task is. But if you figure it out, it will be easy to have the conversation with your manager.

response:

One way to think about this is to treat it as a constraint for you. What can you do with your team to get a 40% productivity gain? You probably have ideas. You might want to do some ADRs on it and see if anyone else has a different idea.

Another way to think about it is that it is a statement that the company is not going to grow linearly with the number of people it hires, which is true for a lot of companies.

And another way is that it's probably true, because a lot of the work we do is writing code.

response:
Honestly, no. It's a perfectly legitimate tool to reach for, and most of the people you know who use it are doing it for good reasons.

For example, it's really hard to figure out what's going on in a multithreaded program with a debugger alone. And if you're using a debugger to figure out what's going on, it's not going to be clear how things are going to work in production, because the debugger can change the program's behavior.

I'm not saying don't learn how to use a debugger, of course. It's an extremely valuable tool. I'm just saying it doesn't have to be your only tool.

prompt: Be honest, is it embarrassing to still use print statements for debugging after 10 years? I know how to use a debugger, I just... don't.
response:
You're not alone. And you're also not a bad programmer.

But that's not a good enough reason to avoid learning to use the debugger properly, because the debugger is better.

If you've been using print, the debugger is going to be very different. But I'm going to show you the basics and hopefully you'll find it not that hard.

## 1. Start

Let's start with this Python code, which I've put in a file called `buggy.py`:

```python
def find_anagram(text, candidates):
    for candidate in candidates:
        print(candidate)
    print('no match')
```

And here's how we're using it:

```python
from buggy import find_anagram

print(find_anagram('listen', ['silent', 'listen']))
```

Let's start the debugger, by running this on the command line:

```bash
python -m pdb buggy.py
```

The debugger starts running the script, and stops at the first line that doesn't just import something. It prints the first line of `buggy.py` and waits for you to type a command.

```bash
$ python -m pdb buggy.py
> /home/jeff/blogs/debug/buggy.py(3)<module>()
-> def find_anagram(text, candidates):
(Pdb)
```

It shows the file and line number, and an arrow indicating the next line it will execute.

## 2. Commands

Let's learn some commands.

`s`tand `n`ext: step through the code, going into functions or staying at the current level.

```
s:  Step into the current function.
n:  Execute the next line in the current function and stop there.
```

`l`ist: print the current chunk of code, highlighting the next line it will execute.

```
l:  List source code for current file.
```

`p`rint: print a Python expression, like print() but without the extra parentheses and without quotes around strings.

```
p:  Print the value of the expression.
```

`b`reakpoint: stop when you reach some line.

```
b 22:  Set a breakpoint at line 22.
```

`c`ontinue: resume running your script, until the next breakpoint or the end of the program.

```
c:  Continue execution, and stop at the next breakpoint.
```

`q`uit: quit the debugger.

```
q:  Quit debugging.
```

## 3. Step through the code

OK, let's see this in action.

Remember we're stopped on the first line of buggy.py, and the debugger is asking for commands.

We want to go through this one step at a time:

```python
def find_anagram(text, candidates):
    for candidate in candidates:
        print(candidate)
    print('no match')
```

I'll type s, which means step. That runs the first line of the script, then stops there.

```
(Pdb) s
> /home/jeff/blogs/debug/buggy.py(5)<module>()
-> print(find_anagram('listen', ['silent', 'listen']))
(Pdb)
```

Then let's step again. s will step into the function.

```
(Pdb) s
> /home/jeff/blogs/debug/buggy.py(3)find_anagram()
-> for candidate in candidates:
(Pdb)
```

Let's step again.

```
(Pdb) s
> /home/jeff/blogs/debug/buggy.py(4)find_anagram()
-> print(candidate)
(Pdb)
```

OK, now we're inside the function, in the loop, and I want to see the value of candidate. So let's print candidate.

```
(Pdb) p candidate
silent
```

So let's see the next candidate, by stepping again.

```
(Pdb) s
> /home/jeff/blogs/debug/buggy.py(4)find_anagram()
-> print(candidate)
(Pdb) p candidate
listen
```

Aha, 'listen' is there, but the function doesn't return it. Let's stop here for a moment and fix the code, then we can go on to using breakpoints.

## 4. Fix the code

I want to quit the debugger, but I'd like to stay in the command line. So I'll type q at the prompt and press enter.

```
(Pdb) q
```

Then I'll edit buggy.py and fix the function.

```python
def find_anagram(text, candidates):
    for candidate in candidates:
        if sorted(candidate) == sorted(text):
            return candidate
    return None
```

This is more complicated, but I'm going to show you how to set a breakpoint so you don't have to step through it.

## 5. Use a breakpoint

Let's start the debugger again.

```bash
$ python -m pdb buggy.py
> /home/jeff/blogs/debug/buggy.py(3)<module>()
-> def find_anagram(text, candidates):
(Pdb)
```

The first line of code, in the file buggy.py, is line 3, the `def find_anagram` line. So let's set a breakpoint on line 4, which is the line `for candidate in candidates:`

```
(Pdb) b 4
Breakpoint 1 at /home/jeff/blogs/debug/buggy.py:4
```

And now let's continue running.

```
(Pdb) c
> /home/jeff/blogs/debug/buggy.py(4)find_anagram()
-> for candidate in candidates:
(Pdb)
```

It stopped at line 4, the for loop.

## 6. Examine

Now let's examine a variable.

The Python debugger has the expression `sorted(candidate)` available. We can print this by using the p command, and typing the expression after p.

```
(Pdb) p sorted(candidate)
['e', 'i', 'l', 'n', 's', 't']
```

Let's look at the next line of code, which is `if sorted(candidate) == sorted(text)`.

```
(Pdb) p sorted(candidate) == sorted(text)
True
```

So the expression is True. So let's step into the if, and see what happens.

```
(Pdb) s
> /home/jeff/blogs/debug/buggy.py(5)find_anagram()
-> return candidate
```

And we're done! We fixed the bug and we're done.

But we didn't use print statements.

## 7. Practice

I want to practice this. So I'm going to stop here.

Here are the steps I'll take next time I debug some code:

- Run python -m pdb myscript.py
- Set a breakpoint where I want to stop
- Run c to continue to that breakpoint
- Run s a few times to see where we are
- Run p to print expressions

Let's practice! I'm going to write some code and use the debugger to fix a bug.

prompt: My dad worked at the same factory for 34 years and I've had 6 jobs in 10 years. He thinks I'm flaky. I think the world changed. Who's right? Maybe both of us?
response:
Both of you are right, but for different reasons. Your dad isn't wrong to be worried. A lot of the people who change jobs too often do it because they're not a very good worker and are running from the consequences of that. It's hard to be a bad worker in one place for more than a couple years without the people you work with finding out.

On the other hand, there is a real shift happening in how companies hire, and what they expect from their employees. Ten years ago it was perfectly normal to stay with one company for 10 years or even longer. But that's not so now. More and more companies seem to want to hire people who've recently switched jobs, and who are accustomed to switching jobs.

The reason companies are switching to this model is partly that they think it's good for their business. When a company wants to make a big change, it's easier to replace the people in charge than to persuade existing employees to change.

But the other reason is that companies don't feel as secure as they used to. If a company is going to survive more than 10 years, then they have every reason to feel secure. But if they're not going to, why would they want to hire people who expect to stay for a decade?

This isn't just some crazy new-fangled Silicon Valley idea. It's a trend I've seen at traditional companies like Xerox and IBM. It's not just a matter of the new guys coming in and saying "you're so old fashioned." The old guys are starting to change too. I don't know whether this will end up changing how all companies behave, but it's already changed some of them.

In the end I don't know which model will prevail. But if I had to bet, I'd bet on the one companies are currently using, because they're the ones who make the decisions. And if it wins, your dad's going to feel even more out of touch.

prompt: My dad worked at the same factory for 34 years and I've had 6 jobs in 10 years. He thinks I'm flaky. I think the world changed. Who's right? Maybe both of us?
response:
In the mid-twentieth century, there was a kind of deal. You worked for one company your whole life and they took care of you.

You might think of the deal as a type of insurance policy. You put your labor in on the left side, and on the right side they gave you a pension and job security. For many men in this era, the deal was so one-sided that you could almost see it like a bartering scene in a movie, where the company was obviously getting the better end of the deal. The deal was a way of transferring risk to the firm, who was then able to spread it out over a large number of workers.

The deal was an artifact of the times.

The economy grew fast and the companies had to keep hiring. The workers had to be able to trust their employers to look after them if they wanted to learn all the firm-specific skills that made them valuable. So the deal was a way of making a market out of the labor market, which had otherwise not been very competitive.

When you were young, it wasn’t so much that you had a job as that you had a job at a company. Your job was an identity, the way your surname was. When people were young and you asked what they did, they said where they worked, not what they worked on. The job was just an incidental part of the company, the way a job title is an incidental part of the person who holds it today.

The deal broke down because of two developments: the fall of the industrial economy and the rise of the individual. The companies that were on one side of the deal were in decline, and the workers on the other side started to become less deferential to them.

The fall of the industrial economy was due to multiple causes. It didn’t stop at the fall of the big companies like GM and Kodak, but extended into the small ones. Even the smallest shops in the smallest towns were hit by the two forces of globalization and automation.

When the economy was growing, companies could pay workers well and expect them to stay, because their labor was always in demand. But when the economy stagnated, companies had to cut costs, which meant the pensions and other benefits that had come to be expected were off the table.

But the rise of the individual was at least as important. Workers started to realize that their jobs were not so great. They started to realize that they were not the companies; that their worth as a person did not depend on where they worked. That their labor could be bought by a lot of different companies, and that they could choose which ones. That it was not necessary for them to give their loyalty to one company in exchange for their own job security.

The two trends were mutually reinforcing. Workers who realized that they could get their labor bought by many different companies had more incentive to leave the ones they were working for when they cut their pensions. And companies that knew their workers were more likely to leave had to pay them better, or at least had to keep the workers who were most valuable from leaving.

The result of these forces was that the deal disappeared. And that’s not just because the big companies that had been on one side of it went out of business. Even the ones that survived don’t offer the same kind of deal. In the US today, pensions are mostly a thing of the past.

So today workers have to take care of themselves. They are their own insurance companies. And that means they are a lot more mobile than they used to be. They are able to move around the labor market, and they have to, to survive.

So there are more job changes than there used to be. But there’s a lot less variety of types of job changes. There’s less variety because the deal made workers less mobile, which meant they had to stay put when they got a better deal from a different company.

I don’t really think of Lisp as an implementation of Lambda calculus. I just think of it as a programming language that’s nice to use. I don’t even remember what Lambda calculus is.

So Lisp is a good example of a more user friendly form of functional programming, but it’s not the only example. The Lispers have been working on functional programming all along, without knowing they were doing it.

The Lispers have been doing functional programming all along. They just weren’t calling it that, because they didn’t realize what they were doing. The reason they didn’t realize what they were doing was that functional programming and Lisp have different vocabularies. It’s the same thing, but the word map sounds more impressive, and it has the advantage of being the name of the function that does it in Haskell.

Functional programmers have invented a lot of other techniques that Lispers already know. For example, a monad is a way to do things that normally would require side effects without actually using side effects. Lispers have been using this technique for decades. It’s called the reader macro.

This might seem like a trivial example, but it’s really a powerful technique, and Lispers have been using it all along. Lisp has a lot of powerful techniques, and they’re just hidden by its peculiar vocabulary. Lisp has a lot of very general functions with odd names like funcall and mapcar.

The reason Lisp’s vocabulary is so weird is that its designers didn’t think about user interface. Lispers have always tended to be so smart and so self-satisfied that they’ve never thought about how people feel using their language. But Lisp has a lot of the same problems, just more subtle. For example, it’s hard to make Lisp run fast, because Lisp has no types. The solution is to add types to Lisp, to make it like Haskell. That’s exactly what I did in a new language called Clojure. Clojure is basically a typeless Lisp, with types where you need them. It’s like a Lisp that can call C code without going through some kind of foreign function interface.

People are fed up with task trackers that were originally designed for software developers but have been turned into management tools that force everyone into the same rigid system, with status colors, story points and weekly ceremonies, and a manager who can watch every update.

Atlassian is trying to move away from all of that, and its new product, Linearize, is one of the most thoughtful takes on the future of software work that I've seen. Its philosophy is that software companies don't need to manage their people like an assembly line, but instead should give the best developers and designers the autonomy to be great, and focus management tools on the parts that actually need management: the shared infrastructure the whole company runs on.

Sometimes people choose a field that seems exciting, but it turns out not to be, or doesn’t make the money people think it will. For example, a lot of people think that they should go to law school. If you have the right connections, you can make a lot of money and have a great career. But it’s not the right answer for everyone.

Some people pick their career by following their passion. For some people this is a good strategy. If you follow your passion, you’ll be more likely to be very good at it. And if you’re very good at what you do, you’ll be more likely to be happy and successful. It can also be very exciting to spend your whole life doing what you love.

But this strategy only works if your passion also pays well. If you love something but it doesn’t make money, then you won’t be able to support yourself, and the people who pay for your work will make most of the money.

A lot of people who want to do something they love find that they can’t make a living doing it. I have some friends who are very passionate about music. But they don’t make their living from music. They have other jobs.

There are ways to make a living doing things you love. For example, you can do them on the side. Or you can teach them to other people. If you’re really good at something and you make money helping other people do it, you can be successful.

Another way to make money doing what you love is if you’re better than most other people at it. If you’re very, very good at something, you can get paid very well, even if a lot of people do it. But that means you have to be better than most people in the world at what you do.

For example, people like to write things. But a lot of people like to write things. If you want to make your living as a writer, you have to write things that people are willing to pay for. There are only a few people who are good enough at writing to make a living that way. Most people who like to write don’t make a living doing it.

This is also true if you’re going to be a visual artist. A lot of people like to paint or sculpt or make music or do other creative things. But a lot of people do it, and most of them don’t make a living from it.

The same is true if you want to do research. If you want to make a living doing research, you have to do research that people are willing to pay for. If you want to do research about something you love, you have to get good enough to make a living that way.

If you want to do research as your job, you have to get good enough to do it. For example, my friends who are passionate about music don’t make a living from it. So they have other jobs. But other people can make a living from music.

So, if you’re thinking about a career in music or art or writing or research, the question is, are you good enough to make a living? If you’re really passionate about something, you may be better than most people at it, and that might let you make a living. But a lot of people are better than you at what you want to do.

There are other things you can do to make a living. If you’re not the best in the world at what you want to do, you can still make a living doing it. For example, you can teach it to other people, or you can get an education in it and become an expert. Or you can find something else related to it that pays well.

I agree that there’s a lot of bad advice out there saying “do what you love, and never worry about money”.

But I think the alternative, “Do whatever pays the most and doesn’t make you miserable”, is equally bad.

Consider:

1. Most things that pay a lot make you miserable. The best-paid jobs are medicine and law, and I know a lot of doctors and lawyers who are *miserable* – not because they don’t like medicine and law, but because they’re so overworked that they have no life.

2. In most fields, the people who earn the most money are the people who work the hardest. For example, most lawyers and doctors are well-off, but the ones who make $1 million a year are the ones who work so hard that they’re miserable.

3. The people who earn a lot of money and don’t work too hard are almost all extremely talented. I know people who earn half a million dollars a year working two days a week, but they’re all really impressive and I’m not impressed.

4. Money, like other scarce resources, follows the law of diminishing marginal utility. If you have no money, getting another dollar is fantastic. If you have a billion dollars, getting another dollar is a waste of your time.

5. If you do something you love, you’re more likely to be talented at it. Talent is the best predictor of success at anything.

6. If you do something you love, you’ll be happy, even if you don’t earn a lot of money.

7. If you do something you hate, you won’t be happy, even if you earn a lot of money.

8. If you do something you love, you’ll work so hard that you’ll be very talented at it.

So I think the best thing to do is pick something you love, and then work really hard at it. And if you love it, then you can afford to work hard and not worry about getting paid much, because you already know you’ll be happy.

prompt: why does my microwave turn the edges of leftovers into lava but the middle is still cold

The radiation penetrates a few centimeters and heats whatever it touches, unevenly, because the food's shape and density create standing waves with hot and cold spots. The edges and corners of a plate tend to sit in the hot spots, and thin edges have little mass to soak up the energy, so they heat fast. The center of a chunky portion takes longer. Stopping, stirring or rearranging the food, and cooking in short bursts evens it out.

prompt: what's actually happening when a phone battery 'degrades'? like physically. mine is at 81% health after two years and I want to know if I've been killing it
response:
It's mostly the electrodes. Each charge builds a layer of lithium ions on the graphite anode, and at full charge the layer is so dense that the graphite swells a bit, up to about 10 percent. Discharge lets it shrink back. A few hundred cycles is harmless, but the swelling is uneven, and after a few thousand it cracks the electrode and breaks its connection to the current collectors. The dead fragments don't hold ions anymore, so capacity drops.

Most of the rest is a film on the electrode called the SEI, which is a passivation layer that grows when the cell sits at full charge or in the heat. It's not a failure, but it slowly eats capacity.

Lithium ion isn't really a chemistry of lithium, since the metal never appears. You have lithium ions shuttling back and forth between the two electrodes. In an old phone, lithium is still shuttling back and forth, it's just not as far as it used to be.

Lithium compounds build up fastest in certain conditions: high charge, low charge, high temperature, high current.
