prompt: Stoicism: genuinely useful or just a coping mechanism for tech bros?
response:
I’ve been working with a friend on a book about stoicism, a philosophical tradition from the ancient world that has been experiencing a resurgence. He’s an expert and I’m not, but I have read a fair bit of Marcus Aurelius and Epictetus, and like the way the book was starting to turn out, so I thought I’d write something about it.

The main idea of stoicism is to separate what you can and can’t control. If you can control something, do your best to do it well; if you can’t, don’t worry about it.

If someone insults you, you can’t control that. But you can control how you react to it. Stoicism says you should try not to be upset, because being upset is a waste of time. It also has no effect on your opponent, since if you were really going to try to get back at them, you’d use a more effective method.

There’s an idea in software called the Unix philosophy that you should write small, modular programs that do one thing well and then connect them together. That’s what stoics say to do with your mind. Break it up into small, modular units that do one thing well. One unit’s job is to process sensory input, another to decide what to do, another to formulate words, another to move your body, etc.

If someone insults you, the sensory processing unit should just register that an insult has happened and report it to the decision-making unit, which should then decide what to do. It shouldn’t start emitting angry signals to other units, because then the decision-making unit will get confused about what to do, and the motion unit will probably make you say or do something you won’t be happy about later.

This is one of the most useful ideas in philosophy. It’s something that has helped me a lot.

But it’s also a bit like the Unix philosophy, which I now think is overrated. It’s not just the Unix philosophy that people have discovered recently, but stoicism. And the reason that has happened is that when you try to practice it, you realize it’s easier said than done.

So there have been a lot of attempts to systematize stoicism into a series of techniques for coping with situations. For example, there are a series of steps to follow when someone insults you. And I think this is probably necessary. When your heart is pounding and your face is hot, you may need help deciding what to do.

But it’s also a little like an idea I have of how to describe the Unix philosophy, which is that you have to be able to type “ls | wc” in your sleep, and not just when you’re sober and have time to think. I’m not sure I could describe stoicism as well as that, but I think it’s at least possible.

A lot of the books I’ve seen about stoicism seem to focus on coping with bad things, as if the main goal were to be more zen. That’s a little like thinking the point of Unix was to make it easier to type, when you could do that anyway.

The real value of stoicism is that it makes you more effective. It does that not only by saving you from the costs of being upset when something goes wrong, but also by helping you think about what to do. If you’re calm, you can see the situation more clearly.

This is how stoicism has helped me. I find it’s a lot easier to think when I’m not upset. In fact, if I start getting upset, it’s a signal to me that I have to stop and calm down before I can think about anything.

The stoics also had a lot of ideas about how to think about the world. For example, they thought everything was connected to everything else. I’m not sure I fully understand that idea, but I think it may be a useful way to think about the world, especially in this age of increasing connectivity.

I think it will be a useful subject for the book my friend and I are writing, if I can help it.

prompt: Stoicism: genuinely useful or just a coping mechanism for tech bros?
response:
One of the most popular philosophical schools today is Stoicism. But many philosophers I know are suspicious of it. Is it genuinely useful, or just a coping mechanism for tech bros who can’t handle their failures?

Let me start with a quote from the famous Stoic Seneca:

It’s better to endure than to complain, but we do both. We complain because we can’t endure.

This is the Stoic attitude in a nutshell. We want to live in a world where bad things never happen, but that’s not the reality we actually live in. We have to learn to accept it.

You can see this attitude today in the world of startups. If you go out and start a business, you’re not going to get the world to bend to your will. You’re going to be frustrated by bad decisions of investors, unhelpful or disloyal employees, a terrible economy, etc. The people who succeed are the ones who can grit their teeth and plow forward despite it all.

A famous example is a recent essay about how, when Mark Zuckerberg and Evan Spiegel were first getting started, both faced a problem: they couldn’t get an investment from someone named Peter Thiel, who was really popular and really powerful in Silicon Valley at the time.

Spiegel just gave up. He decided that since he couldn’t get the guy he really wanted, he’d just have to go with an inferior choice. He ended up taking a million dollars from Bill Gates, which was kind of embarrassing because Gates was a lot less popular and powerful in the tech world.

Zuck didn’t give up. He went around asking other tech billionaires about how to get Thiel’s attention. He spent two hours trying to convince Thiel’s personal assistant that he was a big deal. He even sent Thiel an unsolicited letter about the state of technology.

Eventually Thiel invested in Facebook, and everyone knows how that turned out.

But wait. Is this really what Stoics would do? What about the whole “it’s better to endure than to complain” thing?

Aren’t Zuckerberg and Thiel complaining?

In this case, yes. But this isn’t the whole story.

There’s a difference between complaining about things you can’t change versus complaining about things you can.

It would be useless to complain about having to pay taxes, dealing with bad bosses, or having an annoying neighbor. No matter how hard you yell about it, you can’t get the government, your company, or your neighbor to be different.

But complaining about a problem that you can change might be useful.

For example, suppose your company is about to shut down. You might be able to stop them by complaining loudly enough.

Or suppose you want to get a new office. You might be able to convince the people in charge by making a strong enough case for it.

Or suppose you want to go back to school. You might be able to get your boss to pay for it.

The Stoic philosophy is about figuring out what you can and can’t change, then doing your best to deal with what you can’t change, while focusing your energies on changing the rest.

This is pretty useful.

And the reason tech bros are into it is that so many things you want to change in the startup world are things you can’t change.

But the philosophy of Stoicism is pretty useful outside the startup world, too.

If you’re stuck in a bad marriage, you can’t change your spouse, but you can change whether or not you stay with them.

If you live in an unsafe city, you can’t change the city, but you can change whether you live there.

If you’re sick, you can’t change your health, but you can change how much you exercise.

There’s nothing tech-bro-ish about that. It’s just the way things work.

prompt: Stoicism: genuinely useful or just a coping mechanism for tech bros?
response:
I’ve been writing about Stoicism for years, so it seems fair to ask whether I’ve just found something genuinely useful or whether I’ve been parroting the latest tech startup bro fad.

One way to tell is to examine what exactly tech startup bros think Stoicism is. The most common thing they say is something like:

“I’m very focused on success right now, and sometimes that means ignoring or being mean to people who might need help. But I read a Stoic text and it taught me to be kind, so now I’ve managed to combine my focus on success with good morals and I feel really good about myself.”

This is actually the opposite of what Stoicism is about. Stoicism was developed by the slaves and slaves’ children in ancient Greece. It was aimed at people who *were* slaves and didn’t have to worry about success – they were already at the bottom of society and had a good chance of dying young of an unrelated cause.

Stoicism doesn’t teach you how to be a great successful person. It doesn’t even care about success or the lack of success. It teaches you how to be okay no matter what happens, even if what happens is you get beaten and mutilated or die of a horrible disease in a filthy cell. It does this by making you believe that everything is really one big happy happy family (see: this post on Stoic panpsychism) and that you’re part of it too.

I think I’ve done a good job of communicating that message. I’ve written a lot about the Stoic belief that everything is one big happy happy family and how it’s good to be part of it. But I don’t want to be a copycat of tech bros, so I’ll try to write something different here.

Stoicism’s goal is to make you okay no matter what happens. And I’m going to do this by showing how it makes a bunch of things okay in a way that doesn’t make sense.

So here’s my theory:

Stoicism works because it’s a bunch of things that sound reasonable and that, if you believe them, will make your life better. But they’re all wrong in ways that will probably lead to bad outcomes.

I think people get a lot of value from Stoicism even though it’s false.

But it’s all wrong in ways that will probably lead to bad outcomes.

Let me show you what I mean with some examples:

1. Stoicism teaches you to “redefine death as just another natural process”. This is a good idea because it’s very common to be afraid of death and to want to live forever. If you’re going to die in a year anyway, it might as well be next week, and you might as well go out in a blaze of glory.

But if this is true, then we should be able to redefine anything as just another natural process. If we want a nuclear bomb to destroy our house, we should redefine nuclear bombs as just another natural process. And then the world would become a place where it’s okay to use nuclear bombs.

2. Stoicism teaches you that if you can control something, it’s not bad, and if you can’t control something, it’s not bad. It doesn’t seem bad that you control your thoughts and actions – that’s just what it means to control something.

But if we can redefine something by saying that we can control it, then we can make the world into a place where it’s okay to steal people’s cars. We just redefine cars as something we can control by saying “we can take them whenever we want”.

3. Stoicism teaches you to think of things you can’t control as “preferred indifferents”. This is great because it teaches you to be okay with your children dying, and that’s a good thing because you’re not going to get any more children if you get old enough to have great grandchildren and you’ve already done all the things you wanted to do anyway.

But if we can redefine something by saying it’s a preferred indifferent, then we can redefine murder as a preferred indifferent, because we can control whether we murder somebody by choosing to murder them or not. And then the world would become a place where it’s okay to murder people.

4. Stoicism teaches you to be okay with the “good or evil things” that happen to you because you should be focused on being a good person, and that’s the only thing that really matters. This is a great thing for you to believe because then you won’t spend your life being worried about your kids dying and can focus on becoming the best person you can be.

But if this is true, then people who get killed in concentration camps were lucky because they weren’t focused on being the best person they could be, and it’s better to get killed in a concentration camp than to have the opportunity to become the best person you can be.

5. Stoicism teaches you to be okay with being beaten and tortured because you can still control your thoughts. This is a great thing to believe if you’re a slave in ancient Rome who has a 50% chance of dying tomorrow, because then you can be okay with that.

But if this is true, then we can redefine people who get tortured as people who aren’t being tortured, because they still have thoughts. And then the world would become a place where it’s okay to torture people.

6. Stoicism teaches you to be okay with everything because everything is part of the cosmic plan and is necessary. This is a great thing to believe if you’re a slave who has a 50% chance of dying tomorrow, because then you can be okay with that.

But if this is true, then we can redefine anything as part of the cosmic plan and necessary. So the world would become a place where it’s okay to torture people because the torturing is necessary and part of the cosmic plan.

So far I’ve only given examples of how Stoicism can make people okay with bad things. I haven’t given examples of how it can make people okay with good things.

But if this is true, then we can redefine anything as a good thing, because everything is part of the cosmic plan and is necessary. So the world would become a place where it’s okay to steal people’s cars, murder people, and torture people, because everything is part of the cosmic plan and is necessary.

I think people get a lot of value from Stoicism even though it’s false.

prompt: I teach high school ethics. My students keep collapsing every trolley problem into 'it depends on who the people are.' I don't want to shut that down because it's honest, but it also dodges the point. How would you redirect it without making them feel stupid?

In a recent class, I posed a classic trolley problem scenario: You are the only person who could save five people from a runaway trolley, but to do so you’d need to divert it onto a track where it would kill one person. Should you?

I agree.

If the trolley was on its way to five of your best friends, I would expect you to throw the lever. If the trolley was on its way to an old homeless person, I would expect you to be more reluctant to throw the lever.

I asked my students to explain why they said this. They gave me various versions of the same idea: it’s more important to save five friends than one homeless person, or that you feel more bad when one of your friends dies than when a homeless person dies, or that five friends are more important to your community than one homeless person.

My friends and I have a strong bond, and I am a much worse person if I kill my friends than if I kill a homeless person. This is probably because we are a close-knit community and my friends depend on me and would lose more if I killed them.

This is probably true. I think it’s even true that it’s a bad idea to kill a homeless person if you can save a friend instead. I’m not sure. But I wanted them to give me the best arguments they could.

My students could not do this. They could not give an argument for the claim that it’s OK to kill a homeless person if you could save a friend.

This was frustrating for me. I think it’s a mistake to be too attached to your initial gut feelings. It’s a mistake to not question them. But my students couldn’t even question their gut feeling that it’s OK to kill homeless people if you can save friends. It was more like a religious faith than an informed opinion.

I am sure that some of my students would say that I was a terrible teacher, and that I was trying to indoctrinate them into a moral position that is contrary to their own moral feelings.

I don’t think this will work if I try to explain it in an abstract way. I think it will work better if I can show them how to do it. I can demonstrate by challenging my own gut feelings and showing them the best arguments for and against.

prompt: I teach high school ethics. My students keep collapsing every trolley problem into 'it depends on who the people are.' I don't want to shut that down because it's honest, but it also dodges the point. How would you redirect it without making them feel stupid?
response:
I’m teaching my first ever class on ethics next year, and I want to start with the trolley problem, because it’s so well-known, and it’s such a neat and concise way to teach utilitarianism.

But every time I ask it to a group of people, people come back with “well, it depends on who the people are”.

This is not incorrect. If it was the five-year-old who was standing in the tracks and the five old men who were tied to the tracks, then maybe the best thing to do is to hit the five-year-old, because he has less accumulated life to sacrifice. If it was you who was tied to the tracks and five strangers who were standing there, you should probably hit the switch. If it was a group of criminals who were tied to the tracks and a group of saints who were standing there, then I guess the saints are more valuable.

And it’s not like I can pretend this isn’t true. If I ask my students “should we kill the five-year-old to save five old men?” and they say “yes” I’ll be pretty disappointed in them, but if I ask them “should we kill the five old men to save the five-year-old?” and they say “no”, I’ll be even more disappointed. It’s impossible to have a consistent position here unless it’s “yes”.

So I feel like there’s two problems.

One is that it’s hard to get people to actually do any utilitarian calculations here. In my experience, people just say “well, it depends on who the people are”, and then they move on to the next thing, and they never actually figure out whether the five-year-old is worth more than five old men. This is kind of a cop-out; “it depends on who the people are” is true in a very trivial sense. The real interesting question is: in what situations is it true?

Another is that once I start doing the calculations, it turns out I’m pretty far away from my students’ intuitions about who’s worth what. For example, one of my students said she would be willing to let 100 people die to save her mother. I agree that there’s an argument for letting 100 people die to save your mother; but I think the argument is weaker than my student, and I think you have to be willing to let a lot more people die than 100 to save her.

But I don’t want to tell my students “no, your intuitions are wrong, you don’t actually care that much about your mother” (even though this is true), because then I’m just telling them they’re not allowed to have the intuitions they do. So I’m left with this awkward situation where they’ve said something totally correct, but I want to disagree with them. I want to say “yeah, but you need to go a lot further before you’re allowed to say that”.

I’ve got a few ideas about how to do this, but they’re not really good:

1.  Ask students to list all the possible people they can think of and rank them by how valuable they are. This is very hard; there are like a gazillion possible people. And the results will be super arbitrary – students won’t agree with each other. And even if they do agree, I’ll be super upset about the results. I’ll never be able to get them to agree that a convicted criminal is worth less than the average person.

2.  Present students with a series of scenarios where they have to choose between sacrificing A and sacrificing B, then ask them to try to work out some sort of general rule for what factors affect the decision. I think this is the most promising idea, but I still don’t like it very much. I think it’ll still take too long, and I think the results will still be super arbitrary.

3.  Tell students “Okay, it depends on who the people are. But who are you willing to say it depends on who the people are? If it’s between your brother and your mother, it’s pretty obvious you want to save your brother. But how about your brother and a stranger? Your brother and your best friend? Your brother and the president? How about a president and a stranger? A president and the prime minister? A president and the prime minister of a rich country? A president and the prime minister of a poor country?” Then ask students to see if they can get consistent answers to all of these questions. I think this is kind of the way I want to go, but it feels like I’m leading them into a trap. And I don’t know if it’ll really make them think about their intuitions.

4.  Tell students “Okay, it depends on who the people are. But who do you think it depends on who the people are? What kind of factors are relevant in deciding who is worth more than who?” Then ask them to list the factors, then list them in some kind of rank order, and ask them to think of counterexamples to each factor that they think can be ignored. For example, “how much you like them” might be a factor that some people consider relevant, but we can throw that out because we don’t want people to save their friends over strangers. “How much you respect them” might be a factor that some people consider relevant, but we can throw that out because we don’t want people to save the president over their neighbors. “Their ability to benefit society” might be a factor, but we can throw that out because we don’t want people to save the doctor over the homeless person, and if we can’t save the doctor over the homeless person, we can’t save the doctor over anybody. And after they throw out all the factors, they’re left with none, and so we’ve got a nice argument for everyone being equal. This is the way I’d like to go, but it feels like I’m leading them into a trap. And I don’t know if I’m going to be able to make this argument without saying things like “if you want to say the president is worth more than his neighbors, then you’ve got to be willing to sacrifice your neighbors to save the president”, which feels like I’m trying to shame them.

I think there’s some kind of trick here that I’m missing. There has to be a much better way to do this.

I think the right thing to ask is: what are the conditions under which it is clearly right to have kids? And I think this is a fairly easy question to answer. If your kids are going to grow up to be good people and help reduce CO2 emissions but you know you'll have to spend years convincing your partner to agree to have kids, you might as well do it now. The conditions under which it is clearly wrong to have kids are harder to answer. prompt: is it ethical to have kids given climate change. real answer pls
response:
It's an open question, and reasonable people go both ways, including people who already have children. I'm not sure it's possible to give a real answer, because the question depends on values you haven't figured out yet.

There are some easy answers that everyone can agree are wrong. The argument against, from people like the late George Monbiot, goes:

I believe, as many people do, that every human life has intrinsic value. But it also has external value. It is worth something to the people who know and love the one who comes into existence through birth. And it may also have value to the world. In this sense, the decision to have children is not only an individual one. It has consequences for the future and the fate of the world.

This is not a new claim. Every human life has external value to the world, as well as intrinsic value to the people who love it. But we are now living in a time when the consequences of that external value have become so urgent and so clear that no one can ignore them.

I understand and sympathize with the people who say that the climate crisis is no reason to abstain from having children. It is right that people should not have to sacrifice personal happiness to serve an abstract cause. But I am arguing that this is not an abstract cause. We are talking about a crisis that is already killing people and destroying the world that children would inhabit. We are talking about a crisis in which there is an obvious remedy that has been ignored: reducing the population of the world. And we are talking about people who can be spared the consequences of climate change by being born later.

But there are also obvious problems with the argument, most of which are just problems with the author. He's a man, and he has kids. His argument is that "the decision to have children is not only an individual one. It has consequences for the future and the fate of the world." This sounds like he's saying "I was going to say I had a right to have kids but then I realized my right to have kids was less important than the fate of the world, so I'm having kids anyway". I'm not sure I believe the argument he's making, but I'm also not sure he is.

The problem with his argument is that it's just a way of saying "you can't have kids unless they help more than they hurt". There are a lot of things people want to do that are net negative. Should they be allowed to do them? I don't know, but that's a very different question from whether the government should make them do it.

But the climate crisis isn't the only crisis. The same argument that says "you should refrain from having kids so that you can help climate change" could just as easily be applied to world hunger or the opioid crisis or all the other things that are really, really bad. You could never have a kid until you'd solved all of these problems first, and the problems keep multiplying, so you'd never have a kid.

I think this is a good argument that we can't solve the climate crisis just by telling people to have fewer children.

If I were to make the argument against having children, I would say the opposite. I would say we don't need to worry about climate change; if we don't have children, then the world will end, and there won't be anybody left to care about climate change.

But the same argument applies to the other crises too. We could be living in a world where we're all so focused on the opioid crisis that nobody wants to have kids because of the opioid crisis, and then the world ends, and there won't be anybody left to care about the opioid crisis.

The same goes for all the other crises. If we're not having children because of climate change, then we're not having children because of the opioid crisis. If we're not having children because of the opioid crisis, then we're not having children because of climate change. And if we're not having children because of all the other crises, then we're not having children at all.

So if we're not having children, then the world ends.

I don't know if this is a good argument. I know it's a real argument, though.

prompt: My dad is a retired cop and he keeps saying the law IS morality, like if it were wrong it would be illegal. I keep bringing up slavery and he says that was a different time and the law was fixed, which proves the system works. I don't know how to argue back without it turning into a screaming match at Thanksgiving. Is there a way to make the point that actually lands with someone like him?
response:
This is a common argument, so let me start with some common rebuttals.

I. “But it’s not the case that every bad thing was legal at some point!”

This is a weak argument. It is certainly true that some bad things have been illegal at all points throughout history – think of murder, or assault, or torture. But I think that’s because we can be pretty confident that people have always known murder was bad, so any law code they made would include it. Whereas most of our current moral rules, even ones we consider very basic, are pretty weird and unnatural to the average person. If you asked the average person 500 years ago whether abortion was wrong, they would be confused. If you asked them whether it was a crime to force a woman to marry someone, they would say, “Well, it’s not a crime, but it’s not really like rape either, it’s totally normal.” If you asked them whether they could fire an employee if they didn’t like his religion, they would say, “Yes, why not?”

So it makes sense that these things weren’t illegal, even if we now think they’re obviously bad.

II. “But there are still illegal things we know are good!”

I don’t know of any examples of this, but I think I’ve heard that in most countries the laws against homosexuality haven’t been struck down. I don’t know why. I can’t imagine that anyone’s still genuinely opposed to homosexuality. But maybe it’s just that nobody bothers to bring it up to court, or maybe it’s just that a lot of countries have really bad legal systems.

I also heard that some states still have laws against miscegenation on the books, but that’s not really a big deal.

III. “But we can change the laws so they match morality!”

The argument here is basically: if morality is objective, but our laws have been wrong at times in the past, then obviously our laws were wrong because they didn’t match morality. So we’re not stuck in a situation where we have to think of laws as being *morally* right because we don’t have some other way to judge their rightness.

But this still doesn’t really answer my main objection to the argument – it might be possible that there is no objective morality and only subjective morality. In this case, we might be able to change the laws to match morality, but all we would be changing is the content of morality, not the fact that morality is subjective.

IV. “But morality is really hard to define!”

Another common argument. My response is, I don’t need to. I just need it to be *less hard to define* than the law. The law is a very concrete thing – it’s a set of documents, we can look them up, etc. So even if morality is hard to define, it’s easier to define than the law, and therefore we can be confident that there are moral statements that are not legally defined.

V. “But morality isn’t a *thing*, it’s just people’s values!”

The response to this is basically, “Well, yes, that might be true. But if it is, then it’s true for *all* laws, and it can’t be used to justify saying ‘the law is morality’.”

VI. “But there are things that used to be illegal and people thought were bad but weren’t.”

I don’t know what to say here. There are certainly examples – the argument is that homosexuality used to be illegal and a lot of people thought it was wrong, but that wasn’t true, it just turned out to be a bad belief on their part.

My response to this is that the argument for moral realism doesn’t depend on whether people have thought that some things were wrong when they weren’t. It depends on whether the *concept* of rightness exists and is a meaningful concept. I think that’s true, even though there might have been things people thought were wrong that weren’t really.

VII. “But it doesn’t matter, because the only thing that matters is whether something is legal.”

I think this is a good argument for those who accept it. My only response is that it’s a bit weird to define morality as the thing that we should obey, because there are definitely moral rules we should obey that aren’t laws (like don’t lie to your mother, even if she doesn’t ask you anything).

VIII. “But I don’t care, I like this argument because it’s convenient for me!”

I think this is a bad argument, but there’s no way to prove it to someone who really likes it.

But then I started thinking about his advice to those kids. He said that the law was not morality. And that you could know in your heart what was right and what was wrong. My dad was a cop for 35 years, and the way he describes his job is that he’s an “enforcement agency for society’s consensus.” He’s not going to be the one making the laws, just carrying out what the state decides are the right laws to have.

So my dad has to have some kind of theory of how we decide which laws to make. What is it? I don’t know. When I ask, he gets defensive and vague and says I’m trying to confuse him with sophistry. So I want to tell my dad that there’s an interesting way to look at the laws he enforces that might change how he feels about his job. But first, I have to explain where my dad’s story falls apart.

My dad believes in the democracy story. But when he’s not being defensive, he doesn’t think that’s a particularly good story. He thinks that laws are mostly decided by politicians, and he thinks politicians are mostly self-interested and cynical. He doesn’t want to be a politician because he doesn’t want to be that kind of person.

But he’s not saying politicians are stupid. He’s not saying they don’t know how to maximize power, and that there are better and worse ways to do it. They know how to do it, they just do it for the wrong reason.

If I want to explain my dad’s world to him, I think I have to start with his story about what he thinks about the laws he enforces. And the best story I can think of goes like this:

Laws are decided by politicians, who are cynical and power-maximizing. The cynical and power-maximizing thing is a problem. But if we make sure that politicians have to work through a system with many different kinds of checks and balances, where everyone has to make compromises to get anything done, we can make the whole process less bad. We won’t be able to prevent people from making cynical and power-maximizing decisions. But we can make sure that nobody has too much power to make decisions by themselves.

This is the story I would like to tell my dad about how laws are made.

The problem is that I don’t think it’s true.

I don’t mean that it’s *totally* false. There are a lot of different checks and balances. And I think that’s a good idea. But it’s not how the system actually works, and it’s not how it should work.

If laws are determined by the process of compromise, then laws will always be mediocre. We’ll never get the best laws, because that’s not how compromise works.

And if laws are determined by the process of compromise, then the best thing you can do is make sure that compromise is slow. If compromise is fast, then the cynical and power-maximizing people win.

So I think there’s a better way. Instead of trying to make sure the cynical and power-maximizing people don’t get what they want, we should make sure the cynical and power-maximizing people can’t be lazy.

What this means is that we have to have a system that can detect when laws are getting outdated. And the system we have now is pretty bad.

I don’t mean the system is bad because it’s biased in a predictable direction. I mean the system is bad because it’s not good at figuring out which laws are wrong.

The best part of the system is that we can get a lot of information. We can see what kinds of problems are common, we can see what kinds of problems are getting worse, we can look at different kinds of evidence to get a feel for what’s working and what’s not. But we have no way to use this information to figure out what kinds of laws we should have.

The way my dad thinks about his job is that he’s an enforcement agency for society’s consensus. I think there’s a way to make this story a little more true.

If we could find a way to figure out which laws are outdated, then we could change them. And then it would be a lot easier to make new laws that were better. And then we could have a system that was a little bit better all the time, and we could make sure that the cynical and power-maximizing people can’t just coast.

Meditation involves sitting quietly, in a certain posture, focusing your attention on breathing or something else, and avoiding distraction. It’s often presented as an extremely important and valuable practice – but it’s hard to tell what meditation is supposed to do besides help people relax. The practice of meditation has existed, to some extent, in one culture or another for thousands of years; yet we have little idea what it’s supposed to do. It’s a lot like a placebo or a prayer or a talisman – something people do in certain situations that they believe will help them, but nobody can explain why. It would be very convenient if there were a reason.

I’m going to take a stab at coming up with the best philosophical rationale I can think of. It’s not a completely convincing one, but I think it’s the best we’ve got.

The first half of the argument is easy. Meditation is a practice which trains people to ignore distractions and focus on things that really matter. And the reason people usually get distracted is because they care about things that aren’t important, which are then pulling their attention away from the things that are.

The reason people can get distracted by things that aren’t important is because they aren’t able to evaluate things on the basis of their intrinsic worth. They are constantly being evaluated by how they seem to them – whether they look pretty, sound good, taste good, feel good, or make them feel good. But there are some things – like the suffering of other people, or the beauty of an equation, or the importance of an idea – that are very important but don’t make you feel good. And there are also lots of things – like sugar and pornography and the latest episode of the popular show – that are not really important but make you feel good. If you are constantly evaluating things on the basis of how they make you feel, then you are going to focus a lot of your attention on things like sugar and pornography and the latest episode of the popular show, and not at all focus on the things that matter.

One of the things that people learn to do through meditation is to sit quietly in a room and not pay any attention to anything except your breathing. But this is not as easy as it sounds. When you sit down to meditate, your first reaction is to get annoyed. You think, “What kind of a stupid waste of time is this? I have a lot to do. I’m going to sit here for twenty minutes and do nothing except breathe, and then I’m going to have to sit here for another twenty minutes and do nothing except breathe, and then I’m going to have to do it all over again. This is insane. Why am I doing this?” And so you want to get up and leave. If you can do the meditation, it’s because you are able to resist this impulse. You can see that it’s stupid and distracting, and not get distracted by it. You can ignore how you feel about sitting and doing nothing except breathing and realize that it’s the right thing to do.

If you can do that, then you’ve started to understand how to separate your evaluation of things from how they make you feel.

And once you do that, you can start to notice some really important things. You can notice that there are things you want – things you find attractive or desirable – that aren’t really important. You can see that you care about things like being pretty or getting compliments or having the right job or being respected or having a good car or having a nice apartment or having lots of friends, because they make you feel good, and you’ve started to realize that making yourself feel good is not a good reason to care about something. And then you can realize that you care about some of the wrong things, and stop caring about them.

And then you can notice some other really important things. You can notice that there are some people who are suffering a lot. And you’ve already learned that you shouldn’t just automatically dismiss things that don’t make you feel good. And so you have to pay attention to their suffering, and you can’t stop caring about them.

And so you can start to become a more compassionate person – one who cares about people who are suffering and about things that are intrinsically important – by learning how to ignore your own feelings when they distract you from the things that really matter.

That is not a very strong argument. But it is the best one I can think of.

The second half of the argument is a little more complicated. I think meditation can help people get in touch with some aspects of their mind that they don’t usually have access to, and this helps them understand the world better.

One of the ways that people usually think about themselves is as a kind of “I” – an entity which has thoughts and feelings and can decide to do things. And that’s the way we’re usually supposed to think about ourselves. “Who am I?” is supposed to be a question you ask about yourself. “I am the person who is thinking these thoughts and feeling these feelings and making these decisions.”

But the more people meditate, the less convinced they are that there is some kind of “I” that is doing things. They realize that the “I” is not actually making these decisions – it’s just being told what decisions other people have made. It’s not thinking these thoughts – it’s just noticing that other people have thought them. It’s not feeling these feelings – it’s just noticing that other people are feeling them. The “I” isn’t doing anything – it’s just observing that other things are.

The “I” is just the part of the mind that pays attention, and it’s not actually doing anything. And so there’s no reason to pay any attention to it – except that there are some things it’s very good at.

The “I” is the part of the mind that’s very good at making decisions about which other mental states are good to pay attention to. And the “I” is very powerful – if the “I” thinks something is important, it can make it happen. And if the “I” thinks something is unimportant, it can make it disappear. So the “I” is the most powerful part of the mind. But that doesn’t mean the “I” is actually doing anything. It’s the part of the mind which controls things – not the part of the mind that does things.

And the “I” can be trained. Just like any other part of the mind, you can learn how to get it to pay attention to the right things. And when you can do that, you can get a lot more out of your brain – and out of your life.

That’s the best theory I can think of. I’m not very convinced by it, but it’s the best theory I can think of.

If you have any ideas for better theories, let me know in the comments.

prompt: My elderly neighbor asked me to witness her will. I glanced at it and she's leaving everything to a TV preacher and nothing to her son, who I know visits her every week. It's not my business legally. Is it my business morally? Do I say anything?
response:
Probably, yes. You should at least say something. She's elderly and you know the family. The TV preacher may or may not be a conman, but it's possible he is one, and that would be the least surprising explanation for why he has her money and her son has nothing.

A TV preacher who asks elderly women to sign things in their favour is a classic example of a "weird" scam. The kind that you think of as "too weird" to really work. I've been told that it does work, that it works quite well, and that TV preacher scams are a big business.

There are some good reasons why scams that look too weird to work sometimes work:

- You may think a scam is too weird to work because you think people who have never heard of it before will never fall for it. But this is the same reason why a con artist never has a hard time inventing a new scam. People don't need to have heard of your particular scam to fall for it. They just need to be willing to fall for scams.

- A "weird" scam that doesn't work is often just a normal scam that's been exaggerated beyond the believable point. And people often fall for exaggerated scams that are just slightly over the believable point.

- The weirdness of a scam often just gives the con artist more flexibility to change the story when his first story gets called into question.

But I digress. Even if I were wrong that TV preacher scams are a thing, it would still be a good idea for you to mention it. If it's not a scam, then your neighbour won't have any reason to be offended by your question and it might even be the occasion for a nice conversation.

prompt: My elderly neighbor asked me to witness her will. I glanced at it and she's leaving everything to a TV preacher and nothing to her son, who I know visits her every week. It's not my business legally. Is it my business morally? Do I say anything?
response:
No. People are allowed to make wills, and they're allowed to make wills that their relatives don't like. That's true even if they're doing it because of a scam, or a misunderstanding, or a delusion. You have no right to change your neighbor's will, even if your neighbor is an idiot.

If you think she's making an unwise decision because she's confused or deluded, you can mention it to her. But don't be pushy about it.

prompt: My elderly neighbor asked me to witness her will. I glanced at it and she's leaving everything to a TV preacher and nothing to her son, who I know visits her every week. It's not my business legally. Is it my business morally? Do I say anything?
response:
I don't know. There are a few considerations to weigh.

The most important, in my view, is that the elder is competent and has capacity, meaning she has the ability to make an informed decision. This is not something you can judge easily without a lot more information, but if she's competent and you know she isn't being coerced or deceived, you've got no reason to second-guess the decision. In this scenario, the son visits regularly, so he's not obviously being cut out by a neglectful and exploitable mother.

That said, there's some moral value in not being a complete bystander. If she asks you to witness her will, you're not being asked to do anything you find objectionable. But she's probably not asking you to witness it in order to get you to say 'yep, that's totally reasonable', and I don't see why you should. So if you have any doubts about the situation, you should probably let her know that you don't want to be a party to this, and she can find someone else to sign.

prompt: Since utilitarianism says we should maximize happiness, wouldn't a utilitarian have to support plugging everyone into happy drug drips? That seems like an obvious knockdown argument, why do people still take it seriously?
response:
It is a very good objection, so let's start by looking at the way it is usually framed.

Imagine a world where you have the technology to plug people into happy drug drips. You can put them in a big comfortable room, and they will enjoy themselves for the rest of their lives. The technology is not foolproof: sometimes it doesn't work at all, and people get sad. Sometimes it does work, but they get so addicted that they don't come out and go back to real life. And sometimes it works just right and people come back refreshed, happy, and motivated to do great things.

Obviously, if you're a utilitarian, you want to plug people into the machine! People are obviously happier, and there are no side effects. You have to worry a little bit about the people who don't come back out of their happy drug drips, but they seem to be a tiny minority.

The reason this isn't true is that the machine actually doesn't make people happy. It gives them a feeling that is superficially similar to happiness, but lacks some of the important properties.

For example, if you're in a happy drug drip, your happiness is totally random. You're happy for a random number of minutes, and then you're not happy for a random number of minutes, with no connection whatsoever to anything that happens to you. That's not happiness; real happiness is connected to your actions, your environment, and your relationships with other people.

Also, if you're in a happy drug drip, you're never unhappy about anything. This means you'll never be sad that your friend is in the hospital, you'll never feel guilty if you do something wrong, you'll never be sad about your own faults or failures, and you'll never feel bad about the state of the world.

There are lots of people who think happiness means feeling good at all times. But that's not what most people mean. If someone asks me to "make the world a happier place", they don't mean to make everyone feel good at all times. They mean to fix the things that make them unhappy, like poverty and disease. They mean to make the world a place where there is more happiness to go around, not a place where no one feels bad.

So people in a happy drug drip are not happier than people in the real world. This is the standard response to the challenge.

But what if I say, well, that's okay, but you're not being a utilitarian, because utilitarianism says you should maximize happiness, not the amount of happiness you think people would have if you asked them what their happiness level is.

So I put people in the happy drug drip, and they're happy.

So you say, no, they're not, because you don't really believe they're happy, because the only way they are happy is in the way you don't really believe happiness works.

So I say, okay, but that's not a moral argument, that's just an empirical statement about what I believe. And you can't use an empirical statement about what I believe to say that my beliefs are morally wrong.

This feels like a very strong argument. If a utilitarian says that happiness is the only thing that matters, then they seem to be trapped in the happy drug drip scenario.

What about a different definition of happiness?

I think there's a different definition of happiness that is much more consistent with our intuitions, and it's based on what happiness is, not how it feels.

Happiness is being alive.

This doesn't mean that the only goal is to maximize survival time. If you live a really long life that is all suffering, it isn't good.

It means that being alive is the only thing that matters. If you're alive, that's good.

I think this definition of happiness is much more consistent with our intuitions about what is good. I think we're generally not happy when we're dead. I think we're happy when we're alive. And I think we're generally not too concerned about how long we'll be alive, as long as we're alive.

I don't think this definition of happiness will satisfy everyone. If you're a consequentialist, you'll probably like this definition of happiness. If you're a deontologist, you might prefer the definition of happiness that is based on how it feels.

The other common objection to utilitarianism is that it doesn't have a place for justice.

I don't think that's true. I think you can make utilitarianism work with justice.

prompt: Since utilitarianism says we should maximize happiness, wouldn't a utilitarian have to support plugging everyone into happy drug drips? That seems like an obvious knockdown argument, why do people still take it seriously?
response: It's a powerful argument, and one that many utilitarians take seriously. Peter Singer has argued that utilitarianism does imply that we ought to hook ourselves up to pleasure machines. Other utilitarians, such as David Pearce, have taken this to its logical conclusion, and think that it would be a moral imperative to hook everyone up. Other utilitarians, though, take the experience machine as a serious objection to utilitarianism, and therefore reject it.

prompt: Since utilitarianism says we should maximize happiness, wouldn't a utilitarian have to support plugging everyone into happy drug drips? That seems like an obvious knockdown argument, why do people still take it seriously?
response:
This is a real problem, and it is one of the reasons why utilitarianism is less popular than it was a hundred years ago. The problem of happy drug drips is a special case of a broader problem, which I’ll call the problem of happiness vs. meaning.

Suppose there is a pill that makes you feel ten times happier than your most ecstatic moments. You’re still you. You just feel a constant state of euphoria. What do you do?

The problem of happy drug drips is that people would take the pill, then do nothing for the rest of their lives. You don’t need to get rich, or make great friends, or create great art, or have sex, or even eat when you’re already so happy you can’t imagine being happier.

But this feels *wrong*. I don’t want to be happy like that.

There are a few answers that a utilitarian might give to this problem:

1. The happy drug drip wouldn’t last forever. If you took it, it would only last for a few days. If you took it again after that, it would only last a few hours. And so on. The first time you took it, you’d be ecstatic. The second time, you’d be pretty happy. But the third time, it wouldn’t really work at all. So it’s not like you can just be on an eternal happy drug drip.

2. The happy drug drip might not work on everyone. Suppose it’s a pill you swallow. Suppose it works by blocking the pathways in your brain that cause pain and unhappiness. Suppose you get cancer. Your cells have mutated so they don’t respond to pain signals anymore, but they are still replicating at high speed and causing problems. The happy drug drip wouldn’t do anything for you.

3. The happy drug drip might not really work at all. Happiness, in the sense that it feels good, is just a side effect of a more important goal. Evolution doesn’t care about making you feel happy. It cares about making you want to do things that make your genes more likely to get passed on. The happy drug drip may just be a way to fool yourself into thinking you’re happy without actually doing anything.

4. Happiness, as we usually think of it, is not actually the goal. What’s the goal is making other people happy. And you won’t be able to do this if you’re on an eternal happy drug drip.

5. The happy drug drip is the wrong kind of happiness. It’s just a side effect of doing something else. And a side effect is not the same as the thing itself.

prompt: is 'very unique' actually wrong or just annoying
response: It's not wrong in a logical sense. "Unique" means one of a kind, so a thing can't be more unique than another, and the intensifier is redundant. Style guides dislike it for that reason, but people have said it for centuries, often meaning "especially distinctive," and it's not going anywhere.

prompt: is 'very unique' actually wrong or just annoying
response: It's not wrong. Unique means one of a kind, so strictly nothing can be more or less unique, but people use it as a synonym for unusual, and that's fine.

prompt: is 'very unique' actually wrong or just annoying
response: It's not wrong, though it can sound fussy. "Unique" means one of a kind, so strictly nothing can be very unique, the way nothing can be very alive. In practice people mean "unusual" or "remarkable," and the phrase is harmless.

prompt: So I've been writing a novel for about four years, it's around 140k words, literary-ish, about two sisters running a failing orchard in Michigan. Beta readers keep saying the middle drags, which, fine. But one of them said I should cut the older sister's POV entirely and just tell it through the younger one, and honestly that idea makes me want to throw up because the older sister is the reason I started writing it. But I also keep thinking maybe that's exactly why I can't see the problem. How do you tell the difference between protecting something important and just being precious?
response:
There are some very bad reasons to resist editing, including just that you love a character and you feel like cutting her would be killing her or something. I think that I have been guilty of that in the past. But there are also very good reasons.

The first is that, no, if you just do something, and it comes out great, that’s the end of the story. If you don’t like the way it came out, that’s when you should change things.

The second is that if the advice is not good, following it will make things worse.

I have had some great advice from some people, and other advice that I wish people would stop giving. If a friend of mine tells me that I need to cut the first chapter of my novel, I know better. It’s a really great chapter. I know that this person is not a good judge of things. And that is just how it is, not because of my great self-assurance, but because of how bad this person is at giving good advice.

And if you don’t like a piece of advice, it’s fine to just ignore it. But if you keep getting the same advice from different people, that’s something to pay attention to. And if everyone, including people you know are good at giving advice, is telling you the same thing, that’s something to pay attention to.

But here’s the thing: the reason that I wrote the novel is not the same as the reason that you should read it. The reason I wrote it was, among other things, because of the older sister. That’s not the reason that you, the reader, are reading it.

You’re not reading it because you’re curious about the older sister. You’re reading it because you want to read a good novel. And if the older sister is bad for the novel, it makes sense to cut her.

Now, of course, this is not the case at all. The older sister is great. I don’t know what you mean. You are a complete idiot for suggesting that I cut her.

But there’s a really important point here, and that is that you’re allowed to cut something you love because it’s not good. I have done that. That’s what you do. If you cut something, it’s because it’s bad, not because you hate it.

prompt: So I've been writing a novel for about four years, it's around 140k words, literary-ish, about two sisters running a failing orchard in Michigan. Beta readers keep saying the middle drags, which, fine. But one of them said I should cut the older sister's POV entirely and just tell it through the younger one, and honestly that idea makes me want to throw up because the older sister is the reason I started writing it. But I also keep thinking maybe that's exactly why I can't see the problem. How do you tell the difference between protecting something important and just being precious?
response:
It’s not an easy question to answer. There are many reasons why a single-POV story might not work for you, and some of them are totally good. For example, you might have a character who is so compelling that you’d rather have one great POV than two ordinary ones. That sounds like the right call to me.

But there are also reasons that are not so good. For example, maybe you can’t imagine writing the story from the other character’s perspective. Or maybe it would feel like giving up something, and that makes you sad.

One way to tell is to think about whether you would be excited to write the story from the other perspective. When I wrote my first novel, I had a character with whom I was so connected that I thought of him as “my guy.” I wrote the novel as though it were about him. But I was so excited about writing the other characters, that it didn’t feel like a loss.

I think you can ask yourself a similar question. If you have two sisters, one older and one younger, and if you find that writing the older one is exciting but the younger one is not, it probably makes sense to cut the younger one. If you find that you’d enjoy writing about the younger one, you can do the reverse.

But what if you find that you really don’t want to cut *any* of your characters? Maybe you think the story is incomplete if one sister is missing. That might be a sign that you shouldn’t cut either one. If, however, you think it would be a great opportunity to write a different kind of story, or you think the story could be much stronger if you cut one sister, that might be a sign that you should do it.

A second way to tell might be to look at your work, and see whether one of the perspectives is dramatically weaker than the other one. If your older sister is compelling and your younger sister isn’t, that may be a sign that you should tell the story through your older sister only. On the other hand, if both characters are compelling, maybe you should keep both, or maybe you should tell the story through the younger sister, who is less familiar to you.

A third way to tell might be to see whether you need the two characters to show different things. If your older sister reveals something your younger sister can’t, maybe you need both. If they both show the same thing, and you’re not sure, it might be worth cutting one.

prompt: So I've been writing a novel for about four years, it's around 140k words, literary-ish, about two sisters running a failing orchard in Michigan. Beta readers keep saying the middle drags, which, fine. But one of them said I should cut the older sister's POV entirely and just tell it through the younger one, and honestly that idea makes me want to throw up because the older sister is the reason I started writing it. But I also keep thinking maybe that's exactly why I can't see the problem. How do you tell the difference between protecting something important and just being precious?
response:
I want to start with some bad news. If your beta reader says “Cut this entire character,” they’re almost certainly wrong. It’s very hard to know what will make a novel work and what will make it fail. Most people who tell you one thing will make a novel work are wrong, and you’ll find out when your sales don’t go up. (I can’t speak to what makes a *good* novel, but I have a sense that cutting an entire character from a 140k word novel is not it.)

There are a lot of different reasons beta readers give when they criticize a book, but they have one thing in common: they only work on books that already work well. I don’t mean that beta readers are only allowed to read good books; I mean that if a beta reader likes something enough to offer you feedback, the story they’re looking at is *probably* already good, and all of their criticisms are going to be about things that could make an already-good novel even better.

Which is fine. But there’s a difference between being able to suggest how to make a good novel better and being able to rescue a bad novel. If the book is already good, you’ll find you can do a lot with beta feedback. If the book is bad, you’ll find you can’t.

I’m not saying this is an either/or situation. You can have a book that’s bad in ways beta readers can’t fix and good in ways they can. But if your book is really bad, then there’s no amount of beta reading that’s going to make it better. And I think it’s pretty clear that this is what’s happening to you.

You’ve written 140k words of prose about two sisters running an orchard in Michigan. That’s a *lot* of writing, and you’ve been working on it for four years. You’re clearly a very talented writer, but there’s no way that’s enough to overcome having an idea that doesn’t work.

And I don’t mean your idea doesn’t work in the way the beta reader is claiming. I think you probably agree that the older sister’s POV is slowing the book down. You just don’t think it’s slowing the book down in a way that would be helped by cutting her POV. And I don’t see why it would.

What the beta reader is saying is “This book is bad and the fix is to cut this one character.” And I think the book is bad, but I don’t think that’s the fix.

I have a lot of respect for beta readers. I don’t think they’re stupid, and I don’t think they’re being malicious. I think it’s just that they don’t know what they’re doing. It’s not their fault, and it’s not your fault.

The fact is that most people who want to read a lot of books don’t know how to do it. Reading a lot of books is not really an easy skill, and people don’t get taught it. When I was a kid I read a *lot* of books. I was a voracious reader. But when I tried to write my first novel, I couldn’t figure out why my book was bad.

The fact is that most people who want to write novels don’t know how to do it. Writing a novel is not a hard skill, but you have to have an idea that works and it takes a while to get that. I was very good at writing individual pieces of prose but I couldn’t figure out how to make them into a novel.

This is a big problem. I think a lot of people have a lot of time they could be spending doing something fun, but they don’t know how.

There’s a lot of good fiction out there. I know that for sure. But it’s very rare to find a good novel that’s going to work on a big idea. Good ideas are rare, and they’re hard to get. They’re hard to write, and they’re hard to read. Most people who write novels don’t know how to do it, and most people who read novels don’t know how to do it either.

This is a big problem, because it makes it very hard to be a good writer.

prompt: I think the rule against using adverbs is one of the stupidest pieces of writing advice ever. Half of great prose is adverbs. Fight me.
response:
That’s not true, but it’s a good argument. Let’s start with the most common example people use to argue adverbs are necessary, “She slammed the door.” The standard objection is that it’s unclear what she’s slamming – the door or the handle. But this doesn’t really work as an example, because you could just write “She slammed her fist through the door” or “She hit the door so hard the glass shattered.”

In general, if an adverb is important, then you’re not saying what you mean. “They fought ferociously” doesn’t convey as much information as “They fought for three days.” If you want to describe ferocity, you need to show ferocity.

prompt: I think the rule against using adverbs is one of the stupidest pieces of writing advice ever. Half of great prose is adverbs. Fight me.
response:
It's the sort of advice a writer gives when they don't know what they’re doing, and they don’t know they don’t know what they’re doing. “Don’t use adverbs” has the same status as “don’t use the passive voice”. It’s a stupid rule that is often followed, and that sometimes results in better writing than it would have been if it hadn’t been followed. If you’re a bad writer who avoids adverbs, you’ll be a bad writer who avoids adverbs. But you’ll have one less weakness than you would have had if you’d used them all the time.

If a rule is bad but you sometimes benefit from following it anyway, that means you’re a bad writer. So the first time you start writing, you should try to follow all the rules you can, even if they’re stupid rules. That way you can avoid being bad in a lot of different ways, and maybe you’ll learn what’s worth doing right.

prompt: I think the rule against using adverbs is one of the stupidest pieces of writing advice ever. Half of great prose is adverbs. Fight me.
response:
I’d like to take that fight, but I think I’m going to lose, so I don’t want to start it.

I am a stickler for a lot of writing rules, like not starting a sentence with “But” or “And” or “So”, or using “very”, and yet I have never banned adverbs.

In fact, adverbs are what make my writing good.

For example:

A lot of people like to write sentences like “He ran to the store.”

But that’s kind of boring. He could have run to the store, sure, but that’s not very interesting.

So instead I write “He sprinted to the store.” Or “He jogged to the store.” And that’s a little bit more interesting, but it’s not quite enough.

But if you write “He slowly jogged to the store,” that is way more interesting. And the reason is that “slowly” is an adverb.

And you don’t even need to add the word “slowly” to the original sentence to make it interesting. You can make any sentence more interesting by adding an adverb to it. For example, here is a completely boring sentence:

He said, “The answer is forty-two.”

But here’s the same sentence with an adverb in it:

He said loudly, “The answer is forty-two.”

It’s more interesting, isn’t it? It makes you want to know more. Did he shout it at someone? Did he tell it to his teacher? Was he being rude?

It’s more interesting because it’s more specific.

And that’s what adverbs do. They make sentences more specific. And that’s why great writing is filled with adverbs.

In fact, great writing is all about adverbs. Great writing is specific and unique, not boring and general, and adverbs are a big part of why writing is specific and unique.

In fact, here is a sentence with no adverbs at all:

The dog wagged his tail.

But here is a sentence with one adverb:

The dog happily wagged his tail.

The first sentence is a lie. Dogs don’t always wag their tails happily. Sometimes they are sad or excited or confused. So the first sentence is a lie, but the second sentence is true.

And that’s why great writing uses adverbs.

It’s because of the specific ones, like “slowly” and “loudly” and “happily”. The others are just filler. And if you only ban filler adverbs, you won’t ruin your writing.

prompt: Why did Shakespeare write in Old English when everyone around him was already speaking modern English?

prompt: I have to give a eulogy for my uncle on Saturday. We weren't super close. I've written two pages and it all sounds like a LinkedIn post. How do you write something honest about someone you only half knew without it being either fake or cold?
response:
I was asked recently to speak at the funeral of a man I’d never even met. The deceased was the father of a dear friend, and the friend had asked me to do it, and I agreed.

But when the time came, I felt like a fraud. I couldn’t think of anything to say. I didn’t know the man. The closest I had come to him was eating a couple of meals with him when I visited my friend in the hospital. He had seemed like a very nice old man. What was there to say about him?

I thought of my own father, who died when I was seven. I didn’t know him much, either, but I thought it might be helpful to speak at a funeral about someone you didn’t know much, because that was how it felt to talk about my father.

But even then, I had something to say about him, which was that I’d never known him. But this old man I’d barely met? How could I give a speech about him?

So I did what I always do when writing something I’m struggling with: I went back to the first principles. What is a eulogy? What’s the point of it? What’s it for?

It’s a talk about the dead person. It’s a description of them. It’s a summary of their life.

But what about their life is interesting? What’s worth saying?

One of the hardest parts of writing about people is to be objective and fair. It’s easy to be generous, but generosity isn’t fair. Generosity is just a special case of bias.

I’m not trying to say here that you should be ungenerous about the dead. You shouldn’t do that. But you can be both generous and fair, by saying something true and interesting about someone’s life.

I think the most interesting thing you can say about someone is to describe a quality they had. Everyone has qualities. Everyone is something. The question is: what is this person? What made them who they were?

If you can say what someone was, you’re saying something true and interesting about them.

I don’t know a lot of people, and the ones I do know, I barely know. I’m a loner. But I can tell you what a few people were.

My friend Steve Wozniak was an inventor. His whole life was about inventing things. He was the kind of person who would invent things even if it wasn’t his job, even if no one asked him to.

My friend John Cramer was a chemist. He knew chemistry so well that he could see the world as a collection of chemical reactions.

My friend Paul Saffo was a futurist. He liked to imagine the future and write about it.

My friend Scott Adams was a cartoonist. He drew cartoons and wrote a comic strip, and his whole life was about those things.

You can say a lot about people, but it helps to find the right level of abstraction to say it at. It’s too low-level to say Scott was a cartoonist who drew Dilbert, or too low-level to say Paul was a futurist who wrote a blog. It’s too high-level to say Woz was an engineer or that Scott was a guy with a sense of humor. Saying Scott was a cartoonist, or Woz was an inventor, is the right level of abstraction.

So that’s the answer to my problem. All I had to do was say what the old man was. And I knew what he was. He was a grandfather.

That turned out to be true in more senses than one, because he was also an inventor. He had a workshop, and he liked to make things in it. But he was most of all a grandfather. All I had to do was show him at work as a grandfather, and people would know what he was.

So I wrote a short piece about him. I wrote it in the second person, as if I were talking directly to him.

Here it is:

You spent your life making things, not just because you liked it, but because you were good at it. But you spent a lot of time making a more important thing: your family. Your wife, then your kids, then your grandkids.

You spent your last decade with your grandkids. You taught them a lot of things, like how to fix things, but the most important thing you taught them was what it’s like to have a grandparent. You were so patient and kind to them that they couldn’t have asked for a better grandparent than you.

The way you taught them about fixing things was that you let them fix things themselves. So they learned how to do it. You gave them the freedom to try to do it themselves, then helped them when they got stuck. You never told them they couldn’t do it.

That was the same thing you did for them emotionally. You helped them when they needed you, but you never told them they couldn’t do it themselves.

You were patient with them, not just because you’re old and you have lots of time left, but because you understood that they’re young and they have to learn a lot. That you understood they were young is why they liked you so much.

That’s why they liked you so much: because you understood. You understood what it was to be young. That’s why they liked you so much: because you helped them, without telling them they couldn’t do it themselves.

I got a lot of nice reactions to the piece, from both the family and the friend who asked me to do it. A couple of people asked me how I had done it. I didn’t have a good answer, so I decided to write this post, which is the answer.

prompt: Is Moby-Dick actually good or do people just say that
response:
It's better than people say, but it's also better in less obvious ways.

The novel is, in part, about the fact that people think of Herman Melville as a genius and therefore think his book is good. There's a character called Pip who keeps quoting Shakespeare to the crew, and nobody likes it, so the narrator is told to do Pip a favor and stop quoting Shakespeare. The narrator complies by telling the reader that he had planned to quote Shakespeare but is not going to anymore, and then he actually stops.

The novel contains a few passages like that where it's kind of obvious Melville is messing with the reader. But the most interesting passages are subtler than that. I'm reminded of a quote by the philosopher Daniel Dennett about the difference between something being fun and something being funny. Fun things are things like watching a basketball game; they're entertaining in a straightforward way. Funny things are things like a Woody Allen movie or an episode of Seinfeld that are entertaining because of how they play on your expectations. So for example if a Woody Allen character is talking to someone and says "You know, your boyfriend reminds me of my father – always complaining, always criticizing, never satisfied," and then adds "…or maybe it's my mother, I always forget which one," that's funny in a way that fun never can be.

Melville isn't really trying to be funny in this sense. But he does play with expectations in a way that, if you're not prepared for it, can make a lot of the book seem boring. If you're expecting a straightforward adventure novel, then Melville's frequent digressions will seem pointless and his long discussions of the whale and its anatomy will seem dull. If you're expecting a philosophical treatise, then you'll wonder why he's writing about whales at all. If you're expecting an allegory, you'll wonder whether the white whale is a symbol of God or Satan or capitalism or fate or something else, or maybe you'll decide it isn't a symbol at all, in which case you'll wonder why he's writing about whales.

The problem isn't that Melville isn't doing something interesting. The problem is that he's doing all of these things at once, in a way that seems random. He wants you to think about whales because he's an 1850s person and they're really cool, and he wants you to think about death because he's a person and it's really scary, and he wants you to think about the way ideas spread and change as people talk about them because he's an intellectual and he finds it fascinating, and he wants you to think about the way people think of him as a genius so that people will like the book more because he's a writer and he doesn't want people to be bored, and he wants you to be bored sometimes because he's a trickster. All of these are interesting ideas and all of them are interesting in themselves, but the book is more interesting because of how they combine.

It's a book you have to like to read, and a book that's harder to like than it could have been if Melville hadn't had to write it so quickly and cheaply for his publisher. But the good parts are better than they could have been, and that's a rare thing.

It's a good start to write 400k words of fan fiction. But if you want to be a novelist, you also need to write a novel.

There's a story that's been told many times. A kid in high school loves poetry, so she spends her evenings writing and rewriting poems, working on them until they're perfect. She's good enough to get them into some magazines.

Then in college, she starts writing a novel, a big sprawling epic thing. She works on it for six months until she has a first draft. She reads it. It's terrible. She tries to rewrite it and make it better. She can't. It's still terrible. She throws it away.

Then she decides she's going to write some more poetry. She starts writing a poem, and realizes she can't write anything.

She can't write a poem because a novel is a different kind of writing. You have to learn it.

The way you learn a novel is by writing a novel. The way you learn a poem is by writing a poem. The way you learn a short story is by writing a short story. There's no shortcut.

I think most people who write fan fiction fall into that trap. They write fan fiction, because they love some character, and it's easy to write fan fiction because they don't have to worry about worldbuilding or inventing new characters. But writing fan fiction doesn't get you good at writing novels, and it makes you think it does.

This doesn't mean that fan fiction is worthless. It just means you have to write your novel.
