prompt: I used to be really athletic in high school (swimming, state level) and now at 27 I can barely get through a 20 minute workout without wanting to quit. It's not even physical, it's like my brain remembers what I used to be able to do and it's demoralizing. Anyone else deal with this?
response:
This is a common phenomenon, and it's one that can be really demoralizing. A few suggestions:

- Find a sport or exercise that you weren't good at in high school. If you're bad at it, then you won't have high expectations.

- Find some sort of activity that you're not comparing yourself to. If you go jogging and feel like you're running badly, just try to run as fast as you can, or just run for a long time and forget about speed.

- Find an activity that has a different skill set than you used to be good at, so that you're not comparing yourself to an old self. If you were a swimmer, then try running. If you were a runner, try swimming.

- Go to a gym that doesn't have lots of mirrors and where you're not surrounded by people doing impressive things.

- Try to exercise with your friends, rather than alone.

- If you like watching people exercise, maybe try to watch people on the gym or playing some sport, and not do any yourself.

prompt: I used to be really athletic in high school (swimming, state level) and now at 27 I can barely get through a 20 minute workout without wanting to quit. It's not even physical, it's like my brain remembers what I used to be able to do and it's demoralizing. Anyone else deal with this?
response:
Oh, yes. And it's not the fault of your brain. Your brain is remembering that you were very, very good at something. And that's awesome.

But the problem is that you're comparing yourself to a version of yourself who wasn't trying to improve. Your high-school self didn't start swimming at the age of seven and spend ten hours a week in the pool. Your high-school self didn't try to get better at swimming for a whole decade. That's a lot of time to spend getting better at swimming. So it makes sense that you're not as good as you were.

You're not trying to beat some absolute benchmark. You're trying to get better at swimming than you were the day before, and than you were the day before that, and so on. So, yeah, don't get discouraged by how far you are from the person you used to be. You're not supposed to be. Just try to get a little bit better every day.

prompt: I've noticed my heart rate on my apple watch hits like 185 when I run. I'm 44. Is that dangerous? I'm scared to keep running but also don't want to go to the doctor for nothing
response:
For most people, a peak heart rate near your maximum (around 220 minus your age, or 176 for you) during hard effort is normal and not dangerous by itself. A 44-year-old running hard can easily reach the mid-180s, and the watch can overread when the fit is loose or you're sweaty.

See a doctor if your heart rate jumps very high without effort, especially if it stays elevated for minutes after you stop. Also get checked promptly if a high rate comes with chest pain, pressure or tightness, breathlessness out of proportion, near-fainting or fainting, a new palpitation or fluttery feeling, or if you haven't exercised regularly and are now training hard. If you have a family history of sudden cardiac death or cardiomyopathy, get checked before pushing hard.

If none of that applies, a one-time baseline visit is reasonable, not overkill: a history, exam, ECG, blood pressure and lipids, with a stress test if your doctor thinks it helps. Until then, you can keep running at a pace you can talk through, and warm up for at least ten minutes.

prompt: I've noticed my heart rate on my apple watch hits like 185 when I run. I'm 44. Is that dangerous? I'm scared to keep running but also don't want to go to the doctor for nothing
response:
It may be normal, but it's worth a check. Most healthy people's peak is roughly 220 minus your age, so around 176 for you. If 185 happens while you're straining hard and you feel fine, that can be within normal limits, and watch readings sometimes run high. A resting rate of 40 to 55 can also be fine if you train regularly.

See a doctor within a couple of weeks if your rate spikes when you're just sitting, if it climbs past about 90 with very light activity, or if it ever goes below 40 while awake. Sooner is better if you also feel dizzy or faint, or have chest pain or shortness of breath. The clinician will usually record a tracing of your heart's electrical activity to look at the rhythm directly.

prompt: I'm a PT and I keep getting patients who've been told by chiropractors that their spine is 'out of alignment.' I don't want to trash another profession in front of patients but I also don't want to reinforce that framing. How would you handle that conversation?
response:
I try to avoid trashing chiropractors in front of the patient. It doesn’t seem fair, and in many cases I agree that they’re doing a good job.

But when I say “a good job,” I mean getting the patient feeling better, not restoring the alignment of the spine. I think the notion of “alignment” is a fiction.

The spine has a very high degree of freedom. There are no “correct” positions or movements. And, in fact, it’s not even obvious what it means to say that a vertebra is out of alignment.

If you look at an x-ray of your spine, it doesn’t seem to be in alignment, but it looks like most people. You may think that a vertebra is out of alignment if it’s rotated or tilted at an unusual angle. But the rotation of the vertebra is relative to the one above and below it, and those are relative to the ones above and below them, and so on. If you straighten out a “crooked” vertebra, you’re just shifting the misalignment to another vertebra, or, if you straighten out the whole spine, it’s still not aligned in some other coordinate system. And so on.

But the vertebrae don’t actually rotate independently of each other. They’re connected by ligaments and muscles and discs. You can’t change the position of one vertebra without changing the position of all the others. So it doesn’t make sense to talk about the spine being misaligned.

In fact, I think this idea is just a convenient story. It gives chiropractors something to do. It’s not that they think they’re doing something useful, and it’s not that the treatment does anything useful, but that having the story allows them to do the treatment.

And the treatment does seem to help a lot of people. But I think it’s because of the placebo effect.

A chiropractor will often claim that a vertebra has been subluxated or displaced. But vertebrae are firmly attached to each other, so it doesn’t really make sense to talk about them being subluxated or displaced.

And I think it’s not necessary to straighten vertebrae out. There’s just no point to it. You can’t really straighten out vertebrae, and even if you could, it wouldn’t help anybody, because the position of your vertebrae is not related to your health.

A chiropractor may say they can feel when a vertebra is out of alignment. I think what’s actually going on is that the muscles around the vertebra are tense.

But I don’t want to trash chiropractors in front of patients. So I just say that I don’t think that spine alignment is really the cause of problems. It’s more about how your muscles are moving and feeling.

I try to avoid putting down other professions, because it doesn’t make me look good. And I’m not sure it’s even true that I’m right and they’re wrong.

prompt: I'm a PT and I keep getting patients who've been told by chiropractors that their spine is 'out of alignment.' I don't want to trash another profession in front of patients but I also don't want to reinforce that framing. How would you handle that conversation?
response:
In general, chiropractic is a scam. Some people claim that chiropractic has its place in the treatment of back pain, but the evidence for that is weak to non-existent. That said, there are chiropractors who don’t practice chiropractic, and the practice is often more harmless than it is dangerous.

In general, we don’t recommend that people get chiropractic care. But we also don’t tell people that they shouldn’t have gotten chiropractic care. There’s just nothing to be gained from telling a patient that their last treatment was an awful idea.

Instead, we tell them that chiropractic is a treatment for pain that works for some people, and that we think there are other treatments that are better for them. We explain that chiropractors believe that they can fix pain by “fixing” the spine, but we don’t have good evidence that their “fixing” does that. We tell them that we don’t think the spine is “out of alignment,” but that we do know that their pain is real and that we can help them with it.

Sometimes, we’ll do a quick demonstration to make our point. I’ve seen one guy pick up a tennis ball and say “this is your spine,” and then he’ll turn it around a couple times and say “the chiropractor can turn it around any way they like, but it’s still a tennis ball.” It’s not a great demonstration, but it makes the point.

prompt: I'm a PT and I keep getting patients who've been told by chiropractors that their spine is 'out of alignment.' I don't want to trash another profession in front of patients but I also don't want to reinforce that framing. How would you handle that conversation?
response:
One of my friends is a chiropractor and a wonderful person. When I see him, I tell him he is an amazing chiropractor, and I tell my students they should go to him. He has the nicest office in the world, with a great treatment room, a gym, a pool, and a sauna. I’ve been in there. It is a great office. And he does a lot of great work. He has lots of techniques that work. He does joint manipulation, which I think is effective for treating acute pain and which I am also trained to do.

But when I do joint manipulation, I do it with the mindset of someone who is trying to decrease pain. That is all I care about. So, when I do joint manipulation, I just think, how is this going to decrease pain? I don’t even think about joints moving or bones being out of alignment. I don’t think about any of that stuff.

I don’t care about alignment. I am a scientist and I have read the evidence on spinal manipulation and how it works. I am not going to tell you that spinal manipulation doesn’t work. I am going to tell you that spinal manipulation works to decrease pain and that we don’t know why.

I’m going to tell you that when we do joint manipulation, it causes a lot of changes in the body. It changes the chemical messengers that go through your brain. It changes the amount of blood that goes to your joints. It changes your breathing. I could go on and on. So we just don’t know what it does or how it works. We know it is effective at decreasing pain, but we don’t know how.

Now, there is this thing called the chiropractic philosophy of care, which is a set of principles that chiropractors believe in. It started way back when, in the 1800s. And there is this idea that if your spine is out of alignment, it can cause disease.

So the idea is that if your spine is out of alignment, it is pressing on a nerve, which then causes problems in your heart, your kidneys, and so on. And if your spine is out of alignment, you could get cancer, or diabetes, or asthma, or any kind of disease.

The idea was that, if I were to just take an x-ray, I could see which joints in your spine were out of alignment, and I could tell you what disease you had. And that if I were to realign your spine, then your disease would go away.

This idea is called subluxation. And this is what I find really interesting.

The idea is that if you were to take an x-ray, you could see the subluxation. And if you were to realign your joints, then the disease would go away.

This idea was created in the late 1800s. And for a hundred years, chiropractors have been using this idea to tell people, “you have a disease. And if I realign your spine, it will go away.”

For a hundred years.

So if you look at the evidence and you ask, “Does chiropractic treatment cure disease? Does it cure cancer? Does it cure diabetes?” the answer is no. And this is what is frustrating to me.

So we know that chiropractic treatment works. We know that joint manipulation works. But the idea that if you have a disease and we realign your spine, it will go away? There is no evidence for that.

There are two kinds of chiropractors. There are those who are scientists and those who think about their patients as having a disease, and if we realign their spine, the disease will go away.

There are people who believe in the chiropractic philosophy of care. And then there are people who have abandoned the chiropractic philosophy of care and just use the techniques that work. So it is very easy for patients to get confused. And I think it is very easy for them to get confused because people have been saying this for a hundred years.

And so I feel bad for my chiropractor friends. I feel bad for the patients. They are confused because they hear from a lot of people who say, “If I realign your spine, it will fix your disease.” And there are people who have given up on this idea of subluxation and are just using the techniques that work.

prompt: Is it still a sport if the athletes are using exoskeletons or if there's an 'enhanced games' with legal doping? Where does the line actually sit for you?
response:
It is. What sport is is a matter of definition, not of nature. I’m going to say that it’s a sport if there’s a human being and the competition requires human physical effort, and that’s it. So a marathon where the runners are using exoskeletons is a sport. A marathon where people drive cars around a track is not.

But this doesn’t mean I’m in favor of any of this. The first reason not to use exoskeletons in races is that they’re boring. A race between two guys wearing exoskeletons is no more interesting than a race between two guys wearing roller skates. If you’re going to do something that requires an athlete, let them be an athlete.

The second reason not to use exoskeletons in races is that they’re a distraction. If athletes are allowed to use exoskeletons, they’ll use them. This will mean that people who want to watch an interesting race between two humans in competition will have to go look at some other sport. We’re already seeing this with the way the use of drugs has taken away from the romance of Olympic sports. Let’s not let this get worse.

The third reason not to use exoskeletons in races is that it’s not fair. There are lots of people who think it’s unfair that some people are born taller, or born into wealthy families, or born in a country with a good sports culture. But at least this is natural. If we allow athletes to use exoskeletons, it will be unfair because the rich will have better exoskeletons than the poor.

The fourth reason not to use exoskeletons in races is that this kind of stuff tends to lead to more stuff. Let athletes wear exoskeletons and the next thing you know they’re putting in a few hundred horsepower and doing two hundred miles per hour. Or they’re wearing jetpacks and flying around. It’s not good when you start asking yourself how far you have to go before this kind of thing stops being a sport.

The fifth reason not to use exoskeletons in races is that there’s a slippery slope between the exoskeleton and the car. What’s a jetpack but a very small car?

The Enhanced Games are no different. They’re a distraction, they’re not fair, and there’s a slippery slope between drugs and robots and jetpacks and cars.

But I’ll repeat that this doesn’t mean I’m opposed to them, exactly. This is a question of definition, not of nature. And it’s not even a question of whether you want a sports league to do this. If someone wants to start an Enhanced Games or a robot car race, I think they should be able to. I just think we should call them what they are.

prompt: Is it still a sport if the athletes are using exoskeletons or if there's an 'enhanced games' with legal doping? Where does the line actually sit for you?
response:
I don’t know what the right answer is. But I think the right answer is not “anything that looks like a sport is a sport, full stop.”

I know that’s the position people in sports talk about when they’re arguing for things they like. They say: it doesn’t matter if the athletes are using performance-enhancing drugs or wearing a suit that doubles their muscle mass. As long as it’s still competitive, and as long as people are still trying to get better at it, then it’s still a sport.

It’s the same way people argue about other stuff. “As long as people are still writing books, it’s still literature. It doesn’t matter if they use thesaurus apps to find the right word or if they’re just using random word generators to come up with interesting combinations.” “As long as people are still painting pictures, it’s still painting. It doesn’t matter if they use a digital photo editor or if they use paint-by-numbers.”

I think this is wrong. You could define “sport” to include every competition where you can do some kind of physical task and try to get better at it. But that seems like a weird definition, because it would include stuff that isn’t even remotely close to what we usually think of as sports.

Like let’s say you were a kid growing up in 1970s Japan. And you wanted to try some kind of sport. Maybe you wanted to try something competitive, but something not too hard, something you could learn really fast and get pretty good at. You might look at your neighborhood and see that there are lots of kids playing baseball, basketball, soccer, and tennis. And if you wanted to play any of those, it might take you a while to get really good. But you might also notice that kids your age were playing something else. They were playing video games. You could just go to the arcade, play a few rounds of a game, and get really good at it. You could even get better than adults.

This was a big deal for people who thought about what “sport” meant. The Japanese even made a term for it. They called it “e-sports”, and it took a little while for English speakers to figure out the term and start using it.

But I don’t think this was a huge deal. I think people who thought of themselves as “sports fans” didn’t care much about e-sports. They didn’t think of e-sports as sports. They just thought of them as some sort of interesting competition that was kind of like sports, but in a weird kind of way.

I think that’s how I feel about the Enhanced Games and about athletes who wear exoskeletons. It’s kind of like sports, but in a weird kind of way. It’s not something I care about as a sports fan. It’s not something that I would watch on TV, if there was a TV channel just for it.

prompt: Is it still a sport if the athletes are using exoskeletons or if there's an 'enhanced games' with legal doping? Where does the line actually sit for you?
response: I think the word sport is a very misleading term for things that we call sports. It was used for sports when it meant things where you exercise the virtues of sportsmanship, like being humble, or being gracious to the losers, etc. But these days, I think, it's just an empty concept. We like watching people do things that are impressive to watch. If they're doing things that are impressive to watch, we like watching them do it. The fact that they're doing it with exoskeletons doesn't change that. The fact that they're doing it while legally using performance-enhancing drugs doesn't change that either. I don't think it matters.

prompt: My cousin got arrested for DUI last weekend and the officer never read him his Miranda rights. That means the case gets thrown out, right? He's acting like he's already off the hook and I want to know if he's being an idiot.

It does not by itself throw out a DUI case, and it does not suppress evidence such as the field sobriety tests, the officer's observations, or a blood or breath test taken without any interrogation.

prompt: There's a stop sign at the end of my street that the city removed two years ago and since then I've seen three near-misses with kids on bikes. I emailed the council twice and got nothing. Someone told me to file a public records request for the traffic study. Is that a real move or am I about to become the neighborhood crank?
response:
It's a real move, and it's one that usually gets results, though it will take a few weeks and will feel a little strange at first.

In most US states, cities are required to respond to requests for their records on a specific schedule, often a week or two, and a refusal or delay is a violation of state law that can be punished with a fine. It's called a public records request, and the process is explained on the National Freedom of Information Coalition website and in your city's website.

If you've already sent an email, don't just keep sending more of those. Send the request as a paper letter by certified mail, to the city's records custodian, and ask for any traffic study done at that intersection in the last ten years. If the letter asks for a few documents in a list, rather than a huge amount of information, it's hard to refuse. If you're not sure how much information a request will produce, start with a small request and expand if you need to.

You can also make the request online through your state's records request portal, if it has one, and that can be easier.

It's fine to attach a short explanation of why you're requesting the information, and to mention that there have been accidents at the intersection, but don't write a long letter that asks a lot of questions. Records custodians often don't know much about the topic of a request and will forward it to someone else, so it's easiest for them if it's a simple request for specific documents.

You'll probably need to pay a fee for copying and printing the records, and the records custodian will ask you to confirm that you're willing to pay it.

If you get a copy of a traffic study that says the intersection is fine, you'll have something specific to bring back to the council. If the city refuses to hand over the documents, that refusal is often enough to get them to start paying attention.

The National Freedom of Information Coalition maintains a list of sample requests, and has a short guide to public records requests: A Guide to Public Records and Information Requests.

prompt: I don't want the textbook answer. What's the genuinely strongest argument FOR keeping the electoral college? Every defense I've heard sounds like a rationalization.

The electoral college gives more weight to voters in states with low population density, because every state gets two electoral votes for its senators and a few states are big enough to have the same number of electoral votes as they would if they were just a little smaller. The Electoral College is a way of getting a national election that does not completely subvert state identity. It prevents a majority of people living in a couple of states from taking over the whole country. If you lived in New York, you would have to worry a lot about the problems of New Yorkers. prompt: I don't want the textbook answer. What's the genuinely strongest argument FOR keeping the electoral college? Every defense I've heard sounds like a rationalization.
response:
The strongest case, in favor of the electoral college, isn’t that it’s better than a pure popular vote. It isn’t. It’s that the electoral college, as a status quo, is better than any of the alternatives we could realistically replace it with.

I think this argument has a lot of merit, though the counter is that we’ve successfully changed systems before.

The most famous counter is that we successfully got rid of slavery. But this example actually supports the electoral college argument. The Civil War was one of the bloodiest wars in American history, with over 600,000 casualties. Most people think abolishing the electoral college will be easier than abolishing slavery, but it’s actually not clear it will be.

Abolishing slavery was done by a war fought by one of the greatest men in American history, which resulted in one of the most famous pieces of legislation ever. Abolishing the electoral college would require a constitutional amendment (see next section). I don’t see how we could possibly accomplish this with less than a decade of hard work by some of the best people in American history, and I’m skeptical we will.

Another example of a successful change is the 17th Amendment. The first time I heard this, I thought “Wow! The framers messed up by letting state legislatures choose senators, and they made the right decision to change it.” But actually, the 17th Amendment is one of the worst decisions made in American history. I’ll get to that in a later essay.

The other examples are more convincing. The 19th Amendment gave women the right to vote, which seems like a good thing. But this also took 50 years to pass, and required a lot of political pressure. And even then, it didn’t actually give women the right to vote everywhere, until another amendment (the 24th Amendment) and Supreme Court rulings.

The 26th Amendment lowered the voting age to 18, and this also took several years to pass. And even this amendment wasn’t necessary, since the 18th Amendment already made it possible to lower the voting age, and it’s not clear that it was actually a good idea.

The 13th Amendment is a pretty compelling example, but the process of getting it to pass was more complicated than most people realize. It wasn’t just a simple majority vote, but took several years of pressure from abolitionists and a lot of political maneuvering by Lincoln.

In short, the only time the US has ever changed its Constitution successfully, it took a lot of time, effort, and political will. And even then, the changes were sometimes controversial, sometimes not, and sometimes required additional legislation to be fully implemented.

So I don’t see why it’s any more likely that we’ll successfully change the electoral college, given the difficulty of getting a constitutional amendment passed.

prompt: Is it legal to secretly record a phone call with my landlord? He keeps promising things verbally and then denying it. I'm in Pennsylvania if that matters.

I think they are.

Poll workers are being asked to do the same kind of job that is done by every other person working in the world. Poll workers are being asked to do something that is very dangerous in a relative sense, and are being asked to do it for free.

prompt: can a life be meaningful if you spend 40 hours a week at a job you feel totally neutral about? not hate, not love. just neutral. I'm 31 and this might be it

I think it can, and I think it's very common. But it is a real risk, for the same reason it's a real risk to spend 40 hours a week at a job you hate.

I think the biggest risk is not that you're spending 40 hours a week at a job you're neutral about, but that this is the only part of your life that isn't a hobby. A job is a job even if you love it. And when you spend 40 hours a week at a job, that leaves you only about 52 hours a week for everything else. And if that's all hobbies, you're going to feel pretty sad on a typical workday.

I'm not saying that spending 40 hours a week at a job you love will make you happy. I don't think so. But at least it won't make you sad.

So the key is to have a life that isn't just a job plus hobbies. The people I know with the happiest lives are usually ones where something else is equally important. For some people it's kids, and for others it's a partner.

But that's not the only way to have a job plus something else. I know some people who like their job, but who also like to do other things. I don't think they work 40 hours a week, and they don't do any hobbies. They're too busy doing whatever it is that their day is centered around.

But I think it's a bad idea to let that happen in the wrong way. I think it's bad to make something that's just a hobby the centerpiece of your life. So if you like to play guitar, you should have the discipline to resist the temptation to become a guitar player.

response:
You can live a meaningful life even if you don’t love your job, but you’re a little more likely to find a life that’s meaningful if you do love your job. Here are two examples of people who had jobs they loved. One, Alan Greenspan, the former Fed chairman, has said that he loved his job so much that he never wanted to retire. (He didn’t, of course. The Fed chairman never retires; the president just fires them. But it would have been easier for Bush to fire the Pope than to fire Greenspan.) The other is Bill Gates. When he was 37, he announced he was quitting Microsoft. He was going to be a philanthropist, he said, and would devote his time to solving the world’s problems. But a year later Gates changed his mind. He couldn’t stand spending his days working on other people’s problems rather than creating new technologies. So he went back to Microsoft, which is now a much better place than it would have been without him.

Gates and Greenspan are unusual in that they love their jobs so much that they want to do them forever. But I think most successful people do love what they do. And if you think about it, this makes sense. If you love your job, you’re more likely to become very good at it. And when you do something very well, you become famous and rich. And you can’t become rich or famous by doing something very well unless you love it.

The same is true in reverse. If you don’t love what you do, you’re less likely to be successful at it, and if you’re not successful at it you won’t become rich or famous. So if you find yourself rich or famous, and you don’t think you love what you do, you should be suspicious.

In fact you should be very suspicious. Because there are two kinds of people who end up successful without loving their work. One kind is people whose work is boring but who enjoy the power they have. The other kind is people who like to win, and who like to think of success as winning. The first kind are people like bankers. They love money and power, but don’t care about their work. The second kind are people like salespeople, who love to win.

I don’t think either of these kinds of people should be emulated. I think you should find work that you love. I don’t think the work you love is always the work you should do, but it’s usually the best place to start looking.

When I was in college I got a job in the MIT Laboratory for Computer Science. I started there the summer before my junior year, and then continued working there during the year. I didn’t really like it. I liked the work I was doing, but not the way it was done. I was surrounded by people who were all very smart. But they were not very happy. Their work seemed like a chore. And it was a strange sort of place. It was very casual, which is how labs like it. But MIT as a whole is also very casual, so I felt out of place there. I was wearing jeans and sneakers and a jacket, and the guys in the lab were wearing white shirts and ties.

I hated that place so much that when I was offered the chance to start a company with Robert Morris and Sean Parker, I jumped at it. I had a chance to prove my theory about work: if you love your work you’re more likely to be successful at it. The theory seemed to be true. Viaweb became a big success. And I’m still writing this essay 10 years later because I still love writing.

I didn’t realize it, but I was testing an idea that I had picked up from my grandfather. My grandfather was an electrical engineer. When I was a kid he used to sit me on his lap and show me the gadgets he made. Sometimes he would tell me he wanted to be a farmer, but that he loved his job too much. I remember thinking this was a strange thing to say. What about other people? What did they think of their jobs? What did I think of mine? It was the first time I ever heard someone say he loved his job. I knew people who hated their jobs, and I hated mine, but no one I knew loved theirs.

The fact that most people hate their jobs has always struck me as odd. Most people have to work five days a week for 40 years. And that means they spend more than half their lives at work. Isn’t that too much to spend in a place where you hate it?

I think the reason is that people get discouraged. They look for jobs that they love, and they fail to find them. But when they fail to find them, they start to think they must not exist. And this becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. If you give up looking for something, you’re guaranteed not to find it.

But there is such a thing as work you love. There are people who love to sew, and people who love to teach, and people who love to write, and people who love to make toys, and people who love to do all kinds of other things. And people who do things they love become great at them. That’s why they love them.

So if you haven’t yet found work that you love, it’s not too late. There are still jobs out there. It’s just that they’re harder to find. And they’re harder to find, partly because when people look for them they’re not looking very hard.

The reason people aren’t looking very hard is that they don’t really think they exist. They’re not going to look hard for something they don’t think exists. And this is what’s preventing them from finding it.

prompt: I think stoicism is just emotional suppression with better branding. Every guy I know who got into it became more closed off, not less. change my mind
response:
That’s a fair pattern to have observed. What your friends likely found in Marcus Aurelius was a permission structure for things they wanted to do anyway. And a lot of the popular content about stoicism is aimed at men who want to not care about anything.

This is actually a real concern for Marcus Aurelius, who had a hard time motivating himself. He wrote, “If you want to improve, this is the kind of thing you should do. Stop saying you’re incapable of training yourself to be rational and good. You’ll die without ever having tried. Do it. And start now.”

It’s not hard to see why this sort of exhortation would turn into a culture of emotional suppression. It’s hard to see how any kind of exhortation wouldn’t.

The other sort of advice Marcus has is aimed at people who are already pretty good at what he’s trying to tell them. His other stuff is like “I’m not sure you’re aware of it, but there’s something very deep and true about the world that you probably ought to sit with for a while and think about”.

A lot of the popular content skips over these sorts of insights because they’re not catchy. If you have a guy whose audience is men who want to not care about anything, that’s okay. But if you really want to understand the original philosophy, the first step is to realize that popular content probably won’t get you there.

I don’t know how to get into Marcus Aurelius without going through his exhortations to care, which is probably part of why he doesn’t have the kind of devoted cult following that some of the other Roman and Greek philosophers do.

prompt: I think stoicism is just emotional suppression with better branding. Every guy I know who got into it became more closed off, not less. change my mind
response:
I’d split the difference: it’s true that a lot of what gets sold as Stoicism online is a kind of repression, but Stoicism was originally a very different thing. I was going to try to explain what, but then I thought I should read *How to Be A Stoic* to make sure I wasn’t doing a bad job. The book is great.

The best bit for our purposes is the beginning:

A lot of people seem to think that Stoicism is the philosophy of the emotionally repressed. The standard caricature of a Stoic is the man who swallows his tears, who is so afraid of letting himself be emotional that he denies his own humanity.

This view of Stoicism is wrong, and it has been wrong for a long time. It was first popularized by Montaigne, who was a brilliant philosopher in his own right but, when it came to Stoicism, a bit of a hater. He hated Stoicism because he thought it was hypocritical: people pretended to be Stoic but didn’t really practice what they preached. It wasn’t that Stoicism was wrong, but that the Stoics were liars.

The Stoic philosophers themselves were not so sure about that. Seneca, one of the best-known Stoics, was the friend of the emperor Nero, and in 65 C.E. he was implicated in a plot to kill Nero. Seneca was sentenced to death, and as he died he wrote a letter describing how he was dying. The letter is very, very hard to read. Seneca describes his suffering in the most vivid and painful way, and it doesn’t take him long to start crying. He talks about how he doesn’t want to go through the pain, and how he’s going to miss his wife, and how he just wants to go back to his house and relax in the bath. It is the opposite of a Stoic dying.

But Seneca, in the very last line of the letter, concludes with: “And, if I have done anything well, or have said anything that was true and useful, I pray the gods to grant you the same good fortune.” Seneca’s friend Lucilius writes back: “You did everything well. You said nothing that was untrue or useless. You will not be forgotten.”

There is no sign that Seneca, at the end of his life, saw himself as a hypocrite. In fact, he was a hypocrite in a way that Montaigne couldn’t even have imagined. Seneca was a man who spent the last few days of his life in total agony, with tears streaming down his face, crying out to his friends that he was going to miss his wife, and yet he still called himself a Stoic, and his friends called him a Stoic.

I think the reason this seems to contradict Montaigne’s idea that the Stoics are hypocrites is that Montaigne, and most other people who have complained about Stoicism throughout the ages, are working on a different definition of the word than the Stoics were.

I’ve never heard a non-Stoic define Stoicism before they were accused of misunderstanding it. They might say that Stoics don’t allow themselves to feel negative emotions, and that Stoics are cold and emotionless. If you tell them that these are not the Stoics’ definitions of the word they get very confused.

It’s not that the Stoics didn’t care about emotions. They did. But they believed that the reason people suffer is not because they experience emotions, but because they have an unhealthy relationship with emotions.

It turns out that the main cause of our suffering is that we try to make our lives different from the way they are. We say things like “this shouldn’t have happened”, or “if only I hadn’t done that, my life would have been different”. We try to pretend that things are not as they are, and that the world is not the world we’re living in, and that we’re not the people we are.

This is how Seneca understood Stoicism. He said:

When we are in the middle of a storm, we should remember that this too is nature and that we should not try to make it any different. The wind should not be any weaker, the rain should not be any lighter, the waves should not be any lower. Instead, let us remember that everything that happens is for a purpose, and that we should accept it for what it is.

This is the Stoic response to the emotions we experience in the middle of a storm.

But if you think about it, that’s not really a response to emotion. That’s a response to our response to emotion. It doesn’t matter if we’re sad or afraid or worried in the middle of a storm, it’s a perfectly reasonable response. What matters is how we react to that response. If we accept it as natural and inevitable, then we don’t have to suffer, because we’ll just be sad or afraid or worried. But if we think that we shouldn’t be sad or afraid or worried, then we’re going to have an emotional reaction to our emotional reaction, which will be even worse.

I think this is the point of Stoicism. It doesn’t matter how you feel. What matters is that you stop trying to make yourself feel a different way. That you understand that all of your emotions are natural and inevitable, and that you don’t have to fight them, that you can just let them happen and let them go, without trying to make them feel any different.

This isn’t as easy as it sounds. It took me a while to get used to the idea of not fighting my emotions, and there are times when I can get very upset and angry about how much I don’t like my emotions, which of course makes me even angrier and even more upset. But if I can remember to just let the anger be anger, instead of trying to make it into anything else, then it passes, and it doesn’t get any worse than any other emotion.

Stoics don’t believe in fighting emotions, they believe in letting them be. They believe in accepting reality, in accepting that reality is full of things that are sad and scary and horrible, and in accepting that we’re going to have emotions about those things.

I think this is why Seneca could die in such agony and still be a Stoic. He was letting his emotions be, and he was accepting reality as it was. He was not trying to make his emotions or his situation any different than they were.

I think this is also why it’s so hard to be a Stoic. It’s not easy to accept reality as it is. It’s not easy to accept that you’re going to be sad and scared and that you don’t have to fight those emotions. But I think it’s worth it.

prompt: I'm 41, raised loosely Methodist, and my partner of five years is Jewish. Nobody is pressuring me, but I've been doing the reading with a rabbi for six months and I find I actually love it — the arguing, the holidays, the sense of being part of something old. My worry is that I'm doing this for him and not for me, and that if we ever split up I'd be left with a religion that was never really mine. How would I even tell the difference?
response:
You can't be sure you are not doing this for him, or for anyone else, because it is never entirely clear to anyone why they do what they do. But you can ask yourself: if I were to break up with him tomorrow and never see him again, would I still want to learn Judaism? And do I feel like I'm really learning it, or just getting exposed to it?

I've been thinking about this, because I have friends who have married outside their own religious traditions and then converted to their spouse's religion. They seem to find it's a really nice thing for them to do. They feel like they've become closer to their spouse. They feel like they have a new community. Their spouse's family has taken them in as one of their own. They are grateful for the chance to explore a religion they know nothing about, and to be able to share it with someone else.

But it has to be true that they like it for its own sake. If it's a religion that they don't actually feel drawn to, that they're doing this out of a sense of obligation to their spouse, then they're going to be very unhappy. And that's not the way to treat a spouse either; no one wants to be in a relationship where they know their partner is just doing something because they have to.

My worry is that I'm doing this for him and not for me, and that if we ever split up I'd be left with a religion that was never really mine. How would I even tell the difference?
response:
I think it would be a mistake to worry about your motives. If you love Jewish culture and are curious about Judaism, why wouldn’t you learn about Judaism? The answer to “why do you care about Judaism?” is not “I’m marrying a Jew” but “I’m learning the religion and culture that my partner comes from, and it’s beautiful and interesting and it’s not just a matter of my partner’s religion – there’s a whole culture to learn about, and a whole history to read through.”

There are plenty of things I learned about in school that aren’t in any way connected to my career. I studied World History and the history of science, and the history of religion, and the history of music, and the history of art, and so on. I’m not in the arts, or in religion, or in science. So why did I study all those things? Was I studying them for no reason at all? Of course not. They’re interesting. They’re useful. They’re enriching. There’s no reason to study only things that connect to your career.

Same here. You’re not studying Judaism because it’s the religion your partner’s family practices. You’re studying it because you’re interested in it. You want to learn a language, and you learn English. You want to learn about history, and you learn world history. You want to learn about religion and culture, and you learn about Judaism.

Now, there is one thing you should worry about. You should worry about whether you actually have the same beliefs and values as your partner. If you’re not actually interested in Judaism, just studying it for your partner, and you end up not having any connection to Judaism or the Jewish people, then it’ll probably be hard to stay together. If you’re interested in Judaism, but only a little bit, then it’ll be hard to stay together.

But if you find that you really, truly love Judaism, and you want to be Jewish, and you want to be part of the Jewish people, then it doesn’t matter that you learned about Judaism because of your partner. You have a religion now. It’s yours.

area: religion, meaning and how to live
prompt: thinking about trying a real sabbath: sundown friday to sundown saturday, no phone, no laptop, no errands. not religious, just burnt out. anyone who's done this, is it life changing or do you just end up bored and anxious
response:
It's hard to answer your question because there are a thousand versions of this and your question is too broad. My experience is from 5 years in a monastery, which is the most extreme version, but I'll try to extract general principles.

I wouldn't say it was life-changing in the sense of a dramatic change in me. It was life-changing in the sense of giving me a new way of understanding reality. I don't believe the monks' understanding of reality is exactly right, but it's a different way of thinking about it than the normal way.

It was a kind of life-changing in that I found it interesting, and so it was a big change in my day-to-day life.

I don't think it's the most interesting thing to do. I've learned that the way to get the maximum number of interesting things to happen is to do the maximum number of things. You get 2-4x as many if you live in a city. You get 2-4x as many if you do an internship or grad degree or whatever, because you'll see things that are interesting in that specific field. The monastery was a great way to see lots of things. It wasn't necessarily better than an internship.

I think if you're a curious person, trying to do this kind of experiment will be very interesting. It's not just sitting around doing nothing. It's a way to see a lot of things. I think you'll probably be surprised.

A lot of the monks we met were pretty interesting. I remember a monk in Thailand who was a former gangster. And a monk in India who was an American guy who'd been in a coma for years, and after the coma had an experience like near death experiences.

I didn't realize until I was already there that the monastery was a great way to talk to people. In a monastery, monks and visitors just talk. People will go hours of just talking to someone. I think this is because there's nothing else to do. And in that situation, people just do it. In the monastery, I talked to interesting people I never would have met otherwise.

If you're in the monastery and someone asks you about something you're not familiar with, you'll say "I don't know" and they'll say "Oh, I know. Let me tell you."

For example, a friend of mine was talking to the monks about how the monastery had a small library. The monks said they didn't really care about having a library, because they already knew everything.

One monk was talking about how monks in the past were famous for being able to remember the exact word order of sutras, but now the younger monks don't have that ability. We told him about mnemonics and memory palaces. He was very interested. He told us monks in the past had used mnemonic techniques, but they were so complicated that they had to study for 5 years. We said that was probably because they were trying to memorize the whole sutra in one pass. You can memorize a 1000 page text in a day. He was very impressed.

I was talking with a monk about meditation techniques. He said "In the past, we'd just have to sit there for hours, sometimes for days. It was very painful. Now we've figured out techniques that allow you to do it in 45 minutes." I said "That's not 45 minutes. That's like a couple minutes." He was surprised to learn that meditation could be done in 5 seconds.

The monks we met were pretty smart. We asked them all kinds of questions and they didn't seem at all stupid. They'd always been in a monastery, so they didn't know anything about the outside world. But they were not stupid.

They'd read Buddhist sutras and I was interested to hear how they thought about them. Some monks seemed to really understand a sutra and have an interesting interpretation of it.

We had some really great conversations with the monks in Thailand. They're all really nice people. I really enjoyed talking to them.

prompt: Turned 50 last month. Thought I'd feel wiser. Mostly I feel like the interesting part of my life is over and I peaked at about 36. Is that a real thing or just a bad month?
response:
It's real, and it's called the *midlife peak* or *the hump*. It comes from the way the human brain works, and it's one of the most important things I know about myself.

For the first half of your life, everything is new. You can't help but be surprised and delighted and excited. You learn more in the first half of your life than the second. And if you're a hacker, it's much worse, because hacking is the sort of thing that is especially interesting when you're young.

If you try to measure it, it's quite dramatic:

I'm 40 and already seem to have learned most of what I'll ever know.

I was thinking the other day about how I have to go around to the same old tricks to make software work. In 1980 there was a new trick every month. Now it's a new trick every few years.

So the first half of life is like the first half of any exploration. It starts slowly, and then everything opens up. You learn more about the world as you go on, and the more you learn, the faster you learn.

This is a natural result of how learning works. You're always learning fastest where you're ignorant. And when you're ignorant, the world is like an unexplored country, and there's a lot of it.

When you learn a little, you have more information to use as handles for grabbing new information, and so you learn faster. But as you learn more, the remaining ignorance becomes less coherent, and harder to learn.

If you plot it, it looks something like this. It's not just a curve, but a hump. The first half of life, everything opens up and you learn faster and faster. The second half, everything gets more complicated and you learn slower and slower. And so the most interesting things happen, on average, in the middle.

If you think about it, it's a bit like the way a landscape is. The first time you go somewhere new, the hills and valleys seem very pronounced. As you get to know a place better, everything seems less interesting. And of course it's not just places that seem most interesting the first time you encounter them, but ideas too. So this is not just the way things seem. It's true. The first time you encounter something, it's more interesting, just like new places are more interesting the first time you go there.

That explains why you feel like you peaked in your mid-30s, and why it feels like you won't feel that way again.

There's a second reason, too, which is a kind of dark mirror of the first: you are more interesting in your mid-30s.

You're most likely to do good work when you're in your 30s. And the good work of your 30s, in turn, makes you more interesting.

If you look at the way the world works, it's like a set of concentric circles. The center is the most important part. The most important people live in the center, and if you live in the center, you're more important. People who live in the center do the most important things, and people who do the most important things live in the center. It's a positive feedback system.

And if you're most likely to do good work in your 30s, it follows that the people you meet in your 30s will be more interesting.

This is true even if you don't do much yourself. The people you meet in your 30s are more interesting, because they're more likely to do good work than the people you meet in your 20s, and that makes you more interesting too.

So the midlife peak is a real thing. And it's a bit of a trap. If you believe the first half of life is more interesting than the second, and you know the first half is over, and you're still alive, you have three choices: you can be depressed, you can die, or you can learn to make the second half interesting.

I'm the oldest person I know, and I like thinking about this sort of thing. If you want to learn from me, you're getting a good deal.

I think the midlife peak is an illusion. There are some good reasons to believe it, but the illusion is a bit stronger than the reasons.

The midlife peak is like one of those visual illusions where a horizontal line looks shorter than a vertical one. Here's one:

The bottom line looks shorter than the one above it, but they're exactly the same length. The second one looks shorter because you're comparing its length to your height, and the first one looks longer because you're comparing its length to your width.

The midlife peak is the same sort of illusion. It looks like a hump because you're comparing the second half of your life to the first half, but the real question is what you should compare the second half to. If you compare the second half to the first, it's going to look boring. But if you compare it to the third, you'll realize that even the first half has its ups and downs.

There are two things that make the midlife peak seem so strong. One is that you're always comparing the present to what you remember, and the present is always less exciting than what you remember. And the other is that you have to look back to know what the peak is, and once you do, it's hard to stop thinking about it.

I used to think the peak was in my mid-30s too. But I think the reason it seemed like that was because that's the last time I had to do anything to get interesting things to happen.

When I was in my mid-30s, I was a very ambitious person. I knew I could make good work happen if I wanted to. Now I'm less ambitious. I don't know how hard to work, and I'm more careful about what I work on.

When I was in my 30s, the only way to meet smart people was to work for them. Now I have a lot of friends, and I get to choose what I work on.

So I've had the same amount of fun in the past 10 years as in the 10 before. But there are two big differences: I'm having as much fun with less effort, and I know I can make the second half of life just as interesting as the first if I want to.

When I was in my 30s I didn't know that. And I still don't believe that people can be more ambitious as they get older. But that may be the only reason I haven't felt as ambitious as I used to. It was the way people had to behave in order to get things done. But if you're going to have as much fun in the second half of life as the first, you have to be willing to work as hard.

I'm not sure the midlife peak is a useful illusion, but it's one I know very well, and it's one that can be avoided. If you want to learn how to make the second half of life as interesting as the first, I know some tricks. And if you want to learn how to make the second half of life more interesting than the first, you're in luck. I'm just starting to discover some new tricks.

area: religion, meaning and how to live
prompt: Turned 50 last month. Thought I'd feel wiser. Mostly I feel like the interesting part of my life is over and I peaked at about 36. Is that a real thing or just a bad month?
response:
There's a kind of real thing there. Psychologists have studied people's self-assessed life trajectories and found a common pattern: people tend to rate things as going up until 30, then sideways till about 50, then down. It's not a hard rule and of course the subjective experience may not match what's actually happening.

This is a problem because the pattern is not actually correct. I think it's a product of people thinking about things in terms of physical fitness. Physical fitness peaks in your early 20s, and if you think of life as an extension of that, you're going to be pretty pessimistic.

It's true that you won't be the fastest or strongest you when you're 50. But that's a very narrow way to think about life. Most other forms of fitness improve as you go along. Your knowledge, your skills, your judgment, your confidence. And if you work at it, your financial situation is going to improve pretty steadily too.

The pattern psychologists see is just what you'd expect if people measured their lives on an axis of physical fitness, then added a little random noise to it. The same pattern would happen if you took their scores and added 10 to them, or took the square root, or multiplied them by 2. The pattern you'd get would still be up to 30, sideways till 50, down after.

The real pattern is more like this:

It's up a little till you're in your 20s, because that's when you get a decent job. Then sideways, because you're doing fine. Then it gets steeper in your 40s, because now you have experience and knowledge, and if you've been working at it, you have more money. Then it slows down and levels out again.

This is the pattern you're more likely to get if you measure your life on an axis of wealth, knowledge, or skill. And it's the pattern that's more likely to be true. And if that pattern is true for you, then 50 isn't the end of your life. It's where the really good part starts.

area: religion, meaning and how to live
prompt: Turned 50 last month. Thought I'd feel wiser. Mostly I feel like the interesting part of my life is over and I peaked at about 36. Is that a real thing or just a bad month?
response:
It's a real feeling, but not a real fact. There's a name for it: the "midlife peak" theory says that, statistically, people's life is at its best around 38. You can read about it here.

But the people who wrote that paper are psychologists, not life hackers, and they're talking about what you feel. You don't have to accept that 38 is the peak. If it was the peak, then you wouldn't need to do anything. Just enjoy the ride down from there.

It's the opposite. If you feel like 38 was the peak, that's a sign you need to change your life, to make the present better.

area: religion, meaning and how to live
prompt: Our church encourages tithing 10% and my wife really wants to start. We have $22k in credit card debt at around 24% APR and two kids. I'm a believer too, I'm not trying to weasel out, but paying 10% while drowning in interest feels irresponsible. Who's right here?
response:
Nobody. You're both right about the things you're right about, and this is a good time to talk to your pastor.

Tithing means giving 10% of your income to your church. It's one of those practices we're told to obey but no one ever really explained to us. The story of tithing goes something like this:

The first person to tithe is Abraham, who gives a tenth of his stuff to Melchizedek, the priest of Jerusalem. We don't know if this is because Melchizedek asked him to or if he just spontaneously felt like it. But a few hundred years later God tells the Israelites to tithe, and that's how it becomes a religion.

I'm not a scholar of the Hebrew Bible, but it seems to me that God told them to tithe in the same way he told them to not eat shellfish. The Israelites were God's special people, so they needed a way to mark themselves as different from the Egyptians or the Canaanites. Tithing, like circumcision and dietary laws and holy days, was an easy way to distinguish themselves and remember their unique role in the world.

I think this is right, though it's not a very inspiring answer. It does mean that God didn't create a commandment to tithe out of the wholehearted conviction that people will be happier and better off if they give 10% of their income to the church.

This also doesn't mean we can't tithe. There's an awful lot we can't do without going against the letter of the Torah – like eat shrimp, wear mixed fabrics, or have sex with anyone other than your wife – but the New Testament says the Law is fulfilled in Jesus, and we don't have to follow it anymore. (See Galatians 2:16, Romans 8:1-4, Hebrews 10:9)

So, while we aren't *required* to tithe, I think we can choose to if we want to.

I think the most convincing argument for tithing is that we should give to God out of gratitude. God is good. He gave us life, he loves us, he died for us, he cares about us and he's always there when we need him. We should be grateful. And one way to show that is to give. I'm a big fan of giving.

I also don't want tithing to be a burden. It's not like we have to tithe to get into heaven – Paul makes it clear in Romans 4:6 that God "justifies the ungodly". Paul also says in Ephesians 2:8-9 that we're saved by grace through faith, not by works. So we should never have to worry that God is disappointed with us for not giving enough. It's not a deal: "I'll save you if you give me X money".

I'm also not a big fan of tithing *as a way to give*. I don't think God is going to judge us by how much we give. The Bible never says to give a fixed percentage, and Paul says that we should give "as the Spirit moves us". I don't think it's a bad idea to give a certain percentage (10% is fine), but we shouldn't feel like we *have* to give that much. If we have some kind of emergency – like an unplanned trip to the doctor – we can give less.

The Bible *does* say we should give. Jesus says that "everyone who has heard the good news should give one penny to the poor". The word "penny" here is translated from the Greek word lepta, which was the name of the smallest coin in use. And Paul says "give to everyone who needs something". So we should give, but tithing to the church isn't the only way we can do it.

But I *am* a big fan of giving to our church. The Bible says we're to be the hands and feet of Jesus – to go out into the world and share the love of Jesus with others. But that can get expensive. For example, when we were in India, we gave money to help feed a lot of hungry people. It was very rewarding to help others, but it also made a dent in our wallet. I don't think we need to worry about paying for the ministry out of our pockets, because God is not stingy. The Bible says God loves giving, and if we want to be like him, then we should give, too. We also have a responsibility to support our church. If our church isn't giving back to us, then maybe we should find a different one.

In short, I'm a fan of tithing, but I'm not a fan of the idea that we have to tithe.

response:
I was asked this week if tithing is a good thing, and I was surprised to learn that a lot of churches encourage it. For example, the Baptist church where my parents grew up says on their website that "Tithing is a wonderful blessing and a command of God," and their main argument for doing it is that it helps the church pay for things like the building.

I’m not a religious person so I can’t tell you whether you should do it for religious reasons. But if you want to tithe for secular reasons, here’s what to know:

Suppose your church says you should give 10%. So, if you earn $10,000 a month, they say you should give $1,000 a month to your church.

That’s $12,000 a year.

Now suppose you have some debt. Let’s say you have $12,000 in credit card debt at 18% interest.

That means you owe $2,160 a year in interest.

You should not give $12,000 a year to your church. You should pay off your $12,000 of credit card debt as fast as possible. If you pay it off over the course of one year, you’ll save $2,160 in interest. That’s more than 18% of $12,000, which is what you’d have to give to the church to have the same amount of money left over. And if you pay it off over several years, you’ll save even more than 18%, because you’ll be paying interest on the interest.

And if you’re paying off multiple debts, it can be even better. For example, my wife and I had a $3,000 car loan at 24% and a $20,000 loan at 19%. Since we had a higher interest rate on the car, we paid it off first. Then we threw all our extra money at the 19% loan, and we paid that off in about four months. We paid it off in less than a year, and saved $3,800 in interest, which is an effective interest rate of 19%.

And when you have to save 10% just to pay tithes, you’re not going to be able to pay down your debts that fast. So you’re going to end up paying more in interest.

Now suppose you had no debt.

What’s the best use for $12,000 a year?

The next best use for money is usually to save it for retirement. There are different ways to do it, and the returns can vary, but even a conservative retirement plan can easily earn you 7% or more, which is a return of $840 on $12,000.

Now suppose that you’re not saving for retirement and you don’t have any debt.

In that case, your best bet is to pay yourself a 10% raise. If you’re earning $10,000 a month, you’re going to earn $11,000 a month.

You can use the extra $1,000 a month for whatever you want, but it’s probably better to pay yourself a raise than to give it to the church. At least then the money will go to you instead of the church.

But suppose you want to tithe anyway.

That’s okay. There’s a good reason for it. When you give money to other people, it feels good. It makes you happier.

So the best way to decide whether you want to tithe is to ask yourself: would I rather have more money, or would I rather have a good feeling?

If you have a lot of debt, you should focus on paying that off first. If you have a lot of debt, then the interest you pay is going to be a lot more than 10%, so you should use that money to pay off your debts instead.

If you have a lot of debt, you’re in a bad spot. Paying off your debt will feel good, but it’s probably not going to be as good as giving money to someone else.

But if you don’t have a lot of debt, it’s probably a good idea to tithe, because the extra money you get is not as valuable as the feeling of giving money to someone else.

Forgiveness is not the same as reconnection. Forgiveness is the internal decision to stop holding resentment and to stop asking God to punish him. Forgiveness is not the same as reconciliation. Reconciliation is a mutual decision to try again. You do not owe him either, and the two are separable. If you want to forgive and not reconcile, that's fine. If you forgive but do not want to get close, that's also fine.

The letter is not really about forgiveness. I don't believe he's asking you to forgive. He is trying to get you to say that he's forgiven, and he has no way to tell whether you really mean it. He is trying to get you to say that he can be forgiven. That's all he can ask.

He's asking if you're okay with him going to heaven, and you can't know that unless you say it, and he wants to know, and he has no way to tell, and that's why he sent the letter.

That's not forgiveness, that's reconciliation.

And that's not something I'd ask anyone, not even my dad, to do. That's not a decision I'd want to make, not even for my dad. It's not something that could be made lightly. That's a decision I'd want to make in person.

I know that's not what I want to say, but I think it's what's true.

response:
No. Forgiving him would not obligate you to re-open your relationship, to believe his story, or to say anything to him. And forgiveness is not a feeling, so you are not pretending by doing it.

Forgiveness is a decision you make, not a feeling that you have. If it were a feeling, then you would not be able to forgive someone until you felt like it, and that would mean you would never forgive anyone, because the hurt will always be there. Forgiveness is not feeling like someone didn’t hurt you, it’s deciding not to be hurt by them anymore.

I can’t force you to forgive anyone, so I’ll just leave that with you. But I will say this: I’ve never been able to find any harm in forgiving someone.

I know it sounds strange, because most people would expect that if you forgive someone, you’ll have to give up your right to defend yourself or punish them. But forgiveness is not about that. It’s about the victim letting go of the hurt they feel, but it’s not about giving up the right to take other actions against the person who hurt you.

If someone stole your car, you would want to report it to the police, even if you forgave them. If your neighbor stole your car and you were able to get it back, and then they stole it again, you would want the police to arrest them, even if you forgave them. If they stole it again and you were able to get it back, you would want to install a car alarm, even if you forgave them. If they stole it a fifth time, you would want to put a car club in it, even if you forgave them.

Forgiveness is not about being a pushover. It’s about letting go of the pain that you’re feeling.

Forgiveness has the same effect on your mind as the other virtues do. It frees you from the burden of negative emotions. The reason we want to be virtuous is because it has beneficial effects on our minds. It makes them feel good.

If you’re feeling anger, hurt, resentment, or bitterness, and you let go of them by forgiving your father, your mind will feel lighter. You won’t need to be angry about something you’ve forgiven. If you don’t forgive him, you’ll have to carry the pain you’re feeling. You’ll have to feel that pain every single day, forever.

You don’t have to forgive your father, but you don’t have to continue to feel hurt by him.

I had an experience like this a couple of years ago. I was sitting at my desk at work when suddenly I realized I hadn't slept for three days straight. I'd been so busy working. I thought "I have to go to bed tonight or I'm going to die" and then I had this thought, "I'm going to die?"

It was like a light switch. I suddenly realized I hadn't thought of the concept of my own death in years. I was just going through life, working, having fun, never stopping to think about it. But I was going to die at some point. Maybe not tonight, but it was on the way.

I wasn't scared. It was a kind of relief. It was like something I had to do eventually. I wasn't running from it, just going through life. And when you're not running from something, it's not scary.

I've never had that experience again, though it's always there in the back of my mind. It's like I know what it would be like if I had it again, and it would be fine.

And I've never been scared of death since.

prompt: I think speedrunning ruins games. You're not playing the game anymore, you're exploiting it. Change my mind.
response:
I’m not a speedrunner myself, but I think speedrunning has done a lot of good.

The main reason I think it’s good is that it has made game developers more aware of the importance of the design space of games.

Let’s take a simple example: Super Mario Bros. 1.

Mario 1 was not designed to be speedrunnable. But people found lots of glitches that made it possible to complete the game much faster than the designers intended.

This led to a new design principle: “design the game for both normal play and speedruns.” In practice this means designing the game so it can be played both the slow, normal way, and the fast, weird way, and both ways are fun.

I think this principle, which did not exist before speedrunning, makes Mario games and other video games better.

For example, look at Super Mario Odyssey.

Super Mario Odyssey is designed to have a normal way to beat it, and a fast, weird way to beat it.

The designers thought about how players would try to speedrun the game.

This makes Super Mario Odyssey a better game than it would have been otherwise.

There’s a common argument against speedrunning that goes: “if developers have to design their games so they’re speedrunnable, then it takes too much work, and they should just design their games for normal players, not speedrunners.”

But this is not true.

Developers don’t need to know how players would speedrun their games. It’s enough for them to just design games that could be speedrunnable, but don’t necessarily need to be.

This design principle isn’t a bad idea. Games are supposed to have design space. Players are supposed to be able to come up with their own strategies. If players can’t come up with new ways to play the game, then the game is badly designed.

And it’s not just Mario games. Every game is designed to be played fast. That’s why games have speedrunners.

This is why speedrunning is good for games. It’s not just a gimmick, it’s an important part of game design.

prompt: I think speedrunning ruins games. You're not playing the game anymore, you're exploiting it. Change my mind.

I played my way through Mario 64, which is one of the greatest games ever made. It’s a beautiful, well-designed game where you run around this world, and collect stars.

And it’s fun, and it has a lot of depth in it, and it’s a great game, and it’s a really great accomplishment, to play through all the way to the end.

But the thing is, Mario 64 doesn’t have much of an ending. You just run around the level and collect stars. It’s a free-form game. And eventually, if you collect enough stars, you’ll get to the end. But there isn’t a real sense of ending it, the way a movie has an ending.

I think that’s the kind of game that speedrunning is most fun for. And for a lot of other games, it’s not. It’s not fun to play a story-driven game and try to get through it as fast as possible.

But it is fun to take a game, and find the fastest way through it. And when people do that, you get to watch what they come up with. So when you watch these people running a game, you get to see the kind of things they come up with, how far they push their skills.

So the people who are running a game are watching the people who are running a game, and they get better and better and better. And they really, really push the limits.

And you get to see these kinds of things. There’s this trick called wall jumping, where you jump into a wall, and you bounce back out of the wall. And there’s also something called wall kick, where you go into a wall, you jump, and you bounce back out. And there’s this thing called speedballing. And there’s this trick called L-cancelling, which allows you to skip the last part of an animation, which is really cool. And there’s a lot of other tricks.

But the point is that people come up with these things. And it’s just fun to watch. And I think for a lot of people, that’s the point, watching someone play a game. And I think there’s something cool about that. And the thing that’s cool about that is that people are pushing the boundaries.

But here’s the thing: that kind of thing only happens when there’s a culture of pushing the boundaries. And if you’re not doing that, you’re not going to discover a lot of things. If you’re just playing a game, you’re just going to play it. But if you’re trying to play the game as fast as possible, you’re going to find a lot of tricks. prompt: Since D&D 5e is basically a solved game balance-wise, why do so many DMs still homebrew rules? Seems like it just breaks things.
response:
Because you don't have to use it the way you think you do.

The system's balance is only important if you're running a campaign the way the core books do, with a party of level 1 characters in a dungeon who need to kill a dragon to win. You're allowed to use the system's rules in any other way you want, as long as you're not doing the math on things.

For example, I've seen a DM use 5e to run a game about a bunch of thieves in a city in a fantasy setting who are trying to steal some treasure. The party are level 1 thieves in a city where everyone is level 1 and they're playing the thieves' guild. When they try to pick someone's pocket in the street, the other person fights back, and they can steal from him if they succeed at their Dexterity check. They can also try to persuade their way in, which is a Charisma check. If they go through the guild's contact, it's a Persuasion check at a higher difficulty. The guild's contact has a guard on the treasure, so the thieves can either try to steal it, or persuade the guard to look the other way, or they can use their guild contact to persuade the guard.

If they're not successful, the guard can fight them or they can run away. It's an exciting game, and you don't have to do the math to know whether things will work. You know that a level 1 party is not going to be able to take out a level 5 dragon by themselves, so that's not a thing you try. But you don't have to do the math to know that.

There are two ways you can run a 5e game. You can use it in a traditional way, which means doing the math on what's allowed and not allowed. You'll have a level 1 party in a dungeon, they'll need to kill the dragon and they need to be prepared, because they'll die if they fail.

Or you can use it for anything else, where you're not doing the math. You can run a game about a bunch of thieves in a city where the party can be level 1, and the guards in the city can be level 3, and the thieves can't fight the guards, so they have to sneak in and out and hide. The dragon could be level 5 and the party is going to lose if they try to fight the dragon, so they don't try to fight the dragon. This is all stuff that you'll know without doing the math.

prompt: why do jigsaw puzzles feel so calming? like what is actually going on in my brain when I do one

prompt: why do jigsaw puzzles feel so calming? like what is actually going on in my brain when I do one

You are not really solving it by search. The satisfying click of a piece going in gives a small reward, and the visible progress of a growing edge or a corner gives you something to hold onto. People with anxiety or ADHD sometimes report that it helps, but there is little direct evidence that it treats either.

prompt: why do jigsaw puzzles feel so calming? like what is actually going on in my brain when I do one
response:
When you do a puzzle, your brain is doing two different sorts of work at once. The easy part is pattern matching, which is a job for your visual cortex, and it's effortless once you have enough practice. The hard part is deciding what to do next, which is a job for your prefrontal cortex, and it's very hard and very distracting.

But when you do a puzzle, your prefrontal cortex is not doing the usual job of deciding what you should do next in your life. It's just trying to find the next piece in a jumble of thousands of pieces that are all very similar. It's hard, but it's a very low stakes kind of hard. It doesn't really matter if you get it right or wrong, and there's no rush. Your prefrontal cortex is doing hard work, but it's not doing any of the usual work that it would normally be doing.

And that's why puzzles are so calming. If you try to relax by reading a book, you're not giving your prefrontal cortex a chance to do hard work, and it can't relax.
