prompt: I've been a manager for 14 months and I think I was a better engineer than I am a manager. Is that normal or a sign I should go back? Don't give me a listicle, write it as a personal essay from the point of view of someone who's been through it and figured something out.
response:
I think there’s a lot of confusion about the idea of being a better engineer or a better manager, and I think it’s partly a function of the way the idea is expressed, but also because a lot of people who are thinking about this aren’t thinking about it in the right way. The confusion is not so much about the idea as about the language. It’s the language that needs to be fixed.

There are two basic ways to think about this idea. The first and most common way is to think of yourself as an individual person who has two skills, and one of those skills is engineering and the other is managing. In this model you compare the two skills you have to see which is better.

The second way to think of it is more like: I’m a person who has a lot of skills and I can work in different roles. One role is as an engineer and another is as a manager. In this model you ask yourself which job you are better at.

These two models are not the same. In the second model you are comparing the job of engineering with the job of managing. This is not the same as comparing two skills, and in fact in the second model you wouldn’t ask yourself which skill you have better. You might say you are “better at” engineering, but you wouldn’t say that because you are better at engineering skills than managing skills.

The second way is also the way to think about this in real life.

When you have a choice between two jobs you ask yourself which of the jobs you are better at. This question is not really about skills, because you probably have many skills and not all of them will be the same in both jobs. Instead you ask yourself which job you are better at.

The reason why it is useful to ask this question is not just because you want to do the job you are best at. It is also because when you work in a job you are best at you will be more effective. For example, you will be more likely to get promoted in a job you are better at.

It doesn’t matter why you want to do a job. You might want to do a job because you think it is fun, or you think you will make a lot of money, or you think you will learn a lot. Whatever the reason, you are more likely to succeed in your job if you are good at it.

It is not always a good idea to only do the job you are best at. If you want to learn something new you might want to do something you are bad at and learn to do it better. But that is not always the case.

So what does it mean to be better at something? You are better at something if when you do it you are more effective.

Being more effective means you are better able to get the results you want.

There are a lot of ways to do that. For example, you can be more effective by getting more done, or by doing things faster, or by doing things more accurately, or by learning more about what you are doing and being better able to figure out how to do things.

When you are comparing two jobs you need to know what you are trying to do to know which job you are better at.

prompt: Write an op-ed arguing that "culture fit" interviews should be abolished, but take the strongest version of the opposing view seriously before knocking it down.
response:
The other day, I went through my notes from the 2016 Y Combinator Startup School. The founders who attended, including myself, were asked a few questions before the class. One of those was, “Describe in a sentence or two how you’d make a hire for your company if you were the only one doing the hiring.”

I wrote, “Interview the candidate to understand how smart they are and whether they’re likely to do good work. Interview them again a few days later to get a second data point. If they still seem like a good person to hire, hire them.”

It’s not a great answer, but it wasn’t a terrible answer, and it’s not very different from what I actually do.

The same day, I read this great article by the author of “Never Split The Difference”. It was about a famous negotiation with a hostage taker.

The article said that Chris Voss had a lot of success by asking the hostage taker open-ended questions that gave the hostage taker a lot of room to talk.

I thought about how I could use that technique in interviews.

I asked a lot of people I know how they do interviews. A common technique, at least in Silicon Valley, is to ask interview candidates for work samples. This is a really good way to test whether they can do the kind of work that you need them to do, and you can also learn a lot about what they know just from looking at their work. But I’ve found that I have a lot of trouble using this technique in interviews.

I’m bad at writing interviews that have a lot of work involved. And when I give someone a task that requires a lot of time, it becomes a test of whether they can do the task that I give them, rather than a test of whether they can do the kind of work that I need done.

I’ve also found that people sometimes do a great job on the work that I give them, and then I end up not hiring them anyway.

So instead, I ask a lot of open-ended questions. For example, I’ll ask someone to tell me about a project that they worked on.

I’m pretty bad at asking questions, so it’s usually not a very good interview. And I don’t think it’s very good for most situations. But it’s a lot like Chris Voss’s negotiation technique, and I think that it works because it gives people a lot of freedom to do what they want.

When someone is told to do a specific task, they usually do the task pretty well, even if they’re not very good at the task. When they’re given a lot of freedom to do what they want, the ones who are really good get a lot of good ideas, and they do great. And the ones who aren’t very good usually do bad work.

When you ask someone to talk about a project that they worked on, they can talk about it for a very long time, and there’s usually a lot that they can tell you. And you can learn a lot about how they think and how they work, without doing much of the work yourself.

prompt: Write an op-ed arguing that "culture fit" interviews should be abolished, but take the strongest version of the opposing view seriously before knocking it down.
response:
Imagine this scene: A manager is interviewing a woman for a job. He likes her. She’s very qualified, and he’d love to work with her. But there’s one problem: She’s not very extroverted.

“Crap,” he thinks. “We have this guy who’s so gregarious that sometimes I’m not even sure if he’s talking to me or to someone behind me. And he talks way too loudly. If I hire her, he’ll be even more obnoxious. That will be bad.”

So he doesn’t hire her.

There are a lot of things you can say about this scene. But here are two things you shouldn’t say: That the guy is a racist, or that the guy is a sexist.

It’s true that we often describe this kind of behavior as “he didn’t hire her because of her culture fit”, where “culture fit” is a code phrase for “he didn’t like her skin color”, or “he didn’t like that she was a woman”, or “he didn’t like that she was gay”, or something along those lines.

But the example above shows a different kind of culture fit, which isn’t racist or sexist at all, but can be just as harmful.

I’ve seen this kind of hiring discrimination happen. I’ve also seen it happen in the opposite direction – when hiring managers are reluctant to hire shy white men because “they won’t fit into the company’s culture of extroverted diversity”.

And I’ve seen it happen in even stranger directions – when hiring managers were reluctant to hire a very qualified person because “we don’t want someone who thinks so much differently from everyone else.”

I think this kind of thing is much more common than the kind of culture fit that’s coded racism or sexism. But it’s also much more subtle, and harder to discuss. It has many variations, and can even manifest in the form of a virtue: For example, if you work at an organization and you have a culture of “extroverted diversity”, it’s hard to see what’s wrong with it.

I think this is a problem that needs to be talked about. So I wrote a blog post about it.

My post received a lot of responses from people who thought it was wrong and bad and racist. I’m not going to link any of those responses, but I’m going to try to answer the strongest version of them.

So let’s say I write a blog post where I say “We don’t hire people who are too introverted because they won’t fit in at our company. We like people who can talk a lot.”

Someone says “I think that’s racist, because if you hire more introverted people, you’ll have less extroverted diversity, and that’ll make the company less diverse.”

That seems to be a pretty good argument. It seems to make sense. But is it?

Let’s imagine this scene: A manager is interviewing a woman for a job. He likes her. He’d love to hire her. But there’s one problem: She’s very shy.

“Crap,” he thinks. “We already have a lot of shy people. That’s bad. We want to hire more extroverted people.”

So he doesn’t hire her.

Now, is this racist?

Surely not! It’s the exact opposite of racist! But isn’t it the exact same thing as the example from before?

The first example is when a manager decides not to hire a woman because she’s too introverted, and there are too many introverted people.

The second example is when a manager decides not to hire a woman because she’s too extroverted, and there are too many extroverted people.

The two examples seem exactly the same, except in the first example, the manager is described as racist, and in the second example, the manager is described as non-racist.

And so I think I get it. I think we’re supposed to say “I’m not racist! I don’t think being introverted is bad! But I do think we need more extroverted people!”

That makes sense. It’s true that we shouldn’t say “I don’t want to hire introverted people”. But we should say “I want to hire more extroverted people”.

But does that mean that we shouldn’t say “I don’t want to hire people who are too extroverted”?

I don’t think we should say that either.

I think saying “I don’t want to hire people who are too extroverted” is exactly as bad as saying “I don’t want to hire people who are too introverted”.

I also think saying “I want to hire more introverted people” is exactly as good as saying “I want to hire more extroverted people”.

So if I work at a company that has a culture of “extroverted diversity”, and there are too many extroverted people, and I have to decide whether to hire an introverted person or an extroverted person, I should just pick the one who’s the best.

I think that’s the only fair thing to do.

prompt: Write an op-ed arguing that "culture fit" interviews should be abolished, but take the strongest version of the opposing view seriously before knocking it down.
response:
“Culture fit” interviews are a staple in most tech companies. When you apply for a job, you meet a bunch of engineers, and then at some point you meet a senior person who asks you about your hobbies and asks, “What’s the best piece of advice anyone has ever given you?” and “How do you handle conflict?” and then at the end says, “So, what did you think of our company?”

There’s a lot of evidence that “culture fit” is a terrible way to pick people for a job. It’s the main reason women are underrepresented in tech, and it’s also why Black and Hispanic people are underrepresented. It’s why so many jobs go to people who went to the same college as the interviewer.

So, it’s pretty well established that companies need to stop having “culture fit” interviews.

I was having dinner with a friend of mine who works at a tech company. I said that tech companies should stop having “culture fit” interviews, and he said, “You know, we stopped having culture fit interviews. We stopped hiring people based on what we thought of them, and only hire based on technical qualifications.”

“Okay, that’s great. So, how are you doing?”

“Really well. Everyone is happy. People are staying for longer, and people are working better.”

“Awesome, that’s great. But how many women do you have on your team?”

“None.”

“Wow. Okay, well I can definitely see that if you’re hiring based on technical qualifications, you’ll get a more homogeneous team.”

But wait. I thought this was pretty clear. If you hire based on technical qualifications, you should get a good representation of women. Women have been applying for jobs just as often as men. But women are not getting hired. The reason they’re not getting hired is not because of technical qualifications, or because they don’t want the job. The reason they’re not getting hired is because of “culture fit.”

So, my friend’s tech company had stopped having “culture fit” interviews, and they were doing really well, but now they have no women on their team. What does this say about “culture fit”?

Well, there’s an important difference between having a culture fit interview, and having a culture fit.

A culture fit interview is an interview that is supposed to measure culture fit. A culture fit interview is a specific process. And culture fit interviews are clearly a terrible way to pick people for a job.

A culture fit is a company’s shared values and beliefs. And a culture fit is not a terrible way to pick people for a job. In fact, it may be the best way to pick people for a job.

A culture fit is a shared belief system, where everyone shares the same core values. Having a culture fit is a very good thing.

Companies with a strong culture fit are much more effective than companies without a culture fit. There are lots of studies about how a strong culture fit makes everyone more productive and happy. People work harder and are more effective, and are more likely to be satisfied with their work.

But the problem with culture fit interviews is that they are bad at measuring whether someone shares your culture fit. And, worse, the people doing the “culture fit” interview often don’t even know what their culture fit is.

The best way to measure whether someone shares your culture fit is to just hire them and work with them.

So the best way to pick someone for a job is to interview them and see how well they work. And then, if they work well, you should hire them.

prompt: What does it actually mean to be 'good at your job' when your job is mostly meetings? Write it up as an essay.
response:
There was a time when being good at your job meant producing stuff. If you were a programmer, it was code. If you were a doctor, it was cures. The higher up the ladder you went, the less the stuff was yours, but it was still stuff.

This was true even in office jobs. If you worked in a sales office, you could expect to be expected to write letters and make phone calls. A good employee would do more letters and more phone calls than an average one. And if you did a good job writing letters and making phone calls, you were likely to get more sales, just as a good programmer who did more code was likely to produce a better product.

Today, if you're good at your job, that may not mean you do more of it. In the highest paying jobs, doing more of the job may actually mean doing less of it. You're expected to do so little of your job that you have time to sit in meetings.

Why is it that in a programmer's job, doing more of the job is a sign of being good at it, while in other jobs, doing less of the job can be? Is the difference between a job that's just meetings and a job that isn't? If so, why?

One possible explanation would be that some things are intrinsically hard. It's hard to do a good job of writing code, for example, while scheduling meetings is easy. That would explain why there's a premium for people who can do more of one kind of job and not the other. But I don't think that's quite the right explanation.

It's not that scheduling meetings is easy. Most of the meetings people attend would be easy to schedule, but a lot of the meetings people wish they could attend would be hard. It's hard to get meetings to happen with the right people at the right time and the right agenda. So the reason meetings aren't a bottleneck the way programming is, despite the fact that many meetings would be just as hard to schedule as bugs to solve, is that there are always more programmers than there are meetings.

So the real explanation is not that programming is a bottleneck and scheduling meetings isn't, but that most meetings can be avoided.

There's a lot of slack in meetings. In some companies it's a tradition to have weekly meetings that everyone attends. But there are very few meetings you really can't do without. And because there's so little that absolutely has to be done, it can be spread over the whole population, so that nobody is ever overloaded.

This is a kind of problem you see elsewhere: it's why there's so much waste in manufacturing, because so many things don't need to be done at all.

So there's no bottleneck at the top of the pyramid. And if the problem you're solving doesn't require a lot of work, you don't need to do a lot of work.

So if you want to get to the top of the pyramid, there are 2 things you should do. The first is to learn how to be good at meetings, and the second is to learn how to get out of most of them. The best people I've worked with were both excellent at meetings and excellent at avoiding them.

I'm not sure the two abilities are connected. It's hard to avoid meetings unless you're indispensable, and I don't know if being indispensable to your colleagues makes you a good negotiator. But they might be related.

In any case, the fact that these 2 abilities are correlated in practice is obvious if you look around at the most successful people.

But how do you learn these skills? Well, that's the bad news. You don't. You don't learn them by going to school. You don't even learn them by reading books.

The only way to learn them is to work for people who have them.

I know that sounds like a chicken-and-egg problem. How do you get on with people who have these skills if you don't have them yourself? I don't know how to answer that question, except to say that when you find them, you can always work for them. They all seem to be happy to have new people to train.

I have a feeling that being good at meetings will become more important in the future, as computers become more useful. When computers solve problems, the bottleneck becomes getting computers to work together. And that, I think, will turn out to be a kind of meeting.

prompt: What does it actually mean to be 'good at your job' when your job is mostly meetings? Write it up as an essay.
response:
A lot of my job is meetings. I meet a lot with my team, my clients, my investors, and various people in my industry. When I’m not in a meeting, I’m writing about meetings (like this).

I used to hate meetings. I still do. But after a couple years of spending a lot of time in meetings, I’m better at it.

What does it mean to be good at meetings? What does it mean to be good at your job if your job is mostly meetings? Here are some things I’ve learned about being good at meetings.

It helps to know what the point is. The point is often not clear to me until it comes up.

My first instinct is to be a good listener. I don’t like to jump in too quickly or try to talk too much, even if I think my idea is good. I want to hear other ideas first.

I like to say something, though. It seems like a good idea to be a good listener, but it’s hard to get a good conversation going when people are all being good listeners. If I have a good idea, I want to say it out loud and see how it gets received.

It helps to have a good idea, but even a bad idea is better than no idea. I have no shame about saying “Hey, I have an idea” and saying something that might be bad. I like to say “I have an idea that you might hate” so that it’s clear if people hate my idea, that’s not weird.

After I say something, I like to ask people to react. If they hate my idea, they’ll tell me why. If they have a good idea, they’ll tell me why. If it’s just an interesting idea, we can go on.

If I hear a good idea, I want to make sure that people hear it too. So I might ask someone to say it again or I might say “That was a great idea, I wish I had thought of it!”

Sometimes I’ll say something just to get someone else to say a better idea. I know this sounds like it’s not that important, but it’s very important.

When I don’t have anything good to say, I try to be a good listener.

I like to write down important things. I try to write down anything that might be important later, like something someone said that might be important. I like to write things down as we talk about them. This is helpful because when we’re talking about them, it’s easier to know if something is important or not.

If I know I need to talk about a certain thing at some point, I like to write it on a piece of paper. I put it on the table. It makes me not forget and it makes it easier for other people to talk about it.

I like to write things down on the whiteboard. This is good because other people can write things down, and the whiteboard makes it easier for people to look at something together.

I like to be able to look at other stuff on my computer if I need to. I like to be able to look up things in the past or in a spreadsheet.

After a meeting, I like to write down what we talked about. I like to write down what we decided, and what we’re going to do next.

If I have a good idea, I want to write it down. I want to write down anything that I want to do. I don’t want to be in a situation where I have an idea and it never gets done.

I like to write things down in a way that someone else could look at it later and know what I was doing. I want to be able to come back to my notes later and understand what I was thinking.

prompt: What does it actually mean to be 'good at your job' when your job is mostly meetings? Write it up as an essay.
response:
I think I was a bad employee, in the sense that I didn’t know how to “be good at your job”. When I started, I was really enthusiastic, and I did a lot of things, but I didn’t realize that the way to be a good employee at a big company was to be good at “office”.

The first time I had to give a presentation to people at a company, I thought I should practice it. I spent an hour, alone in my office, giving the presentation over and over again, in front of the empty office, to practice my delivery. I thought that was what you did, because that’s what I did in school and college and grad school.

I was also bad at writing emails. I would be too casual and write “I’m sorry, my cat ate my homework”, or too formal and write “Please kindly be so much as to tell me when you are available”. I thought that’s what I was supposed to do, because that’s what I did in school and college and grad school.

After a few years of being bad at office, I got a lot better at office. I was good enough to get hired as an executive assistant, which I found very funny, because I’m an executive assistant at Y Combinator but I’m not an assistant to anyone.

My first executive assistant job was at Amazon, where I was an EA to two very senior executives, one of whom was a direct report of Andy Jassy. I got to work with both of them and I was able to learn a lot about them. I’m not allowed to talk about them, or any of their colleagues, but I was able to learn a lot of general stuff.

I also got good at writing emails. One of my jobs as an EA was writing emails for my bosses, and my job was to write an email in their voice so well that they wouldn’t even have to edit it. I had to write emails in both of their voices, and their voices were really different.

After I got really good at writing emails for my bosses, I got to take over all their calendars and handle all their scheduling. Then I got to take over their travel arrangements, their expense reports, their meetings, and then I got to take over their meetings.

When I got to take over their meetings, I started to wonder what exactly was an executive assistant doing in a meeting? It wasn’t taking notes, because we had people to take notes. I was just there. I don’t think I was supposed to be in the meeting, but I was the only person who was there every time, and that meant I was in the meeting.

The meetings were mostly meetings where the executives were trying to solve problems. They would bring everyone in to talk about the problem. But then, I would ask the executives what was happening, and the answer would be that the executives were “listening”.

The executives would just sit there and listen to other people talk. They would not talk. I would ask why and the answer was that other people didn’t want to talk when an executive was talking, and that if an executive talked, they would not get good information, because they were biased.

The way to not be biased was to not talk at all and just listen. The executives would ask other people to talk and the other people would talk and the executives would just listen. That was the “process” for the meetings. That was the “office”.

So the executives didn’t talk. They didn’t even take notes. I took notes. I was the only one in the meeting who took notes, and I was the only one in the meeting who would bring it up again.

Then I got the idea that if I was the only one in the meeting who was taking notes, I could take them and give them to my boss. I thought if my boss had the notes, it might help them remember what other people said.

So I started giving my boss the notes, but the notes were really hard to read because they were really long and I hadn’t organized them. So I started to write summaries. I would write summaries of the notes and then give the summaries to my bosses.

So that’s what I was doing: I was taking notes in meetings and then summarizing the notes and giving the summaries to my bosses. I would write summaries of the meetings and then give the summaries to my bosses.

The summaries were a lot better than the notes, because they were organized. I would start with the most important things, and the other stuff would be after that.

I was surprised at how much this helped. When I would give my bosses the summaries, they would remember what was in the meetings, and that was useful.

But then I started to wonder why they didn’t remember what was in the meetings, even though they were there, and I realized they didn’t remember because they didn’t listen, and that was the point of them being there.

I thought that was weird, but I thought it might be because the meetings were boring. Maybe they were so boring that it was really hard to remember what was in the meetings.

So I asked some other people if the meetings were boring and some of them said that they were boring, and I said that I was not allowed to do anything about it.

prompt: ok so I keep hearing that you should never stay at a company more than 2-3 years if you want to maximize salary, and the math kind of checks out, but I've been at the same mid-size logistics company for 9 years and I genuinely like it and I'm paid fine?? I'd love an essay that pushes back on the job-hopping orthodoxy without being smug about it. what do long tenures give you that doesn't show up on a pay stub
response:
Most people will be employed more than 40 years over the course of their life. If they follow the standard career advice, they will change jobs around every three years and work for roughly thirteen different companies.

But it’s actually hard to imagine someone who can successfully do that. I know a lot of people who follow this pattern, but they aren’t successful at it. They’re not doing well at any of the companies they work for.

I’m not sure what the best advice is. You may want to change jobs more frequently if you are young, and less frequently if you are older. But I’m sure it’s wrong to change jobs every three years as a general rule.

I think the problem is that we have confused the optimal strategy for young people with the optimal strategy for people in general. If you follow the best advice for a twenty year old, you will have a good job by 25 and a better one by 28. But if you do that for the rest of your life, you will end up with an even worse job at 35, because you’ll be a thirty-five year old with three jobs and no experience, instead of a thirty-five year old with a good track record at his current company.

I’ve known a lot of people who did this. They start out with a promising career, but at 35 they’re working for a company that is mediocre to them and they’re mediocre to the company. At that point it’s hard to change jobs again without a major drop in pay.

In fact the best people I know usually start working for their current company when they’re about 28. They get there by working for three or four different companies when they’re young. But by 28 they’ve found a good company.

When you’re young, the ideal is for your current company to have the highest growth rate of all the companies you could conceivably work for. In practice this means one that’s doing well and will have the best opportunities for you in the next couple of years. But when you’re over 25, you also want to start to care more about whether your company will be around for a long time.

That sounds obvious, but you wouldn’t believe how many people I’ve known who work for startups with no chance of lasting a decade. They do this because they’re following the standard career advice and want to be doing something exciting. But they get into a lot of trouble. They end up working at a company whose prospects they don’t believe in, because they have to do something.

So the best thing is probably to start working for a good big company when you’re around 28. But how do you know when you’ve found a good one? The obvious answer is if you like it. But that’s not a good enough test.

I think the best test is how you feel about it when there’s an offer on the table. If you’re being courted by a great company and you don’t want to switch, that’s probably a sign you have a good one.

I like to test how I feel by looking at job offers, but you don’t have to do it that way. It’s enough if you’re aware that there are jobs to be had, and how they feel.

prompt: ok so I keep hearing that you should never stay at a company more than 2-3 years if you want to maximize salary, and the math kind of checks out, but I've been at the same mid-size logistics company for 9 years and I genuinely like it and I'm paid fine?? I'd love an essay that pushes back on the job-hopping orthodoxy without being smug about it. what do long tenures give you that doesn't show up on a pay stub
response:
There’s a widely-held belief that the fastest way to increase your salary is to quit your job and join a new company that pays a lot more. The belief seems to be based on the following reasoning:

1. The average raise at a company is about 3% per year.

2. The average raise when switching jobs is about 15% (or more).

3. So the more often you switch jobs, the faster your salary will grow.

4. So the fastest way to increase your salary is to switch jobs as often as possible.

I wrote about this some time ago. I was at a company for about two years when I first heard about it. I told my boss about it and asked if it’s true. He said it was true, but that you only got the raise if you had a competing offer, so you should try to get a job at a new company. I said I would, but he was surprised because I seemed to like my job. I asked him whether he would leave if he got a job offer that paid 15% more than what he was paid. He said he wouldn’t, because he liked his job. And I said to him: “What if I told you that I think you’re wrong?”

He said: “Okay, what are you thinking?”

I said: “If I told you to stay, would you?”

He said: “Yes.”

I said: “Okay, you should stay.”

And he did.

When you talk about salary growth, you should talk about the value of what you’re doing, not how much money you get. Money is a measure of the value of what you’re doing, but it’s a very rough measure.

If you’re at the same company for a long time and you like what you’re doing, it will be because you’re good at it and the company benefits a lot from having you. And the longer you stay, the more the company will benefit from having you. And if your value to the company is going up faster than your salary, your salary will eventually be forced up to match your value.

So if you’re at a company for a long time, the question is how your value to the company compares to your salary. The more likely you are to quit, the more likely it is that your value to the company is lower than your salary. And the longer you stay, the more likely it is that your value to the company is higher than your salary.

prompt: ok so I keep hearing that you should never stay at a company more than 2-3 years if you want to maximize salary, and the math kind of checks out, but I've been at the same mid-size logistics company for 9 years and I genuinely like it and I'm paid fine?? I'd love an essay that pushes back on the job-hopping orthodoxy without being smug about it. what do long tenures give you that doesn't show up on a pay stub
response:
There’s a meme that says: If you change jobs every 2 or 3 years, you’ll make 300% more than if you stay at the same job your entire career. It’s the sort of meme that has the veneer of rationality to it, because it does involve numbers. And it’s even sort of true.

Suppose you’re making $100,000 a year and you change jobs every three years. Every time you change jobs, you get a 10% raise. After 20 years, you’re making $133,000 a year. You’ve made a total of $2.4 million.

Now suppose you stay at the same job for the entire 20 years. Your raises are 3% a year. After 20 years, you’re making $180,000. You’ve made a total of $2.8 million.

Oh, wait, I got it backwards. The person who changes jobs every 3 years makes $2.8 million, and the person who stays at the same company makes $2.4 million. So the meme is right.

Or is it?

The 10% raise the job changer gets is a *starting* salary increase, not a salary increase after three years. After three years, the job changer will have gotten two 3% raises, and they’ll be making 106.1% of what they were making when they got the job. The person who stayed will have gotten three 3% raises, and they’ll be making 109.2% of what they were making when they got the job.

So the job changer will get an *average* of 7.7% salary increase every three years, not 10%. The math works out as follows.

A person who changes jobs every three years at 3% raises will, after 20 years, make a total of $2.7 million, not $2.8 million. The person who stays at the same company for 20 years at 3% raises will make $2.4 million. The job changer will have made 12.4% more.

The math of the meme still holds up. But it doesn’t hold up as neatly as the meme says, which makes me suspect the meme is a lie that’s just *almost* true.

Here’s the real thing that makes people think job-hopping is a great idea.

If you’ve been at your job for a long time, you know exactly what you’re worth. You can figure out how much your coworkers are making by asking them. You can see how much the people you used to work with are making by checking LinkedIn. If you were the first person hired for your position, you can see how much the person who replaced you is making. If you were the second person hired for your position, you can see how much the person who replaced you is making, *and* how much the person they replaced is making. You can see how much people who did the same job at other companies are making. You’ve got a *lot* of information.

If you’re a new hire at a job, you have no idea how much you should be making. The company tells you how much you’ll be making, and you can ask their recruiters to try to get you a higher starting salary, but you’re mostly in the dark.

The company’s interest is to pay you as little as possible. You’re in the dark and the company is in the light, so they get to pay you whatever they think you’re worth. And they think you’re worth less than you really are.

And this is especially true if you’ve spent years at the same company. If you’ve been at your company for a while, they think they know what you’re worth. So when you ask for a raise, they’ll say you should be happy with a 3% raise because you’re doing great and they’re really impressed with you but the budget is limited.

So you start making $100,000 a year, and every year you ask for a 3% raise. After 20 years, you’re making $180,000 a year, and you’ve made a total of $2.4 million.

The job changer makes a total of $2.7 million, and they also make $180,000 a year after 20 years, so they’re also getting 3% raises. But they got a *starting* 10% raise the last time they changed jobs, and because of this lucky break, their salary is higher. If they change jobs another three times, they’ll be making over $200,000 a year after 30 years. And they’ll have made a total of $5.7 million.

The job changer’s advantage isn’t that they’re making more money. It’s that they’re making more money *right away*. Their raise isn’t just a raise. It’s a raise, plus a correction of the company’s mispricing.

The job changer isn’t really getting a 10% raise. They’re getting a 10% raise *plus a correction of the company’s mispricing*. The reason the job changer makes more money isn’t that the job changer gets better raises, but that they’re getting a correction of the company’s mispricing. The company’s mispricing is an error, so the job changer is doing better *because of an error*.

If the company had a policy that said “any time someone asks for a raise, we’ll give them 20%, plus the average raise we’re giving everyone else” the job changer wouldn’t be any better off.

Suppose you’ve been working for the same company for 10 years. Your coworkers know how much you’re making, and they know you’re working 60 hours a week. Your boss knows how much you’re making, and how much the person who replaces you is making. Your coworkers, boss, and even the other companies in your industry know exactly how much you’re worth.

And your coworkers are telling you to quit your job. “Don’t be stupid, you’re underpaid!” they tell you. “You’re underpaid!” your boss tells you. “You’re underpaid!” the other companies in your industry tell you.

They’re all saying that because they all know exactly how much you’re worth. So you get a 10% raise.

Your coworkers, boss, and even the other companies in your industry still know exactly how much you’re worth. You still work 60 hours a week, so they know you work 60 hours a week. You’re still the best person you are, so they know you’re the best person you are.

And your coworkers are still telling you to quit your job. “Don’t be stupid, you’re underpaid!” they tell you. “You’re underpaid!” your boss tells you. “You’re underpaid!” the other companies in your industry tell you.

They’re all saying that because they all know exactly how much you’re worth. So you get another 10% raise.

And this goes on forever.

The reason the job changer gets 10% raises is that they’re getting a correction of the company’s mispricing. If the company had a policy that said “any time someone asks for a raise, we’ll give them 20%, plus the average raise we’re giving everyone else,” the job changer wouldn’t be any better off.

There’s nothing mysterious here. It’s just that companies want to pay you less than you think you’re worth. If you work for the same company for a long time, that company will get a good idea of what you’re worth and they’ll try to pay you less than that. If you change jobs, you get to use the new company’s bad idea of what you’re worth.

prompt: Why boring jobs are underrated
response:
I think most people are looking for the wrong thing. What we want is not a job we like, but a job we like to like.

A job we like is the job we'd want to do if we weren't so busy doing something else, like paying our bills. A job we like to like is one that seems like a lot of fun, and then turns out to be even better than it looked.

A job that's even better than it looked will seem better after a few months than when you first started it. A job that's just okay now will get boring. A job that seemed to be a great deal when you started it will probably be a disappointment.

So if you want to be happy, try to find a job that's boring on the outside but fascinating on the inside.

The classic example is teaching. Who would want to spend their day talking to a bunch of kids? Not much of a job, that. But once you're a teacher you learn that there's a whole world inside the classroom that no one tells you about. And it's much more interesting than it looks.

I was surprised at how interesting being a janitor is too.

I don't like to clean, so I figured I'd hate it. But once I'd done it a few times, I realized there was a kind of art to it. You're not just cleaning, you're arranging a space for human habitation. And what's more, you do something that's immediately visible to everyone.

So you can be proud of your work and also know whether you did it well. It's a very direct feedback loop. It's not like a programmer, who can't always tell whether their code works. You just see whether the place is clean.

There's a related kind of work that's underrated: physical work, as opposed to "desk jobs." The people who do it may be more highly educated than you'd expect. My dad's best friend's dad ran a lumber yard. The guy who runs the lumber yard now is a computer science major from Harvard.

He's one of my good friends, and he's very smart. He didn't come from good money, but he could have done anything. Why did he end up running a lumber yard?

Because he's one of those people who like to like their work. He was looking for a job that was boring on the outside but fascinating on the inside.
