You can do this to some extent with any field. You can find a way to like almost anything. But there's an easier way. You just have to know which fields are underrated, and then work in those.

There's one field that's underrated everywhere: government. I'm not talking about the government job that everyone thinks of, but rather the work you can do in it. When I was in college I was afraid of government jobs for two reasons.

One was the usual reason, that government was bad and so people who worked in it must be bad too. And the other was that I didn't want to be boring. I thought government work would be boring, which I thought would mean I was boring.

I now realize I was wrong about both. Working for the government is the best thing I ever did. It was the most interesting work I'd done, and the people I worked with were some of the most interesting I'd met.

And I still can't believe it.

It's hard to be surprised by a job that's more interesting than you expected, because you never have expectations. You have to be surprised by a job that's more interesting than you expected it to be.

I'm not advocating government work specifically. It's just the most extreme example of the kind of thing I'm talking about. If you think working in government would be boring, working at Microsoft might be just as interesting.

I'm not saying you should work for Microsoft. I'm just saying that you could. It doesn't have to be a choice between government work and being bored.

I think this is a bigger issue than it seems at first. Most people are going to spend a lot of time working. If they do it in jobs they like, that's a very good thing.

And that means we should try to find more good jobs, which I think we can.

I have this vague feeling that there's a way to make jobs more interesting.

I think it's something to do with not doing things the boring way.

I think it's something to do with not doing things the way other people do them.

prompt: Why boring jobs are underrated
response:
I was thinking a lot lately about why I have been so happy with my job as a writer at an investment firm, and I realized the answer was because it was so boring.

I have always liked my job, and I have tried not to overrate that, but I think this is one of the happiest I have ever been in a job. My job is the sort of job that you would not normally expect someone to like. I have a desk in an open-plan office in Connecticut, surrounded by other people with computers. I do not talk to anyone much during the day. Most days I just sit at my computer and type.

The thing that I like about my job is that my life is my own. I have never had a job that gave me this much freedom. Most jobs have some rules about how you can spend your time. Even if the rules are very loose, the fact that you feel as if your time is being watched can be very stressful.

A lot of my friends complain about this at their jobs. Some say they are not allowed to use Twitter, or have to work a minimum number of hours. Others complain that their boss wants them to always be available. The worst is when your boss or coworkers are not just interested in what you are doing during working hours, but what you are doing outside them. That's just creepy.

I think some people are better than others at dealing with having their life micromanaged. But I am not one of them. In my last job, it was very stressful to have someone checking the logs to make sure that I had spent enough time in the office. I felt as if I was being watched even when I was not, and this meant I never fully relaxed when I was there.

I was not the only person who felt this way. I have a friend who is very different from me in personality, but has a strong dislike of being watched. When he was working at a startup, his boss came into his office one day to see what he was working on, and he was so stressed by this that he ended up crying. He thought he would quit and go work in the woods.

I was not the only person who felt this way. I have a friend who is very different from me in personality, but has a strong dislike of being watched. When he was working at a startup, his boss came into his office one day to see what he was working on, and he was so stressed by this that he ended up crying. He thought he would quit and go work in the woods.

At my current job, my only responsibility is to write. The only way they could tell if I was not doing this is if they read my writing, but they never do. I could sit in a hammock all day, as long as I was writing at night. This has never happened, but I don't feel the need to pretend to be working either. I can go on a two-hour walk during the day, or take a nap if I want to. I don't have to sit at a desk and pretend to be working, and I don't have to worry about how much time I have logged on the time tracker.

This freedom is not just about how I can spend my time, but also about the fact that I am not in a position to be judged by others. I don't know whether you think my writing is good, and I never will. It is not like at a startup, where everyone is always judging what you are doing. In my current job, no one ever evaluates me, either positively or negatively.

I have a lot of freedom at my current job, but it has been surprising that this makes me so happy. I don't want a boring life. I want to write and do interesting things. But I think having a boring job allows you to have a more interesting life.

One way to think about it is that there is a difference between what makes you happy and what makes you sad. The things that make you happy are the things that you enjoy doing. But what makes you sad is a constant background stress that you feel from being watched.

I think people have been too worried in the past about making their job fun. I think they should worry more about making their job boring.

prompt: Why boring jobs are underrated
response:
Boring jobs pay well and they rarely cause existential crises.

If you’re looking for a job in your thirties or forties, the best ones are in the boring parts of the economy. Boring things that don’t make good magazine articles, but which are indispensable.

For instance, the economy needs people to check whether the numbers on the invoices match the goods delivered, and people to make sure the right things get sent to the right places on time. These are unglamorous jobs, but they’re indispensable.

The same is true in medicine. Doctors who deal with chronic conditions like diabetes or arthritis aren’t as exciting as those who do surgeries, but they’re indispensable.

Most of the people who write about jobs focus on glamour. What you should be doing is getting a job in something that’s going to be exciting and important. You don’t even need to like it; as long as you’re good at it, you can do anything.

I used to think so too.

I got my first job in tech when I was 13. It was at a company that made software for banks, which I figured was a pretty safe bet. But then when I was in college, I started thinking I was missing out. I should be doing something exciting. So instead of trying to get a job when I graduated from college, I got a PhD. I wanted to do something important.

And I did, sort of. I published 11 papers, which made for good magazine articles. But none of it has been useful to anyone.

What I’d learned is that exciting and important are not the same thing. Indeed, if anything it’s the opposite: exciting is probably a bad sign. People want to write magazine articles about exciting things. So if you want to work on something you think might turn out to be useful, you have to ignore the people telling you what you should be working on. Which is to say, you have to do boring things.

When I got a job at Microsoft, I was told there was a team doing something called “distributed computing.” Distributed computing sounds exciting. But when I got there, I found that it wasn’t so much distributed as broken. The reason people talked about it so much was that it sounded like something you’d want to do. But actually it was terrible.

When I got back to Y Combinator, I was excited to work on startups, because those sounded exciting. But I quickly learned that most startups are terrible too. So I started to notice there was a pattern here.

When you think about it, it’s obvious. Startups are a risky bet. Most startups fail, so the fact that people are talking about them a lot isn’t a sign that they’re good. Indeed, startups are by definition new, and most things are bad at first. The same applies to distributed computing. It’s new. New things are always exciting, because they’re full of possibilities. But exciting is a very poor proxy for important.

So when I started doing consulting, I looked for the boring parts of the economy, not the exciting ones. And it was the best advice I ever gave anyone. People were desperate to have their problems solved, and they were willing to pay a lot.

One of the best examples of this was my experience with Amazon. I knew about Amazon because they were so famous. Everyone was talking about them. They sounded like a very exciting place to work. So one of my first clients was a startup I advised to get into a partnership with them.

It turned out that Amazon was a terrible partner. They were late, rude, and unhelpful. But I realized that if I did this for a living, I’d get paid a lot for being annoyed at them.

I got more annoyed at Amazon the more I had to deal with them. They made it hard to deal with them in every possible way. I would have loved to have worked at a company where people tried to make you as happy as possible. That would have been fun.

But that’s not how Amazon works. They try to make you as unhappy as possible. They want you to pay them a lot of money, so they do everything they can to make it hard for you to get out of it.

I don’t know how they think this will work in the long run. I don’t think it will. But that’s not my problem. It’s not even a problem I care about. I just care about getting paid to be annoyed at them, and that part works.

The same is true of other boring parts of the economy. For instance, most companies have terrible websites. But I don’t care about their websites. I just care about getting paid to work on them.

It’s not glamorous, but it pays well.

The worst jobs are the boring ones that don’t pay well. Those are the ones people should avoid.

prompt: I'm 41 and thinking of leaving accounting to retrain as a nurse. Everyone either says "go for it!" or "are you crazy" and neither helps. Could you write an essay on how a person should actually think about a mid-life career change, the real costs, the stuff people romanticize, and what regret looks like in both directions?
response:
Let’s say you’re thinking about changing careers in a way that will take more than a few weeks to set up. You’re in your mid-thirties, like me. And you have a lot of people in your life who are either very enthusiastic (“Go for it!”) or very concerned (“Are you crazy?”).

I’ve talked to a lot of people about career changes, and this is the best I’ve been able to come up with in the way of advice:

One way to think about this is, if you don’t make the change, how long will you feel unhappy about not doing it? A few months? A few years? A lifetime? If it’s just a few months, you can just wait it out. If it’s a few years, maybe try talking yourself out of it a little harder. If you’ll be unhappy for the rest of your life, you’re going to need a lot more than my blog post to convince you otherwise.

Another way to think about this is, if you do make the change, how long will it take for it to be successful? A few months? A few years? A lifetime? If it’s a few months, you can just try it out. If it’s a few years, maybe try talking yourself into it a little harder. If it’s a lifetime, you’re going to need a lot more than my blog post to convince you.

You can see where these two ideas are going.

If not doing the thing means you’ll be unhappy for the rest of your life, but doing it has a high chance of making you happy within a few months, then you should totally do it.

If not doing the thing only means you’ll be unhappy for a few months, but doing it has only a chance of making you happy after a lifetime of hard work, you should not do it.

But most cases are somewhere in the middle.

Let’s say you’re not super happy in your current job. You like it, but it’s not your dream job and it’s hard to get excited about it. And you have a potential alternative career that might be your dream job, but you’ve never tried it and you don’t know if it will work. If you don’t do it, maybe you’ll regret it, maybe you won’t. And maybe you’ll regret it a little, or a lot. If you do it, maybe you’ll be happy, maybe you won’t. And maybe you’ll be happy a little, or a lot.

If you’re at this point, I’d say that if the new thing is at all interesting and seems like it would be fun, you should try it out. You don’t need to go crazy. If it’s something you can try out without too much trouble – like, if you want to do something in the arts, take a class, or do some volunteer work, or start an online magazine – you should do it. If it’s something that takes up a lot of time or money, but you can do it in a way that doesn’t require giving up your current job – like, if you want to go to grad school, you can do that while you work – you should probably try that, too.

The only time you have to make a big commitment – give up your current job, move, change your whole life – is if you can’t get enough information from the less committed options.

Now, sometimes that makes sense. If you want to become a musician and play gigs for a living, there’s no way to find out if that will work except to become a musician and play gigs. I don’t know of any better way to find out if being a musician is going to work for you than trying it out.

But if you’re thinking of going back to school for something, there’s almost always a way to try it out without actually going back to school. I think this is because people think you have to get a degree to do the thing, but you don’t, you can just do the thing.

Here’s how to do this:

1. If you want to go to school for a particular subject, take a course in that subject. It doesn’t matter if it’s at a big fancy school. Take any course you can. I like online ones. But if you want to be a lawyer, take the first class of the bar review course. If you want to learn Spanish, take a class. If you want to go to medical school, take biology. If you want to go to grad school for philosophy, take a philosophy course at a local community college. (If you want to go to grad school for philosophy and you think there’s no way you could ever take an undergrad philosophy course, that means you’re going to grad school for the wrong reasons and you should talk to your therapist instead of me.)

2. If you want to do a job, do the job. It doesn’t have to be your dream version of the job. It doesn’t have to be at the best company in the world. It doesn’t have to have a good salary. You can even do it for free. But if you want to work for an NGO in the developing world, take some sort of job at some sort of NGO. If you want to be a social worker, work for a shelter. If you want to be a lawyer, work for a legal aid society.

The thing is that you can find out whether you really want to do it before you have to give up your current job. Sometimes the only way to do it is to give up your current job, but often you can find out for yourself.

This is important because if you don’t find out for yourself, you’re going to get a lot of bad advice from people.

People are pretty bad at giving advice about your life. There are two kinds of advice: generic advice, and advice based on their experience.

Generic advice is stuff like “follow your passion” or “don’t do anything you can’t live without”. If I tell you to follow your passion, you can’t be sure that’s what you want to hear. If you wanted to hear something different, I could have said “don’t follow your passion”. If I told you to do whatever you want, you’d still wonder whether you wanted to do what I said you wanted to do.

It’s not that people who give generic advice are bad. I’m just saying it’s easy to give generic advice, and it’s not always helpful.

The other kind of advice is based on someone else’s experience, and it’s usually pretty good advice. But sometimes they give you bad advice because they have bad experiences.

For example, let’s say I want to be an artist, but I have a good-paying job and I’m a little scared to leave it. My friend says “you should be an artist! I did it, and it’s the best thing I’ve ever done”. But I ask “did you like it? Did you like the process of working for a living as an artist, or just the fact that you were an artist?” And they say “Oh, well, I’m not working as an artist anymore. I just quit. But I’m an artist, so I feel like I got what I wanted. It was the best thing I ever did!”

That is not good advice, because this person did not work for a living as an artist. They don’t know how it feels, and it’s not going to be the best thing I ever do if I work for a living as an artist.

But if my friend says “I was an artist, and I worked for a living as an artist, and it was the best thing I ever did”, that’s good advice. But they don’t know about me. I might be terrible. I might not like it. Or I might like it.

Or I might hate it.

Let’s say I do give up my current job and work for a living as an artist. I have a terrible time at it. And then I talk to a friend, who is an artist. And they say “Oh, I’m not an artist anymore, I’m in accounting. It’s the best thing I’ve ever done”. This is not good advice, because this person did not work for a living as an accountant. They know what it’s like to be an artist, but not to work as an accountant. I can’t tell if I would hate being an accountant, or love it.

This is what people mean when they say “I regret that I ever became an artist” or “I regret that I’m not an artist anymore”. The former is bad advice, because you don’t know if they’re talking about working as an artist, or having been an artist. The latter is bad advice, because you don’t know if they’re talking about working as an accountant, or having been an artist.

It’s really hard to think about what it would be like to work as an accountant if you’re not. But it’s easy to think about what it would be like to work as an accountant if you have.

I don’t mean this to sound like a trick. I’m just saying that it’s hard to make good decisions if you don’t know what it would be like to work at something. If you don’t know, you’re going to get bad advice from people who give generic advice, or bad advice from people who don’t know what it’s like to work at the thing.

And if you don’t try it, you might regret it.

There’s a lot of stuff I’ve never tried that I regret not trying, like learning to play guitar, or working for a law firm. I could tell you what I think it would be like, but I wouldn’t know what it’s like.

But there are a lot of things I’ve tried out that I didn’t try to make a career of, and that I don’t regret. I tried it out, and I thought “yeah, I don’t want to do this for a living”, and I didn’t try it again. And I didn’t regret not trying again.

Sometimes, I think, you need to try it. If you want to be a lawyer and you never try it, you’ll always be wondering if you’re missing out. But if you want to be a lawyer, and you work for a law firm and you don’t like it, you can stop. And you can tell people “I tried to be a lawyer, and it didn’t work”. That’s good advice, because you know what it’s like.

The same thing is true about not trying it. If you want to be an artist and you don’t try it, you’ll always be wondering if you’re missing out. But if you try it and don’t like it, you can stop. And you can tell people “I tried to be an artist, and it didn’t work”. That’s good advice, because you know what it’s like.

prompt: I'm 41 and thinking of leaving accounting to retrain as a nurse. Everyone either says "go for it!" or "are you crazy" and neither helps. Could you write an essay on how a person should actually think about a mid-life career change, the real costs, the stuff people romanticize, and what regret looks like in both directions?
response:
It’s a big decision, and it’s not clear what would be best for her. But one thing that’s clear is that a lot of people have strong opinions about what she should do. “Go for it!” one group says. “But you’re crazy,” says another group.

I can’t say whether she should switch careers, because I don’t know enough about her. But I can say a lot about how we think about this sort of decision, and a lot of the advice is pretty useless.

“Go for it!” is the sort of advice you give to someone when you’ve got no idea what they’re doing. It’s the kind of advice you give to a friend of a friend who’s trying to do something really scary, like go live in Russia or take a job with an unknown startup.

This is not a good kind of advice to give someone who’s going to change careers.

Imagine you asked people for a lot of money to give them a business loan, and everyone just said “sure, go for it!” without looking at your business plan or doing any kind of due diligence. You’d know that you’d made a lot of friends, but you wouldn’t have raised any money.

People often say “go for it” because they want to be supportive. But if you think about it, if you were giving really good career advice, you’d be making some kind of prediction, and predictions are scary. So when you want to be supportive, you give noncommittal advice.

But you can’t make a decision like changing careers on the basis of noncommittal advice. It doesn’t help you decide what to do. It’s like when your friends say “you could go into any field you wanted, you’re so smart.” True, but not useful.

“Go for it” is the sort of thing someone might say in an email or on social media, where you can give support at low cost. And that’s fine. But it’s not the sort of thing you should make a big decision on.

On the other side, the “you’re crazy” side of the spectrum.

This is also not useful advice.

If I went on a conference call with my friend to discuss a big career decision, and she said “oh my god, that’s the stupidest thing I’ve ever heard, you’re so dumb, you have no idea what you’re doing, you’re a terrible person,” I would just be like, okay.

You might say, “but wait, there are people who give you negative career advice but do it in a supportive way. They say things like ‘I’m really worried about you’ or ‘that’s going to be so hard, don’t you think?’”

Well, sure, but if someone really cared about you, they would give you *good* advice, not bad advice. And the advice “you’re going to be so miserable if you do this” is not good advice. It’s just a kind of negative advice.

So you don’t want to ask your friends for career advice. It’s not that they don’t want to help you, but they can’t really.

If you want to make a big career decision, you need to think for yourself. That’s not always easy or fun, but it’s the only way.

So how do you think for yourself?

First you need to think about the kind of job you want. I think a lot of people have some kind of vague idea of what they want their life to be, but that’s usually not enough to think about how to make good career decisions.

So let’s make a list of the things you want in your job.

I have a lot of ideas on what you might want in a job. But here are a few of the most common:

1. To feel like you’re learning something interesting.

2. To do work that you’re good at, that you get compliments for.

3. To earn a lot of money.

4. To get promoted quickly and have a lot of influence.

5. To have a lot of autonomy and independence.

6. To have a job that gives you a lot of freedom.

7. To have a job where you can be creative.

8. To do work that you think of as meaningful.

9. To be with people you think are impressive.

10. To be able to spend time with your family or friends.

11. To not have to travel or commute a lot.

12. To have a stable job that will be there for the next twenty years.

Now, if you really want to think about what kind of job you want, you should make a longer list. But these are the most common things people want.

But there’s another thing you should think about: which of these do you want *most*.

This is a really hard question. And I think most people are not very good at answering it.

But if you think about it in terms of career choices, it’s a lot easier to answer.

Here’s a test:

If you got a job that did one of these things *very* well, and did all the other things poorly, would you take it?

For example, suppose you got a job that paid you $10,000,000 a year. You’d make a lot of money, but you’d do something you didn’t like, and you wouldn’t learn anything, and you wouldn’t make any friends. Would you take the job?

Most people will answer that they’d take the job.

So if you want to think about the things you want in a job, and how much you want them, you should think about this.

I think that if you really want to make a good career choice, you should think about this a lot. I think you should think about this question for every single thing you want in a job.

But I’ve talked about this sort of thing a lot before, and it’s not really what you’re asking. You’re asking what you should do.

And that’s a really hard question to answer.

But I’ll give you my advice anyway. It’s not that good, but it’s not nothing.

If you’re really thinking about changing careers, you should try to see what you could get from your current job.

I mean, there’s always going to be some kind of tradeoff between staying in your current job and trying something new. But sometimes you can do something where you can get both.

For example, you can go to medical school at night. It’s a lot of work, but if you go to school at night, you can keep your day job. This means you’ll probably get a better degree, because you’ll be older and more motivated than most people. It also means that if you go to medical school, you can go to medical school and then be a nurse.

If you want to change careers, you should think about the things that you could do that would let you do both.

prompt: I'm 41 and thinking of leaving accounting to retrain as a nurse. Everyone either says "go for it!" or "are you crazy" and neither helps. Could you write an essay on how a person should actually think about a mid-life career change, the real costs, the stuff people romanticize, and what regret looks like in both directions?
response:
I’m sure there are people who would say that the best career decision you could make is to do whatever makes you the happiest. If you’ve got a job that you absolutely love, all the better, but if not, you should go find one that you do.

But happiness isn’t the only thing that matters. You can have the most amazing job in the world and still be miserable if you don’t make enough money to support yourself and your family. You can make a million dollars a year and still be miserable if you feel like your life has no purpose and the work you’re doing doesn’t matter.

I can’t give you some simple algorithm for determining how much happiness is enough, or how much money, or how much meaning. That’s something that you just have to sort out for yourself. But once you’ve decided what the right combination of those things is, you’re left with a much harder question – how do you actually get it?

In most cases, it’s not all that hard to find something that you’re going to be good at, but that isn’t going to make you very happy. Plenty of people have great jobs that they’re very good at, very good at making money, very good at advancing their careers, and yet they’re miserable. The problem is that they never took the time to ask themselves, “is this what I actually want?”

But it’s not that simple either. Plenty of people have the time to ask themselves “is this what I actually want?” and when they answer, “no, it’s not” they find themselves trapped.

For example, there are people who go to a medical school and decide in the middle of their second year that they don’t want to be doctors anymore. But they can’t just get out. They have to finish the rest of the program, which takes 3 or 4 more years. They have to go into practice and work off their medical school loans. And they have to go back and pay off their undergraduate loans. So they can’t just walk away and start again.

Or take a woman who wants to be a lawyer, but is afraid to quit her job to go to law school. She’s not sure she’ll even get in. She’s not sure that it will be a good fit. She’s not sure that she’ll even like law. And when she asks herself if she could afford to just go for it, she realizes that it would be a real struggle.

And that’s why I’m so frustrated when people make sweeping statements like “you should just follow your dreams” or “there’s no such thing as being too old to start a new career.” These are both true but at the same time, they don’t tell you very much.

I know of a lot of people who have made big, impressive career changes and I’ve always admired their ability to do that, to take big, bold steps. But I don’t always have the guts to do the same.

I don’t really know whether that’s because I’m a coward, or whether I’m just being realistic. I don’t know if the people who took big, bold steps had the guts to do it, or whether they just had the money to do it.

I know plenty of people who have the guts to take big steps, but can’t afford to do it. They don’t have the time to spare, and they don’t have the money to spare.

And there’s nothing wrong with either of those people. Some people have the guts to take big steps, but not the resources to do it. Some people have the resources to take big steps, but not the guts to do it. Both of those things make perfect sense.

But then there’s people who have both the guts and the resources to take big steps, and yet they still don’t do it. They tell themselves that “I’ll just wait a few more years. I’ll just save up a bit more money. Then I’ll be ready.”

But then, a few more years later, they tell themselves the same thing. And a few years after that, they’re so far along that they can’t leave anymore.

The problem is that they keep looking for this mythical “perfect moment” to make their big change. The perfect time to leave your job is the same as the perfect time to go on a diet. It doesn’t exist.

If you want to make a big change in your life, you have to start right now. Because that’s the only time you’ll ever get to start.

I know I can’t make the decision for you, but there are a few things you can do to make the decision easier.

1. Make sure that you’ve been thinking about it for a long time. If you’ve been thinking about changing careers for a long time, the decision is going to be a lot easier.

2. Think about the long-term costs. If you can’t afford to do it now, you can always save up some money. But that takes time, and time is the thing that you can’t get back.

3. Think about how you’ll feel when you’ve done it. If you’ve been thinking about changing careers for a long time, you probably know how you’ll feel. It’s just a matter of taking that first step.

prompt: Blog post idea: the hidden etiquette of Slack. Things like who gets a thumbs-up vs. a reply, why "hey" with nothing after it drives people insane, the politics of the green dot. I want it funny but with an actual argument underneath about how status works in remote teams.
response:
I recently moved into a new office. It’s on the fourth floor, in an unremarkable corner of a nondescript office building in Austin, Texas. I like it. It feels like the kind of place where you can work without distractions, and the office has a good atmosphere.

But there are some things I need to get used to.

My desk is on the right, and there’s a long bench on the left. At the far end of the bench is an old, dusty, beige Dell laptop that doesn’t do anything and is probably worth like $10. But someone must have it, because there’s a sticky note on it that says, “THIS LAPTOP IS FOR EMERGENCIES ONLY.”

The sticky note is so boring that no one would ever look at it. But it’s a sticky note, so it will stick around for years. The laptop will stay at the end of the bench as long as the company has any desks left.

This is a small thing, but it tells you a lot about how humans behave.

If I told you that my company was a really good company that cares a lot about the environment, and they had a program for giving people laptops at the end of their useful life, would you believe me?

A few years ago, a friend and I started a company together. It went well, but we didn’t manage our money well, so it failed. Then we started another company that also failed. So I spent about ten years working on ideas that didn’t work, which is pretty common, but I didn’t feel very successful.

Then I started working on the idea of making a tool that would let me and my friends run a company without a lot of overhead and bureaucracy.

So I started writing a tool called Fathom that was a combination of GitHub, Slack, and Trello.

And it did pretty well.

It wasn’t as successful as I’d hoped, but it was enough to be profitable.

So when I left Fathom in 2015, I had the money to pay myself and my friends to work full-time on the company.

And when I got back to work, the company had gotten so successful that it had become a company I could run full-time.

And now, two years later, I’m starting to get comfortable with my new position as CEO.

I’m not sure it will last forever, but for now, we have a lot of momentum.

prompt: Blog post idea: the hidden etiquette of Slack. Things like who gets a thumbs-up vs. a reply, why "hey" with nothing after it drives people insane, the politics of the green dot. I want it funny but with an actual argument underneath about how status works in remote teams.
response:
A while back I was in the middle of trying to get my head around the social dynamics of remote teams. I was in a Slack channel with my co-workers and someone said something that I thought really needed a response. So I wrote one. But it was getting late, and I was in the middle of another conversation, so I told myself that I would reply to the Slack message in the morning.

I woke up and went to reply to it, and I discovered that it had already been answered. In fact, it had gotten about a dozen responses already, some of which were better than the reply I had planned. So there was no point in me replying, and I moved on.

But then I thought about how strange it was that I had intended to reply but hadn’t been able to because I was already a half-day late. I felt like I was late to a meeting where everyone had already discussed the problem without me. I wanted to reply, but I had no way of doing it without being a total weirdo. It was a perfect example of how remote work is going to change a lot of things about social relationships, and I wrote down some thoughts on it.

The first thing that I thought about is how different the social signals are in a Slack conversation from the signals that you get when you’re physically in the room. When you’re in the room, people can see each other’s reactions. I was working on a project with some friends in college, and we spent a lot of time in the library, talking about what we were doing. If one of us said something that the other two thought was stupid, they would laugh. When that happened, we would go over the same topic again, but from a slightly different perspective. But on Slack, even if your friends are online, you don’t get any indication of how they’ve reacted to what you just said.

And of course the green dot doesn’t necessarily mean that they’re looking at Slack, either. It just means that their computer has Slack open, and their computer is on and connected to the internet. I’m constantly looking at the Slack conversation that I’m in, even though my Slack window is on another screen. When I get a new message, the Slack window flashes for a second on the other screen, and then I read it.

And even when they’re looking at Slack, they don’t necessarily have the conversation that I’m in open. If they’re in another conversation, they don’t know that I’m talking in this one. If they have the conversation open, they might not realize that there are new messages, because it’s not always obvious where the bottom of a Slack conversation is. I think it’s because I have a small monitor, so when the conversation scrolls up, it doesn’t always seem like it’s going to the bottom.

So the idea of “hey, what do you think?” is really hard to get right on Slack. If I wanted to ask a question to a large group of people in a Slack channel, I would have to say “hey, what do you think of this?” I have to include the “hey” because it’s the only way to tell people that I’m talking to them. I can’t just say “what do you think of this?”, because they’ll never know that I’m trying to have a conversation with them. And I can’t just say “hey” and wait for them to reply.

I have tried that, just to see how it works, and it’s kind of a disaster.

I think the problem with “hey” and nothing else is that it’s too vague, and that it’s hard for people to know how to respond. I don’t want to tell people to ignore me when I say “hey” on Slack. I want to tell them that it’s a terrible thing to say “hey” with nothing else on Slack, because it’s really hard to know what to do.

I want to tell people that if they really want to have a conversation, they need to say more than just “hey”.

It’s interesting that “hey” is such a big deal. It’s a word that you hear all the time, and people don’t seem to have a problem with it when they hear it, but for some reason it seems like people have a problem with it when they see it on Slack.

Maybe that’s because it’s hard to figure out how to respond to someone on Slack, but easy to figure out how to respond in person. When I say “hey”, someone will usually say “hey” back, and we’ll have a conversation. But if I send someone “hey” on Slack, and they send me “hey” back, it just feels a little bit weird. I can’t help but think that I’ve done something wrong.

I don’t think that’s a good reason to avoid saying “hey” on Slack, though. It’s just a matter of being clear and specific about what you’re doing, and saying “hey” with nothing else is not clear and specific.

There are a lot of small details that are different on Slack than in person, and I haven’t figured them all out yet. There is a whole etiquette of Slack that I’m still figuring out.

A couple of things that I’ve learned:

- When I’m talking to someone on Slack, and they reply, it’s annoying to wait for them to finish saying what they have to say. I want them to say it all at once.

- Sometimes I reply to someone on Slack, and they reply immediately. If they’re trying to have a conversation with me, that’s fine, but sometimes it’s annoying because I haven’t had time to think about what they’ve said, and now I have to reply right away. I don’t want to reply right away. I want to take a little bit of time and think about what they said.

- When I reply to someone on Slack, I want them to say “thanks” or something. Otherwise, I don’t know if they got my message.

I don’t know if there’s anything that I can do about these things. They’re just kind of the way things are.

I know that I can’t expect other people to understand all of these things. I don’t understand all of them myself.

I don’t think that it’s even possible to explain all of them. They’re too complicated, and too subtle.

The only thing that I can do is try to make sure that I’m not doing anything that’s really, really annoying, and hope that other people aren’t doing anything that’s really, really annoying to me.

And when I do something that’s really, really annoying, I just have to deal with it. I’m going to do a lot more things that are really, really annoying in the future. I don’t know how to avoid it, because I’m not a very good person. I don’t know if anyone else is a very good person, either, but I think they’re probably doing a better job at being less really, really annoying than I am.

prompt: Blog post idea: the hidden etiquette of Slack. Things like who gets a thumbs-up vs. a reply, why "hey" with nothing after it drives people insane, the politics of the green dot. I want it funny but with an actual argument underneath about how status works in remote teams.
response:
I’m the kind of person who will happily use Slack for six or seven hours, then log off to avoid checking my phone. But my boss works from home, and he’s on the computer all the time. So he can see that I’m not on, and he can see that I am on. And this is a status game, and it can go very badly.

Here’s the problem. In office work, the status game is pretty clear: you either sit down at your desk or you don’t. If you sit down at your desk, you’re available. If you don’t, you’re not available, and you’ll probably be working in a conference room or with someone else. This is how it was for me when I was working in an office, and it’s how it is in a lot of jobs.

But I work from home. So the office status game has to be translated into home status games. And this is where Slack comes in. Slack can tell you when I’m available, but that’s because I’ve got to turn it on. So I’m in the same situation as my boss – I’m always on. And this means that my boss can see when I’m in the office, when I’m at home, and when I’m not. And it means that he can see when I’m on Slack, when I’m not, and when I’m in the office.

Here’s how it works. When my boss sends me a Slack message, I’m supposed to reply immediately. If I don’t, it means that I’m not on Slack. And if I’m not on Slack, it means that I’m not in the office. And if I’m not in the office, it means that I’m not working. And if I’m not working, it means that I’m lazy. And if I’m lazy, it means that I’m getting a bad review.

prompt: Compose an essay examining whether the four-day work week is a genuine productivity reform or simply a perk that will be quietly rescinded in the next downturn.
response:
The four-day week sounds like a win-win. Productivity goes up, and people have more time for themselves and their families.

But are people actually adopting it in a big way?

The four-day week was a big deal in the US until about 1998, when 24% of American workers had a compressed workweek. After that, it declined steadily to the current level of 18%.

There are also studies showing that a four-day workweek is bad for companies. One study found that when workers had a four-day workweek, their productivity was actually *lower* and they had *more* sick days.

And of course, the four-day workweek is bad for customers. If your doctor or lawyer or accountant doesn’t work on Fridays, and your business is on their schedule, it could cause you a lot of headaches.

There are also downsides to the four-day week for workers. It’s harder to coordinate with your friends and family, since they’re all working on Fridays. If you want to go out on Friday nights, you’re tired after four straight days of work.

I’m sure there are many people and companies for whom the four-day week makes sense, but it’s not a great idea for most people or companies.

prompt: Compose an essay examining whether the four-day work week is a genuine productivity reform or simply a perk that will be quietly rescinded in the next downturn.
response:
Some companies are trialing a four-day workweek, and the results so far seem promising.

The results don’t convince me this will work at scale. The evidence we have on four-day workweeks so far has the same problems as evidence from all the other radical workplace changes that have been proposed in recent years, from flextime to standing desks to no-managers. All the evidence so far suggests they work, but none of it is very good.

It’s a bit of a cliché to say “the future is here, it’s just not evenly distributed.” But it’s true. We’re used to it. We’re not used to this: the present is here, it’s just not evenly distributed.

The best evidence for these radical changes comes from the most radical companies. Some of the companies that have implemented these changes are so unusual that they can’t be representative of the broader population. For example, one of the companies that tried a four-day week, Microsoft Japan, has no mandatory overtime and allows employees to leave at 5pm. The only companies you’d expect to be able to get away with a four-day week are the companies that already have the most permissive work environment.

The evidence so far comes from very different industries. We have a handful of examples from manufacturing, and a few from software and other knowledge work. We have no evidence about whether the results will generalize to other industries. The best examples of radical workplace changes tend to come from the industries where radicalism is easiest. It’s hard to find a good example of a factory where workers are given standing desks.

A radical workplace policy works best when the workers choose it. If a company lets people choose whether or not to work four days a week, the four-day week is a good policy. If a company forces everyone to work four days a week, the four-day week is a bad policy.

The evidence so far has not been collected under any controlled setting. This is a huge problem. If you let people choose whether or not to work four days a week, the people who choose to work four days a week might already be different than the people who choose not to. And if you force people to work four days a week, the results will be confounded by the fact that you forced them to do something they didn’t want.

The evidence so far suggests the policy works in the companies that implemented it. But that’s not enough to prove that the policy works.

All this evidence is anecdotal and uncontrolled. It might be possible to get better evidence by running a large randomized trial. But there are no signs anyone is trying to run a large randomized trial of these policies.

It would be nice to have more evidence. It would be even nicer if it were true.

prompt: Compose an essay examining whether the four-day work week is a genuine productivity reform or simply a perk that will be quietly rescinded in the next downturn.
response:
The four-day work week is one of those ideas that seems almost too good to be true. How can you cut someone’s hours by 20% and have them just be as productive as they were before? Well, the evidence is that they are, at least sometimes, and sometimes they’re even more productive.

The best way to understand why this is is to imagine your job as having two parts:

1. Stuff you actually have to do

2. Stuff that you just have to be in the office doing

Part (2) includes things like standing in meetings to give updates, answering emails, and sitting at your desk for eight hours and pretending to work. These are things that seem productive, but which are not actually doing any of the work that’s needed to do.

The first piece of evidence for this is the existence of part (2) in the first place. If people are spending their entire work day doing useful work, why do we have so many meetings and emails and all this other busywork? If people were spending the entire day doing useful work, we’d have no need for these things.

The second piece of evidence is that when people are told they only have to be in the office for four days a week, they don’t spend the fifth day on the couch. They spend it working from home.

This doesn’t necessarily mean they’re being productive, but it does mean that they’re spending it doing things that look like work.

And the third piece of evidence is that when people have been in the office for a few hours, they don’t necessarily spend the rest of the day working. A lot of people spend the last few hours of the day doing busywork just to fill time.

For example, when my kids were small, I used to pick them up from daycare at 3 PM and then go back to work until 6 or 7 PM. That time was usually a really good time for doing useful work.

But if I didn’t have to pick my kids up, I wouldn’t have had to leave, and the last two hours of the day would have been a really bad time for doing useful work. I would have spent a lot of that time just being present in the office doing busywork and pretending to work.

I don’t know how true this is on average, but there’s at least some evidence that people don’t spend all their time doing useful work, and I think the explanation for the four-day work week is that some people can spend more of their time doing useful work.

And when people spend more of their time doing useful work, they sometimes get more work done. And sometimes they get less.

The best evidence that people can sometimes get more done comes from the United Kingdom government’s four-day work week experiment in 2022. 2,900 companies took part. 92% of the participating companies stayed on the four-day work week after the experiment ended. 71% of employees reported reduced burnout, and 39% reported increased well-being.

But the experiment wasn’t perfect, and it’s hard to figure out if the results are just people liking it more or if they were really more productive. For example, the experiment was voluntary, so the companies that participated were probably companies that already liked the idea.

But I think it’s probably the case that some people can be just as productive or even more productive if they work fewer hours.

But I don’t know if this applies to everyone, and I don’t know if it applies to most people. And I don’t know how much it will apply in the future.

I know there’s some evidence that we’re getting more and more productive as AI gets better and better. So in some sense, we might have some slack in the system right now that we can take advantage of. But as AI gets better and better, and we get more and more productive, we might not have that slack in the future.

I think the most common scenario is that we’re going to keep getting more and more productive as AI gets better and better, so the four-day work week is going to be a temporary thing. But that might be wrong.

prompt: what I wish someone had told me about my first performance review
response:
Your manager is not grading you. They are filling out a form for a meeting with *their* manager. The meeting is not about your performance. It is about their performance and their team's performance, and your review is one line in the story of their year.

You may have noticed that the actual review conversation has been reduced to a formality. Your manager will read you your evaluation out loud and ask if you agree. You're not supposed to disagree, so you agree, and the meeting ends.

This is how it should work. Your manager spent 10 minutes writing your review and a month preparing for the meeting with their manager, and the last thing they want is an argument with you.

You should know in advance how you're doing. Your manager is supposed to give you regular feedback. They are not grading on a curve, so you don't need to try to get ahead of anyone. If you're doing okay, you should know it. If you're not, they should tell you and help you fix it.

If you're surprised by something you hear in your review, you have a problem.

If you have a problem with your manager, you have a problem.

A performance review is a report card. If you fail a subject in high school, there's nothing you can do about it. You're not going to ask your teacher to change it, and they're not going to let you take the test again. You get a bad grade and you have to live with it.

If your report card is bad and you want to argue, you're going to need to find someone to talk to. It's important to remember that a bad review doesn't necessarily mean you have a bad manager. But if you've talked to your manager, and your manager refuses to tell you what you're doing wrong, or won't help you fix it, then you have a bad manager.

prompt: what I wish someone had told me about my first performance review
response: You were hired for your potential, not your results. Your manager can't yet know how you'll develop, so a first review is usually a learning conversation about what they're seeing, not a judgment. If there's something that concerns them, they'll tell you, and there's nothing wrong with that.

prompt: what I wish someone had told me about my first performance review
response:
1) Your manager will want to hear what you think went well and what you think didn’t. This is the part of the review most people fumble, because it’s easy to think that the review is your manager evaluating your work, but the process is intended to involve you talking about how you think you did, too.

2) It’s OK to talk about things you think went well and things you think didn’t. You’re not being asked to grade your manager or your company, or to discuss things that don’t affect your work. This part of the review is about your work, your work in your role. It’s also OK if your review has to be negative – if you’ve been doing something wrong, then you should say so and talk about how you’ll fix it.

3) Be honest. You’ll have more luck if you say you were late to a lot of meetings and say you’ll do better next time, than if you lie and say you never came late to a meeting.

prompt: I run hiring for a 200-person nonprofit. Write a short essay arguing that cover letters are worth keeping, despite everyone hating them. My actual reason is that they're the only place we see how someone thinks when nobody gave them a template, but develop that further than I have.
response:
I have a few things to say on the cover letter question.

I think they’re worth it. You can see from a short cover letter whether the person is articulate, whether they’re focused on the mission (rather than, “I want any job”), and whether they understand our organization.

I’ve seen a lot of cover letters, including a couple that were great, including one that was brilliant in a way I hadn’t expected.

And, I’m not asking for more than a paragraph or two.

But it should be short and on point.

I also think people shouldn’t spend a lot of time on them. I don’t want people to have to spend an hour writing a cover letter. If you don’t have anything to say, or you don’t feel like spending 15 minutes writing it, don’t worry about it.

But if you think it would be good to have a chance to say something about yourself, and you don’t feel like you’d be taking a lot of time doing it, then we ask that you do it.

I think that’s a fair deal.

And for those of you that are already in the field, I think that’s a good way to show that you’re interested in the organization and you know what you’re doing.

I don’t want to sound like I’m being a jerk, but I have seen a lot of people who don’t know much about the sector and are just trying to get in for the money or because they want something to do. I don’t want to discourage them, but I want to discourage them from making it seem like they’re interested in the cause.

I don’t want to encourage the perception that it’s easy to get a job in this field.

So I’m going to ask you to write a couple of sentences about why you want this job.

This is not going to be the end of the world. It will take you maybe 15 minutes to think of something. And if you do a good job on it, I’ll be able to tell you more about you than if you didn’t do it.

And I think it’s probably a good idea to write something that’s going to help you in your career.

For instance, if you write that you’ve been working in the field for 10 years, that might make someone more interested in you. But that’s not going to hurt you either.

prompt: I run hiring for a 200-person nonprofit. Write a short essay arguing that cover letters are worth keeping, despite everyone hating them. My actual reason is that they're the only place we see how someone thinks when nobody gave them a template, but develop that further than I have.
response:
It feels like there’s some kind of social norm against cover letters. You see people on Twitter saying things like:

- I hate cover letters because they’re boring, they’re formulaic, and they usually say nothing of substance about the person.

- I’ve started asking candidates to send me a video instead of a cover letter, where they talk a bit about why they want to work for us, and how they can help.

- Cover letters are just one more thing that make it harder for people to get jobs, especially for disadvantaged people.

I don’t have anything to say about videos, but I think there is a case to be made for cover letters.

When I’m thinking of hiring someone, one of the most important things I want to know about them is: what are their thoughts like? Are their thoughts clear, or fuzzy? Are their thoughts deep, or shallow? Are their thoughts well-structured, or jumbled?

A cover letter is a great place to find out. It’s a place where they’re writing about a topic they care about, they’re writing it for their own purposes, and the topic is one they know well enough to have an opinion about. This is one of the few places we have where someone is trying to express their own thoughts without an interviewer asking them questions.

The first sentence of my cover letter when I applied to Google was: “I have a lot of good memories about Google.” I knew the interviewer was going to read this sentence, and it seemed like a great place to start.

prompt: I run hiring for a 200-person nonprofit. Write a short essay arguing that cover letters are worth keeping, despite everyone hating them. My actual reason is that they're the only place we see how someone thinks when nobody gave them a template, but develop that further than I have.
response:
There are a lot of hiring practices I’m skeptical about, but one of the very few that I think is actually good is cover letters. This is, unfortunately, a bit of a minority position; people seem to really dislike cover letters, and they’re getting increasingly rare in the US (for example, Google has decided to stop asking for cover letters). But the reason people dislike them is the same reason I think they’re good.

Cover letters are boring, they don’t provide much new information, they are usually formulaic, and they often have bad spelling. This is true. But it’s not true for everyone, and you can’t tell who’s going to write a good one until you ask them to.

Cover letters are boring, because people usually write them by filling in a template: “I am a very passionate person and I am very excited to work for your company. My past jobs have given me experience in X, Y, and Z, which will help me be successful at your company. I am sure you will be impressed.” I am not saying this to mock people; this is how I would write a cover letter if you told me to do it, and this is how most people would write a cover letter if you told them to do it. But it’s boring, and it doesn’t say anything new, so it’s annoying for hiring managers to read.

Cover letters are boring, and don’t provide much new information, because they’re not designed to provide information. They’re designed to show respect to the hiring manager. “I am aware of your company’s existence, and I took the trouble to write this letter.” And this is also not really a problem. It’s the same reason we shake hands in business meetings. It’s a ritual, and if we didn’t have it we’d invent something else. In fact, we have *too many* rituals that serve the same purpose.

Cover letters are boring, and formulaic, and annoying, but they’re not always boring. You will sometimes get someone who has a unique voice in their letter, or who can tell you something unique about them. It’s kind of a lottery. 90% of applicants will do exactly what I told them to do, write a boring formulaic letter, and you won’t learn anything from it. But a few, say 2 or 3%, will surprise you in a good way. And you’ll only know who’s going to be in that 3% once you see the letter.

And this is the main reason that I think cover letters are good. There are all these other things you can ask applicants to send, but cover letters are the only one that lets you see their unfiltered voice. You ask for a resume, but that’s just a list of bullet points. You ask for a reference, but that’s just someone else’s voice. You ask for a writing sample, but that’s often someone else’s idea, or something they were trying to sound like. But if you ask someone to write a cover letter for your organization, and that person decides to write it their own way, then you’re going to get something really cool. It’s like the cover letters are a tiny little test. If you fail the test, nothing bad happens to you, but if you pass the test, you get to stand out.

The reason I’m writing this is because of some recent discussion about how some companies have recently started trying to get rid of cover letters. This is a bit of a disaster, because it’s removing the only way to get this information, and it’s very hard to replace it with something else. It’s hard to replace it because it’s not a hard thing to replace. It’s not about skills, or accomplishments, or anything like that. It’s about people’s personalities. And that’s something that’s really hard to test for.

So, if you’re a company, and you’re trying to get rid of cover letters, then you have two choices. You can either stop asking for them, and be a little bit more of a lottery than you need to be, or you can keep asking for them.

prompt: Why do so many people quietly hate their job titles? I'd like an essay exploring titles as a weird kind of currency at work.
response:
There was a time when it would have been normal to have a job title. “Accountant.” “Plumber.” “Engineer.” But it’s become increasingly common for a professional to be unable to say their job title without a long pause, or a shrug, or a long explanation. And increasingly, if you ask someone what their job title is, they will be offended.

This is not the reaction you’d expect if people were just trying to impress you with a fancy title. A lot of people’s job titles are vague. Many people are unable to say their job title because it doesn’t exist, and it’s not hard to think of a reason this might be true.

In fact, the reason is so obvious that it’s surprising we’ve spent so long pretending that it wasn’t true. The reason so many people are unable to say what their job title is is that they secretly hate what their job title is.

What’s the difference between a job title you’re proud of and one you’re not?

A job title you’re proud of is a description of your job. It’s a short, clear, concise summary of what you do. If someone said they were a plumber, you’d know what they did.

A job title you’re not proud of is a kind of currency. It’s not a description of what you do; it’s something that describes your position on some kind of hierarchy.

I recently met a woman who described herself as a “Senior Manager of Customer Happiness.” It would have been hard to tell you what a “Senior Manager of Customer Happiness” did just by looking at that title. But the title was very impressive. It had all sorts of impressive words in it. And it clearly communicated that she was very important.

It was a job title that communicated her rank and importance, not her job.

When I meet people, I sometimes ask them what their job is. Most people respond with a job title.

But when I ask people what they actually do, they often describe a job that is very different from the job that their job title implies. For example, a lot of people whose job title implies that they do a certain thing do almost entirely a different thing.

But the title “Manager of Customer Happiness” sounds much better than “Manager.” “Manager of Customer Happiness” has a certain ring to it.

Most job titles are like that. They’re designed to impress people. They don’t describe your job. They’re not even meant to describe your job. They’re meant to make you look important.

You’re not a “Senior Manager of Customer Happiness”; you manage a team of people who work on the customer experience. Your job title is a kind of lie. It’s a lie that most people are happy to tell, but it’s a lie. And it’s not a lie you’re proud of telling.

So when someone asks you what your job title is, you don’t want to tell them that you’re a “Senior Manager of Customer Happiness”. It’s embarrassing.

prompt: Why do so many people quietly hate their job titles? I'd like an essay exploring titles as a weird kind of currency at work.
response:
A few years back, I was at a conference and was talking to a man who was a vice president of a big company. He said “I am a VP here. But if I told anyone outside of the company that I was a VP they would think I was a VP of a tiny little startup.”

I’ve also known people who are “managers” at large companies, who say that if they told people what they were doing on a daily basis, people would think they weren’t actually managers.

There are a lot of people who have jobs where their job titles don’t describe their actual day to day tasks.

In a lot of cases this is an issue of job titles being inflated.

For example, one company’s job title levels went “software engineer, senior software engineer, senior staff engineer, staff engineer” — meaning the “senior” title was actually less impressive than the title that sounded less impressive.

A lot of companies do this kind of thing.

But there’s another sort of inflation that happens with job titles, which is when people take the job title at face value.

For example, if a person is “VP of Engineering” at a big tech company, you might think that they spend most of their time managing a team of software engineers.

But in practice, they often spend most of their time doing management things that aren’t really about engineering.

I was talking to a VP of Engineering at a large tech company a while back, and he said that if he spent half of his time managing a team of engineers, he’d have failed. He said he had to spend all of his time on things like budgeting and hiring and working with the board of directors. He said if he was spending any time thinking about engineering, he was doing it wrong.

In some sense, this is like the title being *de*flated. If you’re a VP of Engineering, you’d think that the main thing you’re doing is engineering. But you’re not actually doing any engineering.

This kind of thing is really common.

In this article, I’m going to talk about the way job titles function as a kind of currency. And I think when you understand this, you can understand a lot of the weird things that happen with job titles.

## Job Titles As Currency

One reason job titles matter is that they help companies understand what each employee does.

If I have a job called “software engineer”, then my company knows that my role is to make software. If my job is called “head of marketing”, my company knows that my role is to work on marketing.

This can be really useful in a big company where there are lots of different kinds of people doing lots of different things.

Job titles also help people outside the company understand what each employee does.

For example, I used to have a job called “director of engineering”. When someone asks me “hey, what do you do?”, it’s easy to say “I’m an engineering director at a company that does [X]”.

And if you know that I’m an engineering director at a company that does X, that tells you a lot of things about me. For example, it tells you that I manage a group of engineers. I may or may not do my own engineering, but I manage a group of people who do.

So titles can be helpful for both inside the company and outside the company.

But there’s a problem with using job titles as currency.

The problem is that job titles aren’t very accurate.

For example, there’s a lot of variation in what different companies call the same role.

I know a lot of people whose job title says “senior engineer” even though they’re a lot more senior than other “senior engineers”.

I know a lot of people whose job title says “vice president”, even though they don’t really have the responsibilities of a vice president.

And I know a lot of people whose job title says “manager”, even though they aren’t really managing anyone.

Job titles are a little like currencies. When I go to the grocery store, I can buy stuff by giving the store a dollar. And I know that the dollar will always be worth about the same amount.

But when you get to different countries, a dollar isn’t necessarily worth the same amount.

For example, I was in Vietnam a few years ago, and the Vietnamese currency was called the dong. And a dollar was worth 25,000 dong.

In some ways it makes sense that different currencies have different values. For example, maybe the Vietnamese economy has a lot of inflation, and so dong are worth less than dollars.

But there’s a kind of “currency inflation” with job titles too.

For example, I know a lot of people who are “VP”s at startups. A startup with a 10 person team can have a “VP of Marketing”. In a big company with 10,000 people, a “VP of Marketing” might be in charge of a team of 100 people.

## Job Titles Are A Weird Currency

A lot of people are really uncomfortable with job title inflation.

There are a lot of people who get upset when a startup with 5 people calls someone a “vice president”, because they think it’s ridiculous to have a vice president with 5 people.

There are a lot of people who get upset when a company gives people the title of “senior engineer” for doing nothing more than “software engineer”, because they think it’s ridiculous to have a “senior” title that doesn’t actually mean anything.

There’s a lot of anger about job title inflation. And I’m not going to defend job title inflation.

But I do think it’s interesting to think about why job title inflation happens.

One reason for it is that people want to feel like they have an impressive job.

For example, if I were a manager at a company that had 20 people, I’d be managing maybe 5 people. I might not have any reports who have reports of their own.

So if I told people “I manage 5 people”, people might think that I’m not doing a very impressive job.

But if I were a “senior manager”, that sounds more impressive. And maybe I could claim that I manage 15 people, because I’m managing a manager of 5 people and the other people they manage.

Job title inflation is often a way of making people’s jobs sound more impressive.

And sometimes it’s really useful.

For example, some people are really bad at doing the job they’re supposed to be doing, but they’re really good at doing a bunch of other things.

For example, I used to know a person who was bad at doing their job as a product manager, but they were really good at making the other people around them successful. So the other people were really happy that they were working with this person.

So the company gave this person the title of “director of product management”, so that they could focus on helping their team members do well.

I think it’s reasonable for people to get a little upset when they see that people are doing really impressive things with boring job titles. And when they see that people are doing boring things with impressive job titles.

But there’s a reason people are willing to pay extra for job title inflation. And when you understand why people pay for job title inflation, you can understand why it happens in the first place.

prompt: Why do so many people quietly hate their job titles? I'd like an essay exploring titles as a weird kind of currency at work.
response:
A few years ago I got a raise at work and it was a pretty decent raise. I was happy about that. I’d been there a long time, my title had been “director,” and I was going to be “vice director.”

But when the change happened, people who had always been friendly to me, and who had never once referred to me by my title, suddenly started saying “Hi, Vice Director” or “Great meeting with you today, Vice Director.” And it didn’t just happen at work; it happened in private. At parties, friends who knew me as “David” for many years would suddenly refer to me as “Vice Director” and I’d have to correct them.

And it was so weird. It was like someone had handed me a big bag of money – “here’s ten thousand dollars” – and instead of putting it in my wallet or spending it, I had to carry it around in a sack on my back all day.

In a lot of ways my job was the same. The only difference was that the company’s CEO had told other people “he is the vice director” and so other people started telling him “you are the vice director.”

I felt like I was being told something that wasn’t true. I was David, but now I was David the Vice Director, and people started treating me as if I were David the Vice Director. And it made me feel weird.

This experience was a really interesting thing for me, because I hadn’t thought that much about job titles. And in fact, it was interesting because it made me realize I’ve always felt weird about job titles.

In college, I did a lot of internships, and one of my friends always called me “Mr. David” when he talked about me, as if I were some kind of fancy intern. And it made me feel like he was trying to make me feel uncomfortable, as if I were some sort of superior being. I didn’t want to be a superior being. I just wanted to be David, like I was in high school, when I was never “Mr. David” or anything like that.

And as I got older and did more internships and worked in a bunch of jobs, I always felt weird about job titles. It was never something I thought about much, but the idea of getting a title and people referring to me by it always made me uncomfortable.

But then I did a job where my title was actually a big deal. I was an assistant to an important person in the company, so I was given the title “VP.” And a lot of people in the company were impressed that I had the title “VP,” even though I was basically just an assistant.

And this really made me uncomfortable. It’s not like I was working hard, or making decisions that were super important. I was just an assistant. So it felt like the company was trying to make people treat me as if I were more impressive than I was.

And it’s a little like the Vice Director thing, but a lot worse, because I felt like people were trying to make me feel like I was more impressive than I was, and they were actually succeeding.

And it was really hard to deal with, because I would have to sit in meetings with people who were obviously more impressive than me and then have to pretend like I was a VP. And I was really bad at it. And it would be really stressful, because I felt like I wasn’t doing a good job.

And it would be worse at the end of the day, when I’d go home and talk about work with my friends. They’d ask “How are you doing?” And I’d say “I’m doing fine, it’s great, I’m VP.” And they’d be all excited, and I’d have to say “Yeah, I’m great, I’m a VP, I’m doing so great!” And it’s like my friends were trying to make me feel like I was doing great, and they were actually succeeding.

And I’d say “Yeah, great, I’m a VP,” and my friends would get excited, and then it would be over, and I’d go to sleep, and it’d be over.

And then the next day I’d go to work and be a VP again, and I’d have to pretend like I was doing a great job, and it would be really stressful. And I’d come home at the end of the day and my friends would get excited again, and it would be over, and I’d go to sleep, and it’d be over.

And then the next day I’d go to work and be a VP again.

It’s like a game.

prompt: Write something arguing that 'follow your passion' is actually decent advice and the backlash against it went too far.
response:
If I said I got into programming because I wanted to make cool games, everyone would laugh at me. “That’s a terrible reason. You need to have a clear, well thought out business plan. You should study the market. You should talk to a mentor. You should think about what you can do that no one else can do. And then once you’ve done that, you should pick the best option, the one that has the highest probability of success. You shouldn’t follow your passion, because if you’re not successful, you’ll be stuck doing something you don’t like.”

But that’s actually what I did, and I think it’s why I got into programming in the first place. And it’s why I’m still programming now.

I think people got a little too cynical about “follow your passion” in the late 2000s. You’d go on r/programming and see people saying “I want to be a programmer but what should I do with my life?” and the answer would always be “no, you’re just a hack”.

I remember when I was 23, I was really upset about the state of the world and I wanted to fix it. So I said “okay, I’m going to study computer science and work for a tech company and get enough money so that I can hire some people to help me with my mission”. And I found that pretty much everyone who I told this to was like “you’re stupid and your plan is terrible and you’ll fail and you’re just going to get a job and you’ll get rich and then you’ll be sad and you’ll realize you wasted your life”. So I spent about a year and a half not believing that it was possible for me to be successful doing what I wanted to do.

Then some people who I really admired said “hey, what are you doing with your life?” and I said “I’m going to go to college and learn computer science and get a job at Google and then I’m going to use my money to fix the world”. And they were like “yeah that sounds good”. And I was like “how can you say it sounds good when you know that I’m not even a good computer scientist?” And they were like “well, you should do what you’re passionate about, and then hopefully you’ll be successful and then you’ll fix the world”. And that got me thinking: maybe it’s okay to be successful at something that you like and that you’re good at, even if you weren’t supposed to be, like, it wasn’t in the business plan.

I think it’s okay to want to be successful at something that you like, even if you didn’t do all of the “right things” to become successful. And I think that’s true even if you didn’t start as a kid saying “I’m going to be really successful and then I’m going to save the world” – in fact I think the more that’s not true, the more important it is to say “you should do what you’re passionate about and if you’re good at it then maybe you’ll be successful”.

I think that if you like something you do, you’re more likely to keep doing it and therefore become more successful at it. And if you like something you do, you’re more likely to notice opportunities within that domain and therefore become successful at it. So I think it’s a good idea to do things you like.

prompt: Write something arguing that 'follow your passion' is actually decent advice and the backlash against it went too far.
response:
A few months ago, someone wrote an essay criticizing the common advice to “follow your passion.” It was popular on Twitter. Many of my friends retweeted it, and several said it was the best article they’d ever read. I read it and was completely unimpressed.

So, why?

First, I think there was some confusion over what advice was being given. The common advice to “follow your passion” is almost never meant literally. For example, suppose your passion is video games, and someone told you to “follow your passion” and you became a professional video game player. Then you probably wouldn’t make much money, and would probably eventually get bored of it. So this is obviously not the advice most people meant.
