What most people mean is that you shouldn’t be too focused on money when you choose a career. For example, you can earn a lot of money by becoming an investment banker. But this is a boring job, and you’ll probably end up feeling really unhappy if you’re not passionate about it. So it’s better to work in something you’re really excited about.

The criticism I saw of this advice was that you can’t afford to be picky about your job, especially if you’re not a genius. For example, suppose you’re a math genius. In this case, it’s fine to be super picky about your job, because you can get any job you want. So it’s better to work in something you’re excited about, so that you can enjoy yourself. But if you’re an ordinary person, it’s better to take any job that pays well and be happy with it.

This isn’t the only objection I’ve heard. Some people say that the advice “follow your passion” doesn’t work in practice because you can’t know what your passion is. For example, I’ve never heard a person who became passionate about their job because they worked there. It’s always been the other way around – people have picked their jobs because they were passionate about them. So you can’t really choose to “follow your passion” in your career.

I think these objections are too strong.

For the first objection – “you can’t afford to be picky” – I think it’s true that ordinary people shouldn’t be *too* picky about their jobs. But the original advice “follow your passion” isn’t about being super picky. It’s more about being moderately picky. For example, suppose there are two jobs that pay about the same, and one of them is a bit more interesting than the other one. Then the advice “follow your passion” says that you should choose the more interesting one. I think this is fine for ordinary people.

I think this objection is too strong because it’s based on a misconception about how picky you can be. I think most people can afford to be a bit picky. For example, I know someone who lives in San Francisco and works for a tech startup. They like San Francisco, and they like working for a startup. So they’re pretty happy, and they make a lot of money. They’re not a genius, but they can afford to be pretty picky.

Second, I think the objection that “you can’t know what your passion is” is also too strong. It’s true that you can’t predict what will make you happy, and it’s hard to figure out what you’re passionate about. But that doesn’t mean that you can’t follow your passion. For example, suppose there are two jobs that pay about the same, and one of them seems a bit more interesting to you. Then the advice “follow your passion” says that you should choose the more interesting one. I think this is fine, even if you can’t predict what will make you happy.

For example, I know a guy who’s really passionate about video games. He’s not a genius, but he made enough money to pay for his college degree. He also got a really good job. He’s not super picky about his career, but he still has a great job. I think this is fine.

prompt: Write something arguing that 'follow your passion' is actually decent advice and the backlash against it went too far.
response:
When I was in high school and college, I followed the then-fashionable advice to “do what you love.” I’m not sure that’s the best advice for everyone, but it’s a good sign that a lot of people are now against it, because that usually means it was bad advice before.

My experience with this advice was mixed, and I’ve seen the results in others too. The best case: you get to work on what you love and your love for it makes you so good that you become rich and famous. The worst case: you get fired. But it was the middle that got me. If you work on something you love, you will do better than you would otherwise. But it’s also true that if you’re bad at something and work on it for years, you can become quite good at it, even if you don’t love it. What happens when you combine these two things?

If you’re working on something you love, you will do better than you otherwise would, but if you’re also bad at it, the effect of working on it for years may outweigh the effect of loving it. It will only be because you love it that you are willing to work on it for years when you’re bad at it. So the result is that you’re working on something you love, but you’re only moderately successful.

This is not a bad result. But it is not as good as it could have been. You have been fooled by something you love into working on something you’re bad at. If you’d been working on something else that you’re better at, even if it wasn’t something you love, the effect of working on it for years might have been stronger.

I don’t mean to disparage what I did when I was young. I’m not sure what I would have done instead. But now that I understand the risk, I think a better formulation of this advice would be “do what you love and are good at.”

The “do what you love” advice is now so discredited that even the qualified version sounds a little weird. If you tell someone they should work on something they love and are good at, they’re likely to reply that they’re good at something, but it’s not something they love. They can either do what they’re good at, or what they love, but not both.

But this is a false dilemma. This is just another case where people are assuming a false dichotomy because they’re thinking in terms of single-valued attributes, like “good” or “bad.” The real world is more complex. The fact that you have to trade off a little of one thing for a little of another doesn’t imply there’s a single place where the tradeoff is maximized.

A good way to think about this is in terms of a utility function. If you have a utility function that depends on two things, then you don’t necessarily have a single maximum. You may have a whole plateau of equally good options, spread out over some region. There will certainly be a plateau of good options for the two-dimensional utility function that depends on how good and how much you love something.

If you look at a two-dimensional utility function in terms of a single value, as people do, then of course you can’t help thinking there’s a single maximum. But the fact that you’re only thinking in terms of one value doesn’t mean there’s a single maximum, any more than the fact that you’re thinking in terms of numbers means there’s a single largest one.

prompt: My dad worked at the same steel plant for 34 years and never once talked about his career. I've had six jobs in twelve years and I talk about mine constantly. I want a personal essay about that contrast: what the word 'career' even meant to him vs. me, and whether either of us got it right.
response:
I’ve changed jobs six times in the past twelve years, three of those changes in the past twelve months alone. And I can’t stop talking about it.

I’m not just telling you. I’m telling everybody. Everyone who’ll listen.

This is not how my father talked about work. For 34 years my dad worked in the same steel plant, and I never once heard him talk about his career.

I don’t think I ever heard the word “career” come out of his mouth. Maybe he would’ve used the word if I’d asked, but I didn’t ask, and he didn’t mention it. He didn’t have much time to think about his career. He had to work.

When my dad went to work, he went to work. He didn’t talk about it. He didn’t think about it. He did the job.

I don’t know how much he liked it, but I don’t think he ever questioned it. He didn’t have a “career,” he had a “job.” I think he did it because it paid the bills.

I didn’t want that. I never wanted that.

I didn’t want to just work, I wanted to have a “career.”

I don’t know if I did it right. I don’t know if I did it wrong. But I know I tried to do it differently than my dad.

I don’t know how long I’ll do this current job. I don’t know how long I’ll do the next one. And I’m constantly talking about my “career.”

I don’t think this will change.

prompt: My dad worked at the same steel plant for 34 years and never once talked about his career. I've had six jobs in twelve years and I talk about mine constantly. I want a personal essay about that contrast: what the word 'career' even meant to him vs. me, and whether either of us got it right.
response:
When I was 18, I told my dad I had a job. “Oh,” he said, “do you have a career?” “Not yet,” I said. “Just a job.” “You should think about your career,” he said. “How did you get a job?” he asked. “I applied and they hired me,” I said. “How do you know you’re going to like it?” he asked. “I don’t know,” I said. “That was a big mistake,” he said. “You never know whether you’re going to like a job until you’ve been doing it a while.”

When my dad was my age he’d been working at the same steel plant for four years. He worked there for another thirty.

I have six jobs in the past twelve years. And I talk about them constantly. I write about them. The name of this blog is about one of my jobs.

My dad never talked about his.

I think of him as one of my heroes. He was the opposite of a careerist. He wasn’t the sort who talked about his job constantly. He wasn’t even the sort who thought about his job. It was just something he did.

I’ve never had a job that made me think of him. But maybe my dad was the job that made me what I am.

What I love about the past twelve years is the feeling of doing the right thing at the right time. I’m not the best typist or the best programmer or the best writer, but I’ve always been a good typist, a good programmer, and a good writer, and I was doing the right job at the right time.

I didn’t feel that way in the 20th century, though. I had a lot of jobs and didn’t feel like I was doing any of them right. I didn’t feel like I had a career.

I think what makes a career is not just the work, but the feeling of doing the right work at the right time.

prompt: My dad worked at the same steel plant for 34 years and never once talked about his career. I've had six jobs in twelve years and I talk about mine constantly. I want a personal essay about that contrast: what the word 'career' even meant to him vs. me, and whether either of us got it right.
response:
My father worked in the same steel plant for 34 years, and never once, in his whole life, talked about his career.

When he got his first job there, in 1961, I was three years old. I didn’t remember much about him except that he never got promoted, and that he was always complaining. It was the 70s. He was always complaining about the other workers who didn’t do their fair share of work and were getting the same raise. When he got sick, he complained to me about how much it hurt, and how the doctors said he had to keep working anyway. He was always saying he was going to quit, but I never believed it. I always thought he was just going to say that forever.

In 1991, he had a heart attack. He went to the hospital and came back. They put him on medication and said he was fine. They said he could go back to work, but he never did. He retired.

I thought he was going to die right away, but it turned out he had 12 more years of his life to live.

For 12 years, he never worked.

I have been working for 12 years.

For all 12 of those years, I talked about work. All the time.

In 2009, I got my first job, in a factory that made furniture. I made a lot of chairs, and some tables and desks. I hated it.

I didn’t hate it because the work was too hard. The furniture factory was one of the easiest jobs I’d ever had. They gave you all the tools, you just had to put the furniture together. But it was boring.

I had always wanted to work for a company that sold things, so I left the furniture factory and got a job selling things. I hated it.

My first job selling things was selling furniture. I hated it, but at least it wasn’t boring. It wasn’t hard, either. I was a lot better at it than my friends, and the job was easy, so I thought I should just stay there and work my way up to the top. But I didn’t.

I always wanted to be better, so I quit the furniture store and started selling computers. I hated it.

I got promoted. My job was a lot better. I was better at it. But I still hated it.

Then I got even better at selling computers. My job got even better. I loved it. But then I had to learn how to make a website, and the company I was working for didn’t teach me how, so I quit.

I got a job teaching myself how to make a website. I hated it.

Then I made a website. I loved it. Then I quit that job.

Then I sold a website. I loved it. I got a job selling websites. I hated it.

I hated all of the jobs that I didn’t love. I don’t know why. It seems like it should be the other way around.

Maybe I hated them because I didn’t like them, or maybe I didn’t like them because I hated them.

It might sound like I had a lot of jobs. But I don’t think I’ve had more jobs than most people. I think most people have about six jobs in their whole lives.

I’m not sure why I hate most jobs. Maybe it’s because I’m always changing jobs. Maybe it’s because I’m always learning new things, so I never have enough time to get good at my job. But I’ve been doing this for 12 years, and it doesn’t seem to bother me.

I think the real reason I hate most of my jobs is that I hate doing anything more than once. If you do something a lot, you get used to it. If you don’t, you don’t.

I’ve been working for 12 years. I’ve had six jobs. I’ve changed jobs almost every two years. It’s not like I’m a quitter. I’ve been working for a long time.

My father got his first job in 1961. He worked at the same steel plant for 34 years. He retired in 1991. He never once talked about his career.

I’ve had six jobs in 12 years. I talk about work all the time.

prompt: Is mentorship overrated? Most 'mentor' relationships I've seen are a coffee every quarter where nothing happens. Make the case, but be fair about when it does work.
response:
It has been suggested to me that “mentorship” is overrated: people talk about it as if it is some sort of panacea, but actually the mentor-protégé relationship isn’t very effective most of the time.

This was actually my impression of mentorship too before I got a mentor. In fact, I remember reading a while back that the reason the idea of a mentor was invented in the first place was because it’s an easy way to keep a teacher and a student from hooking up. So we have this idea of a “mentor”, but really it’s just a cover for cheating in class.

And that was basically my impression: mentorship is like dating. Everyone says they want to date, but if you just keep going out and going out, you’re probably going to end up alone. And then you have to wonder if dating is actually a good idea at all.

It turned out that I was wrong about dating and it’s turned out that I was wrong about mentorship.

I have had some great mentors: some I’ve asked, and some I haven’t. And now I know a few people who are really good at getting mentors. They have a mentor, and that mentor recommends another mentor, who then recommends another, until you have some kind of chain. And they say they are all mentors that are going to be really helpful.

And that’s what’s been missing from my life: I’ve had mentors, but I’ve never had a mentor chain. And that’s what the people I’m talking about here have. And so that’s the difference.

I know a few people who have a mentor chain, and I think it’s going to be a big advantage for them. The people they’re working with are going to be a lot more helpful to them, because they’re going to have a lot more information and be a lot more experienced.

And I think it’s going to be more than that. I think it’s going to have a very big effect.

prompt: Is mentorship overrated? Most 'mentor' relationships I've seen are a coffee every quarter where nothing happens. Make the case, but be fair about when it does work.
response:
I think it is, yes.

I've had the opposite experience in my life from most. When I was at MIT I was given a mentor, which was a senior undergrad in computer science. My mentor and I met twice. My mentor was nice to me, but our interactions consisted of me telling him about a paper that I was reading and him saying, “oh, I’ve read that paper, it’s good.”

It was a completely useless relationship.

There are a few possible reasons. I was already very smart at 13; my mentor was just 2 years older than me, and I was much more advanced in CS. So he was already not much of a mentor.

He was also very nice. So was I. And nice people are usually very bad mentors. They don’t want to upset you. They don’t want to make a bad impression. They will tell you what you want to hear, rather than what you need to hear.

I don’t think it helps much to try to match the mentor to the mentee. You need someone who isn’t just more advanced than you in a particular subject, but who is also a great person.

I have had two great mentors. The second was a great mentor for me, but I think he would have been a bad mentor for anyone else. In my case, he was someone that I had to fight for his attention.

This doesn’t work for most people. Most people will feel embarrassed if they have to fight to get attention from someone they admire. They will just think that the person isn’t interested in them, and they’ll give up.

But it worked for me, because I am very stubborn.

I think mentorship is a good idea in principle. But it usually works poorly because the mentor is someone nice who will tell you what you want to hear rather than what you need to hear.

And in the cases where it works best, the mentorship relationship is actually one-sided, which means it’s not really mentorship at all.

prompt: Is mentorship overrated? Most 'mentor' relationships I've seen are a coffee every quarter where nothing happens. Make the case, but be fair about when it does work.
response:
Most mentorship programs, in my experience, are a waste of time. In my last job, I was in charge of the mentorship program and tried to improve things. I had a lot of ideas, but the more I thought about it, the more I was stuck on one problem. How the heck would I know whether mentorship was having an effect?

If you ask mentors and mentees if they found it useful, they'll almost always say yes. But that's true of most things. You can't just ask people whether they like something. You have to look for evidence of effect.

How would you measure whether mentorship had an effect? You could try to see if mentees do better in terms of promotions or salary increases, but the time scale is too long and there are too many other variables.

I thought for a while about looking for some more indirect effect. Maybe mentees would say that their work was more satisfying or they were happier with their company? I tried to think of things you could measure that would be both likely to be affected by mentorship and easy to measure. I came up with one: how many new people the mentee brings into the company. I thought that if the mentorship program was going to have any effect at all, it would most likely show up there. But in the end I was too busy to run the experiment.

If it's hard to tell whether mentorship is having an effect, it's no wonder that companies that have mentorship programs usually don't care very much about how well they work. So they don't, and mentorship tends to be a waste of time.

That said, it can be very effective. It depends on what kind of mentorship you're doing. If you're doing "mentorship" where the mentor and mentee meet up for coffee once a quarter or so, and the mentee talks about his or her problems, it will tend to be a waste of time. That's just therapy, and you get more out of it if you pay an actual therapist.

Mentorship has to be more like teaching. For teaching to work, the teacher has to be teaching a real subject. But in most mentorships, there is no real subject.

I don't want to sound like I'm saying that mentoring can't be done on a general topic like "how to do your job." I'm not. I've done it, and it's very useful. What I mean is that the general topics most people have in mind when they imagine mentorship are useless.

What I've found most useful in mentoring is to concentrate on a specific skill. How to give presentations. How to write. How to make things look pretty. How to negotiate. How to be a good manager. All these are real subjects. If you want to mentor someone, pick one of them and concentrate on it.

The other thing that's crucial for mentoring to work is that the mentor have to do a lot of work. Not just show up once a quarter for coffee and listen to the mentee's problems.

If you're mentoring someone on a specific skill, you're really just teaching them that skill. So you have to do all the things you'd have to do to teach anyone anything. You have to learn about the subject; you have to work out how you're going to present the material; you have to actually prepare specific things to teach them. You have to read and think and work.

Mentoring is a lot like teaching. But in some ways it's a lot harder. The biggest problem is that most people don't know what they don't know. And the problem with this is that they're the ones choosing what to talk about.

I once taught a writing seminar at Y Combinator, and at one point a guy said that the only thing he didn't understand about writing was how to fix sentences. How were we supposed to know that was the only thing he didn't understand? He didn't know he didn't know everything else.

This problem gets worse as you go up. The less one knows, the more one tends to realize how much one doesn't know. If you're in high school, you know that there are things you don't know. You get a test, you fail, and you know you should have studied more. So you study more. But if you're a professor, you think you know everything there is to know.

So you get this situation where the people who need mentoring the most are the least likely to know they need it, and they're also the least likely to get it.

And if you're someone who realizes you need mentoring, you have to be careful about how you go about it. You can't just pick someone famous, or someone you like, and say "please mentor me." Chances are you won't be a good match. You need a mentor whose expertise is in the area where you need it, and you need one who understands what you're trying to do.

The most reliable way to get a good mentor is to become their apprentice. Then you're almost inescapably in the right situation. You're in the mentor's field. You're doing exactly what the mentor does. You're doing it under their eyes.

Unfortunately, apprenticeship is no longer common. But it's what I did when I was a student. I went to work for Guy Steele in the Computer Science Department at Harvard, and that was the best education I got there. It was the closest I ever came to having a mentor. I worked for him, and he watched me and corrected me.

Apprenticeship isn't the only way to get a good mentor. You can do it without an apprentice, but the mentor has to be a better teacher than Guy Steele was, which was not very good.

The thing about apprenticeship is that you don't have to be an apprentice to do what Guy Steele was doing, which is watching me and correcting me. You could watch someone else and correct them, without them working for you. And this is what I did with the people I mentored at Viaweb. I watched their work and corrected it. And I've tried to do this in various forms ever since.

The hardest part about being a mentor is to know what to correct. When I was mentoring someone on writing, it was easy. I'd read what they wrote, and there would be things that were obviously wrong.

When I was mentoring people on design, it was also fairly easy. I could see things that were wrong, or could be done better.

But when I was mentoring people on how to manage a company, it wasn't so obvious what to correct. When I mentored someone on managing a startup, that was easy enough, because I knew what we were doing and what they were doing, and I could see where they were doing it wrong. But now I have a mentor on how to run an organization, and it's not so clear. Sometimes I say something, and the mentor will correct me. But mostly I think I'm supposed to be learning from watching the mentor.

The problem here is the same one I mentioned before: I don't realize what I'm not realizing. So I can't say "hey, how do you do that thing I'm doing wrong?" I can only hope that the mentor will realize that I'm doing something wrong, and correct me about it.

So the most reliable way to get a good mentor is to be their apprentice. And the next most reliable is to get someone who does what you do to mentor you, so they understand the context. But that's a pretty low bar. If you're a journalist, I don't think you're likely to learn much by getting a journalist to mentor you.

So if you want a good mentor, you have to choose your subject carefully. The best way to do it is to choose a specific skill you need. The best mentors are the people who are very good at a particular skill, and are willing to teach it to you.

prompt: an essay on the out-of-office reply as a literary form
response:
The most common form of writing I engage in is the out-of-office reply, which I am surprised isn’t more celebrated as a literary form. The best out-of-office replies are like great haiku: terse, evocative, and memorable.

The great ones convey the character of the person who wrote them. I recently received one from a person who was going to be away for a few weeks and had set a reply saying “I will be out on business, but I’m still checking email and will reply to you as soon as I get a chance.” This is so unlike most people that I immediately felt like I knew this person better.

When I was young, people were more likely to write something like “I’m in Paris on business, and will be checking email sporadically. If you want to talk, call me, but it may be the middle of the night.” Now everyone is always checking email, so no one writes that anymore.

The most common form of out-of-office reply is something like “I’m on vacation until the end of the month. I will reply to your message when I get back.” It’s so ubiquitous that if someone wrote such a thing today, it would be a joke.

The next most common form of reply is what I’ll call the “I have an assistant” reply. It says something like “I’m away from the office for the next two weeks, and won’t be checking email. If it’s urgent, contact my assistant, Bob, who knows where I am and can reach me.”

The “I have an assistant” reply is so common that there is an entire category of out-of-office replies that consist solely of variations on that theme. I think it’s because a lot of people are nervous about the prospect of not checking their email, and that’s why they have an assistant. If they’re not checking their email, and there are people who need to talk to them, and they have an assistant, then obviously the assistant must know where they are and have their cell phone number. And so they write this reply.

But there are a lot of variations on the theme.

One person writes: “I am at my home. I do not have email here, but if you are calling for a reason that is sufficiently interesting I will be pleased to come back to my office and retrieve my laptop so that I can reply.”

Another: “I am on vacation. If you have any questions about anything I do, please contact someone else.”

Another: “I am out until the 26th. I will reply when I get back, or if I think you are really important, sooner.”

Another: “I am out of the office until [date]. I won’t be checking email, but I may or may not be available by phone.”

Another: “I’m out for a while. Email won’t get a reply. If you really need to talk, find me by phone, but it will probably be the middle of the night somewhere. I’ve left my cellphone number with the receptionist.”

But by far the most common reply is the “I am on vacation until [date]” type. That’s not surprising, given that most people spend most of their time working, and most of the time they’re not working they’re on vacation. But if you look closely at the replies you can see that there’s a whole spectrum of vacations.

At one end of the spectrum are people who say “I am on vacation until [date]. I will reply when I get back.”

And then there are people who say “I am on vacation until [date]. I will reply when I get back, unless it’s really urgent, in which case I’ll reply sooner.”

The “unless it’s really urgent” clause is a bit of a lie, though. If the person who wrote it really had been going to check email to see if they had any urgent messages during the vacation, they wouldn’t have written the reply in the first place.

At the other end of the spectrum are people who say “I am on vacation until [date]. I will be checking email, but may not be able to reply immediately.”

And I think there are people who write a reply like “I am on vacation until [date].” and then, once they’re there, sit down at their laptop and reply to every message as if they were working.

prompt: an essay on the out-of-office reply as a literary form
response:
There is a genre of writing that is almost as constrained as the limerick, and I’m not sure that it’s been studied as much as it should be: the out-of-office reply. It’s a form that has all the same formal constraints as a poem, which means it has its own aesthetic traditions and problems.

Out of office replies are a type of automatic email reply that you send out when you’re away from your computer. They’re a relatively modern invention, but they’re still evolving. When I was in elementary school, my dad had one of the first out-of-office replies. Mine was just “I am on vacation until the end of the month. Please send all mail to [other email address]”.

Nowadays, it’s common to use your out-of-office reply to send a long paragraph describing the things that are happening in your life while you’re away. For instance, last week I got an out of office reply that said “I’m at a family reunion in the hills with 40 of my relatives, none of whom are related by blood”. This is a great out of office reply. I feel like a part of something. I can picture him having fun at a family reunion, and even though he wasn’t being deliberately humorous, his email was a little bit funny.

But there’s a real problem with this form, which is that you have to make sure that all your emails are going somewhere. So most out-of-office replies have to end with a sentence that’s something like “I will return to email on [date], and if you need to talk to me sooner you can reach me at [phone number]”. It’s like writing a sonnet where you have to end on the line “and it’s a great day for a walk”.

I remember when I read the first out-of-office reply that was a list of all the things that I might be interested in hearing about. I was very excited when I got one. It was from a writer whose name I will not mention, but who I was in contact with at the time. Her email said “I will be away for a few weeks, and this is what I’ve been doing: 1. reading this book, 2. writing this essay, 3. going on this trip”. It made me feel like we were part of a larger community, where we were all sharing our experiences with each other. I wanted to write back and tell her that her trip sounded really interesting and I was glad she had gone.

But I didn’t, because it was an out-of-office reply. This is another problem with out-of-office replies: you can’t write back to them. It’s like talking to a person who has a big mirror in front of them. They’re always showing you their face, but they never show you theirs.

There are some other out-of-office reply formats I’m interested in studying. For instance, I’ve gotten out-of-office replies from people who have gone on long trips. I think they’re probably interesting to study because the trips are so long.

There are also out-of-office replies from people who work in the same field as me, and that can be a bit of a trip.

prompt: an essay on the out-of-office reply as a literary form
response:
When a company I was interested in going to work for had recently been acquired, I was looking for someone I could ask about it. I looked in the company’s directory for the CEO, and found a contact form. I wrote a message, hit send, and got an automatic reply saying that the CEO was out of the office, would be back next month, and would reply to my email after that.

The reply was a bit too fast, but that’s not the point. It was the form that interested me: I didn’t know who I’d be talking to, so the company provided a contact form. But the CEO was the only person who was ever going to reply, and he was out of the office. What was the point of the form? It should have said “I’m out of the office, and I’ll be back next month.”

Out-of-office replies are a kind of literature with their own conventions. The most common kind is the generic “I’m on vacation until date X, and will reply to your message after that.” Some people include instructions about who to contact in the interim, but this is a mistake. There’s no way that instruction is still valid when your reply was written. You may even have forgotten who it was you told people to contact. In my own out-of-office replies I only put instructions like this in if it’s certain they won’t change in the interim. For example, in 2020 when I was writing a book I had one that said “Sorry, I can’t answer your questions now, but you can find answers to most questions about writing software in my new book, The Making of Emacs.” That was true when I wrote it, and I could guarantee it would still be true months later, when people read it.

Out-of-office replies are the most frequent example of an odd kind of writing, in which you have to write not for the people you know will read it, but for an unknown audience. It’s the same problem as writing a README. You don’t know who’s going to read it. You have to make assumptions, and they may be wrong. If you tell people who to contact when you’re out, you’re assuming they won’t change jobs during the vacation you’re on.

The problem with out-of-office replies is they can easily become an excuse not to reply to someone at all. “I’ll reply to your message after I’m back” is a way of saying “if I remember to.” The person writing it knows this. So they usually include an extra sentence, like “Please do not hesitate to contact me directly in an emergency.” But the fact that this sentence has to be there shows how unreliable the promise is that you’ll reply to your messages when you get back.

It’s even worse in the case of a generic out-of-office reply. If you’re not expecting to reply to all the messages that come in, why not say so? A company I was interested in buying had a contact form that sent all inquiries to one person. I sent a message, and got a generic reply that said the person was out of the office until a date about two months away. This was an extremely expensive company to buy, and I would not have paid the price they were asking. I don’t know what the right answer was to my inquiry, but they could have said “Sorry, I’m out of the office until date X. You probably want to read our website instead.”

Out-of-office replies are interesting because they’re a kind of literature with their own conventions. But they’re a bad kind. Because they’re automatically generated, the authors can never see how their replies get read, and so they never have a chance to learn from the results.

prompt: I just got laid off for the first time (tech-adjacent marketing, 8 years in). I'm fine financially for a few months. I don't want advice, I want an essay about what being laid off does to how you think about work. Something I'd actually want to reread in a year.
response:
I got laid off from my last company in late 2013. It was the first time it had happened to me, though I had done a lot of layoffs as a manager.

As with most people, the first reaction I had was fear. Fear of what was to come, fear of what it might mean for my family, fear of what it would mean for me. Fear of what it would mean for my career and where I would end up in ten or twenty years.

I think that’s the natural reaction, and it can be a pretty good motivator to help you find something better, and quickly.

But I think most people are pretty much right to think of a layoff as a terrible thing. It’s just too close to a rejection, and it’s too much of a shock to not feel awful.

But a lot of us spend a very significant fraction of our lives working, and I think we should spend a bit of time thinking about what a layoff means, what it does to us as people, and what it could mean for our future.

Laid off from a company for the first time

I had been working for 8 years at that point, and I’d been at the same company for four of them.

It was a tech-adjacent marketing company, and I was doing a pretty good job as a project manager. I felt like I was making good decisions and that my job was something I was very good at and had to be very good at.

I also had a good relationship with my manager, and she helped me get into a role that was more suited to my interests and skills, and I was excited to continue growing there.

Then we were laid off, all at once.

At first I thought it might be about my performance, but it was actually because of the company. The company had done poorly enough that they needed to cut a lot of people.

The company did not do well, and a month after I was laid off, it was acquired by another company and everyone who was still working there was laid off.

This happened in the same week I got a new job offer, so I got to interview in a new role, and eventually took that job and moved to another city.

What did it do to how I thought about work?

I don’t know if I’d ever had it before, but it was the first time I had felt really insecure about my job, and I think that’s what happened to a lot of people who were laid off and then got a new job, and I think it changed how we thought about work.

Before we were laid off, we thought about work like we always had. We thought we needed to work a lot of hours. We thought it was important to work hard, and to work hard at our job, in a way that was visible to others. We thought we needed to prove to people that we were doing an amazing job.

After being laid off, I think we started to think about work in a different way. It wasn’t about proving how hard you worked. It wasn’t about how well you could do your job. It wasn’t about doing work well, or having the best ideas. It wasn’t about how hard you worked. It wasn’t about doing a good job, or how hard you worked to do that job, or if you had the right skills for the job.

It was about how valuable you were.

It was about whether you could do the job or not. It was about whether you had the right skills for the job. It was about whether you had what the job required of you, and whether you had a lot of skills that were valuable to the company. It was about whether you could do a lot of things, or whether you were good at something, or whether you could do something at a high level that no one else could.

It was about whether you were valuable to the company.

How valuable you were

It was hard to be laid off, but it also made us better at our jobs, and it made us think about how to make ourselves more valuable.

prompt: I just got laid off for the first time (tech-adjacent marketing, 8 years in). I'm fine financially for a few months. I don't want advice, I want an essay about what being laid off does to how you think about work. Something I'd actually want to reread in a year.
response:
I am so excited to be back in the job market.

I mean, I’ve had a lot of job offers in my life, but most of them have been through people I know, like the CEO of a startup saying “we need a marketer, you’re good at that, and we can’t pay you that much.” That’s the kind of thing that happens when you’ve been around the world of startups long enough to know everybody, and you’re not thinking about it very hard, so it’s not quite the same thing as going out into the world and being like “hey, world, I’m a marketer!”

It’s kind of like going to college to take a class you’ve been taking at work for a while. You’ve been working for eight years, so you have all the answers, but going to school and taking classes with a bunch of people who don’t know what they’re doing is a great way to learn more about the subject you’re really good at.

I think what I’ve learned is:

You’re going to make money and do stuff you like and be happy.

You don’t have to be a marketer. I’m so lucky that I’m good at something, and something that a lot of people want, and that you can be good at without working 80-hour weeks. But there’s something comforting about knowing that if marketing were to disappear, there would be other stuff I could do instead. I can do all sorts of things, even though I’m a marketer.

You don’t have to work for startups. There are a lot of different kinds of jobs. When you get laid off and suddenly you’re not working for startups, there are so many options. I could be working for a company that doesn’t care about me, or a company that doesn’t care about their customers. I could work for a company that makes products I don’t believe in, or a company that makes products I do. I could work at a company that believes in diversity and inclusion and sustainability and transparency and the things that I care about, or a company that doesn’t. There’s a lot of companies that are like “hey, we care about this stuff, and we’re going to tell you that we care about it, and you can hold us accountable, and we will probably make a mistake, but we’re going to try.”

You’re going to be able to work for those companies. There are a lot of companies that are like that. It’s not all just the same big tech companies. It’s not just “big tech or the government.” It’s a lot of different kinds of companies, doing a lot of different kinds of stuff.

There are a lot of different kinds of startups. You don’t have to work at a startup that wants to sell everything to everybody, just to make money. There are a lot of startups that are like “we’re going to make this one thing, and we’re going to be really good at it, and then we’re not going to do anything else.” You’re going to make money at those startups.

I think that’s all true, but I don’t think anyone would have told me. I think the reason I didn’t know that is that I didn’t go to college. I didn’t have a college degree or an MBA or anything like that. I just went to work for startups. I didn’t think a lot about what I was doing. I wasn’t going to school and taking classes and having people tell me what was true and what was possible. I just knew what I knew. And I was kind of limited.

I’m so glad to be in the job market now, because now I’m getting to learn all these things. I’m learning that I can have a job and make money and be happy. I’m learning that I can work for companies I like. I’m learning that I can work at a startup and not have to sell everything to everybody, just to make money. I’m learning that I can do all these things, and that there are a lot of different kinds of jobs out there.

prompt: I just got laid off for the first time (tech-adjacent marketing, 8 years in). I'm fine financially for a few months. I don't want advice, I want an essay about what being laid off does to how you think about work. Something I'd actually want to reread in a year.
response:
The first time I got laid off was about eight months ago, and I’ve thought a lot about what it means to be “unemployed.” Here are some thoughts on what it’s like to be without a job, from the person who just got fired:

A lot of people seem to be under the impression that the main issue with being unemployed is that you don’t have any money. But that’s not true, at least not at first. Most people who get laid off have enough money to last at least a few months. And if you’re smart, you should be able to get a job after a few months.

The main issue with being unemployed is not a lack of money, but a lack of status.

When I got laid off, I had enough money to last a year or two, if not more. But the lack of status was devastating.

I spent the first six weeks of being unemployed not looking for a job. I didn’t even talk to other people about being unemployed. I couldn’t look anybody in the eye. I felt so ashamed.

The lack of status was so bad that I wasn’t able to tell people that I’d been laid off. I was too ashamed.

I didn’t want to lose my status, so I spent the first six weeks trying to fake having a job. I lied about everything.

When people asked what I was doing, I’d say I was doing “freelance work.”

That meant I was constantly lying to people about what I was working on and what I was doing.

I didn’t even want people to know that I was unemployed.

I’m not ashamed of that. I was just trying to do what was best for me, at the time. I had a job for eight years and I didn’t want to lose my status. It just felt like the right thing to do.

I felt so awful about being unemployed that I wasn’t even able to look for a job. For the first six weeks I was unemployed, I didn’t even talk to other people about being unemployed.

But after six weeks, I got a bit more comfortable with the idea of being unemployed.

After six weeks, I started applying for jobs. And after two more weeks I got a job offer.

So I was unemployed for about 2 months. I was able to get a job because I knew a lot of people in the industry. And I wasn’t that bad at my job.

But the experience of being unemployed changed me a lot. It made me realize that being employed is more important to me than I thought.

It also made me realize how important it is to have a job that you like.

I was really upset at my company for laying me off, but I also realized that I should have left my job sooner. I was unhappy and I should have been looking for a job.

That’s why I’m really happy to be at Quora now.

It’s a great company to work at. Everyone at Quora is really smart and hardworking, but they’re not stressed out or overworked. Quora is one of the very few companies where people have a good work-life balance and aren’t stressed out.

It’s a great place to work at.

prompt: Explore why the people who get promoted are often not the people doing the most important work. Is that a bug in how organizations work, or a feature?
response:
I read a lot of books, and one of the best is *The Muppet Movie Guide*, where I read the movie *The Secret Life of Bees*. In the movie, a beekeeper explains to a child why the people who get promoted in a beehive are not necessarily the best workers:

The best worker in the beehive is the queen, but the queen bee is never promoted because she’s the best worker.

In a beehive, there is a hive manager who is always promoted. This hive manager is a queen bee who is good at her job, but she’s not the best worker, because that would be a queen bee. If you get promoted to the position of hive manager, your new job is no longer doing the best work but managing other workers.

In other words, the beekeeper is saying that the best worker in the beehive is the queen bee, and the best hive manager is the bee who manages the beehive.

I thought this was interesting because I read a lot of books and movies, and I like to think that the best people get promoted in the bee world.

prompt: Explore why the people who get promoted are often not the people doing the most important work. Is that a bug in how organizations work, or a feature?
response:
It's common for people doing a lot of important work to feel that they're being snubbed when someone else gets promoted over them. But when I was at Y Combinator I thought a lot about this, and it's not as simple as it seems.

For example, there are two different meanings of "important work." There's important to the company, and important to the world. If you're in a big company, those are unlikely to coincide. What's important to the company is generally to make the company more money. The people who do that best are not the same as the people who do the most important work in a global sense.

There are two different ways people can work on problems: bottom-up or top-down. Top-down means you start with the big problems and work your way down. Bottom-up means you start at the bottom, solving whatever problems are at hand, and if the company is lucky they add up to something interesting. Bottom-up work is hard to judge, and hard to judge fairly.

People who work on a problem top-down get rewarded more than people who work on it bottom-up, because when people work on something top-down it's obvious what they're doing. It's harder to see what people working bottom-up are doing, so it's harder to notice.

There are two ways people can work on problems: in a company, or outside it. In a company you're more likely to be rewarded for doing important work. It may be important to the company rather than the world, but there will be someone watching to reward you for it. If you're doing important work on your own, you may get less immediate recognition.

There are different meanings of "important work." If you work top-down, you're more likely to be rewarded. And if you work in a company, someone is more likely to be watching to reward you. So if you want to get promoted, the best way to do it is to work top-down on problems in a company.

That's true, but is it a bug or a feature? Is it unfair that some kinds of work are rewarded more than others? I think it's a feature. The company wants you to work on the important problems top-down, because that's the most efficient way. And the company wants someone watching to reward you for it, because that's the most efficient way to get important work done. So if the company is rewarding you more, that's just the company working efficiently.

prompt: Explore why the people who get promoted are often not the people doing the most important work. Is that a bug in how organizations work, or a feature?
response:
I have seen many organizations in which the most talented people were stuck in the middle, doing the important work, while mediocre people were promoted to positions of power.

I used to think this was a bug, but I’ve realized it’s a feature. It’s not a coincidence that the most effective organizations I’ve seen have the best people doing important work, even when it’s not what they want, and that people aren’t rewarded for doing it.

I used to think that the most talented people in an organization should get promoted. It would be more fun for them. If you think of organizations like companies, it’s also more efficient. The most talented people are the best at doing things, and if you make them managers, they’ll manage better. But in fact you do not want the most talented people to be managers. It’s a feature, not a bug, when the best people in an organization stay in positions doing important work.

This is true for the best individuals, and it’s also true for the best organizations. Some organizations are better than others at doing hard things. It is a sign of a strong organization if the best people stay in it doing hard things, rather than leaving to do what they want. And if the best people stay in an organization, that means it can’t be rewarding people for doing hard things.

You’re not necessarily wrong if you think this is a bug. You may be right that it’s a bug in *your* organization. It’s not an inherent feature that the best people should stay in an organization. If they leave, you probably deserve it. It’s only a sign of strength if the people who stay are better than those who leave.

But on average it is a sign of strength, because it’s hard to be an organization with a lot of talent that also rewards people for doing the important work. It’s not easy to do both, so you can expect a strong organization to make a tradeoff, and in my experience it almost always makes the right choice.

How is it possible that the best organizations, which have to be doing something right, are not rewarding people for doing the important work? How could an organization that does not reward people for doing the important work succeed?

It’s possible because the best people are motivated by things other than rewards, and the most valuable work is usually done by the best people.

The most talented people are usually motivated by things other than rewards. They’re motivated by a sense of achievement, by the desire to work on hard problems, by the desire to work with the best people, by the desire to do good things. In the early days of an organization these are usually enough. They may even be enough to keep people doing the most important work in a large organization, if there are enough of them, and they’re surrounded by people who respect them. But if you want to maximize the chance that people will do the important work, you can do better.

There’s a kind of organization I’ve seen that does better. It’s an organization that does not reward the most talented people for doing the important work, but does reward people for doing other kinds of important work.

You might expect such an organization to be less successful, but in fact it’s often more successful than organizations that reward people for doing the important work. Why?

It’s because of the distinction between work that’s important to the organization and work that’s important to a specific person. An organization can’t just reward people for doing the work that’s most important to the organization. It has to reward people for doing the work that’s most important *to them.* People will do the work that’s most important to them anyway, if it’s also important to the organization. But if you want to reward people for doing the work that’s important to the organization, you have to reward people for doing the work that’s important to them, and that can’t be the most important work to the organization.

It’s a mistake to reward people for doing the work that’s most important to the organization, because it has the side effect of rewarding people for doing the work that’s important to them.

That may seem like a subtle distinction, but it’s really fundamental. It’s the same as the distinction between what the market does well and what it does badly. It’s not a problem with markets that they don’t solve the world’s problems. It’s a problem with markets if they reward people for solving the world’s problems. That has the effect of making them less willing to solve the world’s problems.

If you reward people for solving problems, you’ll get problems solved. But you’ll get problems solved in a way that’s not as effective as it would be if the people solving them weren’t doing it because they were paid for it.

prompt: Please write an essay on the ethics of quiet quitting from the employer's side: is it ever fair for a company to expect more than the job description?
response:
I like to think of myself as a pro-employer. I want to believe that most employers are fair and reasonable. But, like most people, I tend to be biased toward the people I know, who are disproportionately bosses, and biased toward the people in a position to help me, which are also disproportionately bosses. So maybe that’s not entirely surprising.

But, like most people, I’m not great at reasoning from the opposite side, especially when it’s not an individual human being but a corporation. So when I read that quiet quitting – basically, refusing to work past what the job description demands – is all the rage, I started thinking about how hard that was for employers.

The idea is, you shouldn’t feel guilty for only doing what the job description demands. I don’t know why there are people who feel guilty about this. They’re just doing their job. Why would they feel guilty?

And yet, even though I’m supposed to be pro-employer, it’s not that simple.

Most people know the story of the man who gets a job as a taxi driver, and on the first day, the driver who’s supposed to train him tells him, “Here’s the key, have a good job” and leaves. That seems like a terrible employer. But I’ve read some stories of what happened afterwards. Most of the people who got this kind of job actually did really well, they just took a few weeks to figure out how to do it. If you’ve ever read any good advice on how to be a good manager, it tells you to give your employees goals and not directions. And the reason is because, if you give them goals and let them figure out the directions, it will help them develop skills that will help them when they’re given harder tasks. It also makes them more engaged in their work, which makes them better and happier.

Of course, the boss can only do this when the employees know more than he does. In that case, giving them a goal and leaving them alone is the best thing he can do. It’s a bit like when you tell your kid to go out and play with his friends and not to do anything stupid. You know they’re a lot more competent than you are and you’re not even sure what they’re doing in the first place. You’re not going to tell them how to play.

But when you’re not sure they’re competent, it’s important to give them directions. If you just tell them what to do, then if they do it well enough, you can start giving them goals. If they don’t, you can give them more directions.

This isn’t just a good way to manage people. It’s the only way to manage people. If you don’t give your employees a goal or a direction, you’re not managing them. The boss who tells his employee “do whatever you want” isn’t managing them. It’s like if your parents let you do whatever you wanted and never told you to do anything at all, you wouldn’t be able to say they were parenting you.

Most of the time, this is done through a job description. A job description is what the employer thinks the employee should be doing. If you can’t meet their expectations, they can tell you what they’re trying to do. If they can’t do that, then they don’t know what they’re doing.

There’s a lot of talk of companies taking advantage of their employees. Sometimes that’s true. But I think a lot of it’s just that the employee is doing what they want to do and the company is trying to do something else, and neither one knows exactly what the other one wants. That’s the same thing that happens when you’re working on a project with a friend and you don’t agree on what you’re doing.

I don’t know which of those is more common. But it seems to me that the second one is much more common than the first. It’s much more common for someone to be confused about what they want than for someone to want to take advantage of other people.

When I was younger, I used to think that the boss and the employee always had diametrically opposed interests, so that whatever one of them wanted, the other one would never want. But that’s obviously not true.

If the boss wants the employee to do a job and the employee wants to do a job, then they agree on the goal. They might not agree on how to do it. They might not even agree on what exactly it means to do it. But that’s a lot less disagreement than if they disagreed on the goal.

I think a lot of people work for the same company for years, and that’s the main reason. If they worked for different companies, they would have very different goals, and that would be a lot harder to manage.

I think this is why a lot of companies are successful. They’re not that good at managing their employees, but that doesn’t matter much, because the employees want to do the job the same way the company does.

And this is why it’s hard to be a good boss. If you’re just giving directions, you can’t manage people very well. You need to be able to get them to do the job on their own, and that’s hard.

prompt: Please write an essay on the ethics of quiet quitting from the employer's side: is it ever fair for a company to expect more than the job description?
response:
It’s common now to hear about “quiet quitting”. That’s when workers do the bare minimum and no more. It’s seen as an act of rebellion.

Is it a good idea to rebel that way? I don’t know.

But is it fair? I think it’s fair for employers to expect more than the job description, and that quiet quitting is a betrayal of the implicit contract between employer and employee.

Suppose I own a restaurant, and I hire a waiter. I give him a job description that says “take orders, bring food to tables”.

He does exactly what the job description says. He takes orders. He brings food to tables. But he never clears the tables after customers leave. Instead he leaves the plates, cups, and empty bottles on the tables and walks away, leaving that job to my busboys to do.

That’s a betrayal of the implicit contract between us. I hired him to do more than what was in the job description. He knew that. He agreed to it.

This is not a hypothetical situation. This is what happened to me. I owned a restaurant. A waiter did this. It wasn’t even a case of someone doing a little less than I expected, but a case of someone doing almost nothing, which left me having to cover for him constantly.

The job description said “take orders, bring food to tables”. But that wasn’t really the job. That was an attempt to describe the job. It was only an attempt because we didn’t know how to do better. We were both aware that the job description was incomplete and wrong.

The job description is like a description of a person’s face in a police file, where a witness says “the guy is about six feet tall, has a beard, and is wearing a blue coat.” This is a description of a person, but only an attempt, because we don’t know how to do better. If you’re looking for this guy in a crowd, you wouldn’t say “well, he’s got to be somewhere here because there’s someone about six feet tall, with a beard, in a blue coat”. You would look for the guy who seems closest to the description and hope that he’s the guy you’re looking for.

That’s what a job description is. It’s an attempt to describe a job, in a way that we hope is good enough to find people who can do that job. It’s not a precise contract, where you do exactly that and nothing more or less.

The implicit contract between employer and employee is much more like the implicit contract between the police and their witnesses, where the witness says “the guy was about six feet tall, with a beard, and was wearing a blue coat” and the police assume that he’s right, and use that information to look for the guy.

The person who’s “quiet quitting” is someone who’s using the job description to do less than they expected. They’re twisting the meaning of the job description to make it fit their own interpretation of what they want to do. They’re doing that, and then calling it a “quiet” rebellion, because they don’t want to get in trouble for it. They’re betraying the trust of their employers, then calling it a “quiet” act of rebellion.

If you don’t want to do that, don’t do it.

prompt: Please write an essay on the ethics of quiet quitting from the employer's side: is it ever fair for a company to expect more than the job description?
response:
I have seen many articles on the ethics of “quiet quitting” in the last few months, and I am writing this one from the perspective of a company.

First, the definition of “quiet quitting” that I’m using here, which I think is the one that most people intend: “I’m only doing the things on my job description, and nothing more”.

A lot of people are angry about this, because they think that it’s selfish and unfair. But I think most people are not thinking about this issue very well, and I think that the companies that expect more than people’s job descriptions are not fairing people well.

1. People’s job descriptions should reflect all of the things they are expected to do

When someone says “I’m quiet quitting”, they are usually saying “I only want to do the things you explicitly asked me to do”.

This is fine, but it is a bit like a customer buying a house and then getting angry that the bathroom doesn’t have hot water: if you don’t explicitly say “I would like hot water”, then you’re not allowed to complain that you don’t have hot water.

It’s not the customer’s fault that they forgot to explicitly say “hot water”. The house seller should have known that everyone wants hot water in the bathroom. And when people are hiring for a job, they should expect people to ask “do I need to do X” and say “Yes”.

If you think “X” is something that everyone needs to be doing, then it should be part of the job description. And if you are surprised that your employees don’t do “X”, then the fault lies with you, not with them.

2. Most jobs are more difficult than the job description says, but people are not allowed to use this as an excuse to do a bad job

Most jobs are much more difficult than the job description makes them sound. I had a job at Amazon where I was in charge of their entire global customer support system. But my job description says “You will be in charge of improving the customer experience”, and it sounds like something you could do in a couple of days.

But I think that a lot of people use this as an excuse to do a bad job.

For example, at Amazon, they had a lot of people on a team that would write code. When I would ask them to write a particular algorithm, they would say things like “that’s not in my job description”. I would tell them to write an algorithm, and they would write an algorithm that was so inefficient that it would take three hours to run.

I told people that I would evaluate them by how much time their code took.

People who wrote very bad code and tried to blame their job descriptions got fired from Amazon.

If you want to be an ethical person and do a good job, then it’s not okay to say that “X is not in my job description”, when X is something that everyone would consider to be a basic thing that you should do for a job.

When people have a hard time, I tell them to ask me how to do the job better. They should not use “it’s not in my job description” as an excuse to do a bad job, but if they have a problem with the job, I want them to tell me so that I can help them.

3. It’s not fair for companies to expect more than people are paid for

It’s not okay for a company to pay someone the wage of an intern and expect them to do the work of an expert, because then the intern is not getting paid for all the work that they are doing.

This is the problem with Amazon wanting me to run the entire company’s customer support system, but not wanting to pay me more than $100,000 a year, which is what I would have been making as an intern.

When I was at Amazon, I was not allowed to make any decisions about the company unless I was paying for my decisions out of my own pocket. This is how Amazon prevents people from making decisions that cost the company money.

I think that people who have to pay out of their own pocket to run a business are not in a good position to make decisions. It’s really easy for someone to have a good idea for a business, and then not have enough money to make it happen.

The people that Amazon has to pay for their ideas are not in a good position to make decisions.

But it’s a lot easier to get rich if you are running a business that you own, and if you are not paying out of your own pocket, then it’s a lot harder for you to make a lot of money.

People are not very good at deciding what they are worth, but they are very good at deciding what they are willing to pay for.

The easiest way to decide what you should pay someone is to ask them how much they are willing to accept, and if you can pay them that, then you can pay them more.

prompt: short essay on why the best coworkers are usually the ones who say 'I don't know' a lot
response:
I’ve always said I liked working with a certain colleague because he knew more than everyone else. Then I realized that he also said “I don’t know” more than everyone else. It’s the same thing.

If you know more things than other people, you’ll also know more things you don’t know. And if you’re honest, you’ll say so. It feels weird at first, but after a while it’s not hard to imagine why everyone thinks you know more.

I’ve seen what it’s like to work with a guy who says “I know” way more often than he says “I don’t know.” If he says “I know”, then he’s wrong half the time, or at least he’s wrong often enough that you don’t believe him.

The same applies to people who seem to know everything and say “I don’t know” never. It’s a little like the person who always says “I know,” but much worse. In the first case, he’s at least aware of the possibility that he doesn’t know things. But the second type of person is delusional.

The only way to know things you’ve never heard of is to learn them from someone else. And if you’re delusional, you won’t listen to people who know things you don’t. So the delusional not only know less, they’re stuck knowing less.

It’s easy to be overconfident in the presence of people who seem to know less than you do. If you’re surrounded by people who know less than you, you might as well be overconfident. That’s how bad managers get so powerful. They surround themselves with suckers, which makes them seem smarter than they are, which makes them more powerful, which enables them to surround themselves with more suckers.

But the more you know, the more you need to be careful not to be overconfident. The more you know, the more you’ll get things wrong, because you’ll be wrong more often and you’ll say you know more often.

So if you’re a smart person who’s always confident, you’re probably less smart than you think.

prompt: short essay on why the best coworkers are usually the ones who say 'I don't know' a lot
response:
The best people at work aren’t the ones who know all the answers. They’re the ones who ask the right questions.

In the last few years, working with brilliant people has taught me to expect this. When I asked for help from smart people, they often said: “I don’t know. What do you think?”

If you’ve ever said that to someone, you might think that it was a waste of time. They didn’t know anything. They didn’t have an answer.

But I think that was a good thing. Here’s why.

When I talk to people about how to get better at my work, they often try to tell me how to do my work.

They tell me how to write better. They tell me how to take better photos. They tell me how to learn better. They tell me how to code better.

When they do that, I have two choices.

The first is to listen to what they say, and then do exactly what they say. The problem is, if I follow their advice, I’m not getting better. I’m just doing what they tell me to do.

The second is to do what I want to do. If I do that, I can get better, but not by doing what they tell me. I’ll have to discover the lessons by myself.

Both of those are pretty bad.

The first one is bad because I’m wasting my time following someone else’s ideas.

The second one is bad because I’m not benefiting from their ideas at all.

When smart people say “I don’t know. What do you think?” I have a third option.

I can think about what they want to say, but then talk about what I think.

When someone asks me what I think, I have to say something. If I don’t have an answer, I have to think until I do.

After I’ve said something, they ask me to say more about it.

They ask questions to help me think about what I think.

If my ideas were good, they help me see the good in them. If they were bad, they help me find the flaws in them.

When they do that, I learn more than just what they think.

I learn what I think. And I learn why.

I learn more about myself than about them.

That’s better.

It’s not just that I learn more. I learn it faster.

When you work with smart people, they help you think faster. They ask questions that help you answer them better. They ask questions that help you answer those better, too.

That’s not always a good thing. Sometimes you think too fast. You don’t think carefully.

But it helps.

That’s why the best people at work aren’t the ones who know all the answers. They’re the ones who ask the right questions.

prompt: short essay on why the best coworkers are usually the ones who say 'I don't know' a lot
response:
One of the most underrated qualities in coworkers is the ability to say, honestly, “I don’t know.”

This is a lot harder than it sounds, and there’s a good reason: it’s hard to say “I don’t know” in front of someone, because it makes you feel like an idiot. But it’s also hard to say “I don’t know” when you know that you do know: your ego resists.

But saying “I don’t know” is so much better than making something up or faking it, because people can tell. You can fake it for a short period of time. But people get wise to you pretty fast, and then you’re the “I don’t know” person who’s also the “I lied” person, and it’s not a very good place to be.

If you’re honest about not knowing, you can find out. If you’re an honest person, that is.

If you say “I don’t know” and then look it up, you’ll know.

And if you say “I don’t know” and then look it up, and then tell people you know, you’re the only person who knows it.

So when I meet someone who says “I don’t know” all the time, I’m happy, because they can look stuff up.

A coworker who says “I don’t know” is saying, “I have no idea, but I’m willing to figure it out.”

A coworker who says “I don’t know” is saying, “I don’t want to mislead you.”

A coworker who says “I don’t know” is saying, “You can trust me.”

A coworker who says “I don’t know” is saying, “I’m more interested in being right than in making myself look smart.”

I like these people, and so do my coworkers.

prompt: Write a reflective essay on the strange grief of leaving a job you loved because it stopped being the job you loved. Context: I left a small design studio after it got acquired and everything got 'professionalized.'
response:
I used to work at a little design studio. The people who worked there were smart and fun, and the work was cool, and we all had the same goals. We worked hard and got paid well and had a blast.

And then the studio got acquired, and the whole thing changed. The company that bought it was a big, successful, professionalized company, and they tried to take all the things they did well and apply them to the studio. The studio’s work became more “strategic”, the work environment became more “structured”, and the people I worked with became more “professional”.

And it was all really good.

Except, it wasn’t.

The new, professional, structured, strategic work wasn’t the work I loved, and the new, professional, structured, strategic people weren’t the people I liked, and the new, professional, structured, strategic work environment wasn’t the one I liked. But I didn’t want to be unprofessional and unstructured and not strategic.

So I quit.

I’ve been thinking about that a lot. I’m sure there’s some kind of philosophical theory of identity that talks about how the ship of Theseus is still the same ship even if you replace all the planks one by one, but what if the planks are replaced at once? Does it even matter how much you love that boat?

I don’t know if there’s a theory for that, but I’ve certainly felt that weird grief that comes from watching something you love become something you don’t. I know that my job used to be something I loved, and it’s not something I love anymore, but I can’t even describe what’s different!

I feel like that’s how it has to be. I don’t know how to describe the qualities that make people and things worth loving. If I could, I’d just have a checklist: make sure you have 400% of this, 200% of this, and 0% of that. But I can’t, so I’m stuck with my feelings.

prompt: Write a reflective essay on the strange grief of leaving a job you loved because it stopped being the job you loved. Context: I left a small design studio after it got acquired and everything got 'professionalized.'
response:
I worked for a small design studio for four years, and recently left. It wasn’t a breakup. It wasn’t a firing. It wasn’t even a firing in spirit.

I left because it stopped being a place I loved.

The studio is still a place I love, and I’ll always have a fondness for it and for the people there. I’ll have a fondness for the work I did there. But I didn’t like what the studio had become.

I didn’t like the change.

And I felt weird about being sad about that change.

It’s a kind of strange grief. You know the kind of grief where you lose someone, but you can’t really articulate why you’re so sad, because you didn’t even like the person that much. It’s that kind of grief. I can’t articulate why the studio isn’t the studio I loved anymore, but it isn’t.

I loved what it was.

I’m not sure I can describe what the studio was, but I’ll try.

It had a great product. It made an app for making websites that made people happy. It had a great culture. It was very collaborative. The office was a great place to be. It was small enough that you could talk to everyone in the building on a regular basis, and it was big enough that you could be anonymous if you wanted to be. It had a great CEO. It had a great board. And it had a really nice atmosphere. I really felt like a part of it.

I loved the atmosphere of this company, and it’s hard to say what that means. But I think that’s why I left. It just wasn’t a place I felt like a part of anymore.

It had the same people. It had the same great CEO. It had the same great product. But it was different.

It was different because it was now the division of a larger company, and it’s different when you are a division.

I didn’t like what the change was.

It was different because it was now the division of a larger company. The company was a good company. It made good products and it made good money and its CEO was a good CEO. But it was still a different kind of company.

The CEO had a great vision for the studio. I thought he had a great vision. But there was a big difference between working at a small company and a big company.

The culture of a small company is different from a big one.

I didn’t like what the change was. I didn’t like the changes in the culture. I didn’t like the change in who I talked to. I didn’t like the change in what I thought about. I didn’t like the change in who I wanted to be.

It was different because it was now the division of a larger company. It was different because it had to do things the larger company wanted it to do. It was different because it had to be profitable to the larger company, and that was a different kind of profitability than being profitable to yourself.

The culture of a small company is different from a big one.

In a big company you don’t want to talk to your competitors.

In a big company you have to be professional.

In a big company you have to get a lot of things done.

I didn’t like what the change was.

I loved the culture of the studio. It was a culture where we could talk to our competitors. It was a culture where we could be unprofessional. It was a culture where we could get away with not getting a lot of things done.

It was different because it was now the division of a larger company. It was different because the CEO had to be the CEO of a larger company. It was different because the CEO was a CEO of a larger company.
