prompt: I'd love a short essay arguing that open offices weren't actually the disaster everyone says, and that remote work has its own version of the same problem nobody wants to name.
response:
I’ve been hearing people say for years now that open offices are terrible. But I’m starting to wonder if maybe the truth isn’t so clear. Maybe the problem with open offices wasn’t really what everyone thought.

When I hear people say that open offices are terrible, I always picture the same kind of open office. They’re open to the extent that you can hear the conversation at every other desk. You’re in a huge room with hundreds of other people, and every conversation you hear is someone saying something you don’t want to hear.

I’ve never worked in an office like that. I’ve worked in open offices, but they’re pretty small. Like 15 people. It’s not completely silent, but it’s not really that distracting. I don’t have any trouble concentrating.

But I’ve worked in quiet offices too. They’re not really quiet, though. In my quiet offices there are 4 to 12 people. They’re all in separate rooms. The rooms aren’t soundproof. They have glass windows. You can look into any room through the windows, and you can hear what everyone’s saying pretty well.

If you want to know why I’m bringing this up, I think it’s because I’ve been thinking about remote work. I think remote work will have its own version of the open office problem. It’s going to be hard for remote workers to concentrate.

If you work from home, I imagine there are always distractions. It’s hard not to notice the things that are happening around you. Like, you’re sitting at your desk, trying to concentrate, and you hear something from the next room. Maybe someone’s talking on the phone. Maybe someone’s watching TV. It’s hard not to look into the other room and see what’s going on.

I’ve tried working from home, and this is the main problem I’ve had with it. It’s not the distractions outside the house. I don’t have to notice those. But it’s the distractions inside.

So I’m going to try to work from a place where it’s not hard to concentrate. Maybe somewhere that’s a little like a quiet office. A room where I’m alone, but where I can hear other people working. That might help.

I think people who like open offices and people who don’t are right. People who say open offices are too loud and distracting are right. And people who say that closed offices are better are right. But the truth is, if you work from home, it can be really hard to concentrate. So even if you hate open offices, you might still find that working from home has a lot in common with open offices.

prompt: I'd love a short essay arguing that open offices weren't actually the disaster everyone says, and that remote work has its own version of the same problem nobody wants to name.
response:
A couple of years ago, the journalist Gretchen Reynolds wrote a fascinating article for the New York Times on the history of the open floorplan office. I was skeptical about the article’s thesis, which is that open office plans hurt productivity and cause stress. This was, after all, just the latest in a long stream of articles that have been saying the same thing since the mid 1990s. I remember the office of the company where I worked in the mid 90s was open, and I think that was actually pretty good. It made communication easy and I think it helped people work better.

But what caught my eye in Gretchen’s article was this:

When the National Institute of Health and the University of Iowa College of Medicine did a study of open-plan offices in the mid-1990s, they found that the people who had been there for years had higher levels of stress hormones than those in a separate office. They had lower levels of antibodies, suggesting a weakened immune system. But the people who had been in an open office for only a few months didn’t show the same signs of stress. The researchers concluded that the stress response wasn’t to the open office itself but to the stress of moving to a new environment. In other words, it was not the layout that was at issue; it was the lack of stability.

It’s interesting that Gretchen didn’t explore this conclusion further. It suggests that the problem with open office spaces is that they change too often. The problem with open office spaces is not that they are open, or that they are bad for communication, or that they are bad for productivity, but that companies tend to change their floorplans frequently. This means employees get moved around often, and they don’t have a sense of stability.

I think this is right. I think one of the problems with open floorplans is that if a company has a few hundred people, there’s a good chance that you’ll be moved around frequently. And that’s not good. I think it’s much better to have open offices where you have a stable location. If you work in a startup, I think it’s best to have a single room or floor and to never move.

I also think it’s worth pointing out that some companies have done a great job of designing open office spaces. I’ve worked in open spaces at Amazon, Google, and Microsoft, and I liked all of them a lot.

I think the same story is going to be true with remote work. The problem with remote work is not that it’s remote, but that it’s unstable.

A lot of people want to have their own home office. That sounds like a very good idea to me. That’s exactly what I do. I’m sure there are lots of people who like to work at a local cafe or work from a coworking space or whatever, and if that works for you, great, but I think most people will be happier working from a stable location, which is your home office.

When remote work started, people had to improvise, so they were moving around a lot. I remember being asked during the first few weeks, “Where are you going to work from this week?” And I would be like, “Ummmm, I don’t know. I don’t want to work from home. I don’t want to work at a cafe or a coworking space. What am I supposed to do?”

I didn’t know at the time, but now I’ve realized that the problem is that I don’t have a home office yet. I’ve never had one. In the last 20 years, I’ve always had a physical office, and it was great. But now I don’t have a physical office, so I have to improvise.

In retrospect, I think the problem with remote work is exactly the same problem as the problem with open floorplans. People are unhappy because they’re not stable.

prompt: Freelancers: when do you raise your rates? Write an essay about pricing your own labor and why it's so psychologically hard, aimed at people in year one or two of freelancing.
response:
A couple of weeks ago, I was sitting in my car, listening to my podcast, thinking about pricing. And I was thinking about the fact that I’ve never been a person who’s been good at pricing myself.

This was something I was thinking about when I was running my podcast. And this was something I was thinking about when I was doing work as a freelance consultant.

When I was doing work as a freelance consultant, I would always underprice the work that I was doing. I would underprice it because I was trying to get the gig. And I would underprice it, because I wasn’t sure that I was any good at it.

In those early days of my career, I felt like if I quoted too high, and someone didn’t hire me, then I would have to admit to myself that I’m not really that good.

That’s just something that we all do. It feels bad.

But it was even more difficult.

It was even more difficult to price my work higher, when I didn’t know what I was doing, because I knew that I could make mistakes. I knew that I could deliver something that wasn’t great, that I would have to redo, and that would take longer than expected.

So in those cases, I would underprice the work. I would underprice it to compensate for the fact that I knew I could mess up and I knew that I wouldn’t get it done on time, or that I wouldn’t get it right, the first time.

But it was still hard, and that’s why I think about this all the time.

And I think that it’s not just for me, but that it’s something that we do as people.

When I talk to freelancers, and I talk to other self employed people, and I ask them about the process of figuring out how much they’re going to charge, they say that it’s so hard.

They say, when I’m going to talk to someone about a project, and I’m going to have to tell them how much it costs, I’m so scared. And I’m so nervous.

And I know that when I’m having a conversation like that, I’m going to underprice the project.

I’m going to underprice the project, because it’s so hard.

It’s so hard because I think that I’m going to lose the client. I think that I’m going to lose the client, because if I charge too much, they’re going to say, you know, that’s too expensive. And it’s just hard.

And I think this is so hard because there’s this weird thing about money, and our relationships to other people, and our relationships to our own self.

Because the problem is, if you’re underpricing yourself, if you’re not charging as much as you could, you’re hurting yourself.

When I was thinking about this a couple of weeks ago, I was thinking that, when you’re underpricing your work, you’re not just leaving money on the table. You’re not just hurting yourself. You’re actually making everyone else’s lives worse.

And I was thinking about this because of my own experience of this, and how when I would underprice my work, I would do this work for clients, and they would tell me, “Hey, you know, we thought we were going to pay you for a certain amount of work, but then you were so great, we ended up needing more work, and so we paid you more than we would have if we had been working with somebody else.

And so, not only was I not getting the money that I thought I would, but they were also spending more money on the project, than they had thought.

And I think this is just a really interesting thing. And it’s this weird thing about how money works, and how our own self-worth works, and how our relationships to other people, and our relationships to the work that we do.

And I think that there’s a lot of ways that we can get better at this.

But the best thing that we can do to get better at this, is to do the work.

We have to do the work. We have to get better at the work. We have to get better at the work, and we have to get better at talking to other people, and talking about our work, and how we can help them.

It’s only when we’re really good at doing the work, that we’re good at pricing the work, because we’re good at explaining the work, and we’re good at talking about the work, and we’re good at telling other people how we can help them.

prompt: Freelancers: when do you raise your rates? Write an essay about pricing your own labor and why it's so psychologically hard, aimed at people in year one or two of freelancing.
response:
When you’re a freelancer, it’s surprisingly hard to raise your rates. It feels like a betrayal of people you care about, and a loss of identity.

One year into freelancing, I was feeling a lot of guilt about charging $250 per hour, when most of my friends who were employees in the tech industry were making between $70 and $200 an hour. But after a while I realized that I needed to raise my rates to $350. I didn’t want to do it.

There was one project I was working on that I thought was a good candidate to raise my rate. The client was a person I’d worked with for years, but not recently. She was paying me the standard $250, which meant $350 didn’t seem unreasonable.

I’d started this work a few months ago, and it was nearly finished. I sent her a message:

I’m going to raise my rate to $350/hr starting on the 1st of the month. You won’t see any changes in what you pay me for a while, since your current project is about a month from being finished.

She replied a couple hours later:

I’ve been going back and forth on whether to say anything. I’m so happy that you said something. I’ve been wondering why you didn’t say anything, and wondering if you thought I wasn’t a good client or something. I’m just so glad you said something, and I’m so happy to hear about it.

I had not expected to hear something like that from her. I wasn’t sure what to do with this. I hadn’t even expected her to reply in the first place.

I wrote to another friend about it, and she said something like “you’re going to get so much positive feedback”. I didn’t expect that either.

A couple weeks later, I was working with another client on an entirely new project. I told him I was raising my rates to $350/hr starting on the 1st of the month. He was a little upset, but he was fine. He was also happy to hear about it. I was surprised by this again.

My friend from before was right. It was surprising how much positive feedback I got. Everyone seemed to like that I had raised my rates. I was a little nervous that I was going to lose some people, but I didn’t lose any.

One day, a friend of mine who I hadn’t spoken to in a while, reached out. She said that she’d just left a big tech company, and that she wanted to work with me. I said that I’d be happy to help, and that I charged $350/hr. I thought she’d be a little surprised to hear this, but she just said “that’s fine”.

I was so glad that it was this easy, and that I hadn’t hesitated for much longer. Raising my rates felt really hard, but the actual thing that would’ve been hard was if I hadn’t raised my rates and lost people.

The best part of this was that I could work with people I cared about. I could work on things that were hard, and I didn’t need to think about money as much. It was a good time for me.

The next year, I raised my rates again to $450/hr.

A couple years ago, I raised my rates again to $800/hr. I thought about this for a while. I wasn’t sure if it was a good idea to raise my rates that high.

I thought about my favorite clients, and decided to raise my rates with them first. It was a little scary to do this, but the process was just as smooth as it had been before. Everyone was happy to hear that I’d raised my rates.

I had a lot of new clients coming in, and I thought about how to set rates for them. I didn’t really want to have different rates for different clients, so I raised my rates to $800/hr for new clients, too. I was a little nervous about this, but it turned out to be fine.

A couple weeks ago, I raised my rates to $1000/hr.

Raising my rates to $1000/hr was the hardest for me. I thought about it for months, and I kept delaying. I was afraid of what it would mean to do this. What if I lost people? What if people were upset?

I thought about my friends who were getting really excited about raising their rates, and I wondered what they were doing that I wasn’t. I was thinking about a lot of things, but I wasn’t doing what they were doing, which was just raising their rates. I think I was getting really confused about how hard it was going to be. I just raised my rates, and it was really easy. It was like the first time. Everyone was excited to hear about it.

I was relieved, and it made me feel really good to have raised my rates. I’m glad I did it.

It’s been a couple years since I first started freelancing. I was able to learn a lot about pricing, and how to raise my rates. I’m glad I have been able to learn about this.

Imagine you are a successful person. You have made a big difference in the world. You have helped millions of people. You have done something that will last. And you are very rich.

How much of that has luck had to do with it?

I’ve had a lot of conversations with people like this, and most of them will not admit that luck had anything to do with it. They will say that they got where they are purely through hard work and talent. This is not only false, it is a dangerous thing to believe.

I’m talking about the kind of successful person who has helped millions of people. I’m not talking about people who have merely gotten rich. People who have become rich through luck have nothing to feel guilty about. But the people who have accomplished things that benefit others are in a different position. They are taking credit for things that aren’t solely their fault, and if they don’t admit it they are denying their own role in it.

I’ve talked to dozens of people who are very successful, and I’ve found a pattern to their thinking. It’s not that they’re being dishonest. They’re just not thinking about it. They think they’re being honest, but because they’re unaware of how much luck contributes to their success, they don’t mention it.

I asked one person who is very successful in Silicon Valley what role luck played in his success. He laughed and said “none”. I said “really? You think luck had nothing to do with it?” He said “yes”. Then I asked if he thought he was smarter than the average person. He said “yes”. I asked if he thought he was smarter than most people in Silicon Valley. He said “no”. Then I asked if he thought he was smarter than most people in San Francisco. He said “no”. Then I asked if he thought he was smarter than most people in the country. He said “no”.

So he thought he was smarter than most people, but not smarter than most people in San Francisco. He was in Silicon Valley because it happened to be near where he lived.

This is the same pattern I see in almost all conversations about what made people successful. They’re unaware of how much luck contributed to their success, but they also believe that they are smarter than the average person. It’s an interesting combination.

The most successful people tend to be the most oblivious to how much luck had to do with their success. I once asked a very successful investor what role luck played in his success. He said “none”. Then I asked “really? You think it was just luck of the draw that you were born in a place that was on the cutting edge of investing at the right time?”

He thought about it for a moment, then said “yes.”

I once asked a successful venture capitalist what role luck played in his success. He laughed and said “none.” I said “really? You think that you wouldn’t have been as successful if you hadn’t happened to be in Silicon Valley in the 90s?” He said “yes.”

I said “and you think you wouldn’t have been as successful if you hadn’t happened to be born in a certain year?” He thought about it for a moment, then said “yes.”

I’ve had this conversation with lots of successful people, and it always goes the same way. They’re unaware of how much luck contributed to their success, but they also think that they’re smarter than the average person.

This is a dangerous combination. They’re not taking responsibility for their own success, and it’s affecting how they act in the world. They tend to think they’re better than other people, which affects how they relate to other people. They can end up thinking they’re better than people who are actually smarter than them, which can lead them to make bad decisions.

And because they don’t realize how much luck played a role in their success, they can end up thinking that their accomplishments were all because of them. If they don’t realize that they got lucky, they can end up thinking that they were always going to be successful, which can affect how they treat people who aren’t.

prompt: Every company I've worked at says 'we're a family.' Write an essay about why that phrase makes people's skin crawl and what a healthier metaphor for a workplace would be.
response:
It has been suggested that the best way to avoid a bad marriage is to go in expecting to get divorced. I think the same is true for jobs.

A lot of people are surprised to learn that I've worked for myself. They assume I'd never be able to survive in the company of other people. In fact I've been surrounded by other people most of my life. I just never got the notion that I belonged to them.

There are some companies that manage to be great places to work even when you treat them as something you're temporarily working for. But most try to make you feel like you're part of a team or a family. When they do, the first thing I think is, oh crap, what are they trying to do?

The family thing is particularly creepy, because it implies an obligation that has to be kept secret. If they say you have to work for them forever, at least you know what you're up against. But if they tell you they're a family, they're not just implying an obligation; they're implying an obligation that you're not supposed to even think about. They're saying you're part of a family, but not saying how much that means, and hoping you won't think to ask.

You can see what they want by looking at what they think a family member is supposed to do. The standard answer is that you're supposed to support your family no matter what. And I know this because I've actually heard people say so. It's not just a matter of being loyal to a family member; it's a matter of being supportive.

You know what that means. It means if someone in the company is doing something stupid, it's your job to pretend it isn't. If you have the guts to say what everyone else is thinking, the boss will say "you have to support the team," and the boss will always be right.

When I worked at Viaweb, we got to experience a family member behaving badly. A couple of months before the company was sold, we found out the new owner planned to fire all of us. So we spent the next month in a frenzy of activity, trying to get whatever done we could.

There was one problem though. The person they were going to replace us with was a former Viaweb employee who had left in something of a huff, and was now at the company we'd been bought by. He seemed to be using his new position to make our lives miserable, by making sure that all the information we might need to survive the transition was withheld from us.

The CEO was furious with him, and told the whole company so. I'm sure she didn't realize what she'd done. She'd just handed our nemesis a great gift. He was now not only a business competitor, but a family enemy. If we had to choose between our new owner and the man who left us in a bad mood, we'd have to pick the latter.

I don't know exactly what happened next, but I suspect this is how the CEO managed to get rid of him within two months. He had no choice. The company was now in the hands of a group of people who were united against him.

I'm not saying the employees were right to turn on the CEO. But this is what she got for treating the company like a family.

There are other ways companies can go wrong even if they manage to avoid getting too family-like. Some companies are so much like families that they never notice the difference. When I was in high school, the local IBM office did some kind of thing where you had to stand on a chair and jump over a line of people. You weren't supposed to touch the line of people. If you did, you had to do it again.

I don't know what this was supposed to symbolize. Probably something about getting your work done on time. Maybe the line of people were the deadlines. Or maybe they were the customer. I don't know. I just remember everyone doing it.

At some point they must have decided that standing on a chair and jumping over a line of people was a really good way to symbolize a workday. I can only think of one reason for that to be true: the work is to some of the employees. The company isn't using it as a metaphor to motivate the employees; it's an exercise they go through because it's part of the culture.

When I was in college I got a job at a small startup in a garage at the end of a dirt road in the middle of the country. My job was to write a compiler for a new programming language that the company had invented. The compiler had to be done in two weeks.

I was told that I could have a programmer to help me if I asked, but I didn't. I thought I could do it faster by myself. And of course I was right.

But I made one mistake. I spent a couple days writing the compiler, and then went to talk to the boss. I said "I think I know exactly how the compiler should work."

The boss said "that sounds great, you'd better get back to work." So I did.

Then I spent another couple days on it, and came back again. "I'm almost done. I've got everything working except the code generator."

The boss said "that sounds great, you'd better get back to work." So I did.

I finished the code generator, and was really happy. I was very proud of it. It was really neat. I came to the boss and said "the compiler is done."

The boss just stared at me. "What?" he said. "You should still have three days to do it."

I said "what? I thought I should work as fast as I could."

The boss was silent for a moment. Then he said "if you'd asked me, I would have given you another programmer."

And that was how I learned that in most jobs, you're not supposed to get your work done as fast as you can.

You can see what it means to be part of a family just from those two stories. If you're part of a family, you're not supposed to do the work. You're supposed to be supportive. You're supposed to do whatever you're told, and then just hang around, pretending to work, until the boss tells you to go home.

I had a job at Harvard once where I was supposed to be a teaching assistant. The job was supposed to take about six hours a week. But of course you're not supposed to do it that fast. You have to spread the work over the whole term, or what would the point be of being a teaching assistant?

At least in a job where you're part of a family, the work is defined. You know what you're supposed to do. The only problem is you're not supposed to do it as fast as you can. But in a company that really has turned into a family, even that gets lost.

When I worked at Viaweb, the whole company was very family-like, but in the end it didn't really turn into a family. There were things that needed doing, and people who knew what they were. So we knew how to do our jobs, even though we weren't supposed to do them too fast.

But I've seen the next step in the evolution of a company into a family. In one company I worked at, we were so much like a family that we'd lost track of what we did. There were things that needed doing. People just didn't know what they were.

We had meetings all the time. They were supposed to be to decide what to do, but they never resulted in any decisions. I was a programmer, and I had no idea what to work on, or who else had been assigned what.

That company had a problem, which was not doing what companies are supposed to do. I don't mean the usual problem of not getting things done; that's what happens in most companies. I mean they didn't even know what companies were supposed to do.

I don't think they were stupid. I think they had forgotten. They'd lost track of it, just like they'd lost track of what we were supposed to be working on.

I've seen a company do this kind of thing even if the founder is a genius. But if you're a genius, this kind of thing only happens when you're doing something so complicated that you forget what you're doing.

If the company is doing something complicated, it's hard to get things done even if you know what needs doing. The people doing it are smart, but they're not geniuses. So you get into a situation where everyone is working hard, but nothing is getting done. And then it's even harder to notice what you're supposed to be doing.

When I was at a company like this, we had a problem that kept recurring. We were a software company, so of course we had bugs. One day the boss said there was a bug he wanted us to fix. Everyone in the company said they'd fix it. And of course it got fixed. But then the boss said there was another bug. And everyone in the company said they'd fix it. And then another. And so on.

At some point I realized what was going on. Every time the boss said he wanted a bug fixed, people would fix it. So the bug list was always getting shorter. So the boss kept adding more bugs.

The boss was the only one who noticed that bugs existed. No one else in the company was going to go looking for bugs to fix. They were just going to sit around doing what they were told.

So the company couldn't get rid of bugs. They could only get rid of the bugs the boss knew about. Which was a lot, but not as many as the company would have fixed if everyone had gone looking.

I think you can say the point of a job is to get things done. It is certainly not to be supportive. It is not to get whatever things are done that the boss thinks need doing. It is to get things done. And the only way to do that is for everyone to know what needs doing, and go looking for it.

If everyone in a company knows what needs doing, it's very hard to stop them from doing it, even if they're part of a family. When I worked at Viaweb, I knew we had to get our work done, whatever that meant, so I had the idea of working faster, which the boss told me not to do.

But if you don't know what needs doing, being supportive is a good way to spend your time. You can't be supportive of anything else.

When I worked at Viaweb we had a lot of meetings, but they were short. People didn't know what needed doing, so we tried to find out. I don't know if we were ever completely successful, but we got pretty close.

I think you can tell a lot about a company by looking at its meetings. If the meetings are short and frequent, you know people have to get things done, because otherwise they wouldn't be able to afford the time. If the meetings are long and rare, you know the company has turned into a family, because otherwise no one would have time to sit through them.

I once worked at a company where every meeting lasted four hours. You can bet we didn't know what we were doing there.

When I worked at Viaweb we had a few meetings that lasted longer than an hour. One of them was when the company was trying to decide how to fix a problem. It took three hours, because it was complicated and we were smart. But it was not a typical meeting.

I think the meetings at my first job were the longest I've ever sat through. They lasted as long as the people who attended them. At the worst ones, the meeting was just a bunch of people talking about things, and you could see it was all nonsense, because everyone was getting more and more nervous as they tried to make up ideas on the fly.

I don't know how I survived it. Probably I was too stupid to realize that what we were doing was pointless. I think I thought meetings were just supposed to be like that. It wasn't until I was working at Viaweb that I realized that meetings were supposed to result in decisions.

When you're part of a family, you're not supposed to do anything. You're supposed to be supportive. And the only way to know what to be supportive of is if you know what the company is doing.

If you're part of a family, the best thing to happen to you is to become a family. You get to be even more supportive than before.

In a company like that, you're not supposed to do anything. You're not even supposed to pretend to do anything. And it's not a metaphor. It's real.

I think if you get to know people well enough, you'll know if they're part of a family. And if you do, you'll know what to be supportive of.

prompt: Every company I've worked at says 'we're a family.' Write an essay about why that phrase makes people's skin crawl and what a healthier metaphor for a workplace would be.
response:
One of the most common phrases I’ve heard as a junior software engineer is “we are a family here.”

I’m a bit older now and I can explain why that phrase, in addition to being corny, should make you a little bit nervous.

Family, at its core, is the concept of unconditional support. You’re not in your family because you’re good or successful, you’re there because of who you are. And you can’t just leave the family you were born into and join the family of another family.

This is a problem.

If you join a family at work, then you’re supposed to be unconditional with your coworkers. You’re supposed to be loyal and supportive, no matter what.

And if it’s a family, then you can’t just leave if you don’t like it. If you don’t get along with the people, or if the work sucks, you can’t just leave for a different family.

The idea of family is the idea of unconditional loyalty and unconditional support. But you should never have to give unconditional loyalty or support to a company or workplace. And the reason I always bristled when I heard “we are a family here” is that the more I thought about it, the more it sounded like something that should be worrying.

The company that says “we’re a family” probably isn’t saying it with bad intentions. But it does make me nervous because it’s a company that has made it normal for people to feel unconditional loyalty to them.

And there are plenty of companies out there that are doing the exact same thing with bad intentions.

There’s a type of company that tries to take advantage of the concept of family to get away with bad management. They want you to be loyal, supportive, and not leave. They want you to feel like it’s a betrayal to leave or do bad work or complain.

So the family metaphor isn’t just corny. It’s a sign that maybe your company isn’t great.

The problem isn’t that the company isn’t a family. The problem is that the concept of family is a really bad concept to apply to a workplace.

A workplace isn’t a family. A workplace is a place where you and other people are working together to make money.

What we need is a better metaphor, one that better describes what a workplace is and what it’s for.

A lot of people think the word “team” is a better word than “family” to describe a workplace, and I agree. A team is a place where you’re working together with other people.

But “team” has the same problem as “family.” It can be used to encourage unconditional loyalty. There are teams that you join because you want to belong to them, and teams that you should not leave.

A team is a better word than “family,” but it still sounds a little dangerous when you hear it.

The word that would work best for a workplace is a word that describes a group of people who are working together to accomplish something and earn money, and that people can leave at any time. The word I’m looking for is something like “cooperative” or “club,” but that’s not quite right either.

A club is an organization that people are in because they want to belong to it, like a team. And a cooperative is an organization where the members own it together, but that isn’t quite right either.

We need a new word, one that describes a place where a bunch of people are working together to do something. And it needs to be a word that doesn’t make people think “unconditional loyalty” when they hear it.

prompt: Why rewrites fail. Essay.
response:
I’ve spent most of my life in a kind of professional rewrite business, rewriting other people’s writing to make it better. This week I started thinking about why people’s writing needs to be rewritten, and I think I have an answer.

The reason is not laziness. Writers usually work very hard. The reason is the nature of writing itself.

Writing is a kind of thinking, and thinking is a kind of exploration. To explore a territory you have to wander. But a finished essay is not the place where you wandered; it’s the territory you found.

The best essays read like a guided tour through the writer’s head. But you wouldn’t go on a guided tour of someone wandering around in a forest. So the first task in writing an essay is to explore, which necessarily involves wandering; the second is to turn what you learned into a guided tour of the territory you explored.

When you finish an essay, you’ve finished the first part. But the second part takes just as much work, and is just as important. In fact, you could say it’s the part that matters.

The reason is that in the first phase you were the audience for your own essay. The first audience an essay has is the person who writes it. When you’re writing, you’re reading what you’ve just written to see whether it makes sense. If it doesn’t, you have to change it.

So in the first phase you have both the writer’s and the reader’s hat on your head. And in the first phase you’re wearing the writer’s hat most of the time. You’ve got a thing to say, and you’re thinking of a way to say it.

When you write, you’re not just choosing words. You’re discovering what to say. And not just what to say, but where to say it. The essay you end up writing is not just a sequence of sentences, but a sequence of sentences in a specific order.

But you won’t know where the sentences go until you’ve written them. So when you’re writing you’re working on two problems simultaneously: figuring out what to say and figuring out where to say it.

As you write, your essay takes on a kind of life of its own. It has a trajectory that you don’t fully understand, but which you have to follow. In a good essay, this trajectory is a tour of a fascinating place. But it can’t be guided until the exploration is done.

So when you finish an essay you’ve got something that seems like an essay. It’s got the same shape as an essay. But it hasn’t been through the process that turns an essay into an essay.

You’ve got something that seems like an essay because it’s actually a kind of fossilized exploration. What it needs to become an essay is for the parts you wandered through to be rearranged in a form that lets a reader explore efficiently.

I’ve never seen a good essay that didn’t need this. If it looks like it’s in good shape when you finish it, it’s probably not going to be a good essay.

And it’s not just a matter of fixing a few sentences here and there. It’s a second pass that will change the essay’s structure and probably its emphasis.

What changes the structure? As you reread, you’ll notice certain things that are wrong. Maybe a paragraph doesn’t make sense, or a phrase is clunky.

As you write, you’re not just writing down sentences. You’re also thinking about what to write. But you can only think about so much at once. So the thoughts you have as you write are not the only ones. When you reread you find the others, and they often lead to changes.

The most dangerous things are the ones that don’t make sense. When you reread and find a sentence that’s confusing, the instinct is to rewrite it. That’s fine if you don’t know what you meant, but if you do, it’s a sign of something you should be thinking about.

When I reread, I usually have a stack of sticky notes on the desk next to me. When I find something that’s confusing, I write myself a note. “This bit needs to be clearer.” Then I go on.

When I’ve got all the notes, I reread them, and I try to think about how to make the essay clear. But at this point I’m not changing the essay. I’m just thinking about it.

The second time through the essay is when I fix things. But before I start changing anything, I think about what I found during the first pass.

As I reread the first time, I noticed all sorts of things that I didn’t think much about then. But now I see a pattern. This thing I found to be confusing isn’t just one thing. It’s part of a larger problem that’s making this essay confusing.

In the first pass I found a lot of places where the essay was confusing. Now I find the reasons why.

This is what I call the structure of the essay. It’s not about the sequence of words, but the sequence of ideas. The first pass tells me where the essay fails. The second pass tells me why it fails.

The structure of an essay is not just the order of the paragraphs. It’s more like the sequence of thoughts that you have as you read it. In a good essay these form a path through interesting territory.

The structure of an essay is usually the thing that’s wrong with it. In writing, the structure is always going to be the most complicated part.

You can’t change the structure of an essay without changing everything. If you change the order of the ideas, that changes the sequence of words. So to change the structure of an essay, you have to rewrite it.

This is not a big deal for me, since I get paid to do it. But it’s a big deal for the writer. If an essay needs rewriting, you have to tell the writer that.

But people are often resistant to having their work rewritten. It seems to them that their work isn’t good enough, and rewriting it would be a sign of how bad it is.

It’s not.

Rewriting is part of the job.

The best writing in the world all goes through this process. The only difference is that for most people it happens within their heads.

prompt: Why rewrites fail. Essay.
response:
Rewrites are the most commonly prescribed solution for poor writing, and they are also the most commonly ignored advice, because most people don’t realize how hard a rewrite is, or that it’s even necessary.

A rewrite isn’t fixing a few mistakes. A rewrite is throwing out what you have and starting again from scratch. It’s like rebuilding a house, not redecorating. The idea is to start with what you have, but not be afraid to throw out anything that doesn’t work.

Most people’s problem is that they try to improve what they have. If you don’t have a solid draft, a rewrite can’t help you. If you don’t have the right idea, a rewrite can’t help you either. The rewrite is a way of making what you have into the best it could be. It can’t make it something else.

If you want a rewrite to work, you’ve got to give yourself a deadline. It won’t be any use if you can go on forever.

A good rule to go by is to give yourself one day for every 500 words. So if you have 5000 words to rewrite, a day is too little and two weeks is too long. You’ve got to give yourself long enough to get it done, but not so long that you start thinking about it, because you’ll end up just fiddling with it.

The deadline works because it forces you to be ruthless. When you only have a week to rewrite 5000 words, you can’t afford to spend a day fussing with a sentence.

A rewrite is something you do by yourself. It isn’t a group project. It isn’t even a conversation between you and the original writer. A rewrite is something you do in the place of the original writer. If you can’t do it in the time you give yourself, it’s not worth doing.

The rewrite is like the original, except better. There’s only so much improvement to be done on a piece of writing. If it was a bad idea, it can’t be fixed. If it’s about the wrong thing, it can’t be fixed.

What a rewrite can do is make what you have as good as it can be. If you have something good, it can make it better. But if you have something bad, it can’t fix it.

A rewrite is the thing you do to make something good into something great.

prompt: Why rewrites fail. Essay.
response:
I recently read an essay by a guy I respect a lot about how the best approach to writing is to write everything you want to say, in whatever style comes most naturally, and then rewrite it.

This is probably the most effective approach, and I'm pretty sure the guy is right. But I also think that this is a really, really hard thing to do, and that most people will fail at it, and that's why most people's writing is kind of mediocre.

Rewriting is really, really hard.

I think most people think of writing as this one thing: think of stuff you want to say, write it down. But it's actually two things: figure out what you want to say, and then find a way to say it.

The second part is really hard.

Writing well is about more than just saying something. It's about making the words you choose do their job. It's about being efficient. It's about rhythm and flow. It's about making the reader feel things.

If you're a good writer, all of these things will flow from you automatically and you won't have to think about it. If you're a bad writer, these are the things you need to think about most of the time.

But I've been writing for a while, and I've read a lot of writing, so I'm not sure I'm a really bad writer. And yet I still find that I'm thinking about these things a lot of the time.

I think that when you're actually writing, it's really hard to do everything at the same time. You need to be thinking about the stuff you're trying to say, and you need to be thinking about how to say it, and I don't think you can do both things well at the same time.

So what I do when I'm writing is, I write down what I want to say, and then I rewrite it. I think that this is a really good thing to do, but I'm also worried that it's a really bad thing to do. I think that most people will be better off not doing this.

When you write down something you want to say, your brain is working on the task of figuring out how to say it. And as you're writing it down, your brain is still working on this task, and it's still finding a way to say it.

I don't know how to describe this process, but I think this is what happens, and if you rewrite what you wrote, your brain won't do this. And then you'll just have something that's kind of clunky.

I think that most people write in a pretty bad way, and if they rewrite what they wrote, they won't get much better. And so I think if you're a bad writer, you should try to be a really bad writer, and then you'll be a little bit better than you would have been.

prompt: I've been writing software for 22 years and I've come around to thinking that most code comments are an apology for something. Write an essay developing that idea, including the cases where it's wrong.
response:
I’ve been writing software for 22 years, and I’ve come around to thinking that most code comments are an apology for something.

For instance, in one of my programs:

# this is wrong, but it will get replaced when we rewrite it

# this is the least bad way to do it

# I hate doing it this way, but I didn’t have time

In the first case, the comment is apologizing for a temporary hack. The code is wrong in a way the author knows. It will be fixed someday, and the comment is a way of saying “I promise that it will.”

The second comment is an apology for an imperfect solution to a problem, but one that the author believes is the least bad option. The author is acknowledging that what she has written could be better, and saying she’s done the best she knows how.

In the third case, the author is apologizing for a bad solution that isn’t temporary. The author knows the code is bad, but she didn’t have time to do it right. If you don’t have time to do something right, then what you do is not temporary, and the apology doesn’t work.

These are three kinds of comments that I find most often. I’m sure there are others.

But I think that’s just how we talk, not just when writing software. Most comments in life are apologies.

The exception is comments that describe things people don’t already know. But that’s not the kind of comment that’s a bad thing, so that’s not the kind I mean when I talk about comments being an apology for something.

If you can tell, that’s the kind I was talking about when I said that comments are a bad thing. Comments are a bad thing because they are an apology for something.

But comments that describe things people don’t already know are not an apology for something. And so they are not bad.

That’s a really interesting distinction.

response:
Suppose that you had the time and inclination to write an explanatory comment for each of your lines of code. Then some of the time it would be impossible. You'd want to write the comment “increment x,” but you've already written that in the code.

As you write code, you can avoid this difficulty by omitting comments that explain what the code does.

This is a good rule, but I find myself making it into a stronger rule than it can possibly be. Sometimes, if the code is clear, the comment is just noise. But it isn't a mistake.

What are the comments that are a mistake? I think they're ones that exist as a kind of apology for the code.

For example, suppose you have a variable that you can't name sensibly because its purpose is obscure. You might write a comment like

// TODO: refactor so I can give this variable a real name

You don't really expect to refactor that code. You're just trying to ward off criticism for the variable's name.

I think comments like this are the ones people like to hate. There's an obvious class of them: comments that just say something like “this is complicated” or “I don't understand this code.” But I think all comments apologizing for the code are like this, whether they admit it or not.

And this kind of comment is not just noise. It's the wrong kind of comment. It doesn't just fail to be useful; it is affirmatively unhelpful because it will discourage the reader from understanding the code, even though that might be possible.

One of the best pieces of advice I've seen for writing code is to write code that is so good your friends will be jealous. This is a great idea, but it's probably better to write code so good your friends will be impressed by whoever wrote it. If you write code so good people can't tell who wrote it, you'll have a hard time proving you did.

This is not a rule that requires you to write your name in the code. The point is that you shouldn't write code that people will be impressed by because they're impressed that you did it, but they will not be impressed if they think someone else did.

In other words, there are two kinds of impressive. You could write code that someone like Steve Wozniak might write. Or you could write code that only someone like Steve Wozniak could write.

In the same way, there are two kinds of clear code. There is code that anyone can understand, and code that only you can understand.

One thing that impresses people is when they can't figure out how you did something. It's a kind of trick. The code is impressive in the same sense that a magic trick is impressive. But magic tricks are not good code.

The reason magic tricks are not good code is not that they are bad. That would be a strange thing to say, since magic tricks are not even trying to be code. They're a different category of thing. The reason magic tricks are not good code is that they're not trying to solve a programming problem. They're trying to impress people.

The same thing is true of code that is only clear to its author. It's not trying to be clear. It's trying to impress people with how good the author is.

And this kind of clear code can be bad, in the same sense that a magic trick can be bad. If I show you a magic trick, there are two ways for it to be bad. Either the trick could be bad, as in, it fails to work properly; or the trick could be bad because it's too obvious, as in, you can see how it's done.

A magic trick that's too obvious is bad, but not in the same sense that the other kind of bad trick is bad. The second kind of bad magic trick is bad because it fails to do the thing magic tricks are supposed to do, which is to impress people by doing something they can't figure out how to do. The reason a trick that's too obvious is bad is that it fails to accomplish its goal.

So the goal of writing code that only you can understand is to impress people with how smart you are. But if that's your goal, you're doing it wrong, in the same sense that a magic trick that's too obvious is wrong. The trick is bad because it fails to accomplish its goal.

The thing that impresses people is that you did something they can't figure out how to do. So if you can figure out how to do it, you're not impressed. And the same thing is true of code that only the author can understand. It's not impressive to you. If you wrote the code, it's not impressive that you understand it.

So the goal of making code only understandable to the author is just to impress yourself. Which is another way to say that the goal is to avoid being embarrassed.

The same thing is true of comments. If you're writing a comment to make clear what the code does, that's not an apology. It's just noise. But if you're writing a comment to say “I don't know what this code does,” that's an apology. And it will have the same effect on its readers as the comments saying that the code is complicated. It will discourage them from trying to understand it. And that's a bad thing.

But sometimes the code is genuinely bad. Sometimes it's so bad there's no point in trying to understand it.

The solution for code that's bad enough that it's not worth understanding isn't to comment that it's bad. That would only make it worse. The solution is not to write code so bad that it's not worth understanding. But the solution for code that's bad but not too bad is to write better code.

I'm not saying that all the time the best way to fix bad code is to rewrite it. Sometimes you just have to get the job done. The best way to rewrite bad code is not always to rewrite it.

But sometimes you can fix bad code by rewriting it, and sometimes it's worth doing that. And the solution to a lot of bad code is that if you're going to write code that's too bad to understand, you should write it so well that you can understand it.

Write an essay arguing that DRY ('don't repeat yourself') has done more harm than good for intermediate programmers.
response:
DRY is a principle of software development that aims to reduce repetition in source code. It’s usually used to mean that if you find yourself copy-pasting something, it’s a sign that you should refactor. But the principle goes beyond that, to a more abstract meaning of “avoid repeating yourself in a codebase”.

DRY is a great idea, but it’s hard to get right. Intermediate programmers can sometimes take DRY too far, and I think they’ve suffered for it.

The first problem with DRY is that it’s not a rule. If you follow DRY, and you think of it as a rule, you’ll end up with code that’s hard to maintain.

If you want to write code that’s easy to maintain, you need to know your codebase, and that takes time. DRY isn’t about writing code that’s easy to maintain. It’s about writing code that’s easy to maintain if you have an intimate knowledge of the codebase.

In other words, DRY is about writing code that’s easy to maintain when you’re the one maintaining it. That sounds like a good idea, but it’s not. You don’t have to know a codebase to work on it. A good codebase should be easy to work on for people who haven’t seen it before.

If you’re not the one maintaining a codebase, you need to be able to tell how your change will affect the rest of the codebase. That’s not easy if the codebase is very DRY, because when you have a lot of indirection, it can be hard to know what your change will affect.

This problem is so common that it has a name: the shotgun refactoring problem. When you have a lot of indirection, if you need to make a change to one thing, you may have to touch a lot of other things as well.

In a lot of codebases, the shotgun refactoring problem has gone too far. In the worst case, you have to touch every part of the codebase just to make a small change.

The DRY principle is good. But if you follow it too far, you’ll get code that’s hard to maintain for people who aren’t you.

I think a lot of codebases are too DRY, but I’m not saying that all codebases are. There are codebases that are so hard to understand that it’s obvious they need refactoring.

For example, if you have a lot of copy-paste in your code, it’s usually a sign that you need to refactor. Copy-paste is a sign that you’re not thinking about how your code is organized, and that you’re not thinking about how you can use abstractions to make your code easier to understand.

If you have a lot of copy-paste in your code, you should refactor. But if you have a lot of indirection in your code, you should also refactor.

So DRY is a bad rule. But it’s still a good principle. It’s just a bad idea to use it as a rule.

prompt: Write an essay arguing that DRY ('don't repeat yourself') has done more harm than good for intermediate programmers.
response:
DRY, or “don’t repeat yourself,” was originally a principle about software design, saying that if you find yourself repeating yourself, you should find a way to abstract that repetition.

In theory, DRY makes sense. But in practice, I’ve noticed that many intermediate programmers obsess about applying DRY, often to their detriment.

For example, a student of mine has two functions in different files that are very similar. They’re about 20 lines long, and most of the code is identical. She asks me if she should combine them.

When I look, I see that the two functions are used in completely different situations, and it isn’t obvious at all how they are related. If I were forced to guess, I’d bet that one function is just a copy of the other that was copied and modified to do a slightly different job. But if they’re related, I can’t tell how. I can’t imagine any abstraction that would make the code simpler.

The student doesn’t want to make this decision, so she asks me. What do I say? I think the right answer is: keep the two functions separate.

There are three good reasons why.

First, the two functions are related in a way that’s so mysterious that I can’t figure it out. If they’re related, I’d bet that one function is a copy of the other that was copied and modified. If that’s true, that suggests that this kind of copy-and-edit is a normal way of working.

Second, I can’t figure out how they’re related, and neither can I imagine an abstraction that would make them simpler. If I’m forced to guess, I’d bet that the code would be harder to understand, because I’d have to read through the shared code trying to understand the way the two different functions are different.

Third, the code doesn’t need to be simpler. If I understand the code as it is, and if I understand what changes to make, I don’t need any further help. The code doesn’t need to be simpler.

So I think the right advice is to keep the two functions separate.

I worry that intermediate programmers often want to apply DRY, and when they do, it causes them to write confusing code and make it harder to work with. So I worry that DRY does more harm than good for intermediate programmers.

prompt: Write an essay arguing that DRY ('don't repeat yourself') has done more harm than good for intermediate programmers.
response:
The Don’t Repeat Yourself principle was first introduced by Andy Hunt in the book The Pragmatic Programmer: “Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system”. It is a simple enough principle, but like many simple ideas, its simplicity is deceiving. It is a very powerful idea, but like many powerful ideas, its power is deceptive.

A simple principle is one that you can state in a few words or sentences. A powerful principle is one that has very broad applicability, and that can be used to make decisions in a wide variety of circumstances. Simple and powerful principles are the most dangerous: you can’t be sure that you understand them fully, and you’re likely to apply them in cases where they don’t actually apply.

DRY is simple enough, and you can apply it to a huge variety of situations, but the most important part of the principle is not included in the description that is usually given. When people say “Don’t repeat yourself”, they mean that you shouldn’t copy and paste the same code twice. But the most important part of the principle is that you need to figure out what you are repeating yourself about, and that may not always be something obvious. For example, here is a piece of code that you might see in a program:

```python
a = 0
b = 1
while b < 1000000:
    a, b = b, a + b
```

This code, as you might guess, computes Fibonacci numbers. The way that it does this is by storing the last two Fibonacci numbers in variables `a` and `b`, and then replacing `a` with `b`, and `b` with `a + b`, which are the next two Fibonacci numbers. This code is not violating DRY, and yet there is definitely a form of repetition going on here. There are two pieces of knowledge that are being repeated here: there are two places where the relationship between the next Fibonacci number and the previous two is mentioned, and there are two places where the last two Fibonacci numbers are mentioned.

The reason this matters is that this code could be made more DRY by writing it like this:

```python
a, b = 0, 1
while b < 1000000:
    a = b
    b = a + b
```

It’s still possible to make this even more DRY:

```python
a, b = 0, 1
while b < 1000000:
    b += a
```

This is probably the most DRY form of this program, and it is the form that I would normally write. There is no longer a repetition of knowledge. There is only one place where the relationship between the last two Fibonacci numbers is mentioned, and only one place where the last two Fibonacci numbers are mentioned.

The point here is that the most DRY form of a program isn’t always the one that doesn’t contain duplicated code, and sometimes the DRY way to write code means writing it in a way that doesn’t look at all DRY to somebody who is only looking for duplicated code.

DRY is a good way to think about programs, but it is an extremely subtle principle. It is easy to misinterpret it, or to take it to its conclusion in a way that doesn’t actually lead to good code.

It is also very common to over-interpret DRY, by trying to make your programs as DRY as possible. This is a mistake for a number of reasons:

1. Making your program more DRY means adding more abstraction, which means adding more complexity, which is something that you should always try to avoid.

2. It is extremely hard to make your code more DRY. There are many possible abstractions that you can add to your code to make it DRY, and it is not easy to figure out which of those is the right abstraction.

3. Making your code more DRY makes it more likely that you will get things wrong. The best way to write code is to write it in the simplest way possible, but if you are trying to write it in the most DRY way, then you will end up writing code that is more complicated than it needs to be.

4. There is no benefit to making your code more DRY than it needs to be. Your code should be as DRY as it needs to be, but you don’t need to make it DRYer than it needs to be, and it doesn’t make sense to do so.

DRY is not really a principle. If you look at DRY, what you really find is that it is a principle of abstraction: the only thing that DRY really means is that you should use abstraction in your programs whenever you can.

If you use abstraction, then your code is likely to be more DRY. If you use a lot of abstraction, then your code is likely to be very DRY. If you don’t use any abstraction, then your code is likely to have a lot of duplicated code. If you have some duplicated code, then your code is likely to have less abstraction than it could have.

The way that I think of DRY is as a warning sign: if I see duplicated code, then I know that I am not using enough abstraction.

That is all that DRY really is, but that doesn’t stop people from thinking that DRY is a principle. The reason that this matters is that DRY is not the kind of principle that people think that it is, and trying to use DRY as a principle is a very bad idea, because it will lead you to do many bad things.

DRY is a principle that has no power: it’s the kind of principle that everybody agrees with, and that everybody believes, but that nobody really has any idea what it means, and therefore nobody can really use it to do anything.

prompt: Why is naming things so hard? Not the joke, the actual reason. Write it up as an essay.
response:
If you’ve ever tried to give a name to an idea that’s in your head, you’ve probably discovered that it’s very hard. But why is it so hard?

A few years ago I was writing a book on programming and came across the same problem. I wanted to write about how to write code that’s easy to change, but I couldn’t think of a name for that idea. I eventually decided to call it "extensibility". I wasn’t at all happy with that choice, but it seemed like the best option I had.

In fact, it was one of the least good options I had. It meant something completely different and I had to spend a whole chapter explaining how it wasn’t what most people think of when they hear that word.

I’ve been thinking about why naming things is so hard, and I think I have some good ideas. Let’s look at a couple of ways to think about what’s going on.

### Names Are Compression

The first idea I want to explore is that naming things is a compression problem. You’re compressing all the details you have about something into a name, and that’s really hard. If you don’t have a name for something, you can describe it in a long paragraph, but that’s not nearly as effective.

For example, here’s one of my favorite things I learned recently, which has no name:

If a sentence is so complicated that you can’t understand it, you can break it into smaller sentences and then understand them. But if you’ve ever read a good book, you’ve also seen sentences so complicated that it took you a while to understand them. Why?

Because if you break a complicated sentence into smaller ones, you have to repeat a lot of words, and those repeated words are distracting. The more complicated a sentence is, the more distracting it is. If you have the right mental model, you can understand long complicated sentences and skip over the distracting repeated words.

I’m sure you’ve encountered this phenomenon when reading a really complicated sentence.

This is a cool idea that doesn’t have a name. It’s a good compression problem.

### Names Are Search

A second idea I want to explore is that a name is a kind of search. It’s a compressed description of something you’re looking for, and you’re hoping to find other people who’re looking for the same thing.

If there’s no name for something, it’s impossible to find people who’ve also had the same idea, or to find out what they discovered about it. So it’s very useful to be able to come up with a good name for something you’ve noticed.

The thing is, the name you pick has to be one that others people use or are likely to use. So it’s not just a compression problem, it’s a problem of coming up with a search query that’ll find what you want.

You can do a search for what you’re trying to explain, but it won’t help if you’re describing something nobody has explained before. So you need to come up with a name that will match a lot of the things that other people have described that are similar to what you’re talking about.

For example, if I want to say that my idea is about writing code that’s easy to change, then I could use a search term like “writing code that’s easy to change”. That would match some existing work on the topic, but not enough. So I’d need to use a more general search term, like “extensibility”.

### You Can’t Search For What You Don’t Know

The search idea gives me another idea. It seems obvious, but it’s true. You can’t search for what you don’t know. I don’t mean in the sense that you don’t know what to search for. I mean that if you don’t know what to search for, you won’t search for it. You won’t know to search for it.

This is why a lot of ideas take a long time to be discovered. People are searching for what they know, not for what they don’t. If you know that you have a problem with something, and you know the solution involves using a database, then you can search for the term “database” and find out about databases. But if you don’t know that you have a problem, or that the solution involves using a database, then you won’t know to search for those things.

The other thing that makes searching difficult is that you have to pick a term that others people are likely to use. The harder it is to figure out a term that other people will use, the harder it is to search.

### The Best Ideas Are The Easiest To Explain

A few years ago, the famous writer James Clear wrote a blog post about the power of simplicity. The basic idea is that a great idea is one that you can explain in a few words. It’s so good that you don’t need to explain it at all.

There are many examples of this. If I told you that “the universe is expanding”, you’d probably have some idea of what I meant, even if you weren’t a physicist. If I tried to explain it in more detail, it would probably make it less clear.

This is why it’s so valuable to find a good name for something. A name that explains an idea clearly is a name that other people will probably use. So if you find a good name for something you’re thinking about, you’re likely to find that other people are already using it, or that other people are likely to find your work if they search for that term.

This is also why it’s so valuable to find a good name for something you don’t know about. It might be the most important thing you’ll ever learn.

When I was in high school, I was a competitive debater. One of the most important skills I learned in debate was how to use language in a way that was technically accurate while also making the audience feel like they were being told something that was obvious and true.

I was pretty good at this. I won a lot of debates, and won a few national titles.

Years later, when I started programming professionally, I found that this skill was incredibly useful. I was always able to come up with better names than everyone else.

It took me a little while to figure out why this was the case. I had to ask myself, “Am I actually better at naming things, or am I just better at pretending to be good at naming things?”

When I was in high school, I was a really smart kid, but I wasn’t the smartest kid I knew. So, to win debates, I had to learn some things that smarter people didn’t need to learn.

One of those things was how to use language to make the judge believe things.

For example, if my opponent said something that was true, but that I didn’t want to admit was true, I would always be able to rephrase it in a way that was still technically true, but that made it sound like a ridiculous argument.

When I was in college, I learned a word that describes this idea. It’s called equivocation, and it’s one of the most powerful tools in a debater’s arsenal.

Equivocation is an intentionally misleading use of language. A classic example of equivocation is when someone says “I’ve never seen the light,” and everyone thinks they mean “I have never been to heaven,” when really they meant “I have never seen light that isn’t dark.”

Equivocation is a powerful technique because it allows you to say something that is technically true, but that sounds like something else.

And, as it turns out, this is also how good naming works.

Good naming is about saying something that is technically true, but that also sounds like something else.

For example, I once wrote a function called `normalize()` that did a whole bunch of weird things. It turned strings into uppercase. It deleted non-alphanumeric characters. It converted numbers into a weird format. It was pretty complicated, and there were a lot of steps, but I called it “normalize” because that made it sound like it was doing something simple and obvious, even though it was doing something complicated and surprising.

It’s important to understand that this is a bad example of good naming. If you do this all the time, you’ll end up with a codebase that is full of weird surprises, and it’ll be really hard to understand. But it is a useful technique to know about, and sometimes it’s exactly what you need.

Another example of good naming is when you have two objects that are really different from each other, and they do different things, but you name them the same because they are conceptually similar. For example, you might have a `List` class and a `LinkedList` class that both implement the same interface.

Good naming is not about being accurate, or even being clear. It’s about saying something that sounds like what you mean, and that also happens to be true. It’s the same skill as equivocation.

I don’t want to imply that equivocation is a bad thing. It’s a powerful tool, and it can help you accomplish a lot of great things. But it can also be dangerous. I’ve seen a lot of codebases that are riddled with equivocation, and they’re a nightmare to work with.

So the next time you’re writing code, think about how you’re using language. Is it technically accurate? Does it also sound like what you want to say?

prompt: so at work we've had this monorepo vs polyrepo argument going for like 6 months and I've realized the argument isn't really about repos at all, it's about who gets to make decisions and how much teams trust each other. could you write an essay making that point? about 1200 words, readable by non-engineers too since I might send it to our VP

I’ve been thinking a lot about monorepos and polyrepos lately, because that’s the kind of thing I do, and it turns out that the debate about monorepos and polyrepos is not really about monorepos and polyrepos at all. It’s about how much you trust your organization, and who’s in charge of making decisions.

Let’s say your organization has 20 teams, which is pretty small. Each team is about 10 people. If they all used a monorepo, they could coordinate by using code review to discuss their changes, and by talking to each other to decide how to split up work. If they all used their own repo, they’d still have to coordinate. They’d coordinate by talking to each other, and by publishing things like version numbers and API specs.

Either way, 20 teams is manageable. If you have 200 teams, it’s less manageable, and you’ll find that the monorepo approach works less well, and the polyrepo approach works a little bit better. You’ll have to figure out a little more how to coordinate things so that they aren’t broken, but that’s a solvable problem.

There are two big problems that make monorepos harder to use:

1. You have to make decisions about how to structure the code. Monorepos have a lot of code in one place, and if everyone is allowed to put whatever they want where they want, that’s going to be really hard to navigate. There needs to be a team whose job is to decide how to organize the code, and how to enforce that.

2. You have to make decisions about what to do with shared libraries. Shared libraries are used by many parts of the organization. If there are bugs in the shared libraries, there’s a risk that they could cause problems in many parts of the organization. So shared libraries are a risk for your organization, and you need to be careful about who is allowed to make changes to them.

The reason monorepos are bad for organizations with 200+ teams is that you can’t get 200 teams to agree on how to structure their code, and you can’t get 200 teams to agree on who should be responsible for the shared libraries.

The reason monorepos are okay for organizations with 20 teams is that it’s much easier to get 20 teams to agree.

The problem with monorepos is that there are a bunch of decisions that have to be made about how the monorepo works, and if there’s a lot of code, you can’t make those decisions by getting everyone to agree.

Some of the decisions that have to be made are:

- How should the code be organized?

- Who makes the decisions about how the code is organized?

- Who is responsible for the shared libraries?

- What process is used to decide to merge changes into the shared libraries?

- Who makes the decisions about how the build process works?

- Who makes the decisions about how to configure the build process?

- Who makes the decisions about how to configure the test process?

- Who makes the decisions about how to configure the deploy process?

And so on.

If you have a bunch of code and you have to make a lot of decisions about that code, then someone has to be responsible for making those decisions. If the people making the decisions are in charge of the team that has the code, then that’s fine. If the people making the decisions are not in charge of the team, then things can get messy.

A lot of people talk about monorepos as though the whole organization has to agree on things, and that’s not true. If the organization has one big team, and that team has to agree on everything, then that’s fine. If the organization has a bunch of smaller teams, and each team has to make decisions on its own, then that’s also fine. The problem is when you have a bunch of teams in an organization, and the organization is in charge of making decisions about the whole organization’s code. That’s when you run into a lot of problems.

The problem is that the decisions about how the code is organized and how things work are not technical decisions, they’re political decisions. Some people want to have the ability to make those decisions, and other people don’t want to be the people making those decisions. If you’re the person making the decisions, you’ll want to have power, and you’ll be willing to give people the power to make the decisions if you’re going to get to make the decisions. If you’re not the person making the decisions, you’ll want to have power, and you’ll be willing to give people the power to make the decisions if you’re not going to be the person making the decisions.

If you’re the person making the decisions, you’ll want to have a lot of power, because if you have a lot of power, you can make more decisions. If you’re not the person making the decisions, you’ll want to have a lot of power, because if you have a lot of power, you can get the person making the decisions to make the decisions you want to be made.

I keep hearing “tests are the documentation.” It’s a great way to feel like you’re getting two things for the price of one. It feels like a good deal. It feels like a bargain.

And it’s just flat-out wrong.

Tests and documentation serve different purposes. Tests are a way to check that our code is behaving in the way we expect. Documentation is a way to share our expectations with others.

A good test describes one expected behavior, and shows that the code does, indeed, behave that way. A good test says “I expected this, and it was true.”

A good piece of documentation says “you can use this thing to do this.” It may not be true, but that is not documentation’s job.

When tests are wrong, they are broken. And they should be corrected, even if that means changing the way that code behaves, or even removing that code.

The way we handle lies and broken things is very different.

In practice, tests and documentation are even less similar than this.

A piece of documentation may be wrong, but it may also be correct. When it’s correct, you are not certain that it’s correct.

A test is something that checks the code. A piece of documentation is something that helps you understand the code.
