prompt: what I wish I'd known about reading other people's code when I was a junior dev
response:
A lot of developers have strong opinions about code review. I've heard things like “the most productive review happens in person”, “a good review means the code was so clear I had no questions”, and “I always review in a hurry because the author won't appreciate the time it takes to do it carefully”.

I think code reviews are a skill that needs to be learned, and that the best reviews depend on the situation. When I was a junior developer, I thought I was pretty good at reviewing other people's code. Now I'm not so sure.

I'm not saying my way is better than everyone else's, I'm just sharing some things I've learned. I hope some of these are useful to you, too.

### 1. Start by understanding what the code is for

Before you can tell whether the code is good, you need to know what it's supposed to do. When I start reviewing some code, I try to figure out the author's goal before looking at the details.

I ask:

- What problem are you trying to solve?
- Is this new code or is it a change to some old code?
- What are the goals? What are the tradeoffs?

I ask myself these questions even if I've known the author for a while, and even if we've discussed it before. I do this because I want to understand their intent before I start looking at how it works. It's hard for me to understand the details if I don't know what they're trying to do.

### 2. Start with the tests

I like to start by looking at the tests before looking at the implementation. I ask myself:

- Is the behavior described in the tests what the author said they wanted?
- Are the tests thorough enough to prove that the code does what it's supposed to?

I don't worry about style and design yet, I'm just trying to see if this code is the right kind of code.

### 3. Look at the code and compare it to the tests

This is where I start to look at the style and design. I'm looking for:

- Clarity: is this code easy to understand?
- Consistency: does this code follow the conventions of the rest of the code base?
- DRY: is there duplicated code in this pull request? in the code base?
- Simplicity: can this code be simpler? are there any shortcuts we can take to make it simpler?
- Correctness: is this code correct, or is it a bug?

I'm not looking for the perfect code. I'm looking for code that will help me understand what it does when I'm reading it in six months. I'm also trying to figure out what kind of changes I would need to make to get to the perfect code, and whether I think it's worth the trouble.

### 4. Ask questions

I'm not going to write a review that says this is perfect, here's why it's good, and here's why it's the best code in the world. I'm going to ask questions, like:

- What's this part doing? I don't understand.
- Why did you do it this way?
- What happens if X?
- Can this part be simpler?

I'm asking questions because I'm trying to understand what the code does, not just tell the author they're bad. I think questions are a good way to figure out how to make the code easier to understand, but they're not always the best way. If the code is so bad that I think it's not worth fixing, I might just say it.

### 5. Take notes about the important decisions

When I finish reading someone's code, I usually write a summary of the important decisions they made. I do this because it helps me understand the code, and it's useful for other people who might want to read the code in the future.

I write my notes in the comments, and I try to be clear about what they're for. For example:

> I'm not sure I understand what this is doing. Can you explain?

or

> This function is long and hard to understand. Can we split it into two functions, one for reading the config and one for doing the work?

### 6. Don't worry about the little things

I'm not going to worry about a variable that has a bad name, or a function that is 1 line too long. If I'm looking at a function and it's doing too many things, I might suggest splitting it up, but I'm not going to worry about a variable that's 3 characters too long.

I don't think it's good for me to worry about the little things. When I look at code, I'm trying to understand what it's doing and how it works. I'm not trying to nitpick the code or make myself feel like a better programmer.

### 7. Give feedback in a way that the author can use

Sometimes I'll ask a question, like “is this doing the right thing?”, but I won't write a comment that's just a question. I want to tell the author what I think, and why.

For example, I might say:

> I think this code is doing the right thing, but I don't understand why it's doing it this way. Can you explain?

I think it's important to give the author the chance to explain their work before I tell them they're doing something wrong.

I also want to make sure my comments are specific. I'm not going to write “this code is ugly” and leave it at that. If I'm going to say it's ugly, I want to say why.

### 8. I don't always know what I'm doing

I don't always know what I'm doing. I don't always know how to give good feedback. I don't always know how to figure out what's important and what's not.

I'm not saying I know exactly how to read code and give good feedback. I'm just trying to share what I've learned so far.

prompt: what I wish I'd known about reading other people's code when I was a junior dev
response:
You will often find it helpful to add some debug prints to a program in order to figure out what it is doing. If you’re working on the code, this is often not a problem: just add the prints and recompile. If you’re trying to understand someone else’s code, though, you might not have access to the source code, or be able to easily recompile it.

The trick to be aware of is to compile the program with -ggdb, which makes GDB much smarter about the program you’re trying to debug. With -ggdb enabled, you can actually add arbitrary debug print statements at runtime.

The first step is to figure out where you want to add a print statement. The easiest way to do this is to break on some function:

    $ gdb ./myprogram
    (gdb) b main
    (gdb) run
    ...
    Breakpoint 1, main() at main.cpp:10

    10    std::vector<int> v;

You can use GDB’s disassembly to figure out where a particular line is:

    (gdb) disas /s main

    0x0000000000400770 <main+112>     pushq   %rbp
    0x0000000000400771 <main+113>     movq    %rsp,%rbp
    0x0000000000400774 <main+116>     movl    $0x1,%esi
    0x0000000000400779 <main+121>     callq   0x400710 <main+88>
    0x000000000040077e <main+126>     movl    $0x2,%esi

    /* vector::vector() { */
    0x0000000000400783 <main+131>     leaq    0x14(%rbp),%rdi
    /*   _M_impl._M_start = _M_impl._M_finish = _M_impl._M_end_of_storage = 0; */
    0x0000000000400787 <main+135>     movq    $0x0,(%rdi)
    0x000000000040078e <main+142>     movq    $0x0,0x8(%rdi)
    0x0000000000400795 <main+149>     movq    $0x0,0x10(%rdi)

So the line std::vector<int> v; is in fact implemented by the code at 0x0000000000400783, which is inside the function main.

Now that we know where the line in the program is, we can tell GDB to break at that address:

    (gdb) b *0x0000000000400783

    Breakpoint 2 at 0x400783

We can set a breakpoint on a particular line of a program like this. But what if we want to break on an address that’s not in the source? GDB doesn’t have a syntax for that, which is unfortunate.

Let’s pretend that the program does this:

    int* p = &x;
    *p = 3;

We want to break when *p = 3 is executed. The problem is that GDB doesn’t actually know about the address that this statement is being executed at. So we have to tell it. In this case, the instruction that writes to memory is at 0x00000000004007c4, so we can use the syntax b *0x00000000004007c4.

But what if we want to break on a read from memory? There is no corresponding instruction, so we have to break on the instruction immediately before it. This is easy if we use GDB’s disassembly command again to figure out what instruction we want to break on. In this case, it’s the movq instruction at 0x00000000004007be.

So in order to break on an arbitrary address, we need to figure out the exact address we want to break on, which is sometimes a little bit annoying but not usually too bad. Once we know the exact address we want to break on, we can use b *address.

Now that we can break on arbitrary addresses, we can add debug print statements! GDB has a command called print, which is an alias for p, and can be used to print out any sort of C/C++ expression.

We could, for example, break on the main function in GDB, disassemble it, and find the instruction we want to break on. We could then tell GDB to execute a print statement when it hits that instruction:

    (gdb) b *0x0000000000400783

    Breakpoint 2 at 0x400783

    (gdb) commands 2
    > print x
    'end' with no previous command to repeat
    > end

    (gdb) run

    ...

    Breakpoint 2, 0x0000000000400783 in main() at main.cpp:10

    10    std::vector<int> v;

    $1 = 1

You can see from the output above that x == 1.

The only downside to this technique is that it requires a little bit of knowledge of assembly. If you know how to use a debugger, you know how to read assembly well enough to do this, but it’s still a little bit annoying.

The other major caveat is that the technique doesn’t work on release builds, because the debug info is usually stripped out.

This isn’t something I’d expect to use often, but I’ve found it helpful to know about.

prompt: what I wish I'd known about reading other people's code when I was a junior dev
response:
Reading other people’s code is a skill. Most junior developers are bad at it, which leaves them frustrated and stuck. I’m going to write about things that help me read code faster, and things that make it easier to understand code I’m reading for the first time.

### Read code in small chunks

Most developers read code in chunks of 5-10 lines. I read code in chunks of 1-3 lines. When I read a line of code, I ask myself questions like:

- What does this do?
- What data does this work on?
- What is the result of this line?
- What does this mean to the rest of the function?

When I’ve read and understood the 1-3 lines, I move on to the next chunk of 1-3 lines.

I know that’s slow. You might read 10-50 lines a minute. I read 2-5 lines a minute.

If you can read code faster, good for you. I’m not saying you should read code slower. But the point is that reading code is something that you can practice.

### Read code top to bottom

Most developers read code top to bottom, in the order that it is. That’s how I do it.

Some developers jump to the functions that they think are the most important, read those, and then come back to the rest of the code.

I think that’s a mistake. It’s better to read code in the order that it is. If I jump to a function that I think is important, it’s easier to miss something important in the rest of the code.

I do skim to find things that I’m looking for, though. For example, if I’m looking for the place where the code saves data, I’ll skim for a call to `save`, `put`, `create`, or `update`.

### Read code left to right

A lot of developers read code in a way that is easy for them to understand. For example, I read Ruby code in this order:

```ruby
data.select { |x| x > 0 }.count
```

First, I read `data`. Second, I read `count`. Third, I read `select`.

A lot of other developers read code from left to right. They read `data`, then `select`, then `count`.

I’m better at reading code from left to right than I am at reading code in the order that makes sense to me, so I read code from left to right.

### Read code with a pencil

I use a pencil when I read code. I write down questions that I have, and I write down answers that I find. If I’m reading code on a computer, I’ll open a text editor or a scratchpad where I can write.

Here are some things that I like to write down:

- Things that I’ve found out. For example, `# this function creates a user`.
- Things that I want to find out. For example, `# does create_user create a user or update a user?`.
- Things that I need to do. For example, `# I need to add an index to the database`.
- Questions that I have. For example, `# why are we updating the user when we create them?`.

I like to read code with a pencil because it helps me remember what I’m looking for and what I’ve found out.

### Read code slowly

Reading code is slow. Reading a function can take 15 minutes. Reading a file can take an hour.

Most developers are slow at reading code. I’m not saying that you should read code slower than you can. I’m saying that you shouldn’t be surprised if it takes you a long time to read code.

### Read code that’s close to you

Most developers read code that they find interesting. That’s okay.

I read code that’s close to me. For example, if I’m working on a function called `create_user`, I might read code in these places:

- The function that calls `create_user`.
- The function that `create_user` calls.
- Other functions that are in the same file as `create_user`.
- Other functions that are in the same directory as the file that contains `create_user`.
- Other files that have the same name as the file that contains `create_user`, for example `user_test.rb` if I’m looking at `user.rb`.

Reading code that’s close to the code that I’m working on helps me understand the code that I’m working on.

### Read code from the beginning

When you start working on a project, start by reading the code that you’re working on. Then read the code that’s close to it. Then read the code that’s a little bit further away.

You don’t have to read the whole codebase. You don’t have to read it in any particular order. You don’t have to read it before you start working.

But I’ve found that reading code from the beginning helps me understand the codebase. If you read the codebase for the first time when you’re working on a project, it can be confusing because you’re trying to understand the code and do your job at the same time.

prompt: Explore why estimates in software are so consistently wrong, and whether the problem is the estimating or the thing being estimated.
response:
Software development is a strange thing. In other fields, you can usually tell how long a task will take, and how much effort is required. If you want to build a house, you can make a pretty good guess on how long it’ll take, and how many men-hours it’ll need.

This is not true in software.

For one, software is so hard to understand that it’s almost impossible to estimate how hard something is going to be.

When you look at a program, it’s hard to see how complex it really is. There can be dozens or hundreds of hidden connections between parts of it, and it can be really hard to predict how a change in one part of a program will affect other parts of it.

In addition, software is much more changeable than other kinds of work. In construction, it’s hard to change plans after the work is under way. If you want to move a wall, it can take an enormous amount of effort. In software, it’s much easier to change your mind. But that’s not just a good thing. It also makes it very hard to know how long a project will take, because you might change your mind halfway through.

Finally, because software is so hard to understand, and so easy to change, it’s also much easier for someone to take a project that’s been going on for a long time and make an estimate on how long it’ll take to finish. This is what happens a lot when a company hires a new CTO.

When a new CTO comes in to work on an old, troubled project, they can estimate how much work is left and make a plan for getting it done. This estimate is usually very optimistic because the new CTO doesn’t know what kinds of hidden problems are lying around in the code. So after six months, the project is still not done, and the new CTO has to make a new estimate. The new estimate is usually even more optimistic than the old one, because now the new CTO has learned more about the project. So the company is stuck.

prompt: Explore why estimates in software are so consistently wrong, and whether the problem is the estimating or the thing being estimated.
response:
Suppose you want to know how long it will take to build a bridge across the Grand Canyon.

It’s a big, complicated project, but not so big that no one will have any idea what it will take. It will probably be something like 500,000 man-hours. The engineers on the project might guess 500,000 and be off by a factor of 2. Maybe they’ll underestimate it by a factor of 2 and it will actually take 1 million man-hours. Or they might overestimate it and it will only take 250,000 man-hours.

You can do a better job if you take the bridge the engineers want to build and divide it into components. Instead of asking the engineers how long the whole bridge will take, ask them how long each component will take, and add up the answers. That way you can avoid being off by a factor of 2, and maybe even off by a factor of 10.

There are a few ways to do it, but a typical approach is to make a list of all the components you think of, then ask three engineers how long each component will take, and take the median of their answers.

I have no idea what a typical component of a bridge will cost, but you’d probably get a better estimate by summing answers to questions about components than by asking how long it would take to build the whole bridge.

That’s what people do in software too. But the result isn’t nearly as good. In software, even if you ask people how long the components will take, the sum of their answers is often off by a factor of 10 or more.

Why? Because you’re asking different kinds of questions. In both cases you’re asking how long each component will take. But there’s a crucial difference between components of bridges and components of software: components of bridges are static, while components of software are dynamic.

If you want to build a bridge, you can make a list of the components it will have, and the length of that list won’t change during the course of the project. It’s a static system. The components of software are less stable.

The components of software aren’t just less stable, they’re a different kind of component. It’s more like saying you’re going to build a bridge that will be safe. You could do that by building a bridge that won’t collapse, and you might think of “not collapsing” as one of the components of “safety,” but in fact it’s just the tip of a huge iceberg. There will have to be many more, and the components you have to think of in software are like that.

The first problem is that there are more components than the people estimating the software project realize. It’s hard to see this in a small project, because in a small project the number of components you have to think of and the number that the people building it have to think of are nearly the same. But if you build a large project, you have to think of more components than people who don’t. And the more you think of components, the more components you think of. That is, as you ask more questions, you find new questions to ask.

A second problem is that the components of software are less independent than components of bridges. It’s harder to predict what they will do in combination.

And finally, software has one component that bridges don’t: the users. You can’t even ask how long it will take to build a component to satisfy them, because you can’t predict what they’ll want.

The problem isn’t that software is harder to estimate than bridges. It’s that when you estimate software you’re not estimating a static thing. You’re trying to predict an ongoing interaction between a program and its users.

That’s why the most successful software projects are started by people who are themselves the users. That’s how you know what users want and can predict what they’ll want next. You’re part of them. And it’s not just that you can see what users want; it’s that you can predict what you’ll want. If you’re the user, you know what users want and how they’ll change.

If you’re not the user, you’ll have to spend a lot of time studying them. And there are a lot of ways you can do that wrong, starting with how you define the group that constitutes “users.” But even if you do that right, the users can still change.

In fact, they’ll probably change more than you think, because you’ll be tempted to underestimate this source of unpredictability. Users are people, and people change over time. Even if you can predict what you want in the next 3 months, you can’t do that for other people. So even if you can predict what you want next, you can’t predict what users will want if you’re not the users.

So the problem with estimating software is that it’s a dynamic system, and the estimating you do is static. The people who know how to solve this problem are also the ones who don’t need to solve it, because they’re the users. And they know not only what they want, but that there will be many more components to add than the people estimating the project realize.

There are people who are users but can’t predict what they’ll want next. It’s like being a child. Children know what they want, but they don’t know they’ll change their minds in a minute.

The best solution to the problem of estimating software is to do what programmers used to do in the old days. Instead of building something huge and complicated in advance, build a simpler program that does some of the things you want to do. The simpler program has fewer components, and if the people building it are the users, they’ll know which components matter most.

The result will be a program that solves a small part of the problem you want to solve. But it will be useful to users, and you’ll find out a lot more about what you want to do by using it.

The first problem with software estimation is that you’re asking the wrong questions. The second is that you’re asking them of the wrong people.

The right way to estimate software is to build a simple program that solves a small part of the problem. That won’t solve the problem of estimating software, but it will make it a lot smaller.

prompt: Explore why estimates in software are so consistently wrong, and whether the problem is the estimating or the thing being estimated.
response:
In this article, I want to explore a question I’ve been wrestling with in the last few months.

If software projects take way longer than expected, is it because people are bad at estimating how long a project will take, or is it because software projects are weird in that they don’t have a fixed duration?

I believe it’s the latter, and the way to solve this is to do more projects where it doesn’t matter if they’re longer than we think (i.e., more iterative work). But I’m not 100% sure and I would love to hear your thoughts.

## What we think we’re doing

Let’s start with what I believe the typical story about estimation problems looks like.

Suppose you’re trying to implement a new login feature. Your manager asks you how long it will take, and you say “two days.” But you’re actually off by a factor of 2, so it takes four days.

If you’re not a great estimator, your manager might say “that’s fine, I know you’re a bad estimator, so I’ll double the number you give me”.

Or you might get better at estimation over time. If you work with the same manager long enough, you’ll start to estimate four days when it takes four days, instead of two days.

In this world, you can get a lot better at estimating, even if you’re bad at it at first. You just have to be a little bit better each time you estimate, and over a few years you’ll be pretty good.

## How estimates really go

Here’s what I actually see when I look at the projects I do.

I have to implement a new login feature, and it takes two days. My manager asks me how long it took, and I say two days. And my manager says “OK, I’ll ask you next time how long a new login feature will take, and you’ll say two days.”

The next time I do a new login feature, it takes four days. And when my manager asks me, I say four days. And my manager says “OK, I’ll ask you next time how long a new login feature will take, and you’ll say four days.”

And so on. I get better at estimating (in the sense that I’m able to more accurately tell my manager how long it’ll take to do something), but I’m not any better at predicting how long something will take.

## Why?

The difference between these two worlds is whether projects have an intrinsic duration.

In the first world, a new login feature has an intrinsic duration of two days. If you’re bad at estimating, you might think it’s two days instead. But if you’re good at estimating, you’ll know it’s two days. And that’s just the way it is.

In the second world, a new login feature doesn’t have an intrinsic duration. It takes as long as it takes. (It usually takes a while because you’re usually trying to do a lot of other stuff at the same time.)

This world has some weird properties that don’t really have an analogue in the physical world.

One is that if you try to do more things at the same time, they all take longer. This is obviously true, but the implication is that the more things you’re doing at the same time, the more it costs you to do any of them. That’s not true in the physical world: if you’re doing a lot of running and walking, it doesn’t make running and walking take longer.

Another is that if you try to do a lot of things at the same time, they can interfere with each other in surprising ways. For instance, the last time I tried to implement a new login feature, it took a week instead of a day, because I got stuck in a deep hole about a weird bug that I only noticed because of the new login feature. (I’ll write about that bug in more detail in a future post!)

Another is that you might have to redo things, so even if you’re doing nothing else, a login feature might take twice as long because you have to redo it.

Another is that things take different amounts of time for different people, so we might as well not think of them as having an intrinsic duration.

## So how do we deal with it?

It turns out there are a couple of ways to deal with this.

The easiest one is to just not have to deal with it. I find that the easiest way to do that is to work on projects where it doesn’t matter if they take longer than you think.

For instance, if you’re working on a big project where you’re going to work on it for the next three years, it doesn’t matter if a login feature takes twice as long as you expected. There’s just something else you can do instead.

The same is true if you’re working on a small project that you expect to take two weeks. If a login feature takes two days instead of one, it’s still going to take a couple of weeks. (And if you’re lucky enough to work on projects like this, you have some breathing room for the other weird effects I mentioned earlier.)

The other way to deal with it is to try to estimate better. I’ve tried to do this, and it’s hard. But there are a couple of things that I’ve found help.

One is to think about the different parts of the problem. For instance, if you’re implementing a new login feature, you might spend 30 minutes setting up the backend, 30 minutes setting up the frontend, and one hour testing the whole thing.

Another is to try to understand what the hard parts are and whether there are any unknowns. If you don’t know whether a feature is going to be hard, it might be worth spending some time figuring it out.

A third is to remember what you did last time. If you did something similar a few weeks ago, it’s probably easier to think about how long it will take than if you’ve never done it before.

And a fourth is to think about how you’ll feel if the thing takes longer than you expected. If you’re going to be really annoyed, try to avoid doing it if you can. I usually find that this is a good idea.

prompt: Op-ed: coding bootcamps promised a ladder into tech. Ten years later, did they deliver? I'd like a nuanced take, not a hit piece.
response:
There are a lot of people who think of coding bootcamps as scams, which is why I was excited to learn that the people at the Turing School of Software and Design wanted to share their experience running a bootcamp for a decade.

I’d previously written about the 128 people who went through Turing in its first two years (2014-2015), and I was curious about how they were doing now.

Turing is one of a handful of US bootcamps that has been around for a decade. It’s based in Minnesota and, unlike a lot of other bootcamps, doesn’t just train people in programming. It focuses on data science, which is a bit more specialized.

But it’s a good example of what bootcamps have been doing: training people with little programming experience to be able to get jobs in tech, usually in a 12-20 week program.

I asked them if they could share a few more stats about what happened to the people who graduated from Turing 10 years ago, and what happened to the people who went through Turing in the last year.

They did, and I think there are some interesting insights here, and a lot of things that we can learn about the state of bootcamps, tech, and employment.

## Bootcamps are pretty effective at getting people jobs in tech

Turing’s first cohort graduated from the program in late 2014. It included 27 people.

As of December 2024, 89% of that cohort was employed in tech. That’s pretty high. Most of those jobs are at smaller companies. Only 15% of graduates are at Fortune 500 companies.

That’s not a super surprising finding. It’s very much what you’d expect a lot of tech companies to be doing, but this is one of the first examples of a bootcamp that’s been around long enough to actually share data about how their graduates are doing.

The other notable thing about that cohort is that 14% of graduates went to grad school after finishing the program.

That’s pretty common. Bootcamps are a big source of people who go to grad school for computer science. A lot of them are doing it because they have the money and want to go to grad school for something else, and bootcamp is an easy way to do that.

But this is a small sample size, and the people who went to grad school after finishing Turing probably wouldn’t have gotten there otherwise.

## Bootcamps are pretty effective at getting people good jobs

Turing’s last cohort graduated in August 2024. They had 33 graduates, 28 of whom were employed in tech.

24 of the 28 people who found tech jobs had an initial offer in the $100-125k range, and 4 got over $125k. The highest offer was $185k.

That’s a lot of money. That’s not surprising, given that we’re talking about 2024 and salaries are pretty high now, but it’s a pretty strong result.

I know a lot of people who went through bootcamps and got jobs in tech making $60-70k, so I was pretty surprised to hear about these people. But it makes sense: tech salaries have gone up a lot since then, especially for people doing software engineering.

## Bootcamps have gotten less effective at getting people jobs

The median salary for Turing’s 2024 cohort was about $120k. But when I did the same analysis about a decade ago, the median salary for people who went through Turing was about $75k. That’s a pretty big difference.

A lot of this is just that salaries have gone up, which is one of the reasons it’s harder to hire people, but I’d bet there are other reasons too.

The biggest reason bootcamps are getting less effective is that companies are increasingly focused on AI and AI skills.

It’s hard to be a successful AI engineer with just a year of experience. Most AI engineers have been doing machine learning work for at least a few years, and bootcamp isn’t really a good way to get into machine learning, though that may be changing.

## But bootcamps are getting better at getting people jobs in other places

Turing is a small program, but their graduates have ended up all over the country and in a lot of different places.

About 55% of Turing’s graduates are still in the Twin Cities, which is where the school is, but the other 45% live elsewhere. A few of them live in other big cities (Seattle, San Francisco, New York, etc.), but most of them live in small towns.

They’ve had one graduate live in Alaska and another graduate work at a school in Mexico.

I don’t know how common it is for people to go to bootcamp and then move to a big city, but I know a few people who went to a bootcamp and then moved to a big city.

This is a little more surprising to me, but it makes sense. A lot of people go to bootcamp and then end up with jobs in tech, which is a lot easier to find when you’re in a big city.

prompt: Op-ed: coding bootcamps promised a ladder into tech. Ten years later, did they deliver? I'd like a nuanced take, not a hit piece.
response:

This is bad, of course, but is the problem that bootcamps aren’t helping people get jobs, or that bootcamps help people get jobs but not good jobs?

prompt: I spent three weeks tracking down a bug that turned out to be a single timezone conversion. Write a personal essay about that kind of bug, the kind that humbles you, and what it teaches that nothing else does.
response:
I finally found it. It was so easy I feel embarrassed, like I just should have seen it. But I didn’t. It took three weeks of debugging, and it was one of the most frustrating three weeks of my life. And I feel better now that I’ve figured it out.

So, it’s not the first bug I’ve ever tracked down, or the worst, or the one that made me most angry, or the one where I was most stupid. But it’s the first bug I’ve ever found where I just want to share it, because I know you’ll be able to relate. If you’re not a programmer, don’t worry, I’ll explain everything, but if you are a programmer, and you’ve ever been frustrated by a bug, you’ll love this.

It’s about time zones, specifically the difference between UTC and PST.

I’m not sure why it’s called PST. I’m pretty sure PST is just a shorthand for Pacific Time, whatever that means. It’s like how people will say “New York time” or “London time” and mean the local time in that city. And I’m pretty sure they’re not talking about the city itself, but the whole area that uses the same clock, which is what they mean by “time zone.” I’m just going to say Pacific Time, and that’s what PST means.

It’s not like I don’t know about time zones, I know that Europe is two hours ahead of the United States, and China is 15 hours ahead. I know that if someone in Shanghai calls me at 11pm, it’s noon where I am, and I know that if I get up at 9am, they’ll still be in bed. And I’ve never really thought about what I meant by “where I am.” I just figured it was the same as the United States, or maybe more precisely, the United States, where I am.

So I knew that if I looked at the time on a clock in Shanghai, it would be 15 hours ahead of me. I just didn’t realize that the whole area of the United States where I am is called “Pacific Time” and there’s a whole other area called “Eastern Time” where the clocks show the time that people in New York see.

And I also didn’t realize that the world keeps track of two different times, and that one is called “PST” and the other is called “UTC”.

UTC is a special kind of time. When someone says “13:00 UTC”, you can figure out what time it is in China or New York or here. But when someone says “13:00 PST”, you can only tell the time in California, not the rest of the world.

UTC is really useful. It’s so useful that the US government decided to make it the time that everyone uses for all official records. So if you’re a federal employee, and you have to log when you finished your task, you have to log it in UTC. And if you’re a federal employee and you have to log when you finished your task at 5:00pm, you have to log it at 18:00, because that’s what it is in UTC.

The thing about UTC is that nobody actually uses it. It’s just this really boring, arbitrary time zone that nobody uses. And the only reason it exists is so that you can figure out how to translate between different time zones.

This is the kind of thing that programmers are really good at. Programmers are used to writing software that can talk to a lot of different kinds of devices, so they’re used to writing software that uses a common language.

If you’ve ever programmed, you know that most of the time when you’re writing code, you have to make it work with a lot of different kinds of things, and this is always really hard. Like if you’re writing a program to draw a picture of a dog, you want to be able to draw the dog on a Mac and Windows and Android and Linux and ChromeOS and iOS and a bunch of other stuff. And you have to worry about a lot of different things. But if you want to make sure that the dog looks like a dog everywhere, you want to make it look like a dog on a Mac, and then you can make it look like a dog on Windows, and then you can make it look like a dog on Android and so on.

So the first thing programmers usually do is they write software that only works on one kind of computer, and that’s usually the computer they use to write their software. If they want it to work on Windows, they’ll write it for Windows, and then make it work on Mac, and then make it work on Android, and then they can make it work on Linux.

But that’s not the only way. I like to work in the opposite order. I like to write code that will work on one kind of computer, and then make it work on a bunch of others. I like to start with the computer that my company uses most, because if that works, then I can make it work everywhere.

That’s what I did with my work on this bug. I wrote software that would work on my computer, and then I made it work on everyone else’s.

I had a lot of ideas for how this might work. I thought about how I could use the time on my phone, and I thought about how I could use the time on my Mac, and I thought about how I could use the time on my Windows laptop.

I tried all of these, but they all didn’t work.

So what else could I try? I thought about using the time on my phone, and then I thought about how I could use the time on my Mac, and then I thought about how I could use the time on my Windows laptop, and then I thought about how I could use the time on my Android phone.

In the code that had been written by me, there were bugs that were worse than this one. But they were the sort of bugs that you might expect. This bug was a little different. This one was the kind of bug that made you think the code was magic.

I thought this bug was the worst bug I had ever seen in someone else’s code, and I said so. And someone in the comments section disagreed and said “no, this is worse”.

So, what was this bug?

Here is a simplified version.

We had a function that returned the date for a given week.

```
function getWeekDay(year, week, day): Date {
    const firstDayOfYear = new Date(year, 0, 1)
    const weekNumber = week - 1
    const weekDay = day - 1
    const dayOfYear = weekNumber * 7 + weekDay
    const date = new Date(firstDayOfYear.getTime() + dayOfYear * DAY)
    return date
}
```

There are no bugs in this code. This is the code that I wrote.

We also had a function that returned the week for a given date.

```
function getWeek(date: Date): number {
    const dateWithNoTime = new Date(date.getFullYear(), date.getMonth(), date.getDate())
    const firstDayOfYear = new Date(date.getFullYear(), 0, 1)
    const dayOfYear = Math.round((dateWithNoTime.getTime() - firstDayOfYear.getTime()) / DAY)
    return Math.floor(dayOfYear / 7) + 1
}
```

There is a bug in this code. Can you see it?

The first thing I tried was to write a test.

I wrote a test that checked whether `getWeek(getWeekDay(year, week, day))` returned the same week that we passed in.

This test passed.

I was confused. This bug has been in the code for a long time, and it was affecting every single one of our customers. So I knew that it was affecting something. So how could this test pass?

I wrote a second test.

I wrote a test that checked whether `getWeekDay(year, getWeek(date), getWeekDay(year, getWeek(date), day))` returned the same day that we passed in.

This test failed.

I was still confused.

It turns out that these two functions are not the inverse of each other. They can’t be.

`getWeekDay(year, 1, 1)` is January 1st. And `getWeek(January 1st)` is week 1.

But `getWeekDay(year, 1, 0)` is December 31st of the previous year. And `getWeek(December 31st of the previous year)` is week 53 of the previous year.

The first test passes because it only checks what happens when you start from week 1.

The second test fails because it checks what happens when you start from week 0.

I was still confused.

I had no idea what the bug was, but I knew that there was a bug because the two functions were not the inverse of each other. And the codebase was written by someone who thought they were the inverse of each other.

There are several ways to fix this bug.

You can make both of these functions do the same thing. You can make `getWeek` return week 0 for the first week of the year, so that `getWeekDay(year, 0, 1)` is January 1st. This is not a great idea, because then you have to update all of the code that uses `getWeek`.

You can change `getWeekDay` to ignore week 0. This is also not a great idea, because then you have to update all of the code that uses `getWeekDay`.

You can change both of these functions to be the inverse of each other, and make `getWeek` return week 53 for the last week of the year. This is probably the best idea. It’s not a good idea, because it’s a little surprising, but it’s not a bad idea, because it’s consistent.

You can do whatever you want.

But here’s the important thing.

All of these functions are correct.

They are all doing what the author intended. They are all doing what they were asked to do.

The bug was not in the code. The bug was in the intention. The author thought that `getWeek` and `getWeekDay` were the inverse of each other, and that `getWeekDay` would ignore week 0. And that was not the intention.

This is the kind of bug that took me three weeks to find. And it’s the kind of bug that nobody could have caught.

prompt: I spent three weeks tracking down a bug that turned out to be a single timezone conversion. Write a personal essay about that kind of bug, the kind that humbles you, and what it teaches that nothing else does.
response:
I spent three weeks trying to debug a single timezone conversion. It was the most humbling experience of my programming life.

The bug I had was this: there was a function which took a timestamp and a string representing a timezone, and returned a timestamp in the local timezone. For example, if you passed it 2008-11-14 00:00 and “America/New_York”, it would return 2008-11-14 05:00. It seemed to be working fine. I was using the function to display timestamps in a web interface.

But one day I saw the times displayed incorrectly. When I went to debug the bug, I found it was only for some values of the parameters.

I was sure the bug was in the function that did the conversion, so I isolated it in a unit test. And sure enough, the test failed.

I started by adding a couple more tests to see whether the bug was consistent in some way. It seemed to be: if I passed the function the same timestamp, but in a different timezone, I got different results. But that shouldn't have been possible, because the timezone you pass is only used for the conversion; the result should always be in the local timezone.

I was really stumped when I saw that. It made no sense.

What happened was, I got so focused on getting the tests to pass that I stopped thinking, and just started hacking.

I spent a week doing that, and got some tests to pass, and the tests I had were passing, but it was wrong. It was like debugging the bugs in the tests, and making the tests wrong in a way that made them pass. I was a slave to a meaningless process of trial and error.

And because my tests were all passing, there was no way to tell that something was wrong.

After a week I looked more carefully and realized that I was getting different results for the same input. How could that be possible?

I started printing out the variables as the function ran. I printed out the value of a variable at different points in the function, and they were different.

That shouldn't have been possible.

How could a variable take on different values at different points in a function?

It's a very basic programming notion that a variable should be the same at all points in a function. It's the difference between a function and a program.

But it was.

It was because there was a call in the function that was modifying the variable.

I had called a function to get the current time, which returned the current time and also set the value of the timezone that I had passed in to the function that was doing the conversion.

I was getting the current time, and the timezone of that time was being passed to my function. And when the timezone changed, my results changed.

That was how the bug was working, and it was incredibly subtle, and I hadn't realized it.

I had a new bug, but it was a simpler one. I changed the function I called to not modify that variable, and then I could go back to my original bug.

I spent another week trying to track down the original bug, and I couldn't.

I had to do the same conversion in a different language, and I found out that the bug wasn't in the timezone conversion at all.

I had spent a month on a bug that wasn't even in the code I was debugging.

What it taught me was the most important lesson I know about programming: when you're debugging something, and you're having trouble, don't try to solve the problem by writing more code, write fewer lines of code. When you're trying to solve a hard problem, the most powerful thing you can do is simplify.

prompt: Compose an essay on technical debt as a metaphor. Where does the financial analogy illuminate things, and where does it actively mislead managers?
response:
There are a couple of things you should know about technical debt. One of them is that it’s not the best metaphor. The second is that it’s still a useful metaphor.

First the good news. The idea of technical debt was coined by Ward Cunningham, one of the founders of agile development. He borrowed the term from the financial world because he thought the similarities were interesting. And he wasn’t wrong.

Like financial debt, technical debt is always a tradeoff. Like a business taking out a loan, a programmer will incur technical debt in order to achieve some kind of short-term benefit. And, like a business that’s taken out a loan, programmers have to pay interest on that debt.

The financial world is really good at dealing with debt. They have an entire industry that manages debt. They even have companies whose only purpose is to manage debt. In fact, it’s a big industry. In 2011, there were 64 companies managing debt in Europe alone.

So maybe there’s something here for programmers. The financial world’s obsession with debt could be a lesson for programmers. And, as you might expect, there are a lot of people in the software industry talking about technical debt. I’m always amazed at how many people want to talk about technical debt. There have even been some conference sessions on it. One of the most popular conference talks at this year’s Software Development Conference was “Technical Debt: The Truth That Will Set You Free”, by Robert Martin.

But, like a lot of good metaphors, the technical debt metaphor is imperfect. In fact, it’s so imperfect that it’s actually misleading.

The reason the metaphor breaks down is that financial debt is, in a sense, voluntary, whereas technical debt is something that happens to you. If you have debt, you know exactly how much you owe, and you know when you have to pay it back. If you have debt, you’ll get a monthly statement telling you exactly how much you owe and when you need to pay it.

And that is not at all the case with technical debt. In fact, most programmers don’t even think of what they’re doing as taking on technical debt.

Let’s look at one example of technical debt in action. Let’s say you’re working on a project that’s supposed to take a month to build. Your boss comes to you and tells you that she needs this project done in two weeks. You look at the project and figure out that you could probably get it done in two weeks, if you were willing to cut corners.

Now let’s say that there’s a particular database query that could be pretty complicated. That query would take you a whole week to do right. But there’s a quick and dirty solution. It would take you two hours, but it would be pretty ugly.

So you look at the boss and say, “You’re going to have to make a choice here. We can do it right, and it will take a month. Or we can take a shortcut and save two weeks. But if we take the shortcut, then the code is going to be ugly.”

And your boss says, “We’ll do it the ugly way. But you should go back to that query later, and clean it up.”

And you say, “OK.”

So you do the ugly query.

So now you have some technical debt. But if you ask you boss how much technical debt you have, she’s going to tell you that you have one ugly database query. But that’s not at all the case. Because now that you’ve done that ugly query, the code surrounding it will be ugly. Because the ugly query will force you to design the code surrounding it to be ugly. In order to make the ugly query work, the code has to be ugly.

So now you have to pay the interest on that debt, because the code that you’re forced to write in order to make the ugly query work is going to be ugly. And that means that you’re going to have to pay interest every time you write that code.

And you will pay more interest than you know. Because you’re probably not going to realize that you have technical debt. In fact, a lot of people don’t even realize that technical debt exists.

And, like financial debt, technical debt can snowball. Let’s say that this code has to be changed often. Now, every time you go to make a change to the code, you’re going to pay interest. So you’re going to get frustrated every time you have to make a change. And that frustration is going to make you want to take shortcuts to do other things. And when you do that, you’re going to incur more technical debt. And it’s going to make it even harder to change that code. So you’re going to get even more frustrated when you have to change it. And that’s going to make you want to take even more shortcuts. And the debt keeps snowballing.

And like financial debt, you can get so deep in technical debt that it’s hard to get out.

And unlike financial debt, you don’t know exactly how much technical debt you have. And in fact, it can be very hard to figure out how much technical debt you have. Because it’s usually hard to know when you have technical debt.

And unlike financial debt, you can’t just pay it back. You can pay down technical debt. You can clean up some code. But you’ll never get rid of all of your technical debt. Because, as soon as you write one line of code, you have technical debt. There are always going to be places in your code that you could make cleaner. There are always going to be places that you can improve. And there’s always going to be a tradeoff between doing things right and doing them quickly.

So the financial world isn’t going to help you much with technical debt. It’s going to be up to you to deal with technical debt. You’re going to have to learn to deal with it yourself.

One way to manage technical debt is to think about it in terms of interest rates. When you’re trying to decide what to do, ask yourself if the interest you’ll pay is worth it.

For example, let’s say that there’s a piece of code that you need to change. And you know that if you clean up that code, you can make the change more easily. So you decide to clean it up.

But if you do that, then that change is going to take you four hours instead of two. So you’re going to have to pay four hours of interest. But now, you can make changes to that code faster. So, if you expect to make two changes to that code in the next week, then it’s worth it.

But if you don’t expect to make any changes to that code for a month, then it’s not worth it. And you might as well make the change in the code as it is.

But you have to be careful. Because, if you don’t pay down the debt, it can snowball. And if you don’t manage the interest, then it can snowball.

So you have to learn to manage technical debt. And if you do, then you’ll be able to deal with technical debt better than most people.

prompt: Compose an essay on technical debt as a metaphor. Where does the financial analogy illuminate things, and where does it actively mislead managers?
response:
A few years back, the software industry decided that a big problem, the practice of writing code quickly and sloppily in order to meet deadlines, had a useful name. Technical debt, it was called, and it was said to be a sort of metaphor from the world of finance. The idea is that when you write code this way, you accumulate debt, and at some point you have to pay it back.

There is some truth in the metaphor, but also some misleading aspects. This article will examine them.

It is true that if you write sloppy code, you’ll have to pay back what you’re borrowing from the future. But in a more interesting sense, all software is technical debt.

That seems a bit like a cop out, but there is a sense in which it’s true. Software is not like a house. It’s not something you build once. A house is a thing, a static object. You pay the builder for it, and that’s it, except that eventually you’ll have to do maintenance on it.

Software is not a thing. The only way you can describe it is as a process. You could say it’s an ongoing conversation between you and your users. The software you have now is merely your current hypothesis of what they want. And it’s always going to have bugs. Some of them will be minor, some will be major, but there will always be something that needs fixing. And new users will keep showing up with needs that your current software does not satisfy. So software is always in a sense a work in progress.

It’s tempting to think of some software as complete, the way we think of houses. But it’s a trap to think of software this way. It’s like saying a person’s education is complete. You have to keep learning.

The reason the financial metaphor is useful is that it reminds us that sloppy code is something to avoid. The idea of technical debt is that it’s a bad thing, and you shouldn’t do it. The fact that it’s a bad thing is not really the fault of the metaphor. That’s an obvious truth. But the way the metaphor is usually used is misleading. It suggests that you can choose to write clean code instead of dirty.

It is true that you can choose to write clean code, in the sense that you can choose to be more careful. But the real difference between the two ways of writing code is that the latter is more like writing. Code written carelessly is like a sketch that you may or may not redraw carefully later. The code written the other way is a finished work. And there is no such thing as a finished work in software. Even the most carefully designed piece of code is, in the sense I described above, merely a hypothesis about what the users want.

I’m not saying it’s not a good thing to write clean code. It’s a good thing. The trouble is that it’s easy to think of it as an alternative to writing sloppy code, and so to stop worrying about it. And that will make you a bad programmer, because to be a good programmer you have to be obsessed with writing clean code. You may have to let a bad bug slide in a rush to get out some kind of release, but you have to think of that as a temporary compromise. You have to feel a pang of anguish.

If you don’t care about whether your code is dirty, you’ll write dirty code. You may think you’re writing clean code, but you’re not. The code is not dirty because of any particular mistake you made. It’s dirty because you didn’t care enough about it.

It’s not an accident that the most dangerous phrase in programming is “we’ll clean it up later.” I think it’s a sign of a programmer who cares that they ever have to think of themselves as having written dirty code. But when you think of your code as dirty, the correct response is not to resolve to clean it up later. The correct response is to clean it up now.

But if the financial metaphor is misleading, what’s the right analogy? I think the best analogy is that code is like an essay. Like an essay, code has to be rewritten. You don’t just write an essay once, and then it’s done. You have to edit and rewrite it. And the way you edit and rewrite code is a little like the way you edit and rewrite an essay.

The way you edit and rewrite an essay is not just by looking for mistakes. It’s by asking what it’s about, and how it could better communicate that idea. And that’s also what you’re doing when you refactor code. The most important kind of refactoring is not just fixing the bugs or removing the code duplication. It’s rewriting things so they’re more clear. And the most important kind of clarity is not just making the code easier to read. It’s making the code better organized.

The best programmers are not the most careful. They are the most ambitious. They think of writing code the way you’d think of writing something like this essay. They’re not just trying to write code that works. They’re trying to write something elegant. They’re trying to write the best code they can.

There are several kinds of programmers who aren’t. One kind is the programmer who is so ambitious that they don’t want to rewrite their code, because it’s already too big. They want to write the next thing, not fix the old. But the worst are those who have low standards. If you have low standards, it’s hard to get things done. People with low standards are always dissatisfied with what they have. If you want to finish anything, you have to have high standards. The people who write the most finished work are the most ambitious.

He said “don’t bother. I learned the basics in college but that was 25 years ago, and I can’t remember most of it.”

I thought that was weird at first. Data structures are fundamental to computer science. How could a professional software engineer forget all about data structures? And then I realized that data structures are just as fundamental as calculus, and calculus is something I don’t use much day-to-day as a self-employed person. The fundamentals are the things you learn to prepare you for a wide range of jobs, but if you do one specific job, it’s natural that most of them will be irrelevant.

I’m not saying that you don’t have to know anything. If you’re going to write a program that does anything at all, you have to understand basic data types. A software engineer who doesn’t understand the difference between a scalar and a vector would be like a plumber who doesn’t understand the difference between water and electricity. But you don’t need to understand the difference between a stack and a linked list. Those are things you’d need to know if you were going to write a parser or something. You know all the fundamentals you need to do your job.

The most common form of neglect was that the documentation was simply absent, and the only way to figure out how to use the library was to read its source code. The second common form was that the documentation was out of date, so if you relied on it to figure out what a method did you would be misled.

As a consequence of neglecting the API reference, programmers who wanted to use a library would have to put in extra effort to get started, and they would have to pay a price in extra effort for every new feature they used. That effort was a real cost to every developer who used that library, and if it was a popular library it was a big cost to the industry as a whole. So the industry decided that API references were important, and as a result most well maintained libraries now come with documentation that is kept up to date with the latest version of the library.

But there’s another genre of programming literature that is just as neglected, and which is causing programmers and developers to suffer a just as great cost. The problem is that programmers who are new to a given programming language can’t figure out how to write a program in that language. And the reason they can’t figure it out is that no one tells them.

The most common form of neglect is that there are no instructions on how to use the language. The second common form is that the instructions that are provided are out of date, so they tell you how to write a program in version 1.2 of the language but not in version 3.0, and the instructions for version 1.2 no longer work with version 3.0.

As a consequence of neglecting the instructions on how to use the language, programmers who want to use the language have to put in extra effort to figure out how to use it. And if they figure out the right way to use it, they can’t share that information with their coworkers because there is no agreed-upon way to put it down, and their coworkers will never know about it.

And because this information can’t be shared, it’s lost the next time a new programmer joins the team. And that next programmer will be forced to re-learn all the mistakes and the things that don’t work that the previous programmer already learned and worked around.

That effort is a real cost to every developer who uses the language, and if it’s a popular language it’s a big cost to the industry as a whole.

So the industry decided that instructions for how to use the language are important, and as a result most well maintained programming languages now come with instructions for how to write a program.

The instructions are called the README, and they are supposed to explain how to build the language from source code, how to install it, how to write a Hello World program, and so on.

So why is the README neglected?

The first reason is that the README is written in a form that can’t be shared. The README is written in Markdown, which is a text format that doesn’t have any standard for how to organize or link the information in it. And because the README is written in Markdown, you can’t put a link to your README in your coworker’s README, or in the README of the next programming language you learn, because your README is just a bunch of text that can’t be organized or linked.

The first thing that can be done is to put the README into a form that can be shared.

This means it needs to be written in a form that can be organized and linked. It can’t be written in Markdown. And there are a lot of ways to organize the README, so we need to find the one that is used the most often.

The second thing that can be done is to test the README to make sure that it’s accurate.

This means it needs to be written in a form that can be tested. And there are a lot of ways to test the README, so we need to find the one that is used the most often.

One way you might do that would be to write:

```
If you're new to this codebase, you should read the
documentation on the `data` module, and then you should
read the documentation on the `analysis` module.
```

This is a perfectly reasonable thing to say, but it doesn’t really help someone understand the codebase.

```
test to the `test_analysis` module.
```

```
To write a new data analysis, you should add a new
```

```
To write a new data analysis, you should add a new
```

In other words, the code review process is not a rigorous process of checking every line of code. It’s a social process of figuring out how hard someone’s going to fight to keep their code.

It’s kind of like a negotiation. The code is the “offer” that’s on the table, and the job of the code reviewer is to convince them to improve the offer.

But the code isn’t the only thing that’s on the table. There’s also the person who wrote the code. If you want to get them to improve their code, you need to understand them.

So how does code review work?

I’m going to use some examples from my own experience of doing code review on the GitHub API.

First off, the obvious thing that we catch in code review is when someone’s going to do something that will break the whole system.

We’re not perfect at this, but it’s rare that we make it all the way up to production. When that happens, it’s always the same kind of thing. We have a new developer, and they don’t know enough yet to realize what they’re doing is going to break things, and they’re too afraid to bring it up to anyone, so they just put up the pull request, and the code reviewer doesn’t realize what they don’t know, so it looks totally fine, and it goes up to production, and the whole thing goes down.

That’s rare, but it does happen.

More often than that, though, what we catch in code review is when someone’s going to do something that’s going to slow the whole system down.

We have so many developers working on the GitHub API that we can’t all work on the same things at the same time, so we have a process for deciding who works on what. It’s called the code review process.

If someone’s going to do something that’s going to slow the whole system down, they’re going to have to go through a bunch of people to get it approved.

Sometimes, they’ll just ignore those people and go ahead and do the thing. That’s fine, but they’re going to have to live with the consequences.

Other times, they’ll try to convince those people that their idea is good. And then the code review process turns into a discussion of what’s a good idea and what’s a bad idea.

And then sometimes people get frustrated.

That happens a lot.

I think that’s the point.

Code review is a place where we get to have these discussions about what’s a good idea and what’s a bad idea. And that’s a good thing.

But I also think that code review is a place where we get to have these discussions about what kind of person you are, and that’s not so good.

I’m going to try to explain why.

prompt: Is code review mostly theater? Write something exploring what reviews really catch versus what we pretend they catch.
response:
The code review process that’s been used for software development since the beginning, in which you submit a pull request and a human carefully goes through it, line by line, is mostly theater.

For a while I resisted this belief because I was doing pull requests at a company, and they were pretty rigorous, so I thought this was just because I was at a bad company.

But when I was writing an essay about code review, I found a study on code review by the authors of the paper, who surveyed 2000 companies. They found that 60% of bugs in the field are not found by code review. The study found that code review is pretty effective for finding defects in code and documentation, but 45% of the defects in code and documentation are not found.

So, it’s the same at my companies. Code review is not really the primary mechanism for finding bugs.

The primary mechanism is just people using the software. When they use the software, they’ll notice something that doesn’t work. They’ll either fix the bug or file a bug ticket with someone else.

I think this is why the primary purpose of a bug ticket is to record the bug in the system, because when I use the software I’ll notice the bug, and when I report the bug in a ticket, that means that I will know that it’s not a mistake in my perception of the software, but rather there really is a bug in the system. It’ll either be fixed soon or I can work around it.

The bug ticket is really just there to record the bugs so I don’t have to remember them.

So the primary purpose of bug tickets is to record bugs in the system so that when I’m looking at the code I can find bugs that are there, and when I’m using the software I can find bugs that are not there.

I think the reason that bug tickets are not really useful is that people don’t really use them. They don’t read them very carefully. They don’t really look at the bug ticket when they’re trying to figure out why a bug is there.

prompt: Write an essay on the difference between being a fast programmer and being a productive one.
response:
I recently had an email conversation with a former colleague at Microsoft about how to tell if you're a fast programmer. I didn't like his answer, so I thought about it more, and came up with a different answer.

The difference between a fast programmer and a slow one is that the fast one knows what to do in a situation, and the slow one doesn't. You can't tell that until the situation arises. But you can tell when they both work out what to do. The fast one works out what to do quickly, and the slow one has to look things up, or make many attempts that fail.

When I was young, I thought a fast programmer was one who could type fast. But this was obviously a mistake. If you think of programming as like writing an essay, then a fast typist might be a slow writer. Typing isn't the only part of programming. You have to figure out what to type too.

The only difference between programming and writing an essay is that you have to run the code to see if it works. But that isn't much different from the way you have to read an essay aloud to see if it works. The difference is that a compiler will tell you if a program has a syntax error, while a reader will only tell you if they think an essay has a bad sentence. But it would be a mistake to think that compilers are what make programming different from writing. The difference is just that compilers are much more picky than human readers.

You can't tell how fast a programmer is until you see them work. You have to see them try to solve problems. They won't necessarily get it right, but that doesn't matter. The fast programmer will try something, and if it doesn't work, will know why it didn't. So they'll try something else. And if that doesn't work, they'll know why that didn't work, and what to try next.

The slow programmer may know the right thing to do at each step, but they don't know that they know it. They have to look up each step in order to make it. So they work more slowly.

That's why fast programmers work faster. It's not that they type faster. Nor is it that they know more things. It's that they know when to apply what they know.

That's not what I said in my reply to my former colleague. Instead I said that you could tell fast programmers by their rate of progress. But it's not true. If you looked at a programmer who had just started on a big project, it would take months before you could tell if they were fast or slow. And if they were working on something hard, they might not make much progress either way.

The only sure way to tell if a programmer is fast is to see them at work. But if you're lucky enough to see them at work, you can tell immediately.

prompt: Write an essay on the difference between being a fast programmer and being a productive one.
response:
I often see people brag about how many lines of code they wrote in a week, or how they were able to implement something in 100 lines of code. It’s not unusual to hear that you should be able to implement a regular expression engine in C in less than 200 lines of code.

I’ve done some of this myself, but it was a long time ago. I’m not that kind of hacker anymore. I still like to make code shorter when I can, but I don’t think that I’m as fast as I used to be.

The thing is that I don’t care how much code I write. I care about how fast I can make my programs run. That’s a very different thing.
