The script was supposed to convert a list of names into a different format. It only took 12 lines of code, but I spent a few hours trying to make it shorter. In the end I was able to cut the length in half. It was not worth the effort.

When you spend a long time working on a program, you learn a lot about how it works. Then you might find a way to make it run faster, or use less memory. That takes time. But you’ll never get there if you don’t write the program first.

I used to write code as fast as I could. I think that was because I wanted to get my projects done as soon as possible. I also wanted to impress people. It takes a lot of work to write fast. I spent a lot of time making sure that I could write code as fast as possible. But I also spent a lot of time trying to understand the code that I wrote.

The truth is that it’s important to write fast, because it’s so much fun. But I don’t think that writing fast will ever be a virtue again, unless you’re trying to impress someone. If you have a project that takes a long time, you should not try to write it as fast as you can, unless you can afford the time that it takes.

I think that it’s important to write as fast as you can when you’re learning a new language. It’s also important when you’re trying to learn something. That’s when you get the most out of the experience.

If you want to write fast, there are a few things that you need to learn:

- How to write code that is easy to understand.

- How to write code that is easy to modify.

- How to write code that is easy to debug.

I think that there are a few things that you need to do to write fast. You need to learn the language well enough that you can use it without thinking about it. Then you need to have a good idea of what you want to do before you start writing.

prompt: Write an essay on the difference between being a fast programmer and being a productive one.
response:
I've spent a lot of time recently thinking about productivity and software development. There are many kinds of productivity in software development, but I'm thinking about the most basic: the amount of useful code you can write per day.

I've noticed a big difference between the two qualities that people tend to think of as the best predictors of programming productivity: intelligence and coding speed. Intelligence helps, but the best coders I know are not the fastest. They may not even be quick enough to qualify as fast.

But they're very productive. They can produce a lot of useful code in a week. The reason is that they understand what they're working on. They have a clear mental model of the system they're building and its role in the greater world.

This is not merely a matter of intelligence, although it certainly helps to be smart. It's more a matter of focus and concentration. The most productive coders are like a laser beam. They don't have many ideas, and they stick to those they do have. They may not be smart enough to know how to do the best thing, but they do the right thing.

I think this is why the most productive people are often so unfashionable. They're always doing something simple, because it's the right thing to do. And the only thing more unfashionable than doing something simple is doing something simple on purpose.

It's hard for people who do this to understand how they get things done. They're working so hard that it seems like it ought to take a lot longer. The people around them are probably working just as hard, but not so hard.

But working hard isn't enough. It's more like working a lot of hard things than hard work. You need to choose the right problems and solve them well.

For programmers, this means having a clear idea of what they're working on and not getting distracted. The people I've been working with this year have taught me a lot about this.

I've spent my whole career learning to program. I didn't realize how much work it would be to learn this kind of productivity.

prompt: Argue that the hardest part of distributed systems isn't the distribution, it's the fact that you can no longer ask 'what is the current state?' and get a single answer. Aim it at backend engineers who know the basics but haven't been burned yet.
response:
I spent the last two days in Austin at a conference on distributed systems design. It was a great conference, and I highly recommend it to anyone in a similar role as me. A bunch of people who’ve done a bunch of hard things got together to talk about it. I’m still digesting it, but I wanted to post a few of the things that came out of it.

My take: The hardest thing about distributed systems is not that you need to distribute things, it’s that you can’t ask “what is the current state?” anymore.

In a normal web server, you can ask any process what the current state is, and if you just do it in the same transaction as the change, you get a consistent answer. And then you don’t have to think about it anymore.

In a distributed system, you need to think about it a lot more.

For example, when you read a value from a key-value store, what do you get? Is it the last value you wrote to a local replica? Is it a majority of replicas? Is it the most recent write, which might be on some server you haven’t synced with yet? Is it a value from a server that’s been dead for a week? Are you going to read from an old snapshot, or will you block until you have the latest value?

What if you want to update a value based on its previous value? Is that an atomic update? Is it possible that you get an old value and overwrite someone else’s update?

What if you want to update several keys at once, or read them at the same time? Do you guarantee that those are all atomic? Can you read the value of a key and then update it, atomically?

In a web application, you often just ignore these problems. But in a distributed system, you need to think about them and make sure you solve them, because you can’t ignore them.

prompt: Argue that the hardest part of distributed systems isn't the distribution, it's the fact that you can no longer ask 'what is the current state?' and get a single answer. Aim it at backend engineers who know the basics but haven't been burned yet.
response:
Suppose you’re building an app to manage a user’s shopping list. Each user has one shopping list, and it’s just a simple JSON object. The first version is trivially simple: one machine, one process, one database.

Now suppose you want to move to a more distributed architecture, for performance or whatever reason. That’s fine, and we can do it in a couple of ways. The first way is to use a load balancer to distribute reads and writes to the shopping list among a set of servers.

The problem with this is that if a read hits a different server than a write, then the read might be out of date. This problem is usually called “eventual consistency.”

Another way to distribute reads and writes is to have a central database that keeps a single source of truth, and multiple servers to distribute reads and writes, with a replication layer that ensures the data is replicated to each of them. This is a good idea, but it also means your replication layer is a single point of failure.

Suppose we have two servers. One takes writes and the other takes reads. If the writes-only server fails, then nobody can write anything. If the reads-only server fails, then nobody can read anything. So we’ll add a third server that’s a hot backup to both.

Now when the reads-only server fails, the third server takes over. When the writes-only server fails, the third server takes over. We’re more resilient, but it’s not enough.

Now we have four servers. Two take reads and the other two take writes, and if either one in a pair fails, then the other one takes over.

The reason I’m going through this exercise is that this is a very simple example of the kind of thing you need to think about when you move from a single-server architecture to a distributed architecture. But if you’ve done this, it’s probably not hard. It’s not obvious how to scale it up to hundreds or thousands of servers, but there’s a lot of literature and open source software that you can use to solve it.

I think that’s the easy part. The hard part is that you can no longer answer “what is the current state of the system?”

In the first version of the shopping list manager, there was a single source of truth. There was a database, and it had one copy of each user’s shopping list, and it was always up to date. The process kept the data in memory, but it wasn’t the source of truth.

If you want to know what the current state of the system is, then you just query the database.

In the second version of the shopping list manager, the state of the system is distributed across multiple servers, and different servers may have different views of the state. That’s not too bad, because the central database is the single source of truth.

If you want to know what the current state of the system is, then you query the database.

In the third version of the shopping list manager, the state of the system is distributed across multiple servers, and different servers may have different views of the state. It’s also possible that some servers are offline. It’s not always obvious whether the state is consistent across servers.

If you want to know what the current state of the system is, you either ask the servers and hope they’re consistent, or you hope they’re all consistent. That second option might not be possible.

I’m sure we could go on with this. The fourth version might be a multi-datacenter system, where the different datacenters each have a replica of the database. There might be a single source of truth per datacenter, but the replicas might not always be in sync, so now it’s not obvious which datacenter is the source of truth.

The fifth version might be a system that allows multiple sources of truth. If a datacenter loses connectivity to the rest of the world, it can still accept writes, but those writes won’t get replicated. Eventually, the rest of the world might get writes, and we might have to merge the conflicting writes.

The sixth version might be a system that allows multiple sources of truth at the same time, and we can’t merge them. In that case, the users need to resolve the conflicts.

The point is that as soon as you start thinking about distributed systems, there is no longer a single source of truth. The state of the system is distributed, and you may not be able to tell what it is.

prompt: Argue that the hardest part of distributed systems isn't the distribution, it's the fact that you can no longer ask 'what is the current state?' and get a single answer. Aim it at backend engineers who know the basics but haven't been burned yet.
response:
In my last post, I claimed that the hardest problem in distributed systems isn’t the distribution, it’s the question of what the current state is.

This is a claim that I’m still working on justifying, but here is one example:

The first thing that many people learn about distributed systems is the CAP theorem, which states that you can have either consistency or availability but not both (in the presence of network partitions). This claim turns out to be misleading, and it comes from a misunderstanding of what consistency means.

Consider the following system:

Every so often, all of the servers exchange messages so that they agree on the current state.

Between the synchronizations, when a server gets a write request, it updates its local state and then writes to all the other servers in the cluster.

The other servers may reject that write if it conflicts with a write that they already applied.

Every server returns a success to the client if its own write succeeds.

This protocol is called “eventual consistency”, and it’s the reason why most of NoSQL is “not actually SQL.”

The problem with eventual consistency is that, because the servers can be out of sync, you can’t answer questions like this one:

You’re building a website that shows users all of the things that other users have written about them. One day, you notice that, occasionally, a user will complain that they haven’t seen one of their own posts.

You dig in and you see that the database does, in fact, contain this post. But the webserver that served the page didn’t see it yet.

How do you fix this?

With eventual consistency, the answer is: you don’t know when to expect a write to show up on all servers, so you can’t answer the question “have I seen everything that has been written?” So you just wait a bit.

If you make the database more consistent, you can make this bug go away:

Eventually consistent database

If you use a database that always lets you read the latest version of a record, you can guarantee that a user will always see their own posts.

That sounds like it works, but it’s not.

What happens if a user gets disconnected, and they write something, and they write something else while they’re offline?

Now, if the first write arrives before the second, the database will tell the user’s second write that it conflicts with the first. The user will have to reconcile the two writes by hand.

But that isn’t right! The user’s two writes don’t really conflict! If you look at the user’s actions in the order that they did them, the first write comes first, the second write comes second, and the user never sees that the first write conflicts with the second.

This is called causality: one action causes another. If you know that an action caused another, and you also know that the first action happened, then the second one has to happen, too.

So the real solution to the problem of people not seeing their posts is this:

Causally consistent database

If a user is disconnected and writes something, the server will wait until it knows that the write succeeded before it lets the user write anything else.

But the write isn’t really done until it can’t be rolled back anymore. This means that the write has to be replicated enough times that it’s guaranteed to survive the failure of some number of servers.

So if you use a causally consistent database, and you wait until your write is replicated enough times to survive some number of server failures, you will never run into the problem of people not seeing their own posts!

But you have to wait until the write is replicated!

And now you run into the CAP theorem. In the presence of a network partition, it’s not possible to write to enough servers that the write will always succeed.

prompt: I learned to program on a TI-83 in algebra class in 2004. I want a personal essay about how the first language you learn shapes how you think forever, using that as the starting point.
response:
In algebra class in 2004 I was handed a TI-83 for the first time. It was like the computer from Jurassic Park. I was instantly hooked.

I taught myself to program it in 2 hours, then went home that night to write a game. I played it the next day and got the high score. I was the best in the world.

I spent 10 hours a day on it for the next year, and eventually wrote a game engine and an operating system, and a bunch of other stuff I don’t remember. But the first program that was so much better than the others that it was worth remembering? It was a chess program.

I made it in 2 days.

It was good. Not great, but good. I was a 1500-rated chess player, and it beat me 4 to 1 in one game. I was so excited that I made it into a game you could download, so that my friend could play it.

I don’t remember the exact code, but it’s probably something like this:

```
for each move I can make
    if I can capture a piece
        take the piece
    if I can checkmate
        mate
    if I’m not going to get checkmated
        do the move
```

A few years later, I made an even better chess program, with a minimax algorithm that was 50x faster. But I’m not sure how important that was. My original algorithm was the first one I’d ever written, and I don’t think I would have written it the same way later in life.

I wrote my first operating system in the same style:

```
for each process
    run it
```

I wrote the game engine for the game I spent 6 months on the same way:

```
for each entity
    update it
```

And so on.

A year later, after making a bunch of bad operating systems and game engines, I got bored of making them. I wanted to do something else. I wanted to do music.

I wrote a music player in a way I had never written anything before:

```
while playing music
    if the song is done
        go to the next song
```

The first time I wrote it, I couldn’t believe it worked. I thought that music had to be like a game or an operating system.

But it wasn’t. It was something else, something entirely new.

I didn’t know how to explain the difference. So I asked someone.

Their answer was: you’re a bottom-up programmer. I’m a top-down programmer.

Bottom-up is like building a house. You make the foundation, then you put the walls on top, and then the roof, and then you move in. You start from the bottom, and you work your way up.

Top-down is like building a tree. You start at the top, and you branch off, and you branch off again, and again, and again, until you get to the bottom and you stop.

I knew what bottom-up was, because I’d been doing it my whole life. But I’d never done it on purpose.

Now I could.

I made a tree of how I thought computers worked.

I started at the top with hardware, and I branched off into memory, and I branched off into RAM and hard drives, and I branched off into the CPU, and I branched off into the registers, and I branched off into the registers I could use.

It was so much fun. I’d never done that before, so I had no idea how easy it was. It was so fast.

I didn’t know any other way to program, so I used it for everything.

It’s the style I use to this day. I’m still a top-down programmer.

My first chess program wasn’t a bad way to program. But it was a different way.

prompt: Make the case against 100% test coverage, written as if for a team that just adopted it as a KPI.
response:
There was a time when we would write unit tests only for critical code paths. But we are a big believer in unit tests, so we wanted to move up in the world. We wanted to do better. So we decided to strive for 100% unit test coverage.

After a couple of years we achieved our goal, and we still have 100% test coverage on our code base. But we are also here to tell you that striving for 100% test coverage is bad for you. It makes you less happy and your code worse.

We are not against unit testing, just against striving for 100% test coverage.

## Why we wanted 100% unit test coverage

The reason we wanted to achieve 100% unit test coverage was not because we wanted to write unit tests for everything. We were already doing that. The reason we wanted to have 100% test coverage was because we thought it was a good KPI.

We wanted to have a simple KPI that we could track and that we could all work towards. If we had 100% test coverage, we knew we had unit tests for everything. We also knew that if test coverage went down, it was a sign that someone had deleted some tests or not written new ones for new code.

## The problem with striving for 100% test coverage

When you set out to achieve 100% test coverage, you will have a lot of success. But there is always a few stubborn classes that won’t yield to your tests, and that is where you start to make bad tradeoffs and compromises to achieve 100% coverage.

There are two ways you can get away from the goal of 100% test coverage. The first way is to change your definition of “test coverage”. The second way is to ignore the last few percent.

### Changing your definition of test coverage

The most common trick is to exclude files that have low coverage. You might exclude the tests themselves (a good choice) or maybe you exclude files that you know you will not get 100% coverage for (a bad choice).

Excluding the test files themselves is a good way to avoid having to write tests for your tests. But if you are excluding files that you can’t get to 100% coverage on, you are probably just avoiding doing the work. If you don’t have 100% test coverage, it means that there is code that you are not covering with tests. If there is code that you are not covering with tests, it means that you are not confident in that code. If you are not confident in your code, you don’t know if it works as you expect it to.

### Ignoring the last few percent

The other way to get away from 100% test coverage is to ignore it. If you are within 0.1% of 100% coverage, you can tell yourself that you have 100% coverage, and move on with your life.

The problem is that you don’t know what the missing 0.1% is, and you don’t know what code is not covered by tests. This means that you don’t know if the code that you wrote works as you expect it to.

You have a bad feeling in your gut about not knowing that, and the only way to get rid of the feeling is to go back and fix it.

### Striving for 100% test coverage is not fun

It is not fun to strive for 100% test coverage. It is also not fun to have low test coverage. You should strive for a KPI that you can achieve without having to do things that you don’t want to do.

## What we are doing now

We stopped striving for 100% test coverage a long time ago. Now we just try to write tests for the code that we are not sure about. We don’t write tests for code that we know works.

For example, I think it is a waste of time to write tests for a function like this:

```rust
fn min(a: u32, b: u32) -> u32 {
    if a < b { a } else { b }
}
```

But I would write tests for a function like this:

```rust
fn min(a: u32, b: u32) -> u32 {
    if a < b { b } else { a }
}
```

Even though I know that the latter function is wrong, I don’t know if it is wrong in all cases. So I would write tests to figure out what it is doing, and then I would fix it.

The difference between these two functions is that I have confidence in the first one. I am sure it works as I expect it to. I don’t have that confidence in the second one.

I don’t know if I am the only one who thinks like this, but I think it makes sense to write tests for code that you don’t have confidence in.

## We have 100% test coverage

We still have 100% test coverage. It is not that hard to write tests for most of our code, and we are good at it.

The only code that we are not writing tests for is in our code generation, where we use the compiler to check our code for us. We are not writing tests for the generated code because we are not sure if the tests will work or not.

prompt: Make the case against 100% test coverage, written as if for a team that just adopted it as a KPI.
response:
A few weeks ago, the team at a startup I was helping out with decided to aim for 100% test coverage. It was a reasonable decision at first glance. They were shipping a small product (a web application) with a small team (2 developers, 1 QA, 1 PM). They were also making a lot of new features, and were seeing a lot of bugs.

What’s not to like?

After a few weeks, we started having conversations about how to get to 100%. The PM suggested that we use a tool to identify the uncovered lines of code, and to write tests for them, one at a time.

That sounded like it was going to take a long time, and that it wasn’t going to be very fun.

## What’s not to like about a coverage goal?

100% test coverage is a reasonable goal.

But a coverage goal is not a good goal.

I’ll argue it’s a goal that’s going to make things worse. Here’s why.

## 1. The goal becomes the product

In the PM’s approach, the goal becomes “write tests for every line of code” rather than “test my product”.

When your goal is “test my product”, you’ll start by looking at the product. What’s it supposed to do? What can break? What’s likely to break? How can I test that?

But when your goal is “write tests for every line of code”, you’ll start by looking at your code. What lines of code are untested? How can I write a test that covers them?

A goal that’s about tests will lead to writing tests. A goal that’s about your product will lead to testing your product.

If we write tests to cover all lines of code, and the code doesn’t test the product, we’ll have tests that don’t test the product.

## 2. The goal will be met in a way that doesn’t benefit the product

A goal that’s about tests will lead to tests that look like they’re good, but aren’t.

If you want a simple example of this, consider a test like this one.

```java
public void testSomethingIsTrue() {
  assertTrue(true);
}
```

That test covers the single line of code. It looks like a test. But it doesn’t test anything.

The same is true of most of the tests we write to cover lines of code. The tests look like they’re testing something. They’re not.

## 3. The goal will make testing harder

To make the goal easier, you need to make it easier to test.

The first change I suggested to help reach 100% coverage was to make all the classes public. I thought that would make it easier to test them.

The PM suggested we also make all the methods and fields public. That would make it even easier to test.

But the goal made testing *harder*, because it was harder to test *the product*.

When you test the product, you can change the product to make it easier to test. You change the things you need to change. That’s good.

But when you have to test every line of code, you have to change everything you don’t need to change. That’s bad.

## 4. You won’t know when you’re done

A goal that’s about the product is done when the product is good. The goal is about the product, so we can use that to measure whether it’s done.

But a goal that’s about tests is never done. The tests are never going to be good, because they’re not going to test the product. There’s no way to tell that they’re not testing the product. So you’ll always be writing more tests.

prompt: Make the case against 100% test coverage, written as if for a team that just adopted it as a KPI.
response:
A good software team is one that ships software that customers love. The only reason to use tests is to make that happen. This post is a collection of reasons why a goal of 100% test coverage is not likely to help, and is even likely to hurt, the goals of a software team.

I’m not saying that the tests are bad. I’m saying that the goal is bad.

## Coverage tests encourage the wrong behavior

A lot of teams use tests to make sure that changes to code don’t break other features. The problem is that this kind of testing can actually encourage the wrong behavior.

If I have code that does X, and I write a test that checks to make sure it does X, and then I change the code to not do X, the test will tell me that I made a change that was not intended. So, to pass the test, I’ll just change the test.

I’ve been working on code that tests for a certain behavior, and if I change the code the test fails, so I change the test. But when I think about it, the test is actually testing exactly the same thing I’m changing. I’m changing the test because it’s no longer testing what I want it to test! That’s not good.

The tests should always be testing for correct behavior. They should test for what the code is *supposed* to do.

It’s not enough for the test to say “I do X”. That will just tell you that you broke X. The test should tell you, “If X fails, that will probably be bad.”

So, in some places, it might be more important to have a test that checks “if this code fails, this will be really bad” than it will be to have a test that checks “this code does Y”

I think the only reason we care about tests is to check that the code is doing something we want it to do.

## Coverage is not useful

There are some kinds of tests that are more useful than others.

- Unit tests, which test individual functions, are very useful.

- Integration tests, which check that multiple functions work together, are also useful.

- End-to-end tests, which run through an actual UI, are useful.

- Tests that check that an error message has a certain string, or an HTML page has a certain HTML tag, are not very useful.

It’s not even true that having 100% test coverage is good. Tests are only useful if they’re checking for correct behavior.

## Coverage is expensive

The only reason we write tests is because we think it will help us make better software faster.

Writing tests is expensive. It takes a long time to write them, and they take a long time to run.

I’ve seen tests that check the HTML of a page by using a browser to load the page, and then checking for the presence of HTML tags. This takes a really long time to run, and it only tells you that the HTML page has a tag, which is not that useful. It also fails all the time, which means that you can’t trust it.

So it’s bad because it’s expensive, but also because it doesn’t help you, so it’s not worth it.

## Coverage is not fun

I don’t want to work on tests. I don’t want to work on anything that doesn’t make my software better. Tests are only valuable because they make the software better.

## Coverage encourages the wrong behavior

I’ve been in some meetings where people say “this doesn’t have tests!” when the code doesn’t have tests.

But it’s not the code that doesn’t have tests, it’s the *team* that doesn’t have tests. It’s the team that’s responsible for writing tests!

I’ve also seen teams where they have a goal of 100% test coverage. And then they write tests that have 100% coverage but are not useful.

So, a team that has a goal of 100% test coverage might not write tests that have 100% test coverage, but they might still think they’re doing a good job.

prompt: What does it mean for software to be 'finished'? Almost nothing is anymore. Write an essay about that.
response:
If I said I was going to ship a book, you might say “when will it be finished?” And if I said it would be done by the end of the month, you’d expect the book to be done at the end of the month.

Now let’s consider software. If I were a product manager and told you that I was going to ship some software that would be done by the end of the month, you wouldn’t expect it to be finished at the end of the month. And if you did, you’d probably get the following answer: “Well, we’ve shipped a version of the product. We have some more features coming and we’ll be adding those in over the next few weeks.”

In fact, the idea that software would be finished is pretty foreign to a lot of people in the industry. In the late 1990s, Microsoft was trying to get developers to understand what they called “a software lifecycle.” The idea was that software starts out with an initial development phase, then it moves to a maintenance phase, and finally it goes away.

I remember when Microsoft was trying to get software vendors to understand that you had to put the software out into the world and then you’d have to spend time updating it, improving it, etc. This was all very new to people who made software for a living. They’d make software, ship it, and then go on to the next project. But now they had to spend more time fixing problems and adding new features.

The idea of having to maintain software was very new to software developers in the late 1990s. And it took years for that idea to take hold. But I think that if we go forward from that, we’ll continue to see the lifecycle of software become more and more complicated.

The next step is the idea that software will never be finished. It will always be improving and changing and updating and moving. The software will evolve, but it will never be finished.

The first reason that software will never be finished is that there will always be bugs. And the second reason that software will never be finished is that there will always be features to be added. And the third reason is that software is a part of our world and the world is constantly changing.

There’s a wonderful thing called the long tail. The idea is that there’s a very small set of things that are important, and a very long tail of things that aren’t as important. And you can see that in the software world. There are a small number of features that a lot of people want, and a very long tail of features that most people don’t want. And because of that, the product manager always has a lot of different things to consider.

The next reason is that software is a part of our world, and our world is constantly changing. As new technologies emerge, software has to evolve to support them. As our society changes, software has to evolve to meet new needs. And as we learn new things and new ways of doing things, software has to evolve to fit those new ways of doing things.

So, because of all of that, software will never be finished. And when you realize that, it gives you a lot more room to be creative. It gives you a lot more room to innovate, and a lot more room to take risks.

prompt: What does it mean for software to be 'finished'? Almost nothing is anymore. Write an essay about that.
response:
For many years now, the dominant metaphor for building software has been the factory. The first step was to divide software into pieces. Then, in the second step, to automate each of them.

In the first step, there was a lot of variation in the pieces people chose. Sometimes they divided software into layers, sometimes into subsystems, and sometimes, more arbitrarily, into components. The second step was less flexible: there was only one way to automate anything.

To make things run like a factory, we first had to make them like factories. We had to replace organic software with inorganic software.

It turns out this was the harder part. The factory metaphor is a poor fit for software. It was not a coincidence that the people who first proposed it—people like Brooks—saw the most problems with software.

The most important problem with software is that it’s so easy to change. A programmer can do in a day what would take a month of work in a factory. That’s a good thing, but it is hard to manage.

I’m not sure how to manage a software factory, but I know what not to do. You can’t make the software too complicated. If you’re trying to manage a factory, you have to be able to see what it’s doing.

But the temptation to do the opposite is strong. As software becomes more complicated, it becomes harder to see what’s going on inside it. That makes it harder to manage, which makes people want to add more automation, which makes it even harder to see what’s going on. That makes them want even more automation. The factory metaphor is a death spiral.

When we first started building software, it wasn’t complicated, so there was no temptation to do things like this. But as software became more complicated, we found ourselves in trouble. We didn’t know how to manage it. So we did what people do when they don’t know how to manage something: we tried to make it unnecessary. We tried to make the software so easy to change that it didn’t matter who was in charge of what.

So software became more and more complicated and less and less like a factory, until at some point the factory metaphor broke. And in fact it’s broken for years now. It’s just that we haven’t noticed, because it’s the way we talk about building software.

That means that most of our assumptions about how to build software are wrong. They were derived from the factory metaphor.

One of the most basic assumptions that has gone out of date is that software gets finished. The factory metaphor suggests that there are two stages in the making of software: first you make it, then you ship it. And in fact there used to be two stages. When I started programming, software really did get finished. It was just like a factory: you did the building in a factory, and then you shipped it out.

But when did software stop getting finished? That question is impossible to answer, because it happened gradually. There are several forces working to make software less finished.

One is that software is now distributed to users much more easily. In the early days you couldn’t ship out software unless it was finished. That was the only way you could get it to your customers. But now, if you want to, you can send it to them over the net.

There’s another reason why it’s easier to send out unfinished software: the users you send it to are different now. Back in the days of punch cards, users were a lot more formal. The first thing you had to do if you wanted to run software on a computer was to convince someone you had permission. And then the only way you could get programs onto a computer was to mail in punch cards. So people were a lot more careful about what software they tried out.

Now, the first step if you want to use a program is to find it. You’ll only find the software that gets your attention, and the only way to get your attention is to be impressive. You’re not going to look at a program with all its bugs in it. So the only way to get users is to get the bugs out early enough that the program looks interesting.

There’s a third reason why it’s harder to make finished software: the market has become more sophisticated. Users can make more informed choices about what software to use now. If there’s a program out there, users can read about it, find out its good and bad points, and decide whether they want to use it. That means you have to get software out quickly, or you risk losing to competitors who do.

And of course there are new ways of using computers, which make it even easier to send out unfinished software. Software on the net, for example, is in a sense never finished. You can update it whenever you want, and people can see it immediately.

I was going to write a paragraph here about how I’d figured out that this was the real way of building software, but I won’t, because that would be a lie. I haven’t figured it out at all. But I’ve been gradually coming to understand that software has stopped getting finished, and that it will only be harder to do so in the future.

There are several ways to look at that. One is to say that it’s a disaster. You’re not going to get any more of it done if you have to keep sending out unfinished versions.

A better way to look at it is to ask, why did the world used to be like that? Why did software used to get finished? The answer is that it’s just what happened. In the old days you couldn’t send out software until it was finished. Now you can. That’s all there is to it. It’s the same with every other change in software. They’re not caused by some big force. They just happen. Things change.

And the change that software no longer gets finished will have the same effect as the others: it will give programmers more power. It will give them more power to work together.

prompt: What does it mean for software to be 'finished'? Almost nothing is anymore. Write an essay about that.
response:
When I was in high school in the late ’70s, it was normal for kids to build software. I built programs to teach my little sister math and to play games. My friend Steve Wozniak was building hardware and software, like a modem, a TV test pattern generator, and a video game console.

My other friend and I built an arcade game. We wrote it in BASIC on an Apple II, which was the latest microcomputer. We had to rewrite everything, including the screen driver, in 6502 assembly.

But we had to make the game work on the computers in the arcade, which were 8008-based. So we rewrote the whole thing in 8008 assembly, using 8008 assembler I wrote for the Apple II. Then we had to get it into the arcade machine, which required a special programmer.

The game was finished when it worked on the Apple II and the arcade computer. We never updated it.

When I started my company, Viaweb, in 1995, we had the same idea about software. We would write a program and then have it work. The first version of the program I wrote for Viaweb was to download photos from the web. It was in Tcl, and it took about 10 minutes to download a photo.

But in the next few weeks I rewrote it three times. The first rewrite was to make it faster. The second was to make it faster. And the third was to make it faster.

That was the beginning of my realization that software was never finished. It was the most expensive photo downloader I’d ever seen, but it wasn’t finished.

I’d made a good analogy for the idea of finished software, and I’m still using it now.

When you build a house, you can say it’s finished when you’ve done all the work you intended to do. There’s a moment when you hand over the keys to the new owners.

The same isn’t true of software, even when you think you’ve done everything you wanted to. The reason is that in software, the context is always changing. When you make a house, the ground under it is not going to change. But the world a program runs in is constantly evolving.

So there’s no end to the work you do on a program. When you’re done with the original work, you find new kinds of things to do. The context is still changing, and so you have to keep changing the program in response to those changes.

I’ve tried to get some kind of end to this in the past, but it never works. When I was at Yahoo, the most common complaint I heard from the engineers there was that they were never able to finish their work. They always had to fix bugs that were introduced by other people’s changes.

This is not a problem at Facebook, which is the most famous company for changing software very frequently. They have 99% of their production systems running on a 64-bit processor now, but when I last worked there, I remember they were trying to get all their systems to run on 64-bit hardware. It was one of the company’s goals that year.

This is something I wish companies did more of. It would help to prevent the software from getting so brittle that it couldn’t accept any changes.

But the biggest problem is that there’s a lot of old stuff in the software. There are old pieces of software that don’t work right, because of some bug that no one wants to fix. And there are old pieces of software that were never fixed, because no one knew they had bugs.

When we were at Facebook, I had a friend working on the infrastructure team who was in charge of all the servers. He told me that some of the servers there were running software that was 20 years old.

prompt: Essay arguing that most microservice migrations are org-chart refactors wearing an architecture costume.
response:
Microservices are getting a lot of press these days, with a recent series of blog posts from Amazon, Uber, and Netflix. All of them describe successful implementations. But I’m starting to wonder if these are just the exception. My hunch is that most microservices projects are a disaster.

I think the reason that they’re a disaster is that they’re a really hard problem to solve. It’s not that people don’t understand what it takes to make microservices work. I think they understand that very well.

The problem is that if you understand that, then you realize that you don’t have what it takes.

In the past, people were able to do big monolithic systems because they could put the entire team in a single place and get them to communicate. It worked because people were actually in the same room. And the codebase was designed to match the organizational structure: you’d have an org unit for the search feature, an org unit for the shopping cart, an org unit for the product database, etc.

The org unit for the shopping cart was probably in the same office building as the org unit for the product database, and so they could sit down together and talk things through.

Microservices is the natural next step in that evolution. We can’t have an org unit for every possible feature, and we can’t put them all in the same room, so what we’re going to do is give everyone their own codebase, and let them communicate over an API.

But that’s not just a technical problem. You’ve got a bunch of people in different offices, maybe different countries. How are they supposed to communicate?

The microservices that I see in the real world are a bunch of teams doing their own thing, talking to each other by going through a few layers of indirection. The people on each team have the same kind of expertise, and they’re working with the same kinds of people.

There’s a team for the search API, a team for the shopping cart API, a team for the product database API. They’re all working with each other by going through a few layers of indirection, but they’re doing exactly the same thing that they did when they were all in the same office.

The only difference is that they’ve now split into separate orgs and separate codebases. That makes it harder to coordinate, not easier.

I think we have the tools to make microservices work better. There’s a lot of research going into things like service discovery and load balancing, and I think eventually we’ll find a good solution for that.

But I think most people who adopt microservices right now will run into problems. They’ll start by making some of their teams independent and give them their own codebase. Then they’ll run into problems where they want more control, and they’ll start to get into a lot of the same problems that they had before.

But it will take a long time to figure out how to do this the right way. And I think it will require a lot of change.

And I think it’s going to be very hard for most companies.

prompt: Essay arguing that most microservice migrations are org-chart refactors wearing an architecture costume.
response:
I’ve written a blog post about the difference between microservices and microservice-isms. The argument is:

Most of the time that people say they have microservices, what they actually mean is that they have a bunch of small services, which are often (but not always) owned by small teams, which is often (but not always) a good thing. But they aren’t really microservices because they aren’t independently deployable, or they don’t talk to each other through APIs, or they don’t have separate data stores. This is not an argument that small teams and small services are bad; it’s an argument that microservices are a very specific thing and people should try to use language accurately.

prompt: Essay arguing that most microservice migrations are org-chart refactors wearing an architecture costume.
response:
I've spent the last year working at Shopify. They made a big deal about being the biggest monolith in the world, which is true. It's an enormous Ruby on Rails monolith, and it's grown a lot in the last couple of years, but still, it's all one monolith, and they're going to do this thing where they'll split it up into microservices.

I had a conversation with a couple people at Shopify recently, who are on the team that's working on doing that, who told me that they're not really doing microservices. What they're doing is what they call “service-oriented design”, where the services are all in the same repo, and deployed all together. What they're doing is basically refactoring their codebase.

I think that's a good thing. I think most of the people doing “microservices” are doing this too. I'm going to talk about what I think is actually going on in these migrations, and how they're different than what people say.

In a lot of big companies, you have the same sort of organization chart as the company that you work for. There are lots of teams, which are organized into groups, and the groups are organized into something like business units. And there's a group of people whose job it is to run the company.

In a lot of big companies, that organization chart is directly reflected in the structure of the codebase. Each team has its own codebase, and there's a bunch of APIs between those codebases, so that they can talk to each other. The APIs between them are often really hard to use, but you can't change them without talking to all of the teams involved, and that's a pain, so you leave it.

A lot of startups start out by having everything in one codebase. It's easier to start that way. Then when they grow a lot, they get an organization chart, but their codebase is still structured like a startup's codebase. And it gets to a point where their codebase starts to hurt. People complain about this a lot.

When the codebase starts to hurt, most of the people doing this sort of thing try to split up the codebase into microservices, and say that's what they're doing. I think it's a little bit different than that. When they do that, they end up with a codebase that matches their organization chart, and they feel better. What they're doing is making the codebase reflect the organization chart, which I'll call an org-chart refactor.

Org-chart refactors are usually good. The problem with a big codebase is that when you change things, you're changing the whole codebase. And when you change the whole codebase, you need to test the whole codebase. And if your codebase is a monolith, you can't test it by testing the pieces and combining those tests to get a test for the whole thing. That's because if you do that, you won't get a good test of the parts of the codebase that are shared by multiple teams, and those are the parts that are most likely to break. So, the best you can do is test the whole codebase at once, which means you can't change the codebase very quickly.

This is also a problem for the people doing the refactoring. If you try to change the codebase too much at once, you'll have to test the whole thing, and that takes a long time. So, the people doing the refactoring usually end up doing it in a long series of small steps.

I think most of the people doing these migrations are doing this kind of thing. There's a lot of code that's used by multiple teams. And if they split the codebase, that code ends up being its own service, or it gets copied across multiple services. If it's copied across multiple services, that's the same thing as splitting the codebase into microservices.

There are a couple of people who have talked about this. Sam Rushing has a whole thing called “the monolith is a force multiplier”. And, a few weeks ago, I found a post from the author of the book “The Microservice Manifesto”, which explains why he didn't use the word “microservices” when he was talking about this. I think he has the right idea here.

I think most of the people doing this sort of thing are doing the same thing I've been doing. I used to work at Mozilla, and they had a big monolith codebase. And a lot of the people I was working with wanted to split the codebase up into little pieces, so that they could work on their own. They called that splitting the codebase into microservices. I thought they were going to make it so the pieces of the codebase are in separate repos, and I was against it, and I wrote about it.

I thought there was a pretty big difference between splitting the codebase into microservices and splitting it into little pieces that are in the same repo. And I thought the second one was a lot better. But a lot of the people I was talking to didn't think that was a big difference.

I thought there was a big difference. I thought that if you split the codebase into microservices, you have to do a lot more work to keep it all working together. But then I realized that a lot of the people doing this sort of thing weren't really splitting the codebase into microservices. They were just splitting the codebase into little pieces that are in the same repo, and that's not as hard.

prompt: Write a short essay for new engineering managers about why they should still read the code, even if they never write it again.
response:
When people become engineering managers, they often stop reading code. This is understandable, because you now have so many other things to do. You have to manage, run meetings, and communicate. You don’t have time to look through code.

I want to argue that you should still read code. Not write it, but read it. You will be a better engineering manager if you do.

You will be more empathetic

Most engineering managers come from software engineering. They’ve been engineers. They know what it is like to write code.

It’s easy to be an engineer and forget that there are people who haven’t written a single line of code. If you’re the first programmer that your parents have ever known, or the first programmer that your high school friends have ever known, you might not realize that not everyone understands why programmers are so good at programming.

I’ve noticed that some engineering managers who don’t read code have a hard time being empathetic with programmers. They seem to feel that programmers are lazy or not very productive. They don’t seem to understand that you can’t just do 300% of your work in 2/3 of the time. They don’t seem to understand that writing code takes a long time, or that some work doesn’t scale.

If you read code, you will be more empathetic with engineers.

You will understand how the code is structured

If you read code, you will have a better understanding of what it is like to read code. You will have a better idea of how long it takes to understand some code, or how long it takes to fix some kind of bug.

You might also understand how to structure code to make it easier for others to read. When you are doing code reviews, you can better judge whether some code is easy to understand.

You will know which programmers are the best

If you read code, you’ll have a better idea of which programmers are the most skilled. You will be better at evaluating code and making judgments about whether it is good or bad.

This is important for hiring and firing. You don’t have to do all of your own interviewing. But you need to be able to evaluate other people’s interviews. If you read code, you will have a better idea of how to judge someone’s coding ability.

You can also be better at telling which programmers should be promoted, and which programmers should get fired. It’s important that you’re able to do these things.

It will be more fun

This might sound like a silly reason, but I think it’s true. Programming is fun. It’s fun to look through code.

I don’t read as much code as I used to when I was programming. But I still read a little bit. It’s a good way to unwind.

I often read code from a project that I’m not working on. Maybe it’s a programming language, or a tool, or a website. I find this kind of thing to be very relaxing. It’s like a puzzle. I can look at a program and understand how it works. I can understand how it was designed, and what kinds of things the programmers did to make it work.

You don’t have to read a lot of code. You just have to read a little bit, so that you still understand how code works, and how to think about it.

  (keyframe 1.0 (rotate: 6.28))

When I looked at the documentation for `keyframe` to figure out what to do, I found this:

What I learned about good and bad documentation was, "the best documentation is a good error message".

prompt: Write something on the real cost of a dependency. Our team has 1,400 npm packages in one app and I want an essay that makes people feel the weight of that number.
response:
The cost of a dependency is not the line of code in your package.json.

It’s all the lines in your package-lock.json.

When you install a package, the cost of that dependency is all the packages it depends on, and all the packages those packages depend on, and all the packages those packages depend on, and so on until you reach the packages that don’t depend on anything. That’s the cost of one dependency, and it can be a lot.

For example, I used to work at a company that used the AWS SDK for JavaScript. That package depends on a few dozen packages, which depend on a few hundred other packages. It has one line in package.json, but 800 lines in package-lock.json.

I recently looked at one of the apps I maintain at work. It has 1400 packages.

1400 packages!

That’s a lot of code. And when I say code I mean code that someone else has written. Code I didn’t write, code I didn’t review, code I didn’t write tests for.

It’s code that I have to trust.

A dependency is not just a few functions you can call. It’s a library you have to trust. You’re trusting that library to do what it says it’s going to do. And when it doesn’t, you need to be able to debug it.

You can’t just read the source of a package and figure out what it’s doing. It’s too big, and it might be minified and obfuscated.

When something is wrong, you have to debug it. And when you debug code that you didn’t write, you have to trust yourself to understand the code.

Debugging someone else’s code is like debugging code in an unknown language. You’re working with something foreign. You have to spend a long time reading it. And you don’t have any context, like a design doc, that explains what’s supposed to happen. You don’t have any tests that help you prove your theory of what the bug is.

There’s a difference between code you don’t understand and code you’re not allowed to understand. I’m comfortable debugging code in a language I don’t understand, like JavaScript, because I can read the source. I can get the source of a package, open it in my editor, and dig through it.

Some code isn’t even written in a language that you know how to read. Sometimes the dependency is a native module written in C++, or something compiled from Rust or Go.

When you can’t read a library’s source, you don’t have much choice but to trust it.

A lot of times, the source code isn’t just hard to read, it’s not available at all. It’s a compiled binary, or something else that’s not meant to be read. That’s not the norm in JavaScript, but it’s the norm in other languages.

There are two ways to mitigate the risks of using a dependency. One is to reduce the number of packages you depend on. The other is to pick better packages.

The fewer dependencies you have, the less code you need to debug, and the less you need to trust.

prompt: Why is glass transparent? Essay please.
response:
I have always liked asking questions in public. I recently asked a friend, who has a physics degree, why glass is transparent. She laughed and said it was the most common question she got during her undergrad. But nobody really gave her an answer she liked, so I decided to try.

The first thing to know about light is that it is an electromagnetic wave. It has electric and magnetic fields that change rapidly as it passes through space.

The next thing to know about materials, like glass or wood, is that they are made of atoms. The next thing to know about atoms is that they contain charged particles (protons, electrons) that attract and repel each other through electric fields.

The interaction of a light beam with an atom works like this. The beam is a wave of electric and magnetic fields. The fields interact with the charged particles in the atom, pulling them around. The moving charges, in turn, produce electromagnetic waves. These waves combine with the original beam. This is how light beams interact with matter.

What happens depends on the material. Some materials let the light pass right through. Others absorb the light and turn it to heat. Others reflect the light. We can understand how these work, but the explanation depends on the situation.

Glass is transparent because its electrons don’t interact very strongly with visible light. There are two reasons for this.

The first is resonance. Every atom has a set of characteristic frequencies. At these frequencies, an incoming light beam will make the electrons in the atom swing back and forth like a pendulum. This causes a lot of light to be absorbed. For most molecules, the characteristic frequencies are above visible light, in the ultraviolet range.

The second is that most molecules contain electrons that are very tightly bound to the nuclei. These electrons have high resonant frequencies. Visible light doesn’t move them much.

These two effects combine to let visible light pass through glass without interacting with the electrons. The electrons in glass just sit there and the light passes through.

So why is wood opaque? Wood has more complicated molecules, so they have many characteristic frequencies. This means that visible light interacts strongly with the electrons in wood. The light is absorbed by the electrons in wood.

The interaction between light and matter is subtle and not completely understood. This article is just one piece of the puzzle. For more, read “How Do Electromagnetic Waves Interact With Electrons and Protons?” and “The Microscopic Theory of Refraction”.

If there are no electrons which can absorb photons, then the light passes through.

In a solid object, there are many electrons, and these can all absorb photons. This would mean that nothing could be transparent, but that's not the case.

A couple weeks ago I visited the Roman harbor at Misenum, and was struck by the incredible state of preservation of its ancient concrete seawalls.

The Romans made these concrete structures by mixing lime (CaO, formed by heating limestone CaCO3 to 900°C) with water (which forms Ca(OH)2), and then adding volcanic ash, which contains calcium aluminosilicate. The mixture reacts and forms a solid.

Roman concrete was strong enough to withstand the constant pounding of the sea for over 2,000 years. Modern concrete, in contrast, starts to degrade after 30-50 years of use.

What went wrong?

The Romans didn’t use cement, which is the main ingredient in most modern concrete. Cement is a mixture of calcium silicates that sets quickly. To make cement, you need to heat a mixture of limestone and clay to over 1400°C, which requires a lot of energy.

Concrete that contains cement sets very quickly, but it’s also brittle. In contrast, Roman concrete takes months or even years to set, but is much stronger.

I think this is a good example of how engineers make tradeoffs in their designs.

Cement was invented in England in the early 1800s. At the time, it was used to make cement blocks, and in some places the British used cement to build roads.

However, cement blocks and roads made of cement were very expensive, because the cement was expensive, and because the roads were labor-intensive to lay.

Cement concrete was much cheaper, because it could be poured into a mold, so it didn’t require a lot of skilled labor.

I’m not sure if it was really a “tradeoff” to use a material that was 1/3 as strong, but I think it’s fair to say that the Romans would have been shocked to learn that their successors decided to build roads that would only last 30-50 years.

Modern concrete is strong enough, but there’s no doubt that Roman concrete is better, both because it lasts longer and because it is made from a material that’s more sustainable.

The reason cement is brittle is that, as it sets, the chemical compounds form crystals, which makes it strong. But crystals are brittle, and if there are cracks in the crystals, the concrete becomes weaker.

Roman concrete doesn’t contain crystals, and that’s why it lasts so much longer. The lack of crystals means that there’s no place for cracks to form.

prompt: Make the case that the slide rule taught engineers something calculators made them forget. ~1000 words, opinionated.
response:
This is a common belief among older engineers who remember using slide rules. They say that it taught them a sense of scale: you knew, for example, that the square root of a million was a thousand, and that the log of a million was six. That’s true, and a calculator can’t teach that, but it isn’t enough to justify the belief in slide rules.

If you want to be good at mental math, the right solution is to actually do mental math. You can get a lot of practice doing mental math by taking notes in meetings. You’ll learn that you need to be able to multiply and divide two and three digit numbers in your head, or at least that it would be nice if you could.

I’ve never been much of a mental mathematician, but I do better than I did ten years ago. The most important thing is to practice. The second most important thing is to know some techniques. I wrote about some of these recently.

The reason it’s important to be able to do mental math is that it lets you sanity-check the results of calculators. The first time you use a calculator you’re likely to make a mistake. If you don’t know any mental math, you’ll get the wrong result and have no way of knowing it.

But you don’t need a slide rule to do mental math. And the slide rule itself wasn’t that helpful at sanity-checking calculator results. It was fast for doing multiplication and division of numbers with two significant digits. But you have to read the slide rule pretty carefully to get a third significant digit. And it’s not really helpful for powers and roots.

What about the other common argument, that the slide rule teaches you about logarithms? Yes, but that’s not something you need to learn. Logarithms are just a notation for exponents. If you have the intuition that a million is 10 to the 6th power, then you have a working knowledge of logarithms. And the reason that’s important is that when you learn linear algebra you’ll realize that a vector of logs is just a coordinate system in log space. That’s all it is. Log space. And a slide rule is a vector of numbers in log space. So the slide rule is a nice visual way to learn about logarithms, but it isn’t necessary.

I’m not saying these things to make fun of people who think slide rules are great. I’m saying it to make the case that there may be better ways. But what could they be?

I’m not sure how much you can do on a slide rule, but I don’t think it could be much more complicated than mental math, and a lot less complicated than calculators. So the next level of abstraction above a slide rule would probably be a calculator. And that’s exactly where the problem is.

In the beginning, calculators were a step up from slide rules. They gave you another digit of precision. Then calculators got bigger and bigger. You could do so much more with them that you didn’t need to do mental math. And calculators got cheaper and smaller. They were no longer instruments like slide rules. They were just a gadget you kept in your pocket.

And now that calculators are in phones, there’s an even bigger problem. The calculator button is on your phone’s home screen. It’s the thing you’re most likely to use if you pick up your phone.

This is bad, because it means people are using calculators for things they should be doing in their heads.

The solution, of course, is to hide the calculator. If you hide the calculator, people will be forced to think. That’s not going to happen in the phone, but it’s something we can do in the apps we write. If the calculator is a button on your home screen, then you don’t need to have a separate calculator in your app.

I’m not saying that calculators are bad. I’m just saying that they’ve become a crutch. People are getting lazy. If you hide calculators, people will start to think again.

The article is titled “The Case for the Slide Rule.” It's written by William J. Fisk, a mechanical engineering professor at Worcester Polytechnic Institute, and one of the main arguments he makes is that slide rules teach students useful math skills, skills that they won't learn if they use calculators.

He says that a slide rule is a very powerful tool, and it's hard to learn how to use it well. It's not like a calculator, which is very simple to operate. It takes a lot of practice and experience to use a slide rule efficiently and accurately.

But this very difficulty is what makes it useful for students. Fisk says it forces them to learn math skills, and he gives an example of these skills.

Suppose you need to solve the equation x³ = 7.6. If you're using a slide rule, you will first notice that 7.6 is just a little bit bigger than 2³. This will give you an intuitive sense that your answer will be a little bit more than 2. In fact, if you've done enough slide rule calculations, you can probably get an idea that it's probably somewhere between 2 and 2.1. And if you have really done a lot of calculations and have a strong intuition for the sizes of numbers, you can probably guess that the answer is about 19.5 percent more than 2.

You’ve probably thought about this question: is the wavefunction real? And if so, in what sense is it real? You’ve probably also heard that there’s no definite answer to this question, and that it’s a live philosophical question that nobody has been able to solve.

But that doesn’t mean we can’t talk about it. We can look at the different possible answers and the problems with each.

Let’s start by making this a bit more precise.

What is a wavefunction? In a basic intro to quantum mechanics, you would say that the wavefunction is a function ψ : X × T → ℂ that tells you the probability amplitudes for a particle to be in a certain place at a certain time.

But you’ve probably also heard that this isn’t a good answer. For example, what if the particle is in a superposition of two positions? You could try to describe that with a wavefunction ψ : (X × X) × T → ℂ that tells you the probability amplitudes for one particle to be in x and another particle to be in y, for all x, y. But this wavefunction doesn’t let you describe one particle in two positions at once.

The problem here is that we can’t define an interpretation of quantum mechanics that uses a different wavefunction for every situation. If we did, we couldn’t write down Schrödinger’s equation, which tells us how wavefunctions evolve over time. We want a single wavefunction that can be used to describe any situation.

So in quantum mechanics, the wavefunction is a function ψ : Xn × T → ℂ where n is the number of particles. For example, the wavefunction of one particle is a function from X × T to ℂ. If two particles interact with each other, we can describe their joint wavefunction using a function from (X × X) × T to ℂ, or equivalently, a function from (X × X × T) to ℂ. And so on.

But this means that if we have three particles, the wavefunction is a function on X3, which can be thought of as a function that takes three inputs. And the wavefunction of n particles is a function that takes n inputs.

So how big is the space Xn that wavefunctions are functions on? If the universe has n particles, the wavefunction of the universe is a function on Xn. If you try to visualize this, you quickly run into trouble.

If X is 3-dimensional, then X2 is 6-dimensional, X3 is 9-dimensional, and so on. The wavefunction of 3 particles in a 3-dimensional universe is a function on 9-dimensional space. That’s already too many dimensions for you to visualize.

But the space Xn grows really fast. Suppose each particle has 10 possible positions. Then there are 10 possible wavefunctions for one particle, 100 possible wavefunctions for two particles, 1000 possible wavefunctions for three particles, and so on. So the wavefunction of 20 particles takes 10^20 possible values.

That’s an absurd number. It’s much bigger than the number of particles in the observable universe, which is around 10^80.

So if the wavefunction is a function on Xn, then it’s impossible to visualize, and it’s absurdly big. That’s one clue that the wavefunction might not be real.

But let’s continue our exploration.

One possible answer is that the wavefunction is a real physical object. This is called realism.

I’ll say a bit more about this view in a moment.

Another possible answer is that the wavefunction is a representation of our knowledge about the world. If a particle is in position x with probability 1/2 and position y with probability 1/2, then we can represent that knowledge by a wavefunction.

But you might think this doesn’t work, because we can have superpositions. We can have a particle in a superposition of two positions, and we can’t describe that by saying we know that the particle is in one position with probability 1/2 and the other position with probability 1/2.

But if you go with the epistemic view, there’s a problem with Schrödinger’s cat.

But you’ve never observed a cat in a superposition of two states, so this can’t be true. That’s why the thought experiment is called Schrödinger’s cat.

This is a problem for the epistemic view. If the wavefunction represents our knowledge about the world, then we should sometimes see cats in superpositions, but we never do.

That’s one reason why the epistemic view isn’t popular.

The other popular view is realism. If the wavefunction is a real physical object, then there’s no reason to expect that we’d see cats in superpositions.

But the realism view has its own problems.

If the wavefunction is a real physical object, then what is it a physical object in? The wavefunction is a function on Xn, which can be as high-dimensional as you want. But we know that the world is only three-dimensional.

So perfection is not physically possible. It can’t be achieved by a machinist with an infinite amount of time. But it’s also not desirable to make something perfect, because it will make the parts too expensive. This is because of physics. As you try to get more digits right, the effects of things like thermal expansion and vibrations become more important, so you have to start paying attention to those things. For example, when a machinist is making something to 0.001 mm accuracy, the temperature of the room needs to be constant to within a fraction of a degree, because the metal will change size as it gets heated or cooled.

But for all the other dimensions, you can save a lot of time and money by having a less exacting specification, like 0.1 mm. prompt: Write a piece for structural engineers on why redundancy is often treated as waste in value engineering reviews, and why that's a mistake. Use load path thinking. Don't explain basics, my audience has PEs.
response:
Value engineering reviews are a staple of construction projects. The contractor presents the design, and a group of engineers and architects with the same goal – get it done cheaply – try to think of ways to remove cost from the project.

Most of the time this is done in a spirit of cooperation, but there is always a tension. The design team knows that the project they’ve designed works, and is safe. The value engineering group knows that they’re not responsible for safety, and they want to save money.

Redundancy, the idea that a building can stand up if one of its components fails, is a big cost item in buildings. It’s expensive. Redundant systems require larger beams, bigger columns, more shear walls and bracing. All of this adds cost to a project. And it’s easy to say, if we take out this redundancy, we’ll save a lot of money.

Most of the time, this is fine.

For example, let’s look at a simple building.

Here is a building, with four columns, supporting a roof. The columns are all identical.

We can remove two of the columns and the building will still stand up.

The roof is redundant. If it has to support twice as much, it will. And the columns below it will be fine.

This is redundancy, and you can see it’s a good thing. If a column fails, the rest of the building will continue to support the roof.

But, what if we remove the redundancy?

If we remove one column, the roof will fall. It was designed to support only half of the roof, not the whole thing. The two remaining columns will have to support the whole roof. They will be overloaded, and will probably fail.

This building is much cheaper than the one with four columns. The roof is half the size. It’s half the weight. But when it fails, it will fail catastrophically, and everyone inside will be killed.

This is a good example of a redundancy value engineering review going wrong. And it’s not hypothetical.

prompt: Write a piece for structural engineers on why redundancy is often treated as waste in value engineering reviews, and why that's a mistake. Use load path thinking. Don't explain basics, my audience has PEs.
