prompt: Argue that fever is underrated and we treat it too quickly. 800ish words.
response:
A friend recently sent me a link to a New York Times article about fever, which has been a bit of an obsession of mine lately. It was called “The Fever That Doesn’t Want To Be Treated” and was written by a woman named Rachel Aviv who was in the middle of a fever herself at the time. It’s a wonderful piece of writing, and it’s a great article in its own right, but it also made me want to write down my fever-related thoughts.

This is not a medical article. I am not a doctor, I don’t give medical advice, and you should go see a real doctor if you have medical questions. This is just me thinking out loud.

Rachel Aviv writes that she was suffering from a fever of 102.4, that she took an aspirin that lowered it to 100.3, and that she still felt miserable. And then she describes what she did next:

I turned off my phone and decided to do the only thing I could think of that might make me feel better. I would lie down in the sun.

The article ends with:

I’m still feverish, but I feel much better now. If I had another fever, I would do the same thing, and then I would do it again, and then again, until it went away.

That’s an unusual thing to say. Most of us, at that point, would probably take another aspirin, maybe switch to ibuprofen to make sure we’re attacking the fever from all angles, and then call a doctor.

But that’s the point I’m trying to get at. I think that fevers aren’t taken as seriously as they should be, and I think it’s a big mistake to treat fevers aggressively with antipyretics like aspirin and ibuprofen. I don’t say this to encourage people to take dangerous fever-adjacent illnesses like sepsis for granted – if you’re worried that you have an illness that should be treated, go see a doctor. This is a plea for those of us who are sick but not very sick, for those of us who are sick but not dangerously sick, to take our fevers a little bit more seriously.

In 1881, a French doctor named Félix Alphonse Calmette discovered that fevers can kill bacteria in your blood. This is a common feature of fevers, and there’s a lot of evidence for it. In 1970, doctors at the University of Wisconsin discovered that fever made it harder for salmonella to reproduce.

In 1967, a study found that mice with fevers had more resistance to cancer, and a 1998 study found that the same thing is true of human cancer cells in vitro.

In 1994, the CDC published a study showing that children who took antipyretics for their fevers took longer to recover from the illnesses that caused those fevers. This result has been replicated many times. For example, this 1997 study found that kids who were treated for fever took longer to recover from pneumonia than kids who were treated for fever. This 2000 study found that kids with bronchiolitis who were treated with antipyretics took longer to recover.

The CDC’s study looked at the difference between fever treatments and no fever treatment, but a 1999 study looked at two different types of fever treatment, paracetamol and ibuprofen. It found that paracetamol had a negative effect on recovery time, and ibuprofen had a positive effect. That seems a little weird, but I’ll take it.

I think these studies are pretty impressive. They show that fevers are helpful in a wide range of situations, that antipyretics can slow recovery from these situations, and that they do this even when you are treating someone with a very dangerous illness.

I am not a doctor, but one possible explanation for these results is that fevers help the body fight infection by boosting the immune system and killing bacteria. This doesn’t work on every pathogen – some bacteria like salmonella are less good at reproducing at high temperature, but some viruses like rhinovirus are more good at reproducing at high temperature. But fevers can also make it harder for viruses to infect cells. I also think this could be why paracetamol slows recovery but ibuprofen doesn’t, since the former is a more aggressive treatment.

In addition to all of this, I like to take my fevers a little bit more seriously because I find that I don’t usually feel great when I have them. I don’t think fevers are as good at fighting infection as they used to be – it used to be that people had high fevers that killed all kinds of bacteria, but now we have antibiotics and the only pathogens that can survive are the ones that can survive antibiotics. So I think the body doesn’t need to mount as big of a fever response to them as it did before.

But I also think that the body sometimes throws up fevers unnecessarily. Like, when I get a fever I usually have to lie down in a bed, in a dark room, with a blanket over my face, and I have to not do anything for eight to twelve hours. This is usually a pretty good thing, because I’m usually too sick to do anything else anyway. But sometimes my fever is the only symptom of a pretty minor illness, and I still feel pretty good. In that case, I think it’s really important to listen to your fever, to lie down in bed and rest and take care of yourself instead of trying to push through. You might be able to push through, but it might not be worth it, and it might make your illness last longer.

If you’re sick but not dangerously sick, and you have a fever, and you feel like you should probably lie down in bed and rest and take care of yourself instead of trying to push through, listen to your body and do that.

Fever is an underrated part of the body’s immune system. The immune system’s ability to defend the body from invading pathogens is a complex, well-organized process involving many different components working in concert. Some of these components are immune cells, while others are proteins like the interferons and cytokines. Other factors are not components of the immune system itself, but rather play a supporting role. One of these is fever.

Fever is a common symptom in infection. When a person is infected, the body releases cytokines that trigger fever. This occurs by signaling to the brain to increase the set point of the body’s temperature. In this way, fever is one of the body’s defenses against pathogens.

The first indication of a pathogen’s presence is the inflammatory response. As the immune system identifies pathogens, it activates various types of immune cells. Neutrophils are the first immune cells to arrive. They release chemicals to kill pathogens, and their death releases even more chemicals that trigger inflammation. This leads to a local fever, which is felt as heat and redness.

Fever has been shown to reduce the ability of many pathogens to reproduce. This is true of viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites. Fever may also increase the ability of immune cells to destroy pathogens, but this remains less certain. As a result, fever plays an important role in the immune system’s fight against pathogens.

Although fever is beneficial, the body keeps it within a limited range. This is due to the risk of damage to the body itself. This may explain why we are so inclined to reduce fever with medications like ibuprofen and acetaminophen.

A common belief is that fevers above 104°F should be treated in children under 5. In fact, fevers up to 106°F have been shown to be harmless. The only concern is the possibility of seizures, which occur in only 1-2% of children with fevers and which are usually not harmful.

Fever can be beneficial even when it is not caused by infection. A recent study of mice showed that the ability to increase their own temperature in response to injury led to faster healing. This suggests that fever may also speed healing in humans.

Given the benefits of fever, we may be overly aggressive in treating fever with medications. While it is reasonable to treat a person with an infection to relieve discomfort, it is not always necessary to do so. If a patient can tolerate a fever, there may be no need to treat it.

A good example is a 2003 study of patients with acute lower respiratory tract infections. The patients in the control group were allowed to retain a fever, but were not given medication to treat it. Patients in the other group were treated with ibuprofen. The results of the study show that those who retained their fever did not have a worse outcome than those treated with ibuprofen.

Another example of the benefits of fever is the use of fever-inducing drugs in the treatment of cancer. Patients receiving this treatment have a reduced tumor size after treatment, which is believed to be due to the body’s immune system destroying the cancer cells.

Fever is an important part of the body’s immune system. We may be over-treating fever with medications, especially in situations where the patient can tolerate the fever without suffering. More research is needed to determine whether it is safe to forgo fever medications in certain situations.

prompt: Argue that fever is underrated and we treat it too quickly. 800ish words.
response:
Fever is so effective that it seems to come with a cost.

But it seems to come with a surprisingly small cost.

Fever, or pyrexia, was long considered a disease, the disease of a burning body. Hippocrates called it “king of fevers”.

But this is now well-understood to be a mistake, and instead a normal response to illness.

A fever is a body’s attempt to fight off a virus or bacteria, by making its body’s internal temperature more like that of its attacker’s preferred environment. For example, in a fever of 40 degrees C (104 degrees F), bacteria such as salmonella will have a harder time surviving and multiplying. Viruses also seem to be negatively affected by fever.

When the human body senses the presence of an invading virus, its immune system sends out alarm signals to tell the hypothalamus to raise the body’s temperature. The hypothalamus is the brain’s thermostat, and so it works by turning up the thermostat a few degrees. The body’s temperature rises until it matches this new set point.

Fever is also a sign that the immune system is doing its job, and that the body is fighting off an infection. For many illnesses, the presence of a fever is an indication that the disease will resolve more quickly and with fewer complications.

There are two ways of measuring how effective fever is. The first is how often fevers occur, and how often they are effective. The second is whether fever is a “real” process in evolution, or a byproduct.

Fever, it turns out, is extremely common. There are hundreds of different causes of fever, and it is common to get a fever at some point in life.

A study on 250 adults in Africa found that, on average, they experienced about 26 fever episodes in their lifetime. Most of these fevers resolved in under two days, and 85% of the time did not require any treatment.

But if a fever didn’t respond to treatment, or lasted more than two days, it was a much more serious condition.

Fever is also a common disease in children. Studies show that up to 75% of children will experience a fever in their first year of life.

But despite this, fever is generally a good thing. In an analysis of 123 studies on fevers, most found that fever helped the body to fight infections. Some found that fever increased the ability of immune cells, such as macrophages, to kill bacteria.

In one study of rats, when researchers suppressed the rats’ fevers with acetaminophen, they became more susceptible to infection by a bacterium called E. coli.

Fever may be a “real” process in evolution, and not a byproduct. Some animals have natural fevers. In a study of 12 species of wild animals, researchers found that most of them had natural fevers.

But it’s also true that animals can develop diseases that suppress their fevers, and that some animals can develop diseases that increase their fevers.

Fever is, overall, a normal response to illness.

prompt: Why do humans have such a long childhood compared to other primates? I'd like an essay exploring the competing explanations, especially the grandmother hypothesis, and whether any of them are fully convincing.
response:
Humans are the only mammals to have an adolescence. Adolescence is the stage of development between puberty and adulthood, and is defined in primates as the period between the age of first sexual activity and the age of first reproduction.

This is a little more complicated than it sounds, since some primates have two phases of adolescence, called prepubertal and peripubertal. But the point is that many primates have a prepubertal adolescence, even if they don’t have a peripubertal one. And yet, humans are the only species that reliably has *both*.

I think adolescence is a pretty important part of human life, and we don’t have much of a reason to explain it.

One common explanation for the long human childhood is that human brains are so large that it takes a long time to grow. But this is a little circular, since we don’t really know why human brains are so large in the first place.

But in this case, the circularity is pretty acceptable. We don’t need to explain why human brains are so big, so long as we know why humans have a long childhood. If we explain it in terms of brains, and we explain brains in terms of childhood, it’s still a complete explanation.

But what is that explanation?

One idea is that human infants are born too underdeveloped, so they need a long period to reach maturity.

The common explanation for why human babies are born so underdeveloped is that human skulls are too large to pass through a normal-sized vagina. But if you look at the skull sizes of other primates relative to their bodies, human babies aren’t that unusual, so this explanation doesn’t really work.

The common explanation is the obstetric dilemma, which says that human infants are born underdeveloped because bipedalism makes human hips smaller.

There are a few problems with this.

First, human hips are *huge* compared to the hips of other apes. In fact, human hips are so big that we can walk around with a very inefficient gait.

Second, even when a baby is born underdeveloped, it’s still a long time before it’s mature enough to reproduce.

The reason is that we’re born underdeveloped in two different senses. One is that we can’t walk, and this is presumably because our skulls are too large. The other is that we don’t have the brain capacity to take care of ourselves, and this is presumably because our brains are too large.

We have an underdeveloped body because of bipedalism. We have an underdeveloped brain because of a large brain.

The underdeveloped body explains the first 3 years of our lives. The underdeveloped brain explains the next 20 years.

But why do we have an underdeveloped body in the first place?

Well, this is a little complicated.

It could be that bipedalism is the main constraint. It could be that bipedalism made our hips small, and we couldn’t evolve larger hips because they would have made walking hard.

It could be that bipedalism was a constraint that made our hips small, but that we *wanted* larger hips anyway. We wanted larger hips, because we wanted to have larger brains.

But why do we have larger brains?

One idea is that having larger brains gives us more of a chance of surviving in our environment, so we evolved larger brains.

Another idea is that having larger brains allows us to be smarter, and having more intelligence gives us a chance of being better at finding food and mates.

This second explanation is the one we use when we talk about humans having a bigger brain. But the first is the one we use when we talk about the fact that we have to have a long childhood.

So the second explanation is the one that makes sense when we talk about brains.

But it doesn’t really explain why we have a long childhood.

The real explanation for why we have a long childhood is that our brains are underdeveloped.

We have to have a long childhood because we have to be born underdeveloped.

And we have to be born underdeveloped because our brains are too big.

prompt: Why do humans have such a long childhood compared to other primates? I'd like an essay exploring the competing explanations, especially the grandmother hypothesis, and whether any of them are fully convincing.
response:
I recently read a review paper on “why humans have such a long childhood”. It was pretty interesting, and here are my notes on it.

Humans have much longer childhoods than other primates. Chimpanzees wean after a couple years, while our kids spend more than three years on their mothers’ milk. Chimpanzees reach adult size in about twelve years, while human kids are still far from that at that age.

But there’s a lot of variation in exactly how long human childhood lasts. In the West, the average age for women’s menarche is thirteen or fourteen. In Africa it can be as early as nine. Some people consider childhood to last until the age of majority, eighteen in the West but as low as thirteen in some other places. Others consider childhood to last until the average age of first reproduction, which in the West is twenty-five, and in traditional cultures is usually closer to sixteen.

Why does this happen? Why don’t we mature faster? There are three main competing hypotheses:

1. The big brain hypothesis says that human childhood is long because we’re so smart. There’s an evolutionary tradeoff between how big your brain is at birth, and how long your childhood lasts. Bigger brains have to be born earlier so they fit through the mother’s pelvis; this makes children more vulnerable to infant mortality, but lets us have more babies in a row without having to space them out. This hypothesis argues that we’re smart because we need to be (eg to invent tools and develop language), but this made our brains so big that we had to have a longer childhood to compensate.

2. The grandmother hypothesis says that human childhood is long because humans have grandmothers. In other words, we can spend so long being kids, because our parents’ parents help out with the childcare. Chimpanzees don’t have grandmothers; their mothers die long before their kids reach the age of independence. If humans have grandmothers, they can devote more time to childcare without worrying about starvation or exhaustion.

3. The social brain hypothesis says that human childhood is long because we’re so social. Being social is great, but it requires a lot of learning: you have to understand the roles, the rules, and the politics of your society. This takes a lot of time, but it’s worth the investment.

The authors of the review paper argue that the big brain hypothesis and the social brain hypothesis are circular. They don’t answer why we’re smart, or why we’re social, they just say that we’re smart and social, and that this causes long childhoods.

The grandmother hypothesis is more interesting. It has two parts: 1) there’s an evolutionary advantage to having a long childhood, 2) grandmothers make this possible.

The review paper spends most of its time talking about the first half. It argues that it’s probably true, since longer childhoods seem to lead to better outcomes later in life, at least in the West. It gives a few examples, but most of them are kind of confusing:

- One study looked at a population in the Congo that’s so impoverished that most children die before their fifth birthday. The children who survived past their fifth birthdays lived longer, but the authors don’t say whether this is because they were more fit or because they were better able to withstand the stresses of the community.

- A second study looked at children who were abused early in childhood; they were more likely to be violent and/or depressed in adulthood. Again, we don’t know whether the abuse itself was the problem, or whether the abusers were bad people who were also bad parents.

- A third study looked at children who were abused early in childhood, and found that their brains were smaller than normal. This seems more convincing, except that there’s no way to tell whether the abuse caused the smaller brains, or vice versa.

The authors of the paper think that these are convincing, but I don’t. If you really want to see whether there’s an advantage to longer childhoods, you need to do a comparative study: look at children who were abused early in childhood, and children who were abused later in childhood, and see which group has worse outcomes. But this doesn’t happen because children who are abused early are more likely to have their abuse discovered, and be removed from the household. So the people who are abused early end up having less abuse than the people who are abused later, and this confounds the results.

I’m also not sure that this kind of data is useful. Maybe it’s true that having a longer childhood is good for you, but that could be because longer childhoods let you learn more things. It might not be the length of the childhood that’s important; it might just be the learning.

The second half of the grandmother hypothesis – that grandmothers help make this possible – is more interesting. It’s based on two different studies.

First, a study of the Ache people in Paraguay found that children with grandmothers available lived longer and had fewer illnesses than children without grandmothers available. They also had more siblings, which means that grandmothers probably made it easier for their children to have more kids.

Second, a study of hunter-gatherers in Botswana found that when grandmothers took care of their grandchildren, they were less likely to die.

Both of these studies seem to show that grandmothers help out, but they don’t really show that grandmothers help out very much. Ache children who had grandmothers lived an average of 45 years; those who didn’t lived an average of 41 years. Botswana children who had grandmothers had a 57% chance of living to age 5; those who didn’t had a 47% chance.

I’m not sure this is a lot. I don’t know how many other factors would be needed to raise the average age of Ache children by 4 years, or how many would be needed to increase the survival rate of Botswana children by 10%. It’s possible that grandmothers are doing a lot, and it’s possible that they’re doing a little.

The grandmother hypothesis is also complicated by the fact that it’s not always clear who’s doing the childcare. In the Botswana study, the grandmothers were taking care of their grandchildren, and the children who had grandmothers were less likely to die, but the grandmothers were also more likely to be married and to have more children. It’s possible that the grandmothers helped out by giving their daughters and sons-in-law more money. But if you don’t know what the grandmothers are doing, you don’t know how much they’re doing.

The authors of the review paper argue that the grandmother hypothesis is the most convincing explanation for long childhoods. They think that the other two hypotheses are circular, and that the grandmother hypothesis isn’t. I’m not sure I agree.

I think it’s true that grandmothers help out, but I don’t know if they’re the main reason we have such long childhoods. And I’m not sure that the grandmother hypothesis is really less circular than the other two. Maybe we have grandmothers because we’re social, and maybe we’re social because we’re smart, and maybe we’re smart because we have long childhoods.

prompt: Why do humans have such a long childhood compared to other primates? I'd like an essay exploring the competing explanations, especially the grandmother hypothesis, and whether any of them are fully convincing.
response:
A child, in human terms, is anything under about thirteen or fourteen years old. If your daughter is nine, you have a child. If your daughter is fifteen, you have a teenager. A teenager is not a child.

By these standards, human childhood is unusually long. We spend more time as children than any other known primate.

Why?

I.

The most well-known hypothesis is the “grandmother hypothesis”.

The grandmother hypothesis says that the reason human children take so long to grow up is that they have access to resources provided by their grandmothers.

For example, the grandmother can help take care of the child. When the mother is out foraging, the child isn’t left to fend for itself; the grandmother can look after it and make sure it’s safe. So the mother can spend her time gathering more resources, and the child doesn’t have to take care of itself or even worry about being neglected or left alone to die.

Or the grandmother can directly help with food. She can gather fruit, prepare it, and feed it to the child.

Or the grandmother can help in more abstract ways. She can look after the child so that the mother can rest, and the rested mother can take care of the child better.

Or the grandmother can help in still more abstract ways. She can teach the mother how to be a better mother. The mother will probably have a lot more children, so it’s in her interest to be a good mother. But if she’s never been around other mothers, she might not know the best way to do this.

The reason the grandmother hypothesis is popular is because there’s an obvious objection to it: you’d think that the child would want to get off the grandmother’s back sooner, and not wait till adolescence. If the grandmother is taking care of your needs, why not have the grandmother take care of all your needs? Why not let her take care of you for life?

The grandmother hypothesis solves this by pointing out that grandmothers are themselves older than usual. They’re not around as long as they ought to be. If the child could grow up faster, it would want to. But it can’t because there’s an evolutionary trade-off.

This is because, in modern humans, grandmothers are almost as productive as mothers. When a woman gives birth to her first child, she’s usually about nineteen. Her child’s grandmother is about forty, and about to enter the years of her life in which she is most productive. The grandmother will probably live to be about seventy, and in the meantime she’ll take care of lots of grandchildren.

This is a trade-off. If grandmothers were productive for more years, this would be better. But then mothers would have to be productive for more years, and the grandmother would have to start working before she was even born. That would mean women would start being fertile earlier. But the body would have to grow faster to reach that age, and that would mean childhood was shorter.

This trade-off could work in either direction. But it turns out that in modern humans, the system has settled at a place where mothers are fertile for about forty years, and grandmothers are productive for about thirty years.

II.

There are other hypotheses too.

One is that humans take so long to grow up because of our big brains. Our brains are so big that our children come out of the womb with underdeveloped brains, and they have to spend more time growing and developing those brains in order to grow into a successful adult.

Another is that human children need to learn so much that they need to spend a lot of time learning.

Another is that human childhood is long because our bodies grow in an odd way. In some species, the body reaches its adult shape quickly but then grows slowly for a long time afterwards. That’s not us. We grow fast at first, then slow down, then grow again at puberty. We’re weird.

Another is that human children have to learn culture. They have to learn the norms of their society, so they have to spend a lot of time learning those norms.

Another is that human children need to learn how to make decisions. They need to be able to figure out what to do in different situations, and they need to learn how to do this before they’re on their own.

The grandmother hypothesis is probably the most convincing, but none of these is really fully convincing.

Your gut is not a second brain, though it does have its own nervous system.

prompt: I'm a second-year med student and I'm honestly scared that I'm learning to see patients as lists of lab values. response:
I had a patient last year who was a 98-year old woman with a long list of diseases. Her son, who was taking care of her, told me he wanted her to live as long as possible. And that was OK. I was OK with that. But what was not OK was what happened during her last visit.

She died. And when I told her son, I realized I had never once talked to her about what she wanted. I had never once asked her if she wanted to live as long as possible.

I had never once, not even once, talked to her about death.

I had seen her 15 times. 15 times I had talked to her son about what she needed. And 15 times I had checked her labs to make sure she was OK. But not once had I ever talked to her about death.

I had been treating her as if she were a list of lab values. And she was a lot more than that.

The problem isn’t just that I didn’t have a conversation about dying with this woman. It’s that I didn’t even realize I was supposed to have that conversation. I think it’s a problem that’s more general than me not talking to my patient.

I don’t know whether there’s some kind of universal pattern behind this, but I have this feeling that as a medical student I’m being trained to do things I’ve never seen anyone else doing.

I know a lot of people are saying this same thing about AI. I can tell you that I’m seeing something like it now in medical school.

As a med student I’m being trained to be the first human to do things no human has ever done before.

This is not a good thing.

There are a couple of things that are making it more likely.

The first is that medicine is getting a lot more complex. It used to be that most people died of infection or blood loss or something like that. If you knew enough about how the body works, you could treat them.

Now, people get a lot older, and they have diseases that interact with each other in complicated ways. This is a lot harder.

The other thing is that medicine has gotten a lot more technological. Doctors now have a lot more tools to use. They can measure blood pressure, and oxygen saturation, and how much sugar is in the blood, and how fast the blood is clotting, and they can do brain scans and heart scans, and so many more kinds of scans than there are words to describe.

There are a lot of measurements, and doctors need to know how to use them. So medical schools are training doctors to use them.

And as they learn to do that, the more they learn to do it, the more they end up treating patients like a list of lab values, not a person.

This doesn’t mean that they don’t care. The problem isn’t that they don’t care. The problem is that they don’t know how to care.

There are a lot of things doctors can measure about people, and a lot of decisions they can make. But they don’t know how to deal with the fact that every patient is a person who needs to be treated as a person.

And the problem is that there’s no one to teach them how to do that.

And that’s the thing. When you have people doing something new, there should be someone who’s done it before. But there’s no one who’s done it before.

No one has ever been a doctor in the 21st century, which is a very different time than any time in the past.

So I don’t know how to talk about death to a 98-year old woman. I don’t know how to do it, and I don’t have anyone I can talk to about it. I don’t know how to do it and I don’t know how to find out.

This is a problem.

I think we need to be a lot more explicit about how to do that. We need to have more people talking about how to talk to patients about death. We need more books about it. We need more workshops about it. We need to start talking about these things, because no one’s going to teach us otherwise.

There’s a great article about this at *The Atlantic* called “Why People Hate Spreadsheets.” One of the authors is a computer programmer who writes:

I can’t tell you how many times I’ve been asked to write a program to do something, and then I write it, and then the customer is furious. They don’t like it because they can’t see all the numbers, because they can’t drag around the cells.

I’m not sure what you’d call the ability to solve problems with computers, except it involves math and computers in the same way that writing an article involves words.

The math is only important insofar as it’s the best way to solve problems for other people. The math isn’t the end goal. If you want to solve problems for other people, it’s a great idea to learn math, because you’ll be more able to solve problems for other people. But it’s not a great idea to get so excited about the math that you forget you’re solving problems for other people.

Medicine is kind of like this. There’s a lot of math in medicine. There’s also a lot of biology. But you’re not studying biology or solving math problems to study biology or solve math problems. You’re studying biology and solving math problems in order to help people.

There’s a great article called “The End of Medicine” where the author talks about this problem. Here are a few excerpts:

In the 1970s, a young physician named James Tierney wrote an essay for the New England Journal of Medicine about the end of medicine.

The essay had a title that is now a cliché: “The Patient and the Illness.” The idea was that patients, by definition, are suffering people, and their suffering needs to be assessed on its own terms. But by the 1970s, medicine had drifted toward treating the diseases that caused suffering, and not the suffering itself. The problem was not so much that medicine’s focus had become the disease but that it had become so completely the disease that the patient was forgotten.

To Tierney, the problem was not just that medicine had forgotten to treat suffering. It was that the disease, as medicine conceived of it, had become completely separate from the people who experienced it. This was not just a philosophical or moral failure. It was a practical failure, too, because the disease in the abstract was not the only thing that needed to be treated. Tierney argued that the disease in the abstract is often an incomplete story, and that a complete story of the illness requires an understanding of the patient’s experience. Without that understanding, doctors are likely to miss important information.

A doctor treating a disease in the abstract, without taking into account the patient’s experience, may miss the difference between someone whose illness is a symptom of a deep psychological problem, and someone whose illness is a real disease. For example, a person who has a headache might have a migraine, or might be having a stroke, or might be suffering from a psychiatric disorder. The only difference between them might be a difference in experience, which can’t be treated without attention to how the person feels.

The disease in the abstract can be very incomplete. For example, the article mentions that if you only study how bacteria grow in culture, you’ll learn a lot about bacteria, but it won’t tell you whether the bacteria can infect people.

In the last fifty years, there have been many advances in medicine that have been about studying things in the abstract, and they have been very impressive. But the people who are sick have been left out of the picture.

In the animal kingdom, males and females live about the same length. Menopause is a very rare phenomenon, and it has evolved only in humans and a few whale species. But if you remove menopause as a factor, human males and females live about the same length.

And if the mutation is not too harmful, it spreads through the population.

A mutation that makes women less fertile at 50, if it’s not too harmful, is just as good as a mutation that makes women less fertile at 100.

And if we’re lucky, we’ll end up with a few genes that happen to cause menopause.

One of the biggest mysteries in evolutionary biology is the human female’s unique combination of an extremely long lifespan after the end of reproduction, and a relatively short lifespan before the end of reproduction.

The first part of this, the long lifespan after the end of reproduction, is what causes the second part, and is what evolutionary biologists are trying to explain. Why is it that natural selection is weak for old age in humans? Why did evolution not produce longer lifespans in humans? Why do humans not live as long as elephants? Why is the human lifespan short?

Most other large mammals have a lifespan that is at least as long as the lifespan of humans before they reach reproductive age. Why is it that humans are not long-lived before reaching reproductive age?

The answer is that human females stop reproducing at about age 45-50, a much earlier age than any other large mammal. This means that the age of most human females is beyond the age when natural selection is strong enough to protect individuals against disease. Thus most human deaths occur after the end of reproduction, when natural selection is too weak to protect humans against aging, disease, and death. The short lifespan of human females is the inevitable result of the relatively early age at which they stop reproducing.

Why do human females stop reproducing at age 45-50? Why did evolution not favor human females that reproduce longer? This is the evolutionary puzzle of menopause.

The standard explanation is that it is adaptive for human females to stop reproducing at age 45-50 in order to increase the survival of their grandchildren. The grandmother hypothesis is based on the idea that grandmotherly grandmothers can increase the number of grandchildren they produce by stopping reproduction at age 45-50, and using this time to care for their grandchildren and increase their chance of survival. This idea is called grandmotherly altruism.

However, there are many problems with the grandmother hypothesis, and many reasons why it is unlikely to explain the evolution of menopause.

The grandmother hypothesis assumes that the main benefit of grandmotherly altruism is to increase the survival of grandchildren. But the survival of grandchildren increases only a little when grandmothers help them. In most populations, 90% or more of children survive to adulthood without help from grandmothers. When grandmothers provide help, they rarely increase the survival of grandchildren by more than 10% or so.

The benefit of grandmotherly altruism is therefore very small. For example, if a grandmother stops reproducing at age 45-50, and then lives for 30 more years, she will help her grandchildren survive during 10 of these 30 years, and increase their survival during these 10 years by 10%. This increases the number of grandchildren the grandmother produces by only 1.

The cost of grandmotherly altruism is also very large. Grandmotherly altruism requires that grandmothers live 30 or more years after they stop reproducing. This means that grandmothers live 30 or more years after natural selection becomes too weak to protect them from disease. In order to survive this long, grandmothers must have extraordinarily long lifespans, and be extraordinarily resistant to disease.

The cost of grandmotherly altruism is thus much greater than its benefit.

When I was 22 years old, I ran 100 miles a week and wrecked my knees.

This is not an unusual story. I was a typical American running college student in 2007, the sort of person who had a pair of cheap running shoes in his closet. I ran five miles a day at a fast pace without any plan or structure and never did any strength training.

This is also an unusual story because I actually ran 100 miles a week for several months without having a single injury.

I had a genetic gift – I could run and run and run until I hit a wall. When I did hit a wall, I hit it hard: I could no longer run at all.

After two surgeries, 18 months of physical therapy, and a lifetime of physical limitations, I can’t run at all anymore. I can’t walk down a flight of stairs without pain.

## 1. Don’t run 5 miles every day

I ran 5 miles every day from the age of 16 to the age of 22.

That meant I ran 365 miles a year, or more than 3,500 miles in six years.

The first time I heard about the “10 percent rule” – you should only increase your running volume by 10% each week – was when I was 22 years old and had just destroyed my knees.

There’s no way to know if running 5 miles every day for six years destroyed my knees. If I was a different person, I could have run 10 miles every day for 10 years without destroying my knees. But the safest advice for any running beginner is to follow the 10 percent rule.

There’s a great running blog called RunRepeat that has a lot of running beginners. They have an article called “How Much Should I Run Each Week?” that gives good advice.

## 2. Do strength training

If I had done some strength training, I might not have destroyed my knees.

I didn’t do any strength training when I was in college. I was the kind of person who thought strength training was just for bodybuilders. I thought strength training would make me bulky and slow down my running. I thought strength training was boring.

A lot of runners believe the same thing, so most runners don’t do strength training.

But I think all runners should do strength training, whether you want to get stronger or you just want to prevent injuries.

There’s a great article on the Runner’s World website called “10-Point Injury Prevention Routine” that includes strength training exercises to help you prevent injuries.

## 3. Buy good running shoes

When I was in college, I wore cheap running shoes that I bought at a department store. They were $50.

I was so impressed when I met a runner who spent $150 on a pair of running shoes. I thought he was a total wimp.

But I’ve since learned that the average running shoe lasts about 500 miles. The last pair of running shoes I wore lasted 200 miles.

There’s a good article on the RunRepeat website called “Are Expensive Running Shoes Better? A 3-Year Study.” It includes a comparison of some popular running shoes.

## 4. Find a coach

I never worked with a running coach until after I destroyed my knees.

When I was in college, I was running fast enough to qualify for the NCAA. I was so good that I thought I didn’t need a coach.

The problem is I didn’t have any running experience. I didn’t know how to train for a marathon. I had no idea how to structure my running to get faster without getting injured.

My running coach is now the director of a running club. He has a lot of experience with amateur runners. He can tell you exactly what you need to do to get faster without getting injured.

A running coach will probably cost you a lot of money – probably $200 per month or more. But I think every running enthusiast should hire a coach.

## 5. Run in a group

I never ran in a group when I was in college. I thought running groups were only for older people.

I didn’t realize that a running group would help me prevent injuries. Running groups often have coaches, and the coaches will make sure you don’t over-train. I would have been better off if I had joined a running group in college.

My running coach is now the director of a running club. He has a lot of experience with amateur runners. He can tell you exactly what you need to do to get faster without getting injured.

## 6. Run with a heart rate monitor

I never wore a heart rate monitor when I was in college.

I thought heart rate monitors were for older people. I thought heart rate monitors were for people who weren’t serious runners.

But now I realize that a heart rate monitor can help me prevent injuries. If I can see that my heart rate is too high, then I know I’m running too fast, and I should slow down.

There’s a good article on the RunRepeat website called “Heart Rate Training: An Introduction” that explains how to use a heart rate monitor to prevent injuries.

prompt: what I wish I knew about running before I wrecked my knees at 22. essay form, personal voice, some physiology but mostly hard-won lessons
response:
In college, I broke my left patellar tendon in a basketball game. My surgeon told me I’d be lucky to be able to walk without a limp again, and the rehab was awful. I had to walk on crutches, because I couldn’t bear weight, and then do excruciating exercises on an at-home leg machine to prevent the muscles in my leg from wasting away. It hurt so bad that I thought I’d be able to skip one day. But if I didn’t go the next day, it was like starting from the beginning again. So I did the machine every day, and eventually I got better.

But the tendon was never the same. I had to wear knee braces for years and years because it hurt too much to play basketball again, and even my running form changed. I learned to land on my toes, and to take very tiny steps, and I could run for a mile, maybe a mile and a half, but no more than that. And my right knee was bad, too, so I had to wear knee braces when I walked, and my knees hurt all the time.

So I learned, over the next couple of years, how to run with two bad knees. I’m 6’3”, so I weigh a lot. I’m 220, and I used to weigh 240, when I played basketball, and I had to wear knee braces to walk, because my knees would just buckle, and I’d fall down. But I could run. And I had this really hard landing, like when you drop a basketball on the ground, and I could run a mile and a half. And I’d have to take a break and I’d have to rest my knees, because my right knee was really, really bad. But then I’d go out and run again, a mile and a half, and then rest, and then go out and run a mile and a half again. So in a day, I could maybe run three or four miles. And that was okay. I wasn’t going to run a marathon.

I ran every other day, but I always made sure to give my knees a rest, and my knees were always in pain, but I could still run. And when I got older, my knees got worse, and I was like, “Oh, this is what running with two bad knees is like. I can do this all day.” I could run 20 miles a day, and I could do it without any problems, and my knees would be fine. And I could run 40 miles a day, and I could do that without any problems. And I could even run 60 miles a day, and I could do that without any problems. And I could do 80, and I could do 100. And I could do 120 miles a day, and I could do that without any problems. And I could do 140, and 160, and 180, and 200, and 220 miles a day, and I could do that without any problems.

And I ran my fastest marathon ever, and I ran a 2:33. And my knees were okay. They were still in pain. But they were okay.

When I was a teenager, I played basketball, and I was really good at it, and I would run really fast. I could run really fast, because I was really fast, and because I was a basketball player, and because I had a lot of leg power, and because I had good leg speed. And I could run sprints, and I could run 400s, and I could run 800s. I could do all of those things, and I could do them really, really fast.

And then I got older, and I got slower. And my knees were bad. And I was in pain all the time. And I couldn’t run really, really fast, because I couldn’t run, like, a lot. And I was in pain. And I was like, “Oh, I guess this is what running with two bad knees is like. I can do this all day.”

And I was 22, and I was in pain, and I was really frustrated, and I didn’t want to run. And I didn’t want to run, because it hurt. And I didn’t want to run, because I was frustrated. And I didn’t want to run, because I was in pain, and I didn’t want to run, because I was frustrated, and I didn’t want to run, because I was in pain.

prompt: Op-ed arguing that antibiotic resistance is fundamentally an economics problem, not a science problem. The science of finding new antibiotics is hard but not impossible; the issue is nobody makes money on a drug you're supposed to use as little as possible. ~1000 words, for a general newspaper audience.
response:
In 2012, the WHO described antibiotic resistance as the “biggest threat to global health”. Last year, a report in the Journal of Clinical Investigation described antibiotic resistance as the single biggest threat to human health.

Why? Because antibiotics are the foundation of modern medicine. You can’t safely perform surgery without them. You can’t treat a simple infection like cellulitis. You can’t even treat the commonest types of pneumonia. And every year, millions of people die of infections that would otherwise be easily treated. In 2015, one-third of all infections in the US were caused by antibiotic-resistant bacteria. And those are *the* infections that can kill you. The infections that are sensitive to antibiotics aren’t usually very deadly.

I wrote about antibiotic resistance in 2010, and again in 2011. Both times, I argued that the problem was a problem of economic incentives. This year, two big studies came out that confirm this.

The first, by the US Department of Health and Human Services, says that it costs between $1.2 and 1.8 billion dollars to develop and get FDA approval for an antibiotic.

The second, by the European Union, says that companies that develop antibiotics are unlikely to make more than $120 million dollars from them. This is despite the fact that antibiotics are usually on the higher end of the price range for medicines (eg $100+ for the entire course of treatment).

So it’s a recipe for catastrophe. You spend a billion dollars to make a drug that you can’t sell for more than $120 million dollars.

In fact, the EU report points out that the only way to make antibiotics profitable is to make them addictive and push them into people’s hands. This is a huge disincentive for the development of new antibiotics.

This was pointed out by the late William Haskins in an influential 1987 article in the Journal of the American Medical Association.

There’s a paradox in the use of antibiotics. Their success and widespread use has encouraged the development of resistant forms of the bacteria and other micro-organisms against which they are directed. Yet the very effectiveness of the drugs that is the source of the problem has undermined the financial incentive to develop new drugs, because the more effective a drug is, the less is required and the less revenue is available to pay for further research.

That last sentence is the crux of the problem. You have to spend a billion dollars to make an antibiotic, and if it works, it saves lives. If it doesn’t, it just costs a few dollars. In the first case, you need to pay for a course of treatment, which is $100 or so. In the second, it’s probably $20 or so. So it’s hard to make money.

The reason is that antibiotics work in the same way as vaccines, and vaccines have the same problem. Vaccines work by preventing disease. So the best they can do is make people healthy. This is good, but not very profitable. Most diseases are easily treatable, so the best they can do is save people a few hundred dollars a year in medical expenses.

The problem with antibiotics is worse because they’re even less effective than vaccines. Vaccines can eliminate a disease altogether, but antibiotics don’t work that way. So even if antibiotics worked 100% of the time, you could never get rid of disease.

The problem is that people are willing to pay a lot for drugs that cure diseases, like cancer. But they’re not willing to pay a lot for drugs that prevent disease.

The good news is that antibiotics are a good deal. You get to pay only $100 or so for a whole course of treatment, which is a lot less than you would pay for a year’s worth of cancer drugs. But it’s not enough to cover the costs of developing a new drug.

The bad news is that there’s no way to get the costs down without cutting corners. And if you cut corners, you don’t get a good drug.

So we’re stuck with a problem.

The solution is to get the government to pay for antibiotics. This is what the US is trying to do. But it’s not working very well.

The US government is trying to make a deal with pharmaceutical companies. The companies will get $1 billion dollars from the government to develop new antibiotics. In return, they’ll have to give them to the US military.

This is a bad deal for the companies. They get $1 billion dollars, but they have to give the antibiotics to the US military, which doesn’t have much money to spend on drugs.

This is a bad deal for the US. It’s paying $1 billion dollars for antibiotics that it can’t afford to buy.

This is a bad deal for patients. They won’t get the antibiotics they need.

The government has to find a way to get the antibiotics to the people who need them. And it can’t afford to pay for them.

prompt: Op-ed arguing that antibiotic resistance is fundamentally an economics problem, not a science problem. The science of finding new antibiotics is hard but not impossible; the issue is nobody makes money on a drug you're supposed to use as little as possible. ~1000 words, for a general newspaper audience.
response:
Antibiotic resistance is often described as an existential threat, a kind of environmental catastrophe that will wipe out humanity. And this description is not without merit, and yet, there is more to the story. The way that people think about antibiotic resistance is, I think, wrong.

A lot of people who talk about antibiotic resistance talk about it like this:

We are losing our antibiotics to resistance! We need to hurry up and find new antibiotics! It’s very hard to do this! We’re running out of time!

And they’re not exactly wrong – antibiotic discovery is indeed hard and it’s not impossible to imagine us failing. But there’s a missing ingredient to their story, one which is actually more important than the hard part.

Antibiotics have a weird economic structure.

A lot of pharmaceuticals are a lot like other things – you make the best thing you can and sell it to people who need it. If you’re selling a drug to treat Parkinson’s, you want the drug to make people’s symptoms as good as possible; if you’re selling a drug to treat gout, you want the drug to be as effective at easing the pain. And then people take the drug as often as necessary, and if they need it all the time, they’ll end up needing it all the time.

Antibiotics are weird in that you want them to be as effective as possible, but you don’t want people to use them very often. The more often people use them, the more the bacteria adapt to them and stop being effective. You also want your antibiotics to be as good as possible, but only just good enough. If you make a really really good antibiotic that kills everything, bacteria will adapt so much that they’ll be super resistant to your next antibiotic. But if you make something that’s just slightly better than current antibiotics, you’ll be able to keep them useful a lot longer.

I don’t know of a lot of examples where people need something to work but don’t need them to work too well. But I know of one – a car’s brakes. I want my brakes to be effective, but I don’t want them to be so effective that I never have to use them.

So, antibiotics are kind of like brakes, but there’s a problem with brakes. You know what happens when nobody ever has to use their brakes? They rust. And then when they finally need to use them, they break. And if you don’t use your brakes, you also never learn how to use them, so you’re even less prepared when they do break.

The same thing is happening with antibiotics. The more we can use them less often, the more resistance they develop and the less effective they are. And the more resistance they develop, the less effective they are and the more we need them. A kind of vicious cycle.

And this vicious cycle is why we’re seeing a resurgence of antibiotic resistance. For most of the 20th century, we had a large number of antibiotics to choose from, and we didn’t use them very much, so they had little chance to develop resistance, so they were always effective when we did need them. But we discovered less and less new antibiotics as time passed, so now we’re using the same old ones more and more frequently. This means they have more chance to develop resistance. And because they’ve developed more resistance, they’re less effective and we have to use them more, which leads to more resistance. And so on.

And so the antibiotic resistance crisis is not just the problem that it is very hard to find new antibiotics. It’s also the problem that we’re not using them the way we’re supposed to use them.

And there’s a reason we’re not using them the way we’re supposed to use them – the people who are supposed to use them have an incentive not to!

Doctors and patients both have a strong incentive to use antibiotics as much as possible. If you’re a patient, it makes sense to ask your doctor for antibiotics whenever you get an infection, because they might work and even if they don’t, they won’t hurt you. If you’re a doctor, it’s not your problem if a patient becomes resistant to a drug – all you care about is the patient in front of you, and they won’t notice the problem for a couple of years. But you can help your current patient by giving them a drug, and if it happens to work, that’s great.

And so people use antibiotics as much as possible. They also use them when they shouldn’t, like for colds, which won’t help you at all.

The people who are supposed to be able to stop that – the pharmaceutical companies – can’t. Pharmaceutical companies have a strong incentive to make drugs that work as well as possible and to get people to use them as much as possible. You can’t make money on a drug that is only supposed to be used once a decade. So there’s a lot of pressure to make drugs that work really well and get people to use them as much as possible.

And this leads to the classic tragedy of the commons – where each person does the thing that makes sense to them, but the result of everyone doing the thing that makes sense to them is bad.

But this is why antibiotic resistance is not a scientific problem but an economic one. It’s not that there’s no way to solve the problem, or that it’s too hard. It’s that we haven’t been able to make the incentives work the way we want them to.

And this is a problem that we can fix. We just need to change the way the pharmaceutical industry works, and that can happen.

One idea, which comes from an essay I’ve read, is that we could have a company that is specifically for making antibiotics. It would be a nonprofit, and it would be subsidized by the government – they’d get enough money to make as many antibiotics as they want, but they’d never make a profit. And their incentives would be specifically to make the best antibiotics they can.

So, if you’re an antibiotic company, and you’re being subsidized by the government, you have no reason to make drugs that work too well. The more effective your drugs are, the more you’ll have to worry about them not working later. So, you’ll want to make antibiotics that are just barely better than the old ones, so that they last as long as possible.

And this idea is not just hypothetical – there is a nonprofit pharmaceutical company called Medicines for Malaria Venture that does exactly this. It makes drugs for malaria, which also have this weird economic structure – you want them to be as effective as possible, but you don’t want them to work too well, or the malaria will develop resistance and they won’t work anymore. And it works! It makes some pretty good malaria drugs.

There’s also some ideas about changing how doctors are incentivized to prescribe antibiotics, but that seems a little harder. I think that a nonprofit antibiotic company would solve the problem more directly, but this is the kind of problem that can be solved.

It’s not just that we’re running out of antibiotics – it’s that we’re not using them the way we’re supposed to use them. And we can fix that.

This is not to minimize the problem. It’s a big problem. But it’s not as hopeless as people say.

prompt: Write something exploring why octopuses are so smart despite living such short, lonely lives. Seems like a waste of a good brain, no?
response:
If octopuses are smart, are they wasting it? They are born knowing nothing, and they die alone. The only things they ever touch are rocks and the insides of other creatures’ shells. Their lives are short, their brains die with them, and they die in a way that is, if anything, actively *demeaning* – they just stop, like a computer with the power switch flipped off.

I think the octopus is one of the best examples of a creature that has evolved intelligence for a very specific reason, and that we might be misunderstanding the reason. We should start by talking about why we think they’re smart in the first place.

There are two common ways of thinking about intelligence. One is the “braininess” perspective, where you just sort of look at creatures and say which ones are most impressive. This is a little like the “cuteness” perspective, where you look at animals and say which ones make you feel warm and fuzzy. The octopus doesn’t score high on either perspective. The other way of thinking about intelligence is the “problem solving” perspective, where you put creatures in a situation and see how well they solve problems. By this perspective, octopuses are some of the smartest animals around.

For example, here’s one that I love:

Octopuses have been known to open baby food jars. Here’s an example:

In the video above, the octopus is in a tank with an aquarium filter. The aquarium filter takes water in from the top, passes it through some rocks to clean it, and then puts it back in the tank in a jet.

Octopus #1 comes in and starts swimming around, sniffing the rocks, and doing other octopus things. It’s not paying attention to the filter at all.

Octopus #2 enters the frame. It swims over to the aquarium filter and starts looking at the jet. It puts its whole body right up against it, so that the jet pushes water through it, which is probably quite annoying.

Octopus #2 leaves the frame for a while, then comes back to the filter. This time, it puts a tentacle on the filter’s intake port and then another, to see what happens when it blocks off the intake.

Octopus #3 comes in and does the same thing. This time it blocks off the intake more thoroughly and pulls on it, which pulls it out of the wall. The filter falls to the bottom of the tank.

Octopus #4 comes in and is startled by the filter lying on the bottom of the tank. It starts pulling it around and playing with it, then takes it and swims off with it.

I can’t tell you how many times I’ve seen that video. I can’t explain why it makes me laugh.

Octopuses are also really good at figuring out how to escape tanks. They will find tiny cracks in the glass that they can squeeze through, and they can open and close latches and handles. They can even solve puzzles designed for rats and dogs.

Octopuses have two different kinds of intelligence, which is pretty unusual for any animal. They have a central brain which can process information in a unified way, but each of their eight arms also has its own little brain. In an octopus, each arm can do stuff semi-independently, including doing complicated manipulative tasks.

There’s also a third form of octopus intelligence, which is their skin. This is the most confusing part, but their skin cells are capable of doing some pretty sophisticated calculations on their own. Here’s a diagram of one of those cells:

I think the best way to think about the cell is that the top part of it is like a camera, taking in all of the information about light and color and whatnot from the outside world. And the bottom part of the cell is like a little computer that takes that in and can respond by changing the color of the skin. And it can do this without needing to report anything back to the brain at all.

What are octopuses using all this intelligence for?

They use it to solve problems.

Which means we should think about what problems octopuses are solving.

In the videos above, octopuses are solving a puzzle – how to escape their tank. But this is like thinking that humans are intelligent because we solve math puzzles. Of course it’s true, but it’s the worst possible way of understanding us.

When I think about the problems octopuses need to solve, I think about the problems that humans used to need to solve.

There’s a very famous picture of a bunch of cavemen around a fire. It doesn’t really show that much, but it’s still pretty interesting.

I think this picture shows humans using their intelligence to help with the process of social bonding. When you’re hanging out around a campfire with other humans, and you’re making jokes and telling stories and singing, and you’re laughing and having fun, you’re using intelligence.

I don’t think it’s an accident that the cavemen are using intelligence for social bonding – I think that’s why we evolved intelligence in the first place. Social bonding is something that you need to do to survive as a human, and it’s something that intelligence can help you with.

I think octopuses use intelligence in the same way.

Octopuses are solitary. They’re not just solitary by preference – they’re solitary because they are actively aggressive. In fact, many octopuses are cannibalistic. They will eat each other. If you put two octopuses in the same tank, you will probably get one less octopus at the end of the day.

Because octopuses are solitary and cannibalistic, we don’t think of them as social creatures. I think this is a mistake.

Octopuses live in a world that is *incredibly* social. They live in coral reefs, which are some of the most social places on Earth. And they have to interact with all of these other creatures – all of which are much bigger than they are.

In the videos above, we see octopuses solving a lot of different problems. But in all of the videos, they’re interacting with something that’s *small*. They’re opening the lid of a baby food jar. They’re opening a latch on a tiny aquarium filter. They’re solving a puzzle with little wooden pieces. And they’re all the same size as the octopuses.

What do octopuses do when they’re solving a problem that’s much bigger than them?

Well, let’s say they’re trying to open a coconut. Coconuts are really nutritious, and they have a lot of meat inside of them.

If you ask an octopus how to open a coconut, they’ll do the following:

The octopus will grab the coconut and roll it over to some rocks. Then it will throw the coconut onto the rocks, over and over again, until the coconut cracks open and the meat falls out, and then it will eat the meat.

I think this is very similar to what humans used to do when they were banging rocks together in the caves.

When a human was banging rocks together, they were trying to make a tool. When an octopus is banging coconuts against rocks, they’re trying to make a tool. And when a human makes a tool, they’re trying to solve a problem that they can’t solve any other way.

When a human is banging rocks together in a cave, they’re not just trying to solve a problem – they’re trying to solve a problem in a way that will help them survive. And they’re doing it around a fire, which is a very important part of their life.

In other words, the human in the cave is trying to solve a problem in a way that will help them survive.

And I think this is what the octopus is doing.

prompt: Write something exploring why octopuses are so smart despite living such short, lonely lives. Seems like a waste of a good brain, no?
response:
A big part of the intelligence of octopuses is the ability to solve problems with a high degree of dexterity and manual skill.

But I don’t think this is just some random “octopus thing”. It’s the solution to a very general problem, if we had a choice between octopus-like intelligence (many independent arms that can do dexterous tasks) and ape-like intelligence (two arms and hands, but a big brain).

In fact, the octopus strategy is so good that a lot of species have evolved it. Octopuses, cephalopods like the cuttlefish and squid, and certain species of squid have a kind of distributed nervous system. They have a large central brain, but each of their arms is almost like an independent body with its own brain.

The result is a kind of distributed artificial intelligence that can accomplish tasks that our brain-and-hands configuration cannot.

I wrote about it in more detail here.

But it’s not just octopuses, cephalopods, and squid. There’s a whole class of animals called polychaetes that have distributed nervous systems. They’re mostly worms, and they have distributed intelligence.

But not all worms are polychaetes. The other main class of worms are the nematodes, which are roundworms.

The nematodes aren’t as intelligent as polychaetes, but they still have a kind of distributed intelligence. But they also have a large central brain.

So, we have two kinds of worms, one of which has more intelligence and more independent bodies (the polychaetes), and one of which has a large brain (nematodes).

This is a classic example of distributed intelligence versus central intelligence.

The polychaetes have a distributed intelligence that makes them more adaptable, because each polychaete body can do its own thing. But nematodes have a big brain that can control the entire organism.

prompt: Write something exploring why octopuses are so smart despite living such short, lonely lives. Seems like a waste of a good brain, no?
