One of the strangest animals in the world, the octopus is a cephalopod, a group that includes squid and cuttlefish. They’re the only mollusks — mollusks! — that are smart, having evolved an intelligence comparable to that of a domestic cat. This has produced an animal that is not just clever, but also creative, resourceful and mischievous, all qualities that seem wasted on creatures that live solitary lives, rarely see other octopuses, and die within two years.

But that’s not quite the whole story. Octopuses are not just clever, they’re clever at a surprising range of tasks, and those tasks seem to be very different from the tasks that make other animals smart. It’s as if evolution, having already designed the brain of a smart cat, then decided to put that brain into an octopus, then added a few more clever things on top of that.

This is not a new observation. In a 2013 paper, the biologist Martin Gardner wrote about his experience of working with octopuses at the Monterey Bay Aquarium. Gardner was interested in whether octopuses could figure out how to open a container. Gardner found that when he offered octopuses a container, they would immediately start picking at it. They would try to lift it open, or turn it over, or even suck up its contents. But they would never open the container. Even when they had spent a whole day trying, they would never figure out that they could open the container by removing its lid.

The next day, Gardner returned to the aquarium and found that the octopuses had figured it out overnight. He hypothesized that octopuses were clever, but not very good at learning, and would figure out novel problems in their sleep. This seems to be supported by recent research showing that octopuses do a lot of their learning while they’re sleeping.

Octopuses have a few things in common with humans. In particular, both have a brain with lots of neurons, which is why octopuses can be smart. But most of their similarities are superficial. In fact, the more we think about it, the more we can say that octopuses are nothing like us.

Octopuses live in a world that is completely alien. We, and most other animals, live on land. Octopuses live underwater. We live on a planet where the air is a gas. Octopuses live in an environment that is liquid. This matters a lot, because it makes it much easier to do things underwater than it is on land. For example, it’s easier to move around underwater, which is why many animals have evolved to be aquatic. It’s also easier to build things underwater, and this is why many animals are able to build things underwater. Octopuses, for example, are able to build things underwater, and they do it with ease.

The octopus body is very different from ours. It’s made mostly of muscle and tissue, and has no bones, so it’s very flexible, able to squeeze through gaps and holes that would be too small for us. It’s also very light, which makes it easy for octopuses to swim, which is why they can swim so quickly.

Octopuses’ brains are very different from ours too. Our brains are mostly made up of nerve cells, which are the cells that do most of the work in the brain. Octopus brains are mostly made up of a type of cell called a glial cell. This is a type of cell that is not found in human brains.

prompt: I'm an epidemiologist. Write an essay for a lay audience about why "correlation is not causation" is a slogan that does more harm than good, because it teaches people to dismiss observational evidence entirely rather than think about confounding. Mention smoking and lung cancer as the obvious case where we never had an RCT.
response:
I wrote yesterday about the smoking/lung cancer study, how it was one of the most important pieces of research ever, and how it was *not* an RCT. It was an observational study, with a big flaw: confounding. People who smoke also tend to have other behaviors that can cause lung cancer. And yet the study was still strong enough to convince everyone in the world that smoking causes lung cancer, and this is a big deal.

This is because “correlation does not imply causation” is not a principle, it is a warning label on a *specific kind* of study.

When you do an RCT, you can control for confounding. And then you don’t have to worry about confounding. So an RCT can show causation.

When you do an observational study, you can’t control for confounding. And so you have to worry about confounding. But as long as you think carefully about what confounders could be there, and control for them as much as you can, then you can still have some evidence for causation.

But when you have an observational study, and you don’t control for confounding, and you don’t even try to think about what confounders could be there, and you conclude it is a real effect, then you will have a lot of problems.

I don’t know where the idea that “correlation doesn’t imply causation” came from, but if it came from that, it’s not very well phrased. The problem is, that’s the kind of study everybody’s mom does. And so the slogan ends up teaching people to dismiss observational evidence *entirely*.

In a lot of cases this is the right thing to do. A lot of observational studies *are* so bad that they deserve to be dismissed, and people’s moms do deserve to be dismissed.

But some observational studies are very, very good.

The best observational study is one that controls for as many potential confounders as it can.

And the second-best observational study is one that *doesn’t* control for confounders, but *thinks very hard* about whether the results could possibly be due to confounding.

That’s what the smoking/lung cancer study was. It didn’t control for anything, but it did a really good job thinking about how much you would have to confound it in order to make it go away.

prompt: I'm an epidemiologist. Write an essay for a lay audience about why "correlation is not causation" is a slogan that does more harm than good, because it teaches people to dismiss observational evidence entirely rather than think about confounding. Mention smoking and lung cancer as the obvious case where we never had an RCT.
response:
I am trying to remember if I mentioned this before: correlation is not causation?

This was a great slogan for its day. It warned us that we had to think hard about our methods to get good results. It warned us that some studies might be misleading. But we’ve gone so far as to make it into a meme. We say it to people like: “I know you found some correlation, but correlation is not causation.”

If a study is well conducted, it is an estimate of causality. It is not a test of causality. You can’t just take an estimate of causality and say “well, correlation is not causation”.

And if you think you can do this, then you are making a serious mistake. I’m not sure how to say this in a way that is clear and not confusing to people.

One way to say it might be:

If you find a correlation between A and B, you might be seeing an effect of A on B. You might also be seeing an effect of B on A, or some third variable C causing both A and B, or some other weird thing. So you have to think really carefully about whether A could affect B, and what other explanations are possible.

If you do all that, and still think there is a causal effect, then you have an estimate of causation. You can’t say “correlation is not causation” anymore.

Now, this was not a problem back when epidemiology was young. You had a study that was supposed to show that smoking caused lung cancer. You could say “correlation is not causation” and the study might be wrong. There might be some other explanation. So you could ask for an RCT.

But now epidemiology is much more sophisticated. You are not going to get any studies which say “smoking causes lung cancer” anymore. You are going to get studies which say “smoking causes lung cancer. We adjusted for every possible confounding variable. And we used instrumental variable models. And we did the thing where they look at the gene which makes the enzyme that metabolizes nicotine. And all of it is consistent. We are confident.”

And you can’t say “correlation is not causation” to that. And even if you did, that is not a useful reply.

The only useful reply is to question the assumptions of the study. Maybe they didn’t adjust for all the possible confounders? Maybe they have some kind of bias that is unaccounted for? Maybe there is some weird interaction effect or something?

But those are specific arguments that depend on the specific study. They are not “correlation is not causation”.

prompt: I'm an epidemiologist. Write an essay for a lay audience about why "correlation is not causation" is a slogan that does more harm than good, because it teaches people to dismiss observational evidence entirely rather than think about confounding. Mention smoking and lung cancer as the obvious case where we never had an RCT.
response:
The most common reaction to seeing some observational study, or hearing that observational studies show some link between X and Y, is “correlation is not causation”. This is technically true, but it’s a slogan that is often used incorrectly, and that causes people to dismiss observational evidence entirely.

I think most people have the idea that the scientific method involves doing observational studies, then testing your hypothesis with randomized controlled trials. For example, they think doctors studied that aspirin lowers the risk of heart attacks by studying populations of people with and without heart attacks and measuring the risk in both. When they see observational studies showing some link between X and Y, they think “ah, they haven’t done a proper RCT yet, I’ll just wait for the definitive answer”.

But that’s not true. RCTs are only done when you already have some reason to think the intervention might work. And the reason is always observational studies.

Take aspirin. People noticed aspirin seemed to be associated with lower heart attack risk. Then they did an RCT to make sure. The aspirin story was a little complicated (see my post on the aspirin controversy), but at least it involved an RCT.

What about smoking? Nobody would have thought to do an RCT of “should we smoke cigarettes or not?”. The evidence for that is purely observational. The same is true of most things. We never randomized people to see if they would or would not get colonoscopies, and the evidence for colonoscopies being useful is purely observational.

It’s even more complicated than that. The observational studies on aspirin were themselves based on previous observational studies of aspirin and other drugs like it. This process can go back several generations, so by the time you get to the aspirin RCT, you’re several steps removed from any particular observation.

So in practice, observational studies are not the first step in the scientific method. The first step in the scientific method is observational studies of observational studies of observational studies of observational studies.

And in practice, observational studies are the most important part of the scientific method. They are the part that generates new knowledge. RCTs are mostly there to double-check that observational studies are right, and they almost always do.

It’s not even true that RCTs can be better than observational studies. I wrote an article in which I claimed observational studies might be the only type of study we could ever do on things like the safety of anesthesia, because it’s not ethical to randomize patients to the different anesthetics. But someone wrote in and said “no, you can always do retrospective observational studies, where you look at people who happened to get different anesthetics and see who was more likely to have bad results”. This is also true. In this case, the observational study is not an observational study of a randomized trial, but it is still a study of something that was *almost* randomized, which may have similar virtues.

I don’t want people to stop being skeptical of observational studies. I want them to understand that they are the main way we learn things, and so the question of whether something is proven should not be “whether we have done an RCT yet”.

The question of whether something is proven should be “how many observational studies are there, and how well do they match up?”

If you want some examples of how the system works, see my posts on the aspirin controversy, and on how observational studies of the aspirin controversy were able to explain why it didn’t work.

There’s an internal biological clock in every person’s body. In the 1980s, a scientist named Jeffrey Hall discovered a few genes in fruit flies that controlled the clock. One of these genes makes a protein called PERIOD, or PER. If you mess with the PER gene in fruit flies, they don’t sleep on a 24-hour schedule, but a shorter or longer one.

PER protein accumulates in the cell during the day, and is destroyed at night. When enough of it accumulates, the cell decides it’s time to sleep. When it’s all gone, the cell decides it’s time to wake up. This cycle takes 24 hours.

But it’s not just travel that makes our bodies tired. Anything that throws the clock out of sync with our usual schedule makes our bodies tired. And that’s what happens to nurses who work on the night shift. They’re working from 11pm to 7am. When they finish work and go home and try to sleep, it’s 7am. But their bodies don’t know that. Their bodies are still on a 24 hour cycle, and the PER protein is still accumulating in their cells. And they’re tired. So even if they manage to fall asleep, they can’t sleep well, and they wake up feeling tired. And then they have to work again. So they get more tired, and they can’t sleep as well. But when the nurse goes to sleep at 7am, his body is still in the day-time mode, and his blood pressure and heart rate are high. His body is working overtime to keep him awake, and he’s tired.

There’s also evidence that having a messed up PER cycle makes you gain weight. Nurses who work the night shift are 30% more likely to have high blood pressure, and 20% more likely to be obese, than nurses who don’t.

So how do we fix this?

prompt: Write an essay considering whether the placebo effect should be thought of as a treatment in its own right, including open-label placebo studies, and what that would mean for informed consent.
response:
Placebos are usually thought of as an ethical evil that makes it hard to properly test treatments.

But it’s possible to treat the placebo as a useful treatment on its own. For example, in one study, patients who got a placebo and were told they were getting an actual treatment were more satisfied with their pain management than patients who got no treatment at all.

This raises the question of whether we can ethically exploit patients’ desire to believe they’re getting some sort of real treatment for their own benefit.

A paper in PLOS One describes an experiment that explores this idea. It’s not the first open-label placebo study, but it is pretty thorough.

They recruited 158 patients with chronic knee pain. All of them were told they were going to get placebo pills for 12 days. 85 were told that their pills were “inert substances” that wouldn’t produce any treatment effects. 73 were given an additional explanation that “there is a large placebo effect in the human body. We know from several studies that placebo treatment can improve symptoms.”

As you might expect, the placebo effect was much stronger in the group who was told about it. 35% of the “inert substances” group reported any improvement compared to 62% of the “placebo effect” group. The “placebo effect” group also reported greater reduction in their pain level.

There is a question of how to interpret this result. In a normal double-blind study, you might say that a treatment is better than a placebo if it works better in patients who think they’re getting it. But here, if we assume that the placebo effect group would be better off getting an actual treatment, then we can’t say they were treated better because they think they’re getting something. If we assume the placebo effect group would be better off not getting a treatment at all, then we can’t say they were treated better because they think they’re getting something. And if we assume that they were indifferent between getting the placebo effect and not getting a treatment at all, then we can’t say the placebo effect treatment is better than the inert substances treatment.

So what does this have to do with informed consent?

Informed consent means giving patients information about the risks and benefits of their treatment. In this case, that means telling them that there is a 35% chance that they will experience some improvement. This is the same in either group.

prompt: Write an essay considering whether the placebo effect should be thought of as a treatment in its own right, including open-label placebo studies, and what that would mean for informed consent.
response:
I’ve seen a lot of discussion about the placebo effect recently. Most of it has centered around the “nocebo effect”, the phenomenon where a placebo can actually make you feel worse. This is a fun new area to investigate, but in this post I want to consider what it would mean to think of placebos not merely as a side effect to be investigated, but as a legitimate treatment in their own right.

I.

Suppose I have a condition that responds to a drug. The doctor gives me that drug, and the condition improves.

There are two ways to think about this.

One way is to say “The drug worked. The drug was the cause of the improvement”. This is the standard view, and the one that is the most convenient and most often invoked.

The other way is to say “The placebo effect worked. You were told that a drug would work, and the power of your own belief was enough to make it work”. This is the view that some people (including me) hold to a degree.

I would never say that the placebo effect works every time, or even most of the time. There are times when you need a drug because your condition is so serious, and the placebo effect isn’t even the slightest bit helpful. But there are also times when you don’t need a drug because the placebo effect is enough.

This might seem to violate our intuition that the placebo effect doesn’t work, since we don’t have a lot of placebo treatment options. But we also don’t have a lot of options for treatment in general. The vast majority of people with chronic pain are told it’s incurable, and there’s no treatment. If you can offer them a treatment that’s 10% as effective as a painkiller, that might be worth a lot.

I’ve been arguing for the placebo effect as a treatment option for years. It’s the main reason why I don’t think it’s wrong for doctors to pretend they’re doing something to make things better. You might think it’s wrong for doctors to pretend they’re doing something, but actually they *are* doing something, and it’s helping.

I also used to think this made placebo effects easy to test. If you’re skeptical of the placebo effect, and someone asks you to do an experiment to disprove it, just give people placebo drugs and see if they get better.

But I recently learned there’s a new area of placebo research that challenges this. The idea is called “open-label placebos”.

Open-label placebo treatment is when you give someone a placebo and tell them you’re giving them a placebo. This seems like it would be useless, since it relies on telling people they’re getting a treatment that doesn’t work. But there are now two studies suggesting it works anyway.

The most well-known was a small study from the University of Massachusetts in 2014. In the placebo group, 41% of patients said their chronic pain improved, while in the no-treatment group only 8% of patients said their chronic pain improved. It was a small sample size, and they didn’t have a good control group, but still.

Then this week another larger, more carefully controlled trial out of Harvard came out, with similar results.

II.

There’s a lot more to say about these studies. There are concerns about the exact experimental setup; there are concerns about the sample size; there are concerns that the participants were motivated to please the researchers; and there are concerns about the fact that open-label placebos may be a different kind of placebo than the ones we usually think about. But I’m going to leave these aside for now and just consider the implications of open-label placebos.

It’s not that surprising to me that open-label placebos work, even though they seem to conflict with the standard placebo story. I’ve always believed that the placebo effect doesn’t work because of people’s mistaken beliefs about their treatment, but because of a more complicated mechanism that I’m not sure I really understand. But this story is consistent with the observation that open-label placebos work, and also with the observation that placebos sometimes work even when people know it’s a placebo.

The problem is that, if open-label placebos are a legitimate treatment, then we have to think about what it means to test open-label placebos.

I said before that it was easy to test the placebo effect, since all you had to do was give people placebos and see if they got better. But now it turns out it’s not that easy after all, because sometimes people get better even if you give them placebos. That means if we give people placebos, we can’t distinguish between open-label placebos and a placebo effect caused by open-label placebos, which is a problem.

If we want to figure out whether open-label placebos really work, or whether it’s just the placebo effect of open-label placebos, we’d need to have a control group where people know they’re getting open-label placebos, but they’re not actually given any.

That control group would be a lot harder to put together. You could do something like:

1. Give the subjects a fake appointment to get an open-label placebo treatment.

2. Tell them “this is a research study on the power of the placebo effect, and the treatment will be completely fake”.

3. Have the subject come to the appointment, but instead of giving them the open-label placebo treatment, tell them there’s been an emergency and you’ll have to reschedule, and apologize.

This is an experimental design I’ve seen suggested elsewhere, and I think it could work if done well. But I think it’s going to be a lot harder to do well than just giving people placebos, and so it’s probably not going to happen.

I think we’re going to get a lot of open-label placebo trials that don’t control for placebo effects, and that are going to be very hard to interpret.

I think we’re going to get a lot of open-label placebo trials that claim to control for placebo effects, but that don’t control for placebo effects very well, and that are going to be very hard to interpret.

I think we’re going to get a lot of open-label placebo trials that are going to be very hard to interpret.

And I’m not saying this is a bad thing, because it’s hard to think of anything harder to interpret than placebo effect trials.

III.

A lot of people think of the placebo effect as a confounding factor that makes it hard to figure out if a drug works. But I think it would be interesting to consider the opposite view: that the placebo effect is a legitimate treatment that we’re not giving people enough of.

If you don’t want to use the term “treatment” for the placebo effect, you could also call it a “complement”. Just as vitamins are a kind of complement that’s missing from a lot of diets, the placebo effect is a kind of complement that’s missing from a lot of treatments.

One thing that would help make this treatment more effective is to have doctors tell their patients that they’re giving them a placebo, rather than pretending it’s a real treatment.

Doctors can tell patients they’re giving them a placebo, and they still think it will work because of the placebo effect. This would allow doctors to be more honest with their patients, which would be nice.

But this also means that open-label placebos become a real treatment, and we need to test it.

This is going to be very hard to do, and I think we’re going to get a lot of studies that are going to be very hard to interpret. But I think it’s going to be an interesting field.

prompt: Write an essay considering whether the placebo effect should be thought of as a treatment in its own right, including open-label placebo studies, and what that would mean for informed consent.
response:
If you were in the grip of depression, you’d be happy to hear that the following treatments are effective: “taking a daily dose of Prozac,” “getting 5 hours of sunlight a day,” or “doing 3 hours of yoga a week.”

But suppose you were instead told that the best treatment would be to “take a daily dose of sugar.” You might be happy to hear that. But you might also be suspicious – if you didn’t know any better, you might think your doctor was either incompetent or trying to swindle you. If you knew better, you might think your doctor was trying to make fun of you.

I say all this because there’s some evidence that placebos do work. A lot of studies have tried to compare the effects of taking sugar pills to taking real pills (usually a fake treatment to a real one). When done properly, these studies always show that people who take sugar pills get better. Not as well as people who take real pills, but better than they would have without any treatment at all.

There are other reasons to think that placebos can be effective treatments. For example, if you take pain medicine and it works, but then you tell your friend that the medicine is really just a placebo, your friend can take the same medicine and find that it no longer works.

There’s also a long history of people taking placebos and getting better. The placebo pill is the oldest and most universal treatment in medicine. If you go to a doctor in any society in the world, there’s a good chance you’ll get a placebo. The sugar pill is a universal drug, and doctors everywhere use it to treat everything.

I think all of this is interesting, but there’s also an opportunity for more work in this area. This essay will attempt to outline some of these opportunities, including how to do studies to determine whether placebos really help, and if so how to make them even more effective.

1 – The Placebo Effect

There’s a famous story that during World War II, a British doctor gave a morphine drip to a wounded soldier and then ran out of morphine. He gave the soldier a saline drip and told him it was morphine. The soldier said he felt better after the saline than he had after the morphine, and the doctor was shocked.

Unfortunately, this story is probably apocryphal, but there’s a lot of other evidence to suggest that placebos can be very useful. For example, a recent study in the American Journal of Gastroenterology compared the effect of placebo pills to placebo injections, and found that placebo injections were much more effective. And a recent study in the journal Pain found that placebo pills were very useful for relieving chronic pain in patients with fibromyalgia.

2 – Placebo Effects in Clinical Trials

There are a lot of studies that compare placebo to real drugs, and they’ve all found that placebos work, although they don’t work as well as real drugs. There are a lot of different ways to study the placebo effect, and most of them find that people who take a placebo get better.

One study, however, found something really surprising: people who thought they were taking a placebo were actually better off than people who thought they were taking a real drug!

The researchers in this study divided people into two groups. One group took a sugar pill, and were told that it was a sugar pill. They were also told that the sugar pill would help them. The other group took the same sugar pill, and were told that it was a real drug, and that it would help them. Both groups got better. But the group who thought they were taking the placebo got better than the group who thought they were taking the real drug!

This is a surprising result. It’s surprising because it means that people who think they’re taking a placebo get better than people who think they’re taking a real drug. But this is not a very surprising result, because we know that people who take a real drug get better than people who take a placebo.

prompt: Why do we get goosebumps from music? Write it up as an essay. I'm interested in the evolutionary weirdness of it, a leftover hair-raising reflex triggered by a chord change.
response:
I remember my first time hearing *Thriller*. It was at a high school talent show, and everyone was standing in the hallways, waiting for the curtain to go up. I was standing in front of the bathroom. And when it started, I was like, *What is that?*

I knew it was a recording, but I was like, “Why does this make me feel like I want to scream?”

There are some things about music that are mysterious, including why it makes us feel so powerful. I don’t want to get into that here. I just want to talk about one part of it that we know quite a lot about: the goosebumps.

I remember my first time getting goosebumps from music, and it was also at a high school talent show. In fact, it was at the same one as *Thriller*. I had been in the band all year, and I was going to go out to join a few friends in the audience when the band started playing.

It was a guy playing guitar, and he was playing something in a minor key. Then there was a chord change, and I didn’t know what chord it was, but I knew it was a different chord. And it made me feel like my hair was standing up. And I didn’t know what the hell was going on, and I didn’t know what chord it was, and I don’t know how to talk about it, so I’ve been thinking about it for fifteen years, and I want to write a post about it.

I think my favorite description of the feeling I get from these sorts of music is from *Soul Searching* by Michael J. Miller:

I was listening to a CD of Chopin’s music in a friend’s living room. She was doing the dishes and I was lying on the couch and just listening. She had this wonderful record of Chopin’s nocturnes. And I was really feeling it.

And then there was this piece that had a chord change that just got me. I was like, oh my God. I’m getting goosebumps from a chord change. I’m getting goosebumps from a piece of music.

I had never thought of this before. I had never thought of this before in my life. This is so strange, and yet here I am, lying on this couch, and I’m getting goosebumps.

And then I just kept listening, and I was just like, *Oh my God, this is incredible*. And I just lay there, and my friend was doing dishes, and it was just such a magical moment. And then there was another chord change, and I just started crying. And then she came over to me and she was like, “Hey. What’s going on? Why are you crying?”

And I just said, “I’m just getting goosebumps. I’m getting goosebumps from a piece of music. And it’s so incredible, I’m just crying.”

And I think this is a really important point. That this feeling is so much stronger than any other emotion. When something happens to me in my life that’s really sad, or really happy, I’m not like, “Oh my God, I’m going to cry.” It’s just like, “Yeah, I’m sad.” But if a chord change happens, and I’m getting goosebumps, I might cry.

So why does this happen?

It happens because of our evolution.

You know how if a tiger comes out of the bushes, your hair stands on end? Or if someone is really angry at you, and you get this feeling? It’s because our body has this reflex of raising our hair. That’s why people who have hair all over their body get goosebumps. When a lot of people get scared, or angry, their hair stands up, but not in a way you can notice.

This reflex probably evolved because, if your hair is standing on end, you look bigger. If you look bigger to a predator, they’re less likely to eat you.

But if you have a tiger in your backyard, and your hair is on end, your body doesn’t know why your hair is on end. That’s why people get goosebumps from music. When they get goosebumps, their hair is on end, but they don’t know why it’s on end.

And we don’t even have enough hair to make this work. The last time I tried to make a cat afraid of me, I failed.

There’s a lot of evidence that this is why we get goosebumps from music. For example, if you listen to music with a lot of sudden changes in intensity, you’re more likely to get goosebumps. And people who are really sensitive to sudden changes in intensity get more goosebumps.

So, I think that’s why.

prompt: Every few months there's a new superfood or a new villain food (eggs, then butter, then seed oils). Write an essay on why nutrition science seems to flip-flop so much, and whether that's a failure of the science or of how it gets reported. I'm not looking for "it's complicated" as the conclusion.
response:
There are three types of nutrition advice. The first is about whether a particular food will cause harm if you eat too much of it. The second is whether a particular food is healthy, meaning that it will make you more healthy if you eat more of it. The third is whether an ingredient or nutrient has positive or negative effects on health.

These three types of advice sound similar, but they have different strengths and weaknesses and are treated differently in science.

Type 1 advice is the most common: “eat less salt”, “eat less fat”, “eat less red meat”, “eat less alcohol”. It comes from epidemiological studies, which are large-scale studies looking at the health of thousands of people, and they have an obvious strength: they’re really big.

Epidemiology is also the weakest form of study in medicine. The standard hierarchy of medical evidence is randomized controlled trial > prospective study > epidemiology.

A randomized controlled trial takes a group of people and randomly assigns them to two groups. One group gets the thing under study and the other doesn’t. Then you see what happens to each group. For example, in a trial of a new drug, the first group would get the new drug and the second group would get a sugar pill.

A prospective study is very similar to a trial, except instead of randomly assigning people to the two groups, you just let them choose what they want, and then see what happens.

An epidemiological study is very different. Instead of studying one disease in thousands of people, it studies hundreds of diseases in tens of thousands of people.

The strength of epidemiology is that it’s really good at finding associations between things. For example, it discovered that smoking causes lung cancer.

Its weakness is that it doesn’t prove causation. It can say that people who smoke have lung cancer more often than people who don’t. It can’t say that smoking is causing lung cancer. Maybe people who smoke get lung cancer because they like both smoking and lung cancer. Or maybe there’s something in cigarettes that protects them against lung cancer.

The only way to prove that one thing causes another is a randomized controlled trial. But you can’t do randomized controlled trials on smoking or any food because that would mean you had to force people to eat things that you thought might kill them, which would be immoral.

So, you can’t prove by trial that smoking causes lung cancer, and instead you have to rely on epidemiology, which has a lot of problems.

But even though epidemiology is weak, it works really well in some cases, such as smoking and lung cancer.

That’s because smoking and lung cancer have a large effect. If smoking had a small effect, it would be very difficult to find. Since it has a huge effect, the epidemiologists find it easily.

If a food or nutrient has a very small effect on health, it’s very hard to find in epidemiology, and even if you find it, you probably won’t be able to trust it.

For example, suppose that drinking water is slightly good for you. Then epidemiologists might find that people who drink a lot of water are healthier than people who don’t. But if you ask why, they might say, “Well, people who drink a lot of water are probably more health conscious than people who don’t, so that’s probably why they’re healthier.”

In other words, there are many things that people who drink a lot of water are likely to do that will make them healthier, such as exercise and eat well and avoid smoking. So it’s hard to tell if drinking water is what’s making them healthy, or if they’re healthy for other reasons.

That’s the problem of confounders: other things that are correlated with what you’re studying that also have effects on health, so it’s hard to tell what is causing what.

Confounders are a big problem in nutrition epidemiology. If you ask people to list what they eat every day for a week, and then see if people who eat more fish have higher IQs, you might think fish makes people smart. But there are lots of other things correlated with eating fish that could also make people smart, such as living in a wealthy family, having a parent who’s smart, or being in a culture that encourages eating fish.

So, type 1 epidemiology studies are okay for large effects, but not for small ones.

The second type of advice is about whether a particular food is healthy. For example, it might say that eggs are healthy or that avocado is healthy.

These studies are done by measuring a few biomarkers, such as blood pressure or cholesterol levels, and comparing how they change when people eat more or less of a particular food.

They are not as good as randomized controlled trials, but they are better than epidemiology.

The problem is that it’s very difficult to prove something is unhealthy, because it takes a long time to show that something is harmful. It can take years or decades for something to cause a disease.

For example, it took decades to prove that trans fat was bad for you, and even today, some people still doubt it.

That means that it’s really hard to prove something is unhealthy. If you’re eating something every day for a few years, and your cholesterol levels stay the same, that doesn’t mean that it’s not making your cholesterol go up. It might just take longer to see the effect.

So, type 2 studies are very good at showing that something is healthy. They are not good at showing that something is unhealthy.

The third type of advice is about whether a particular nutrient is good or bad for you. For example, it might say that saturated fat is unhealthy or that omega-3 fatty acids are healthy.

This is a harder problem. It’s much harder to study nutrients than foods. This is because we don’t understand very well how our bodies work.

There are many different nutrients in a food. For example, an egg has protein, fat, cholesterol, some vitamins and minerals, etc. If you eat an egg and your cholesterol goes up, you don’t know if that’s because of the protein, the fat, the cholesterol, or something else.

Also, nutrients interact with each other. For example, vitamin C helps your body absorb iron. So if you want to know if vitamin C is healthy, you need to take into account that it might be helping your body absorb iron.

The fourth type of advice is about how much of something you should eat. For example, it might say that you should eat 200 grams of protein every day, or that you should drink eight cups of water.

This is the hardest type of advice. There are lots of different nutrients in your food, and they interact with each other. It’s very hard to figure out how much of each one you need.

We know that we need protein and carbohydrates and some fats and vitamins and minerals, and we know how much of each of those we need. But it’s very hard to say how much of each one we need, because it depends on how much of the others you’re eating

prompt: Every few months there's a new superfood or a new villain food (eggs, then butter, then seed oils). response:
I was reading an essay by nutrition researcher Gary Taubes, who’s done a lot to popularize nutrition science (or more accurately, to popularize his own personal opinions about what’s right and wrong in nutrition science). One of the things that always comes up in the discussion of nutrition science is how it seems to flip-flop all the time.

For example, Taubes points out the following:

The first time it was published in a scientific paper, a paper in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, in 1998, the conclusion that eggs are bad was based on 16 studies that looked at 192,000 people. A study in 2001 of more than 34,000 people found that those who ate two or more eggs a day had higher rates of cardiovascular disease. This was a pretty big study, but then a study published in 2006 found no link between eggs and cardiovascular disease. It was a big study: 78,000 people. The 2006 study was more than twice as big as all 16 studies that had been combined in 1998. A 2007 study of 102,000 people found no link between eggs and cardiovascular disease. In 2008 another study of 30,000 people found no link between eggs and cardiovascular disease. And another study in 2009, this time of 190,000 people, found no link between eggs and cardiovascular disease.

In other words, the egg study situation seems to be like this:

1998: eggs bad.

2001: eggs bad.

2006: eggs not bad.

2007: eggs not bad.

2008: eggs not bad.

2009: eggs not bad.

And it’s not just eggs. Butter is another good example. It used to be bad because of its high saturated fat, but more recently a lot of researchers have been saying it’s actually pretty good. And seed oils used to be considered pretty healthy, but recently people are saying they’re bad.

All this makes for a pretty good argument against nutrition science, because it looks like the best people in the world are arguing among themselves about the most basic facts. The best people in the world should be able to figure out whether eggs are bad or not.

But there are three important points that need to be made here.

1. The scientific community is not a single monolithic body. Different scientists have different opinions. Sometimes their opinions change over time. That’s not the same thing as the scientific community flipping back and forth. For example, it’s not like there was a 2005 study that said eggs weren’t bad that was then repudiated by a 2006 study that said they were. The first two “eggs are bad” studies were actually kind of out in the left-field, and I’m not sure anybody took them very seriously.

2. If you look at the actual studies, the evidence is pretty clear that eggs are not bad. The two studies that said eggs were bad were much less certain in their results than the four that said they were not. For example, a study of 190,000 people that found eggs were not bad gives much more weight than a study of 34,000 people that found eggs were bad.

3. This is mostly a problem of how nutrition science gets reported in the media, rather than with the science itself.

Here’s the thing. Nutrition science is a really tough and controversial field. It’s a field where you’re trying to figure out the health effects of some really small thing (eggs) that everybody does in the same way (eat). So it’s hard to figure out, and you need really big studies to get it right. In fact, most individual studies don’t prove very much. It takes a lot of studies together to say something like “oh, eggs are definitely not bad.”

But the media wants to talk about one study at a time. So every time a new study comes out, there’s always a big news story about it. And when you put all those news stories together, you get a jumbled mess that looks like “eggs bad, eggs not bad, eggs bad, eggs not bad.” So you end up with the impression that nutrition science is a field that constantly flips back and forth on the most basic facts.

prompt: Every few months there's a new superfood or a new villain food (eggs, then butter, then seed oils). Write an essay on why nutrition science seems to flip-flop so much, and whether that's a failure of the science or of how it gets reported. I'm not looking for "it's complicated" as the conclusion.
response:
Last week, a New York Times article called “The New Superfood Is Butter? Scientists Say Yes, It’s Complicated” got a lot of attention. The article is based on a new study from the Harvard School of Public Health (HSPH) which concludes that butter is fine for most people to eat (I’ll get to the qualifications in the “it’s complicated” part later). The study found that eating 14 grams of butter a day (a tablespoon) doesn’t raise cardiovascular disease risk. This was a big deal, because it directly contradicted the results of the HSPH’s own previous study, which found the same thing except that it increased cardiovascular disease risk.

The New York Times article doesn’t mention the previous study, but it does mention the general principle that nutrition studies are inconsistent, and that we should interpret the new study in light of the previous studies, including those that disagree with it. The article points out that the previous studies were observational studies, in which researchers observed what people were eating and then measured the results. Observational studies can be confounded by other factors – for example, if people who eat lots of eggs tend to also be overweight and sedentary, an observational study might incorrectly conclude that it’s the eggs rather than the sedentary lifestyle causing health problems. The article also mentions that eggs have changed, so that they now have lower cholesterol than they did in the past, and that a lot of the previous studies looked at eggs that were worse than the ones people eat now.

But the Times article does not say anything at all about the previous HSPH study. That was an observational study with the same methodological flaws, using the same type of eggs, and concluding that eggs are bad.

Why does the media ignore this? It’s probably because the article isn’t trying to present a nuanced and complicated picture of the evidence around eggs. It’s trying to tell you something – namely, that eggs are good. This is a pretty standard way of talking about nutrition – pick an issue, and tell you what you should think.

This kind of article is fine – if you believe the Times’ nutrition experts. But this isn’t science. Science is supposed to be based on evidence, and the evidence on eggs is pretty mixed. I’m not a cardiologist or nutrition scientist, but I’ve been studying the egg problem for the last few months. And I think the evidence that eggs are bad is much stronger than the evidence that eggs are good.

In the past couple of years, eggs have gone through a pretty weird transformation. They used to be bad – everyone agreed on this – and then they started getting pretty good press. The Times article I mentioned above is the most recent in a whole series of articles claiming eggs are good. There was also an article about eggs that was pretty widely shared on Facebook, and a New York Magazine article that said that eating 3 eggs a day might be a good idea.

So I decided to look for myself at the evidence around eggs. I’m not a medical researcher or nutrition scientist. I know very little about nutrition and I’m not qualified to give medical advice. But I am able to read studies, so I decided to see what they say about eggs.

It turns out that eggs are a little tricky. There’s a lot of research that’s relevant to eggs, and a lot of it is hard to interpret, because eggs affect health through so many different mechanisms. But I think the main question to ask about eggs is whether they’re good or bad for your heart. There’s a lot of evidence that eggs increase cholesterol (we’ll look at this in more detail below) and high cholesterol is associated with increased heart disease risk. That’s the main question.

There’s a lot of evidence that eggs are bad for your heart. The evidence that eggs are good is much weaker. The studies I found supporting the claim that eggs are bad outnumber the studies supporting the claim that eggs are good by 15-20 to 1.

I’m not going to go into all the studies here. But the short version of the story is that eggs are probably bad for your heart. But there’s enough uncertainty that I can’t be completely sure, and it might be possible to eat a few eggs a day without increasing your risk of heart disease. I can’t be completely sure because eggs are complicated and there’s a lot of uncertainty about how they work.

Eggs affect your health through a bunch of different mechanisms. The main one is that they’re high in cholesterol, and it’s possible that high cholesterol causes high blood levels of LDL, which is one kind of cholesterol. High levels of LDL are associated with heart disease risk, although there’s some controversy over whether high LDL levels cause increased heart disease risk or whether high LDL levels are just associated with it.

There’s also the possibility that eggs have anti-inflammatory effects (although eggs are pretty low in omega-3 fatty acids, so this is questionable) and that the choline in eggs increases homocysteine levels.

The choline in eggs has an interesting effect. It increases your levels of homocysteine, a type of amino acid. High homocysteine levels are associated with increased risk of heart disease, although it’s not really known whether high homocysteine levels cause heart disease. Homocysteine levels in humans are much lower than they are in other animals, probably because of vitamin B12 supplementation (this is a very recent phenomenon). The average homocysteine level in humans is around 10 micromoles per liter, and the average in mice is around 30.

This might be why eggs haven’t been associated with increased heart disease risk in observational studies. Humans might just not be able to increase their homocysteine levels enough from eating eggs to notice a difference.

Eggs also affect your health in a lot of other ways. They’re high in protein, which is good. They have a lot of vitamins and minerals. They might reduce your risk of eye disease. They might improve your memory and your mood. They might cause acne. They might make you fart more.

This means that eggs can be good for you in some ways and bad for you in other ways. It’s possible to eat eggs and have good health, or it’s possible to eat eggs and have bad health. It depends on a lot of different things.

There are a lot of studies that say that eggs are bad for your heart. But there are also a lot of studies that say that eggs are good for your heart, or that they don’t affect your heart at all. I think the studies showing eggs are bad are much more persuasive, but it’s possible that eggs don’t affect heart disease at all.

prompt: Write an essay on CRISPR's origin story, how it came from people studying yogurt bacteria and obscure DNA repeats, as an argument for funding curiosity-driven research that has no obvious application.
response:
CRISPR-Cas9 is one of the most transformative discoveries of the past decade. It is a system for precisely editing the DNA of living organisms. It is widely considered a key technology in the development of genetic engineering in a way that will have major impacts on health, agriculture, and biology.

CRISPR-Cas9, like many other technologies, came out of a long chain of serendipitous discoveries that began with an entirely different field of research. And it makes a great story for what we might lose if we cut research funding to areas with no apparent application.

In the 1980s, Francisco Mojica and a few other researchers were studying bacterial and archaeal genomes. Mojica was interested in why bacterial genomes were so much smaller than eukaryotic genomes. He found that bacterial genomes had some short sequences of DNA that repeated over and over at different places in the genome. He was particularly interested in one of these repeats in a bacterium called Haloferax mediterranei, which had 42 copies of a 29 base-pair long repeat.

The repeats were a very consistent part of the bacterial genome. They were present in all strains, and they were all exactly the same. But between the repeats there were other sequences, which varied. And they varied between strains. The sequences were always 30 base pairs long, but the actual bases were different.

This made Mojica very curious. In bacteria, most of the genome consists of genes that encode proteins. But these 30 base pair stretches were too short to be genes. And they didn't look like regulatory sequences. So what were they?

Mojica noticed that the 30 base pair stretches weren’t just randomly different – they were related to some viruses which infect bacteria. In 1995, he published a paper titled “Identification of clusters of highly similar repeats in prokaryotes might reveal a new mechanism for gene expression”, where he suggested that these repeats were somehow involved in the expression of some genes. He speculated that they might be related to how bacteria deal with viruses.

Mojica was a tenured professor, so he could continue studying this for a while without worrying about funding. But in the mid-1990s, funding for basic science research was being cut, and in 1997 Mojica was fired from his university and had to stop working on the problem.

A few years later, Sylvain Moineau started working on CRISPRs. Moineau was studying phage-resistant bacteria, and was wondering what the mechanism of resistance was. He had noticed the strange repeats and speculated that they might be related to the resistance mechanism, but he didn’t know why or how.

Moineau and a few other scientists started to figure out what was going on. They found that CRISPR repeats are found in about 40% of bacterial and archaeal genomes. And they are usually followed by genes called Cas genes.

CRISPRs, they discovered, are a natural immune system in bacteria. When bacteria get infected with a virus, they capture some of the virus’s DNA, chop it up into 30 base pair pieces, and incorporate the pieces into their genome between CRISPR repeats.

When the bacteria reproduce, they make copies of the CRISPR repeats and the captured DNA sequences. This gives each daughter cell a record of all the viruses that have infected their ancestors. They also make copies of the Cas genes. When these bacteria get infected by a virus, the Cas genes encode proteins that cut apart the virus’s DNA and destroy it. They do this only if the DNA of the virus matches one of the DNA sequences in the CRISPR, so that they don’t accidentally destroy their own DNA.

So CRISPRs are a way for bacteria to remember which viruses have attacked them, and to make it easier to defend against those viruses.

This discovery, though, was not the end of the story.

CRISPR-Cas systems are complicated and diverse. There are different types of CRISPR-Cas systems that work in different ways.

One of the most common types is called Cas9. In 2012, Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed that they could use Cas9 to edit the DNA of bacteria by changing the DNA sequence of the CRISPRs. In 2013, George Church and Feng Zhang showed that CRISPR-Cas9 can also edit the DNA of yeast and mammalian cells. And in 2015, the Nobel Prize for medicine went to Doudna and Charpentier for their work on CRISPR-Cas9.

CRISPR-Cas9 is a system for precisely editing the DNA of living organisms. It is widely considered a key technology in the development of genetic engineering in a way that will have major impacts on health, agriculture, and biology.

The development of CRISPR-Cas9 involved several people studying basic questions about bacterial genomes, some of whom weren’t even able to continue their research because of cuts in funding for basic science research. This is not an isolated case. Many of the most transformative technologies of the past century came out of areas of research with no obvious application, including nuclear fission, the transistor, the World Wide Web, and the Internet.

In a 2014 essay titled “The Death of Science”, David Zuckerman discusses how funding for basic science research has been cut in recent years. He argues that this is a mistake, because basic science research is where many of the most transformative technologies come from. He writes:

We are living in a world where we are being told that we need to make science more productive, and that we should focus on applications rather than basic research. But this is a mistake. The most transformative technologies of the past century came out of areas of research with no obvious application.

Zuckerman argues that we need to fund basic science research because we can’t predict which areas of research will lead to the most transformative technologies. He writes:

We don’t know which areas of research will lead to the most transformative technologies. We can’t predict which areas of research will be most productive. The best we can do is fund a lot of different areas of research and hope that some of them will lead to transformative technologies.

The development of CRISPR-Cas9 is a great example of this. It came out of an area of research that had no obvious application, and that was being cut because of a focus on productivity and applications. And it led to one of the most transformative technologies of the past decade.

We need to fund basic science research.

prompt: Write an essay on CRISPR's origin story, how it came from people studying yogurt bacteria and obscure DNA repeats, as an argument for funding curiosity-driven research that has no obvious application.
response:
I spent the last few weeks looking into the origin of CRISPR, and there was something that struck me as really interesting.

In a typical origin story, someone is studying the subject in question and makes some surprising discovery. For example, in 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen was experimenting with cathode rays and accidentally discovered X-rays.

CRISPR doesn’t have an origin story like this.

The first CRISPR paper, by Francisco Mojica, was actually a paper on obscure DNA repeats. In 1987, researchers discovered some strange repeats in a bacterium called Haemophilus influenzae. These sequences had a few different components: a long string of DNA that repeated over and over, with some slightly-longer strings between each repeated sequence. The longer string seemed to have no purpose, and the repeats themselves didn’t seem to code for anything either. It seemed like a strange mistake, some sort of DNA mutation, and researchers stopped studying it.

This was not true. The repeats were called *clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats*, or CRISPR. There were 11 of them, and the intervening bits of DNA, called spacers, were 28 to 38 base pairs long. Mojica was studying these repeats in bacteria like E. coli, and he noticed that some of the spacers matched other bacterial genes. This seemed like a pretty cool thing, and he published a paper on it.

Mojica went on to study CRISPR for years. In 2000, he was studying *Bacillus halodurans*, a type of bacteria that was in the process of being sequenced. He was looking at CRISPR sequences and noticed that one of the spacers was a DNA sequence that was in a bacteriophage, or a virus that infected bacteria. This was a new development, and he published a paper on it.

At this point, CRISPR research was still just the study of these strange sequences. In 2005, Mojica was studying CRISPR sequences in bacteria. He noticed that some of the spacers were *newly acquired*, meaning they weren’t in the bacterial genomes when the bacteria were first discovered. This suggested that there was something more to these sequences, but he still didn’t have any idea what.

Then he noticed something interesting. The new spacers had a lot in common with bacteriophage sequences. In fact, the most recent spacers were usually the ones that looked the most like phage sequences. This suggested a new hypothesis: CRISPR sequences might actually be a *bacterial immune system*, and spacers might be part of the bacterial immune response.

This hypothesis seemed weird, but a few years later, in 2007, a different researcher named Rodolphe Barrangou showed that it was probably true. He was studying yogurt bacteria, and he noticed that if he infected yogurt bacteria with a bacteriophage that didn’t infect them, they wouldn’t be infected by the bacteriophage the next time. This suggested that they had an immune system. He found out that this immune system was related to CRISPR, and he published a paper about it.

After this, there was a lot of research about CRISPR. Researchers figured out that bacteria could store new CRISPR sequences in response to a bacteriophage. They also figured out how CRISPR worked, and how to use CRISPR in other organisms. Now we use CRISPR a lot.

It’s kind of strange that someone studying obscure DNA sequences accidentally discovered a bacteria immune system, but it makes sense if you think about it. Bacteria have to fight off bacteriophages all the time. It seems like they would have an immune system that fought off phage sequences. And it would make sense for this immune system to have DNA sequences in it that looked like phage DNA. So the CRISPR sequences, which seemed to be random DNA that didn’t code for anything, might actually be a bacteria immune system that stored phage DNA sequences.

But this was a wild guess. In fact, it was even a weird hypothesis when Barrangou and his team published their yogurt paper in 2007.

And if you think about how hard it is to come up with this hypothesis by yourself, it makes sense why someone would have to be studying CRISPR for a long time before it occurred to them to hypothesize it. And that’s what Mojica did. He spent 20 years studying CRISPR. That’s a lot of time, and he got a lot of publications from it. It was a really long time to study something that had no obvious purpose.

I think this is a good example of why it’s good to study things that don’t have obvious purposes. If you don’t study things that don’t have obvious purposes, you won’t discover the interesting stuff. And there are always interesting things that we don’t know about, and it’s impossible to guess what they are. So the only way to discover them is to do a lot of research and look for the interesting stuff.

Mojica was able to make a big discovery by just studying CRISPR. There is no way to predict what someone studying CRISPR will discover, so I don’t think anyone could have predicted his discovery. So the only way to have discovered CRISPR is to spend a lot of time studying CRISPR.

And I think this is a really important thing to think about, because a lot of people think that if we do research on things that don’t have obvious purposes, we’re wasting time. And I think that if you look at some of the big discoveries that have happened in the last 100 years, like X-rays, you can see that people studying things that had no obvious purposes are how we make big discoveries.

prompt: Write an essay on CRISPR's origin story, how it came from people studying yogurt bacteria and obscure DNA repeats, as an argument for funding curiosity-driven research that has no obvious application.
response:
In the last few months, two scientists from University of California San Francisco, Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier, have won major awards for developing CRISPR, the new gene editing technology which is going to revolutionize biology. This has become a new favorite example of the kind of research we should fund: basic research without obvious applications, which later becomes a revolution.

Here’s an example of the kind of essay that got written after the Nobel Prize (I’ll leave out the name of the author since I’m not trying to single them out, just illustrate a style of writing):

When the Nobel Prize was announced, I thought of something I learned about the discovery of penicillin. I didn’t know it had come from studying mold. I didn’t know it was discovered by a man named Alexander Fleming, who had been looking at a different mold on a petri dish, which was growing on top of staph bacteria. And I didn’t know the story of Fleming’s discovery had been told in the same way that we are told of the discovery of CRISPR:

Fleming noticed that the mold was killing the staph bacteria around it. So he went back the next day to see if this was really true. He was told that it wasn’t true, and that it had been a coincidence. But he was really sure about it, so he went back to the lab the next day to repeat the experiment. The people told him that they had cleaned the room, and he would never be able to replicate his experiment. So he gave up, and forgot about the whole thing.

He went to work on another project, and he made a petri dish with staph in it, and he left it in the corner. But then he went on vacation. When he came back, he noticed a new mold growing on top of the staph bacteria. So he repeated his experiment again, and realized that the mold was killing the staph bacteria.

This kind of story is why we need to fund basic research. We don’t know what new discoveries are going to come from basic research. We don’t know how they will change our lives. But we know they can change our lives.

I’m not going to take a firm position on whether this is a true story (it’s not even on Wikipedia) but it is *a story*, and it does a good job of conveying the spirit of a lot of the research I’ve read on. If you want to learn about the real story, the story of the discovery of CRISPR, that’s a lot better.

In the 1980s, Francisco Mojica was a young biology professor in Spain. He wanted to study the genetics of a species of archaea, an odd group of organisms which look a lot like bacteria but are neither. The particular organism he was studying was Haloferax volcanii, which lived in the Great Salt Lake.

Mojica found a strange pattern of DNA sequences repeated over and over again, separated by bits of unique DNA which he called spacers. He had no idea what these sequences were doing. He wrote a paper about this strange DNA repeat that no one had ever heard of before. The reviewers thought the paper was interesting, but they couldn’t understand why anyone was doing this research. It wasn’t important, so it didn’t belong in a prestigious journal. So they rejected it. He resubmitted it to a more obscure journal.

Mojica spent a few years trying to figure out what CRISPR was doing, and couldn’t. Then he gave up and went to Canada.

About ten years later, Sylvain Moineau was a microbiology professor at the University of Quebec in Montreal. He was studying phage resistance in bacteria. Bacteria were being attacked by phage (viruses that attack bacteria) and he wanted to understand how they were resisting the phage. His graduate students were using a technique called transposon mutagenesis to knock out random bacterial genes and figure out which genes were important for phage resistance.

Moineau had read Mojica’s original paper about CRISPR, and he thought it was kind of interesting. He told his graduate students that if they knocked out the CRISPR gene, it might have something to do with phage resistance. They knocked out the CRISPR gene, and it did have something to do with phage resistance.

Moineau published a paper about this. He figured out that bacteria were taking DNA from phage that they had eaten, and they were putting it in their genome in the CRISPR regions, and they were using the CRISPR regions to recognize the phage.

Moineau and Mojica were both interested in CRISPR, and they met in 2012 and talked to each other for several hours. Mojica told Moineau that he had been working on a different kind of CRISPR in archaea, which had something to do with DNA methylation. Moineau told Mojica that he had been studying a different kind of CRISPR in bacteria, which had something to do with phage resistance.

CRISPR was becoming interesting, but it was still not very interesting. It was an obscure DNA repeat that didn’t do anything important, and it was a bit weird that there were three different kinds of CRISPR in different organisms. But it was still an interesting topic.

Emmanuelle Charpentier was a microbiologist in Sweden, and she was interested in CRISPR. She read Mojica’s and Moineau’s papers and got excited. She decided to study CRISPR in Streptococcus pyogenes, the bacteria that causes strep throat. She discovered that CRISPR was used in the bacteria to attack phage. She realized that CRISPR was a gene editing tool, and she thought she could use it to edit the genome of bacteria.

prompt: I've been a vegetarian for 12 years and recently started eating fish again because my iron and B12 were tanking and honestly I feel a bit like a hypocrite. but it made me think about how much of what we call "natural" diet is really just a story about evolution we tell ourselves. could you write an essay about that? not about whether vegetarianism is right or wrong, more about how people (me included) use biology to justify choices they've already made for other reasons
response:
I’ve been vegetarian for twelve years, and recently decided to allow myself to eat fish again.

This was a decision made on scientific rather than ethical grounds. It turns out my iron and B12 levels had been plummeting, and it wasn’t a big deal until I realized I’d been on the wrong side of the median for B12 deficiency. It also turns out my diet had been pretty bad for most of my vegetarianism and I was basically subsisting on rice and cheese, which wasn’t great.

I still don’t eat meat. But I feel like a hypocrite. I remember being vegetarian for a long time without even questioning it. I never knew a reason to. It just felt right.

But as soon as I started thinking about the ethics of meat-eating, I realized I had no good answer. And so I went vegetarian, and then I felt guilty that I’d been a meat eater for so long, and I’d been eating meat for so long, and then people started telling me that I was probably wrong, and I was wrong, and they told me to stop worrying about it and just make the decision I felt most comfortable with.

I don’t know. I can’t decide, and I don’t know how to decide. And the reason I know that is, I have a vague recollection of having a similar feeling about meat eating when I was very young, which is that I never really questioned it. It just seemed like something you did. And I think that I have a lot of other beliefs that are the same way.

And I’m starting to realize that a lot of my beliefs are more like “I’ve already made up my mind and I need a justification for it.” And I think that is a very common phenomenon. People will use science to justify a belief in a way that’s basically just confirmation bias. They’ll pick out the pieces of scientific evidence that they like and ignore the rest.

And this is a very common theme that comes up here, and in fact, it’s something I’ve been thinking about a lot. This is the idea that people will often use science to justify a belief, or more generally, to justify an idea that they have already decided to believe in for reasons other than science. And then they’ll act as if science had been the basis for their decision.

This is the story of evolution that people tell themselves. There are two kinds of people who believe in evolution. The first kind of people are the scientists and science-y people who believe that evolution is a good idea, that it’s important that people believe in evolution, and that people should be made to believe in evolution by any means necessary. These are the people who are most comfortable with the phrase “just because” when they’re talking about how evolution is true. And the second kind of people are the people who believe that evolution is a good idea, but they don’t care very much if other people believe it, and who don’t really understand what evolution is all about, but who like the fact that it’s not creationism.

And the people who believe in evolution but don’t really know why are the people who use evolution as a justification for something else, and it’s very common to hear them use evolution as a justification for some kind of thing.

response:
*The following is an excerpt from my upcoming book The Rationalist’s Toolkit: Think Better and Change More.*

I used to be a vegetarian. For years, I was so vegetarian that people would think I was vegan. I didn’t care about animals; I cared about the environment. And it seemed so easy and convenient. I ate vegetables and grain. And I didn’t have to think too much about my food.

And then my health began to decline. My B12 levels began to drop. I felt tired all the time. I had a really hard time sleeping. I had terrible digestive problems.

So I took a big risk and started eating fish again. I knew the risks involved in eating fish – mercury, etc. But I knew that I was going to eat fish anyway, so I decided that I was going to do it in a way that I thought would minimize the risks. So I was going to limit myself to just two fish meals a week, and I was going to eat salmon and tuna only.

I didn’t expect anything to change. But within a few weeks of eating fish, all my problems were gone. I was sleeping fine. I was not tired all the time. And my digestive problems disappeared. I thought, wow, that’s amazing.

And then I looked up the connection between B12 and sleep, and I learned that you can get insomnia and other sleep problems if you don’t have enough B12. That was really interesting, but I thought, how do you not have enough B12? That’s not a big deal. You just eat some meat.

So I looked up the vegetarian B12 connection. And I learned that vegetarians and vegans can have a lot of problems, and that B12 is a big problem. You have to supplement if you’re a vegetarian or a vegan.

And then I thought, what a weird connection. It’s kind of a weird coincidence that vegetarians and vegans have problems, but I thought, okay, let me just look at this for a few minutes, and I’ll be done with it.

And I ended up spending an hour learning about this connection, and I realized that there was a connection between the B12 deficiency and the other problems that I was having as a vegetarian. And I was thinking, well, maybe it’s just a coincidence. But it wasn’t a coincidence. It’s actually that when you’re low on B12, all these other problems show up.

This is just one example of how the human brain is really, really good at finding patterns, and how our brains are really, really bad at rejecting false patterns, and how we just need to be really, really careful.

prompt: An essay, please, on the history and ethics of the HeLa cell line, focusing less on the well-known story and more on what it should change about how we handle tissue donation today.

In the 1970s and 1980s, cell cultures of the HeLa cell line were freely traded between biolabs. Researchers could mail in their samples, and labs would grow the cells for them. The problem was so widespread that the National Institutes of Health (NIH) formed a working group, and a year later a journal article called “HeLa Cell Contamination of Other Cell Lines” was published in Nature, and described how 13 different human cell lines in the collection were contaminated.

This kind of mistake is bad. It’s bad because the HeLa cells were contaminating research in other areas. It’s bad because it meant researchers were wasting their time studying cells they thought were something else but actually weren’t.

But it’s especially bad because it was a breach of trust.

The HeLa cells were obtained without consent from a woman, Henrietta Lacks, who was dying of cervical cancer. Her doctors took some of her cells and put them in a culture. This was, at the time, very unusual, and there was no expectation at the time that cells would continue to grow indefinitely.

The cells were so hardy that scientists could easily get them to grow. Researchers were able to make copies of them, share them with other researchers, and so on. And as this story is well known, I’ll skip past it.

The cell line became very profitable for a company called GIBCO, who were selling them to researchers. A large part of the profits went back to Johns Hopkins hospital. But there was little to no money given to Henrietta Lacks’ family. This caused controversy.

Henrietta Lacks’ family eventually settled with the university for an undisclosed amount in exchange for a right to be consulted before any patents are filed using HeLa cells.

But what would have been a better result?

It seems to me that there are three basic options:

1. Do not give the researcher access to the tissue.

2. Give them access, but the researcher must pay a fee.

3. Give them access, and they are able to charge whatever they want for it.

The third option is what happened to Henrietta Lacks’ cells. Her doctors gave them away for free. Then they went around sharing them with other labs. Then they started selling them for money.

The second option was adopted at UCSF:

A researcher at UCSF had access to a collection of rare samples from a variety of rare diseases. These samples came from various donors who donated their tissues for research purposes. But they were so rare that other researchers wanted to use them, and the lab was spending a lot of time growing the cells for them. They started to think that the people using these cells should have to pay them, because they were spending a lot of time growing them.

So they came up with a fee schedule. If the samples were hard to grow, they’d charge a bigger fee. If the samples were easy to grow, they’d charge less. If the samples had to be grown for a long time, they’d charge more.

I have no way of knowing which of these is most common. But I think the third option is probably the most common, because the HeLa cells were given away for free at first, and that’s what everyone expected to happen.

And you will become a whole mouse, with a nose and ears and eyes and a brain and a body and limbs with five digits on each.

When a cell gets a signal that tells it to become a nose, or an ear, or an eye, or a toe, it knows when it is supposed to do it, it knows where it is supposed to do it, and it knows what to become.

The human body is a miracle. And yet, if you know a little about biology, it’s not so much a miracle as a puzzle. The miracle is how a single cell (the fertilized egg) becomes a human being. But the puzzle is how a single cell knows how to become a human being.
