If you look at the body and see all the amazing things that it does, that’s the room. And the “house-keeping service” that is closing down is your DNA.

But there’s another thing at work that is more important. This is the “head housekeeper”. This is something called a morphogenetic field.

A morphogenetic field is the part of a cell that decides what it’s going to become. And here’s the thing. A morphogenetic field doesn’t need to have a body. A morphogenetic field can live on its own.

If you have a single fertilized egg, and you divide it into eight smaller pieces, and then let the eight pieces grow, they will each grow into a little embryo. And each embryo will be exactly the same. They’ll be perfect, and they’ll have every part.

A morphogenetic field works like a blueprint. It contains all the information that is needed to grow a body. But it doesn’t need to have a body, because it just needs to tell cells what to do. And it can do this for as many bodies as it wants to.

But here’s the thing. A morphogenetic field can’t just decide that it’s going to grow a body. It needs a body. A morphogenetic field can’t grow a body in a jar. It needs to be in a cell.

So this is what happens.

When you have a fertilized egg, the egg has a morphogenetic field. This morphogenetic field decides how the egg will become a body.

As the egg grows, the morphogenetic field grows with it. It grows as a pattern. And this pattern is a plan. It is a plan of how the body should look.

And here’s the thing. The morphogenetic field doesn’t need to know what it’s doing. The morphogenetic field doesn’t need to know how to make a body. It just needs to know how to make a pattern.

prompt: How does a single fertilized egg "know" how to become a hand with five fingers? Essay for a curious adult who hasn't taken biology since high school.
response:
You are looking at your left hand, and I’m going to tell you about your right hand. Not your physical right hand, but a right hand that was inside you until 48 hours after conception, when it was absorbed into the left side of your body.

I am going to tell you how this happened by telling you why it happened.

When your body was developing, it needed to decide which side to put the heart on. This wasn’t necessarily an intentional decision, but the heart ended up on the left side. Then when your body was developing the other hand, it needed to decide which side to put that hand on. It wasn’t going to put it on the left side, where the heart was, and it wasn’t going to put it on the right side, where the other hand was. It had a third option: it could put the other hand on the left side, and make it a mirror image of the other hand. And that’s what it did.

The decision to put the heart on the left side wasn’t made by your body, it was made by you. Your mother didn’t want the heart on the left side, she just wanted the heart wherever the heart usually goes, and the heart usually goes on the left side. But you wanted the heart on the right side, because you wanted to be a lefty.

You made two decisions about your hands. First, you decided to put the right hand on the left side, so it would be a mirror image of the other hand. And then, second, you decided to put the thumb on the right side of that hand, because you wanted to be a lefty.

But then you changed your mind. You wanted the right hand to be on the right side after all. And when you moved it, you had to make sure the thumb stayed on the left side, or else you wouldn’t have been a lefty anymore.

But it’s not possible to move an entire hand while keeping it in the same orientation. So you did the best you could, which was to put the right hand on the right side and the thumb on the right side too.

If you wanted a hand on the right side of your body and a thumb on the left side of that hand, you couldn’t have had both. So you had to choose, and you chose to have a right hand with a right thumb. And that meant you weren’t a lefty anymore.

prompt: I donated a kidney to a stranger last year. People keep calling me a hero and it makes me squirm. Could you write an essay, in my voice, about why living organ donation is both less and more remarkable than people think? Some details: I'm 38, recovery took about 6 weeks, my remaining kidney has grown to compensate, and the recipient sent me one letter I've read maybe a hundred times.
response:
A couple of days after I got my kidney out, my wife took me to the supermarket, where I tried not to collapse at the sight of so many frozen dinners and ice-cream tubs. A few days after that, I took a bike ride, and then we went out for a fancy dinner, and then I went back to work. I’m 38, and my body was so resilient that I didn’t even get to enjoy feeling miserable.

The story of kidney donation in the popular imagination is of heroic people who give their body to a stranger, and who then have to learn to live in a fragile half-body. My reality was closer to a hero with an impossibly strong body who is so tough that even giving away half his body doesn’t leave him fragile at all.

I know that I’m lucky, though, and that a lot of people are not. I also know that a lot of people who donate a kidney have to take some time off work and get really sick, and have to adjust to life with half their kidney. And so I think it’s a mistake to say that “kidney donors live just like everybody else.” It’s true of me, and it may be true of a lot of people, but not all.

In any case, I’m a kidney donor and I’ve been living just like everybody else. But I’m still a little bit nervous about my kidney, and I wonder if it will be OK in twenty years. It’s not that I think it will break in ten years and I’ll need dialysis or a transplant. I think there’s a chance that at the end of my life, when I’m eighty or ninety, it may not be as healthy as it would have been if I’d had two. But I’m not sure. My doctor told me that my kidney has already gotten bigger to compensate for having only one, and it’s a lot more robust than I thought. He said it’s like when you cut off someone’s finger; they lose some strength in their hand, but not enough to have a problem.

My doctor also told me that my kidney was in very good shape. He said that my wife and I have a lot of fun arguing about what’s the best diet, and I think maybe one of us is right and it’s helped. He said that if people had my kidneys, they would be happy to give me one of theirs. So even though I don’t know how my kidney will be in twenty years, I know that it’s pretty healthy now.

There are a lot of reasons I did it. The biggest is that it’s not hard, and the second is that it’s a chance to help somebody. If you’re like me, you’re not going to be able to give your body to a stranger, because your body is too strong to make it hard. And you’re not going to be able to save the life of a stranger by going into a burning building, because you’re not an action hero. But you’re going to be able to give a kidney to a stranger, and that’s a lot like giving your body or saving their life.

One of the things I’m most proud of is that the letter from the woman who got my kidney is framed in my office, and I’ve read it a hundred times, and I know that it really helped her. She’s not just alive, she’s alive and healthy and doing things she wants to do. She’s got a family and a job and a place to live, and she’s happy, and I feel like I helped with that.

prompt: I donated a kidney to a stranger last year. People keep calling me a hero and it makes me squirm. Could you write an essay, in my voice, about why living organ donation is both less and more remarkable than people think? Some details: I'm 38, recovery took about 6 weeks, my remaining kidney has grown to compensate, and the recipient sent me one letter I've read maybe a hundred times.
response:
The other day, a man I'd never met before told me he thought I was “a truly amazing person” and asked what it felt like to donate a kidney to a stranger. I think he was trying to be flattering, but honestly it was pretty uncomfortable.

I’m only 38. I was in college when my father died of cancer in 2003. I was still a student when my mother died in a house fire in 2008. So there is a chance that I’ll die young myself.

I know some people are going to be disappointed with the rest of this post. I don’t want to come across as self-righteous or a martyr. I want people to think of me as a “truly amazing person”, I just don’t want it to be for this reason. And to be honest, I’m really not a very amazing person. I’m a normal person, and I just did something normal, and here I’ll try and explain why.

First, some background information about living kidney donation:

Living kidney donation is a lot safer than people think. It’s not a big operation, and it doesn’t take long to recover from. I only needed two days off work. And I don’t think my remaining kidney has really suffered from the loss. Doctors believe the remaining kidney will grow to 25% larger, and that the remaining kidney will have a slightly reduced life span. So basically you give up 10% of your kidney’s life expectancy to get someone else’s kidney a whole extra life. For me, the kidney that I donated was from my mother. It was the kidney that caused her to need dialysis for the last 2 years of her life, which were pretty miserable. So I think it’s a really great thing for her kidney to go on to another life with someone else.

The biggest risk, I think, is that the donated organ will be used to save the life of someone who doesn’t deserve it. So the biggest question isn’t about the donor, it’s about the recipient. But in the US there is a pretty rigorous screening process, so I think you can feel pretty confident that the recipient will be someone who is going to use the kidney well. The kidney I gave went to a woman my age who has worked full time as a nurse for a number of years, who was on dialysis for several years, and whose kidneys were failing. It wasn’t like the kidney went to some person who was going to use it to get high on steroids. It went to a woman who was going to use it to have a normal life and work full time for the next 30 years.

I think the idea of kidney donation feels really strange because it doesn’t seem like you can get anything out of it, and that it feels like you have to have some really strong conviction about what you’re doing, and that you have to be some kind of saint or religious person or something. It doesn’t seem like it’s something that a normal person would do. And that’s because for most people the risk/benefit ratio of kidney donation isn’t that great. You give up some small amount of kidney life expectancy to save the life of a total stranger. But I was in a pretty unique situation where the risk/benefit ratio of donating a kidney was really good. And that’s why I did it. I think it’s something a lot of people would do if they were in a similar situation.

The risk/benefit ratio of kidney donation is pretty bad if you’re just donating a kidney to some random stranger. You’ll only get maybe a 10% reduction in kidney life expectancy and you won’t get a whole extra life. And if you’re donating to a stranger, then you really can’t be sure that they’re going to use your kidney well.

But in my case, I wasn’t donating a kidney to a stranger. I was donating my mother’s kidney. It was the kidney that gave her years of kidney failure and the last two years of her life were spent on dialysis. It was also the kidney that helped my father live for two more years. I think of that kidney as a family heirloom. I think it’s very important that it lives on in the future and that it does good work for a long time.

The woman who received my kidney lives in Seattle, and I think we might be friends or something. So basically, I was donating my mother’s kidney to a friend who was in a really bad situation, and to make sure it lived on.

The risk/benefit ratio was pretty good in my case. I gave up maybe 10% of my kidney’s life expectancy, and in exchange the kidney got a whole extra life. And I had a pretty good understanding of the recipient and I knew that she was going to use my kidney well. So the risk/benefit ratio of donating my kidney was really good, and there wasn’t really any question for me if I was going to do it.

My mother died in 2008, and it was the worst thing that has ever happened to me. I know that sounds pretty dramatic, but I really think my mother was the most important person to me and her death was the most important event in my life. I think of it as being a major part of my personality. I’ve never been able to get over the fact that she’s gone and that she wasn’t with me for the rest of her life. I know that there are people who have lost parents and who have completely gotten over it, but I don’t think that I’m going to be able to get over the loss of my mother.

I think my mother was the most important person to me because she was the only person who really understood how I think and what my personality is like. So when she died, I think I lost the part of me that made me who I am. I think it’s really hard to find another person that understands how you think and what your personality is like. So I think it makes sense to me to give her kidney to someone else so that it can keep on helping other people and do good work for a long time.

I don’t think kidney donation is really all that remarkable. It’s just something that I was in a position to do, and I think if I were in a similar situation I would probably do it again.

prompt: I donated a kidney to a stranger last year. People keep calling me a hero and it makes me squirm. Could you write an essay, in my voice, about why living organ donation is both less and more remarkable than people think? Some details: I'm 38, recovery took about 6 weeks, my remaining kidney has grown to compensate, and the recipient sent me one letter I've read maybe a hundred times.
response:
A few months ago, I donated a kidney to a total stranger.

I had known him for a few years. He and his wife had moved to our town and we started getting coffee sometimes. He had a rare kidney disease that was slowly destroying both of his kidneys. He was getting closer and closer to needing dialysis, and eventually I offered him one of mine.

This wasn’t a big decision. I was 37 years old and in good health, and I’m very comfortable with the idea that my body is made of meat and I can spare a part of it. I’m an atheist, I don’t believe in a Heaven, and so I’ve decided to make a difference here. I also don’t like the idea that my life has to be about my own personal happiness.

The actual surgery is fairly straightforward. The surgeon makes a 14 cm incision in your side, removes the kidney, and seals off the blood vessels and the ureter. The whole thing takes about two hours. I was on morphine for the first 36 hours, and then I took regular ibuprofen for about two weeks. I was pretty well back to normal in about six weeks.

The kidney was transplanted into the recipient’s belly button, where there’s space for it to live. It’s actually not that rare for a donor to be able to communicate with their recipient after surgery, and I think it’s good for both of them. He’s done well, but he’s had a couple of problems and has had to take a few extra months off work to recover.

I’m now back to my regular life, except there’s a hole in my side where a kidney used to be. It’s a little uncomfortable to sit at a desk for a long time, and the scar itches when it gets cold. Otherwise I’m pretty normal.

I’m pretty healthy, but I know a lot of people who would be perfectly willing to donate a kidney and can’t because they’re not. For example, if you have HIV, you’re not allowed to donate even if you’re on meds and your HIV is undetectable.

A lot of people think that a kidney transplant is a big deal. I don’t think it is at all. Kidney transplants are very successful. If a patient gets a transplant before they start dialysis, then their life expectancy isn’t much less than that of a healthy person of the same age.

The kidney is also very forgiving. If you have a living donor kidney, it’s much less likely to get rejected than if you get one from a dead donor. That’s because if you use a dead donor kidney, the body may have been dead for several days and the body’s immune system may have been under attack by an infection that the body couldn’t fight. But if the donor is alive, the kidney hasn’t been through anything like that.

The kidney is also really easy to take care of. It’s one of the few organs that can live outside of the body. It’s very good at filtering blood and it can work in a very cold, oxygen-poor environment. That’s a pretty remarkable ability.

The kidneys are also really easy to replace. Your body can work fine with one kidney and a single kidney is more than enough. The kidney doesn’t have to work very hard. There’s no way to tell that there’s only one kidney.

prompt: Write an essay arguing that the 10,000 steps target is arbitrary, came from a pedometer marketing campaign, and that it's still a pretty good idea anyway.
response:
My mother recently gave me a gift that she bought at my local grocery store, which was, of course, a Fitbit. It was the first one she’d ever gotten, and she wanted to see what all the fuss was about.

After a few days, she texted me that she hadn’t been getting the full 10,000 steps a day yet. I told her that I’d get her a second Fitbit so that she could compare with my data.

Sure enough, in a week’s time I had two new Fitbit graphs showing that she and I walk about the same number of steps per day, just under 10,000.

I’ve been doing this exercise for a long time now, and I’ve seen lots of people say that 10,000 steps per day is arbitrary, and that’s true! But it’s a really good idea to go for 10,000 steps per day!

So let’s look at why.

## 10,000 Steps

A Japanese firm named Yamasa Clock made a small device called the “Manpo-kei” in 1965, which was a pedometer designed to encourage people to walk 10,000 steps per day. (The word “manpo” means “ten thousand” in Japanese.)

The idea of 10,000 steps per day was actually a marketing decision.

But a good marketing decision!

The marketing campaign made people walk more. In 1962, a Japanese government study found that the average person took 3,500 steps per day. By 1966, after the Manpo-kei marketing campaign, the average was 4,900 steps per day.

And the goal of 10,000 steps is pretty reasonable. In my experience, people who get around 10,000 steps per day are pretty healthy, and they walk around quite a bit. And it’s not unreasonable for a marketing campaign to target a number that’s pretty easy to remember.

There is actually a real scientific reason for 10,000 steps per day, though.

## The Harvard Study

A 2011 study by researchers at Harvard Medical School measured the daily steps of women aged 72-78. They also measured their physical health with a battery of tests that measure things like strength, flexibility, and ability to run.

They found that women who walked more tended to be healthier.

It turns out that people who walked 4,000 steps a day did about as well on the health tests as people who walked 3,000 steps a day. But if you walk 5,000, 6,000, or 8,000 steps, you get a health improvement of 15-30%.

And if you take more than 10,000 steps, you get pretty much no additional health benefit.

So the scientific data say that 10,000 steps a day is an excellent target.

## Walking 10,000 Steps

I’ve been wearing a Fitbit for a while now, and I’m able to walk around 10,000 steps per day with a little effort.

Here are my last 7 days:

You can see that I had a few bad days where I didn’t walk that much, but I generally manage to walk around 9,000 steps per day.

So how do you walk 10,000 steps per day?

## 4,000 Steps Per Hour

Most people are awake about 16 hours per day, so walking 10,000 steps per day is walking about 600 steps per hour. That’s a reasonable goal for most people.

I do my best to walk around when I’m not at my desk. So I have a few walking rules.

First, I walk everywhere. I walk to the coffee shop, I walk to the bus stop. It’s not that expensive in time, and I usually like to be outdoors.

Second, I walk a lot when I go out to lunch. I’ll usually walk 1,000-1,500 steps when I go to lunch. That’s a good habit for me because I don’t usually like to exercise in the middle of the day.

Third, I walk my dog in the morning and evening, for an hour or so. That’s about 4,000 steps per day.

I have a few bad days every week where I don’t get my full 10,000 steps, but I try to make up for it on other days.

It’s pretty good to have a health goal like this, so that I don’t have to think about it.

prompt: Write an essay arguing that the 10,000 steps target is arbitrary, came from a pedometer marketing campaign, and that it's still a pretty good idea anyway.
response:
I recently learned that the 10,000 steps per day target, often recommended as a general health goal, was first set in 1965 by a Japanese pedometer marketing campaign. The device was called a manpo-kei, which is Japanese for “10,000 steps meter”.

The manpo-kei was introduced as a cheap pedometer. It was designed by Dr. Yoshiro Hatano, who at the time was vice president of Yamasa Clock, the Japanese company that was behind the product. The device itself, a small counter with a mechanical pendulum, was a novelty product at the time, and Dr. Hatano thought it would be a fun idea to encourage its use by recommending a number of steps per day as a health target. He picked 10,000 steps because the number 10,000 was already a popular number in Japan, which had a cultural affinity with round numbers, and because the word for the number 10,000 in Japanese had a shape which looked like a person walking.

Dr. Hatano said that he wanted to encourage people to be active, and that he wasn’t sure if the exact number of steps mattered. It turns out that he was right that the exact number doesn’t matter, and it’s not a coincidence that this number got adopted in the West without any scientific basis.

In 1996, a study led by Dr. David Bassett at the University of Texas at San Antonio looked at how many steps per day people took, and found that the average American was taking 4,300 steps per day. Dr. Bassett’s group was investigating how many steps were required to get the health benefits of exercise, and their research was based on the idea that 30 minutes of brisk walking would count as moderate exercise. Based on this research, they recommended that people take at least 7,000 steps per day, though the average number taken by Americans was still well below 7,000 steps.

More recently, a 2015 study led by Dr. I-Min Lee at Harvard University studied 16,741 older women, and looked at the effect of walking on their risk of mortality. They found that the women who took 4,000 steps per day had a lower risk of death than women who took fewer steps. This is a much lower number than the 10,000 step target, and even lower than the number Dr. Bassett recommended. Dr. Lee’s study also found that people who took more than 7,500 steps had the lowest risk of death, and their risk did not decrease any further even though some people in the study took more than 20,000 steps a day.

Even though it’s clear that the 10,000 steps number isn’t scientifically meaningful, it is still a good idea to try to walk 10,000 steps a day. In a 2010 study by Dr. Daniel Moore at Penn State, it was found that 10,000 steps corresponds to about 8 miles, and people who walked 10,000 steps were in the highest level of fitness for their age. In other words, if you’re trying to be generally healthy, it’s a good idea to try to be in the healthiest group of people your age, and trying to take 10,000 steps is a good way to get there.

I think the 10,000 step goal is pretty useful, and I’m glad it’s still around, even though its origins were completely arbitrary.

prompt: Write an essay arguing that the 10,000 steps target is arbitrary, came from a pedometer marketing campaign, and that it's still a pretty good idea anyway.
response:
A couple of months ago, I read this essay about the 10,000 steps a day standard, and I thought it was pretty compelling. But I had a couple of questions, so I asked some researchers.

First, here’s the basic argument from the essay:

A researcher at Stanford University named James Levine has studied the number of steps needed to lose weight and found there’s no magic number. In fact, the most successful weight losers had the most variable numbers of steps from day to day. He also found that the 10,000 steps a day figure was arbitrary.

Levine and his colleagues found that people with the 10,000 steps a day goal tended to exercise more, but that was because they were already more physically active to begin with.

Levine also says that the 10,000 steps a day goal may not even be scientific. He says it was actually a marketing campaign in the 1960s by a Japanese pedometer manufacturer, Yamasa Clocks, which was trying to sell its pedometer called 10,000-step counter.

So the 10,000 steps a day goal is arbitrary and came from a marketing campaign, but people who walk that number of steps tend to be physically active anyway, so maybe it’s a good goal to have after all.

My questions:

1. If 10,000 steps is arbitrary, why 10,000 and not 8,000 or 12,000?

2. What does “more variable” mean here? Do the most successful weight losers walk more steps on average, or less?

3. How does Levine think that people with a 10,000 steps a day goal tend to walk more steps *because* they’re already more physically active?

4. How would you define “physically active”?

5. If 10,000 steps is arbitrary, are other numbers? For example, could someone walk only 8,000 steps a day and still be physically active?

6. If 10,000 steps is arbitrary, is there a number of steps that would be an even better goal?

7. What other studies have been done on the 10,000 steps a day standard?

8. Is walking an important activity in terms of health?

9. How do you feel about the 10,000 steps a day goal?

I emailed James Levine, and he said he’d be happy to answer, but he was traveling this week and he’d get back to me next week.

So I emailed two other researchers, Dr. Mark Pereira and Dr. Robert Motl at the University of Illinois, and they were able to answer.

1. If 10,000 steps is arbitrary, why 10,000 and not 8,000 or 12,000?

Dr. Pereira says that “there are many other numbers that might work.” He says that “10,000 steps seems to be a reasonable goal to encourage people to move more during the day.” He also says that “10,000 steps would be a reasonable daily step goal for people who are not currently walking much.” He explains that “we don’t really know the dose-response relationship between steps and health outcomes.”

He also says that it’s probably more important to “move more,” rather than to hit a specific number of steps.

2. What does “more variable” mean here? Do the most successful weight losers walk more steps on average, or less?

Dr. Motl says that people who lost weight were “very inconsistent” about their activity levels. He says that “they may have walked 10,000 steps one day and 4000 the next.” He adds that “this was true for all of the successful weight losers we studied.” He says that “it may be that those who were able to lose weight had other healthy behaviors like dieting and exercise.”

3. How does Levine think that people with a 10,000 steps a day goal tend to walk more steps *because* they’re already more physically active?

Dr. Pereira says that “people who are more active have a greater chance of hitting the 10,000 steps per day goal.”

4. How would you define “physically active”?

Dr. Pereira says that “I’m not sure what this means.” He explains that “some studies show that people are able to maintain weight even if they are sedentary, so physical activity is not required for weight maintenance.”

Dr. Motl says that “we consider people physically active if they walk at least 5000 steps per day.”

5. If 10,000 steps is arbitrary, are other numbers? For example, could someone walk only 8,000 steps a day and still be physically active?

Dr. Pereira says that “we don’t know how many steps are enough for health.” He says that “there is evidence that a range from 4,000 to 14,000 steps can help with weight control.”

6. If 10,000 steps is arbitrary, is there a number of steps that would be an even better goal?

Dr. Pereira says that “a reasonable number might be 10,000.” He says that “people who are not currently active should walk more to get to this level.”

7. What other studies have been done on the 10,000 steps a day standard?

Dr. Motl says that “the 10,000 steps per day goal was studied in a 1999 paper by Tappeiner et al. They concluded that 10,000 steps per day is a reasonable goal for improving health.”

8. Is walking an important activity in terms of health?

Dr. Pereira says that “there is strong evidence that physical activity can reduce the risk of many diseases, and improve many aspects of physical and mental health.”

9. How do you feel about the 10,000 steps a day goal?

Dr. Motl says that “I think it’s a great idea!”

So, to sum up:

1. 10,000 steps is an arbitrary goal.

2. Other goals could work, too.

3. Walking is good for your health.

4. People who walk more tend to be more physically active, but we don’t know if that’s cause or effect.

So it’s a pretty good goal to work toward, even if it’s not the perfect goal.

prompt: Essay for clinicians: why the decline of the physical exam matters even when imaging is better at finding things. I'm an internist with 25 years in practice, so write with that authority and don't romanticize the old days.
response:
The physical exam is dying, and the cause is technology. But this trend is a bad idea, and we should push back against it.

I think the physical exam is a really good idea for three reasons.

First, it’s a great diagnostic tool. It’s true that, like with other tests, the physical exam has false positives and false negatives. But it’s a low-cost test, so a positive result will usually be true. And when you combine all the different things you can check, it can detect a huge range of problems. If you have the training, you can tell just by looking at a patient’s hands whether they’ve got diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis. I can usually diagnose the type of cancer just by looking at the biopsy specimen under a microscope.

Second, it’s a great screening tool. A lot of diseases are treatable if caught early, but have almost no symptoms until they’re pretty far along. But you can often detect many of these by looking for early signs. It’s rare to catch cancer in a biopsy unless it’s already pretty far along, but if you’re a pathologist, you can often detect precancerous lesions and get them removed before they have a chance to become cancer. There are hundreds of other examples like this. The physical exam is an amazing way to prevent disease before it happens.

Third, it’s a great way to get to know your patients. I think one of the most important things a good doctor can do is to know what her patients are like. Not in terms of their disease, but in terms of their goals and values, their lifestyle, their personality, their relationship with their family, their finances, their work situation, their hopes for the future, and so on.

The physical exam is a great way to build a relationship with your patients. It’s a time when you’re both focused on a common goal, and when you can get to know each other without having to force the conversation.

But the physical exam is dying. And the reason is that it has been replaced by technology.

The physical exam is a great diagnostic tool. But it’s not the best diagnostic tool. Imaging has become extremely good, and is better at diagnosing most things than the physical exam. This is a good thing, and we should take advantage of it.

The physical exam is a great screening tool. But it’s not the best screening tool. The physical exam was a great screening tool because it was the only screening tool. But now there are many different screening tests, and they can find things much better than the physical exam. This is also a good thing, and we should take advantage of it.

But the physical exam is the only way to get to know your patients, and the decline of the physical exam means that we are losing this.

We need to change this. We can’t let the physical exam die.

We have to make it happen. We have to make time for the physical exam. We have to make it part of our practice. We have to make it a priority.

prompt: Essay for clinicians: why the decline of the physical exam matters even when imaging is better at finding things. I'm an internist with 25 years in practice, so write with that authority and don't romanticize the old days.
response:
I’ve been an internist for 25 years. As a resident, I was asked to perform a careful physical examination of the patient in front of the consulting physician. My examination would be checked off with a simple note, “PE performed, no pertinent positives.” Now, as a consultant, I often get asked what is in the physical examination that is important. I think about this question a lot and I have a few thoughts.

When I was a resident, the physical examination was a central part of the diagnostic process. The attending, a resident, and an intern would perform the examination, then sit at the bedside to discuss the findings. The patient was the central part of the diagnostic process and the examination would often take a few minutes.

The physical examination was the most important part of the diagnostic process because imaging was unreliable. X-rays and CT scans could detect things, but we could not always tell whether what we were seeing was related to the patient’s symptoms. The physical examination was the only way to determine whether the problem was important.

In 1995, I started an emergency medicine fellowship and learned how to use ultrasound at the bedside. Ultrasound was better than imaging, because I could control the probe and correlate what I was seeing with the symptoms and physical examination findings. I could tell whether what I was looking at mattered. I was able to use ultrasound to diagnose the problems I saw most often, which allowed me to manage many patients without imaging.

Imaging and ultrasound were better than physical examination in some ways. Imaging and ultrasound could detect things that I could not find on physical examination. But ultrasound and imaging were also less precise than the physical exam in a few important ways.

Imaging and ultrasound are not specific, because they do not have access to the patient’s symptoms. For example, imaging can tell you that the patient has a gallstone, but it cannot tell you whether it is causing the patient’s pain. Ultrasound is better than imaging in this way because ultrasound can correlate the patient’s symptoms with the anatomy being examined, but ultrasound also has limitations. For example, ultrasound can show that the patient has an inflamed appendix, but it cannot tell whether the pain is caused by the appendix or something else. Ultrasound can also tell that a lump is a lymph node, but it cannot tell whether the lymph node is causing the patient’s symptoms or just a bystander. In other words, ultrasound and imaging often have the same limitations. They can tell you what something is, but not whether it is causing the patient’s symptoms.

The physical exam is not as sensitive as imaging, but it is much more specific. It takes into account the patient’s symptoms, so we know if the problem matters. I have a patient who is worried that she has a tumor. Her examination is normal, and there is no way to prove that she does not have a tumor. The examination cannot find a tumor if it is small, but it can rule out the large tumors that we worry about. We can tell the patient that the examination does not show anything concerning, but we cannot say that she does not have a tumor.

When I am trying to decide whether to do a CT scan, I think about how much information I will gain from doing the test. If the CT scan will tell me something I cannot find on physical examination, then it may be worth doing. But if the CT scan will only confirm what I already know, then the test does not add much value.

I think a lot about the role of the physical examination. I was trained to rely on the physical exam as the basis for diagnosis, but I have learned to rely on imaging and ultrasound instead. I worry that many doctors are doing this and that the physical examination is not as important as it used to be. The physical examination is the most precise tool we have. We can use it to find and rule out a large proportion of important medical problems. We should use it as much as possible.

prompt: Essay for clinicians: why the decline of the physical exam matters even when imaging is better at finding things. I'm an internist with 25 years in practice, so write with that authority and don't romanticize the old days.
response:
I had a patient a few years ago who came in with a cough. Chest x-ray was normal, but I could tell from his physical exam that he had a pleural effusion, so I sent him for an ultrasound. He had a large pleural effusion, but not enough for it to show on the x-ray. We tapped it, found it to be blood, and did some more workup which eventually proved he had mesothelioma. He got treatment for that. If we had waited until the effusion was big enough to show up on the chest x-ray, he might have died.

It is tempting to think of the physical exam as a substitute for more high-tech testing – when we had no CT scanners, we had no choice but to rely on the physical exam. But I think that’s a mistake. The physical exam is not a worse version of more expensive tests – it is a fundamentally different form of testing, and the two can complement each other.

There are some reasons why the physical exam is less effective than modern technology, and I will talk about those in a bit. But I think there are some reasons why the physical exam is more effective too, and that it can be used in ways where other technology is simply useless.

There is a lot of evidence that physical exams are getting less effective. A study of 512 patients with low back pain found that 27% of them were told they had degenerative disc disease based on x-ray, and 28% were told they had a herniated disc based on MRI. But when they got a surgical biopsy of the relevant region, only 2% of them had anything at all wrong, and none of them had herniated discs.

Another study tried to determine how often a physical exam would show a positive result for “tumor” in patients with no history of cancer. They found that it happened in 1% of patients. And a lot of these were false positives, which means that the actual rate of positive exam in patients who were healthy is even lower. This seems pretty low – in a hospital full of patients, we’re getting a few false positives a year from each physician.

I don’t know how to interpret the low rate of false positives. I know that physical exams are imperfect – I have made my share of false positives, and probably my share of false negatives as well. I have found that the more I do an exam, the more likely I am to get it right. And I think that’s one of the major problems with the current system of medical education.

In the 1960s, students would spend four years at the bedside, and learn to take physical exams from their superiors by doing physical exams. Now, students spend two years in class, learn about the physical exam by reading about it, and then do a quick rotation in internal medicine. That’s about 10% of the time they used to do. And the rest of the time is spent in class or on the wards, which are not great places to do physical exams.

In my experience, the physical exam is not very good at finding disease that hasn’t affected the patient’s life yet. A patient who has been having problems for a few weeks and is getting worse is a good candidate for the physical exam. A patient who has been having problems for several years and is stable is not a good candidate.

prompt: Why are there no green mammals? Write an essay that starts with sloths and works outward.
response:
In 1931, a British scientist named J.S. Haldane wrote a paper titled “On Being the Right Size.” Haldane was a very good scientist, but he was not a good writer and his prose is difficult. However, it’s packed with ideas, many of which have since proved useful.

Haldane’s big point is that animals are constrained by size in ways that are counter-intuitive to us. We like to imagine that if we found the right solution, we could make a giant horse or a flying whale or a giant bird, but in reality there are some hard and fast limits to what’s possible. Haldane’s example of an impossible animal was a green mammal.

The only reason an animal would be green would be to camouflage itself as a plant, but Haldane notes that mammals and other homeotherms are very inefficient. You have to eat a lot of food to keep your body warm. This is fine for a lion – there’s a reason lions are yellow. But it’s not possible for a green mammal. The plants that a green mammal could eat don’t have enough energy to support it, so a green mammal could never evolve.

The only possible exception would be a giant green mammal, since big mammals are less inefficient – they can radiate less heat for a given volume. So Haldane asks: could we evolve a giant sloth?

He concludes no. This is because the bigger you are, the weaker you are relative to your size. That’s because your legs are three-dimensional, so as you increase your size they increase in weight faster than they increase in strength. That’s why elephants have very thick legs and giraffes have very thin ones. Haldane argues that a sloth big enough to get away on plants would need to be so big that it couldn’t support its own weight.

But what about a sloth the size of a giant tortoise?

A giant tortoise would work, except that tortoises are cold-blooded. So Haldane asks: could we make a giant tortoise-sized cold-blooded sloth?

Yes! And it would look something like this:

In fact, there’s a pretty good example of a giant tortoise-sized cold-blooded sloth in Jurassic Park. It’s called Dilophosaurus:

I’m not really sure whether this is possible in principle, but this is not the kind of question that is answerable through experiment. Instead, we have to rely on what we know about the biology of mammals, the biomechanics of limbs, and the physics of heat radiation. If we can imagine a Dilophosaurus with the metabolism and body temperature of a tortoise, and with the same basic body plan as a sloth, we can be pretty sure it would work.

I think this is a good example of a thought experiment. It’s not really an experiment – we’re just looking at what we know about how the universe works and concluding that a giant tortoise-sized cold-blooded sloth should be possible. However, it’s like an experiment because it tells us something we didn’t know about how the universe works – that a Dilophosaurus with the metabolism and body temperature of a tortoise, and with the same basic body plan as a sloth, would work. It’s also interesting because we can see how it leads us step by step through our understanding of the universe: we start with a lion, and we know a lion can’t be green because it’s inefficient. But then we realize we can use this knowledge to make something that would be possible, because as we learn more we can make it more efficient.

This kind of thought experiment is possible because the universe works in a very understandable way. It’s easy to imagine a lion, a sloth, and a giant tortoise, because they’re things we see a lot. And it’s easy to know a lion can’t be green, because lions eat a lot of meat. It’s harder to know a sloth can’t be as big as a tortoise – you would need to know a lot more about biomechanics. But you could probably still do it with a little thought and experimentation.

This is a good time to talk about thought experiments in general, because there’s a lot of confusion. Some people think of thought experiments as things where you try to imagine an experiment that you can’t do, like Einstein thinking about what would happen if he rode a beam of light. But that’s not what thought experiments are. In fact, if you try to imagine an experiment that you can’t do, you’ll usually end up with something that’s really hard to understand, because you can’t do the experiment to see if you’re right.

I think the best way to think of thought experiments is as a way of learning about something you already know by imagining a new situation. For example, you can learn about the universe by imagining a giant tortoise-sized cold-blooded sloth. You know how the universe works, you know what would happen to this creature, and so you can conclude that it would work.

You can also do thought experiments with things you already know about. For example, you might think about how your brain works by imagining what would happen if you suddenly lost the ability to see. Or you might think about how a business works by imagining what would happen if one of your employees quit. The key thing is that you’re trying to learn something by imagining a new situation, not just by imagining something that you can’t do.

There are no green mammals.

I know, I know, the green monkey, the green monkey, the green monkey. But they aren’t, they’re only green by the most aggressive stretch of the word. The green monkey is a monkey of a sort of greenish gray color that might almost pass for “green” if you were really desperate. Why is there no true green mammal, like the green monkey?

Let’s start with the sloth.

Sloths have algae growing on their fur. That makes them look green, sort of like a mossy tree.

Why do the algae grow on the sloths and not on, say, the tree frogs? The tree frogs live in trees too. Well, sloths live in the trees, but they also do not really go anywhere else, because they’re so slow. They get up to eat a leaf or a twig, and then climb back into the trees. They don’t go to the ground, where they would wash off, so their fur stays wet enough for the algae to grow on it.

Now, why are tree frogs green, but not green mammals like the sloths?

There are three answers that you could think of.

The first is “because tree frogs are frogs, and frogs can be any color, while mammals can’t.” This is not true. There are some mammals which have really weird colors. I don’t know about you, but I never knew that the echidna was that purple. So the first explanation is wrong.

The second explanation is “because mammals have fur, and fur can’t be green.” This also isn’t true. The echidna has quills, which are a type of fur, and they’re purple. So the second explanation is wrong.

The third explanation is “because the sloths have algae growing on their fur to make them green, which tree frogs don’t do.” This is true, but it’s not the whole story. It’s not *just* algae, it’s algae and also the way that the sloth hangs upside-down in trees, and not having to go down to the ground, and not needing to look green to eat.

Why are sloths green, but not the green monkey? Why are tree frogs green, but not the green monkey?

Because the green monkey is a monkey. It doesn’t do anything special. It isn’t a sloth, it isn’t a tree frog. It’s a monkey. It lives in trees, but it’s not hanging upside-down in trees. It doesn’t have algae growing on its fur. It doesn’t need to look green to eat the fruit on the branches. It’s just a monkey, who is greenish-gray, who is lighter on its back than on its face and hands, and whose hands are darker than its face.

prompt: My daughter is 9 and has quit piano, soccer, and Girl Scouts in the span of 18 months. Everyone keeps telling me I'm teaching her to be a quitter if I let her stop. I'm not so sure. response:
There was a period, about five years ago, when I was convinced that every child should be required to stick with every activity they start.

This is what I believed: if you are a child and you start a sport, you must do it for an entire season. If you start a musical instrument, you must practice it until you master it. If you start a school activity, you must stick with it until you can’t go on.

The reason I thought this was that I thought children were, at their core, lazy and pleasure-seeking, and that if you let them quit anything, they’d quit everything. My mother and my father both went to college on full athletic scholarships, and it was not a matter of either of them being the best at anything, but of them simply being willing to do what everyone else quit doing. My mother and father believed in a simple formula: work really, really hard, and then the results will take care of themselves.

My children, I believed, were not going to become Olympic athletes, but they were at least going to be able to stick with some difficult things for long enough that they could develop some skills.

This is how I started out. But I’ve changed my mind.

I don’t believe any longer that children are, at their core, lazy and pleasure-seeking. I think children are very, very, very sensitive to the world, and that it’s hard to be a child, and that children do not want to be in situations they think will make them unhappy. If a child says she wants to quit, she means it.

In fact, the last time I insisted that one of my children stick with something they really didn’t want to do was back in 2010. It was my middle child, and we were in third grade. She had started taking piano lessons, and within a week she had decided she hated them. I said she had to stick with them for a few months, at least, but she didn’t want to do that. She cried and cried and cried.

So, in 2010, I was still stuck on the belief that children should be required to stick with everything. But that child, who is now 13 years old, has had a lot of success at a lot of things, and I don’t think that’s because I forced her to stay with piano lessons. I think it’s because she likes to be around people and she likes to make things and she likes to be smart and she likes to do a lot of really hard work.

When you’re a child, you get to decide what you want to do. I think it’s important for parents to understand that. And I think it’s important for parents to be aware of the fact that if a child says they don’t want to do something, they usually mean it.

That said, I think that children should be required to stick with things they don’t want to do if they’re good at them. If you’re doing well in school, you should stick with school. If you’re making a lot of friends and you have a lot of fun, you should stick with that school. If you’re really good at playing the piano, you should stick with that.

This is what I mean: I have two children who are really good at playing the piano. I think they are going to continue to play the piano for the rest of their lives. I think they are going to become concert pianists.

My daughter, who is 9, is not a concert pianist. She does not want to be a concert pianist.
