prompt: Op-ed, 800 words or so: the case against homework in elementary school is weaker than people think.
response:
I’m a teacher of a third grade class in an elementary school in New York City. I’ve been thinking a lot lately about homework. The debate on homework, particularly at the elementary level, has gotten a lot of attention recently. A recent New York Times article, “For Elementary Schoolers, Homework Is a Waste of Time”, describes how the city of New York eliminated homework entirely for second grade students, while the New York City Board of Education has decided to ban homework for all elementary students in New York City.

The argument for eliminating homework for elementary schoolers, or at least limiting it substantially, is usually that children need more time for play and other non-academic pursuits, and that research shows that homework doesn’t actually improve students’ academic performance. These arguments seem pretty good, but are actually somewhat less compelling than they might seem at first glance.

There are some pretty interesting studies suggesting that homework doesn’t actually improve students’ performance. In 2012, an Education Week article summarized one study, which found that there was no relationship between homework and achievement in elementary school, but did find a relationship between homework and achievement in middle and high school. The study found a small correlation between the amount of homework in high school and achievement, but the correlation was even smaller in middle school.

This study is probably right that homework doesn’t correlate with achievement in elementary school. This study also makes a couple of points that we should keep in mind when considering the research on this topic. First, there’s a very weak correlation between homework and achievement in high school, where we generally believe that homework matters a lot, and a very weak correlation in middle school, where we might believe homework matters somewhat less. And third, the study only measured the correlation between the amount of homework and achievement, not the correlation between the amount of homework and the achievement students actually learned. If the study measured the correlation between the amount of homework and the amount of achievement students got from their homework, it might be a lot higher. And the reason that students aren’t getting a lot of learning from their homework might be because the homework assignments are not well designed. For example, if students are doing a bunch of homework problems that are all the same and repetitive, that might be a waste of time, but that doesn’t mean that homework in general is a waste of time.

I think there’s a lot to be said for the idea that students in third grade and below shouldn’t have a lot of homework. This is partly because young kids have a lot of fun learning things, and homework takes away some of the time they can spend doing those things. But there are also more specific reasons not to give young children homework.

First, homework is probably not very effective for young children. Young children often can’t do things without help, and they can’t do things as quickly as older children. So if a third grader is practicing addition, it might take them an hour to do 20 problems, whereas if they were doing it at school, it might take them 15 minutes. The amount of time it takes young children to do their homework is often a lot more than the amount of time they would need if they were doing it at school. So the time they spend on homework is not the time they would have spent doing fun activities, but instead the time they would have spent doing more schoolwork.

Second, young children are very bad at completing their homework. I often have to follow up with students that don’t bring their homework in, and if I follow up with their parents, their parents tell me that the children didn’t do it. This is because young children are very bad at managing themselves, and they will forget to do things that they need to do unless someone forces them to. So if they forget to do their homework, they might not even realize that they need to do it until they’re trying to put their homework in their bag for school. In addition to this, kids can be pretty lazy, and a lot of them just don’t care about their homework. I think that a lot of kids would do homework if they were forced to, but I would argue that forcing kids to do homework is not a good solution. Kids have a lot of time to be bored at home, so if they do their homework, they have less time to be bored. That sounds good to me! But forcing kids to do something they don’t want to do is a bad idea, and will probably be counterproductive, because kids will hate homework even more, and will spend less time doing it. I would also argue that kids are doing other things at home that are more productive than homework.

There’s a lot to be said for giving students a few homework problems as a way to see if they understood what the teacher taught them. If students are going to do their homework, it’s a great way to see if they understood what the teacher taught them. I do sometimes give students homework to see if they understand something, but I don’t usually do this, and I usually don’t give students too much homework.

There’s also a lot to be said for giving students homework to learn something they aren’t going to learn in class. I do this sometimes, but I try not to do it too often, because young kids are very bad at learning new things without help.

prompt: Op-ed, 800 words or so: the case against homework in elementary school is weaker than people think.
response:
I’m not a huge fan of homework in elementary school, but a lot of people who want to ban it seem to have overstated their case.

In this article, the American Federation of Teachers writes:

If we take seriously the idea that the primary goal of education is to help students learn as much as they can, then it seems reasonable to conclude that schools should not require homework in elementary school.

…

What’s the research on this? As one of my favorite educational websites, The Education Blog, pointed out, a 2006 meta-study of studies of the impact of homework on academic achievement found that homework is beneficial for middle school students and high school students, but not for elementary school students. This study is one of the best summaries I’ve read of the evidence on the impact of homework on achievement. It makes a number of important distinctions, but it finds that homework has a positive relationship with achievement for middle school students and high school students, but not for elementary school students.

I’d be interested to see more studies that break out the effect of homework on achievement by grade level, but I’ll take this as my best guess.

In this article, a columnist for the Houston Chronicle writes:

A meta-analysis of 60 studies found that homework in elementary school has no positive impact on academic performance.

…

And this is just elementary school. The same 2006 review found that homework in middle school had “a small positive effect on academic performance” and homework in high school had “a medium-sized effect on performance.”

…

What I find interesting is that the same study found that doing more homework does not correlate with better results. So even in the best case, there’s a limit to how much homework helps you.

I’m not entirely sure how to interpret this. Maybe it means there’s no effect at all on academic performance, or maybe it means there’s a small positive effect at first which levels off. Either way, this is a pretty strong claim.

So we have this great study by Harris Cooper and colleagues that concludes homework helps in middle school and high school, but not in elementary school. Then, in the Houston Chronicle article above, it’s mentioned in passing that Cooper’s study found that “doing more homework does not correlate with better results.”

I’m not sure how to interpret this. Maybe there’s a small positive effect of having some homework that quickly levels off. Or maybe there’s no effect.

But either way, I think it’s pretty clear that homework is not a huge deal in middle school or high school. The idea that homework is the main reason students succeed or fail, or that a school district that assigns more homework will have better test scores, is just not supported. It’s interesting that teachers seem to believe that homework is important, because their own data suggests they’re wrong.

So why should we even have homework? Well, it’s pretty clearly not helping with achievement. But maybe it’s helping students learn how to study and how to manage their time? Or maybe it helps students practice what they learned in class?

This would all be totally reasonable if it weren’t for one problem:

There are other reasons for students to do homework. They can work on homework because they want to know more. They can do homework because they want to get good grades. They can work on homework to prepare for a test. They can work on homework to improve their college application. They can work on homework to keep their parents from yelling at them.

If it helps kids develop good study habits, we can just have them do homework.

I’m sure we can just figure it out.

prompt: Op-ed, 800 words or so: the case against homework in elementary school is weaker than people think.
response:
I recently finished reading Alfie Kohn’s *The Homework Myth* (review here), which is a persuasive argument for eliminating homework altogether in elementary schools. Kohn’s case is a good one, but I think there are still legitimate reasons to assign some homework in elementary school, which is what I want to talk about here.

I’m not saying there aren’t good reasons to eliminate homework in elementary school. Kohn is a good writer, and he’s convinced me that a lot of homework in elementary school is useless or actively harmful. But I still think that there are some useful things that children learn by doing homework. For example, they learn how to prioritize. There’s a difference between learning how to prioritize in theory, and learning it by doing it. A lot of people don’t learn to prioritize until they’ve been working a job for a while, but I’ve had a sense of what prioritizing involves ever since I was about ten years old, because I had to do it all the time in high school. And I think it’s a skill we should be teaching children as early as we can.

Of course, if the purpose of elementary school is to teach children how to do well in school, then I don’t see why we should be doing this in the classroom. Why not just give them a lot of different subjects and make them figure out how to do well in them? The fact that children in elementary school have to be in the classroom for eight hours a day doesn’t mean that all of those hours have to be spent learning how to do well in school.

One of the reasons for doing school in the classroom is that it’s where children learn how to socialize. But socializing isn’t the only reason children should be in school. We want to teach children to learn and prioritize, and we should be using all eight hours of class time we can to do that.

And this doesn’t mean that elementary schools should stop teaching children how to read and how to do math, or any of the other things elementary schools are supposed to be teaching children. It just means that the curriculum should be much more demanding than it is now. In fact, the curriculum should be as demanding as it needs to be, if we want children to learn how to prioritize.

A lot of people think that a demanding curriculum is a bad idea, because it causes children to feel stressed, and because it leaves them too tired to do anything else. There’s no denying that children who are pushed hard in school are more stressed than children who are pushed less. But this is true of children in other situations too. We don’t have to teach children to learn in a classroom that has a fixed number of hours in a day. They can be pushed hard in any situation. But we do have to teach them in a situation where we can control the amount of stress they’re experiencing. And if the situation is a classroom, then it only makes sense to push them as hard as we can.

It’s also true that children who are pushed hard in school don’t have as much time to do other things as children who are pushed less hard in school. This is why the best children are often children who aren’t interested in anything outside of school. But this is a problem that we can solve by making sure that children who are pushed hard in school get the same opportunities as children who aren’t.

We want to teach children how to learn and prioritize, but we want to give them the same opportunities as children who aren’t pushed hard in school. We can do this by making sure that they have the same opportunities as children who aren’t pushed hard in school, and by making sure that they’re given the same opportunities.

prompt: I taught 7th grade math for 11 years before leaving for a tech job. The thing nobody tells you is how much of teaching is crowd control dressed up as pedagogy. Write an essay about that gap between what teacher training says the job is and what it actually is day to day. Honest but not bitter, if you can manage it.
response:
I taught 7th grade math for 11 years. Then I left to do tech work, and I’m a lot happier than I was.

If you’ve never taught, you may not appreciate the amount of crowd control that is involved. And if you’re a teacher, you may appreciate it a lot.

I used to go to a lot of teacher trainings, where they’d try to teach us how to be better teachers. They’d say things like:

Teach students in ways that will help them learn better!

But it’s not just teaching that’s hard, it’s controlling the crowd. A student may be interested in learning about some thing. But if their classmate is trying to distract them, or another classmate has thrown a paper ball at their head, or another classmate has said “I hate you, you’re worthless,” it’s hard to learn about that thing.

If a student is having trouble learning a thing, you can try to help them learn it, but that’s not always enough. You also need to control the crowd so that they can learn the thing. And that’s where a lot of the difficulty of teaching lies.

I’ve taught 7th grade for a long time. I know how to control the crowd. But I’ve spent most of my career doing things that are not the most important things to do in 7th grade. I spent time teaching about the square root of 2 to make sure that it was not a rational number, but that’s not something I need to worry about. There is no math test in the world that has questions about the square root of 2. It’s not the most important thing.

So what is the most important thing?

The most important thing about teaching 7th grade math is that students learn how to add and subtract fractions. That’s important, because they’ll need to do it when they’re taking algebra.

If you can’t add and subtract fractions, then you can’t take algebra. And you need to be able to do algebra, because you’ll need to take trig and calculus in high school. And you need to be able to do trig and calculus, because if you want to be an engineer you need to be able to do engineering. And if you want to be a software developer, or if you want to be a scientist, you need to be able to do calculus. And if you can’t do calculus, you won’t be able to do science.

I didn’t realize this until I had been teaching for a long time. But I did. And I was good at teaching it. But I never thought it was the most important thing to do.

And I didn’t even have time to do it. I had to teach the whole curriculum. And I didn’t have time to do it.

prompt: I taught 7th grade math for 11 years before leaving for a tech job. The thing nobody tells you is how much of teaching is crowd control dressed up as pedagogy. Write an essay about that gap between what teacher training says the job is and what it actually is day to day. Honest but not bitter, if you can manage it.
response:
One of the things people don’t talk about when they’re talking about education is how much of what teachers do is crowd control. They spend a fair amount of time talking about what kids need to learn in math class, or in history class, but they talk much less about how you’re going to get them to sit quietly and listen to you, because that’s not the “real” job.

It’s a lot like a restaurant. We talk a lot about the food, and how the restaurant is going to get that food to the diner, but we hardly talk about the fact that restaurants are also in the business of controlling crowds. The people who have to deal with the crowds are usually called “hosts” or “managers”. They’re not usually chefs or waiters.

I think this is a good metaphor for how teachers think about teaching. The real job is to get the information to the students. The crowd control is the job of the administrator, the dean, the discipline specialist. But, like the restaurant, they don’t think that their job involves any real crowd control.

The other day I was talking to my friend, who is a math teacher, and I asked him why he wasn’t in the room, when it was supposed to be math class time.

He says, “Oh, I’m not teaching today. It’s discipline day.”

And I said, “Huh?”

He said, “Once a week we don’t have class, we have a discipline lesson. Like ‘if you throw food you will lose recess privileges.’”

And then we laughed about it, because it was really funny. But then we talked about it a bit more, and he said that even though he didn’t have to teach, he was in school the whole day. The only difference is that instead of his classroom he was in the office, helping the dean write up kids for things they did wrong.

And, well, he’s right. But it’s not the only difference. If he was in the office for the whole day instead of in the classroom, the kids in his class would not be having a math class.

This happens a lot more than people realize. We have a lot of teachers that are not in the classroom.

And this is one of the things that is hard for people to understand about teaching. People will say, “You have to have a college degree to be a math teacher? I could teach that stuff.” And it’s true that most people could explain to a room full of students what the Pythagorean Theorem is.

But most people don’t have a lot of experience keeping a bunch of young people who want to be somewhere else in the room and listening to what they have to say. And most people don’t know how to keep 25-30 kids in a room from getting in fights with each other for several hours a day. And most people don’t know how to teach the class a new skill, then help them practice that skill, then evaluate their progress. That’s what teaching is.

This is one of the reasons that teacher training is so important. It’s not just about learning the material. It’s learning a whole new discipline that is different than everything else you’ve done in school before.

And it’s one of the reasons that the teachers who stay in the profession for 20 or 30 years are so valuable. They’ve spent years learning how to do that kind of crowd control, and they have the experience to help the people who are just starting.

prompt: I taught 7th grade math for 11 years before leaving for a tech job. The thing nobody tells you is how much of teaching is crowd control dressed up as pedagogy. Write an essay about that gap between what teacher training says the job is and what it actually is day to day. Honest but not bitter, if you can manage it.
response:
I was teaching seventh grade math, which means I was teaching thirteen year-olds. This was, at first, an exciting prospect. Thirteen year-olds are full of questions and energy and wonder. I wanted to share all the cool stuff I knew about the mathematics of curves with some bright-eyed students who hadn’t been jaded yet. I wanted to be able to tell my friends that I had taught them to think about curves like curves, not like the straight lines and squares their school had tried to cram them into.

But there was one thing I didn’t know until I was doing it. There was one thing I learned really, really fast.

I was not teaching mathematics.

I was crowd control.

I mean, obviously I was trying to teach mathematics. But the problem is that teaching mathematics is the easy part. The hard part is getting thirteen year-olds to sit still and listen to you. The hard part is telling them to open their books to page 107. The hard part is making sure everyone is listening when you’re talking. The hard part is getting them to do the work that you assign. The hard part is making sure they’re not talking out of turn.

It’s not like I didn’t know all this before I started. I knew it. But I was naïve. I thought that if I just really, really made it clear that I was teaching mathematics, and that I was a really good mathematics teacher, and that this was really, really cool, and that I was doing it for them, and that it was their responsibility to listen, they would all suddenly fall silent and open their books and do the work.

I was naïve.

So my first year was a complete disaster. I had three sections, two of which consisted mostly of boys who had a system for distracting each other. I had a fourth period section which was all girls, and which I thought would be a walk in the park. I mean, it’s not like girls don’t listen.

The first thing I did was teach a lesson on parabolas.

I wrote “y = x²” on the board, and then I drew a parabola. And I said, “Look! This is a parabola! And look, if you move this point along the parabola, the y-coordinate is always equal to the x-coordinate squared. This is the defining property of a parabola! This is what parabolas are! And parabolas are important. They’re the shape of the mirror of the Hubble space telescope. They’re also the shape of the solar cookers you can build for 20 bucks. They’re the shape of the satellite dish on your roof. Parabolas are important.”

Then I said, “Now, let’s do a few problems about parabolas.”

I wrote out some equations and asked them to graph the parabolas.

Then I said, “Alright, now you do this problem on your own.”

Then I said, “Let’s see what you got.”

And this is what they got.

And this is what I got.

The class was so noisy that I couldn’t even hear myself talk. I was the teacher. I was responsible for the class. It was my fault. I didn’t know how to control them.

The girls I thought would be a walk in the park were even worse. They had a system for distracting each other too. There was no way to tell who was talking out of turn. Everyone had a partner they whispered to. They would always be sitting down, but they would never work, and I never knew if they were talking about the work or not.

I got into the habit of walking around and telling everyone to work on the problem I was supposed to be teaching.

Then they started asking me questions about the problem, and I would say, “It’s on the whiteboard. I wrote it down.” And then they would ask me the same question about the next problem, and I would say, “It’s on the whiteboard. I wrote it down.” And then they would ask me the same question about the next problem, and I would say, “It’s on the whiteboard. I wrote it down.”

The next year I realized that I couldn’t rely on them being able to read.

I wrote the problems on the board and then I copied the problems on the whiteboard.

Then they didn’t know which problem was the current problem.

So I wrote the problems on the board and then I copied the problems on the whiteboard, and then I highlighted the current problem with a bright yellow marker.

Then they forgot about the highlighted problem.

So I wrote the problems on the board and then I copied the problems on the whiteboard, and then I highlighted the current problem with a bright yellow marker, and then I circled it.

Then they forgot about the highlighted and circled problem.

So I wrote the problems on the board and then I copied the problems on the whiteboard, and then I highlighted the current problem with a bright yellow marker, and then I circled it, and then I drew an arrow to it.

Then they forgot about the highlighted and circled and arrowed problem.

So I wrote the problems on the board and then I copied the problems on the whiteboard, and then I highlighted the current problem with a bright yellow marker, and then I circled it, and then I drew an arrow to it, and then I asked them to do it.

This worked for a few weeks.

I did it the same way every class. I wrote the problems on the board, and then I copied the problems on the whiteboard, and then I highlighted the current problem with a bright yellow marker, and then I circled it, and then I drew an arrow to it, and then I asked them to do it.

I wrote the same thing on the board every day. I drew the same thing on the board every day.

And after a while it got so boring that it just got ignored.

After the first year I had a system for controlling the students. I was really good at it. It worked really well.

After the second year I had a system for controlling the students that I was really good at that worked really well.

After the third year I had a system for controlling the students that I was really really good at that worked really really well.

After the fourth year I had a system for controlling the students that I was really really really good at that worked really really really well.

By the fifth year, I could walk into a class and have everyone sit down and be quiet in under a minute.

I was a really, really good crowd controller.

But I never got as good at teaching mathematics as I wanted.

I mean, I was really good at it. I thought it was really cool. But I wasn’t as good at teaching mathematics as I was at crowd control.

And the thing nobody tells you about being a teacher is that it’s mostly crowd control.

You’re not teaching mathematics. You’re controlling the students. The mathematics is just a way to give them something to do while you control them.

And if you think about it, this is the way it has to be. The reason for the school system is to teach kids how to work in an organization, not to teach them any particular subject. You need to learn how to listen to other people, and to do what they tell you to do, and to work on things that you find boring. And that’s what school is really for. That’s what it’s actually for.

And it’s a shame. Because if I was in charge of the school system, I would be really good at it. I would teach everyone the coolest things I know. I would make it so exciting that people would actually want to learn it. And that’s why I would never make a boring lesson about the history of the French Revolution.

But I’m not in charge of the school system. I’m in charge of crowd control. And that’s the job I’m really good at.

And I think it’s okay to be really good at crowd control. But I wish I could be as good at teaching mathematics.

prompt: Is reading aloud to kids who can already read themselves a waste of time? I keep doing it with my 11 year old and he still wants it. Write it up as an essay, I'm curious what the argument would be.
response:
The day after I posted *Why We Read Aloud* I got a few emails saying “yeah, but that’s for little kids who can’t read yet.”

I’d already written a *Why We Read Aloud To Kids Who Can Read Themselves* (which is, like, the more obvious post), and I think I’ve mentioned in the past how I’m always surprised how many parents think that the moment a child can read, they should read by themselves.

I’ve never seen it written up explicitly, but I think a lot of parents who don’t read aloud to their older kids are thinking something like this:

1. I used to read to my kids when they were small and couldn’t read yet.

2. My kids can read now.

3. My kids don’t need me to read to them now.

4. Therefore, I don’t need to read to my kids now.

But that’s like saying

1. I used to carry my kids when they were small and couldn’t walk yet.

2. My kids can walk now.

3. My kids don’t need me to carry them now.

4. Therefore, I don’t need to carry my kids now.

Obviously that’s a non sequitur – I still carry my kids sometimes, not because they need it but because they like it.

Similarly I read aloud to my kids not because they need it but because they like it, and it feels nice to spend quality time with them, and it helps them enjoy the stories more.

In fact, I still read aloud to my 11 year old, and he’s still into it.

I have a few friends who think I’m a complete idiot for doing this, because “my son is 8 and he’s not interested in reading aloud anymore”, which is true, but not at all a reason that *I* should stop.

This is the way – you have to do what your kids like, not what the other parents tell you to do.

prompt: Is reading aloud to kids who can already read themselves a waste of time? I keep doing it with my 11 year old and he still wants it. Write it up as an essay, I'm curious what the argument would be.
response:
I keep reading aloud to my kids. When my daughter was two I used to read her a book every night. My son has just turned seven and is the first of my kids to have learned to read, but he also likes to have books read to him.

My parents have been concerned that I’m wasting my time. They argue that reading aloud is a good thing for small children who can’t read yet, but that once the kids can read on their own then reading aloud is just a waste of everyone’s time.

They’re wrong. Reading aloud is a very good thing to do no matter how old your kids are. In fact, the older your kids are, the more valuable reading aloud is.

I’ve been reading aloud to my kids for several years. Here are a few reasons why it’s a good thing:

1. I’m not really teaching my kids to read.

I don’t think that reading aloud to a small child teaches the child to read. I think reading aloud to your small child teaches your child that books are fun, and that they can learn new things from books. But, it doesn’t really teach them to read. Kids learn to read, either by going to school or by teaching themselves.

Reading aloud is not just about teaching kids to read, it’s about teaching kids to love books.

2. You can pick better books than the kids.

If I leave my daughter with a book to read, she is going to pick books with a lot of pictures and not much writing. When I read aloud to her, I get to pick books that I think she needs to read.

My son is the same way. He has a taste for fantasy books, and when I read aloud to him I can pick books about science or history or something else he might not be interested in.

3. Reading aloud is relaxing.

Reading aloud to your kids is a relaxing, low energy way to spend time with your kids.

When I read aloud to my kids, I read slowly, and I read the words that are in the book, word for word. My kids love this. They like to hear the words that they know from the books.

My daughter and my son can read on their own, but they still love when I read aloud to them.

4. Kids can have a sense of accomplishment.

When I read aloud to my kids, they get a sense of accomplishment when the book is done. They feel like they did something, and that they have learned something.

My kids know a lot of things from the books that I read aloud to them. They know about dinosaurs, and stars, and planets, and many other things.

My kids love to tell their friends about things they have learned from books.

5. Kids can get excited about books.

Kids love to hear about new books. My kids love to hear about new books, and they love to hear about new stories.

My kids get excited when they hear that there are new books coming out. They know that they are going to get new books soon.

When I read aloud to my kids, they get excited about books.

But I don’t think this explains all of it. If it did, it would imply that people who are very cynical wouldn’t have this tendency. I suspect that most people are at least a little cynical, so they wouldn’t get a GPA above 4.0.

V.

Another possibility is that students want good grades because they feel it is right to get a high GPA. They don’t think that the world is fair or that good people get good grades. But they know that it is right to get good grades.

prompt: What I wish I knew about the teenage years before my kids hit them. Two boys, now 19 and 22. Write it as if I'm passing it on to a friend whose kid just turned 13.
response:
So, my friend's son just turned 13. He's the first in his family to be that age.

I have two boys, now 19 and 22, and there are a bunch of things I wish I had known before they became teenagers.

1. I should have spent more time with them when they were young.

I spent a lot of time with them when they were toddlers, and a lot of time when they were in college and away at school. And I spent a lot of time on them when they were in middle school and high school.

But when they were about 5 to 10, we did a lot of activities that I really regret not doing, because they are the most fun. My older son has a great relationship with his own children now, and he has told me that what he wants to do is to go swimming with them every day.

I was never in that position when my kids were little, and it's really unfortunate. I think that, as you spend more time with kids, you become a better parent, because you get better at dealing with them, and they have a lot less power over you.

I know that's not true in some cases, because there are parents who spend an enormous amount of time with their kids and who really lose control. But for most people, I think that spending more time with kids is a good thing, and I wish that I had spent more time with mine.

2. Kids really are different as they grow up.

We knew this, but it's not something I had fully accepted. When I had my first two boys, I expected that they would both be very similar, but it didn't turn out that way. My youngest son is a very different person from my older son.

There are lots of people who tell you this, but you don't hear about it as much as you should, because people's children usually turn out pretty well. So you hear about a lot of people who tell you that it's hard to be a parent, and how you should spend more time with your kids, but you don't hear people telling you "I thought my kid was going to be this way, and he turned out totally different."

When you have two kids, you get this really fast, which is great, because then you can have two different kids and have both of them. You know, the more you know about the kids, the better it is.

3. There's a big difference between being a good role model and being a role model.

Being a good role model is something you do automatically. Being a role model is something you're aware of. When you're aware that the kids are watching you, you behave differently. You're more careful.

So it's not just that you're more conscious of your behavior, it's that you're more conscious of how your behavior is perceived. You're a little more aware of what you say. So I think that it's really important to be a good role model, but being a role model is more effective.

And when kids are watching you, you know what? You're going to make mistakes. But if you're aware that you're a role model, you'll make fewer mistakes.

4. Kids do better when you're consistent about things.

When you're consistent, kids feel more comfortable. And, I think, kids do better when they feel comfortable, because it's easier for them to concentrate on the things they're supposed to be doing.

I think that there are some kids who like it when the rules change a lot, or they like to push boundaries. But I think, on average, kids do better when they have some consistent rules.

So I don't know if it's important to have a consistent bedtime or not, but when I was a kid, I had a consistent bedtime, and I think it was a good thing for me. I went to bed early. But there are a lot of kids who don't like to go to bed early.

prompt: What I wish I knew about the teenage years before my kids hit them. Two boys, now 19 and 22. Write it as if I'm passing it on to a friend whose kid just turned 13.
response:
There are things I wish I’d known.

The first is that the transition into adolescence is a hell of a lot less abrupt than most people expect.

Most of the things we think of as adult traits are really adolescent traits, and most of the things we think of as adolescent traits are really childhood traits.

For example, in adolescence your friends become more important than your parents and family. This isn’t really a transition to adulthood, it’s a transition from childhood. Kids don’t care about their friends very much – they’re too busy with their parents. Adolescents care a whole lot about their friends, which seems weird to their parents because they don’t understand that it’s the next stage in a normal and natural process, rather than a complete reversal of their kid’s values.

Adolescents become more independent from their parents. This is also not really adulthood, it’s just what happens when kids grow up.

Most people think of independence as something that comes late in the transition to adulthood. This isn’t right. Adolescents become independent from their parents long before they become independent in general. And this independence is not something parents can or should prevent – it’s not a rebellion against parents, it’s just the natural process of children growing up.

And so on.

In other words, the transition from childhood to adolescence is very different from the transition from adolescence to adulthood.

The second thing I wish I’d known is that kids don’t need parents as much as they think.

I know this sounds obvious, but what I really mean is that parents think they do things for their children which are really not all that important to them.

I think I know the best example, though I have no idea why I know it.

In the late 1940s, the British government decided to send some of their children out to Australia to live with Australian families. This was not a very good idea, but it’s kind of interesting in a few ways.

The most interesting thing for me is that the children who went to Australia, in the end, didn’t really think about it in terms of losing their family.

A lot of the children went because they had lost their fathers, who had been killed or injured in World War II. So they weren’t going away from their family – they were already away from their father, and their mother was struggling to take care of them.

The children who went away thought of it in terms of their future – they were going somewhere they could have a better life.

When you were young, you depended on your parents for all of your needs. When you grew up, you became more independent. And the kids who went to Australia became independent from their parents a bit earlier than they would have otherwise.

I’ve always thought this was a really interesting insight about adolescence and growing up. Kids don’t think of their parents as the center of the universe – they see them as just another step in a long line of steps that will eventually take them to their own independence.

The third thing I wish I’d known about adolescence is that most of the things you want your kid to do are actually things you want your kid to do.

This is, I think, the best explanation of why adolescents are so hard to understand. The world they live in is not a world designed for them. In the modern world, most things you want to do are things that are either forbidden or not allowed by your parents.

A teenager wants to go out at night. This is not allowed. He wants to go to a concert. This is not allowed.

I think the most important thing to understand about your teenager is that he wants to do things that are forbidden or not allowed. If he could do everything he wanted to, he would live an entirely different life from the one he’s living now.

And I think this is the most important insight of all:

Your kid does not want to be an adolescent. He wants to be a young adult. And that’s not the life he’s living right now, because the world is not set up to allow him to do what he wants to do.

If he lived in a world where he could do what he wanted to do, he would be a very different person.

The fourth thing I wish I’d known is that it’s a lot easier to get your kid to do what you want if you make the consequences of doing it clear to him.

When your kid hits adolescence, you don’t have much power over him. And this is true even if he’s in a situation where he has to listen to you – for example, he has to do his homework to get a good grade.

prompt: What I wish I knew about the teenage years before my kids hit them. Two boys, now 19 and 22. Write it as if I'm passing it on to a friend whose kid just turned 13.
response:
A friend asked me the other day what I wished I had known before my kids entered their teens. I was going to try to write this, but it was way too long, so I’ll just put it right here, and hope that at least some of it’s useful:

The first three years are the worst, and then it gets better. It seems like forever when you’re in the middle of it, but it really does get better. The kids are way more manageable when they’re 17-18 than when they’re 13-14.

I’d say 15 was the best of the bad years. They’re not old enough to have a car, or to be able to go out to nightclubs, or to get jobs, or to drink alcohol.

The kids are way smarter and more aware than you might expect. You don’t have to treat them like small children.

You can’t stop them from having sex. But you can make it harder by not letting them have a car until they’re 16 or 17, and by not letting them hang out unsupervised with other kids.

A car can help a kid get into trouble. But it can also save him from trouble. If he doesn’t have a car, he can’t go anywhere when he’s in trouble and has to leave the house.

Your kids will do a lot of dumb things that you wish they hadn’t done, but they’ll probably survive. And you can’t prevent the dumb things.

You can’t prevent them from experimenting with drugs, but you can try to prevent them from getting addicted.

It’s easier to get kids interested in school if they see you as someone who cares about school.

Kids will do well in school if they think their parents are paying attention.

Kids can’t really have a good relationship with their parents while their parents are busy trying to control them.

It’s a lot harder to get kids into trouble when they’re working.

If you tell your kid that you’re always there for him, you will be there for him.

It’s not just parents who can get kids into trouble. Other relatives are dangerous too.

Kids aren’t going to make good decisions about their friends. You can’t choose their friends for them. You can’t even really tell them who their friends are. But if you can, you can make some decisions for them by making sure their friends aren’t within their reach.

It’s much easier to prevent kids from doing bad things that you don’t like than to try to deal with the consequences.

If you want your kids to be good and successful, you have to surround them with good, successful people.

When it’s time for them to get a job, they’re going to want to work at a job they really like. But if you try to get them a job they like, it’s probably going to be a dead-end job, and they’ll get stuck.

Don’t tell them that they’re going to regret something. That will make them do it.

Don’t say you’ll punish them for something they haven’t done yet. They’ll find a way to do it anyway, and then when you punish them, they’ll feel like they’re being punished for something they didn’t do.

It’s hard to be a good parent when you’re not happy.

It’s important to be honest with your kids. But you also need to realize that some things you know about the world will be more of a burden for your kids than you.

The more you try to control your kids, the more they’ll rebel.

When your kids do things that upset you, you have to decide whether or not to let them slide. It doesn’t matter what you decide, as long as you’re consistent.

When your kids get in trouble, you need to talk to their friends’ parents.

If your kids want you to pay for something expensive, they have to get a job first.

If your kids want you to pay for something expensive, you have to know exactly how much it costs, and what it’s for.

If your kids want you to pay for something expensive, they have to earn it by getting good grades.

It’s a lot easier for you to deal with the world if your kids don’t have lots of friends.

Kids will get their education outside of school. You need to make sure the education they get outside of school is good.

You need to be very careful about what you buy and how you live. Your kids will want to copy you.

You should try to get them to be interested in doing things they can do on their own.

prompt: Everyone loves 'growth mindset' but I've watched it turn into a poster on the wall and nothing else at my kids' school. Short essay on how a decent psychological idea gets flattened once it enters schools?
response:
I spent a week last week at my daughter's school, which turned out to be a great opportunity for a study of the flattening of psychological theory.

I was in the office of one of the teachers at a middle school where my daughter was taking classes, and there was a huge poster on the wall about “Growth Mindset.”

I’m a big fan of growth mindset research, so I asked if she could tell me about it. And she could. And it was great. And it had been an important insight that had changed the way she taught her classes. I was so happy.

But then she told me that the poster had been hanging on the wall for a while, and it had become just sort of a decoration, not something that anyone was thinking about anymore. It wasn’t like she had forgotten about growth mindset, or that she no longer believed in it. It was more that it was so obviously true that she didn’t really think about it consciously anymore.

This is a really fascinating phenomenon. It’s like a process where you start with a great idea, and then you try to convince people about it, and then you find that the idea has been flattened into a poster on a wall. And it feels good. But not as good as when it was an idea.

But the thing is, this isn’t just something that happens in schools! This is what happens to a lot of ideas. You start out with a great idea, and then you try to get everyone to agree with it, and eventually you’re just left with a slogan on the wall. It feels good, but not as good as it used to feel.

There are two obvious reactions to this phenomenon. The first is to think that the idea must be a bad idea, because it got flattened out into a poster. But that’s not true! Great ideas get flattened into posters too.

The second is to think that the idea has to be good if it got flattened into a poster. But that’s also not true! Bad ideas get flattened into posters too.

The only thing that you can know for sure is that if an idea gets flattened into a poster, it’s a big deal.

prompt: Everyone loves 'growth mindset' but I've watched it turn into a poster on the wall and nothing else at my kids' school. Short essay on how a decent psychological idea gets flattened once it enters schools?
response:
“Growth mindset,” the idea that children can cultivate intelligence, is one of the most powerful ideas in all of modern psychology. It’s also one of the most powerful ideas in education. It’s so powerful that I would not be surprised if it was, eventually, the idea that makes education itself obsolete.

It’s also a terrible idea.

I don’t mean that in the sense of “a terrible idea that no one ever would have thought of and which you shouldn’t have thought of either.”

I mean that in the sense of “a wonderful idea that no one can actually do right.”

Growth mindset was invented by Carol Dweck, a researcher at Stanford University. She showed that children who believe their intelligence is fixed (“I’m a dumb person, and there’s nothing I can do about it”) do worse in school. Children who believe their intelligence is flexible (“I’m dumb right now, but I can work to get smarter”) do better.

So what happens when people take the idea out of the research lab and try to apply it to the world?

I don’t mean this as a generalization. This is literally what happened at my kid’s school.

They had an assembly, which included an explanation of the theory of growth mindset. They got an exhibit, which included a lot of posters about growth mindset. They had a big campaign, which included an emphasis on growth mindset.

And then they did some follow-up studies, which showed that kids had absolutely no idea what growth mindset was, and their attitudes about their own intelligence hadn’t changed at all.

Growth mindset is the idea that kids believe their intelligence is fixed. And if kids believe their intelligence is fixed, they have a hard time getting motivated to do anything because they think that if they fail, then they’re stuck with that failure forever. They also feel like they can’t do anything to change the world because they don’t have the ability to change the world.

The school had an assembly, which was a big part of the growth mindset campaign. But then the school also had a bunch of other assemblies. And if you were trying to get kids to believe that their intelligence was fixed, you would just tell them that, right? So the school probably had an assembly on “intelligence is fixed.”

The school also had an exhibit on growth mindset. But they had lots of other exhibits. And if you were trying to get kids to believe that their intelligence was fixed, you would have an exhibit on that, right? So they probably had an exhibit on “intelligence is fixed” too.

prompt: Everyone loves 'growth mindset' but I've watched it turn into a poster on the wall and nothing else at my kids' school. Short essay on how a decent psychological idea gets flattened once it enters schools?
response:
Growth mindset is a wonderful idea that’s been flattened into a poster on the wall at my kid’s school, and this isn’t even the first case of this kind of thing that I’ve noticed.

The idea of growth mindset was developed at Stanford University, most notably by Carol Dweck, but is based on a lot of work by psychologists. Growth mindset is the idea that intelligence isn’t innate and unchanging, but that the way you learn can make it seem like it is.

In my experience, most school kids don’t have a growth mindset. Most school kids believe they are either smart or stupid, and they have no idea how to make themselves smart. They think it’s something they are born with, like height. They think it’s something you either have or you don’t.

This is unfortunate because school is mostly about learning, and if you think you can’t get better at something, you won’t try hard to get better at it. If a kid thinks they are stupid, they won’t put in the effort needed to learn a difficult subject, and they’ll end up bad at it, which will confirm their belief that they are stupid.

But the research has shown that if you talk to kids about growth mindset, they do better in school, especially in math and science.

The first idea I want to talk about is how growth mindset got flattened into a poster on the wall at my kid’s school.

The second is that this happens to all ideas, not just growth mindset.

I’ll try to explain the process, and maybe we can figure out how to avoid it.

Growth mindset is an interesting and nuanced idea. It’s not simply the idea that kids can get smarter, it’s about how kids are taught and about changing how they think about their abilities and learning.

I’m not sure how my kid’s school learned about growth mindset, but I think it’s probably something like this.

1. Someone read about growth mindset.

2. They told their colleagues about growth mindset.

3. They talked about it for a few months.

4. Someone asked “Okay, but what does this actually mean?”

5. Someone answered “You know, you know, it just means that we should tell the kids that they’re capable of getting better at everything and they should believe in themselves.”

6. Someone asked “How do we tell the kids that?”

7. Someone said “A poster on the wall.”

8. The poster was printed.

9. The poster was put on the wall.

10. The school has growth mindset.

I think that growth mindset is a good idea. It’s just that if you want growth mindset to work, it can’t just be a poster on the wall. You have to talk to the kids about growth mindset, and the teachers have to believe it and teach it. And I think that’s not what happened here.

This might seem surprising, but it’s just a generalization of what happens every time people try to change something, whether it’s a school or a company or the world.

The basic process for changing something is that you need a good idea, and then you need a bunch of people to believe the good idea and try to make the good idea happen.

This is easy to understand when it’s a person doing something that only takes a couple days, like getting an idea for a book and writing it.

It’s harder to understand when it’s a group of people trying to change an institution, like a school trying to implement growth mindset.

There’s a lot of work involved in changing the way that an institution works. You have to change the policies, the way things are taught, the way people communicate with each other, etc.

In a lot of cases, you have to change the way that people feel and think.

This is hard, and people will try to make it easier by changing as little as possible.

So, when I see a poster on the wall, I think that people didn’t want to put in the work to change the school. They just wanted to put a poster on the wall so that they could feel like they’ve made progress.

But this is really easy for a group of people to do. The school doesn’t really need to do anything other than put the poster on the wall.

I think this is an example of what I call “change theater.”

Change theater is when you pretend to do the hard work of changing something, but instead you just do the easy work.

Change theater is common in schools, companies, and everywhere else.

The idea behind change theater is to get the credit for doing the work without having to do the work.

prompt: Essay: the strange disappearance of the school librarian.
response:
There is a story in which a professor at Harvard asks a class to write a story about a man who disappears from a hotel room in London. The students write stories about a man who is kidnapped, about a man who is murdered, about a man who is a secret agent. The professor’s own story is the story of a man who goes out to buy cigarettes and never comes back.

The story of the school librarian who disappears is a little different. She does not go out to buy cigarettes and never come back; she simply disappears. No one sees her leave. One day she is there, and the next she is not. And when you go to check the school library database, her account has been deleted. As if she had never existed.

The librarian is a small figure, and not very interesting. It is hard to imagine that anyone, even the librarian herself, could be interested in her story. But there are two things about her which make her story more interesting than they might otherwise seem. First, she is a school librarian. Second, she has spent thirty years working in the same school library.

A school library is a strange place. It is like the intersection of several different worlds. There is the world of students, who are always looking for ways to waste time, and who are not necessarily interested in books. There is the world of teachers, who are looking for ways to help students read books, and are not necessarily interested in wasting time. There is the world of the books, which exist for their own sake, and which are not necessarily interested in students or teachers. There is the world of librarians, whose interest is to serve the other three worlds, but who often are not very interested in any of them.

There is no reason to assume that this librarian, or any school librarian, is personally interested in books. It is not like she got into this job out of passion for literature. She is there because the school needs a librarian, and she is the person who was available when the school needed a librarian. Her interest is in getting through the day and getting her kids off to school.

And yet she works at a school library. What is she doing there? And why?

The first thing to understand is that libraries are a very important part of how schools work. Schools are a place where teachers meet students to teach them how to read, but they are not the only place where this happens. There are many other places where people can learn to read. There is home, where your parents may try to teach you to read. There is church, where your pastor might teach you the Bible. There are books that are written to be read by non-readers, which you can pick up and start reading if you are motivated enough. And then there is school. And then there is the school library.

The school library is a place where students can go when they are not in class. They can go there to read, but they can also go there just to be there. They can go there to have lunch. They can go there to meet friends. They can go there to get away from the rest of the school.

And this matters. It matters because schools are a place where students learn to read, and when they learn to read they are going to start to think in ways that are different from the way they thought when they were children. And when they start to think in these different ways, they are going to feel different, too. They are going to feel that they are different from other people. And this is going to make them feel lonely.

And the school library is a place where they can go to feel less lonely. They can go there to find other people who are reading, or who are trying to read, or who are trying to understand the world in the way that they are trying to understand it. They can go there to find a place where they can be themselves, and not have to worry about being judged by other people for being themselves.

And this is why the school librarian matters. She is the one who takes care of the school library. She makes sure that the books are in good shape. She makes sure that the shelves are organized. She makes sure that the library is a place where students can go and feel at home. She is the one who makes the school library a place where students can go when they are feeling lonely, and find that they are not as lonely as they thought.

prompt: Essay: the strange disappearance of the school librarian.
response:
I have never been happier to be wrong than when I predicted that the school librarian was going to go out of business, like the school book store did, and like the school newspaper did.

A few years ago, there was this whole movement to get rid of school libraries, on the grounds that they were just places where students could go to avoid doing work. They had too little value to be worth keeping. I agreed with them. They said that the librarian was just a glorified copier and printer. If you needed a book, you could go to the public library. I agreed with them.

It turns out that they were wrong. It turns out that the librarians are a real force for good in the world, and if you remove them you’ll lose the books, too. This isn’t obvious, though.

Librarians can be pretty boring people. When you’re not working with them one-on-one, they’re often invisible. I knew several of them when I was a kid, and I remember them all being old ladies who were obsessed with order. I think this is what makes them seem so useless – they’re boring and invisible and obsessed with order, which are all characteristics you associate with people who do unimportant work. But they actually have a really interesting role.

A librarian is not just someone who organizes books. The librarian is a person who’s going to have some kind of relationship with every student who goes through the building. In my last post, I talked about how we need to be more willing to make a personal commitment to every student who comes into our buildings. But the truth is, we need to make a personal commitment to every student who comes within a mile radius of our building. If you do that, it’s hard to imagine an easier way than to give every student a personal commitment from the librarian.

The librarian has a very different role from everyone else who works in the school. She is a person who does not have to have power over anyone. She does not have to have any authority to punish or reward people. She doesn’t have to grade anyone, or discipline anyone, or do any of the many unpleasant tasks that teachers and other staff have to do. She can just be a person. She can just be a person who knows all the students and is interested in all the students and is willing to give all the students a listening ear, even the ones that no one else wants to listen to.

This is a very important role. The librarian is one of the only people in the school who doesn’t have a reason to be afraid of students. The librarian is one of the only people who can just be a person to students, instead of having to play the role of judge or disciplinarian or boss. And in particular, the librarian is one of the only people who can take students seriously, even when the rest of the school can’t. The librarian can take a kid’s questions seriously, even when it’s a question that no one else in the school will bother to answer. She can listen to students, and take students seriously, even when they’re really annoying.

The reason is that the librarian can afford to do that. She can afford to take time to have a conversation with someone who’s going to leave the school in a few days. She can afford to take time to listen to someone who is in the bottom 5% of the class. She can afford to be nice to someone who is going to have an attitude. She can afford to do these things because she doesn’t have to deal with the problems that come up when you do it in the classroom. She doesn’t have to worry about whether the student is going to be disruptive in her class. She doesn’t have to worry about whether she’s going to have to spend time on an annoying student at the expense of her other students. She can just be a person to a student.

I’ve worked with a bunch of librarians, and I think they all have something in common. They are all pretty boring people. They are all people who love their work a lot, and who are very, very good at it. And all of them are people who are willing to take on the task of being a person for every student who comes through the building, even if it means doing something that’s not really their job.

The problem is that when you get rid of the school libraries, you get rid of the school librarians. If there’s no school library, there’s no school librarian, and if there’s no school librarian, there’s no one who has to do that work of just being a person to every student who comes through the building. This is a big loss.

I know this because I spent a lot of time talking to librarians. And I know that this is what they’re willing to do.

prompt: Essay: the strange disappearance of the school librarian.
response:
A school librarian is something I’ve never encountered before. I’m sure that’s because I haven’t been to school in a very long time, but I also think it’s because school librarians are a kind of endangered species.

When I was a kid, my school librarian was a big deal. I had a lot of friends who were also librarians, and we had a lot of fun, and I’m glad I got to spend so much time with her.

But it seems like she’s gone, and I don’t know what happened to her.

prompt: Something exploring why siblings raised in the same house by the same parents can turn out so radically different. Not the genetics lecture, more about what 'the same house' even means when you're the oldest vs the youngest.
response:
It’s a question I was asked recently:

Why are people who are raised in the same family so different?

I’ve noticed it too. My mom has three kids: one who’s a really nice person who will help you when you’re lost, one who’s an incredibly successful careerist, and one who is the sort of person who will steal your lunch or yell at you on the Internet.

My dad has two kids: one who likes to make friends and talk to people and go to parties, and one who likes to sit alone in a room and read.

I’m a weirdo, but I’m not the only one.

If you’re a member of an online community that has more than, say, ten members, you probably have seen some sibling rivalry. And it’s always surprising. One sibling is always so good, and the other always so bad. Sometimes it’s one person who is good in one way and bad in another. Sometimes the good person is so good that the bad one’s badness is almost embarrassing, and sometimes the bad person is so bad that the good one’s goodness is almost embarrassing. I’m always amazed at how siblings who seem to have the same parents can be so different.

There are two common explanations. The first is that people are born that way. The other is that people are made that way.

I don’t know whether there’s some kind of genetic explanation for this, but I have read a lot of interesting stuff about how children can be different in families. One of the most interesting explanations of this is about birth order and parenting style. I read it in a book called *The Biology Of Belief* (which has a lot of interesting stuff).

In the book there are some studies which have shown that parents are very different in their parenting style based on whether the child is their first or later child. The most interesting part of the study that I remember is that when parents have a first child, they are very anxious and try very hard to do things right. They are especially anxious about whether their first child is being properly disciplined.

When a parent has their first child, there is no reference for how to raise a child. They have to try to learn from books or friends or relatives, and they have to be very cautious. If they are too lax, their child will become too spoiled. If they are too strict, they will be afraid. They also want to be fair and don’t want to treat their child in an unfair way.

prompt: Something exploring why siblings raised in the same house by the same parents can turn out so radically different. Not the genetics lecture, more about what 'the same house' even means when you're the oldest vs the youngest.
response:
I was recently talking to someone who has a brother, and they said that as kids they used to argue about who was “basically their mom’s favorite.” My mom is the sort of person who loves kids a lot, so I guess she was.

I think the answer might be that she loved them the same amount. But she had different relationships with each one of them, and they were each her favorite in a different way.

It’s funny how many people talk about how weird it is that siblings raised in the same house by the same parents can end up so different.

There’s an evolutionary explanation for this: the oldest child will get more parental investment, but less investment per child, than subsequent siblings. So natural selection has favored a personality type in first-borns that takes advantage of this advantage to try to cement a higher social status. And it has favored a type in later-borns that doesn’t take this route, and does something else instead.

This is not really a satisfying explanation for the enormous differences between siblings. If I had a sister, we would probably have a lot of the same values, but one of us would be a little more conservative, and the other a little more progressive, or one of us would be a little more ambitious and the other a little less ambitious, or something like that. But that’s not really the kind of differences that make people ask “How can two people raised in the same house by the same parents end up so different?”

What I really want to ask is why some kids in my family are so very religious, and some are completely atheist, when it’s the same family. Why do some have a passion for the environment, and others have a passion for economics.

Why am I a person who is passionate about writing, and my sister is not?

Why is my brother interested in science, and his wife is interested in art?

Why do some people in the family have big families, and others don’t?

This is not a question of genetics. My brother and sister, who are identical twins, have very different personalities. And if you really think about it, the evolutionary explanation doesn’t really account for most of the differences between siblings.

The answer, I think, is that the “same house” that kids grow up in is not really the same house. My parents had four kids, and when my parents had five, my oldest brother left home for college.

If there were five kids, and the oldest had left home, my parents would have four kids. But if there were four kids in a house, and the oldest had just left, my parents would have three kids. It’s not just the number of people, it’s the number of siblings. I’m the oldest person my mother has ever had a child, but I’m also the youngest of the four people she’s had children with.

My older brother and I are two years apart in age, so he was nine years old when I was seven, and we didn’t have a lot in common. When I was nine, he was eleven, and we didn’t have a lot in common. When I was eleven, he was thirteen, and we didn’t have a lot in common.

It’s not just the same parents. It’s different parents. The parents who had me were the parents who had my older brother when he was two years older than me.

When I was seven, my parents were not yet the parents who would have my older brother when he was a toddler.

I’m the youngest of my mother’s four kids, and she had a big family, but when my mother was younger she wanted to have more kids. She was young enough to have a child when she had four kids. She had a lot of kids, and when she was younger she wanted to have more. My sister and I are both a little bit too old to have a child together.

This is a very interesting thing about my mother. She had four kids, and when she was young she wanted to have more, but she never did. She had four kids, and she never got to have five.

And it’s interesting because she also got married young, and when she was young she wanted to be married for a long time, but she was never married that long. And she wanted to have a lot of kids, but she never got to have that many.

I think the reason I have such a big family, and my siblings don’t have very big families, is that I’m the youngest, and I’m the youngest of my parents’ kids, and when my parents had me, they had a lot of kids.

I also think it’s interesting that my older brother and I are very different, and that my parents are very different.

prompt: I'm a pediatric occupational therapist. I want a piece for our clinic newsletter (maybe 1000 words) arguing that handwriting instruction still matters even though kids type everything now. The audience is parents, not clinicians, so keep the motor-development stuff accessible. Don't oversell the research, some of it is mixed.
response:
I’ve been seeing more and more questions in my practice about whether handwriting instruction matters in a typing world. And more and more kids are arriving in my office with letters in the air (a “d” with the round part on the left; an “f” with no cross-bar; a “k” with two sticks).

I’ve been thinking a lot about what handwriting instruction looks like these days. And I’ve come to a few conclusions.

First, we need to be careful not to oversell handwriting’s benefits. Some of the studies that are floating around on the Internet are actually showing the opposite – typing and handwriting are about equally effective for learning. And when we look at studies with more powerful methodologies, the handwriting advantage is smaller than people think.

Second, we need to be careful not to undersell handwriting’s importance. Handwriting is a complex motor task that develops over several years. We know that handwriting fluency is connected to literacy and school performance. And even if a kid will never use handwriting again (I’m talking about the future here, not today), writing is a really good way to learn to read – and handwriting fluency is still connected to learning outcomes.

So how do we put this together? What does this mean for handwriting instruction?

Handwriting is a complex motor task

Writing is a very complicated task! It takes a lot of work to plan letters, hold a pencil, write on paper and make letters in the right place. It takes a lot of effort to do that, and it takes time to get good at it.

I was reminded of this today when I helped my daughter write a Christmas card. She’s 6, and it took her a really long time to write “Happy Holidays” on a piece of paper. I think that was 40 letters. And she got really frustrated.

And that is exactly the kind of thing we need to be thinking about.

There are lots of things we can do to help kids write better. We can make them practice. We can change their pencil grip. We can make them use larger paper. And of course we can teach them how to form letters.

But we should be clear about what these interventions are going to accomplish. Most children won’t be writing long passages of text. They’ll be writing their names, or a sentence, or two, on a piece of paper.

And they’ll probably be doing that for a few years.

That’s fine. That’s not a bad amount of time to spend learning how to write.

But it’s important to be realistic about what we can accomplish.

Handwriting fluency and literacy

There are studies showing that handwriting fluency is connected to literacy outcomes. But what we really need to know is whether teaching handwriting causes literacy. And those studies are hard to do. And they are still not completely settled.

But there are reasons to think that teaching handwriting helps kids learn to read.

When you write letters you have to plan them. You have to think about the sequence of movements, and the shape, and the size, and so on. And when you’re learning to read, you need to do the same sort of thing.

And handwriting is a very active way to learn letters. When you read a letter, you’re just sitting there looking at it. When you write a letter, you’re doing something with it. And that’s a lot more powerful than just looking at it.

So teaching handwriting is really important. But it’s not the only way to learn letters. And it’s not the only thing that will help kids learn to read.

What does this mean for handwriting instruction?

I’m not sure I have a lot of advice here.

I think we should be careful not to oversell handwriting’s benefits. It’s not the magic bullet that some people think it is.

And I think we should be careful not to undersell its importance. Writing is a complicated motor task that takes years to learn. And we know that handwriting fluency is connected to literacy outcomes.

So what does that mean?

I think it means that we should think carefully about how we teach handwriting. We should be aware of what we’re trying to accomplish, and what it will take to get there. And we should be clear about what we can and can’t do.

And I think it means that we should be careful not to get too focused on the letter of the law.

prompt: I'm a pediatric occupational therapist. I want a piece for our clinic newsletter (maybe 1000 words) arguing that handwriting instruction still matters even though kids type everything now. The audience is parents, not clinicians, so keep the motor-development stuff accessible. Don't oversell the research, some of it is mixed.
response:
I am often asked why my pediatric occupational therapy practice still includes handwriting instruction. “Everyone uses computers now,” says my interlocutor. “Children can type. They barely ever write with pencils. Why should we waste time teaching them to write?”

This question is reasonable. But we know that handwriting is not a skill that can be thrown aside. There are many reasons why handwriting still matters, but here are a few of the most important.

Learning to write by hand is a key part of childhood development.

Children are born ready to explore their world with their hands. At 6 months, they can grab and hold small objects. At 12 months they are able to scribble. At 18 months they begin to draw pictures. By 4 they are able to draw a stick figure with a few limbs. These are all signs that their hands, brains and eyes are working together to accomplish complex tasks.

In fact, learning to write is one of the first things a child can do that they cannot copy. Scribbling and drawing are imitation. But writing involves learning a new form, the alphabet. Children learn to make the letters A through Z, and then they begin to put them together to make words.

Learning to write is an exciting milestone in childhood. It also gives children the tools they need to learn how to read. And it is a wonderful way for children to express themselves through their own writing.

Handwriting is the foundation of handwriting.

Children who can write fluently have a huge advantage when they begin writing longer compositions. They can concentrate on their ideas instead of thinking about each individual letter. They can write faster and more clearly. And their words tend to be better organized because their handwriting is easy to read.

Handwriting is also a powerful tool for learning. Children who can write well are able to write their notes by hand. And they are able to review what they have learned by writing things down over and over.

Studies of handwriting and learning have shown that children who write by hand tend to remember more of what they have learned. One study found that children who wrote notes on paper outperformed those who typed on a laptop by a significant margin. And a recent study found that even children who are not good at writing by hand remember more when they write their notes by hand. This is because writing is slow. Writing by hand forces children to slow down and think about what they are writing. And thinking about their ideas helps them remember them better.

Handwriting is useful for the rest of life.

Even though writing is being replaced by typing in many places, handwriting is still an important skill. Children who are in school need to be able to write their schoolwork. They also need to be able to write for tests. In fact, writing is one of the ways students are tested for their state exams. And most high school students have to write their essays by hand.

Children who are in college need to be able to write their notes by hand. They also need to be able to write their essays. Even children who are in graduate school may need to write by hand. In fact, writing is still required for graduate school entrance exams. And many universities require students to write their theses by hand.

There are many places where handwriting is still required, and children who can write well have a big advantage.
