response:
Handwriting may not be as important in the twenty-first century, but it’s still important. Here are some reasons why, from our perspective as pediatric occupational therapists.

1. Handwriting is a fine motor activity, which means it engages the small muscles of the hands and arms. This is a valuable part of overall motor development, which builds strength and coordination. It is also fun, which makes it a good part of play.

2. Some children find writing helpful as a way to process information. This may be because it’s a more physical activity, or because it’s slower than typing and you have to think about what you’re doing.

3. Handwriting is a skill that children need for school, especially in elementary school. Teachers expect students to write in many subjects, even if the children use a computer for most of the work. 4. Writing well takes a long time to learn. Many children struggle with handwriting during the first few years of school, but they can learn how to do it better with practice. If they don’t get this training when they’re young, it can be harder to learn later.

5. Most children do better in school if they have good handwriting. Teachers are happier if their students have neat, easy-to-read handwriting. Students like it when their teachers give them more positive feedback.

6. Children learn to write better when they have a lot of practice and a good method for writing. This takes time, and it’s not easy. Children who are struggling with handwriting need help from a teacher, a parent, or a pediatric occupational therapist.

So, should you be concerned about your child’s handwriting? I think that’s up to you. Here are some reasons why you may want to help your child learn to write better:

- Your child’s handwriting is getting in the way of doing other things. For example, if your child has a hard time writing during class, or if your child can’t keep up with the rest of the class, or if your child can’t finish work before the time is up.

- Your child is struggling to write, but there’s no particular reason why. For example, if your child is writing a lot, but the writing is slow, painful, or messy.

- You have time to work on your child’s handwriting, and you’re interested in helping them.

If you’re interested, here are some ways to help your child learn to write better:

1. Give your child a pencil that they find comfortable. This is an important part of the process, because it’s hard to learn how to write when you’re having to fight with your tools. There are a lot of different pencils that children like, and it can take a while to find one that works for your child.

2. Give your child a lot of practice. The only way to learn to write is to write a lot.

3. Be patient. Learning to write is hard work, and it takes time to learn.

prompt: why is it that every generation of parents thinks the next generation is being raised too soft? write me an essay on that
response:
I recently stumbled on an essay called The Soft Generation, in which the author complains that modern kids are being raised too easy, that we don’t let them do enough hard things anymore, and that we should be trying to teach them to be stoics. I found it amusing because this is something people have been saying for a long, long time.

The Stoics themselves had a saying: every generation is less able to bear hardship than the last. The Stoic philosophy of accepting pain and being tough was invented precisely to counter the supposed decadence of the previous generation. It was the latest answer to the ever-present problem of people complaining that they don’t have to do anything hard anymore and so they’re getting too soft.

This was not merely a Roman thing. It was a Greek thing. Plato and Aristotle complained that today’s kids are no good, too easy, too soft, and too undisciplined. The Greeks complained that *the* *Persians* were too soft. Xenophon wrote a whole book about how his fellow Greeks had the advantage over the Persians because the Greeks grew up being able to suffer and the Persians couldn’t stand anything.

The Persians themselves complained that today’s kids are too soft. In the Avesta, the old Persian holy book, they say that the previous generation of Zoroastrians was better than theirs, and they had to do more to become good.

Then the Persians became the empire. The Greeks became a colony of the Persians, and the Greeks complained that *they* were too soft and weak compared to the Romans. The Romans complained that *they* were too soft and weak compared to the Scythians.

Even the Scythians had people who complained that the kids were getting too soft. The Scythians, the people whose name means “soft”, had their own version of a Stoic philosopher, Anacharsis, who complained that people weren’t tough enough and had to be taught to bear pain.

I’ve gone pretty deep here, but this has been going on at least since the 13th century BCE. In the Code of Hammurabi – one of the oldest written legal codes in history – King Hammurabi complains that his predecessor King Samsuiluna has “softened” the legal code and made it too easy.

It seems to have gone on as far back as human history goes.

There is a common story among evolutionary biologists about how our ancestors’ brains got larger. A hundred thousand years ago or so, early humans lived in groups with a few other humans and a dozen or two lions. In order to survive in such a harsh environment, they had to be able to work together, plan ahead, and solve complex problems. But a hundred thousand years ago, a genius inventor managed to make spears, which were so deadly that lions could no longer compete with humans. As a result, humans were able to grow in ever-larger numbers and eventually became the top predators in the world.

But now that humans no longer needed to compete with lions, they could afford to specialize. Some humans were able to concentrate on growing crops, instead of hunting. Other humans could concentrate on making spears better, or making shelters, or making better tools. All of this specialization required more complex communication and cooperation. And the need for more complex communication and cooperation was an evolutionary pressure in favor of bigger brains.

This story is not true. Evolutionary biologists don’t actually believe it. But I find it useful as a metaphor.

The first few million years of human evolution were really tough. Most of us died of disease or starvation, or were killed by other animals. We had to be smart and tough and cooperative just to survive.

But then – perhaps because of the invention of cooking, perhaps because of the invention of the spear – humans became the top predators in the world, and the pressure became less. In fact, as our population increased, it became harder and harder to survive. We had to be able to cooperate with larger and larger groups of people, and this required ever-greater cognitive ability. But in terms of the actual ability to survive day-to-day hardship, it got easier and easier. People in a rich society didn’t need to be as physically strong, or as good at planning and hunting, as people in a poor society. But they did need to be able to cooperate with a lot more people.

In this sense, it is probably true that today’s kids have it easier than their ancestors. It is also true that today’s kids have to be better at cooperating with larger groups of people. But this is not the same thing.

The fact that kids have it easier than their ancestors has nothing to do with the fact that every generation is thought to be weaker than the one before. In fact, the fact that every generation is thought to be weaker than the one before is probably just the fact that every generation is thought to be weaker than the one before.

It is a fact that people think that the young are getting too soft. It is a fact that the young are getting too soft. These are two different facts.

But the fact that people think that the young are getting too soft might be true. And if so, it might be useful to investigate why.

One reason could be that the young are actually getting too soft. But I don’t think this is true, for the reason that the young are actually getting too hard.

People think that the young are getting too soft because they don’t understand that the young are getting too hard.

People think that the young are getting too soft because it is true that the young are getting too hard.

prompt: So my kid's school just switched to standards-based grading (1-4 instead of A-F) and the parent meeting about it was chaos, half the room was furious. I actually think the idea makes sense in theory but I also kind of get why people hate it? Like a 3 means 'meets expectations' and that just feels like a C to everyone over 30. Can you write an essay that takes both reactions seriously and tries to figure out what grades are really for in the first place.
response:
If you’ve been to the parent meetings at my kids’ school this year, you’ve seen what’s known as “standards-based” or “standards-aligned” grading. Students in kindergarten through fourth grade are no longer given letter grades. Instead they are given a number on a scale of 1 to 4 for each of 30-40 different standards they’re supposed to meet, for a total of something like 600 grades per semester. A 1 means a student doesn’t understand the standard, a 2 is developing an understanding, a 3 is meeting expectations, and a 4 is exceeding expectations.

The parent meeting was a disaster. The new system is supposed to be really cool, and it is, but the teachers were unable to communicate it in a way that wasn’t infuriating to most parents. I’m going to spend this post explaining why I think the new system is really great, and what the teachers should have said. And then I’ll spend the rest of this post trying to figure out why the system is so hard to explain and to understand, and why it’s so difficult to change, even when it makes sense.

I’ll start with the new system, since that’s easy.

I.

In the old system, a teacher would give a kid something like 100 test questions, and he might get 90 right and 10 wrong. He’d get a 90%, which would correspond to a B+.

In the new system, a teacher might give the same kid 100 test questions, but instead of counting how many he gets right, she’d look at which he gets right and which he gets wrong. She might notice that he answers all of the first 30 questions right, all of the next 30 questions wrong, and then a mixed bag of right and wrong on the last 40 questions. In which case he might get a 4 on the first standard, a 1 on the second standard, and a 2 on the third standard.

I’m oversimplifying here. In reality, teachers might take a more holistic view, or have kids demonstrate their understanding of the standards through projects or class activities or whatever. But it’s pretty similar.

This isn’t just a cosmetic change. In the old system, the kid would get a 90% no matter which 90 of 100 questions he got right, so the grade would convey no information about what he had learned. In the new system, the kid would get a 4 on the first standard, a 1 on the second, and a 2 on the third.

And this matters. My kid, who was getting 95%’s and A’s, got a bunch of 2s in the new system and was pretty shocked. But she had never learned to do fractions, and the new system made this abundantly clear.

The new system also has better incentives for both kids and parents. A kid who’s getting 90%’s and B+’s is more likely to say “I don’t care about learning anything more, I have an A and I’m happy with it”. But a kid who’s getting 1s and 2s on a bunch of standards knows she’s doing something wrong. A parent who’s seeing B+’s is probably going to be pretty confident that her kid is learning, and is unlikely to take an active interest in what’s happening in school. But a parent who’s seeing 2s and 3s is going to be more motivated to talk to the teachers about what they’re doing.

The new system also has better incentives for teachers. If a teacher is teaching a bunch of 9s to kids who have no idea what 9s are, a letter grade system doesn’t tell her anything about that. But in a standards based system, she’s going to see the kids getting 1s on a standard and will know that she needs to teach that more.

It’s a really good system.

But nobody seemed to like it. There were a lot of things that made people angry, but here are the two that I hear most often:

II.

One thing people really hated is that a 3 is considered good. A 3 means that a student is meeting expectations, and that’s supposed to be great.

But it just feels like a C to everyone over 30.

I had this conversation with a friend who’s been an elementary school teacher for about 20 years. She told me that in her school, the kids who get 3’s are the ones who are usually getting A’s.

I said, “That can’t be right. If most kids are getting 3’s, then that’s going to make all the other kids really angry. They can’t accept that getting a C means they’re doing well.”

She said, “It’s a different culture now.”

I said, “But the parents still hate it. They’re the ones who set the cultural norms for their kids!”

She said, “Oh, the parents don’t care. They never care.”

I asked, “How do you know?”

She said, “Because I’ve been a teacher for twenty years, and I have never heard a parent who cared about their kid’s grades.”

I was surprised by this. I thought that I had always heard parents complaining about their kid’s grades. I thought parents were always saying how important grades were.

But it never came up when I talked to people’s parents about it. And it wasn’t until recently that I realized that parents are actually pretty apathetic about grades.

And this might be a really important reason why the new grading system has failed.

A lot of us got good grades in school, and if you got good grades in school you probably got A’s, which were really cool. And you were pretty sure that your kids would get A’s too, because kids get A’s by default. And even if your kid didn’t get A’s, he was probably still doing just fine.

I think the reason that I thought parents cared about grades is that I was confusing myself with other people. I do care about grades, I’m just not a representative example of parents. I’m someone who went to college to study philosophy of mind and logic. And then I wrote a very successful blog. And then I published a book about how to make better decisions. And I’m not a representative example of parents.

And I think the reason that people hate standards based grading is because they think that getting a 3 is really bad, but really it’s just fine.

And I think the reason that people think that a 3 is really bad is because most people in the country don’t care about grades. They care about them because they’ve heard that parents care about grades, and they’ve heard that parents say “A’s are the only good grades”.

But they’re wrong!

And we need to talk about this, because getting A’s is not a goal. It’s a good thing to learn things, and it’s a good thing to be able to get A’s on tests if you learn things. But getting A’s is not a goal, and it doesn’t matter as much as most people think.

III.

There’s another reason why people hate standards based grading. They hate that the system is really confusing.

I think the old system was actually confusing too, even though everyone pretended that it was easy to understand.

A letter grade is supposed to tell you how well you did.

If I got a B+, I’m supposed to be really happy. If I got a C+, I’m supposed to be pretty disappointed. If I got an F, I’m supposed to be really angry.

But I never really understood what this was supposed to mean. I don’t know what it is to do really well on a test, and I don’t know what it is to do really poorly. I just know what it is to get an A, and I know that that’s really good, and I know what it is to get an F and I know that that’s really bad.

But what does it mean to do really well on a test? I don’t know.

And I think this is one reason why people hate standards based grading.

I think this is why people think that a 3 is bad, even if the teachers say that 3 means meeting expectations, and it’s supposed to be pretty good. The teachers say that you’re doing well if you get a 3, but the kids are going to hear it as “I’m only doing okay”, which makes them pretty disappointed.

And I think this is also why people hate the idea of getting an A in a test in which they only got 60% of the questions right. They’re going to feel bad about getting 60%, even though it’s supposed to mean that they’re doing great.

And I think this is also why people hate the idea of getting an F in a test in which they got 90% of the questions right. They’re going to feel bad about getting an F, even though it’s supposed to mean that they’re doing really well.

But if we think about what it means to get a letter grade, I think this makes a lot more sense.

IV.

If we’re going to get a letter grade for something, I think that we should be asking what it is that we’re being graded on.

A letter grade is supposed to tell us how well we did.

prompt: So my kid's school just switched to standards-based grading (1-4 instead of A-F) and the parent meeting about it was chaos, half the room was furious. Can you write an essay that takes both reactions seriously and tries to figure out what grades are really for in the first place.
response:
I’ve been on a school’s school-parents committee for a while now, and we’ve just had one of those big public assemblies to talk about grading. This school has switched from A-F grading to standards-based grading, and the assembly was basically one long conversation between a few of the teachers and the parents explaining how it works and why, and asking for questions.

Most of the time it was pretty good. And most of the questions were very reasonable.

But sometimes it was like a horror show.

Some parents were just furious. They’d say something like “A 3 is basically a C, right? How am I supposed to get into a good college with a bunch of Cs in my transcript?”

And then the teachers would patiently explain that a 3 doesn’t really mean a C, that it means “meets expectations” and that most kids in most subjects get 3s.

And the parents would say “I’m sure most kids in most subjects get Cs” and they’d continue to be furious.

And then we’d move on to other things, and some of the other parents would go “Why are they so angry? This system is clearly better than A-F.”

And the teachers would say “Yeah, I get the feeling like this was a bad idea.”

So basically it’s a really confusing situation where half the room thinks the teachers are just trying to fool them, and half the room thinks the other half is just clueless. And I’ve been thinking about it a lot.

I think the parents are right that the school was a little disingenuous. I think the teachers were right that standards-based grading is better than A-F. And I think both sides are missing what the other is talking about, so there’s no way to reconcile their opinions. And I think both sides are also missing what grades are for in the first place, which might be a lot more complicated than any of us would like.

I.

First: why are the parents so angry?

It’s hard to get a handle on. I went to the meeting with my wife, and she said that the parents who were yelling at the teachers had very nice kids, and were just trying to get their kids into college. She said that when you talk to them, they’re not dumb and they’re not evil, just…confused. And she said that the thing she wanted most was just to get the teachers to explain the system in a way that would make them stop screaming, but that the teachers just weren’t willing to do that.

I don’t think this is an issue of “the teachers were just too much of a bunch of idealists to admit that the system is stupid”. I think there’s a more complicated issue here.

A lot of people have the opinion that you should have a 4.0 GPA to get into a top-tier university.

And in the A-F system, getting a 4.0 GPA means getting straight A’s.

And in the standards-based grading system, a 3 means “meets expectations”.

This creates a situation where parents who have heard that they should aim for a 4.0 GPA are going to be very confused.

I think a lot of the parents were just trying to translate the standards-based grading into the A-F system, and the teachers were just trying to explain the standards-based grading on its own terms, and that’s why they were fighting.

I think that’s why the teachers were getting so frustrated with the parents. I think the parents are just trying to do something simple, and that’s translating their understanding of the grading system into a new set of grades, and the teachers are just trying to explain why this system is different, and the parents are just refusing to do that.

II.

What are grades for?

I think there are at least three reasons to have grades, and they don’t always line up.

First, you need grades to know if you’re doing well or not. If you’re doing well, you want to keep doing what you’re doing. If you’re doing badly, you want to change something.

Second, you need grades to know how you’re doing compared to other people. Maybe you’re doing well but everyone else is doing better, in which case you need to up your game. Or maybe you’re doing badly but everyone else is doing even worse, in which case you can relax a bit.

Third, you need grades to get into college. A good grade is a good thing, and a bad grade is a bad thing, and you need good grades to get into a good college, which is a good thing.

prompt: So my kid's school just switched to standards-based grading (1-4 instead of A-F) and the parent meeting about it was chaos, half the room was furious. Can you write an essay that takes both reactions seriously and tries to figure out what grades are really for in the first place.
response:
The first thing to say is that standards-based grading sounds great.

A-F grading, the kind of system that most of us know, is kind of a mystery. You start out at A-, which is like 97-98%. If you lose 3%, you drop to A. Lose another 3%, you get B+. Lose another 2% and you’re at B. Lose another 2% and you’re at B- . Lose 3% and you’re at C+. Lose 2% and you’re at C. Lose 3% and you’re at C-. And so on.

The system is confusing and arbitrary. If a kid gets 98%, they get an A-. If they get 97%, they get an A. This means that in some sense an A- is better than an A. And yet an A- is worse than an A, because you can’t get anything lower than an A-, whereas you can get something lower than an A.

I don’t know when or how it happened, but at some point grades became an all-or-nothing system. If you got a B+ on one test and a B- on another test, you averaged to a B. But if you got a B- on one test and a B on another test, you averaged to a B-. You couldn’t get a B unless you got at least two Bs. And if you got a B- on one test and an A- on another, you averaged to a B, so you couldn’t get a B- unless you got at least two B-s.

There are some things that are great about this system. I like it because it encourages me to work really hard on everything. If I can get an A- on a paper, I will work very, very hard on it. If I can raise my grade by 0.1%, I will try to do that.

But standards-based grading does away with all this. In standards-based grading, you get grades from 1 to 4, with 1 being below standard, 2 being standard, 3 being above standard, and 4 being way above standard. The idea is that the teacher grades a paper according to how well the kid has learned the skills taught in class. For example, a 4 paper would be something the kid wrote really well and also used in interesting ways. But a 3 paper would just be something the kid wrote really well, like a normal good essay.

And the really great thing about standards-based grading is that it doesn’t matter whether you get 99% or 70%, as long as you understand the material. You can miss tons of details and still get an A, as long as you understand the big picture. And if you understand the big picture but can’t figure out the details, you can still get an A, as long as you ask for help.

I think standards-based grading sounds great. I like it a lot.

And yet, the other night I went to a meeting with my kid’s teachers about how to grade him. And the parents were furious. They hated the system. I understand why.

A 3 is a good grade. It means you meet standard. It means you understand the material. It’s great. But if my kid is doing great, if he is understanding the material, then he should get a 4, right? And yet my kid is not getting a 4. Why is that? What does it mean to get a 4? And if he gets a 3, that means he’s doing well but not great, right? He’s okay, but not great. And that’s not very good.

And my kid’s teachers have to explain that it’s really hard to get a 4. It means you’re in the top 5% of the class. It means your paper was so good that the teacher wanted to show it to other teachers and use it as a model for the class. And yet, they keep giving my kid 3s. Why? They keep saying my kid is doing well. He’s doing great. But he’s not getting a 4.

The problem, as I understand it, is that standards-based grading really does seem great, but people are used to getting A’s, and they want to keep getting A’s. They want to know they’re doing great. And if they’re doing great, they should get A’s. And yet the teachers keep saying they’re not giving A’s.

But this isn’t the fault of standards-based grading. This is the fault of A’s. It means something that is too vague and ambiguous. It’s too easy to get. And yet people want to keep getting them.

But if people want to keep getting A’s, then why do they want standards-based grading? I think it’s because standards-based grading does away with some really bad parts of A-F grading. Like, why is a B- worse than a B? If you miss one detail, you drop a grade, even if you’re still learning the material. And why is an A- worse than an A? If I get 98% I get an A-, but if I get 97% I get an A. But I should get an A if I do great!

This is why the parents at the meeting were upset. They didn’t want A’s. They wanted to get great grades. They wanted to be told they were doing well. And they wanted to know they were doing well.

I learned that, and I think it’s a shame, because I could have learned how to fill out a job application in 30 minutes, and that would have let me spend an extra 45 minutes learning something else, like how to read a lease.

But I’m a terrible customer service rep, and that’s because I didn’t learn how to talk to customer service reps in school, I learned it in life, and that’s a waste of time.

response:
We’ve come a long way, as a society, since the days of writing our own letters by hand. First we had typewriters. Then we had computers. Now it’s just the laptop or smartphone in our hands all day, every day. Typing is fast, efficient, and, more importantly, legible. The only thing that makes cursive writing still worthwhile is the fact that some people have trouble reading block letters.

If you think that’s not an issue, just try to read this.

You probably can read that just fine. But if you can’t, cursive is a must-have skill.

What are the odds that your kid is going to become someone who can’t read block letters?

What are the odds that your kid is going to have to hand-write a check?

What are the odds that your kid is going to have to hand-write a thank you card?

What are the odds that your kid is going to have to hand-write a grocery list?

What are the odds that your kid is going to hand-write something else at all?

We’ve gotten really good at teaching cursive, so much so that we’ve turned a simple skill into a whole course. The course covers not just how to write the letters, but how to connect them, how to write them fast, and how to make them look pretty.

And that’s fine if you want to be an artist. But if you just want to survive in the modern world, you don’t need to know how to write “the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog” in cursive. You don’t even need to know how to write it in block letters, because you’ll just type it into a computer instead.

What you do need to know how to do is read a lease, understand a contract, sign a check, and talk to a customer service rep when you have a problem with your car insurance.

That’s a lot more practical than learning to write cursive, isn’t it? And yet no school is teaching this.

I’ve thought about this a lot, and I’ve come up with what I think is a better solution.

Let’s keep teaching cursive in first and second grade. Kids will learn the skill.

Let’s make it a requirement that third through fifth graders write thank you notes and letters to their grandparents in cursive. They won’t lose the skill.

Let’s make it a requirement that sixth through eighth graders write short essays in cursive. They won’t lose the skill.

Let’s make it a requirement that high schoolers handwrite some short essays. They won’t lose the skill.

And then let’s use the time we saved to teach kids how to fill out a job application, how to write a cover letter, how to read a lease, how to understand a contract, and how to talk to a customer service rep.

That’s a lot more important.

prompt: Write an opinion piece arguing that schools should stop teaching cursive and start teaching kids how to fill out forms, read a lease, and argue with a customer service rep.

When my daughter was in kindergarten, she was introduced to cursive, an ornate style of writing that was used by scribes a thousand years ago, and was designed for people with quill pens and parchment.

She had a very hard time with this, and she was not alone. A survey of the teachers who had introduced cursive to her grade said that most kids couldn’t write cursive by the end of the year, and that 20% still couldn’t even two years later.

Now, I’m not sure why my daughter ever needed to learn cursive in the first place. Most people aren’t quill and parchment scribes. Most people don’t have to deal with anything that requires cursive. I can’t think of anything I’ve ever had to write in cursive in my life.

There is no reason for anyone to use cursive in this day and age. And yet every kid in America is taught cursive. Why?

The main reason is tradition. We have a habit of teaching kids things like cursive that are useless, because they have always been taught.

The only reason we teach kids how to do long division, for example, is that we’ve always taught them to. Long division is a completely useless skill. People don’t do long division anymore. Nobody does. We’re not even sure why long division is useful. Nobody does long division. But we teach it because we’ve always done it.

We teach kids how to write essays. This is probably useful, but it’s not very useful. And it takes so much effort, and most people don’t do it very well, and they get so frustrated by it. We teach them to write essays because it’s an easy thing for teachers to assign, and because we’ve always taught kids to write essays.

We teach kids how to do long division, and write essays, and do all sorts of other things that are hard to learn and not very useful, just because we’ve always taught those things.

So when we think about what we should teach kids, we should look at the things that are most useful to them. What are the things that people really need to know in order to function in the world?

It’s not cursive. It’s not long division. It’s not essays.

There are much more useful things that kids should learn:

1. How to fill out forms.

This is the first thing that everyone has to do, and yet most people don’t know how to do it.

People don’t know how to fill out a check. I don’t know how to fill out a check. I had to learn it this summer because I needed to open a bank account, and I still don’t know how to do it correctly.

People don’t know how to fill out a lease. When my friend moved to a new apartment, the person who was leasing her apartment told her that she could fill out her lease. She didn’t know how to fill out a lease. She didn’t even know how to figure out which numbers to put where.

The person who leased her the apartment was a college professor. She was a college professor who couldn’t fill out a lease.

We should be teaching kids how to fill out forms. It would help them.

When you’re getting an apartment, they give you a lease to sign. It’s a really complicated contract.

You don’t know what you’re supposed to do with a lease. The landlord who gives it to you just expects you to sign it and pay your rent. They don’t tell you that you need to read it.

We need to teach kids how to read a lease. It would help them.

3. How to argue with a customer service rep.

When you’re arguing with a customer service rep, they’ll ask you for your information. They’ll say things like “I’m sorry, but I can’t let you do that.”

But they won’t tell you that you can just say “I’m not going to let you do that.” They won’t tell you that you can ask for a manager. They won’t tell you that you can threaten to sue them. They won’t tell you that you can ask for a manager.

They won’t tell you any of these things.

We need to teach kids how to argue with a customer service rep. It would help them.

These are all things that we should be teaching kids. They’re all useful things. They’re all things that we should teach kids.

It’s not cursive. It’s not long division.
