I was home, always. My mother would sit in her home office, writing. I would sit in the living room, writing. We would read a lot.

In the summers, my mother and I would spend a lot of time in the library. I loved the library. I would check out as many books as the librarian would allow, and bring them home in huge bags. I would read them one after the other, and return them to the library in huge bags, the next time I went back.

I was always hungry. There were no lunch hours, and no cafeteria. My mother would make lunch for me, and then I would eat lunch in the living room, and read while I was eating lunch.

I never had a group of friends. I had no group of friends. I didn’t have friends. I had no friends. I had a friend who I liked. That’s all I had.

When I was in high school, I started going out a lot. I started going out to bars. I started going out to clubs. I started going out with boys. But then I got back to a normal routine.

When I got back to my normal routine, I started going to college.

I was homeschooled for all 12 years of school.

It’s not like my childhood was perfect. I was very lonely. I was very sad. I was always crying. I would cry a lot. I would cry because I was always hungry. I would cry because I was always lonely. I would cry because I didn’t have any friends. I would cry because I didn’t have any group of friends.

prompt: Essay arguing gifted programs do more harm to the kids in them than to the kids left out.
response:
In the last few years, I have been very critical of gifted education. In particular, I have criticized the idea that “gifted education” is a good idea, or that gifted children are in some special need of extra help.

I’ve also noticed that the people in gifted education who disagree with me – in a field where I am considered an expert – all say that I’m being mean and unfair, and that I’m “hating on gifted kids”. This is not something I would usually do: I don’t have an axe to grind about gifted children, I just happen to be interested in gifted education and I think it’s a bit weird.

So I thought I’d take a quick detour and explain why I am NOT mean and unfair to gifted kids, and why I think that even if I were, that wouldn’t be much of a problem.

1. Gifted kids have the most self-esteem of any group of children.

The most common criticism of gifted education is that it creates an unhealthy focus on IQ scores and academic performance. But if gifted education makes a lot of people feel like they’re smart, it also gives those people a lot of self-esteem.

This is a good thing.

People with high self-esteem do better in school, have more successful relationships, are less likely to smoke or drink or commit crimes, and – in some cases – are less likely to be depressed.

It’s pretty common to talk about self-esteem as an “empty calories” type of idea – a superficial and temporary boost that won’t change anyone’s life. But this seems to be a misreading of the data, which suggests self-esteem has real benefits.

If the most common criticism of gifted education is that it makes people care about academic success, then it seems that gifted education is actually making people care about something that is correlated with success in life. That’s not a bad thing.

2. Gifted kids have the highest levels of parental education, income, and involvement in their education.

Gifted children are more likely to come from wealthy, educated, involved parents. That is, they come from an environment that is good for children.

Gifted programs seem to do a few things that make the children in them even more likely to have good environments. They make parents pay money and get involved in school activities, they make parents spend time on education-related things, and they make parents be aware of gifted education in particular.

This is also a good thing.

3. Gifted kids are more likely to be male than female.

This is true for gifted education in general, and in particular true for STEM gifted programs.

This is because boys are more likely than girls to have high and/or variable scores in math and science.

I don’t know what to do about this. There doesn’t seem to be a great way to help the problem of fewer girls being gifted in science. But if anything, it seems to help with the gender gap in the sciences.

4. Gifted kids are more likely to be white than black.

This is a fact.

I have no idea how to fix this.

But it’s probably not too bad, given that white people have better life outcomes than black people.

5. Gifted kids are more likely to be rich than poor.

This is also true.

This seems less bad, since rich kids are better off than poor kids.

6. Gifted kids are more likely to be Jewish than non-Jewish.

I don’t know that this is true, but it is true that Jews score higher on IQ tests than everyone else, and Jewish people have higher education and wealth levels than everyone else, so I assume this is true.

This seems like a good thing, for Jews.

7. Gifted kids are more likely to be Asian than non-Asian.

This is also true.

This seems like a good thing for Asians.

8. Gifted programs do not seem to make children in them any happier or more successful than their non-gifted peers.

Some studies seem to show a positive effect of gifted programs. But there’s a lot of selection bias here. Gifted children probably come from more educated and wealthier families, and those families are probably more supportive of their children, and have more resources to spend on their children. Also, gifted programs are often run by enthusiastic teachers who are more committed and effective than average. And children who get extra help may be more motivated than the kids who don’t. So we don’t really know if gifted programs are good for gifted kids. But even if they are, this is a good thing.

9. Gifted programs may be bad for kids who are NOT in them.

I am not sure that this is true, but it is possible. There are a couple of reasons that I think it might be true.

First, when you take a bunch of gifted kids and put them together, the other kids who don’t get selected for gifted education are probably more likely to feel like they’re not as smart as everyone else. That could be bad for their self-esteem.

Second, when you spend a lot of time on gifted education, you probably spend less time on helping the other kids.

prompt: Essay arguing gifted programs do more harm to the kids in them than to the kids left out.
response:
There are good arguments for the idea that gifted programs do more harm to the kids who get to go to them than to the kids who don’t, and I’ve tried to make them before. I’m not going to rehash the full argument, but I just saw a study that gives new evidence supporting it, so I thought I would post about that.

This is from a Swedish study on gifted education. They had a school that did a “within-grade enrichment” program. I’ll quote from the abstract:

The aim of the present study was to evaluate the effect of within-grade enrichment on students’ academic development and satisfaction at school. The study included 280 students, of whom 108 participated in the enrichment. The students in the enrichment program had higher grades in the subjects Swedish, Mathematics, and Social Studies compared to those not included in the enrichment. Students in the enrichment group reported a higher degree of satisfaction with school compared to those not included in the enrichment.

This seems to be a study that would find a positive effect of gifted education if one existed. The children in the enrichment program are the same age as the children who don’t get it, which means their only advantage is having a smarter peer group – they’re not benefiting from having older kids, who tend to be a little more advanced. They’re the same age, same school, and so on. They just get some special enrichment program instead of doing the same curriculum as everyone else. And this study, done by an obviously neutral group of researchers who were just trying to evaluate the program, found that they were happier and had better grades than their non-enriched peers.

And yet this study does not show that gifted education does any good. Because it doesn’t have any kind of control group. If you compare the enriched kids to a control group of kids who were not gifted enough to qualify for the program, you might find that the enrichment group was happier. But that could be because they were naturally happier to begin with. If you compare the enriched kids to a control group of kids who were gifted but who were not enriched, you might find that the enriched group did better. But that could be because they were naturally smarter to begin with. And if you compared the enriched kids to a control group of kids who were enriched but who were also not gifted, you might find the enriched group did better. But that could be because they were naturally smarter and happier to begin with.

The only way to find out whether enrichment programs work is to randomly assign children to enriched or non-enriched groups. Then you can compare the enriched kids to the non-enriched kids and know that the differences are due to the program. This study, as well as most of the other studies I’ve looked into, has no such group.

A study of the Swedish program is not going to tell us anything about US gifted education programs, which are vastly different. But I’m going to assume that the Swedish program is pretty good. In fact, it probably has more support from the public than most programs have, so if this program, with a lot of support, is not able to produce good results, then I don’t have high hopes for anything else.

I just found a recent study of gifted education in the US. They were trying to see whether gifted students in a gifted program, compared to regular students in a regular classroom, got better results.

They found that the gifted students did better.

But again, that’s not a fair study. The gifted students in the gifted program may be better off than the regular students in the regular classroom, but that’s not because they’re in the gifted program. It could be because they were naturally gifted in the first place. So again, this study does not prove that gifted programs work.

I found another study which looked at gifted students who were not in a gifted program, and compared them to non-gifted students in a regular classroom. They found the gifted students did better.

This makes it harder to believe that gifted programs work. If the gifted students who aren’t in the gifted program are doing as well or better than the regular students, then the gifted program isn’t doing any good. If you put those kids in a regular classroom, they’ll do just fine. And if you put them in a gifted classroom, they’ll probably do just fine too. So the gifted classroom is not helping those kids.

And if the gifted classroom is not helping the gifted students in that classroom, then what is it doing? It’s taking all the good students and putting them in a separate classroom, leaving the regular students to learn from a teacher who is not used to dealing with advanced students. The teacher can’t spend extra time on them, because he has a full class of regular students. And the gifted students in a regular classroom are usually not allowed to advance at a faster rate than their classmates. If they do the work fast, they get a 100 and sit around doing nothing.

So the gifted students in the gifted program are not helped by their program, because they do just as well in regular classrooms. And the regular students in the regular classrooms are hurt by the gifted program, because their teacher has to spend so much time on the gifted students that he can’t help the regular students as much as he could.

prompt: Essay arguing gifted programs do more harm to the kids in them than to the kids left out.
response:
I know I’m late to this. But I recently started teaching kids in a gifted program and it’s gotten me thinking about gifted education.

I had a very gifted childhood – 133 percentile, the kind where you know everyone else is less smart than you and you’ve known it since elementary school. In my experience, gifted programs were mostly a waste of time. We got more work to do (like memorizing all the US state capitals) and sometimes a chance to skip a year of school, which I did. But most of the time it was like a normal program. The kids in the program weren’t necessarily more advanced. The teachers weren’t necessarily better than other teachers. There wasn’t always much of a curriculum.

And of course, it was a bit of a status game – I didn’t like it much as a student, but I loved it as a teacher (I can’t help myself).

But when I thought more about gifted programs, I thought maybe they aren’t that bad. Sure, the kids in the program aren’t getting much extra help, but at least they’re not being held back. And the kids not in the program have a bit of a challenge to work off.

That’s how I’ve always thought about gifted programs. I thought they were a bit of a scam, but a harmless one.

But the other day, I had a revelation. Gifted programs aren’t a harmless scam. Gifted programs are a harmful scam. The kids in the gifted program are getting nothing, but the kids in the normal program are getting less. And in fact, it’s not just less – it’s a lot less. The kids in the normal program are worse off than they would be without a gifted program.

How do I know this? I’m teaching in a gifted program, but I’m teaching a normal class as well. And I was a gifted child, but I was a normal child as well. I was in a gifted program, but I was in a normal program as well. In fact, I was in a gifted program and a normal program at the same time (I was in a gifted program in 4th grade and a normal program in 5th grade – I skipped a year).

And in my experience, the kids in a normal program are worse off than the kids in a gifted program. In fact, the normal program is a lot worse.

I don’t think it’s fair. I don’t think it’s good for the kids either. I think it’s better to have no gifted program at all. And in fact, I think it would be better for the kids in a gifted program to be in a normal program.

But gifted programs are a bit of a status game. If I stopped teaching the gifted program, everyone would be in a normal program. But then I wouldn’t be teaching the gifted program. And I’d get a status penalty. So I’m going to keep teaching the gifted program.

prompt: Why do we teach history to kids chronologically? It seems backwards to me, starting with the ancient world when they have zero context for anything. I'd love a short essay on whether there's a better order.
response:
There are three main ways to organize a school’s history curriculum: by geography, by time, or by theme.

By geography means you learn the history of one place, like Greece or England, and then move on to the next. By time means you start with the ancient world and work your way forward, like starting with the history of Egypt and moving on to Greece, then Rome, then the Middle Ages in Europe, and so on. And by theme means you do one unit on war and then one on economics and so on, using events from all over the world as examples.

The geography approach was most popular until the 1950s. Most kids learned the history of their own country first, then Europe and other developed countries, and then the rest of the world. This made sense at the time, since most countries were teaching their schoolkids to be citizens of their own country.

The time approach was invented in the 1950s by a group of people called “the 3Cs” – Carl Becker, Herbert Feis, and Charles Beard. These people were all American, and were very interested in trying to teach history in a way that made it relevant to America. They believed that America was the most important country in the world, so they wanted to start with that. They thought they could do this by teaching kids the history of the world from earliest times up to the present day, so they could learn about everything that happened before America became a country. But they realized that they couldn’t cover the whole world in enough time.

They decided that they could solve this problem by teaching kids about the history of the world, but focusing on Europe, because Europe was the most important place in the world. They thought that this would be a good way to teach kids how to think about the world and be citizens of the world.

This approach has become more and more popular. Most schools in America and most schools in Europe have moved towards this approach.

prompt: Why do we teach history to kids chronologically? It seems backwards to me, starting with the ancient world when they have zero context for anything. I'd love a short essay on whether there's a better order.
response:
I’m going to start with a very contrarian thesis: chronological history is the best way to present history to people.

When I was in school, the first history class I had was about ancient civilizations. I remember this as being really confusing. I couldn’t get a handle on how people lived in ancient times or what their world was like. I didn’t have much of an intuitive sense of what things were like in my own time and place, and trying to extrapolate that into ancient times only made things worse.

By the time I got to the American Revolution in seventh grade, I was a lot better. I could picture the period and the people and the ideas involved.

And of course the more recent the subject, the easier it was to understand. World War II was easy because I knew a lot about it from movies and from hearing my parents talk about it. It was really interesting how it all worked out when I saw it in a historical context.

So when I heard people talking about teaching history “backwards”, starting from the present and going back, I was really excited. This had to be a better way.

I was disappointed when I realized how bad it was.

The history class I took was basically structured as:

1. Modern times:

a. US history, especially recent history

b. World War II

c. World War I

d. Industrial Revolution

2. Early modern times:

a. American Revolution

b. French Revolution

c. Thirty Years War

d. Reformation

3. Ancient times:

a. Roman Empire

b. Greek City-States

c. Persians

d. Egyptians

e. Mesopotamians

I was in the middle of the class when I noticed something interesting. I was better at the recent material, but I was also better at the older material. There was a big valley in the middle.

I started thinking about why, and it’s kind of interesting.

Recent material is easy because it’s familiar. You’ve seen it in the media, you’ve heard about it, you have a lot of context and associations and can fill in the gaps. It’s easy to imagine and understand.

Ancient history is easy because it’s not like today. It’s easy to imagine what it’s like to be an ancient Egyptian. They had gods that we don’t, they had pharaohs, they had a completely different set of institutions. It’s easy to remember their institutions as different from ours. The more different they were, the more I could see them in a new light and learn from them.

Modern history, say the past century or two, is really hard because it’s not familiar *and* it’s not different. The world we live in is basically an outgrowth of the world of a hundred or two hundred years ago. You can’t imagine it like the ancient world because the world is so similar. But it’s not familiar enough to fill in the gaps. You get all of the drawbacks of ancient history with none of the benefits.

This is why it’s so much easier to learn history chronologically. When you’re starting out, you have no context to work from, but you don’t need it, because you don’t have to worry that you’ll confuse ancient history with modern times. You get a good feel for how different the ancient world was, and the next time around you have a good framework for understanding how the world changed over time.

By the time you get to the recent stuff, you’ve got a ton of context, and the only thing you need to fill in is what’s different about the recent world from the modern world. But that’s not so hard, because it’s not so different.

I think that’s why chronological history is so good. It gives you the right context for understanding each period.

I think it would be interesting to see what happens if you did a history class that started in the middle of modern history. If you could somehow give people the right context for the modern world, without the rest of history, you could start in the modern world, then go to the ancient world, and skip the most difficult part of history, the recent past.

prompt: Why do we teach history to kids chronologically? It seems backwards to me, starting with the ancient world when they have zero context for anything. I'd love a short essay on whether there's a better order.
response:
Kids are taught history, when they are taught history, in chronological order. First Egypt, then Greece, then Rome, then medieval Europe, then the Renaissance, then the Enlightenment, then the French Revolution, and so on. This makes sense to us adults, because the way we understand history is as a sequence of events, with the events of today being the direct result of events in the past. This way of thinking is called “historicism”.

I’m not sure the kids have the same thought process as we do. Kids don’t think of themselves as living in a long unbroken timeline with events before they were born being causal ancestors of their current situation. When they think about history, they’re thinking of the world as a series of stories. They want to know about things like “What was it like to be a kid in ancient Egypt?”

If kids learn history the way I remember learning it, they’ll get a lot of stories. But the story they’ll get about medieval Europe won’t be about the same Europe as the story they’ll get about ancient Greece, even though they may not realize that. They’ll probably learn that there were kings and queens in medieval times. They’ll probably learn that there were kings and queens in ancient Greece. They’ll probably not realize that they’re two totally different things.

I think kids have a much better idea of what’s going on when we think of history as a set of stories about places and times that are interesting to them. If we want them to learn about ancient Greece, we can tell them stories about ancient Greece. If we want them to learn about medieval Europe, we can tell them stories about medieval Europe. We don’t need to put it in chronological order, because they don’t need to.

I would think that kids would do better with a history class where we start with ancient Greece, and tell them a bunch of cool stories about the ancient Greeks, and get them interested in learning more. Then we’d go to medieval Europe, and tell them a bunch of cool stories about medieval Europe, and get them interested in learning more. Then we’d go to ancient Rome, and tell them a bunch of cool stories about ancient Rome, and get them interested in learning more. The kids will probably learn more, and have a better understanding, this way.

prompt: Write a personal essay about the moment a parent realizes their child has become someone they wouldn't have chosen as a friend, and loves them anyway.
response:
It’s an odd kind of sadness that has been with me for a few weeks, though it’s also kind of beautiful, so I can’t complain too much.

I was at the library with my son, who was in his usual spot looking at books that were a few years beyond his reading level. And I was standing at a bookshelf browsing. And I saw a book that looked interesting, and I pulled it off the shelf and read the blurb on the back cover. And then I saw that the author was someone I’d met online, and we’d had a brief conversation about writing and life and things. And I got a little excited, and started thinking that it would be really cool to get the book signed.

Then I looked up, and realized that my son was watching me and had seen who the author was. And he was smiling a little bit with a sort of smug grin.

And I just knew what he was thinking. He was thinking: “Oh my god, mom likes this woman?”

I know how hard it is to say something like this out loud, but I am really happy that I am friends with a lot of people I met online. I think about how I would have met some of them if I hadn’t been online. Would I have seen that woman who wrote that book? It’s not impossible, but it’s a long shot. Would I have made friends with the guy who teaches a course I love? It’s not impossible, but it’s a long shot. And if I hadn’t been online, I wouldn’t know that he exists. I wouldn’t know that the author of that book I liked exists.

And I don’t want to go on and on about how I met this author, or what we talked about. I don’t think I’d be allowed. But the point is, I know a lot of people online who are not just cool, but kind of amazing. People I love.

But then I realized that my son would never get it.

And that he would never make friends with this author or the teacher or the other people I’m friends with.

And I realized that when I’m in a conversation with someone I met online, my son would be thinking: “What the hell is mom talking about?”

And I thought: this is going to be so hard.

My son is in first grade. And he’s not really thinking too deeply about how he’s different from me, or how we have different friends.

I just realized that it will be a little hard to explain to my son that there are people out there who are amazing and interesting and funny, but he won’t ever be friends with them.

It’s not that I would be friends with them.

But I can’t explain why that doesn’t bother me.

I guess I can say this: it would be so easy to say, “But, I am going to have friends when I am older, and I will have all kinds of friends, and I will make friends with everyone I meet.” And I think this would be true, in general, but not in this case. I know some of the people I met online.

I think it’s going to be hard for my son to get it.

prompt: Write a personal essay about the moment a parent realizes their child has become someone they wouldn't have chosen as a friend, and loves them anyway.
response:
A month ago, my son turned 18. And it was the first time I had ever met someone who was not my son, that I would not have liked as a friend.

When he was small, I thought his friends were kind and fun, but not as smart or interesting as he was. When he was in high school, his friends were kind and fun, and about as smart and interesting as he was.

When he was in college, his friends were not kind and fun, and not as smart and interesting as he was. But they were my son’s friends, and he was my son, so I loved them.

Now he’s all grown up. He lives in a different country, with a wife I don’t know, and a life that is very different from my own. And his friends are not my friends.

And I know this is supposed to be a good thing. It’s supposed to mean that my son is making his own life, and finding his own people. And that his choices about where to live and what to do and who to be around are not going to be based on what will make his parents happy.

And that’s right, and it’s good, and I’m happy for him.

But I’m a little sad. I’m a little sad because my son and I don’t share anyone. He’s my son, and he loves me, and I love him, and that’s all that I have now.

I used to live in San Francisco. And I loved San Francisco. And it was where I had friends, and it was the place that I was part of.

And it’s hard to leave somewhere that’s where you live. But I have to leave it, because my son is in a different country, and I want to know his life, and I want to be near him when he needs me. So I have to move away from where I live.

I don’t want to be the person who tells you how much it’s going to hurt. I want to just tell you what it’s going to be like.

It’s going to hurt, in the way that leaving a relationship hurts. And it will hurt because you’re going to leave behind the people who love you, and you’re going to have to leave behind the city that you live in, and you’re going to have to learn to live somewhere else.

prompt: Write a personal essay about the moment a parent realizes their child has become someone they wouldn't have chosen as a friend, and loves them anyway.
response:
One of the things I love most about my son is how he can look you straight in the eyes, ask you a question, and then just stand there, waiting.

He’s not shy, but he has an innate sense of not being too much. Not talking too much, not wanting too much, not being too needy. If I say something like “Oh, can you give me your mom a call on Monday?”, he nods and then goes off to do whatever he was doing, never needing any more than that.

But when he asks me something, I know I’m expected to give him my full attention until I answer him. There’s no rushing him and no rushing the conversation.

This was part of why I was so pleased to have been able to have him over the day my parents were here. They’d come to the house early Monday morning to help me set up for my conference that started on Wednesday. I was a little nervous that I wouldn’t have a chance to see my son for two days, but then I found out his dad would bring him over.

My son and I were playing a video game and he was really into it. My parents were sitting in the corner, talking to each other. I could see that they were really enjoying watching us, but they were trying not to make it too obvious.

And then suddenly my son got up from the couch and walked over to them. “I’m going to go play with my grandparents now,” he said.

And I watched as my parents were so happy about it, and I realized they were happy in a way that I don’t often see them happy.

I was really proud of him, and I’m proud of him all the time, but that was a really big moment for me. It felt like a culmination of all the things I was proud of him for, but it was also an affirmation of something I’ve never been able to put into words.

I love my son in a way that I can’t explain. I love him more than I love myself, or my friends, or my partners. I love him in a way that I’m pretty sure I’ll never be able to explain to him.

And I feel like it’s because I know him so well. I know all of his strengths, and all of his weaknesses. I know that he can be really mean to people and really kind to people. I know he’s super sensitive, but also really good at getting what he wants. I know he loves to watch TV all day, and I know he wants to be a doctor.

When I think of all the things I love about people, I can think of a few. They’re funny, they’re nice, they’re kind, and they’re interested in interesting things. But when I think of all the things I love about my son, I can’t think of any.

And the thing is, if I really, really thought about it, I think I would know exactly what I would want a friend to be like. And it wouldn’t be anything like my son.

But I don’t have to think about it. I don’t have to decide how I feel about him. I just love him and that’s that.

prompt: Teacher shortages get blamed on pay, but nurses and police are underpaid too and their shortages look different. Write an essay that tries to pin down what is specifically wrong with teaching as a job right now.
response:
Teaching is widely regarded as a terrible career choice. The median high school teacher salary is just under \$55,000. The median nurse salary is \$68,000. The median police officer salary is \$66,000. It’s hard to say what exactly teachers are doing that’s so hard that the profession has to be so badly underpaid, but the government’s decision to pay them worse than nurses or police officers makes it easy to conclude that teachers are being exploited. And yet teachers have it worse than nurses and police officers. Teachers are in a state of crisis that doesn’t affect nurses and police officers. Teachers don’t have shortages, they have a collapse.

In 2019, 40% of school districts said they had difficulty finding teachers. In 2021, 81% did. 14% of schools in one Texas district were understaffed by more than 50%. The number of people going into teacher education programs is down 45% from its peak. The median teacher age has risen from 33 to 48. We’re talking about a full-blown collapse, not a shortage.

The US has a nursing shortage, but this looks like what you’d expect from an underpaid profession. Nurses are overworked; hospitals have no budget to hire more nurses than they need; there’s a lot of turnover, meaning hospitals have to keep hiring new nurses to replace the ones who left; the new nurses get bad reviews, and that gets passed on to them by existing nurses. But the nursing shortage is a manageable shortage. Nurse education programs are full. The median age of nurses has risen from 40 to 45, which means it’s taking nurses a little longer to retire, but not that the profession has collapsed.

The US has a police shortage, but this is a shortage that only appears in certain parts of certain cities where the crime rate is high. These shortages are often not as serious as they appear, because they’re due to a bunch of cops going on disability at the same time for one reason or another. The number of people in police academies has actually risen in the last five years.

Teachers are not a profession in shortage. They’re a profession that people can’t get into.

Why are teachers underpaid? The answer everyone gives is that the supply of potential teachers is so high that teachers have no bargaining power to ask for more money. There are always lots of people who want to teach, and they’re willing to take a big salary cut for the social prestige that comes with teaching children.

I think that’s wrong. There are lots of people who would be willing to take a 10% salary cut for a job that they find meaningful. But there aren’t lots of people who would be willing to take a 25% salary cut for a job that they find meaningful. And I think the 25% salary cut that teachers are being made to take is part of what’s causing the teacher collapse.

But I’m not going to try to solve the teacher salary problem. If we want to fix teacher salaries, we can do that by taxing teachers less or by increasing the tax on doctors, lawyers, and other wealthy professions. I don’t know enough about how taxes work to have an opinion about which of those is a better idea. Instead, I’m going to focus on the problems that exist even at current teacher salaries.

I’ve heard lots of people say that teachers are underpaid compared to other professions, and that’s what is causing the teacher collapse. I’m not going to argue with that claim. But I’m going to say that I think the teacher collapse is more serious than the teacher salary problem. If the teacher collapse were a result of the teacher salary problem, it would be possible to fix the teacher collapse by fixing teacher salaries. I’m going to say that I don’t think that’s true. I think even if we fixed teacher salaries, we would still have a teacher collapse.

To understand why I think this, it helps to understand what teachers do.

Teaching a class is a really weird job. There are parts that are fun. There are parts that are boring. There are parts that are hard. There are parts that are easy. And there are parts that are boring and easy, but you’re not allowed to do them, because it’s cheating. There are other parts that are fun and hard, but you’re not allowed to do those either, because it’s cheating. And there are parts that are fun and easy, but you’re not allowed to do those either, because the teacher is not supposed to be having fun.

The first part of teaching a class is giving a lecture. I’m going to pretend that I’m teaching a math class, so my lectures are probably about theorems. I can give a good lecture, but it doesn’t work the same way that it would if I were giving a talk at a conference. A talk at a conference is for the audience to learn from me. A classroom lecture is for the students to learn from me. When I give a conference talk, I get to talk about the most exciting parts of my field. When I give a classroom lecture, I have to start at the beginning and work my way up, because my students need to understand everything I’m talking about.

Teaching theorems is a lot of work. It’s like explaining things to a very slow friend. I have to be careful not to go too fast, and I have to make sure that everything I say is understandable. Sometimes I have to go really slowly. Sometimes I have to repeat things many times. And I have to do it for several hours every day. That’s tiring. But there are ways to make that work.

prompt: Teacher shortages get blamed on pay, but nurses and police are underpaid too and their shortages look different. Write an essay that tries to pin down what is specifically wrong with teaching as a job right now.
response:
I don’t know exactly what the problem is, but it’s not “teachers are underpaid”.

In 1990, teachers earned 98% of median wages. Today, they earn 77%. This is bad, but nurses, police officers, and social workers also earn about 77% of median wages.

There is some shortage of nurses, police officers, and social workers. But none of it is like the shortage of teachers. In most schools, teachers quit at such rates that school districts can’t even fill every position at the end of the year.

There is an important difference between teachers and police, nurses, and social workers. Nurses and police can do their jobs without a degree. Yes, most police have a degree, and some are even graduates of the police academy, but it’s not a requirement.

But you *can’t teach without a teaching credential*, and you *can’t get a teaching credential without going to a university*. This is true in the US, but I think it’s also true in most other countries, and even if it wasn’t, it’s an important part of the US problem.

The US Department of Education reports that 10,600 fewer people graduated from teaching colleges than in 2000. In 2000, 8% of college graduates got degrees in education. Today it’s only 4%. This is despite the fact that the US Department of Education says there will be a deficit of 300,000 teachers by 2026, and it’s even worse when you consider the fact that education has become a more specialized field with more opportunities for specialization.

So there are fewer teachers because fewer people are going into the field. But why? There are many reasons – teachers are underpaid, teachers are overworked, the work is too difficult, the work is not fulfilling, there’s not enough respect in society.

But I think the reason people aren’t entering the field is because they don’t think they are going to be able to do it.

Let’s think about why someone chooses a college major. They think about their interests, but they also think about whether they will be able to finish and succeed. If I wanted to be a neurosurgeon, but I know that I have low grades and am not that smart, then I might be interested in neurosurgery but still choose a different major.

The same applies to teachers. Maybe you want to be a teacher, but you know that you have low grades and a short attention span and you don’t want to spend two years in teacher’s college. Maybe you’re not sure if you’re going to pass the teacher’s credential exams.

So you don’t enter teacher’s college. Even if you want to be a teacher.

This means that the teachers that *do* enter the field are the ones who think they are going to be able to do it. They are smart, they have good grades, they want to be teachers. This means that the quality of teachers is higher. But this also means that these teachers have more choices.

Let’s think about this with a game theory perspective.

Let’s say we have a teacher who is smart, wants to be a teacher, and knows that they are going to pass the credential exams. But she has a lot of choices. She could be a high school teacher, or she could go to medical school, or she could become a lawyer. Or she could become an English professor.

The teacher has a choice of which job to take. But the school doesn’t. If she quits, the school might not be able to replace her.

This gives the teacher a lot of bargaining power. She can demand more money, more freedom, more respect, and more support. And the school has to comply.

This makes it harder and harder for teachers to keep doing their job. If a teacher makes a mistake, she might lose her job, but there’s no penalty for not doing the job well. Teachers can demand to be able to work in a place that doesn’t expect them to work, and no one will say anything because they can quit.

In other words, the school is in a prisoner’s dilemma with the teacher. If the school gives the teacher a lot of respect and support, but the teacher doesn’t do the job, the teacher wins and the school loses. If the school doesn’t give the teacher respect and support, and the teacher does the job, then the teacher loses and the school wins. But if the teacher quits, the school loses *no matter what*.

So the school gives the teacher more and more support, and the teacher gets better and better at getting it, and the teacher gets less and less motivated to do the job.

prompt: Teacher shortages get blamed on pay, but nurses and police are underpaid too and their shortages look different. Write an essay that tries to pin down what is specifically wrong with teaching as a job right now.
response:
There’s a new study from the New York Times looking at why there’s a national shortage of teachers. It blames low pay. I find this argument confusing, because there are a bunch of other jobs with similar pay and very different shortages. For example, teachers make about $40,000 a year. Nurses make about $40,000 a year. Both of them are in very high demand. But there’s no nurse shortage (I can get a nurse to give me shots at my favorite local hospital any time I want), while there is a teacher shortage (a lot of school districts are struggling to find people to fill their positions).

Police officers make about $40,000 a year. They are in very high demand. But there’s no police shortage (I can call the police any time I want, and if there are a lot of crimes in a neighborhood, they will send more cops to keep patrolling the area).

The nurses and police are in high-demand, well-compensated, socially-valued jobs that can be filled at the market rate. Teachers are in a high-demand, well-compensated, socially-valued job that can’t be filled at the market rate. What is different?

I think this is a really interesting puzzle. I’m not sure I can solve it, but here are my ideas.

A lot of the pay is tied into tenure. Teachers who leave their job lose that. This might mean that teachers, unlike nurses and police officers, will tend to be more conservative, and more likely to want to stay in the same district their whole lives. It seems like this might have some effect on the shortage, but it’s hard to say how.

The article claims that teachers are working longer hours and with greater stress than other comparable professions. But this seems a little bit hard to believe. Teachers get 12 weeks of vacation a year. Teachers get a four hour lunch break. Teachers have summers off. I don’t know how much of this is true, but it sounds pretty good to me.

The article talks a lot about how teachers are overworked. But in my experience, many of them are also very badly paid for the work they do. Teachers are constantly doing things like making complicated, time-consuming, and beautiful PowerPoint presentations, and they don’t get any credit for it.

It’s hard to imagine nurses having to do that, or police officers having to do that. But in school, it’s a constant demand.

I’ve heard that a lot of teachers in the past were in it for the pay. And a lot of teachers in the past were also in it for the summers off. I don’t think you can find that kind of teacher anymore.

I’ve heard that people who care about this issue think that teachers should be given the ability to earn more money by doing well. But this is a terrible idea. It’s like trying to make a job better by making it more stressful and high risk.

The way to make teaching a good job is to make it a good job. To make teaching a good job, make it more fun, make it less stressful, make it less work, and make it a place where people are appreciated for the work they’re doing.

I don’t think it’s a coincidence that most of the teachers I’ve liked the most were the ones who were most fun to work with.

There’s a lot of work that needs to be done in the field.

prompt: Is screen time actually the problem or is it just the thing we can measure? 3 kids, I'm exhausted by the guilt. Write something that takes the question seriously without reassuring me just to make me feel better.
response:
I don’t know. We don’t really know.

I mean, I’ve been a dad for over a decade. I’ve written about parenting in The Corner Office and The New York Times and other places. And I know I have no idea what I’m doing.

But what I do know, I know with the certainty of lived experience, is that I would rather spend time with my kids than just about anyone else in the world.

I also know that when my kids are on their iPads or watching TV or playing video games, I am *not* spending time with my kids.

Which brings us to our original question. Is screen time the problem?

There are two kinds of people who ask this question, and they are almost never talking about the same problem.

The first type of people are those who are so concerned about their kids being exposed to too much screen time that they have cut it out of their kids’ lives entirely. These people are so terrified of technology that they’ve basically raised their kids like it’s 1920.

The second type of people are parents who are worried about how much time their kids are spending on technology, but who also think that technology is a great thing. They just want to make sure their kids are using it responsibly.

The first group is probably right, in the sense that they are doing exactly what they should be doing: taking their kids’ safety very seriously. But they have also created an unlivable life for themselves.

The second group is wrong, but in a more interesting way. They want to spend more time with their kids, but not in the way that their kids might want to spend that time. They want to spend that time doing fun things that are good for the kids, not things that might be fun for the kids but not necessarily good for them.

I’m not sure which group you fall into. But I am sure that, when you think about what you want to do, it looks a lot like what a lot of other parents do.

The only problem is, we don’t really know what other parents do. We just have a lot of stories in our heads about other parents and how they do things.

We know that other parents are doing things that we think are bad. But we don’t know if they’re doing things that we think are good.

I’m not going to tell you what you should or should not be doing with your kids. I don’t know either.

But I will tell you what you should be doing about your kids’ screen time.

When you ask your kid to do something, you are telling them what you think they should be doing, and they will do it or not.

When you ask your kid to *try* to do something, you are telling them what you think they *might* be doing, and they will do it or not.

You don’t want to tell your kids that they should be doing something.

You want to tell them that they might be doing something.

This is an important distinction.

If you tell them what they *should* be doing, they will know you are wrong, because they know they are not doing it.

If you tell them what they *might* be doing, they will know you are right, because they know they are doing it.

prompt: Is screen time actually the problem or is it just the thing we can measure? 3 kids, I'm exhausted by the guilt. Write something that takes the question seriously without reassuring me just to make me feel better.
response:
I know a lot of parents who are exhausted by the “Is screen time bad?” question. They don’t want to be told that it’s okay or that it’s bad. They’re tired. They just want to be told what to do, what’s going to make their kids turn out okay.

The problem is that’s not what we know.

There have been several large studies that have looked at screen time and whether it predicts how well people do. The results of these studies are mixed.

The first was done by psychologists at the University of Pennsylvania in 2015. They found that spending lots of time on social media predicts that people will feel worse.

The second was done by the University of Oxford Internet Institute in 2017. They found that screen time does not predict how well kids do.

The third was done by the University of Toronto in 2018. They found that spending lots of time on screens predicts worse mental health outcomes in kids.

There’s also a big study by psychologists at Michigan State University from 2015 that shows that screen time doesn’t matter, but that’s a smaller study, and they didn’t have a lot of measures.

These studies are all big. So you’d expect that they’d agree with each other, right? But they don’t. And we can’t tell which one is right.

So we don’t know if screen time is bad for kids or not. And that’s frustrating, and it makes people think that the whole question is just “what is the scientific community making up to get funding?” It’s not, but we do genuinely have a problem here.

There are a few explanations for why the studies are so different. One is the possibility that some of the kids who spend the most time on screens are spending it in harmful ways, and some are spending it in healthy ways.

The second is that the research doesn’t capture the kind of media people are using.

In this study, they asked people to keep track of the different things they do. They found that playing video games and watching TV was associated with higher wellbeing, but that social media and internet use wasn’t associated with wellbeing.

I think the research on video games is probably a good guide. It shows that playing video games makes people feel better. So if the people who are spending more time on their phones are spending it on social media, and the ones who are spending less time are spending it on games, then we’d expect to see that the people who spend more time on their phones are doing worse. And in fact, we do.

The third is that the studies are looking at the wrong thing. In this study, they looked at whether screen time predicts how well people do in life. They found that screen time doesn’t predict how well people do in life. So maybe the studies that show that screen time is bad are just measuring the wrong thing?

prompt: Is screen time actually the problem or is it just the thing we can measure? 3 kids, I'm exhausted by the guilt. Write something that takes the question seriously without reassuring me just to make me feel better.
response:
I spent this weekend trying to answer the following question:

What is the effect of the average American kid spending 5 hours a day in front of a screen?

Is this a good or a bad thing?

I tried to answer this question seriously, the way you would try to answer a scientific question.

The answer was, sort of, neither.

That’s because, when I actually tried to answer the question, it turned out that there was no answer to give! There was no way to know.

This is a very frustrating place to be. I wanted to be able to answer this question. I have three kids. This question is not academic to me. I care about it a lot.

And when I thought about why I couldn’t find an answer, I realized that this is an unusually frustrating question, but it is a question that a lot of people really want to ask.

When I started my podcast, the topic I got the most questions about was screens. What should I do about screen time? How much is too much? Why do I feel so guilty about screen time?

The reason I felt so guilty about screen time is that the research is really hard to do, but it isn’t zero. There are lots of people who feel like they’re doing this research, but they’re really just doing something else.

This is a really common problem in science. And, it’s a problem that has been especially severe in psychology and in public health.

Here’s how it works. There are all sorts of things that we know are correlated with things that we don’t want. For example, smoking is correlated with lung cancer.

But there’s no way to prove that smoking causes lung cancer. This is because smoking is just one thing that smokers do, and so maybe it’s something else that smokers do that is causing lung cancer. Maybe it’s the cigarettes, or maybe it’s the coffee or the stress or the poverty.

To get around this problem, researchers try to do a lot of studies, and show that all of the studies agree. For example, you might study smokers, and show that they get lung cancer. Then you could also study a bunch of other people who are like smokers in different ways, and you could show that they also get lung cancer. Then you could try to rule out other possible explanations for your results, and you could try to show that it isn’t the coffee or the poverty. If all of these studies agree, then maybe you can conclude that it’s the smoking that’s causing lung cancer.

This strategy usually works, but sometimes it doesn’t, and that’s why I spent the weekend being frustrated about screens.

When I started this research, I thought that the results would be like this. But they weren’t like this.

There was a lot of evidence that screen time was bad for children. But this evidence was all over the place. Some studies would show that a little screen time was good for kids, other studies would show that a little screen time was bad for kids.

Sometimes screen time would make people smarter, sometimes it would make them dumber. Sometimes it would make kids more violent, other times it would make them less violent. It would make kids more obese, less obese.

I was really hoping that I could figure out what was going on. I was hoping that maybe a couple of these studies were wrong, and that I could rule them out. But they were all done in the same way.

I spent a lot of time trying to figure out how to make this work. But I couldn’t.

So instead of just concluding that the science is bad, I tried to figure out why the science was so bad. Why was it so much worse than other science?

And what I found out was that the scientists who did the science on screen time and its effects were doing it in a way that was very different from the way that they did other science. They did it in a way that made it very easy for them to get bad results.

It turns out that the way that you do science really matters, and if you do it in the wrong way, then you get bad results.

This is a problem that I want to talk about in a lot more detail. I think it’s really important, and I’m going to try to explain it as well as I can.

prompt: I'd love a reflective essay on the ethics of praising children. When does praise stop being encouragement and start being a form of management?
response:
There was a time when it would have been impossible to tell children the words “You are so good at this!”, and it wouldn’t have been possible to make them feel uncomfortable and indignant.

Now it is possible to do it.

I think it is because in a few years the idea will become so popular that it will be normal. And in another few years it won’t be possible to say such things to children anymore.

When I was a child, if a woman who didn’t know me would give me a candy and ask if I like it, and I would answer yes, she would say: “Oh, I’m so glad to hear this! It is so nice to see that you like it! It is a pleasure to know that you are happy!” And I would not feel uncomfortable, because everyone was doing this, and because no one would ask me if I like it.

It is so different now. When someone asks me if I like something (like a candy), it’s not a simple question, it’s a trap. If you answer “yes”, it is like you are saying that you are not a real human being, because there is nothing you like, you just obey. And you can’t say “yes” to anything, because then you are a slave.

If you say “yes” to anything now, it’s an insult to your dignity.

prompt: I'd love a reflective essay on the ethics of praising children. When does praise stop being encouragement and start being a form of management?
response:
A few years back, I was at a dinner party when one of the guests told me he had decided to stop praising his young daughter. “I realized I was using praise as a way to manage her, and I didn’t like the effect it was having on her.”

I’ve been thinking about this for years. What is praise? Why do we praise children? How does praise turn into manipulation? What’s the difference between praise and a reward?

I think we praise children for two reasons. First, to encourage them. Second, to control them.

I don’t mean that parents who praise their kids have nefarious motives. Most of the time, we are encouraging them. But sometimes we are controlling them. And sometimes we don’t even know which one it is.

It’s easy to tell the difference between a reward and a punishment. If my daughter says, “I’m going to make a drawing of the cat if you buy me a puppy,” that’s a reward. And if I say, “If you don’t clean up your toys, I won’t let you go to the park,” that’s a punishment.

Praise and criticism are a lot less clear-cut. Are you encouraging a child when you praise her, or controlling her? The same question applies to criticism.

For example, suppose I say to my daughter, “Wow, that’s a great drawing!”

Am I encouraging her, or manipulating her? I think I’m encouraging her.

On the other hand, suppose my daughter draws a picture of a cat and says, “Can I show this to Grandpa?” and I say, “Sure, but first you have to clean up your toys.” I’m manipulating her. I’m saying, “If you do what I want, I’ll give you what you want.”

Now let’s go back to praise. Suppose my daughter draws a picture of a cat and says, “Can I show this to Grandpa?” If I say, “Wow, that’s a great drawing!” I’m encouraging her. I’m not saying, “If you do what I want, I’ll give you what you want.”

But what if I say, “Wow, that’s a great drawing! Now let’s clean up your toys”? I’m manipulating her.

I think the same goes for criticism. Suppose my daughter draws a picture of a cat and says, “Can I show this to Grandpa?” If I say, “That’s a great drawing! Now let’s clean up your toys,” I’m manipulating her.

But what if I say, “You know, that drawing is a little messy. Maybe you could redo it”? I’m encouraging her. I’m not saying, “If you do what I want, I’ll give you what you want.”

What do I mean by “manipulating”? I mean controlling her, but in a sneaky way. I’m not telling her what to do. I’m not even threatening her. I’m manipulating her by saying something that makes her want to do what I want her to do.

I don’t think this is necessarily bad. Sometimes I manipulate my daughter. But I think it’s important to know when we’re doing it. And to make sure we’re not doing it so much that it becomes our default mode of communication.

I think praise and criticism can be good ways to encourage children. But they can also be good ways to control them. And I think the second is more likely than we realize.

prompt: I'd love a reflective essay on the ethics of praising children. When does praise stop being encouragement and start being a form of management?
response:
I think I was a pretty good student in elementary and junior high, if I’m going to judge by things that seem to be valued today like enthusiasm, engagement, and the desire to please the teacher. When I started high school, all the teachers seemed to be saying is that I should be more serious. I was still pretty enthusiastic and engaged, but they had somehow figured out that that was a bad thing, and I’m not sure how. I think I would’ve been pretty bad at getting along with most of their current students.

But I have to admit I think that my experience with praise and criticism as a kid was pretty much the ideal. I was mostly praised and encouraged and told that I was good at something. And I didn’t have parents who praised me so much that it stopped sounding like praise. I think it’s possible to overdo things like this, but I think most parents would be more likely to underdo it.

I think of praise as a way of helping a kid see that something they did was the right thing to do and they can keep doing it. I think of criticism as a way of helping a kid see that something they did wasn’t the right thing to do and they should try something else. I think of praise as more fun and criticism as less fun, but I don’t think there’s any reason not to use criticism as much as necessary. I’m sure there are some kids who have to be criticized more than others, but I would imagine that most kids would benefit more from praise than criticism.

And yet I’ve been reading a lot lately about how you shouldn’t praise kids. I don’t know if this is because people have discovered something new, or because there’s an old idea about praise that they want to get back to, or if they’re just saying what they’ve always said but now I’m finally listening. Either way it seems like an important idea.

So here are some things I’ve learned about why you shouldn’t praise kids:

- Praise can be used as a form of manipulation, which I don’t think is very nice of a parent to do.

- Praise can lead to children who are more interested in getting praised than in actually doing the thing.

- Praise can make kids think that they’re doing a thing only because they need to be praised to do it, and that if they’re not praised, they shouldn’t do it.

- Praise can make children less willing to try new things that they aren’t good at yet because they don’t want to do something they won’t get praised for.

- Praise can make children more interested in doing things because of praise than because of how interesting the things are.

- Praise can make people think that they are good at something because they are always praised for it, even if they aren’t.

- Praise can make people think that they are only good at something when they are praised for it, and if they aren’t praised, they aren’t good at it.

- Praise can make children think that they’re not good at something if they aren’t good enough to get praise, even if they’re actually good at the thing.

- Praise can make children think that they need to be praised for what they do, and if they aren’t, they’re not doing it right.

I don’t want to sound like I’m saying you never, ever, ever should praise your kids. I’m not sure how to get them to do anything without either praising or criticizing them. I’m sure there are a lot of ways to do it. I think of praise and criticism as things you use when your kids do something wrong or right. There are a lot of other ways to help your children, too.

Praise can be a really powerful tool. I think I got away with it because I was a little bit lucky and got good parents. I’m not sure how it would have worked for my friends who were not so lucky.

I think I’m probably going to be more careful about praising kids from now on.

prompt: Underrated: the school bus. Essay.
response:
A few weeks ago, in a small town in the Czech Republic, I got off a plane with a couple of hours to spare and headed out to look for something to eat. I was in the middle of the Czech countryside. The nearest decent restaurant was about a half-hour away. The nearest train station was about the same distance. I took a bus to the town, which was the same amount of time as either the restaurant or the train.

I got on the bus, and it drove for about ten minutes and stopped at a stop on the road where no one was waiting. A man got on, and he got on at a stop where no one was waiting. The bus kept driving until it reached a stop where no one was waiting, and then stopped. Two women got on. The bus kept driving until it reached a stop where no one was waiting, and stopped. Another man got on. The bus kept driving until it reached a stop where no one was waiting, and stopped. No one got on. It kept driving until it reached a stop where no one was waiting, and stopped. No one got on. It kept driving until it reached a stop where no one was waiting, and stopped. No one got on. It kept driving until it reached a stop where no one was waiting, and stopped. No one got on.

Finally, after about forty-five minutes, we made it to town, and I got off the bus.

I think people often think that buses are slow, and they are slow, but I don’t think people realize how slow they are. On a bus, you can go nowhere in a hurry.

But that’s OK. Because sometimes, you don’t need to go anywhere in a hurry.

I know a guy, who lives in a small town, and he wants to go to a different small town to meet a friend. But there is no train between the two towns, and there is no bus between the two towns, and there is no direct flight between the two towns. But he can take the train from the first town to a big city, and then get off the train, and take a bus to a different big city, and then get off the bus, and then take a plane to a third big city, and get off the plane, and take a train to a fourth big city, and get off the train, and then take a bus from the fourth big city to the second small town.

But, there is a better option for him. He can take a bus from the first town to the second small town. That is what buses are for, and it’s what buses are really, really good at.

I know some people who want to go from their hometown to a big city to go to school, and then go home to their hometown for the winter break. They can get there by plane, but then they have to get to the airport, and they have to get to the airport at a certain time, and they can’t change their schedule, because the plane won’t change its schedule. And they have to go to the airport at 7 am, and their mom is not going to take them. So, they have to take a bus to the airport, and get on the bus at 6 am, and get to the bus stop by 5:55 am, because the bus will not wait if they are late.

But there is a better option for them. They can go home by bus.

Buses are not good at getting you to big cities quickly, or getting you to airports on time. Buses are good at getting you to small towns that aren’t on a train line, on a schedule that matches your own schedule.

I’m not trying to say that buses are good at everything. Buses can’t get you to a city like Beijing from a city like Chicago. If you want to do that, take a plane.

I don’t think people realize how much of the world is made up of small places, connected by small roads. I know a lot of people who want to travel to a place, but don’t think they can get there. But they can. They can get to a place that is on a highway, and then go to a smaller place that is on a smaller road.

And a lot of people who want to travel to small places don’t know that you can. But you can.

prompt: im a senior in high school and my teacher said we could pick any topic for our final essay as long as it argues something. i want to argue that group projects teach the wrong lessons about working with people. can you write a model essay i can look at to see how an argument like that should be built? around 1200 words
response:
There are many ways in which group work is valuable. It can simulate the dynamics of real organizations, teach us to manage conflict, and so on. But for all its virtues, it’s not the best tool for teaching the people skills that will actually matter to us as adults.

The most important people skill I learned in school was how to negotiate. In college and beyond I was able to get most things I wanted because I learned, as a kid, how to make a convincing case for why they were good ideas. It also helped to be prepared with counterarguments, and in some cases I had to make sure I didn’t come across as too pushy. And then at some point I discovered that it was more effective to just ask what people wanted, and try to figure out a solution that was win/win.

All of these are things you learn from playing with kids. That’s where I learned to negotiate, and the reason I was so effective at it was that I’d had a decade of practice.

It’s the same with all the other important people skills. Most people who are effective at it learned in childhood how to make others laugh. Most people who are effective leaders learned by playing with kids how to get others to do what they wanted.

It’s not an accident that most people learn these things from playing with kids. Kids naturally gravitate to games that teach them these skills.

But the one that teaches you how to cooperate with others, which is the one I want to talk about, is also the one that’s least likely to come up in games kids play. Most of the time kids don’t cooperate. If they have to, they’re usually just trying to avoid the teacher’s wrath.

So what do we learn from the group work that teachers make us do?

First, we learn that we have to deal with jerks. This is certainly an accurate lesson about life. But it’s not necessarily a useful one. The right response when a jerk is working on a group project is to tell a teacher. The right response when a jerk is working on a project in the real world is not to be in a position to have to work with them.

Second, we learn that we have to deal with people who don’t care. We usually don’t have this problem in childhood. The only time it comes up is when we’re made to do group work by someone else. So we learn that it’s something we have to put up with, and that it happens when we’re forced to work with others.

The problem is that that’s not at all what happens in real life. People with good ideas attract people who care.

Third, we learn that we have to deal with free riders. Again, this is something that happens a lot in group work. But again, that’s not at all what happens in real life. Free riders are a problem in group work because we’re made to work together. In real life you choose your coworkers.

The best coworkers I’ve had weren’t my friends. They were usually people I hadn’t even met, and who had a reputation for doing good work, and who had an idea I wanted to work on.

I’ve been a free rider myself. When I was a freshman in college, I was a free rider in 1 out of every 3 or 4 groups I worked in. I did it on purpose. I was not trying to be a good citizen.

But I think most free riders are trying to be good citizens. I was too. I just had a different idea of what that meant. I believed it was more important to be productive than to work well with others. I don’t know if that was true then, or if I was just rationalizing not having to share my ideas. But it’s a good thing to be rationalizing, because it means you’re trying to be productive.

I would have been more productive if I’d had the chance to work on my own, but that wasn’t an option. I had a choice between being a free rider and being mediocre, and being a free rider seemed the lesser evil.

Nowadays I would not choose between those two options. I would just find better coworkers, or start a project on my own. But as a freshman in college, that wasn’t something I thought about. I hadn’t learned it yet.

So what should we learn about cooperating with others when we’re kids?

One thing we should learn is how to get people to work with us. It’s a great feeling, being the kind of person people want to work with. But I don’t think there’s a way to make people practice that.

The way I learned to get people to work with me was by doing interesting work. I’d hear about some kid who’d started a website, and I’d think, I want to be the person who runs that website. Then I’d start one, and get others to work on it.

The other thing we should learn about working with others is how to get people to do what you want. I learned that as a kid too. But that’s a skill we have to practice, and we only practice it when we’re forced to work with others.

In the real world you learn by trial and error. But I think we could teach it to people. It’s not as complicated as it seems. You don’t have to be pushy or rude to get people to do things.

The most common mistake kids make is trying to push other people around. It’s the most obvious way to do it, and it’s not too hard. But it’s also the least effective. It’s better to make people want to do what you want. And the easiest way to do that is to give them a reason to.

But there’s a more subtle form of manipulation that’s more effective than pushing people around, but is also not good. The trick is to make people think they want to do what you want. But then they’ll often get angry and refuse to do it. It’s better to just tell people what you want, and to explain why it’s a good idea.

And then at some point you realize that there are ways to do something that are better for you and the other person. But by then you’ve already been able to get the other person to do things you wanted.

And at that point, you realize you don’t have to be good at pushing people around. In fact you don’t want to be. You just want to have good ideas. And if you have good ideas, people will want to work with you.

That’s the lesson you really learn about working with others. That you don’t have to push people. You just need to have good ideas.

And that’s an incredibly valuable lesson, because it means you can just focus on the work.

prompt: im a senior in high school and my teacher said we could pick any topic for our final essay as long as it argues something. i want to argue that group projects teach the wrong lessons about working with people. can you write a model essay i can look at to see how an argument like that should be built? around 1200 words
response:
Group Projects Teach You the Wrong Lessons About Working With Other People

Group projects are a staple of American education. Students spend countless hours working together on projects and assignments in order to learn the essential skill of cooperating with others. Unfortunately, group projects teach students the wrong lessons about working with other people.

In a group project, there are always a few people who put in the work and a few people who just show up and take a free ride. The people who are actually doing the work get frustrated with the people who aren’t doing anything. So the people who are doing the work do the work faster and better, while the people who aren’t doing any work take the credit for the other people’s work.

This may seem like a bad thing, but it’s how it works in the real world. Some people get ahead by working hard, while others try to take the credit for the other people’s work. If group projects taught students that the way to succeed is to work with other people, students would be confused and disappointed when they realized that’s not how the world works.

Students have no idea how to work with other people. They don’t know how to communicate with other people, or how to make sure that they’re all on the same page. They also don’t know how to deal with problems when they arise. And they don’t know how to work together to produce high quality results.

So the only way to get something done on time and to a high standard is to ignore the other people in your group and just do the work yourself.

The people who are good at doing work are usually not the people who are good at taking credit for other people’s work. So the people who are good at doing the work will just have to do the work themselves.

The people who take credit for other people’s work will never do any work of their own. They’ll just sit there and wait for other people to do the work, then take the credit for it.

It may even make it harder.

If you’re skeptical that the group project teaches how to work with people at all, think of the things you learned from your group projects. You learned how to deal with people who don’t do their share of the work. You learned how to deal with people whose work is inadequate. You learned how to deal with people who don’t show up when they’re supposed to. You learned how to deal with people who don’t care about the quality of the work.

These are certainly lessons. But they’re negative lessons. They’re lessons about how to deal with people you don’t like, not how to work with people you do. And I don’t think the group project teaches these negative lessons all that well either. I think it teaches students to hate people who don’t care about the quality of their work. I think that’s a bad lesson, too.

I have a friend who has a job where she sometimes has to work with people who don’t care about the quality of their work. She says it’s one of the worst parts of her job. It can be very demoralizing to work with people who don’t care about the quality of what they do. It can even make you feel like you’re being dragged down, as if the quality of your own work was lowered by proximity to theirs.

I used to feel this way too, until I realized it was a mistake. I started to see the people who didn’t care about the quality of their work as people to whom I could help. If I could make them care a little, then their work would be better and the project would be better. This turned out to be easier than it sounded. Most people would be happy to improve the quality of their work if you’d just tell them how.

It was only a year or so ago that I learned to see people who don’t care about quality as people to help, not people to hate. But if my experience is typical, I had already learned to hate them long before that, in the group projects of high school and college. And I don’t think that lesson was all that valuable. If anything, it was harmful, because it made it hard for me to see them as people I could help.

When I was in college, I once spent an entire year working on a group project. We were 4 people, and we spent every day together for that year, talking and working and arguing. I remember it pretty well because it was the hardest year of my life.

The group projects I remember in high school were just small exercises. We would be assigned a group of 4 or 5 and then we would make a poster about something. It was too short to get to know the other people, and too small to learn anything about working with them. I don’t think I learned anything from those group projects.

The group project in college was a real project. It was too bad I didn’t realize what a good thing it was at the time.

2. Make it an opportunity to work with people you like.

I’ve learned to work with people in a better way than the group project taught me: with friends. Working with friends is not a new idea. It’s the reason we have offices in the first place.

The group project is not a good way to learn to work with people because it’s a way to be forced to work with people you don’t know and don’t like. It’s the worst possible way to learn to work with people.
