prompt: Why did so many medieval people go on pilgrimage when it was dangerous, expensive and took years? Write it as an essay. I feel like 'religion' is too easy an answer.
response:
The most basic reason was to fulfill the terms of an oath or vow. People who swore to make a pilgrimage were expected to go, and often were compelled to do so, either through social pressure or even the threat of imprisonment.

Medieval people made vows, and had their vows enforced, because they had no access to the modern legal system. They needed a way to ensure people kept their promises, and swearing to God was the closest available substitute for a court system. (I should note that the modern system is itself just another form of vow-taking. For example, when you take a job you promise to work and not steal and not murder your boss. When you buy something you promise to pay for it. And so on. But you do not have to make this promise to God, and the enforcement mechanism is not divine intervention or social pressure but instead the power of the state. So it’s different.)

This was especially common in a world where people were much more prone to take oaths. People had the same basic moral impulses we have, including wanting to keep promises; but they had fewer ways to keep promises other than promising to God. For example, in the modern world I can pay you money to ensure that you’re going to do what you said you were going to do. Or I can hire a lawyer who will go after you in court if you don’t. But in the medieval world, neither of these would necessarily have been available. The best I could do was say “Do this thing, and if you don’t, I will curse you”. If the other person was sufficiently religious, this might work. But if they were not, there wasn’t much else I could do.

For this reason, oaths, promises, and vows were taken very seriously. If you had made a vow, and failed to keep it, you were committing a serious sin. You might want to try to make it up to God in some way – for example, by making a pilgrimage to a holy place. This was not so different from the modern day, where if I break a promise to someone, I might try to compensate them in some way.

Another reason was simply to ask for divine favor. For example, a medieval peasant might make a pilgrimage to a church or monastery, and then ask for God’s blessing. God might grant it, or might not. But it was worth trying.

Similarly, people often asked for the blessing of saints. A person who was very pious, such as a monk, would become a saint after they died. People could then ask that saint for a blessing. For example, if someone was suffering from a disease, they could go to a monastery dedicated to a saint and ask for help. If the saint happened to be a healer, they might actually help. But if the saint had been a warrior, or a bishop, or someone else who was not famous for being a healer, then the answer would probably be no. But it was still worth trying, because it was a way to ask for God’s favor.

Finally, people sometimes went on pilgrimages as a way to make up for sins they had committed. It was considered a bad thing to go around committing sins, and people needed a way to make it up to God. One way was to make a pilgrimage to a holy place and ask for forgiveness. This was the opposite of the modern world, where we don’t go out of our way to do bad things. But medieval people did, and had no way of making it up to God other than to ask for forgiveness in some way, so they did.

prompt: Essay: the Library of Alexandria didn't burn the way you think.
response:
I had no idea that the Library of Alexandria was destroyed in a single catastrophic event. I learned this at a dinner party where a man described how “Caesar’s soldiers burned the entire Library of Alexandria during the Roman conquest.”

This is not what happened. The Library of Alexandria was gradually diminished over a period of many centuries, with only the last few years being definitively tied to specific events.

The Library of Alexandria was founded around 295 BC when Alexander the Great conquered Egypt. A group of scholars who accompanied Alexander founded the museum in Alexandria in his honor. Ptolemy I, Alexander’s general and successor in Egypt, wanted the library to be the most prestigious collection of knowledge in the world. It started with the books that were in Alexandria at that time, but the Ptolemies went much farther. All ships entering Alexandria’s port were required to stop and allow inspectors to board and copy their books. In return, the owners got the copies while the Ptolemies kept the originals.

This was a massive undertaking. The library contained between 40,000 and 400,000 scrolls by 30 BC, according to different sources. If you assume 1,000 words per scroll, that’s 40,000,000 to 400,000,000 words, which is 80,000 to 800,000 books.

The Library of Alexandria survived Ptolemy and the rest of his dynasty, but suffered from lack of funding during the Ptolemaic civil war around 80 BC. It survived Julius Caesar, who burned part of Alexandria and the harbor around 47 BC. Julius Caesar’s men, not Caesar himself, are usually given the blame for setting fire to the books in the harbor, but there is no good source confirming this story. It’s possible the fire did not spread to the Library.

The Library of Alexandria was damaged when Octavian, Augustus, and Cleopatra VII fled Alexandria in 31 BC. The Library’s scrolls were scattered as the city was sacked.

The Library of Alexandria was diminished over time as the Ptolemies’ power decreased and the Library of Alexandria was no longer the center of learning in the ancient world. In AD 391, Christians who wanted to destroy the pagan temple of Serapis in Alexandria also destroyed the Brucheion, which was the last branch of the Library of Alexandria.

Some scholars have also blamed Caligula for burning the Library of Alexandria, but most of the primary sources contradict this claim.

prompt: Essay: the Library of Alexandria didn't burn the way you think.
response:
Most people believe that the Library of Alexandria was destroyed when Julius Caesar’s troops accidentally set fire to the city. It was a devastating loss, but nothing like what it’s often presented as. It’s said to have had all the knowledge in the world, and that it was a huge repository of ancient wisdom lost forever.

But the Library was probably destroyed over a long period of time. And it never had all the knowledge in the world in it.

The Library was first built in 283 BC by Ptolemy I Soter. Ptolemy I Soter wanted to bring all the wisdom of Greece into one place, and the Library was a way to do that. The library was a physical location where people would store books, but it was also a kind of brand: Alexandria was known as the intellectual centre of the world.

Ptolemy II Philadelphus, son of Ptolemy I Soter, was the most ambitious of the rulers of the Library. He wanted to collect every book that was ever written, and he ordered that every book that entered Alexandria was to be copied and the copy sent to the Library. He also had agents going around the world looking for books.

This is a fantastic idea! You have a copy of every book ever written, and your capital city is known as the intellectual centre of the world.

The problem is that most books in Alexandria were Greek books. Most of the other cultures around the world didn’t have much in the way of literature to be copied into the Library.

It was also not a place where people went to read books. It was a place where books were stored, and people would request a book from the librarians and they would bring it to them.

The Library of Alexandria had a reputation that was way beyond what it could deliver.

prompt: My grandmother was one of the women who worked at the Bletchley Park codebreaking operation and she never told any of us until she was 86. Write a personal essay about what it does to a family when a person keeps a secret like that for 60 years out of duty, and what it means that she finally decided to tell.
response:
I was in my 30s when I learned a remarkable fact about my grandmother. It was not that she had done remarkable things in her life. It was that she had never told us.

The story was something I would have known long ago if she had told it, but I learned it for the first time in 2016, from a man I'd never met, who contacted me on LinkedIn. He'd seen on the web that my mother was named "Wendy Milner." He knew of a "Wendy Milner" who had done something remarkable, and so he wanted to reach out to her.

He explained who she was. She had been one of the codebreakers at Bletchley Park during World War 2. She had not talked about this in public. The book The Women of Bletchley Park is dedicated to her memory, but the author never knew her name. She died in 2010 at the age of 85, without ever telling me anything.

She was 86 when she finally told my uncle, my mother's younger brother. This was not a casual conversation. It was the culmination of a long process of coming out. He tells it like this:

In the autumn of 1996 my aunt called me and said that she had something to tell me. She had always kept things to herself and didn't like talking about her life. I was very surprised, as I thought she had nothing to tell me that I didn't already know. My uncle said that the information was extremely important and he would need to sign an NDA before I would tell him the information.

She sent me a document to sign, which I signed and returned. Then she called me again and told me, "You'll never believe what I did when I was young." My uncle asked what, and she said that she had worked at Bletchley Park during WWII.

My uncle asked "You must have known the amazing people who worked there." She said "Yes, I met Alan Turing and Hugh Alexander." My uncle asked "What was it like working there?" She answered "I'm not allowed to tell you that." He asked her again. "It is not allowed. I can't tell you anything more." She was very insistent and would not let me ask her any more questions.

My uncle was delighted by this story, but he was surprised that she had not mentioned it. He was also surprised by her reluctance to discuss the topic further. He thought she would have talked about it if she wanted to. She was the kind of person who would have wanted to talk about it for weeks, months, years even.

My uncle also said that he knew she had not told me about it, and that she had never talked about it in public.

Why would she never talk about such an amazing thing? She would have been able to talk about it openly from the day she learned that the codebreaking effort was declassified in 1974, and could have talked about it with even more enthusiasm since the 2009 release of the Turing book. She didn't talk about it until she was 86, and then only a little.

The answer to this mystery is a little disturbing. She was not the sort of person to enjoy the feeling of having a secret. She told me things about her childhood that I think she was embarrassed about. She was not the kind of person to hide things out of pride.

No, she never talked about Bletchley Park out of a sense of duty. It was not allowed to talk about it. She was under an obligation to keep it secret, and she kept it secret, out of a sense of duty, for over 60 years.

I think she felt a little uncomfortable about it when she finally told her family. It was a secret and she'd been told not to talk about it, but she was 86 and her life was ending, and she wanted her family to know about the things she had done. But still, this was not how she felt about it until the very end.

My father was born in 1937. He would have been 6 when she left Bletchley Park. So he might have been able to ask her about it, had she told him when he was younger. And he might have been able to tell us in turn. But that never happened.

I don't know what it means that she didn't tell us until she was 86. It is a very important thing, and it was not a secret any more. But maybe she was waiting for an official OK before she talked about it. Or maybe she thought that if she told anyone, the secret would spread, and she did not want to spread it.

The fact that she never told us this, and never told anyone, and never talked about it, is a mystery that I am still trying to understand.

prompt: My grandmother was one of the women who worked at the Bletchley Park codebreaking operation and she never told any of us until she was 86. Write a personal essay about what it does to a family when a person keeps a secret like that for 60 years out of duty, and what it means that she finally decided to tell.
response:
One of the things that surprised me the most when I first read about Bletchley Park in 2010 was how much of the story was about the women.

I think this is partly because of a tendency in historical accounts of World War II to leave women out of the story if they don’t seem to have done something very impressive.

For example, the women who ran the Enigma machine at Bletchley Park were very important, but not as cool as the people who built the Bombe.

So the story tends to focus on the people who built the Bombe. And, as far as I know, all of them were men.

Another reason why we focus on the men is that it’s easier to do so.

If we look at the people who ran the Enigma machine, it becomes much harder to tell a coherent story.

These are just people. They didn’t invent anything, or come up with a brilliant idea that changed history. They just worked, and did a job they were very good at.

That’s why the men are more interesting. We want to hear about the people who made the breakthroughs, not the ones who did the work that made those breakthroughs possible.

And so it’s easy to forget that without the women at Bletchley Park, nobody would have been able to build the Bombe.

So why did the people who built the Bombe, and all of the people who worked on the Bombe, and all of the people who built the Colossus, and all the people who broke the Lorenz code, and all the people who did the cryptanalysis on the Bombe results, and so on, never tell anybody what they did?

It was because they weren’t allowed to.

The work they did at Bletchley Park was top secret. They couldn’t talk about what they did, or even say that they were there.

And the secrecy was not just for a few years. It was for the rest of their lives.

It wasn’t until the 1970s, after the men and women who worked at Bletchley Park got into their 50s and 60s, that they could start to talk about their jobs during the war.

But the secret was still very important, and the government was afraid that people would be able to work out what they had done and use that information to build a better Enigma machine or something.

So they told people to keep their secret. And they did.

I don’t know if the people who worked at Bletchley Park were very happy to keep their secret, or whether they just did it because they were told to. But they did.

I know about this because of my grandmother. She was one of the women who worked at Bletchley Park, and she never told any of us that she had been there.

I think she was about 23 when she left Bletchley Park, and she was 86 when she told me. So she was only able to tell me about 60 years after the fact.

And I think the reason she didn’t tell us earlier is because she was told to keep her secret. And she did.

I don’t know if she was happy about that, but she did it.

So I think it’s really important that we remember the people who worked at Bletchley Park. They didn’t just keep their secret for the rest of their lives, but they also gave up their chance to tell anyone what they did.

And the story of Bletchley Park is so much more interesting if we remember the women who were there.

prompt: My grandmother was one of the women who worked at the Bletchley Park codebreaking operation and she never told any of us until she was 86. Write a personal essay about what it does to a family when a person keeps a secret like that for 60 years out of duty, and what it means that she finally decided to tell.
response:
My grandmother was one of the women who worked at Bletchley Park during World War II, and she never told any of us until she was 86.

When she did tell, it was because the secret had become her burden, and it wasn’t just that she didn’t want to keep it anymore. It was that she felt that if she told it to my father, he would pass it on to me. She felt it was important that I know.

She didn’t have to tell anyone else. She could have told just me. She could have waited until my father was dead. But she didn’t do that. She felt it was important for him to know too, that his mother had done something important during World War II. And she didn’t want to be dead when he found out.

My father and his sisters didn’t know about it. They’d never asked her, because she didn’t seem the type, or at least that’s how she told it to me. She was the sort of woman who’d have been too shy to talk about such a thing.

There are two ways she could have handled it. One is that she could have told everyone her family when she came home after the war, because this is something you’d want to tell your family. And she could have said “I worked at Bletchley Park during World War II”. But she didn’t want to do that, because it was a secret.

Or she could have told no one and kept it to herself.

But she did something else, which was to keep it from everyone, and not even to think about it, for about 60 years.

The secret had never been mentioned in the family. It had become invisible. My father and my aunts didn’t know. No one knew. And then, when she told, it was like the secret had come back to life.

She wasn’t 86 when she decided to tell. She decided a year or two earlier. But she was 86 when she told, which is when it really happened.

It was an important moment, but no one could have known that, because she wasn’t making a big deal about it. She told my father and his sisters, who were very surprised, but they didn’t know how important it was.

And she told me when I was 26. I’d just started doing a project with her, and one day I was walking to her house. I was going to ask her to come to New York to help me on the project, which would take a lot of work. So I decided to say hi to her first. So I walked up to her front door and rang the bell.

And this is when she told me about Bletchley Park.

I didn’t know how important it was. I’d never heard of Bletchley Park. I thought it was a small operation. I was interested, but I didn’t know if I should be really interested. It was like this thing that could be a very big deal or it could be kind of nothing.

And she was so uninterested in telling it. She said “I worked at Bletchley Park”. And I said “really, what did you do there?”. And she said “I worked on the Enigma machine”. And I said “Oh that’s cool”. And she said “Well it’s not much of a secret anymore”.

She told it like it was the most boring thing she had ever said. And that’s how it was in her mind. She’d told herself she didn’t want to keep the secret anymore, but she didn’t know what the secret had become. She didn’t know how important it was. She didn’t know what she was doing.

She thought it was a secret, and she’d kept it for 60 years. And now it wasn’t a secret anymore.

It was like the secret had been locked in a box that no one could get into. And then, when she said she’d worked at Bletchley Park, the box opened and the secret came out. But no one could have known that it was so big.

prompt: Write an essay on why the Roman Republic's institutions, which had survived for nearly five centuries, collapsed within roughly one hundred years. Focus on the norms rather than the laws.
response:
The Roman Republic was one of the great political systems in human history. It was created in 509 BC and it survived, basically in the same form, until 133 BC. After that, it started to break down and was finished off by Julius Caesar in 44 BC. It lasted for nearly five centuries.

And then it collapsed within the space of a century.

Why did the Roman Republic collapse? And what can we learn from its collapse?

I’ve been thinking a lot about this recently, and I think I’ve come up with an explanation that’s pretty different from what I’d expect.

The Roman Republic was based on a few key ideas. It had an executive, a senate, and some popular assemblies. The senate was the center of political power. Senators were supposed to have the right to make their own decisions about policy – but they were expected to consult and compromise with each other.

The people who ran the state were supposed to be the “best and brightest” – the most skilled people.

This sounds like a lot like American politics (and it was a big inspiration for American politics) but it wasn’t really. It was a much, much looser system.

The Roman Republic had a lot of rules. But it didn’t have an effective judiciary. And so the rules were often ignored. It was more like the rules in a game that you play with friends and family – you can’t enforce them, but you’re supposed to try to follow them.

But a few people started to violate these rules a lot. One was a guy named Sulla.

Sulla was a guy who was really good at being a general. And he got his own army, and his army followed his orders. So he used the army to get himself elected. And then he made himself “dictator”.

Then there was a guy named Marius, who was a little bit like Sulla.

Then there was a guy named Caesar who was a lot like Sulla.

These guys were all very successful. They got what they wanted. And they had more power than anyone else. And they had all these people who wanted to be like them.

So a bunch of other people did what Sulla and Caesar did. And then they all fought each other. And then Caesar won and he set up a “monarchy” of sorts.

And that was the end of the Republic.

I’m oversimplifying here a lot. But that’s roughly what happened.

I think the collapse of the Roman Republic is a pretty good case study of how norms work.

Norms can be pretty strong, and you can do a lot of bad things and still be okay if you follow the right norms.

But they can also be surprisingly fragile. And sometimes the only thing standing between “normal” and “everyone breaks the rules” is one guy who breaks the rules once.

So if you want to keep your society from collapsing, make sure there’s no one who can get away with breaking the rules.

prompt: Write an essay on why the Roman Republic's institutions, which had survived for nearly five centuries, collapsed within roughly one hundred years. Focus on the norms rather than the laws.
response:
I am a big fan of the Roman Republic (see my article, Rome and the American Constitution), and this is one of the biggest questions in Roman history. Why did it fall so quickly?

A big part of the answer is that the Republic was a system of norms rather than laws, and those norms were fragile. The Constitution of Rome had been established over a long time, in response to specific crises, and had never been written down. For example, the Roman Republic had no written Constitution, and yet the Roman Senate was able to rule the entire world. The Senate was just a group of old guys who met in a particular room and made decisions. They had no real legal authority, but everyone just agreed to obey them.

Norms are more flexible and resilient than laws, because you don’t need a formal institution to change them. A norm can be changed by a single person acting in a certain way, as long as other people find that behavior persuasive.

A law is a norm that has been formalized. This makes a law easier to enforce, because you have institutions dedicated to enforcing laws. But laws are also much less flexible, since it takes a lot of work to change one.

Norms can be surprisingly resilient. In the early Roman Republic, you needed to be a noble to hold office, but the Plebeians overthrew the monarchy and didn’t have much money or prestige. Over a few decades, the Plebeians were able to establish a norm that they could hold office too. This was despite the fact that there was a law (the *Lex Ogulnia*) that said they couldn’t.

But norms can be surprisingly fragile too, because if a single person breaks a norm and gets away with it, it can become acceptable.

The Roman Republic was established around 500 BCE, but only began to fall apart around 130 BCE, which is when Gaius Gracchus proposed the first major land reform and tried to use force against his opponents in the Senate.

In this article, I’ll explain some of the main norms of the Republic, how they developed, and what made them collapse.

## Why Norms Were Needed

The Roman Republic needed norms to work because its Constitution was too small.

The Constitution of the Roman Republic was about as simple as the Constitution of the United States. The Senate and Assembly could make laws. The Senate was in charge of foreign policy, and had power over the courts. Magistrates were responsible for the execution of laws, and were given a year’s term in office. Each magistrate had a veto, and some (like the consul) had the authority to command armies.

The Roman Constitution was much more limited than the Constitution of the United States. It didn’t define civil rights, didn’t include a bill of rights, didn’t have a judicial branch, and didn’t have anything like the federalist structure of states.

The Roman Constitution was written over several hundred years, and so it was much more detailed than the original Roman Constitution. For example, the original Constitution didn’t have a Senate. The Senate was created in 509 BCE in response to a crisis. There wasn’t a good process for electing kings, so the Romans decided they would stop electing kings. The Senate would be composed of the most experienced people in Rome, and they would have the authority to make laws. They would have the power to veto the decisions of magistrates.

The Senate became very powerful, and the magistrates didn’t have much authority. This created a new crisis, where the Senate would use their veto to block laws that were obviously good ideas. So the Romans created a new branch of government: the people’s Assembly. The Assembly was created around 300 BCE and gave the Roman people a lot more power. They could pass laws, make declarations of war, and elect magistrates.

The power of the Roman Senate and Assembly was limited by a system of checks and balances. A magistrate’s veto could stop the Senate or Assembly from passing a law. But if there were two magistrates, like the consuls, each with veto power, then you’d need both to agree to stop the Senate from passing a law.

You can see that the Roman Constitution was a hodgepodge. It had a bunch of institutions with overlapping and unclear authority. This is typical of constitutions written in response to specific crises. But it meant that there were many open questions about how the Constitution worked, and that the Romans had to make up new rules to resolve those questions.

For example, the Constitution never specified how often the Senate would meet, or what sort of agenda they would have, or how many votes it would take to pass a law. Instead, the Senate just made up these rules as they went along. These rules weren’t laws, but they were still binding, because if you broke them the Senate could declare you an enemy of the state.

The Roman Senate had no legal authority to declare you an enemy of the state. It was just a group of powerful people who decided to do it. So this was a norm.

A big part of Rome’s power was that it had a lot of very smart people. They were able to solve the problems with the Constitution by establishing new norms, and the Romans were willing to accept those norms, because they thought they were just.

The norms of Rome were also very flexible. They weren’t very well-defined, so if you broke one, you might get away with it.

This is one reason Rome was so successful. The Roman Constitution was flexible and able to adapt to new situations. The people in charge of the Roman Republic were willing to make changes to their government when they needed to, and they had very few laws that prevented them from doing this.

But it’s also one of the reasons Rome’s government eventually broke down. Because the norms were so loose, it was easy to break them, and once someone started breaking the norms, it was hard to stop them.

## The Norms of the Republic

The Romans had a number of norms that they expected their leaders to follow. These norms were never written down, but everyone knew them, and if you broke them, you would be punished.

These norms were mostly enforced by the Senate and the people, rather than by any formal institution. This means that it was up to other Romans to decide whether you were breaking the norms, and whether they would punish you. If you broke a norm but people thought you had a good reason for doing it, they might not punish you.

Here are some of the main norms of the Republic.

### You should be just and humble

Roman leaders were expected to be humble and to care about the good of Rome. You were supposed to be fair and just, and not do things to benefit yourself at the expense of others.

Roman leaders were expected to have a sense of civic duty. They were expected to be willing to give up their wealth and comfort for the good of Rome. In fact, Roman leaders were expected to be poor. If you were wealthy and in charge of Rome, people would accuse you of being a corrupt aristocrat.

The Romans didn’t really believe in democracy. They were aristocrats, and they expected that the most successful and virtuous people would be in charge. The Roman government was an oligarchy: only the wealthiest people could hold office. But the Romans believed that they were a just oligarchy, because they thought that the best people in Rome were naturally virtuous and wealthy.

This was a norm, rather than a law, because the Romans didn’t have any formal institutions to enforce these norms. prompt: Write an essay on why the Roman Republic's institutions, which had survived for nearly five centuries, collapsed within roughly one hundred years. Focus on the norms rather than the laws.
response:
In 509 BC, the Romans overthrew their king, Tarquin the Proud, and founded a republic. For the next 500 years, they fought wars, expanded their power, and became the dominant power in the Mediterranean, while retaining a system of government that was, at least by the standards of the time, surprisingly democratic.

The Roman republic was based on three institutions. First, there were two consuls who served as heads of state. They were responsible for running the day-to-day administration of the government, but they didn’t have much real power. Their term lasted only one year, and the power of the consulship was shared with its fellow consul, so that neither could act without the other’s consent.

Second, there were the various popular assemblies, whose members were the Roman citizens. These included the Comitia Centuriata, a sort of upper house, whose members were selected in a way that heavily favored the wealthy, and the Comitia Tributa, a sort of lower house, which voted by geographic region. These assemblies were supposed to have the power to elect the consuls, approve laws, and declare war, but in practice they were controlled by the aristocracy.

Third, there was the Senate, a sort of advisory council of about 300 members. Senators had no formal powers, but they were all former magistrates and other prominent Romans, and it was customary for the consuls and assemblies to defer to their advice. Senators served for life.

These institutions, though imperfect, were effective enough to hold together for 500 years. But then, in 44 BC, Julius Caesar was assassinated. After that, Rome was torn apart by several civil wars, and, in 27 BC, Octavian defeated his rival Mark Antony and took control of the Roman government. He took the title of “Augustus,” and ruled as a dictator for the next 40 years. In the process, he transformed Rome from a republic into an empire.

The Roman republic didn’t collapse all at once. The civil war between Octavian and Antony was just the last in a long series of civil wars. Rome had also been under dictatorial rule for 20 years before Octavian came to power, when Julius Caesar ruled as dictator.

There were, in fact, two periods during which the Roman Republic was under dictatorial rule. The first began in 82 BC when Sulla, another general who had defeated his rival in a civil war, came to power. The second was when Caesar was killed in 44 BC. In between, there was a short period in which the republic reasserted itself.

How did the Roman Republic, which lasted for 500 years, collapse within a century?

I want to start by saying that the way people think of the Roman Republic is misleading. There were several important events, such as the rise of Julius Caesar, that caused major shifts in Roman politics. But the way that Rome was actually governed changed much more gradually, over the course of a century.

For example, we might think of the Roman Republic as being a democracy, at least for some definition of the term, that was replaced by Caesar’s autocratic rule. But that’s not the way it worked. Caesar’s rule was an extreme example of a trend that had been growing for the entire century.

The trend was a concentration of power in the Senate. In the early centuries of the republic, the Senate’s power was limited. It had no formal power at all, just the ability to advise and influence the consuls. The consuls were the real heads of state.

However, the Roman assemblies were very corrupt. They were rife with bribery, and their voting was not secret, so voters were subject to coercion. The result was that, while the assemblies nominally elected the consuls and other magistrates, it was actually the Senate that was in control. They would decide on the right candidates, and then they would use their influence over the assemblies to ensure that those candidates were elected.

The assemblies did not only have the power to elect the magistrates, but they also had the power to pass laws and declare war. The Senate would also influence the assemblies in those cases. So the Senate’s formal power to advise the consuls was, in practice, a lot more than that.

But, as the centuries went on, the Senate became more and more powerful. It gradually became less necessary for the Senate to use the assemblies to get what they wanted. By the time of Caesar, the Senate had become the dominant institution in Roman politics.

One reason for this was that Rome had become bigger and wealthier. The assemblies were designed to be used by the original 30,000 Roman citizens. But, in the centuries after the founding of the republic, Rome conquered several hundred thousand new citizens, who were added to the assemblies. This caused a lot of problems.

The assemblies were supposed to meet in the Forum, the central square in Rome. But there wasn’t enough room there to hold more than a few thousand people. So the assemblies had to be divided into multiple smaller groups that would vote on different days. This made the assemblies slow, cumbersome, and easy to rig. So they gradually lost their importance.

There were other factors at work, too. As Rome became richer, the assemblies became more corrupt. And the Senate also became more corrupt. Senators began to be selected not just by virtue of their office, but simply because they were rich. This made the Senate a more powerful and more entrenched institution, and it helped to marginalize the assemblies.

Another trend that worked against the assemblies was the rise of powerful military generals. In the Roman Republic, the army was not a standing army. It was assembled for each war and then sent home again. So it wasn’t possible to have a permanent military class. But, as the centuries went on, the wars became longer, so the army became more permanent, and the generals became more important.

The generals had no official place in Roman politics, because they weren’t supposed to be permanent. But the generals were able to use their influence over their soldiers to gain power. Soldiers would campaign to get their generals elected consul, or to win some other political office. Generals would use this influence to control Roman politics, and they would do this in alliance with members of the Senate.

The last part of this story is the rise of the “populares” (popularists). These were a faction of the Roman Senate that used the popular assemblies to win influence, and they tried to undermine the power of the Senate by passing laws to redistribute the wealth of Rome and grant citizenship to new Romans.

The populares were led by men like Julius Caesar. Caesar was actually a member of the patrician aristocracy. He was a member of the Senate. But, like other populares, he was an ally of the people. He tried to undermine the Senate by passing laws that were popular with the citizens.

The populares were not only opposed to the old aristocracy, they were also opposed to each other. Julius Caesar and the populares won a civil war against Pompey in 48 BC, after which Caesar ruled as dictator. But then, in 44 BC, Caesar was assassinated by members of the aristocracy who were opposed to him.

A lot of people think that Caesar was assassinated because he threatened to declare himself king. But I think this is a myth. Caesar had no interest in being king. He had no interest in undermining the Roman Republic. He had been a member of the aristocracy his whole life, and he wanted to preserve the traditional institutions of Rome.

The populares were just a faction within the aristocracy. Caesar was a member of the aristocracy, and he didn’t want to destroy Roman politics. He wanted to reform it, and he wanted to make the Roman state more democratic.

But the populares were very corrupt and they had very little control over themselves. They had been able to control the popular assemblies, because the popular assemblies were very corrupt and very easy to control. But this meant that they were able to get what they wanted without any constraints. So they ended up trying to do too much, and they ended up undermining their own power.

They didn’t just want to reform Roman politics, they wanted to take over Rome. This was a recipe for disaster.

When Caesar died, his faction lost its leader. The populares had already been too corrupt and too out of control before his death. Once he was gone, they had no hope of regaining power.

So the populares, who were the most powerful faction in the Roman Republic, lost their power, and the Roman Republic collapsed.

prompt: I've been on a kick reading about the 1918 flu and the weird thing is how little anyone seemed to remember it afterward? Like it killed more people than the war but there are barely any monuments, barely any novels about it, my great-grandparents lived through it and apparently never mentioned it. Can you write an essay about why some catastrophes get remembered and others just vanish from the collective memory?
response:
In 1918, the deadliest flu pandemic in recorded history struck the world. It killed tens of millions of people, possibly more than the First World War itself. But unlike the First World War, it doesn’t appear in very many novels, doesn’t feature in many movies, and doesn’t inspire many wars of memory.

It’s not just the flu, either. The 1890s and 1900s were a time of enormous social and economic upheaval in the United States, and many of the major political changes of the 20th century were decided in this era. And yet it is so little remembered that historians have a special word for it – the Gilded Age.

The Gilded Age is not a metaphor like The Age of Reason or The Age of Enlightenment. It means that the era is so badly forgotten that all we have left is the gold leaf on its monuments – just a thin, shiny layer of gold covering a mostly forgotten history.

But why? What determines whether some things become major historical landmarks, and others fade into obscurity? I’m going to talk about four factors:

I. A Good Story

The most important thing about an event is whether it makes a good story.

I don’t mean that the event has to be dramatic in any way, or that it has to be about interesting people, or even that it has to be true. I mean it has to be a story that people are interested in hearing.

If it is – think of things like the Battle of Agincourt or the French Revolution or the Civil Rights Movement – then it will be remembered.

If it isn’t – think of things like the 1890s Gilded Age or the 1918 flu – then it will be forgotten.

There is a famous anecdote about this. When World War II was just starting, there were a lot of people worried that it would be as big a disaster as World War I had been. In 1939, a group of British writers published a book called They Fought Alone. It was a compilation of stories about heroic actions taken in World War I – brave soldiers who stood against hopeless odds, or who kept fighting after their commanding officers had ordered a retreat.

The book was intended to remind people of how important it was to stand up to tyranny, and to tell people what was possible when they did.

It failed. They Fought Alone did not sell at all. There was no demand for it.

Why? Because people were not interested in stories about World War I. It had been a disaster, a bloodbath, a meaningless waste of time and energy. If World War II was like World War I, then we didn’t need to be told. We would remember on our own.

Instead, people wanted stories about how World War I had been a huge mistake – like the stories in John Keay’s book, The Great War, which sold very well at the time. And this was true even though it had been a century since any of them had been alive to witness it.

And so it is with all historical events. If they make a good story – if they teach us something, or give us inspiration, or entertain us – then they will be remembered.

If not, they will be forgotten.

II. A Good Lesson

But not all stories are interesting. A lot of things make stories that people don’t want to hear.

For example, it’s a bad story if you’re going to tell people they’re stupid.

This is true of any story that makes people feel bad about themselves. Stories that make people feel bad about their own past are usually bad stories, because people usually don’t want to hear them.

The reason is that there’s usually nothing people can do with them. If you tell people they’re stupid, they won’t do anything about it. If you tell people that their ancestors were bad, there’s nothing they can do about that. If you tell people that the way things are isn’t as good as it could be, there’s usually nothing they can do about that, either.

People like to be able to learn from history. They like to hear stories about how things happened in the past and what that means for how they should act now.

They don’t like to hear stories about how their ancestors were stupid and that there’s nothing they can do to prevent their descendants from making the same mistake.

And this is why so many historical lessons aren’t actually learned. They are stories that tell people they’re stupid. People don’t like stories that tell them they’re stupid. So they don’t learn them.

But when historical lessons are useful – when they can tell people something about how they should act now – people like them. And they remember them.

Consider the lessons we learned from the Cold War. The Cold War wasn’t a very interesting story. It involved mostly boring people making boring decisions that had mostly boring effects. But it gave us some very useful lessons about how to deal with nuclear weapons and how to handle international relations.

So it’s a very good example of a story that taught us something we could use in the future. And so it’s a story that we remember.

This is also true of stories about things that happened in the very recent past, where there are people alive who can learn from them. If there’s a story about something that happened to your family in the past, and there are still people in your family alive to hear it, they will remember it very well.

This is why stories about the Holocaust are still being told today. There are still people alive who remember it, and people are still interested in hearing the stories they have to tell. And because people are interested in hearing them, they will keep telling them, and they will keep being remembered.

But once everyone who experienced them is dead – and that’s true now – then people will probably lose interest in them.

prompt: I've been on a kick reading about the 1918 flu and the weird thing is how little anyone seemed to remember it afterward? response:
A century ago, the world was gripped by a deadly new disease. It spread through military camps and cities, bringing down millions of people in their prime.

In 1918, one-third of the world’s population was infected and at least 50 million people died.

You probably know the disease I’m talking about. It was, of course, the Spanish flu.

Or was it?

I remember hearing that story as a kid, but somehow I didn’t remember it as an adult. I think I’ve even heard this story from my parents. It seems to be a popular anecdote in a lot of the books I’ve read about the twentieth century.

But what about my parents? They were born and raised in 1940s Australia. They could have heard stories about the flu from their grandparents, who were adults when it happened. And my grandparents lived long enough to tell stories about it to their children.

So why don’t I remember it?

Why don’t I know any novels or plays about it? I know some novels and plays about World War I, World War II, the Black Plague, and the American Revolution. I’m not sure I know any novels or plays about the Spanish flu.

There are a couple of small buildings and plaques dedicated to it. But I can’t name any monuments bigger than a building dedicated to it. I can’t name any monuments to World War I or World War II in any country I’ve ever been to. But I’ve never seen a monument to the Spanish flu.

There are no holidays commemorating it. I can’t name any holidays commemorating World War I or World War II. But I’ve never heard of a holiday commemorating the Spanish flu.

I don’t know of any popular songs about it. I can name lots of popular songs about the American Civil War or the Vietnam War. But not the Spanish flu.

I don’t know of any jokes about it. I know lots of jokes about the Titanic, and I’ve heard of a few about World War I and World War II. But not the Spanish flu.

What’s going on?

We might be able to learn a lesson here about the difference between events that stay in the public consciousness and events that fade away.

The Spanish flu wasn’t even the biggest catastrophe of the 20th century. World War I killed about 17 million people and injured another 20 million or so. World War II killed over 50 million. The influenza outbreak killed fewer than those wars.

So why is it forgotten?

A couple of days ago, I had the chance to talk to one of the leading experts on the subject.

Michael Belfiore is a professor of history at the College of Charleston, who has published a book about the Spanish Flu. He’s also written a blog about the Spanish flu.

When I first asked him, he told me that he was surprised at how little the Spanish flu was known, even though it killed more people than World War I. But after a few more questions, he became more confident that the reason was that the Spanish flu wasn’t really a single event.

When World War I or World War II happened, the whole world focused on them. Every major newspaper reported them. Everyone in the world watched the war.

But the Spanish flu was a worldwide outbreak. It affected different countries at different times. It lasted for a couple of years. It was spread around by soldiers moving from place to place.

It wasn’t even the biggest outbreak that happened at the time. There was also a smaller flu outbreak that swept through Europe in 1915, killing millions of people.

The Spanish flu, as a single event, didn’t really exist in the public consciousness. Each country remembered its own outbreak, but that was it.

If you look in a newspaper, you might see a lot of news about the outbreak.

But if you talk to someone who lived through that era, they’ll only remember their own outbreak. The people who lived through that outbreak probably don’t have any particular memories of the outbreaks that happened in other countries.

And that’s probably why we don’t remember the Spanish flu very much now.

My grandparents lived through it, but it didn’t happen in Australia, so they didn’t remember it very well. My parents heard about it from me, but not from their parents. And now I don’t remember anything about it.

prompt: I've been on a kick reading about the 1918 flu and the weird thing is how little anyone seemed to remember it afterward? Like it killed more people than the war but there are barely any monuments, barely any novels about it, my great-grandparents lived through it and apparently never mentioned it. Can you write an essay about why some catastrophes get remembered and others just vanish from the collective memory?
response:
I think there’s an obvious explanation for this. We have a tendency to remember things which resemble things we already know how to categorize.

So the Second World War seems like a more obvious thing to remember than the First. They’re both wars in the same place, fighting the same countries, with the same generals. The only thing they don’t have in common is that the second one ends differently. So if you have a mental category of “big war in Europe involving Britain and France”, then it’s pretty easy to put both of them into it.

But if you’re trying to figure out how to describe the 1918 flu, there’s no category to put it in. So far as I know, there’s never been another pandemic before. So it’s not even like it resembles other pandemics, it’s just… a weird thing nobody else has done. So it’s pretty hard to categorize.

This is true to some extent in all domains. The 1970s recession is pretty hard to remember, because it was so different from other recessions. The first Gulf War is pretty hard to remember, because it was so different from other wars.

The second Gulf War, in contrast, is pretty easy to remember. It resembles other wars, it’s got all the usual components. You don’t need to learn a whole new way of thinking about wars to understand it, you can just use all the frameworks you already have.

I wonder if there’s a similar pattern in individual memory. Is it easier to remember things that you have a category for?

And can we do anything with this? If we want to remember something, should we try to connect it to something else we already have a category for? If we want to forget something, should we try to make it look like something we don’t have a category for?

prompt: what's the most underrated invention of the 1800s and why is it the refrigerator car? write an essay making the case
response:
The refrigerator car was an innovation that enabled Americans to eat meat all year.

It also helped to enable urbanization, because people who lived far from farms and cattle could eat the food they raised.

This is one of the most important innovations of the nineteenth century that people know nothing about.

The 1800s are a period that we think of as full of technological revolution. We remember the steam engine and the telephone, the lightbulb and the airplane.

But if you ask a historian or an economist, they’ll tell you that the greatest innovation of the nineteenth century was the railroad.

It’s not hard to see why.

The railroad enabled a huge growth in manufacturing and commerce. It enabled urbanization and growth of big cities, because it made transportation of goods fast, cheap, and reliable.

In the 1850s, the railroads were so popular that people were predicting that they would make canals obsolete. Canals were one of the greatest engineering feats of the eighteenth century and a huge boon to the American economy.

But the railroads were much faster, and the railroads took over.

By the early 1880s, the railroad boom was in full swing, and people were getting excited about the future of railroads.

Railroad companies like Pennsylvania Railroad, New York Central, and Chicago and North Western had become massive organizations, and they were able to hire the very best minds of the era to improve their operations.

These companies could afford to pay top salaries to the very best engineers, and the very best engineers were excited about the possibilities for innovation in the railroad space.

In 1878, a famous inventor named James Earle, who had invented many important technologies, including the telephone switchboard, the safety pin, and the first practical electric light bulb, went to work for the Pennsylvania Railroad as a consulting engineer.

Earle was a very creative person, and he was excited to work with one of the most forward-thinking companies of the time.

Soon, he came up with an idea for a refrigerator car.

Refrigerator cars were not new. The idea had been around for a long time.

People had known for a long time that meat could be preserved by freezing it. In the early days of meat preservation, people would simply freeze the meat and store it in a cold place.

As the railroad network grew, it became possible to ship meat from one place to another. But meat could spoil, so people needed a way to keep it cold in transit.

This led to the invention of the refrigerator car.

prompt: what's the most underrated invention of the 1800s and why is it the refrigerator car? write an essay making the case
response:

The sewing machine is an excellent invention: it made it much easier for people to sew things. But you could sort of argue that it didn't change the world so much as the automobile did. The refrigerator car is another story.

Before the refrigerator car, people would only eat meat from animals that had died near them, and they'd have to eat it quickly. If you lived in a town, you could have meat from the animals slaughtered in the nearby slaughterhouse. If you lived in the countryside, you could eat some meat from the animals that you killed yourself, but you'd have to eat it immediately.

This was a problem in a lot of ways. You couldn't eat fresh meat for a couple of weeks in the middle of the winter, because it wasn't warm enough outside for animals to live on the farm. You couldn't eat beef from the West Coast if you lived in the East. You couldn't easily feed the thousands of people who were working in the big cities, since the meat couldn't travel from the countryside to the city.

Then someone invented the refrigerator car. Suddenly, meat could travel long distances on trains and not spoil. The price of meat dropped a lot, which meant that people could buy more meat. The farmers in the West Coast could sell meat to the people in the East, and the people in the cities could buy fresh meat.

That sounds good, but the refrigerator car didn't just make people more able to buy meat. It also had a lot of effects that people didn't expect.

First, the meatpacking industry could make a lot of money selling meat all over the country. So the meatpackers became some of the richest people in America.

Second, when the meatpackers became rich, they started buying land out West. And when they got more land out West, they could make even more money. This led to a lot of land in the West being bought up by the big meatpacking corporations.

And that had an impact on the whole West.

The people who used to live on the land got pushed out, because the meatpackers had more money than them. The big meatpackers also bought cattle to put on the land, which helped them make more money.

But the cattle changed the environment a lot. Cattle eat grass, but they eat so much grass that they deplete the land. So the land out West, which used to be full of grass and trees, got covered in dirt.

And it was all because of the refrigerator car.

prompt: Blog post: things historians wish the public understood about how little we actually know about most of the past.
response:
I’ve mentioned before that my job as a historian is not to write the most interesting history. It’s to write the most *accurate* history. The most interesting history, for most people, is probably the one with the most characters and plot twists; the most accurate history is the one with the most characters and plot twists *for which we have evidence.*

The result is that the most accurate history of most things is much less interesting than the most interesting history of those same things. For example, the most interesting history of the Roman Empire would be a long, detailed biography of Nero. The most accurate history of the Roman Empire would be a long, detailed history of the Roman Empire in which Nero gets a few brief mentions. Nero’s life was interesting, but our sources are much better on, say, Augustus and Hadrian, and those are also interesting.

But the most accurate history of the Roman Empire is also not the most accurate history of most of history. In 2013, the Journal of Interdisciplinary History published a survey of all of the major history textbooks in the US, and found that 93.8% of the world’s history took place in a part of the world about which we know essentially nothing. We know about the history of China and Europe, and we know a little about the history of Egypt, Mesopotamia, and India. But for most of the world and most of history we have no idea what’s going on.

If we want to know how accurate our history is, we have to look at one of the fields we know a lot about, like Rome, and see how little information we have even in those fields.

Historians are very bad at knowing what they don’t know. Most of us are taught to be very careful about what we assert we do know, but we rarely get a chance to reflect on how much more we don’t know. For example, a famous recent piece of Roman history is the recent discovery of an ancient inscription recording that the famous emperor Marcus Aurelius, when he was a baby, ate 120 pounds of meat in a month. We have found a few other similar inscriptions, but we know that a large number of others must have existed. For example, there are a few other inscriptions recording how much Marcus ate when he was a child, but we know he had an entire childhood, so we know there must have been many more inscriptions recording the same thing that we’ve never found. We know that Marcus was born in 121, so if we were very lucky we could find inscriptions covering all of the years in his childhood, and if we got even luckier we could find a few inscriptions covering some of the months of his childhood. So we know that the inscription that says he ate 120 pounds of meat in the fourth month of his life must have been one of many dozens of similar inscriptions from his early years that are now lost.

If we want to understand how little historians know, we should think about the kinds of questions we would like to have answered.

The most obvious kind of questions are questions about the fate of famous people after we lose track of them. The best known example of this is Cleopatra. We know a lot about Cleopatra’s life, but we know essentially nothing about what her kingdom turned into after she died. We don’t know who her children ended up with or how their descendants turned out.

A less famous example of a historical dead-end is the story of the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius’s son Commodus, who killed his father and inherited the throne, but then was assassinated by a group of palace guards after only eight years of rule. They killed him and then tried to make it look like he’d been a bad emperor. But the people of Rome liked Commodus too much, and so they killed the assassins and made sure the assassins’ actions never happened. Historians today say it didn’t happen, but we know it did, and we know the assassins did a bad job of covering up the evidence. Commodus had a son and a daughter, who lived on. What happened to them?

Another kind of questions are questions about the fate of the descendants of people we know. For example, we know a lot about Charlemagne. But we know nothing about what happened to the descendants of his younger children. We know that his sons divided up his lands between them, but those lands were later taken away by the Vikings, and there are no records about the descendants of Charlemagne’s sons after that.

A third kind of question is questions about the fates of people who were only briefly famous. The most famous example of this is Jesus. We know that he died, but we know almost nothing else about him. We know nothing about what happened to his family after that. We know that he had a mother and four brothers and a sister, and we know that they were there when he died. But we know nothing about what happened to them after that.

A fourth kind of question is questions about the fate of people we know about who died young. For example, we know that the famous Roman poet Horace died at the age of 57. This is unusual for Roman poets, who typically died around the age of 40, but it’s still a fairly young age. He died in 8 CE. But what happened to his descendants? We don’t know.

A fifth kind of question is questions about the fates of people who were only briefly famous, and who were only briefly famous because they were in one of those situations where they were famous for a while and then disappeared. The most famous example of this is Jesus, but there are others. For example, we know that there was a Roman poet named Martial who was only briefly famous, and who was famous for a while and then disappeared. We know that he died in 104 CE. But we know nothing about what happened to his descendants after that.

prompt: Blog post: things historians wish the public understood about how little we actually know about most of the past.
response:
It’s often said that we know about 0.1% of the past and 99.9% of the present. That’s true in the sense that most people are aware of most other people’s lives, and there’s a huge amount of media coverage of the things that happen. But if we know a lot about the present, what about the recent past?

The recent past is not that well covered. I’ve written about this in terms of journalism, but this is also true for the academic disciplines that study history and culture. Here are a few examples.

There are very few academic studies of the world in 2005. The most detailed work I know of is a book called The World in 2005 by Paul Collier. It is based on data collection by the World Bank and the United Nations, so it describes the world in terms of economic growth, life expectancy, GDP, and so on. But the data isn’t collected for every country, so the book is full of statements like “we don’t have good data about these countries.” This is despite the fact that these countries existed just twenty years ago.

There is also the World Development Indicators, which collects a lot of statistics about every country every year since 1960. The data is a bit sparse for the early years and it doesn’t have everything you’d want, but it’s a lot. If you want to learn about the world in 2005, you can find a lot of information here. But the data is mostly about things like income and mortality, so if you want to know how people actually lived their lives, the WDI is useless to you.

There’s also an important paper by Robert Lucas called “The Industrial Revolution in Global Perspective” (1992). Lucas’s paper is about the industrial revolution and the rise of capitalism, but one of the most interesting parts of the paper is the way he talks about the 20th century:

The 20th century was a period of great growth in income. It was also a period of great growth in our knowledge of history and economics, so we can now understand the world of 1913. In fact, we can understand the world of 1970 just as well. But the same is not true of 2000. For a variety of reasons, we know almost nothing about the world of 2000, and the reasons are not just that data collection has not been completed and that we are still in the process of making the best use of available data. The reason is that the world of 2000 is a new kind of world in which there is much more interdependence among countries, in which information is much more important, and in which the importance of the market place of ideas is much greater than in the past. We can only begin to imagine how we will study the world of 2000 in the future, after we have developed the appropriate tools.

There are no historians studying the present. This doesn’t mean that we don’t know anything about it. It just means that there’s not a discipline of academia that studies it in the same way that we study the Roman Empire.

We have a lot of material from the 20th century. We have newspapers and photographs and books. We have radio and television and the internet. But there are a lot of different formats and different sources. It’s very difficult to search through everything. And it’s even more difficult to find the things that we need if we don’t know what we’re looking for.

So the 20th century is not well covered. There are many books about the 20th century, and they are very good. But they’re not written by historians. They’re written by journalists and writers and people who were there. They tell us about the events of the century, but they don’t tell us about the whole world.

We know a lot about the 20th century because we’re still living in it. But it’s not well covered.

prompt: Blog post: things historians wish the public understood about how little we actually know about most of the past.
response:
History is so full of gaps and uncertainty that it would be almost embarrassing to publish it in the style it’s normally published.

Imagine an historian’s article saying:

“Historians know that a Roman emperor called Trajan ruled Rome for fifteen years, from 98 to 117 AD, and that this was during the second century, and that this was the third century before the beginning of the common era. They also know that he did a lot of things, because emperors do things. They think that these things were probably not all good things and that he was probably not as good as they’d prefer. He probably died in 117 after ruling for fifteen years and was probably replaced by another emperor. Historians also know that the Roman Empire lasted a lot of centuries after that, until around the time of the seventh century.”

This is how the normal style of history would read if we added explicit error bars on every claim.

I like the style of history that’s been popular in the last few decades and I like the style of history that’s been popular in the last couple hundred years. But if we can only have one, I would prefer the style that admits uncertainty.

In most of history, we don’t know much about what happened. When we find a book in a library, we can read it word for word, but this is rare in the ancient world. Often we only have second-hand summaries, and sometimes third-hand. Even then, we have to worry about all sorts of biases. If I find a text written in praise of King John, it might be because it was written by his court poet, or because it was a copy of a text written by his court poet, or because it was a copy of a copy of that text, and maybe it’s been edited and censored a couple times, and maybe there was a second source that was critical of King John, but it got lost because the church burned all the copies.

And what about the people who lived their lives without writing any books? How do we know they existed? Often we can’t tell, except when a text mentions them. And if a text mentions them, it’s probably because something interesting happened to them, and we don’t know much about them at any other point.

Sometimes we can find archaeological evidence. But this isn’t very reliable. There are tons of biases. We know way more about the ancient world in Egypt, for example, because Egypt’s climate preserves things really well. In most places, most organic materials have rotted away, so it’s hard to know what they did. Also, we tend to dig only in places where we think something interesting might have been. And when we do dig, most things are hard to find. If a city has a thousand residents and we find a few thousand skeletons in the ruins, we can’t really tell if the city had a population of a thousand, a million, or ten million.

The situation is a little better when we’re closer to modern times. But we still have a lot of uncertainty. We have a lot of texts, but texts are very unreliable. We have a lot of archaeological evidence, but it’s still unreliable.

We tend to know more about the lives of the rich, because they wrote down what they did, or they owned things that archaeologists can find. We don’t know much about most of the lives of the poor. We know that they were born and that they died and that they were born in the same place they died. But we don’t know what they did in the intervening years. We know some things about what the rich did, but we don’t know most of the things they did.

History is full of uncertainty.

prompt: People love to say 'history is written by the victors.' Write an essay testing that claim against actual examples. I suspect it's mostly wrong, or at least badly incomplete.
response:
It has been suggested that the best way to learn anything is to look for counterexamples to things people tell you are true. Here’s a great example of this.

There’s a popular saying that “history is written by the victors”. It’s often used to explain why people say things about history that are obviously false. For example, why it’s not well known that Christopher Columbus’s landfall in America was not the first time Europeans came there.

The saying seems very convincing: after all, if you win a war and you want to be able to brag about it later, you can just make sure everyone knows how awesome you were. And if you lose, there’s not much you can do about it.

But it doesn’t seem to be true. The history of Rome is probably the best documented period of ancient history. But it’s not written by the Romans. It’s written by the people who conquered Rome. When the Goths overthrew the Western Roman Empire, they took a lot of Roman scholars with them.

This makes sense if you think about it. When you conquer a place, you want to learn from it, not destroy it. A common mistake of conquerors is to think that if they can take a place, it must be less sophisticated than they are. But usually that’s not the case. The Greeks were conquered by Rome, but they took their culture with them. The Romans were conquered by the Goths, but they took their culture with them. And the Goths were conquered by the Franks, and they took their culture with them. In each case the conquerors learned from the conquered. And that meant that it was the conquered who wrote the histories that survive to this day.

It seems that history is written by the conquerors, and what the conquerors want to learn from the conquered is their history.

In fact the history of Rome is so well documented because it was the first time the pattern of one civilization conquering another, and learning from it, started. It’s also the first time we have good documentation, because it was when the culture being transmitted finally included historians who wrote down what was happening.

response:
History is written by the victors. This is a cliché that’s repeated so often people believe it without thinking. But the more you examine it, the less sense it makes.

In the 1860s, the Confederacy was trying to secede from the Union. In the 1880s, the Union won, and the Confederacy lost. But the most well-known history books about the Civil War were written by Southerners: *A March in the Snow* by John Pendleton Kennedy, *Battles and Leaders of the Civil War* edited by Robert E. Lee’s son and *Mary Magruder*, *The Causes of the Civil War* by Clement Evans, and *The Story of Robert E. Lee and of Gettysburg Campaign* by Douglas Southall Freeman.

The Confederacy was crushed by the Union. But the Confederacy’s story of the Civil War won out in the books. And not just in the 1800s. In 1998, the Library of America published *The Story of Robert E. Lee and of Gettysburg Campaign*, the last of the books I listed. And in 2008, the Civil War book that won the Pulitzer Prize for history, *The Killer Angels* by Michael Shaara, was written from the Confederate point of view.

It’s true that the Civil War is sometimes called a “Civil War” rather than a “Confederate War of Secession.” But there were plenty of Northerners who called it the latter, and I don’t know whether either side would be happy to hear it called “the Civil War.”

The most famous historical text, Thucydides’ *History of the Peloponnesian War*, was written after the war ended with Athens’ defeat. Athens lost, but the city whose victory was being celebrated did not write the history book.

If anything, it looks like history gets written by the losers, not the victors. When you win, you’re busy running the empire and keeping it running, and you have no time to sit down and write books. When you lose, you have nothing else to do, so you sit down and write books. The victor gets busy building the empire, and the loser gets to explain what went wrong and why they deserved to win.

Of course, victors write history books about their own victories. But the most interesting history books are about defeats, and in most cases, the losers write the history books.
