prompt: I teach a survey course on early modern Europe. I want a short essay (~900 words) I can assign in week one that makes students feel how strange the 17th century actually was, so they stop reading it as 'people like us but in wigs.' Pick a handful of concrete things: how they experienced time, darkness, pain, distance. Avoid the Enlightenment-progress narrative.
response:
It is hard to imagine how different the world of our ancestors was from ours. It’s not merely that our ancestors had no automobiles, no electric lights, no refrigerators. These are obvious things, and once you’ve noticed that they didn’t have them, it’s hard to forget. But there are more subtle differences, which are so easy to forget that we sometimes forget them even in the middle of an argument about them.

For example, consider the question of time. To us, the idea that time is divided into minutes seems so self-evident, we almost can’t imagine it any other way. But our ancestors had no reason to divide time so finely. They didn’t have clocks; they didn’t have jobs with a nine-to-five schedule; and they didn’t have public transportation. Time was a vague thing, which they kept track of by the sun and the moon, the seasons, and a few landmarks in their daily routine.

A person born in 1600 would have been used to a world where everyone was illiterate. We’ve been living in a world where everyone is literate so long now, that it’s hard to imagine it any other way. But most of our ancestors couldn’t read. This isn’t just because we didn’t have schools then. It’s because we couldn’t see any reason to go to the trouble of educating the illiterate masses.

To us, the idea that it’s a bad thing for a child to have to work is so obvious, we forget that it’s not. The idea that children are precious and innocent is a product of the nineteenth century. Before that, it was common to send children to work in the factories. Children weren’t considered to be fragile things needing special care. If you sent a child to work in a factory, he was not much different from an adult worker.

For us, the idea that the world is round is so obvious, it’s hard to imagine it any other way. But our ancestors didn’t know the world was round. It wasn’t even the idea of educated people like Aristotle that the world was round. It was only the idea of educated people like Aristotle that the world was round.

We think of our ancestors as simple, ignorant, and unenlightened. But the world of our ancestors was not simple. It was complex and subtle, full of ideas we have forgotten.

We often imagine that the medieval world was a world of darkness, where people lived in caves. But it wasn’t. The people of medieval Europe lived in castles, churches, and houses. They had food, clothes, and furniture. They had tools and weapons. They had money and markets. They had armies and kings and emperors. They had music and art and literature. They had universities and libraries. They had science and philosophy. They had all sorts of things we take for granted.

prompt: I teach a survey course on early modern Europe. I want a short essay (~900 words) I can assign in week one that makes students feel how strange the 17th century actually was, so they stop reading it as 'people like us but in wigs.' Pick a handful of concrete things: how they experienced time, darkness, pain, distance. Avoid the Enlightenment-progress narrative.
response:
We are not very good at imagining the world before the nineteenth century. We read about the past in the present tense. A king is crowned, a peasant is punished, a courtier is flattered, and we experience it as if these events were taking place right now in our world. It is hard to imagine the experience of life in the past. When you try to imagine life in past centuries, the best you can do is to imagine people like us, living in a world like ours, but wearing clothes we have never seen before.

The experience of life in the seventeenth century was not like our own. This is an important point to remember when you read about events like the Thirty Years’ War or the Glorious Revolution. The people who experienced these events did not live in a world like ours.

Consider the experience of time in the seventeenth century. We can tell time pretty precisely, down to the second, because of the clocks that hang on the walls or that are built into our computers and phones. These clocks are powered by electricity and the battery that powers them is a storehouse of energy. The electricity comes from burning coal, oil, and gas. All of this energy was put into the ground by the sun. We use it because we can. We are able to tell time, precisely, because we can.

In the seventeenth century, time was experienced in a very different way. Clocks had been invented, but they were expensive and inaccurate. They needed to be wound, and if they weren’t, they stopped running. The only timepiece most people had was the sun, which rose and set in the same place every day, and which was very accurate.

The sun is very bright in the daytime, and at night the sky is very dark. This is not something we think about in the modern world, but it was an important part of life in the seventeenth century. You couldn’t do anything at night. The stars were very bright, and they provided a little light. You could also burn candles, or oil in a lamp, to make a little light, but this was expensive. You had to buy candles, and oil for your lamps, and this took money. The sun, on the other hand, was free. It’s very bright in the daytime, so you could do all sorts of things. You could see very well in the daytime, because of the sunlight, so you could read. You could walk down the street, because you could see where you were walking. At night, by candlelight, you could see very little.

In the seventeenth century, people didn’t have to be awake at night. They slept at night, and were awake during the day. They couldn’t work or travel at night, and they didn’t want to, so they slept.

When we are injured, we can take a painkiller, like ibuprofen. This was first invented in 1964, and is now a household name. You can’t imagine life without it, and it’s very cheap. There are two theories. One is that Jesus and his apostles decided they didn’t like Saturdays, which were a Jewish tradition. So they changed the Sabbath to Sunday. This is true in some Christian communities, where people go to church on Saturday. But in most Christian communities, people go to church on Sunday, so this theory is not correct.

The other theory is that Jesus and his apostles were not trying to change the Sabbath, they were simply saying that Jesus, the Messiah, was alive, and that was a really good thing. And that was true not just on Saturday, but all the time. And so the first Christians just celebrated every day, not just Saturday.

And so this is true of most Christians: they don’t have a Sabbath, or a holy day of rest. They just try to live a good life all the time. And so that’s why most of them go to church on Sunday. And that’s why it’s not a Jewish tradition, but a Christian tradition.

The first Christian communities lived in Roman cities, and in those cities, people worked six days a week. But in the Roman Empire, the day of rest was the eighth day of the week, which we now call Sunday.

prompt: Write an essay on the history of the weekend. Who actually won it, and how fragile is it?
response:
The weekend is a strange phenomenon. It’s a feature of the modern economy that most of us take for granted. But it didn’t exist for most of history. It was only established in the last century. And it’s not even universal: in much of the world, people don’t get weekends, or if they do, they’re shorter or different. So what’s the story of the weekend? How did it come about? How did we end up with weekends as long as we have? And how much does the weekend depend on particular decisions?

It’s hard to tell the story of the weekend because it depends on a lot of little decisions by a lot of different people in a lot of different places. Most of these decisions are so small that no one wrote them down or even thought about them consciously. So there is no official record and we can only guess.

Still, there are a few things that seem obvious.

Weekends didn’t exist until the Industrial Revolution

In traditional agriculture, there was a lot of downtime when people couldn’t do anything. Winter was a big downtime. Rain was a downtime. In addition to these longer stretches, there was a day each week when people stopped for a religious holiday.

The Industrial Revolution changed this. Machines could work continuously, regardless of rain or winter. As a result, factories often did run continuously. Some even operated twenty-four hours a day.

However, factories could only operate as long as workers were available. So the new factories needed a way to motivate workers. They couldn’t rely on religious holidays, because people would be reluctant to work on days they thought were holy. But they could rely on other holidays. So many of the earliest factories gave workers one day off per week on a weekday. This gave them an incentive to work the other days.

This was a major change. In traditional farming, there was no reason for people to have one day off per week – it was just an accident of religion. But the factories gave them a real reason to have one day off per week.

So it’s probably true that the Industrial Revolution invented the weekend.

Most workers in the US were already getting weekends by 1910

The US was an early adopter of the Industrial Revolution. So the US was an early adopter of the weekend. In 1899, 58% of US factory workers were getting a Saturday off. By 1910, 70% were.

The remaining 30% were working on Saturdays. But they were usually getting a half-day off, and by the 1920s they’d mostly switched to the full-day Saturday off.

Why Saturday?

The first weekends were on weekdays, not weekends. This was because there wasn’t yet any consensus on what days were weekends.

In most places, the first day of the week was Sunday. It’s always been a religious holiday. But some places used Monday as the first day of the week. So the last day of the week could be Sunday, Monday, or Saturday, depending on where you lived.

The Industrial Revolution was happening in a lot of different places. And different people in those different places chose different days as the weekend.

The US eventually decided to make Saturday the last day of the week. So the US weekend was Saturday.

But Britain made Sunday the last day of the week. So the British weekend was Sunday.

And France made Monday the last day of the week. So the French weekend was Monday.

The US, Britain, and France are all major economic powers. And all three of them had different weekends. So it wasn’t obvious how the rest of the world was going to get its weekend.

It’s not clear why the US and Britain chose their particular days. But we can tell that it was a very close race. The US and Britain almost chose different days. And the rest of the world was almost all going to choose a third day.

In fact, most countries chose Sunday as their weekend. France didn’t, but neither did Spain. And some countries, like Russia, didn’t even have weekends at the time.

But the US, Britain, and France were the biggest economic powers of the time. And all three of them chose their weekends based on their own traditions. The US and Britain chose based on Christian traditions. And France chose based on secular traditions. So all three of them chose different days.

And it was a very close race. In 1930, the US and Britain were still very different. The US had a Saturday weekend and Britain had a Sunday weekend. But France, which was a much smaller country, had a Monday weekend.

So it was a very close race, and the US and Britain ended up with different weekends. And this was a major event, because it meant that the US and Britain, the two biggest economic powers of the time, had different weekends.

The modern weekend, in which work stops on Friday evening and resumes on Monday morning, emerged from a series of accidents in the late 19th century. It is a recent phenomenon, and it may have only a limited future.

The earliest recorded weekend was observed by a textile mill in Manchester, England, in 1828, after its owners agreed to close on Saturdays for one hour, so that the workers could attend religious services. This was part of a movement to give workers a shorter Saturday and a full Sunday for worship. As the century went on, workers fought to close factories on Saturdays for longer periods, and then for the whole day. In 1900, the International Workingmen’s Association demanded a “weekly holiday, free from all labor, of one complete day and one complete night, as well as a free half-day on Saturday.” This was not a new idea — the Sabbath goes back thousands of years, but the fight for it continued.

In 1926, a newspaper owner in Gary, Indiana, closed his paper on Sundays and Saturday nights. Soon after, the Ford Motor Company, headquartered in Detroit, followed suit. They argued that the workers who spent their Saturdays buying cars on credit didn’t have enough time to spend them.

Other companies followed. Eventually, the weekend became a universal part of American life, though not everyone agreed. In 1938, the New York Times reported on a study finding that the Saturday half-day “seems to cause a marked depression of productivity for two or three days of the week.” Other industries argued that it was too inefficient to shut down so often. But the weekend spread, especially among factories and the stores they served.

The weekend is an accident. It’s not even the most efficient way to distribute rest throughout the week, as a study in 1938 found that people were less productive after a weekend than after shorter breaks. It was originally created to allow workers time to worship on Sundays, but in the intervening century it has become a secular institution.

This is a problem. The secularization of the weekend means that people have lost their sense of obligation to it, and the workweek is beginning to expand. In 2005, the average American worked 44 hours a week, compared to 40 hours in 1989. The weekend is disappearing.

prompt: The Dark Ages weren't dark, fine, everyone knows that now. But write the essay arguing the correction has gone too far and that something real was in fact lost after 500 AD.
response:
In the past 100 years, historians have moved away from calling the five centuries between the fall of Rome in 476 AD and the start of the European Renaissance in 1000 AD the “Dark Ages”. The term is a bit insulting to those who lived then, and is misleading in suggesting that the West was a dark and empty place in this period while the East (or China, or India) were all light and full of life. The modern term “Early Middle Ages” is much more accurate.

But I think this is one of those cases where we have gone too far. There was something lost in the centuries after Rome, even though it wasn’t the entire West that was lost.

1. The West

I’ve been reading this article by historian David McCandless. McCandless argues that we need a new word for “Europe”, because the current meaning of “Europe” is a mess. He wants to get rid of “Europe” entirely and replace it with the term “the West”.

In the past, “Europe” has been used to mean a lot of different things. For a few centuries, it meant just the Roman Empire, and later just the Byzantine Empire, and still later just France. It’s been an attempt to separate Christian Europe from Muslim North Africa. It’s meant “the West” in the sense of Catholic Europe, as opposed to Orthodox Byzantium. At one time it meant just the British Isles. And today, “Europe” usually means the EU, though sometimes it includes the Balkans, sometimes it doesn’t, and it’s hard to tell without asking a specific European.

McCandless wants to use the term “the West” to refer to the Western Roman Empire as opposed to the Eastern Roman Empire. This is similar to the way historians today talk about “the East” and “the West”.

2. The West was lost

The West was not entirely lost, but it was mostly lost. When we talk about the “Dark Ages” in the US or UK, we mean the whole world, not just Europe or the West, and this is wrong. When China lost the West in 476 AD, they didn’t lose Rome. They only lost the West.

But the West was a pretty good deal. The Roman Empire had invented the modern legal system, the Roman Republic had invented democracy, and the Greek city states had invented philosophy. The West had been the world center of culture and innovation for the previous 500 years.

China didn’t invent philosophy until the 5th century, and they didn’t invent democracy or the modern legal system until they encountered Europe. China had a lot of great ideas, but most of those came from India.

3. A few centuries of decline

After the fall of Rome in 476 AD, Europe declined for a few centuries. There were still empires, but they were less successful. The Roman Empire had conquered most of Europe and the Middle East. The Byzantine Empire, which was the successor state to the East Roman Empire, lost most of its territory. The Byzantine Empire was a great deal smaller than the Roman Empire.

When the West was lost, the European empires lost. When the West was lost, the legal system was lost. When the West was lost, the Roman Republic’s ideas about democracy were lost. When the West was lost, the Greek ideas about philosophy were lost.

4. But it was not a complete loss

Some things were not lost. The Byzantine Empire continued to exist. The Byzantine Empire was still powerful, and it had some great ideas. The Byzantine Empire was a Christian empire, and Christianity was still around.

The Byzantine Empire was not the same as the Roman Empire, but it was still an empire. The Byzantine Empire was not the same as the Roman Republic, but it was still a place where people had some ideas about democracy.

5. And it was not all that long

The West was not lost for very long. It was lost for 500 years, which is a long time, but it was not forever.

6. And we got it back

When the West was lost, we got it back. The Renaissance was when we got it back. The Renaissance was not just a cultural movement, it was a political movement. When the West was lost, the Renaissance was when we got it back.

7. And we did it all over again

When the West was lost, we did it all over again. The Renaissance was when we got it back, but we didn’t just get it back, we got it back in a new way.

prompt: The Dark Ages weren't dark, fine, everyone knows that now. But write the essay arguing the correction has gone too far and that something real was in fact lost after 500 AD.
response:
In the West, the collapse of Rome in the late 400s led to the period most historians call “the Dark Ages” (500-1000). It’s a bit of a loaded term, since it suggests a period of cultural and technological stagnation. Most people who know about it know that it wasn’t all that stagnant or backwards, and there was a lot of interesting stuff going on in other countries like the Abbasid Caliphate and China. It was also just a couple centuries. If we think of the Middle Ages as 1000 years, the Dark Ages were a third of it.

And yet, I think we *should* think of it as a period of decline. It wasn’t a decline of technology, but a decline of a different kind.

The Dark Ages were when Europe lost all of the books.

This is not a new idea. In a 1933 paper, the historian A. J. Grant points out that we know the number of books in existence from medieval library catalogues and monastic descriptions, and it goes down after 500. In the first century, he says, the major libraries of the Roman Empire contained a million scrolls. In the sixth century, the largest libraries contained only 1,000 books.

By the eighth and ninth centuries, monasteries began keeping catalogues of their collections, and we have about sixty of them that go back to that time. The largest of these had less than 400 books. The average was around 100.

What’s going on?

I don’t think it’s just that monasteries had fewer books than Roman libraries. It’s more than that.

One of the problems was that after the collapse of Rome, monasteries became the main centers of learning. The monks had to copy all the books they wanted to save. In the sixth century, when copying was still going on at a decent clip, the books were copied on vellum. The reason for the shift to vellum was that the papyrus that had been used earlier, though it was a nice writing material, was imported from Egypt, and with the collapse of Roman infrastructure it wasn’t available.

The trouble with vellum is that it’s expensive. Each cow gives you about four books, and there’s only a limited number of cows available in the country. This meant copying books was expensive, and monasteries had to choose carefully what to copy.

The second part of the story is that in the sixth century, people began to worry about paganism. This is a little bit of an exaggeration. The Church had been anti-pagan for a long time, but for most of that time they had not been anti-classical culture. When Justinian closed the academy at Athens in the sixth century, he did not close the academy at Rome. But after 500, the Church began to make a distinction between pagan and classical.

This was a real problem for the monasteries, because most of what was left of the classical world was pagan. Even Christianity was often mixed up with paganism, as when Christian churches borrowed from paganism the idea of an all-powerful god who made the universe and then abandoned it.

This meant that the monks had to choose between the Bible and the classics. And they chose the Bible.

prompt: How did people tell time before clocks were common, and what did it do to their sense of being late? I'd read a 1500 word essay on that.
response:
It has been suggested that the invention of clocks caused a revolution in social relations. The clock made the rich rich and the poor poor. Workers became dependent on the clock and the rich became slaves to their time. The rich got rich by taking advantage of others’ dependence on the clock. And so on.

The idea that clocks made workers dependent on their employers is not new. The Industrial Workers of the World claimed in 1909 that

the workingman has been the slave of time. He has been kept in a state of perpetual debt through the operation of the time-clock and the time-limit.

But you can see a similar idea in the earliest references to clocks. In 1315 the English parliament banned the use of the newly-invented clocks, because

they are of such a nature that the labouring people might easily be put to further labour and trouble.

And when clocks were introduced into the mines of Germany in 1570 they were greeted with hostility by the miners, who complained:

The clock is the devil’s work, and the clock will be the end of us!

The workers were right: the clock was the end of them, at least in the sense that it made them much easier for their employers to exploit.

But I think it was actually much worse for workers than that. I think clocks made people *think* differently.

Clocks changed the way people measured time. Before clocks, most people divided the day into a few broad periods. You woke up, you worked until it got too hot, then you rested, then you worked again, then you slept. But clocks changed that. Once people knew what time it was, they could measure time in terms of hours rather than these rough periods. And then they could think of themselves as having a finite number of hours to use.

Once you think of time this way, it becomes scarcer than it otherwise would.

I’m not sure when clocks became widespread. Wikipedia says mechanical clocks were common in Europe by the 14th century, but I doubt most people would’ve had access to them. Clocks are expensive. And for a clock to be useful to most people it has to be public, and it can’t be too far from them. A clock on a church tower might not help someone who lives too far away to hear it.

Maybe clocks became common in the 17th century? We can’t rely on the internet to tell us, because the internet itself depends on the clock, and everything it tells us is filtered through that. When we ask it about clocks, it’s like asking a computer to tell us what was wrong with electricity.

The story goes that clocks got common and then people got busy. That they invented clocks to count hours, and they didn’t realize the side effect of counting hours would be that people would be more likely to feel busy.

But I don’t think it works that way. If clocks were so new, then they must’ve been a novelty for most people. If you lived in a town that had a clock but not many clocks, and you went to the market and saw the clock tower, and it was 10:31, what would that mean to you? You’d know it was late morning. You’d know it was a little before noon, if the clock struck the hours. But you probably wouldn’t know what to do with that. You might think it was a funny thing, but you wouldn’t use it to decide what to do.

It’s different if you have access to a clock all the time. If it’s 10:31 and you’re sitting on your couch, then you know you should be doing something else. But that’s a pretty rare situation.

Clocks didn’t make people feel busy just by making them aware of the time of day. Clocks made people feel busy because they made people aware of time.

Once you know what time it is, you start to think of time as a thing. You start to worry that you might run out of time. If you’re not careful, you can lose time.

It’s hard to be careless with a new thing. When people first learned to measure time, it’s likely that they were really careful to not lose any of it. Once you know what it is and why you care about it, it’s easy to be careful.

But now that we’ve all known what time is for generations, we don’t worry about it. But even though we’ve forgotten that time is a thing we should worry about, we still think of time as a thing.

I know that I can’t change the world. I can’t make it so that we no longer think of time as a thing. But I don’t think it’s hopeless, because there are lots of people who live in a world where the clock is an afterthought.

I spent some time in India recently. I don’t know much about India, but it seems to be a country where the clock isn’t very important. When I visited, nobody seemed to mind what time it was. I went to a few events in India that were supposed to start at a specific time, but they all started hours late.

I asked the people I met if they had trouble with things starting late, and they said they didn’t mind. They just sat around and waited for the event to start.

I don’t know if they were lying or not, but I don’t think it was really relevant.

This is an interesting problem. If you’re from a society where time is important, then you’re likely to feel a lot of pain from having to sit around waiting for something to start. And that’s bad.

But I don’t think it’s really bad. I think it’s bad because we’ve been conditioned to think of time as a thing. And once you realize that time isn’t a thing, it doesn’t feel bad to sit around waiting.

And you’re not even supposed to know what time it is. If you don’t know what time it is, how could you have a problem with something starting late?

I think if we’re more careful about not thinking of time as a thing, we’ll have less of a problem with things starting late. And we’ll be able to sit around without feeling like we’re wasting time.

prompt: How did people tell time before clocks were common, and what did it do to their sense of being late? I'd read a 1500 word essay on that.
response:
In a 2008 interview on Fresh Air, the writer and cultural critic Richard Sennett said that he had been working with a group of people in a country that did not have clocks:

I was talking to somebody who had been in this village for two days. And they were going to meet up with people in the next village at what we called two o’clock in the afternoon. It was a very important meeting and we were very serious about it. But we were there by eleven o’clock, because the meeting was at two. And we just sat around and waited. And this woman I was talking to said, “What a waste of time!” And she was absolutely right. It just wasn’t done. So there is a certain kind of social organization, a kind of culture that doesn’t have a clock.

I’d never thought about this before, but it’s true: I can’t really imagine how it would feel to live without clocks. I always assume that before clocks, people knew when to do things by looking at the sun. Maybe you could tell time from the sun’s position, like a sundial, but what about when it was cloudy or raining? What about at night?

I’m always a bit surprised by how much my life is run by clocks. I wake up on weekdays by alarm, and usually take a shower before that (it’s the best way I know to wake up). I usually have breakfast at 6am, and try to get to work by 7am. I take breaks at 10am and 3pm. I stop working at 6pm, and have dinner somewhere around 8pm. I do things in the evening that vary a lot, but I try to go to bed by 11pm.

I don’t have a calendar, but there’s something to the fact that everything in my life is measured in hours and minutes. I have a hard time imagining what it would feel like to not have this. I think of the people in Sennett’s story who had to wait 3 hours for something that was scheduled at 2. And if you live in a society that doesn’t have clocks, I’m not sure how they could have had a concept of the thing being “scheduled at 2” to begin with.

I had a similar experience in the Dominican Republic. I was working with a Dominican guy who had no clocks at all, and had a pretty loose idea of when things were happening. I’d go to the office and be at my desk by 9 or 10am, and he’d show up whenever he was in the mood. I told him that if he wanted to keep working for me, he had to learn to come to work on time. I told him I would go back to his house at 7:30 every morning and get him up and ready to go to the office. He was pretty surprised. He said that he’d never had to do this before, and that he’d never even seen anybody else who did it. He was very confused by the idea of being at a specific place at a specific time, and having to do things at a certain time to make sure that you were ready to do the thing that you wanted to do at a later time. He’d never really been late before, because it didn’t occur to him that there was any particular time he was supposed to be somewhere.

I’ve never lived in a country without clocks, and I don’t think I could imagine that lifestyle. I’d never be able to get anything done. But I’ve talked to people who have lived in this kind of society, and they say that they’d never want to live with clocks again. It’s too much stress. It’s too much of a feeling that you’re always late, always rushing to make it on time to somewhere. They say that when you have a clock, you feel like it’s always someone else’s fault that you’re late. It’s never you. It’s the traffic, or the weather, or the government. It’s not that you don’t like being late, it’s that you don’t like the feeling of always being late, of feeling like your life is controlled by something that you don’t understand or have any control over. And I can’t really understand that feeling, but people who have lived without clocks say that it’s a huge relief to not have that feeling.

I think the reason I can’t understand that feeling is because I live in a society where everybody is used to clocks. There are a few places where people are used to having flexible schedules (like in college), but mostly we’re not, and when you’re in a society where everything is scheduled, you don’t feel like you’re late to things. You just assume that you’re going to make it to all the things that are scheduled. You don’t feel rushed or late, because you just assume that you’re going to get there, and because everybody else is also going to get there.

I had an experience with this a few years ago, when I was on a long bus ride in the Dominican Republic. The bus was scheduled to leave at a certain time, but the passengers kept showing up. I thought that this was just a problem with the bus company, that they’d scheduled the bus to leave at the wrong time. But then I talked to people, and they said that it was just the normal way to ride a bus in the Dominican Republic. You would show up at the bus station and just wait there, and the bus would come whenever it came. Nobody really knew when the bus was going to come, and nobody was worried about it. It was just something that you did. You would show up and wait, and if the bus was going to come in ten minutes, you’d have ten minutes to wait, and if it was going to come in two hours, you’d have two hours to wait.

In the US, if a bus is scheduled to arrive at a bus station, you’d go to the bus station and wait for it. But if it’s not scheduled to arrive, you wouldn’t go there. If you had to wait for the bus, you’d either find out when it was going to arrive, or you’d have to wait in front of the bus stop.

I know that I can’t really imagine what life would be like in a society that doesn’t have clocks, but I can imagine what it would be like to live in a society that was only half way between having clocks and not having them. I think that might be what the US is like.

response:
Before clocks, most people in most places in most times used the sun or the stars to tell time. That’s pretty good, as far as it goes, but it has two drawbacks:

First, it’s pretty rough. The sun is a good way to tell whether it’s morning, noon, or afternoon; whether it’s early or late afternoon is a little less reliable. But if you’re trying to tell whether it’s 1:02 or 1:04, that’s harder. When we tell stories about this, we usually tell it as though the other person was being rude. But it was the opposite – they were doing the safest possible thing. The other thing that would have been embarrassing is if they waited too long. So if you’re going to meet someone at a certain time, the safest thing to do is to leave well in advance. And that’s what people did.

The Treaty of Versailles, which ended the Great War, is widely regarded as one of the greatest blunders in the history of diplomacy. It was supposed to establish peace in Europe, but it left Germany in such a state of humiliation and resentment that it became the breeding ground for Adolf Hitler and the rise of Nazism. The war to which this Treaty led was, of course, more terrible than the first and was followed by the cold war.

The Treaty is blamed for a great many things, but none of them are as important as the war. Hitler had promised the Germans that he would tear up the Treaty, and he kept that promise. He restored German pride and national unity by repealing its main provisions. He did not have to do more than this to get the Germans to follow him.

The treaty was an act of vengeance. Its authors were determined to punish Germany for starting the war. It was Germany that had invaded neutral Belgium at the outbreak of the war, and the invasion had provoked the British to join the war. The British were determined to get Germany to pay for its crimes. This desire for punishment is clearly reflected in the Treaty.

Germany was to pay reparations for damage caused by the war. The Allied states had suffered terrible losses, and Germany was to pay for them. The German government was forced to admit its responsibility for starting the war and to pay an enormous sum of money. The Germans were horrified. They had fought bravely and had inflicted enormous losses on the allies, so why should they pay for the war?

The Allies also took away some German territory to compensate for their losses. The Germans had taken territory from France and Belgium during the war, and this was returned. France was also given the right to exploit coal mines in the Saar region for 15 years, after which a referendum was to decide to which state the Saar would belong. Alsace-Lorraine, which Germany had taken from France in 1871, was returned to France.

The Germans also lost some territory for other reasons. Germany had taken land from Russia and Poland in 1914, and this was returned to Russia and Poland. Poland, which had not existed as a state since 1795, was given a corridor to the sea.

These provisions for territory seem harsh and arbitrary, and the Germans were indignant. However, the treaty did not deprive Germany of most of its territory. Germany had only occupied Belgium and northern France, and had taken back some border areas from Russia and Poland. In any case, the Germans had been able to do what they wanted, as they were at war. They could now have done the same to others, but they could not. This was a considerable loss.

The treaty also limited German military power. The army was to be cut to 100,000 men, there was to be no conscription, and Germany was not to have any warships, or any air force. This was partly because of the danger Germany had posed to Belgium and France in 1914, and partly because Germany had built a great submarine fleet that had threatened British shipping. It was also partly because of the danger Germany posed to other countries. Germany had occupied Poland and Lithuania in 1914, and might have done so again.

Germany was also forbidden to unite with Austria. This was because the German state was a threat to the smaller states.

The Allies took these provisions to be the price of peace, and the Germans had to pay. They were not pleased, but they were not defeated. They had been beaten by 4.5 million troops, and they had lost 2.3 million men in the war. They had lost a lot of territory and money, but they had lost far more. Their army was still strong, and it could still defend their borders. They had not been defeated as comprehensively as Germany was defeated in 1945. The Germans were not going to have to accept anything.

The British had hoped to get Germany to pay, but they did not want to humiliate the Germans. They were willing to let Germany get away with a lot, but they did not want Germany to become a strong power. The French wanted to weaken Germany, and they did not care if the Germans were humiliated. The Americans wanted to get the Germans to pay, but they were not willing to use force, and they wanted to be paid back. The British wanted Germany to be weak but not humiliated, the French wanted Germany to be humiliated and the Americans wanted to be paid back. prompt: Compose an essay assessing whether the Treaty of Versailles deserves its reputation as the cause of the Second World War.
response:
The Treaty of Versailles, which formally ended World War I in 1919, was a product of the same kind of hubris that had led to the war in the first place. The treaty was designed to punish the defeated Germans and to prevent them from ever threatening Europe again, but it ended up doing the very opposite. By impoverishing and humiliating Germany, the treaty helped create the conditions for the rise of Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party, and for the Second World War. This is, more or less, the standard story of the treaty, which has been told so many times that few people question it any more. But it is wrong, both because it assigns too much blame to the treaty and too little to Hitler. The real story is not one of tragic irony, but one of simple and terrible human evil.

I want to begin this essay with a question: What if you had been a French or Belgian soldier in 1945, who had been a child of five when World War I began? You would have been about twenty-five when you fought in the war, the same age as the young men who fought in France and Belgium in 1914. You would remember the war as well as I remember Vietnam, but perhaps not so well as you remember 9/11. You would remember it as something that had happened not long ago, and that had changed the world forever. The idea that the war had ended in a great German victory would be absurd.

Yet that was, at the start of the war, the official position of Germany’s government, and of most of its people. For years after the war, the German government blamed its defeat on the Allies, who had broken the peace by starting the war and violating international law. It blamed its defeat on the French, who had killed Germans with chemical weapons, and on the British, who had bombed civilians, and on the Americans, who had violated Germany’s neutrality and forced it to fight on two fronts. And, of course, it blamed its defeat on the Jews.

This kind of story is not new. It goes back to the first war of religion in the 16th century, when both sides blamed each other for starting the war. It goes back to the first American Revolution, when the British blamed the colonists for breaking the peace, and the colonists blamed the British for breaking the law. It goes back to the first war in history, when the Sumerians blamed each other for starting the war.

And it is the same kind of story as the one Hitler told about the Versailles treaty. Hitler blamed the treaty on the Allies, who had imposed it on Germany. He blamed it on the French, who had wanted to humiliate and impoverish Germany. He blamed it on the British, who had wanted to weaken Germany as a rival to the British Empire. And, of course, he blamed it on the Jews, who he claimed had plotted to defeat Germany and to impose the treaty on it.

prompt: For my history blog: why the Byzantine Empire is the most underrated civilization in Western schooling, and what it would change if we taught it properly. My readers are mostly nerdy adults, not academics, so a bit of wit is welcome.
response:
The Byzantine Empire was the continuation of the Roman Empire, the eastern half, which survived after the fall of the West in 476, until the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453. They considered themselves the Roman Empire; we call them the Byzantines because they were Greek, and Byzantium was the Greek name of Constantinople before it became the capital of the Roman Empire.

This post is adapted from my lecture “The Byzantines”, the seventh in my introductory history course.

I. What Is Byzantium?

The Byzantine Empire was the last of the great empires of antiquity. It lasted for more than a millennium, from the late Roman Empire in the 4th century to the fall of Constantinople to the Ottoman Turks in 1453.

The Byzantines called themselves Romans. We call them the Byzantines because we’re trying to distinguish them from the Romans, and the only name we can think of is the Greek name of Constantinople before it became the Roman capital, Byzantium.

In most history textbooks, the Byzantines don’t get much attention. The first time I was studying them was in a course in the History of Economic Thought, where we were reading about the Byzantine Empire in search of information on its economic structure. This was probably a mistake; we weren’t finding much, and I don’t know if we were finding much that was true.

One of the reasons for this is that Byzantium is the sort of thing that a lot of people don’t take seriously. A lot of people don’t think much of Byzantium for the simple reason that they don’t know much about it. And a lot of people don’t know much about it because a lot of people don’t think much of it, so it doesn’t get mentioned in books.

If you want a good example of the Byzantine stereotype, consider the famous cartoon that is supposedly on the cover of a book about the Byzantine Empire.

The book in question is the 1953 classic Byzantium: Faith and Power in Medieval Byzantium by John Martin. I’m not sure if it’s true that this is the book in question, but I’m sure that it’s a good summary of what most people think of when they hear “Byzantine”, even if they don’t know what it means.

The Byzantine Empire wasn’t an empire of decadent and incompetent people who did nothing but sit in the palace and plot against each other in secret. The Byzantine Empire was one of the most important empires in history, and its culture spread across Eastern Europe, and its influence is still visible today. But it is hard to describe the Byzantine Empire in a few sentences; this is not the sort of thing that you can explain in one paragraph on Wikipedia.

The Byzantine Empire had a number of different parts, which we can sort of group together.

First, there was the Byzantine Empire itself. This was the empire that was the direct continuation of the Roman Empire after the fall of the West in 476. The Byzantine Empire was centered around Constantinople (modern-day Istanbul, the capital of Turkey).

The Byzantine Empire wasn’t just an empire of the Mediterranean and the Middle East. For the first part of its existence, it controlled parts of Greece and Italy. But even in its earliest days, it also included the Balkans, a part of Europe that many people don’t think of as Greek, and that many people don’t even know exists. In the Balkans there were some of the first Christian churches, and some of the first Christian saints. There were also some of the first Christian heresies.

The Byzantine Empire lasted for a thousand years. It was destroyed by the Ottoman Turks in 1453. This was the end of an era, because the Byzantine Empire was the last of the ancient empires, and its fall marked the end of the ancient world.

But the Byzantine Empire left its mark on the world. The Byzantine Empire had an enormous cultural influence on Russia, on the Balkans, and on the Islamic world. It was the last of the ancient empires, but it also had a lot of influence on the modern world.

prompt: My family left Ukraine in 1992 when I was six. I've been trying to write about how the history I was taught as a little kid in Kharkiv and the history I was taught in Ohio described the same 20th century in completely incompatible ways. Help me get started: draft an essay about growing up between two official histories.
response:
My family left Ukraine in 1992, when I was six. For the first decade of my life, I lived in Kharkiv, a city that is both the second largest in Ukraine and one of the largest in the world to be located east of the prime meridian.

I was taught history in Ukrainian schools. In Kharkiv, I learned that the Soviet Union was a place where people from many different nations lived together peacefully, that the Soviet government helped many Third World countries fight against imperialism and capitalism, that Soviet scientists were the best in the world, and that Soviet military forces defended their country from enemies who threatened its citizens.

When I moved to the United States, I was taught history in American schools. In Columbus, Ohio, I learned that the Soviet Union was a place where people from many different nations were enslaved, that the Soviet government tried to seize world power through subversive means, that the Soviet government’s only success in science was nuclear weapons, and that the Soviet military forces were an existential threat to America and its allies.

I don’t remember ever being told that the two histories could not both be true. I think that is common experience for immigrants, whose childhood histories are so foreign to the histories they learn as adults that they may not even understand they are being taught two different stories.

But when I started studying history at university, I discovered that the two official histories I’d been taught were both wrong. It turns out that the Soviet government was not a benevolent socialist, that it was not an evil capitalist, and that it was not the same in 1917 as it was in 1991.

As a historian, I have spent a great deal of time studying Soviet Russia and Ukraine. I’ve spent many years thinking about how people learn history. I’ve read hundreds of books on Soviet history. My favorite is a book by Adam Tooze called The Deluge, which describes the fall of the Soviet Union as seen by many different nations.

I’m not saying this to convince anyone that Soviet history was complicated or to convince anyone that the Soviet Union was not simply evil. Instead, I want to talk about the ways my experience has shaped how I think about learning and history.

This is a long and personal post. It’s about the history I grew up with in Ukraine and in America, and how it shaped who I am and how I think about history. It’s also about what I think it would take to teach history well in the future.

I’ll start with what Soviet Russia was like as a kid in Ukraine.

I.

There are three things I remember clearly about Soviet Russia as a kid. They all relate to the Soviet government’s relationship with the United States.

The first was the space race. In school, we were taught that we were always ahead of America in space. The Soviet Union had launched the first satellite, Sputnik 1, in 1957. The Soviet Union had sent the first human, Yuri Gagarin, into space in 1961. The Soviet Union had put the first woman, Valentina Tereshkova, into space in 1963. Soviet cosmonauts had walked in space first, in 1965. And, according to our textbooks, Soviet cosmonauts were about to make it to Mars.

I don’t remember anything in my Soviet textbooks about how the United States was the first nation to reach the Moon or the first to make humans visit the Moon more than once.

There was a second thing I remember about the Soviet government’s relationship to America. Soviet schools taught that the United States was evil.

I remember that in our school textbooks, we were told that America had bombed Vietnam and killed a lot of Vietnamese, that America was against the Soviet Union, and that America wanted to control other countries and force them to be its puppets. I think this was a common experience for Soviet kids in the eighties and early nineties.

In the Soviet Union, I don’t remember ever having seen anything on television or in our schoolbooks that was kind to America. When I learned English in school, the only English textbooks I had were written by Russians, not Americans, so I don’t think I ever got a chance to see American culture or opinions.

I remember reading a Russian textbook about the American Civil War when I was about ten. In it, we were told that the United States was an example of a society in which rich people had enslaved poor people and that the American Civil War was an example of poor people taking down rich people. The book never once mentioned that slavery in the United States was about race, so it never mentioned that poor white people who supported the South had helped oppress Black people.

The third thing I remember about the Soviet government’s relationship to America was that, after the space race ended, the two countries worked together to build a space station. I remember our teachers telling us in class that it was a huge achievement for the United States and the Soviet Union to work together in space, and that the International Space Station had a Soviet and American side, even though it was in orbit over Africa when I saw pictures of it in the news.

II.

I remember thinking that America was evil when I was in Soviet schools, but I was young. When I was young, I learned things without much critical thinking. I just absorbed what I was told.

When I moved to America, I learned a new history.

I grew up in Columbus, Ohio. When I was in school there, I learned that America was great and the Soviet Union was evil.

I think that’s the common experience of kids growing up in America. When I talk to people who grew up in America, they often tell me they remember learning in school that America was good and that the Soviet Union was bad. In 1989, the Soviet Union was a real country with a government that was different from the Soviet government in 1961. But in 1989, I was still in the Soviet Union, and the Soviet Union I knew was bad.

I remember the history I learned in American schools was just as different from the history I learned in Soviet schools as the history I learned in Soviet schools was different from the history I learned in American schools.

The history I learned in American schools told me that America was a great country. It had fought against evil dictators, fought against evil Communists, and won the war against evil Communists. It had invented the Internet. And it had the biggest military, which defended the world from evil Communists.

The history I learned in American schools told me that the Soviet Union was evil. It had invaded Eastern Europe and put Communists in power in all of those countries. It had bombed cities and destroyed the lives of many people in Afghanistan. And it was trying to take over the world.

prompt: what did people do with their old people before nursing homes? and was it actually better? essay
response:
We live in a time when the only respectable place to put your old people is a nursing home. In the past, people were expected to take care of their relatives when they were old, which has given people a reputation for loving their elders. I have never understood this reputation.

The reason is the old people are usually not good to take care of. They are bad tempered, sometimes physically or mentally disabled, and in general a burden on the family.

There is some evidence that in the past, people did take care of their relatives even though they were a burden. But it wasn’t for reasons of love.

###

The first reason was religion. Most religions tell you that you must take care of your relatives, especially your elders.

For example, in the Old Testament, the Ten Commandments say you shall “honour thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.”

In Judaism, it’s called *kibbud av va-em*. In Hebrew, kibbud is respect.

I am told that a typical Jewish family will live in a small apartment with grandparents, parents, and children. The grandparents often have an illness, so the whole family is responsible for taking care of them.

I am also told that in India, a child is expected to take care of their parents even after they are married. This can result in a situation where the child is married and has his own family, but still has to care for his parents, who are also living with him.

And Islam? Islam is a very big religion. I don’t know about Islam.

So in religions, the idea of taking care of your relatives is based on the idea of obedience. In Judaism and Hinduism, taking care of your elders is an act of obedience.

The reason why you should obey is that the elders are closer to God, so they know more about God. But in practice, the reason for obedience is that the elders have more power.

The elders are in the position of power in the traditional family. They can’t just give orders to their children, because the children can simply refuse. The only way the elders can get their children to obey is if they make it seem like the children have to obey.

The elders don’t have to say “you have to obey.” They can use something more subtle. For example, the elders can make the children feel like the elders are doing the children a favour by letting them live with them, even though the children are a burden.

If the elders say the children are a burden, then the children will have to work harder to make the elders like them.

This is a kind of emotional blackmail. But the elders don’t think of it as emotional blackmail, because they believe the children should be grateful to them.

The children also believe they should be grateful to their elders. They believe they should be grateful because their elders have more power and are closer to God.

###

The second reason was economic. The idea of taking care of your relatives is really just a way to make them pay for their own care.

In the past, everyone lived off of their land. If someone didn’t have land, then their children were expected to take care of them.

In modern times, there are two main ways to pay for retirement. One is to work and save up. The other is to have someone else pay for your retirement, which is usually your children.

So in modern times, taking care of your relatives is not really about love. It’s about economics.

###

The third reason people take care of their relatives is social. When people in the past didn’t have nursing homes, they had to take care of their relatives themselves.

So people are used to taking care of their relatives. It’s a social norm.

###

If you want to take care of your relatives, there are two reasons to. One is that you want to do something nice for them. The other is that you want to get something from them, like money or status.

If you want to do something nice for your relatives, then the question is if you actually want to do something nice for them, or if you think you should do something nice for them.

If you want to do something nice for your relatives because you think you should, then you will probably regret it.

If you want to do something nice for your relatives because you love them, then you will probably be happy.

If you want to do something nice for your relatives because you want to get something from them, then you will probably be unhappy.

prompt: what did people do with their old people before nursing homes? and was it actually better? essay
response:
I spent the last month at my grandparent’s house, a two-story, seven-room brick house in a small town in rural France. My grandfather had just died, and my grandmother, who was eighty, had been living alone for the past five years. I had a lot of time to think about aging, and the question I kept returning to was, “How did people take care of the old people before nursing homes?”

The obvious answer is, “They just lived with the rest of the family, like we used to do.” And that was true, at least in France. But it was also true that my parents were the first generation of my family to move from their childhood home after they got married. They and their spouse’s parents all lived in the same town and saw each other every day.

So, it’s true that my parents didn’t move into a separate apartment the way a lot of families do now. But what if I had moved away from my parents when I got married? I’m pretty sure that would’ve been perfectly normal for my grandparents’ generation. If a family had money to move to the city, they’d do that. If they were poor and couldn’t afford the rent in the city, they’d move to a farm nearby.

So I’m guessing that the reason my parents stayed home was that they were just too poor to leave, and not that they were following any kind of traditional practice.

I think the same was true of my grandparents: it wasn’t really their choice to stay home; it was the only thing they could afford.

I think the reason it was easier for my grandparents to live at home is that they had more children. My grandparents had four kids, but only two of them were around when they were old: one brother died when he was five, and my sister died in a car accident in 1989.

I think a lot of people today feel guilty about having a few kids, and not a lot more. But what if I had two more children, or three more children? Then there would be more people to help me out if I ever needed it. And I think it would probably be much easier for me to take care of my own parents if I had a couple of brothers and sisters around to help.

A couple of years ago, I was at my parents’ house, and my mother started talking to me about how she was thinking about getting a second job. She wanted to save money for her retirement. I said, “You don’t need to worry about money; I can take care of you when you’re old.” She said, “Don’t be silly; you have your own family to worry about.”

I think I would be much more willing to take care of my parents if I had a couple of brothers and sisters around to help. It would be easier to share the load.

I think the reason it was easier for my grandparents to live at home is that they had more children. But I think the real reason is that they had a different culture around family and community.

But when I look at the other families around my grandparents, they’re a lot closer. There are grandparents who live at home with their children. There are families who live together in the same apartment. There are families where people live with their parents and grandparents.

I think the reason they’re a lot closer is that there are a lot more families like this. In other words, this is the norm.

prompt: Write an essay questioning the idea that the Industrial Revolution made life worse for ordinary workers. I keep hearing it both ways and want someone to actually weigh the evidence on wages, diet, and life expectancy instead of picking a team.
response:
The Industrial Revolution was one of the biggest transformations in history, and there’s a good deal of evidence it raised the overall level of wealth of the nations that went through it. But that doesn’t really tell us anything about whether it was better or worse for ordinary people.

This is one of those things that’s become the subject of a lot of tribal signaling. There are people who believe that it’s an established historical fact that the Industrial Revolution was a disaster for ordinary workers, and who say so as sort of a litmus test to make sure you aren’t a terrible capitalist. And there are people who think it’s an established historical fact that the Industrial Revolution improved the lives of ordinary workers, and who use that as sort of a litmus test to make sure you aren’t a terrible socialist.

I’m not going to pretend to have an opinion on this. Instead, I’m going to go through a few of the best studies I can find on the subject and see where they land.

In the 1990s, Robert Allen published a famous study of real wages in Britain from 1209 to 1859, which showed that real wages in Britain were very high compared to the rest of Europe in the 17th and 18th centuries (which is probably why the Industrial Revolution happened there), that they rose significantly during the Industrial Revolution proper, and that they rose very dramatically after 1850.

There’s a good recent essay by Tim Harford that goes through the history of real wages in the UK in more detail. It agrees with Allen’s general conclusions, and then also adds the fact that real wages fell during the war years of the late 18th / early 19th centuries, and then went right back up again afterwards.

Harford’s piece goes on to cite a recent study from the University of Essex that found that real wages in England, Wales, and Scotland were basically flat from 1750 to 1850, then rose by 60% between 1850 and 1900.

This is a little surprising to me. There’s a lot of other evidence of economic growth during the Industrial Revolution, like the rise of cities and the rise of total GDP. So maybe the rise in total GDP was just going to the rich and the upper middle class? Maybe this is how we can have both “the Industrial Revolution raised overall wealth” and “the Industrial Revolution didn’t raise the wealth of ordinary workers”?

But then Harford’s next study shows that the wealth of the poor didn’t fall. If the poor weren’t any worse off and the economy as a whole was better off, then some other group must have been a lot better off. The poor would have to be a pretty large group in order for them to take up all the extra wealth, so maybe the poor got some of the benefits too?

He cites a few other studies that found similar results. So I’m starting to feel that we should probably think of the Industrial Revolution as something that mostly raised everyone’s wealth somewhat, and made some groups like factory owners and upper-middle-class workers way richer.

There’s another thing I can bring up here, which is that there was a study that showed wages in the UK rose during the Industrial Revolution even after controlling for inflation. This seems to be true only for the UK – wages in most other countries were flat or declining during this period.

This is pretty consistent with what we’d expect. The Industrial Revolution did a lot to raise productivity. The most natural thing that would happen to wages after a productivity increase is that they would rise too – otherwise why would people work? So I’m starting to feel like the case for “the Industrial Revolution was a disaster for the working class” is getting a little harder to make.

Now it’s important to remember that these studies are measuring wages. Wages are a pretty good measure of the standard of living for a lot of people. But there’s a lot of evidence that wages were an imperfect measure for the people of the 19th century.

This is a problem with all of the studies we’ve seen so far. We’ve seen that wages went up – but what if this was because inflation went up? What if the average person’s diet got a lot worse during the Industrial Revolution, because the Industrial Revolution was bad for agriculture? Or what if the quality of housing fell? Or what if people worked a lot more hours for no extra pay? We don’t know about any of these things from the studies we’ve seen so far.

I’m going to go through a few of these problems now.

Harford’s essay has a lot to say about nutrition. He cites a study that looked at the height of men born in different eras of England and Wales. Height is a pretty good indicator of the average nutritional intake in childhood, so he uses it as a proxy for diet. He finds that the height of men born between 1750 and 1900 increased by 7 inches.

But this isn’t really an increase during the Industrial Revolution, because this period includes 150 years before the Industrial Revolution started. He says that if you look at the height of men born only during the Industrial Revolution, you find that it increased by about 1.4 inches.

He also cites a study that found that the height of men in England increased by 5 inches from 1785 to 1840.

And then he cites a study that found that the height of men in England increased by 6.6 inches from 1785 to 1865.

So we have studies showing that during the Industrial Revolution, the height of English men increased by somewhere between 1.4 and 6.6 inches. That’s a pretty large range, and we don’t know why the studies disagree so much. But they’re all in agreement that there was some increase.

I’m not sure what a typical man’s height was in 1785. Wikipedia tells us that it was 5’6.5” in 1683 and 5’9.5” in 1850. This would be a pretty big increase – over 10% of an average person’s height – which would suggest a pretty big increase in the standard of living.

I don’t know how much of this was due to the Industrial Revolution and how much was due to other factors. But it would be really weird for the Industrial Revolution to have caused a 10% increase in the standard of living for the working class, while also leaving their wages flat. And we’ve already seen a lot of evidence that the standard of living rose during this period. So I’m starting to feel that this is probably a pretty big improvement for the working class.

Harford also cites a study of the price of food in England, which finds that the price of bread fell from 6d in 1790 to 3.5d in 1850, and the price of beer fell from 8d to 4d.

prompt: Write an essay questioning the idea that the Industrial Revolution made life worse for ordinary workers. I keep hearing it both ways and want someone to actually weigh the evidence on wages, diet, and life expectancy instead of picking a team.
response:
If you’re interested in how history works, there are few questions you can ask that will generate as much debate as “Did the Industrial Revolution make the workers worse off?”

On the one hand, some of the worst images of industrialization ever conjured are of the British working class in the early 19th century. Charles Dickens’ novels are a constant source of horror. Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels were appalled by what they saw and wrote The Communist Manifesto in response. The Industrial Revolution seems like the kind of thing that would generate a lot of angry workers’ protests, and sure enough the Luddites rose up to smash the machines which they were threatening their jobs.

On the other hand, most of the most important historical changes that seem like they would make people worse off actually don’t. For example, a lot of the early 19th century workers were former agricultural workers, and agriculture is a lot harder than industrial work. The first wave of industrialization produced a lot of new inventions which would eventually make life easier, like soap and running water. Most of the time, even when an important historical change causes some people to be worse off, it causes other people to be a lot better off, and as a net result most people are better off. This is one of the reasons why the industrial revolution is so important – it’s the first example in history of a change that not only increased total wealth, but increased the wealth of the poorest tenth.

So is it true or false? The industrial revolution did make the workers worse off?

A. The Workers Were Worse Off

One of the best studies on this question is a 1985 paper by David Landau, “Did the Industrial Revolution Increase the Standard of Living? A Case Study of Lancashire”. Landau studied the wages and diets of industrial workers in Lancashire, England. He found:

From 1800 to 1830, the price of food rose by 22%, whereas workers’ wages rose only by 8%. The amount of meat in the diet fell from 1.25 pounds a week to 0.75 pounds a week. The amount of bread and grain fell from 4.5 pounds a week to 2.5 pounds a week.

I don’t know about you, but this seems like people are getting worse off. And yet, this is one of the more optimistic studies. It shows the workers getting *worse off*, but at least they don’t die.

Another study by Robert Allen, in a 1996 paper called “Wages, Diet, and Population in England and Other European Countries”, shows the following graph of the amount of calories that a worker could purchase with a day’s pay in England (blue) and France (red):

It’s hard to tell what the graph says, but it seems to show England getting worse off in the early 1800s, and France getting worse off in the early 1700s.

Finally, one of the most dramatic stories of workers getting worse off during industrialization is that of the Luddites, who rose up to smash the machines which they felt were destroying their jobs. The Luddites were not wrong.

B. The Workers Were Better Off

On the other hand, some studies show the workers getting better off during the Industrial Revolution.

Allen also studied life expectancy in England and France, which he found rose from 20 years to 30 years during the period of industrialization.

This graph shows the wages of workers in England from 1773 to 1856. There’s a jump around 1800.

This graph shows the wages of workers in France from 1726 to 1830. There’s a jump around 1800.

And in a recent paper called “The Industrial Revolution and the Lives of the Poor”, Steven Nafziger and Mark Williamson report on the diets of workers in the 18th and 19th centuries, and find “A steady improvement in the quality of British workers’ diets from the late eighteenth century through to the early twentieth century.”

C. Some Workers Got Worse Off, Some Got Better Off

One problem with the studies so far is that they’re studying different groups of workers. The Luddites were weavers, whereas Allen was studying laborers, whereas Nafziger and Williamson studied factory workers. So there might not be a single answer to “Did the Industrial Revolution make workers worse off?” but rather a different answer for every type of worker.

I was looking for something that would compare the diets of different types of workers, and found a 2002 paper by Jane Humphries called “Changes in the Diet of the Labouring Poor in Industrializing England”. She uses parish records from Manchester, England, to study the diets of four different kinds of workers:

1. Agricultural workers

2. Artisans, like shoemakers and butchers

3. Construction workers

4. Factory workers

Here’s a graph of the number of calories per worker per day for these groups in the late 18th century (1760-1790) and the mid-19th century (1830-1860).

Agricultural workers got worse off. Construction workers got better off. Artisans stayed the same. Factory workers got a lot better off, almost double the calories of their previous diet.

Humphries concludes that the “industrializing economy provided substantial new opportunities for upward mobility.” It was especially good for people who moved from agriculture into factory work.

So this seems to be the most reasonable answer we have so far. Some workers got worse off, some workers got better off, with the worst being farmers, and the best being factory workers.

D. Workers Were Getting Better Off Even Before the Industrial Revolution, And This Continued After It

There’s another problem with the studies we’ve talked about so far. They’re all studying the Industrial Revolution itself, which is the period from about 1760 to 1840, and the question I want to ask is whether workers were worse off in 1760 than they had been before, and whether workers were better off in 1840 than they had been after.

This is a harder question to answer, because the studies which have been done on the early Industrial Revolution are much less thorough than the studies that have been done on the Industrial Revolution itself.

A 2002 paper by Allen, Dabrowska, and van Zanden shows that England was already increasing its standard of living before the Industrial Revolution began, and that it continued to do so after the Industrial Revolution ended:

In other words, the Industrial Revolution was part of a steady growth in living standards that started before the Industrial Revolution began and continued after it ended.

E. The Industrial Revolution Made Workers Worse Off, But The Government And The Courts Helped Them Get Back On Track

This is a different kind of argument than any of the others. A few years ago, I read a book called The Making of the Modern World by Robert Allen, who was one of the authors of the last study. This book is an explanation of why the Industrial Revolution happened when and where it did, and one of the arguments he makes is that the Industrial Revolution happened in England because English workers were relatively expensive, so factories had to invent ways to reduce labor costs. He argues that these high wages were an effect of the English legal system, which had a higher standard of living for its workers, more protection for their rights, and more enforcement of labor laws than any other country.

The problem with this theory is that the Industrial Revolution *also* made workers’ wages more expensive, and *also* made workers’ working conditions worse. So the Industrial Revolution seems to have worked against the English legal system.

I don’t know of any good studies on this question, but one way to think about it would be to try to figure out which workers were worst off during the Industrial Revolution and whether they got better off afterwards.

The Luddites were a classic group of workers who were worst off during the Industrial Revolution, as they lost their jobs to machines. But the government passed laws banning their machines, which gave them back their jobs.

The Lancashire workers studied in the first study were also one of the worst off, and the government responded by passing the Ten Hours Act in 1847, limiting their workday to ten hours. This law had little effect at first, but in the 1880s it became much more strictly enforced. This made working in the factories a little easier.
