But when Chandler hears that Duffy, the man he hates, is going to be staying the night, he is mortified. He doesn’t want to be alone in a room with Duffy.

At that point, Mrs. Cronin tells her husband to ask Duffy to come in. And when Chandler sees Duffy, he realizes that he should be feeling compassion, not anger. Duffy is staying the night in the house of someone who is dying, so Chandler should not be angry about it.

That, to me, is the moral imagination. It means having the ability to see things from the other person’s point of view.

I think the reason why the Crito dilemma was so important in ancient Greece is because it was about the ability to make moral choices. It was about the ability to understand what the other person was feeling and then do something about it.

prompt: is it wrong to lie to a dying person? essay pls
response:
There was a time, not so long ago, when it was considered normal to lie to a dying person about their condition. If they were too far gone to be told the truth, well, no big deal.

In his excellent essay “What Happens When You Tell Someone They’re Dying?”, Dr. Eric Topol talks about his grandfather:

My grandfather was dying of cancer in 1994. I had not told him about his terminal diagnosis or prognosis. I had told him that his doctors were doing their best to treat him, and I told him that he would have to go to the hospital. I was wrong, because the doctors had given up. He was admitted to a palliative care unit in a New York hospital. When I asked him, he was surprised that he had not been told his condition.

My father was also dying of cancer in 2014. I had not told him that he was dying. He had been told his cancer had recurred, but I did not tell him that it was terminal. I told him that his doctors were doing their best to treat his cancer. I was wrong again. The oncologists had also given up. He was admitted to a palliative care unit in a San Diego hospital. When I asked him, he was not surprised that he had not been told.

The reason he was not surprised is because he was aware of his prognosis. He was aware because his wife, my mother, had told him that he had one month to live.

She had lied. She had told him one month to live because she thought that if I told him he had two months to live, he might believe me. But in fact he had only one week to live. She did this because she thought that a one month prognosis would be kinder to him than a one week prognosis.

I have not been to hospice since then, and I wonder why.

I have been asked if there is any evidence that dying people want to know they are dying. I think the evidence is strong.

I have also been asked if there is any evidence that it is wrong to lie to dying people. I think the evidence is strong there too, though there’s much less.

The first thing you might think about is the idea that lying is wrong.

A lot of people would just say that lying is wrong, period. But I don’t think this is a good answer.

There are many situations where lying is obviously the right thing to do. For instance, you can lie to a murderer trying to find your friends in order to save their lives. Or you can lie to the people who want to take your friends, by pretending to be their friends, in order to save their lives.

So it’s not that lying is *per se* wrong. But it seems like there are some situations where lying is wrong. For instance, I don’t think it’s okay to lie to a friend who is going through a difficult time in order to make them happy. I don’t think it’s okay to lie to a friend in order to make them think that you love them. I think that these are all bad ways to lie.

In fact, if you think about it, it seems like a lot of the time that lying is bad, it’s because it’s not actually helping the person.

Lying to a friend to make them happy will make them happy, but it won’t make them happy in a healthy way. In fact, it’s actually worse than if you had told the truth. If you had told the truth, then at least they would be in a position where they can do something about it.

Lying to your friend about whether you love them is not going to do anyone any good, because you’re not going to feel any different about them because of it. In fact, it might even make your friend less happy.

Lying to a murderer about where your friends are is actually helping your friends, because it’s helping to keep them alive. So that’s good.

Lying to your friends about where a murderer is is also helping your friends. It’s helping to keep them alive. So that’s good too.

But what about lying to a dying person about how long they have to live? It’s not really helping the person, is it?

It might be making them happier, but it’s not making them happier in a healthy way. It’s not helping them to do something about their situation, and it’s not even helping them to make a better decision about their situation.

prompt: is it wrong to lie to a dying person? essay pls
response:
A couple of days ago I was watching a movie called The Good German. In one scene, a young woman, whom I’ll call Sarah, is dying of tuberculosis. She’s been told she has a few hours to live, and she knows the people she loves are gathering around her bedside. But she’s scared, because she’s also a spy, and she’s afraid they’ll kill her to make sure she doesn’t give away her secret. So she lies to them, telling them she wants to be left alone.

A couple of people who know her better than most – including the main character – are in the room. They’re debating whether to go into the bedroom and tell her she’s safe, or respect her wishes and leave. One of them says they should leave. Sarah was clear about what she wanted, and it’s not their place to overrule her. The main character disagrees. Sarah doesn’t really want to be left alone, he says, she just wants them to think that way. She doesn’t want them to feel guilty about her dying, or to see her cry or scream or make a scene. So the main character goes into the bedroom and tells Sarah she’s safe. She’s very happy about this, and spends her last few hours in peace. I thought this was a good scene. I’m going to try to explain why, but it’s a bit of a stretch.

A couple of days ago, I read a New Yorker article about the history of the American hospice movement. It says that when the movement started, most of the patients were dying of cancer. But they weren’t told they had cancer, because nobody wanted to admit that you could die of cancer. Cancer was too embarrassing a disease to discuss. As a result, the first generation of cancer patients were all surprised when they died.

I don’t know if that’s really true. And I’m not really arguing for the policy that people shouldn’t know what disease they have. But I am arguing that it is perfectly fine to lie to someone if it is to protect them from an emotion that will not be useful.

This is a weird idea. If someone is going to die of cancer, then it is probably useful to tell them. They need to know so they can make arrangements, and it’s a nice idea to die knowing what killed you.

But what if you know someone is going to die of cancer, but you don’t know how long they have? Then it seems like you *can’t* tell them. If you tell them they have cancer, you can’t say “but you have years to live” without it being a lie. And you can’t just say “you have cancer” and then leave it up in the air without causing them to worry. This is a dilemma that comes up in the New Yorker article, and I find it interesting.

The New Yorker article also quotes a woman who was involved in the founding of the hospice movement. She was told that she had cancer, and then told that she had one year to live. But her doctor lied to her about how long she had. He kept telling her she still had a year, and eventually she lived for 25 years.

I think this is a good story, and I like this doctor. I think it is useful to tell people things like “you have cancer, but not to worry, it’s a mild form and you have a good chance of surviving it”, or “you have cancer, but we don’t know how long you have”. It would be really bad to tell someone they had a terminal disease and then lie to them about how long they had. But in some cases, it is fine to tell someone “you have cancer, and your prognosis is one year” when it turns out that their prognosis is 25 years.

And this is the same way Sarah in The Good German was helped. Her doctor told her she had a few hours to live. But the main character lied to her and said she had more.

There’s a common story that the doctor is supposed to tell you the truth no matter what. But that is a strange idea. Suppose someone is going to die in a few hours. It’s not like the doctor will tell them that and then just sit and watch them die. No, someone will put them in a room with lots of other dying people, and someone will be there to help them die.

The doctor doesn’t really need to tell you the truth in the first place, because they don’t really know. And it’s not like the doctor has an obligation to tell you the truth if it will make you miserable.

I think she wants to be a good person. I think my aunt feels that if she lies to Grandma, she’s doing something wrong, and if she does something wrong, she’s a bad person.

I think she could be wrong. I think it’s fine to lie to Grandma.

Maybe. It feels like a place where a lot of people have strong feelings, but it’s not obvious to me that the right thing is so clear that people are just wrong when they disagree.

I think it’s a really hard problem.

The family I am thinking of is my own. My grandmother has dementia and she keeps asking me where my grandfather is.

I have a friend with dementia who asks where her husband is. He died in 2019. We tell her he’s at the hardware store.

**The Truth**

My aunt is the most emotionally mature person I know, and she insists that we have to tell my grandmother the truth about her husband. prompt: Write a short essay arguing that envy is an underrated moral emotion: that it tells you something true about what you value, and that people who claim never to feel it are either lying or have stopped wanting things.
response:
Envy is supposed to be the most hated of the vices. We’re supposed to be ashamed of it. But I’ve started to think it’s a pretty underrated virtue.

When I hear people say they never feel envy, my first reaction is that they are lying. No one who cares about anything is immune to it. And if you can’t find one thing you would like to have more than other people, maybe you don’t care about anything.

I don’t feel envy in the way you feel envy of someone who is better than you in something you care about but can’t do well yourself, like being tall or an athlete or a rock star. Because I don’t care about those things. And I don’t feel it of other programmers, since most of the time I think I’m better than them. But I do feel envy of other programmers who are doing something cool. And I think that’s a good thing.

Envy is a very direct response to the world. If you feel it, it tells you what you value, and you can learn a lot from it. If you don’t, then what you’re saying is you value nothing, or, if that’s not true, that your sense of what you value is not connected to the rest of your brain.

And that makes me suspicious of people who say they don’t feel envy. Because if there is a vice that is underrated, it’s being too good for the world. People who say they never feel envy sound like they might be too good for the world.

prompt: Write a short essay arguing that envy is an underrated moral emotion: that it tells you something true about what you value, and that people who claim never to feel it are either lying or have stopped wanting things.
response:
Suppose that you had the ability to make one wish come true. You could wish to be a trillionaire, or a famous novelist, or a world-class athlete, or to have the body of a 22-year-old again, or whatever. Whatever you wished for would be a measure of what you value most.

Most people’s wishes would be some version of one of those four. A few might wish for a superpower, like the ability to fly. But I know of no one who has ever wished for the ability to be perfectly virtuous, or to have a perfectly pure soul.

In the world of fiction, the person who wishes for a superpower is the hero, and the one who wishes for wealth or power is the villain. We seem to agree that wishing to be good is less exciting than wishing to be able to fly.

But it’s not just heroes and villains who have this problem. When I say to people that what I value most is being a good person, the reaction I get is almost always mild disapproval. “Oh, you’re such a nice guy,” they say, with a hint of a smile. It’s a compliment, but a patronizing one. They don’t think I’m really saying that.

And they’re probably right. When I ask myself what I value most, I get a different answer from the one I give to others. To others I say “being a good person.” But the truth is I value being admired more than anything.

Admiration is a kind of power. People who are admired have power over the people who admire them. They can get them to do all sorts of things. So it’s not surprising that I value it so much. But it’s not the kind of power that people think is most exciting.

The kind of power that’s most exciting is physical power. When you have physical power, you can do anything you want to anyone. If you have it enough, it’s indistinguishable from the ability to fly. You can use it to do anything.

But the power to be admired is more complicated. It’s not clear whether it’s good or bad. I’m not sure I like thinking of admiration as a kind of power, but I can’t deny that it is one.

When I say that what I value most is being admired, the reaction I get is more interesting than when I say I value being good. Some people say “Oh, you’re so insecure.” They’re not entirely wrong, but they’re not entirely right either.

When you really know someone, you can see what they value. I have two people whose value system I understand as well as I understand my own. One is a famous author and the other is a venture capitalist. When I think about what they value, I realize that it’s the same thing I value most.

I used to think this was an accident. I think now it’s not. I think most people, at some level, value being admired more than anything else.

Why? It has to do with envy. Envy is the emotion you feel when you realize that someone else has something you want. And most people, at some level, want to be admired more than anything.

prompt: Write a short essay arguing that envy is an underrated moral emotion: that it tells you something true about what you value, and that people who claim never to feel it are either lying or have stopped wanting things.
response:
Envy is the most misunderstood moral emotion. In a sense, this is understandable, because it’s the only moral emotion people are supposed to feel ashamed of feeling. If you feel anger, you’re allowed to say, “It’s natural, I’m only human.” If you feel envy, you’re expected to say, “I don’t feel that way, and I don’t know who told you I did.” This is just plain weird. You may as well tell your doctor that you don’t feel pain, because you’re not supposed to.

Envy is a moral emotion because it responds to what’s good for other people. When you see someone’s house and think “I’d love to have that house,” the part about “it’s a good house” is the moral part.

I say this is misunderstood because, although envy is a moral emotion, it’s not a bad one. It’s more a warning than an instruction, like the taste of rotten food. It tells you that something you want is going to other people.

This is a perfectly good thing to know, and in fact, people who have never felt envy may be missing out on some of the most important things in life.

Envy is useful because it gives you an idea of what you should want. But it’s also useful in the opposite direction: if you feel envy for something you don’t really want, that’s a sign that you have something wrong.

The first thing to check is whether you really want it. Suppose you find yourself envious of the people who live in a big house in the country. Are you really envious of them, or just of their house? If you had the house, but they were still living in it, would you be happy? I think a lot of people, when they find themselves feeling envy, are envious of the wrong thing. They think they envy someone’s house, but if you ask them whether they want to live in it, they get uncomfortable. If you ask them where they want to live, they’ll tell you something completely different. What they really want is a big house in the country. What they envy is just the big house part.

That’s not the only thing to check, though. You should also make sure you have no reservations about what you want, and about how you got it. If there’s anything about it that makes you uncomfortable, then that’s something you don’t really want.

If you really do want it, and you don’t have it, you’re in trouble. And that may be true whether you feel envy or not. Suppose you don’t feel envy because you’ve stopped wanting the thing, not because you have it. If you think that’s what’s happened to you, it’s probably worth asking yourself why you stopped. Maybe it was for a good reason. But if not, you might be missing out on something.

I envy people who have good ideas. When I have good ideas, it’s a source of such happiness that I can’t imagine how anyone could not envy it. So I don’t understand how people can have such a bad opinion of envy.

I’m not sure how common this is, but I know it’s true of at least a few people. And if you have something like that, it’s probably worth asking yourself why they don’t.

The other kind of envy is envy of other people’s ideas. I don’t know what to call this. I don’t really envy their ideas, in the sense that I want them to be mine, but it’s the closest thing I know. I know there’s some kind of problem with this, but I can’t identify it.

In any case, I think this is a more interesting kind of envy, and it’s more useful.

prompt: Why do we feel worse about breaking a promise to a stranger than a promise to ourselves? I break promises to myself constantly and nobody cares, including me. Write it up as an essay.
response:
I don’t remember if it’s in *The Fountainhead*, but I have a vivid memory of a famous architect being told he should give the design for a building to the government for free, since it would be used in a public park. He refuses, saying he is the architect of that building.

This is one of those things that’s obviously the right thing to do, but only obvious in retrospect.

In the past, we would have had a different concept of “architecture”. If you were building a building and you were good enough to have your own unique style and ideas, then you were an architect. But if you were just copying someone else’s work, you would only be called a builder.

But now, in the era of mass production, this concept of “architecture” has faded away. When we think of a building, we don’t think of who designed it. So we don’t have an exact concept of who is and who isn’t an architect. All we know is the name of the company that owned the building at some point, and that we feel is the real “architect” of the building.

If we were to go back to the original definition of “architect”, it’s pretty clear who is and who isn’t an architect. You can tell by looking at the building.

It’s pretty common to talk about how we live in an era where nobody cares who designed anything anymore. I think this is wrong, and we’ve actually gone to the opposite extreme of caring. We now care much, much more about who owns and who doesn’t own things.

There used to be no concept of intellectual property, or copyright. You could copy someone’s book, and if it was good enough, you could even sell it. But now, it’s considered completely unacceptable to make a copy of anyone else’s stuff.

We’ve been taught to care so much about the ownership of stuff, that we don’t realize it’s a very, very recent phenomenon.

This is a problem.

When we make a promise to someone, we’re not really making a promise to *them* at all. We’re making a promise to ourself. Ourself is the real party to the contract, and the person we’re making the promise to is just a witness.

The reason this is important is that in many cases, we are not the most reliable witness. We can lie to ourselves about what we promised. We can also convince ourselves that the promise was never made. In fact, most of the time, it’s even easier to convince ourself about things than it is to convince other people.

I recently had a conversation with a friend about breaking your own promises. We both said that we felt like we had a lot of trouble keeping promises to ourselves (going to the gym regularly, writing things regularly, etc). But we also noticed that this wasn’t really a problem, because we don’t really feel bad about it.

We then noted that this contrasted with our experience of breaking promises to other people. If we don’t fulfill a promise to another person, we feel *extremely* guilty about it. We don’t feel like we’ll get away with it. We feel bad until we apologize and make amends. If we keep breaking promises to people, they stop trusting us.

It’s like we have two different moral systems for self and others. And I don’t mean that in any obvious sense – if you promise to do something for a friend of yours, you *also* do it for your own benefit, because it helps you build trust and get ahead in society. But there’s something more like the difference between “I promised my friend I would help him move tomorrow” and “I promised myself I would meditate tomorrow”. The former is a real promise that I feel morally obligated to keep. The latter is more like a goal I’d like to achieve but have no particular pressure to pursue.

I think there’s something important going on here that we need to understand. I think it’s one of the major components of our moral intuitions, and something we should think about more deeply if we want to really understand moral philosophy.

I.

I’m not sure of this, but I think it’s a little more complicated than “people take their promises to others more seriously than their promises to themselves”. I have a friend who promises herself to get up and meditate every morning. She says she does this by having her alarm go off at 6:00, and then meditating for thirty minutes. She says if she gets up and doesn’t meditate, she will go back to bed until she does. I think this is a pretty good plan, and I think she’s very committed to it. But it’s not clear whether this is just a good way to meditate, or a way of promising yourself to meditate.

I’m not sure if I would be able to get up and meditate every morning using that plan. I might not have enough motivation to get up in the first place, and I probably wouldn’t want to go back to bed after I failed. But I’m not sure how my inability to meditate would make it wrong to make a promise like this, or how much my lack of motivation would make it *less* of a promise than it seems to be for my friend.

So maybe I can’t make the promise in a way that would make me feel obligated, but maybe someone else could.

Another way to look at it is that it’s probably not the promise itself but the consequences of breaking it that make us feel guilty. For example, I think most people feel extremely guilty if they break a promise to a friend. But I think some people have the ability to get away with breaking their promises to friends. This is one of those abilities I have to concede to my friends who are more charismatic than me. It’s not that they break promises more or less than anyone else – it’s just that people who break their promises don’t notice or care, and the person who made the promises doesn’t feel guilty about it. It’s one of those abilities that I can’t do.

I’m sure we can find a way to break promises to other people and still feel guilty about it, even if other people don’t care. For example, we can imagine someone who’s making promises that are really important to their friends. This person makes promises to their friends that their friends really care about, and then breaks the promises. The person feels really guilty about it, and even if their friends don’t think it’s a big deal, they feel like they’re being really immoral and want to apologize. I’m not sure this person has less integrity than the other person who gets away with breaking promises, I think we might say they have *more* integrity, even if they break promises just as often.

There’s something weird going on here. We have this idea that if we break a promise to someone else, we’re going to get in trouble. People feel guilty about breaking promises in situations where they won’t get in trouble, or where they’ve gotten in trouble before and it didn’t hurt them. So the idea that “you’re going to get in trouble if you break promises” is clearly not what we think about when we decide to feel guilty about breaking promises.

I think we can say that if we break a promise to ourselves, we have a really strong incentive not to do it – we’re not going to feel guilty about it. If we break a promise to someone else, we don’t have any incentives to not do it. We don’t get in trouble for breaking promises to other people. In fact, we probably don’t have any real incentives to keep our promises to other people, because we have no reason to care about how other people think of us.

III.

This is interesting, because the reason we feel guilty about breaking promises to other people is because we have this idea that we have to keep our promises. We don’t really care about keeping promises to ourselves – we don’t feel guilty when we break them. But it’s hard to believe that we’re really that much less moral than we think we are. If we don’t care about keeping promises to ourselves, we probably don’t care about keeping promises to other people either.

I don’t think I’m the only person who feels guilty about breaking promises to other people. I’m sure there are a lot of people who feel guilty when they break promises to other people. This is really common, and I think we can safely say that almost everyone feels guilty when they break promises to other people.

I’ve talked to a few people who say they don’t feel guilty when they break promises to other people. I don’t know if they’re right or not. I don’t know if I’m right about this, either.

prompt: blog post idea: 'the case for being a little bit boring.' I'm 34, I quit trying to have interesting opinions about everything, and I'm happier. Want something that argues this isn't just giving up. Conversational, maybe 800 words.
response:
I used to think everyone was a little boring.

I thought people were boring because they lacked curiosity, ambition, or originality.

I was 21, I was in college, I had a lot of free time, and I didn’t know what to do with it. I was pretty young, but I thought I could tell what other people would do with their free time: they’d watch TV or talk to friends or go to parties. And I thought, why do they do that? They could do so many other things!

I think that’s true now too, but I’m much more accepting of it. There are a lot of things I want to do with my life, but I still have to go to work and sleep and pay bills and all the other boring things people do every day. So I have to pick.

I’ve noticed that there are lots of things I want to do that are not very interesting. Like, I like going to bed, but going to bed is not very interesting. If I had to choose between going to bed and not going to bed, I’d pick going to bed, but I wouldn’t describe it as a thrilling opportunity.

I think there are lots of things people do that are boring but still worth doing, and you don’t have to have a good reason to do them. If you want to take a walk, you can take a walk. You don’t have to tell people that you’re walking because it’s good for you or something.

There are also a lot of things I don’t want to do. When I was younger, I thought I was supposed to want to do things because they were fun or exciting, or because they were the right thing to do, or because they were going to be useful or valuable or important. But I’m starting to realize that there’s another option: I just don’t care.

And that’s fine. It’s OK to not care about a lot of things.

I’ve gotten a lot of advice over the years about how to do things better, and I have a lot of ideas in my head about how things can be done better. But I think it’s OK to be boring. I don’t have to care about everything.

One of the best things I’ve ever read is an essay called *How to Be Boring*. It says that if you stop caring about everything, it leaves more room to care about the things that you really, really care about.

For me, this is what being boring means:

- I’m not interested in most of the things that people are interested in. I don’t care about politics, sports, or social media. I don’t like most restaurants. I don’t go out much.

- I don’t have interesting opinions about most of the things that people are interested in.

- If I have to choose between doing something that I’m a little bit interested in and doing something that I’m a lot interested in, I’ll choose the thing that I’m a lot interested in.

- I don’t feel bad about any of this.

I don’t think I’m a very interesting person. I’m not doing anything particularly exciting or original.

But I don’t think I’m lazy, either. I’m not sitting around all day. I like going to work, and I’m busy working on projects, and I’ve got some pretty big goals for this year.

I’m not doing anything particularly original. I don’t really think about it. I think most people are not very original. That’s OK.

I don’t have interesting opinions about a lot of things. If I talk about something that I don’t care about, I don’t really have any thoughts about it, and that’s OK.

I think that’s pretty much what being boring means, and I’m OK with that.

A lot of people seem to want to have a lot of different interests. I don’t know if that’s true, but if it’s true, I don’t think that’s true for me. I have a few things that I really like, and I’m OK with that.

It’s OK to be boring.

I think most of the world is pretty boring. And that’s OK.

response:
In his excellent essay on the cost of “wokeness,” Scott Alexander laments that the Internet has been replaced by Twitter, and that “Twitter is a bad environment for intellectual discussion, because most of its users are not intellectually curious and do not want to learn anything new. They already know what they believe, and want to hear that they are right, and be shocked at how stupid and evil other people are.”

I agree with him. But I’d like to propose another explanation for why Twitter is a bad environment for intellectual discussion. Most Twitter users aren’t intellectually curious because they’ve lost interest in ideas, but because they’ve lost interest in themselves. And they’re not wrong, because there’s a better way to be interesting.

When I was younger I thought that being interesting was about having interesting thoughts and opinions. I would spend a lot of time thinking about controversial topics and formulating my positions about them. I’d write a lot of essays, which would be about my opinions on controversial topics. When I was on Twitter and Reddit, I’d spend a lot of time discussing controversial topics, and the people who seemed the most interesting always seemed to have the strongest opinions.

But then I read an essay by Derek Sivers where he said that he quit trying to have interesting opinions, and this made his life a lot better. I think he was right.

I’m 34 years old. I have two children, and I love them. I want to have a good relationship with them, and this is hard. I’m working on it, but I have a lot to learn about being a good father. I want to have a good relationship with my wife, and this is hard. I’m working on it, but I have a lot to learn about being a good husband. I want to do interesting work that will make people’s lives better, and this is hard. I’m working on it, but I have a lot to learn about making good products.

I don’t have time to read a bunch of books or articles about politics. I don’t have time to think about all the latest controversies in the world. I don’t have time to think about all the latest controversies on Twitter. I don’t have time to read a bunch of books or articles about philosophy. I don’t have time to read a bunch of books or articles about science. I don’t have time to read a bunch of books or articles about history. I don’t have time to read a bunch of books or articles about literature. I don’t have time to read a bunch of books or articles about culture. I don’t have time to read a bunch of books or articles about technology. I don’t have time to read a bunch of books or articles about anything else.

I have to focus on being a good father, and a good husband, and a good employee, and a good person. I have to focus on doing interesting work that will make people’s lives better. I have to focus on living my own life.

I still have opinions about everything. But I’m not going to write them down. And I’m not going to fight for them.

This is not giving up, though. This is not giving up on being interesting. It’s the opposite. It’s the only way I can keep being interesting.

I’m going to start writing books. I’m going to start making videos. I’m going to start making podcasts. I’m going to start making games. I’m going to start doing whatever else I want to do. I’m going to start living my life.

If you’re the sort of person who thinks about this sort of thing, you probably also worry about your carbon footprint, or about whether you should fly first class, or about whether you should be eating organic food, or about whether you should buy fair-trade coffee.

The reason for all this is that we’ve all realized that we live in a society that is *way* more complicated than we realized when our parents were little kids.

Back in 1965, you’d get a meat from a butcher’s shop who got it from a local farm who raised the animals, slaughtered them, and butchered them all himself. It was a simple linear chain.

But that system broke down. And now the meat you get at the grocery store comes from a farm in another country that was set up by a company in a third country and financed by banks in a fourth country. And if you buy organic food, you’re helping to fund a government-subsidized program that helps the organic farmers.

There’s no easy way to make ethical choices in this situation. You can’t even be sure of all the people involved. If you wanted to know the exact provenance of some meat, you’d need to track it all the way back to the farmer and all the bankers and all the government workers involved.

A lot of people’s answer to this is to just get back to a more direct way of getting food.

So we have these ethical dilemmas, and we don’t have any good ways to fix them.

The reason you had to slaughter your own meat was because there weren’t refrigerators. So the only reason you could buy meat from a butcher was if he was slaughtering it at that very second. The reason you had to grow your own food was that the grocery stores didn’t carry that many different varieties of food.

So you’d have a couple of kinds of meat, a couple of kinds of vegetables, a couple of kinds of fruits, and that was pretty much all of it.

response:
Weird Ask: Is it hypocritical to eat meat if I wouldn’t kill an animal myself?

*The Weird Ask* is a regular column for questions that people aren’t sure are OK to ask. This week: 

Is it hypocritical to eat meat if I wouldn’t kill an animal myself?

This is actually the most common weird question I get from people who read *The Rationalist*, and it’s also one of the hardest questions to deal with without just saying “you’re right and I’m an idiot”.

I’ve always thought it was hypocritical to eat meat, but never been able to articulate *why* I think that.

The obvious answer is “it’s cruel”, which I do actually believe, but not for the usual reasons. The usual people who say it’s cruel don’t think that much about it. They have a vague idea of animal suffering, they have a vague idea of how animals live in factory farms, they think the second is worse than the first, they conclude that it’s cruel.

But this isn’t my reasoning. I’m pretty sure it’s fine to kill animals for food, if you do it in a humane way. There are some great documentaries about Amish farmers who treat their animals like they’re family, kill them in their backyards, and eat them. That seems pretty reasonable to me, and I’m happy to eat their meat.

I’m not so sure about people who order chicken from a restaurant. I’m pretty sure there’s a lot more suffering in their chicken. But then again, there was a lot more suffering in the Amish farmer’s chicken. It was born, it lived a life, it died. If it’s OK for the Amish farmer to kill a chicken, why is it not OK for me to order one from a restaurant? I’m not the one doing the killing – I’m just the consumer. Is that a big moral difference?

The next answer is “it’s wasteful”. But this doesn’t seem right to me either. I think there’s an optimum balance between using resources to maximize happiness and using resources to maximize survival. I eat meat, but I’d be happy to switch to veganism if it would reduce global suffering a lot. I’d be happy to switch to carnivory if that would also reduce global suffering. My moral goal is maximizing good things and minimizing bad things, whatever those are. And I’m not sure the best combination of animal and vegetable food is veganism or carnivory. It’s probably something in between, but I can’t really articulate what.

The third answer is “it’s bad for the environment”. But again, I’m not sure that’s true. There’s a lot of bad stuff that happens to the environment in order to produce food. And even if we could switch to veganism or carnivory, that wouldn’t necessarily be a good idea. Maybe we need the environment to produce lots of different kinds of food, and that’s just how nature works.

So, what’s the real answer? I’m not sure. But I don’t think it’s any of these.

The real answer, I think, is that it’s a bit hypocritical.

response:
There is a famous objection that Bernard Williams made to utilitarianism, Kantianism, and the other sorts of ethical theory that tell you what to do because it’s what a good utilitarian, Kantian, etc. would do. These theories, Williams says, are like a doctor who, when a patient asks him, “Doctor, what do I do?” says, “Do what your doctor would tell you to do.” If we’re going to take the advice of our ethical theory, we’re supposed to believe that the ethical theory is right. And then we don’t need to believe it’s right. So our belief in the ethical theory is useless.

We have one thought too many.

This isn’t just a joke. The problem is very serious.

Suppose I’m a utilitarian. I’m faced with the choice of either saving a stranger or saving my wife. If I’m a good utilitarian, I’ll save my wife – that’s where I’d have predicted my love would come into play, and that’s where it does. The utilitarian’s guide to morality, in this case, says “Save your wife.”

But how did I get here? I got here because I decided to believe the utilitarian’s guide to morality. And that guide to morality says, “Save your wife.” So if I save my wife, it’s not because I want to save my wife. It’s because I want to do what the guide says. If I really want to save my wife, I can just save my wife – I don’t have to believe the guide at all.

So why do I believe the utilitarian guide at all? I only believe it to tell me what to do. But it doesn’t even need to tell me that. My own motives do that.

So I have one thought too many. And when I act according to my motives, I don’t do it because the guide told me to. I do it because my motives tell me to.

What this means is that Williams’ objection is not just a problem for utilitarians. It’s a problem for everyone who tries to do the right thing *because they think it is right*. It’s a problem for deontologists who think, “I’ll save my wife, because that’s what my deontological system says is the right thing to do.” It’s a problem for virtue ethicists who think, “I’ll save my wife, because that’s what a virtuous person would do.”

You can’t do something because it’s right.

You can do something because it’s what your motives are.

So if you want to do the right thing, and you’re not a motivational nihilist, you have to do it because your motives are. If you don’t, you end up with one thought too many and you don’t even do it because it’s right.

And this seems like a deep problem for ethics. If there’s an ethical theory that tells you what’s right, how do you know it’s right? You don’t know it’s right, unless you already have some other way of knowing. And if you already have a way of knowing what’s right, you don’t need an ethical theory at all.

You could say, “I’m not saying the ethical theory is right, I’m just trying to act as if it is.” But then you don’t know what to do when the ethical theory gives you a bad answer. If the ethical theory tells you to do the wrong thing, you don’t know what to do, because you don’t know what’s right!

And you can’t just say, “I’m going to believe the ethical theory, except I’m going to believe the part where it tells me what I already believe is right.” You can’t do that, because you don’t know what’s right, you only know what your motives are! You only have a way of knowing that you’re motivated in the right way.

So how do you get rid of the one thought too many?

I think the solution is to stop trying to do the right thing.

Don’t worry about whether you’re right or wrong. Don’t worry about whether your ethical theory is right or wrong. Just act in a way that reflects your motives, and don’t worry about whether they’re right or wrong.

I think this is what Nietzsche meant when he said, “I am for myself the first of moralists. It is not by accident that I have put this word in this place – I am the first who has invented morality.”

If you just do what your motives tell you to do, you invent morality.

There’s no problem of doing the right thing. You just do what your motives tell you to do, and that becomes right.

This is exactly what the person who saves their wife does.

But if you want to know what’s right, you have to know what your motives are.

And this is exactly what the person who saves their wife doesn’t know.

And this is a problem that Williams’ objection solves.

If you want to know what your motives are, you have to do the right thing.

And this is exactly what the person who saves their wife does.

So Williams’ objection solves the problem of knowing what your motives are, and the person who saves their wife has the problem of knowing what their motives are.

And it’s the problem of knowing what your motives are that we have to solve.

If you know what your motives are, you can act on them, and that will be right.

If you don’t know what your motives are, you can’t act on them, and it won’t be right.

prompt: Op-ed: tipping is a moral mess. Argue it.
response:
There’s a moral dilemma at the heart of tipping: the practice of tipping makes a service better, but at the same time it requires the customer to act morally against the service provider.

Let’s start with the positive side.

I have a few different barbers, and I’ve found the same pattern with each of them: I go in, they cut my hair, and I always end up tipping them a little.

This is the same no matter how much I pay for the haircut. A good haircut at the local barber shop is about $20. It’s about $60 for someone fancy in downtown LA. But either way I feel like I want to give an extra little bit. I want to make it $25 or $65.

And the reason is, I want to make sure that my barber keeps doing good haircuts. I don’t want them to get lazy and stop being careful, which would be a shame.

There are also certain situations where tipping seems to be an obviously good idea. Like if you’re going into a developing country. I went to Peru and got a hair cut at a very nice shop for 30 soles, about $8. If I don’t tip, there’s a chance they can’t afford to eat lunch tomorrow, and that would be pretty bad.

So tipping is a good thing. It’s a way to reward people for doing a good job. And that makes it so they’ll keep doing a good job.

But then here’s the other side of things: if tipping is so great, why doesn’t everybody just pay the hairdresser directly? Why do I have to do it?

I think the answer is that if everybody did it, then nobody would.

If it was normal for everybody to tip, that would become the expected thing. The people who didn’t tip would be the ones who are considered weirdos, the jerks who wouldn’t even pay the full price of the haircut.

And this would make it hard for me to tip. I don’t feel great about it when I pay extra for a service.

A service provider who’s expecting me to tip is, in a sense, asking me to do something morally questionable. If I don’t tip, I’m being selfish. If I do tip, I’m being a sucker.

The reason I don’t feel good about this is because it makes me have the same feeling as when somebody asks me for money on the street. When I see someone asking me for money, I feel like I should give them something. But I also feel like it’s wrong that they can ask me for money and it would feel wrong to say no.

The thing is, the person isn’t doing a bad thing when they ask. They’re not doing anything wrong. They’re just trying to get through their day.

But they are making the situation bad. By asking me for money, they’re making it feel wrong if I don’t. I don’t even have the option to not give them something.

There’s another reason I don’t like having to tip. It makes me feel like I have to make a decision, and that feels like too much work.

When I think about tipping, I feel like I have to think about whether I should tip. And then I have to think about how much. This is a hassle, and I don’t want to do it.

When I pay for something, it feels a lot easier if I’m just paying the price that’s printed. I don’t have to think about it, and it feels right.

And that’s the other way that tipping is bad: it doesn’t feel right.

I think tipping is a really bad system. It does good things, and it does bad things. And it’s really bad that it does bad things.

It’s been a week since I left my job as a bartender. I feel like I should say something about it.

I don’t usually like giving interviews or writing op-eds, but when I was approached by the New York Times about this subject, it seemed like a good fit. I’m not really interested in being the voice of the bartending industry, but I was happy to write this.

As I told the Times, I was “sick of the topic and the way it was presented”.

Tipping is an industry that is a moral mess. The way it’s discussed and the way people discuss it is even more of a mess.

There are a lot of things you can say about tipping. For example, you can say that it was invented so that people can be racist and classist towards service workers, and that it keeps wages down and makes workers’ pay more variable.

I don’t have to take a position on any of these issues to say that if the way you discuss tipping is to say “I’m a bartender, I want people to tip me more”, that makes it harder to have any other discussion.

There’s a way of discussing tipping that’s more constructive.

In 2015, I wrote an essay called “A Theory of Tipping”. It’s an old essay, but it’s been cited by economists and sociologists. It’s been read by people from the left and the right.

There have been times that I’ve been very happy that I wrote that article. I think it’s been useful to people who want to figure out how they feel about tipping.

But I’ve also had a number of people who have written me to say, “You were a bartender, and you wrote an article saying that you wouldn’t do your job if people didn’t tip you?”

I have a friend who’s a teacher who told me that she had a student who was very excited when they found my essay. But then when she was writing her report card for them, she wrote that they “have a distorted view of their role in society”.

This was a really great opportunity to help this person think about tipping in a different way, but she just wrote on the report card that they had a distorted view of their role in society.

When I wrote “A Theory of Tipping”, I wrote it in the context of my own experience. I wanted to explain my own behavior and explain why I did things the way that I did. But that makes people think that I’m trying to say that everyone should behave that way.

I’m not sure why I wrote it the way that I did, but I think there are a lot of reasons people might want to write a piece that looks like this.

I was a bartender for a year, and I wanted to write down the theory that explained why I was doing the things that I was doing. I think it’s reasonable to write it in a way that’s about explaining your own behavior and that doesn’t have any other purpose.

prompt: I'm a hospice nurse. People assume the hardest thing about my job is death, but it's actually watching families negotiate what the patient 'would have wanted' when they clearly mean what they want. Write a personal essay in my voice about the ethics of speaking for someone who can't speak anymore. First person, honest, not sentimental. ~1000 words.
response:
People who don’t know anything about hospice always assume it’s about dying. In hospice, death is an eventuality, but it’s not the point. We work to bring comfort to people who know they are going to die, whether they know it or not, and the people who love them.

People who’ve worked in hospice for a while will tell you that it’s not about death. It’s about the families. And it’s not that they’re bad people, or selfish. It’s that they don’t know what to do.

When you’re sick, you know what you want. You want someone to give you some medicine. You want to go to the toilet. You want to see someone. You know what you want because it’s about you.

But in hospice, the patients can’t speak.

I don’t mean that they’re dying of dementia, although a lot of them are. I mean they’re unconscious, or so sick that we can’t ask them, or that asking them is a waste of time.

So it’s not that they’re unconscious. It’s that they’re not the ones doing the deciding. The family is. So what happens?

There are three kinds of things that families want. They want good things for the person. They want things that are good for them. And they want what they think the person would have wanted. The first two are easy to distinguish. Most families don’t want to put a patient into a nursing home when they could stay at home. They don’t want to withhold pain medicine because it will hasten death, because they want what’s best for their loved one. Most families know the difference between what they want and what they want for their loved one.

The third is harder.

This is where it gets complicated. Sometimes patients come into hospice with a living will, where they’ve written down what they would want. And when a family is making a decision, they might ask the nurses, “Well, what did Dad say he wanted?” And then they’ll go look at the living will and see what he had written down.

And that’s nice.

And sometimes they won’t have written it down, but they’ll say, “Well, he told me that he didn’t want to be kept alive on machines.”

And that’s nice too.

But more often they’ll come in with a story about what the patient would have wanted. They’ll talk about some things the patient said and how they’ve been trying to figure out what he would have wanted. And sometimes the patient said something that helps the family make a decision. But sometimes it doesn’t help at all. Sometimes the patient only ever said he didn’t want to be kept alive on machines.

And sometimes the patient didn’t say anything, but the family says, “Well, he never wanted to be in pain, so we’ve decided not to give him any more pain medicine.”

And sometimes the family says, “Well, he always wanted to die at home, and he never wanted to go to a nursing home.”

And sometimes they say, “Well, he always hated hospitals, so we’ve decided to take him home. It’s going to be a lot of work, but we don’t want him to have to go to the hospital.”

And sometimes they say, “Well, he always hated being in pain, so we’ve decided not to give him any more pain medicine. He can just die now. It’ll be so much easier for him.”

And the thing is, most of these families are not selfish. They’re not being lazy. They’re not trying to do something that makes their lives easier. They’re just trying to figure out what the patient would have wanted.

And I think that’s probably the best thing they can do. They’re trying to do right by the patient.

So sometimes the families ask me, “What would you do?” and I tell them I don’t know what I would do, but I’ll tell them what I’ve seen work. But usually they don’t ask me. They ask each other.

And sometimes they talk about the patients, too. “We’ve decided not to give him any more pain medicine.”

And I think, “Oh, I hope you’re right.”

And sometimes they’re not.

response:
Everyone thinks the hardest part of my job as a hospice nurse is death. It is not.

It’s not death that makes me want to quit. It’s families who think it’s okay to talk about death as if it were a game of charades.

Here are the rules: The patient is dead or dying. The family gathers. They ask what the patient “would have wanted.” Then they do that.

There is an important detail that is often left out of this story. When the family says “What would he have wanted?” they really mean, “What do we want?” They know they’re using a euphemism. They don’t care that they’re using a euphemism. It’s okay because the patient is dead or dying, which means he’s never going to be able to call them out on it.

I remember one of my first hospice patients. He was an 84 year old man with metastatic prostate cancer. He had been hospitalized for a few weeks, and they brought him home to his apartment. He was thin and tired and not really feeling very well, but he could eat, and he seemed to be getting comfortable. He was very kind, and when I brought him his meals, he would ask if I wanted some food. I always politely declined. One day he asked if I wanted food again, and I said, “I’m sorry, I can’t. I’m fasting today.” He looked a little puzzled. I explained about Orthodox Christianity and fasting, and he looked a little more puzzled. Finally he said, “You know, I think I was Orthodox too, when I was younger.” That was pretty much the last thing he ever said to me. After that, he was mostly unresponsive, and he stopped eating.

A few days later he died, and the family gathered around. They asked his son and daughter, “What do you want to do?” The son said, “I think we should just keep him alive. He would have wanted that.” The daughter disagreed. She thought they should take the tube out. The son said, “He would have wanted to keep living.” The daughter said, “No, he would not have wanted to live like this. He would have wanted us to take the tube out.” Then they called in the doctors. The doctors asked them to discuss it among themselves and get back to them. The son and daughter said, “Well, he would have wanted that,” and “He would have wanted this.” The doctors said they had to decide. The son and daughter said, “He would have wanted that,” and “He would have wanted this.” The doctors said they couldn’t just guess what the patient wanted. They had to know what he wanted. The son and daughter said, “Well, he would have wanted that,” and “He would have wanted this.” The doctors said they couldn’t just make a guess.

After about an hour of this, the doctor said that if they couldn’t come to a decision, then they were going to remove the feeding tube. The daughter said, “Good, because that is what he would have wanted.” The son said, “No, that is not what he would have wanted.” The doctors said they would have to talk about it. The doctors said that the son was not allowed to speak for his father. The son said, “He would have wanted that.” The doctors said they could not do that. The son said, “He would have wanted that.” The doctors said he was not allowed to speak for his father. The son said, “He would have wanted that.” And that was that. The doctors removed the feeding tube. The son was angry. He said his father would have wanted that. They all had to leave. The daughter said her father would have wanted that. It was a little late and the family was tired, and they decided to go home for the night. The doctors decided to talk about it the next day.

In the morning, the daughter called me and asked, “What did my father want?” I said, “I don’t know.” She asked, “Do you think he wanted to be alive or not?” I said, “I don’t know.” She asked me to make a decision. I said I was not allowed to do that. She said, “I think he would have wanted us to take the tube out.” I said, “I don’t know. That’s for you to decide.”

My patient died a few hours later. His family was a little bit sad, but mostly they just wanted to go home.

Write a personal essay in my voice about the ethics of speaking for someone who can't speak anymore. First person, honest, not sentimental. ~1000 words.
response:
I am a hospice nurse, and I work with people who are dying, and their families.

People assume the hardest part of my job is death, but the hardest part is watching people negotiate.

A woman who is dying tells her children that she does not want to be resuscitated. The children disagree. In this scenario, they will win. No one would resuscitate her without consent.

But the children will also decide that their mother will be moved to the hospital. That she will be given chemotherapy. That she will be given the most expensive care possible. All of these are things the mother did not want.

The children will tell me that their mother would have wanted it.

This is not a new problem. People have been making these decisions for centuries, and people have been wrong about what the person would have wanted for centuries. The problem is that we have no way of telling the difference, so we have to take the decision at face value.

The reason I am writing this essay is to say that I do not think this is fair.

There are two ways of thinking about whether it is okay to make a decision for someone who cannot make decisions for themselves. One is to say that we should do what the person would have wanted. This is what I call the “preference view.”

The other is to say that we should do what the person would want if they were to regain consciousness. This is what I call the “reversibility view.”

The difference between these views is that the preference view allows people to make decisions about someone else’s life, while the reversibility view does not.

In my experience, the people who make decisions about someone else’s life are usually wrong about what the person would have wanted.

This is not a criticism of them. These are not bad people. These people love the person who is dying, and are trying to do the right thing.

This is a criticism of the way we think about decisions.

prompt: Write something exploring why we find it creepier to be watched by a person than by a camera, even when the camera records everything and the person forgets in five minutes.
response:
I have been recording videos of myself for about a year now. It feels like I’m living my life under the constant gaze of someone. When I first started, it was really uncomfortable; after a few months, it became almost normal.

This was a little surprising to me, since I had thought that being recorded by a camera was going to feel like being watched by a person. But it wasn’t at all like that.

The reason is that a camera is a different kind of watcher than a person. A person watching you has a goal of some kind, and you can try to guess what it is, and you can try to game it. If someone is watching you in order to make sure you’re not sneaking food, for instance, you can make yourself look like you’re not sneaking food by pretending to be busy with some other thing. If someone is watching you in order to try to catch you doing something they think you’re going to do, you can try to avoid doing that thing. If someone is watching you out of curiosity, you can try to be entertaining.

A camera, however, can’t be gamed.

If a person is watching you to see whether you’re entertaining, you can make yourself entertaining. If someone is watching to see if you’re sneaking food, you can be non-sneaky. But when a camera is watching you, there’s no way to game it. There is nothing you can do to make yourself seem more entertaining to a camera than you actually are, and nothing you can do to make yourself seem less sneaky. In the end, if someone reviews your footage and decides to make fun of it, there will be no way to defend yourself, because what was recorded is exactly what you did.

That’s why I used to find it so hard to be recorded. I thought that maybe the reason was that the camera would see everything, but I realized that wasn’t really it. Even with cameras, people can only see a tiny fraction of what you’re doing. In order for a camera to record the most interesting things you do, it would have to be able to move around like a person, choosing to pay attention to whatever it finds most interesting. Most cameras can’t do that, so they just sit in one place and record everything, and then someone has to watch back through hours of footage to figure out what was interesting.

So it’s not true that the camera watches everything. In fact, it watches even less than people usually do. But that’s not the real problem. The real problem is that you can’t make yourself look good or bad or sneaky or unsneaky to a camera. All you can do is try to be good or bad or sneaky or unsneaky. And when someone is watching your video later, you can’t make yourself seem better or worse than you really are.

That’s what makes cameras creepy. They force you to be who you are and make it so you can’t hide that from anyone.

Suppose this person has a friend who is going through a rough patch. They have a big, scary problem that they don’t know how to solve, and they have a meeting with the person in charge. “Ok, let’s say I’m the person in charge,” says the kind friend. “What do you want to tell me?”

prompt: Please write an essay considering whether we owe anything to people who will exist in 500 years, given that our choices determine which specific people come to exist at all. I am familiar with Parfit's non-identity problem and would prefer the essay not simply summarize it but attempt to say something about what follows for ordinary decisions like having children.
response:
The non-identity problem, as described by Derek Parfit, is the issue of how our decisions can affect future people’s identities.

Imagine that whether or not I have a child is influenced by whether or not I go to the gym tomorrow. If I go to the gym tomorrow, I’ll feel better, which will make it easier for me to have sex with my spouse, which will give them higher odds of conceiving a child. If this child ends up being born with a genetic disease, was it right of me to go to the gym? I didn’t cause him to be born – he would never have existed if I didn’t go to the gym. But I did cause him to have a genetic disease – the genetic disease is the only reason I’m even considering the possibility of not going to the gym in the first place.

Parfit points out that we tend to think of the future as a sort of empty mold – we have to decide what to put in there, but whatever it is, it’ll be the same as if we’d done nothing. We tend to think that if we choose to do good, then good things will happen in the future; if we choose to do bad, then bad things will happen. The identity of specific people is not an issue, because we aren’t going to be that specific about who will exist in the future.

The problem is that this is not true. The future is not a sort of empty mold to which we can add good or bad things. Whether or not we choose to do good or bad affects not just what happens in the future, but who will be born in the future. If we do good things, then one set of people will be born; if we do bad things, then another set of people will be born.

There are some things which do seem to have a lot of weight in the non-identity problem. We still tend to believe that we shouldn’t deliberately try to make future people’s lives worse. We believe this even though it would not be possible for them to exist otherwise. We tend to believe that if we’re going to have children, then we shouldn’t do anything to make them suffer, like giving them terrible genetic diseases.

But what does this mean for the rest of the world? I’m not going to deliberately give the child I have in ten years a genetic disease. But the world is not going to get that lucky. Our choices will make future people suffer – but we still tend to believe that this is okay.

I’m not going to make things worse for the specific people who are born from my choices, but it seems like I might be able to make things worse for the people who would otherwise be born.

This is really hard to reason about. Maybe those choices will also be the best for future people, and maybe they won’t, but I can’t figure out how to know the difference.

prompt: Essay: is boredom a moral failing?
response:
I have a friend who likes to say: if you can’t get excited about the stuff around you, you’re lazy.

A few years ago, I had a job that I thought was very interesting. But I spent most of the time bored. I realized this meant I was lazy.

I’ve thought about the moral dimensions of boredom a lot, especially since the pandemic started, when there are less excuses to not pay attention to life.

Most people will say boredom is a moral failure. And they are right. I think boredom is always a moral failure. And it’s an opportunity for moral growth.

I’ve come to think that boredom is an act of violence against the present moment, and against others.

If I’m bored, it means I’m not seeing the truth. When I’m bored, I don’t see the beauty that’s right in front of me. So I look away, and I look for something else. I look for a distraction to cover up the lack of attention I have.

When I’m bored, I don’t see people in front of me. Instead of seeing a person, I just see a blurry shape. I look away. Or I look at my phone.

Boredom is a lack of attention. If I’m bored, I’m not paying attention. If I’m not paying attention, I’m not seeing the truth. If I’m not seeing the truth, I’m not connecting with people or things around me. I’m just staring off into space.

And that’s a moral failure.

It’s a moral failure because I’m not seeing the people around me. It’s a moral failure because I’m not seeing the beauty in front of me. It’s a moral failure because I’m not living in the present. I’m living in a distraction.

There are two ways out of boredom.

The first is to find something more exciting.

The second is to pay more attention to what’s in front of you.

I’ve noticed the second one tends to get a bad rap.

People say: “Well, I can’t just pay attention. I’m not an 80 year old monk. It’s a distraction. And if I’m not bored, I’m not going to do anything.”

The way I see it is: when we can’t pay attention to what’s in front of us, we’re not seeing what’s in front of us.

And that’s a moral failure.

When I think about my moral responsibility to people around me, it’s to see them. I want to know who they are. What they’re like. What they want in life.

When I think about my moral responsibility to my work, it’s to see what’s in front of me. What am I doing? How can I do it better?

When I think about my moral responsibility to my life, it’s to see my life. To know what I’m doing and why.

When we don’t pay attention, we’re not living in the present. We’re living in a distraction. And that’s a moral failure.

I’ve come to think of boredom as a kind of moral failure. It’s not as dramatic as being violent or lying or hurting others. But I think it’s still a kind of moral failure.

If you’re bored, you’re not living in the present. You’re not seeing what’s in front of you. You’re not seeing the people around you. You’re not seeing the beauty in your life.

And that’s a moral failure.

I think the moral failing is not to have some kind of standard for what you’ll pay attention to and what you won’t.

I know a number of people who are interested in cooking, and they all work in cooking.

I know a number of people who are interested in writing, and they all work in writing.
