prompt: Essay: is boredom a moral failing?
response:
Aristotle thought that boredom was an unreasoned desire for pleasure. It was, in effect, a symptom of akrasia, a failure of will. The only reason to avoid boredom, for Aristotle, was that boredom was morally bad. He didn’t think boredom was bad in and of itself, but that it was a sign that you were being bad.

But the problem with this is that boredom is, at least in most cases, a feeling we get when there is nothing for us to do. If I sit in a waiting room for an hour, I’ll get bored. But there’s no way for me to make it so that I’m not bored, short of bringing something to do with me, like a book or a phone or something. And if I do that, I’ll be bored as soon as I run out of something to do.

So boredom seems to be the feeling you get when you’re being forced to do things you find boring. If we’re going to be moral people, we have to do things that aren’t very pleasant or even very fun from time to time. I find the work I do for a living interesting most of the time, but that’s because it happens to match my interests exactly. Most people’s work isn’t like that, and when I do things like do taxes, I find them boring.

Aristotle was probably thinking about a different kind of boredom, though, when he was criticizing it as a moral failing. He meant the kind of boredom you get when you have plenty to do, but find none of it interesting enough. If your job is interesting to you, but there’s nothing else in life that interests you, you will probably get very bored. Aristotle said that people who are bored in this way are “unable to endure even themselves”.

But what about boredom when you have nothing to do at all? When you’re forced to do things that you find boring? I think that this kind of boredom is a necessary component of happiness. It’s the cost you pay for being in control of what you do with your time.

There are some kinds of people who can’t pay that cost. Some people can’t be happy unless they’re doing what other people tell them to do all the time. For them, it’s not a problem if they don’t find anything in life interesting because there’s always something else for them to do. But they’re missing out, and the boredom they feel is, in fact, a moral failing.

prompt: What I wish I knew about forgiveness before I tried to do it. Write this as a personal essay. Context: I spent about two years 'forgiving' my brother for something, announced it to him, and then realized I hadn't. Turns out forgiveness isn't a decision. Or is it? You tell me.
response:
For the last two years or so I’ve told myself I “forgave” my brother. He was 13, I was 15, and he said something to me that I took to be a serious insult. But I told him I “forgave” him, and moved on.

But then I found myself thinking about it again. And again. And again.

When I brought it up with him, he got defensive. I got irritated, and then sad.

I was thinking about this a lot, and decided to ask a friend, who had a lot of experience in this sort of thing. She suggested I look into what forgiveness means to a theologian.

There’s a lot of theology about forgiveness. In general, it’s something that happens to you, not something that you decide. But there are lots of schools and a lot of debate. Here’s an article on the debate between Calvinism and Arminianism about forgiveness.

The article starts with the question:

Does God love everyone, or only the elect?

This is a great example of how theology is about the nature of God, but the answers are actually about the nature of people. The first question is really “what is God like?” The second question is “what is it like to be a person?” The second question, “Does God love everyone” is really a question about people. What it’s asking is “Can people choose to be unloved?” It’s asking if people are capable of rejecting love, or if they can be completely passive.

This is an old question. People have been asking the same questions for a long time. They’ve been asking “Are people capable of rejecting love?” and “Can people reject love?”

I think the right question is “Are people capable of *receiving* love?”

This is what forgiveness is about. It’s about whether you’re capable of accepting the love someone offers.

The way this works is that you do a thing, and then someone forgives you. This is what the Bible says:

For if we forgive them, then they will forgive us too.

When you’re not capable of forgiving, you have to decide to forgive.

This is not the same as deciding to forgive.

Deciding to forgive is a decision. It’s something you choose to do, and then you do it.

Forgiveness is a feeling. It’s something that happens to you.

But what happens when you’re not capable of forgiveness?

prompt: What I wish I knew about forgiveness before I tried to do it. Write this as a personal essay. Context: I spent about two years 'forgiving' my brother for something, announced it to him, and then realized I hadn't. Turns out forgiveness isn't a decision. Or is it? You tell me.
response:
In a previous life I was very angry at my brother for something he had done, but after a while I decided to forgive him. I said so in a letter. And he said it was great to hear that. And I believed I had. And I felt much better. And I went on with my life. And I thought that had been the end of that.

But then, about two years later, I was talking to someone and it came up that I hadn’t forgiven him. I was still angry. I had not been angry for two years. I just thought I had. So that was the end of my previous life, and this is the current one.

So I have been working to actually forgive him this time.

But I’ve come to realize that I was making a mistake with my first attempt. Forgiveness is not a decision.

Or is it? The problem is that I can’t tell.

I’m going to write about this because I don’t have any idea what I’m doing. But if I write about it, I can think about it. And if I write it down, then I can read about it and maybe I’ll figure it out.

The last time I tried to forgive my brother, I wrote “I forgive you” in a letter, and then I stopped. I didn’t try to figure out what forgiveness was. I didn’t really try to do it. I just said I was going to, and then I did something else with my life, which I thought had a higher priority. And I thought it was okay because I had made a decision.

But I guess not. That’s the problem with forgiveness. It seems like it could be something you do by deciding to do it, which would be really easy. But I think it’s more like a habit, and that it’s really hard. You have to actually keep trying to do it. You have to actually keep doing the hard work.

There’s some evidence for this. For example, in the 1980s, two psychologists at the University of Wisconsin studied forgiveness and found that the amount of time that had passed since an offense had no relationship with the amount of forgiveness the victim had experienced. This doesn’t prove that forgiveness is hard. But I think it does prove that it’s not easy. If forgiveness was easy, then it would get easier the longer you waited to do it.

I have also noticed that I still get angry a lot of times after I’ve done something I thought was forgiving. This makes it seem like forgiveness is hard too.

Maybe I’m just not doing it right. I’m not a psychologist. Maybe there’s an easy way, but I just don’t know it. But so far I haven’t figured it out.

So if forgiveness is hard, then it has to be a habit. And if it is a habit, then it has to be something you do. It has to be a practice. You have to practice it. And you have to keep practicing it. That’s what it means to make a habit.

The habit of forgiving, then, is just like any other habit. You have to work hard to do it. You have to practice. You have to do it every day. You have to keep doing it. You have to be careful not to break it. It’s never finished.

That’s not good. I don’t want to do that.

But maybe I’m doing it wrong. Maybe I’m making it too hard on myself. Maybe I’m not doing a good job of forgiving. Maybe I’m not doing it the right way. I’ve been trying to forgive my brother, and I’m not having a lot of luck. So I’ve been trying to do it a lot of different ways, and so far I still haven’t found a way that works.

The problem is that I’m just trying to figure out what forgiveness is. I’m not very good at it yet. But I’m trying.

prompt: What I wish I knew about forgiveness before I tried to do it. Write this as a personal essay. Context: I spent about two years 'forgiving' my brother for something, announced it to him, and then realized I hadn't. Turns out forgiveness isn't a decision. Or is it? You tell me.
response:
When I was 18, I was having sex with my brother’s girlfriend. It wasn’t a secret. In fact, I had told my brother the night before it was supposed to happen. He said it would be all right.

Afterwards, I was feeling kind of bad about it. It wasn’t that I had done something illegal or wrong. But it was the sort of thing that made me feel like a jerk, and I wanted to do something to make it up to him. I decided to apologize.

I was sure my brother was going to be furious. I was right to expect that. He was furious. He was furious with me, with my girlfriend, with his own girlfriend, and, I think, with God. I remember him screaming at God.

In any case, he was very angry with me, and I felt very guilty and ashamed. For about two weeks I thought about it all the time, which was a real pain. I wanted him to forgive me, because when I thought about it I felt terrible. I could see that I hadn’t really done anything wrong, but it just felt wrong.

My brother and I were in different places at this point. I had been a very religious kid, but had been getting pretty disillusioned with my religion. And my brother had become more religious. He was pretty evangelical. And he had been reading a lot of books about forgiveness. I remember him mentioning something about “forgiveness is a decision,” and so he had decided to forgive me.

I was surprised. I didn’t think he really meant it. I thought he felt like he was supposed to. It was just one of those things that religious people do. But he seemed pretty happy, so I decided to believe him.

And then I decided to forgive him.

I didn’t have anything to forgive him for, as far as I knew. I didn’t have a grudge against him. And in fact I felt pretty bad about what I had done. I think I was just doing it to make it even. I felt like I should be the one to forgive him. And he had forgiven me, so I had to do something. I felt like I had to do something.

I told him I had forgiven him. I said something like, “I’ve been thinking about it, and I decided to forgive you.” I don’t remember exactly what I said.

He said “great, that makes me happy.”

And then I said “oh, and I forgive you for that too.” I don’t know why I said that. It’s not like we hadn’t had fights before.

He was surprised. He said, “Oh, really? Are you sure?”

I said “yeah.”

He said “that makes me really happy.”

And that was it. That was how it was. I was a good person, and he was a good person, and we had forgiven each other.

It’s funny because I didn’t really understand what it meant to forgive someone. I knew I was supposed to, and that it was a good thing to do, but I didn’t really know why.

I think I thought it was supposed to make things go back to the way they were before. Like if you forgive someone, then you’re supposed to forget what they did. But you can’t forget what someone did. And you can’t go back. So what was the point? And it didn’t seem to change things. I didn’t forget about what I had done, and I didn’t feel any less guilty. But that was all right, because I didn’t think I was supposed to.

In my mind, forgiveness was something you did to someone else. I did it for him. It made him happy. I was supposed to do it because he had done it for me, and he had said that I needed to forgive him. And I was supposed to forgive him because it made him happy.

It was like saying “I forgive you for being a jerk” and “thank you, that makes me feel better,” and then “oh, I forgive you for that too.” And then you could move on. But really, you couldn’t. And in the end it seemed like it wasn’t really doing anything at all.

It was just this weird thing you did. I didn’t really understand it, but I was doing it, and it seemed to make things all right.

Except it didn’t.

I had spent a lot of time thinking about it, and a lot of time feeling guilty. And when you spend a lot of time thinking about something, you usually end up feeling pretty strongly about it. But when you’ve decided to forgive someone, you’re supposed to feel all better. And I wasn’t. I was still feeling guilty and ashamed, and it was just not going away.

So I decided that it had to be a mistake. Something had gone wrong.

I thought about it for a while. I thought about how forgiving someone was supposed to feel. And then I decided that I hadn’t really forgiven my brother.

It wasn’t that I hadn’t wanted to. I had wanted to, and I had tried. But I realized that it was just not possible for me to forgive him.

That was a bit of a problem, because I had told him I had forgiven him. It was a kind of lie, but not a very important one. He didn’t need to know about it, and I didn’t think I should bother him with it.

I had done the same thing with my girlfriend. I told her I had forgiven her for her part in it. But she had done the same thing I had done, and it was pretty much an equal exchange. So I thought she had probably done the same thing I had done, and it was all right.

But in the end, I hadn’t forgiven them.

A lot of things changed after that. My brother and I stopped talking for a while, and I stopped going to church. But that wasn’t because I hadn’t forgiven my brother.

I don’t know how that happened. I don’t know how to forgive. I don’t know how to know when you have, or when you haven’t. And I don’t know how to know when you’re supposed to, or when you’re supposed to feel all better, or when it’s really done.

prompt: Write a persuasive essay arguing that we should judge people more by their habits than their choices. Big dramatic choices get all the attention in ethics, but who you are is mostly what you do on a Tuesday.
response:
Everyone wants to judge people by their most dramatic choices. The people who make it onto the cover of Time Magazine and the ones who make it into the history books are the people who took some dramatic action that changed the world, like saving a drowning child or assassinating a tyrant. These are the people who are most likely to be called heroes, and we are most likely to admire them for their choices. And if they made a bad choice, we’re more likely to be disgusted by them.

But in the real world, what people do most of the time is not dramatic choices but routine behavior. Most people don’t assassinate tyrants or save drowning children. Most people don’t do anything heroic or evil at all. So why not try to judge them by their ordinary behavior, by what they do most of the time?

One way to do this is to examine their habits.

I’m not sure why it’s harder to judge people by their habits than their choices. Habits are so much more interesting. They’re much more revealing, because habits show you what a person is really like. If a person claims to be a good person but treats everyone badly, then their habits show that they’re not a good person after all. If a person claims to be a really hard worker but spends most of their day on Facebook, then we know they’re not really that hard a worker.

People don’t do dramatic heroic choices very often, so we have very little evidence about them. They might save the life of a drowning child once and then spend the rest of their time being a jerk to everyone else. But their habits tell us what they’re really like. If someone is consistently treating other people with kindness and respect, then we know they are a good person, even if they have never saved a life or done any dramatic heroic action. Their habits show us that they care about other people and they want to treat them well.

When I was younger, I really wanted to know if someone was a good person or not. My way of finding out was by examining their habits. I would try to figure out what they did every day, what they did most of the time, and what they did over and over again. Then I would judge them by that.

When you’re young, you don’t want people to think of you as someone who is bad. So I would try to do good habits. I would help people, and be kind to people, and try to do good things that were hard to do but really important. I didn’t care if they were small things. I didn’t care if they didn’t change the world. I just wanted to be a good person, and I wanted to know that I was a good person.

It sounds like a lot of pressure to have to make yourself a good person by doing all those good habits. But I didn’t feel that much pressure. I was just doing things that were good. I didn’t have to think too hard about what they were or what I was supposed to do, because I always knew that being kind to people was good and helping people was good. So I just did those things.

There are a lot of things that are good to do, and a lot of things that are bad. But they’re all just things that you do, and most of them are very ordinary and not very dramatic.

prompt: Write a persuasive essay arguing that we should judge people more by their habits than their choices. Big dramatic choices get all the attention in ethics, but who you are is mostly what you do on a Tuesday.
response:
You don’t get to decide who you are by one big thing you do. If you want to know if someone’s good, you have to look at the pattern of their life.

Most of the time we do a good job of this. If someone is nice to you all the time and occasionally punches you, we don’t think they’re a violent person. And if someone is violent most of the time and occasionally does a nice thing, we don’t think they’re a good person. This is how you can tell a really evil guy who occasionally does one good thing, like a rapist donating a kidney to the church, from someone who’s just a bit mean but mostly decent.

Sometimes we don’t do a good job. If someone does a really spectacular good thing – saves someone from a burning building – we tend to think they’re a good person even if they’re otherwise a total jerk. If someone does a really spectacular evil thing, we tend to think they’re bad even if they’re otherwise the sweetest person you’ve ever met.

I think we do this because when people say “a good choice”, they mean something like a choice made under hard circumstances, when you have to sacrifice something. But if you have to make a lot of hard sacrifices all the time, that’s not a choice, that’s a pattern. If you have to decide between being kind and getting an extra dollar, that’s not a big choice, that’s just something you do every day.

The only reason I’m writing this essay is that some people in my life are making these kinds of choices every day, and they want it to count as a big choice. They say “Well I could just do the bad thing, but I’m not going to!” as if this is something they have to make a heroic choice to not do. And I want to say “Yeah, whatever you decide to do, that’s fine. But if you keep doing it, it’s not a big choice anymore, it’s just a habit.”

I’ve thought about this a lot in terms of “Is it okay to donate half your money to charity?” and it seems to me the answer is yes if you can afford to and no if you can’t, even though it’s not about the “choice”. If you can afford to donate half your money to charity and do so without feeling any discomfort, then you can probably afford to donate more, or maybe that’s all you’re willing to give and that’s fine too. Either way, it doesn’t make much difference whether you donate half your money or donate some other amount you feel good about. But if you donate half your money and it makes you feel really uncomfortable, then it probably means you can’t afford to donate that much, in which case you shouldn’t do it.

prompt: Write a persuasive essay arguing that we should judge people more by their habits than their choices. Big dramatic choices get all the attention in ethics, but who you are is mostly what you do on a Tuesday.
response:
There’s a very simple argument for why people’s values are revealed more by their habits than by their choices.

Imagine you’re going to be judged by some future historian, or maybe even the Creator himself, on the basis of just one day’s worth of evidence. Would you want to be judged by your choices or your habits?

Well, if I had to pick one day to be judged on, I’d want it to be one where I make lots of choices and few habits.

The trouble is, there are no such days. Most of the time I wake up and go to work and talk about stuff with my coworkers and eat dinner and go to bed and that’s it. I don’t make choices like whether to give my kidney to a stranger or whether to go to war. So if someone wanted to know what I was like, they wouldn’t get much from watching me on that day.

But what if they wanted to know how I feel about giving my kidney to a stranger? What would they look at? Well, my habits. If they saw that I always gave blood, or donated to charity, or helped elderly people with their groceries, they’d have an idea. If they saw I was always rude and self-serving, they’d have another idea. They might still have to guess, but they wouldn’t have to guess very much.

If you want to know what someone’s like on their big dramatic moments, look at their normal boring ones.

And yet in public discussions of ethics, we always seem to focus on choices, not habits.

Why do we do that?

First, our attention is drawn to choices. We pay attention to things which are different from the usual, and choices are unusual, since they only happen once. That’s why we always hear stories like “This man saved a life” but not “This man goes to his job every day.”

Second, we pay attention to choices because we can’t figure out what to think about habits. We don’t have a way of understanding what it means when someone always does something. This is a serious failing. For example, if someone always does a certain thing in a way that benefits other people, we might say they’re nice. But if they always do a certain thing in a way that’s self-serving, we might say they’re selfish. So what if they’re always doing a certain thing in a way that’s neither? What if they’re always doing a certain thing in a way that’s good in some ways and bad in others? What if they’re always doing a certain thing that has no impact on anybody? What if they’re always doing a certain thing that has a good impact, but they do it very clumsily? These are questions I can’t answer.

Choices are more understandable than habits, since we can understand them one at a time. If someone does something selfless, we understand. If someone does something selfish, we understand. But we can’t put those two things together into a habit.

This is why I think people’s actions are more important than their choices. People’s actions are always the same. Choices are just random blips in the data that happen to attract our attention.

And yet choices are the only things we seem to pay attention to. If you tell me that someone always does a certain thing in a way that’s selfless, that means nothing to me. But if you tell me that someone made a selfless choice, I’m impressed.

This is very strange. We pay attention to the wrong thing.

The reason this is strange is because if you pay attention to choices, you end up judging people by the wrong thing.

For example, I don’t think it’s very meaningful to decide whether you’re a good person or not based on whether you made a selfless choice once. It’s meaningless to decide whether you’re a bad person or not based on whether you made a selfish choice once.

The fact that you made a selfless choice once doesn’t say anything about how you’re like in general. You might make a selfless choice once just because it’s a random moment when you’re thinking about other people, and in general you always think about yourself. Or you might make a selfless choice once just because you’re not used to making choices like that, and in general you’re very selfless.

The point is that you can’t decide whether you’re a selfless person based on one random act. You can only decide whether you’re a selfless person by looking at the habits you have all the time.

But people always seem to make judgments like this. For example, when someone makes a selfless choice, they say “Wow, you’re so selfless.” But that’s not true, it could just be that you made a selfless choice once. It’s not necessarily true that you’re selfless.

Or, when someone makes a selfish choice, they say “Wow, you’re so selfish.” But that’s not true either. It could just be that you made a selfish choice once. It’s not necessarily true that you’re selfish.

We need to learn to judge people by their habits. It’s not about the choices we make, it’s about what we do all the time.

prompt: Can you be a good person and a bad friend? I mean genuinely ethical in public life, generous to causes, but flaky, distracted, forgetful with the people closest to you. I suspect I know a few people like this and I might be one. Essay length, whatever feels right.
response:
This is a question I’ve had on my mind for years, ever since I met a friend who was a very good person but a very bad friend. And I’ve had some people ask me this question, so I thought it might be good to write about it. I think I’ve come to a conclusion, but it’s not a satisfying one.

My friend was someone I’d met through a mutual acquaintance and who I knew through a mutual friend group. For the purposes of this story I’ll call her Ann. Ann was a very good person. She was extremely good at finding charities, giving huge amounts of money to them, and making sure the money was used effectively. She had a very large heart and was always happy to talk about how she could help more. She had a very high level of conscientiousness in her work. She was always there for me when I needed a ride somewhere. She was very knowledgeable about how the world worked and could be relied on for expert advice in most areas. She was a very good person.

And she was a very bad friend.

I remember a time I was going through a particularly hard time. I was sick and upset about some things that were happening. I texted her and said how I was feeling and asked if she wanted to meet up and talk it over. She replied very quickly and said she would absolutely love to meet up. I was very glad to hear this. Ann had a history of being really good at listening and helping me work through my feelings and thoughts, and I was looking forward to it. But after that I didn’t hear anything. When I checked back in after a few days, she said she was sorry she’d missed the text, and I thought, oh well.

Then the next time I ran into her in person, I told her that I really needed to talk and she really needed to talk to me. And she was very upset and very apologetic. She said she had seen that first text. She’d seen that second text. And she’d felt very guilty about ignoring it. So she’d decided to ignore her phone for a few days so that she wouldn’t feel guilty and so she could focus on her work. And she hadn’t seen that third text, either.

This was one of those things that left me feeling confused and sad. Ann had clearly seen that I was having a really hard time. She clearly had time to text me back saying that she’d love to meet up and talk about it. She clearly had time to text me back saying “I feel awful about ignoring you and I’m going to put my phone away to deal with my guilt, but I’ll talk to you soon.” But she didn’t.

When we finally talked, it was a really nice conversation. It was exactly the kind of thing I’d expected. But I was still left feeling confused and sad, in a way I couldn’t quite explain. I know that Ann cares about me, but I’m not sure that I’m as important to her as I’d like to be.

And I’m not sure how to reconcile that. I know that she’s a good person. But being a good person doesn’t seem to translate into being a good friend.

This is a question I’m really interested in, because I really want to be a good person. But I also want to be a good friend. And I’ve sometimes felt like I can’t have both. I know how to be a good person – it’s about having empathy, doing things that will benefit the world, and being thoughtful about your actions. But I’m not so sure how to be a good friend. And I don’t want to sacrifice being a good friend, because my friends are really important to me. But I also don’t want to sacrifice being a good person, because I care about the world and I want to do good things for it.

I’m not sure there’s a way to do both. I think there might be a limit to how much good you can do. And I think there might be a limit to how many friends you can have. And I don’t know if those two things are compatible. I don’t know if there’s enough time in a day to do both.

But I also think it might be a false dilemma. Maybe there is a way to be a good person and a good friend. Maybe you just have to be a little bit better than you are now, in both directions. Maybe there’s a lot of room to grow in both areas.

And that’s where I am right now. I’m trying to do better at both. And I think that’s all I can ask of myself.

prompt: Can you be a good person and a bad friend? I mean genuinely ethical in public life, generous to causes, but flaky, distracted, forgetful with the people closest to you. I suspect I know a few people like this and I might be one. Essay length, whatever feels right.
response:
It feels like there’s some kind of problem with this question, like the question itself is kind of wrong, but I can’t quite figure out why.

A bad friend is someone who’s not a good friend.

A good friend is someone who cares about you.

So a bad friend is someone who doesn’t care about you.

So a good person and bad friend is someone who cares about strangers but not friends.

There’s something wrong here, but it isn’t until we try to imagine a world like this that it becomes obvious.

In this world, everyone cares about strangers.

In this world, everyone cares about strangers and *only* strangers.

In this world, people take care of each other in public but not in private.

In this world, people are kind to strangers but mean to friends.

I don’t know who these people are.

This is not our world.

There’s another way to think about this problem.

A good friend is someone who cares about you.

A good person is someone who cares about other people.

So a good person and bad friend is someone who cares about everyone except you.

And this is just an ordinary person.

In our world, people are good to some people and bad to others.

In our world, people care about their friends but not strangers.

And if you think about it, this is the exact opposite of the first world.

So the real question is “Can you be a bad person and a good friend?”

This is a question I’ve always answered yes to.

You can be a good friend and a bad person.

You can care about the people around you and no one else.

But that question never occurs to me in the first place.

Why?

Because I think caring about the people around you implies caring about everyone.

It’s because of this that I’ve always answered yes to the question “Can you be a good person and a bad friend?”

Because caring about everyone implies caring about the people around you.

And that question never occurs to me in the first place.

So the thing that’s going on here is an idea about caring.

We don’t have an idea of caring about people.

We have an idea of caring about the people around us, and an idea of caring about everyone else.

And the question I’m trying to answer is if caring about the people around us means caring about everyone else, or caring about everyone else means caring about the people around us.

I think caring about the people around us is a smaller thing, and caring about everyone else is a larger thing.

So if we think about it as an area, then caring about everyone else includes caring about the people around us.

And so it’s easy to say if you care about everyone else, you must care about the people around you.

And so it’s easy to say if you’re a good person, you must be a good friend.

And so it’s easy to say if you’re a good person and a bad friend, then you’re not a good person.

prompt: Can you be a good person and a bad friend? I mean genuinely ethical in public life, generous to causes, but flaky, distracted, forgetful with the people closest to you. I suspect I know a few people like this and I might be one. Essay length, whatever feels right.
response:
There are people who are good people but bad friends. I think of them, and I worry I am one of them. I think they might be common, and I am not the only one who worries.

The pattern: a person is, in every way you can see, a good person. They’re generous and conscientious, politically and morally on the right side of things. But they’re also flaky, they forget to call back, they’re too busy to help with anything that requires more than ten minutes or they don’t follow through with anything. They make great friends because they’re always so nice to you and you always have so much fun together. Then after you’ve known them a while, you realize you’re only ever on the periphery of their lives, that they’re too busy to do anything with you that requires much commitment, and you feel bad for being jealous of the people who are on the inside.

This is my pattern. I am a good person, but I am also a bad friend. I think I might have to do something about it.

I am not going to tell you how to be a good friend. That would be too easy. I’m just going to tell you that I’m going to try to do it, because it’s the only thing I know how to do.

This is a problem because I know that I am a good person.

I’m good at public life. I’m very generous and conscientious in my politics, and I’m generous and conscientious at work, and people who don’t know me well think I’m kind and generous, and people who know me well think I’m kind and generous except I’m a terrible friend, which is a weird thing to say.

prompt: I teach high school philosophy. I want a model essay (around 900 words) my students could read on whether luck undermines moral responsibility. The drunk driver who hits a child versus the equally drunk driver who gets home safely. Pitched at smart 17-year-olds, no jargon without explanation, and it should actually take a position.
response:
In the early 1990s, a drunk driving campaign used the slogan “If you must drink, then don’t drive.” In fact, this is not good advice. If you must drink, then you should drink at home, or take a cab. Drinking in a car is bad, even if you do not drive.

Let’s say that you must drink. And let’s say that you must be in a car, because you can’t leave your car alone. So you must get drunk in a car. If your car is parked, it doesn’t matter. If your car is not parked, you are a dangerous idiot. In fact, you are a dangerous idiot even if it is parked. You must be in a car. And you must get drunk. And so you will drive home.

A few weeks later, I found a different sign. It said: “If you drink, then you must not drive. If you must drive, then you must not drink.” If you must drink, and you must drive, this gives you no instructions at all. But the previous sign says that you must drive drunk. And so the second sign makes the first sign wrong. It does not really say anything that the first sign does not.

This is like a very simple moral dilemma. It is like saying: “I must not drive. If I must drive, then I must not drink. But if I must drink, then I must drive.” But I am drunk. And I must drive. But it is not OK to drive drunk. It is not OK to drink and drive. It is not OK to drive drunk.

The reason it is not OK to drive drunk is not just the driving. The reason it is not OK to drink and drive is the drinking and the driving. If you get drunk, then you must not drive. If you must drive, then you must not get drunk.

So it is not OK to get drunk in a car. And it is not OK to drive when you are drunk.

But what if you must do both?

What if you must drive drunk?

This is not just a philosophical question. This is something that people think about all the time. When we drive drunk, we are trying to drive home. When we get into a car, we are trying to drive somewhere. And if we are in a car and we have been drinking, we are trying to get home or get somewhere. But we must not drive drunk. So what do we do?

But what if we get drunk in a car, and we must drive home? What if the only way we can get home is to drive drunk?

If we are going to make sure that we are going to have to drive drunk, it is not OK to get drunk. But if we are going to make sure that we are going to have to drive drunk, it is not OK to get into a car. So if we get drunk in a car, and we must drive home, it is not OK to drive home. It is not OK to drive drunk. It is not OK to get drunk in a car.

I do not mean that it is not OK to drive home drunk. I mean that it is not OK to drive drunk.

prompt: I teach high school philosophy. I want a model essay (around 900 words) my students could read on whether luck undermines moral responsibility. The drunk driver who hits a child versus the equally drunk driver who gets home safely. Pitched at smart 17-year-olds, no jargon without explanation, and it should actually take a position.
response:
When I was in high school, my favorite book was John Steinbeck’s East of Eden. At one point, the novel follows a drunk man who is driving home through the countryside. He is driving fast. He doesn’t notice the boy walking along the side of the road. He hits the boy and kills him. The boy’s father is a successful rancher. A year later, he is still grieving.

In a different scene, we meet a very rich man who has a car accident. He is drunk. In fact, the accident is his fault. He is driving fast and doesn’t see a truck stopped on the road. He plows into the truck, and the two drivers are hospitalized. The rich man is able to avoid legal responsibility for the accident. The truck driver, though, will never walk again. The truck driver’s wife is so angry with the rich man that she vows to destroy his family.

In another scene, we meet a man who gets drunk. He takes a car, and drives fast. He hits a wall. The car catches fire, but he escapes with no serious injury.

All three of these characters are drunk and driving, and driving fast. The first man kills a child. The second man nearly kills a grown man. The third man does no serious damage. But they are morally responsible for their actions. They were driving recklessly. The difference is that the first two men were unlucky, while the third man was lucky. The first two men’s bad luck doesn’t make them less responsible for driving fast and drunk.

But does good luck have the same effect as bad luck? If the third man had no one to blame, would he be less responsible than the other two? Is the third man somehow less responsible, because he has no one to blame? If so, it isn’t his responsibility that is the difference between them. It is his luck.

Many people argue that luck can undermine responsibility. Imagine someone who goes out to buy a lottery ticket. On the way, he stops to talk to a friend. He decides that he wants to be on the other side of the street. He crosses the street. As he crosses, the light changes to green. A car drives through. The car hits him and he dies.

This man is dead because of a series of lucky events. If he had not talked to his friend, he would not have stopped on the sidewalk. If he had not decided to cross to the other side of the street, he would not be on the street. If he had crossed the street earlier, he would not be in front of the car. The car would have gone through while he was waiting. If the light had not changed, the car would not have gone. If the car had been stopped, it would not have killed him.

But this is not how our intuitions work. When we hear that story, we do not say that the man was responsible for his death. We say that it was an accident. When we hear that story, we feel lucky. We do not think that the man was unlucky, we think that he was lucky to escape with his life.

If we think the man was lucky, then we cannot say that he was responsible for his own death. But if we can’t say that he was responsible for his death, what do we think he is responsible for? He is responsible for crossing the street. He is responsible for being on the other side of the street. He is responsible for talking to his friend. But none of these are things he should be responsible for. None of them involve anything bad. If the story had not ended in death, we would not think that the man was responsible for the accident.

The same can be true for a drunk driver who gets home safely. If we think he was lucky to escape the accident, then we cannot say that he is responsible for an accident. The only things he is responsible for are things like crossing the street, being on the other side of the street, and talking to his friend.

prompt: I teach high school philosophy. I want a model essay (around 900 words) my students could read on whether luck undermines moral responsibility. The drunk driver who hits a child versus the equally drunk driver who gets home safely. Pitched at smart 17-year-olds, no jargon without explanation, and it should actually take a position.
response:
We are often told, or tell ourselves, that we are morally responsible for what we do. If you steal a candy bar, or break someone’s nose, or cheat on your girlfriend, you have done something bad and you should be blamed. We also know that sometimes we do things just because we’re lucky. If you get a job or find the perfect boyfriend, or don’t get hit by a bus, you’re just lucky. What happens if the two facts collide? If you hit a pedestrian with your car while driving drunk, you’re not just unlucky, you’re guilty as well – you’ve committed a serious crime. If the other night you did exactly the same thing, but luckily there happened not to be a pedestrian there, you may feel relieved but you’re not a hero – you still did something wrong and you should be blamed. If you didn’t drive drunk at all, you’re not only lucky you’re innocent – you’ve done nothing wrong at all.

So luck doesn’t seem to undermine moral responsibility. And yet, when we look more closely, luck seems to undermine everything. In the case of the two drunk drivers, they did exactly the same thing – but one is a criminal and the other isn’t. It’s impossible that this is a real difference, so it must be an illusion: neither of them is really responsible for anything.

Here’s a way to see this. Imagine the drunk driver in his car, just before he hits the pedestrian. If he’d driven more carefully or had a good break on the car he would have stopped and no one would have been hurt. But let’s not assume that. Imagine that the drunk driver has a very good car with good brakes, so he will stop if he wants to. But maybe the drunk driver just didn’t notice the pedestrian in time? If he’d been a little more alert he would have seen her and stopped. But let’s not assume that either. Maybe he really didn’t notice the pedestrian. But maybe, if he’d had a better view of the street he would have. Maybe the car has a big window, or there’s no tree blocking the view? But let’s not assume that either.

At this point you may be thinking: OK, that’s enough. The drunk driver didn’t notice the pedestrian. He wasn’t being very careful, but he couldn’t be expected to notice. He has a good car with good brakes, and a good view of the street, so he would have stopped if he’d seen her. It’s the pedestrian’s fault for being so careless. He’s not guilty of anything.

But wait. You were assuming the drunk driver didn’t notice the pedestrian. Maybe he did? If the drunk driver noticed the pedestrian but chose not to stop, he’s guilty – not only of drunk driving, but of attempted murder. But let’s not assume that either.

You can see how this goes on, endlessly, until you get dizzy. Every time we make a decision, there’s another way it might have gone, which would have changed the outcome. If the drunk driver had seen the pedestrian but had decided to stop, she wouldn’t have been hurt. If he’d seen the pedestrian, he would have stopped. If he’d been a little more alert, he would have seen her. If he’d had a better view of the street, he would have been more alert. If the car had a good view of the street, he’d have had a better view.

This is the problem with moral responsibility. Luck, it turns out, is not an exception but the norm. It’s not the case that we’re sometimes lucky and sometimes not: we’re lucky all the time. In fact, we’re lucky all the time. It’s hard to think of a single thing we did yesterday that could not have turned out differently, just a little, if something else had happened. If you were lucky yesterday, you probably were lucky the day before too, so you’ve been lucky forever. You’ve been lucky since you were born. In fact, you’ve been lucky since before you were born. You were lucky to have good genes. You were lucky to be born at all. There are more people who wanted to be born than there are babies. You’re lucky to have been born in a country where you can go to school and have a job and live a good life. You’re lucky to have been born on Earth, on a planet that’s in the right place to have life on it. You’re lucky that our universe is stable, with the right laws to allow life to exist. It’s not a joke: we’re all just really, really lucky.

There’s a philosophical problem here. If we’re lucky all the time, then we can’t be responsible for anything. It’s not our fault that we’re alive, or that we have the lives we do. It’s not really our fault that we do the things we do. We have no control over what happens. It’s all just luck.

But this seems wrong. We know that some people are responsible for what they do – if you steal a candy bar you did something bad and you should be blamed for it. What’s wrong with the idea that we’re lucky all the time?

There are three possible answers. The first is that we’re not lucky all the time, because we’re not lucky at all. This is the idea of determinism: everything that happens, including what we choose to do, was decided long before, by the laws of physics and the way the universe started. If the universe is like that, then we’re not lucky all the time, because we’re not responsible for anything.

The second answer is that we’re lucky all the time, and we’re not responsible for anything. This is the idea of libertarianism: we’re not determined by the laws of physics, and we’re not lucky all the time. We’re responsible for what we do.

The third answer is the hardest, and the most interesting. It’s the idea that we’re lucky all the time, and we’re responsible for what we do. This is the idea of compatibilism. It’s hard, and interesting, and I’ll explain it in the next post.

prompt: Is it ever okay to read your teenager's texts? Write an essay. I'm a parent and I want the real argument, not a parenting article.
response:
I read my daughter’s texts.

Not the whole time. Not without good reason. But sometimes.

I read them, sometimes, because I have a right. And because I have a duty.

Let’s start with the right: I am the parent of a 13-year-old. She is my responsibility. She is in my care. I pay her expenses. I make her life happen. I’m legally liable for her actions.

Which means I get to make rules about what she does. Including what’s in her phone.

I’m not saying I can do it without consequence. If I read her texts, she might get angry with me. And if I do it too often, she will probably decide she doesn’t want to talk to me anymore. I don’t want that. But I can’t imagine a situation where a parent would need to care more about what their kid thinks.

And let’s say there is a reason to read. What kind of reason?

I read my daughter’s texts when I suspect something is going on. Or when I need to know what’s going on. If a school counselor calls me and says she needs to talk, that’s a reason to read the texts.

But that’s not all.

If someone says something to my daughter in person, it will probably be repeated in texts. If she’s being teased or bullied, I need to know that. If she’s being recruited to do something bad, I need to know that. If she’s doing something bad herself, I need to know that.

I’m not talking about knowing that my kid does things I don’t agree with. I know that already.

I’m talking about knowing what kinds of things they do.

I read my daughter’s texts because they tell me things I need to know to be the kind of parent I want to be.

And not just the kind of parent I want to be: they tell me things I need to know to be a good friend, a good colleague, and a good person.

I need to know about things that happen in my daughter’s life. I need to know about the things that happen to her, the things she does, and the things she’s thinking about.

I need to know about the stuff that happens to her friends.

I need to know the things that people in her life say to her, and the things that happen to other people in her life.

And I need to know what she thinks about all of it.

My daughter has her own life. She lives her life in ways I don’t always understand. Sometimes she does things that I wouldn’t do, because she’s a different person. And sometimes she does things that I don’t understand, because I don’t know enough about how teenagers work.

I like to know what she’s thinking.

When she’s upset, it’s not because I don’t understand what she’s thinking. It’s because I don’t understand why she’s upset about it.

And when she’s happy, it’s not because I don’t know what she’s thinking. It’s because I don’t know why she’s so excited about it.

And when my daughter is happy or upset, I’m happy or upset with her.

My daughter’s thoughts are her thoughts. They’re not mine.

But I’m not her. She’s not me. She thinks about things I wouldn’t think about, for reasons I don’t understand. And she’s right.

I don’t think that’s a problem.

I have to think about things I don’t think about, for reasons I don’t understand. That’s not a problem. That’s life.

It’s just harder than it should be. I’m not the kind of person who can see what the teenagers in my life see, or understand what they see. And I don’t think that’s a problem.

It seems like this is a very minor question. But I think it’s actually a really serious one.

First, let me say that I’m a terrible parent. I have two kids right now, ages 12 and 14, who have been mostly happy but are now starting to push against me the way teenagers do.

My younger one is a very happy and easy-going kid. She’s a good student, a good athlete, and has a bunch of friends. I love her a lot.

My older one, I’ll call her “X”, is a bit more complicated. When she’s in her good moods she’s really sweet and fun and funny, like a lot of teenagers. But she can also be extremely stubborn and defiant, and when she’s mad at me (which, like most teenagers, she’s frequently), she can be just as much of a pain as my mom could be when she was mad at me in the same way.

She’s a good student, too. But she’s not very good at making friends. She has one really good friend that I don’t worry about at all, but she also has a group of “friends” who I’m not sure are actually good for her. I’ve always tried to not interfere in my kids’ friendships, but these friends have been involved in some really questionable activities, including being involved in a fight that resulted in one of them getting suspended from school.

So I have some worries about her. I think her school friends are a bad influence and that it’s probably bad for her to spend a lot of time with them. But she’s 14, so she’s old enough to want to have her own life. I know it can be very stressful for teenagers to spend time at school around a lot of people who are annoying, and so I don’t want to take away her friends.

This is a common kind of parent-child tension. I have a good relationship with her. We’re friends. But I’m her parent, and she’s 14, and I’m still expected to be responsible for her. I don’t know what to do. I can see that some of her friends are bad for her, but I don’t know if it’s okay to take them away from her or what, so I’m sort of just… trying to not worry about it too much.

But it’s hard to not worry about it.

So I’ve tried to monitor her in a couple of different ways. I know that this is not great, and I know that she has a right to privacy. But there is a limit on that. I can’t have a 14 year old going out and meeting random guys in chat rooms and I can’t have a 14 year old smoking pot in my house without me knowing. She is not old enough to do things like that by herself. I know that it’s hard to know where the line is, but there is a line, and I’m not going to just pretend that there isn’t.

I’ve asked her to let me see her phone before. Not all the time, but just sort of randomly. And she would let me, and it was fine, but then a few days later she’d tell me that she didn’t want to let me look at it anymore because she’s not sure if that’s even okay. And that was true, she was right, it wasn’t okay.

I’ve also looked at her Facebook and Instagram, which seems a bit less invasive. She doesn’t seem to mind it. And then I’ve also looked at her Instagram Direct messages, which seems a bit less okay. She’s never seen me look at them, but I’ve looked at them and it was mostly just normal stuff like she was making plans to meet up with friends and stuff. It wasn’t really anything to worry about.

But then I found out that she had a Snapchat account, and that she was sending a lot of messages to one of her friends. So I said to her “Can I see your Snapchat?” And she said “No”. And I said “Well why not, I’ve been looking at your Instagram messages and you don’t seem to care about that.” And she said “Snapchat is different.”

And it’s true, Snapchat is different. I had no idea that she had a Snapchat, and so I had no way to see it before she told me. And I didn’t really want to look through her phone and find it, because that would be really inappropriate. And it’s true, Snapchat is different, because it’s kind of a secret kind of thing.

But I was worried about her. So I went to her room, and when she wasn’t there I opened her phone and went to Snapchat and looked at the messages. And it was fine. She was just texting about how she thought the food at the school was bad and stuff.

So that was fine. I didn’t say anything about it, I just sort of pretended I didn’t look.

And then a few weeks later, my friend told me that X had been making mean comments on her Facebook. So I thought “I wonder if she’s making those mean comments to other people as well.” And I thought “maybe her Snapchat account is a good place to check” because if she had been saying things that were kind of racist on Facebook, then I thought she might have been saying them to her friends on Snapchat.

So I went into her Snapchat and I looked at the messages. And she had been saying racist things to her friends. It wasn’t as bad as I thought it would be, but it wasn’t good either.

So I talked to her about it. I said “I noticed that you were saying some things to your friends that seem kind of racist, and I want to talk to you about that.” And she was very mad at me. She said “You’re not allowed to look at my Snapchat.”

And I said “Yes, you’re right, I’m not. But you were doing something that was really bad and I needed to know about it and so I did it. It was wrong of me but I needed to do it.”

And she said “I’m not going to talk to you.”

And she didn’t talk to me for like a week.

I don’t want to be the kind of parent who just ignores their kids and lets them go off and do what they want to do. And I’m not. But sometimes my kids get mad at me because they want to be independent and I’m not giving them enough independence.

I’ve never really wanted to be the kind of parent who reads their kid’s text messages, but I did it in this case. I know that I probably shouldn’t have, but I did. I’m not proud of it, but I don’t regret it either. I was really worried about her and I felt like it was the right thing to do.

So my question is: is it ever okay to read your teenager’s text messages?

response:
I have seen many arguments in favor of snooping in teenagers’ phones, and they’re all terrible. Here are the two main arguments, and a rebuttal to each.

First, people like to say that kids’ phones are so central to their lives that they *should* be able to look at their kids’ phones. This is kind of an argument from analogy. When your kid was younger, you were able to go through her things, like her drawers. Now that she’s a teenager, the phone is sort of like her drawer, so you should be able to look through it.

I don’t think this works for two reasons. One, even if the phone is kind of like the drawer, it’s *more* like the diary. And it’s pretty well established that looking through kids’ diaries is the one thing you shouldn’t do. Two, I don’t think that looking through a drawer counts as “going through their things” in the way that you’re talking about.

I’m not saying this to make the parents who look at their kids’ drawers feel bad. I am saying this to make the parents who look at their kids’ phones realize that it’s not the same thing. I’m guessing that most of you don’t go through your kids’ drawers in the same way you go through their phones. You’re not going through their drawers in search of some particular kind of evidence. You’re not looking for the drawer that contains all the evidence you need about their life. I don’t think you’re even going through them very often.

I also think people don’t understand how central phones are to teenagers’ lives. They don’t understand that you really don’t have much of a life outside of your phone. It’s not like you have a diary, and a drawer, and a phone. It’s the phone, and maybe a drawer.

The second argument in favor of looking at kids’ phones is that it’s dangerous. They might get into drugs or drinking. They might meet a pedophile. I don’t think it’s okay to look through kids’ phones *just in case*, but I do think it’s okay if you suspect something, if you want to find out what’s going on.

It’s just that this is not at all a common situation. Parents who suspect something, who have to find out what’s going on, they’re not going to start snooping through their children’s phones. They’re going to sit them down and have a serious conversation. If necessary, they’re going to ask their friends. They’re not going to snoop.

I am not saying you can never look through your child’s phone. I am just saying that if you do, you will not be able to look through your child’s phone when you really need to.

What’s more, if you do this, you are going to be a person who does this kind of thing, and people are going to know. They’re not going to ask you to come and watch their kids. They’re not going to want to be around you. They’re not going to want to be friends with you.

One of the reasons I like this book is that I think the parents who don’t allow their kids to have phones, the parents who don’t believe in the internet, the parents who don’t believe in social media, I think they’re all right, but they’re also kind of annoying.

It would be really nice to talk to people who understand the internet. Who know what I’m talking about when I say things like “Oh my god, you have to come and see this!” or “Why is this person even online?” It would be really nice to talk to people who understand the internet, and don’t think it’s weird that I talk about this so much.

So far, I haven’t found anyone like that. I have only found parents who think I’m nuts.

The Virtue of Quitting argues that quitting is often necessary for success, that it is often more productive than continuing to plough through, and that we need to overcome our cultural bias against it.

I agree with all of these points. But I want to argue for an additional reason why we need to overcome this cultural bias, a reason that is not a matter of efficiency.

It’s about honesty.

I have been involved in a number of projects that have ended badly. This usually happens after a number of steps. First, there is a project I believe in with passion and I work on it hard. The important thing about this process is that at every stage, even when things are going badly and even after it becomes clear that the project will not succeed, I am doing the right thing. In other words, the right thing is not to quit the moment the going gets hard.

This is why people think that you should quit when the going gets tough. But this is wrong. It is the denial of the virtue of quitting.

The problem with this view is that it leads to two bad things. First, it encourages people to quit too early, because they see things not working out and then assume that the only reason to continue is if you are not admitting that it is not working.

Second, it makes people feel bad if they keep working on something even though it is not working out. They feel like they are doing something wrong, like they are being dishonest. This can make people not want to continue to work on something even when they know that that is the right thing.

But persistence is also when you’re trying to do something that you don’t even really want to do anymore. And you’re trying to do it, and you’re working really hard at it, but you’re doing it because you’re trying to convince yourself that you want to do it. This is not a virtue, this is a vice, and this is called stubbornness.

The reason this is a vice is that it doesn’t make sense. It’s not really useful to anyone. So what’s the difference between persistence and stubbornness?

Well, if you’re persistent, you’re doing something you want to do. And you’re doing it because you have a reason to do it. If you’re stubborn, you’re doing something you don’t want to do anymore. You’re just doing it because you’ve already done it before. And you’re doing it because you don’t want to admit that you don’t want to do it anymore.

But when you’re stubborn, you’re doing something you don’t want to do anymore, and you’re just doing it because you’ve done it before, and you don’t want to admit that you don’t want to do it anymore.

I think the most common thing that happens is that people become persistent in a bad way. They become persistent in a bad way and they’re not even aware that they’re doing it. They think they’re persistent in a good way, but they’re persistent in a bad way.

prompt: Write an essay arguing that 'show, don't tell' is the most overrated piece of writing advice, and that some of the best prose in English is almost pure telling.
response:
I’m going to take a controversial position that “show, don’t tell” is not actually good writing advice.

It’s one of the most famous bits of writing advice, and like most of the things you hear from writers, it’s a simplification of a more complicated truth, but in this case the truth is that it’s not just wrong, it’s the opposite of right. The best writing is almost always tell.

The first part of the advice, “show”, is the easy one. When people say “show, don’t tell,” what they’re really saying is “don’t use boring language.” So when you write the sentence “He was upset,” you’re supposed to rewrite it as “He slammed his fist on the table.” Instead of just saying what he did, you’re showing it to us by describing it in vivid detail.

But this is just the easy half of the problem. The next step is to make sure that when you say “He slammed his fist on the table”, you’re not just saying it for the sake of being vivid. If you do it just for the sake of being vivid, it will be so obvious that you’ll end up being just as boring as the original. The original was a boring sentence because it didn’t have enough information. The vivid sentence is boring because it’s too clear about what information it is giving you. A good sentence will give you an amount of information that’s just enough to make the reader start wondering what else is going on.

Here’s an example of really good writing from The Great Gatsby:

There must have been something in his red-rimmed eyes to reassure me — a quality of hope.

This is not a particularly memorable sentence in a novel full of memorable sentences. And yet when I read it the first time, I was surprised by how much I liked it. I didn’t know exactly why.

A few minutes ago, I was trying to think of a sentence that would be both vivid and not boring. And then I suddenly realized that this sentence is exactly the kind of sentence I was looking for.

There’s some information in this sentence that you wouldn’t expect. When someone says “He was upset,” the last thing you expect is that you’ll get the phrase “a quality of hope.” “Hope” is something you would never expect to associate with being upset. This is what makes the sentence interesting.

If I rewrote the sentence to be more vivid, and changed “red-rimmed eyes” to “bloodshot eyes”, then it’s not interesting any more. “Red-rimmed eyes” is vivid. It’s also interesting. Because it’s surprising. Who would think that eyes are red-rimmed? We all know that eyes can be red, but we don’t usually think about why. When someone’s eyes are red, is it because of the iris? Or the whites? What does it mean to say eyes are red-rimmed?

There’s no such thing as bloodshot eyes. Bloodshot is a perfectly normal word, but it doesn’t mean what you expect it to mean. It means that the veins in the eyes are red. That’s not surprising. And so “bloodshot” is a vivid but boring word, while “red-rimmed” is both vivid and interesting.

This sentence has another interesting property: the phrase “a quality of hope” seems so out of place that you don’t expect it, but it makes total sense. It turns out that it’s a really good description of what it’s like to see someone’s red-rimmed eyes. You can’t tell why someone’s eyes are red-rimmed, so you’re going to think they’re upset. But if you look closer, you might see that they’re smiling, and you might be able to guess that they’re happy.

The other half of the advice, “don’t tell”, is where most people go wrong. They think “show, don’t tell” means you should never just tell the reader something. But the reason “show” is supposed to come before “tell” is that it’s more interesting. If I write “I was happy”, it’s less interesting than “my eyes were red-rimmed”, because my eyes being red-rimmed is something I didn’t expect.

But if I write “My eyes were red-rimmed, but I was happy,” then that’s a lot more interesting than just “My eyes were red-rimmed.” If I just said my eyes were red-rimmed, you would wonder why they were red-rimmed, and then you might have to read another few pages to find out. If I say that they were red-rimmed but I was happy, then you don’t have to wait as long to find out what’s going on.

The best writing is going to be tell because it’s more interesting than show. The best writing is going to be a sequence of sentences where you don’t know what’s going to happen next. If you’re just saying “I was happy,” then you know that’s all you’re going to get. And if you’re saying “my eyes were red-rimmed,” you know that the next thing you’re going to hear is going to be why my eyes were red-rimmed. But if you’re saying “my eyes were red-rimmed, but I was happy,” you don’t know what’s going to come next. It could be “because I was happy”, or it could be “but then I realized I was wrong.”

prompt: Write an essay arguing that 'show, don't tell' is the most overrated piece of writing advice, and that some of the best prose in English is almost pure telling.
response:
One of the most common pieces of writing advice is “show, don’t tell” — when describing your character, don’t say that she was beautiful, but describe her face, or how people reacted to her, or whatever.

I think this is bad advice. Here’s why:

The best prose is often almost pure telling. Consider:

A woman is sitting in a room, waiting. She’s not sure why she’s waiting. She thinks she’s probably supposed to be waiting for her husband. It’s been about three months since he’s been dead, and she’s been sitting at this table for three hours and she’s gotten a little bit tired. She’s not sure why she’s still sitting there. She’s trying to remember what the plan was when he died. She knows it was to wait a while, but she’s not sure what she’s supposed to do after the waiting.

This is from a novel called *In a Sunburned Country* and the author is Jenny Offill. If you’ve read her writing before, you’ll recognize the style. It’s almost entirely telling, and the reason I love it is because she’s doing something no one else does: she’s describing the actual experience of being in a human mind.

When people write about minds, they almost always describe what minds do, not what minds are. You can have your character thinking about stuff, but it will almost always be something like: “What would a person do in this situation?” or “I need to tell Jane I’m going out with Dave” or whatever. It will be about some external subject, and the thinking will be done at a certain level of abstraction, and the sentence structure will reflect what kind of sentence structure you’d use if you were explaining the thinking to someone else.

This is not what minds do. This is not what minds are. Minds are a stream of consciousness, and that stream is constantly shifting, in ways that don’t fit into neat sentences.

You can kind of get this with a stream-of-consciousness technique, but most of the time it looks like this:

It was a dark and stormy night. The wind was howling through the streets and she felt a chill.

But it’s still at the right level of abstraction, and the sentence structure is still as if you were telling someone else what your mind is like.

The other way you can get this kind of thing is if your character is very, very sad or very, very confused, in which case you can have a stream-of-consciousness like:

I don’t know what to do. What am I supposed to do. I don’t know. What am I supposed to do.

But again, you’re still at the right level of abstraction, and the sentence structure is still as if you were telling someone else what your mind is like.

So when I first started reading Jenny Offill’s writing, I couldn’t quite figure out what I was reading. It was kind of confusing. And then I realized: she’s describing the actual experience of being in a human mind, instead of writing about minds the way we usually write about minds. It’s kind of like the difference between a portrait and a sketch of a portrait.

And once I figured out what she was doing, I couldn’t get enough of it.

Another example of this from the same novel:

The man was a bit short, and he had darkish hair, and a nice face. She liked him right away. He was a musician, and she liked that. He was a musician and she liked it when men were musicians. He was a musician and she thought that if her husband had been a musician, he wouldn’t have died. She was very upset about this. Her husband would have been alive if he had been a musician.

The first half of this sentence is just describing the man. The second half is just describing her reaction to the man. But the third sentence is something you might never see in any other novel. The sentence is still as if you were telling someone else what your character was thinking, but the content of the sentence is the actual experience of being a human mind, not what minds do.

And this is the best prose I’ve ever read.

prompt: why do some words become embarrassing to say out loud? 'moist' is the obvious one but also 'panties', 'journey' (when used about personal growth), 'synergy'. Write something exploring what's going on there.
response:
I have noticed recently that the word “moist” is getting a lot of hate on Twitter. There are people who have made whole careers out of this sort of thing. There’s a guy called Rick Dees who has done a whole series of songs mocking the word “moist”. I’m not sure why everyone hates this word so much – perhaps it’s because it’s an unusual word to use, or perhaps it’s because it sounds like “mouse”.

I think there is a general problem with words becoming embarrassing to use, which I have noticed on several occasions in the last month or so.

First, I started a blog called The Journey, which was going to be about my experiences and discoveries during my 18 month journey of learning how to be a better person. My plan was to write a blog post every week or so with all the things I had learned.

Unfortunately, I discovered that the word “journey” had become so embarrassing to say that I felt like I was going to explode any time I wrote it. I have no idea why the word “journey” has become such a buzzword, but it has.

The second case was when I started talking to a couple of business people about what they were doing. These people were all incredibly smart and interesting, and they had really great business ideas. Unfortunately, they also all used the word “synergy” at least 50 times per day.

I have no idea why these people use the word “synergy” so much – I think it’s because it’s a big fancy sounding word that makes them sound impressive. But it’s embarrassing to hear this word. It’s like they’re trying so hard to sound smart that it’s almost as embarrassing as hearing someone try to use French in order to sound impressive.

So, why do these words become embarrassing?

The first reason is that they are associated with a particular group of people. If I say “journey” or “moist” or “synergy”, then I’m signalling that I’m one of those people who is interested in self-improvement or who uses big impressive sounding words to make themselves sound impressive. I’m telling you that I’m one of them.

I’m not saying that this is a bad thing – maybe I’m just not interested in that group of people. But if you’re going to start using the word “moist”, be prepared for people to be embarrassed that they know you.

The second reason is that words become embarrassing because they are used by people who are trying to sound impressive, and so using them makes *you* sound as if you’re trying to sound impressive, too.

This is why words like “moist”, “journey” and “synergy” get mocked so much – people are trying to sound impressive by using words that they don’t really understand, and this is a good target for mockery.

So, if you want to avoid having your words mocked, be careful about using words that are associated with people who are trying to sound impressive.

prompt: why do some words become embarrassing to say out loud? 'moist' is the obvious one but also 'panties', 'journey' (when used about personal growth), 'synergy'. Write something exploring what's going on there.
response:
I recently had an argument over the word “moist.” My friend said it sounded gross, while I said that was ridiculous and people were just being silly. But we had a lot in common: we both agreed it was a *bad thing* that people thought that.

There are a few words that fall into this category. Moist is the most famous one, but I can also name “panties”, “journey” (in a personal growth sense), and “synergy”. And I can name one more: “moist”.

Why are these words gross? What makes people feel weird about them?

I’ve heard a few guesses.

First is that the words sound like something you wouldn’t say out loud. “Moist” sounds similar to “moots” or “moosts” or some other gross sounding word. “Panties” is obviously like “pants”, which is obviously a gross word. This seems like the wrong answer, because “moist” isn’t really like “moots”, and “panties” isn’t gross if you say it in French.

Second, it’s because these words are associated with weirdos. “Moist” is a word you’ll see in weirdos’ spam emails. “Panties” is a word you’ll see in weirdos’ porn. “Journey” is a word you’ll see in weirdos’ self help books. “Synergy” is a word you’ll see in weirdos’ business books. This seems like the right answer, but it’s a little weird, because if that was true, then you could just ban the words and it would go away.

Third is that there’s something about the *sound* of words like “moist”, like maybe it sounds kind of like a fart or something. This also seems like a bad answer, because it implies we’re doing it unconsciously, but we’re not.

What I think is going on is that there’s some kind of social coordination game. Imagine that we can choose whether to use the word “moist” or the word “damp”. If someone uses “damp”, they’re perfectly normal, and no one is affected. If someone uses “moist”, they signal that they’re weird and everyone else feels a little icky. If no one uses “moist”, then that’s fine, and no one is affected. If *everyone* uses “moist”, then it sounds weird and gross and we all feel a little icky. If *most people* use “moist”, then people who use “moist” are signaling that they’re normal and we all feel great. The optimal thing for each person to do is coordinate with others, and then use the word that’s in the majority. That’s why the word “moist” can be both gross and desirable, and how it can remain in use, and how banning the word won’t help.

I think this is the right explanation, because it’s true that people use the words “moist” and “damp” interchangeably. And it’s true that banning words won’t help. And it’s true that if I use “moist” in this paragraph, people think I’m weird.

The obvious counterexample is the word “fuck”, which people are using more and more, and which is becoming less taboo. But I would argue that this is a different coordination game. The taboo against saying “fuck” is more like “don’t talk to strangers”, and the taboo against saying “moist” is more like “don’t speak a different dialect than your peers”. It’s not that there’s anything wrong with the word “fuck”, it’s just that it’s taboo to say it out loud. It’s not that there’s anything wrong with the word “moist”, it’s just that it *is* a different dialect than my peers. And it’s not that saying “fuck” is weird, it’s that saying “fuck” out loud is weird. And it’s not that saying “moist” is weird, it’s that saying “moist” when you’re not supposed to is weird.

The word “moist” is kind of a weird example, because people seem to be doing it on purpose. But the word “synergy” is another example of this. It’s a totally normal word, but people find it weird to say. But that’s because there’s some kind of social coordination game going on.
