Finally in college I figured out that the word was supposed to be neutral. It had only become taboo because I’d heard people using it in the wrong way and I hadn’t known how to separate the word from the taboo.

I think this is the right story for “moist” in particular. But I’m not sure that’s the whole story.

The word “moist” is a weird word. It’s not very common. It’s not a word you see in everyday conversation. It’s not a word people use to talk about things like “I like moist cake”. It’s a word you mostly find in technical descriptions, like on the back of boxes of crackers. It’s a word whose normal uses are so rare that when someone says it, it really draws attention. And the word that draws attention is the word that gets turned into a taboo word.

I think the same story applies to “journey”. It’s a pretty common word, but it’s a bit unusual. You probably won’t use “journey” in normal conversation. And when you use it in the weird self-help “I’m on a journey of personal growth” kind of way, it draws attention. Then it gets turned into a taboo word.

I think the same story applies to “panties” too. I think a lot of people just don’t like using the word. It’s a common word and I don’t think there’s anything weird about using it. But it just sounds a little funny.

prompt: I would appreciate an essay on whether a translation can ever be better than its original, and if so, what 'better' could even mean. Examples from poetry welcome, but I'm more interested in the conceptual question.
response:
Can a translation ever be better than the original? And if it can, in what sense of the word better?

I’ve seen it suggested that in some cases, a translation can be more beautiful than the original – more beautiful in the sense that it’s a more successful work of art. But I can’t imagine what it would mean for this to be true.

Suppose I write a poem, then a translator translates it into another language. The translator’s job is to produce a version of the poem in another language that, as far as possible, evokes the same feelings in its readers that the original evokes in mine. They can’t do this perfectly, because of the impossibility of perfect translation.

But the translator’s job isn’t to write a different poem. They’re not allowed to take liberties, make their own aesthetic choices, and try to produce something that evokes different feelings. If they did that, they wouldn’t be writing a translation of my poem, they’d be writing their own poem.

The closest analogy I can think of is this. Suppose I write a poem, and then a copyist makes a copy of the poem. In some cases, the copyist does a good job; in other cases, they do a bad job. It’s not an interesting question to ask which is better, the original or the copy; obviously the original is.

A translation is a very complicated copy, with a lot of latitude to succeed or fail. But it is still a copy, and a bad copy, and that’s the best case.

There is no reason to assume that this sort of copy would be better than the original. The copyist is probably not as good a poet as I am – in fact, probably not a poet at all. They might be able to find a few better words for the poem, but this would be at the expense of losing many other things that are good in the original.

This is what it would mean for a translation to be a “more successful work of art”. A more successful work of art would be one that evoked the same feelings in its audience, but did it with less effort, or less money, or less time. That would mean that some version of the poem in another language would evoke more feelings per unit of effort than the original does.

This seems impossible. I don’t mean that it’s hard to imagine such a translation. I mean that it’s logically impossible for it to be better, in the sense of more successful at evoking feelings, than the original.

prompt: I would appreciate an essay on whether a translation can ever be better than its original, and if so, what 'better' could even mean. Examples from poetry welcome, but I'm more interested in the conceptual question.
response:
I was recently talking with someone who was translating from Italian to English. I asked whether the Italian was better or English. She answered with a story about the time she worked on the book *The Name of the Rose*. She was translating a passage, and after a couple of drafts, she thought she had translated the passage so well that she had made it better than the Italian. But then she went and looked at the Italian again, and she had to admit that the Italian was better, because the Italian was the way the author had *intended* it to be. She went back and forth a couple of times, but eventually had to admit that even though she had improved the prose, it was no better than the Italian.

I think this is a very important insight, and it’s one that I’ve been trying to work through for a while. I’ve come to realize that I’ve had a lot of conversations like this over the last few years, with a lot of different translators, and the general conclusion has been that a translation can never be better than the original.

I don’t think this idea will be obvious to many people, because we’re used to thinking of a translation as a copy of the original. The more faithful the translation, the better. So I’m always curious how they think about this idea, and why they don’t think of their job as copying. But I also think that the general idea of “faithfulness” is a misleading way to think about translation, and I think there are a number of important ideas in translation theory that have to do with this.

So let’s say that a translation is a copy of the original. If the translator gets every little detail of the original text right, then the translation should be identical to the original text. But then we’re no longer talking about a translation, we’re talking about the original. A translation is a copy, but a copy of something else. The translation is in English, but it copies an Italian text.

What this means is that the translation is a copy, not of what the author intended to say, but of the way in which the author expressed those words. If we think of the original author’s intention as the original “text,” the original author’s Italian expression is an imperfect copy of that.

This means that the “faithfulness” of a translation is not about how well the translator understood the author’s intention, but how accurately the translator reproduced the author’s *mistakes*. The translator’s job is to reproduce the mistakes in the original text. This is not always a job that a translator wants to do, and there are cases where it’s not even possible. But in general, the translator’s job is to reproduce those mistakes.

But I’m not a translator, and so I’m not going to try to explain all of the different considerations involved in translation. So instead, I’m going to try to explain this from the point of view of poetry. I’m going to use a poem that I wrote, called “Losing Your Memory.” It goes like this:

I am losing my memory.

I was supposed to be here yesterday.

I remember it was yesterday.

I remember I was supposed to be here,

and that I was not.

I remember that I forgot.

I have never been more sure of anything,

and I don’t even know where to begin.

I can’t even remember the end.

Now, this poem is in English. If I tried to translate it into French, I’d probably get a translation that sounds something like this:

Je perds ma mémoire.

J’étai censé être ici hier.

Je me souviens que c’était hier.

Je me souviens que je devais être ici,

et que je n’y étais pas.

Je me souviens que j’ai oublié.

Je n’ai jamais été aussi sûr de quoi que ce soit,

et je ne sais même pas par où commencer.

Je n’arrive même pas à me souvenir de la fin.

I don’t speak French, but I know enough to know that it doesn’t sound right. It’s a bit stiff, and it doesn’t rhyme or have any rhythm. And there are a couple of things that I’m not quite sure how to say in French, like “I was supposed to be here,” and so I just made a guess there and left it for a translator to fix.

If you’re a translator, you might find this funny, but I think it’s important to understand what it’s like when someone who doesn’t know the language tries to translate something. And the reason I think it’s important is because a lot of people are surprised to hear how much work goes into translation. And when someone is surprised about the amount of work involved in translation, the reason is that they’re assuming that the process is just about copying, and that if you just have a really good dictionary, then it should be easy to translate. And I think that’s a really common way of thinking about translation.

So the reason I’m going to use my own poem is because I can explain what I was going for. I wanted the poem to have a certain rhythm, but also to rhyme, and to be easy to read out loud. And the poem also has a few things that I think are interesting. I wrote “I was supposed to be here yesterday,” which I think sounds funny. It sounds like “yesterday” should go at the beginning of the sentence. “I was supposed to be here yesterday,” I wrote it in that order.

And then there’s the last line, “I can’t even remember the end.” It’s a line that refers back to the line from earlier in the poem, “I don’t even know where to begin.” That’s supposed to be funny, but there’s also the fact that “begin” and “end” are a pair of words. I’m sure that there are better words for those words, but for some reason, I didn’t think of anything else when I was writing this poem.

So now let’s try translating it. I’m going to try to translate this poem into French. I don’t know French, but I’ve had a bit of practice with translation, and I’ve got a translator’s dictionary, so I’m going to try to do it the best I can.

I’m not just talking about the obvious case where the original is a great work in a dead language, and a translation makes it accessible to modern readers, who would otherwise be shut out from reading it at all. Nor am I talking about the obvious case where the original was written in some obscure language, and a translation into a major language will make it far more widely available. These are both cases where the translation is more widely available, but I don’t think they are cases where the translation is “better” in any sense.

No, I’m talking about a much stronger claim.

I think that a translation of a poem can be better than the original. Not more widely available, not more readable, not more understandable, but better.

This is a strong claim. To prove it, I need to show that there is some kind of quality where the translation is better, and I need to show that this quality is what we mean when we talk about how good a poem is.

My argument will proceed by two examples of cases where this happens. I hope that if I can come up with two examples where the translation is better, it will be hard for you to imagine any third kind of poem that wouldn’t be subject to the same argument, and I’ll have demonstrated that translations can be better than the originals.

I.

In her essay, Guedj gives an example of a passage of poetry where the translation is more beautiful than the original.

Here is the English translation:

The wind and the sea had carried me to the land of the Cyclops, to the lawless, wild-eyed Cyclops, who eat meat among their people and neither plow nor sow, nor know anything of the fruit of the wheat, which when it grows in the field nourishes all men.

Here is the Spanish version:

El viento y el mar me llevaron a la tierra de los Cíclopes, los desalmados de ojos torcidos, que comen carne entre su gente y no aran ni siembran, ni saben nada del fruto de la espiga, que al crecer en el campo nutre a todos los hombres.

And here is the Greek original, transliterated:

hē anemos kai thalassa hēgesato eph’ ho genos kyklopōn aphronōn, phthōron aithōn, hoi d’ en laois ktemnesin esthiōsin, oud’ arousin oud’ arousin, oud’ oiden thespos arthra, to th’ en agreisai phutōn pant’ anthrōpous trphei.

It would probably take a while to explain why the Spanish version is better than the English one, or why both the Spanish and English versions are better than the Greek. But I hope you can understand this at least: I think the Spanish version is more beautiful than the English version. I would be pretty surprised if anyone disagrees.

Now. If we say that the Spanish version of this poem is better than the English one, what do we mean?

It’s not that the Spanish version is more accurate. It’s not that the Spanish version makes a more compelling case that Odysseus is lost and alone, or that the Cyclopes are wild savages, or that the wind and the sea are uncontrollable. These are all facts about the original text that the translation can only preserve, not improve. It’s not that the Spanish translation is more accessible or more readable.

The Spanish translation is not more beautiful than the English translation because it does a better job of communicating what Homer meant, or what Homer’s poem is about. It is more beautiful because it is more beautiful. And if we can accept that “more beautiful” means “better”, then the Spanish translation is better than the English one.

II.

Guedj’s example shows that a translation can be better than the original in the sense of being more beautiful. But is beauty the kind of thing we should be thinking about in poetry? Is a poem that is beautiful but not profound really better than a poem that is profound but not beautiful?

I think the answer is yes, and I can prove this with the example of the poet Thomas Hardy, whose poem “The Darkling Thrush” is both beautiful and profound.

This poem has been translated into many languages, some of them with more beauty than others. Here is a translation into Spanish:

El sol se hundió en el ocaso,

La última luz se apagó.

Un pájaro cantó en la negrura.

¿Qué le dirías,

Pobre viejo año,

Que estabas tan triste?

¿Por qué te dejaste a la deriva?

En el invierno,

Con el aire que respira

Casi helado y la noche

A punto de caer

Sobre la tierra muerta,

Con un campo dormido,

Con una arboleda que cruje y crujirá

Cuando el viento bala

La última rama del pino

Y la última hoja del roble.

Y el cielo se cierra

Como un pájaro que desciende,

El sol se aleja.

La noche cubre el suelo,

Los últimos pájaros se alejan,

Las últimas estrellas se apagan.

¿Qué me dirías,

Pobre viejo año,

Que estabas tan triste?

¿Por qué te dejaste a la deriva?

The poem is not very beautiful, but it captures what is important in the original. If you read this translation, you will know what Hardy’s poem is about, and you will understand its profound meaning. But it won’t sound like a poem, and it won’t be any more beautiful than the average prose.

In Spanish, I think “The Darkling Thrush” would be a pretty bad translation. It is probably the worst translation I know of, and if I can show that the Spanish translation of *The Odyssey* is better than the Spanish translation of “The Darkling Thrush”, then I will have shown that the Spanish translation of *The Odyssey* is better than the English translation of “The Darkling Thrush”, and I will have shown that a translation can be better than the original.

Here are the first few lines of the Spanish translation of “The Darkling Thrush”:

The sun is setting in the west,

The last light is gone.

A bird sings in the dark.

I think this is a more beautiful translation than the original. It’s also not very accurate. If you read the Spanish translation, you’ll know that the sun is setting and the light is going away and a bird is singing in the dark. But you won’t know what the original poem is about, because it’s about something different.

This is a case where a translation is better than the original because it’s more beautiful, but it’s not a case where the translation is better because it’s more accurate.

prompt: for my newsletter (mostly librarians and teachers, ~3k subscribers): an essay on rereading. why the second time through a book is often the first time you actually read it. warm but not twee, 800ish words
response:
I have spent the last three weeks rereading books. I am a compulsive rereader. For the last 30 years, I have probably read a third of my books more than once. Some more than twice.

When I was young, I read a lot of books more than once because I didn’t have enough books to go around. When I was 10, I read the entire collection of children’s books at our local library and had to start over again, and I kept doing that until I got old enough to read the adults’ stuff too.

There’s something about rereading that has been a constant in my life, even in the era when I had enough books to go around. For the last 20 years, my partner and I have been rereading the books that we first read together. We have reread them because we loved them. But we have also reread them to reestablish a shared history. We reread them because, as the years pass, the world becomes less predictable and more frightening, and we want to remember what we have in common.

But this time, I reread books because I wanted to remember why I like reading in the first place.

Rereading has taught me an important lesson, one that’s been slowly seeping into my consciousness for a few decades now.

When you read a book for the first time, you are busy with the task of figuring out what’s going on. You are trying to keep track of the characters, where they are, what they are doing, why they are doing it, what’s going to happen next. The task of figuring out what’s going on takes up most of your mental bandwidth.

When you read a book a second time, you already know the story. When you reread, you don’t have to figure out what’s going on. So your attention goes elsewhere. You notice the details you missed the first time. You pay attention to the style. You notice what the author is really trying to say.

The second time through is often the first time you actually read a book.

I had always known that I loved to reread books. But now I have noticed that rereading is something that people do for all kinds of things. People reread their favorite songs. They reread their favorite movies. They reread their favorite television shows. I think most people who love a song, or a movie, or a TV show, will tell you that they love it because they’ve listened to or watched it more than once.

When you first listen to a song, you may not notice the words. When you listen to it a second time, you hear it more clearly. When you listen to it for the third time, the words have sunk in. When you listen to it a fourth time, you may notice that the singer doesn’t quite hit the same notes every time. When you listen to it for the fifth time, you start to understand how the lyrics relate to the music. You start to understand what the song is saying.

The second time through is often the first time you actually listen to a song.

When you first watch a movie, you don’t notice the details. But if you watch it again, you notice things. You notice details that you didn’t notice the first time. You start to understand the relationship between the movie and the novel it was based on. You start to understand how the characters relate to each other.

The second time through is often the first time you actually watch a movie.

When you reread a novel, a lot of things happen. You notice that the book you read when you were 10 is not the book you are reading when you’re 30. You start to understand what the author is trying to say. You start to understand how the author’s style differs from the styles of other writers. You start to understand that there’s a reason why the book was written the way it was.

The second time through is often the first time you actually read a book.

I reread books for the same reason that people reread their favorite songs, their favorite movies, and their favorite television shows. I want to know the things I love better. I want to understand the things I love more deeply.

When I reread a book, I get to know it better. When I reread a book, I discover new things. When I reread a book, I notice the details that I missed the first time.

When you reread a book, you can learn more about the author’s life. You can learn more about the author’s craft. You can learn more about how to read a book.

I think there’s something important that rereading can teach us about learning.

prompt: for my newsletter (mostly librarians and teachers, ~3k subscribers): an essay on rereading. why the second time through a book is often the first time you actually read it. warm but not twee, 800ish words
response:
I recently finished my second read of a novel. Not a re-read, mind you. A second read. A completely fresh, first-time encounter with the words. My first read of this book was years ago. I’d been asked to write a review of it for a school magazine, so I read it in a single sitting on the train back from an all-day conference. I remember thinking it was a bit confusing and slightly disappointing. I was annoyed because the character I was supposed to identify with was just so unlikeable, and I thought the author was a bit smug in how he presented certain things. I wrote a review that was basically just “this book was pretty boring and the main character wasn’t that likeable.” Then I forgot about it.

Several years later, a friend told me that she’d reread it and thought it was really interesting, and I said, “Oh no, I didn’t like it.” And she said, “Well, it’s pretty short. You should try reading it again.”

So I did. And it wasn’t even a little bit the same book. It was so much richer. The plot made so much more sense, the characters were more likeable. It wasn’t even just that I had forgotten how boring it was. It was that I wasn’t even noticing the things that had previously bothered me. I think I was thinking of the book in terms of the things that I hadn’t understood the first time I read it. The things that I hadn’t liked. And so now I was thinking of it in terms of the things I had understood, the things that I had liked. I think I was thinking about the book in terms of its successes rather than its failures. And that had an enormous effect on my perception.

I didn’t realize until I was halfway through that the main character was the same age as me now, not like he had been when I was reading the book for the first time. I’d been fifteen then, and so I had been thinking about how this character was a few years older than me, and I’d been thinking about what it meant that he was slightly older than me. And now that I was twenty, the book was a lot more relatable to me. And so the character was a lot more likeable.

I have a new rule now, which is that when I’m trying to read a book that is supposed to be for kids or teens, I try to read it first at the age it was intended for. Then I read it a second time as an adult. And then I read it a third time when I’m old. It’s interesting to see how it changes, and how much more I can understand of the book on a second and third reading.

I have a bunch of books that I’ve reread that I had thought I’d hated the first time I read them. The first book that comes to mind is *The Hobbit*. I hated it the first time I read it. I was about ten, and I was really into fantasy, but I just found it annoying. I hated that Bilbo was so reluctant to go on the adventure. I hated that the dwarves were all so stupid. I hated that Gandalf kept going off to do mysterious things and never explained what he was doing, or why he was doing it. I hated that the elves were so snooty and condescending. I hated that the whole thing was basically about a bunch of elves giving a bunch of dwarves a bunch of treasure. I thought it was a silly, overwrought story, and I didn’t like it at all. I think I was pretty disappointed.

A few years later I read it again, and I thought it was wonderful. I could understand exactly why Bilbo was reluctant to go on the adventure. I understood exactly why the dwarves were so stupid. I understood why Gandalf had to be so mysterious and cryptic. And now I really liked the elves and the dwarves and the hobbits and the whole plot, and the whole book. I thought it was a really amazing story.

And then later, when I was an adult, I read it a third time and thought it was still amazing. And now I can’t imagine why I hated it the first time.

I think the second time you read something is often the first time you truly read it.

prompt: for my newsletter (mostly librarians and teachers, ~3k subscribers): an essay on rereading. why the second time through a book is often the first time you actually read it. warm but not twee, 800ish words
response:
Rereading: The Best Time To Read A Book Is The Second Time

The first time I read Harry Potter was in the summer before seventh grade, 1999, and I was so impressed and thrilled that I read it again the next summer, and again in 2001, and then stopped. I don’t know why, exactly. I’ve read some books so many times that they become a sort of ritual or habit, but I never got that with Harry. For me, the books I reread are the ones that I can return to for any reason: nostalgia, boredom, the need to remember something I’d forgotten. I reread the Harry Potter books because I loved them, but I can’t quite find the words to say why. I don’t think that I have a favorite Harry Potter book. I remember reading them in a hurry when I was young, and the feeling I got was a sense of urgency and excitement: I wanted to know what was going to happen next. I still think the books are wonderful, but when I reread them I am looking for something I can’t quite put my finger on. I don’t think that it’s nostalgia, since I don’t reread every book I loved as a child. But there’s some combination of magic and excitement in those books that I can’t find elsewhere.

This is a bit of a digression. The point of all this is that I don’t think that rereading is all the same, and I don’t think that everyone rereads the same books for the same reasons. But I do think that the first time we read something and the second time are different, and that this difference is one of the things that makes rereading so much fun.

The first time you read a book, it’s all new. The words, the characters, the style. You have to make sense of it all, which takes effort. You have to decide what to pay attention to, and you have to figure out what to pay attention to. It’s like reading in a foreign language.

The second time you read a book, you don’t have to worry about understanding it. You don’t have to figure out who is who. You know what happens at the end, so you don’t have to worry about that. You’re just reading, which is something very different than trying to understand. If you’ve read a book so many times that you can recite it, then you can just read it the way you read poetry. You’re not trying to understand it, you’re just trying to remember.

I don’t know if this is exactly right. But I do know that the second time I read a book is the first time I can really enjoy it.

There’s a famous passage from The Great Gatsby where Nick Carraway says that he’s “promiscuous” in his reading, meaning that he reads a lot of different things and doesn’t really care which. But I think he’s saying something else. I think he’s saying that he reads a lot, and that he’s not very good at it.

When I read The Great Gatsby for the first time in school, I thought it was one of the worst books I’d ever read. It was so confusing and boring, and I couldn’t understand why anyone would like it. I had a lot of problems with the writing, the style, and the way Fitzgerald used words. I just couldn’t get into it, and it took me forever to finish.

I didn’t reread it until the last week of the semester. By that point I’d already done all my homework, and I had some time on my hands. I sat down to read The Great Gatsby, and I was surprised to discover that it was actually pretty good. It was still boring at times, but it was interesting in a way that I hadn’t noticed the first time around. I still have problems with the writing, but I’m not quite so bothered by them anymore.

I don’t know why I liked it the second time. It’s the same book. It’s just that the second time around I was able to read it without worrying about whether or not I was supposed to like it.

prompt: I've been writing a novel for six years and I'm starting to think finishing it would ruin it, because right now it can still be good in my head. Is that cowardice or is there something real there? Could you write an essay on the unfinished book as a kind of comfort? I don't need encouragement, I need someone to think about it with me.
response:
I finished a novel recently. It’s a long novel, and I’ve been writing it for six years. It took me almost as long to write it as it did the four novels before it combined.

When I was finished writing, I read it in a single sitting, as I did for all my previous novels. This time, though, I felt like I was reading somebody else’s work. I wasn’t sure it was good. It wasn’t as good as I remembered it being. It wasn’t as good as I imagined it could be. I wasn’t sure it was even finished, really.

I’ve written about finishing a book before. It’s always been hard. But this time, something new happened. I realized I might never write another one.

I’m forty now. I’ve spent the last fifteen years writing novels. That’s 30 percent of my whole life, already. The idea of spending another fifteen years writing another novel is really starting to feel heavy.

What’s more, I’ve been writing novels since I was a teenager. I’ve already written ten, plus two others that are half-finished. The first one I wrote was *The Book of Dragons*. I finished it when I was seventeen. I think it’s a very good novel, but when I read it now I can see where it came from. It’s a work by a teenager who loves Tolkien and the fantasy genre.

The first novel I wrote after that, *The King of Night and Day*, was a big step. It’s not just fantasy. It has more complicated ideas and characters. I was 18 when I wrote it.

After that, I went on to write novels that were a step from *The King of Night and Day*, but not as big a step.

And that’s still the case now. My latest novel, *The Book of Accidents*, is a step from *The King of Night and Day*. But it’s a pretty small step.

I’m not sure what to do with that fact. It makes me wonder: what if writing a book is not an exercise that makes you better? What if writing a novel is something you can only do a certain number of times? What if every time you do it, it takes something away from the well?

It could just be a coincidence. My novel-writing abilities have been increasing steadily for twenty years. Maybe they’ll keep increasing. But what if they’re not? What if *The Book of Accidents* was the best novel I’ll ever write?

What if that’s already happened?

What if, right now, there’s a great novel in my head, but I’m not going to be able to write it?

I don’t know.

But it makes me want to think more about the idea of an unfinished book.

The idea of an unfinished book is a really interesting one. It’s a book that could be great, but never will be. It’s a book that is a ghost, a phantom, a possibility. It’s a book that is an idea. It’s a book that is a dream.

There’s a book like that in my head. I think about it a lot. But I’m not sure I can write it. And even if I can, I don’t think I’ll have the energy to finish it. I have too much going on. My life is too full. I’m too busy.

But the idea of it is always there. It’s like a star that shines forever. It never goes out. It’s always there.

I don’t think I’m the only person who has an unfinished book in their head. I think a lot of people do. I know a lot of writers who’ve told me they have a novel they want to write, but they can’t write it. It’s just there, waiting.

There’s something comforting about that. It makes me feel like I’m not the only person who’s thinking about books that don’t exist. It makes me feel like there’s a community of people who are thinking about ideas that will never become books.

I don’t know why that’s comforting. I don’t know why having a book in my head that I can’t write makes me feel better. But it does.

It might just be a trick my brain is playing on me. It might be a way of saying: this book is really great, but it will never be as good as I imagine it. And that’s okay. It will always be as good as I imagine it.

It might be a way of making excuses for why I haven’t written a novel in six years. And that’s okay, too.

Or it might just be a really good idea that I’m not going to write. And that’s okay, too.

But it’s also just an idea. It’s not a book. It’s not going to be a book. It will never be a book. But it’s still an idea. It’s still there.

And that’s kind of beautiful, too.

Or you could do whatever else you want.

The second book does not replace the first book. And not finishing the first book is not a sign of moral turpitude.

A half-finished novel can be as good as a completed one, or it can be better, depending on what you like.

prompt: I've been writing a novel for six years and I'm starting to think finishing it would ruin it, because right now it can still be good in my head. response:
The book is always better in your head.

I mean, you know it’s going to be better in your head. You’ve been writing it in your head for ten years, and you’re pretty sure there’s going to be a better version somewhere in that space of possibilities. You’re pretty sure it’s going to have the perfect ending, the perfect dialogue. It’s always going to be better in your head. And maybe the best you’re going to do is get something as good as the one in your head. But I’m not saying it’s likely.

The best you’re going to do is get something as good as the one in your head.

And that is a really tough thing to deal with. I’ve never been able to deal with it. I’ve never had the guts to deal with it. Every time I’ve had the guts to start writing something, I’ve lost my nerve and I’ve gone back to the place where the book is going to be perfect.

So I’m going to try to write about the book that’s always going to be perfect in your head. I think I can write about it.

I’m going to write about the book that’s always going to be better in your head.

The book is always going to be better in your head. That’s what makes it so hard to write it. That’s what makes it so hard to write anything.

That’s what makes it so hard to write anything.

prompt: Draft an essay making the argument that the em dash has quietly replaced the semicolon as the default mark of a 'literary' sentence, and that this shift reflects a change from logical to conversational prose. I'm a copyeditor of 15 years so don't be cute about punctuation; I want an actual argument with examples.
response:
When I started my job as a proofreader in 2007, I would often find em dashes in manuscripts. I never much liked them. They were too dramatic for my tastes, too much like a raised eyebrow or a gasp. I found them distracting.

Today I find them irresistible. I like to use them when writing. I like to see them in other people’s writing. And I like to find them when editing, because they’re a kind of reward, the same way I like to find a good sentence or a great metaphor.

What happened?

I think the em dash and the semicolon have swapped places. The semicolon used to be the literary mark. You could spot a good writer by how well they used semicolons. Nowadays, it’s the em dash.

I think this is because of a big change in the style of writing. In the early 20th century, there was a shift from ornate sentences to plain prose. You can see this in a simple comparison of two authors, George Bernard Shaw and Mark Twain.

George Bernard Shaw wrote like this:

There are two ways to spread the light of truth, and both are equally efficacious: by teaching it to those who want it, and by teaching it, against their will, to those who don’t want it.

Mark Twain wrote like this:

You can lead a horse to water, but you can’t make him drink.

Shaw’s sentence is a classic example of a formal style. It’s elegant and symmetrical. It uses the phrase “equally efficacious” as a kind of hinge that balances the two parts of the sentence.

Twain’s style is conversational. It’s the kind of sentence you might hear someone say. It’s also an idiom, which is probably the reason it sounds conversational.

In this article, I’m not talking about formality vs. informality, or about what’s good or bad. I’m just noting that there was a shift in prose style at the beginning of the 20th century, from the ornate to the conversational.

When that shift happened, it changed the way that people use punctuation. Writers started using fewer semicolons. I think this is because semicolons make a sentence more ornate.

The em dash is the mark that’s taken over the semicolon’s old job. It’s used when a writer wants to make a sentence ornate.

Here’s an example of the em dash in place of a semicolon.

It could be a book club — but it’s not.

Here’s another example:

She told me something important — something that I need to know.

Both examples use the em dash in place of a semicolon. The semicolons make the sentences more formal, while the em dashes make them more ornate.

I think that the em dash has taken over the semicolon’s job of making a sentence ornate. But there are a couple of differences.

The first difference is that semicolons are hard to use. If you try to use a semicolon, you’ll probably do it wrong. Most people use semicolons incorrectly, because they don’t know how.

On the other hand, it’s easy to use an em dash. Just put one in.

A second difference is that em dashes can be used for a couple of different things. The most common use is for emphasis. They’re used to make a sentence more ornate, and to add a little emphasis.

Em dashes are also used to make a quick aside. This use makes an em dash sound conversational, while a semicolon makes a sentence sound formal.

I’ve also seen em dashes used to make a sentence more formal. For example:

The committee — which has been working on the issue for months — will meet today.

I’ve seen that sentence written both ways, with or without the commas.

I think I’ve talked enough about semicolons. Let’s talk about the em dash, because I think it’s interesting.

There are three main uses for the em dash. The first is to make a sentence more ornate. The second is for emphasis. The third is for a quick aside.

prompt: Is Moby-Dick boring on purpose? Essay.
response:
Herman Melville’s Moby-Dick is a famous novel, but it is also a famously difficult read. In the first chapter, Ahab, the ship’s captain, doesn’t even appear. The second chapter is a description of a whaling harbor in a small Massachusetts town. The third chapter describes a local tavern, and the fourth one describes the local whalers. The first 24 chapters describe things other than the plot.

I recently read Moby-Dick for the first time, and I was surprised by how much I enjoyed it. It’s an unusual novel that has a very different flavor from most books you’d read in college or high school. But it was hard to get through because of the language and setting.

I started writing this essay thinking about why Melville wrote the way he did. I think that Melville deliberately included boring content in Moby-Dick, but not for the reasons most people think. In fact, I think his boring content made Moby-Dick more interesting for me than it otherwise would have been.

Melville writes about whaling in a way that makes it look extremely boring. A lot of the chapters contain information about whale anatomy, the history of the whaling industry, and the structure of a whale ship. I’m not sure how much of this information was actually useful to whalers, but it certainly wasn’t information that other writers of his day considered interesting to their readers.

Some people might be tempted to say that Melville was just writing for his friends, because there wasn’t anything else he could do. But that’s not true: Melville wrote novels before and after Moby-Dick that were designed to be popular. He probably wasn’t writing for his friends at all, but for the general public.

Melville wrote in the 1850s, so he had to compete with a lot of other writers. Melville probably considered the best writers of his time to be people like Mark Twain and Nathaniel Hawthorne, both of whom were publishing new books at the time.

Moby-Dick is a very difficult novel to read. I read it for the first time after reading many books that have been written by literary critics or by novelists trying to imitate a literary style.

The language is full of long-winded sentences and archaic vocabulary. It takes a lot of work to understand what the book is saying.

I think Melville knew this and wrote in that style on purpose. Melville was interested in making Moby-Dick a great novel in the way that Shakespeare is a great play, and he was trying to write something that would make people think about how much language affects our perception of the world.

The story is about a man who goes mad trying to kill a whale. In some ways it’s a pretty typical adventure story. A character named Ishmael joins a whale ship and is taken on a voyage to find the whale that Ahab wants to kill.

Melville’s writing doesn’t make the plot sound exciting. He tells it in a very detailed and matter-of-fact way, and that doesn’t create much suspense.

But Melville wanted to write a realistic story. He wanted to make the story sound as if it were being told by someone who was actually living it. He also wanted the story to be told in such a way that the details would seem real and plausible.

Melville’s characters are real people who do things that real people do. That makes the story seem like it’s not very exciting, and it doesn’t make it easy to read. But I think it makes Moby-Dick a better novel.

It’s hard to say why, because there isn’t a good way to explain how language works. When you read a story, it’s hard to understand how it works. It’s easy to notice if something is wrong, but it’s hard to explain why something is interesting.

I think Melville was trying to write in a realistic style in order to make his story seem real. But he didn’t just write about things that were already real. He was trying to make things that were real seem more real.

prompt: Is Moby-Dick boring on purpose? Essay.
response:
It’s often said that Moby-Dick is one of the most boring books ever written. I don’t know if it’s true, but the claim is so widespread that it’s practically a meme. It’s also often said that it’s not really as boring as it looks. I have never read the entire book, though I have read quite a lot of it, so I can’t speak to this, but I do think there’s a good case for it being at least a little bit boring on purpose. And I think this is important.

Suppose we take a novel and add a bunch of boring material to it. For example, we could take Shakespeare’s Othello and every few pages insert a lengthy discussion of the taxonomy of flies. Most people would agree that this was a horrible idea, and would agree that the result was far worse than the original. And most people would think that, whatever the original had going for it, the new version was definitely worse because it was so boring.

But now suppose we take another novel and add a bunch of boring material to it. This time, however, we insert our boring material in a particular kind of place. We take any scene that would have had a happy ending, and we insert a bunch of boring material right after the protagonist has done something that’s going to make everything turn out okay. And then, after the boring material, we have the boring material cut off, and the next thing we see is something horrible happening to the protagonist that makes everything bad.

I think most people would agree that this was a great idea. I think most people would agree that this was better than the original. And I think most people would agree that the new version was probably better because it was more boring.

So the question of whether a novel should be boring or not is not straightforward. There are at least two relevant ways to be boring. You could be boring in the sense of taking a long time to get to the good parts. Or you could be boring in the sense of putting a bunch of boring things in between the good parts. The first kind of boring isn’t good. The second kind of boring is a powerful tool in the author’s arsenal.

Moby-Dick, in particular, has the latter kind of boring all over the place. Here’s an excerpt from the chapter titled “The Doubloon”:

In the midst of the excitement arising from the strange occurrence of the doubloon, the ship’s carpenter, who had been busy working away at his bench, at the end of the forward cabin, suddenly let fly a tremendous profane oath, and, rushing out of the cabin, ran on deck, and, seizing the foretopman by the collar, pulled him by a long jerk from the cross-trees, where he had been standing, and in his excitement struck him on the head.

The carpenter, I learned afterwards, had been so absorbed in his work, in carving a small ivory model of a whale’s bone, which he had been making for the captain’s children, that he was wholly unconscious of all the hullabaloo on deck about the doubloon. But the first glimpse of the men in such a state of excited curiosity, staring at one another and at the gold, made him think that the ship was on fire; and, rushing to the door, he saw the captain, who was leaning against the bulwarks, staring at the doubloon. This sight, together with the excited air of the men, convinced the carpenter that the ship was on fire; and in his excitement he flew into a violent paroxysm, which ended in his seizing and striking the foretopman, who, fortunately for him, he had not seriously hurt, as the foretopman had on his iron helmet.

The carpenter’s wife and children are on the ship. Ahab’s children are also on the ship. The carpenter is making Ahab’s children a little whale bone to play with. Ahab’s children are on the ship. I can’t really remember what else Ahab’s children did in the book.

But I remember this. And I remember this because it was boring. I remember it because the boringness made me pay close attention to it, so I could get through it quickly.

This is exactly the kind of scene that Melville would want to be boring. The scene itself is not the point. But you have to remember it. Because here’s the next paragraph, from the same chapter, only a little bit further down:

When, after a time, the carpenter recovered his senses, he went back to his work, and was very busy for a considerable time, but without saying a word.

The carpenter’s wife and children are on the ship. Ahab’s children are on the ship. The carpenter was making Ahab’s children a little whale bone to play with. Ahab’s children are on the ship.

And then, later, the whale bone gets cut off. Ahab cuts it off in order to use it as a peg on his leg.

I remember this because it was boring. I remember this because Melville wants me to remember it. I remember it because the boringness made me pay close attention to it. And I remember it because it makes it so much more tragic when the whale bone gets cut off.

So, if boring is so important, why do people say Moby-Dick is boring? Because Melville puts in boring material that you don’t have to remember. He puts in boring material that isn’t the point. He puts in boring material that you can forget.

This is why he starts the book by making it clear that the name Moby-Dick is not important:

There are various names for the great white fish described in these pages. By some, it is called the Albino; by others, the White Whale. But this I know – that, whether white or otherwise, it is the most terrific and appallingly majestic of all created things. I will therefore call it Moby Dick.

And the reason he puts this here is so that when he later calls the whale by any number of other names, you don’t have to remember them all.

He also puts in boring chapters that are irrelevant to the plot. Here is an excerpt from the chapter titled “The Whale as a Fish”:

The Whale as a Fish. The whale is a mammal. He is not a fish. He breathes air, has lungs, gives birth to living young, and nurses them with milk. His skin is smooth and rubbery. He has no scales. His fins are paddle-like. He has no gills. He has no fins on his back. He has a tail fluke, which he moves up and down, not side to side.

I remember this because it was boring. I remember this because Melville wants me to remember it. I remember it because the boringness made me pay close attention to it. And I remember it because it’s interesting to know that whales are mammals.

Melville also puts in a bunch of chapters where he makes it clear that he’s being a jerk. He writes:

I am not going to tell you that the whale is a fish. I am not going to tell you that the whale is a mammal. I am not going to tell you that the whale is neither a fish nor a mammal. I am not going to tell you anything about the whale. I am going to tell you about the whale’s bones.

This is an excerpt from the chapter titled “The Whale’s Bones”. The chapter is about the whale’s bones. It is not about whether the whale is a fish or a mammal.

prompt: Is Moby-Dick boring on purpose? Essay.
response:
On the last day of high school, my history teacher asked me, in front of the whole class, “Who here has read Moby-Dick?” I raised my hand. My teacher had a complicated look on her face, which was my first sign that I was doomed. I was going to be the kid who, having finished reading the book, said “It’s boring.” This was, after all, an English class.

There’s a reason I can still remember it so vividly, thirty years later. Because I was wrong. Moby-Dick is not boring. It’s one of the greatest novels ever written. It’s just that I read it when I was too young to appreciate it. I didn’t read anything better for the next twenty years.

I had read other books that were more complicated, but Moby-Dick is the first book I read that felt like it was trying to say everything. It had a lot of ideas packed into it. I thought I could understand all of them, but I couldn’t. I was reading a book that had things in it I wasn’t old enough to understand.

Moby-Dick has become the poster child for “books that are too hard for kids.” I read it in high school, and most of the kids I knew who read it did so in college. The first time I was asked to review a book that people were complaining was too hard for kids, it was Moby-Dick. The kid who wrote the review had never read it. It turns out that’s not hard to do, because it’s in almost every school library.

I didn’t read Moby-Dick when I was 19. I read it again in my mid 20s, which was just about when I started to write essays. It’s not a coincidence. When I finally understood Moby-Dick, I understood how to write. It was the book that taught me that, like all great literature, good essays are dense. That you don’t just say one thing in an essay, you say several.

One of the things I learned from Moby-Dick is that it’s good to be able to put a lot of ideas into your head at once. If you can’t, you will think that things that say a lot of things are boring. I used to think that when I was a child. When I read Moby-Dick the first time, I thought it was boring because I couldn’t tell the ideas apart. They all seemed to be one giant mush. When I read it again, I could understand each one individually. I could tell which was about the whale hunt, which was about the meaning of life, and which was about the philosophy of law.

I think I would have had the same trouble with most books if I hadn’t read Moby-Dick. It’s the book that taught me that books were allowed to have a lot of ideas in them at once. Moby-Dick taught me how to hold several ideas at once.

The reason I think I’m a writer now is that I learned that trick from Moby-Dick.

I was surprised to learn that Moby-Dick is considered a classic. I thought it was just a good book, not a classic. Most people don’t seem to understand that either, because they talk as if they don’t know the book. They ask me how I feel about it.

I feel like I read a very old book. I feel like the ideas in it are so important that I would have had to read them anyway. It seems like Moby-Dick is going to be the most important book to have come out of the 19th century, but it doesn’t seem to have taken the country too long to realize that.

The book is very complicated, and it is very hard to understand. There are many things I still don’t understand about it. I don’t even know how to make the most important decision about the book, which is whether it’s about whales or God. I think it’s about whales, but I’m not sure.

prompt: What I wish I'd known about writing before my MFA, which cost me $68,000 and taught me mostly how to sit in a circle. Personal essay, funny but not bitter. Or a little bitter.
response:
In college, I was a journalism major. When I graduated in 2008, a year before the Great Recession, the job market was already bleak. I was in a good place to start a family, so I got a job at a marketing agency and married my wife, who was a few years older. I didn’t have much of an interest in writing fiction, but as a journalism major I’d always wanted to write a book. I figured, if I’m not going to make a career out of writing, it’s as good a time as any to write a novel.

My first novel idea was a fantasy novel about an old man in his 70s who gets a superpower. It was a terrible idea, but I didn’t know that. After a few months I had a few chapters written and I was excited about it. I sent the first chapter to a few friends who were writers and asked what they thought of it.

It was the wrong time to ask. It was right after I had started an MFA program, and a lot of my friends were in the program too, and we were all going to the same workshop. We were writing these stories for the first time and we didn’t have an idea what we were doing. In the workshop, we would read these stories out loud to each other, and then we’d ask each other questions about them. This was supposed to be the way that writers were supposed to get better. I was very excited about this. I knew there were writers who thought it was useless, but it seemed like a great idea!

One of my friends read a short story in our workshop that was about a guy who was writing a novel about an old man in his 70s who got a superpower.

I didn’t realize at the time that this was the sort of thing that people might do. I thought maybe they were both working on it, which was just a coincidence. I kept working on my novel.

After a few months, I decided to stop working on the novel. The idea was too stupid. I was also just not that interested in writing fiction. I didn’t like the idea that if I wrote the wrong thing, people would laugh at me. It was better to write something practical, like a blog post or a newsletter that had some value to readers.

So I just wrote my newsletter for a few months and then I decided I wanted to do something with the idea of an old man getting a superpower. I wrote about it in my newsletter. I said, “hey, here’s an idea that I’ve been thinking about, and I’m not sure if I’m going to write a book about it or not.” I asked my readers what they thought of the idea.

I got so many responses saying they were excited and that I should absolutely write it. I decided to do it. I wrote it in 2011. I was 27. I was working full time at a marketing agency. It was my first novel.

I’m not going to tell you everything that happened to me in my MFA program because it’s not a fun story. It’s about how I was really happy for the first year and then things got kind of bad for me and then it got kind of better but then I just wanted to leave and so I left. I’m not going to tell you that part. The point of this essay is to tell you about what I learned about writing, and what I wish I’d known about writing.

I’m not sure why I wanted to go to an MFA program. I knew a lot of people who went to MFA programs, and I thought it was interesting, so I thought I’d go to one. I also knew that there were a lot of writers who went to MFA programs, but I didn’t know that it was so common that it was almost a requirement, like if you don’t have one, you can’t be a writer. I didn’t know that that was the deal, but after I went to one, that’s what I thought.

In the first year, I got a lot of feedback on my writing. I thought my writing was really bad because I was really new to writing. I had written a novel, but I hadn’t written any short stories, which were what we were supposed to be writing in my program. I think everyone else in the program thought my writing was pretty good. I didn’t think so, but I think I was just being too hard on myself.

prompt: Write an essay about why villains get the best lines. Milton's Satan, Iago, Hannibal Lecter. Is it because evil is more articulate, or because writers secretly side with them?
response:
Villains are better speakers than heroes. Think of Milton’s Satan, Shakespeare’s Iago, or Hannibal Lecter. Why is this?

There are three explanations: 1. Evil people really are smarter and more articulate than good people, so when writers write about them, that shows in the dialogue. 2. Evil is more interesting than good, and the more interesting the character, the more interesting the dialogue. 3. Writers secretly support the villain, so they make the villain sound better.

I think the truth is mostly the second explanation and a bit of the third, with only the tiniest bit of the first.

The first explanation is tempting. Evil people seem smarter. And it’s true that some great villains, like Satan, are great villains because they’re smart. But if we try to apply the first explanation to all the best villains, we run into trouble.

Iago is the villain of Shakespeare’s Othello. He’s not smart. He manipulates people, but he doesn’t come up with novel ideas. He uses the old techniques of manipulation. He’s not a smart villain, he’s a devious villain.

What makes Iago interesting is that he’s a really bad person. He’s not smart, but he does what others won’t do. Shakespeare makes him sound good so that we’ll understand him, and maybe so that we’ll like him a bit.

The same is true of Hannibal Lecter. Hannibal is not smart, he is evil. What makes him interesting is that he is so bad that he has no limits. What makes him interesting to write about is that he doesn’t do the ordinary, he does the extreme.

So the second explanation is probably right. It’s not that evil people are smarter, it’s that when you write evil people, the more evil they are the more interesting they are. And the more interesting the character, the more interesting his speech.

But there’s a bit of the third explanation too. When you write a villain, you have to understand him. And the best writers, when they understand their villain, like him a bit. Shakespeare liked Iago a bit. He wrote him to be interesting and to have good speech.

This is not just true of Shakespeare. It’s true of many writers, including mine. If you read my blog, you’ll probably see it.

I have been writing a book called The Nature of Politics. The book starts with a section on the villain, and in it I give a list of villains. When I was writing it, I was surprised by how many of the villains I liked. I didn’t like Hitler. I didn’t like Stalin. I did like Iago, Hannibal Lecter, and Satan.

I like a lot of the bad guys. That’s not a surprise. They make for interesting stories. It’s more of a surprise that it happens in nonfiction. The reason for this is that writers have to understand their subject. And if you understand someone, you understand their motives and why they do what they do. And if you understand why someone does something, you like him a bit.

prompt: Write an essay about why villains get the best lines. Milton's Satan, Iago, Hannibal Lecter. Is it because evil is more articulate, or because writers secretly side with them?
response:
The best villain lines in all of literature come, I believe, from Satan in Paradise Lost.

When Satan first appears in the poem, he’s been defeated by the angelic army in his war against God, cast out of Heaven, and left floating in Hell. The reader is given a close up of him in his “solar empire”:

Himself lost in a place of endless night,
The most remorseful of the loss he mourns;
The next thing to be seen of him is
Sitting alone; and in the dark
He looks at a little light shining on the ground
That comes through a crack in the rock,
As if the sun were shining through a crack
In the roof of the world.

He looks at the sun and says

So shines a fragment of the sun
On the earth, a little world
That mirrors the great sun’s brightness
In its own small circle of light,
So shines this light on the ground of Hell.

It is the most beautiful passage in all of Milton. Satan’s words are poetic, graceful, and deeply moving.

And then Satan realizes he shouldn’t be staring at the sun, because the sun makes him think of Heaven, which makes him feel really sad. So he decides to go back to work.

Milton wrote this poem when he was old and blind. The best of Satan’s lines are some of the most beautiful passages in the entire poem. But they don’t describe Satan as being nice, or even really good at being bad. Satan is the villain of the poem, and he’s bad. So when he goes off to do bad things, Milton writes about him in a much more neutral style than he does when Satan is looking up at the sun.

And the best lines in the book about Satan’s work as the villain are when he’s being an asshole to the angels.

This is the only time Satan speaks directly to an angel in the poem, which is surprising because he spent the first half of the poem working really hard to make it seem like the angels were all on his side. But he does, and when he does, it’s just the most horrible thing ever.

He says:

And you, who were the most beautiful of God’s creations
Are now the most hideous of all things.
It is hard to believe that the gods created you,
Because they would be stupid to create anything that looks like you.

This is not the kind of thing a person would say if they were trying to get on somebody’s good side. The angels’ leader, Michael, who was in charge of the entire angelic army, and has been fighting Satan for a while, doesn’t know what to do.

The best of the villains in literature are all like this. They are always smarter, more articulate, and more confident than anybody else.

Iago says “honest” about 120 times in Othello, and is really good at being sneaky, and always has the perfect comeback. He gets the best lines.

Aldous Huxley wrote a great essay about why writers secretly side with the villain. He says that every novel has two heroes in it. The first one is the actual hero, who is always doing the right thing. The second hero is the villain. He writes that the reason why the villain always seems so smart is that the writer is secretly on the villain’s side. The writer wants us to be interested in the story, so he makes the villain smart and interesting.

So the villain has the best lines because the writer wants to get on their good side.

prompt: Write an essay about why villains get the best lines. Milton's Satan, Iago, Hannibal Lecter. Is it because evil is more articulate, or because writers secretly side with them?
response:
I have a hunch that this is partly an illusion: the reason good guys don’t get the best lines is that we don’t want them to. We’ve had a lot of bad guys, but not very many good ones, and they get better lines, and people love them.

But the reason people love them is because writers write good lines for them.

Writers know they’re going to be hated, and want to be loved back. They make their good guys bad.

prompt: Argue that the second person ('you') is the most manipulative point of view in fiction, and that this is exactly why it works.
response:
If you’ve ever wanted to write in the second person, here are my thoughts on why it’s so hard, and also why it can work.

This is a longish essay. It takes a few examples from a lot of stories, and then I try to explain why second person is so hard to pull off and what it’s good for.

I.

If you’ve ever tried to write in the second person, you know how unnatural and jarring it is.

You walk to the door. You open it. You step outside. You go down the stairs to the basement, where you can feel the cold and hear a low buzzing. You switch on the lights, and see a room full of servers.

If you try to do this in the first person, it becomes much less awkward:

I walk to the door. I open it. I step outside. I go down the stairs to the basement, where I can feel the cold and hear a low buzzing. I switch on the lights, and see a room full of servers.

Or third person:

He walks to the door. He opens it. He steps outside. He goes down the stairs to the basement, where he can feel the cold and hear a low buzzing. He switches on the lights, and sees a room full of servers.

These all work fine. But the second-person version is just wrong somehow.

II.

I recently finished a novel called You by Caroline Kepnes. The plot is: a very attractive and successful man named Gaz is obsessed with his college roommate, who he calls “You”. One day he kidnaps you.

You are a writer and you are not very successful, but Gaz is so charming and self-assured that you are drawn to him. But you also know that you’ve made a mistake. You need to get away. But you can’t get away.

Gaz is the one who is writing your story, and his goal is to make you think he’s right. This is where the second person is useful. It’s easier to believe “You should have known that you had made a terrible mistake. Gaz is right. You should just trust him and give up” if you’re talking about the protagonist as “you” than as “the writer” or “the protagonist”.

The book is very short. This is a common feature of second-person novels. There’s not enough room to do anything more complicated than make you feel like Gaz is right.

III.

I recently finished a novella called The House With a Clock in its Walls by John Bellairs. The plot is: an orphaned boy named Lewis lives with his uncle, who is a wizard. One day Lewis finds a magical house that has a clock that runs backwards, and he has to fix it before it kills everyone.

Lewis is the protagonist, but it’s written in the second person. It’s not trying to make you think Lewis is right, it’s trying to make you understand what he’s like. The book doesn’t have much of a plot. Lewis goes to the house, sees what’s there, tries to fix it, does some things that don’t work, and then succeeds at the end.

The House With a Clock in its Walls isn’t a very good story. It’s not trying to be. It’s an easy story to read, and the main purpose seems to be to teach you how to read.

IV.

I recently finished a book called You by Richard Powers. The plot is: a group of people with very high IQs gather in a house on a cliff in the ocean in order to decide who deserves to get a new island that they built. One person is missing, and he comes back after a while. Then they all die.

The book is very short. It isn’t trying to tell you who is right or who is wrong. It isn’t trying to make you feel like one of the characters. It’s trying to make you feel like they’re all in the same room together.

V.

I recently finished a short story called The Yellow Wallpaper by Charlotte Perkins Gilman. The plot is: a woman with a mental illness is taken to a new house by her husband. She is supposed to be resting there, but it makes her feel worse. She becomes convinced that there’s a woman in the wallpaper.

The story is written in the first person. It’s trying to make you understand what the woman is like, and why she can’t get better.

There’s also a version of this story in the second person, called You Can’t Help Feeling That She’s There. It’s trying to make you think that the woman is right.

VI.

I recently read an article called The Second Person as Narrative Device. It talks about some other examples of second person being used to make you feel like someone else.

One example is a book called You by David Mitchell, which is about a man who is obsessed with finding the person he thinks he’s reincarnated from.

Another example is a book called A Monster Calls by Patrick Ness, which is about a boy whose mother is dying.

VII.

I recently read a book called You by Ian McEwan. The plot is: a man named Joe is trying to get the attention of a woman named Laura. He’s not very successful, but he doesn’t give up.

Joe is the protagonist. The book is written in the second person. It’s trying to make you understand what Joe is like.

VIII.

I recently read a book called The Girl With All the Gifts by M.R. Carey. The plot is: a lot of people have a fungus that turns them into zombies, and it’s spreading. A scientist named Melanie has a plan to fix it, but she’s not very successful.

Melanie is the protagonist. The book is written in the second person. It’s trying to make you understand what Melanie is like.

prompt: Argue that the second person ('you') is the most manipulative point of view in fiction, and that this is exactly why it works.
response:
Second person, the form that begins “You wake up, still groggy with sleep. Your head hurts.” It’s the most underused of the three basic forms of first, second, and third person, and yet the most effective.

Most of the time we use first or third person because those are more comfortable. In first person, the protagonist is in control of the information that the reader gets. “I didn’t tell her what I was thinking because that would get me in trouble.” Third person is like a God’s-eye view that lets you see what’s going on in several heads at once.

Second person is different. You’re not in control of your own character. You’re not sure you’ll even get to the end of the chapter before you die. You don’t get to think what you want.

Second person is the point of view that lets you play with your reader like a cat toying with a mouse. It lets you do anything you want with them, which is exactly why it’s so powerful.

This is not to say that second person is manipulative. It’s not manipulative any more than the way you’re a manipulative parent when you make your child do something because you know they’ll benefit from it. The second person form, like the good parent, does it because it cares.

Second person is not the most common form. It’s not even that common. But if you can master it, you can do things with it that no one else can.

prompt: Argue that the second person ('you') is the most manipulative point of view in fiction, and that this is exactly why it works.
response:
Second person is the least common point of view in fiction, and I think it is the most manipulative. In first person, the author is hiding behind a character. In third person, the author is still hiding, but behind the character and an additional level of abstraction. In second person, the author is talking directly to you.

Second person is like the difference between being accused of a crime in a police report or in a court indictment (third person), being told you’ve been accused of a crime (first person), and being told you are being accused of a crime (second person).

Second person can be very hard to do right. It’s the most vulnerable and transparent of all the points of view. You can do it in a police report or a court indictment, but the language is very formal and it’s hard to really feel that you are being accused. In most fiction, if I say something like “you are a person”, I feel that I am reading a story about somebody else and I stop feeling the second person.

The most famous example of successful second-person fiction is The Housemaid by Fredric Wakeman. You have to read it in its original version, when the housemaid was a man. I read it in the 2000s, but I can’t say anything about it without ruining the ending.

You’re not necessarily reading a first-person story, but you are reading a second-person story. In a first-person story, you are reading the words of a character. In a second-person story, you are reading words that were written specifically for you to read. It can be more difficult for the author to write to you directly than to write about somebody else.

A successful second person story will make you feel like it’s written just for you. The characters are you and the author.

I wrote a story about how to do second person fiction. It was my first time doing it, and I did it badly. My story was written in the second person, but it was really in the third person.

The most common way of doing second person fiction is to use the first person and the second person together. You are writing about somebody else, but at the same time you are talking to them.

It’s harder to do second person well. The best example of successful second-person fiction is The Housemaid.

prompt: My kid is 8 and has started reading graphic novels exclusively, like Dog Man on loop, and the other parents at school talk about it like it's junk food. I read comics as a kid and I turned out fine (I think?). But I also notice I can't concentrate on long books anymore and wonder if that started somewhere. Can you write a thoughtful essay on whether it matters what kids read as long as they read? Something I could maybe share with the other parents, not preachy.
response:
I recently read a New York Times article about how kids today are reading less, which led to a discussion with a friend about what kids read. She’s the mother of two elementary schoolers and said her son and daughter were both obsessed with Dog Man, a popular graphic novel series. They read it over and over again, which she seemed to view as a failure.

I can’t really remember when I read comics for the first time but I definitely did. I remember reading them a lot as a kid. And then one day I discovered that there were books. And I liked those too.

I’m not sure why it’s such a surprise that kids would read comics. It’s a natural progression from cartoons to comics to novels.

The NYT article is a bit depressing. It cites a 2017 report by the National Association of Book Publishers which says that the percentage of American adults who read at least one book for pleasure in the previous year has dropped from 78% in 1982 to 68% in 2017.

But the article is misleading because it uses the phrase “read at least one book” when it means “read at least one non-graphic novel.” That’s a weird definition of “read a book.” The average 15-year-old reads 100,000 words per day, which is about 2.7 books. But if it’s comics then you don’t count. If it’s the Bible then it doesn’t count either.

I’m sure the report would have found that most 8 year olds read at least one book per year if they had included comics.

And that would be okay. I read comics for years and it was fine. And now I read a lot of long books and that’s fine too.

The reason I read comics was that I loved them. The reason I read books was that I loved them. I wouldn’t have read books if I hadn’t loved them. And I wouldn’t have read comics if I hadn’t loved them either.

I didn’t read comics because I couldn’t read books. I read books because I couldn’t read comics. I couldn’t read books when I was a kid, but I could read comics. And when I was old enough to read books, I realized I was interested in stories and wanted to read more and better stories. And that’s why I read books.

A lot of my friends read comics too, so we talked about comics. That turned out to be a really good thing. I didn’t talk about comics with my friends in high school. But the comics we read as kids really helped prepare us to talk about comics in high school.

If I hadn’t read comics as a kid, I probably would have read books as a kid. But I doubt I would have liked them as much. I probably wouldn’t have thought of them as my favorite thing to do. And I definitely wouldn’t have talked to my friends about them.

Now I like reading a lot. I like reading comics. I like reading books. I like reading a lot of different kinds of books, but I prefer fiction. I read nonfiction sometimes, but mostly fiction. I prefer short stories, but sometimes I read novels. I read both books and comics, but mostly books. I read a lot of things for my work, but I read more fiction than I used to. I don’t read as much as I used to, but I’m not sure I want to.

If my friends had talked to me more about comics, I probably would have liked them more. And if I’d liked comics more, I probably would have liked books more. I don’t know how I’d have liked books more. But I know I wouldn’t have liked comics less if I’d talked about them more.

prompt: My kid is 8 and has started reading graphic novels exclusively, like Dog Man on loop, and the other parents at school talk about it like it's junk food. I read comics as a kid and I turned out fine (I think?). But I also notice I can't concentrate on long books anymore and wonder if that started somewhere. Can you write a thoughtful essay on whether it matters what kids read as long as they read? Something I could maybe share with the other parents, not preachy.
response:
A few days ago I went on a podcast and discussed the value of graphic novels as reading material for kids.

The host said, “But I hate graphic novels. I can’t imagine reading one.”

I said, “Then you’ll never understand my children. I have no idea why they’re reading *Dog Man*.”

He was surprised that I’d even admit that. I said, “I love the fact that the kids enjoy it. It makes me wonder if I’m being too rigid about the kinds of books we should read.”

He asked, “Does it help them?”

I said, “I’m not sure if it does or not. I’m not even sure what you mean by ‘help’.”

The host said, “I’m sure it does. It gets them to read.”

He wasn’t joking. He said it sincerely, with the confidence of a man who has always read traditional novels. He said it’s enough of a virtue to encourage kids to read *Dog Man* if they won’t read anything else.

And this got me thinking:

Is it enough to encourage kids to read if it means they’ll only read *Dog Man*?

I think I know the answer, but I’m going to lay out the arguments on both sides to make sure I’m not fooling myself.

The case for reading *Dog Man* is pretty easy to make.

First of all, it gets kids to read. This is important because kids who read tend to do better in school. So by reading *Dog Man*, kids will do better in school. This is a huge thing.

Second, reading *Dog Man* is better than not reading at all. It gives kids something interesting to do with their time, so they won’t be staring at their phones. This is a huge thing.

Third, reading *Dog Man* teaches kids how to read. It gives them practice with the process of reading and helps them build reading skills. This is a huge thing.

Fourth, reading *Dog Man* might make kids like reading. If they read enough *Dog Man* comics, they might like them and enjoy reading in the future. This is a huge thing.
