prompt: An essay, please, on the ethics of publishing a dead writer's work against their wishes. Kafka asked Max Brod to burn everything. Brod refused, and we have The Trial. Was Brod right, and does our gratitude settle the question?
response:
We do have Kafka’s *Trial*. Max Brod, the writer’s friend, published Kafka’s novels against the author’s dying wish that they be burned. Brod was right, but he wasn’t necessarily right *for Kafka*.

There’s a famous debate about whether it’s ever okay to break somebody’s will. Suppose you’re in a coma, and a doctor who knows you very well says that he knows you very well, and that in fact you would want to be kept alive and treated no matter what. If you’ve made a living will, should that win, or the doctor’s claim?

I’ve never been a big fan of the principle that “if somebody has said something, that’s always final and you can never override it.” I’ve talked a bit about how if we take the idea of “the right to choose” too seriously, it leads to really bad results (for example, “if you said you want to stay in a hospital room for 300 years, that means you must stay in a hospital room for 300 years, no matter what happens”). If we have a good, strong reason for believing someone else is doing a better job of figuring out your preferences, it seems like that should win out.

But that’s just an example of how I’m skeptical about the idea of “the right to choose” and its implications. It’s a very complicated idea, and I’m not sure I could defend it very well.

But if I were going to defend it, the case of Max Brod and Kafka’s papers would be my strongest example. I can’t imagine that anyone’s choice is more important than their choice about what to do with their own works after they die.

Kafka was a very anxious and paranoid man. He spent much of his time worrying about the things he wrote, whether they were good enough, and whether he would be shamed if anyone saw them. His father was abusive and often belittling, and Kafka feared his father would hate or be ashamed of his work. And his brother-in-law was an accomplished writer himself, and Kafka worried he would look like a fraud in comparison to him.

Kafka’s friends were very loving and supportive, and he had a very strong desire to please them. So he wrote a lot, and gave his works to his friends. But every time he did this, he also asked his friends to burn them, or to only read them in private and never let anyone else see them. If they asked him why, he gave the standard anxieties and worries that I outlined above.

At the end of his life, Kafka had a friend, Max Brod, who was very close to him. When Kafka died, he left a will saying that if his will was still unfulfilled, his friend Max Brod should burn all his manuscripts. This seemed like a very good idea for a will – it was a will written by a very sick person, with a very close friend who was very dedicated to him, and it was pretty clear that Kafka’s desire to be ashamed was just as strong as it had been all his life. It wasn’t like Kafka had suddenly changed his mind and decided he was a genius and everyone had to read his work – it was just like he had been for the last 30 years, very sick, and still worrying a lot about what everyone thought of him.

Brod didn’t burn the manuscripts. He published Kafka’s work, and it became very famous. Kafka’s reputation has improved over the years. Today, he’s not quite at the level of the greatest writers in history, but he’s pretty near it.

There’s a famous story about a woman who was on a plane to New York, and she was reading *The Trial*. She had never been to New York before, but she wanted to go, because she wanted to go to the exact spot where the protagonist of *The Trial* had been when he realized he had been arrested and would spend the rest of his life going to court.

Kafka was a very depressed person. But he also had a very strong sense of what was good and what was bad in his writing. He had some good and some bad writing, and he knew which was which. In his will, he didn’t ask Brod to burn everything, but to burn everything that was bad, and to publish everything that was good.

Kafka was a very depressed person, but he also knew that depression distorted the way he saw the world. And he knew that his depression would not just end at death. He knew that his depression would be so strong that it would keep his mind from seeing the things that he loved. So he wrote a will, and said “when I’m dead, let someone else who doesn’t share my depression read my work, and let them figure out which of these things are good and which are bad, and publish the good ones and burn the bad ones”.

Brod didn’t burn Kafka’s work, but he followed the spirit of Kafka’s will. He published what he thought were Kafka’s best works, and he burned what he thought were Kafka’s bad works. He kept only the books that were written before Kafka had a very bad year where he wrote a lot but it was all bad. He kept the books that were very good, and he kept some things that he thought were good but were actually bad. He burned what he thought was bad. He kept *The Trial*, which was definitely a good work.

Brod was right.

The people who are alive today were right to keep reading Kafka, even after he died. The people who are alive today are right to keep reading Kafka even if he had been alive today. They are right to keep reading Kafka, and to keep reading him if he were still alive and trying to stop them.

Brod was right to publish Kafka’s work and not burn it, and he was right to keep publishing it after Kafka’s death. He was right to publish it, and he was right to keep publishing it.

prompt: An essay, please, on the ethics of publishing a dead writer's work against their wishes. Kafka asked Max Brod to burn everything. Brod refused, and we have The Trial. Was Brod right, and does our gratitude settle the question?
response:
The writer’s dead. He’s left you a manuscript. He’s told you to destroy it. Do you?

This happened to Max Brod, who was Kafka’s only close friend. Kafka asked Brod to burn all his work, and Brod refused. Brod published Kafka’s work, including *The Trial* and *The Metamorphosis*. I can’t imagine being more grateful to Brod for that. I love Kafka, and the world is a better place for having *The Trial*. I’m not sure if I would have been so sure of myself a century ago. Maybe you’d think it was an obvious question. Then again, it was Kafka who said “the most important thing a person can do is to be honest with themselves.”

Kafka was a religious Jew. He may have been worried about what would happen to his soul if he published anything. He was Jewish and he lived in Prague, where there was always a threat of anti-Semitic pogroms. Maybe he was afraid to become famous, or even just visible. Maybe he was afraid of his work being misread and misunderstood, or of how it would be received. Maybe he wanted the world to have no literature.

There are lots of reasons not to publish something after the fact. If the author died too young, you might be short-changing an entire oeuvre that never had a chance to develop. If they’re too old, it might be a bad last-ditch attempt at fame. Maybe you think it’s their last attempt at suicide, and they’ll be happier without the world knowing it.

This week I got a book in the mail from an acquaintance who passed away in December. She’d given me her manuscript, and asked me to publish it. She was working on it right up to the end. It’s an interesting book about some interesting subjects. If I didn’t publish it, no one else would, and it would never see the light of day.

What did Kafka mean by being honest with himself?

I think being honest with yourself is more like telling the truth. Being honest with yourself is more like being true to yourself.

I think being true to yourself is being true to the way you feel. If you’re a good person, this is the same thing as being true to the truth. If you have lots of bad habits, being true to yourself might not be good.

So what would Kafka be true to in asking Brod to burn his manuscripts?

The reason for being true to yourself is that you can’t be a good person without being true to yourself. If you can’t be true to yourself, you’re not free.

Maybe the most important thing a person can do is be honest with themselves. Maybe the most important thing a person can do is be true to themselves.

Maybe Brod should have burned the manuscripts. Maybe he should have burned them all, without reading them, and then felt really bad about it.

prompt: An essay, please, on the ethics of publishing a dead writer's work against their wishes. Kafka asked Max Brod to burn everything. Brod refused, and we have The Trial. Was Brod right, and does our gratitude settle the question?
response:
Kafka wrote to his friend Max Brod, the last time, “Dear Max, my burning wish, after my death, is that all my writings, letters, diaries, manuscripts, etc., and whatever is left of them, should be collected, and burned unread without exception.” Brod refused.

Kafka’s letters were not burned, and we have The Letters to Felice. They’re pretty good, and I would have missed them otherwise. They’re not as good as The Trial, but I’m pretty sure nobody will miss The Trial.

I am also sure that, if you told me that one of the major literary works of the twenty-first century had been deliberately burned, I’d be pretty sad about it. I’d also be pretty sad if one of the major literary works of the twenty-first century were a suicide note that had been published against the wishes of the deceased and their family.

There is a line somewhere in the literature that says “the dead are the dead”. It’s a way of saying that the only reason we care about the dead is insofar as our actions affect the living. I’m sympathetic with the idea, but I don’t think it fully solves this problem.

One could argue that we have a responsibility to do what the dead wanted us to do, as long as it doesn’t conflict with a greater responsibility to do what the living wanted. If I asked someone to burn my diary after I died, it would be immoral for them to publish it. If the living world somehow depended on the publication of my diary, they could do so without being immoral. Otherwise they should do what I want.

I’m not sure if this is the right view. But let’s assume it is. How do we know that Kafka didn’t want to publish his work after all?

I mean, there’s a few things I want done after my death. But some of them are things I want done, even if I had the choice, and other things are things I want done if I can’t control them myself. For example, I want to be buried in a cemetery in my hometown – but if I could arrange it now, I’d do it. But I want my friends to be notified of my death as soon as possible, even if I could arrange it now.

The latter sort of wish seems more like “if I don’t do something now, I want this to happen”, whereas the former sort of wish seems more like “I want to be in a place where I would want to be if I had the choice”. And in the latter, the desire is really just about the world being a certain way; if the world is already that way, there’s no reason to do it.

I think the former sort of wish is much more important than the latter sort of wish. It seems to me that this is how the world would work if we didn’t have a strong presumption against violating dead people’s wishes.

This makes sense if you think of the dead as having no preferences at all. If I make a wish, and the people I love fulfill it, that is good, even if I no longer exist and cannot appreciate the goodness of it. But if I make a wish, and the people I love do it even though it’s not necessary to do it, then that’s not so important anymore.

It seems to me that most people don’t care that much about the dead, at least the very-dead. We don’t think of them as conscious beings with preferences of their own. We think of them as ghosts who need our help, or we just think of them as people who are no longer here. And it seems to me that our moral intuitions are mostly built around these notions.

I think there’s something to this notion of the dead as ghosts who need our help. It’s not just that I want my friends to be notified of my death – I want them to be notified *by me*. And if I can’t do that, I want them to be notified by the people I trust the most. And if I can’t do that, I want them to be notified by whoever, because it’s the right thing to do.

A diary is a mirror. It's a mirror that makes the light of twenty years shine on you.

prompt: Clichés are underrated. Write an essay defending them, the way a carpenter might defend a standard screw.

A carpenter might say that they’ve always thought screws were underrated. People always talk about nails, about glue, about nails, but what do they know about screws? Screws are great. And it’s not just carpenters who like screws. They’re everywhere. They’re the first thing you put in when you build something, they’re the last thing you put in before you’re done. And they’re cheap. And they’re easy. And they’re so common that you don’t even notice them, or think about them, or care about them. They’re just there.

And the same can be said for clichés. They’re everywhere. You hear them every day, in every conversation, in every book, in every movie, in every song. They’re cheap. They’re easy. They’re common. You don’t notice them.

prompt: Clichés are underrated. Write an essay defending them, the way a carpenter might defend a standard screw.

There are also many other reasons to appreciate the cliché. For example, they’re the most reliable way to get a point across quickly and concisely. You can take a whole paragraph to say what you could just as easily have said in a cliché.

prompt: Clichés are underrated. Write an essay defending them, the way a carpenter might defend a standard screw.
response:
The standard screw.

We tend to think of them as a failure of imagination. The only reason to use a screw, we think, is because someone has already done the work of making the screw and we’re too lazy to do it ourselves. But this isn’t true, because the best screws aren’t the standard screws.

The best screws are the ones the carpenter makes himself. The best screws are made from the best materials, and fit the particular joint they’re going into perfectly. They are often not standard at all. They’re the size and shape that the carpenter needs them to be, down to the micron, and they’re custom made to order.

But the carpenter doesn’t use the best screws. He uses the standard screw. He might have a drawer of special screws, and he’ll use them when he needs to, but usually he’ll just reach for the standard screw.

Why?

The carpenter has learned a valuable lesson. If he’s going to make a thousand joints, he doesn’t want to spend the time making a thousand custom screws. He wants to make the custom screws if he can get away with it, but he’ll only spend the time if it’s really worth it. And it’s almost never worth it.

The carpenter has learned the value of a good compromise. The standard screw isn’t perfect, but it’s 99% of the way there. And it takes 5 minutes instead of an hour to make.

If you think about it, this is kind of amazing. We are able to produce a single screw, and then use it in a thousand different situations. The screw has to be pretty good to do that!

The best screw would be made to order and custom fit for each joint. But the screw would take an hour to make, and it would only be used once.

It’s the standard screw that makes this possible. We can make a standard screw, and then use it in a thousand different situations, and it’s still pretty good.

This isn’t just true of screws. This is true of a lot of things.

I run a translation agency. We’ve been in business for over 30 years, and one of the most important things I’ve learned in that time is that translating jokes is so hard that nobody should expect it to work.

This is true no matter how talented the translator is or how similar the two languages are. It’s so bad that I’ve been able to prove it empirically. In 2009 I ran an experiment, using a sample of 250 jokes, on whether professional translators could successfully translate jokes across 30 language pairs. They couldn’t.

There are two kinds of reasons why translating jokes is so hard. One is that most jokes are written to play on the specific structure of the particular language they are written in.

A joke like “I’m reading a book on anti-gravity. It’s impossible to put down.” doesn’t work in any language except English. That’s why I put it first, as the most obvious case. But even jokes that don’t rely on English as much as that often rely on the structure of particular words that only happen to exist in English.

A good example of this is the joke “A bear walks into a library and asks for books on bears.” This depends on the word “bear” doing double duty. There is no equivalent of this joke in French, because “bear” is “ours” and “book” is “livre”. French translators are forced to choose between “un ours entre dans une bibliothèque et demande des livres sur les ours” or “un ours entre dans une bibliothèque et demande des ours sur les ours”, and neither is funny.

It’s a miracle that jokes survive across the English-speaking world at all, because there are a lot of jokes that rely on words that only have the right connotations in American English. For example, “I’m sure he’s guilty,” said the man, “but I have no proof.” “You have proof,” said his wife. “You’re holding his shirt.”

That joke doesn’t work in British English, because there the word “shirt” doesn’t imply “the shirt of the person who is wearing it.” It’s not an American idiom for “shirt” to refer to the wearer, but it is a British one. In British English you can say “I’m wearing a nice shirt today”, but the more idiomatic thing to say is “I’m wearing a nice shirt today.”

But even when a joke isn’t relying on the structure of a particular language, translating it is still hard. Jokes are usually written to be funny in one language, but not for a particular country. A joke like “What do you call a fish without eyes? A fsh.” is funny in all English-speaking countries. It doesn’t depend on anything that’s specific to American English. And yet there’s no version of that joke in any other language.

There are two reasons for this, and both are related to something I call the joke translation gap. A joke is a piece of writing with two meanings. One meaning is funny. The other isn’t. In an English joke, the funny meaning is usually in English, and the unfunny one is in whatever language it was translated from.

The translation gap is the distance between these two meanings, and the bigger it is, the funnier the joke is. The most common type of joke is the pun, and the joke translation gap is the distance between the two words in a pun.

But if the translation gap is the distance between the funny and unfunny meanings, it’s also the distance between the funny and unfunny languages, which is why jokes can’t be translated.

To translate a joke, you have to keep the funny meaning funny and the unfunny meaning unfunny, but in another language. And that’s impossible, because the funny and unfunny meanings have to be the same distance apart in the other language as they are in the original language. But there aren’t any languages where the words in any particular joke are the same distance apart as the words in the corresponding English joke.

There are so many reasons why jokes are hard to translate that it’s not clear why they’re ever translated at all.

And yet they are.

Jokes get translated all the time, and the ones that do get translated are often funny. But they are also translated badly.

The joke translation gap is a measure of how good a translation of a joke is. The bigger the translation gap, the worse the translation.

Most people can tell that a joke translation is bad, even if they don’t know why. If someone in your audience laughs at a joke translation, they’re probably laughing because they can feel it’s funny.

But sometimes you can’t tell from the face of a joke whether it’s been translated or not, and that’s when the translation gap is most useful.

Sometimes you can tell that a joke has been translated, but not why. If you can’t tell why a joke translation is funny, it’s probably because of the translation gap.

The joke translation gap is useful to people who write jokes, as well. If you want to write a good joke, you can use the translation gap to figure out where the joke is coming from.

A joke is the best kind of writing. It’s the only kind of writing that’s always funny. If you write a joke, you can always be sure your audience will laugh.

prompt: I run a translation agency. Write an essay on why jokes are the hardest thing to translate, harder than poetry, and what that suggests about what humor actually is. Use real-ish examples (puns, timing, cultural reference) but keep the focus on the idea. 1200 words.
response:
At the end of the last century, my translation company had a client, a large software company, who wanted a very large project translated. I said, OK, we have the capacity to translate anything. The client asked: “Can you translate jokes?” I said, sure. “OK, here are 4000 of them.”

This client was selling a program that allowed people to store jokes on a computer. They had hired people to write jokes, and then wanted them translated into 10 languages. I asked for a sample. Here it is:

When the police came to arrest the inventor, he had the nerve to ask, “Who are you?”

We tried a lot of different people on this project, and I think everyone gave up. Not because the joke above was so bad, but because it was so easy to see how much work it was to translate the ones it wasn’t.

I think jokes are the hardest thing to translate. Even harder than poetry. If you want to know why, think about why poetry is hard to translate. I’m going to try to answer this question by starting at the level of poetry and working my way down to the simplest case, which I hope is humor.

Poetry is hard to translate because it relies so heavily on specific words. A poem is a lot like a program that has been hand-optimized. A poem is composed word by word, each word chosen for maximum effect. It can be quite different from what an ordinary English speaker would say to express the same idea. And this makes it hard to translate, because there’s no point at which you can safely leave the original text behind and start working with your own words. If you translate a poem one sentence at a time, you’ll get something very different from the original.

But why is a poem worded so unusually? It’s worded unusually because a lot of its effect is in the sound of the words. The poet wants the words to have a particular sound when read aloud.

But why does the sound of the words matter? Because words have multiple meanings, and a good poet can exploit this fact. The sound of a word can make you think of words that sound like it. This is why words in poetry often rhyme. And the sound of a word can also trigger images. The word “splash”, for example, is an onomatopoeia, so the sound it makes when you say it sounds a bit like the thing it means.

The meaning of words in poetry isn’t limited to the things the words directly refer to. The sounds of words can also trigger associations.

The sound of words can even be used to create an atmosphere. That’s why poems are full of “s” and “z” sounds, and why when you read one aloud you feel a bit sleepy.

And so it’s easy to see how much meaning there can be in a poem, and why it’s so hard to translate. Translating a poem means not just preserving the direct meaning of each sentence, but also reproducing the associations that the sounds of the words trigger. And these associations are very language-dependent. The associations that words trigger in one language have no relation to the associations that words in another language trigger, except by accident.

But why do words have these associations in the first place? What’s the point of exploiting them? The point is to convey some meaning that you can’t convey by just saying what you mean. The point is to create surprise.

So the hardest thing to translate is anything that relies on surprise. And the most extreme form of this is the joke.

There’s a famous essay by Vladimir Nabokov called “The Enigma of the Reincarnation.” I think of it as one of the greatest essays ever written. It has a lot to recommend it, but the main reason it’s so great is that it is, as far as I know, the only essay that ever managed to make reincarnation sound plausible. I’ve read it many times, and every time I finish it I think, “Well, I guess it could be true after all.” But the next day I forget how plausible it sounded.

How could a non-fiction essay about a controversial subject manage to make its readers believe something that they forget a day later? It’s not the facts presented that convince you. It’s the way the prose flows. The prose sounds so true, that you believe whatever it’s saying.

Nabokov’s essay is an object that has a different effect depending on how you interact with it. It’s not the same thing to read it as to just hear about it. It’s not the same thing to read it in English as to read it in a translation. The same thing holds with jokes. A joke is a special kind of object that behaves differently from other things that carry the same information.

What’s the difference between the joke above and a non-joke version of it?

When the police came to arrest the inventor, he asked, “Who are you?”

A joke seems to be a kind of trap. It takes you in one direction, and then suddenly reveals something you didn’t expect. That’s why a good joke is surprising.

But why do people like to be surprised? I think one reason is that it feels like winning. I think it’s the same reason people enjoy being surprised by the punch line of a mystery movie. In a sense, you have beaten the movie to the punch, just like when you know the punch line to a joke.

But you can’t enjoy being surprised by the punch line of a joke or movie if you already know the punch line. A joke that is explained in advance is not a joke. This is what makes jokes so hard to translate. In translating a joke, you’re trying to recreate something that by definition can’t be explained.

It’s not just jokes that behave this way. There are lots of things that work like jokes. A good joke is like a good poem, and a good poem is like a good scientific theory. The best theories seem to make something surprising sound obvious. But it’s not the information you’re trying to convey. It’s the way you’re trying to make people feel when they hear it.

In 1985 I wrote an essay called “The Hacker Ethic.” It’s the first thing I’ve ever written that people have quoted, and it’s still one of the things I’m best known for, despite being one of the least successful of my essays. I think it did well because I found an angle that made what sounded like an outrageous claim sound obvious. The angle was that hackers were like the ancient Greeks. I don’t think this essay is a work of art in the same way as Nabokov’s, but it works in a similar way. The angle is so surprising that it can be used to convince people of something they otherwise wouldn’t have believed.

I’m not suggesting that the idea of the hacker ethic is a joke, or that the essay was intended to be funny. But it has one of the same properties. It’s not just the information you’re trying to convey, but the way it makes people feel when they hear it.

If you want to know what kind of thing humor is, it’s something that behaves more like a good scientific theory than it does an ordinary statement. The reason people are fascinated by it is that it is so counter-intuitive.

The fact that humor is harder to translate than poetry is probably not an accident. It’s probably related to the fact that it’s not just information, but that it behaves like a joke.

prompt: what's the deal with people who say they 'don't read fiction because it's not real'? I want an essay that takes them seriously for a minute before explaining what they're missing
response:
It’s a bit of an old-fashioned thing, and I think it’s slowly dying. But it’s still not uncommon for people to be a little proud that they don’t read novels. The usual claim is: “I like non-fiction because it’s real, I don’t like fiction because it isn’t”.

I’m going to try to take this seriously for a minute. I think there’s something to it, though it’s not what people usually mean by it. And I think fiction’s advantage is what we might call *moral imagination*.

Imagine a man who lives on a farm in 18th century Europe, with only a few books. If he likes non-fiction, then they’re going to be about farming, philosophy, religion, and politics. If he likes fiction, they’re going to be about kings and knights and witches. In this situation, the non-fiction is *more* real. It’s describing the world the farmer actually lives in, and the fiction is describing a world so far away from his that it might as well be a dream.

Now imagine a man who lives in modern-day New York City, with a library card. If he likes non-fiction, they’re going to be about the Manhattan subway system, the philosophy of John Dewey, religion in Harlem, and the politics of New York State. If he likes fiction, they’re going to be about a woman who works as a doctor in a small hospital in rural Nebraska, or a young man who gets trapped in a magical portal to another world, or a man who travels back in time to live in 18th century Europe. In this situation, the fiction is *more* real, because it’s describing the world the rest of the country lives in – the world that will eventually become the majority of the US population – and the non-fiction is describing a world so small that it might as well be a dream.

The first man’s choice of non-fiction is good. He lives in 18th century Europe, and he’s reading books about 18th century Europe. He has no reason to read about other countries. And he has even less reason to read about a fantasy world with wizards and dragons and magic portals to other worlds.

The second man’s choice of fiction is good. The Manhattan subway system is important, but it’s also just a very small part of the world. He can’t understand the United States without knowing what life is like in Nebraska, or for that matter what the philosophy of John Dewey might be like if it was practiced in rural Nebraska instead of in New York. And if he’s going to be an artist or a politician or an entrepreneur who needs to be able to create new things, he can’t understand the United States without knowing the sorts of fantasies that people have.

But it would be bad for the second man to say: “I like non-fiction because it’s real, I don’t like fiction because it isn’t.” The fiction he should be reading is more real than the non-fiction he would read, and it’s even more necessary if he wants to be able to create new things.

So I think there’s a kind of “moral imagination” that’s created by reading a lot of fiction. It’s not that you’re imagining anything in particular – it’s that you’re imagining in a more imaginative way than you would otherwise.

prompt: what's the deal with people who say they 'don't read fiction because it's not real'? I want an essay that takes them seriously for a minute before explaining what they're missing
response:
You don’t read novels because you’re “not the reading type”? It’s not that. You don’t read novels because you “hate fiction”? It’s not that either. You don’t read novels because of a very particular reason, which is that you think it’s bad to read things that aren’t true.

I have been told that this is a common attitude among some of the people who don’t read novels, and I can believe it. I have seen plenty of people who wouldn’t read a novel because they don’t like fiction. And I understand where they’re coming from, because I have a lot of the same feelings.

But I think those feelings, even though they’re understandable, are misguided.

First of all, it’s not true that novels are less valuable than nonfiction just because they’re fiction. That’s like saying that a story of the kind you tell at Thanksgiving dinner isn’t interesting because it’s not a story you’d read in a newspaper. The fact that something is made up is no guarantee it’s not interesting.

Secondly, you can learn more from fiction than nonfiction, because you can learn about the way things work without being limited by your own experience. Fiction is a machine for generating interesting stories about how things work. It’s a machine for making things that aren’t true, but are more true than what’s true.

I learned more about politics by reading George Orwell’s novels than I did by reading nonfiction. I learned more about what it’s like to be poor by reading John Steinbeck’s novels than by reading nonfiction. I learned more about what it’s like to be an animal by reading Ursula K. Le Guin’s novels than I did by reading nonfiction.

The reason why you can learn things like this from novels is because you’re never limited by your own experience. You can learn what it’s like to be poor without having been poor. You can learn what it’s like to be an animal without having been an animal.

This is not something nonfiction can do for you. Nonfiction can’t make up a story that teaches you what it’s like to be an animal, because that would be fiction. It can only tell you what it’s like to be the kind of animal that the nonfiction writer has been. And most nonfiction writers have never been an animal.

I have a good friend who has never read a novel. He told me recently that he reads all kinds of nonfiction, including books about animals. I asked him if he had ever read something that taught him what it’s like to be an animal, not just what animals do. I asked him if he had ever learned about his experience of being an animal, what it feels like to be an animal. I asked him if he had ever learned what an animal’s mind is like. He said no.

I think that’s not too surprising. There’s very little nonfiction written by animals, and very little nonfiction written about animals by people who’ve been animals. So there isn’t much nonfiction about what it’s like to be an animal.

But there are novels about what it’s like to be an animal. And they’re not just made up out of thin air. They’re informed by science. The authors of novels about animals know a lot about what animals do. But they have the advantage that they can also imagine what it’s like to be an animal. They can write a story about it. And they can teach you what it’s like to be an animal.

I’m sure my friend has read novels about animals, even though he’s never read a novel. I’m sure he’s read books by other people who are animals. And I’m sure he’s read books about what it’s like to be an animal.

prompt: what's the deal with people who say they 'don't read fiction because it's not real'? I want an essay that takes them seriously for a minute before explaining what they're missing
response:
I’m going to take the “I don’t read fiction because it’s not real” argument pretty seriously here. Not because I’m a dumbass who thinks people like this are being smart, but because even the smartest people have bad habits, and it’s worth understanding and fixing them.

A. If you’ve read too much nonfiction, your brain might be on lock and unable to process fiction

I remember when I was a teenager, I got so into the Bible that I read it from start to finish in a couple weeks. I was pretty excited about this. I thought it would be a revelation.

But what actually happened was that it didn’t have much of an effect on me at all. I didn’t have any crazy religious epiphanies or anything. I just went about my normal life, reading a few books a week, trying to figure out if there was anything more interesting than that.

I didn’t think too much about this at the time, but now I wonder if it was just that I had read so much stuff that my brain couldn’t handle it anymore. I read the Bible in 10 days, but it’s over 1,000 pages. That’s more than 100 pages a day. That’s more than two novels a day.

When I got to the end, I wasn’t ready for more. My brain was like a stuffed pig’s stomach, and I couldn’t digest anything for a few weeks.

And that’s why, when I read nonfiction, I feel like my brain is on lock and I can’t understand it. I don’t like to read nonfiction, but when I do, I find that I can’t really get anything out of it. I’m not really paying attention, and I don’t remember what I just read.

And then when I try to read fiction, I can’t really enjoy it either. I think that’s because my brain is stuck in “nonfiction mode” and I’m not really paying attention.

B. I’m not sure I believe the “I don’t read fiction because it’s not real” thing

I know a lot of people who say this. I know people who say they’re too busy to read fiction, or that they don’t have time, or that they’re not interested. I know people who say they don’t read because they don’t like it. And I know people who say they don’t read because they can’t get anything out of it.

But I don’t know anyone who says they don’t read fiction because it’s not real.

C. Maybe I’m reading too much nonfiction?

I’m not sure.

prompt: Op-ed for a regional paper: our town's library is replacing its reference desk with self-checkout kiosks. Write an essay about what is lost when you stop being able to ask a stranger a question about a book. 600-750 words, no nostalgia porn.
response:
A few weeks ago, I was at the public library with my daughter, who was seven at the time. She was in the kids’ section, searching for a book, when a librarian walked by. The librarian asked my daughter what she was looking for and told her exactly where to find it. My daughter and I were so impressed that I told the librarian that she had a gift.

The next day, we went back to the library. This time, my daughter couldn’t find a book she wanted. A librarian walked by, and my daughter asked her for help. The librarian said she didn’t have time to help her.

The day after, we went back a third time. My daughter didn’t find the book she was looking for this time either. A librarian walked by, and my daughter asked her for help. The librarian said, “Ask someone else,” and walked away.

This was not a big deal to me at the time. Maybe the librarian was busy. Maybe she didn’t like kids. Who knows?

The next time we went to the library, I realized there wasn’t a librarian at the reference desk anymore. The desk had been replaced with a big pile of books, some computers and two kiosks. The computers and kiosks were for looking up things online and checking out books without having to talk to a human being. I asked the woman at the front desk why there weren’t any more reference librarians, and she said the library had been closed for renovation for the last two years, and they hadn’t put any reference librarians back.

My daughter had been asking librarians for help at the library her whole life. She never had a problem, except for that one time, when one librarian was too busy to help and one didn’t like kids. But this time, there were no librarians to ask.

My daughter asked me if I could find the book she was looking for. I said I would try, and I started asking the computers for help. The computers told me that the book my daughter wanted was in the library, and that it was in the kids’ section. But I couldn’t find the book in the kids’ section. I tried to use the kiosks to find out more, but the kiosks didn’t know where the book was.

So I tried asking my daughter to help me. She was seven. She couldn’t do very much. I asked her if she could remember where the book she wanted was. I asked her to think about what kind of book it was. I asked her if she had ever found it before. I asked her if she remembered the cover. She thought and thought, and I thought and thought, and we still couldn’t find the book.

I gave up and told my daughter that we had to go home. She was very upset. I think she was more upset than I was.

After we got home, I thought about how we had gone to the library three times in a row that week, and we hadn’t found a single book my daughter wanted. It was the first time this had ever happened to us. I had never seen my daughter so upset about not finding a book in the library.

I don’t think anyone in the library is bad. In fact, I think everyone there is nice. I think the reference desk would probably have helped us find the book my daughter wanted, if we’d tried it. But there was no reference desk.

I don’t think it’s a big deal that I can’t find the books I want in the library. I can order any book I want online. I’m not interested in finding books I don’t already know I want.

But my daughter is interested in finding books she doesn’t already know she wants. She’s only seven. She doesn’t really know what she likes yet. I don’t know what she will like in a few years. And I really want her to be able to find books she loves.

prompt: Op-ed for a regional paper: our town's library is replacing its reference desk with self-checkout kiosks. Write an essay about what is lost when you stop being able to ask a stranger a question about a book. 600-750 words, no nostalgia porn.
response:
For a while, I thought the best books I had ever read had been found by chance, because I was wandering around a library, looking for something I knew I wanted to read, and I would end up picking up a book that looked interesting, read a few paragraphs, and put it on the shelf. And then I’d wander around some more, and pick up another book that looked interesting. It would take me a couple of hours to find the one book I was looking for, and by then, I’d have about thirty other books in my arms.

It was only after I started doing this for years that I realized it had been the librarian who found them for me. I was the one wandering around, looking for something I knew I wanted to read, but it was the librarian who had been pulling books from the shelf and telling me, “You should read this!” And then I’d wander around some more, and pick up another book that looked interesting, and they’d tell me, “You should read this!” And after a couple of hours, I’d have about thirty other books in my arms.

The librarians didn’t just pick random books and hand them to me. They knew what I was looking for, because I’d come to the library with a list of questions about it, which we’d discuss as we wandered through the stacks. I asked them about books I was interested in, and they told me where to find them, or if they weren’t there, I could order them from other libraries, or they’d find me other books that were just as good. We’d go back and forth, and after a while, they’d pick up a book that had nothing to do with what I’d asked for, and say, “You should read this!” and I’d say, “Why?” and they’d explain why, and I’d say, “Okay, I guess I will!”

When I moved, I started going to my new library, and I thought I’d try to get as many books as I could from there. I’d ask them about books I was interested in, and they’d tell me where to find them, or if they weren’t there, I’d order them from other libraries, or they’d find me other books that were just as good. We’d go back and forth, and after a while, I’d have about thirty other books in my arms.

But the librarians at my new library weren’t going to just hand me a book. They’d give me a book with a note on the back that said, “I found this for you” and a link to my list of questions about it. I didn’t know what to do with the note, so I put the book on the shelf, and when I got home, I put the note in my bag.

prompt: Write something exploring why we read the same bedtime story to children a hundred times and they never get tired of it, while adults find repetition unbearable. What are kids getting that we've lost?
response:
My son’s bedtime story is *The Gruffalo*. It’s very good. A mouse walks through a dark forest. He meets a fox, who wants to eat him, but the mouse is not afraid. He tells the fox that he’s going to meet a Gruffalo, a monster with poisonous claws, and the fox, thinking he can eat the Gruffalo, agrees to go with him. They meet a snake, who wants to eat them both, and she joins them. And they finally meet a Gruffalo, who wants to eat them all. So the mouse, having made up the Gruffalo story out of thin air, is now in real danger. But the Gruffalo is easily fooled, and the mouse talks him into thinking that there are worse monsters in the forest, which he has to eat first. And then the mouse gets away.

*The Gruffalo* is a very good book. But it’s not a good book to read over and over again. We’ve read it 42 times. I’m getting annoyed.

A friend asked me recently whether my son would like to read *Harry Potter*. I said I didn’t know, but I didn’t really want to spend two hours a night for a year reading the whole series to him.

But he’s not the first kid I’ve known who gets really into one book and then wants to read it again and again and again. I’ve had a child read *Charlotte’s Web* to me a hundred times, another kid wanted to read *The Phantom Tollbooth* for the entire summer.

Why do kids want to read the same book over and over, but adults don’t?

I was talking to someone about this recently, and she said that kids are like that because they want to learn it all by heart, and the more they read the book, the more they know it by heart. But when I suggested that to my son, he was confused.

And that’s true. It’s not that kids read books a hundred times to learn them by heart. I know some kids who know books a hundred percent by heart, but they don’t do that by reading it a hundred times. They’re just very good at memorization.

I can’t explain why kids do this. But it’s not just them. Adults also read books over and over again. I’ve read *The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy* four or five times, and *Fahrenheit 451* three or four times. I’ve read *The Old Man and the Sea* twice, and *The Lord of the Rings* twice. *The Hobbit* a hundred times.

But that’s not the point. I like reading a book I’ve read before. But I really like reading new books.

My son doesn’t. It’s not that he doesn’t like new books. He likes new books. But he likes them for about 10 minutes, then he wants to go back to the one he knows.

My son’s bedtime story is *The Gruffalo*. It’s very good. A mouse walks through a dark forest. He meets a fox, who wants to eat him, but the mouse is not afraid. He tells the fox that he’s going to meet a Gruffalo, a monster with poisonous claws, and the fox, thinking he can eat the Gruffalo, agrees to go with him. They meet a snake, who wants to eat them both, and she joins them. And they finally meet a Gruffalo, who wants to eat them all. So the mouse, having made up the Gruffalo story out of thin air, is now in real danger. But the Gruffalo is easily fooled, and the mouse talks him into thinking that there are worse monsters in the forest, which he has to eat first. And then the mouse gets away.

Why do kids want to read the same book over and over, but adults don’t? I don’t know. I can’t explain it.

But there’s something going on.

prompt: Write something exploring why we read the same bedtime story to children a hundred times and they never get tired of it, while adults find repetition unbearable. What are kids getting that we've lost?
response:
I read my daughter a picture book called Goodnight, Gorilla. It’s a little over a year old now. I’ve read it a hundred times and she still wants me to read it every single night. She’ll point at a picture on the bookshelf and say, “That one!”

I think that it’s a perfectly nice book. I like it. But I’m a grown-up. I can read an entire book in a few minutes, and if I like it I’ll read it again, and again, and again. But I can’t do it one hundred times, let alone one thousand times.

Kids, though, seem to love repetition. And I think that’s the point.

A few years ago I read about a study where people who were learning Spanish had a difficult time distinguishing between the sounds of “b” and “v”. They couldn’t tell the difference between “bueno” and “vino” or “bajar” and “vivir”. And a researcher found a way to help them. He had them listen to recordings of native Spanish speakers speaking these words for a total of ten minutes. And afterwards they could distinguish between the two sounds perfectly.

But here’s the twist: he had them listen to the same two words over and over again.

The researchers didn’t think that this could possibly be enough practice to learn to distinguish between the two sounds, so they tried it with a second group of people. They gave the second group ten minutes to practice distinguishing between “bueno” and “vino” in whatever way they wanted, and they failed. The only group that succeeded was the one that had practiced distinguishing between exactly the same two words over and over again.

I think kids have found the secret to learning things. If you learn by repetition, then you need to repeat something many many times. Kids can’t do that with just any old thing, but if you make the repetition exciting and fun – and it’s hard to make reading a picture book with funny animals on it boring – they can do it over and over and over again, hundreds and thousands of times.

That’s why kids can memorize poems and songs and stories and things like that so well. And it’s also the reason that repetition is so effective for adults too. When we get excited about a topic we’re studying – say, programming – it’s not that hard to read the same thing over and over again.

prompt: Write something exploring why we read the same bedtime story to children a hundred times and they never get tired of it, while adults find repetition unbearable. What are kids getting that we've lost?
response:
A friend told me about a study of young children who had just learned a new word like “tummy”. The researchers told them a simple story using the new word, like “Bob’s tummy was hungry”. A few days later, they gave the children a test and asked them to pick out the picture of the hungry tummy from three similar pictures.

The children had learned the new word, but they couldn’t pass the test.

The researchers tried again with the same children and gave them another new word to learn, like “silly”. This time, they gave them a whole series of stories using the word “silly” in different ways. After the series of stories, the children passed the test with flying colors.

The difference between the first and second time was that the first time, they learned a new word in an unfamiliar story, but the second time, they learned a new word in a familiar story. The children had heard the story many times before and knew it well.

The difference between the two experiments is that the second one is what we do every night at bedtime. We read the same story over and over again, until our children know every word. And we do this without realizing that it is a powerful learning technique.

When we read to our children, the story they hear in their heads is a combination of our voice and their imagination. The first time they hear a story, their brain is trying to make sense of it. They are learning the meaning of new words and working out how the sentences fit together. And they are learning the story, which is a kind of sequence of actions, thoughts, and situations. It’s a lot of new information for their young brain to take in, and their brain is using most of its power to get the job done.

But the next time we read the story to them, they have already worked out all the meaning and all the sequence. So their brain doesn’t have to use any power on this. That means they have more spare power to use for other things. They can listen to their parents’ voices and learn all about the subtle meanings and rhythms in speech. They can listen to the sounds of speech and learn how to pronounce every word. They can listen to their parents’ emotions and learn how to tell the difference between a grumpy voice and a loving one.

They can also use their brain to imagine all the things that were left out of the story. This is where the magic happens. We all have an internal model of the world. It’s our mental picture of what things are like and how they work. When we hear a story about a character walking through a forest, we have to imagine the forest. We imagine all the things we have seen and learned about forests, but the story didn’t mention. The trees, the leaves, the animals. We also imagine how the character is going to feel, because we know how it feels when we walk through forests.

All of these imaginings are made up of things we have seen and heard before, and are stored in our brain. But they were probably not mentioned in the story. We have to work out what it looks like, and what it sounds like, and what it feels like. So the first time we hear a story, our imagination is not working very hard, because most of our brain is busy with the new information. But the second time we hear a story, most of our brain is free, so we can use it to imagine the things that the story left out.

When we read bedtime stories to our children, we are teaching them to imagine. We are using their brains to fill in all the things that we left out of the story, and they are learning to do this by themselves.

This is why children never get tired of hearing the same story again and again, while adults can’t stand repetition. Children never get tired of it because it teaches them how to imagine. Adults have already learned how to imagine, so they don’t get anything out of hearing the story again.

It’s not just in stories that imagination helps us learn. It helps us in everything we do. When we imagine something, we use our memories to build a picture. This helps us to learn because the memories we use to imagine something get strengthened by the act of imagining. The more we imagine something, the better we remember it.

If we imagine what it would be like to be an astronaut in space, we use our memories of astronauts in space, and our memories of astronauts, and our memories of space, and our memories of being in strange and different places. If we imagine what it would be like to be a bird in the sky, we use our memories of birds, and our memories of the sky, and our memories of flying. If we imagine what it would be like to be a superhero, we use our memories of superheroes, and our memories of being brave, and our memories of being admired by other people.

If we remember all the things we have imagined before, we are going to have a huge amount of memories in our brains. And memories are the building blocks of knowledge. The more memories we have, the more knowledge we have.

Imagination is not just fun. It is a powerful learning technique. And we teach it to our children by reading them bedtime stories every night, and letting them listen to the same story again and again and again.

prompt: An essay arguing that the best writing advice ever given is 'read it out loud' and that almost every other rule is a special case of it.
response:
The most effective writing advice I’ve ever been given is “read it out loud.”

The best way to do this is by recording yourself and listening back, because the first time you read it out loud it’s hard to catch problems. The easiest way to find a problem is when you find yourself reading the same sentence twice, because that indicates the first reading was ambiguous.

This is not the first time I’ve written about reading out loud. But I was reminded of it by a recent essay about editing, which said that editing is reading what you’ve written and asking yourself “wouldn’t it be better if I said this or that?”

I think that’s true but misleading. When you read out loud, you don’t need to ask yourself what it might be better to say. If you’re reading out loud with any care, you’ll immediately realize whether something you’ve written sounds wrong.

The reason this works is that writing is a form of speaking. The words have to go through the same circuits in your brain that are used for speech. The brain is very sensitive to patterns, and has a good model of what words usually sound like. If your writing deviates too much from that model, the brain will complain, just as it would if you spoke a sentence in an unnatural order.

Writing out loud, then, is just a kind of syntax checking. It’s checking your words against the model of English that’s already in your head.

This is why it’s useful to read out loud even when you have no idea whether something’s wrong with what you wrote. Even a bad sentence sounds bad. When you read something out loud and something goes wrong, it’s because something went wrong when you were writing it, not when you were reading it. The problem was in the words the moment you wrote them, and reading them out loud is just what detected it.

There are a lot of specific pieces of writing advice that are special cases of read out loud. For example, one common piece of advice is that you shouldn’t use adverbs. I’m often asked “but why not?” And the answer is that it usually sounds bad when you do. If you read your writing out loud, you won’t need to be told not to use adverbs. You’ll realize that they sound like what they are, a kind of verbal wallpaper.

When someone suggests a new rule of writing, my first question is “does it sound good when you do that?” I think this question is sufficient. You don’t need to look up how to pronounce adverbs in French before deciding you don’t need to use them.

The reason this is true is that good writing has a certain sound to it. When you write well, you can hear it. And that’s why, if you want to get good at writing, you should read a lot of good writing. You’re not just learning new words. You’re building up a mental model of what good writing sounds like.

I was reminded of this recently while editing a student’s paper. It was pretty good, but I couldn’t quite say why it was good. But when I read it out loud, I realized why: it had the kind of sound that good writing has.

I can’t precisely describe what I mean by good writing sounding good. I’m not even sure whether it’s an independent variable. It’s possible that good writing sounds good for the same reasons good music sounds good. It could just be that a good sentence has a certain musicality, like a good melody. Or maybe that’s a red herring, and what I mean by writing sounding good is just that it has the sound of writing that was written well.

I’m also not sure how much of this can be learned consciously. For example, I think the reason it’s bad to end a sentence with a preposition is just that it sounds bad. But it’s not just that it sounds bad to you, it sounds bad to everyone, because English sounds different to everyone. So you can’t just make a list of what sounds good to you.

The best you can do is to develop your ear. Read and write a lot, and you’ll learn what sounds good.

prompt: An essay arguing that the best writing advice ever given is 'read it out loud' and that almost every other rule is a special case of it.
response:
Some rules are good. But they’re hard to keep track of. For example, the rule against starting sentences with “and” or “but” is a good one, but a hard one to remember. You end up writing sentences like

And he went into the room, and then he saw what it was, and then he started screaming, and then it was all over.

And it’s hard to know which words to put in parentheses to make it right.

But if you read that sentence out loud, you can tell that something is wrong. Then you can change it until it sounds right.

It’s a little hard to know if this is a coincidence, or a rule that covers all the other rules. But I’ve had good results following it.

prompt: An essay arguing that the best writing advice ever given is 'read it out loud' and that almost every other rule is a special case of it.
response:
I am going to make a shocking and heretical statement. I’m going to say that the best writing advice is to read your writing aloud. Yes, the best writing advice is not to use passive voice, or to write short paragraphs, or to avoid beginning sentences with “And” or “But”, or to make your sentences the length of waves. The best writing advice is to read what you’ve written out loud and see how it sounds.

In this essay I want to talk about why the best writing advice is to read your writing aloud, and then why the other common writing advice is actually just a special case of that.

When you read something out loud and it doesn’t sound good, you usually know why it doesn’t sound good. I can write a sentence that is technically perfect, but when I say it out loud I realize it sounds like something a lawyer would write.

Here is an example of a sentence that is technically fine, but doesn’t sound right:

I am not saying you should always write short paragraphs.

Here is the same sentence when I rewrite it to sound better out loud:

I’m not saying you should always use short paragraphs.

The first sentence has no obvious problems. I didn’t use passive voice. The sentence was short. I didn’t begin the sentence with “And” or “But”. But when I say the sentence out loud, it doesn’t sound right. It’s probably because of all the letters that rhyme: “not say-you should”. In English that’s very hard to say out loud.

Here’s another example:

When people say the world is more dangerous now, I often wonder if they mean that it’s more dangerous than when they were young.

That’s a perfect sentence. There’s no passive voice, it’s not too long, and there are no “And” or “But” at the beginning of the sentence. But when I say it out loud I hear “I often wonder if they mean”, and it sounds a little weird.

Here’s a better version:

When people say the world is more dangerous now, I’m often wondering if they mean that it’s more dangerous than when they were young.

This sounds a little better, although I could also change “when they were young” to “they were young”, or to “it was”. When you’re writing, you’ll often have several ways to make a sentence sound better out loud, and you may need to experiment a little to see what works best.

### Read your writing aloud

There’s a good reason the best writing advice is to read your writing out loud. When you read something out loud, you are actually using the part of your brain that processes sounds. Your brain is really good at processing sounds because our brains evolved that way.

If you read your writing out loud, your brain will tell you that the writing doesn’t sound right, even if you don’t know why. That’s the most important thing you can know. You can then try to rewrite the sentence until it sounds right.

You can also use the same technique to find problems with your writing in general. If you read an essay out loud and something sounds weird, then your brain is telling you that something is probably wrong with that part of the essay.

I think the reason the best writing advice is to read your writing out loud is that it’s so rare to see writing that sounds good out loud. Most writing is meant to be read silently.

There are a few exceptions. When you write a speech, you need to read it out loud before you give the speech to see if it sounds good. When you write a song, you need to sing it out loud to hear if it sounds good. And when you write a script for a movie, you read it out loud so that you can hear if the lines sound good out loud. But most writing is not written to be said out loud, and that’s probably why people forget to read their writing out loud when they’re writing.

### Other writing advice is a special case

I think the reason you often see other writing advice instead of “read your writing out loud” is that people have figured out patterns in what makes writing sound good out loud.

For example, short paragraphs sound good out loud. I know that for sure because I have read a lot of essays out loud, and I know that the ones with short paragraphs sound better. But if I had never read an essay out loud, I wouldn’t know that short paragraphs sound good. And if someone else had told me that short paragraphs sound good, I probably wouldn’t believe them.

But once you have read a lot of writing out loud, you start to notice patterns. You start to notice that short paragraphs sound good out loud. You start to notice that long sentences don’t sound good out loud. You start to notice that “And” and “But” at the beginning of a sentence sound good. You start to notice that passive voice sounds weird out loud. You start to notice that most of the writing advice is just a list of patterns that you’ve found from reading your writing out loud.

### The reason to read your writing out loud

I think the main reason you should read your writing out loud is that it can help you find problems with your writing. But there’s another reason I like reading my writing out loud: when you read your writing out loud, you get to hear the music in your writing.

I like hearing the music in my writing, but most of the time I’m writing for the reader, not for myself. If I write something that sounds good to me but not to the reader, then the reader won’t understand what I’m trying to say.

I think a good way to use the technique of reading your writing out loud is to write first for the reader. That’s the most important thing you can do when you write.

Then you can read your writing out loud, and if it sounds good to you, that’s great, but it’s not the most important thing.

prompt: I'm a court stenographer. For 22 years I've typed other people's words exactly, including their ums and broken sentences, and I've come to think spoken language is far stranger and more beautiful than written. Write a personal essay from my perspective about what transcription teaches you about how people actually talk.
response:
I’ve been a court stenographer for 22 years. I report people’s words exactly, and sometimes I’m not sure if I’m going to end up a lawyer or a poet.

In my job I write other people’s words down as I hear them. I don’t fix grammar or spelling. I don’t change sentence structures or delete “um.” If you say “um, I really think I should maybe, maybe, maybe try and talk about, like, um, the new policy that was just passed yesterday and, um, you know, that everybody, everyone in town, everyone in the whole world is, you know, talking about and, you know, is very interested in how it’s going to affect them, and so I think that we need to talk about how it’s going to affect us and what we should do,” I write that down.

It’s not easy.

I don’t like to talk about the things I’ve seen in the courtroom. They’re people’s problems and I’m not supposed to know about them, but I have to listen to everything and then remember it all.

I don’t like to talk about what I’ve learned in the courtroom, either. It’s not like I’ve discovered something no one else knew. It’s more like I’m surprised by the things I know. It’s like I have this information in my head and I can’t quite believe it.

But I know that if you say something about 55 to 60 percent of the time, it will happen. If you say something about 90 to 95 percent of the time, it will happen and it will also be the truth. If you say something a lot of the time, it will happen.

I know that you’re more likely to get pregnant if you have sex on your back, that you’re more likely to have a boy if you have sex on your back. I know that.

I know that some men get really really really excited by feet and toes and socks.

I know that the world is a really crazy place and that there’s a lot of crazy stuff going on and that most of the time it’s going to seem crazy and that you’re not crazy. I know that.

I know that people have been going to their therapist and saying “I’m really, really anxious and I don’t know why and I’m really really scared of something but I don’t know what it is” and their therapist says, “Well, what do you think you’re scared of?” and they say, “I don’t know! I don’t know! I really want to know. I really, really want to know. But I don’t know.” And they go through this long process and they have these huge breakthroughs, and they learn all the secrets, and they say, “Oh, I’m scared of something and I know what it is,” and they’re all excited about what it is they’re scared of, and they come to court to testify about it and they say, “I’m really scared of being alone.” And then their lawyer says, “Is this true? Have you always been scared of being alone?” and they say “No, I’m scared of being alone now.” And the lawyer asks, “Is that a change?” and they say, “Yes, it’s a change.” And the lawyer says, “Okay, why are you scared of being alone now?” and they say, “I don’t know.” And the lawyer says, “That’s okay. You don’t have to know. But I’m asking you, why are you scared of being alone now?” and they say, “I don’t know.” And the lawyer says, “Okay, do you want to guess?” and they say, “I don’t know. I don’t want to guess.” And the lawyer says, “Okay, are you scared of being alone because you think you’re going to be alone for the rest of your life?” and they say, “Yeah, I think I’m going to be alone for the rest of my life.” And the lawyer says, “Is that true?” and they say, “I don’t know. Maybe. I don’t know.”

And I’ve seen people say that’s true.

And I’ve seen people say it’s not true.

And I’ve seen people say, “I don’t know.”

And I’ve seen people say they’re really really really excited about being alone for the rest of their life and they’re going to be great.

I’ve seen people say all of these things.

prompt: I'm a court stenographer. For 22 years I've typed other people's words exactly, including their ums and broken sentences, and I've come to think spoken language is far stranger and more beautiful than written. Write a personal essay from my perspective about what transcription teaches you about how people actually talk.
response:
I am a court reporter, and for 22 years I’ve been listening to people talk. My job, in this profession, is to type out what someone says verbatim, and that means that I’ve transcribed a lot of broken sentences, lots of “ums” and “ahs,” and a lot of people saying things like “I don’t know. I don’t know if that’s the right way to say it, but . . .”

I am a writer by another job, and I was surprised to discover that I’d become a better writer after working in the court. Because the more I transcribe, the more I realized that people talk in a much stranger and more beautiful way than we do when we write.

I wrote about it in an earlier post, but I have a new example. I was transcribing a trial today, and the lawyer was trying to ask the jury a question. This is not a transcript of a trial, which would be boring. It’s a transcript of a lawyer talking about a trial.

I have no idea what a lawyer is supposed to say, but he was trying to ask the jury about their thoughts. He started like this:

I’m going to ask you something that might seem a little odd, and that is, what do you think about the word “beyond”?

And then he stopped for a while. He had his hands clasped together, and he looked like he was trying to remember something.

He said, “I’m going to ask you what do you think about the word ‘beyond.’”

And he started again. “Beyond” is not a normal word, is it? And I would like to ask you, does the word “beyond” strike you as normal or not normal?

He was not quite right, but he had gotten it in his head that “beyond” was the word he was going to focus on, and he was not going to stop thinking about that. The rest of the conversation wasn’t about whether the word “beyond” was normal or not. Here’s a sample of what he said after that:

It’s an interesting word. When we say beyond, we can’t really define what beyond means. We can’t. I mean, there’s no limit, there’s no measurement that you can say. This is beyond. This is beyond. This is beyond. We can’t say, beyond means. There’s no measurement for beyond. You can’t really put a definition on the word beyond, and that’s what we’re asking you to do.

He was talking about the phrase “beyond a reasonable doubt.” I think he was trying to say that, beyond a reasonable doubt, is not a phrase we can define. There’s no way to measure reasonable doubt. There’s no point where you can say, this is reasonable doubt. This is beyond reasonable doubt.

But he said this a lot of times, and he kept coming back to it again and again.

That’s what you can’t do. You can’t define beyond.

He asked the jury to think about it.

It’s an interesting word, and it’s an interesting concept. When you hear the word beyond, where does your mind go?

I’ve always thought that the phrase “beyond a reasonable doubt” is a really bad way to say what we mean. I don’t think people understand it. I don’t think the jury has a good way to think about what it means.

But what was interesting to me was how the lawyer said it. He tried to say something, but he didn’t do it in the way that we write. He did it in the way that he talked.

And that was the point that I wanted to make. When I write, I try to write in the way that people talk, but I usually do a bad job of it.

I think the reason that I do a bad job of it is that we usually think that we’re talking in the way that we write. And it’s not true. We do not talk in the way that we write.

I have always thought that we talk in a more complicated way than we write, but I think that the way that we talk is not more complicated. It’s different.

We talk in a way that is more emotional.

We write in a way that tries to make sure that people will understand us.

We talk in a way that we don’t always understand.

And when we talk, we use the same words over and over again.

We talk in the way that we do because talking is a way to get what we want.

prompt: I'm a court stenographer. For 22 years I've typed other people's words exactly, including their ums and broken sentences, and I've come to think spoken language is far stranger and more beautiful than written. Write a personal essay from my perspective about what transcription teaches you about how people actually talk.
response:
I have been a court stenographer for twenty-two years, and in that time I have written down the spoken words of thousands of people, from the president of the United States to the least articulate witness I can imagine.

My work is, on the face of it, dead easy. You listen to people talking and you write down what they say. But in practice it is anything but simple. You must learn to type 130 words a minute, because that is the speed at which some people talk. More than that, you have to be accurate 99 percent of the time. That’s because you are writing down what people say under oath, and their words may be crucial to the outcome of the case.

The thing that most surprises people about court stenography is that I write down everything the witness says, including his or her ums and ahhs, broken and awkward sentences, and all the rest. If the witness is a child who can’t tell you much more than “Yeah, that’s right, I don’t know,” I write down “Yeah, that’s right, I don’t know.”

This is not the kind of writing that people think of as beautiful. I write down the spoken words of people with all their faults. Yet after twenty-two years of this I find myself saying, “I wish people would stop trying to be so eloquent.” If you really want to appreciate language, you should try listening to the way ordinary people talk.

In the first place, there is something fascinating about the way people use language. We like to think of language as a means of communication, and in fact it is. But it is also a game that people play, and it is this game aspect of language that makes it so interesting. I have spent my whole career watching people play with language and I have come to think it is the most fascinating game that humans have ever invented.

For example, I often find myself thinking, as I write down the words of a witness, that this is a very interesting way of saying what you mean. Here is a typical example.

The witness is a 64 year old woman who is testifying about a business she owned. I ask her, “Did you ever go to a lawyer about your business?”

She answers, “Well, we did, but I don’t think the lawyers are all that great.”

And I think, wow. I’ve heard lots of things said about lawyers before, but this is the most interesting. She isn’t even complaining about her own lawyer, or the lawyers she went to. She is saying something much bigger. She is saying that the entire profession is suspect. And the way she puts this sweeping judgment is “I don’t think the lawyers are all that great.”

There are other fascinating aspects of spoken language that I have learned about in my job.

For instance, one thing I’ve learned about people who are good at playing the game of language is that they never say what they mean. They say a little more than they mean, and a little less, and a little different than they mean, but they never mean exactly what they say.

The best example of this is my father. He was very good at this. He always said something interesting that was just a bit off. He never said what he meant, and yet it was always obvious what he meant. But the most fascinating thing to think about was the gap between what he said and what he meant.

It was never just a bit off, though. Sometimes it was a lot.

For example, my father would often ask me, “What did you do to yourself?” This was usually when I had cut my knee or had my arm broken or something. And if I said, “I fell down,” my father would say, “Well, what did you do to yourself?” He was trying to elicit a confession, because he thought I must have done something to cause the accident.

And of course I was always guilty. I had done something wrong. But it wasn’t exactly what he said. I hadn’t done anything to myself. I had done something that caused me to fall down and get hurt.

There was always a gap between what my father said and what he meant. But he was so funny, and so obviously affectionate, that I never even noticed. He would say, “Well, what did you do to yourself?” and I would say, “Nothing. I just fell down.” And he would say, “Oh. OK.”

The second thing I’ve learned about the spoken language of good players is that the only thing they never say is the boring stuff. They never say “hello” and “thank you” and “I hope you are well.” They always say something interesting.

For example, instead of saying “hello,” my father would say “Hi, what’s going on?” or “Hey, are you still alive?” The second time I heard him say that, I said, “Dad, what’s the deal? Why do you always say ‘Are you still alive?’”

And he said, “Well, I thought it was funnier to say that.”

The third thing I’ve learned about the spoken language of good players is that they never say what other people say.

For example, most people would say “good-bye.” My father would say “Well, I’ll see you later.”

If I say “good-bye” to him, he says, “What’s that? Say ‘bye-bye.’”

He would say “Oh, you’re right,” when he meant “No, you’re wrong.”

He would say “I thought maybe maybe you could do that” when he meant “Please do that right away.”

If I said, “I’ll see you at the airport,” he would say “Yes, but I can’t find my pants.”

The thing that is most fascinating to me about this is that he never said what other people said. He said something different, but he never said the same thing that other people say.

I think it’s one of the most interesting things I know about language. And I think this is what makes good speakers good. They always say something different.

The fourth thing I’ve learned about the spoken language of good players is that they never say what they mean.
