This is the most important thing, and it’s the hardest to explain.

I know that when I’m listening to a speaker I really like, I’m listening to the words they are saying and I’m listening to what they mean and I’m listening to the gap between what they are saying and what they mean.

This is what’s fascinating about good speakers. They always say something different than what they mean, but it’s always obvious what they mean.

I think this is why good speakers are so fascinating to listen to. They say something different than what they mean, but it’s always obvious what they mean.

That’s what I love about language. And that’s why I’m a court stenographer.

prompt: Write an essay about the words that exist in one language and not in another, but skip the usual listicle stuff (hygge, saudade, etc). I want to know whether lacking a word actually stops you from feeling the thing, or just from talking about it.
response:
I was thinking the other day about the words that exist in one language and not another.

I don’t mean the usual “saudade” and “hygge” stuff. I mean things like “hymn” or “yodel” that don’t translate easily into other languages because they’re based on practices specific to a particular culture.

But then I realized I’m not sure how true this even is. “Hymn” is a perfectly understandable word, just a bit weird and unfamiliar. If I’d heard it before, it would just be an old-fashioned way of saying “song”. If someone had told me it meant “church song” I wouldn’t have been surprised.

But what about a word that has a meaning that’s more than just a matter of style?

What about “holy”? It’s in the Bible, so it’s not a Christian word in the same way “hymn” is. But it is a Christian word in the way that it’s based on a Christian concept. The word “holy” means “set apart as sacred”, but “sacred” means “the God who exists and cares for us”.

If I were to explain that concept to an atheist, the best I could do would be to give a vague description of what a believer in “sacred” would think. But I wouldn’t be able to give them the word “sacred”, because it doesn’t exist in their language.

Is this a case of someone who lacks a word for something not being able to feel it? Can an atheist not feel holy?

I was thinking about this yesterday when I was talking to someone who was describing what it was like to take a class taught by a woman professor.

She said the professor would sometimes make a little sound when she was excited. Not an exclamation like “Ooh!”, but a little high-pitched “hmm” sound. It was a little cute, she thought.

The word I would use for this kind of sound is “squeal”. But she didn’t use the word “squeal”. I don’t think she even thought to use it. She just said “a little sound”.

I think there’s a reason for this. It’s not that “squeal” is the only word I could have used. But it’s a word that fits her description better than any other one I know of.

I think there’s a reason for this.

prompt: Write an essay about the words that exist in one language and not in another, but skip the usual listicle stuff (hygge, saudade, etc). I want to know whether lacking a word actually stops you from feeling the thing, or just from talking about it.
response:
In her book “A Field Guide to Getting Lost,” Rebecca Solnit writes that she once lived in a small town in the mountains of northern California and would often walk along the ridge in the woods. One day, when she was walking in the woods, she found a word in her head that she had never heard before. At the time, she thought that she had invented it: “It was *murrum*, and it meant the sound of walking on the gravel trail, and it had never been said before, I thought, until it was in my head.”

Solnit later learned that she hadn’t invented the word, that *murrum* was a standard word in Aboriginal Australian.

Solnit’s example of a word that she had never heard before is a good one to start with, because I want to talk about how it feels to encounter a new word, and how that feels to encounter a new word when it is the name for something you already know.

I’m going to talk about the way people say that some experiences are hard to explain because they don’t have a word for it. This is usually brought up in the context of words like *saudade* or *hygge* that people use to describe a feeling. I don’t want to talk about those because they aren’t that useful.

Let’s say that *hygge* means “a cozy feeling that you get when you are surrounded by soft blankets and candles.” I think that *hygge* is probably a bad word, and it’s hard to imagine an experience of hygge that you could not have explained in the words I already gave. I have a friend who lives in Denmark who says that she likes the word *hygge* but that there is something missing about it. She said that there is a Danish word that describes the feeling of sitting down to eat a meal that you have been waiting to eat for a long time, and it’s a word that she wishes existed in English.

I think that’s a much better word to talk about, because it’s clear that it is talking about an experience that you can’t easily express without that word.

The first thing that I want to say is that we have a lot more words than we think we do.

If I want to talk about that feeling of sitting down to a meal that I’ve been waiting for, I can say “It was the feeling of *savoring* the meal.” The word *savor* is already in English, but I don’t think that many people are aware of it. I think that there are thousands of words like that, that people don’t know about because they don’t use it in their day to day speech.

I was talking to a friend about this idea, and they said that they would like to know why it is that we can’t remember words that we know. I think that this is because we have a lot more words that we know than we remember. I have a hard time remembering whether I know a word like *savor*, but I know that I can write it down. And then, after I write it down, I remember that I used to use that word.

I think that the same is true for words like *hygge*. I think that you might know that *hygge* is a word, but you can’t remember how it’s spelled or how it’s pronounced. I think that if I tried to look up a word like *hygge* in a dictionary, that I would remember that I knew it.

So, when people say that they can’t explain their feelings because they don’t have a word for it, I think that’s probably not true. I think that they can just say that they feel a sense of savoring.

The other part of this idea that I want to talk about is that I think that it’s a mistake to think that words are just names for things that you can already know. I think that there is a lot of truth to the idea that words shape the way that you think about the world.

In Solnit’s story, she thought that she had invented the word *murrum*, and she said that it meant “the sound of walking on the gravel trail.” I think that that is wrong, that she was just guessing at what the word meant.

I think that what was actually going on was that she had heard the word before, and that it shaped the way that she thought about the sound of walking on gravel. I think that when she heard the sound of walking on gravel, that she was reminded of the sound of murrum, and so she remembered that word.

In her book “The Myth of Sin,” Robin Hanson talks about how she thinks that the word *soul* is a really bad idea. Hanson’s argument is that the word *soul* is a word that people use to talk about a thing that they feel like they can’t quite understand. I think that the word *soul* is a mistake because the only way to talk about something that you can’t quite understand is to use the word *soul*. I think that using the word *soul* just makes it harder to think about the thing you are talking about.

I think that Hanson is right that words can shape the way that you think about the world.

When you hear a new word, that it can shape the way that you think about the thing that you are talking about. I think that when you hear the word *murrum*, that it gives you a sense of what it’s like to walk on gravel. I think that this is true even if you know that *murrum* is just a word that Aboriginal Australians use to describe the sound of walking on gravel.

I think that the same is true of the word *hygge*.

prompt: Write an essay about the words that exist in one language and not in another, but skip the usual listicle stuff (hygge, saudade, etc). I want to know whether lacking a word actually stops you from feeling the thing, or just from talking about it.
response:
One of my friends recently told me that she was trying to learn Icelandic. I’ve had a bit of Icelandic myself, but I’m nowhere near fluent, so I asked her about it and she told me the hardest part had been learning words that didn’t exist in English.

I asked her what kind of words those were. She gave me “feginung”, which apparently means the kind of sadness you feel when you’re happy about something for someone else.

I asked her if she thought I could have feelings for this kind of sadness before she’d learned the Icelandic word for it. She said that she didn’t know, but she thought she’d had the feeling before. I thought it was possible, but I had a different theory.

I’m going to start by talking about a really neat thing that’s going on in a new language called Toki Pona.

Toki Pona is a new language invented by Sonja Lang. She wanted to make the smallest possible language, so she made one with only about 120 words. The words are really simple; “water” is “telo”, “tree” is “kasi”, and “bird” is “lape”.

The word for “book” is “lipu”. You can say things like “lipu pona” (good book) or “lipu lape” (book about birds), but if you want to say “this book is about how to be happy”, you say “lipu sona pona” – “book knowledge happiness”. You don’t really need a word for “instructional manual” because you can just say “lipu sona” – “knowledge book” – and that gets the idea across well enough.

Toki Pona doesn’t have a word for “sadness”, so how do you express that feeling? You don’t. You have “pona” – happiness, and “ike” – badness, and I think Sonja just wants you to use “ike” to mean both sadness and other kinds of bad things.

This brings us to an interesting question.

A couple of years ago, a guy at my church was giving a talk about the importance of prayer, and he was telling us to be careful not to use words like “God”.

It’s not the word “God” that matters, he said. It’s the idea of God that matters.

And the problem is that once you use the word “God”, you might start to think you understand God. And if you think you understand God, you might start to think that you don’t need to ask for help in understanding. And that’s bad.

So instead of using the word “God”, he suggested we use the word “the Thing”.

The next morning, I was trying to pray. And I couldn’t figure out what to say.

“I want to understand the Thing”, I thought, but that doesn’t work.

What’s the difference between “God” and “the Thing”? “God” has a lot of meaning behind it. “The Thing” is just a placeholder for something that hasn’t been thought about yet.

And I realized that the word is the thought.

When I think of “God”, I get ideas like “Jesus died for us so we don’t go to hell” and “the Trinity”.

When I think of “the Thing”, I get ideas like “I don’t know what I’m talking about” and “please make this work”.

And “God” isn’t just some word that we’re using as a shorthand for “Jesus died for us so we don’t go to hell” and “the Trinity”. “God” actually means those things. They’re the only meaning behind the word “God”.

I don’t think “God” is a better word than “the Thing”. I think they’re both useful, but they mean different things, and I like having more options.

I think the same thing is true of the Icelandic word “feginung”.

Maybe I can feel that kind of sadness without knowing the word. I don’t know. But I don’t think I can talk about that kind of sadness.

And I think I’ve been talking about all the wrong kinds of sad.

prompt: Blog essay: why I stopped finishing books I don't like, and why it took me until 41 to give myself permission. Light tone, but I want a real point about what we owe authors (if anything).
response:
I have started to stop reading books that I’m not enjoying. I used to feel guilty and try to force myself to finish them, even though it was a waste of time.

I know this because I read books that I really like and finish them in a few days. If I read a book that’s not good for me at my normal speed, I would finish it in a month.

I am 41, and I’ve been reading my whole life. So, it’s a little embarrassing that I only realized this a few weeks ago.

I started thinking about it after finishing a long novel that I didn’t really like. I read it in a month, which was really slow for me. I had tried other books, and they had been too complicated.

I’ve been a big reader of fantasy novels and have read 40-50 of them. Some of them have been so good that they’ve been life-changing and opened up a world that I wanted to visit again.

But I’ve also read many fantasy novels that have been so bad that I couldn’t get into them, and I just didn’t enjoy them.

I think that many people read a lot of books that they don’t like, but they feel like they should finish them. They might be thinking that they owe the author, or they might be thinking that they’ll like it later.

I read books that I don’t like because I think that I’m not getting something. I want to know what it is that I’m missing. I think that the book is good, but it just doesn’t speak to me.

I also read books that I don’t like because I’m not sure that they’re bad. I’ve read a lot of fantasy novels, and I’ve realized that I have a lot of taste and I know the best fantasy novels. But I’m not sure that I have the same taste in other kinds of books, so I want to give them a chance.

I have read books that I didn’t like and then realized that they were bad. I have also read books that I didn’t like and then realized that they were good, but they didn’t speak to me.

I read many books that I don’t like because I’m not sure that they’re bad. But I think that this is not a good reason to read a book that I don’t like. If I don’t like a book, I should stop reading it. I don’t owe the author or the book anything.

I don’t want to feel like I have to read a book that I don’t like because I’m not sure that it’s bad. I want to be able to stop reading a book that I don’t like and not feel bad about it.

I think it’s great to be able to choose what I read. I don’t want to feel like I have to read a book that I don’t like because I’m not sure that it’s bad.

prompt: Blog essay: why I stopped finishing books I don't like, and why it took me until 41 to give myself permission. Light tone, but I want a real point about what we owe authors (if anything).
response:
This past summer, I bought a novel by a favorite author. I read two chapters and put it down. I’d read something better the night before and it was still going through my head. I was in a hurry because I’d taken this summer trip on purpose, to spend some quiet days with no kids, no house chores, no work. I didn’t have time to read a mediocre novel.

I didn’t finish it. That was the first time I’d done that in the 33 years I’d been an avid reader. I didn’t feel any worse for it.

In the last few years I’ve become more comfortable with quitting books I don’t like. But I’m not sure why it’s been so hard, even though it seems like such a small change.

When I was a kid, I was pretty good about quitting books I didn’t like. I was a voracious reader, so I wanted to get to the next one as fast as possible. If the book I was reading wasn’t working, I stopped reading it.

In school, though, we had to finish what we started. In my eighth-grade English class, I had to write reports on two books, one of which I really didn’t like. I remember being angry that I’d been forced to spend time on a book I wasn’t enjoying. I also remember being ashamed, because I thought that not liking a book might mean I was too shallow or stupid.

I also think I had a lot of shame about how much time I spent reading. I was very interested in books and very good at reading, but I didn’t feel like I could spend too much time on it because it wasn’t a good use of time.

This was the late 80s. I was in the same age group as the kids in The Breakfast Club. It was the 80s, which was a time when the people in charge felt that it was very important to make us feel bad about the kinds of things we were interested in.

For the kids in The Breakfast Club, that meant their interests in music. The kids in my grade were interested in reading. I think the idea was to make everyone feel bad about what they were into, because we were all “wasting our time.”

My parents never told me that reading was a waste of time, but I felt like there was something wrong with me because I liked it so much.

I don’t remember when I stopped feeling bad about reading. Maybe it was in college, when I noticed that I could get good grades by doing just enough work in all of my classes, and then using my extra time to read.

It was in the late 90s and early 2000s that I decided that I was going to try to read every book I started. I think that was mostly about feeling like I had to finish what I started, but also about how much money I was spending on books. I’d buy them on the assumption that I’d get a lot of pleasure out of them. If I stopped reading them halfway through, I felt like I was wasting my money.

I thought that reading a book to the end meant I was more likely to finish it before giving up. So I’d keep reading it for a while longer. But I’d get pretty far into a book before quitting it. I never finished a book just to finish it, but there were times when I would have gotten more out of my time by doing something else.

I think I thought I had to finish books because of respect for the author. When I read a book, the author was putting a lot of their attention into me. I was spending time with that person. If I quit the book, I was ending the relationship.

And now I’m 41 and I’ve realized that the author doesn’t care.

If I don’t finish a book I don’t like, the author doesn’t know I’m reading it, so it’s not like the author is losing the opportunity to put their attention into me. If I stop reading, it’s not like the author loses me as a friend.

If I like the author’s other books, I can tell my friends to read those. But I’m not going to read a book that I don’t like.

I’m not going to read a book I don’t like, no matter how many times the author tells me they’re very excited about it, how much it means to them, or how much time and effort they put into it.

I don’t owe it to them.

I don’t think this is true only for books. I don’t owe anything to the people I’m interacting with. I don’t have to finish watching a movie I’m not enjoying, or read a blog post I’m not interested in. I don’t have to go through an entire workday at a job that isn’t working, or spend an hour with someone I don’t like.

I don’t owe it to them. I don’t owe it to myself.

I’m sure there are things I could do that would make me feel better, and there are things I could do to help the people around me. But I don’t owe anyone anything, so I can do those things if I want to, but I can also not.

prompt: Blog essay: why I stopped finishing books I don't like, and why it took me until 41 to give myself permission. Light tone, but I want a real point about what we owe authors (if anything).
response:
It’s not an exact science, but I like to say that when I’m a third of the way through a book and still not enjoying it, I stop.

A couple weeks ago I did this with *The Great Alone*, and I was sad that I’d only been able to get through 20% of a book I’d already paid for. But then I remembered that I’d already read most of it, which was kind of nice.

I’ve been reading this book for years. I started it when it first came out, then I read a couple chapters and put it down. A few months later I started it again. I read a few more chapters and put it down again. Every time I’ve started it, I’ve read 10-20% of the book and then put it down. I always thought I’d get back to it eventually, which I didn’t realize I’d been doing for the past five years.

It was hard to admit that I wasn’t going to finish it, but I was excited to not have to spend any more time on something I didn’t like. I’m still not sure I’m going to put down every book I start, but I’m trying to become more comfortable with that.

I didn’t realize I had a lot of feelings about finishing books I started until I noticed I was trying to finish this one for the fifth time. I feel like I owe it to the author to finish what I start. I don’t know why, but I’ve always felt like that. I guess I’m kind of a people pleaser, and I’m always trying to do what I’m supposed to do. I’m not sure where the idea comes from, but I’ve had it for a long time.

I think it comes from my parents. My mom has never been a reader, but my dad has read a lot, and he’s always finishing books he starts. I think he likes to finish things.

When I was in college, I started taking my reading more seriously. I started reading more serious books, and I found it hard to put them down when I didn’t like them. I always felt like I had to finish a book if I started it. I was always worried about wasting my money, but I was also worried that if I didn’t finish a book, I wasn’t going to be able to talk to other people about it, so I wasn’t being an equal partner in my friendships.

I was also worried that if I didn’t finish a book, I’d be missing out on something important. I thought if I didn’t finish a book, I’d never understand something really important about life. I thought if I didn’t finish *Moby Dick*, I’d never understand why people get obsessed with things. I thought if I didn’t finish *The Great Gatsby*, I’d never understand how the rich live. I thought I would miss out on all the good things life has to offer.

When I was in college, I read a lot, but I didn’t finish a lot of books. I started reading *The Sun Also Rises* and couldn’t make it through two pages. I started reading *Ulysses* and couldn’t make it through two pages. I started reading *The Catcher in the Rye* and couldn’t make it through two pages. I was really bad at finishing books I started.

The longer I stayed in college, the more I started to realize that some people didn’t finish books, and that was totally okay. I was still really bad at it, but I didn’t care as much anymore.

I was still worried that I wasn’t being a good partner in my friendships. I would start reading books my friends were reading, and I would never finish them, and then I would never be able to talk to my friends about the books. I would be out of the conversation, and I would miss out on a really important part of my friendship.

I’ve talked a lot about how I’m a people pleaser. I’ve talked a lot about how I’ve always been a people pleaser. I don’t know where that came from, but I’ve always been a people pleaser. I think it comes from my mom. My mom is a really nice person, but she’s not really assertive. My dad is really assertive, but he’s not really nice. I think I’m kind of a mix of my parents, but I’m not sure which way the balance goes.

I’m really bad at being assertive. I’ve always been really bad at being assertive. I think that’s why I was so worried about being out of the conversation. I always wanted to make sure I was doing something that was socially acceptable, so I would always start reading books my friends were reading, even if I didn’t like them.

I never really talked to anyone about this. I never told anyone that I was struggling with finishing books I started. I never told anyone that I was struggling with not finishing books I started. I never told anyone that I was struggling with starting books I started. I never told anyone that I was struggling with being out of the conversation.

prompt: Please write an essay of approximately 1,000 words on whether an author's private morality should affect how we read their work. I want to avoid the usual 'separate the art from the artist' framing and instead ask whether some works are actually changed, as texts, by what we learn about the person who wrote them.
response:
A lot of people are talking about whether we should separate the artist from the art. I don’t think that’s really the right question. It’s not the question people are asking – even the people who want to separate the artist from the art know that art is not *separated* from the artist in any real sense. It’s also not the question that we should be asking – even if we could separate art and artist and only judge the art, we’d probably want to know about the artist and let our knowledge of them affect our judgment of the art.

But it *is* a good question whether we should let the artist change the art. It’s a good question whether some texts actually become different texts when we know more about who wrote them.

I remember hearing people debate this when the author of a children’s book got outed as a sex offender. One camp said the book didn’t change, that it was the same words in the same order, and that we shouldn’t let what we knew about the author change the words in the book.

The other camp pointed out that it *was* changed in some way – maybe not literally, but we knew something about it that we didn’t know before, and that changed the way we read it. They said things like “I know that he was a child rapist when he wrote that lovely, innocent story about a boy and a bear going on an adventure together”, which certainly has a different feel to it than “I know nothing at all about this author, but it seems that he’s written this lovely, innocent story about a boy and a bear going on an adventure together”.

I think this camp is right, and that there are a lot of ways the author can change the text. I think most of these effects are probably *desirable* changes.

The most obvious way is that the author’s behavior can prove or disprove claims the author makes in their text. This is obviously relevant to nonfiction. If you’re reading an article by a prominent author on the topic of “how to tell if a guy is gay”, you might not even need to know he’s gay, just that the author is a prominent person in a position to know. But if you read that article by a gay man, that makes it a lot more credible.

Likewise, if you’re reading an article by a prominent author on the topic of “how to make sure your son doesn’t end up gay”, you might not even need to know that the author has no children at all, just that the author is a prominent person in a position to know. But if you read that article by a man who has never had children, that makes it a lot less credible.

The author’s behavior can also provide a counter-example to a general claim the author makes. For example, if you’re reading a blog post by a prominent author arguing that “I never ever lie to my friends, I’m an honest person”, you might not even need to know that the author has previously lied to you, just that the author is a prominent person in a position to know. But if you read that article by someone you know has lied to you before, that makes it a lot less credible.

Even if a text doesn’t make any general claims about the author’s behavior, the author’s behavior can give it a certain ring of truth. I can’t give a specific example, because I don’t think I’m qualified to talk about this, but I remember reading about a prominent blogger who was involved in a controversy about whether he was a racist. One of the arguments against him was that he was too quick to criticize anyone who wasn’t black for a lot of small things that were just barely racist, while he had a lot of friends who were clearly racist and he never criticized them. I don’t remember enough of the details of this to remember whether that blogger actually wrote a post defending his behavior, or whether it was just something people talked about in the comments.

It was hard for me to think of that as a really strong argument against him, though. I mean, yeah, he was being inconsistent, which made him seem like either a jerk or a hypocrite. But I didn’t know enough to judge whether he was racist, or whether his behavior was more a matter of him wanting to avoid offending other black people or wanting to come across as less racist. I don’t know the right answer to this, and I don’t know whether I would have thought differently about that blogger’s writings after reading about him, so I won’t give this as a clear example. But I can see how it might work.

I have a feeling this type of thing is really common in nonfiction. I think it’s less common in fiction, but I can imagine ways it might happen. If you read a work of fiction by a character who’s very similar to the author, it’s not really surprising if the character makes some mistakes that are also mistakes the author has made. But if the author is very different from the character, you might take it as a strike against the author if the character makes the same mistakes. For example, if you read a story about a woman who makes a decision to be more open and vulnerable with people, and then later has a conversation where she does something that is really not open and vulnerable at all, you might not care much. But if you find out the author is an open and vulnerable person who makes a point about how important it is to be open and vulnerable, you might think “wow, what a hypocrite”.

I can’t give a specific example of this, because it’s too easy to just think of something that doesn’t fit, and then people will say “oh, here’s a real example that proves the point is stupid”. But I can see how it could happen.

Another way an author’s behavior can change a text is that it can make you understand why it says what it says. I mentioned a blog post by a blogger who was accused of being a racist. I didn’t give an example of how a blogger’s behavior could change how we read a text, but I can imagine how it might. For example, if you read a blog post by an author who says “there’s no such thing as racism, we shouldn’t talk about it, it’s just a concept that people have invented”, you might think the author is being either racist or very naive. But if you read that same post by an author who you know has suffered a lot of racism, you might think “oh, they’re just trying to get people to stop talking about racism so they don’t have to suffer any more of it”. That would probably make the post more credible.

I don’t think we should let the author’s behavior completely change how we read a text. For example, I have a feeling that the “I never ever lie to my friends, I’m an honest person” post I mentioned earlier would be less credible if the author lied to me. But I don’t think it would be *completely* unbelievable – maybe he’s just changed his mind and now he’s an honest person. Maybe he used to lie to me, but not so much anymore. Maybe he lied to me when he was angry and he’s changed a lot. I would probably be a lot more skeptical, but I wouldn’t go from “oh, this sounds very true” to “oh, there’s no way this is true”.

I also don’t think it’s right to say that the author’s behavior shouldn’t change the text at all. I don’t think that’s the way we read or understand things. I think we do let them change the text, and I think that’s usually a good thing.

prompt: Please write an essay of approximately 1,000 words on whether an author's private morality should affect how we read their work. I want to avoid the usual 'separate the art from the artist' framing and instead ask whether some works are actually changed, as texts, by what we learn about the person who wrote them.
response:
When it comes to the work of a deceased or absent author, the question of whether a work is tainted by its author’s bad character is easy to answer, since the author can’t be there to be harmed by the accusation. For a deceased author who is also an important historical figure, as with Martin Luther, a bad reputation is sometimes even helpful. For a living author, it depends on whether the author is trying to make money from the work in question. If an author is an important figure in his own time, as with Salman Rushdie or the late Christopher Hitchens, the author is often more hurt by his own actions than by anyone else’s. If an author is making money from a work but is not a major figure in his own time, as with the late Larry Summers, he may be hurt by having his work disavowed by publishers or readers. But if the author is not making money from the work in question, then it is hard to see how a bad reputation would be an important enough consideration to override the author’s own desire to be read. The same goes for the question of whether we should avoid works whose authors are accused of bad things without any evidence. In my experience, the only times that works have been widely avoided for this reason are when they’ve been accused of bad things by other works, which are themselves widely avoided for the same reason, and I don’t think we should take this too seriously.

The only situation where the question of whether an author’s bad actions are a reason not to read his work is interesting is when the author is an important figure in his own time, but not making money from the work in question. This situation seems to arise most often for authors like John Stuart Mill, whose actions are the main way to know him, but who has other work worth reading. If we disavow the work because of the author’s bad actions, it is not because we want to punish the author – he doesn’t seem to care either way – or because we want to avoid money going to the author or his heirs – no one cares about that either. It is, instead, because we care about the content of the book.

This situation also arises for works that were written by groups that had some bad people in them. I think this is usually a bad idea. For example, when I was in college in the late 1990s there was a lot of talk of how we should avoid reading the works of the Frankfurt School because they had a lot of antisemitic people. I never thought this made sense, since it was not as if reading a book by Theodor Adorno would make me think that antisemitism was a good thing.

A stronger version of this argument is to say that, in addition to not wanting to hurt living authors, we shouldn’t read works by authors with bad reputations because the work could be used to defend the author. For example, if you have a good work by a racist author, you might be able to use the good parts of the work to defend the racist author.

I don’t think this works either. If you try to use a work to defend the author, the people you’re arguing with will have the advantage of context. For example, if someone tries to argue that you should read Mill’s *The Subjection of Women*, you can say that it has a lot of good points, but that we shouldn’t forget that he wrote it in order to convince his wife that it was okay to marry him after the death of his first wife.

prompt: Please write an essay of approximately 1,000 words on whether an author's private morality should affect how we read their work. I want to avoid the usual 'separate the art from the artist' framing and instead ask whether some works are actually changed, as texts, by what we learn about the person who wrote them.
response:
In the last few years a growing number of prominent writers have been disowned by their readers, usually because of some shocking new fact about their private lives. The author who caused the most controversy was J. D. Salinger, whose private life had become known through his letters published in The Catcher in the Rye (Simon & Schuster, 2005). Salinger was once the most beloved living American author, but his letters revealed a man who had been a fascist supporter, and many of his readers felt betrayed.

When writers are disowned, it’s usually said that the writer should be separated from the work. But I find that a misleading formulation. The question is not what we should think about the writer. It’s what we should think about the work. And that depends on whether we think the work is different now. Does the work change?

Some works certainly don’t. It seems hard to imagine that anyone would read the Iliad in a different way because of something they’d learned about Homer’s private life. In the 20th century too, some books were not affected by their authors’ private lives. I have never heard of anyone changing their mind about Kafka’s work because of something they’d learned about him personally.

But sometimes we think a work has been changed because of what we’ve learned about its author. The most famous example is The Diary of a Young Girl (Random House, 1949), which was so much better than anyone would have expected. When it was published, most readers must have felt that Anne Frank must have been a genius, because she must have been able to write a great book in just a couple of years. But then people realized she was only 13 when she started writing it. So the book didn’t change. The change was in readers’ understanding of its author.

When the author is older than a child, the change is usually in the work, not the author. For example, Salinger’s The Catcher in the Rye (Little, Brown & Company, 1951) was considered a masterpiece. But once people learned about Salinger’s private life, they started thinking it was a terrible book. They didn’t change their minds about Salinger. They changed their minds about the book.

If the work is unchanged, then it doesn’t matter what we learn about the author. If we read The Catcher in the Rye with the same thoughts as we did before, it doesn’t matter who wrote it. So the key is not to ask whether the work is changed. But then how can we tell?

What’s happened, I think, is a change in our expectations. When we learned about Salinger’s private life, we suddenly thought we could see how it influenced his writing. But we can’t really see any influence. We just think we could, if we looked hard enough. It’s a change in expectations, not understanding.

When we first read a book, we have certain expectations about what we’ll see in it. If Salinger’s private life had been unremarkable, we would have had certain expectations. And when we got to know him, our expectations changed. But the work was unchanged. We just expected to see something new in it.

We are not the first people to be surprised by authors’ private lives. The first to be shocked by an author’s private life were readers of the ancient Greek epic poet Homer. In the Homeric Hymn to Apollo we read “Homer, you bard, son of Cleitus of Smyrna” — as if Homer were some minor poet who’d merely written one song. But everyone knew Homer as the author of the Iliad and the Odyssey.

The Homeric Hymns are a collection of poems attributed to Homer. The Homeric Hymn to Apollo is attributed to another Homer, which seems like an obvious joke. And it’s not the only joke in the poem. For example, Apollo is addressed as the lord of the island of Delos, but Delos was not the seat of Apollo’s cult until the 7th century BC.

The Homeric Hymn to Apollo is not the only Homeric poem that makes jokes. The Odyssey contains a joke that’s been lost on modern readers. In Odyssey 21.292 Penelope tells Odysseus, “I have heard that you are the best archer in Ithaca.” Odysseus then shoots an arrow through twelve axes, a feat no one else could perform. But there’s a problem here. Odysseus is the greatest archer in Ithaca? But in Odyssey 8.76 Odysseus says, “I am not a singer or a bard; I am only a middling warrior.” If Odysseus can’t sing or tell a story, why does he sing and tell a story for an hour in Odyssey 8.76?

In Odyssey 8.73 Odysseus says, “I am not a singer or a bard. But I can do many things. I am skilled at all kinds of singing, and when I am at home I like to sing. But I am not a singer or a bard.” Odysseus is saying that he’s not a professional. He is merely a dilettante. He likes to sing. He is good at it. But he is not a professional singer. He is just an amateur who sings for his own pleasure.

Penelope’s description of Odysseus as the greatest archer in Ithaca is not a mistake. It’s a joke. Odysseus is like Homer. He’s not a professional. He’s just an amateur who likes to shoot arrows for his own pleasure.

response:
At the airport in Reykjavik I saw a poster for Icelandair, which was a picture of an empty road in Iceland, with a caption explaining that it was the road to the Blue Lagoon, Iceland’s touristy hot-spring spa. The road was so empty that it looked like it was a road on the moon. The only other person who was there was a guy in a suit taking the picture. It was hard to tell what the picture was, so it wasn’t much of an advertisement for the Blue Lagoon. But it was a beautiful picture. It was beautiful in the same way that all airports are beautiful.

When we were kids, I used to think it was just a coincidence that I liked airports, because that’s just a weird thing to like. Airports are full of people who are stressed, sad, and angry, and that isn’t something I want to be around, and they also have terrible food. But I’ve figured out what it is about them that I like. It’s not just a coincidence. It’s the same reason I like the moon.

The airports in Reykjavik and the moon look the same way for the same reason. It’s because nobody wants to be there. When you’re in the desert, you don’t see people. If you go into a town, you see people. People like towns because it’s good to be around other people. People like towns so much that it makes the towns pretty. The buildings and roads in towns are beautiful because people spent a lot of time making them beautiful. The desert is empty because nobody spent any time making it beautiful.

In the same way, airports are empty because nobody wants to be there. That’s why airports are all the same and why they’re kind of beautiful. Nobody spends time making airports beautiful, so they all end up looking the same. There is no reason for the airport in Paris to look different than the airport in Los Angeles, and so it doesn’t.

There are lots of people in airports, but they’re all just there because they have to be. They aren’t really in the airport. They’re all in their heads somewhere else, thinking about the place they’re going to or the place they’re coming from. If you get on a plane, you can see the person across the aisle staring into space and thinking about something else.

That’s not what it’s like in most cities. The people in cities want to be in cities. So cities end up looking different from each other because everyone in the city is trying to make it into a city that they like. Cities with a lot of immigrants end up being interesting because they’re a mishmash of everybody’s ideas of what a city is. That’s why you can tell what city you’re in.

The airport in Paris and the airport in Los Angeles are both the same because they’re both a mishmash of nobody’s ideas of what an airport is. That’s why they all look the same. Nobody cares about them, so they’re empty and boring and beautiful.

You can see how this works by looking at the airport in New York. The airport in New York is different from other airports because people like New York so much that they want to be there. The airport in New York is full of people who like the city, so it feels like a city, and it’s a mess because it’s a mishmash of everybody’s ideas of what a city is.

There are a lot of different airports in the world. There are airports in cities where a lot of people like to be, like New York, and airports in cities where nobody wants to be, like Reykjavik. But the airport in Reykjavik is actually nicer than the airport in New York. It’s cleaner, nicer, and more beautiful. That’s because nobody wants to be in the airport in Reykjavik.

If nobody wants to be in an airport, the airport doesn’t have to be very good. It can be pretty much just a building with bathrooms. It doesn’t need to be a city, because nobody wants to be in it. That’s what makes it so beautiful.

It’s the same thing with the moon. The moon doesn’t have anything on it because nobody cares about it. You could have a million people living on the moon, and it would still look the same. It would still look like the moon. The moon isn’t pretty because it’s full of cool people. It’s pretty because it has nothing on it.

That’s why airports are beautiful. They’re all the same because nobody cares about them. But that’s exactly what makes them so pretty.

response:
It used to be that you’d arrive in a foreign city, walk through its airport, and instantly feel the culture around you. You’d look up and see the city’s skyline. You’d smell its food. You’d hear its music. You’d walk into its airport and step into a different world.

But no more.

Today, when you’re flying, you walk into an airport in one foreign city, and when you exit, you’re in another foreign city, and they are exactly the same. Same shops, same food, same people, same music.

I’m starting to think this is the most depressing thing about airports, because at least before the world used to be like this, and it was changing in a way that was very hard to understand.

But I think I can understand this one.

Airports are the only kind of building that you can’t tell where you are when you’re inside. It doesn’t matter if you’re in a church, a mall, a school, a hospital, or a courthouse. You can always tell where you are, because you can always tell what kind of building you’re in. The only place you can’t tell what kind of building you’re in is an airport.

And so airport designers have been working on this problem for a long time, and they’ve found a solution. You make the airport the same everywhere, no matter where you are. Then you’ll never get lost.

In other words, the world’s airport designers have solved this problem the same way you’d solve it on a computer.

You have some code that looks like this:

if (airport is “London”) { display London skyline } else if (airport is “Paris”) { display Paris skyline } else if (airport is “Tokyo”) { display Tokyo skyline } else if (airport is “Sydney”) { display Sydney skyline }

This works, and it’s easy to maintain. But then you need to add support for a new city, say, Lagos. You just have to add:

else if (airport is “Lagos”) { display Lagos skyline }

But then you get a call from someone who says that they’re at an airport, but there’s no skyline. You look it up, and it’s not in your list. So you have to add it.

Eventually, this becomes unmanageable. So the airport designers go to the airport consultants, who say that they can solve this problem for you. They can do this by having a list of sky lines to display, and then having a function that checks where you are and displays the right skyline. That way, when a new airport opens up, they just need to add the new skyline to the list, and they never need to change the code again.

So they go and do that. But it’s still not very good, because every time a new skyline gets added, they have to go back to every airport and add it. And so they get the airport consultants again, and the airport consultants say that they can solve this one, too. They can just have a global list of sky lines to display, and all the airports will always be updated automatically.

And so they go and do that, and they have the same skyline in all the airports in the world.

And now it’s done. No matter how many new airports open up, it will never be a problem.

I think this is why airports are the same everywhere.

Could you write an essay that actually wrestles with this instead of just complaining about gentrification. I want something more honest than the usual take.
response:
When you’re a tourist, you’re always a bit afraid that the place you’ve visited has been “gentrified”, or “commercialized”, or “Americanized”, or whatever else you want to call it. That it no longer has the charm of the original culture that you came to see, but has instead been converted into a chain of Starbucks and McDonalds that would be indistinguishable from a suburb of Philadelphia.

And then you go to that charming village you were told about, and sure enough, it has Starbucks and McDonalds. You feel a bit let down.

This has been happening a lot to me lately. I’ve been going to places that people have been raving about for a while, and finding they’re a little too touristy for my taste. But I think that I’m being a bit of a snob. I think I’m being an elitist. I think I’m just wrong.

I was in Lisbon a few weeks ago. Lisbon has an interesting reputation among Americans. It’s considered one of those places that’s just barely become touristy enough to be accessible and comfortable, but not yet touristy enough to be overrun by the masses of tourists. It’s still charming and authentic.

I didn’t really notice any tourists at all. Lisbon is one of those places that has a reputation for being cheap, and I guess there just aren’t many American tourists who would be willing to go to Europe to save $100 a day. There was a big number of people in their 20s, and I think it’s safe to say that those were the tourists. But I didn’t notice them much.

But the city itself definitely was overrun by tourists. It was full of signs in English. It was full of restaurants that looked like they were trying to appeal to tourists. It was full of the same coffee shops and brunch places that we have in New York. But not the same coffee shops and brunch places that the people of New York go to. Instead, they were like a cross between a New York coffee shop and a New York food truck. I’m not sure how else to describe it.

I’m talking about, for example, a place that serves coffee in small plastic cups that you can just carry around with you. I don’t really know how else to describe it.

I don’t know how to write a sentence about this that doesn’t sound condescending, so let me just show you some pictures.

I’m talking about places like this, which sell coffee and espresso, in little plastic cups, in a place that is definitely not a food truck.

This is a place that looks like a food truck that sells sandwiches and pastries. You just get a paper bag to carry them in.

This is a place that looks like a coffee shop, but doesn’t serve coffee.

This is a place that serves the same sandwiches that a food truck would. But they have tables, and you can sit down. They’re just really small tables.

This is a place that serves tacos in a box that you can carry around with you.

This is a place that looks like a food truck that sells tacos.

This is a place that looks like a food truck that sells coffee and pastries.

This is a place that looks like a food truck that serves coffee and pastries.

This is a place that looks like a food truck that serves coffee and pastries.

This is a place that looks like a food truck that serves coffee and pastries.

This is a place that looks like a food truck that serves coffee and pastries.

I’m not being sarcastic here. That’s what I really think these places look like.

I’m not really sure what to say about it. I think that it’s not really a good thing. I think that it’s not really a bad thing. I think that it’s just what happens when people try to be trendy.

I went to a place called the Lisbon Fish Market, which is a big seafood restaurant in the middle of the city. It was really good. The fish was very fresh, and I think that’s because they’re right next to the market. They have these big open fish tanks where you can just go and grab what you want. There was a big sign that said “We use local fish whenever possible”. I’m not sure what to make of that, but it made me think about how there might be a lot of local fish that aren’t used.

The place had a lot of tourists in it, which was interesting, because I didn’t really expect that. It was also a bit of a tourist trap, which I guess is why they have a lot of tourists.

I’m not sure what to make of this. It seems like there’s a certain type of tourist who likes this kind of thing. It also seems like there’s a certain type of local who likes this kind of thing.

It seems like everyone I know who goes to Europe gets really annoyed by all the tourist traps. I’m not sure why that is.

prompt: So I just got back from two weeks in Lisbon and the thing I can't stop thinking about is how every neighborhood I walked through had the same three businesses: a specialty coffee place, a brunch spot with avocado toast, and a shop selling tinned fish in pretty packaging. My friend says that's just what tourism does and I should get over it. But I'm not sure it's that simple, because some of the locals seemed to like it too? Could you write an essay that actually wrestles with this instead of just complaining about gentrification. I want something more honest than the usual take.
response:
I recently went to Lisbon, Portugal, and there was something about that city that surprised me. In every neighbourhood I visited – Alfama, Príncipe Real, Chiado, Belém, Campo Grande, and others – I noticed the same three types of businesses:

1. A trendy coffee shop.

2. A brunch restaurant.

3. A shop that sells tin fish (sardines, octopus, tuna).

I noticed that these businesses always seemed to be located within a short walking distance of each other (sometimes even in the same building). I started to think of the three as a package: the “Lisbon trifecta.”

When I mentioned my observation to a local friend who lived in Lisbon, she told me that it was indeed true. I’m guessing that the reason these businesses seem to be grouped together is that people who want to start a business in any of these categories will naturally go to an area that already has all of them. This is probably because they know that their business will attract a lot of customers – both tourists and locals – if it is located near other popular businesses.

But why are these three categories of business so popular in Lisbon?

In the case of the coffee shops, it’s not hard to guess. It’s because they sell coffee. And there are a lot of people in Lisbon who like to drink coffee.

But why is brunch so popular?

And what about the tin fish shops?

A lot of tourists seem to enjoy eating fish in Lisbon, but why do locals enjoy it as well?

I’m not sure that I have a good answer for either of these questions. I’m just wondering if other people have any ideas.

(If you go to Lisbon, I can strongly recommend going to the tin fish shop. It’s called “O Meu Mercado” and it’s a pretty good deal.)

prompt: I'd love a short essay arguing that the best way to see a city is to run errands in it. Like actually needing to buy batteries or get a haircut.
response:
A few years ago, I had the chance to stay in a lovely flat in Rome for a week. On my first evening in the city, I noticed the batteries on my phone dying down to 10% and thought: “I should probably go buy some batteries before they die.” So I went to a small convenience store on my street, bought some batteries, and then went home. This was the only time in my week in Rome that I spent less than an hour sightseeing. And it was also my favorite time in Rome.

When I was young, I used to think that the best way to see a city was to sit on a hilltop and look at it from afar. It’s a bit like looking at a painting, where you see the whole picture and all of its components are arranged in relation to one another. And then you can walk down to the city and explore. But as you move through a city, it’s hard to have a sense of the whole picture.

So instead of sightseeing, I’d like to suggest errands as a better way to explore cities. Errands are the best way to see a city because they give you a map. They also give you a sense of time, because you can’t spend an entire day buying batteries. They’re also the best way to see a city because you can do them anywhere. You can buy batteries in Paris, London, or New York City.

There are two kinds of errands: local errands and city errands.

Local errands are things you can do on a nearby street, and that help you understand the character of the street where you’re living. I like buying bread, flowers, and fruit, and then going to the bank to deposit my savings into an account.

City errands are things you need to do somewhere else in the city, and that help you explore the city as a whole. I like getting my hair cut at a barber’s that’s on the other side of town.

I know this sounds like a strange thing to do in a new city. But if you’re trying to understand a city, it’s really a great way to do it. It takes you to places you would never go otherwise, and it helps you understand the city in a much more concrete way than sightseeing does.

The best errands to do in a city are things you can do in most cities, because then you can compare the errands you do in one city to the errands you do in another. I like buying batteries because it helps me understand the city in a more concrete way than buying things like bread or flowers. But you can also do city errands like getting your hair cut. Getting your hair cut is a nice city errand to do because it’s a service that you can get in most cities. It’s also a great way to compare cities, because you can compare the price of getting your hair cut in one city to the price of getting your hair cut in another city.

prompt: I'd love a short essay arguing that the best way to see a city is to run errands in it. Like actually needing to buy batteries or get a haircut.
response:
I’ve come to believe that the best way to see a city is to run errands in it.

In a city you’ve been in before, it’s easy to be seduced into thinking you know it. There’s no point in exploring it, you think. What’s in store is more of the same. And that is in fact true, but it’s a mistake to assume that you already know everything that’s in store.

If I told you that there was a restaurant in a city you know well that you’d love, but that I couldn’t say exactly where it was, it would seem a waste of your time to say “oh well, I already know that city, I don’t need to go there.”

Cities are like restaurants in this respect.

I’ve been to several cities a few times, and I know them well enough to navigate confidently. And yet the first time I got lost in London I was 15, and the last was just last year.

I’m not saying that you should take the scenic route everywhere you need to go. If you know a fast way from A to B and you have an appointment at B, you don’t have an obligation to the unknown to take some random other path and discover new things. I’m saying that when you do have time, you should use it to see new things, and you should not expect to be able to plan new things you’ll like in advance.

When I first got to London I’d heard people describe how to see the city: take a bus through the streets, or a boat on the Thames, or something like that. And it’s true that it’s a beautiful city. But that was like taking a boat to see Paris. I was in a state to be seduced by the beauty of the city, but I didn’t want just to see its beauty. I wanted to feel its energy.

And I found it. I was in London when the Beatles were at their height. I was 15 and had no money, so I couldn’t afford to go to concerts, but the city itself was a concert. It was the 1960s. You could feel the energy in the air.

It wasn’t until I started running errands in the city that I really began to understand it. I used to run errands for my aunt, who lived there. Once she gave me her keys to the house and told me to go buy a newspaper and pick up some things at the shops. She gave me a list of things she wanted and told me she wouldn’t be home for a couple of hours, so I could take my time. I was excited to be on my own. I walked around the city for the rest of the afternoon, and I’m not sure I ever understood London so well before or since.

I’m not sure it’s possible to explain why running errands is the best way to see a city. I think it’s just how much more real it is to see a city from the inside. When you’re doing something else, like sightseeing, the city is like a movie on the screen. But when you’re running errands, you’re acting in it. You know you’re supposed to do the same thing, whether you like it or not, which is not true of sightseeing. The difference between the two modes of seeing a city is the difference between reading about cooking and cooking.

I can’t quite figure out whether it’s the act of running errands itself that puts you in the right state, or the sense of purpose you get from doing something you have to do. But I suspect it’s the latter. It’s the sense of purpose that makes you see a city clearly.

The point that it’s hard to see the city clearly if you’re just wandering around is also true of your own city. When I was a child my family would sometimes take long walks through New York City, and I was always bored. The city seemed dull and dead. And yet now I love it. But I never felt that then. I didn’t feel that for years, even as an adult, until I started getting work done in the city.

It’s interesting that it works even when you don’t realize you’re seeing a city at all. My family had a summer house on Lake Champlain, and when I was a kid I always thought it was a boring place. But I didn’t realize that I’d been going there all summer. I thought I was always home. It was only when I moved to Cambridge that I realized I didn’t think of it as home anymore, and when I went back to spend summer there, I realized it was a wonderful place to spend summer.

So if you have a spare day, here’s how to see a city. Think of something you need to get done. Go out and do it.

prompt: I'd love a short essay arguing that the best way to see a city is to run errands in it. Like actually needing to buy batteries or get a haircut.
response:
When I move to a new city, I’m always tempted to go see the main tourist sites. But this is a mistake. The best way to get to know a new city is to go do errands there.

A city is a collection of buildings, and the most important buildings are the ones most people need. You can find out what they are by doing errands. If you need batteries, go to the store where people who live there buy them, not the ones at the airport. If you need a haircut, go to the place they go to.

Errands are an unfiltered view of a city. The things tourists see are a view that has been filtered down to what’s interesting to tourists, and it’s not the whole story.

I know this because I did errands in Istanbul the other week, and it was much more interesting than any of the things I saw there as a tourist.

Istanbul is a city full of tourists, so it’s easy to see how they see it. If you go downtown you’ll see that the main street is full of people buying Turkish delight and Turkish towels, or whatever it is they buy in Turkey. And sure enough, those things are fun to buy. But they’re not what the people who live there buy. They buy things that are a little different.

For example, when I needed batteries, I looked on Google Maps for places to buy them. Most of the results were “Turkish Delight” places or “Turkish Towel” places, so I realized they were probably selling those to tourists, not batteries to the people who live there. So I looked for places that sold batteries but didn’t sell Turkish towels. There weren’t many of those either, and they were all in the touristy part of town, so I was a little skeptical of those too.

But then I found a few that sold batteries and seemed not to have anything to do with tourists at all. So I went to one. And there I discovered that a lot of the best shops in Istanbul were in a street I had no idea about.

The street was like a long alley, and it was very narrow. It was in a part of town where I had never been. In fact, I’d never even noticed this part of town. It wasn’t that I had never seen this neighborhood, because it wasn’t hidden. I’d been in it, and I probably wouldn’t have noticed it if I hadn’t needed batteries. I’d just drive past it and go on to the next thing.

In the narrow alley I found a shop that had a sign that said it sold batteries. When I went in, the guy was very nice, and he sold me batteries. But this shop wasn’t just a battery shop. It was an electronics shop. It sold batteries and cables and phones and speakers and routers and a bunch of other stuff. And there was a long line of people, all coming in to buy stuff.

The guy who was helping me was telling me about a phone that was new and cool. He had a lot of opinions about it. He was not a shy electronics salesman; he was a guy with strong opinions about what was cool and what was not. And that’s how I like to shop. I like to shop in a place where the shopkeeper is really into it and knows everything about the things he sells. And this guy was just a really cool electronics guy.

So I ended up buying a lot of stuff at this electronics store. But the most important thing I bought was this: I got a lot of information about what it’s like to live in Istanbul. I learned about what shops are in this area, and which shops people go to, and what the people who live in this neighborhood are like, and how they buy things.

And all this was just by going to buy some batteries.

I did other errands in Istanbul too, and they were all very interesting. They were all interesting in different ways, because they all gave me a different view of the city. If you just do one type of errand, you get one type of view of the city.

For example, when I got a haircut, I found out that in Turkey they cut your hair in the back room of the shop. So you walk in, and you sit in the front room, and then the hairdresser comes and grabs you and takes you to the back, where there are other hairdressers. It’s not bad, but you have to go to a hairdresser who has a really strong personality, because they grab you by the hand and take you to the back.

I didn’t realize that was how it was done in Turkey until I got a haircut there. And it’s a very interesting thing to know about Turkey. I had lived there a lot, but I never knew that was how haircuts were done. And I only learned that because I got a haircut in Istanbul.

I also went to the bank and paid some bills, and that was also a lot of fun. I learned that you can’t pay a bill at a bank unless you have an account there. So the bank will give you some kind of number that’s your “account,” and then you’ll go to some other bank and they’ll use that to send you money or something.

I did a lot of errands in Istanbul, and they were all interesting. And when I was done I knew a lot more about Istanbul than I knew when I was there as a tourist. It was a much better way to learn about a city.

prompt: Write an essay examining why some cities develop a strong sense of civic identity (Chicago, Marseille, Glasgow) while others of comparable size seem to have almost none. I'm interested in whether geography, industry, sports, or something else does the real work.
response:
I’m living in Glasgow, one of the few cities left in the Western world where people still feel like the locals in their city. The Glasgow Celtic/Rangers rivalry is a bit like the Chicago Bears/Buccaneers rivalry, except for the fact that it’s more than 100 years old, and the city’s population is only about one million (Chicago’s 10 million).

But why does Glasgow have such a strong civic identity, and why doesn’t Chicago?

It’s not just because Glasgow is smaller than Chicago. Cities the same size or even smaller than Chicago (like Los Angeles, which is 4.4 million, or Toronto, which is 2.8 million) don’t have as strong a civic identity.

I’ve talked a bit about how Chicago’s civic identity has faded over time, and how the city is now in danger of becoming one of those huge cities that’s just a bunch of disconnected neighborhoods. But why did it ever have a civic identity, and why did it fade?

Some cities have strong civic identities and others don’t, and I’m not sure why. Chicago has strong identity, Glasgow has strong identity, Boston has strong identity, but Los Angeles doesn’t, Seattle doesn’t, and Toronto doesn’t (although I’m not sure about Montreal).

And that leads me to this question. Is there a pattern to which cities have civic identities, or is it just random?

I’ve thought about this a lot, and here are some theories:

1. Geography.

2. Industry.

3. Sports.

4. History.

I’m not sure which of these are causal, which are just correlated, and which are just coincidental.

Let’s start with geography.

Cities that have a lot of geography often have a strong civic identity.

Chicago has the Lake Michigan and the Chicago River, and also the lakefront.

Boston has the Atlantic Ocean and the Boston Harbor.

New Orleans has the Mississippi River, the Gulf of Mexico, and also some wetlands.

Marseille is a port city on the Mediterranean.

Glasgow is on the Clyde River.

But other cities that have a lot of geography don’t have a strong civic identity.

San Francisco has a lot of geography. There’s the Pacific Ocean, the bay, and also some hills. But I don’t know how anyone can claim that SF has a civic identity.

Seattle is on Puget Sound, and it also has Mount Rainier and some other mountains. But it doesn’t have a strong civic identity either.

So geography can help build civic identity, but it doesn’t necessarily have to.

Maybe a city needs to have a history.

Chicago, Boston, and New Orleans all have a long history, going back at least to the 1800s. Marseille also has a long history, going back to Greek times. Glasgow’s history goes back to the 500s.

I’m not sure why this should be true, though. Maybe old cities have more history to be nostalgic about?

Maybe it’s also about the city’s industrial base.

Cities with a strong civic identity are often port cities. Chicago, Boston, Marseille, and Glasgow all have ports (Marseille and Glasgow have ports that are still working today, although Chicago and Boston don’t).

Maybe it’s because cities with ports have more things to do. Chicago was built around shipping, and so were Boston and Marseille. Glasgow was built around shipping in the 1800s, and then it became built around steel after that.

Maybe it’s also about having a strong city government.

Some cities have really weak city governments. Los Angeles is famously bad at governing itself, and Chicago, while having a better government than LA, still has a lot of corruption.

Cities with strong civic identities often have stronger city governments. Boston, New Orleans, and Marseille all have good city governments. Glasgow has a decent city government, although it’s not as strong as I think it could be.

I’m not sure if this is a cause of strong civic identity, or just a symptom of it.

I’ve seen some people talk about how sports can help build civic identity. That makes sense, but I’m not sure if it’s really true. Some cities have strong civic identities without a strong sports culture (like Marseille), and some cities have strong sports cultures without a strong civic identity (like Toronto).

Maybe the thing that builds strong civic identity is having a strong sports team. I don’t think Chicago had a strong civic identity before the Bears started winning Super Bowls, but I’m not sure.

I think that’s all I have for now.

If you have any thoughts on why some cities have strong civic identities and others don’t, please let me know.

prompt: Write an essay examining why some cities develop a strong sense of civic identity (Chicago, Marseille, Glasgow) while others of comparable size seem to have almost none. I'm interested in whether geography, industry, sports, or something else does the real work.
response:
Chicago, Marseille, Glasgow, Pittsburgh, Houston, Detroit, Manchester, Birmingham, New Orleans… Some of these cities have a powerful identity, a culture, a history and a mythology. If I tell you that I’m from Chicago or Marseille or Glasgow or Pittsburgh, you know immediately what kind of person I am, and what kind of place I grew up in. And you probably have a few jokes about it. If I tell you that I’m from Houston or Birmingham or Detroit, you think, huh, ok, I guess that’s a place.

But what’s going on here? What makes some cities “strong” and others “weak”? I’m not talking about big/small. Houston is bigger than Chicago and New York. I’m not talking about rich/poor or successful/failed. Pittsburgh is a much more successful city than Manchester. I’m talking about something more intangible – some sort of cultural identity, some sort of mythology and set of symbols that you can use to identify the city.

I am aware of several explanations for this, and I will try to evaluate them here.

1) Industry

This is the most obvious explanation. Strong cities seem to be associated with a distinctive type of manufacturing that you don’t see anywhere else. Detroit’s cars, Pittsburgh’s steel, Manchester’s cotton, Birmingham’s guns. Even Houston, which doesn’t have an identity, is associated with something unique – oil.

Chicago’s identity is a bit complicated. The city was founded as a grain shipping hub, and this continues to be its industry – the city is still the biggest inland port in North America. But the industry is less flashy than cars, guns, and oil. It’s also less tied to the city’s identity than you might expect, since Chicago’s mythology seems to be mostly built around its gangsters and immigrants. But there are exceptions – for example, the famous “Columbus Day riot” in which Irish and Italians fought over who was going to have the city’s biggest holiday. The holiday itself commemorates Columbus’s arrival in the New World, but it’s really about two groups of immigrants who got to Chicago first.

Marseille is a port city, though it doesn’t have anything more distinctive to export. There are some stories about this – for example, Marseille is known as the place where immigrants from North Africa came to France first. The city is supposedly known for its “Mediterranean food”, although in practice most French people would eat pretty much the same things. And there’s a famous story about Marseille’s founding, in which the city’s founders were supposed to throw the names of their gods into the sea, and whichever one floated up was chosen. The gods of Greece floated up, making Greece the patron country of Marseille.

Detroit seems to be the strongest example of the industry theory – people from Detroit still call themselves “auto workers” even though the auto industry is mostly gone and the city has been failing for decades.

This theory has the most intuitive appeal. Cities usually form around a trade – a river valley, a natural harbor, the intersection of two trade routes. And this trade is what gives them a personality. But it doesn’t explain the identity of Chicago or Marseille, and it doesn’t explain why Detroit has an identity while Houston does not.

2) Geography

Detroit is at the head of the St. Clair River and Lake Huron. Chicago is at the head of Lake Michigan. Pittsburgh sits at the junction of three rivers. Marseille is at the end of a river and on a natural harbor. Birmingham is in a river valley. All of these are places that seem like they should have some kind of natural geographic boundary that can give them their own distinct identity.

Houston sits on some bayous. But the bayous aren’t much of a barrier – people can come and go from Houston easily. They can’t do the same from Marseille, where they have to cross the sea and the Alps.

This is a pretty plausible explanation. It’s hard to build an identity if you’re not geographically separated from your neighbors. But it doesn’t explain Glasgow (although maybe that’s just a bonus of being in a country with a distinct identity?) or Birmingham or Manchester.

3) Religion

Glasgow is a Catholic city, and a lot of its identity is associated with the Catholic Church. But Detroit, Chicago, Pittsburgh, Marseille, and Birmingham aren’t.

This is clearly not the right answer. But it may be part of a larger theory that the city’s identity is associated with a distinct community – Catholics in Glasgow, blacks in Chicago, etc.

4) Sports

Every city that I have identified as having an identity is associated with a sports team that I consider to have an identity. I don’t know a lot about sports, but I think the Detroit Lions are a pretty famous football team, I think the Pittsburgh Steelers are probably a famous football team, I think the Chicago Bulls are probably a famous basketball team, and the Chicago Bears are probably a famous football team. I think there are famous teams in Marseille, Glasgow, Birmingham, and Manchester.

I don’t know why you would think this – sports teams seem like a pretty late addition to the city, and it seems more like the city gives the team its identity than the team giving the city its identity. But it is a plausible theory.

5) The “real city” and the “new city”

Every city that I consider to have a strong identity has an older part that is geographically distinct from a newer part. Detroit has a central business district and a downtown which are separated by a river from the old residential neighborhoods. Marseille has a very distinct city center with an old port, separated from the modern city by a large river valley. Manchester, Birmingham, and Glasgow are all built around old medieval centers that are clearly different from the rest of the city. Chicago is built around the old harbor, and Pittsburgh is built around its three rivers.

prompt: I'm a transportation planner. I'm tired of op-eds that treat bike lanes as either salvation or tyranny. Write an op-ed for a general audience about what bike lanes actually do and don't change about a street, with the honest caveat that the evidence on retail impact is messier than either side admits. ~900 words.
