The most important part of transportation planning isn’t planning the system, it’s talking about what it means.

I’m a transportation planner. I spend a lot of time talking to people about bikes. Some people are angry, and think bike lanes are going to turn the whole world into a dangerous bike-pedestrian dystopia where everyone has to ride bikes and nobody can drive. Other people are happy, and think bike lanes are going to turn the whole world into a utopia with no more cars. Neither view is particularly realistic.

I wish I could tell you that bike lanes will make the world a better place. Or that they won’t. But they’ll do what bike lanes have always done, which is make some people happy and some people angry.

Here’s how bike lanes work. A road is 40 feet wide. Right now it has 4 lanes for cars – two in each direction. Let’s say you want to add a bike lane on each side of the road. So that’s two bike lanes to add, and the 40 feet is going to have to cover that too.

One way to do this is to make the lanes smaller. Instead of 8 feet, you’ll have to fit 8 lanes in 40 feet, which means 5 feet for each lane. A typical car is 7 feet wide, so 5 feet is a bit tight. You might get more traffic accidents. But it might also be worth it to get more people riding bikes.

Another way to do this is to add a third lane of cars in each direction. That makes 6 lanes of cars and 2 bike lanes, which gives 5 feet to each. It also makes it harder to cross the road – there’s an extra lane of cars to get through. But it also makes the road more convenient, which might make it more popular, which might increase car traffic, which might make it worse. But it might also mean more people driving means more people stopping their cars and going into shops instead of just whizzing through.

Or you could add another lane of cars in one direction and make the lanes a little smaller. You’d get 7 lanes of cars and 2 bike lanes, with about 5.7 feet for each lane. This might make the road more convenient for people going in one direction, which might increase traffic, which might increase traffic accidents. But it might also mean more people driving means more people stopping their cars and going into shops instead of just whizzing through.

There are all these possible options, and none of them are obviously better than all the others. So what people think is best is a lot like what people think is politically expedient – people are going to make up stories about what’s good for them, and what’s good for the city.

In practice, adding a bike lane often makes people who own or manage businesses happy. But it’s not a sure thing. There’s a famous study that looked at bike lanes in Toronto and concluded that they didn’t affect retail sales at all. But there’s a more recent study that looked at bike lanes in Portland and found that bike lanes increased retail sales. There’s a study that looked at bike lanes in Chicago and found they increased retail sales in the short term but not the long term. And there’s a meta-study of studies on bike lanes in cities across the United States that found an increase in retail sales of 6% on average.

The studies on how bike lanes affect the overall environment are about as consistent – that is, not at all.

But there are a couple things we can say with some confidence. First, people who like bikes are happy about bike lanes. That’s pretty much tautological. Second, people who hate bikes are angry about bike lanes. Again, tautological.

So the question is, which is more important?

I don’t think it’s a question we can answer. I’m sure some people will be happy and others will be angry, but it’s hard to know in advance who those people will be. It’s hard to know who the winners and losers will be.

There’s no obvious right answer.

prompt: Essay: the case for visiting places in their off season.

You’ll get the most from traveling if you go when there are few tourists around. That means going in the off season.

The off season in a place is when it’s not a good time to visit. That could mean it’s raining, or cold, or hot, or there are lots of bugs, or you can’t swim in the ocean because it’s full of jellyfish, or something else.

The off season can be a long time. In the Caribbean, for example, most people think of it as a place to go in the winter. But actually the Caribbean has 4 different seasons. From December to April it’s the high season and it’s not a good time to go. The islands are so popular at this time that the hotels charge as much as you can pay. If you don’t have a boat, you also have to fly to get to the islands, which makes it even more expensive.

From April to May is shoulder season. The prices are lower, but the islands are still very busy.

From May to November is hurricane season, and you probably won’t find too many people to travel then.

The best time to visit the Caribbean is November. At this time the weather is good, the price of hotels are low, and the islands are empty.

The off season varies from place to place. I don’t want to go to New England in winter, but I do want to go to Hawaii then. I don’t want to go to Florida in summer, but I don’t mind going to Alaska.

The off season for each place can vary a lot. For example, most of Canada’s national parks are open only from late May to late September. That is 4 months. In winter you can see snow-capped mountains, but you can’t drive to them.

If you really want to see a lot of different things, then you can’t be too fussy about the off season. That’s the reason to go to places when no one else wants to. You can see things that you couldn’t see if you went when the weather was nice.

For example, I went to the Canadian Rockies in November. It had been snowing for several days. I had a snowshoe and a set of crampons, and I walked around in the snow. I was the only person on the mountain. I could see where the sheep had been and where the elk and mountain goats had been. I could see where they had eaten the grass and bushes, and where they had left their footprints in the snow. I was able to see things that you could never see in summer.

The weather was so bad that there were no other people at the park. The mountains were all covered in snow. It was a magical place. I had no idea that it was such a beautiful place. I had been to the Canadian Rockies before in summer, and I didn’t know that it was so beautiful in winter.

In general, you will get more out of visiting a place if you go in its off season.

There are different kinds of loneliness. The one that’s most likely to kill you is the loneliness of being surrounded by strangers all the time. That one’s rare in cities. It’s more common in small towns, where everyone’s a stranger until someone tells you who they are. And that’s the kind of loneliness people usually mean when they say small towns are depressing.

The problem is just that they’re strangers. But there are so many of them that if you know how to find them, you can turn a lot of them into friends.

But that’s the kind of loneliness that’s not usually fatal, and that many people enjoy.

There are a few reasons cities are lonelier.

One is that in small towns, everyone knows you, so there are more people you see who know you. It’s a lot like living in a small town if you grow up in a place where everyone goes to the same school. When you were young you had more friends than you needed, and as you got older you were always bumping into people you knew.

Another reason cities are lonelier is that everyone in them is so busy. Another reason is that it’s easier to find people in cities who have your interests. There are a million people in some big cities, so even if something you care about is pretty obscure, it’s probably true of a few thousand of them. In a small town it’s unlikely any of the 1000 people who live there will be like you, unless you’re very typical.

I know someone who used to live in a town of a few hundred people in rural England. He’s very religious, and it didn’t bother him to live in a town of that size, because there was a church there with 100 members. But even in a place where I went frequently, it was rare to see anyone I knew. There are few places where you’re likely to see anyone you know. That leads to the third reason cities are less lonely than small towns, which is that you’re more likely to see someone you know in a small town. And so you’re more likely to be reminded of your friends.

I have a lot of friends in New York, but I can’t remember the last time I met one of them by chance. They’re all in the city, but it’s like they’re invisible. The reason is that the number of people you see on any particular day is so small compared to the number who are in the city. In a small town you see a large fraction of the population every day.

So if you live in a small town you’re probably less lonely in the sense that there are more people you see who know you. But you’re much more likely to be lonely in the sense of not having enough people you can relate to.

That’s the reason a lot of people enjoy the kind of loneliness that comes with living in a big city. They get the good kind (the kind introverts enjoy) and not the bad kind (the kind that kills you). They enjoy being surrounded by strangers. And in a big city they can find enough other people who share their interests to make up for not having a bunch of people they see every day.

So if you want to move to a big city for work, you should probably do it, if you can. But when you get there, you should make sure you spend some time finding people you can relate to.

prompt: Every travel influencer says 'travel like a local.' I think that's mostly a fantasy and kind of condescending to actual locals. Write an essay that takes this seriously: is it possible, is it even desirable, and what's the more honest alternative?

I’m on my way to the airport in a taxi. My driver tells me about his daughter. She’s a big fan of a famous musician whose name I know. “We’re going to her concert this month,” he tells me. “I will be taking my daughter.”

This is the closest I’ve ever come to traveling like a local.

The phrase “travel like a local” seems to be a staple of travel writing. It’s so common you can even buy travel books with this exact title. The meaning, for those who don’t know, is that when you go to a new city, don’t go to the big touristy places, don’t take the tour, and don’t buy the postcards. Instead, get out and explore on your own. Find places that only the locals know about. Live like a local.

I think this is a bit of a fantasy.

The problem is that a lot of local knowledge is very hard for an outsider to get. It’s not just that it’s hard to find a good restaurant in the local area. It’s that even if you find the right restaurant, you won’t know what to order. You won’t understand the jokes in the local TV show. And so on. The reason the locals know where to go and what to order is that they’ve spent their whole life there.

And yet there are people who actually travel like a local. It’s easy to find examples. I know a woman who moved to India, and who now cooks and talks about food like an Indian. Another woman I know has lived in Germany for years, and can talk about German food and culture better than most Germans. And so on. It’s a skill. If you have the skill, it’s easy to learn about the local culture. But the people who do it well have the right skills and interests.

I think one reason people like to talk about traveling like a local is that it’s a nice story. It’s a great story to tell. It makes it sound like you’re being open-minded and humble. “I’m not just a tourist,” you say. “I’m getting to know the locals, and they’re letting me.” That makes a great story.

But it’s also a bit condescending to the locals. It makes the locals sound like extras. You, the tourist, are getting to know “the locals”. The locals, for their part, have no idea you even exist.

I’ve lived in a lot of cities, including some pretty big ones, but I’ve never been introduced to anyone else’s friend or co-worker. That would be traveling like a local, but I don’t know why that would happen. I’ve never seen it. The closest I’ve come is my taxi driver, who told me about his daughter. It was a little like it, but not quite.

There’s another reason to like the idea of traveling like a local. It makes it sound like you’re getting a better experience. Tourists don’t get the best experience. Tourists just see the sights. The real experience is in the local culture, which is only available to the locals.

That’s not true. The best tourist experience is to go to the big tourist places.

If you like music, then going to the big concerts is a great experience. If you like museums, then going to the big museums is a great experience. If you like food, then going to the big restaurants is a great experience. If you like architecture, then going to the big buildings is a great experience. If you like art, then going to the big galleries is a great experience.

It’s not hard to see why. The big tourist places are where the best stuff is. That’s why they’re the big tourist places. The people who run the big tourist places are the people who care the most about it, and they’re the people who have the best things.

For example, if you like music, you might think you’ll get a better experience going to a small club where the locals go. That’s true. Locals don’t have a choice. They have to go to the places near them. But you have the advantage of not being a local. You can go to the places where the best stuff is. So, if you like music, go to the big music venues.

The same is true for museums, restaurants, galleries, and so on. If you want to have a great experience, go to the big tourist places.

The only advantage of traveling like a local is that it’s interesting. It’s an interesting story. It’s an interesting life.

If you want to have an interesting life, it might be worth it.

prompt: I teach 8th grade geography and my students genuinely do not believe that where you're born shapes most of your life. Write a short essay (maybe 700 words) I could read aloud to them that makes the case without being preachy or making them feel guilty.
response:
A couple of years ago I was sitting with a woman who was from Lagos, Nigeria. The two of us were discussing how the place where you live affects everything about you, from the food you eat to the music you listen to to the things you worry about.

She told me a story about the time she moved back to her home village in Nigeria for a few days. She was surprised how much she had forgotten in just five months away. She walked into the village and her cousin said, “You haven’t visited this place before, have you?” and she said, “Actually, I grew up here.”

The world we live in has gotten bigger, and it seems like we’ve forgotten how much of an influence a place has on a person. I don’t mean the obvious things, like what language you speak, or what you wear. I mean the things that shape how you look at the world.

When you look at someone from another culture, you may think that you’d be the same person if you’d just been born there. That’s not true. We are shaped by the world around us, and it’s much easier for us to change that world than it is for us to change ourselves.

There are some people that are just different than the rest of us, that have a rare gift and they don’t need to worry about any of this. For most of us though, where we live, and the people around us, play a huge role in how we think and live.

I know a guy named Sam, who grew up in California. When he was in his twenties, he moved to New York City. He was working at the same job and living in the same kind of apartment, but when he got there, he immediately started going to the gym every day.

Why did this happen? In New York City, everyone goes to the gym. So he started going too. Sam is a very different person in California than he is in New York City.

The only reason he is different in those two places is because there are a lot of people in New York City who go to the gym every day, and there aren’t many people in California who do. When Sam moved to New York City, he just picked up a new habit, because that was what everyone else around him was doing.

This is true of everything. When you live in a big city, it’s normal to be able to ride bikes all over the city, because you’ve had bike lanes and bike paths your whole life. When you live in a small town, it’s normal to walk to school, because that’s what everyone else does.

People tend to think about where they live like it’s just the place where they sleep. But where you live shapes everything about you, from the way you think about your body, to the way you think about what’s possible.

I’m sure that in a hundred years, people are going to be surprised that we couldn’t even see that this is true.

When people think about moving, they worry about the boring stuff. How far is it? How much rent? What’s the weather like? Those are the easy decisions, but there’s another decision that is much harder to make, and that’s where you’re going to live your life.

If you’re really going to think about it, that’s the hardest decision you’ll ever have to make. Where you live shapes every day of your life. It’s the most powerful influence on who you will be.

prompt: I teach 8th grade geography and my students genuinely do not believe that where you're born shapes most of your life. Write a short essay (maybe 700 words) I could read aloud to them that makes the case without being preachy or making them feel guilty.
response:
This year at school I’m teaching a course on “the geography of life,” which is a fun way to talk about the things we’ve known all along about how geography affects us, but in a new way. The course starts with a quote from Carl Sagan’s Pale Blue Dot. He describes the Voyager 1 probe taking the most distant ever picture of Earth:

We are a speck. On that dot, everyone you ever loved or knew, lived and died. All the triumphs and failures of our species, every religion, ideology, economic system ever conceived, every hunter-gatherer, every hero and coward, every maker and destroyer of civilization, every king and peasant, every young couple in the throes of love, every mother and father, hopeful child, inventor and explorer, every teacher of morals, every corrupt politician, every supermodel, every Supreme Leader, every saint and sinner in the history of our species lived there – a grain of dust suspended in a sunbeam.

That’s beautiful, and a lot of people will tell you that it means we are one species, we are all equal, we are all the same, and no matter where you’re from we all belong together.

But that’s wrong, and in the rest of this article I’m going to explain why.

The problem is that while we are all one species, we live in very different circumstances. Imagine two people: one lives in an apartment on a skyscraper in New York City, the other lives on a farm in Montana. Both are the same species, both are human beings. But in terms of daily life, their circumstances are so different they might as well be different animals. One person lives in a building with no windows, the other in the open sky. One person eats at a restaurant the other eats what they raise or buy. One person lives surrounded by hundreds of other people, the other lives surrounded by no other people. One person sees their own kind of people almost all the time, the other sees hundreds of different kinds of people, and their own kind only occasionally. One person lives in a world of concrete and glass and steel, the other in a world of dirt and trees and animals.

They’re both human, sure. But they’re not living the same life. They live in different worlds.

This isn’t even an exaggeration. This is the difference between two cities in the same country. The difference between two countries will be even more dramatic.

If you were to go to the most remote corner of the world, and meet the most different people there, they would still be human beings. You would still be able to communicate with them and understand them. But they would live in such a different world than you, with such different circumstances, that they would be almost completely unrecognizable. They would be as different as the skyscraper dweller in New York and the farmer in Montana, multiplied by ten.

The world of these people, their culture, is not something they choose. They didn’t choose the city they live in, or their country. They live where their parents lived, their grandparents lived, and their great-grandparents, and all the way back until their people first got there. You can’t choose your world. You’re stuck in the world you were born into.

If you are born in the world of the skyscraper dweller in New York, you are going to live a completely different life than the farmer in Montana. If you are born in a world in another country, in a different part of the world, you will live an even more different life. If you are born in the most remote part of the world, your life will be the most different of all.

And that’s where the geography of life comes in. Where you are on the globe doesn’t just determine how different your life is from someone else’s – it determines how rich or poor, healthy or sick, happy or unhappy, you are. Where you’re born determines your world. It determines your life.

I know this doesn’t sound like a happy thought. But it’s an important one, and it’s the first thing we have to understand in order to make the world a better place.

prompt: Why index funds are boring and why that's the point. Short essay.
response:
I’ve been working with an asset management company, and one of the first things I learned from them is that index funds are the most boring kind of investment.

The reason index funds are boring is that, by design, they’re not supposed to be exciting.

Index funds are the opposite of hedge funds. Hedge funds have managers who try to make exciting decisions that will beat the market. Index funds have managers whose job is to do nothing but keep their portfolios identical to the market.

There are only two kinds of fund: index funds and all the others. All the others are just attempts to beat the index funds.

So it’s actually an achievement to have an index fund. If you can find a company that runs one, it means they know what they’re doing. They know that they can’t beat the market, so they don’t try to. They just give you the market.

There are 2 types of index funds:

- Active, which are index funds managed by humans who make occasional small adjustments to their portfolios (like 1-2% a year),

- Passive, which are fully automated index funds.

I don’t like active index funds, though I’ve never invested in one. They’re a weird hybrid between a real index fund and a mutual fund, with a lot of the downsides and none of the benefits.

Passive index funds are the best thing. They are literally just an ETF (or something similar) with no human in the loop.

ETFs are really cool, because they’re just baskets of stocks (or other things). You can buy 5% of the S&P 500 in one second, and that’s exactly how the stock market behaves, which is great.

A passive index fund doesn’t make any decisions, it just holds assets.

So the real reason index funds are boring is that they make no decisions. They have no opinions. They don’t have a worldview. They just hold the market, whatever that is.

That’s great, because it’s really hard to beat the market.

This is the real reason to have a passive index fund. It’s a good default, because it’s hard to do better.

This is why I’m in favor of them. I don’t like active index funds because they’re not passive. I don’t like any other kind of fund at all, because they’re not index funds.

prompt: Why index funds are boring and why that's the point. Short essay.
response:
I’ve been writing about index funds for years, and it seems to me that a lot of people still don’t get it. They think investing in index funds is an alternative to investing in stocks. But it’s not. Index funds are simply a way to invest in stocks.

If you were to invest in stocks the way most people do – picking individual stocks or buying stock picks from a broker or financial advisor – then you would be investing in stocks.

The difference is, you’d likely be doing so at a significant disadvantage. Studies show that most individual investors and financial advisors underperform the stock market. The Vanguard study I cited last week found that most individual investors lost money after fees while the stock market gained 10%.

And that’s the whole point of index funds. An index fund lets you capture the market return with low fees and without the need to pick stocks. It’s not about not investing in stocks. It’s about investing in stocks in a way that gives you a better chance of earning the market return.

In fact, a lot of people still don’t understand the basics of index funds and mistakenly think they’re something other than stocks. The term “passive investing” can be confusing, and the word “passive” suggests an investment that will not do anything. So I’m going to try to explain how index funds work in a way that people will understand.

First of all, they’re not passive. Index funds are actively run by fund managers – that’s why you pay a management fee.

What an index fund is is a fund that aims to reproduce the performance of an index. The index is just a collection of stocks. There are all sorts of indices: the S&P 500, the Russell 2000, the Dow Jones Industrial Average, the NASDAQ, and so on. Indices are used as benchmarks. The S&P 500, for example, is the benchmark used for large-cap U.S. stocks.

When I talk about index funds, I mean index funds that track an index. These are also called “passive” index funds. (The other type, which are “actively managed,” don’t need to track an index.)

Let’s say you wanted to buy into the S&P 500 – the index that covers the largest 500 U.S. companies.

If you did it the normal way, you would have to pick 500 stocks – the companies in the S&P 500 – and then invest an amount in each company so that you invested the same amount in each stock that the stock represents in the index. For example, ExxonMobil is a pretty big part of the S&P 500, so you’d have to invest about 4% of the total into ExxonMobil.

That’s exactly what an index fund does for you. It invests an equal amount into each company according to that company’s weight in the index.

So if you buy shares of an index fund that tracks the S&P 500, you’re investing in the S&P 500. You’re investing in the same 500 companies, in the same proportions, as if you had to pick the 500 companies yourself and figure out how much of your money to invest in each one.

And that’s it.

There’s nothing passive about it at all. A fund manager is constantly buying and selling stocks to make sure the fund’s investments match the index.

It’s not like you’re investing in a fund that just sits there and does nothing. It’s a fully active investment in stocks that just happens to be an investment in stocks designed to match the return of an index.

So when you buy shares of an S&P 500 index fund, your investment is doing exactly what an investment in the S&P 500 does.

And if the stock market goes up 10%, you earn about 10% minus fees (in reality, you earn a few hundredths of a percent less because the fund doesn’t track the index perfectly).

So if the stock market rises 10% over a year, you’ll also rise about 10% over that year. You’ll earn the same return as the market.

If the market falls 50%, you’ll fall 50% (minus a small fee).

And that’s the point.

prompt: I'm 41 and I have $11,000 saved for retirement. I see these articles saying I should have 3x my salary by now (I make $68k) and I feel like a failure. I don't want a financial plan, I want an essay about the whole 'you should have X by age Y' genre of advice and whether it helps or hurts people like me. Be honest, don't just tell me it's fine.
response:
When I was young and single, my mother’s rule was that I should have a certain percentage of my income saved by a certain age. 10% by twenty, 25% by thirty, 75% by forty, 100% by fifty.

This was a good idea, and I followed it pretty well. When I was twenty-one, I worked as a research assistant on a medical study for a year. I had no college student debt, and was living with my parents. When I got my first paycheck of about $1000, I was able to save $100 in one week. I was thrilled.

But when I was thirty and working as a medical researcher at a university for around $40,000 a year, saving 25% a year was a bit tougher. I had a $35,000-a-year mortgage and a car payment, and lived in a city where I paid $1,500 for an apartment (which is still cheap by current standards, but was quite high for a medical researcher). I tried to be thrifty, and got a second job when I could, but I wasn’t really able to save 25% of my income.

So in my thirties I started to feel bad about not being able to follow my mother’s rules, even though I was doing my best. Then when I was thirty-three, I was offered a job as a teacher at the University of Pennsylvania, where they said they could only pay me $30,000 a year. I thought, *this is a really great opportunity, but there’s no way I can afford it*. I said no.

At the time I was in a pretty good position as a researcher – I had tenure at my university and a good job. But I thought of it this way: I was thirty-three and hadn’t saved 25% of my income. It seemed like I was falling further and further behind, and that if I took this job I would never be able to catch up.

The University of Pennsylvania job would have been better for me, financially and otherwise, than the job I took instead. But my mother’s rules didn’t make that clear.

The thing is, the rules were written for a specific time period – the late 1970s and 1980s, when my mother was young. And my mother is not like most people. She started working when she was sixteen, had a college degree in journalism by twenty, and was working as a reporter by twenty-three. At twenty-six, she started working at the university, in a position that was very well-paid. She was able to save 10% of her income as a junior reporter, and 25% as a university administrator.

And she didn’t take into account that in the intervening years, college education had become more expensive, that there would be a housing bubble and a recession, that wages for people like me would stagnate while the cost of living would rise, that there would be a housing crisis that forced people to buy houses at the top of the bubble and then lose those houses after the bubble burst.

I was not as careful as my mother was, and I made some bad decisions, including buying a house during the housing bubble. But I think if I had taken the University of Pennsylvania job, I would have been in a much better place than I am now.

So I don’t want to make my mother’s rules a big deal, or say that everyone should save a certain amount of their income by a certain age. I think I did well by them at the time, and I think they were good advice for her. But things have changed. I think it’s good to save as much as you can. I think it’s good to think about what you’re going to do when you’re older, and how you’re going to pay for your healthcare. I think it’s good to have a plan. But I don’t think you should follow a formula, or feel bad if you don’t.

prompt: Write an essay examining why people who win the lottery so often end up no better off, and what that says about wealth as a skill versus wealth as a quantity.
response:
Suppose that I win a $10 million lottery jackpot, but it’s payable in $100,000 a year over a hundred years. Suppose that I spend the first $100,000 on nice things, which leaves me with $0. And then the next year, the next $100,000 shows up, and I spend it on more nice things, and I have $0. And then the year after that, the next $100,000 shows up, and I spend it, and I have $0. I repeat this cycle for a hundred years, enjoying a constant stream of money.

Suppose that my friend John, on the other hand, takes that same $10 million, deposits it all into a bank account with an interest rate of 4% per year, and then takes out $100,000 a year to spend. At the end of the first year, he spends $100,000 and has $10,400,000. At the end of the second year, he spends another $100,000, has $10,816,000. At the end of the third year, he has $11,248,640. He continues like this until the hundredth year, when he has $37,299,317. At that point he can withdraw his entire balance, spend it all on nice things, and still have another $28 million remaining, which he can leave to his children, or use for his own retirement, or donate to charity, or do whatever he wants.

Both my hypothetical self and my friend John can enjoy $100,000 a year in luxury for a hundred years, but one of us has the luxury of *having* more money and one doesn’t. This is a really neat way of showing the difference between money as an ongoing stream of goods and services, and money as a stockpile of wealth. And when I imagine it like this, I realize it’s also a really neat way of understanding why people who win the lottery often end up no better off than people who lose it.

The reason is this: people who win the lottery get $10 million in cash, but they don’t get the financial skills to deal with it. They can live off their $10 million for the rest of their lives, but they can’t live off the $10 million *and still have some of it left*. And if that happens to them, then even though their lives will be better than the lives of people who don’t win the lottery, they’ll be much worse off than they could have been if they had the skills to live off their $10 million while still having more of it left.

I think a lot of the time, people think of wealth as something that can be measured in dollars and cents. If I make $100,000 a year and someone else makes $1,000,000 a year, they think the other person is ten times richer than me, and therefore ten times more well-off. But wealth isn’t something you can measure in dollars and cents. Wealth is something you do with money, and it’s a skill that has to be learned. If you have $10,000,000 in your bank account, and you’re bad at wealth, then you can just as easily end up with nothing.

There’s no single “money skill” that controls everything, but there are lots of different skills and habits that people with more money have in common.

Money is a kind of energy, and like all energy, it’s always changing forms. Some forms are easier to manage than others.

Cash, in the sense of liquid money you can use right away, is the hardest form of money to manage. It’s the same as raw energy, and the reason is that it’s always changing. You have it one day and by the end of the day it’s gone.

Most people aren’t good at handling a lot of liquid money. They don’t have the skills, and they don’t have the habits, and they don’t have the values to handle it. If you have $1 million in liquid cash in your account, you’re probably going to spend it in a few months, either all at once or in little pieces. And when you run out of liquid money you’ll probably try to go back to making it, and you’ll have to start from the very beginning, and you’ll never have another $1 million liquid again.

The second easiest form of money is real estate, like a house or land. The reason it’s easy is because it doesn’t change. It doesn’t come and go. It’s hard to spend it. You can sell it, but it’s a lot of work, and you can’t sell it if you need the money now. This is a good thing, because it means you can’t sell your house when you get drunk, or when you get a stupid idea, or when you get desperate for some kind of distraction. If you have a house, it’s a very slow process to get rid of it.

Real estate is a good way to manage money. People who have money and don’t know what to do with it usually end up buying a house with it. And if you have a house and you have a lot of money, your money is a lot safer than it would be if it were just liquid.

This doesn’t work very well for people who aren’t good at managing money, though. If you don’t have the skills to manage money, you can’t manage money in the form of real estate either.

The third easiest form of money is investments, in the form of stocks, bonds, funds, and so on. People who have money and don’t know what to do with it usually end up investing it. They buy some stock or a fund, or they put it in a savings account, and then they never think about it again. This is the best way to manage money if you have money and you don’t know what to do with it.

prompt: is it actually rational to keep an emergency fund in a savings account earning 4% when the market averages like 10%? I keep going back and forth. write me something that thinks this through like an essay rather than a listicle
response:
If you have $100,000 saved, you might be wondering whether to hold it in a savings account earning 4% or invest it in the stock market, which earns 10% on average. If you go for the market, you might worry that it’s not safe for the emergency fund.

A common way to think about this is to ask what the minimum emergency fund needs to be for someone. If you need at least $50,000, then you can invest the other $50,000 without worrying that your emergency fund is in danger.

In that case, you might ask why not invest the whole $100,000? If you invested the whole $100,000, you could expect to have more than $50,000 with 95% confidence. The odds of not having $50,000 are so small you could just go for it.

The odds that your $100,000 will fall below $50,000 after 3 years, or even 5, are small. It would require a 50-60% crash in the market. This sort of crash has happened only twice or so in the last 150 years.

You might feel a little nervous about this. If you’re a bit nervous, that’s fine. You can just invest 80% of your money in the market. In that case, if you had a bad year, you’d have a little less money in the market, but that might not be so bad. The worst year in the last 150 years is -50%. If your $100,000 invested 80% in the market has a bad year, you’ll have 40% less than expected. This is something you could deal with.

Or you could invest 50% of your money in the market. In that case, you’d have only a 10% chance of having less than your expected savings after a year.

So you’re in pretty good shape. If you’re willing to accept a 10% chance of having less money in your savings account after a year, you could just put half your money in the stock market and half in a savings account. This might make sense, for instance, if you’re thinking about buying a house in a few years.

If you want to be more conservative, you might want to put just a third in the market. Then you’d have only a 5% chance of having less money in your account after a year.

One problem with this is that you’re going to have a lot of money that you’ve saved for emergencies, but are going to have to use for a house. This would mean that you’re not going to have any money for emergencies.

Another problem with this is that if you invest a third in the market, you’re going to be pretty nervous about the market. If the market crashes, you might panic and sell your investments.

prompt: is it actually rational to keep an emergency fund in a savings account earning 4% when the market averages like 10%? I keep going back and forth. write me something that thinks this through like an essay rather than a listicle
response:
A friend recently emailed me asking whether it was “really” a good idea to have a big emergency fund. He was thinking in terms of opportunity cost. He figured if he had, say, $100k, he could be earning 10% per year (assuming the S&P 500 is a good enough proxy for the entire market) instead of 4% in an interest-bearing savings account. So by keeping that $100k in the bank, he was costing himself 6% of $100k, or $6,000 per year. That is, he would have $600,000 more in the future if he invested that money instead.

I wrote him back to say I think this was a good thing to do. Here’s why.

One of the things I love about this blog is that when I say something here and people disagree with it, they’ll often write in with their perspective. I had a long exchange with my friend about this issue, and I thought it might be worth writing an essay about it.

The core of his argument was this:

> I’m a bit surprised by your reaction. I think of this as an opportunity cost argument. If I’m going to save $50,000 in the stock market, it will be worth $100,000 in 20 years. By keeping it in the bank, I’m only earning about 4% a year, so the money will be worth only $90,000 in 20 years. That’s an opportunity cost of $10,000.
>
> You could argue that the emergency fund will never be used, but if so, then it’s not really an emergency fund, is it? If it will almost certainly be used for the emergency, it’s not worth keeping it around. If it will never be used, then it’s just sitting there in the bank doing nothing.
>
> The only way to justify having an emergency fund is to calculate the probability that the emergency fund will be used, and the expected cost of not having it, and make sure that the expected loss from not having it is more than the opportunity cost from having it. If I never have a financial emergency, I’ll end up with $90,000 instead of $100,000. If I have a financial emergency and need to sell my investments to deal with it, I’ll end up with $90,000 instead of $100,000. So the emergency fund doesn’t help me out much.
>
> On the other hand, if I keep my money in the stock market and have an emergency, I’ll have to sell part of it to deal with the emergency. Let’s say I only need $10,000. So I’ll end up with $10,000 less than I otherwise would have, or $90,000 instead of $100,000.
>
> The only way to make the emergency fund worth it, in this analysis, is to argue that it saves me from some really bad outcome. But the only way I can avoid that bad outcome is by never using the emergency fund at all. Which means it’s not really an emergency fund.

I wrote back:

> I think it’s worth it for a couple of reasons. One is that the emergency fund isn’t the same thing as saving for retirement. You can save for retirement and have a separate emergency fund. For example, I have a retirement account that I’ve invested in stocks. I also have money in a checking account. You could say that the money in my checking account is an emergency fund.
>
> Another thing is that the stock market will go down sometimes, and you won’t always have a choice about when you need your money.
>
> Also, you don’t have to have a huge emergency fund, and if you don’t have a huge emergency fund, then the opportunity cost of keeping it in the bank isn’t that big. For example, if I have $10,000 in the bank, then I’m only losing $1,000 a year in opportunity cost. That’s a reasonable amount to lose for a lot of extra peace of mind.

I think it’s important to distinguish between saving for retirement and having an emergency fund. Those are two different things. If you’re saving for retirement, you’re trying to maximize the amount of money you’ll have by the time you retire. You don’t care what your money will be worth in the next five years. If you’re saving for an emergency fund, you’re trying to maximize the amount of money you can immediately get your hands on in a crisis. You don’t care what your money will be worth in five years.

If you’re thinking about how much you can save for retirement in twenty years, then I’m glad to concede that your idea is better. If you’re thinking about how much money you can get your hands on in a crisis, then I’m glad to concede that my idea is better.

I don’t think there is any way to reconcile these two ideas. If I need to get my hands on $20,000 in an emergency, it doesn’t matter whether I have $20,000 sitting in the bank or $40,000 invested in the stock market. If I have $40,000 invested in the stock market, I have to take that $40,000 and sell all of it before I can get my hands on $20,000. If the stock market has gone up in the meantime, then maybe I’ll be able to sell it for $45,000 and get my hands on $20,000. But if the stock market has gone down in the meantime, then maybe I’ll only be able to sell it for $35,000 and still not get my hands on the $20,000.

This is what the stock market does sometimes. It goes down. Sometimes a lot. In 2008, the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) fell from 14,000 to 7,000. That means if you had $14,000 invested in the DJIA, you’d have $7,000 after one year.

This is why you don’t want to have to sell your investments in a financial crisis. You want to be able to take your money out of the bank and give it to the hospital, or pay the rent, or whatever. If you have to sell your investments to get your hands on that money, and the stock market has gone down in the meantime, then you’ll lose money.

Another reason why I don’t like the idea of selling my investments in a crisis is that it is a hassle. I have to call my broker. Then I have to wait for the money to be transferred into my account. This can take several days. If the crisis is something like a medical emergency, then I can’t afford to wait several days to get the money.

I don’t like having to wait several days to get my hands on money. That’s why I keep some money in the bank. It’s not a huge amount, but it’s enough that I don’t have to worry about it.

If I have, say, $10,000 sitting in the bank, and it’s earning 4% a year, then I’m losing $400 a year in opportunity cost. That’s fine with me. I’m willing to lose $400 a year to be able to get my hands on $10,000 in a crisis.

prompt: is it actually rational to keep an emergency fund in a savings account earning 4% when the market averages like 10%? I keep going back and forth. write me something that thinks this through like an essay rather than a listicle
response:
Suppose you’ve got $100k sitting in the bank account earning 4%. Maybe you’re thinking, hey, the market has always returned more like 10% on average, I should move this money into the stock market. You know, you’re not crazy for thinking this, since the stock market *has* always returned more like 10% on average, and you’re not crazy for thinking your $100k would be worth $106k after one year in the market, versus $104k in the bank account.

But it’s not exactly right, either. The *average* market return is 10%, but *some* years it will be much higher than 10%, some years it will be much lower, and some years it will be negative.

If you’ve got $100k and you’re not going to need the money for a while, then it makes sense to put it in the stock market. You have to wait years and years before the market makes up its losses, but you’ve got the time to wait. So you should do it!

But if you’ve got $100k and you’re not sure when you’ll need it – it’s your emergency fund, your “just in case” savings – then it does *not* make sense to put it in the stock market. In 2008, the market lost 40%. Suppose you had $100k, and you lost a job in 2008, needing that emergency fund. You’d have to go to the market to get it, and you’d only be able to get $60k, not $100k, just because of a one-year market fluctuation.

A market return of 10% on average is not the same as a market return of 10% every year. If you’re sure you can leave your money in the market for years, then yes, you’re going to do fine. But if you don’t know, if it’s your emergency fund, you might need to get the money back out in a year when the market does badly, and then you’re going to do much worse.

So, is it better to put your money in the stock market, or in the bank?

The stock market, on average, returns 10% a year, with a standard deviation of 20%. The bank account returns 4% a year, with a standard deviation of 0%.

If you put your money in the stock market, you have a 50% chance of doing better than the bank account, and a 50% chance of doing worse. But if you put it in the bank account, you have a 0% chance of doing better than the bank account, and a 100% chance of doing worse.

If you need to make sure that you have your $100k, the best thing you can do is put it in the bank account.

Suppose your $100k was your emergency fund, and you lost a job and needed it back after a year when the market did badly. You only got $60k back, so you had to start over from scratch. You had to save $100k over the course of a decade, just so you could go back to the same point you’d started at.

So, yes, the stock market does return 10% on average. But that means it’s going to do badly some years and really, really well other years. If you can wait, then sure, you can do fine in the stock market. But if you need to make sure you’ve got your money back, it’s a bad idea.

prompt: I'd like an essay questioning the FIRE movement. Not dunking on it, I followed it for years. But I've started to think 'retire at 40' is a strange goal for people who mostly like their jobs. Around 1200 words.
response:
I was at a meetup this weekend and a guy was talking about how he had quit his job to become a software consultant. He was a really nice guy and I felt for him, because he was a little nervous about whether people would think he was a failure. And I just want to say here for the record that he is not a failure. He is not a failure for leaving a job he liked less for one that he liked more.

I’ve been thinking about this a lot because I’ve been talking to a lot of people who left work to do consulting and they all seem like good people and are not failures. And it’s made me realize that I don’t like the phrase “retiring from work” at all. And I wish people would stop saying it, because it’s not just wrong, it’s really harmful.

I don’t think it’s right for a few reasons. First of all, I think the people doing it do it because they like their work, not because they dislike their work. A lot of these people are people who really want to be independent and they have a lot of ideas that they want to try out. And it feels good. I know some people who are doing this now and they are all happy. It’s not like they are sitting around their living room bored out of their minds wishing that they had a job. They’re actually doing things. And if you tell them that they are “retired” it makes them feel uncomfortable, and that’s bad. They’re not retired, they’re just doing something different.

And also it’s wrong because, I think, most people like their work. And if you tell them that the end goal is to retire from work, it makes them feel like they should not like their work. And that’s wrong.

And also it’s harmful because when you tell people that they need to retire from their job, then it makes them not like their job. If you tell a kid that they should eat vegetables then it makes them not want to eat vegetables. And if you tell people that they should want to leave their job then it makes them not want to work there.

And I think this is one of the things that makes work worse. A lot of people think of work as this horrible thing that they just have to do. And if you tell them that their job sucks and that they should quit, then it makes it worse. And it makes them not want to work at all, which is bad. And it makes them feel guilty about working, which is also bad.

So I think we should stop telling people to retire from work. We should tell them to do whatever they want. And if they want to do consulting, that’s great. But if they want to keep doing what they are doing, that’s fine too. And I think it’s important for all of us to understand that it is okay to like your work, and that you are allowed to be happy about that, and that it doesn’t mean you are a slave.

I think a lot of these guys who are doing this now are doing it because they want to be independent. And I think that’s a really good thing. It’s really important to be independent. And I don’t think it’s okay to do this to your family. I don’t think it’s okay to make your kids pay your bills. And I don’t think it’s okay to do this to your spouse. You have to think about what’s best for your family. And if it’s better for your family if you keep your job, then you should keep your job.

I think this is a big deal. If you tell people that they need to be independent, then you tell people that they should not work at all. But if you tell people that they can do whatever they want, then you tell them that they can be independent or they can work. I think that’s a big deal.

prompt: I'd like an essay questioning the FIRE movement. Not dunking on it, I followed it for years. But I've started to think 'retire at 40' is a strange goal for people who mostly like their jobs. Around 1200 words.
response:
In his excellent essay on the FIRE movement, Nick Bostrom writes that he believes that most people in the FIRE community aren’t really interested in retiring, but in having more leisure time, more freedom, more autonomy, and more room for creativity.

I’ve been in the FIRE movement for a while, and I’ve met a lot of FIRE people, and he’s right. Most of the people I’ve met who are planning to retire at 40 are not *thrilled* at the prospect of not having to work a job anymore. In fact, they’re kind of ambivalent about it.

It makes sense that Bostrom is right about this, because most people enjoy working. They enjoy being creative, doing interesting things, and interacting with other people. When someone tells you “What would you do if you didn’t have to work a job anymore?” most people get confused or ask follow-up questions. This is a problem for the FIRE movement.

In fact, I’ve started to suspect that “I want to retire at 40” is one of those things that most people say because they think they’re supposed to say it, or because their boss told them to say it.

Like, the other day I was talking to my boss about something that wasn’t work-related. And I said “This is not work, I’m just talking to you because we’re friends.” He said “No, this is work, and it’s on the clock.” And I was like “What do you mean, it’s on the clock?” And he was like “I mean, if you were working for someone else, I would have to pay you.”

This was not a problem, because I was working for him, and so he didn’t actually have to pay me. It was just some weird thing that happened when I was not thinking about what I was saying, and just saying the things I think other people think I’m supposed to say.

When someone tells me “I want to retire at 40”, I have to think about whether they’re just saying that because they think I’m supposed to say it. Like, if my boss told me “I want to retire at 40”, that would be weird. And the only reason that someone like my boss would say that is if they thought I was supposed to say it.

So when someone tells me “I want to retire at 40”, I think to myself: are they just saying that because they think I’m supposed to say it? And if so, what would they say if they weren’t thinking about what they’re saying?

In the last several years, I’ve started to suspect that most people don’t think that they should be saying “I want to retire at 40”. Instead, I think that most people think that they should be saying “I want to work hard and make a lot of money.”

And I think that’s because of the story we tell each other about retirement. In the story, retirement is this amazing thing that you get to do after you’ve “worked hard your whole life”, and it’s what you get to do after you’ve “earned” it. And in the story, you work hard for 40 years, and then you retire, and then you don’t have to work anymore. And you get to do all the things you always wanted to do, like travel, and write books, and do whatever.

I think that we tell ourselves this story because our grandparents told us it.

prompt: I'd like an essay questioning the FIRE movement. Not dunking on it, I followed it for years. But I've started to think 'retire at 40' is a strange goal for people who mostly like their jobs. Around 1200 words.
response:
I’m not trying to dunk on FIRE, because I think there are legitimate reasons why someone might want to retire early, and I followed the rules for a few years. I still believe in the general idea: you should try to have financial security and not worry about work. But I don’t think most people actually want to “retire at 40”, or at least not for the reasons they think.

I think this is another case where the popular conception of something is very different from the actual reality of that thing, and the popular conception is much more appealing.

Most people’s concept of “retiring” is something like “I’m going to be able to spend all my time with my family” or “I’m going to be able to work on that side project I always wanted to”. If you ask them what they’ll do with all that free time, you’ll get some sort of vague and generic answer like “hmm… I don’t know, I’ll have to figure it out”. I can’t remember the exact quote, but I feel like there’s a famous quote about someone asking a young king what he was going to do with all his power and the young king replying “I don’t know, I’ll have to think about it.”

It’s a mistake to think that you can figure out something as important as what you’ll do for the rest of your life later. If you’re really going to retire at 40, you need to have a good idea now of what you’ll spend the next 40 years doing. And this is where it becomes very easy to get confused.

If you want to spend your time with your family, you don’t have to quit your job to do that. Most jobs offer PTO, you can take a week or two off to spend time with your family, or if it’s really important you can do remote work and spend more time with them. I think most of the people I know who want to spend more time with their family could do that without having to completely give up their jobs.

And if you want to work on your side projects, well, you don’t need to give up your job to do that either. I know this because I work at a startup and I spend all my time working on my side projects. This is just what it means to be a startup founder, I’m not saying this is always the case, but there are a lot of options. And if you do have to give up your job to work on your side projects, then it doesn’t really matter if you retire at 40 or 65. It’s better to work on them now than to wait until 20 years from now, when you might be older, more set in your ways, and less creative.

There are other reasons I’ve seen for why people want to retire early that aren’t about quitting work. Sometimes people want to retire early because they have a very specific hobby that they want to focus on. This is a good reason to retire early, I just think it’s pretty rare.

Sometimes people want to retire early because they hate work or the idea of work. I don’t think this is very common, but I know it happens. If you hate work, then retiring early might be a good idea. But most people don’t hate work, at least I don’t. I’m a software engineer and I really like programming. I’ve talked to a bunch of software engineers and almost all of them like programming too. In the last 10 years of my life, my parents and grandparents have died, I got married, and had a kid, and I still think programming is the most interesting thing I’ve ever done.

The other reason I’ve heard for why people want to retire early is that they want to have freedom and not have to work for someone else. I get this, and I think it’s pretty common. I definitely have this feeling. I like programming a lot, but I hate the idea of having to work for someone else.

But I think this desire is more of a misunderstanding than something you can actually achieve. I don’t think you can be completely free. If you retire at 40 and then go do something for the next 40 years, then you’re probably going to end up working for someone. If you’re running a business, then you’re going to have to work for your customers. If you’re working on a book, you’re going to work for your readers. And I don’t think this is so bad.

There’s a lot of freedom in this. If you’re working for someone, they’re going to make you do some things that you wouldn’t otherwise do, but they’re going to be very limited in what they can make you do. If you work for me for a while, I might make you work on things that you don’t like, but I’m not going to tell you to go jump in a lake or anything crazy like that. And when you have your own business or are working on your own book, you can choose who your “boss” is. You can choose whether your boss is your readers or your customers, and you can decide how much you care about them.

I think you can get most of this freedom without having to retire early. I think if you’re an entrepreneur, you already have a lot of freedom. You might not have as much freedom as a person who is 100% retired, but you don’t have to work for someone else, and I think that’s the big thing. And if you’re not an entrepreneur, I think you can still get some freedom, you can just have to put in more effort. If you work for a big company you probably don’t have a lot of freedom, but you can probably get more freedom by working at a startup or by quitting and starting your own company.

I think a lot of this is a matter of attitude. I think people who are always thinking “this is my job” have more trouble than people who are thinking “this is my life” and I think a lot of people are just not used to the second thing. And I think once you’ve had this attitude for a while and gotten used to it, you’ll never want to give it up.

prompt: I'm a CPA. Every January clients ask me whether they should pay off their 3% mortgage early. Write a blog post that explains why the math and the feeling point in different directions here, and why the feeling isn't necessarily wrong. Audience: smart non-specialists.
response:
I get a lot of questions from readers about mortgages. A typical one is:

*Should I pay off my house early?*

In this post I’ll explain why the math and the intuition point in opposite directions here. And I’ll explain why the intuition is not necessarily wrong.

1. Suppose you have a mortgage with interest rate R. Every month, you pay a certain amount (call it P) towards your mortgage. Suppose you want to pay off the mortgage early. One way to do this is to add an extra amount E to your monthly payment and apply it to the principal.

Now, suppose that your mortgage is 3% and that you pay the normal amount plus an extra $300 a month. If you did that for a month and then quit, you’d have paid an extra $300 towards the mortgage. But next year, you’d have paid $3600. If you kept doing it for 30 years, you’d have paid $108,000.

But you can do something even better. If, at the end of every month, you took that extra $300 that you didn’t pay on your mortgage, and put it into an account that pays 3% annual interest, then you’d have the same number as if you’d just added the extra $300 to your mortgage. You’d pay the same total amount of interest, and you’d end up with no mortgage left. In both cases, if you started with $100,000, you’d finish paying after 21.6 years.

It doesn’t matter how much the interest rate is. If it’s 3% or 7%, you’ll get the same result either way.

So here’s the lesson: paying extra on your mortgage doesn’t really save you anything. You get no advantage over just taking the extra money and investing it at the same interest rate as the mortgage.

2. Now suppose you have a 30-year mortgage with interest rate R. One day, you think, “I’m going to save an extra $500 a month to pay it off faster.” You’re not going to add this to your mortgage payment – you’re just going to put it in a savings account. You figure you can invest it at a return of R, so it’s just like paying it on the mortgage, and you’ll save all the interest you’d save by paying early.

You’re wrong. Suppose R is 3%. After one month you’ll have $500 in your account. After two months, you’ll have $1000. After two years you’ll have $12,000. If you had just been adding $500 a month to your mortgage payments, you’d have paid off the whole mortgage in 20 years. But in your savings account, you’ll have only $12,000, and you’ll still have most of your mortgage left.

Here’s the problem. When you add $500 a month to your mortgage, you pay off the principal faster. That means you owe less each month, so you pay less interest. After two years, you’ve only paid $12,000 of the principal, but you’ve also saved more than $1,000 in interest.

When you put the extra $500 in a savings account, you don’t get any of this advantage.

3. Here’s another way to understand it. Suppose you have a 30-year mortgage with interest rate R. If you add an extra $500 a month to your payments, you’ll pay off the whole mortgage in 20 years. If you do that, you’ll save a total of $122,400 compared to just paying your normal payment for 30 years.

Now suppose you just pay your normal mortgage payment for 30 years and put the extra $500 into an investment account. At the end of the 30 years, you’ll have $300,000. If you invested it at the same interest rate as your mortgage, you’d earn $122,400 of interest, the same amount as if you’d paid your mortgage early.

The problem is that you’re not going to invest it for 30 years. As soon as you have enough, you’re going to pay off your mortgage. That means your investment only has about 20 years to earn that $122,400.

4. Here’s the moral: If you’re trying to save as much interest as possible, the best thing to do is just pay your normal payment and invest the extra. But only if you really want to save as much interest as possible.

It’s not clear that this is what most people want. For instance, suppose you have two mortgages. If you paid one off early, you’d save a ton of interest. But if you paid the other off early, you’d save almost none. Suppose the first one has a 30-year remaining term and the second one has only a 2-year remaining term. In that case, the two choices seem very different to me.

I don’t know what the right way to think about it is. prompt: I'm a CPA. Every January clients ask me whether they should pay off their 3% mortgage early. Write a blog post that explains why the math and the feeling point in different directions here, and why the feeling isn't necessarily wrong. Audience: smart non-specialists.
response:
In the last few years I’ve had a lot of clients asking whether they should make extra payments to pay off their low-interest mortgage. My advice, in this case, is always to say no.

You could put that money in a low risk investment (like a savings bond) that would earn a much higher interest rate. If you don’t invest, you’re giving money to the bank for free.

There are two problems with this advice.

First, it’s very hard to get a lot of people to invest. People who are financially well off are already investing, but most people don’t even have a Roth IRA account. So if you don’t invest and your mortgage rate is low, you’re probably not missing a lot of money by paying it off.

Second, the question isn’t just what’s mathematically best. The best choice might be to put the money in a 529 plan to use for the kids’ college. But what about the feeling of being debt free? What about the security and peace of mind? It doesn’t pay a high interest rate, but it might be a great investment.

I’ve had a lot of clients ask me whether they should pay off their mortgage. They want to know if they’re wasting money by paying it off. I’ve always given the same answer: no, because the math is clear. But I’ve been thinking about it for a while and I think I was wrong.

The math is clear in some ways. If your interest rate is below the average return on stocks, you shouldn’t pay off your mortgage. If your rate is higher, you should. I have a 3.4% mortgage, and the average return on stocks is 10%, so mathematically I should invest my extra money and not pay off my mortgage.

But people can be risk averse. If you’re too afraid to invest in stocks and your mortgage rate is low, it doesn’t make much difference whether you pay it off early or not. If you’re risk averse and your mortgage rate is high, then you should definitely pay it off early.

But paying off your mortgage might be the best investment of all. It might be the best investment for most people.

I had a friend tell me that he had just paid off his mortgage. I thought about how great it was that he was debt free. Then he said “and now I can pay off my car”.

The reason why I have never paid off my mortgage is that I don’t think it’s financially smart. I have a 3.4% mortgage. I could invest the extra money and earn a much higher return. I’m not going to pay a bank 3.4% a year.

But when he said he was going to pay off his car, it made me think, if I pay off my mortgage, how much money could I save on other things? I would be able to pay off my car. I could pay for my kids’ college out of pocket. I could invest the extra money in a low risk way.

Paying off my mortgage might have been the best investment I ever made, even though mathematically it would have been the worst.

If you pay off your mortgage, you get a much higher return on your investments than if you keep paying the mortgage. You can invest the money you were saving for the mortgage in low risk investments. If I paid off my mortgage, I could invest my $1,100/month in an S&P 500 index fund. The return on my investments would probably be a lot higher than my mortgage rate.

I think it’s a common mistake to compare the return on investments to the interest rate on your mortgage. You can get a higher return on investments than your interest rate, but it’s not that simple. You have to think about what you’ll do with the money you saved by paying off your mortgage.

I’m glad I didn’t pay off my mortgage. It’s been a lot of work, but it’s made a lot of money for me.

prompt: Essay on the strange morality of tipping, and why the tip screen at the self-checkout coffee kiosk feels like a small moral crisis.
response:
I am not a big fan of tipping. It feels like the restaurant should just charge what they want, which would be more efficient. But it is not just about efficiency. There is something strange about tipping – or maybe the moral confusion about tipping is just the tip of the iceberg of a larger problem.

There was a recent *NYT* article about how restaurants are now experimenting with “no tip, no service”. This is not so unusual – restaurants have always had the option to add a 18% gratuity for parties of six or more, and a lot of them do. And I have heard of a few restaurants that charge a 20% tip on everyone.

But this is not about the 18% tip, or even the 20% tip. I am not talking about tipping at all. I am talking about the tip screen at the self-checkout coffee kiosk.

Imagine that you buy a coffee at a big chain coffee shop. Instead of going through the normal line, you go to a kiosk. You punch in your order on the screen, and pay with your credit card. Then a barista comes along and makes your coffee and hands it to you.

Now, at some point, I think after you pay and before your coffee is made, a tip screen comes up. It says something like “You are purchasing a $3 latte. Would you like to leave a $0.75 tip to the baristas who prepare your order? That is 25%.” It gives you four options. 25% – $0.75, 20% – $0.60, 15% – $0.45, and 10% – $0.30. There is no zero option.

What are you supposed to do with this? It is not really a question about money. I am not going to care about paying 30 more cents. And the barista is not going to care about receiving 30 more cents. It is a question about what we think is fair, and what we want to signal.

Let’s say that I choose 10% – $0.30. What is that saying? It is not saying “I want to reward you for good service”, because you have not done anything yet. It is saying something more like “I am not willing to give you anything more than 10%. That is the bare minimum. I am just giving you the bare minimum, because I have to”.

But there is a problem with that. When we say something about money, it is often because we are saying something about what we think people are worth.

When we say that a waiter should get a 15% tip, we are saying that the waiter is worth at least 15% of the bill.

When we say that we are going to give a waiter 25% or 30% tip, we are saying that the waiter is worth at least 25% of the bill.

When we say that we are not going to tip a waiter at all, we are saying that the waiter is worth at most $0, that the waiter is not worth anything.

I know that this sounds a bit ridiculous, but this is how it works.

Let’s say that I choose the 10% option. I think that this is saying that the barista is worth 10% of the bill, or at most 10% of the bill. I am giving the barista the bare minimum. That seems a little low, especially for a coffee shop, where the baristas are the main laborers. But it is not crazy.

Let’s say that I choose the 25% option. I think that this is saying that the barista is worth at least 25% of the bill.

Now, if we are thinking about what we are signaling, I think that I would choose the 25% option.

But there is another question. If you think that you are going to give a barista 25% of the bill as a tip, why are you giving a barista 25% of the bill as a tip?

It seems a little weird to me. The barista is not going to be making your latte. You are going to pick it up from a counter, and the barista is not going to see that. There is no way for the barista to know how much you tipped, and there is no way for the barista to give you a reward. So there is no reason to think that tipping is going to affect anything.

So why tip the barista? If we want to think about the barista’s welfare, then there is a reason to think that we should give the barista as much as we can, so that they can have more money. But I am not sure that is the right way to think about it.

It is worth asking why we tip at all. Why do people tip?

There are two main reasons: to reward good service, and to show our approval. When we tip a waiter, we are saying “I like what you did”, or “You did a good job”, or “I am happy with your service”.

But why do we say this in money? Why not just say it with words?

I am not sure. Maybe we think that money is more meaningful than words.
