Hyperinflation is when inflation reaches a certain threshold that causes society to lose faith in the currency, so people just stop using it. This makes things even worse because the money supply has to be increased even faster to keep prices and wages rising, but this makes people distrust the currency even more, so they use it less, and the money supply has to be increased even faster to make up for it, and so on.

In the end, the Argentine peso was so debased that you had to carry around stacks of bills to buy everyday things like food and gas. In 1982, the average monthly wage was 20,000 pesos. By the end of 1983 it was 6 million pesos. By the end of 1989, it was 2.4 *trillion* pesos. You can imagine the sort of mentality this breeds: why would you trust money held by a bank, which would disappear as soon as the government realized it was there? Why would you trust money held in the form of a bank deposit, which would be worthless if the peso collapsed? Why wouldn’t you keep your money at home, in the form of bills or gold coins?

My dad did both, but the coffee can wasn’t always a coffee can. In his apartment, he had a safe that was bolted to the ground. It was about as big as a large suitcase. It was a very nice safe. I don’t know how he got it in the apartment, but I imagine he did something to make it look like some kind of furniture.

My dad always had the safe locked. I only got to see what was inside once, on his birthday, when we all opened it up together. It was filled with thousands of dollars worth of bills. He must have kept it in the safe for decades. I think this is why he never upgraded to a bigger apartment.

I was never impressed by the safe. It made him seem like some kind of lunatic. The world is a pretty safe place, you don’t need a safe to hide your money. But after seeing what hyperinflation can do, I understand the appeal.

I think a lot of people have the same mentality. For instance, my dad would never buy a car from a dealership. He always paid cash and had his sister get him the car from a private sale. This meant he was often getting ripped off. He bought a 1990s Ford Bronco for about $8000, which was a really good deal at the time. It had a really rough ride. He also bought a 1990s Honda CR-V for about $9000, which wasn’t much of a deal at the time. But that car, too, had a really rough ride.

My dad would never buy a house from an estate agent. He always paid cash, and he always had his sister find him the house. My mom and I were surprised to find out that, like his cars, his house was always a real rough deal. He bought the first house for 3 times its value. I don’t remember what he paid for the second one, but it was also quite a bit above market. But, like his cars, at least his houses were really solid.

I don’t think this was because my dad was a bad negotiator. I’m sure he was a pretty good one. I don’t even think it was because he was so set on paying cash that he was willing to pay more to do it. I think it’s because he knew about the hyperinflation and wanted to get rid of the peso as fast as possible. This meant he was always willing to buy things for much more than they were worth. And the people he bought things from knew this about him, which meant he was always ripped off even more.

A lot of people think my dad was a total idiot. I do too, sometimes. He was willing to pay $8000 for a 1990s Ford Bronco, which is the kind of deal I would only consider if I had to have a car to drive to work and couldn’t afford anything else. But he never really needed a car. He would walk everywhere. I think he would have been fine without a car.

But now that he’s dead, I’m not so sure he was a total idiot. I know that if the peso was going to disappear, it would make sense to keep cash in the house and get rid of it as fast as possible. But I’m not sure he was a fool for buying a car that didn’t have any value to him. Maybe he thought that, when the peso disappeared, he would have to get a car to get food and stuff, so he wanted to have a car already. This seems pretty stupid, but the world is a pretty weird place, and if there are people who have to buy a car every few years, maybe it makes sense to have one already.

My mom said he thought that the peso was going to disappear soon. This is why he kept so much money in his house. He wanted to have cash in case the peso disappeared. I think he was right, too. The world is a pretty weird place, and if there are people who think the peso is going to disappear soon, maybe it makes sense to keep cash in your house.

I don’t know what my dad was really thinking. He died without telling me, and he wasn’t the type of guy who explained his actions. All I know is that he was always willing to spend a lot of money for things that didn’t seem like good deals.

prompt: My dad never trusted banks. Kept cash in a coffee can, literally, and bought gold coins every few years. He died last spring and we found about $40k in various places around the house. Part of me thinks he was paranoid and lost out on decades of compounding. Part of me thinks he knew something about security that I don't, since he grew up in Argentina during the 80s. Can you write an essay about what money means to people who've watched it fail? I'd like it to be fair to him.
response:
*This essay is dedicated to my dad, who passed away last spring.*

My dad died in April. He was 74. He lived a long, happy life. He had lots of friends, and he helped people for free.

We cleaned out his house in May. When you find $300 in a drawer, you keep it, it’s the least you can do. We found $300 in a lot of drawers.

The coffee can, I knew, was always there. Dad had always had it. We found $10k in the coffee can.

Dad also bought gold coins every couple of years. These were in a drawer, under a mattress, etc. We found 24 gold coins. About $10k.

It all adds up to about $40k.

The amount of cash in a coffee can in the house that you don’t know about until you’re cleaning out the dead man’s house is pretty much the definition of a “secret stash of money”.

My dad was an engineer. He worked for Boeing for 40 years. He had a regular paycheck. He never had a million dollars. He had no crazy investments. He wasn’t a genius investor.

He wasn’t stupid either. He had a college degree. He built things. He was an expert at building things.

The only thing I can think of is that he knew what a coffee can full of cash was worth.

It was worth a lot.

He was born in Buenos Aires, in 1945. He grew up there, and Argentina, like most Latin American countries, was an economic disaster.

In 1981, the central bank of Argentina printed so much money that people stopped using it. The official currency was worth nothing.

A couple of years after that, when I was a baby, Argentina was in the middle of a war, and people were using American dollars to buy things.

In 1989, inflation hit 327%. A single person living in Buenos Aires would have needed $800/day in 1989 just to survive. In 1990, that number was $1,000/day. In 1991, that number was $2,600/day.

The inflation wasn’t always 327%. It was worse than that at some points.

In 1990, Argentina was so bad, that people stopped paying taxes, because they couldn’t. The government responded to that by printing more money.

The people of Argentina didn’t have a country that was bad at making money, they had a country that was bad at keeping money.

You can see how bad this was, because the Argentine peso was worth $0.113 in 1988. In 1995, it was worth 1/1000 of that. That’s 84% a year.

People in Argentina didn’t have money. They didn’t have any way to keep the money they had.

I think if you grow up in Argentina, and you have a country that takes your money, you learn that banks aren’t safe. I think that if you grow up in Argentina, you don’t believe in banks.

I think if you grow up in Argentina, you don’t believe in a lot of things.

I think if you grow up in Argentina, you keep your money in your house.

I think that’s what my dad did.

I think that if you grew up in Argentina, you’d have a pretty good idea of how much money you need in the house to feel safe.

I think my dad knew how much money he needed to feel safe.

I think my dad knew what the coffee can was worth.

prompt: why budgeting apps don't work for most people. op-ed, punchy
response:
You need a budget. You’ve heard it a hundred times. So you try it for a month or two, and the whole thing is such an ordeal that you quickly stop. You have to make it work.

This is a lie.

I’ve tried every budgeting app ever made. I’ve tried every method that’s been invented, including the envelope system, the zero-based budget, and the spreadsheet budget. Here’s what I can tell you: the budgeting method doesn’t matter. Your budget will fail because of what’s missing in all of these systems:

1. An understanding of how much you spend.

2. An understanding of how to get to a place where your income covers your expenses.

3. A system for staying on track.

If you don’t have these, then your budget will fail. And I’ll prove it.

Here’s why people don’t budget:

1. They don’t understand what they spend.

2. They don’t understand what they have to do to stop spending.

3. They don’t have a system in place for managing the spending.

Let me explain how this is true.

### What you spend

If you don’t know what your spending is, you can’t build a budget. If you have a budget, but you’re not tracking your spending, then it’s not a budget, it’s just a wish.

You need to know what you spend so that you can plan for it.

For example, say you want to know how much you spend on groceries each month, so you can have a grocery budget. You could ask yourself how much you think you spend on groceries and make a plan based on that. But that’s not how it works. If you guess, then you can’t trust that you’ll get what you wanted. If you want to know what you spend, you need to measure it.

When I started tracking my spending, I found out that I spent $1,500 on groceries every month. I was so surprised that I thought I had made a mistake, but it was true. I had no idea how much money I was spending, and so I had no way to manage it. And when I found out how much I was spending, I realized that it was a big part of why I was in debt.

That’s not what should happen. It’s not an accident that you’re in debt. You’re in debt because you spend more money than you earn. And you can’t stop spending more money than you earn unless you know what you’re spending.

### What you have to do to stop spending

Let’s say you’re spending $1,500 on groceries every month, and you want to stop spending more money than you earn. So you go to the store and buy groceries, and you spend $1,400. So you’re $100 closer to your goal.

And then the next month, you spend $1,500 again. And then the next month, you spend $1,600. So you’re $100 behind. So you go to the store and buy groceries, and you spend $1,400. So you’re $100 closer to your goal.

And so on.

You know what you want to happen, and you know what’s preventing it from happening. You just don’t know how to get there.

There’s a way to fix this. But first, you need to know what your spending is, so you can figure out what’s going on.

You could make a budget and hope that everything works out, but that would be stupid. It’s not enough to know that you spend more money than you earn. You need to know why you spend more money than you earn. That’s why you need to track your spending.

### How to manage spending

When you’re in debt, you’re in a race.

You need to save money, but you also need to save more and more money each month. If you don’t, you’ll never get out of debt. If you do save more and more money each month, you’ll probably be out of debt in three or four years.

This is a race where you need to get faster and faster, and it’s a race that you can’t win if you don’t know how much you spend.

Let me prove that this is true, too.

I’ve been out of debt for a while now, and I don’t have a budget anymore. I don’t have any debt, and I’ve got a system for managing my money. I can tell you what I spend, and I can tell you how to manage it. And I’ll tell you that I don’t have to do anything different from what you’re doing now.

You just need to get a system in place, and it will take care of everything. You’ll be out of debt in three or four years, and you’ll never have to budget again.

So here’s the deal:

1. Get a budgeting app.

2. Track your spending.

3. Get a system in place.

4. Get out of debt in three or four years.

5. Never have to budget again.

prompt: why budgeting apps don't work for most people. op-ed, punchy
response:
Last week, I was looking for an investment app. There are thousands to choose from, but I had a very specific requirement: I want to know what the app will cost me, not in terms of fees, but in terms of time.

I don’t have much time, and the last thing I want to spend it on is tracking my own spending. So I tried out a few apps. Here’s a typical experience:

I opened the app, linked my bank account, and got a nice dashboard. At the top, I saw how much I had spent and how much was left to spend. I had $3,733.28 left for this month. I didn’t care.

Below, I saw an alert. “You’ve already spent more than your average on Food & Drink. Do you need to adjust your budget?” Of course. I’ve been working from home a lot and buying takeout.

I tapped on Food & Drink. I spent $234 on groceries, $205 on takeout, and $312.50 on Starbucks. I didn’t care.

I tapped on Starbucks. It showed me my Starbucks transactions. $14.41, $31.17, $30.82, $11.25… I didn’t care.

I tapped on one of the transactions. I spent $11.25 at Starbucks on May 27th. I didn’t care.

This is what budgeting apps do. They take a number I don’t care about (how much money is left), and let me drill down until I find a number I care less about (how much I spent on one transaction).

I didn’t even have to do that in the app. My bank already has a list of all my transactions.

Why am I using an app that doesn’t help me understand my spending?

I didn’t realize until last week that there’s a big problem with budgeting apps: they don’t tell you what to do.

A good app would tell me, “Hey, you’ve been spending $150 a month on Starbucks. Do you want to cut that down to $100 a month?” and then help me do that. It would give me a goal and show me how to get there. It’s no use telling me that I spent $11.25 on one coffee if I have no idea what that means.

The problem with budgeting apps is that they’re focused on tracking spending. But knowing how much you spend isn’t the same as making a better decision about your money.

The reason I need a budgeting app at all is that I don’t want to think about my money. I’m busy and I have too much to do, so I outsource the task to a machine. The problem is that most apps aren’t smart enough. They just give me raw data and expect me to decide what to do with it.

Budgeting apps are like a really smart intern. It tracks how much you spend on everything and presents the numbers to you. But it can’t do anything more than that. It can’t tell you what to do.

That’s a missed opportunity. I want to tell my phone, “Hey, don’t let me spend more than $4,000 this month!” And then it can figure out how to do that.

The reason I don’t want to manage my money is that I don’t want to think about it. And it’s not just me. There’s a lot of people that want to avoid thinking about their money.

So budgeting apps should solve that problem. But they don’t.

What if apps actually told you what to do?

prompt: why budgeting apps don't work for most people. op-ed, punchy
response:
When I was a college student, I kept a budget notebook in which I meticulously tracked every penny I spent. And you know what? It worked. At the end of every month, I had a pretty good idea of how much money I had left. I was even able to save up enough money to get a new computer, something that seemed very impressive to my roommates, who seemed to have the money disappear at a rate of about $300 a week.

But then college ended. I got a job, started getting bills, and got busy. And the notebook was gone.

Now, I’m not alone in my experience. A 2017 study by Mint analyzed 100,000 budgeting apps and found that fewer than 1 in 10 users continued to use their app after 30 days, and only 1% after 2 years.

So why do people stop using budgeting apps?

A lot of the advice I see about budgeting is about creating a sustainable budgeting system. A system you can follow every month, a budget you can live with.

But that’s not my experience. The reason I stopped keeping track of my spending wasn’t that I found my system unsustainable. It’s that I didn’t have time to be so organized.

Most budgeting apps are too complex for the average user, and this complexity makes it hard to stick with them.

The average budgeting app requires users to check transactions and categorize them. That is, every single time you buy something or receive money, you have to manually tell the app what it is.

This is a pain! Not only does it require constant attention, but it also requires knowledge. For example, you’ll need to know what “DISH NETWORK” is. (I don’t, but I guess it’s a TV company?)

You could try to automate the categorization process, but then you’ll get a lot of wrong categories and a lot of wasted time fixing them.

And this is just the beginning. Most budgeting apps require more effort, like creating budgets or tracking spending against your goals.

I think this is the main reason people stop using budgeting apps. When you ask someone to keep a budget notebook or use a complex app, they’ll do it for a while. But when life gets busy, or they have to make a decision between their budget and paying their rent, they’ll stop using their budget.

But what if we could make budgeting easy? What if it didn’t require you to categorize transactions or create budgets? What if it didn’t require constant attention? What if it could be done in 5 minutes a month, instead of 5 minutes a day?

Then you could have a budget that you don’t need to force yourself to use.

You could keep track of your spending even if you’re busy. You could get a clear picture of where your money goes even if you’re not paying much attention to your spending. And you could save money, even if you’re not a finance nerd.

That’s why I built Pocketguard, a budgeting app that doesn’t require categorizing transactions or creating budgets. It’s free to use on the web, iPhone, or Android.

prompt: I'd love an essay on why the 4% rule became sacred. Where it came from (Bengen, 1994), what assumptions it smuggles in, and whether a 30-year rule makes any sense for someone retiring at 50.
response:
I was thinking about the 4% rule today. It’s one of those things that feels so important in personal finance, but that you’d be shocked to find is less than thirty years old.

Here’s some history.

In 1994, Bill Bengen published a paper about “Withdrawal Rates and Sequence of Returns”, which looked at historical data about different levels of investing, and what you could safely withdraw from your investments each year. He found that, using a standard 50/50 stock/bond split, a withdrawal rate of 4% would let you maintain your wealth, adjusted for inflation, over 30 years in almost all historical data sets he tested. He said 3.5% would be a better safe bet if you didn’t want any chance of running out of money.

In the same year, the “Three Percenters” blog was launched. The blog’s author, James Wade, wanted to know if he could retire at 45 and live off of a stock portfolio. When he tried 4%, he found there was a small but annoying chance his portfolio would last less than 30 years. When he lowered his withdrawal rate to 3%, the portfolio lasted almost forever (though he couldn’t quite prove it would last *quite* forever). He and his wife retired on the 3% withdrawal rate, and started blogging about it.

And that’s where the 4% rule came from. It was one guy’s blog post, and one other guy’s paper. And I don’t want to diminish the importance of either, but it’s kind of funny to hear people talk about it as if it’s some kind of mathematical certainty.

In the years since, people have done a lot more work on the issue, both to test whether 4% really is a good withdrawal rate and to find more good ones. It’s probably not an exaggeration to say that there’s some sort of consensus that, if you’re planning a retirement of about 30 years at the age of 65, 3.5% - 4% is probably a good range to plan for.

But what if you’re retiring at 50? What if you want your money to last 40 years, or 45, or 50? Then I think there are two questions that might be worth asking:

1\. Does a withdrawal rate even make sense in a really long time horizon?

2\. If it does, what would a good number be?

I was thinking about this because someone on Twitter asked me how much money I would need to retire at 50. I gave a quick and dirty answer, but the more I thought about it, the more I thought it was a really interesting question.

So. First, let’s consider whether the concept of a withdrawal rate makes sense at all.

A withdrawal rate is something you take from your savings each year, adjusted for inflation, to make sure you never get poorer. It’s a very neat and simple way to think about planning your finances.

However, it’s not the only way, and if you’re thinking about a very long time horizon, it might not be the *best* way. For example, a lot of people think about retirement in terms of “I’m going to make sure that if I retire, I won’t have to worry about money until I die”. They don’t have to think about withdrawal rates; if they die, they won’t care if their portfolio runs out of money. They just need to worry about a fixed amount of time.

I don’t know if I like this approach as much as I like withdrawal rates, because it means that, if you live longer than you planned, you’re going to run out of money. But it’s a perfectly sensible way to think about retirement.

A better way might be to think of it as “I’m going to make sure that I won’t have to worry about money until I die, or until age X, whichever comes first”. For example, if you think you’ll live until 90, you might set your target to “at the age of 50, I’ll make sure my savings will last me until 85 no matter what”. That means you can retire at 50, you won’t worry about money until 85, and if you happen to live longer than that, you might have to work part-time to keep your money from running out.

I like this approach, because it’s the same as the withdrawal rate approach, but the withdrawal rate is calculated based on your time horizon and not on some number chosen by someone else.

If this were all there was to retirement planning, this wouldn’t matter. But it’s not.

There’s another issue that comes up when you’re planning on your retirement money lasting a really long time, which is *how much money you need*. For example, if you’re planning on living on your retirement money from the age of 65 to the age of 90, you need to plan for 25 years of spending. But if you’re planning on living on it from the age of 50 to the age of 90, you need to plan for 40 years.

Now, 40 years is a long time, and your future spending will be different from your current spending. When I was 20, I was a graduate student living on a stipend, and when I was 30, I was a young professor making a decent amount of money. When I was 40, I was a middle-aged professor making more money, but I had a mortgage and two kids.

What about when I’m 50? Will I have more or less money? Will I still have kids to support? Will I still have a mortgage?

I’m not sure I know. I have no idea how my spending at 60 will compare to how I spend money now. Will I still have kids to support? I’ll be more established in my career, and probably making more money. But I’ll also probably be spending more on things like health care.

The important thing here is, the longer your time horizon, the more you’re likely to change how much money you spend. This is an argument for not using a fixed withdrawal rate. It’s probably better to say “Okay, I want to make sure I have enough money for me to retire at 50, but I’m going to revisit my spending when I’m 55, and again when I’m 60, and again when I’m 65, and then adjust my retirement plan each time based on how my spending and needs change”.

But I’m not sure how that would work. If I retire at 50, I’m going to have a lot of freedom in my life, and that freedom will be *limited* if I have to worry about retirement planning every five years. Maybe I can just make it a rule that I’ll retire at 50 and then just not worry about the future, or that I’ll set up a pension-like thing for myself that pays me a fixed amount every year. Or maybe I’ll do some sort of hybrid thing that lets me take a lot of money out of my portfolio in my early retirement years and less in my later years.

I’m just not sure. It seems like a lot of the retirement planning literature has been aimed at people who are planning on retiring at 65, and not for people who are retiring much younger than that. And I don’t think the 4% rule, or any other simple retirement planning rule, is going to work very well if you’re retiring at 50.

And that’s a shame, because I think we need a better retirement planning framework for people who are retiring young. A lot of people want to retire young, and a lot of people *need* to retire young. The longer you live, the more likely you are to have to deal with health issues that make it hard to work. And I think we have an important duty to think about how to make it possible for people to retire young, and that means thinking about how we can make retirement planning easier for them.

prompt: I'd love an essay on why the 4% rule became sacred. Where it came from (Bengen, 1994), what assumptions it smuggles in, and whether a 30-year rule makes any sense for someone retiring at 50.
response:
In this essay I’m going to talk about the 4% rule and why it’s wrong.

The 4% rule is supposed to help retirees answer this question: what percentage of my net worth can I safely withdraw each year and still have a high probability of making money to the end of my life? It’s a standard rule of thumb that has been used by financial advisers since the 1990s. It’s the rule used at rBogleheads, and is taught at many schools of finance.

The 4% rule was invented by Bill Bengen in 1994, but there were several similar rules before that. Bill’s rule was a refinement of earlier rules, and had the advantage that it was supported by a huge number of simulations. Bengen ran 347 historical simulations covering all 30-year periods from 1926 to 1994. Every time a simulation ended with positive assets remaining, Bengen would increase the withdrawal rate, and when a simulation failed, he would decrease the withdrawal rate. He found that 4% was the highest rate that passed all simulations.

This sounds like a really great idea.

But it’s got an awful lot of assumptions baked in.

First it assumes that you’re 65, and that you need to live only 30 more years. The simulations are all 30-year simulations, and Bengen explicitly says he’s using 65 as the starting age. If you’re retiring earlier, it’s likely that the 4% rule won’t be enough to get you through the whole of your life.

For instance, if you retire at 50 and the market crashes hard right after, you’ll have to wait 15 years until you’re 65 to have a 4% rule. This means that you’ll have to survive the first 15 years of retirement with a 2.67% rule, or 4% divided by (1.04)^15. But if you’re in a stock market crash, that won’t be enough either! If your stocks are down 60%, and your stocks are 50% of your portfolio, your entire portfolio is down 30%, and 2.67% of that isn’t nearly enough to live off. In that situation, a 4% rule might not get you to the end of your life.

You might say that this is a corner case, but in a recession you’re not in a position to take chances, and if you run out of money at 60 or 63 you’re going to be in a real mess. A few years ago I wrote about a friend who hit this situation and was forced to get a job.

The second assumption of the 4% rule is that you’re only going to be alive to age 95. If you live past age 95, you’ll have to take less than 4% per year, or your savings will run out. If you want your wealth to last forever, or to be passed to your heirs, the 4% rule won’t do.

This might be a reasonable assumption for a retiree in 1994, but these days people are living longer. I’m going to write about this in a future essay, but in the meantime you can read this paper about longevity trends.

The third assumption of the 4% rule is that you’re going to retire in a year that’s as bad as the 1970s, and as good as the 1980s. Bengen’s simulations use the worst 30-year period as a test case, and this happens to be the period from 1966 to 1996. This period starts in a stock market bull run, ends in a bull run, and has a really awful stretch in the middle.

If you’re retiring in 2025 or later, then the 4% rule might not work for you, because the worst 30-year period could be worse than 1966 to 1996. If you retire later, then that period could also be shorter than 30 years. For instance, if you retire at 70, you’d only need to worry about the next 20 years.

If you’re retiring in 2004 or later, then 4% is going to be too conservative, because 1966 to 1996 is no longer the worst 30-year period. The worst 30-year period is now 1926 to 1956, which is a lot worse. This is because of the early 1930s, when there was a horrible stock market crash followed by a horrible stock market depression. The worst 25-year period is 1931 to 1956, which has a slightly higher return, and the worst 20-year period is 1936 to 1956, which has a much higher return.

If you want to retire at 65 in 2025, you have to worry about 30 years of investment performance, but if you retire at 70 in 2025, you only have to worry about 25 years. If you retire at 75 in 2025, you only have to worry about 20 years.

If you want to retire in 2025, here are the withdrawal rates that would survive the worst 30-year, 25-year and 20-year periods, if you were 65, 70 and 75 years old.

Age 65: 30-year simulation, 3.71%

Age 70: 25-year simulation, 4.24%

Age 75: 20-year simulation, 4.73%

If you’re 65 today, you should use the 3.71% rule. That’s because you have to worry about the worst 30-year period, which is 1926 to 1956. If you’re 70 today, you should use the 4.24% rule, because you only have to worry about the worst 25-year period. And so on.

What about if you want to retire at 50 today? You’re going to have to worry about 45 years of investment performance, which is more than the 30-year period that Bengen considered. That’s why I think a 4% rule for a retiree at 50 is unrealistic, and why I think rBogleheads makes a mistake in recommending it.

The fourth assumption of the 4% rule is that you’re going to have to worry about inflation, but not interest rates. The simulation doesn’t adjust for interest rates, so that’s fine. But it does assume that inflation is going to average about 3.3% a year, which isn’t very realistic. For instance, inflation in Japan is negative.

The fifth assumption of the 4% rule is that inflation and interest rates aren’t going to change. If you’re going to worry about inflation, then you also have to worry about interest rates, because when interest rates go up, inflation goes down, and vice versa. If inflation goes up, interest rates go up, and vice versa.

So I think a 4% rule for a retiree at 50 is unrealistic.

prompt: I'd love an essay on why the 4% rule became sacred. Where it came from (Bengen, 1994), what assumptions it smuggles in, and whether a 30-year rule makes any sense for someone retiring at 50.
response:
One of the most sacred rules in the financial world is the 4% rule, or in other words, if you retire with $1 million and withdraw $40,000 a year, the chances are very high that you won’t run out of money.

The rule was first published by William Bengen in his 1994 paper “Determining Withdrawal Rates Using Yield Adjustment Factors”. It became the de facto standard for retirement planning. It has been refined and improved upon by other people (including Bengen), and even with the 2008 financial crisis it’s still alive and well.

The 4% rule is not perfect. There are ways to improve it. It assumes you’re retired for 30 years, and if you’re retired for longer, you need to adjust it downward. It assumes your portfolio has a lot of equity, and the more bonds you add the more it needs to be adjusted.

The reason it is so successful is that most of the people using it don’t care about all of those fine details. They want to know the answer to the question “Can I retire?”. So the rule tells them that if they have $1 million and want to spend $40,000 a year, they can probably retire. This answers the question they care about.

Most of the time it’s enough for you to be able to retire. Sometimes it’s not. If you have $1 million and are 50, you may need the money to last more than 30 years, so the standard rule doesn’t work for you.

You don’t need a lot more than $1 million. But you need more than $1 million.

prompt: My wife and I combined finances after 6 years of marriage and it was weirdly harder emotionally than the wedding. Write a personal essay on merging money in a relationship, what it reveals, what it costs. Can be from a generic 'we' perspective.
response:
The day I moved my last paycheck to our joint account was one of the most stressful days of my life. I was 28 years old, and we had been married for six years.

My wife and I are both pretty open about money in our relationship, so I’ve written about this before, in a couple of posts. But we did not merge our finances at our wedding, like many couples do.

When I was 13, my parents divorced. My father was the breadwinner and he lost custody of me. We lived a long, nasty divorce for six years until he died in a house fire. So my first instinct was to keep things separate. And my wife’s first instinct was to combine everything.

For six years after our wedding, we did this thing where we had a separate account, and I put 20 percent of what I made into a joint account and she put 20 percent of what she made into the joint account, and we paid bills from the joint account.

At the beginning of the year, we would make an annual budget together and decide how much we were going to put into our joint account. And it was always like, “Okay, I’m going to put 30 percent of my paycheck into this account, and you’re going to put 30 percent of your paycheck into this account, and we’re going to put the rest into our separate accounts.”

And my wife and I are very good friends, but it did not work.

Because it felt weird to put money into our separate accounts, which felt like a kind of betrayal to me. So even though I was supposed to be putting 30 percent into our joint account and 70 percent into my own, I was always kind of guilty about it.

I was always kind of like, “Hey, I’m putting money into my own account, and that feels a little bad, because we’re supposed to put all this money together in this big pile and spend it together.”

And my wife and I both have pretty different tastes. I was always like, “I want to spend money on X,” and she was like, “No, I want to spend money on Y.”

So I would put money into my own account, and then I would go buy the things that I wanted to buy, because I wanted to avoid having these arguments where she was like, “No, why did you buy that?”

But at the same time, I hated doing it. I always felt guilty about having my own account.

I would be like, “I want to buy this thing, but I don’t feel good about spending money out of my account, I want to spend money out of our joint account.”

So then I would ask my wife to go buy it for me. And she would be like, “Okay, but that makes me feel weird, because I’m just like, ‘Oh, you want me to spend money for you on that thing?’”

So that was really awkward. It was like a bad marriage, in a lot of ways.

After six years, we decided to combine our accounts.

I was really excited about it. It made me very happy.

I was like, “Okay, I’m going to move everything from my separate accounts into the joint account, and I’m going to pay off all of my credit cards, and I’m going to pay off all of my loans, and it’s going to be great.”

And my wife was excited about it, too.

But it did not go very well.

The first night I paid off all my credit cards and loans, I went to bed and my wife was crying. She was crying because I had just paid off $100,000 of debt.

And I was really confused. I was like, “Why are you crying?” And she was like, “Because it’s really sad that you had $100,000 of debt that you didn’t tell me about.”

And that really, really hurt. It was like the worst thing I’ve ever heard anybody say to me.

And that was a really hard night for both of us.

And then I had to move all of my money into the joint account, which was kind of a scary thing for me, because that means I don’t have access to money that’s separate from my wife anymore.

And that was really scary for me.

Because I was like, “What if we’re in a bad fight and she doesn’t want to give me any money? What if we’re in a bad fight and I don’t have access to money and it’s really scary.”

I didn’t want to have that kind of a relationship.

And I was really nervous about it.

I remember I was like, “Okay, I’m going to move all of my money into the joint account, and I’m going to go to bed.”

And I did that, and then my wife was like, “Okay, so, do you want to move all of my money into the joint account?”

And I was like, “No, let’s not do that right now, let’s do that tomorrow.”

And she was like, “Okay, let’s do that tomorrow.”

And I went to bed, and my wife did not sleep at all. She was really sad about it, because she wanted everything to be in the same account.

And I was like, “I’m really nervous about doing that, I don’t want to do it.”

And I was kind of like, “I can’t believe my wife is so sad about this, this is so weird.”

And she was like, “I can’t believe you’re so nervous about this.”

And that was the weirdest part of it.

I was like, “I’m nervous about this, because I’m worried about what if we get in a fight.”

And she was like, “I’m sad about this, because we’re supposed to do this as a married couple, and you’re not doing it, and that’s really sad.”

And I was like, “I can’t believe you’re so sad about that.”

And it was really weird.

So then I thought, “Okay, let’s not do this right now, let’s think about it for a while.”

And after a few days, I was like, “Okay, I think I’m going to do this now.”

And I moved all of my money into the joint account, and I paid off my credit cards and loans, and I was really happy about it.

But my wife was not happy about it, because she was like, “You don’t want me to do that, I don’t want you to do that.”

And it took us a couple months to get through that.

And I think it was pretty painful for both of us.

Because it meant that I was like, “I’m not going to do this, because I don’t want to do this.”

And she was like, “I really want you to do this.”

And that was pretty hard for both of us.

And it took us a couple months to get through it.

But it was pretty painful, and I think that’s kind of the point.

Because when you’re getting married, you’re making promises that you’re going to put everything together, and that’s kind of a scary thing to do.

And it’s also kind of an expensive thing to do.

And I think people have a lot of pain with that, because it’s scary and it’s expensive.

And it’s like, “Hey, I don’t want to get divorced, but I really want my money back.”

prompt: Argue that buying individual stocks is mostly a hobby, and that's fine, as long as people are honest that it's entertainment.
response:
There are a couple of things that make the stock market more than a hobby. First, you can put in more time and effort, and get a better result. But this is a limited effect. Second, and more important, even a dumb person can put in minimal effort and still make a little money.

There are all kinds of other things that are more than hobbies. But they're more than hobbies in the same ways as the stock market.

This is what makes the stock market an unusual place to learn things. Most people think of it as one of those places that you need to be especially smart to do well in. But I think it's closer to the other way around.

In fact, the people who get rich on Wall Street seem to me to be less than average intellectually. I don't believe this is because they're stupid. It seems much more likely to me that the average IQ of people on Wall Street is high because being high IQ helps you get rich in ways that don't depend on understanding markets.

It's a common misconception that the stock market is some kind of contest between smart people. But it's not. The stock market is not a contest at all.

You could say that the stock market is a kind of contest, if you meant that it's a contest between different forms of investing. You're really competing against people who buy stocks, not against other people who buy stocks. And you're competing against them because there is a limited amount of money to be made from stocks. It's not a zero-sum game in the strict sense, because stocks can increase in value over time, and that creates new money. But at any one time, there is a limited amount of money to be made. And you're competing against all sorts of different kinds of investors. Most of the money in the market is not being managed by the kind of person who buys individual stocks. It's not just the mutual funds. The biggest part of the market is the index funds. And that's not even most of the rest of the market. The rest of the money is not necessarily managed by professional stock pickers. There are all kinds of money in the market: from the superstitious investor who buys stocks ending in a 7, to the fund manager who buys stocks on the basis of their carbon footprint.

The market is not a zero-sum game, and so there can't be an equilibrium, but if there were one, it would be some sort of weighted average of all the different types of investors, and the people buying individual stocks would only be one of the inputs.

When people try to make money by buying individual stocks, they're not trying to outsmart a specific opponent. They're just trying to be smarter than the average investor. And that average doesn't include them.

The average investor is the type of person who buys the S&P 500. And you can be smarter than that by buying the S&P 500. That's why you don't have to be especially smart to make money in the stock market.

But this means that if you want to do better, you don't have to be especially smart either.

What does it take to do better than the average investor? It takes knowing something that the average investor doesn't know. This can be an inside edge. Or it can be an idea that's been disproved, like buying stocks with a lot of debt. Or it can be that you just believe something that the average investor doesn't believe, like that a certain industry will do well. If you believe it and the average investor doesn't, you can make money by buying stocks in that industry.

So there are all kinds of things you can know that will make money in the stock market. And a lot of them aren't even things you can know. You can make money by believing something that isn't true, as long as it isn't true for the average investor either.

But the average investor believes things that aren't true. The average investor, if you're not careful, is even an investor that doesn't exist. There are all sorts of ways that investors can make money. And the average investor is a kind of Frankenstein's monster made up of all these different investors. And he believes all sorts of weird things.

So there are all sorts of ways you can be smarter than the average investor. And a lot of them are not things you can know.

prompt: Argue that buying individual stocks is mostly a hobby, and that's fine, as long as people are honest that it's entertainment.
response:
A lot of people who say that they invest by picking individual stocks, are actually investing to get a kick out of picking individual stocks. They’re doing it to have fun. And there’s nothing wrong with that! They just need to be honest with themselves about the fact that they’re doing it to have fun, because it’ll be more fun that way.

When people talk about “investing”, they almost always mean “buying stocks”.

And when people talk about “buying stocks”, they almost always mean “buying individual stocks”.

And when people talk about “buying individual stocks”, they almost always mean “picking individual stocks”.

And when people talk about “picking individual stocks”, they almost always mean “picking individual stocks based on my analysis of whether they look like they’re likely to go up”.

When you look at people doing this, it’s easy to conclude that they’re doing it for fun, and they’re not really making money.

But I’d like to suggest something more subtle: that a lot of them are doing it for fun, but they’re not even admitting that to themselves.

This might come off as a little weird, because I’m a big proponent of stock picking. But I mean it. I’m not saying it’s bad. I’m saying that people who do it should be honest with themselves about what they’re doing, because it’s more fun when you’re honest.

Let me tell you about a guy who was honest about it.

In the late 1980s, a friend of mine got a job working at a Wall Street investment company. His job was to talk to CEOs of companies he thought were good investments, and ask them to have their boards make the shares available for buyback, so that he could make more money. He had the best job ever. He was working at the center of power, talking to CEOs of big companies, and it was all to benefit himself.

One of the CEOs he talked to asked him “what kind of person are you?”

And he answered “well, I’d say I’m an investor.”

And the CEO replied “oh, no, you’re not an investor, you’re a gambler.”

And he said “no, I’m not a gambler, I’m an investor.”

And the CEO said “you are a gambler, you’re just not smart enough to admit it.”

The CEO was right.

And this guy wasn’t a bad guy. He was a smart guy, and a good guy. He did some great work at that company. But he was still a gambler.

If you want to be an investor, you can just buy an index fund. That’s what people do when they’re investing.

I’m not saying it’s wrong to pick individual stocks. In fact, it’s a great way to have fun. But it’s even more fun to admit it’s a hobby, rather than pretending it’s a job.

prompt: Argue that buying individual stocks is mostly a hobby, and that's fine, as long as people are honest that it's entertainment.
response:
I think I can make the case, in a short paragraph, that buying individual stocks is a hobby, not a financial strategy.

1. Individual stock pickers, on average, under-perform the market. This is, in fact, the point that the efficient market hypothesis is trying to make.

2. If stock picking underperforms on average, then it can’t be a reliable strategy to make money, or people would all do it.

3. So if people do stock picking anyway, the most likely reason is that it’s fun to them.

So the question becomes: is it okay to spend your time and money on entertainment? And the answer to that question is, obviously yes.

And it’s okay to spend *too much* time and money on it too, as long as you acknowledge it’s for entertainment. I’ve written a lot about this, so I’ll just link some examples.

The trouble comes when you say that a thing which is actually a hobby is also a strategy.

For example, I’ve written before about the people who make the case that “the market is too efficient for most people to beat, so we shouldn’t teach people how to invest.” I think this is wrong. I’m not saying people should be taught some magic strategy that beats the market - I’m saying they should be taught how to think about risk and reward, how to set aside an appropriate amount of their wealth for risk-taking, how to think about their own risk tolerance, and how to choose between different risks. This is what people actually need, and they can apply it to any risk they want, from individual stocks to cryptocurrency to real estate to starting a company to going to graduate school.

But I’m not saying that individual stock picking is an example of this, because it’s not. It’s not a strategy. It’s a hobby.

prompt: Essay: is frugality a virtue?
response:
A few weeks ago, in a comment on a post about a different virtue, I wrote:

If you're an effective altruist, then frugality isn't just a virtue but a moral imperative: every dollar you spend on anything non-essential is a dollar you could have spent on saving a life.

This was an uncharacteristically strong statement for me, which was probably why it drew so much attention.

It's a hard problem to evaluate whether frugality is a virtue or not. The most obvious reason for it to be a virtue is because it reduces your needs, which reduces your suffering. It's also a way to reduce your consumption and therefore your environmental impact.

The most obvious reason for it not to be a virtue is the same reason that it makes frugality a virtue in my statement above: if your money can be used to help people who need it, and you are so rich that saving a life by donating is easy for you, but so poor that spending it on yourself is not easy for you, then frugality might be bad.

My friend Will MacAskill, in his recent book Doing Good Better, argues that frugality is indeed bad, because you should donate your excess income. I don't know if I agree with him, but he's certainly much more qualified to talk about this topic than I am.

But I don't think I agree with Will, because I think that frugality has some other benefits that I don't see mentioned in Doing Good Better.

A couple of my friends are really frugal. They're not rich, but they are able to live without spending a lot of money. They live in a small apartment, and they have few possessions.

They both describe living frugally as something that makes them very happy. When they are not living frugally, they are not so happy.

I think this may be due to something that Will and I are both very familiar with: having the ability to choose.

When I was in high school, I worked at a grocery store that was one of two stores in a very small town. My manager at the time said that the reason we always had the most customers was because we had the best selection.

If you have the choice between a dozen kinds of cereal or one kind of cereal, you'll probably choose the former. But if you only have the one kind of cereal, you might not notice that it tastes bad, because you're used to it. And if you only have one kind of cereal, you won't notice that you're missing out on the other eleven, because you never see them.

If you have the choice between a house in the countryside and a house in the city, you'll probably choose the former if you live in the countryside. But if you've never lived in the city, you probably won't be as aware of that. And if you only have the countryside house, you won't be as aware that you've missed out on living in the city.

So if you live a frugal life and you have the ability to choose, you can choose to have a frugal life and be happy. If you don't have the ability to choose, you can't be as happy, because you can't be as sure that you're not missing out.

I don't know how many of us have the ability to choose a frugal life.

prompt: Essay: is frugality a virtue?
response:
A couple of months ago, I wrote an essay on how I learned to live on less than $50,000 a year and what I learned about frugality.

In response, I got a lot of mail from people who were confused. They didn’t seem to get the difference between my idea of frugality and what the word “frugal” usually means to people. So in this post, I’ll try to explain what frugality is to me.

What’s Frugality For?

To make money? If you spend less than you earn, you can save up money and grow your wealth.

To be able to do more than you could before? If you spend less, you have more money left over for things you like better.

But I think those are the two main justifications for frugality. If you don’t believe that spending less helps you either make money or spend it on something better, I can’t really see why you would want to spend less.

What’s Frugality Not For?

To feel good about being frugal? Sometimes people get a weird kick out of being frugal. They brag about being able to do things for less than other people, or brag about how they spend less than other people, or brag about how little they spend.

I can’t do this. I don’t like to brag, and I’m not sure being frugal is an accomplishment you should brag about.

To be able to say that you are frugal? I think you can be frugal without feeling like you are frugal. I try to spend less on stuff I don’t like than I would have before I started frugality, but I also spend more on stuff I like than I would have before I started frugality. For instance, if you read the frugality post linked above, you’d know that I spend $60,000 a year on housing, which is kind of expensive by American standards. But I like the house I live in, so I feel like I’m doing okay.

To have a sense of accomplishment for spending less than you could? Some people feel really good about spending less than they could. It makes them feel virtuous or something. But I don’t.

I don’t like wasting money. It feels bad to me. But I think this is the wrong way to go about it. I think there’s something more subtle than “I hate wasting money” that I want to understand.

The Virtue Of Frugality

The reason I think that frugality is a virtue is because it’s a part of having a sense of your own values.

I think the reason people say things like “I’m not going to spend all that money on food, it’s not worth it” is because they don’t feel that they value food enough to spend that much money on it. I think this is a good thing.

I know someone who spends $300 a week on good food. They like it and they can afford it, so I guess they must really like their food.

I think I would be able to eat that food, but it would be like eating a $100 pizza. I like pizza, but I don’t like it enough to spend $100 on a pizza. I’d probably eat it, and I’d probably like it, but I’d probably feel bad about having spent so much on it.

So, you might say that frugality is a virtue because it forces you to pay attention to your own values. You might say that it’s a virtue because it forces you to pay attention to what you like.

The problem with frugality is that if you do it wrong, it can be a terrible way to spend your time. People who spend their lives trying to find ways to save a few dollars on the little things that they don’t care about are wasting their time.

I think the way to do frugality right is to pay attention to your own values, and to spend less on things you don’t care about, and to spend more on things you do care about.

prompt: Essay: is frugality a virtue?
response:
I read a good essay today by Bryan Caplan called “Frugality, Virtue, and The Virtues”. I don’t agree with it at all, but I think it’s worth talking about anyway. Here are the basic ideas from the essay, with some commentary of my own:

The essay starts with a story about a friend, who used to work at a very high-end restaurant. He’s now a student at the Wharton School of Business, but he still cooks every day, often for his roommates. He has become known for his amazing ability to create gourmet meals from cheap ingredients. For instance, he once threw a dinner party for twelve guests for only $2.75 per person.

As Caplan puts it, he’s “a real-life superhero”. The ability to create gourmet meals out of thin air is “something I can’t do and never will. It’s a special skill.” He describes how he got a taste of it when he met him, and how he was immediately “overwhelmed”.

He goes on to say that he doesn’t see his friend’s frugality as a virtue. He writes:

Frugality is a virtue in my model only if we can make money from thin air, or at least in an amount large enough to do some good.

So he doesn’t think his friend has achieved some sort of virtue by making his elaborate meals on the cheap. He thinks he just has a useful skill, which he probably picked up at the high-end restaurant. But he does think that this is something we should celebrate.

Caplan then proceeds to argue that frugality is a virtue. I don’t think he argues it very well, but I want to try to reconstruct his argument as much as possible.

He quotes Aristotle’s definition of frugality:

Frugality, Aristotle says, is “a disposition to act according to a mean, relative to us, with a view to the avoidance of excesses both in expenditure and in acquisition, and in fact in all cases in which one thing is being given and another received.”

He then goes on to describe a “virtue of the mean”. In this model, virtues are defined by the fact that they represent a balance of excess and deficiency. For example, generosity is a virtue because it balances being too stingy and too reckless.

Caplan goes on to say that this isn’t true of the usual definition of frugality. He quotes from Wikipedia:

In economics, frugality refers to a lifestyle in which the individual tries to use as few resources as possible, especially financial resources. Frugality is usually considered a good habit, as it is the opposite of extravagance and squandering.

This doesn’t represent the virtue of a mean. Caplan says that if you try to live as frugally as possible, then you’ll end up with less money than you need to support your family. So the virtue of frugality isn’t “to use as few resources as possible.”

He then proposes this definition:

Frugality, like other virtues, should consist of the best balance of spending and saving.

This doesn’t quite work though, because it’s not the best balance of spending and saving that is the virtue. It’s the best balance of spending and saving that is the virtuous action. Virtue is a character trait that results in virtuous actions. It’s like the difference between courage and bravado. Bravado is the act of risking your life for a good cause. Courage is the trait that will cause you to do the right thing.

The best balance of spending and saving isn’t the same for everyone. Some people have a lot of money, and for them the best balance would probably be to spend it all. Other people have very little money, and for them the best balance would probably be to spend very little. So, the virtue of frugality can’t be a fixed value. It can’t be spending only $50 a month, or it would not be the best balance for everyone.

Caplan then proceeds to argue that the virtue of frugality is a fixed value. This is how he argues it. First he says that we need to have a single virtue that represents the balance of spending and saving. He writes:

For there to be any virtue at all, the “best balance” has to be the same for everybody. Otherwise, there will be no way to distinguish the virtuous from the not.

The problem is that this is not true at all. There are lots of virtues that are not the same for everybody. If someone has a lot of money, then it is virtuous for them to give more to charity. If someone has a lot of power, then it is virtuous for them to use that power to help others. And it is virtuous for a soldier to fight in war, but it is not virtuous for a civilian to do so.

If the virtue of frugality is not the same for everybody, then we can’t use it to distinguish the virtuous from the not. In other words, if everyone has their own personal level of frugality, then everyone will be frugal. There’s no point in having a virtue that everyone has. It will give you no information.

It’s not hard to come up with a definition of frugality that solves these problems. The virtue of frugality is to spend money on things that give you the most pleasure for the amount of money you spend. This will vary from person to person, but it will always be the same value. And it gives us a way to distinguish the virtuous from the not.

I think this definition is very similar to the one Caplan uses. He says:

For the frugal person, the question to ask about any purchase is whether or not it adds more to your life than it takes away.

This is the question of marginal utility. I’ve never seen anyone use this definition of frugality, but it seems like it could be useful.

response:
You just got your first pay check. It feels weird in your hand. It’s $2,340 after taxes. That’s a lot of money, especially if you’re not 100 years old. And you’re not.

This is a good time to think about what you should do with your money.

Let’s start with what you probably should do with your money.

### 1. Put It All In A Roth IRA

There are two kinds of IRAs: Traditional and Roth.

Traditional IRAs are tax deferred. In other words, you don’t pay taxes on it until you take it out when you retire. This sounds great, but it’s really not.

Roth IRAs are tax-free. If you put money in today, you don’t pay taxes on it, and you never will.

I could explain more, but I think you already get the idea. If you have a choice, pick a Roth IRA.

This is a huge advantage for you because your pay taxes will probably be low now (and you’re a young person so your tax rate is likely to be lower for a while). That means it’s a great time to make Roth IRA contributions, because you’re saving on the lowest possible tax rates.

So that’s why you should put it all in a Roth IRA.

You won’t have access to that money until you’re at least 59, but that’s fine. You probably won’t want that money until then anyway. It’s a lot of money to have lying around. It would just make you want to spend it.

This sounds great.

So why wouldn’t you put it all in a Roth IRA?

### 2. Save For College

This is a good reason not to put your money in a Roth IRA.

If you save this money now, you might not have to go into debt for college.

If you can get into a good college without any debt, you’ll probably get a good job after you graduate. That might mean you have more money than people who don’t get good jobs, and if you put it in a Roth IRA, you’ll have more money than people who get good jobs, and maybe more money than people who don’t get good jobs but also got a lot of money from winning the lottery.

This is what happens when you save your first paycheck.

So you could save for college. That would be a good idea.

But I don’t want to tell you exactly what you should do. So here’s what I want you to think about.

What do you think your chances are of getting into college? Do you think you’ll have enough money to get there without putting up any money from your parents?

If your chance of going to college is low, it’s probably not worth saving for it.

If you have a good chance of going to college and you still have to borrow money to do it, maybe it’s worth saving for.

If you’re pretty sure you’re going to college and you won’t need to borrow any money, it probably isn’t worth it.

So, again, this is what you might think about.

### 3. Buy A Used Car

This isn’t a very good way to spend money. Cars are bad.

But maybe you really want a used car.

So buy a used car.

### You Decide

I don’t want to tell you exactly what you should do. I just want you to think about what you want to do.

I just want to tell you what you might want to think about.

You can’t.

The decision that’s right for you is the decision that feels right to you right now.

And that’s the decision that I made.

I invested the money and I was happy. I saved the money and I was happy. I spent the money and I was happy.

It’s not about making the right decision.

I think about what made me happy.

prompt: Why lifestyle inflation is underrated. Hear me out: if you never spend more as you earn more, what was the point?
response:
When people hear of a lifestyle inflation, they think of some extravagant behavior. They say “You have to control it, or you’ll end up with the highest salary and the least savings of anyone”. But the fact is that you’ll need a lot of savings to retire, and that you’ll be working for years before you can retire, so you’ll have a lot of time for your lifestyle to improve.

This is the point that everyone who tells you to avoid lifestyle inflation misses.

I’ll explain with some examples.

## Example: The person with no lifestyle inflation

Suppose you start work at $50,000 per year, and you have no lifestyle inflation, that is, you don’t adjust your spending up as your income goes up.

Let’s make it even more extreme: Suppose you start work at 18, with no savings.

You’ve been making money for 10 years now. You’ve been living on $50,000 a year the whole time. Your savings are zero.

So you’re 28 now. You have $0.

## Example: The person with a lot of lifestyle inflation

I like to think of lifestyle inflation as a percentage of your income that you spend. If your lifestyle inflation is 100%, that means you spend 100% of your income. If your lifestyle inflation is 10%, you spend 10% of your income and save 90%.

Here we’ll take a very high lifestyle inflation: 95%. That means you spend 95% of your income, and save 5%.

We’ll suppose that you start out at $50,000, and it goes up 5% each year.

Now you’re 28, and your income is $80,600 a year. You spend 95% of that, which is $76,570.

You’ve only saved 5%, which is $4,030.

But it’s not that simple, because you saved less in the past when you were earning less.

If you start earning $50,000 and your income goes up 5% per year, and you spend 95% of it, then you’ll have $25,350 by the time you’re 28.

That’s 6 times more savings than the person who doesn’t have any lifestyle inflation.

## Example: A normal lifestyle inflation

Here, you start earning $50,000, and your income goes up 5% a year, and you spend 70% of it.

By the time you’re 28, you have saved $90,000.

You can do a lot better if you have a lower lifestyle inflation. For example, if you spend 40% of your income, and it goes up 5% a year, you’ll have saved $180,000 by the time you’re 28.

So here’s how you can get $180,000 by the time you’re 28:

- Start earning $50,000 at 18
- Your income goes up 5% a year
- You live on 40% of your income (which starts at $20,000 a year)

That’s not an extravagant lifestyle at all. It’s just that you save 60% of your income.

This is the point that I think people who talk about lifestyle inflation miss. The idea of “living on $20,000 a year” is so far removed from reality, that it’s easy to overlook the fact that if you do that, you’ll have a lot of savings.

But in this scenario, your lifestyle is growing 5% a year. It’s not static.

## Example: Someone with a lot of savings

Now I want to get to the point where I can retire.

I know from the FIRE community that to retire, you have to have 25 times your annual expenses.

If I spend $20,000 a year, that means that to retire, I’ll have to have $500,000.

But I’m 28, and I have $180,000. That’s not enough.

So I work another 5 years, and in that time I increase my savings to $514,000.

I’m 33 now.

So this is the plan:

- Start earning $50,000 at 18
- Your income goes up 5% a year
- You live on 40% of your income (which starts at $20,000 a year)
- You’ll be able to retire at 33

That’s not even the end of it, because this scenario assumes you don’t get any interest on your savings.

## What this means

If you want to retire young, you don’t have to live like a monk. All you have to do is:

- Start working when you’re young (maybe 18)
- Make sure your income grows 5% a year (or more)
- Live on 40% of your income (which starts at $20,000 a year)

That’s not an unusual lifestyle. You’d have a $500/month lifestyle inflation.

prompt: Why lifestyle inflation is underrated. Hear me out: if you never spend more as you earn more, what was the point?
response:

prompt: An essay on inheritance: should parents leave money to their children at all, or does it do more harm than good? I'd like it to take Warren Buffett's 'enough to do anything but not enough to do nothing' line as a starting point and push against it a little.

A few years ago I was sitting with Warren Buffett. He was talking about leaving money to his kids, and said that the right amount was “enough to do anything, but not enough to do nothing”.

I liked this idea, so much that I thought about it for years. But the more I thought about it, the more I started to wonder about it. And a couple of months ago I finally decided that it’s wrong. Not totally wrong, but just wrong enough that I want to write down why.

The idea that you should leave kids enough to do anything but not enough to do nothing comes from an assumption that most people do not have enough money to do what they want to do. It’s a reasonable assumption.

Most people are not rich. They have to work to make money. So the idea that leaving them a bit of money will free them to pursue their dreams makes sense.

But the more I think about it, the less it seems to make sense. If a kid doesn’t have enough money to do anything, what’s he going to do with money that isn’t enough to do nothing?

This brings us to the other half of the equation, the part about not enough to do nothing. The assumption here is that people who are not doing anything are lazy. That there is a natural tendency toward laziness, and that money encourages this tendency.

And this seems to be a good assumption to make. If you give somebody enough money so that he doesn’t need to work, chances are he won’t. So the idea that money will make people lazy, that it’s something to watch out for, that you should leave just enough to make a kid comfortable but not so much that he might become lazy, this seems like a good idea.

So on one hand, you assume that most people don’t have enough money to do what they want, and that leaving some money to your kids will free them to do what they want. And on the other hand you assume that money makes people lazy, and that you should leave them just enough to make them comfortable, but not so much that they become lazy.

The problem is that you’re assuming that laziness and wanting to do something are opposites, and that’s just not true. It’s possible to be lazy and to also want to do something, and this is how most people are most of the time.

Most people don’t have a dream they’re chasing. They don’t want to be a writer or a scientist or a musician, and they don’t want to start a company or write a book or do any other kind of creative work. But they also don’t want to sit on the couch and watch TV all day.

They want to get up in the morning and do something, but they don’t have something they want to do. And this is the kind of people who will most benefit from a trust fund, but they’re exactly the kind of people who, according to Warren Buffett’s theory, you shouldn’t leave any money to.

The best reason I can think of for why Buffett says this is because he’s really rich. He’s too rich to know what it feels like not to have anything to do.

If you’re very rich, like Buffett is, you have to think about what to do all day, every day. He’s not sure what to do with his money, so it’s reasonable that he’s not sure what to do with his kids’ money.

But for most people, it’s really hard to get to the point of “having so much money you don’t know what to do with it”. For most people, the problem is the opposite, that they don’t have enough money to do what they want, and the reason they don’t know what to do is that they’re not sure how to get enough money to do anything.

And this is the kind of people who will benefit from an inheritance. They’ll get up in the morning, and they’ll know exactly what to do.

They’ll have a plan. They’ll know what to work on, what to learn, what to make, and how to make it. They’ll know how to get what they want, and they’ll go get it. And this is the kind of people you want to leave money to, because money is a very powerful force, and it can take people in very different directions.

A small inheritance will never be enough to do anything for somebody who doesn’t have anything he wants to do. But it will make it possible for people who have something they want to do to actually get what they want.

That’s the real reason to leave money to your kids. It’s not about making them comfortable, it’s not about being lazy, and it’s not about doing anything but not doing nothing. It’s about doing exactly what they want, and making sure they have the resources to make it happen.
