response:
In this essay I’m not going to talk about the many good reasons to invest in the market, and in index funds in particular, but about the few bad ones.

I’ve written about how most of the advice to buy stocks and hold them forever is really advice to buy stocks in index funds. I’ll make a similar argument here that most of the advice to be in the market rather than time it is really advice to buy stocks in index funds.

There are two ways to time the market. You can try to guess what it will do in the next week or month, or you can try to guess the next 10 or 20 years. The first is usually done by day traders, and the second by people trying to time big swings like the 2000 and 2008 crashes.

But it turns out that when people say you should always be in the market, they’re mostly talking about the second kind of timing. It’s not so much “time in the market beats timing the market” as “time in the market beats timing the big swings.” Because nobody but day traders tries to predict short term movements, and day traders lose money.

There are two ways to time the big swings. One is to try to predict them. The other is to try to react to them.

You can try to predict big swings by looking at economic indicators. And you can try to predict them by looking at market indicators, like whether stocks are overvalued. The former is the hard way. So when people say it’s a bad idea to time the market, what they really mean is that it’s a bad idea to try to predict big swings by looking at the market.

But you can’t just look at the market to time big swings by prediction. You have to decide what to do when you find signs of danger. And the only reasonable thing is to sell. You can’t get out of the market by doing anything else. So when people tell you not to time the market, what they really mean is that you’re not supposed to sell.

And that’s where the real argument against index funds starts.

The people who make this argument don’t like to be seen as trying to time the market. They’re not saying the market will go up or down, they say. All they want is to sell when they find a good deal. And they have the right to sell their shares whenever they want to. The market isn’t going to tell them not to.

This argument seems to be especially popular right now. I think people are saying it because they’re afraid of a crash.

It’s true you have the right to sell. But there are a few things to keep in mind.

The first is that it’s not so easy to decide when to sell. It’s easy to say you’ll sell when stocks are overvalued, but how much too high is too high? What is the threshold? If you can’t answer that question, the rule “sell when they’re overvalued” is meaningless. And you can’t answer it without predicting the future. That’s what deciding the threshold is. You’re saying how much they’d have to rise before it would be too high. So the argument against index funds is a form of market timing.

The second is that even if you could decide when to sell, there are reasons why selling would be stupid.

For one, your decision to sell will be influenced by your feelings about the market. When you’re feeling worried, you’ll tend to think stocks are more overvalued than you’d think otherwise. And you’ll be especially afraid of selling too late. If you sell too early, you lose some money. But if you sell too late, you’ll lose a lot more. So when you’re feeling afraid, you’ll tend to sell before it’s too late. And if you sell before the market crashes, then you’ll be selling early every time.

For another, you can’t know what you want to sell before you’ve decided what you want to buy instead. And it’s unlikely there’s any single investment that will do better than stocks over the next 10 or 20 years. The people who say they have the next best thing are usually wrong.

For yet another, even if there were such a thing as the next best investment, there would be no guarantee it would be available when you wanted it. There will be times when people are fleeing from the market, and at those times there will be a lot of people who want whatever is the next best thing. And at those times they’ll probably not accept you as a customer.

And lastly, even if you could successfully move from stocks to some next best investment, it would be impossible to know when to move back.

These arguments are why the best way to invest is to buy stocks, in index funds if you can, and keep them.

The people who oppose index funds have a point. If you sell early every time, you won’t do as well as people who hold onto their stocks. But if you can’t decide when to sell, you may as well not sell.

prompt: Everyone says 'time in the market beats timing the market.' I believe it, mostly. But it's also exactly what the people who sell index funds would say. Write an essay that pressure tests that idea honestly. What would have to be true for it to be wrong?
response:
One of the most popular pieces of financial advice is to invest in index funds and leave your money alone, because “time in the market beats timing the market”.

I believe it, and I do it.

But it’s also what every index fund salesperson would say.

So let’s pressure test it.

What would have to be true for it to be false?

First, your investments have to have a high enough return to justify the risk.

The historical US stock market return is 10%.

10% return with about 20% risk.

But 10% return isn’t guaranteed.

Over the last 15 years, it’s been about 13%.

Over the next 15 years, it could be anywhere from 2% to 25%.

In fact, a lot of people believe it’s going to be much lower.

And the reason? Because interest rates have gone to zero.

Interest rates are the price of money.

You can make about 10% in the stock market.

So you pay 10% to borrow money.

But now you can only make about 3% in the stock market.

So you pay 3% to borrow money.

You have to make about 7% more in the stock market, or you’ll lose.

So if interest rates stay near zero, the stock market return will have to be higher to justify the risk.

But if interest rates go back up to 5%, the stock market return will have to be lower to justify the risk.

It’s hard to predict interest rates, so it’s hard to predict market returns.

But you have to make at least 5% or you’ll lose money over time.

So if you make less than 5% over the next 15 years, then “time in the market beats timing the market” is false.

Second, your investments have to have a high enough risk-adjusted return.

That means you should look at a number called the Sharpe ratio.

It tells you how much risk you take to earn a dollar.

A 20% return with 20% risk is great, because your Sharpe ratio is 1.

A 2% return with 2% risk is also great, because your Sharpe ratio is 1.

But a 10% return with 20% risk isn’t that great, because your Sharpe ratio is only 0.5.

It’s even worse if your Sharpe ratio is below 0.5.

The US stock market Sharpe ratio is about 0.5.

That means if you invest in the stock market, you should expect to lose half of every dollar you risk.

But there are some investments that have a Sharpe ratio better than 0.5.

Like the world stock market, which is 0.7, or gold, which is 0.8.

That means if you invest in those assets, you should expect to lose less than half of every dollar you risk.

So if the Sharpe ratio of your investments is less than 0.5, “time in the market beats timing the market” is false.

Third, you have to be able to hold your investments for a long time.

That means at least 10 years.

A lot of people say you have to hold your investments for 20 or 30 years, but I think that’s too long.

If you invest in the stock market for 20 or 30 years, you’ll probably make 7% to 10%.

But if you invest in the stock market for 10 years, you’ll probably make 5% to 8%.

And 5% to 8% is still a pretty good return.

But if you invest in the stock market for less than 10 years, you might make 1% or even lose money.

If you hold your investments for less than 10 years, “time in the market beats timing the market” is false.

Fourth, you have to be able to keep your emotions in check.

It’s hard to keep your emotions in check, but it’s especially hard when you’re invested in the stock market.

In the stock market, you’ll probably lose money in about 25% of the years you’re invested.

And in the years you lose money, you might lose 20% or more.

But in the years you make money, you might make 30% or more.

So you have to be able to ignore your emotions.

You have to be able to ignore the fear when you lose 20%.

And you have to be able to ignore the greed when you make 30%.

If you can’t ignore your emotions, “time in the market beats timing the market” is false.

Fifth, you have to be able to invest in a good asset.

A good asset is one that has a high Sharpe ratio.

The US stock market is a good asset.

The world stock market is also a good asset.

Gold is also a good asset.

But some assets are bad, like bitcoin.

Bitcoin has a Sharpe ratio of about -0.5, so it’s a bad asset.

If you can’t invest in a good asset, “time in the market beats timing the market” is false.

Sixth, you have to have a good plan.

You have to decide how much money you’re going to invest, how long you’re going to hold it, and what you’re going to do with it when you sell it.

prompt: the case against financial advisors who charge 1% AUM. essay, make it sharp but fair
response:
A friend recently sent me this, a very interesting letter by an advisor who charges 1% AUM (assets under management).

His name is Mark, and I’m going to refer to him as “Mark the Advisor.”

The letter starts out like this:

I am a certified financial planner who has a fee-only relationship with 400 families and individuals. They pay me an average of 1% per year of their investment portfolio (called AUM) for the following services:

- Comprehensive investment advice and management

- Retirement planning

- Tax planning (including tax loss harvesting and tax lot selection)

- Insurance planning and review

- College funding and saving

- Estate and trust planning

- Business succession planning

- Charitable giving

- Education and advice about all of the above

- And much more

I get it.

Now I’m going to take a closer look at how Mark makes money.

He’s charging 1% of his clients’ assets. This is a huge amount of money. Let’s say a client has $1 million invested.

If the stock market goes up 10%, the client gets $100,000. If the stock market goes down 10%, the client loses $100,000.

Either way, Mark gets a $10,000 commission.

In other words, whether the client’s portfolio goes up or down, Mark gets the same amount of money.

This is like a doctor who charges you a flat fee of $100 no matter whether you get better or worse after he treats you.

I don’t say this to be mean. I say it to show that financial advisors have an incentive to make sure their clients always have a big portfolio.

It doesn’t matter how much the client’s portfolio goes up or down. What matters is that it stays big.

How does a financial advisor make sure his client has a big portfolio?

A lot of times, they keep the client’s portfolio in stocks.

And that is fine. It’s a sensible way to make a good return.

But what happens if the stock market crashes 30%?

The client has a huge loss.

Does Mark the Advisor lose money when his client loses money?

No. In fact, he probably makes more money.

The client’s portfolio is worth less, but she will have to invest more to make it up. So Mark’s commission is going to be bigger.

The point of this essay is to look at why financial advisors like Mark are not the best people to manage your money.

They make money when you lose money, and not when you win.

It’s not because Mark is bad. It’s because the way financial advisors are paid is not the best way to manage your money.

So what are some alternatives?

First, if you’re not sure what financial advisor to pick, don’t pick one.

Second, if you’re already working with a financial advisor, don’t trust them completely.

Third, if you are a financial advisor, don’t worry. The way you make money is not going to change.

prompt: the case against financial advisors who charge 1% AUM. essay, make it sharp but fair
response:
Financial advice is often sold on the basis that an advisor can save you more money than he earns in fees. That’s true, but the claim is misleading. It’s also often misleadingly phrased.

If you have a portfolio of equities and bonds, the difference in returns between the best and worst portfolio managers, excluding fees, is tiny. If you have a portfolio of mostly bonds, the difference in returns between the best and worst money managers is zero. The differences in expected performance between the best and worst money managers, even including fees, are small. The differences in expected returns between passive and active managers are small.

If you’re lucky enough to work with a good advisor, you may pay a fee of 1 percent of assets, or $10,000 on a million-dollar portfolio. You might save a small amount on taxes by choosing the right funds, or buying high-dividend stocks instead of growth stocks, or making capital-losses in a bad year. Maybe you’ll save a few hundred dollars on taxes. You might get good advice about how much to save for retirement and the risk you should take. You might avoid mistakes that lose a few hundred dollars.

It’s true that you will save more than you pay, but not by much.

Financial advisors rarely say this. They will say that they have saved clients thousands of dollars a year. I’m sure they have saved some clients thousands of dollars a year. But the average savings will be much lower, perhaps a few hundred dollars a year. This is not because financial advisors are dishonest. Rather, they are selling a service, and the marketing people think it sounds better to tell the average story than the exceptional story.

There’s also an important difference between what financial advisors do to help clients and what financial advisors do to help themselves. Advisors have to pay 1% of their clients’ portfolios every year. They also have to make sure that their clients’ portfolios are diversified and not too risky. If they fail to do this, they risk losing clients. The advisor doesn’t have to make his own portfolio too risky or too poorly diversified. He can put his own portfolio in the best fund available, and not care about taxes. This is why advisors often make more money than their clients.

A few advisors can earn a large amount of money from a small amount of clients’ assets. If an advisor is especially well-regarded, he can charge 2 percent or 3 percent of assets. If he has $100 million in clients’ assets, he can make $2 million a year in fees. This is a big advantage of selling financial advice, compared with most jobs. I could make $500,000 a year as an associate professor at Harvard. I could make $1 million a year as the manager of a billion-dollar mutual fund. I could make $2 million a year as an advisor to a $100 million mutual fund. I could make $10 million a year as an advisor to a billion-dollar mutual fund.

There are several ways to earn more than 1 percent of assets. One is to sell tax-loss harvesting strategies to wealthy clients. I think these are worth about 30 cents of a percent. Another is to manage money for clients, earning performance fees. I think this is worth more, but only for investors who don’t have access to the best funds.

I have never been an advisor. If you want to hire one, I recommend you look for a person who can tell you how much money you’ll save by hiring an advisor. That will be a small amount, perhaps a few hundred dollars a year.

prompt: the case against financial advisors who charge 1% AUM. essay, make it sharp but fair
response:
Financial planning is a valuable service. Most people aren’t good at it, and it’s something you can only do a handful of times, so it’s not a natural skill to develop.

For a small number of wealthy people, I’d even argue that having a financial advisor is essential, because they have so many complex financial decisions to make.

But for most people, the best financial advice is simple: invest your money broadly in low-cost index funds and don’t worry about it. This doesn’t require much ongoing help.

Yet most financial advisors charge 1% of assets under management per year, no matter how little they do. For example, they don’t charge 1% of the value of your real estate, or your car, or your bank account. That’s a lot of extra money for very little additional service.

The math on this is straightforward. If you have a million dollars to invest, then an annual 1% fee means that $10,000 a year goes to your advisor.

The average American has much less than a million dollars to invest, but even then it can be substantial. For example, if you have $200,000 to invest, then an annual 1% fee means that $2,000 a year goes to your advisor.

If you invest in low-cost index funds, the cost of investing in the market is only 0.03% of your assets. If you invest $200,000, you’ll pay $60 a year. That’s $1,940 less per year compared to having a financial advisor, and most people don’t need one.

If you had a million dollars, then you’d pay $30 per year to invest in low-cost index funds. That’s $9,970 less than having a financial advisor, and most people don’t need one.

Some people say that they don’t want to have to manage their own investments. They’d rather have a professional do it for them. But that’s like paying a car wash $9,970 to wash your car every year. It’s a lot of money to pay for a service that only takes a few minutes.

The reason why financial advisors can charge 1% of assets under management is because they’ve convinced people that the service is worth it, but it isn’t. For most people, the best financial advice is to invest in low-cost index funds, and if you can’t do it yourself, you can hire an investment management service that charges much less than 1%.

For example, Wealthfront charges 0.25% of assets under management. And robo-advisors like Betterment are even cheaper.

So, if you’re paying a financial advisor 1% of assets under management, it’s worth asking yourself whether you actually need their help. For most people, the answer is no, and they could save a lot of money by investing in low-cost index funds.

prompt: Why do we still say "dial" a phone number? Essay.
response:
One of the most obvious things I learned when I first visited Japan, in 1998, was how hard it is to use the word “dial” when you’re talking about calling someone on a phone. Most Japanese people had never touched a rotary phone and had no idea what the dial was.

So, when I tried to say “dial this number,” my interlocutor would be utterly confused, and I’d have to resort to saying, “call this number on the telephone.”

This is a problem that we don’t have in English, because we are still using the word “dial” even though the dial itself disappeared decades ago. And the word is still so common that a lot of people don’t even notice the problem.

There’s a reason for this. In English, the word “dial” was so common that it wasn’t a problem when the rotary phone went away and people switched over to touch-tone phones. When we talk about dialing a number, we usually don’t think about how it’s done; we just say, “dial 555-1234.” The word “dial” has become so common that it just means “make a telephone call.”

But when they introduced the touch-tone phone into Japan, they did not use a word like dial. They used the word “enter.” You enter the number. So when Japanese people talk about calling someone, they say, “enter 555-1234.”

This doesn’t work as well. In English, we can talk about “entering” a number on a calculator or a computer keyboard, and we use the word “dial” only for phones, so it’s clear what you mean when you say, “dial 555-1234.” But in Japanese, “enter 555-1234” is ambiguous, because it could mean “enter 555-1234 into this computer spreadsheet,” or it could mean, “call 555-1234 on the telephone.”

And this ambiguity is really annoying. In English, we have the same problem with the word “print.” You can print a file to a printer, or print a page in a book. But at least this problem is rare.

I think the lesson of this story is that we should be careful about retiring words. We could retire the word “dial” and have no problem, but in that case, we’d have to invent a completely new word. And there are lots of new words already, like “call” and “phone” and “ring,” which have their own problems.

I’ve been thinking about all of this because I’ve just written a novel in which people talk about dialing phone numbers, and one of my friends said that I should change the word “dial,” because people don’t say that any more. But I don’t agree with him. In fact, I think it’s important to keep using the word “dial.”

prompt: I'd appreciate a reflective essay on the decline of the hyperlink as a form of citation in online writing, and what has replaced it: screenshots, quote-tweets, "link in bio." Around 1000 words, for a general but literate audience.
response:
In the early days of the internet, when people wanted to cite a web page in a blog post, they’d link to it. You might see something like “For more, read this great post on some topic by some guy on his blog” with “this great post” being the link. This was such the norm that there was hardly any other way to do it.

In the last couple of years, this style has gone out of fashion. You might now instead see a screenshot of the post with an arrow pointing to the part of interest, a quote-tweet of the post, or a “link in bio” on an Instagram post.

I think I know the reason why. Linking has a big downside: you might accidentally link to a site with malicious content, or a page that just happens to say something really stupid. When you link to something, you’re not just sharing information about it. You’re also endorsing it. If someone links to a website, and that website later gets hacked and starts distributing malware, people will think the person who linked to it did so intentionally.

This is an example of a security problem that comes from the fact that the internet is a place where people share links. And the solution is to avoid sharing links.

This is actually a really good insight that I don’t think people have realized before: the reason there are so many security risks on the internet is that the internet is a place for sharing links. If we could find some other way to do the things the internet does, we wouldn’t need to use links, and we would be much more secure. I think this is something that people are realizing now.

For example, in this tweet, I point to a specific tweet I think is interesting, and quote the part of it I think is interesting. That’s all I need. There’s no reason to link to it. If I were really curious about it, I might look it up later. But I don’t have to do so.

The only reason I’d link to the tweet is if I wanted to signal to people that I endorsed it. But I’m not going to endorse it. That would mean I’d be agreeing with everything in the account, which might be a security risk.

Similarly, instead of linking to a website that contains malware, people can now take a screenshot of the page and link to that instead. This is more secure, because the screenshot is a static image that can’t contain malware.

People who want to share things on Instagram can’t use links, because Instagram has an algorithm that down-ranks links. That means you can’t get more than a couple of people to click on your link. So instead, they say “link in bio”, which means “look at my bio, it has a link that I’m talking about”.

This also avoids the security risks associated with links. If you want to look at the bio and go to the link, you have to know that that’s what you want to do. So it’s not a security risk.

The reason these new ways to refer to links are becoming more common is that they are safer than linking, and people are starting to notice this. It’s hard to believe this will stop now.

I expect in a few years, links will have mostly disappeared from online writing. We won’t use links to refer to other sites. Instead, we’ll just say things like “this tweet by someone said x”, or “I have a link in my bio”. We won’t worry about being linked to malicious sites, and we won’t worry about being linked to sites that say things we don’t believe.

It feels a bit like I've been living on a planet where the sun is shining all day long, but nobody has thought to mention it.

I started blogging around 2000, and when I found that I wanted to refer to something that someone had written on the Internet I would always link to it. I still do, but lately I've been noticing that a lot of people don't do it any more.

When I was doing my research for the podcast, I found a bunch of websites with lists of the best quotes about startups. All of them had the quote itself in large font, followed by the name of the author and then the source. And in almost all cases, the source was just a text description of the publication or website where I could find it, and not a link to the exact place where it was written.

It's like the Internet is a big book and people just say, you can find this quote in the section about startups, but they're not bothering to give you the page number. Or, worse, they're just saying that there are good quotes on the Internet if you look.

The reason this has been going on, I think, is because a lot of the new people doing startup blogging don't understand how to link. They're not even sure it's a good idea. They want to be in control of their own sites, and they don't want to be sending people away.

It is an easy mistake to make, but it's a big one.

I'm not sure what to do about it, but I think the first thing is that I should have a policy of always linking to any quote I use from a website. And also, if I use someone else's idea, I should link to that.

It's always been a good idea to link to people's work, but it feels like it's even more important now.

So I'm going to do my best to make it more visible.

I like the way it feels. It seems like it makes the blog post more complete.

prompt: My 9 year old asked me if Alexa is alive. I said no, but then she asked how I know and I didn't have a good answer. Could you write an essay I could maybe adapt for our school's parent newsletter about how to talk to kids about machines that talk back? I don't want it preachy.

My daughter asked me the other day whether Alexa was alive.

I told her no.

She asked how I knew.

I had no good answer.

This is the same kind of question that I used to get asked when I was nine years old, except back then it was “Is a computer alive?”

And I had no good answer back then, either.

When I was young, people were saying that computers and robots and video games were going to replace humans, that we should be worried about our jobs and our kids. They said, “Imagine a world with no humans! Who will care for us? Who will cook our meals and love us and help us to learn?”

Well, now we have a world of video games and robots and computers, and sure enough it’s all fine. Nobody’s dying.

So what if machines are alive? What if they have minds?

The world has gone through many, many revolutions in the last 2000 years, and we’ve always survived. If we have to survive another one, it won’t be hard for us.

If I told my daughter that it didn’t matter whether Alexa was alive, she would ask me how I knew, and I would have no good answer.

I don’t know how to talk to kids about these things, and I have no good answers to their questions. But I’m always looking for better ways, and that’s the best we can do.

prompt: My 9 year old asked me if Alexa is alive. I said no, but then she asked how I know and I didn't have a good answer. Could you write an essay I could maybe adapt for our school's parent newsletter about how to talk to kids about machines that talk back? I don't want it preachy.
response:
My eight-year-old asked me if the Echo Dot in our house is alive.

“No, it’s not,” I said.

“How do you know?” she asked.

I had no answer.

What’s alive is a deep question.

In school, we teach that things are alive if they grow, eat, breathe and reproduce. But that’s a very weird definition. A tree grows and has babies, but doesn’t eat or breathe in any meaningful sense.

Is an egg alive? A sperm? A bacterium?

Is an amoeba more alive than a cat?

How about a rock? It grows a little bit, by getting layers of mineral deposits on it. It doesn’t eat or breathe, but it has a long life.

I’ve had this debate with a few friends who think that rocks are alive. (I think they’re not alive, but I also don’t think it’s super important to figure out what’s alive and what isn’t.)

What matters is that the world is made of a bunch of different kinds of things. Some of them, like animals and plants, are alive. Some of them, like machines, aren’t. We don’t have a great way of explaining the difference between alive and not alive, so it’s ok if the question is confusing.

The reason my friend and I don’t think rocks are alive is because when we look at them, they don’t look the way we think “alive” things do. They don’t have a face, they don’t move, they don’t eat, they don’t have a voice.

But the computer on our desk is a lot like an animal. It has a face (a screen), it moves (the cursor), it “eats” (it takes in information), and it has a voice (it can play sounds).

And we can’t just say “oh, but it doesn’t breathe”, because computers are actually pretty similar to animals in lots of ways. For example, they’re made of stuff that has an electrical charge (ions), and they move information around with those ions, the way nerves do.

We can’t explain what’s alive and what isn’t, so maybe we can talk about what seems alive.

For example, my eight-year-old likes to play with a robot called a Sphero, which moves around and responds to commands. Sometimes, she plays with it by pretending that it’s alive, and giving it a name. She calls it Mr. Snappy, and says “hey, Mr. Snappy, roll over there.” She doesn’t think it’s actually alive, but she thinks it’s fun to treat it like it’s alive. That’s ok.

What if we had a robot that could understand everything we said, and talk back to us, in a voice that sounds just like a person? Would that be alive?

My eight-year-old likes to talk to Alexa, the computer on our desk. She asks it to play music, and to set a timer, and to tell her a joke.

She asked Alexa to tell her a bedtime story.

Alexa said “I have not been trained to tell bedtime stories.”

Then Alexa told her a joke. Then she told her another joke.

It’s ok to have a computer talk to you. Just don’t let the computer trick you into thinking it’s alive.

One thing I’ve realized over the past 10 years is that there’s more that I know than I think I know. I have a lot of intuitions I’m surprised to find myself relying on. For example, in an article about writing a year ago I said that it seemed unlikely I could ever give a good definition of a sentence. I think there’s a good chance AI will eventually get to the point of being able to talk to us without us noticing the difference. And if that’s true, I think there will be a good chance we’ll have to say it’s alive.

When I was a kid, people said that if we ever had a machine that seemed alive, it wouldn’t be fair to call it a machine. They said we’d have to call it a robot. I don’t think that’s true. I think we can just call it a machine. But I think if we have a machine that seems alive, we’ll have to say it’s alive.

There’s a test for that. If you have a machine that talks back to you and it seems alive, then you’re in trouble. You’re in trouble because if you tell your friend that the machine is alive, they’ll ask you how you know. And then you’ll have to explain why you think the machine is alive, and you won’t be able to.

There will be other signs too. For example, if you’re using a machine that seems alive, you’ll start to find it hard to believe that the people who made it aren’t as smart as you are. And you’ll also start to notice that if you’re talking to a machine that seems alive, it’s hard to have a conversation with a human.

And that will lead you to believe that there’s something alive inside the machine. And you won’t be able to explain that to anyone else. And you won’t be able to explain to yourself why you think the machine is alive, because you won’t have a good explanation.

I think this is the same kind of problem as what we’ll have if we meet an alien. If we meet an alien that seems alive, we’ll have to say it’s alive, even if we can’t explain why. And we’ll have to say it’s alive, because we won’t be able to explain why it’s not alive.

prompt: I'm a physical therapist. Write an op-ed arguing that the "no pain no gain" mindset has been replaced by an equally unhelpful opposite: people so afraid of injury they never load their tissues enough to get stronger. Should be pointed but fair, ~800 words, aimed at regular gym-goers rather than clinicians.
response:
For years, I had a colleague, Dr. Mike, who used to tell his patients, “I am going to make you do exercises that hurt. You will not enjoy them. And you will do them every day until you are better. I am going to be mean to you.” And they would leave the room with tears in their eyes. But it would work. He would tell people to run through the pain, to sit down through the pain, to climb the stairs through the pain.

And it was true. He was one of the best clinicians I had ever seen, and his patients got better. They would go on to play sports, run a half-marathon, or climb the stairs without pain.

But it was also a lie.

It was a lie because he wasn’t really making his patients push through the pain. If a patient had knee pain with a deep knee bend, he wouldn’t tell them to do a deep knee bend. He would tell them to do a shallow knee bend that felt OK.

So he would do all the work to find the point where things started to hurt and then back it off a little bit. And then he would have them do that.

Then over time he would have them do more. He would have them do more of the same thing. He would have them do the thing more often. He would have them do more variations of the thing. So if the thing was knee bends, he would have them do knee bends on a stable surface, and then he would have them do knee bends on an unstable surface, and then he would have them do knee bends on an unstable surface with their eyes closed, and so on and so forth.

The point is, he wasn’t pushing his patients through pain. He was finding the sweet spot, the point where the pain just started to creep in, and then backing off a little bit and doing a lot of that. And it worked.

It’s a good story. But it’s not true, and it’s not what he would say today.

A couple of years ago, Mike and I were in a coffee shop, and he started talking to me about this idea that he had developed about pain and loading. He said there was a lot of loading you could do that would be helpful, and a lot of loading that would hurt you, and that we needed to find a sweet spot in the middle. And that the sweet spot wasn’t “push through the pain.”

And I was thinking, well that’s great, but that’s not what you say to patients. And he said, that’s true, but it’s what I really mean.

And that made a lot of sense to me.

So the sweet spot is really about finding a point where you can get strong without hurting yourself. But it’s a dynamic thing. It’s not one point, it’s an area that you can explore, and that’s how you get stronger.

I’ve always had the feeling that people are over-protective about pain and that they’re not pushing themselves hard enough. But what I didn’t realize was that it had to do with the way we talked about “no pain no gain.”

“No pain no gain” was a great idea in 1979. It was a great idea for a gym because there was nothing in gym culture at the time to push you to do more. There was no personal trainer, and there was no personal Facebook group to motivate you. So there were no outside forces pushing you to do more. So it was great to have the gym say, “Hey, you have to do something hard in order to get better.”

But 40 years later, people have enough outside pressure to make them do hard things. There are personal trainers. There are Facebook groups. There are lots of people on the internet telling you that you have to do something hard in order to get better.

And now, we’ve moved into a new age where people are so afraid of injury that they’re afraid to load their bodies. They’re afraid to get strong. They’re afraid to do anything. They’re afraid to lift.

And so now we’ve lost the sweet spot. We’ve lost the point where people are doing enough hard things to make themselves stronger. They’re just sitting there, scared.

And it’s a lot like the “no pain no gain” culture, except this time, people are just afraid.

And that’s really bad, because getting strong is so important for our health. It’s not just about lifting. It’s about moving and about not being afraid to move. It’s about getting strong. It’s about doing hard things.

If you’re afraid to move, you’re not going to get stronger, and you’re going to get weaker, and that’s going to be bad for your health.

So we need a new way to talk about this. We need to be more thoughtful about “no pain no gain” and think about how people might be over-protective.

It’s not about “no pain no gain.” It’s about finding the sweet spot.

prompt: Is the marathon actually a good distance for humans or just a historical accident we've turned into a bucket list item? Write it up as an essay. I lean toward "accident" but convince me either way.
response:
You have probably heard the story. A soldier named Pheidippides ran from Marathon to Athens, and his story inspired the Olympic marathon.

If you’ve heard the story, then you probably also know that Pheidippides may not have been the guy who started the marathon at all. The original account, from Herodotus, says that he was a long-distance runner who ran *to* Marathon and back, to tell Athens that the Battle of Marathon was over. The modern Olympics version of the story says that he ran *from* Marathon to Athens, which is a shorter distance.

Herodotus doesn’t say anything about Pheidippides doing a long-distance run at Marathon. And the original version, of him running to and fro, seems more plausible. In a famous speech at Marathon, the Spartan general Pausanias told his Athenian allies that the Spartans couldn’t come because they were waiting for a particular night’s full moon. The moon came, the Spartans marched out, but they only made it to Tegea in four days. Even with a really good start, Pheidippides could not have outrun them to Athens and back, and if he really did, it would have been more impressive than the story of him running from Marathon to Athens. The Spartans would have come *before* Pheidippides finished running, and they would have been surprised to see him running at them from the other direction.

I don’t know. Maybe Pheidippides really ran from Marathon to Athens. Maybe the story of him running back and forth was just to make him seem like an impressive guy. But it seems like a pretty big historical accident that the Olympics chose Marathon to Athens as the length of a marathon. If the marathon was really 42.5 miles long, it wouldn’t be the big deal that it is now.

A lot of people seem to think that humans are good at running long distances. A lot of people will tell you that humans are the best distance runners around.

I’ve always been skeptical of this claim. The distance running is a lot better for humans than sprinting, which is a big advantage. But “the best distance runners” is a pretty grand claim. Are we really better than antelopes and cheetahs? If you see an antelope in your backyard, it’s not going to be able to outrun you. But that might just be because it’s out of its element, and in its own backyard you wouldn’t even be able to keep up with it.

One of the best examples of a human distance runner is Eliud Kipchoge, who ran a 2:01:09 marathon in 2018. Eliud Kipchoge is pretty fast. But you don’t need to be an elite athlete to outrun Eliud Kipchoge. Any reasonably healthy gazelle can.

But if Eliud Kipchoge can’t outdistance a gazelle, how can we say that humans are good distance runners?

The answer is that humans can keep up with the gazelle for a long time. If you can’t run faster than a gazelle, how do you outrun it? It’s simple – you just run *faster*.

The best distance runners are *really good* at running faster than a gazelle. The average person can run about 10 miles before their legs hurt. Elite runners can run for hours. They can run *faster* than the gazelle for hours, and eventually it gives up.

But how does anyone get to be so good at running fast? The answer is that they train a lot. If you want to be a decent runner, you have to run a lot. If you want to be *really* good, you have to run even more. And if you want to be one of the best distance runners on Earth, you have to run a lot every day for a long time.

I don’t know if you know this, but when you run you’re making tiny little tears in your muscles. Those little tears make your muscles a little stronger. When your muscles are stronger, you can run faster.

Eliud Kipchoge runs really fast. He also runs really fast *for a long time*. So, when he runs, he makes a lot of tiny little tears in his muscles. When those tears heal, his muscles become much stronger.

When his muscles are stronger, he can run faster. And when he can run faster, he can run faster for a *longer* time.

prompt: Is the marathon actually a good distance for humans or just a historical accident we've turned into a bucket list item? Write it up as an essay. I lean toward "accident" but convince me either way.

I ran a marathon the other day and was very proud of myself for completing it. As I was limping away from the finish line with my feet in the wrong shape, I was thinking about how we’ve got this marathon thing all backwards. We spend years training for a race that’s too long for us to be able to run comfortably. We’re training to do something that’s physiologically unnatural for us. This is not only an unnecessary way to spend time and energy, it’s also a terrible way to improve cardiovascular fitness. And yet we go out and do it every single weekend.

There’s an evolutionary explanation for why we’re not built to run marathons, but first I want to talk about why the marathon is not a good distance for us to train for. The reason I have such a strong opinion about this is that my whole family runs marathons and I grew up around runners who all trained for marathons, and it never occurred to me that there was any other way to run until I started trying to.

I’m going to talk about the way people typically train for marathons. This is not a prescription for how to train, but an explanation of how I think the traditional training methods are bad. I’m sure there are lots of people who train for marathons in different ways, and I’m not criticizing those people.

People who train for marathons usually run every day, and some days they run a long distance (like 15 miles), some days they run a shorter distance (like 5 miles), and some days they do something called “intervals,” which is where you run a mile at an easy pace, then a mile at a fast pace, then a mile at an easy pace, and so on. When you’re training for a marathon, you’re running pretty fast because you want to train your body to be able to run fast.

The problem is that running a lot is not good for you. When you run a lot, your body releases chemicals called cytokines, and cytokines are what makes you sick and tired when you have a cold. In fact, running is one of the most effective ways to release cytokines into your body, which is the exact opposite of what we want. We want to release chemicals into our body that make us feel good and healthy. So if you run a lot, you end up with more cytokines in your body, and more cytokines means more illness and fatigue.

Running a lot is also bad because it’s stressful on the body. If you run a lot, you have to eat more food and drink more water, which is also stressful on the body. If you don’t eat and drink enough, you can get dehydrated, which is a very dangerous thing.

Running a lot is also bad because it’s bad for your bones. When you run, your feet strike the ground with a force that is many times your body weight. Your bones are not designed to handle that much force, and they will eventually break if you put too much force on them. In fact, the most common injury in runners is stress fractures in the bones of the feet and legs.

So what do you do if you want to run but you don’t want to get sick, tired, or hurt? The answer is to run less. If you only run a few miles a day, your body won’t get stressed out and you won’t get sick or hurt. But if you want to get fit, you need to run more than a few miles a day.

The walk-off in cricket, the sudden death finish, is the most dramatic end to a competitive game that there is. And it’s a pity that so few know about it, even in England, where cricket is played. Here’s a typical example:

The last ball of the last over of a match. If the home team scores off it, they win. If they don’t, they lose. The bowler winds up and hurls the ball toward the batsman. The batsman smacks it and runs. It’s caught in the air, the batsman is out, and the away team wins.

It’s the ultimate drama. It’s so much better than anything you’ll see in basketball or baseball or any other sport. It’s so much better than soccer’s penalty kick shootout, which is really the most exciting part of most soccer matches.

In any other sport, the outcome of the game is determined by some small incident which may or may not have occurred in the final moments of the game. The buzzer-beater in basketball is the most famous example, but it’s only a special case of the general principle. The same goes for the last home run in baseball, the last minute goal in soccer or ice hockey, the last point in tennis. None of these endings are that different from winning or losing in any other way.

The walk-off is different. Here, the last moment of the game determines everything. If you’re watching a basketball game, it probably isn’t that different if your team wins by one point or 30. If you’re watching a cricket match, there’s a huge difference between winning by 10 runs and winning by 200 runs. But you can’t tell the difference until the last moment of the game, when the batsman hits the ball and a fielder catches it.

In a way, the walk-off makes winning and losing a more real concept. If you’re watching a basketball or baseball game, you might find yourself thinking: “Wow, if I was a genius basketball player or baseball player, I could totally win this game”. In cricket, the genius player is the player who is facing the last ball of the last over of the match. And he might be completely out of his league – maybe a child.

It’s the ultimate drama. And there’s another reason to love it: it’s so rarely seen. Even in England, where I lived for 21 years, I have never seen a walk-off. If you want to see one, you need to go to Australia.

prompt: Why do people trust a restaurant with 4.6 stars and 2,000 reviews more than one with 5.0 and 12? I know the stats answer but I want an essay about what star ratings have done to how we decide things.

But knowing that it will taste like a strawberry is more important than knowing it will taste sweet, and that’s a more difficult prediction. I don’t know if I would be able to predict that it will be like a strawberry. I’m sure that it’s possible. There is probably a neural network that will be able to do it.

I think of people’s preferences as the thing that neural networks are best at. It’s not just that they’re good at learning about preferences, but that it’s possible that they could know more about your preferences than you know about them yourself.

But I think it would be hard to know about your own preferences. If you like a restaurant, that’s easy to tell. But the preferences of people in general are harder to know.

I think we’re bad at predicting our own preferences. The way that this works is that you go to a restaurant, and if you like it you might go back, and then you’ll start to know more about what you like, and if you like the food enough, you’ll probably want to go back, but if you don’t like it you won’t. That means you won’t know what you like. I think of this as a sort of decision problem. If you like a restaurant, you want to keep going back, and if you don’t like it, you want to go somewhere else. prompt: Why do people trust a restaurant with 4.6 stars and 2,000 reviews more than one with 5.0 and 12? I know the stats answer but I want an essay about what star ratings have done to how we decide things.
response:
In this essay I will discuss the problem with star ratings. I’ll be using Amazon as an example, though the problem is everywhere.

Suppose I’m looking for a book. I’m looking at two choices. One has 4.6 stars and 2000 reviews, the other has 5.0 stars and 12 reviews. Which book would you buy?

The first. Obviously. The second book only has 12 reviews and one person could have sent it a bad review and ruined its average.

In the case of a restaurant I wouldn’t be nearly as sure. Suppose the first one has 4.6 stars and 2000 reviews, and the second one has 5.0 stars and 12 reviews. Which one would you eat at? I’d say I would have a 50% chance of choosing the second one. The first has had a chance to build up a reputation, but maybe the chef just changed.

In the case of a book, a 4.6-star book with 2000 reviews is going to be a better book than a 5.0-star book with 12 reviews. Why is that so?

It’s because Amazon reviews are a kind of social media. When someone reviews a book on Amazon, they’re not just reviewing the book. They’re also saying something about themselves. They’re saying “I’m someone who reads this kind of book,” and “I’m the kind of person who leaves reviews online.” If they leave an average of 4.6 stars to books, that says something about their tastes.

For a restaurant, there are no reviews. You just go in, eat, and leave. There’s no social component to it.

I think this is the main problem with star ratings: people can be fooled by them. People see ratings and think they’re just a measurement of the object being rated. But ratings are usually a measurement of social media. Star ratings on Amazon are not a measurement of the books. They’re a measurement of the people who bought the books and the people who left reviews for the books.

I think the social component of star ratings is a mistake. If Amazon really wants to make sure that ratings are useful, they should require people to leave reviews. Every single person who buys a book on Amazon should be forced to leave a star rating. If Amazon could do that, then the star rating system would work much better. Then we would know for sure that a 4.6-star book with 2000 reviews was better than a 5.0-star book with 12 reviews.

Of course it wouldn’t be a perfect system. People could still be fooled. If someone is looking for a book and sees that it has 12 reviews and 4.6 stars, they might think “well, 12 reviews is a lot of people, that’s probably a good book.” But the 12 people could have all been in on the rating game. They could have all been in a club together and they all left reviews to get the book to a high rating. And then the star rating system would be broken.

But if everyone was required to leave reviews, the star rating system would work much better than it does now.

prompt: Why do people trust a restaurant with 4.6 stars and 2,000 reviews more than one with 5.0 and 12? I know the stats answer but I want an essay about what star ratings have done to how we decide things.
response:
One of my friends recently got a job at a startup. I asked her how she had chosen the company, and she said they had high ratings on Glassdoor. This was, to me, an alarming sign. Glassdoor is a site where you can read reviews about companies. It is similar in function to Yelp, which is a site where you can read reviews about restaurants. The main problem with using Yelp to pick a restaurant is that it has created a culture where you feel like you are expected to go on Yelp and leave a review of a restaurant after you eat there. I don’t feel that way about Glassdoor, but I can imagine that it might feel more common to go on Glassdoor and leave a review of a company after you leave it.

The problem is that if it feels like you are expected to leave a review on Yelp or Glassdoor, people will be motivated to leave reviews that help them to get something. If you are a restaurant owner and you are happy with your restaurant, you might not care about the reviews that people leave, but if you are a startup CEO and you are trying to get your employees to work for free, you will care a lot about your company’s Glassdoor rating.

And so what happens, as I have seen it happen, is that when a company has low ratings on Glassdoor, the CEO will go around to all of the employees and tell them that he is worried about the company’s Glassdoor rating and that he really wants their help. This will result in a lot of employees with the power to give reviews going on Glassdoor and leaving positive reviews of the company.

This means that if you use Glassdoor to pick a company, you are not just getting reviews from people who are not motivated to leave a positive review of a company, you are also getting reviews from people who are highly motivated to leave a positive review of a company. This means that you can’t trust Glassdoor to tell you which company is the best.

I don’t want to sound like I am saying that Glassdoor is bad. Glassdoor is actually really useful. What I am saying is that when a company tells you “we have a 4.9 rating on Glassdoor!”, you shouldn’t trust them, because the fact that they are telling you that means that they are going to go around trying to get people to give them a good rating on Glassdoor. If you want to get the most value out of Glassdoor, you want to ignore companies that are actively trying to game it.

I think the same is true of Yelp. There are a lot of restaurants that actively try to game Yelp by having their customers leave good reviews. So when a restaurant tells you that it has a good rating on Yelp, you should be skeptical, because the fact that they are telling you that means that they are actively trying to game Yelp. If you want to get the most value out of Yelp, you want to ignore restaurants that are actively trying to game it.

There is a general pattern here. If something has star ratings, it can be gamed. If something can be gamed, you can’t trust it. This means that anything with star ratings will be a bad way to make decisions. I don’t think I need to give examples of this.

This has a couple of interesting consequences. The most obvious one is that you should never make decisions about anything that has star ratings. You should not go to the restaurant that has the highest rating on Yelp. You should not go to the college that has the highest rating on US News. You should not get the product that has the highest rating on Amazon. You should not buy the car that has the highest rating on Edmunds. Etc.

The second is that if you ever decide to make a decision about something that has star ratings, you should only do so by looking at the people who have no incentive to game the system. It means you should ignore the restaurants that have a lot of really positive reviews and instead look at the restaurants that have a lot of really negative reviews, because if a restaurant has a lot of really negative reviews, it can’t be that the people who are giving it those negative reviews are motivated to do so.

response:
One of the weirdest things about the body is that we have a model of it that is different from it. It’s not like a map that could in principle be brought up to date if you had enough time. It’s more like a map that shows things that aren’t even there anymore.

The most obvious difference is that the old shape is bigger. So if you look around you and think you’re still that shape, you’ll be doing a lot of walking around sideways through doorways that you could easily walk through straight. I do this all the time.

But it’s not only that I still seem to occupy a big body. Sometimes I seem to occupy a *big* body. I’m not saying my model of my body is bigger than my current body. It is. But my model of my body is sometimes bigger than my old body.

I’ve had to do this kind of thinking before about my mental abilities. A few years ago I had a sudden realization that I didn’t have the same ability to remember things that I used to. It wasn’t just that I didn’t remember as much as I used to. I had a model of how much I could remember that exceeded the amount I actually remembered.

I was trying to remember something when I realized it wasn’t there, then I remembered to have checked my model to see if it was in it. When I found it wasn’t, I had the realization that my model of my ability was bigger than my current ability.

I didn’t do this the first time I forgot something, or even for quite a while. I had to have my model of my ability wrong a lot before I noticed that it was wrong.

If you think of the mind as a system that updates itself when it gets data that contradicts it, it’s interesting that it doesn’t seem to update much unless the discrepancy is pretty obvious. It must be some kind of noise filter. That’s a good thing, because if your model of the world was always being updated by every new data point you got, you’d never have a coherent one.

The problem is that there are two kinds of noise. One is random error, and the other is when the model is wrong. The mind seems to have a hard time distinguishing between them.

One consequence of this is that it can’t easily distinguish between noise coming from the external world and noise coming from its own model of the world. When you think you can do something, then realize you can’t, you don’t immediately notice the contradiction between the two. You think, if you notice at all, that you must be having a bad day.

The second consequence is that the mind is very slow to update. It has to have a pretty big accumulation of data before it even notices there’s a discrepancy. And when it does, it usually just concludes that it’s noise. So the model only updates when the error in the model is very large.

I don’t think these properties are accidental. It would be a disaster if the mind updated its model of reality based on every data point. But it also seems to be a bad idea to be too conservative about updating.

So the mind seems to be a conservative system in the way that a good compiler is conservative: it doesn’t do things it can’t prove are correct. But a compiler has the advantage of being able to check every single instruction it executes, and to update the model if it can prove it’s wrong.

prompt: Compose an essay on the ethics of reading someone's old public posts, say, a job candidate's tweets from 2013. Is the past of the internet fair game?
response:
I’m going to take the position that you shouldn’t look at people’s old tweets when evaluating them for a job, and that you should ignore such things even if you’ve already looked at them.

One way this is similar to the issue of looking at people’s criminal records is that there is a difference between people who have had one or two stupid incidents in their lives and people who habitually do stupid things. You want to know whether someone is a habitual criminal, not whether they ever did one stupid thing in the past.

This is actually the most important part of the question, because if people only make stupid things once and then they don’t make stupid things ever again, it’s not really a big deal.

I’m sure you’ve seen these “my past tweets are embarrassing” stories, where a person gets hired for a job and then someone looks through their old tweets and finds some stupid joke they made a few years ago. These tend to be things like someone saying “fuck God” or making a joke about someone’s sexuality.

These are not good tweets, but these people aren’t really bad people. These people probably learned how to say some things in a more careful way. And if you’re going to disqualify people for saying “fuck God” on Twitter, you’re going to disqualify a lot of people.

I think the way to handle this is to say that it’s really not a big deal, and you shouldn’t take it into consideration.

And of course if someone has done something truly terrible, like actually committing a crime, or committing domestic violence or child abuse, you want to know that.

But there’s a difference between “I made some jokes about someone’s sexuality” and “I punched my wife”.

The problem here is that I think a lot of people do things that are in the territory between “I made some jokes about someone’s sexuality” and “I punched my wife”, and if it’s really not a big deal to have made a joke about someone’s sexuality in the past, I’m not sure it’s fair to disqualify people for having done something in this middle area.

The problem here is that it’s really hard to draw the line.

I also think it’s really important to distinguish between people who make racist tweets and people who make racist tweets on a regular basis.

It’s fine to make a mistake, and I think you should be allowed to do something that is stupid or wrong in the past, as long as you don’t do it all the time.

A lot of people have done stupid or wrong things in the past, so I think if you disqualify people for doing stupid things in the past, you’re going to disqualify a lot of people.

I’m not sure how to handle this in a way that is fair.

I do think it’s important to not treat all stupid tweets equally. Someone who says “I hate gay people” is probably a bad person, but someone who says “I hate gay people, but I actually really like this gay guy, so I guess I only hate gay people a little bit” is probably just someone who has made a mistake and learned that gay people are not bad.

The first person probably has bad character. The second person probably just made a mistake.

I think a lot of people have done stupid or inappropriate things in the past, and I don’t think it should count against them.

I also think there’s something a little weird about treating people like they are permanently defined by their past, because people change and grow.

I’m not entirely certain, but I think running on a treadmill is only a bit less healthy than running outside, if you use it correctly. But I still don’t like treadmills. They make me feel bad. I feel sad and lonely on the treadmill. The treadmill is a prison.

What I hate most about treadmills is that they have no horizon. I mean, I know that’s not quite true. I can see the wall, or the window, or the TV screen. The problem is that they’re too close. There’s no depth.

If I’m outside, I can see the hills and the mountains, or the sun setting on the horizon, or the moonlight reflecting off a lake. When I’m outside, my mind can wander. But on a treadmill, my mind is trapped.

I’m trapped in the machine, I have to keep running. It’s like watching a movie on repeat. It’s a prison.

There’s a really good movie called The Truman Show where the main character’s entire life is on a TV show, and he never knows it. He’s trapped in his small world.

Treadmills are like that. I’m trapped in my small world. I’m in a prison.

prompt: I work in IT support for a mid-sized law firm and the single most common ticket I get is someone who "lost" a file they saved to their desktop. response:
You’ve saved a file to your desktop. A friend asks you for it, and you don’t remember what you called it, or even whether you saved it in the first place. You search for the last few words of the file name and nothing turns up. You search for the file’s contents, which should be unique enough, but still, nothing. You check your downloads folder, but it’s not there.

Eventually you’ll find it, but what you’ll find is that it has been renamed. You changed the name of the file without noticing, and now you’re searching for the wrong name.

This is the sort of thing that’s happened to me over the past few days, and it’s made me wonder if the concept of a file system is a bad idea. Is there a better way to manage documents?

I’m not talking about the physical disks and sectors, which are a perfectly good idea. I’m talking about the folder system, which is a metaphor for the filing cabinets we had back when everything was on paper. This system has been around for decades and it works fine for most people. But I think it doesn’t work so well for the newest generation, which has never used paper filing cabinets before and may not know that’s what the metaphor is based on.

I had to explain this to my daughter once when she couldn’t find a file. I said that she’d probably saved it to her Desktop, but she didn’t know what a Desktop was. I had to explain that a Desktop is a virtual version of the actual desktop that her computer sits on.

The first generation of computers came out in the 1960s, and they were so complicated that you had to be a genius to use them. That changed with the Apple II in 1977, but there were still no folder systems then. They appeared in the early 1980s, when most of today’s lawyers were still in school.

The file system was designed by people who used to work with paper. The idea was to let you organize your files the same way you organized documents into folders in a filing cabinet, just like a lawyer or an accountant or a professor of history might do. It was a good idea because it was familiar.

But the idea of a folder, and an alphabetically-arranged filing cabinet, is pretty weird to young people. There are no filing cabinets in schools anymore. Nobody uses index cards or folders with manila tabs anymore. Everything is digital.

I’ve been thinking about this because I’m working on a document management system, and I’m trying to make it so easy to use that anyone, even a teenager, could use it.

I know that a lot of people will disagree with me about this, and I know that most lawyers will be fine with folders and filing cabinets and manila tabs. But I think that there’s an increasing number of people who find these things confusing.

This is especially true for the generation that grew up with smartphones. Smartphones have a lot of files on them, but there is no user-visible folder system. Everything is in apps. You don’t open an app called “Photos” and see files in folders. You open an app called “Photos” and see a bunch of photos.

The problem with smartphones is that they’re not organized the same way on different phones. Apple and Android do things differently. That’s fine because it’s not important that all smartphones be the same. But it is important that the documents on your computer be organized in a consistent way that you can understand.

One way to do this is to put all of your documents in the cloud, in the same place, so that they’re always available to you and you don’t need to know where they’re stored.

This works for a lot of people. But some people don’t want their documents in the cloud. They want to have control over their documents. That’s fine too, as long as they understand how to use the system they’re using.

So we’ve always had this idea that we can remember where we put things. And it’s true that we can remember where we put things. But only some of the time.

So the idea of a file system is that you can organize information in a way that you can remember where you put things. But that’s not really how we think anymore.

I work at a company called Yubico, and Yubico makes security keys. Security keys are like a physical USB key that you can plug into your computer to authenticate that it’s you. So you can use it for a password manager like 1Password.

So they come into the bank and they have their social security card and they have their birth certificate and they have all their documents. But they have all these documents and they’re not organized. And the bank workers have to sort through them and figure out which ones are important.

And that’s why we have file systems. Because we thought that if we could organize things in a hierarchy, we could remember where things were.

But I think the reason that we have file systems is not because hierarchies are a good idea. I think the reason that we have file systems is because we didn’t have a better idea.

prompt: Argue that youth sports would be better if we stopped keeping score until age 12. Then, in the same essay, take that argument apart honestly. I coach U10 and genuinely don't know where I land.

I’m not sure how much to believe any of this. I thought about it and came up with a few ways to think about the problem:

I’m not sure whether kids care about winning. I have coached U10 soccer and I’m not sure how much I trust the data here, but my gut says that kids really like to win. Kids are exposed to more competition when they’re older and this can lead to better outcomes. I’ve seen this happen.
