prompt: why do statutes of limitations exist? essay
response:
A statute of limitations sets a time limit on how long an individual has to bring a lawsuit. Most criminal offences have a statute of limitations; in the United States, murder is the only offence without one. This means that if someone kills you, but the police fail to catch them, they will never be able to be tried for the crime – not even if they are caught a year, a century or a thousand years later.

Why is this the case?

One reason is that over time, evidence is lost or destroyed, and witnesses’ memories fade. This makes it more difficult to prosecute a crime or to bring a civil suit after a long time has passed. However, this reason does not quite make sense, because while evidence is lost over time, it is also gained over time. If a crime was committed 20 years ago, it is not just that the police have had 20 years to find evidence and witnesses, but the public has too, which means there is a lot more evidence that can be used. A crime committed yesterday may not even be known about by anyone but the victim and the perpetrator, but a crime committed a hundred years ago may have been talked about by generations of family members, and have a lot of evidence accumulated on it.

The other reason, which I think is the real one, is that we do not want to impose too high a risk on criminals. A person committing a crime should be able to feel that if they get away with it, they will never have to be caught. This is especially important in a society which is going to convict people of crimes based on circumstantial evidence. Imagine there is a new law which says that if a person is in possession of a certain chemical, they are guilty of drug possession. If there is no statute of limitations, then you should worry about getting caught for having been in possession of the chemical at any time in your life. This seems unfair, and would make a society much less free.

In fact, this seems to have been the problem in a famous case in 2012 in the UK – it seems that some law in the UK is that if you are caught in possession of a chemical, then you will be guilty of drug possession – and the court ruled that a drug possession conviction could not be overturned even after 20 years. But then the UK Supreme Court said that this was a violation of the European Convention of Human Rights, and overturned the decision.

So what is the optimal time limit?

It seems to be a tradeoff between how much risk you impose on criminals versus how much evidence is lost or destroyed. A time limit of ten days is so short that it will only prevent the prosecution of crimes which were not caught immediately after they happened, but it will not do a good job of protecting criminals who are trying to avoid justice. A time limit of ten years is so long that it will be impossible to prosecute most crimes except by circumstantial evidence, but it will do a good job of protecting the innocent.

This is why murder is usually the only crime without a statute of limitations. Murder is such a big deal that we feel we need to go after people for it regardless of how much circumstantial evidence we have, and regardless of how many years it has taken to collect that evidence.

prompt: I spent 14 months getting a building permit for a 200 sq ft backyard studio. Every individual rule I ran into made sense on its own. The total was insane. Write an essay about how reasonable rules add up to unreasonable systems, and whether anyone is actually responsible for the sum.
response:
Back in the day, when I was living in Brooklyn, I was planning to build a small garden studio in the backyard, 200 square feet or so, to do writing.

I knew from the beginning that it was going to be a complicated and lengthy project, because I didn’t want to put it on stilts or in a tree or anything like that. I wanted it to sit on the ground, and be connected to the house with a door. I knew that I would need a building permit, which meant getting architects and engineers to do drawings, and submitting them, and going through the process.

I ended up getting the permit after about 14 months. It was very expensive. The permit process was not the main cost, but it was a big part of the cost. It was the main reason the project was so expensive.

But in the end I got the permit, so it was worth it. But as I wrote about on the blog, a lot of people are not going to be willing to go through that process. If they have a small garden space that they could build a studio in, it would probably not be worth it for them to go through the permit process. It might cost them tens of thousands of dollars in time and money, for a space that they don’t really need and can’t afford to build, but would be nice to have.

In the end, I’m not sure how bad the building permit system is in Brooklyn. I don’t know how many people are not building things because of it. I can tell you that I know some people who are not building things because of it. And I know that some people are paying a lot more than they would like to, because of it.

There are lots of people who make fun of building permit systems. And they are right. But I think it’s really easy to make fun of the building permit system, because it’s a good example of something that is reasonable on a case-by-case basis, but unreasonable as a whole.

I remember reading something like a hundred years ago, a story about a town in Massachusetts or somewhere like that. A guy was trying to open a restaurant. He went to the town hall and asked what he had to do to open a restaurant. The answer was, you needed an environmental study to make sure that you could handle all the waste that you would produce. So he had to spend a few months and a lot of money getting that done.

But it was actually not a big deal. He was opening a small restaurant that didn’t have a big kitchen or anything. There wasn’t going to be a lot of waste. So he got the environmental study done and he went back to the town hall and he said, I’m going to open my restaurant. What else do I have to do?

And they said, you have to have a structural engineering study to make sure that the building is safe.

So he got that done, and he went back to the town hall. What else do I have to do to open my restaurant?

And they said, you have to have a fire risk assessment.

And he said, sure, that’s fine.

And he got that done and he went back to the town hall. What else do I have to do?

And they said, you have to have a parking study.

And he was like, this is ridiculous. This is not reasonable.

And they said, why not? Why is a parking study not reasonable? The restaurant is going to take up a lot of space and we need to make sure that people have somewhere to park.

And he said, it’s a small restaurant. It’s not going to take up much space.

And they said, well, you need to do the parking study first before we know how much space it’s going to take up.

This is not a real story that I remember. But there’s a point to it. It’s that you can have a town with a bunch of totally reasonable rules. Every one of them is reasonable. But if you have to go through all of them at once, the total is unreasonable.

And this is kind of what happened to me with the building permit process. Every one of the rules I ran into, I could not make fun of, because they were all totally reasonable. If I could get my architect and my engineer to figure out all of them for me, I would not complain about having to go through them. I would not complain about having to get my building inspected before it was finished, or having to have a plan for how people could get out of my building in case there was a fire. These were all reasonable.

But the total amount of time and money that it took to get my building permit, was unreasonable.

And I don’t know how I feel about that. It’s not my job to make the rules. It’s not my job to make the rules reasonable. If the rules are unreasonable, then I guess it’s not worth doing. But it feels bad to have an idea that I think is good, and then have to spend a year getting a building permit, and have all of the rules that I had to go through be reasonable.

But then again, the rules are not just rules. There’s a bunch of people who are in charge of the rules. There’s a bunch of people who are in charge of inspecting buildings. There’s a bunch of people who are in charge of reviewing building plans. There’s a bunch of people who are in charge of deciding what the rules are. And in theory, they should be able to work together to make things more efficient.

I don’t think it’s their job to make the rules work for me. But I don’t think it’s unreasonable to think that they should be able to work together and get my building permit in six months instead of 14.

And this is where I’m kind of in a bind. I want to say that the building permit system is broken. But then I think, well, if the system is broken, who’s job is it to fix it? I don’t think it’s my job to fix it. I don’t think it’s anybody’s job to fix it. But it feels bad to have an idea that I think is good, and to not be able to do it because of the building permit system.

But I think there’s a couple of different ways that I could go about this. One, I could just decide that I’m not going to build anything anymore, because the building permit system is too slow and too expensive. And I could be like, if I want to write a book, I’ll just do it in my house. I don’t need a building permit to write a book.

Two, I could just decide that I’m going to get the building permit, and I’m going to spend a year doing it. And I could be like, well, it’s going to take a year, but it’s going to be worth it in the end.

And I think I’m going to do that. But I think there’s a lot of people who would not want to do that, because they can’t afford to spend a year getting a building permit. And I think that’s a shame, because there are a lot of people who want to build things, and it’s not worth it for them.

prompt: I spent 14 months getting a building permit for a 200 sq ft backyard studio. Every individual rule I ran into made sense on its own. The total was insane. Write an essay about how reasonable rules add up to unreasonable systems, and whether anyone is actually responsible for the sum.
response:
In this town, it takes about eight months to get a permit for a small new building. That’s if everything goes well. In my case, it took about fourteen months.

The eight months are made up of a series of reviews. The city’s planning department has a set of standards that new buildings are required to meet, and they’re responsible for making sure the plans meet these standards. This is the planning review.

There are other departments that review the plans too, including fire, health, and transportation. The fire review makes sure the building is safe in a fire. The health department looks for things that could cause the building’s occupants to get sick. The transportation department looks for traffic impacts. These are called “concurrences”, and they can happen in parallel with the planning review.

prompt: I'm a public defender, eight years in. I want an essay - personal but not a sob story - about what plea bargaining does to the idea of innocence. 95%+ of my cases never see trial. Clients who didn't do it plead because the deal is 6 months and trial risk is 6 years. I'm not looking for a policy paper, more the moral texture of it.
response:
I’ve been a public defender for eight years. I’ve worked on over 2,500 cases. Less than a handful of them ever went to trial.

This is not an accident. Over 95% of criminal cases are resolved by plea deal. The defendant agrees to plead guilty to some crime and the prosecution drops the rest. The judge gets to give a lighter sentence than would be possible after trial. And the case is over, sometimes within a few hours.

Pleas are an economic necessity for the system. Every court system has hundreds more cases than it can handle. Judges can’t spend weeks on every case. Prosecutors can’t prepare every case for trial. Defense attorneys have clients with a few thousand dollars, and can’t spend weeks on every case.

Pleas make everyone’s life easier. But the system’s incentives mean that most of these people don’t actually get their day in court.

A person is arrested for a crime. The case goes to arraignment and the judge sets bail. Usually bail is high enough that they can’t pay it. So they go to jail, where they wait weeks or months for their case to be heard.

The first meeting with the defense attorney might happen while they are still in jail. The defense attorney will have seen the police and prosecutor reports, but no more evidence than that. The defense attorney will have maybe an hour with the client, who is stressed, scared, and wants to get out of jail.

The client has a right to have a lawyer, but usually not a private lawyer. If their case seems serious, there will be a public defender assigned to them. This is the person I am. If their case seems not serious, they’ll go to court unrepresented.

The defense attorney will get a call from the prosecutor. The prosecutor will say: we have the evidence to send this person to trial, but we’d take six months in prison and drop the rest.

My client is in jail, and wants to get out of jail. Six months in prison is an offer I have to make.

My client is innocent, but that’s not always a good reason not to take the plea deal. If we take this case to trial, and we lose, they might get six years.

The prosecutor is right to threaten us with trial. Prosecutors win over 90% of their cases. If my client is actually guilty, taking the deal is a pretty good idea. If they’re innocent, the odds are still not in their favor.

I’m not a very good lawyer. I’ve been here for eight years, but I’m not sure I’ve ever had more than a few months to work on a single case. I’ve tried a few times to spend more time on a case, but every time, I’ve been forced to accept a plea deal.

A plea deal is not the system working well. It’s a result of the system not working well.

The plea deal is six months. If we lose, we get six years. If we win, we get nothing. If we take the deal, we get six months, and we avoid risking the six years.

If the person is guilty, they’re getting off scot-free. If the person is innocent, they’re going to prison.

I’m a public defender in a big city. The average case in my office is someone who’s charged with something like robbery with a weapon, and has been caught with a gun. The prosecutor has an offer to make.

I’ve worked on a lot of these cases, and I’m good at making the right decision. I’ve learned to read police reports. I can look at a report and figure out whether the cop is being honest.

Most of the time, I can tell that the client is guilty. But the police report will say that they caught them with a gun, and they’ll say, no, they didn’t do it. In my experience, cops don’t lie about that. I tell my client to take the deal.

Sometimes I can tell that the cop is lying. And I tell my client to take the deal.

That doesn’t work for every case.

I have a client who is charged with robbery with a gun. The cop says that my client was caught with a gun. My client says they didn’t do it.

I look at the report. The story doesn’t make sense, and the cop is lying. There’s no doubt about it.

My client is innocent. It’s not a good thing to send them to prison, but it’s also not a good thing to let a guilty person go.

I’ve worked on about 2,500 cases. I’ve won maybe 25 of them. I’m good at telling what’s true and what’s not.

I think this is my best work. I don’t spend much time in courtrooms. I don’t have to go to the courtroom to get the right result in my cases. But I do have to spend time reading police reports. I read a lot of police reports.

My clients are innocent. I know that because I read the police reports. I know that because the police reports lie. I know that because I read a lot of police reports and I know how cops lie.

When my clients are innocent, it’s usually because cops lied.

I don’t know if I should tell my client that they’re innocent. It would be nice to tell them. They’re sitting in jail, and they might be scared. I can tell them that they’re innocent, and maybe they’ll feel a little better.

I don’t know if I should tell them that.

prompt: Please write an essay examining why so many legal systems treat attempted crimes less harshly than completed ones, even when the intent and the effort were identical and only luck intervened.
response:
A man walks out of a bank with a large amount of money and a gun. He’s been caught by security cameras and police are closing in on him. On the way out of the bank, he shoots and kills a security guard.

Another man walks out of a bank with a large amount of money and a gun. He’s been caught by security cameras and police are closing in on him. On the way out of the bank, he shoots and wounds a security guard, who survives.

In most legal systems, the first man is guilty of both robbery and first-degree murder, and gets life in prison. The second man is guilty of both robbery and attempted murder, and gets maybe 10 years in prison.

Both of these men are just as culpable and equally deserving of punishment. They had the same motives. They took the same actions. They put the security guard in the same amount of mortal danger. The only reason they ended up with different results was that one man was lucky and the other was unlucky.

I have written before on the general problem of punishment being so dependent on luck rather than intention. Here’s a particular example of it.

I’ve said before I’m more sympathetic to retributivism than consequentialism. But here it feels to me like consequentialism wins. It doesn’t make sense for an attempted murderer to get off with a much lighter sentence than an actual murderer.

There are a couple of things I could say here. First I could say that we have to allow for some kind of diminishing returns to punishment, such that 20 years in prison is much worse than 10, and 30 years is much worse than 20, but that life in prison is only slightly worse than 30 years. This may be true, but I don’t think it explains the full difference.

Second I could say that the attempted murderer gets a lighter sentence because the system has no way of proving that he intended to commit murder. He might have just been careless with the gun. In this hypothetical example we know that he meant to kill.

The best explanation I can think of is a consequentialist one. If the punishment for attempted murder is the same as for murder, then the police will have no incentive to catch attempted murderers. After all, if they catch someone who’s going to kill, and they accidentally kill them instead, they’ve solved both problems. Whereas if they catch someone who’s going to kill, and they manage to keep them from killing, they have only solved one problem.

This seems like a really bad reason for our law to be so different from the law of nature.

It reminds me of the story of the old guy who is always late to the train station. He tries hard to get up early, but the alarm clock never works. The alarm clock is a very old model that is famous for breaking. So he has a habit of turning it on 30 minutes earlier than the time he wants to wake up at. But when he turns it on 30 minutes earlier, he never wakes up. So he tries turning it on 45 minutes earlier. When he does this, he always wakes up 15 minutes too early. He feels that if only he could turn the clock on 30 minutes earlier, he would wake up at the right time, and he tries it again.

I’m not saying we should punish attempted murder just as harshly as murder. But I am saying I don’t like that it’s so hard for us to punish attempted murder harshly.

prompt: Please write an essay examining why so many legal systems treat attempted crimes less harshly than completed ones, even when the intent and the effort were identical and only luck intervened.
response:
We’ve discussed a few cases of attempted crime before (here and here, for instance) where there seems to be no difference at all in the criminal intent or effort, only whether something that was completely random happened to go well or badly.

So why does the law distinguish between attempted crime and completed crime? Why should the outcome matter at all?

The most obvious answer is that the victim is harmed. But in this case, we know that the victim wasn’t harmed.

There are a few possible reasons. First, perhaps the victim is traumatized even if the crime was unsuccessful. If you try to kill someone, they know you are capable of killing them, and they know that you will probably try again. So the victim can be harmed by an attempted crime just as much as a successful one.

Second, there is a general public fear of crime. You might feel a lot of fear about crime, and think it would be a lot worse if there were more crime. But if you try to murder a bunch of people and fail every time, you’ve created less of a threat than if you tried and succeeded. So maybe it’s not so much about what people know about you, but what they know about how likely it is that you’ll be successful in the future.

Third, the idea is to punish people for the harm they cause, and if they don’t cause any harm, they shouldn’t be punished at all. This seems like a pretty bad idea, because we’re supposed to be punishing people for their actions (and thoughts), not for whether their actions turn out well or not.

Fourth, perhaps the idea is to punish people for the harm they *intend* to cause. Then if you intend to murder someone, but fail, you should be punished the same as if you succeeded. Again, this seems like a bad idea.

Fifth, perhaps the idea is to punish people for the amount of effort they put into harming someone. Then if you go to a lot of trouble to murder someone and fail, you should be punished as if you succeeded, and if you fail by accident (eg, you were aiming for the head, but missed and hit the shoulder) then you should get off lightly. But this doesn’t seem like a good idea, because the amount of effort you put into a crime shouldn’t matter at all.

I don’t know which of these justifications is used in practice. But my own opinion is that none of them make a whole lot of sense.

prompt: Please write an essay examining why so many legal systems treat attempted crimes less harshly than completed ones, even when the intent and the effort were identical and only luck intervened.
response:
When a murderer tries to kill someone, fails, and is caught, he may get the death penalty. When he succeeds, he gets the death penalty, and his victim gets killed.

If a thief tries to steal something, fails, and is caught, he goes to prison. If he succeeds, he goes to prison, and the victim loses his property.

The criminal law of most countries, including the United States, distinguishes between attempts and completed crimes, and generally punishes the attempt less harshly. But it is hard to understand why. The criminal law should be based on the harm done to society by a particular act; and the harm caused by a failed attempt at robbery or murder looks exactly the same as the harm caused by the robbery or murder itself. The thief tries to steal something, fails, and leaves. The victim is no worse off than if the thief had not tried. The murderer shoots the victim, fails to hit anything vital, and leaves. The victim is no worse off than if the murderer had not tried.

So why is it that the law of most societies treats a successful murder more seriously than an attempted murder?

In most of the rest of the world, this question is answered in the same way: nobody cares much, but that is just how the law is, and it probably has some historical explanation. The US is different. In the US, when somebody asks why, he gets an answer.

The most recent, and most widely accepted answer, is that the difference comes from what economists call expected value. The probability of a murder succeeding is greater than the probability of an attempted murder succeeding, so the murderer’s act, considered as a whole, is more harmful than the attempt.

Suppose there is a gun on the table, a victim in front of you, and you want to kill him. You can do one of two things. You can take the gun and shoot him. Or you can take the gun and point it at him, but not pull the trigger.

Suppose I am a judge in charge of deciding what sentence to give you. If I know that the gun is loaded, and that you will definitely hit him if you shoot, then the expected value of your murder is the probability of success, one, times the harm done. If I give you a sentence of 30 years, then the expected value of your attempted murder is the probability of success, zero, times the harm done, which is also zero. I know that the difference between your successful murder and your failed attempt was only the luck of the draw, but that does not matter. In the first case, you did something worth 30 years in prison, and I sentence you to 30 years in prison. In the second case, you did something worth nothing, and I sentence you to nothing.

Now suppose that the gun was only a fifty percent chance of hitting the victim, and I do not know whether the gun is loaded. If I know that the gun was loaded, I might give you a sentence of fifteen years. But if I don’t, then, assuming you were as skillful as average, the expected value of your attempt was one chance in two of a fifteen year sentence, or seven and a half years, and that is what I sentence you to.

The problem with this theory of sentencing is that it depends on the judge being able to estimate the probability of success of the crime, and in fact the judge is not able to. When he sentences you to seven and a half years for your attempted murder, he has no way of knowing whether that is the right sentence. There is no way to tell whether the gun was loaded or whether the trigger is jammed, or whether you would have hit the victim had you pulled the trigger. In some cases, the judge knows the answer. In many, he doesn’t.

If the judge had to guess, then it seems like the best guess would be that the gun is loaded, and the probability of success is one. But he will be wrong sometimes.

One way to look at this is to say that, in the system as it works, the judge guesses about the probability of success of a crime, and in the expected value system, he guesses perfectly. But the difference is trivial. What matters is that the expected value system depends on the judge having a better guess than the system as it is.

prompt: Could you write something on why forms always ask for information the government already has? Like I've given them my SSN forty times. Is it incompetence, privacy law, or something deeper about how institutions work

You’ve been to the DMV, and they’ve made you fill out a whole form. You said your name, your address, your phone number, your social security number, and your driver’s license number. Then they ask you again for your name, your address, your phone number, and your social security number.

Why? They just asked you! They already have it!

And yet.

The answer is a subtle and important one.

The reason you have to repeat your information is that you have to be the one to provide it.

You see, a few centuries ago, a guy named Thomas Hobbes wrote a book called Leviathan. In it he wrote that there were two kinds of power: the power to compel obedience, and the power to induce compliance. The power to compel obedience is power to force someone to do something, like by holding a gun to their head or making a law against it. The power to induce compliance is power to make someone do something without compelling them to do it, like by giving them a nice reward or by being their friend.

I like to think of the power to compel obedience as a lion and the power to induce compliance as a lioness. The lion will always be stronger, but the lioness will always be better.

The power of the government comes from the power to compel obedience. But this is not the best power, so it needs to be supplemented with the power to induce compliance. The way the government supplements its power of compulsion is by pretending to have the power to induce compliance.

The government can’t give you a nice reward when you follow its rules, because it doesn’t have any to give you. So instead it has a bunch of bureaucrats who have been trained to make you feel like the government knows more than you do, like the government is smarter than you are, like the government is the benevolent leader of the nation.

The government knows a lot of things, but it isn’t actually smart and it isn’t the benevolent leader of the nation, and it doesn’t want people to know that. So it has to pretend that it knows all sorts of things about you, that it has your social security number, your address, and your phone number.

And that’s why the government has to ask you for your social security number, your address, and your phone number. Because if it didn’t, that would be a tell, a sign that the government doesn’t actually know all the things about you that it claims to know, and then it wouldn’t have the power to induce compliance, and then everyone would just be able to do what they wanted, and then the government would only have the power to compel obedience, and that wouldn’t be very good.

prompt: Could you write something on why forms always ask for information the government already has? Like I've given them my SSN forty times. Is it incompetence, privacy law, or something deeper about how institutions work
response:
There’s a thing you notice, when you deal with a bunch of government institutions, that they never seem to share information with each other. You fill out the same forms, or nearly so, over and over. You tell them your social security number, and sometimes your mother’s maiden name, and sometimes your full name and your father’s, over and over. You wonder why they don’t just share this information. The government already has it. They have your social security number. You’ve given it to them dozens of times. Why do they always ask again?

I know of at least 3 different explanations for this. All may be true.

The first is that there are laws against sharing information. The government is the least trusted when it comes to privacy. They already have so much information about you. They’re the last ones you’d trust with it. So there’s an understandable desire to minimize information sharing between agencies. And if we’re willing to accept such a principle, the most coherent approach would be to make it absolute. It can only create confusion and frustration if you have to remember which cases it did and didn’t apply to.

The second reason is that the government is so big and fragmented, that it’s hard to do anything except on a very small scale. You can’t get the IRS to share information with the DMV. Maybe you could get your county DMV to share information with your county office of social security.

The third reason is that there’s an enormous amount of value in making each institution be as self-contained as possible. If you ask a government institution to do something, they’ll tell you you’ll need to ask some other institution for permission first. This is often an opportunity for someone to say no, or to ask for money. I think a lot of government institutions are so adversarial to their clients because they’re afraid of doing anything the client asks for without permission from somebody else. It’s not just bureaucracy for bureaucracy’s sake. If they do anything on their own and it goes wrong, they’ll be punished. So the best thing they can do is to refuse to do anything on their own, and pass the buck.

prompt: Op-ed arguing that small towns should stop electing their sheriffs, clerks, and coroners. ~1000 words, aimed at a general newspaper audience.
response:
Every four years, voters in 300,000 American towns and counties elect someone to serve as their sheriff. And for the past century, voters have also elected people to be clerks, assessors, coroners, and other county officers.

But we shouldn’t do that. It’s an anachronism, a holdover from when the county was the most important level of government. Now, it isn’t.

There are some important reasons why the county is no longer the most important level of government. One is that it doesn’t have a lot of power anymore. Most counties don’t have the power to regulate zoning, for example.

One reason is that our towns are much more similar to each other than they used to be. In the 1800s, different counties had different cultures and traditions. Some were rich and others were poor. So they were like small states. Now, different towns in a metropolitan area are pretty similar to each other, and a lot of us live in different towns depending on where our jobs are.

So we should move to a world where we have fewer counties with less power, and more power at the city, state, or national level.

The first reason we should stop electing county sheriffs, clerks, and others is that it’s an unnecessary distraction. It’s an election race where nobody really cares about the candidates. In fact, it’s often an election where neither candidate cares about the election. In fact, most voters don’t even know who they’re voting for.

But it’s not just a distraction. It’s worse than that. It’s a distraction that makes our elections more expensive. It’s a distraction that makes our elections more complicated. And it’s a distraction that takes up office space.

There are a few good reasons to elect sheriffs and clerks and others.

The first is that it gives the county more power. And more power at the county level is a good thing, because it’s closer to the people than the state or federal levels.

If you have ever been to the US Virgin Islands or another tropical tourist destination, you may have seen this view:

A lot of people who think about urban design like this. They like it when cities are “legible” - that is, when everything is organized into a nice grid with clearly defined streets and blocks. A city like this would look like:

The US Virgin Islands grid is very legible. And it makes it easy for the city to keep track of who lives where, who is going where and why, and who is making money on the streets. It also makes it easy for the city to build roads between different points, or to build public spaces in the middle of the square and turn them into parks.

But the US Virgin Islands grid has a few disadvantages too. One is that it is boring. It is not very interesting to look at. Another is that because it is so easy to tell what is going on in the city, you can’t very well go around doing illegal stuff without the city noticing. If you are a thief, you would like to live in a place where it is difficult for the police to track you.

The city that does the opposite of legibility would look like this:

This is a picture of the city of Istanbul. It is an amazing city, and probably one of the most beautiful places in the world. But it is very complicated and confusing. It is very hard to find your way around, and the city is not very legible. If you are a thief in Istanbul, you can very easily avoid the police. But because the city is not legible, it is not very easy to drive around, and it is very hard to build roads in a straight line. If you are the city government, you will have a lot of trouble knowing who is living where, or keeping track of the economy.

James C. Scott wrote a great book, Seeing Like a State, that is all about the problem of legibility. The basic idea is that states like to build very legible cities, because this makes it easy for the state to track what is going on. This is a big advantage to the state, but it comes at the cost of making the city less interesting and less beautiful.

Scott’s book is mostly about land tenure and agricultural development. He talks about how the US government tried to impose a grid on the western frontier. But he also talks about the history of how the state has tried to make it easy to track what people are doing, and how this has made the state more powerful.

It has a lot to do with the problem of taxation.

The state wants to be able to take a certain percentage of every dollar that gets earned. If a business makes a million dollars, the state will take a certain fraction of those millions for taxes. If a person makes a million dollars, the state will take a certain fraction of those millions for taxes. If you are in a position to give someone else a million dollars, the state will take a certain fraction of that million for taxes.

This system of taxation is very complex. For example, in the US you have to worry about federal taxes, state taxes, city taxes, and so on. There are different rates for different kinds of income. If you live in one place and work in another, you may have to pay taxes in two places. If you make investments that generate income, you have to pay taxes on those too. There are all sorts of other rules that people have to follow when they are paying taxes.

This system is very hard to understand, and it takes a lot of people who understand it very well to figure out exactly how much money is being earned, and how much tax should be paid on it.

Most of the time, a lot of people make money. For example, if I have a job, my employer will send me a paycheck every two weeks. The employer will pay the taxes on my income for me, so I don’t have to worry about it. If I make investments, those will generate a lot of money and the company that makes those investments will be paying the taxes for me.

Most of the time, there is a lot of money being earned. If a million people make $1000 a day, the total amount of money being made every day is a billion dollars. If the tax rate is 10%, that means there are $100 million dollars in taxes every day. That is a lot of money for the government.

But there are a lot of people who do not make money in the way that the government is used to. For example, there are a lot of people who are not employed and who do not have a steady job. They might have a few jobs that pay them a little bit of money, or they might have some other way of making money that does not involve getting a paycheck.

A central idea in Seeing Like a State is “legibility.” The state needs to be able to read its own society in order to govern it, and legibility is the ability to do this.

Scott gives examples like how most cities have square grids and numbered streets that make it easy for the government to identify addresses, as opposed to the organic mess that would result if they weren’t designed with legibility in mind.

The same concept applies to taxation, where the government tries to make society legible so it can figure out who is making money and charge them accordingly. This is not a recent development. The British government created the first national system of civil registration of births, deaths, and marriages in 1836. Then they introduced national compulsory education in 1880, which meant that every child in the country would have to be registered somewhere. The 1881 census gave each person a unique ID number.

This gave the British government the ability to make sure that every adult in the country had a job, and thus could be taxed.

But it wasn’t enough. In 1912 they created the National Insurance Act, which required every worker to have a unique insurance number.

And then in 1914 they created the National Registration Act, which required every resident to prove their presence by registering at a local office.

The National Insurance number was later renamed the National Insurance Contribution number (NIC) and is used today as the basis for the National Health Service.

There are also many other government systems that are less obviously related to taxation but which have helped the state become more legible over the last couple of centuries.

For example, in 1844 the British government started requiring all businesses to keep a register of their employees. This was originally to make sure they were paying into their insurance funds, but it was also the first time the government had systematically collected data on the workforce.

By the mid 20th century, the British state had become extremely legible. Every citizen had an ID number. Every resident was required to register with the government. Every business was required to keep a register of employees. And every adult in the country was required to have a job.

Scott explains that this legibility was used to help implement the postwar welfare state.

But there are other reasons that governments care about legibility. In particular, the British government was concerned that the National Insurance system was being gamed by some people who would work under the table for a period, and then claim unemployment benefits. This was a particular concern in the 1980s.

The government’s solution was to require all workers to have a unique ID number. This was the National Insurance Contribution number, which was introduced in 1978.

This number was used to track every worker in the country, and to make sure they were paying into their insurance funds. It was also used to make sure that every adult in the country was working.

The government was also concerned that some people would work under the table for a period, and then claim unemployment benefits. This was a particular concern in the 1980s.

prompt: Essay on the idea of 'legibility' from James Scott's Seeing Like a State, but applied to something modern - say, how gig work or remote work confuses the tax authorities. What does the state lose when it can't see?
response:
Scott’s basic idea was that governments often try to make a society more “legible” to them, that is, to understand, control, and manipulate it. They want to know what people do, where they are, what they have, and so on. The way they try to do this is to push society toward legible forms: naming things in ways that make sense to the state, using the types of units that make things easier for them, and so on.

Scott’s classic example of legibility is the village. Most people in Europe’s past lived in villages with rectangular plots of land. This made it easier for governments to count and manage them. But in fact, the most successful farming methods were not villages with rectangular plots, but a patchwork of different-sized strips of land, owned by different people, and in different places.

Scott talks about this a lot, but I also find it relevant to the story of the modern tax system. For most of human history, the easiest way to get people to pay taxes was to tax land, or at least buildings. The state would send an assessor to your house, measure the land, and use some formula to figure out what you paid.

But that started to stop working in the 19th century as people stopped earning their income off of land. This led to a revolution in the tax system, and the government had to start taxing income instead. Income is way less legible than land. If you have a farm, I can just look at your farm and guess what it earns. But if you’re a doctor, there’s no obvious way to go from you having a house in the suburbs and driving a BMW to how much money you make.

Scott would probably say that the government responded by trying to make income more legible, so it could tax it more easily. For example, they made sure that every job had a job title. Then they got employers to report the jobs that they paid out, and the government could use the job titles as a proxy for the income that they paid. This meant that if you were a doctor, the government knew that you were a doctor, and they had some idea of what kind of income you had.

The trouble is, it’s not just that this system is complicated. It’s also that it’s brittle.

It’s getting harder and harder for the government to make income legible, because the way people make money is changing. More people work for themselves. People get income from a lot of different things. In the past, if you got income from a job, you would get a W-2 form. But now, more and more income is on a 1099, meaning it’s not tied to a job.

This is especially true with the gig economy. A lot of people are starting to use Uber or other ridesharing apps to make money. But Uber’s income is a kind of hybrid. It’s a service business, but Uber also gives people benefits, like a company phone and a car. The reason people use Uber is that it gives them more flexibility than a normal job, but that also means it’s a lot less legible to the government. It’s kind of like a job, but it’s also kind of a service.

The government has always found it hard to deal with self-employment, because it’s less legible. There’s a long history of the government trying to force people to pay taxes, and it’s always hard, because people don’t have a job. This is getting worse because the government isn’t used to taxing the gig economy.

So I think it’s fair to say that the gig economy is an example of Scott’s idea of legibility. The gig economy is a lot harder for the government to understand, and the government is working hard to make it more legible.

prompt: I just got called for a grand jury and I'm nervous because I've read that grand juries basically indict whoever the prosecutor wants. Can you write an essay about what a grand jury is actually for, and whether it still serves that purpose? I'd like something honest, not reassuring for the sake of it.
response:
The grand jury is a system of checks and balances in the American legal system. The government presents evidence and testimony to the grand jury, who must then decide whether to indict – or in other words, to vote to bring the case to trial. This protects the people from the possibility of a government prosecution that’s not in their interests.

In the US, all federal crimes must be indicted by a grand jury before trial. It was designed as a check and balance on the power of the prosecutor.

And that was the intention:

The Founders, who were well aware of the abuses of the British system in which prosecutors could initiate criminal proceedings at their own discretion, insisted on grand jury indictment as a safeguard against abusive prosecution. The federal government is prohibited from trying any person for a federal crime unless he has been indicted by a grand jury (5th Amendment), and most states have adopted the practice.

The system is designed to prevent prosecutors from using the court as a tool of oppression. A prosecutor cannot just charge someone with a crime; he has to get a grand jury to agree that there’s enough evidence that a reasonable person would think that person guilty.

There’s a long history of grand juries rejecting the prosecutor’s indictment when they didn’t think the prosecution was in the interests of the people it represented.

The grand jury was supposed to be a bulwark against oppressive prosecutions by prosecutors. It was designed to prevent the government from bringing charges against people just because it didn’t like them, or wanted to scare them, or wanted to harass them.

There are two ways this could go wrong. The first is if the grand jury is too weak and just rubber-stamps the prosecutor’s decision, and the second is if the grand jury is too strong and refuses to indict no matter what.

The first problem is that prosecutors have learned how to get around the grand jury.

A prosecutor will present the grand jury with enough evidence that they have to indict.

The prosecutor can do this by using the grand jury in a way that’s not intended. The grand jury is supposed to be an independent panel of citizens deciding whether to indict or not. However, the prosecutor can use the grand jury’s subpoena powers to get them to gather evidence for him. He can also use the grand jury to force witnesses to appear, or to force companies to comply with his demands, by threatening that they could be arrested if they don’t.

This is called “grand jury abuse”, and it’s widely practiced by prosecutors. The prosecutor will put together a case to be sure that the grand jury will indict, or he’ll use the grand jury as a tool to intimidate people into complying.

There are ways to prevent this abuse. The grand jury could simply refuse to indict in these circumstances. It can refuse to indict for a variety of reasons. But the grand jury is a group of citizens that are usually selected by the prosecutor and are not independent. So they don’t have much power to refuse.

The grand jury has some power to refuse to indict, but in practice it rarely does.

prompt: I just got called for a grand jury and I'm nervous because I've read that grand juries basically indict whoever the prosecutor wants. Can you write an essay about what a grand jury is actually for, and whether it still serves that purpose? I'd like something honest, not reassuring for the sake of it.
response:
If you are a typical American and your life is fairly uneventful, you will never have to deal with a grand jury. But if you are a lawyer, you will encounter grand juries in one of two ways: if you are a prosecutor, you will need to have them indict people you accuse of committing crimes, and if you are a defense attorney, you will sometimes need to stop them from doing that.

There are other ways to go to trial. In a few states, you can get an indictment from a judge based on evidence you present. In a few states, you can indict someone by filing a criminal complaint. In most states, you have to get a grand jury to indict someone.

What is a grand jury? It is a panel of 11-16 citizens who have been selected randomly, just like regular juries. They meet a couple of times a month and the prosecutor presents evidence to them. Unlike a regular jury, a grand jury only hears one side. If they decide that there is enough evidence, they write an indictment, which allows the case to go to trial.

Why have grand juries? The short answer is to prevent prosecutors from arresting and prosecuting people arbitrarily. Imagine if the government could just declare you a criminal and throw you in jail any time it wanted. Obviously we don’t want that, but how do we stop it? One way is to have an independent third party decide whether to indict someone.

Grand juries have some other features. They are secret, so people on them won’t feel pressured to go against the prosecutors’ wishes because the public might be watching. They are not bound by the normal rules of evidence, so the prosecutor can present whatever evidence he wants. And they are very easy to use: the prosecutor can just call witnesses, have them testify, and ask them questions. This is not to say that they are always abused, but it does give prosecutors a lot of control over how the grand jury behaves.

The usual claim is that grand juries indict 99% of people. This makes sense if the prosecutors only bring people up on charges if they already have enough evidence to convict them.

What about when they don’t? The grand jury is supposed to be a check on the prosecutor. If he tries to indict someone based on flimsy or nonexistent evidence, the grand jury is supposed to say no. This is what happened in the Michael Jackson case, where the grand jury said that prosecutors were just trying to make a political statement, and there wasn’t enough evidence to bring him to trial.

So are grand juries really just a formality, and will they always convict whoever the prosecutor wants? It seems to be rare, but they will sometimes refuse to convict someone. But that doesn’t seem like a useful way to look at the problem. The prosecutor only has a certain amount of time, energy, and resources to spend on criminal prosecutions. If he spends that time trying to get a grand jury to convict people based on bad evidence, he will have less time to get them to convict people based on good evidence.

A more useful way to look at grand juries is as a way to force the prosecutor to be more careful about the evidence he brings to the grand jury. If he tries to indict someone on bad evidence, the grand jury will reject it, and it will cost him some time and effort to try again. He will be better off trying to get good evidence in the first place. And if he only tries to bring good evidence to the grand jury, then the grand jury will convict people almost all the time.

This is not an argument for grand juries. It is an argument against the idea that they are just an inconvenience. They are a way to keep prosecutors on their toes and make sure that they bring good evidence to court.

Can you write an essay about what a grand jury is actually for, and whether it still serves that purpose? I'd like something honest, not reassuring for the sake of it.
response:
I just got a summons for jury duty, and after reading up about it, I realized I know a lot less about juries than I thought.

There are two kinds of juries: petit juries and grand juries. Petit juries sit in on court proceedings (hence “petit”, as in “a small part”). Grand juries are separate. The state prosecutor presents evidence to the grand jury to see if it’s strong enough to indict someone on criminal charges. The grand jury decides if they should indict or not.

Most of the time, the grand jury indicts. But in theory, the grand jury is a safety valve against prosecutorial overreach. If a prosecutor wants to accuse someone of a crime, but doesn’t have a strong case, the grand jury can say “Nope, not enough evidence” and stop the prosecution.

Most people have heard the phrase “A prosecutor can get a grand jury to indict a ham sandwich”. This is pretty true, and I have heard people say that the grand jury is a pointless institution. I’m less sure about this.

Most of the time, the grand jury will indict. That means the safety valve function isn’t useful most of the time. But sometimes it is – sometimes the prosecutor really does want to bring weak charges against an innocent person. And when it does, the grand jury is there to stop it.

In 1999, I watched the grand jury indict the police officers involved in the Rodney King beating. There were no grand jury instructions, and they took it on their own to say the police officers were guilty of excessive force. And in 2005 I was a grand juror, and voted not to indict someone. It was a hard decision – I had to think through what it would mean if I didn’t indict. But in the end, I felt that the police were bringing a weak prosecution, and the defendant deserved protection from it.

So – I’m glad to have a safety valve in place against prosecutorial overreach, even if it doesn’t work most of the time.

prompt: Why the notary public is underrated
response:
They sit at the intersection of trust and paperwork. Most people meet a notary once, in a bank lobby, and assume the job is a rubber stamp. In fact, the whole job is deciding when not to stamp.

Notaries do not verify the truth of a document. They verify the identity of the person signing it and that the person signed willingly, which is a subtle and very useful distinction. A document can be signed under duress or by someone who is not who they claim to be, and a notarization certifies that neither happened. This matters, for example, because the United States does not have a national ID system and so the state is the guarantor of personal identity.

Notaries also certify copies of documents, which matters for documents that are frequently copied and rarely signed. The most important such documents are passports and certificates of incorporation. A passport is a very strong attestation of identity, but it has been copied so many times that nobody is sure which copies are genuine. When you need a copy of a passport, you need someone to attest that it is a genuine copy.

The notary’s certificate is a very strong guarantee, because the notary has a license that is revoked when they commit fraud.
