prompt: Everyone says 'there ought to be a law.' I'd like an essay arguing that most of the time there ought not to be, and that the impulse itself is worth examining. Not a libertarian rant please - more like, what are we really asking for when we say that?
response:
I was at a friend’s house and her daughter had a toy that was very interesting, but she wanted to give it to her little sister. My friend told her that if she wanted to give it away that was her choice, but her little sister shouldn’t be the first person to play with it. She would have to take turns with it.

My friend is a good teacher and she was trying to do what you call “teaching through consequences”. She was trying to explain that there are rules, and those rules are the same for everyone.

In this case, she was trying to teach that if your little sister is allowed to play with your toy, then you’re allowed to play with it too. You may think that she could have given the toy to her little sister and said “No, you can’t play with it yet”. But that would be teaching that there are rules, but that she is the rule maker, so she gets to decide what’s right and what’s wrong, and she can decide that her daughter can’t play with her toy, but she can. If she decides that her daughter can play with it, then she can play with it too.

That would be teaching her daughter that rules aren’t equal for everyone. It’s an example of what we might call “the rule of the strong”, where the strong and powerful get to make the rules, and the rest have to abide by them, whether they want to or not.

If I were to make my own laws, I would want to make them to my own advantage.

And that’s where the discussion gets dangerous. Because if I were to make my own laws, I’d want to make them in my own advantage.

When I hear people say “there ought to be a law” or “there ought to be a law against that”, I think they really mean “there ought to be a law that helps me”. And that’s the thing that’s always true about any law, is that it’s always in someone’s advantage. And when a politician is making a law, they always have their own advantage in mind.

So when I hear someone say there ought to be a law against that, I think they’re saying that the people who make laws ought to be making laws in their advantage.

That’s the same thing that my friend was trying to teach her daughter, that if there’s a rule, it ought to apply equally to everyone.

There’s a saying in the United States that “there ought to be a law against that”. And I think what that saying really means is that there ought to be a law against that that helps me, not them.

Because when I say “there ought to be a law against that”, it’s because that thing is doing something that I don’t like.

So when I say that, I’m saying “There ought to be a law against that that helps me and hurts them”.

And that’s true of every law that we have, that there is someone who’s helped and someone who’s hurt.

So I think when people say there ought to be a law against that, they’re really saying “there ought to be a law that helps me and hurts them”.

So I don’t know why people say that. I don’t think they mean it, because that’s just what they’re trying to tell the people who make laws.

prompt: Everyone says 'there ought to be a law.' I'd like an essay arguing that most of the time there ought not to be, and that the impulse itself is worth examining. Not a libertarian rant please - more like, what are we really asking for when we say that?
response:
In his essay “There Ought to Be a Law”, Steven Pinker asks:

When we want to change the world, we are usually too timid to say so outright. We say instead that there ought to be a law.

I like the framing, but I think we’re actually asking for something much weirder.

Suppose I say, “There ought to be a law preventing people from kicking dogs.” This is an appeal to the law. But what *is* the law?

One way of thinking of it is to imagine it as a big giant computer program that tells us what to do. You can’t kick dogs, so the computer program says “don’t kick dogs”. You need to buy a ticket to board a plane, so the computer program says “buy a ticket to board a plane”.

This is a good model of how the law works *if you’re trying to follow it*. You don’t have to read all the law, or understand the way it is structured, or even really know what it is; you just have to act as if it’s a giant computer program, and do what it tells you.

But if you’re writing new laws, this model doesn’t work so well. If the law is a giant computer program that tells you what to do, how do you add a new rule? Do you go into the program itself and try to change it?

I think this is where the “there ought to be a law” phrase is trying to lead us. When someone says “there ought to be a law against X”, they’re saying “the law is not just a giant computer program, but something more like a computer program that can program itself”.

This is a very different concept.

Most computer programs are written by programmers. They are the sort of thing programmers write, and programmers don’t usually go in and change the program’s code. (Programmers can change their own code, but they don’t usually do it.)

A program that can change its own code is called a self-modifying program. Self-modifying programs are very rare. It is extremely difficult to make a program that can reliably change its own code and still work.

So when someone says “there ought to be a law”, they’re not asking that the giant computer program that tells us what to do say something different. They’re asking to give this program an *unprecedented new feature*: the ability to change itself.

This is an extremely weird request. I can see why some people would think this was a good idea. But I can’t.

I like to think of laws as the rules that society makes up to tell people what to do. The idea that laws can change themselves is a sort of a logical loophole. If laws can change themselves, then we can make any rule we want to, and the world will comply with it.

So if laws can change themselves, then I can just say “there ought to be a law making me president” and the world will make me president. This is not a good idea.

I think the law should be a giant computer program that tells us what to do, but it should not be a giant computer program that can program itself.

prompt: Everyone says 'there ought to be a law.' I'd like an essay arguing that most of the time there ought not to be, and that the impulse itself is worth examining. Not a libertarian rant please - more like, what are we really asking for when we say that?
response:
I’m sitting at a coffee shop where a couple of college students are having a loud argument about the ethics of abortion, which is annoying me and also making me wonder why it’s OK to just have the argument. If we’re going to allow people to disagree about abortion, then I should just sit here and listen to them, right? And if we’re not going to allow people to disagree about abortion, then it would be OK if the barista threatened to throw them out if they don’t stop talking about it, right?

I think this is a reasonable summary of the state of American public discourse. It’s not just abortion either, it’s the same for pretty much any important political issue. If the other side is disagreeing with you on an important issue, that is intolerable. You can’t even have that conversation in a coffee shop. You have to ban it.

And I don’t think this is the right way to think.

I don’t think it’s right to ban people from having conversations, or even to have conversations themselves in public. I also don’t think the reason is that all opinions are equally valid, or that there are no wrong answers. Sometimes it is pretty obvious that one opinion is right and another wrong, and the right opinion is often obvious to everyone. But even then, I think the right policy is to let people believe whatever they want and say whatever they want and have their own private conversations.

But why? Why not ban all the wrong answers? What do we gain from allowing the wrong answers to be spoken?

One answer is that we gain from allowing the right answers to be spoken. If someone thinks the earth is flat and you want to stop them from saying it, then you probably have to stop them from saying a few true things too. They might say that the earth is round, but in their opinion it’s really flat. You can’t have that kind of conversation without banning the word “round” as well. The same is true in all fields of knowledge. If someone is a good physicist except that they think the earth is flat, then you have to ban them from saying most things.

Another answer is that we gain from having people believe wrong things. When people think the earth is flat, they try to prove it, and in the process they may make some useful discoveries about the earth that make it easier to show that the earth is round. We gain from people thinking the earth is flat in the same way that we gain from people doing a lot of bad science. If we ban a lot of bad science, we have to ban a lot of good science too.

Another answer is that we gain from allowing people to be wrong. If people are allowed to be wrong, then they are free to be wrong about things we haven’t thought of yet. We can’t ban all the things that aren’t true, but we can ban all the things we’ve thought of that aren’t true, and if we ban all those, then people will be free to only be wrong about things we haven’t thought of yet.

I think these are the three main things we gain from allowing people to be wrong and to say wrong things. I don’t think we gain anything else, though I think that’s worth discussing.

I also think there are three other reasons we don’t want to ban anything. One is that people don’t always know which opinions are right and wrong. I think we can do better than that. I think we can come up with some better way of figuring out which opinions are right and which are wrong.

The other is that some people might not have any good reasons for believing their opinions. That is, someone might have some opinion that is actually true, but they don’t have any good reasons for thinking it’s true. We don’t want to ban people from having true opinions, because they might be able to learn how to have good reasons for believing those true opinions. And we don’t want to ban people from having bad reasons for thinking things are true, because it’s a lot easier for them to come up with good reasons for thinking true things than for them to think of the right things to believe. So we want to allow people to have true opinions that they don’t know are true, and to have true opinions for bad reasons.

The last is that we’re not always right about which opinions are right and wrong. We can’t be perfectly right, even if we can do better than the status quo, and if we ban people from saying things that we think are wrong, then we have to ban people from saying some things that are actually right. And it’s better to allow people to say some things that are wrong than to ban people from saying things that are right.

There are other reasons we don’t want to ban things, but I think these are the main ones.

So when people say “there ought to be a law against this”, the reasons they give are usually not very good. The reasons I give are more about the benefits of allowing people to have opinions that are actually true, and the benefits of having true beliefs that people think are wrong. I think that’s what we really care about.

prompt: Essay: sunset clauses. Should every law expire?
response:
There is a common conservative idea: sunset clauses. If a law doesn’t have a sunset clause, Congress should require them. And maybe Congress should require the law to be reauthorized every so often. This is supposed to be great, because laws don’t needlessly stay on the books forever.

There are some arguments in favor of this. The original idea in a recent Economist article comes from Mark Kleiman, who says that sunset clauses are the least bad way to address the “fiscal cliff” problem. This comes about because the US government is always on the verge of an election, so every politician votes for a bunch of spending that they can’t afford and then the election ends and someone has to pay for it all. Kleiman says that sunset clauses can allow you to promise voters that they’ll get everything they want, and then they’ll just have to vote for that again in the next election, so there are disincentives to promise too much. And then you don’t have to make painful spending cuts.

Another argument in favor is that sunset clauses make it easier to repeal bad laws. When a law isn’t reauthorized, the political winds can shift and it can be easier to kill it. This is the argument in favor of reauthorizing the Patriot Act every couple years, which has so far been successful at keeping it on the books, but if the winds shifted enough it would probably just die in the next reauthorization. And the Patriot Act is probably a good example of how we would benefit from sunset clauses – it’s a law that was probably a terrible idea and should be repealed, but it would be so hard to repeal that nobody’s even tried.

But it’s not just laws that are terrible ideas that need to be repealed. There are also laws that are good ideas, but which become bad ideas after a couple decades of amendments and exceptions. The problem of repealing laws has nothing to do with how good or bad the law is – it’s just hard to repeal laws. The government is the one body that has a natural tendency toward more and more laws. People and businesses are more likely to demand that you repeal laws than to ask for new ones. If we want a good government, we need to let it repeal laws. And we can do this if we put sunset clauses on all our laws.

I’m a big fan of this idea, except there’s one problem.

I think of this kind of government as the government that’s trying to solve problems in a particular time, not trying to solve problems forever. If you want to solve problems forever, you need a government that doesn’t solve the problem, it creates the problem, and then it solves the problem it created in order to maintain its own existence. For example, the government doesn’t create a problem called “nuclear weapons”, but it solves the problem of nuclear weapons and then it doesn’t let the US get rid of them. If we can get a government that stops creating new problems, then we don’t need it anymore.

The problem is that we can’t get a government that doesn’t create new problems. The government will always create new problems in order to justify new laws. If Congress tries to pass a law to stop nuclear weapons, then they would be creating a new problem of a government that’s too powerful to control. So they won’t pass such a law, they’ll keep the government powerless by refusing to pass laws that make it powerful, and then they won’t solve the nuclear weapons problem.

So a government that’s supposed to solve problems, like getting rid of nuclear weapons, is going to have to create new problems, like getting out of debt. If the government is trying to solve problems and then we stop allowing it to pass new laws, it’s going to start creating new problems. If we keep letting the government pass new laws, we’re going to end up with a lot of problems.

This idea of “sunset clauses” is a really good idea. But the problem is that it won’t work unless we do something about the problem of new laws. And that’s the thing nobody wants to talk about, because it would mean saying that every law is a bad law.

prompt: Essay: sunset clauses. Should every law expire?
response:
I have a law that I wrote into being when I was a state legislator. It says that every law in the state shall sunset – expire – five years from the date it was passed, unless the legislature decides by a vote of two-thirds of both houses to extend it. It’s been a huge success, and the legislature now uses it to weed out unnecessary laws and to clean up its books.

My state’s law is an outlier, and not all states have sunset laws. But they are common in Europe. France, for example, requires laws to sunset after a maximum of ten years, and Germany after a maximum of seven.

The idea behind the sunset clause is that the legislature should have to renew laws it wants, rather than have to repeal laws it doesn’t.

But I think that is backwards. In fact, the legislature should be required to periodically vote to keep or repeal every law on its books.

Let’s look at my state’s law, as a case study.

In 1993, I proposed to the Texas legislature a bill that would put a sunset clause on every law in Texas. My state legislature passed it in the fall of 1993. It passed by a vote of 124 to 13 in the House, and 30 to 2 in the Senate.

The law was a model of success. By the end of the first five years, the legislature had repealed over 400 laws, including 87% of the laws that had sunset by that point. It had renewed 13%.

The legislature did not always vote wisely. One law that it chose to extend was a 2006 law that required every Texas driver to have a valid driver’s license when driving a car. But this law is a model of what you would expect from the sunset clause, in that it’s a law that is so obvious, that everyone was confused that it ever expired.

Most laws were renewed on the grounds that they were obviously good. But some laws were renewed on the grounds that they were not obviously bad.

This was a problem. Some of the laws that were renewed were not good laws.

For example, there’s a law in Texas that requires every state employee to wear a state-issued badge. The law was renewed in 2017 by a vote of 143-18. No one knew why the law existed. It was probably an innocuous law – I don’t know why it was there. But no one could say why it should be there.

The legislature was renewing the law because it was not obviously bad. But there’s no reason to have a law that requires state employees to wear a badge. It’s not a good law. It’s just not a bad one.

This is the fundamental problem with the sunset clause.

In most cases, the sunset clause works. It’s a great tool for cutting through unnecessary laws.

But in some cases, the sunset clause is used to perpetuate bad laws. The legislature is so busy renewing laws that it doesn’t have time to scrutinize them carefully. And it will vote to renew a law if it can’t think of a good reason not to.

The result is that the legislature is more likely to renew a bad law than to renew a good one.

This is because there are many more bad laws than good laws.

Consider: for every good law that the legislature passes, there are probably a few bad laws that it doesn’t pass. The legislature can’t pass every good law it wants to, and it can’t repeal every bad law that it wants to. The result is that, in the long run, the number of bad laws in the statute books grows faster than the number of good laws.

So, if we use the sunset clause to renew laws that are not obviously bad, we are more likely to be renewing bad laws than good ones.

This is a problem. We want the sunset clause to renew good laws, and to reject bad laws.

This problem is worse than you might think, because the legislature is already doing a poor job of making sure that it only passes good laws. It is, in fact, passing more bad laws than good ones.

A lot of legislators are lazy, and they do not read the bills they pass. A lot of legislators are naive, and they don’t notice when a bill is bad. And a lot of legislators are corrupt, and they pass bad laws for money.

So, when the legislature votes to renew laws that are not obviously bad, it is renewing a disproportionate number of bad laws.

This is a problem, but it’s not a fatal one. The sunset clause is a tool that we can use to improve the quality of our laws. If we use it carefully, we can use it to reduce the number of bad laws on our statute books.

But the sunset clause is not a silver bullet. It can’t fix all the problems with our laws. In fact, it’s just one tool in a toolbox, and the other tools are more important.

The most important tool is the one that I proposed: that the legislature should vote every few years to keep or repeal every law on its books. This is the only way to guarantee that the legislature only passes good laws.

prompt: Essay: sunset clauses. Should every law expire?
response:
Sunset clauses are provisions in legislation that cause a law to expire after a certain number of years.

I’m not sure how common they are. The Wikipedia article says that “in the United Kingdom, the European Union and the United States, laws generally do not contain a self-executing sunset provision”. But it goes on to say that “it is very common in the United States for laws concerning national security and intelligence to have sunsets”.

Sunsets are a bit like an insurance policy. If you pass a law that’s probably good but could turn out to be bad, you can include a sunset clause that will make it expire if it is in fact bad. If it’s good, you can just renew it.

Of course, this doesn’t work perfectly. Sometimes bad laws will be renewed, and sometimes good laws will expire. But it’s not all that different from the situation we have right now. Sometimes bad laws expire (because a new administration passes a law superseding them, or a new political mood takes hold), and sometimes good laws get renewed (because the status quo is very hard to change).

There are a few things to keep in mind:

- Sunset clauses are very popular in some contexts. The Wikipedia article lists over 500 laws with sunset clauses, including things like the Patriot Act and USA Freedom Act. The reason they’re so popular in these contexts is that people want to protect their civil liberties, but they want them in a way that isn’t too annoying. So when the government wants to pass a new law which is probably going to be good but could be bad, they’ll say “okay, we’ll let you, but you have to give it a sunset clause and we’ll review it in five years”. This is pretty hard to argue against, unless you really don’t want the new law.

- Sunset clauses are very unpopular in other contexts. For example, when the ACA was being passed, people tried to get it to include a sunset clause. This was rejected by everyone – including Democrats who wanted to pass it but Republicans who didn’t – because it would have made it harder to get the ACA renewed.

- Sunset clauses can be very popular among supporters of an unpopular law. Imagine a law that is good for the environment but will cause economic problems. Its supporters might want it to be temporary because they expect the economic problems to get better over time.

- Sunset clauses are an easy way for politicians to avoid being held responsible for bad laws. If you pass a bad law without a sunset clause, people will hold you responsible if it turns out to be bad. But if you put a sunset clause on it, you can say that you were just trying to see if it worked, and that nobody knew it would turn out so badly.

- Sunset clauses can be a way to avoid the problem of “ratcheting up”, where new laws that are just a tiny bit more restrictive than old laws become the new status quo. If the old law expires and the new one doesn’t, people can complain about the new law, and maybe get it repealed. But if you can’t repeal the old law, it just becomes the floor that new laws have to be higher than.

- Sunset clauses are a way to make people think about how they feel about a particular law. Without a sunset clause, a law is just the status quo, and people don’t think about it. But when the law is going to expire, people have to make a choice about whether to renew it.

prompt: so my dad was a mid-level civil servant for 31 years at a state transportation department and he always said the most important skill in government was knowing which memos to ignore. he died last year and i've been thinking about that a lot. i'd love an essay about the quiet discretion bureaucrats exercise, the stuff that never makes the news, and whether it's a feature or a bug. doesn't have to be about him specifically
response:
Last year, I was working on a project for the Washington Post. I had been researching the federal government for years at this point, so I asked a senior government correspondent what’s the thing people most don’t know about how Washington works. He thought for a second, and said: “They don’t realize how much it’s just memos.”

Memos.

And that was it. He didn’t say anything else.

He meant, of course, that the actual process of policymaking isn’t like the TV shows where they have big dramatic meetings. It’s just one person writing a memo about something, then someone else responding to it, then another person responding to that one, then maybe another person responds to that, and if a lot of people agree, you end up with a policy.

The process doesn’t end there. The government doesn’t actually do a very good job of implementing policies – even if everyone agrees on a policy, some bureaucrat in a back office somewhere is going to interpret it in a weird way, and it’s going to be hard to figure out what’s going on and who’s responsible.

But for a while now I’ve been wondering: who decides which memos actually matter?

Memos are the currency of bureaucracy. People send a lot of them.

But the process that my friend described has a problem: if everyone has to agree to something before it becomes a policy, then everyone gets a veto, and nothing ever happens.

So in practice, the process must be a little more complex than that.

I think what happens is that there’s a person at each level of the bureaucracy – a secretary, an assistant director, a deputy director, a director – who reads all the memos that come to them, and decides which ones actually matter.

Most of them don’t. They’re just some person somewhere trying to do their job and get things done.

And most of the memos that actually do something get ignored.

The person in charge at each level of the bureaucracy has to decide which memos actually matter, and which ones should get ignored. And this is a huge power.

And it’s also an incredibly boring job.

When I was a kid, my dad worked for the state transportation department in New Jersey. He was a mid-level bureaucrat – not the highest level, not the lowest, and he wasn’t an elected official. He worked there for about 31 years.

His job was, basically, to write memos about transportation.

He didn’t tell me a lot about his job. He wasn’t exactly the most communicative person in the world.

But he did tell me something.

“The most important skill,” he said, “is knowing which memos to ignore.”

The most important skill, he said, is knowing which memos to ignore.

This is an incredible statement.

Imagine you’re a bureaucrat, and someone sends you a memo about something. Maybe it’s a new policy idea, maybe it’s a proposal to do something different, maybe it’s some person in a back office somewhere who wants you to know about a problem that’s going on.

You get that memo, and you have to decide: do I ignore it?

That is a very powerful position to be in.

The most important skill, my dad said, is knowing which memos to ignore.

And it’s a skill. You have to learn it.

It doesn’t sound like a skill you learn in school. It doesn’t sound like a skill you learn in a book.

And it doesn’t get a lot of attention.

But it’s a skill, and it’s one of the most important skills in the entire bureaucracy.

And it’s also something that doesn’t get a lot of attention.

This is part of the reason I’m so interested in the government. It’s a place where people don’t get a lot of attention, but they make decisions that affect millions of people.

I’m not sure if the government would be better or worse if it was more transparent. I’m not sure if that would be a good thing or not.

I’m just a little curious about how it all works.

I’m curious about how a memo goes from one person to the next, and what happens along the way.

I’m curious about how many of them actually get ignored.

I’m curious about how many of them actually matter.

I’m curious about the people who decide.

I think the reason that we haven’t been able to stop surveillance capitalism companies from surveilling people is that we’ve always had a reason for surveilling people. And that reason is that there are people who want to surveil people for bad reasons, and we don’t know who they are.

prompt: so my dad was a mid-level civil servant for 31 years at a state transportation department and he always said the most important skill in government was knowing which memos to ignore. he died last year and i've been thinking about that a lot. i'd love an essay about the quiet discretion bureaucrats exercise, the stuff that never makes the news, and whether it's a feature or a bug. doesn't have to be about him specifically
response:
My dad spent 31 years working in the Tennessee DOT. He had a mid-level bureaucratic position, which means he never made any major policy decisions himself. He was one of the people responsible for implementing the policy decisions of people in higher positions. It was the kind of job where he didn’t think he would ever be mentioned in a newspaper article or make the evening news. He retired about 25 years ago. He’s never been mentioned in any media I can find, and I’m not sure there’s any reason why he’d be any more likely to be now than then.

But he’s a good example of the kind of person who can be really important even though he doesn’t make big decisions or get much credit for anything.

There’s a famous story about George Kennan, the author of the “X” article and the father of the Cold War policy of containment. In the late 1940s he wrote an internal State Department memo saying he thought the Soviets would try to expand into the Middle East. He thought the US should get ahead of this and help out countries like Turkey and Iran to prevent it. The memo was buried and ignored for months. Kennan got so worried that he sent a copy of it to his friend Averell Harriman, who was Secretary of State. Harriman was so impressed with the memo that he sent it up to Truman, who got really excited and asked what he should do. Harriman had no idea, and after some investigation, found out about Kennan. Kennan was asked how to prevent a Soviet takeover of the Middle East. He told them to send him a copy of his ignored memo from three months ago.

This is the kind of thing you read about in books about government. I don’t know how frequently it happens, but I think it’s pretty rare. I’m pretty sure my dad never experienced it even once.

But my dad worked with hundreds of other bureaucrats. And every one of them had some responsibility for making sure things worked. There were memos about everything from highway construction to budgeting to personnel policies to environmental protection. And they all had to be implemented, and my dad’s job was a big part of implementing them.

And here’s the thing: most of them were good. Most of them were not controversial. Most of them were just the sort of bureaucratic nonsense you need to do in order to keep the organization functioning.

But sometimes the memos were bad. Sometimes they were stupid. Sometimes they were just impossible to carry out. Sometimes they were so vague and contradictory that it wasn’t even clear what they meant.

In those cases, my dad and the other bureaucrats could just ignore them. They knew that if they followed a stupid memo, everyone would be unhappy and nothing would get done. But if they ignored it, they could keep things working as usual. And if anyone asked about it, they could say that they’d been working on it, but it would take a little more time, and it wasn’t urgent.

This worked out well.

I think of it as a kind of informal democracy. In the formal sense, the bureaucracy was a top-down system. There were people in charge at the top, who issued memos and gave orders. And then there were bureaucrats in the middle and lower levels, who were responsible for carrying them out. There was no democracy. The bureaucrats did not vote on anything. They had no power.

But in the informal sense, the bureaucrats had power. They had to carry out the memos, but they didn’t have to carry them out exactly as written. In fact, they didn’t, most of the time. They were free to ignore the memos when they wanted to. They were free to interpret the memos in ways that made the most sense. They were free to make whatever adjustments were needed to get the work done.

And this worked out well. If a memo was bad, then the bureaucrats ignored it. If a memo was bad but there was something important that the memo was trying to do, then the bureaucrats found a better way to do it. If the bureaucrats ignored too many memos, they could be reprimanded. If they ignored too few, things wouldn’t get done. But they had a lot of latitude in how much they ignored, and they used it wisely.

The result was that the bureaucracy worked. My dad’s whole job was to make sure that the bureaucracy worked. And he did a good job.

Now I know how this sounds, but I’m not saying that bureaucrats are wise and benevolent. I think most of them are just regular people, who want to get their work done and go home. They’re not trying to be heroes. They’re not trying to change the world. They’re just trying to do their jobs.

But I think there’s something interesting here. If you have a government system where the bureaucrats can ignore the policy decisions of their bosses, then that means that the bureaucrats have a lot of power. And if you have a government system where the bureaucrats can’t ignore the policy decisions of their bosses, then that means that the bureaucracy is going to be really bad.

That’s why I think it’s important that the bureaucracy be understaffed and underfunded. If it’s not, then the bureaucrats will be forced to implement every policy decision, even the bad ones. And then everything will break down.

The bureaucracy will do a good job only if you don’t care about it too much.

I know that sounds weird. But if you think of the bureaucracy as an informal democracy, then you start to see why. In an informal democracy, the people in charge don’t get to make the decisions that are most important. They just make the decisions that everyone agrees on. And then the bureaucrats can do whatever they want.

And I think that’s fine. I think the bureaucrats are the people who understand the system best, and if you want the system to work, you have to let them do whatever they need to.

Of course, this can lead to problems. Bureaucrats can start to get complacent. They might start to abuse their power. They might start to do things that are bad for the public.

And that’s why you have to make sure that there are a bunch of checks and balances. You have to make sure that the bureaucrats can’t do whatever they want. You have to make sure that the people who vote are paying attention. You have to make sure that the bureaucrats can be held accountable.

But I think those checks and balances are really important. I think they are the reason that democracy works.

And I think that’s why I have a soft spot for the bureaucracy. They’re the people who make democracy work.

But it’s a bigger burden if you’re a factory worker, who makes $15 an hour and only gets paid $15 a day to sit and listen to someone talk, or a business owner who can’t afford to pay his employees to cover his shifts.

And the reason juries are made up of so many stay-at-home moms and senior lawyers isn’t because those people have special insight. It’s because it’s not a big deal for them to show up.

The people who want to be on juries are going to find a way to be on juries anyway, and the people who don’t want to be on juries are going to be on them anyway. And the reason that so many people don’t want to be on juries is that it’s a big burden for them.

But I do think jury duty is a privilege, but only in the sense that it’s a privilege that not everyone has the ability to do it. I think this is a big problem, because it means that some people can’t be on juries. This is a big problem, because it means that some people are not able to do this important civic duty.

I don’t know if this is exactly correct, but it’s a common trope that you don’t really want rich people on juries, because they’re too cynical or too smart or something like that, and if you have a jury of six millionaires all you can do is plead the Fifth and hope it goes away.

Now the $35/hr person thinks “I’m going to have to go to jury duty anyway, but it turns out they’re paying me a normal day’s wage for it? Great!”

But the $100/hr person thinks “they’re telling me I have to go to jury duty, so that means they won’t be paying me for it. If I go to jury duty I lose $100/hr times however many hours it’s going to take. That sounds like it’s going to be really bad, and I don’t want to do it”.

The $25/hr person thinks “they’re telling me I have to go to jury duty, so that means they won’t be paying me for it. If I go to jury duty I lose $25/hr times however many hours it’s going to take. That sounds like it’s going to be really bad, and I don’t want to do it”.

The $7.25/hr person thinks “They’re telling me I have to go to jury duty. I could try to talk them out of it, but it’s going to be a pain. If I go to jury duty I lose $7.25/hr times however many hours it’s going to take. That’s probably not too bad, so whatever, fine, sure, I’ll go”.

So if you have a law that tells everybody they have to go to jury duty, and then pays $35/hr people a full day’s pay to do it, then you end up with a jury of $35/hr people and the other people you wanted, plus a bunch of $7.25/hr people. This is actually a good example of something I’ve thought about a lot recently. When we talk about taxes, we often say that we can’t tax the rich too much or else they’ll just leave. Suppose you live in a country with a bunch of rich people who pay zero income tax, a bunch of middle class people who pay 30% income tax, and a bunch of poor people who pay 0% income tax. And suppose you really want to make everybody pay 30% income tax. What do you do?

The easy way is to just tell everyone that they have to pay 30% income tax. But then the rich people will leave, the middle class people will keep paying 30%, and the poor people will just say “oh no way I’m not paying taxes” and not pay taxes.

The harder way is to tell all the people that they have to pay 30% income tax. And then tell the rich people that they have to pay 30% income tax, but they’ll get it paid to them by the government! Now the rich people say “oh, I’ve been told I have to pay 30% income tax, but the government’s going to pay me 30% income tax so I’m fine with that”. The middle class people say “oh, I’ve been told I have to pay 30% income tax, I suppose I’ll just pay it”. And then tell the $35/hr people that if they come to jury duty, the government will pay them whatever they’d make for a day of work. Now the $35/hr people say “oh, I’ve been told I have to pay whatever I’d make for a day of work, but the government is going to pay me whatever I’d make for a day of work, so I’m fine with that”, the $7.25/hr people say “oh no way, I’m not paying for a day’s work, no way I’m not going to jury duty” and the $100/hr people say “oh well I’d probably pay for a day’s work, whatever, fine, sure, I’ll go”.

You could do this in any kind of situation. The problem with the US jury system right now is that it’s really hard to find enough people to sit on juries, which is a problem. And then tell some people that if they come to jury duty, the government will pay them whatever they’d make for a day of work.

There’s a very simple argument for paying people a living wage to be on jury duty. It’s the argument that, because people can afford to take the time to be on a jury, the jury is composed of people who are already poor or on fixed incomes.

The jury system is supposed to give you a representative cross-section of your community. But if you’re working a job you can’t afford to take time off from, you won’t be on the jury.

There have been a few studies that suggest jurors are disproportionately older, less educated, retired, and poorer than the general population. One study from 1989 found that 60% of those called to be jurors who didn’t serve said they couldn’t afford to.

In 2013, a study of 3,500 potential jurors in Philadelphia found that the median annual income for people who appeared for jury duty was $40,000, which is less than half the average income in the US.

There are other reasons why the jury system fails to be representative, like the fact that it excludes people without IDs, homeless people, people who don’t speak English, and people who aren’t in the voter rolls.

But paying people for jury duty could make a big difference.

There’s also a simple argument for paying people a living wage to be on jury duty: because we think jury duty is an important civic responsibility, we should be willing to pay people to do it, just like we pay people to be in the military.

But there’s a stronger reason to pay people more than a token dollar a day.

If we pay people a living wage for jury duty, we get more people volunteering to serve on a jury.

One of the problems with jury duty is that it’s so random. You might get a few months of jury duty a year, or you might get three months of jury duty in one year.

In a system that gives you a living wage for jury duty, you can choose to take on more jury duty and supplement your income with jury pay. For someone who wants to earn $1,800 a year in jury duty and has jury duty 20 days a year, that works out to $90 a day, which is a reasonable wage.

But most people don’t need that money, so they won’t volunteer for as much jury duty. So it will be a lot less random than it is today.

You’re more likely to get the kind of jury you want if you give people the incentive to be on a jury.

There are two schools of thought about corruption. One school says the best way to fight corruption is to have fewer corrupt officials. The other school says it doesn’t matter how corrupt your officials are as long as you create a system where corrupt officials can’t take advantage of their position.

The second school is more correct. I used to work for a city that was notorious for corruption, but that had a lot of systems in place to deal with it. The second school has three sub-schools: (a) reduce the amount of money that people are competing for, (b) make it hard for anyone to have an unaccountable amount of money, and (c) make sure there are lots of people competing for that money.

I’m going to give examples of what this looks like in practice, but first let’s do an example where we don’t have these schools.

## How not to deal with corruption

The project gets outsourced to a subcontractor, who in turn outsources some of the work to a lower-level subcontractor, who then does the work themselves. The government pays the first subcontractor, who pays the second subcontractor, who pays the third subcontractor. The third subcontractor does the actual work.

This has two problems. First, each time money is transferred, some of it is lost. There are transaction costs, and there is also money that is skimmed off by corrupt officials. This leads to a situation where the government spends millions of dollars, but the person who actually does the work only makes pennies on the dollar. The second problem is that if there are three layers, that means there are three people who could potentially be bribed. This is a lot of risk.

I’m going to make this concrete by giving a specific example. This is not from the government that I currently work for, but the government that I used to work for.

In the end, the project was outsourced to some guy who was a very good friend of the councilperson’s. The project ended up costing about $2.4 million, which was a lot more than it should have.

## The fewer-bids school

One way to deal with this is to have fewer bids. In other words, the city would require any construction project that costs over a certain amount to go out to bid, which is a process where you send an email out to everybody who wants to get the contract and then pick the person who gives you the best price. But then I started thinking about my kids. I wanted to give them a moral foundation, and I didn’t want to wait until they were teenagers or worse, adults, to try to teach them that. So we started going to church again. And we started saying grace before meals. I wasn’t sure if that was hypocritical, but it seemed better than not having any morals at all.

Now we’re a little older, and I’m not so sure anymore.

My friend has a great point: we were raised to believe that if you don’t believe in God, you’ll be an immoral person. We’re supposed to feel a bit ashamed of our atheism.

So if I start telling my daughter, “you know how Mommy doesn’t believe in God? Well, she still says grace because she’s a good person and she likes to pretend,” I’m teaching her that atheism is shameful, and if you really want to be seen as a good person, you should pretend. And that’s not exactly the kind of moral foundation I want to give her.

I’m also not sure that I want to teach her that she needs to pretend to be religious to be a good person. I would rather teach her to be a good person because it’s the right thing to do.

I know some people think that having God at the center of your life will help you be a good person, and that’s true for some people. But for me, it’s not. If God isn’t real, then I won’t be a good person just because I believe in God.

So I’m starting to think that maybe I don’t have to say grace.

But then my partner is worried that if I stop saying grace, we’ll lose the sense of ritual.

The way I see it, you can have a sense of ritual even if you don’t believe in God. You can still do something every day to mark the passing of time.

I can imagine doing something every evening to show that it’s dinner time. But I think there’s a bit of a risk that it’ll feel like busywork. I want to do something that feels like it’s really worth it, not something that’s just because it’s a routine.

I think maybe we should try it out for a month or so and see how it feels.

prompt: I stopped believing in God around 30 but I still say grace before dinner with my kids. My partner thinks it's hypocritical. I'd love a short essay on whether rituals can survive the death of the beliefs behind them, and whether they should.
response:
The other day my mother was telling me that she has given up on believing in God and has been “on the fence” on whether to keep praying. My response was that this is a silly question. Of course you should keep praying, and not because you have to or because it makes you a better person. Praying is good because it’s good, and I can’t imagine it being a bad thing.

My mother’s question is very common. People who stop believing in God often wonder whether they should continue to attend church or go through religious rituals. Most atheists who have grown up in Christian homes will tell you that they feel guilty about not praying. Even though they don’t believe it helps, they still wonder if they should do it to keep God happy.

Some religious people also wonder if they should continue with their practices if they no longer believe in them. It is hard to say what to do about that. What is certain is that people who stop believing in God but keep doing religious things are not being hypocritical, as some people like to say. There’s an important distinction between a person who does a religious thing because she believes that it will make a higher power happy and a person who does the same thing because she likes doing it. The latter is not doing the religious practice *religiously* but for the other benefits that come with it.

The atheist prayer

I am an atheist. I am not religious. I am not going to church and I do not think that God exists.

And yet, I still pray every morning.

I say it in a way that doesn’t sound very different from what you would say if you were praying to God. “Lord, help me…” and so on. I do this because I like the feeling of praying. It’s calming and it’s fun.

And I think it works, too. Not the way you would expect – I have not been miraculously healed of any disease or had a miracle occur in my life – but it makes me a better person. And if that’s not enough for you to want to pray every morning, then I don’t know what is.

I also say grace before every meal, even though my kids can see that I’m not religious. My partner says that I’m being hypocritical because I don’t believe in God but I act like I do.

And this is one of the things that is always said when people do something religious even though they don’t believe in it. They’re being hypocritical. I always think this is a weird argument to make.

I would like to be clear here. I do not believe in God. I don’t believe that there’s a higher power that I’m praying to. When I go through my morning prayers, I know that no one is listening. And yet, I still feel like it’s the best thing I do every day. I feel better and I am more focused and I have more energy after praying. And I think that makes me a more successful person.

I have thought about this a lot and I think that the best way to put it is this. There are a lot of things that work in ways that we don’t quite understand, but we don’t always have to understand why something works in order for it to be real.

If you don’t believe in God, but you still say grace or pray or go to church or whatever, it does not make you hypocritical. If anything, you’re doing a good thing, and you’re doing it for the right reasons – not because you’re supposed to, but because you like it and it helps you.

area: religion, meaning and how to live
prompt: I stopped believing in God around 30 but I still say grace before dinner with my kids. My partner thinks it's hypocritical. I'd love a short essay on whether rituals can survive the death of the beliefs behind them, and whether they should.
response:
I stopped believing in God somewhere in my mid-20s. This isn’t unusual; I think a lot of people lose their faith in their 20s, and some people are religious and then just have the light go off at some point.

For a long time, my belief in God was the most important thing in my life. I prayed every night, read the Bible every week, went to church. When I became an atheist, my first reaction was that my life would be worse because I’d lost this important part.

But it turns out that losing faith didn’t have much of an impact on my life. I don’t pray anymore, but I’ve found meditation helpful instead. I don’t read the Bible anymore, but I read a lot of other books instead. I don’t go to church anymore, but I go to other gatherings instead.

I also still say grace before meals. This is a ritual that I’ve practiced since I was four, and my kids are now old enough to be able to join me. I find that saying grace is a helpful way to focus my attention on eating, and a nice way to start the meal with a moment of gratitude.

It’s not that I think I’m talking to God. It’s not that I think saying grace makes the food more nutritious or delicious. It’s not that I think my life would be worse if I didn’t say grace.

It’s just that saying grace is a ritual that I’ve been doing since I was very young, and it doesn’t really matter to me that I don’t believe in God anymore. It’s like the habit of locking the front door, which I learned as a child. It doesn’t matter to me that burglars are unlikely to bother with my house. It doesn’t matter to me that I could be safe if I didn’t lock the door. It’s just a ritual I learned when I was small, and I keep doing it.

My partner says it’s hypocritical for me to say grace when I don’t believe in God. I think she has a point, but also not.

When I was little, I used to get scared when I saw a bird. My mother would tell me that it was God’s messenger, and I would calm down and go on with my day.

Now, I don’t believe in God. I don’t think I have any special connection to birds. I don’t have a problem with birds.

But if I saw a bird right now, I would still think of it as God’s messenger. This is a ritual that I learned as a child. It doesn’t matter to me that I don’t believe in God anymore, just like it doesn’t matter to me that I don’t think my house is particularly vulnerable to burglars.

And if one of my children saw a bird and got scared, I would tell them it was God’s messenger, just like my mother did. I wouldn’t want them to be scared, and if I told them it was God’s messenger, I would be more likely to calm them down.

I’m not doing that because I think it will help them get into Heaven. It’s just a ritual I learned as a child.

Rituals don’t require you to believe in the reasons they were originally invented. You can believe in the rituals themselves. You can find them useful. You can just be comfortable doing them.

prompt: Essay on the Sabbath as technology
response:
On the third day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, in a room on the second floor of a small house in the village of Capernaum, a group of twelve men gathered around a long table. They were poor, mostly uneducated fishermen and a few tax collectors and a zealot, and their leader, the Rabbi of Nazareth, was about to explain to them that a new age was beginning.

For the first time in recorded history, a prophet from Galilee, the backwoods of Israel, had come into the Holy Land itself and begun to preach a new understanding of God, challenging the established priests and teachers of the Law, and drawing to himself a crowd of followers. And now the twelve apostles had followed him from Galilee to the village of Capernaum, where he had taken a room in Simon Peter's house, and had spent the last few days teaching them the true meaning of the Law of Moses, and warning them that the time was at hand when the Kingdom of God would appear.

On this third day of Passover, he had invited his twelve apostles to a Passover meal, in which a lamb would be sacrificed, and unleavened bread and bitter herbs eaten, and the events of the Exodus from Egypt remembered. But in the midst of the meal, he said, "I have greatly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I tell you, I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God." Then he took the bread, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying, "Take and eat, for this is my body." And he took the cup of wine, said the blessing, and gave it to them, saying, "Drink from this, for this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins."

The disciples had been astonished. They had heard Jesus say that he would go to Jerusalem and die, but they had thought that he was speaking of some other prophet, not of himself. And now he had told them that he was about to die, and that he would give his disciples his body and his blood to eat. It was a shocking statement, and they could not understand it.

But Jesus had told them not to worry about what he was saying, but to remember the words he had spoken and the way in which he had broken the bread and poured out the wine. They would soon have the chance to remember, and to see the meaning of what he was saying.

For a few days after that night, Jesus would continue to teach, and his disciples would continue to argue among themselves about who among them was the greatest. But soon there would come a night when he would sit down again with his disciples, and the meal would be interrupted by the arrival of Judas, and then the soldiers and police, and Jesus would be arrested and condemned to death. And then they would remember what Jesus had said to them, and they would know that he was not only the prophet but the Lord.

When they would gather together and remember the night on which Jesus had broken the bread and poured out the wine, and given them his body and blood, they would eat bread and drink wine, and remember his sacrifice, and know that he was the Lord. And when they did this, the body and blood of Christ would be given to them, not by the breaking of bread and the pouring out of wine, but by their faith in the work he had done for them. And so, by faith, they would share in the sacrifice of Christ, and be united with him in his death and resurrection.

The Last Supper had been an ordinary Jewish Passover, the first of many in which Jesus ate with his disciples. But in the midst of the meal, Jesus made the statement which changed everything. He had told his disciples that he was about to die, and that he was going to give them his body and his blood to eat, and that they were to remember this when they broke the bread and poured out the wine. And when the disciples remembered, and when they ate the bread and drank the wine, they would remember his death, and they would know that he was the Lord.

And so the Passover was transformed. No longer was it simply a meal to remember the Exodus from Egypt. Now it was a meal to remember the death and resurrection of Christ. And so the Passover became the Lord's Supper.

The Lord's Supper is the only memorial of the New Testament which is based on an event in the life of Christ. The Feast of Tabernacles, which we have just celebrated, commemorates the time when the Israelites wandered in the wilderness for forty years, living in booths or tents. But the Lord's Supper commemorates the death of Christ. And so the Lord's Supper is the most important of the feasts of the New Testament, and it is the only one which is commanded by the apostles to be kept.

prompt: Essay on the Sabbath as technology
response:
When we hear the word “technology,” we usually think of machines and gadgets. We forget that the word originally meant an arrangement of ideas that makes a particular outcome possible. And it is the outcome that matters.

A technology succeeds when it does what it’s supposed to do. The wheelbarrow is good technology because it moves loads faster than a person on foot. It’s not good technology because it has wheels. You can have a wheelbarrow without wheels, and that can still be good technology.

What’s the point of the Sabbath?

In the most straightforward reading of the Bible, the Sabbath is God’s way of providing the same sort of benefits people get from the rest of the world. The Sabbath is technology. It’s a technology of rest.

Why would God create the world, then sit down and rest? Why would he give the Sabbath to his people? Because rest is good for you.

The Sabbath is one of the most surprising things in the Bible. It’s a religious practice that makes no sense until you see it as a technology.

The idea that the Sabbath is technology is not mine. It’s in the first chapter of a wonderful book called The Sabbath by Andrew Goldsworth.

The Sabbath is God’s technology of rest. It’s a device for making people rest, by giving them a day when it is considered normal to do nothing.

response:
I’m not an expert on the Sabbath and I’m not writing an essay on the Sabbath, so if this gets you riled up I’m not sure what else you want from me.

It’s easy to understand why the Sabbath was important to the ancient Israelites, who had just been liberated from slavery in Egypt. The Bible says of the Israelites, “Because thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt, the LORD thy God brought thee out thence with a mighty hand and with a stretched out arm: therefore the LORD thy God commanded thee to keep the sabbath day”.

It’s also easy to understand why the Sabbath was important to the ancient Israelites, who had just been liberated from slavery in Egypt, from a purely technical point of view. The Israelites had just been through a very hard labor-intensive task and probably weren’t in the best shape to do it again right away, so taking a few weeks to rest was the obvious next step.

But the Sabbath wasn’t just a thing that the Israelites did for a few weeks to recover from their trip out of Egypt. It became a permanent feature of their religion, a requirement to keep up with for the rest of time. It wasn’t just a way of getting them rested up, it was a way of keeping them rested up.

This wasn’t the only example of the Sabbath being used as a technology to achieve a goal. In the Ten Commandments, the Sabbath is connected to the idea of property rights. The Sabbath wasn’t just about keeping the Israelites rested, it was about giving their servants and slaves time to rest too. In order for the Israelites to keep their slaves and servants rested, they had to have a way of preventing themselves from working on a day of the week. So they had to invent a way of preventing themselves from working on a day of the week, and they called that thing the Sabbath.

The Sabbath as technology is a very interesting thing to think about, because it’s one of the earliest examples of a technology that was invented not to make a physical thing but to make a human behavior. Invention is often described as a way of making new physical objects, but the Sabbath was one of the earliest examples of a technology that was invented not to make a new object, but to make a new behavior.

response:
If you’ve ever fasted, you know it’s the worst. Not eating is a terrible experience. But people do it. Why?

A few hundred years ago in the Christian world, fasting was so common that even non-religious people fasted regularly. You’d hear a phrase like “after the Lenten fast” meaning “in March”. You could expect to be hungry every Thursday. And you could count on the whole Christian world observing a month of fasting every year.

Fasting is a way of saying: I can make you feel like an idiot and you’ll still be thankful to me.

It’s not just Christians. It’s not just religious people. It’s just people.

Fasting is so universal that people try to come up with some universal reason why we fast, and it’s always something like: “well, maybe we fast to give us some common rituals, so we can have community”.

That’s obviously true. We have tons of rituals that make us feel like a community.

But if that was the main reason, you’d expect fasting to look like any other ritual, right? You’d expect it to have no more emotional power than anything else we do. But fasting is different.

Fasting is a way of saying: I can make you feel like an idiot and you’ll still be thankful to me.

And that makes it powerful. It makes it feel like you’re doing something for God, and if it’s not real, it at least feels like it is.

Why does fasting make us feel good? It’s because it makes us feel stupid, and that’s a great feeling.

There’s no better feeling than knowing something that other people don’t know. It’s a great feeling to be smarter than everyone else. If you know the secret to making money and everyone else is doing the opposite, it’s an amazing feeling.

And this feeling is the best when you’ve gone through the suffering of learning. That’s why people feel great when they get good grades, even though they know the teacher is going to forget everything they taught.

That’s why fasting is such a powerful ritual. It makes you feel smart in a way that normal rituals don’t.

Fasting is a way of saying: I can make you feel like an idiot and you’ll still be thankful to me.

That’s the only way you can say that about something. And that’s why people feel like it’s real.

It’s not just Christianity. It’s not just religious people. It’s just people.

Fasting is a way of saying: I can make you feel like an idiot and you’ll still be thankful to me.

It’s not just Christianity. It’s not just religious people. It’s just people.

When you fast you feel smart. You’re not like everyone else who thinks they can get by without suffering.

You’re smart because you know the truth about suffering. You’ve made it into something good.

And that’s a great feeling.

One of those things is fasting. The majority of religions require their followers to fast at various times. Islam has the month of Ramadan, Judaism has Yom Kippur, Christianity has Lent, Hinduism and Buddhism both have a bunch of fasting holidays. The only major religion I can think of which doesn’t have fasting is Sikhism.

I don’t think this is a coincidence. The people who started religions may have disagreed about how the universe worked, but they were all the same kind of people and noticed the same things. They probably noticed that not eating for a while had some interesting effects, and incorporated them into their new religions.

A lot of religions have other interesting rituals which might have some nonreligious value – for example, Catholicism has confession. I don’t think this is an accident. The people who started religions probably tried all sorts of interesting things, and the more effective ones got codified into ritual.

area: religion, meaning and how to live
prompt: Why do almost all religions have fasting? Write an essay that tries to get at what not eating does to people, beyond the obvious health stuff.
response:
One of the strangest features of religion is fasting. The idea of deliberately going without food for an extended period of time strikes me as pretty weird. It seems the sort of thing that people who are already depressed, or in the process of being institutionalized, might do. Yet almost every religion has some kind of fast. Muslims have the famous Ramadan; Christians fast during Lent; Jews fast on Yom Kippur; and so on.

A lot of fasting in religions is just part of a ritual that does something else (like fasting during Ramadan before the revelation of the Quran), so we should probably ignore them. But I think there are other cases where the fasting itself does something. So what’s going on here?

Obviously fasting is good for your health. But that seems too shallow. Why would ancient religions make their followers deliberately go without food? It’s too specific, too hard, and too complicated. If religions were concerned with health, they would just say “don’t eat too much”, and let people work out exactly how much too much is on their own.

I think fasting is part of a pattern of religious practices where you deliberately do something unpleasant in order to get some kind of spiritual benefit from it. So the practice is less the thing you do, and more the process of making yourself do the unpleasant thing, and the spiritual benefit comes from the process.

Fasting, in particular, is about breaking your attachment to your own body. Most of the time, you are attached to your own body: if it’s hungry, you eat, if it’s tired, you sleep, etc. If you are willing to go without food, you have to consciously detach yourself from your body’s desires. You have to realize that you are not your body, and that your body’s desires are not your desires, and that there is some kind of self that is separate from your body.

The idea of “the self is separate from the body” is an important idea in most religions. It’s the idea that makes people believe in souls, which is why religions so often believe in the afterlife. The idea is also useful in a more mundane way – if you are not your body, and if your body’s desires are not your desires, then you can choose to ignore some of your body’s desires.

It is much easier to detach from your body if you do it gradually. If you just eat a little less every day for a few months, you will gradually get used to feeling hungry, until you don’t feel it very much any more. This is the idea behind Lent, and some of the other Christian fasts. In addition, if you occasionally eat less in a single day, this can also help you detach from your body, because you can practice being in control of your body for just that day.

I think some of the fasting in Islam is for this purpose. There are a lot of times that Muslims are told to fast: during Ramadan, when the Quran was revealed, but also during Ramadan and Muharram, when Muhammad was born and died. So if Ramadan and Muharram were the only times Muslims fasted, then we could say that the fasting was for some other purpose related to the Quran and Muhammad, but because there are other times Muslims fast, it seems more likely that the fasting is for the purpose of detaching from the body.

I think the most common explanation for fasting in Judaism is that it’s a form of repentance. For example, in Numbers 9:13, the text says that if you sin, you have to fast and bring an offering to God. This makes sense: when you are fasting, you are not enjoying yourself. Your body feels sick, you can’t do your normal activities, etc. When you fast, you are telling God you have repented of your sin. You’re saying “I feel bad about what I did, and you should forgive me”.

But it’s not the only explanation. In Leviticus 23:27, the text says you have to fast on Yom Kippur, and in Leviticus 16:29-30 it says that if you fast on Yom Kippur, God will forgive your sins. It’s not entirely clear whether the fasting is the repentance, or whether the fasting makes God more likely to forgive you. It may well be both.

In any case, fasting is probably one of the earliest practices in Judaism. In Genesis 2:17, God tells Adam that he can’t eat from the tree in the Garden of Eden, and in Genesis 3:1-6, he and Eve eat from it. This seems to have been a big mistake that got them expelled from the Garden of Eden, so they probably shouldn’t eat from that tree again, even if they get it back. But when they get it back in the future, they might be tempted to eat from it again. So the solution is to fast, which means you will never be tempted to eat from the tree because you’re not going to eat anything else anyway.

I think some of the fasting in Hinduism is to detach from the body, but there are other types of fasting as well. Some Hindus fast as a kind of meditation or yoga. This means they are not thinking about their body or their physical environment, and they can concentrate on spiritual stuff. I’m not sure if the fasting is for the detachment or the meditation, but it probably is for one or the other.

Some Hindus fast to make their prayers more effective. This is not the same thing as repentance: you don’t have to feel bad about anything, you just have to do a bad thing, like fast. This probably has something to do with the idea that God is paying attention to your body, and if your body is suffering, he might be more likely to pay attention to your prayers.

Some Hindus fast to break their attachment to food. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says he is the “Lord of Food”, and that you can get food from him, but if you don’t want to, you can fast. This is a pretty interesting idea, because it’s not just saying that you can get food, it’s saying that if you’re not eating, you don’t need to eat. You can go without food, and Krishna will make sure you don’t starve.

prompt: I'm 52 and my career peaked about five years ago. Nothing bad happened, I just know I won't go higher. Write a personal essay about the second half of ambition: what you do with drive once it has nowhere to go.
response:
I have noticed recently that the best career I could expect is the one I already have.

This is not the same thing as being content. I would not be content if I were a barista, or a janitor, or a middle-level manager for a company selling boring products. I want to be at the top of something I care about, and I don't always manage to be.

In the last couple years I've been thinking about what we might call the second half of ambition. The second half of ambition is when you know what you want, but also that you can't get it.

In the first half of ambition, your aim is clear. You just do what you need to do to get where you want. You may not always succeed, but at least you know what to do. In the second half of ambition there's a new uncertainty in your life. You know what you want, but you don't know how to get it.

In the first half of ambition, you're on the move. You don't have to ask yourself what you want, because you're just trying to get the thing you already know you want. In the second half of ambition you're not on the move, and you have to face a new kind of question. What do you do when you're not moving?

When you're in the second half of ambition, there are three things you can do. You can aim higher; you can try to stay where you are; or you can turn ambition sideways.

If you aim higher, you have to decide to be unhappy for a while. You will be unhappy, because you're going to be trying to get something you can't get. It may seem odd to decide to be unhappy deliberately, but people do this a lot. They set ambitious goals they won't reach just to have the excuse not to worry about more mundane matters. And if you get lucky enough to reach some of them, all the better.

Aim for as far outside your reach as you think you can manage.

If you try to stay where you are, you also have to decide to be unhappy for a while. In a way you're doing the same thing as the people who aim higher, except backwards. You're saying "I don't want to change, but I know I have to, so let's see how long I can get away with not doing it."

Aim for as far into your comfort zone as you think you can manage.

Aim for something as ambitious as you can get away with not pursuing.

The last option is to turn ambition sideways. That means to apply ambition to something that seems unrelated to your original goal. It's sort of the opposite of what most people do. Most people, if they can't get what they want in one field, give up that field and move to another. But you can go sideways.

If you're trying to turn ambition sideways, how do you decide what to do? I have two suggestions. One is to start by doing things you already enjoy. If you're already doing some things you like, then you're halfway there. The second suggestion is to keep in mind that the goal is to turn ambition sideways, not to do what you already like.

If you're like me, you already have some things you like, but that's not the same thing as something that makes you ambitious. Ambition is not merely liking something. It means doing it and trying to get better at it, not merely to be happier, but because it's something you want to do well.

I don't know exactly what my sideways ambition will turn out to be. I know I want to be ambitious about something, but I'm not yet sure what.

So I'm starting by doing things I like. I recently started taking a class in Mandarin. I like Mandarin, but I've never been ambitious about learning it, because I've always assumed I would end up using it.
