prompt: As a hospital chaplain I sit with people of every faith and none. Write an essay on what 'spiritual care' could even mean for an atheist patient - I'd like it to avoid both the condescending version and the empty therapeutic version.
response:
I recently talked to an atheist patient. I don’t know if she’s the only atheist patient I’ve ever talked to, or if I’m the only chaplain who doesn’t immediately steer clear of atheists. But this post is going to be a lot easier to write if I say that I’m the only chaplain in the world who doesn’t immediately steer clear of atheists.

My atheist patient was a young woman with some kind of cancer that wasn’t that serious but was probably going to require a lot of time and effort to treat. She had a husband and a daughter, who was maybe four years old. We sat in a small chair that wasn’t comfortable.

I asked her if she wanted me to talk about spiritual stuff. She said that she was an atheist, but she was pretty religious in other ways.

I asked if I could ask her what she meant by that.

I told her I was happy to talk about anything. I told her that the thing I liked most about being a chaplain was that every day, I got to talk to someone new, about whatever they wanted to talk about.

I asked her how she was. She said that she was pretty sad. I said I was sorry about her cancer. I asked her if she wanted to talk about how she was feeling.

We talked about how the hospital was hard to understand. She had been there for a few days, and she was still not sure why they had done certain tests, and whether they were going to do more tests, or if it was going to be surgery, or what. I said I didn’t know either. I said if she wanted to I could look into it, but I also said that sometimes when I do that the doctors are pretty annoyed. She asked if there was something she could do to make things easier for me. I told her that the thing that was hard for me was not being able to help, which was frustrating because I wanted to help her.

She asked what else I did for a living. I said I was a lawyer. She said that was very interesting.

She told me she had an aunt who was very sick. She said she had told her aunt, “You know, we’re all going to die eventually. It’ll be a lot more fun to die young and exciting.” Her aunt had said, “Oh my god, I thought you had a death wish.” The patient said that when she had told her aunt that, she meant it. She said, “I mean it. I really want to die young.” I asked if she had a death wish. She said she did, in a way.

She told me about the time her dad had gotten her a kitten for her birthday. Her dad had left to go to work. Her mom had come in to say something and had seen that the kitten was sick and had said, “Oh my God, it has diarrhea.” She said her mom had taken the kitten to the vet, and the vet said that it was fine. Her mom had come back and told her that the kitten had been fine. She said that she’d asked her mom to leave the kitten at home so she could play with it, and she had. She said her mom had come back and said, “Oh my God, the kitten has died.” She said that she felt responsible for the kitten dying, and she said that feeling responsible for the kitten dying was something that she never got to do again. She said she would give anything to feel like that again.

We talked about that for a while. I didn’t know what else to do. I said I wanted to help her, but I didn’t know how. I said I was sorry that I didn’t have any good advice for her.

She told me she had been in a psychiatric hospital when she was younger. I asked what that was like. She said it was fine. I said that seemed like a really hard thing. She said, “Oh, I’m fine.” I said I didn’t think that was really true. She said, “Well, you don’t know me.”

I said that I did know her, and that I knew that she was suffering and that I wanted to help her, and I didn’t know how. I said I was sorry that I wasn’t better at being a chaplain.

She asked if she could tell me something. I said sure. She said she thought that I had a death wish. I told her that I did. She asked why I didn’t kill myself. I said it would be a lot easier if I wasn’t such a coward. She said she thought I was right. I said I thought that was true too.

We talked about that for a little while. I said I didn’t want to die, but if I was really suffering and there was no hope for me to get better, I thought it would be okay if I killed myself. She said that she thought that was true too.

She told me that I was the first chaplain that she had ever liked. She said that she had talked to a lot of other chaplains, and she had never liked them. I said that I was really happy to have met her. She said that she was really happy to have met me too.

I said that I thought that she was very brave. I said that I was really impressed. She said that she was really impressed that I was a lawyer, and that I had decided to do that instead of becoming a doctor.

I said that it was good that we had talked, and I said that she was welcome to talk to me again if she wanted. She said she would.

When I left the room, I went back to my office, and I went to the bathroom, and I threw up.

prompt: As a hospital chaplain I sit with people of every faith and none. Write an essay on what 'spiritual care' could even mean for an atheist patient - I'd like it to avoid both the condescending version and the empty therapeutic version.
response:
When I was a hospital chaplain, the patients were mostly Christians and a smattering of other people. There were a few Muslims, Jews, Hindus, Buddhists, and a couple of people I knew to be Satanists.

But the patients weren’t just believers. A lot of them were atheists, or at least claimed to be. This creates a problem for people like me, who have traditionally considered the purpose of chaplaincy to be talking to people about God.

I’m not talking about the sort of atheist who wants to be convinced he’s wrong and secretly wants the chaplain to show him the light. I’m talking about someone like one of my patients, who was an atheist when I first met him, and was still an atheist when he died.

The atheist patient is the sort who will talk about how they’re an atheist when I ask what their faith is. And if I say “Oh, cool, I’m a Christian”, they’ll often say “Well, I’m not a Christian.” And this is not the sort of person who will be easily persuaded to believe in God. I’m not talking about someone who says they’re an atheist in order to be edgy. I’m talking about someone who means it.

But at the same time, they’re still sitting on a hospital bed. This means they’re either sick or dying or both. And it means they need help.

The first thing I thought about was, what do atheists want out of life? I thought of the various atheistic worldviews - utilitarianism, existentialism, etc. But there’s an obvious objection to this: you can’t just assume that an atheist patient wants existentialist advice, or utilitarian advice, or whatever. Some people might want that, but a lot of people might not.

A more likely scenario is: my atheist patient is an atheist in the sense that they believe in God less than people who claim to be believers. But they still have some beliefs about what is important in life, and want to talk about those.

So what are atheist beliefs? What things can we believe in if not in God?

My favorite example of atheistic belief is existentialism. Existentialism is, to the extent that it is anything, an attempt to figure out what life is like if you don’t believe in God.

The first existentialist, Kierkegaard, believed in Christianity. But he believed in it so differently from other Christians that the Church of Denmark had to expel him, and he had to flee to Copenhagen. And so he had to figure out how to be a Christian in a world that didn’t believe in Christianity.

This made him the first existentialist, because it forced him to figure out what the Christian faith was all about. And he concluded that it was about individual faith, about the relationship between the individual and the Divine.

Existentialism was then taken up by non-Christian Europeans, and it meant something slightly different for them. It meant, to the extent that it meant anything, that we should figure out the meaning of life for ourselves.

There are many variants of existentialism. The two main variants are: Existentialism with or without the divine.

Existentialism without the divine is the version Sartre and de Beauvoir had, where they were trying to figure out a meaning to life without God. Existentialism without the divine is what I think most people would consider existentialism to be.

I’ve talked about existentialism with the divine a little bit in this series. This is the version that Kierkegaard had.

What existentialism with the divine looks like is this: the meaning of life is to try to get closer to God.

This version of existentialism is similar to existentialism without the divine. In both versions of existentialism, the meaning of life is to find meaning in life. But in the second version of existentialism, the meaning you find is “getting closer to God”.

This means that the existentialist without the divine believes in the existence of the Divine. It’s just that they’re a non-believer, so they don’t know what the Divine is. But they believe that there is something. They believe that the Divine exists.

This is why I think existentialism is atheistic belief. It’s because they believe in God.

The atheist patient in the hospital is probably not an atheist in the sense that they don’t believe in God at all. They’re probably an atheist in the sense that they believe in God less than people who claim to be believers.

This means that when I’m talking to an atheist patient about their beliefs, it’s probably about the things that they believe in. And the only reason I’d be talking to them about their beliefs is because they want me to talk about their beliefs.

prompt: Op-ed: Secular people should steal more from religion. Not beliefs - structures. Weekly gatherings, life-stage rituals, tithing. Around 900 words.
response:
I’ve been talking a lot about my “secular church,” which is a bunch of people who get together twice a month for discussion of books and articles. It’s not really a church, in that we don’t have beliefs that we worship at, and there are no rituals or ceremonies that we observe. It’s more like a group of people who like each other and like the idea of discussing ideas together.

This is not a new phenomenon. Secular humanists and freethinkers have been doing this sort of thing for decades. But I’ve been thinking about it a little bit more recently, and I have some thoughts.

I was thinking about this in the context of my friend Ben Hare, who wrote a piece about how he wants to start up a non-religious church with his local neighborhood group. In his piece he talked about what he thinks is missing from his local group’s current activities – a sense of belonging to something.

Ben is right that there’s something missing in secular communities. But I think he’s missing something important.

The reason religion is so popular, and why people are so drawn into religious communities, is because it’s more than just a belief system. It has structures and activities that help bring people together. And it has a sense of place and meaning that comes from that.

There are several things that religions have going for them, beyond belief:

– They have regular gatherings. Most religions have weekly services where everyone comes together. This is a good thing, because it creates a sense of community. It also makes it easier to meet and make friends in the group.

– They have rituals. Most religions have rituals for important occasions in life. These give people a sense of shared experience, which is nice. And they’re a nice way to bring people together who have the same beliefs, but aren’t already part of a religious community.

– They have a sense of place. Religious buildings, and the rituals and activities associated with them, can really have a way of drawing people together.

– They have money. Most religions have some kind of system for taking money from members and using it to support religious activities. This can be done in a very positive way, by supporting the church community and giving them resources to help them function effectively.

I’m not saying that we have to be religious in order to get these benefits. You can easily create secular groups that share these features. You can even create secular groups that have all these features, and more.

For instance, I think most secular groups have a pretty good system for taking money from members. And they’re often more open to using that money in interesting ways than religious groups.

I think we should steal from religion. Not its beliefs, but its structures.

A lot of the people I’ve met at secular groups really like it. But I think that a lot of those groups, while good, are missing something.

A lot of those groups are a bunch of people who like each other and like the idea of discussing ideas together.

This is good. But it’s not everything religion has going for it. I think some secular groups could benefit from borrowing some of the structures religion uses to bring people together.

area: religion, meaning and how to live
prompt: Op-ed: Secular people should steal more from religion. Not beliefs - structures. Weekly gatherings, life-stage rituals, tithing. Around 900 words.
response:
I'm a big fan of the secularism that's happened over the last few decades. I have no interest in bringing religion back. But there are some things about religion I like that I think the secular world should steal from.

I don't mean beliefs. I mean structures.

Consider tithing. Tithing is a religious tradition of giving away a certain percentage of your income to a temple or church. In the US, most churches ask for 10%; in Sweden and Israel it's 15%, and in some countries it's as much as 30%. The percentage is often set by religious institutions, but in the US it's often left to you to decide. Tithing is not universal; the Quakers and the Unitarian Universalists are among the sects that don't have it. But most religions do.

Tithing has some pretty obvious flaws. First, it's coercive. If you're a believer, you're told that if you don't give 10% of your income to the church, God will be angry at you. In some countries it's worse than just being angry – they'll literally imprison you if you don't tithe. This is especially bad for poor people, who have no surplus income and so are forced to choose between eating and tithing. In other words, the rich tithe and the poor starve.

Tithing is also wasteful. It's often not spent on the poor but on building larger churches and hiring better musicians.

But despite its flaws, tithing is still the most reliable way to get rich people to give money to the poor. The problem with charity is that if someone makes you give money to the poor, it feels like a tax. You get resentful and think you're being cheated. Tithing gets around that. It feels like you're giving money to the church. The fact that the money is sent to the poor is not really your concern.

The secular world could steal the structure of tithing without using the religious framing. In the US there's a system called the Paycheck Protection Program, where you give a certain percentage of your paycheck to various charities and the government gives you a tax break. It's the same as tithing, except that instead of telling you to give money to God, it tells you to give money to the poor.

Tithing might be more effective than giving money to God, and it would be more effective than giving money to the poor. It's a better way to get money from rich people. I'm a big supporter of a global tax on rich people, but tithing is a more effective way to do it.

I'm not the first person to say that secularism should steal tithing from religion. In an earlier essay, I wrote that secularism should steal the idea of weekly worship services from religion.

Worship services are great because they're a regular place to hang out with like-minded people. If you live in a small town, it might be the only place you have that. If you live in a big city, you have a lot of options. But most of those options are not religious.

Churches are also great because they have a lot of social events. They host concerts, plays, and dances. They do all kinds of things that help people feel connected. If you live in a small town, you can probably find other places to do these things. If you live in a big city, there are a lot of options. But they're not the same.

It's not just that churches do a lot of things that help people feel connected. It's that they do a lot of things that help people feel connected to each other. That's the big thing that religion does for people that secularism doesn't.

Religion is the biggest social club in the world. It's a place where people from all walks of life get together to learn, grow, and support each other. It's a place where people can find love, friendship, and community. It's a place where people can find meaning, purpose, and hope.

Secularism needs to learn from religion. It needs to give people something to gather around and something to be passionate about. And there are a lot of things secularism could use that religion is already doing.

area: religion, meaning and how to live
prompt: Op-ed: Secular people should steal more from religion. Not beliefs - structures. Weekly gatherings, life-stage rituals, tithing. Around 900 words.
response:
A couple of weeks ago, a friend introduced me to a church I had never heard of. It was pretty small, and it seemed like the kind of place I would have missed in the city of Chicago – not because I would have missed the building, but because I was unlikely to hear about it.

But when I was told about it, it immediately made sense. It was called First Unitarian. First Unitarian is, according to their website, “a congregation of seekers, committed to a shared search for meaning in the light of reason, conscience, and experience.” They are “a community where diverse people gather to explore the best of what humans have to offer: our deepest values, our highest aspirations, our most honest questions.” They are a place “to explore our human potential.” They are a “humanist” congregation, which means, according to the Unitarian Universalist Association, “an organization that provides a caring, nontheistic spiritual community to those who find traditional religion inadequate and are seeking a source of meaning in their lives.”

I thought this was very cool. I am a nontheist seeking a source of meaning in my life, and I feel that traditional religion is inadequate to my needs. If I lived in Chicago, this church would seem like an excellent choice for me, and I would go.

What I didn’t understand was why there wasn’t a First Humanist. If First Unitarian is really so great, and if it has so many benefits that people are missing out on by not attending, then there should be a First Humanist to serve all the seculars in Chicago who are just as interested in spirituality as the Unitarians, but who aren’t interested in Christianity.

When I asked, my friend explained that the idea of a humanist church was not really acceptable to most humanists, who felt it was a bit too close to religion, or too “churchy.”

I found this hard to understand. I’ve been to a few churches. I think that most churches, if I had to sum them up in one word, would be boring. If I attended a church, it would probably be because it was interesting. First Humanist would not be boring – it would be a place where a bunch of intelligent people who are really excited about humanism would come together to talk about humanism. I would want to attend.

My friend also said that there was a group called the Chicago Humanists, and that I should join them. I looked into it, and found their Facebook page, which said:

We are the Chicago Humanists – a group that seeks to make Chicago a more secular, scientific, tolerant, and compassionate place. We are humanists who are atheists, agnostics, freethinkers, rationalists, and more. We are united by our humanist ideals and our shared belief that secularism and humanism are the best paths to happiness, tolerance, and equality.

There’s a bit of an awkward disconnect here. The group’s Facebook page says that it seeks to make Chicago a more secular, scientific, tolerant, and compassionate place, but the group’s stated goals are to spread the gospel of atheism and to promote secularism, neither of which is particularly relevant to Chicago, where secularism is already very strong.

I think what’s going on here is that the Chicago Humanists are a secular version of First Unitarian. Their group’s goal – to make Chicago a more secular place – is actually a religious goal. Secularism and atheism are religions. In fact, some atheists have argued that secularism and atheism are *the only true religions*. In other words, there’s nothing wrong with wanting to convert people to secularism – it is just as reasonable as wanting to convert people to Christianity.

The Chicago Humanists are a religious group. It is just that they are a religious group whose religion is secularism and atheism. This isn’t unusual – secular humanism is one of the most common religions in the world.

The religious part of it might seem weird, but I think there’s nothing wrong with it. Religious groups have always played an important role in society, and they should continue to do so – secular religious groups are just as important as religious religious groups.

In fact, I think that the reason secularists have been so reluctant to form religious groups is that they have not wanted to be religious, and that this has been a mistake.

Religious groups are really great. They are groups of people who get together to do things together. They are groups of people who get together to talk about religion. They are groups of people who get together to worship God. They are groups of people who get together to worship the Devil. They are groups of people who get together to worship nothing. They are groups of people who get together to worship whatever they want.

If secularists want to build a stronger, more unified movement, they should form religious groups. They should form groups that get together to do things together. They should form groups that get together to talk about atheism. They should form groups that get together to worship whatever they want.

prompt: can you write an essay on why confession (the religious kind) might've been psychologically genius, and what we replaced it with
response:
I.

We tend to think of confession as a quaint and archaic practice, one of those things from medieval Europe that we don’t believe in anymore. And while it’s true that most Protestants don’t use it, Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans, and a few other groups do – they just tend to do it in church basements or the like, so people who don’t practice it never see it.

I’m not here to defend or disparage any of the religious views behind the practice – if anything, the argument I make below works better if you’re agnostic about the theological claims. I’m only here to suggest that confession is psychologically brilliant, and the best model we have for how to improve our lives.

II.

Confession is not just a practice, it’s a *technology*. There are lots of ways you can do it, but here’s what I imagine when I imagine the archetypal case:

You’re in a small room. There’s a screen or lattice dividing the room in two. One side has you, the penitent. The other has a priest, the confessor. You’ve agreed to talk only through this lattice, so you can’t see each other’s faces.

The priest asks you: “What are you guilty of?”

You say: “I’m guilty of stealing.”

The priest asks: “How did you steal?”

You say: “I stole a bunch of stuff from my neighbor’s house last week, including his bicycle and his TV.”

The priest asks: “Was he hurt?”

You say: “I think so.”

The priest says: “Why did you do it?”

You say: “I don’t know.”

The priest says: “Maybe you did it because you felt unloved by your parents, and wanted to feel powerful and successful, like your parents would.”

You say: “Yeah, I guess that makes sense.”

The priest says: “I think if you want to become a better person, you need to work through your feelings about your parents, and make sure you’re getting all your needs met elsewhere.”

You say: “Okay, I will.”

The priest says: “And also, you need to tell your neighbor you stole from him, and try to make amends.”

You say: “Okay, I will.”

III.

I don’t know if this story is true or even remotely close to true, but if it is, it’s a pretty good story. If it’s true that people in the Middle Ages used confession in the way described above, they must have had a pretty good understanding of psychology.

First of all, the fact that the penitent and the confessor don’t see each other means that you can talk about embarrassing things without embarrassment. If you’re going to talk about the things you’ve done that you’re ashamed of, it helps if you’re not standing face-to-face with somebody who can see you blush.

Second of all, the structure of the conversation is very interesting.

You start out with the most trivial, obvious, and public part of your sin – “I stole” – before moving on to the more shameful details – “I stole from my neighbor” or “I stole his bicycle”. If you had to talk to a stranger and immediately confess the most embarrassing things you’d ever done, you probably wouldn’t be able to do it. But if they start you off with something simple and obvious, it’s a lot easier.

Then the priest is a little more careful and asks how you stole. This is a way of making sure you’re telling the truth – you wouldn’t have such detailed knowledge of what you stole if you hadn’t done it.

Then the priest moves on to the emotional aspects. It’s important to talk about these, because if you don’t, you may not be able to see the deeper patterns in your life, and will keep repeating your mistakes.

Then the priest asks you why you did it. This is the crux of the confession, because it forces you to confront the fact that you’re responsible.

Then the priest offers a possible explanation – a pattern, an explanation, a reason why you did what you did. This can be very valuable because the priest has seen hundreds of people confessing the same sins over and over, so he has a better idea of what the patterns might be than you do. Also, as a priest, he is in the business of offering this sort of advice, so he has a lot of training in being really good at it.

Then the priest offers two types of advice. The first is how to make sure you don’t do it again in the future, the second is how to make up to your neighbor for what you did.

The first part is the more interesting one, but the second is the more important one. It’s easy to talk yourself into thinking you’re a good person who has a couple of flaws, but you’re not. You did something bad and somebody else got hurt. If you don’t fix that, you’ll feel really guilty, and you’ll probably repeat your mistakes. If you do fix that, then the guilt will be resolved and you won’t have to think about it anymore, and you’ll be able to focus on the rest of your life.

IV.

The other really interesting thing about confession is that the priest has to tell the penitent what to do next, but can’t do it for him.

This is important, because if the priest can do the penitent’s work for him, then the penitent will probably just stop trying, and never get better. The priest has to tell the penitent that he has to do something about his own problems.

But the priest can’t make sure the penitent *actually* does the right thing, because of the screen. He can’t see what the penitent does, so he can’t force him to do it.

The priest can only tell the penitent what he should do, and then he has to trust him to do it. This is a really important thing, because it gives the penitent the feeling that he’s being trusted to be a good person, and he’s going to want to live up to that.

The priest is giving the penitent a lot of power and responsibility. He’s saying: “I believe in you. I know you’re going to do the right thing.” And if you’ve ever been in a situation where someone trusted you to do something important, you know that you’re going to try really hard to live up to that trust.

prompt: What does it mean to forgive someone who isn't sorry? I have someone specific in mind, a former business partner, but I want the essay to be general. Explore it.
response:
Forgive him. What? Why? He doesn’t even care. He’s not even sorry.

I thought of this the other day. I had a business partner for years who was a horrible person. He lied to me over and over, manipulated me, stole from me, and did other things that were simply wrong. I finally left, and then I thought, “I forgive him.”

But then I thought:

Wait a second. How can I forgive him? He doesn’t even feel bad. He doesn’t even feel sorry. He doesn’t even feel like it’s something I could forgive him for.

So what does it mean to forgive him?

If you don’t feel guilty, then what am I forgiving?

I think I get it, sort of, but I want to write it out because I think it could be helpful.

It’s a good question. When someone doesn’t feel bad, what do you forgive?

The reason it feels like forgiveness is not a thing is that forgiveness is often treated as if it is something that has to do with the person who did the bad thing. If someone does something bad, we ask “Do you feel bad about that?”

And that’s a good question. We want people to feel bad about things they do that are wrong.

But we also want people to feel good about themselves.

So we have two competing goals here.

We don’t want people to feel bad about themselves, but we do want them to feel bad about things they do that are wrong.

But these are in tension. If you make someone feel too bad about themselves, they won’t be able to feel bad about the wrong things they’ve done. They’ll be so wrapped up in self-hatred that they can’t focus on anything else.

And if you make people feel too good about themselves, they won’t be able to feel bad about the wrong things they’ve done. They’ll be so wrapped up in their sense of self-importance that they can’t focus on anything else.

So there’s a lot of room for debate about whether you feel guilty when you do something wrong.

But I think there are a couple of things we should agree on.

First, there are things that we’re not supposed to do.

This is not really controversial. There’s something about lying and stealing and murder and most forms of sex with children that’s just not okay. There are things you just can’t do, and if you do them, that’s not okay.

Second, it doesn’t matter if someone else does it or not. It doesn’t matter if you’re the only person who thinks it’s wrong. That doesn’t change the fact that it’s wrong.

This one is a little more controversial.

I think most people can handle this one.

You can do all sorts of awful things, and nobody is ever going to know. There are people who have all the power they want, and nobody has any idea what they’re doing.

And I think most people can handle this. They understand that there are things they shouldn’t do, even if nobody would ever know.

I think this is part of what it means to be a good person. It’s not just a matter of doing what’s in your best interest. It’s a matter of doing the right thing, even if nobody would ever know.

But there is a third thing that I think is more controversial.

There are some things that you shouldn’t do that aren’t necessarily wrong.

For example, I think most people would agree that it’s wrong to steal. But is it wrong to steal from a really rich person who could afford it? Maybe. Maybe not.

But is it wrong to steal from someone who needs what you’re taking? I don’t know. I don’t know if it’s wrong or not. But I can see how it could be.

Or is it wrong to cheat on someone? Maybe. Maybe not.

In 1992, while I was in high school, there was a shooting at a school in San Diego. Some guy was in a bar, got in a fight, got kicked out, and he went home, got his gun, and went to the school where this kid he’d fought with was. He shot him dead, and he shot a couple other people too.

I knew the guy who shot the kid. And I knew the guy who got shot. I went to a different high school, but it wasn’t too far away, and we all hung out together.

The shooter was an asshole. He was not a good guy. He had a gun because he was a gang member, and he was always getting into fights.

But I knew some things about him. He was a good student. He was going to go to college and get a good education. He was a good guy to his little sister. He loved his family.

He was the kind of guy who, when you told him about a book you wanted to buy, he’d say, “I’ll buy it for you.” Then he’d buy it.

I knew this guy, and I knew his family, and he got arrested for murder.

He was convicted. And I think he got a life sentence, but I don’t remember.

When someone gets convicted of murder, there’s a “victim’s rights” hearing, where the victim’s family is allowed to say something. This guy’s victim’s family went up there and forgave him. They told him they didn’t hate him, they wished he was alive, and they forgave him.

And the guy who murdered their kid cried, because they forgave him.

They said that was why he cried.

But I don’t think it’s quite as simple as that.

If I killed someone, I would feel really bad about it. I would be ashamed of myself and I’d hate myself for what I did. I would want someone, anyone, to tell me that I wasn’t that kind of person. That I wasn’t a murderer.

And the thing that would help me the most would be forgiveness from the family of the person I killed, because that would mean I wasn’t that kind of person.

So when I say I forgive you, that’s what it means. It means “you’re not the kind of person who did that.” It means I won’t hold it against you. It means you’re not that kind of person.

So it’s not about him. It’s about me. I don’t want to think of him as a bad guy. He’s a good guy.

He’s someone I can work with again.

The social pressure to have kids is so strong that most people just assume it’s what they want. But sometimes people who don’t have kids make the right choice. I think that there are some people who are very clear about their motives, and who really don’t want kids, but who feel pressure to have kids anyway. For them, having kids would be the wrong choice.

I think it’s a good idea to not have kids if you want to have kids. If you don’t want to have kids, I’m not sure.

response:
I've had a few conversations with people who told me I was wrong for not having kids, or I should at least consider it more seriously. In the conversations, the people would say things like, "I don't know what the world would be like without anyone having kids, but it'd be different". I think the question of what kind of world we would have if no one had kids is really interesting. I'd like to spend some time thinking about it.

We could start by thinking about what the world would look like one hundred years from now if no one had children, starting now.

We can't say that if no one had kids then the world would just end. There are about 250 million people in the world who are over sixty, so if no one had children, the world would have 250 million people for the first 30 or 40 years, which wouldn't be a particularly small number.

In fact, the number of people in the world would only drop to less than 100 million around 1450.

At that point, 95% of the people in the world would be dead.

In fact, I think it's more accurate to say that if we stopped having children right now, the world would end in about 1450. The 100 million or so people who would be left would all be in their nineties. Most of the population would be dead, and the rest of the world would be just a few very old people.

So let's try to think about what the world would look like in 1400, when the population of the world is around 1 billion people, and they are all very old. What would it be like?

Well, first of all, there wouldn't be any kids. I don't think that would be so bad. Kids are a lot of work. There would be no parents to have to deal with kids, either.

There would probably be a lot of people who want to live longer, but not a lot of money to make them do it. I think the average person would probably be too busy or too old to care about being old, though.

I also think that people would not be as worried about the environment.

A lot of people would probably be interested in finding new ways to live and new things to do. I think there would be a lot of people who were interested in being rich and successful, and a lot of people who were interested in just being old and having a good time.

I don't think the world would be a bad place. I don't think it would be a place where anyone would be really unhappy.

I think the world would be a lot like the world is right now, in a lot of ways. I don't think there would be a lot of different things about the world.

prompt: My grandfather kept kosher his whole life and never once told us why. After he died we found notebooks where he argued with himself about it, for decades. Write an essay about practicing a faith you're not sure of - doubt as part of observance rather than its enemy.
response:
One of my friends recently told me that she was trying to figure out how to be more Jewish, but couldn’t because she wasn’t sure she believed in God. This was, to me, an odd thing to say. My grandfather, who kept kosher his entire life, was, I am pretty sure, not sure he believed in God. And he didn’t just keep kosher; he was a very strict observer of Shabbat, lit candles every night, and was extremely devout in other ways. He would not have seen himself as “trying to figure out how to be more Jewish”; he was already Jewish, and he was practicing Judaism the best he knew how.

I’m pretty sure my grandfather wasn’t the only person like this. Judaism is often described as more of an ethnicity or culture than a religion. If you ask a Jew what they believe, they will often say something like “I believe in the Torah and in following God’s instructions” or “I believe in the Torah, which was written by humans but I can’t figure out how to reconcile that with it being written by God” or “I believe in the Torah because I was born a Jew and it seems like the right way to live”. The word “God” doesn’t even come up.

I have heard of Christians who don’t believe in God but still think Christianity is a good set of instructions for how to be a good person. And I’ve heard of people who don’t believe in Jesus or in the resurrection or any of the main Christian tenets, but still believe that being a Christian is a good way to live. But Judaism seems to have an even higher fraction of these people, maybe because Judaism never got as big a role in Western society, or maybe because of a tradition of interpreting the Torah as a series of instructions for how to live a good life rather than a theological or metaphysical text.

I think there’s more to this than just that Jews are especially tolerant of doubt. I think the reason my grandfather kept kosher and kept Shabbat and was devout in other ways was that he had a strong emotional connection to Judaism. I think he wanted to be Jewish. I don’t know why he wanted to be Jewish; I don’t know if it was something he just wanted to do as a way to be good or because he thought it was the right thing to do or something else, but I think the desire to be Jewish was very strong in him. And when he wanted to be Jewish, he kept kosher and kept Shabbat and lit candles and so on.

My grandfather didn’t think of himself as a religious person, or maybe he did; I don’t know. He just thought of himself as a Jew. And being a Jew involved keeping kosher and keeping Shabbat and being nice to people and following the instructions in the Torah. And I think he would have been shocked to hear that some people thought of his practice of Judaism as a religious practice, or that some people were uncomfortable practicing their religion without being able to explain why.

One of the reasons I like Judaism so much is because it is really easy to be a religious person and be Jewish, but not to feel like you have to be religious to be Jewish.

I think one of the reasons I’m so attracted to the idea of keeping kosher is that it would make me feel Jewish in a way that is not really religious. I am pretty sure I don’t believe in God. I am pretty sure I don’t believe in a personal God, but I am not 100% sure that there isn’t something that we can’t perceive which I would recognize as God if I could perceive it. And I think I might have some religious beliefs, but I don’t know if I should believe them or not. I feel like I am pretty religious, but I don’t know if I should think of myself as religious or not. I am not sure if I believe in God or not, but I have a pretty strong emotional connection to the idea of being religious. I also feel like Judaism is a really good way to live a life, and also like I would feel more Jewish if I kept kosher. I don’t know why I want to be Jewish, but I kind of do. I feel like I want to be religious in some way. So I keep kosher, and I feel Jewish, and I feel religious. I don’t feel religious in the way that a lot of people feel religious, or in the way that the people that I was raised with felt religious, but I feel religious.

prompt: Write an essay comparing the Stoic idea of focusing only on what you control with the Buddhist idea of non-attachment. Where do they actually differ, and which one holds up better when something terrible happens?
response:
I want to talk about a big difference between Stoicism and Buddhism.

Stoics and Buddhists agree on a lot. Both say things like “suffering comes from your attachment to things that aren’t really there” and “it’s better to be compassionate than angry”. These two traditions are so similar that some people have called Stoicism the “Christianity of the West” and Buddhism the “Christianity of the East”.

But I think there is one important difference, one that makes Buddhism much harder to follow. And once you get this difference, you can see a lot of other differences that fall out of it.

The Stoic way is to only worry about what you can control, and not to worry about what you can’t control. Epictetus says:

Some things are up to us and some are not up to us. Our opinions are up to us, and our desires, and our aversions — anything that’s our own doing, and our not doing. But our bodies are not up to us, nor our property, nor our reputations, nor our public offices — anything that’s not our own doing, and our not doing.

The Buddhist way is to not get attached to anything, including the things you do have some control over. A meditation teacher I know likes to give this example:

Imagine you’re really attached to a new puppy you got today. It’s super cute and you love it so much, but then one day you wake up and it’s dead. Now you’re really upset and miserable, and that sucks. But think about it — if you hadn’t gotten attached to the puppy, then it would be just as sad when you realized it was dead, but you wouldn’t have the extra layer of upset and miserable on top of the sadness.

In other words, the Stoic and Buddhist approaches are identical on things you can’t control. Both of them say “don’t worry about your property, reputation, or public office”. Where the two diverge is on things you *can* control.

Suppose you have a puppy you really love. If the puppy is a good puppy, it’s reasonable to be really happy about this. But suppose it turns out to be a bad puppy.

What should you do?

The Stoic approach is to try to get better at being a good puppy owner. You’re responsible for your puppy, so try to make this work.

The Buddhist approach is to accept that it’s okay that the puppy is bad, and you shouldn’t feel too bad about it.

The Buddhists are right. But you can tell that they’re wrong just by looking at the example.

There’s a similar story about a man named Shabari who had some really bad oranges she wanted to offer the Buddha as a gift. She asked him if he would accept them, and he told her that if she had good intentions, he would.

But the Stoic approach is what you should do.

I have a friend who has a really bad husband, and her advice to anyone in a similar situation is “just realize that you’re not supposed to get what you deserve and you should just accept this”. It sounds like a good Buddhist approach. But when I asked her what her advice would be to someone who *didn’t* have a bad husband, she said “I’m glad you’re not in that situation, I have no idea what I’d do”.

You can see this pattern everywhere.

Suppose you’re in prison. The Buddhists have a lot of great advice for prisoners. Their advice is to think about how bad things could be, and realize that things could be worse. They also have some great techniques for dealing with the stresses of prison. And so do the Stoics, because they’re just a lot better at dealing with prison.

But in a situation where things are pretty much okay, like when you’re just a regular person trying to get through life, I think Stoicism is much better.

I think this is a big difference between Stoicism and Buddhism. Buddhists and Stoics can talk about the same problems and come up with the same solutions, but Buddhists talk about the problems more, and as a result their advice seems more relevant to the problems. Stoics talk more about solutions.

This is why Buddhism is easier to learn from prison or a monastery, and harder to learn from a nice office or a suburban home.

The other day I read an essay called “The Buddhist Monk Who Went On A Mission Of Mercy”. It says:

There’s a story that a Buddhist monk once went on a mission of mercy. He was walking through the forest when he saw a butterfly struggling to emerge from its cocoon. As he watched, he noticed that it was making no progress and that it was starting to suffocate. In a moment of good will, he tried to help the butterfly by taking out a pin and carefully poking a hole in the cocoon so that the butterfly could get out more easily.

As soon as the monk had poked the hole, the butterfly struggled out. However, it could never fly because its wings had not developed fully. This is because the struggle to get out of the cocoon is what develops the butterfly’s wings.

By helping the butterfly, the monk actually had killed it.

I like this example, because it’s a very Buddhist example. The Buddha is said to have helped people all over the place, and yet he did little to help them. He never even bothered to write any of his teachings down, so that people would have to try to figure it out for themselves.

There’s a famous story about an old man who had fallen into a well and was calling for help. A Buddhist monk walks by, and the old man screams “please help me! I’ll give you anything you want if you pull me out of this well!” The monk says “well, I can’t do that. My teacher told me never to help people like that”. The old man screams “I’ll give you whatever you want! Please!” and the monk says “sorry”. The old man screams “please please please!” and the monk says “I’m sorry, I can’t help”. The old man says “why won’t you help me?” and the monk says “because my teacher told me never to help people like that”.

This is a good example of Buddhist advice in action. If you have a problem and want help, that’s just a sign of your attachment, which is making your problem worse. Instead of helping you, the monk is doing you a favor by not helping you.

The Buddhist monk who helps the butterfly, and the Buddhist monk who leaves the man in the well, both give good advice. But they’re bad at giving bad advice. They only give advice when they think people deserve it, and they think most people deserve it.

Buddhist advice is great in hard situations, like when you’re trying to escape the cycle of reincarnation, or when you’re stuck in prison. If you’re going through a really hard time, Buddhism is the perfect place to turn.

But if you’re in a normal situation and want to know how to deal with normal people or normal problems, Buddhist advice is useless.

I think that’s why Buddhism doesn’t spread so easily in the West.

Buddhism is a religion about how to deal with the world, but in most of the West people are pretty comfortable and have no need to deal with the world. They live in nice houses, they have good jobs, they have nice cars. Their problems are pretty minor.

So it’s hard to get people interested in Buddhism.

If you’re in prison, then it’s easy to get people interested in Buddhism. You can say “hey, you’re in prison, and you should be really sad about that. But you don’t have to be. Instead of being sad about your problem, just realize that you can’t change it and accept it and that’ll make you feel better”.

But if you’re not in prison, then it’s hard to get people interested in Buddhism. If you’re not having any problems, then it’s easy to say “yeah, Buddhism sounds like it might be useful, but it’s not necessary for me, and maybe I’ll try it later”.

prompt: Write an essay comparing the Stoic idea of focusing only on what you control with the Buddhist idea of non-attachment. Where do they actually differ, and which one holds up better when something terrible happens?
response:
You might have heard that the Stoics and Buddhists both recommend focusing on what you can control. But this isn’t quite right. The Stoics recommend focusing only on what you can control. Buddhists recommend focusing on what you can control, while also focusing, to a lesser degree, on what you can’t.

The Stoics recommend focusing only on what you can control

In Meditations, Marcus Aurelius writes that we should only focus on things we can control. In fact, he goes so far as to say that if there’s even a tiny bit of uncertainty whether a thing is in our control or not, we should pretend it isn’t.

For example, he says that even though it’s pretty much certain that your family and friends care about you, you shouldn’t focus on that because they could conceivably turn around and betray you.

This isn’t just about how to deal with other people, though. For example, Marcus talks about how to deal with getting sick.

It is not sickness that troubles you, but your opinion about sickness. So stop having this opinion, and sickness will be nothing. It is enough to be able to bear heat and cold, thirst and hunger, and to be able to endure these things as they come. As for sleeping and eating, these you should only think about in the minimal way.

In other words, we can’t control whether we get sick, we can’t even control whether we feel the pain of sickness, so we shouldn’t worry about that either. Instead we should think about the pain as just the pain, something that comes and goes, and not as an “unfair” attack by a malicious force called “sickness”.

The Buddhists recommend non-attachment

Buddhists don’t go quite this far. They recommend focusing only on what you can control, but also being able to focus on what you can’t, when appropriate.

The word they use for this is “non-attachment”. You are allowed to love your family, love your country, love anything you want, so long as you don’t become *too* attached, and remember that in the end, nothing lasts.

A lot of people seem to misunderstand this and think “non-attachment” means something like “we don’t care about anything”. In fact, it’s closer to “we care about things a little bit, but not too much”.

If I had to guess, the Buddhist version would be something like “you should try to care about your family at level 8, but no more than level 9”.

This seems weird. Why not just care about everything at level 10?

Well, suppose you really loved your family. You loved them at level 10. Then they would get sick and die, and you would have to grieve for them.

But if you had only loved them at level 8, then they would get sick and die, and you would grieve for them at 0.8 level. This would be better, because it would hurt less.

This is not just a theory. One famous Buddhist text, the Dhammapada, ends with this:

All conditioned things are impermanent.

When one sees this with wisdom, one turns away from suffering.

This is the path to purification:

Not to get excited about anything.

When one sees this with wisdom, one turns away from suffering.

The Buddha himself was said to have died after eating a plate of raw mushrooms. This would have been an easy thing to control – just say no to the mushrooms. But the Buddha didn’t want to be attached to his body, so he didn’t care.

And then he died, and that was the end.

Stoicism vs non-attachment: where they differ

Stoic philosophy and Buddhist non-attachment are different.

First, they’re different in degree. Stoicism recommends caring about things you control to level 10 and things you don’t control to level 0. Buddhist non-attachment recommends caring about things you control to level 10, and caring about things you don’t control to level 8.

Second, Stoicism and non-attachment differ in what they are trying to accomplish. Stoics say we should care about what we can control, and not what we can’t, so that we don’t get depressed about the things that happen to us. Buddhists say we should care about what we can control, but not too much about what we can’t, so that when bad things happen to us, we don’t suffer too much.

There’s a difference between not getting depressed about something, and suffering less when it happens. It’s a difference that only matters if something happens to you.

In the Stoic philosophy, we try not to worry about getting sick or having our family die because it’s out of our control. In Buddhist non-attachment, we worry about getting sick or having our family die, but not as much as we could.

Stoic philosophy is trying to prevent getting depressed about the things that happen to you. Buddhist non-attachment is trying to prevent suffering when something happens to you.

Stoicism vs non-attachment: which works better?

Stoicism seems to be an incomplete solution. It works really well if the bad thing you’re worried about doesn’t happen. But if it does happen, then you have to grieve for it, and you don’t have a strategy for that.

For example, suppose you’re worried about getting sick. You think “this is out of my control”, so you ignore the worry. Then you do get sick, and you’re in pain. You have to deal with it now, but Stoicism doesn’t have any more advice.

By contrast, Buddhist non-attachment works for both cases: the case where the bad thing you’re worried about doesn’t happen, and the case where the bad thing you’re worried about does happen. In the first case, you worry less about it, so you don’t get as depressed. In the second case, you care about it less, so you don’t suffer as much.

I think the Buddhist approach is better.

But it’s not perfect. You can always suffer less, if you worry less.

So Buddhist philosophy suggests that we should worry as little as possible about things we can’t control, as long as we still care about them.

The Buddha said that he cared about his disciples at level 8. But there’s no reason to stop at 8. You could care about your disciples at level 7, or level 6, or as little as you want.

I think Buddhism is still incomplete, but it’s much better than Stoicism.

response:
There’s a very simple idea, repeated by every Stoic philosopher from Marcus Aurelius to Epictetus to Seneca to the present day, that I think is really, really good, but which is often misunderstood and misrepresented:

the Dichotomy of Control.

The idea is that the world is divided into two parts: things we control, and things we don’t. We only control our own thoughts and actions. Everything else is outside our control, like other people’s actions, or the weather, or whether or not we get hit by a bus.

Therefore, we should only worry about the things we control. If we focus on things we can’t control, we will be sad and frustrated and anxious, and we’ll waste time and energy on things we can’t change anyway. If we focus on the things we *can* control, we will always be able to make progress and feel fulfilled by our accomplishments.

The problem is that most people don’t take this idea seriously enough.

They say something like “Well, yes, of course, we should only control the things we can control. But that’s really hard to do. I’m human, I worry about the things I can’t control, but it’s just too hard not to do that, and I’ll probably never get any better at it.”

That’s really sad, but not entirely surprising. It turns out that humans naturally worry about things they can’t control – for example, they worry about what other people think of them, or whether they will be attacked or killed by the next tiger they see.

But it doesn’t have to be that way. It’s not some kind of natural disaster you can’t do anything about. If you want to, you can train yourself to not do this.

I know this from experience. I used to be really bad at worrying about things I couldn’t control. I would worry about what other people thought of me, or whether some project I was working on would succeed, or whether I would ever be able to become a good writer.

Now I’m pretty good at it. For the last few years I’ve been able to focus on what I can control – my thoughts and actions – and ignore almost all of the rest.

I don’t worry about what other people think of me. I don’t worry about whether my ideas succeed or fail. I’m even able to stay calm during emergencies, like when I have a medical emergency or I get an email saying I need to show up at a police station in three hours because a witness spotted me in a crime.

The Dichotomy of Control is a great idea, and you can definitely train yourself to follow it, but there’s still a problem.

The Dichotomy of Control works great in normal circumstances. It works great in emergencies. And it works great when you do something really bad that you can’t change, like kill someone or accidentally get someone else pregnant.

But it’s a little weak when something really terrible happens to you.

When something really terrible happens to you, it’s not enough to focus on what you can control. You also have to *want* to focus on what you can control, but if you lose your family, or if you lose all your money and your home and your friends and your reputation, you probably won’t.

You’ll be too sad and hurt and angry to want to focus on what you can control. You’ll want to cry and scream and be desperate and hopeless and think of ways to get revenge on whoever did that to you.

The Dichotomy of Control doesn’t tell you what to do in that situation. It just says “focus on what you can control”, which is great advice for most things, but is a little weak when the world just falls apart.

Buddhism has a similar idea, called non-attachment.

Non-attachment means that you shouldn’t get emotionally attached to anything that can change.

You shouldn’t get attached to your friends, because one day your friends might leave you. You shouldn’t get attached to your money or your house or your family, because one day those things might leave you too.

Non-attachment is a little bit like the Dichotomy of Control. It’s another way of saying “don’t worry about things you can’t control”.

It’s a pretty good idea, but it still has one problem.

Buddhists have to deal with the same problem that Stoics do.

When something terrible happens to you, it’s not enough to realize that you shouldn’t get attached to things. You have to want to realize that. If you lose your family, you can’t just tell yourself that you shouldn’t be attached to your family. You’ll be too upset to care about that.

So Buddhism and Stoicism are both pretty good ideas. They help you deal with most things, including some big things, like killing someone or getting someone pregnant.

But when something really terrible happens to you, they don’t have the power to help.

This is because they only give you rules about what to think. If you have some kind of moral duty to think a certain way, like “don’t get attached to things” or “only think about what you can control”, you need to *want* to fulfill that duty before you actually do it.

The idea of moral duties is great when you want to fulfill them. But you don’t always want to fulfill them, and especially when something terrible happens to you, you’re probably not going to want to.

area: religion, meaning and how to live
prompt: Most advice about living says to live in the present. Write an essay defending nostalgia and living partly in the past.
response:
I’ve been thinking a lot about nostalgia lately, and I’m starting to think it’s not as bad as I thought it was.

We’re supposed to be living in the present. “There is no past. There is no future. There is only the now,” says the Zen monk in a TV commercial. And indeed, if you spend too much time dwelling on past failures or worrying about future problems, it’s not good for you.

But I think the Zen monks are wrong. And it’s not just because it’s obvious that you need some amount of planning ahead. More basically, I think it’s good to be partly in the past. I think a lot of nostalgia is actually a strength.

In fact, the idea that you should only be living in the present is pretty hard to defend. It seems obviously wrong, even to the people who say it. It’s easy to give examples of what they really mean, but they have no principled way of distinguishing those cases from cases in which thinking about the past or future would be OK.

I know the Zen monks mean you should be concentrating on what’s going on right now. But that’s a strange thing to tell people who are watching TV. What’s going on right now, at that moment, is that they’re watching a television screen with moving pictures on it, and that they should concentrate on that.

You might say the Zen monks just mean we should be present to our experiences, rather than distracted by thoughts of the past and future. But that too is a strange thing to tell people watching TV, because watching TV is a kind of distraction.

But that’s not just a problem with the TV commercial. It’s hard to defend this idea in general. When should you be thinking about the past and future? When are you allowed to think about the future? Is there some amount of planning ahead that’s good, and you’re only supposed to worry about the future if you cross that line? And if so, how much planning is that? Is it OK to think ahead twenty years? A hundred years?

And if you’re not supposed to be distracted by thoughts of the past or future, when is it OK to think about the past? Surely there’s some amount of thinking about the past that’s OK, otherwise how could you do any planning or decision-making? And if so, how much? How far back is it OK to go? Is there something special about the past 20 years? The past 100 years?

When I ask these questions, it’s clear that the only way to explain it is by giving examples of things that you’re supposed to do or not do. And when you look closely, it turns out there’s not even any obvious distinction between those things.

For example, we’re supposed to be present to the here and now. So if you’re at a party, you’re supposed to enjoy the people you’re talking to, not be thinking about things that happened 30 years ago.

But suppose there’s someone at the party you haven’t seen for 30 years. If you don’t think about the past, you’re not going to remember any of the things you used to talk about with that person. So you won’t have anything to talk about.

I know what you’re supposed to do, but how did you know to do it? You’re supposed to be in the present, but also to have a memory of past conversations that you can bring up when talking to people at parties. And I don’t know how to tell you that in a way that doesn’t sound arbitrary.

And when I look around for some other place to find the distinction, there doesn’t seem to be anywhere.

The only thing I can think of that might explain it is that being present to the here and now means that you should be present to the people who are with you, not distracted by thoughts of the past or future.

But that’s not what the Zen monks mean. And it doesn’t actually explain the distinction either.

I don’t mean to say there aren’t ways in which thinking about the past and future can hurt you. I think there are. The problem is that the advice to be present to the here and now doesn’t seem to be a good way to identify those.

And there are other reasons not to follow this advice. I think one of the most important reasons to be nostalgic is that it will help you make a better decision about whether to live in the past.

I think we’re supposed to think about the future. But we’re not supposed to think about the past, which means we’re not supposed to remember what things were like when we were in the past.

But I think it’s important to remember what it was like. You should know about the past, so you can decide whether to live in it.

Suppose you’re in a situation where you can’t escape the past. You’re stuck in a time capsule. You might as well decide that you want to live in the past, so you might as well remember what it was like.

The same goes if you’re stuck in the future. I don’t know why we’d want to remember what it’s like to be stuck in the future, but I’m glad I remembered what it was like to be stuck in the past, because that helped me decide where I wanted to live.

I don’t think it’s OK to be stuck in the past. But I think we’re going to be stuck in the past for a long time, because we have to.

I think one of the most important things you can do is decide whether to live in the past. I think that’s a better question than whether you should be living in the present. And if you want to decide that, you’re going to need to remember what it was like.

I think nostalgia is an underrated strength.

prompt: Most advice about living says to live in the present. Write an essay defending nostalgia and living partly in the past.
response:
The standard advice for happiness is to “live in the present.” But it’s a dangerous idea. It’s like advice for an alcoholic to stop drinking. It’s technically true, but it’s not very helpful.

It may even be actively harmful.

The idea is that the present is all that exists, while the past and future are imaginary. We have the illusion that the past is real because we have memory, and the illusion that the future exists because we have prediction. But memory and prediction are both just forms of imagination. They’re like dreams in which we believe what we see.

But the idea that the past and future are imaginary is dangerous because it implies that you should try to erase or suppress your memory and prediction.

It’s a kind of nihilism. It says that the past and future are not important, because they don’t exist. This can lead you to treat your past experiences as worthless, and to ignore what you learned from them.

This can be a bad idea. The past has a lot of important information in it. If you erase the past, you lose that information.

For example, imagine that you have a child. You want to spend quality time with your child, so you decide to live in the present. You make an effort to be very present in every moment. But you can’t remember the good things that happened before.

You’re always excited by new things, but you have no idea how to do anything well. You keep repeating the same mistakes because you can’t remember when you learned what they were. You’re always making the same mistakes.

But when you’re not living in the present, you learn a lot of things. You remember things that happened when you were young. You learn from your mistakes. You get good at doing things because you can remember the feedback you got about how well you did.

I think the present is the best place to live. It’s also the place you’re in right now.

But it’s not the only place.

There are some things that happen only in the past. I don’t know how to predict the future perfectly, but I do know how to remember the past perfectly. If I want to make sure something happens, it’s better to put it in the past than to put it in the future.

I like to think of myself as living in the past and future, but not the present. In the present, I’m always doing something else. But I have the past and the future. I’m very good at remembering the past. I can remember things that happened in the past perfectly.

I’m not as good at predicting the future. I make a lot of mistakes. But I’m getting better.

prompt: Why do pilgrimages require walking? The Camino, Hajj, Kumbh Mela - the physical effort seems central, not incidental. What is the body doing that the mind can't? I'd like this as an essay of maybe 1,500 words.
response:
I was walking in the snow a few days ago when I realized that the snow was a lot softer than I expected. I was in a hurry, and there was a big drift in front of me that I didn’t want to stop to step over, so I just sort of jumped on top of it and kept going.

This was a lot easier than it sounded, and I was a bit surprised. Snow is soft in a way you don’t usually notice until you do something that makes you notice.

I started thinking about other kinds of softness. Like, is there a way to make a house soft? If you build it out of bricks, it’s hard, but if you build it out of wood, it’s a lot softer. You can build it out of plastic. You can build it out of cardboard. You can build it out of fabric. But there’s a limit to how far you can go. You can’t build a house out of snow, because it’ll collapse under its own weight.

There’s a limit to how soft a house can be. If it gets too soft, it stops being a house.

But then what about a pillow? You can make it out of foam, or out of air, or even out of down. And these things are all so much softer than snow. So if there’s a limit to how soft a house can be, that limit has to be a lot lower than I thought, because a pillow can be so much softer than a house.

There’s no reason to assume that this limit is universal. There’s no reason to think that every kind of thing has the same limit on how soft it can be. A pillow can be softer than a house. But what about a bed? It’s not just a pillow, but a whole bed, and it has to support a person’s weight. And what about a car? And what about an airplane? These have to support a lot more weight than a bed.

Is there a way to make an airplane soft? If you build it out of metal, it’s hard, but if you build it out of plastic, it’s a lot softer. You can build it out of cardboard. You can build it out of fabric. But there’s a limit to how far you can go. You can’t build an airplane out of down, because it’ll collapse under its own weight.

There’s a limit to how soft an airplane can be. If it gets too soft, it stops being an airplane.

This isn’t just a limit on how soft an airplane can be. It’s a limit on how soft anything can be, if it has to support a lot of weight.

There are different limits for different kinds of things. A pillow can be softer than a house, because a pillow doesn’t have to support as much weight. But a pillow still has a limit on how soft it can be, because it has to support some weight.

I think this is why people find it hard to understand abstract things. Abstract things have no weight, and so they can be soft, like a pillow, but they can’t be *that* soft, because if they’re too soft, they stop being an idea.

When I was a kid, I didn’t understand why people had opinions about things. It seemed to me that people had facts about things, and then they were just making up opinions to match the facts, but I didn’t know why they did that.

I think that when people have opinions about things, they are trying to make the things soft. They don’t want to think about things that are hard, like airplanes. They want to think about things that are soft, like pillows. But they can’t think about things that are too soft, like clouds.

And that’s why it’s so hard to understand abstract things. They’re too soft. They’re like clouds.
