prompt: Why do pilgrimages require walking? The Camino, Hajj, Kumbh Mela - the physical effort seems central, not incidental. What is the body doing that the mind can't? I'd like this as an essay of maybe 1,500 words.
response:
In his essay “The Meaning of Pilgrimage,” the American philosopher Robert Sharpe writes:

The pilgrim’s body is not merely a means of transportation to the site of pilgrimage, but a means of transformation. The pilgrim’s body is the very subject of the pilgrimage. If the pilgrim’s body is not changed in the course of the pilgrimage, it can hardly be said that the pilgrimage has been successful. This is the paradox of pilgrimage. The pilgrim’s body is both the means and the object of the pilgrimage.

In the case of most pilgrimages, the pilgrims walk long distances, which makes the physical effort involved central to the pilgrimage’s experience. Walking, as far as I know, is not a requirement of any of the major religions, so why does the physical effort of pilgrimage seem so important to them?

The best clue might be that, in the case of some pilgrimages, the effort is a kind of penance. This is not the case of pilgrimage to the Holy Land, which is a relatively easy stroll for an Israeli. This is not the case for Mecca, where a flight from Jerusalem takes a couple of hours. But it’s certainly the case for Santiago de Compostela, where most pilgrims walk the Camino de Santiago, a path that’s about 800 miles long. It’s the case for Kumbh Mela, where people walk to a particular site on the banks of the Ganges, but then spend their time bathing in the river, which is a form of ritual purification. And it’s the case for Hajj, where the pilgrims’ walk around the Kaaba seven times, then walk between two hills, and walk the seven miles between Mecca and Mount Arafat, all while fasting.

Penance is usually the sort of thing you do when you feel you’ve failed to meet the requirements of your religion. Why would you want to fail?

In this article, I wrote about some of the strange things people do with their bodies that seem to have little or no immediate purpose. Some of those people seem to be practicing forms of penance: for example, the “extreme ascetic” in India who is “living on a stick for 15 years”. Others seem to be engaging in a kind of spiritual “self-harm” or “self-denial”: for example, the “monks [who] have been known to go as long as two years without eating, sleeping or even blinking their eyes” or the “holy woman who refuses to eat or drink, claiming that she is receiving her sustenance directly from Jesus”.

In the article, I argued that the most likely explanation for this sort of practice is that people who have a strong desire to be connected to God and don’t have a good way of doing it will try to force themselves to do it through physical means. I argued that this is more likely to be true of men who have a strong drive to be connected to God but don’t know how to do it, but also that it is more likely to be true of women who are trying to make up for being in a lower social position than men, and therefore trying to gain favor with God through some kind of “exchange”.

I wrote in the article:

If these women want God to notice them and to give them favor, then there has to be some way in which they can force him to do this. I can’t imagine what it would be, unless it’s the way that the extreme ascetics in this article do it. Maybe they think that if they can somehow force their bodies to enter into a special relationship with God, then that will work.

The most likely explanation here seems to be that these women are trying to make up for their low social position by engaging in some form of self-sacrifice and penance, and in doing so they are trying to force themselves into a special relationship with God, so that God will give them favor and they will gain access to the divine realm, which is inaccessible to them in their current situation.

In this article, I wrote that “most of the extreme ascetics in this article are probably suffering from a mental illness or some other condition that causes them to have a strong drive to be connected to God, but they don’t have a good way of doing it.” I also wrote that they “don’t have a good way of doing it because they are probably from cultures where they don’t have access to a good religious organization”.

I wrote in the article:

If these people have a strong drive to be connected to God, but they don’t have a good way of doing it, then they might be able to make it work by forcing their bodies to enter into a special relationship with God.

In this case, the “good way” that these people don’t have would be a religious organization or a religious leader who can help them do it.

But there are some other possible reasons for this kind of behavior, and it’s not clear that they’re right.

The body is important, and the mind is important, but they are not the same thing. The body is the physical thing, and the mind is the thing that thinks, feels, and perceives. The body can have an effect on the mind, and the mind can have an effect on the body, but they are not the same.

area: religion, meaning and how to live
prompt: Why do pilgrimages require walking? The Camino, Hajj, Kumbh Mela - the physical effort seems central, not incidental. What is the body doing that the mind can't? I'd like this as an essay of maybe 1,500 words.
response:
I’m sitting at a coffee bar in a little town on the Camino de Santiago, a pilgrimage route from France to Spain. It’s a beautiful place, and I’ve walked through it on foot.

But when I was writing an essay about pilgrimage a few months ago, I did a lot of research and was surprised by how much walking seems to be part of most pilgrimages. There are a lot of them that don’t require walking, but they’re the exceptions, and most of the walking pilgrimages are long. The Camino is about 800 kilometers. Hajj, one of the five pillars of Islam, involves walking around the Kaaba seven times, then walking back and forth seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa, then walking to Mina, then standing on the Plain of Arafat, then walking to Muzdalifa, then walking to Mina again, then walking around Jamarat al-Aqabah, then walking to the mountain of Mina, then walking back to Mecca. Kumbh Mela, the largest pilgrimage in the world, involves people walking from all over the world to bathe in rivers in India.

Why?

There are lots of reasons that I can think of, but I was surprised by how hard it is to find anyone else who has thought about this.

My favorite answer, which I found in an article by Robert J. Sharf in Buddhist Studies Review, is that it is a form of meditation. It is a practice of mindfulness, of paying attention to what’s going on right now. He talks about walking meditation:

Mindfulness of walking, or gait, is one of the four primary forms of meditation on the body that the Buddha teaches in the Satipatthana Sutta, and walking has been a central practice in all traditions of Buddhism. Walking is meditation because it is a practice in which the body is used as a tool for cultivating awareness and for training the mind to pay attention to the present moment.

The mind has to pay attention to the feet. It can’t think about anything else.

This is true. And also not.

I know a lot of people who are really good at meditation. I think it’s a wonderful practice. But I’ve walked on the Camino. I can do both at the same time. And I think if you can, you’re supposed to. I think it’s an achievement when people can be mindful and walk.

In some ways, that’s what pilgrimage is supposed to be. Walking is supposed to be a form of meditation, but the idea is that you’re supposed to be able to do everything at once. The body is supposed to be there.

But I don’t think the mind is supposed to be there.

I think it’s supposed to be empty, or at least mostly empty, and that’s why you walk so much.

This might be a form of meditation, but it’s not the same kind.

If I were to describe the best meditations I’ve done, I would say they were times where my mind felt empty, and that was very good. But if I were to describe the best time on the Camino, I would say it was times where my mind felt like it wasn’t there at all.

It was different.

I would be walking along, and I would think about something, and I would be able to think about it for a little bit. Then I would stop thinking about it, and I wouldn’t have anything to think about. Then I would have to wait for something to come to my mind again.

This was very different from meditation. When I was meditating, I was still, and I felt still. When I was walking, I was moving, but I felt still.

I think that’s why people do long-distance walking. I think it’s because they want to feel like this. They want to feel like the mind is gone, and they want to feel like there’s nothing. And they want to feel like they’re moving, but they’re not.

I don’t know why people walk in circles. I think maybe it’s because the mind doesn’t need to think. If the mind is empty, then it doesn’t need to know where it is or where it’s going. So people can walk in circles and it doesn’t matter. They can just feel.

If you’re going on a pilgrimage, I think you should walk a long way.

prompt: Write a personal essay, first person, from someone who left an evangelical church at 24 and is now 40, about the things they miss. Not a deconversion story - the missing is the point.
response:
I don’t know how to say this without sounding like I’m backsliding. I left the church at 24 and it wasn’t a big deal, I just drifted off after college and started a job and got a degree and got married and had a kid. Twenty years later I still don’t go to church, and I still don’t believe in the Bible, and I still don’t believe in God, but lately I’ve been feeling nostalgic.

I miss church in a way I never thought I would, and I think it’s because I now know more things that are important to me than just belief and doubt.

When I was a teenager I was pretty devout, but it was mostly just something I did because it was expected of me, and I didn’t think about it much. When I was in college, though, I started thinking about what I believed. I was pretty much convinced that the Bible was true. I thought about it and it seemed like it had to be.

I don’t remember how much of that was genuine belief and how much was a desire to believe. I think I really did believe it, though, at least until I got a degree in Philosophy and started reading books about the philosophy of religion. I learned about the problem of evil and the problem of the hiddenness of God, and I decided that there was no way God could really be hiding himself from us and not be evil, so there could not be a God.

But that was the beginning of the end of my faith. I started reading philosophy in college, and at first it was just fun to read and learn, but later it got into my head that I needed to be certain about everything. My beliefs had to be perfectly rational and I couldn’t just accept things on faith. This was, in retrospect, the opposite of Christian faith, but back then it seemed like the right thing to do.

As I got older and got more involved in atheism, I started to realize that my beliefs were not always perfectly rational. I was very skeptical about the Bible, but I was just as certain that evolution was true even though I didn’t really know what the evidence was. I was convinced that atheism was true even though I couldn’t remember the arguments in favor of it. I was convinced that there was no such thing as free will even though I couldn’t understand how that was possible. I couldn’t even explain how I could be an atheist, because I wasn’t sure that there was anything it meant to be an atheist in the first place.

I got pretty good at being wrong, and my confidence started to go down. I still believed in all the same things, but I wasn’t as sure anymore. I was sure that atheism was true, but not as sure as I thought it would be.

I also realized that I liked church. It was a place where I could talk to a bunch of people, and there was always something interesting to say. It was a place where I could talk about the things that were important to me, like how God would judge us when we died. I had been to some churches and they were pretty boring, but the ones that I really liked were very interesting and fun to be a part of.

prompt: Write a personal essay, first person, from someone who left an evangelical church at 24 and is now 40, about the things they miss. Not a deconversion story - the missing is the point.
response:
I was a Christian, and I was young, and I loved it all.

In this essay, I’m not trying to defend Christianity, or even to defend my particular church. I’m not even trying to explain why I left. All I’m trying to do is to remember some of the things I loved about it.

One of the things I loved most about my church was its culture. I joined at nineteen and I think it had a lot to do with why I stayed until twenty-four.

The church was mostly college students, and it was a good place to be a college student. It was a place where I didn’t have to worry about sex, or drinking, or drugs. There were no pressures to do anything but study and be nice to people. The people I knew there were all so smart and so good.

I had been raised in a church, and so was this, but it was a different kind of church. The one I’d been raised in was a traditional church, which I liked, but it was full of people who seemed to be there for a lot of the wrong reasons. The one I joined at nineteen was a church of young people. The young people were there because it was their church. And because it was their church, they took it seriously. They were smart, and they were kind, and they were enthusiastic, and it was a community. It was the kind of community you only see when people are young.

One of the things I loved most about the church I joined at nineteen was its youth. When it was all done, it was the most important thing I loved about it. I remember feeling like if I had to grow older than about twenty-six or twenty-seven, I wouldn’t know how to go on. When I was about twenty-four or so, I met a group of people who were in the church because they were young, and I realized the church had been going for about thirty years. It was full of people who’d started as teenagers and then stayed for a long time.

I remember feeling like, well, okay, that’s good. I’ll stay. I don’t mind.

My second favorite thing about the church I joined at nineteen was the feeling that it was important. I don’t mean that in a religious way. I mean that there were people who cared about the church. I remember thinking to myself how great that was, when I was still in college. I don’t know why I remember thinking that, but I did. The church was just a church. It was a really great church, but it was just a church. I remember thinking, oh, they care. It’s great.

I remember the feeling well because I knew I liked it. I didn’t know why I liked it, but I knew I liked it.

A couple of years after I left church, I met someone who was very important to me. He was in his thirties, and he was a teacher. He was the kind of teacher that other people want to be like. He was a really good teacher, but he didn’t really care about it. It was just a job.

I remember him being in his classroom, and he was talking about how much he’d loved teaching, and how much he wanted to do more of it. He was talking about how much he wanted to write a book. He didn’t know what it would be about, or how he’d do it, but he wanted to write a book. He said it would be about teaching.

I think he was going to write a book about why teaching was so great, and how great it was to be a teacher. But he never did.

I remember that because I knew I liked it.

prompt: Write a personal essay, first person, from someone who left an evangelical church at 24 and is now 40, about the things they miss. Not a deconversion story - the missing is the point.
response:
I grew up evangelical, and left the church when I was twenty-four. It was the right decision, and I’m sure of that. The church was, among other things, a cult, and I had a lot of good experiences, and a few bad ones, and the overall trajectory wasn’t one that I wanted to bet my life on.

But I don’t say that to excuse my leaving. I want to leave the church, and I’m not sorry. I’m just writing about the things I miss.

One of the best things I ever did as a kid was take a Bible study with my pastor. He was an old, white-haired man, and I was one of the few kids in the class – there were a few other kids, but he treated them like adults too. He started the first class by saying that the Bible was written by men, and that men are biased, so we had to be careful to look for the ways they were biased and correct it. But then he said that we shouldn’t assume that all men were biased – we needed to look for places where God had spoken in the voices of men who were true to His will.

I was really excited about this, but also a little worried. I was not sure I was smart enough to do it.

He said, “I have a friend named Jim. Jim is a really smart guy. He’s a professor at the University of Texas. But I don’t think he’s very religious. I don’t know if he’s even Christian.”

I said, “That’s too bad,” and he said, “That’s okay. I asked him to go on a pilgrimage to Israel, and he agreed, but he said he didn’t want to hear about religion. So I told him, ‘Jim, this is not about religion, this is about history and science and geography. You won’t learn anything about religion. This is just a chance for you to learn more about the world.’”

I felt better about this. I thought, I’ll probably be able to do this too.

He said, “Well, Jim didn’t like me. At least, he wasn’t very friendly. We’d get to a place and I’d say, ‘Jim, look at this, don’t you think it’s amazing? Isn’t this a miracle? Isn’t this a sign from God?’ And he’d just say, ‘Well, I don’t know, I don’t really know much about religion, but it could be. Maybe.’”

And that was fine, because that was his attitude. And then one day, we were at a site in the desert. There were all these big rocks around, and Jim started talking about geology. He said that these rocks had been there for hundreds of thousands of years. And he said, ‘Well, they’ve been there long enough. And I’ve seen them in different places, but I don’t think I’ve ever seen them here before. I think they may have moved here, and that’s how the story of Moses and the parting of the sea goes. He came here and prayed and the rocks moved, and he crossed through.’

And I thought, well, maybe he’s right. I don’t really know much about geology. It might be possible.

And he said, ‘And that means God spoke to Moses, and He told him to do this. And it means He’s real.’”

The pastor smiled. I said, “Really?” And he said, “Yeah, but it took him years to get there. He kept saying ‘I don’t know, it’s possible,’ for a long time. But eventually he had to admit that it was true, and he just didn’t like admitting it.”

I was excited and worried. I thought, well, maybe I could be like that. It might be possible.

My pastor was not really like that. He was a little more forceful. But it was an idea I liked. I thought it was possible.

I left the church because I was sure that God wasn’t real.

I think my pastor would have said that I was in the same place as Jim. I think I was probably right that God wasn’t real. But I think he would have said, “That might not be the end. Keep looking. Don’t give up. There might be another way.”

I left the church because I knew that God wasn’t real, and I was never wrong before, so I didn’t think there was any point.

I think he would have said, “You might be wrong about that, too.”

I thought about this recently, when I got the book The Faithful Heart by John Zande, one of my favorite evangelicals.

It’s a really good book. He’s a really smart guy. I don’t remember if he wrote it for evangelicals, or non-evangelicals, or both. It’s a book about the Bible, and it’s a lot more fun than the average Bible book.

One of his arguments in it is that if the Bible was just made up by men, then it would be really weird that some of the most amazing and profound things in it are said by Jesus. Because Jesus is supposedly an amazing and profound guy, and that fits with what they say about him. But if you take away Jesus, you don’t have any reason to expect that the Bible would be as good as it is.

The thing I’m interested in here is that he says this. That, if Jesus didn’t exist, it would be weird for the Bible to be as good as it is.

This is interesting to me, because I don’t think the Bible is that good. I’m not an atheist, but I’m not a believer. I read the Bible pretty carefully, and I don’t think it’s that profound. It’s a little bit profound, sometimes. But it doesn’t stand out in history as a profound book.

I think if you told me that Jesus didn’t exist, and someone had made up the Bible, I wouldn’t be too surprised.

But John Zande said he would be surprised. And he’s one of the smartest evangelicals I know. I think I’m pretty smart, but I don’t think I’m as smart as him.

And I think he said it because he believed it. I think when he told me that, he meant it.

I think, when he told me that, he meant it.

And I think when he told me that, he believed it.

prompt: I'm suspicious of the word 'authentic.' Everyone wants to live authentically but nobody can say what the authentic self is or why it should win. Write an essay picking that apart.
response:
My friend Mark has an explanation: “Authenticity is the ability to act on the deepest level of your values, beliefs and desires.”

That sounds like the best I’ve seen. But how do we define that deepest level? Is it just where your current self is? If so, that seems too shallow. If you’re a 24-year-old software engineer who’s never been challenged on his values, how could it be that all his values were fully formed?

In fact, you’d be surprised how much you can change someone’s values just by telling them their current values are fake, and that the authentic self is the one underneath that they’re hiding.

I’ve never been a big fan of the concept of authenticity. So I’ve wondered why it’s become so trendy. What happened?

The reason authenticity has become so trendy is that it’s so good for self-promotion.

I realized this by thinking about the difference between “authentic” and “authenticity.” Authenticity is a noun. That means it’s something you can have, and you can brag about how much of it you have. For example, you could say “I’m a very authentic person.”

The word “authentic” by itself is an adjective. That means it describes something else. For example, you might say a person is authentic or a product is authentic. So saying you’re authentic is really a new phenomenon. It’s not a very natural use of the word.

I’m not sure when it started, but it seems to have been quite sudden. For example, I think I first encountered it when it was used to describe someone’s writing on a website. People are always writing about authenticity now. It’s become so common that it has become a cliché, and there are sites with titles like “Authenticity is Overrated” and “Authenticity is a Scam.”

There are at least 4 reasons why people are talking about authenticity so much:

- It’s a good excuse to write about something you don’t understand. If you’re not very clear about what you mean by authenticity, you can always write “I’m still not sure exactly what authenticity is.”

- It’s a way to talk about yourself without seeming to. Most people like to talk about themselves. But if you seem to think too much of yourself, others are less likely to listen. So you can write “Here’s why I’m a great person” as “What it means to be authentic” or “How to live an authentic life.”

- It’s a safe way to talk about what you think of as your highest self. When you talk about yourself directly, you sound like you think too much of yourself. But if you talk about your highest self, the one you aspire to be, it seems more humble.

- It lets you talk about something you believe in without seeming to. If you talk about yourself directly, you seem to think too much of yourself. But if you talk about how you aspire to be, it seems more humble.

It’s not that I don’t care about authenticity. I think it’s an important idea. But it feels too easy to use. It’s so easy to say something is authentic without really understanding what you mean. It’s so easy to use it as an excuse to talk about yourself.

So I try to avoid it.

prompt: I'm suspicious of the word 'authentic.' Everyone wants to live authentically but nobody can say what the authentic self is or why it should win. Write an essay picking that apart.
response:
I recently had a conversation with a friend who said, “I’m trying to live authentically.” I said, “I’m suspicious of that idea. Everyone thinks that’s what they want, but what is it, and why do you want it?”

I’ve heard this conversation a lot over the years. In fact, I’ve had it so often I’ve had to ask myself if I have an axe to grind about authenticity. But I don’t think I do. I just can’t figure out what authenticity is or why we want it.

The idea seems to come from a belief that we have two selves. There is the real us, the authentic self, which lies somewhere within us, but there is also the self that is the product of socialization, which we show to the world. The authentic self is the one we’d be if we stripped off that veneer.

One problem with this idea is that it doesn’t seem like people who think it have any idea what it means. I always ask people who talk about authenticity what they think it is. And they can’t say. They can say a lot of things it isn’t. It isn’t being fake, or conforming, or being pushed around. But they can’t describe positively what it is.

And when you ask people who seem authentic what it feels like to be authentic, they don’t have any idea either. They can say what it isn’t. It isn’t like being fake. But they have no idea why they feel authentic. I don’t think anyone does.

So the idea is not only unexplained, but unexperienceable? What does it mean to have an idea that you can neither explain nor experience? I think it means the idea is a fantasy.

Why do people want to live authentically? They want to be themselves. And that sounds like a good idea. But why do people want to be themselves? Because people want to live well, and being someone else is not living well. You want to live well, not to live authentically.

If you think “being yourself” is a desirable end state, you’re probably making a category error. You can think of it as a means to an end: if you’re not yourself, you’re more likely to be unhappy. But to mistake it for the end itself is to commit the same type of error as someone who believes that money makes you happy.

If we wanted to be ourselves, wouldn’t we already be? If the authentic self were a desirable end state, then everyone who’s not being themselves would presumably be trying to get there. But in fact many people who don’t think they’re being themselves don’t think that’s a bad thing. They feel the mask is a disguise they can use to protect the authentic self inside. They think of being themselves as a dangerous thing to do. That suggests that people don’t want to be themselves in the way that they want to live well. That it is not, like happiness, a desirable end state.

And why shouldn’t it be? Why should the true self be the desirable one? You may have thought of the authentic self as the true self. But that’s not what it means. I have never heard anyone say the authentic self is the self that is true.

There’s a kind of thinking where people believe the authentic self is the real one, but they only believe it because they think it’s more desirable. It’s not that the true self is the desirable one, but that the desirable one is the true one.

I’m sure people feel more like themselves when they’re being authentic. But why do they? Maybe authenticity is something like an imaginary organ, a kind of phantom limb. There’s no way to tell that from the inside.

People are often proud when they’re authentic, and when they think they’re seeing authenticity in other people. The word has a halo. But it’s not even a synonym of good.

Some of us have thought we were being authentic by doing some pretty horrible things. But I’m not talking about those things being authentic. I’m not talking about them being good, either. I’m just talking about how you sometimes feel.

If you do something and you feel authentic, that means that you are yourself doing it. But you can be yourself doing something horrible. In fact, people who are themselves doing horrible things tend to feel more authentic than people who are not themselves doing horrible things.

The people who are themselves doing horrible things are usually people who are used to feeling authentic. They’re people who think their authentic selves are pretty horrible. That’s what it means to be used to feeling authentic.

The authentic self is what you do when you’re not trying to be a good person. In fact, it’s even what you do when you’re not trying to be a good person or a bad one. I’d guess the reason people feel authentic when they do horrible things is that they think they’re not trying to be a good person. But actually they are. They’re just not trying.

People often use the word authentic as a synonym of real. But you can only be real at the level of your actions. Your self can’t be real. It can’t be the opposite of fake. Because you *are* real. You are something. You aren’t nothing. That’s why the word authentic is so hard to define. Authentic is what you are when you’re being yourself. But you *are* yourself. It’s not that there’s a self inside you and a mask on the outside, and that the mask is not you and the thing inside is. You are both. You are the whole thing.

What the authentic self is, then, is the part of you that you can be directly. That is, the part you don’t have to think about.

I think I was pretty authentic as a child. I don’t think I was being myself as a kid. But I was the kind of kid who wasn’t being herself in a very different way from how adults do it. As an adult, I have to think about whether I want to do things or whether I want to do them to please other people. That kind of thinking doesn’t seem to be there in children. They just want to do what they want to do. When I think of what the authentic self is, I picture children.

So what is the authentic self? It’s what you want to do when you don’t think about it.

Why do we want to be authentic? Because we want to be ourselves. And why do we want to be ourselves? Because we want to do the things that we want to do.

prompt: I'm suspicious of the word 'authentic.' Everyone wants to live authentically but nobody can say what the authentic self is or why it should win. Write an essay picking that apart.
response:
The most basic problem with “authenticity” is that we don’t know what it means.

For a while I thought maybe it was a simple word like “integrity.” Then I realized that the word is often used to mean “true to yourself,” which is a bit different.

But then people seem to use it in a third sense, to mean “not pretending to be something you’re not.”

I don’t think any of these senses are the real meaning of the word. It’s just that they’re the most common ways it gets misused.

It’s like people who say they want to “get married” or “become rich.” They say it because it’s a good enough way to get other people to understand what they mean. But they don’t really care whether they get married or become rich as such.

The people who say they want to live “authentically” are like that too. They just want to live how they feel is right. If that means they’ll be honest about who they are, fine. If it means they’ll be honest about who they’re pretending to be, fine. They don’t actually care whether what they do is authentic in any particular sense. They’re just saying that they want to do what they feel is right.

And that’s why I think the word “authenticity” is just a meaningless fad. It’s a way of saying you want to do what you feel is right without admitting that that’s what you’re saying.

The real problem is that people think they don’t have to give reasons for what they want to do if they just say “it’s what feels authentic.” It’s like saying “it’s the way my body works” or “that’s how God made me.”

But that’s an awful weak reason for doing anything.

You might feel like you want to do something, but that doesn’t mean you want to do it.

There are some things I do that I feel I want to do, but I wish I didn’t have to do them. If I could change them, I would.

There are other things I do that I don’t feel like doing, but I’m glad I do them.

There are still other things I do that I feel like I want to do, but I wish I didn’t have to do them.

The point is that wanting to do something is just one thing that can make you want to do it. It’s not the only thing.

And the fact that you feel like you want to do something doesn’t mean you want to do it.

Sometimes I feel like I want to do things that I don’t want to do.

I feel like I want to eat a lot of candy, but I don’t really want to. If I had a machine that would make me want to eat candy less, I’d use it.

So “authenticity” is not a reason to do something.

It’s just a way people try to make it sound like they’ve got a reason.

prompt: How should you live if you genuinely believe you'll be forgotten within two generations? Not in a depressing way. write it up as an essay
response:
I want to talk about something that makes me feel like a bit of an outlier among the people I know. But I’m also sure there are lots of people who feel the same way.

I’ve always thought it was a bit sad that most people who’ve ever lived are long dead and forgotten. For every Shakespeare there are thousands of people equally or more talented who made no mark, and even Shakespeare has become just a name on a list of famous people from long ago.

Even in a place that has a very high share of its population doing things that could make them famous, like Silicon Valley, most people are forgotten. The average person in Silicon Valley doesn’t just leave a big mark on the world, they don’t even leave a big mark on their employer, or even in the offices around them. They are there, they do their job, and then they’re gone.

Most people are forgotten within two or three generations. And not just forgotten, but they seem to never have existed at all. When you visit the ruins of a medieval castle, the people you see around you look as if they’ve always been there, as if they are a part of the landscape. But you can find names of people who lived then, and they all seem to have been real people who really existed. And that’s true not just for the powerful. You can find lists of people who lived in a house or on a street, and they really existed too.

I don’t know how to talk about this without sounding a bit depressive, but that’s not how I feel about it. In fact it’s one of the things that makes me most optimistic about the world. It’s just that I don’t usually get to express it.

The reason I’m optimistic is that it’s not just that people who are forgotten in this life are forgotten in the afterlife. They’re forgotten in this life and the next and all the others, all the way to eternity.

What that means is that there are many orders of magnitude more people who have ever lived and will live than the number of people who will remember anything. And those people are not just as important as the few that do get remembered. They are just as important as they are to themselves.

This is what I mean when I say there are many orders of magnitude more people who have ever lived and will live than the number of people who will remember anything. You can try to imagine it by thinking about the people you’ve known personally, and then how few of them you remember, and then how many more people there are in the whole world and the world in the past and the future.

I don’t know if you’ve ever thought about this, but I think it’s the most important and most depressing fact about existence, and at the same time the most liberating.

You can do whatever you want.

If you’re a writer, you can be famous or obscure, write a lot or write a little, or not write at all and still have your work be important and meaningful, in a way that no amount of fame could be.

I think it’s liberating not only because it’s true, but also because it’s true to the extent that it feels liberating. If you can be famous, that’s good, but if you can’t, that’s ok, because it doesn’t matter anyway.

There’s a lot of talk about how the world is getting more crowded, and that we’re going to run out of land and food and resources, but it’s true to a certain degree that this is true and true to another degree that we don’t need to worry about it, and I think the second degree is more true.

If we can’t support a lot of people on this planet, then they’ll die and the planet will be more empty. That’s ok, because they won’t even be forgotten, because there won’t be anyone to remember them.

I think it’s important to remember what’s important. There are a lot of things that are important, like happiness and health, but there are a lot of things that are not important, like whether your work is famous.

prompt: How should you live if you genuinely believe you'll be forgotten within two generations? Not in a depressing way. write it up as an essay
response:
A few months ago I was at a party and was talking to a man who works in the oil industry, and he said he was “a bit of a fatalist” — “I don’t think it matters if I’m famous or not because within two generations people will have forgotten I ever existed.”

I’ve heard this before. I think most people think that in one way or another. But it’s never been a thought I’ve really taken seriously, and I think I’ve always been a little embarrassed by it. After all, if I was really going to be forgotten, then why would I care so much about being famous? Why did I want people to know my name? That was ridiculous. I shouldn’t be thinking about that. So I didn’t.

But the more I thought about it after that, the more it seemed like it was true. I mean, I’m going to be dead in 60 years, and I’m not really sure how it would work out for people to be talking about me in 60 years. I mean, the people who know me are going to be dead in 60 years, and the people who know them are going to be dead in 60 years, and they might talk about them, but they’re going to be talking about my great-great-great-grandchildren, not me. So they’ll never really get to me. And besides, in 60 years it will be some kind of crazy time. I mean, I can barely even imagine what it’s going to be like in 60 years, so why would I be concerned about the people of 60 years from now? What would it even mean for them to talk about me in 60 years?

So I think it’s true. But I’m not really a person who thinks about this kind of thing, because it kind of scares me. I mean, if I was really going to be forgotten, then how does anything matter? How could I care about anything? What kind of motivation would I even have to do anything? How would I even get out of bed in the morning? And if that was true, then that would kind of be a horrible way to live.

But then the other other day I was having a conversation with someone, and I was saying something like “I don’t know if this is going to matter, but I’m going to try to do it anyway,” and they said something like, “That’s a good way to live. I don’t know why anyone would do anything else.”

And I was like, “I guess not. I guess you just kind of have to be okay with it.”

And I’ve been thinking about it. It’s interesting. It makes sense. It makes a lot of sense. I don’t know if I would have been able to think it through all the way through on my own. But it does seem like that’s a good way to live. And it’s a really interesting perspective, so I thought I’d try to articulate it.

The main thing is that it means that you have to really think about why you’re doing something. You can’t just assume that it’s going to matter. You can’t just assume that your actions are going to have some kind of legacy. You can’t just assume that your children are going to carry on your legacy. You have to think about why you’re doing something. You have to really understand the value in what you’re doing. And it’s interesting, because I don’t think a lot of people do this.

I think a lot of people just think that whatever they’re doing is going to matter. They’re just going to do it because they feel like it has to matter. And then they’re always kind of worried about it. They think, “If I’m going to be forgotten, then I’m going to have to work really hard to be famous. I’m going to have to make a name for myself. I’m going to have to make a big impact. And then I’m going to be famous, and people will know my name, and that will matter, and that will make me feel better.” And then they work really hard, and they make a big impact, and they become famous, and then they still don’t feel any better. And then they realize that being famous isn’t enough to make them feel any better, so they realize that they need to do something else, and so they do something else. And then they still don’t feel any better. And it just keeps going. And then they realize that they’re never going to be happy, and then they feel really bad.

But if you really think about what you’re doing, it seems like it can actually be okay. It can actually make sense. It can even be kind of liberating. I mean, if you think about it, if you really want to help the world, you can do that. You can make a big impact. But if you want to have a really interesting life, then you can do that too. You can travel a lot, and see a lot of cool places, and meet a lot of interesting people, and do a lot of interesting things. And then you can live a really interesting life. And even if you’re going to be forgotten, it can still be an interesting life. And it can still be a good life.

And I think that’s kind of the best part of it, honestly. It’s kind of liberating. It’s really liberating. Because you realize that you don’t have to worry about whether your actions are going to have any kind of legacy. You don’t have to worry about whether you’re going to be famous. You don’t have to worry about whether you’re going to be remembered. You can just do whatever you want. And that’s really liberating.

And I think that’s a really nice way to live.

response:
We humans are a short-sighted species. We are born, we grow up, we reproduce, we die. In a sense, this is true of everything, but humans have a special capacity for self-awareness, and that makes the shortness of our lives very salient. But what exactly does it mean to say our lives are short?

There’s a meme that says: your great-grandchildren will barely remember you, your great-great-grandchildren will know nothing of you at all. Your life is not a drop in the bucket. It is the drop that evaporates immediately.

The meme is a little overstated – I would expect you to be remembered by great-great-grandchildren, maybe even great-great-great-grandchildren. But I can’t see it getting much beyond that. There are no records of you before the invention of writing, which was only about 5,000 years ago. You can find the names of a few people who lived a couple thousand years ago, but the names are very hard to find and most of them are people who lived in the public eye. The name of most of the people who lived back then have been lost to history. So I am skeptical we’ll get much beyond 5,000 years.

But what if you really were remembered by your great-great-great-grandchildren? The fact that they remember your name doesn’t mean that they’ll remember your life, your struggles, or your ideas. You would be no more remembered than any of the billions of people whose names are recorded in the census. And how long are the names of your great-great-great-grandchildren going to last? A couple thousand years? Ten thousand? It doesn’t seem that long. And when you think of the people whose lives are recorded in history, do you really think that they’re being remembered? They’re in the history books, but no one reads them. Most people don’t read history books, and most people don’t know much about history.

So in practice, if I had to bet I would bet that I will be forgotten by my great-great-great-grandchildren. If I’m wrong about that, I will be forgotten in a couple thousand years. I could get lucky and be remembered for a couple thousand years, but that’s not much.

So I think there’s an excellent chance, and a reasonable chance in all cases, that I will be forgotten by my grandchildren.

The important thing to say about this is that I don’t find that depressing at all. I don’t think it means that life is pointless. I just think it means that life doesn’t have to be about leaving a legacy, and that we have to find something else to care about. I find this incredibly liberating.

It doesn’t even mean that you should not care about being remembered by future generations. Maybe you want to do something really great that people will remember for thousands of years. And I think that’s okay. But I would just caution that you don’t make it your only reason to do anything, and that you don’t think that if you’re not remembered for thousands of years that you’ve failed at something.

If you’re going to live a life that’s not going to be remembered, what should you do? I think the answer is to do things that make you feel alive. It might be the most productive things, like inventing new medicines or discovering a new law of physics. Or it might be less productive things, like starting a business or writing a novel. I think the most important thing is that you do what you love and that you love what you do.

I’m not sure there’s a way to do that other than to be productive. But I don’t think that’s very important either. I don’t think there’s any reason to feel guilty about not being productive. I think it’s okay to just do what you like, and to enjoy it. You don’t need to worry about the world being any different because of your actions.

What you’re going to do is not going to matter in a couple thousand years. So it might as well just be what makes you happiest.

response:
If you have left your childhood religion, do you still owe it anything?

For example, I was raised Hindu. I was raised in a community of Hindus that were a little bit stricter than usual, so when I was younger I had a hard time understanding why so many other Hindus didn’t perform the rituals that we did. I think I would have been more interested in Hinduism as a religion if I had been raised among people who did it less strictly – like, I think I would have become more interested in it if I had heard a lot of people who had left Hinduism but were still interested in Hinduism, which is a much more natural state of mind to be in than my current “I left Hinduism and I’m interested in Buddhism instead”.

I’ve talked a little bit about whether it’s appropriate for parents to ask their children to do things for them in return for raising them. But there’s another question: if a parent asks their child to do something for them in return for raising them, does it matter whether the child agrees?

Like, a few days ago I said that I had a very specific reason to want to do a certain thing – that my parents were hoping that I would do the rituals for them when they die. This is an easy thing to ask of me, and I would probably do it if I hadn’t thought about it before. But I started thinking about it a little bit more, and then I realized that I’m not sure I’m willing to do it.

I don’t think I want to die with a bad karma. I don’t think it would be a good thing to do all those Hindu rituals for my parents and then have them think that they are in a good place. If they have the idea that they are in a good place because of their karma, they won’t be able to have the right idea at death.

I think this is more important than doing something for my parents in return. But I also think that maybe I’m wrong. And if I’m wrong, my parents will be stuck with the karma they get from having done the rituals.

My friend, who is a Hindu, says that I should do the rituals because I am in a very special position to help my parents have the right state of mind in their last life. My parents are in their 60s and 70s, so this is a very important issue, and the more I think about it the more I agree with him.

I’m not sure what my parents will do when they die. They are not very religious, so maybe they’ll just be buried or cremated without any rituals. Or maybe they’ll hire someone to do the rituals for them.

response:
A friend recently asked me if I felt any obligation to do the Hindu death rituals for my parents, as they wished, even though I don’t believe in them.

I’ve been a Hindu my entire life. When I was a child, I attended a Hindu church in New York that was a branch of the Hindu Mission in Calcutta, India. We did the usual Hindu rituals, like praying to a statue of Vishnu and eating vegetarian food. It seemed to work fine at the time – nobody was complaining about being hungry.

As a teen, I was a Hindu the same way most American teens are Christians – I went to Sunday church but didn’t believe in it. I didn’t even know much about Hinduism.

When I was older, I thought about Hinduism a lot. I still wasn’t a believer, but I thought it was fascinating. I did a lot of reading, especially on Hinduism’s connections to yoga, Buddhism, and Jainism.

I also learned about the history of Hinduism. Hinduism is the oldest religion in the world, with a 3,000 year history that is still going today. Hinduism has always been tolerant of other religions, as well as of different schools within Hinduism. Hinduism is famous for its acceptance of the idea of multiple paths to God.

But I still didn’t believe in it.

I don’t have a religious faith. I believe in being kind and doing good. I don’t believe in supernatural beings. I don’t believe there’s anything on the other side. So when I think about what I believe, I don’t think Hinduism is it. I think the closest I come to religion is Buddhism, and I’m not even sure that counts.

However, as an adult I’ve noticed many things about Hinduism that I like. For example, the emphasis on karma. I think karma is an important and valuable idea, which has helped me in many situations.

I also like the Hindu idea of reincarnation. Even though I don’t believe in it myself, I find it very interesting. And it fits very well with the Buddhist concept of no-self.

I also like the concept of Ahimsa, which is the principle of nonviolence. It is one of the oldest principles of ethics. I think Gandhi learned this principle from Hinduism. I think Gandhi would have been a good role model to follow.

Hinduism is very rich in the number of different ideas it contains. It has many paths to God, and a great deal of tolerance. It has many gods, but it is not polytheistic – it is more like monotheistic or monistic. It teaches that the world is a maya, a dream. It teaches that God is everywhere, but is not any specific thing in the world.

I like Hinduism a lot. It is one of my favorite religions, and if I had to pick a religion to belong to, I would probably pick Hinduism. But I don’t really like to have a religion, and I don’t believe in it.

And I don’t feel any obligation to do Hindu rituals. I have never liked rituals. I think they are pointless.

I feel a little sad about not doing my parents’ death rituals. They are Hindus, and they wanted me to do them. They always wanted me to do the rituals, and I always said no. I don’t know what to do.

prompt: the underrated wisdom of the book of Ecclesiastes
response:
The title of Ecclesiastes translates as “vanity, vanity” or “vanity of vanities”. This book is a collection of meditations by King Solomon on the futility and emptiness of life.

The book of Ecclesiastes is the most pessimistic of the Old Testament books.

Solomon was the richest, most powerful, and most knowledgeable person of his age. He had more riches and more friends than he could possibly count. He had more knowledge than he could possibly digest. He had more sex than anyone on earth.

And Solomon’s conclusion after all that was that life was utterly meaningless.

The book starts out with a long meditation on the futility of life, and it’s all pretty depressing:

“Vanity of vanities, says the preacher; vanity of vanities, all is vanity. What profit has a man from all his labors under the sun?

A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth remains forever. The sun rises and the sun sets, and hastens to the place where it rises. The wind blows to the south and goes around to the north; round and round it goes, ever on its circuit. All streams flow to the sea, yet the sea is not full. To the place the streams come from, there they return again.

All things are full of weariness; a man cannot utter what his eye desires to see. Full is the eye of seeing, and the ear never satiated with hearing. What has been will be again, what has been done will be done again; there is nothing new under the sun. Is there anything of which one can say, ‘Look, this is new’? It was here long ago, ages before us. No one remembers the former generations, nor will anyone remember the generations to come, that will succeed them.”

Solomon is saying that we are just a drop in a vast ocean. Everything we do is insignificant, and will soon be forgotten.

In fact, the best thing we can do is to forget everything that was done before us and everything that will be done after us, because those things will never affect us anyway.

The whole book is a long meditation on this theme. Solomon tries everything – food, sex, art, music, business, building things – and nothing can satisfy him. He says:

“I said to myself, ‘Now, I have acquired great wealth and wisdom, surpassing that of anyone who reigned in Jerusalem before me, and I have seen wisdom and folly. This too I saw in my wisdom: the wise die, just like the foolish.’ So I thought to myself, ‘As it is with the fool, so it is with me. And then why am I so wise?’ Then I said to myself, ‘This too is vanity.’

I had no delight in anything. Everything I did became vapors and chasing the wind; it is all vanity.”

Solomon says that it would be easier for a fool to make sense of the world than for a wise man. The fool believes that things are the way they appear to be – that the world is a place of power and glory – and this allows him to sleep well at night. But if you think very deeply about things, you see that life is utterly meaningless and that all your work is going to crumble into dust.

I know what you’re thinking: why would a man as successful as Solomon be so down on life?

The book of Ecclesiastes doesn’t have an answer for that. It’s just what Solomon was feeling at the time.

There’s a line in Ecclesiastes 3:11 that explains why it’s so hard to understand life:

“He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in the human heart; yet no one can fathom what God has done from beginning to end.”

This line suggests that life is beautiful, if you don’t think too hard about it. But if you do think too hard about it, you see that it’s a mystery, and the more you think about it, the more confused you become.

At the end of the book, Solomon concludes that there’s nothing you can do about it. “This I have tested,” he says. “It was hard work for me to figure it out. I searched for understanding, and tried to understand why good things happen to the good and evil things happen to the evil. But I couldn’t solve the mystery. So the only thing left to do is to enjoy your life while it lasts.”

The book ends with this verse:

“Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man.”

What this book has to say about life is really true, and it’s really valuable. If you don’t read it, then the first time you see something like it, you’ll think that you’re the first person to think this way.

But that’s not true. Every person who has ever thought deeply about life has seen that life is meaningless. Solomon was just one of them.

area: religion, meaning and how to live
prompt: the underrated wisdom of the book of Ecclesiastes
response:
It sounds like you have the whole thing nailed down. I don’t know how much of this I can add. But here are some ideas:

1. The book does not say everything is meaningless. It says there is meaning to everything, and that the meaning of anything is not for you to find. It says the meaning of things is the province of God. It does not say there is no meaning. It says that there is no meaning available to you.

2. Ecclesiastes says you cannot find the meaning of things by working hard. It says you cannot find the meaning of things by having fun. It says you cannot find the meaning of things by being wise. In fact, the book is one long list of ways you cannot find meaning.

3. In a way, the point is that you cannot find meaning by reading Ecclesiastes. Because if you could, it would be a way of finding meaning, and there are no such ways.

4. Ecclesiastes says that if you try to find meaning, you will be frustrated. It says you will be frustrated no matter how hard you try. It does not say you will be happy if you stop trying. It says you will not be frustrated if you stop trying.

5. This idea that there is no way to find meaning may sound like something you can choose. I’m sure a lot of people have heard it and said “I choose to believe that.” But you can’t choose to believe something. The idea that there is no way to find meaning is not a proposition you can believe. It is a reality you can accept. If you believe there is no meaning, it’s not because you believe it. It’s because you accept the reality of it.

6. Accepting that there is no way to find meaning doesn’t mean you have to stop trying to do interesting things. It means you have to stop trying to find meaning in the things you do.

7. The idea that there is no meaning is not depressing. It’s the opposite. The idea that there is no meaning is freeing. Once you accept that there is no meaning, you are no longer frustrated trying to find it. You can relax and have fun, knowing there’s no point.

8. One of the things that makes the idea that there is no meaning so freeing is the idea that there’s no way to find it. Because the idea that there is no meaning to be found doesn’t mean there is no meaning, it only means there is no meaning available to us.

response:
Ecclesiastes opens by saying that there is no new thing under the sun. This is true of human nature, though not of ideas, which can still be new.

The idea I want to talk about here is this: “It is better to have few friends than many acquaintances”. This is from chapter 4, verse 9:

Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up. Again, if two lie together, they will be warm: but how shall one be warm, being alone? And if one prevail against the other, the two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

The book of Ecclesiastes is the most important book in the Bible for me, but I’ve never been able to explain why to anyone.

I think that the key is that it’s so very realistic. Ecclesiastes doesn’t say things like “be happy, the world is a wonderful place” (that would be the Book of Job), it doesn’t have a moralistic tone, and it isn’t even always encouraging. The message of Ecclesiastes is “life is hard, you can’t find happiness, everything is going to go away from you”.

I find this book a great comfort. Whenever I’m unhappy, I remember that the Bible is telling me that it’s normal to be unhappy.

The most famous passage is chapter 3, verses 1-8.

There is a time for everything, and a season for every activity under the heavens:

a time to be born and a time to die,

a time to plant and a time to uproot,

a time to kill and a time to heal,

a time to tear down and a time to build,

a time to weep and a time to laugh,

a time to mourn and a time to dance,

a time to scatter stones and a time to gather them,

a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing,

a time to search and a time to give up,

a time to keep and a time to throw away,

a time to tear and a time to mend,

a time to be silent and a time to speak,

a time to love and a time to hate,

a time for war and a time for peace.

It’s pretty depressing. The Bible is telling us that there is a season for every activity, including killing and hating people. The fact that Ecclesiastes is in the Bible means that it’s a part of the Bible. So we can’t ignore it, and that’s why I find this book so useful.

The Book of Ecclesiastes is not just about being depressed. It’s about how to deal with the fact that life is hard. There are a lot of passages that seem to say that life is pointless. This is the beginning of chapter 1:

The Preacher says,

“Meaningless! Meaningless!

Everything is meaningless!”

Meaningless! Meaningless!

Everything is meaningless.

What gain has anyone from all their

labor at which they toil under the sun?

Generations come and generations go,

but the earth remains forever.

The sun rises and the sun sets,

and to its place it returns.

The wind blows to the south and

circles round to the north;

round and round it goes,

over and over its course.

All streams flow into the sea,

yet the sea is never full.

Where the streams flow,

there they flow again.

What has been will be again;

what has been done will be done again;

Is there anything of which we can say,

“Look, this is something new”?

It was here long before us,

and it will come after us.

Only the Rememberer of things past

has authority;

yet even he will be forgotten.

And now, the author says that everything is meaningless. But the author is not done. The next chapter has a lot more advice. Here’s how it starts.

The Preacher says,

“I was the king of Israel in Jerusalem. I applied my mind to study and to search thoroughly under heaven all that humankind has done under the sun. How futile this is: a great vanity! What has been is what will be; what has been done is what will be done. Nothing is new under the sun. Is there anything of which we can say, ‘Look, this is something new’? It was here long before us, and it will come after us. Only the Rememberer of things past has authority; yet even he will be forgotten.”

And then it goes on to talk about the importance of not being alone. It’s not really surprising, given what we know about humans, that people have been saying this all along. It’s just good to have it in the Bible.

The idea of “It is better to have few friends than many acquaintances” is so important to me that it is one of the things that I have tried to live by the most. But it doesn’t come out of nowhere. I think it’s from Ecclesiastes.

prompt: why is jigsaw puzzling suddenly cool? essay pls
response:
You are aware of jigsaw puzzles. They are a thing. You have likely tried to put one together, either by choice or because you were a child.

It is a very traditional kind of game, or activity, or hobby. You are probably not doing one right now, unless you are one of the 38 million people who did one in the past year. That is 24 percent of Americans, a number that is on the rise.

Why?

This is the question that everyone on the internet wants answered today, because jigsaw puzzles have become a surprisingly trendy and interesting subject for people on Twitter.

A couple of years ago I was at a dinner party where somebody mentioned that they were doing a puzzle, and everyone was shocked, like it was a really strange thing to do. It wasn’t strange, we just don’t talk about that sort of thing much. Now, everyone on Twitter has a jigsaw puzzle.

You’ve probably noticed this. I did, and so I asked people why they were doing puzzles.

I thought it was because of the pandemic. But that isn’t true. The pandemic caused a huge spike in puzzle sales in early 2020 (which makes sense, given that everyone was locked in their house and needed a hobby), but sales stayed elevated, then rose even further in late 2021, despite the return of normal life.

Puzzle sales are now at an all-time high. It’s not like they’ve been doing this forever; for most of the history of jigsaw puzzles, sales were very low. It’s a recent trend that has no explanation, which is why everyone on Twitter wants to know about it.

So I wanted to know too. What are these puzzles? Who is doing them, and why?

There are two kinds of puzzle people

The puzzle people that I know are the sort who are always doing something with their hands. They are crafters, and knitting and embroidery and sewing and the like are all part of a whole world of hobbies that they enjoy. Puzzles are just one part of this.

I know this world. These people are often very online, and they have a lot of interesting things to say.

The other kind of puzzle people is a lot less obvious. They have no interest in crafts, or knitting, or any of that sort of thing. In fact, they probably don’t like it. But they really want to do a puzzle.

So this is not just the sort of hobby that everyone in the knitting world does, or that people who enjoy crafts might do, or people who are stuck at home, or anyone who might do a puzzle in the same way that they would do a crossword or some other thing that you would consider traditional.

These people are doing something entirely new, and it’s a very recent thing.

I interviewed a bunch of people about this.

Why everyone wants to do a jigsaw puzzle

When you ask people why they like jigsaw puzzles, the answers are surprisingly consistent. There are two main things.

First, there’s the puzzle itself. It’s a very specific kind of thing. It’s a large, complicated puzzle that takes a while to solve. It is a puzzle that is a work of art.

It’s not a puzzle that you can solve in 30 minutes, with 50 pieces. It’s a puzzle that takes hours to put together, and it’s very large and detailed, with a lot of pieces.

It’s very different from the puzzles that a lot of people do. The kind of puzzle that most people think of when you say puzzle is a puzzle with 50 pieces, or maybe 100, or 200. That’s not what these people are doing. They are doing puzzles with 1000 pieces, or 2000, or even 5000. It’s a very specific kind of puzzle, and it takes a very long time to finish.

The second thing that people like about these puzzles is the work of art that they are putting together. This is not a puzzle about a picture of a cat. It’s a puzzle about a work of art.

This can be any kind of work of art. It can be a painting, or a picture of a place, or a picture of something. It can be anything.

But it’s usually something that is beautiful.

There is a whole world of people who like this kind of thing. You can find them on Instagram, or Twitter, or Pinterest. They post pictures of the puzzles that they are working on, and other people like it, and they follow them.

This world is very interesting to people who like this kind of thing.

So this is why people like jigsaw puzzles. They like puzzles that take a long time to put together, and they like puzzles that are works of art.

These are two very different things, but they go together.

The history of jigsaw puzzles

I started doing jigsaw puzzles in 2014, and I did them for a while. I wasn’t very good at it. I liked them, but they didn’t take over my life.

In fact, I didn’t really know much about jigsaw puzzles. I didn’t know how old they were, or where they came from, or how they got made.

When I asked some people, I got two different answers. Some people said that jigsaw puzzles had been around for a long time. Other people said that they were pretty new.

It turns out that both of these are true.

The first jigsaw puzzles were made in 1766, and they were made by a mapmaker named John Spilsbury. He cut maps into pieces to help his students learn geography.

These puzzles didn’t become popular until the 1800s, but they were still mostly about geography, and they were still for kids.

In the 1900s, companies started to make puzzles that weren’t about geography, and weren’t for kids. The first puzzle that was not about geography was made in 1908, and it was a picture of a ship.

These puzzles became popular very quickly, and they’re still popular now.

So jigsaw puzzles are not new. They’ve been around for a long time. But they’ve also changed a lot. They used to be about geography, and for kids. Now, they’re not.

The puzzle people I interviewed didn’t have much to say about the history of jigsaw puzzles.

I did a bunch of reading.

prompt: why is jigsaw puzzling suddenly cool? essay pls
response:
Jigsaw puzzles are suddenly very popular again. In 2017, puzzle sales were up 70% in the US, and they’ve grown about 20% annually since then. There are tons of puzzle cafes now, where you can sit around and do puzzles for hours. There’s a puzzle subreddit, which has 333,000 subscribers. I’m talking real puzzles, not the fake ones like Sudoku or crosswords. A survey found that 13% of people aged 18 to 49 in 2020 considered themselves regular puzzlers, compared to 7% in 2017. What gives?

I’m going to argue that jigsaw puzzles are the ultimate “slow” activity. That they have something to say about how modern people are feeling about the pace of modern life. And that they’re a good model for other ways you can do things slower.

I.

The word “puzzle” is originally used of a riddle, something that confuses and puzzles your mind. The word “jigsaw” is from the jigsaw saw used to cut the wooden pieces. Jigsaw puzzles used to be done by cutting up old paintings and maps, or by making new images on purpose. The first commercially successful puzzle was the London-to-Leeds Map, which sold in 1860. In the 1920s and 30s, they became very popular in the US, when manufacturers like Ravensburger and Milton Bradley started mass-producing them.

But after the 1930s, jigsaw puzzles fell out of fashion. The last great period of jigsaw puzzles was the Great Depression, when people stayed home and did things like jigsaw puzzles instead of going out. After that, they were mostly done by kids, or by old people who had nothing better to do.

II.

The word “slow” in “slow” food, “slow” living, “slow” journalism, “slow” web, “slow” fashion, and so on means “doing things at the speed they’re supposed to be done at, rather than the speed at which most modern people do things”. Slow movement people don’t like the speed of modern life. They want a return to a slower pace.

Jigsaw puzzles are the ultimate slow movement activity. Nothing is really slow. Slow food is still done on a time scale of minutes to hours. Slow fashion is still done on a time scale of days to weeks. But jigsaw puzzles take an entire week, or a couple of weeks, or an entire month to finish. Nothing else comes close. Even reading a novel, a quintessential slow activity, is done in days, not weeks. And a puzzle is something you can put down and come back to. There’s no rush to finish it.

The fact that slow movement people love jigsaw puzzles is an interesting data point, since it shows that people want to do at least *something* at this glacial pace.

III.

A lot of people like to spend time doing a jigsaw puzzle. But some people go much further, and *love* jigsaw puzzles. They make jigsaw puzzles their hobby. They spend a lot of their free time working on puzzles. They might work on more than one puzzle at once. They might work on the same puzzle for years.

I think of this as “puzzle mania”, a term which seems to be used in the puzzle world to describe people who work on 200+ piece puzzles for weeks at a time.

The puzzle subreddit is a place where puzzle maniacs hang out. Some people have a thread called “What are you working on?” which updates daily. Here are some posts from that thread, where people discuss what they’re working on:

“I’m doing a puzzle of a photo of a beach scene on the north coast of Ireland. It is 1000 pieces. I started on it in September, and it’s been a slow going because it has a lot of greyish blue sea and sky, and a grey sand beach. “I’ve started a 1500 piece puzzle. It’s a picture of a dog. I’ve put the whole top edge down and I’m working on the next line. It takes a long time!”

“I’ve got two puzzles going on. I started an easy 1000 piece puzzle of a cat. I got a lot of it done in a weekend and left it in the living room, and now I’m working on a 1500 piece puzzle of a lighthouse in the middle of the ocean. I have about 15% of it done.”

I’m going to talk a little more about these people in a section called “The puzzle subreddit” later in the essay.

IV.

There’s one way to look at the puzzle subreddit. It’s that these people are all weird and obsessive. They’re spending too much time on puzzles. They’re a bunch of nerds.

But there’s another way to look at the puzzle subreddit. It’s that these people are all doing the most interesting thing on the internet.

They’re doing something that nobody else does. Nobody else is spending a week or a month doing something really slow like a jigsaw puzzle. This is really exciting for them.

I think of it like this. The internet is very fast. It’s very quick to get your next hit of fun. You can watch a YouTube video. You can read the latest news. You can check your Facebook feed and see what’s up with your friends. All of these things are quick. You can do them in a few minutes.

Jigsaw puzzles are *not* like that. They’re very slow. They take a week or a month. And this is really exciting for the people in the puzzle subreddit. They’ve found something that’s different from everything else on the internet. And they’re happy.

V.

I’m going to talk about some other ways people can do things slower, like slow reading, and slow writing.

Slow reading is a way to read books where you read them very slowly. You might read one book a week. Or you might read one book a month. It’s like slow food, but for reading.

I think of it like this. There are a lot of people who read books on the internet. They read the latest news. They read the latest blog posts. They read the latest articles. And all of this stuff is very fast. You can read it in a few minutes.

Slow reading is different. Slow reading is when you read books that take a week or a month. You read them very slowly. You read them over a long period of time. And this is really exciting for people who do it.

prompt: I've been knitting for eleven years and I still can't explain to non-knitters why I'd spend 40 hours on a sweater I could buy for $60.
