response:
The day I knit my first scarf, a hand-knitted scarf, the world opened up like a flower. For a long time afterward I kept thinking about that feeling. It was something like: Oh! That’s *how* that was made!

I don’t know if you’ve ever felt that way about anything. I think it’s a kind of magic, the kind of magic you feel when you realize something’s been true the whole time, and you’ve just never noticed it.

I can’t tell you why it happens. The magic of the world is a secret. I can only tell you the times I’ve felt it.

I’ve felt it about cooking. For example, I’ve always liked to make bread, ever since I was a kid. I liked making bread because it was kind of a science experiment, and when you opened the oven it was either a success or a failure, and either way it was fun. But when I learned to make bread the way I make it now, I felt a kind of magic. When you make bread, you can watch the dough rise. It takes a couple of hours, but you can watch it. It’s like watching a time-lapse movie. If you know what to look for, it’s really beautiful. The dough seems to *live*.

The first time I made soup, it was magic, the same way. You add all the ingredients to the pot, you heat it up, and the flavors combine. If you make it the way I like, you don’t add the cream until the end. When you do, the soup changes color and flavor, just like a chemistry experiment, and you can’t tell what it’s going to taste like until the cream melts in.

I’ve felt this magic about other kinds of making things, too. For example, the first time I sewed a dress. I had a pattern and I’d bought the fabric, and the pattern said to cut out these pieces. And when I tried it on, it was a dress! I couldn’t believe it. And the pattern had even given me some nice instructions, like “sew in the pockets first, before you sew the sides, and they’ll be easier to sew in.” I’d never thought of that, and I’d never seen it done before. I still can’t believe it, that those little flaps of fabric that I can’t even see are in there, and they’re pockets, and I can put things in them.

I’m not a very good writer. I’m a worse writer than I want to be. I try hard and sometimes I do okay, but usually I’m not very good. I don’t know how much I could improve with more practice. But I *like* to write. Sometimes, when I write well, I have that magic feeling.

And the other day, in the middle of a knitting class, I suddenly remembered that feeling. I realized that I had felt it about knitting, too.

I’d made a sweater. It had taken me a month, and it had been hard. But when I put it on, I *understood* the sweater. I felt like I knew how it was made, and what it was for, and I understood why it worked. I understood how the fabric moved, and how the stitches held together, and why it fit me the way it did.

It was a good sweater, but it wasn’t magic. It was an ordinary sweater. It looked like any other sweater you’d see in a store, though it didn’t feel like any other sweater. I’d never seen a sweater that felt like that before. It was soft and smooth, and it didn’t seem to have seams, like most sweaters do.

I didn’t know what I’d done that was so good. I’d never seen any other knitters’ sweaters that looked and felt like that, and I didn’t even know what I’d done that made it that way.

But the feeling I had when I put on the sweater was that magic feeling. I could only describe it as, Oh! That’s *how* that was made!

Then I realized that I couldn’t explain that feeling to anyone else. I couldn’t explain what I meant. I’d never told anyone before, but I’d felt that kind of magic about knitting. It was too exciting to be true, and I hadn’t even realized it myself.

So I asked my knitting teacher, “Do you feel that way about your sweaters?” And she said yes. She said it was the reason she made sweaters. She said that when she finished a sweater and put it on, she had that feeling. It was like the sweater was a new idea, and she had just figured it out.

That felt like such a good reason to make a sweater. If you didn’t feel like that when you finished it, you probably wouldn’t have enough reason to spend a month making it.

But I didn’t know what she meant, and she didn’t know what she meant. I’ve been knitting for ten years, and I still don’t know what she meant. I’ve been trying to figure it out, but I don’t think I know yet.

I don’t even know if everyone feels that way. I don’t think everyone does.

But a lot of knitters I know do feel that way. Some of them are good knitters, and some of them are great knitters. They’ve been knitting for a long time. They make nice sweaters. But they tell me that when they make a sweater and put it on, they don’t feel that way.

They make nice sweaters, but they don’t feel like the sweater is a new idea they just figured out. That doesn’t seem right to me, because that’s what I feel.

It’s hard to explain.

I’ve been trying to write about this for a long time. I still don’t know what I’m trying to say. I’m going to keep trying.

prompt: I've been knitting for eleven years and I still can't explain to non-knitters why I'd spend 40 hours on a sweater I could buy for $60. response:
I’m a knitter. I knit sweaters for myself and for people I care about, and for eleven years people have asked me why I would do this when I could just buy a sweater. They’re usually polite about it. But it’s the one question I’m never able to give a satisfying answer to. I can’t really explain why it’s so fun and why I do it. When I’m explaining knitting to people, it’s not enough to say “it’s relaxing” or “it’s made with love” or even “I like how it looks.” It doesn’t satisfy the people who ask me. I wish I had a satisfying answer.

Today I think I have one. I knit because I like being able to answer questions about my sweaters.

There are all kinds of questions people could ask about my sweaters. Questions like “how did you make this?” and “who made this?” and “how do you know how to make these?” and “how long did this take?”

Some questions people could ask about my sweaters I *can* answer. But some I can’t.

A question I can’t answer is “how did you make this sweater?” I can’t answer that because there’s no simple, straightforward, accurate answer to that question. There are all sorts of complicated questions I could ask about a sweater that would be hard to answer, but “how did you make this?” is the easiest of the impossible questions.

If I asked you “how did you make this sweater?”, you might answer “by knitting it” or “by sewing pieces together”. But those answers don’t really explain how a sweater is made, in the way that the questioner would want.

You can’t make a sweater just by knitting it, or just by sewing pieces together. Those are just the tools you use to make a sweater. You have to *know how* to knit a sweater, or how to sew pieces together into a sweater.

So if you asked “how did you make this sweater?”, I might answer “by knitting it, using a knitting pattern I found online.” But that doesn’t really answer the question either, because a knitting pattern isn’t a simple, straightforward, accurate description of how to knit a sweater. It’s a set of instructions, and instructions only work if you understand how to do the things the instructions are telling you to do.

A knitting pattern might say “cast on 164 stitches”, or “knit 4 purl 2 repeat 26 times” or “knit to the end of the row”. A pattern that tells you to knit to the end of the row isn’t really answering the question “how do you make a sweater?” because it’s just telling you to do something that you already know how to do.

The best description of how to make a sweater would be a description of how to make every single piece of the sweater, down to the last stitch. But a description of how to make the last stitch in the sweater is going to be like “insert needle into this loop of yarn from the right side to the left, wrap the needle around the yarn, then pull the needle back through the loop”. And that description isn’t going to be very useful if you don’t already know what a loop of yarn is, or what it means to wrap your needle around it, or what it means to pull the needle back through the loop.

So the only way to really answer “how did you make this sweater?” is to explain how to knit a sweater down to the last stitch, and then explain what it means to make each stitch. And even then, that’s not going to be the whole story, because you still have to explain how to hold the needles and how to hold the yarn and how to make the first stitch and so on.

So you see, there’s no simple, straightforward, accurate description of how to make a sweater.

I’ve made sweaters for other people, and when they ask “how did you make this sweater?” I don’t know how to answer that question. I *think* I understand how to make a sweater, but there are all sorts of questions about how to make a sweater that I can’t answer. For example, if you asked me “how do you knit this row?”, I would say “I don’t know”. I don’t understand how to knit a row, even though I can knit a row.

But there are some questions about my sweaters that I *can* answer.

For example, if someone asked me “how long did this sweater take?”, I can answer that. I know how long my sweaters take because I keep track of how long they take. And if they ask me “how much did this sweater cost”, I can answer that. I know how much my sweaters cost because I can keep track of how much they cost.

Or if someone asked me “how do you know how to make this?”, I can answer that. I can’t explain exactly how I know how to make a sweater, but I know that I learned how by practicing. I learned how to knit by practicing, and I learned how to make sweaters by practicing.

Or if someone asked me “where did you get the idea for this?”, I can answer that. When I make sweaters, I look at a lot of different sweaters, and I take pictures of the sweaters I like. And when I’m making a new sweater, I look at my pictures and I choose the pictures that I like the most. I like the pictures that look like my sweater.

But there are some questions about my sweaters that I can’t answer.

For example, if someone asked me “how did you make this?”, I can’t answer that. I can’t answer that because I don’t really understand how I make sweaters. I know how to make a sweater, but I don’t understand *how* I know how to make a sweater.

Or if someone asked me “who made this?”, I can’t really answer that either. I know I made it, but I can’t really explain how I did it.

I’m not good at answering questions about my sweaters. But that’s okay. It’s not what I knit for.

I knit because I want to make sweaters. When I knit, I’m *learning how* to make a sweater, but I’m not trying to understand how I make sweaters. When I knit, I’m learning how to make a sweater. I’m learning how to hold the needles and how to make stitches and how to read a knitting pattern and how to do all the other things you have to do to make a sweater.

I don’t know how to explain how to make a sweater. But that’s okay. I’m learning.

That’s what I love about knitting. I can’t explain how to make a sweater.

prompt: Make the argument that chess engines made chess more human, not less. Op-ed length, maybe 900 words.
response:
For a long time, computer chess engines were more powerful than humans, but the nature of that power was different. Engines played like cold, efficient machines: they found the objectively best move for every position, and never got distracted or tired or overconfident. Humans, by contrast, were a bundle of flaws and contradictions, but they were full of style and imagination.

Today, engines are more powerful than ever. And yet the style of the best human chess players today is more machine-like than it’s ever been. Magnus Carlsen and his peers can make the same sort of brilliant long-range calculations that engines do, and can even make the same kind of quiet, mysterious-looking moves that look like errors but are really hidden threats. They’ve become so good at playing like engines, in fact, that the world top 10 are so similar to each other that no one is ever a clear favorite.

There are two stories you can tell about this. In the first, the best chess players of the past were all great in a way that engines will never be. The new generation is just copying the machine, and as a result, we’ve lost something essential. In the second, the best chess players of the past didn’t realize what they were doing, but engines have taught us what that really means, and now human beings can be as good as they can be.

I’m not going to try to answer which story is really true, but I’m going to argue for the second story anyway.

The first story is very simple. In the past, chess players would try to outsmart each other through a sort of mind game. In the new era, they’re just trying to outcompute each other.

I’m not really sure what that means. Engines have been outcomputing humans for decades. If the new era was just engines getting smarter, then the first story would have started decades ago and the game would have been “solved” long ago.

There are at least two more complicated and more accurate stories. In the second, engines didn’t just solve the game – they gave players new tools. For example, they gave players a new way of thinking about opening theory.

Suppose there’s a position where one side has a slight advantage. In the old days, the strong player would try to maintain this advantage until the weaker player makes an error that lets them win. They would keep making the most obvious good move until their opponent either makes a mistake, or the computer evaluates their advantage as “decisive”, and the game ends.

But in the new era, the strong player can choose more subtle moves, and make it look like they’re giving up their advantage. If they do this well, then even the weakest chess player would be unable to tell that they still have an advantage. And if they can keep the evaluation this low, then the advantage never becomes decisive, and the weaker player can never win!

In the old days, the best move was also the most obvious. If you’re playing a grandmaster and you play the best move, then your opponent will be able to see that they’re in trouble and start defending carefully.

Now, the best move is no longer the most obvious. If you play the best move, then your opponent won’t even know that you have an advantage! And because they don’t know that they’re in danger, they won’t be as careful, and they’ll eventually make a mistake.

In this way, the new era of chess has changed the style of the top players. They don’t just play the best moves – they play the most unexpected best moves.

This seems less like chess has gotten more machine-like, and more like chess has finally gotten smarter.

The third story is even more complicated. In the old days, the best move was the most obvious. That meant you could always tell how dangerous a position was, and you could always tell when you were in trouble. The best move was the most obvious, but it was also the best move.

But now, the best move is no longer the most obvious. If you play the best move, then your opponent won’t even know that you have an advantage. So if you play badly, then the evaluation won’t even tell you that you’ve made a mistake!

In this way, the new era of chess has made the game more difficult. The best players now have to know their opponents better, and they have to be able to play well even when they don’t even know that they’ve made a mistake.

This also seems less like chess has gotten more machine-like, and more like chess has finally gotten smarter.

prompt: Make the argument that chess engines made chess more human, not less. Op-ed length, maybe 900 words.
response:
I want to make an argument which may seem strange, but I think is actually true:

Chess engines made chess *more* human, not less.

This is not to say they didn’t make chess more complicated and harder to play. They absolutely did. But the game they created is a more interesting, exciting, and humane one than what we had before.

When people talk about “humanizing” a game, they usually mean increasing the degree to which it rewards style and creativity over technical perfection. They’re right to do this. The goal of any art form, any competitive game, any intellectual pursuit, is *not* to find a single perfect way of doing it. Otherwise, the pursuit would be boring. It is to find a way of doing it which can be done well in a great many different ways.

Before the engines, chess was not that. It was a game with a huge number of interesting possibilities, but only a tiny number of them were really optimal. There were some great players, like Kasparov, who could create miracles – but these were a kind of heroic last stand against an inevitable fate. Kasparov could create miracles because he was a brilliant human with a brilliant mind. But Kasparov was just a man. The game itself was slowly but surely being conquered by computers, whose brains could analyze millions of positions in seconds. This was the era of Kramnik vs Deep Blue, and although it ended with the humans’ victory, it also ended with the beginning of the end of human dominance.

The engines came to the game, and they made it more complicated.

For a while, this was a bad thing. The engines found new moves in the opening which were much more complicated than anything humans could handle. It’s not that the new moves were obviously better. But because they were so complicated and the best players were so used to the old openings, the new moves were at least as good as the old ones. And because the best players were so used to the old openings, the new moves gave the players who adopted them the edge. This was the era of the Berlin Defense and the “Nina Move”, and it was not good.

But then the human mind caught up. Players studied the new moves and found ways to respond to them. The new ways were even more complicated than the old moves. Players studied those. New ways were found to respond to those. And so on.

The result is that today, the game is even more complicated than it ever was. The average chess player, the one who plays chess for fun on the internet or plays chess at the local club – their games still look the same as they always have. But the best games in the world have become more complicated. Players who used to be able to rely on their ability to calculate and their knowledge of the opening in order to avoid serious trouble in the middlegame are now finding that their middlegames are getting more and more complicated. They have to work harder to survive them. They are forced to be more creative. And so is their opponent.

The best games in the world are now more complicated than ever. They are not just games of strategy and tactics, they are games of art. There is a kind of beauty in them, a kind of elegance, but they are also wild and unpredictable. The engines are helping to drive this creativity.

This is the era of the “humanized” game. It is the era of the game where the best players can’t rely on perfect knowledge of the opening and middlegame to win. It is the era of the game where the best players have to be *creative*. And it is the era of the game where the best players are the most creative they have ever been.

prompt: Make the argument that chess engines made chess more human, not less. Op-ed length, maybe 900 words.
response:
A few years ago I was teaching chess in a school in Chicago, and after every lesson I played the kids for an extra round. There was one kid, a girl, who I was never able to beat. She had this little trick that she loved, which was to put me in a position where my best move was to trade off a bunch of material and end up with a position that is theoretically a draw, but in practice is a draw only if I am extremely careful, and I wasn’t being careful enough.

This was before chess engines got so good that they would just beat me outright. If we had played this game back then I would have lost, because the engine would have helped her play those positions with perfect precision.

But I think there is a good argument that the best chess positions are the ones where human intuition has the biggest effect on the result, and that chess engines have made chess more, not less, human.

I like the story of how Kasparov beat Deep Blue. After the opening, Deep Blue played a move that Kasparov said later would have been impossible for any human player to see, because it was so counterintuitive, so strange. Kasparov saw the move, and he knew Deep Blue had found something interesting, but he couldn’t work out how to respond. Deep Blue played that move with its normal 10-minute per move thinking time. Kasparov had 50 minutes for his reply, and he spent all of them trying to figure it out.

Kasparov said later that he had spent 45 of those 50 minutes staring at the position, and then he realized that Deep Blue’s move was just a random move, and that he had been able to prove that by playing the move himself and seeing that Deep Blue’s reply was random as well. He had figured out that the only reason Deep Blue had spent ten minutes on that move was that it didn’t have a good way to decide when to stop thinking and move on. So he had just made a random move, and his move had also been random, and all he had to do was make another random move and Deep Blue would eventually run out of good moves.

Kasparov then played another random move and won the game.

I think about this story a lot. It’s not just that Kasparov is so much smarter than me, and Deep Blue is so much smarter than me, and that’s just the way it is. It’s that there is something about the way Deep Blue thinks that it can find random moves that would be great in the future, but that only humans can see that that isn’t the case.

And I think this is true even about the latest engines, the ones that beat everyone. Kasparov’s trick was that he understood that the reason Deep Blue was making random moves was that it had a very bad way to decide how long to think about a move, and that wasn’t true of modern engines, but I still think human intuition can beat computer intuition sometimes, just like it can in other games.

I have played chess games where the engine thinks the best move is to do something weird and unintuitive, like make a random move or throw away material that I can’t even see how to win back, and the computer plays it, and I don’t know why the computer made that move, and I think the computer must be right, and I can’t work out a better strategy, and I’m just going to play the computer’s moves. But the computer keeps doing things like that, and it doesn’t seem to be helping it, and I have a feeling that the computer is actually just making random moves, and that I’m just going to make random moves, and it’s going to eventually fail.

I think this is true, and I think this means that the latest engines make chess more human, not less. When I was playing against a human, I could always see how they were thinking. When I’m playing against an engine, I have no idea what is going on, and sometimes I can figure out how to win by understanding something about the engine’s process that humans just wouldn’t understand.

prompt: Essay idea I can't stop thinking about: board games with a 'take that' mechanic (Munchkin, Sorry, etc.) teach kids something genuinely useful about losing gracefully, and the modern co-op game trend is quietly removing that. Is this true or am I just old? Write it up and let the argument go where it goes.
response:
This is one of the most important lessons I learned as a kid.

Back then, there were two big categories of games: competitive games, where the player who made the most points won, and “take that” games, where each player would occasionally do something to mess up all the other players.

In the competitive games, you’d do your best to make the most points, and maybe feel a little bad if you beat your friend by a lot, but mostly it was pretty fair.

Take That games were different.

If you played a good card in Munchkin, your friend would get to steal it, and now you’d have to go without. If you made a really good guess in Sorry!, your friend would be able to send all your pieces back to the start. If you were in a really good position in a game like The Settlers of Catan, your friends would all team up to prevent you from winning.

This was a lot more frustrating than just playing a competitive game and losing. If you lost a competitive game by a lot, you could always tell yourself it was because you didn’t pay attention, didn’t understand the rules, made some bad luck move, or some other explanation that wasn’t that embarrassing.

But in a take that game, your opponent literally just took a piece from you! There was no excuse! You could blame bad luck, but it was bad luck that was so bad you’d been able to build a pretty good position to begin with.

And not only were you going to lose, you were going to lose because someone else wanted to see you lose.

I used to hate take that games. I would lose, and get angry about it, and then lose more, and get angrier, and eventually my dad would tell me that I really needed to get over it, because that was just the way the game worked.

At some point I realized that he was right. I got over it. And now I’m pretty sure it has helped me be better at getting over the stuff that happens in real life.

Like, I know I’m going to lose a lot of stuff.

I’m going to lose fights that I should win.

I’m going to lose to other people in competitions.

I’m going to lose my job.

I’m going to lose my house to foreclosure, and lose it to fire, and lose it to a lawsuit by a neighbor who wants to get even with me, and lose it to a government regulation.

I’m going to lose elections and lawsuits and fights with my friends.

And every time, I’m going to feel like it was really unfair, because it was.

And I’m going to get really upset about it, because it was.

But I’m going to have to get over it, because it’s life.

And now that I’m a grown up, I’m pretty sure that this is something I learned from Munchkin.

prompt: Essay idea I can't stop thinking about: board games with a 'take that' mechanic (Munchkin, Sorry, etc.) teach kids something genuinely useful about losing gracefully, and the modern co-op game trend is quietly removing that. Is this true or am I just old? Write it up and let the argument go where it goes.
response:
The biggest problem I see in modern boardgames is the trend away from “take that” mechanics.

Take that mechanics, also known as “sabotage” mechanics, have been the main way that boardgames have been played for a very long time. If you think about what the most famous boardgames are – Chess, Checkers, Sorry, Risk, Munchkin, Monopoly – all of them have some take-that element, a way that you can directly interfere with the other players.

I remember when Monopoly came out in the late 80s, there was a big controversy about how much more evil it was than other boardgames. It was the first boardgame with sabotage mechanics that kids were allowed to play, and they hated it.

But it worked. By the time I was in high school, everyone was playing Monopoly and I think the general attitude was that it was a perfectly normal boardgame.

And I think there’s a lot to learn from Monopoly.

First: how to win. If you can win Monopoly, you understand the basics of strategy and tactics. You’ve been able to plan ahead, make sure you were in a position to win, and make sure you weren’t being sabotaged by your opponents. This is a pretty good skill set to have.

And second: how to lose. This is the more important skill. If you lose Monopoly, you get the feeling of having lost to a very specific person, the person who beat you, who you could see in real time doing the things that beat you. They might have taken all your cash when you were down, or sold all their houses to build hotels so that you could never buy anything, or whatever. You understand exactly what they did, and how you could have prevented it. You’re not going to feel bad, because you can see what the other player did wrong and you can see your own failings. It’s a great learning experience.

Compare that to losing a game of Settlers of Catan. You lose because the other player just was lucky and got more of the thing you needed and you didn’t. That’s a little more frustrating, and not as instructive – the other player might not have done anything at all to cause you to lose, and you probably couldn’t have prevented it.

This is why I’m a little concerned by the trend toward cooperative boardgames. There are some cooperative games, like Forbidden Island, that you can learn from. But the most cooperative games – like Pandemic or Flash Point Fire Rescue – the kind that you play together with your kids or partner – I’m not sure how much you learn from them.

I know that when we played Pandemic last night, we had a very satisfying victory – and we had the same satisfaction we do in games like Munchkin. But when we lost, we just sort of felt bad for a while. There was no one to blame but ourselves, and it was not a super great learning experience.

I think that this kind of loss, where you have to work together to overcome the challenge, is actually a very valuable skill to learn. And I think that cooperative games are the only way to teach kids that skill. But I don’t know if they are good at teaching kids anything else.

The good news is that I don’t think we need to completely abandon sabotage games to make room for cooperative games. My son is about seven. Last week he learned how to play Sorry, and he loved it.

Sorry is a good game to learn because it teaches all the basic skills that I think you need in a boardgame. It teaches you how to plan, and how to make your move count. It teaches you that you can lose even if you do everything right. It teaches you how to deal with losing. And, most importantly, it teaches you that you can beat somebody else and have that count for something.

prompt: Speedrunning is a form of literary criticism. Discuss. (essay, not too academic)
response:
A few years ago I was at a conference where people were discussing how speedrunning games was different from just playing the game. “It’s kind of like literary criticism,” said one.

I was confused and thought this was a joke. “Speedrunning?” I said. “Literary criticism?”

But I realized they were right, and it wasn’t a joke. And it was a really important observation.

I’ve played through *The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time* three times now:

The first time, I was playing a game. I was having an adventure, meeting new characters, and exploring new areas. It was a great experience and I loved it.

The second time, I wanted to see what was missed the first time. So I started paying attention to new things, like secret doors that I could open by pushing blocks, or the fact that you can use an empty bottle to grab items. It was still a fun game, but I had to put in a lot more effort to enjoy it.

The third time, I was speedrunning it. I wasn’t trying to have an adventure. I was trying to beat the game as fast as possible, which meant I had to learn the best path through each area, how to manipulate the RNG to get the right items, and how to use tricks to break through some of the walls. I ended up doing it in 1 hour 30 minutes, versus over 100 hours for the first two times.

It’s not like I had any interest in seeing if I could do it faster. I just wanted to understand the game at a deeper level. I was trying to see how it was constructed, and how all the parts fit together.

This is very similar to literary criticism, which is about understanding what an author did when they wrote a book, rather than just reading and enjoying the story.

When I was speedrunning *Ocarina of Time*, the goal was to break through a wall and get to the next level. When I was doing literary criticism on *The Hobbit*, the goal was to understand Tolkien’s intentions in creating a particular passage. And in both cases, my goal wasn’t to understand the author’s intentions but to see what I could learn from their work.

This is what I want to do with my writing. I want to write things that people can analyze and learn from, whether that’s by thinking about them or by using them to speedrun my ideas.

prompt: Speedrunning is a form of literary criticism. Discuss. (essay, not too academic)
response:
In speedrunning, you play a video game over and over to try to set a record for how fast you can beat it. It’s a form of literary criticism.

Suppose you’re playing an adventure game. The first time through, you’ll be careful to make sure you don’t miss any clues or hidden items. The second time through, you might try to be more efficient. The third, you might try to do the things in a different order to see if that lets you skip some steps. If you do this enough times, you’ll start to notice how the game works. You’ll learn things about how it was programmed.

In some games, you’ll eventually find glitches that let you break through a wall or skip a room. In other games you’ll find ways to use the game’s mechanics to skip most of the play through. In *The Legend of Zelda* you can make Link stand on the edge of a hole and then turn right. He doesn’t fall, and if you do this fast enough it looks like he’s flying. Some people get so good at it that they can fly through a maze faster than walking. This is not cheating. This is a new way of interacting with the game.

Speedrunners who work together on a game will produce a record-setting route and write it up. They’ll describe exactly how you have to play the game to beat it as fast as possible. They’ll describe how to trigger certain glitches that let you do this.

I think you can understand speedrunning as a form of literary criticism if you think of a video game as a sort of novel. Just as there are many different kinds of novels, there are different kinds of games. Some of the games that get speedrun most often are adventure games. In an adventure game you play as a character in a fantasy world. Your goal is to collect objects, and the objects you collect will determine how many points you get at the end. But your ultimate goal is not to get the highest score. You want to solve the game: figure out the puzzle and find the ending.

Adventure games are the sort of thing that could be written as a novel. In fact the best one, the 1983 version of *Zork*, was written as a novel. *Zork* is set in a dungeon. The dungeon is the thing you have to solve. It’s a sort of puzzle.

*Zork* is not only the best adventure game, but also one of the most popular novels ever written. In 1989 a 1983 *Zork* speedrunning record was broken. The new record was 1 hour 46 minutes. The runner wrote up his strategy in 12,000 words.

When I read his record writeup it was like reading a book about the novel. I read about the dungeon. It was a sort of guide, but a very different sort of guide than anything else you would expect to read about *Zork*.

I was surprised how well it read. It wasn’t just a guide. It had a personality. The runner had clearly put a lot of work into it. He’d thought about how to make it readable. It read like a story. There was a kind of excitement in it, and you could feel the excitement of the runner.

It was a sort of guide to the game, but a different sort of guide than the guide written by the authors. He wasn’t explaining how the game was intended to be played. He was showing how it actually was played. He was showing how a game would be played if you played it enough times.

I think speedrunning is a way to explore a game. When I read a writeup of a game I feel like I’ve played it. I’m not playing the game that was intended, but I think the game that was intended was a mistake. I think the best adventure games are the ones that can be beaten.

I think speedrunning is a new kind of criticism. I think it is a criticism of the game’s programming. And I think it’s a criticism of the game’s story.

prompt: Speedrunning is a form of literary criticism. Discuss. (essay, not too academic)
response:
Speedrunning is the practice of playing through a video game as quickly as possible.

But it’s not as simple as “try to get through the game as fast as you can”, because it’s really hard to do that. In fact, I was doing this in The Witcher, and I was pretty bad at it. I had a lot of trouble, and I only just got the game beaten at all.

The basic trick for speedrunning is to skip parts of the game. But you can’t skip the whole thing. There are still some parts that you have to do. The goal is to find as short a route through the game as possible.

The Witcher is a big game, and the best routes are really complicated. The people who have beaten it fastest are probably experts at this game.

So, it’s sort of like when people speedrun Mario games. They can get a lot of power-ups, so they can break through walls that regular players can’t break through, which lets them cut big chunks out of the game. They can find secret rooms that regular players never notice, with shortcuts that save them a lot of time. And they have to do this so fast that they can’t even pause the game to think about it.

This is a good metaphor for the way to read a book, but it’s not a good metaphor for the way to read a poem.

You’re not supposed to read a poem all the way through. You’re supposed to read it once, really fast, just to get the idea. Then you go back and re-read it again, and again, and again. And every time you re-read it, you see more of it.

You don’t re-read a poem to look for things you missed on the first time. You re-read it to get more out of the things you saw on the first time.

When you read a poem a second time, you know what it’s about, so you can stop trying to figure that out, and you can pay more attention to the words and how they make you feel. And then you read it a third time, and this time you know what it’s about, and you already know the words, and so you can pay more attention to the structure of the poem, and how the words and the structure make you feel. And then you read it a fourth time, and now you know everything, and you can just sit and let it wash over you, and see what you feel, and maybe you’ll feel something new.

So, I think this is an important thing to know when you read a poem. You’re not supposed to read a poem all the way through.

prompt: Could you write something exploring why model railway hobbyists spend years on scenery for trains that just go in a circle? My dad has a 4x8 layout in the garage that's been 'nearly finished' since 2009 and I've started to suspect the unfinishedness is the point.
response:
There are a lot of people who like to play with train sets. There is a very specific kind of person who spends years and years of their life making the landscape of a small model train set as beautiful and realistic as it possibly can be, and then lets the trains go around on their track, doing what trains do.

These people are sometimes called “scenicists” or “scenics guys”, depending on whether they prefer to speak in a slightly formal or slightly informal way.

I’m a scenics guy. When I was about 10 I got my hands on a box of model trains that I think I bought at a garage sale, and now I’m 35 and I’ve spent a lot of my life making tiny landscapes. My latest project is 4’x8’, and it’s been “nearly finished” since 2009.

I am going to try to explain why I spend so much time on this stuff.

First of all, there is the pleasure of making a beautiful thing. I find it very enjoyable to make a tiny landscape, and then to sit back and take a photo of it and appreciate how beautiful it is. This is an obvious enough thing that I don’t need to belabor it.

Second of all, there is the pleasure of learning all kinds of random skills, most of which have nothing whatsoever to do with miniature train sets. In fact, a lot of the time I’m working on things that have nothing to do with my train set at all, just on the grounds that it seems like a fun thing to try. The last year has included making a miniature steam locomotive, making tiny bridges, building a 3D printer, and learning about a new kind of glue that has a lot of applications I haven’t thought of yet.

Third of all, there is the pleasure of seeing how far you can push realism. This is sort of a natural consequence of the first two points. Making a beautiful miniature landscape requires learning a lot of skills and techniques, and as you learn new skills you discover new ways to improve the realism of your miniature landscape. Sometimes you discover that one technique is better than another. Sometimes you discover that combining two techniques in a new way gives better results. Sometimes you discover an entirely new technique.

This is one of the things that makes this hobby so addictive for me. For the last year I’ve been playing with a new technique for making tiny trees. I got some pretty good results with my first experiments, and I’m still working on it.

Here’s a photo of a small mountain that I did last year. There’s a lot going on here. I made a lot of tiny trees and planted them. I took a photo of the mountain, printed it on black-and-white film, and then used a photochemical technique to etch a relief version of the photo in a thin piece of copper. Then I used the copper piece as a mask to etch a relief version of the photo in a piece of acrylic. Finally I placed the acrylic mountain in the landscape, and used tiny pieces of copper to create a very realistic looking rock texture on its surface.

This is a photograph of the mountain with the copper mask in place, taken before I placed it in the landscape.

Here’s another mountain that I built using the same technique. This is the one on the left side of the photo of the whole layout.

I think I’m going to continue playing with this technique for a while. I’m sure I can make the results even better. I could make it even better if I learned how to etch metal with a laser, but that would require getting a laser, which would be expensive, so I’m not sure if that’s something I’m going to do.

Fourth of all, there is the pleasure of doing something that nobody else is doing. I’m probably the only person on Earth who is doing this particular combination of techniques on a miniature train set. I find that I’m continually surprised by the things that other scenics guys have done, so I’m sure I’m wrong about this, but as far as I know I am the only person on Earth who is doing this particular combination of techniques on a miniature train set.

I like doing things that nobody else is doing because it feels a bit like being a pioneer. I think it’s because I’m very competitive, and I like doing things that other people don’t want to do because it lets me win.

I also like doing things that nobody else is doing because it makes it more likely that I can come up with new ideas. If I spent all my time copying what other people had done, then it would be very difficult to come up with new ideas.

Fifth of all, there is the pleasure of making something that is beautiful and realistic, and that other people like. I’m pretty good at making beautiful and realistic miniature landscapes, so sometimes I get paid for this. That’s nice.

I’ve also made tiny landscapes for a lot of my friends, and that’s nice too. This is one of the ways that I can make other people happy.

I think that when you have a lot of friends who you really like and care about, and you’re really good at doing something that makes them happy, you should take advantage of that and do it as much as you can. This is what I’m doing.

I find it very rewarding to make things that make my friends happy. If I could just keep doing this and making my friends happy forever, that would be great, but it’s not possible to do that forever.

This is the last thing I’m going to mention today. I think that when you’re very good at doing something that makes other people happy, you should try to do it as much as you can.

prompt: Short essay: the case against 100% completion in video games.
response:
Some years ago I was a bit obsessed with the games in the *Final Fantasy* series. In addition to playing through the original seven games, I also bought the *Final Fantasy* series complete box, with all of the games for the PS2. At the time the series was at eleven games, but they were only giving away a twelve-disc box, so presumably they had plans to release more games.

Anyway. I was playing through *Final Fantasy IX* for the third time, and I was on the path to get a 100% completion rate, the same way I had in the last two games. This involved getting all of the optional items, all of the optional weapons, all of the optional magic, all of the optional sidequests and so on. In the case of *FFIX* this meant getting 100% of the rare monster kills, and this meant getting 100% of the rare monster drops. In addition to the rare monster drops there were 64 magic spells to collect. 100% completion meant getting all of these.

I was almost done with the 64 spells. I had 63/64, with only one left. Unfortunately the spell was called “Bolt,” which I needed in order to defeat some of the last rare monsters. It was a kind of a catch-22, because I had been avoiding the rare monsters that I couldn’t kill with the spells I had already collected, but now there was only one left and I couldn’t kill it without Bolt, which I couldn’t get without killing it.

I had to give up on 100% completion. I ended up getting 63/64 magic spells and 99% of the rare monsters, which was fine, I guess. The real reason I give up on 100% completion is that it’s really boring, and I have a lot of better things to do with my time.

This is the case against 100% completion in video games.

First of all, it is not even a well defined concept. It means a different thing in different games. In the case of *FFIX* it meant collecting all of the optional stuff. In other games it can mean killing all of the enemies in a particular level, or getting all of the secrets. In *Super Mario Bros*, it means getting all of the coins in every stage. You can’t really get 100% completion in *Mario*. There are just too many coins in there, and it’s impossible to get them all without dying.

Secondly, there is no reason to want it. There is never any reward for getting 100% completion. I have never gotten any kind of bonus or reward or anything for doing it, not even a special message. It is the only thing in gaming that really seems to have no purpose. If it had a purpose, then it would be a more reasonable goal.

Third, it’s very tedious and boring. This is obvious, and I’ll just give an example.

In *FFIX* I had to get 100% of the rare monster kills, which meant collecting a huge number of rare items. In order to kill the rare monsters, I had to get very, very powerful equipment. In order to get this equipment, I had to buy it with gold, which I could only get by farming enemies to get drops.

One of the rare monsters drops an item called the Dragon Fang, which you need in order to make some very powerful weapons. Unfortunately, it only drops 1% of the time. That means that I have to kill about 100 of these rare monsters to get one Dragon Fang. But killing a rare monster isn’t as easy as it sounds. I have to be wearing specific equipment.

I need to be wearing the Phoenix Down equipment, which gives me a 100% chance of reviving from death. I also need to be wearing the Angel Wing equipment, which gives me a 100% chance of avoiding death. Finally I need to be wearing the Lucky Charm equipment, which gives me a 50% chance of getting double the drop rate.

This is all so I can kill the rare monsters and get the Dragon Fang.

I have to do this because of the game’s economy. I need to be wearing the Phoenix Down equipment because it makes it so that I can’t die, which is a problem because the rare monsters are really strong. I have to be wearing the Angel Wing equipment because the rare monsters can do so much damage that I will always die before the Phoenix Down equipment kicks in. I have to be wearing the Lucky Charm equipment because the rare monsters only drop the item I need 1% of the time and I can’t afford to kill 1000 of them.

If you want 100% completion, you have to be wearing these three pieces of equipment at all times. This means that you can never use any other equipment, so you need to get the best equipment that will work with the Phoenix Down, the Angel Wing, and the Lucky Charm.

The Angel Wing equipment costs 3000 gold, the Lucky Charm equipment costs 5000 gold, and the Phoenix Down equipment costs 20000 gold.

Getting 3000 gold in *FFIX* is not that hard. I can get 3000 gold by going to the desert and killing a bunch of enemies. It’s kind of boring.

Getting 5000 gold in *FFIX* is a little bit more difficult. I need to go to a more difficult area with better enemies, which means that I need to have better equipment. The only way to get better equipment in *FFIX* is to get better equipment from other enemies.

Getting 20000 gold in *FFIX* is a real pain in the ass. There’s nowhere in the game where you can get 20000 gold that isn’t also hard. In order to go to those difficult areas you need even better equipment, which you can only get from even harder areas, and so on and so forth.

Getting 100% completion means I have to get all of the optional things. In order to get the optional things I need all of the best equipment, which I can only get from all of the most difficult areas, which I can only go to if I already have all of the best equipment.

I can’t get 100% completion. It’s impossible.

I think that’s really unfortunate, because these games are really cool and really fun. I think it’s a shame that there’s a big part of the game which is impossible.

prompt: Short essay: the case against 100% completion in video games.
response:
I have played many games. I have not played all of them completely. In fact, I have not played any of them completely.

I know this because, when I look at my Steam library, I see things like “72% of achievements” or “88% of the content” marked next to games I have played a lot. Some games are marked as 100% complete, but that is because they have no content that Steam can recognize. I’ve played a lot of games, but never once finished any of them.

But I have seen other people who have. I know of people who play games all the way through and get every achievement, and it seems to work fine for them.

So, why haven’t I ever played a game completely?

1. I don’t like to.

I want the most fun possible. If a game has a boss fight that is challenging and fun, I want to do it. If a game has a boss fight that I can’t win, I want to find a way past it. If a game has 99% of its content in the main campaign, I want to play that. And if a game has 5% of its content in an optional side-quest that is boring and tedious, I don’t want to do it.

I’ve had to do lots of boring and tedious things in games. I’m always happy to do the fun and exciting things. But I don’t need to be bored just because I’m playing a video game.

2. It isn’t fun.

The best part about playing video games is that I get to do things I enjoy. The worst part is that, even though I’m playing a video game, it’s still sometimes not fun.

I like to think that the best games are fun the entire time. If a game isn’t fun the entire time, then it’s probably not as great as I thought. So I want to spend my time playing the parts of games that are fun to me.

But I’ve played a lot of great games that aren’t fun the entire time. They’re still great games. Sometimes great things are hard to enjoy.

For example, *Dark Souls 2* is a great game and I loved playing it. I also hated it. There was a lot of grinding in the game and I hated that. I wanted to skip over that.

*Dark Souls 2* is still a great game. I like that I get to choose how I play my games.

3. It’s a waste of time.

I’m a busy person. I have a lot to do. I have to work and go to school. I have family and friends.

I like to play video games. I think that video games are important to the world. I think we need more great video games. I want to see what’s possible with video games.

But I want to get the most value out of my time. If I don’t have to play video games, I want to play games that are fun to me.

So I don’t play every part of games. I play the parts I like.

Sometimes I play things that are boring and tedious. But I don’t want to play things that are boring and tedious. I have enough of those.

4. I don’t care about achievements.

There’s not much more to say about this one. I don’t care about achievements. Achievements don’t matter to me.

I know some people who care a lot about achievements. I know some people who get every achievement in every game they play.

I’m not those people.

5. I play for the sake of playing.

I play games because I like to play games.

I want to play games that are fun to me. I want to play games that I can understand and that I can be happy playing.

prompt: Short essay: the case against 100% completion in video games.
response:
When I was a kid and I finished a game, I would play it a second time, looking for things I had missed the first time. I wanted to see if there were more enemies than the game had told me, or more items, or more secrets.

The first time through, I had tried to clear the game as quickly as I could. This was, after all, an arcade game, and the people who were best at it were always the ones who got through it the fastest. I was not one of the people who got through it the fastest, but I was proud that I always got through it the fastest that I ever got through it.

I would play the game a second time for this reason and also to see if there was something different about it. This was an important question, and it was not one that my brother and I would ever ask of one another.

I was not a fast enough player to earn an extra life, or a new power, or any other kind of reward that might come for playing the game well enough. I could never beat the fastest times, or the strongest bosses, or reach the hardest levels, and my brother and I could never get any further than I, or beat me in any way. I always thought there might be something I had missed in the game, because I was too slow or dumb to reach it the first time, and this was why I played them a second time.

I was never very good at video games, but I had a few of my own games that I could beat. I was good at video games of a particular kind, and it was not the same kind as my brother. He was good at arcade games, and I was good at adventure games. When he got bored of an arcade game, he would put the coin back in his pocket and move on to the next one. This was not my way.

I always tried to get 100% of the games I played. I didn’t want to have anything left in the game that I didn’t have. This was not just about collecting more items, or unlocking more levels, or finding out more secrets. I was just looking for something to do, and the more I could do in a game, the longer it would last.

I had two games that I beat 100%, and I am still not sure how to beat the rest of them.

The first was Manic Miner. I didn’t have a game manual for it, so I didn’t know what the rules were, or what I was supposed to be doing. I just knew I had to get through the game, and if there were things I could collect, I was supposed to get them.

I had never played the game before, and I didn’t know anything about it. I knew very little about video games, which is why I didn’t know it was an arcade game. It had a lot of levels, and a lot of the levels looked the same, but I knew this game well enough to know that I wasn’t supposed to beat it the way I beat other games, and that I was supposed to play it again, and that if I played it again, I would get more lives than before.

The second was Knight Lore. I had a game manual for it, and I knew what the rules were, and I knew what I was supposed to be doing. I knew I was supposed to get the sword, and the shield, and the amulet, and the lamp, and the ring, and the book. I knew I was supposed to collect all the items, and then go to the final level and get the crown, and then I would have beat the game.

I knew it was an adventure game, and I knew it was not like arcade games, because arcade games were supposed to be played until you won, and adventure games were supposed to be played until you figured out how to beat them.

I didn’t know how to beat either game.

prompt: i do crosswords every morning and my partner thinks it's a waste of time compared to reading actual books. write me an essay defending the crossword as a serious intellectual activity. not a puff piece, address the strongest version of her argument
response:
I do my crossword every morning, before the coffee is finished brewing. I’m in a hurry, so I usually get it done in less than 15 minutes.

My partner thinks this is a waste of time. She wants me to read a book in the morning.

She’s not wrong. But I’m not wrong either.

She makes two points:

1. Crosswords are easy to learn, so once you’ve learned them, they stop helping you learn something new.

2. She can think of other activities that are equally fun, but involve learning more.

I think both of these are true, but also not very strong arguments.

On the first point: I don’t need crossword puzzles to help me learn something. I have books and YouTube videos and a computer. I don’t do crosswords for their educational value.

I do crosswords because it’s fun and it’s a good way to start the day.

It’s also a skill. Like any other skill, it has a learning curve. If you don’t know how to do crosswords, then you’ll struggle. If you’ve been doing them for a while, you’ll get better. If you’ve been doing them for many years, you’ll get better still.

But the first step is to learn how to do them.

For me, this is a new skill. I’ve been doing crosswords for a week. I’m still getting better at it. It feels like a new skill.

On the second point: I don’t know if reading a book is more fun than doing a crossword. Reading a book can be fun, but it’s also easy to get bored. If I’m reading a book and I’m not interested in it, I’ll stop reading. If I’m doing a crossword and I’m not interested in it, I’ll stop doing the crossword.

Reading a book can be fun. So can doing a crossword.

If you want to learn how to do a crossword, I recommend doing one every day.

prompt: i do crosswords every morning and my partner thinks it's a waste of time compared to reading actual books. write me an essay defending the crossword as a serious intellectual activity. not a puff piece, address the strongest version of her argument
response:
In defense of crosswords

prompt: Why are Dungeons & Dragons campaigns so hard to finish? Write it up as an essay. I've been a DM for six years and have finished exactly one.

My best friend and I are on a bit of an adventure: I’m DMing them through the classic adventure module Ravenloft. I’ve been a DM for over six years. I’ve DMed through a dozen campaigns, most of them homebrew, some of them premade adventures. And I’ve *finished* exactly one campaign. Why is it so hard to finish a campaign? I think I know.

### 1. There are too many choices

One reason is that there are just too many choices, and it takes a long time to get the choices right.

When I started, I was trying to run a premade campaign. I had been playing since I was eleven years old, and I was ready to give it a try and see what it was like. But I got stuck early. We’d made our characters, but I couldn’t get through the first session. I’d bought a premade adventure, but I couldn’t figure out how to run it, and then I got stuck in a debate with a friend about how it would be better to just make up my own. And so I did.

It took me a year to get my first session off the ground.

I don’t know whether I did this because I was too young, or because I was too old, but I decided to go through the classic adventure module Ravenloft and make my own adventure. I spent months writing down every little piece of lore that I knew, in order to decide how I was going to run it. Then I got into a bit of a debate with a friend about whether the evil villain should be a guy or a woman, and whether we should use the classic version or the recent version, and whether the classic version should be changed because it was a bit sexist. And then I got stuck.

It took me three years to get my Ravenloft session off the ground.

The problem with running premade adventures is that there are a lot of decisions to make, and it’s hard to figure out how to make them. If I run Ravenloft, am I supposed to make my own backstory and tie in my own character names? If not, do I run it exactly like it’s written, even if it seems a bit dated or sexist? If I do change it, how far am I allowed to go? Do I have to run it exactly like it’s written, or can I tweak it? Do I run it in the setting that it was written for, or can I move it into a different setting? Is there a way to move it?

I didn’t know the answers to any of these questions.

I also didn’t know how long I was supposed to run a campaign for. I didn’t know whether I was supposed to run a premade adventure in a single session or whether I could spread it out across a dozen sessions. I didn’t know whether I was supposed to run a campaign for a few hours or for months or for years. I didn’t know how long I was supposed to make each session or how often I was supposed to have sessions.

I was making all of these decisions for the first time, and I was trying to make all of the decisions at once, and I had no idea how to do it, so it took me a *really long time* to figure it out.

### 2. There are too many things that could go wrong

The second reason that it takes so long to run a campaign is that there are a lot of things that could go wrong. If I’m running a premade adventure, then there are a lot of things that I don’t know, and that means there are a lot of things that could go wrong.

When I’m running a premade adventure, I don’t know anything about the characters that I’m supposed to be playing. I don’t know who they are or what they like or what their goals are or what their backstories are. I don’t know why they want to do what I’m supposed to make them do. I have to make up all of this on my own, and there’s a lot of it. And if I make the wrong decision, or if I make a decision that doesn’t make sense, or if I don’t make enough of a decision, then things might go wrong.

When I’m running a premade adventure, I don’t know anything about the setting that I’m supposed to be in. I have to make up the world and the NPCs and the factions and the history and the geography and the culture and all of the little details that make a setting feel real and that make it seem like there are more things going on than just the ones in the adventure. And if I make the wrong decision, or if I make a decision that doesn’t make sense, or if I don’t make enough of a decision, then things might go wrong.

When I’m running a premade adventure, I don’t know anything about how I’m supposed to run it. I don’t know how long I’m supposed to make the sessions or how much I’m supposed to improvise. I don’t know how I’m supposed to make the players feel like they’re playing together and how I’m supposed to make them feel like their decisions matter. I don’t know what the players are supposed to do in between sessions or how I’m supposed to help them keep track of what’s happening.

The thing is that when I’m playing the game, I don’t usually have to think about any of this. When I’m playing the game, I’m just playing the game, and I don’t have to think about any of this. But when I’m running a campaign, I have to think about all of these things, and there are a lot of them. And if I make the wrong decision, or if I make a decision that doesn’t make sense, or if I don’t make enough of a decision, then things might go wrong.

### 3. The players might not like it

There’s another reason that I don’t like running campaigns: I’m always worried about how the players will react.

I’m a DM who has only ever played with people that I know. I always DM my friends and my family. But my friends and my family are all pretty different from each other, and it’s hard to figure out what everyone’s going to think. I always try to make sure that everyone has a good time, and that means I always have to worry about what everyone thinks.

If I’m playing the game with a group of players that I know, then I know what they like and what they don’t like. But I don’t always agree with them about how to play the game, and sometimes I end up making decisions that aren’t really good for the group. I have a tendency to want to make sure that the players get to do whatever they want, and that sometimes means that I don’t make it clear what the story is supposed to be or what they’re supposed to be trying to do, or that the story isn’t really interesting or fun or meaningful or whatever.

If I’m playing the game with a group of players that I don’t know, then I don’t know what they like or don’t like, and that means I might make a lot of decisions that aren’t good for them. That means that there’s a lot of pressure on me to make sure that I make the right decisions, and that means that I have to worry a lot about what everyone thinks.

### 4. There’s not a clear way to win

I think there’s one more reason that I don’t like running campaigns. I don’t know what it means to win.

When I started playing the game, I was looking for a clear way to win the game. I wanted to know what it meant to win. I wanted to know that if I made the right decisions and did the right things and played the game the right way, then I would win. But I didn’t find that. I didn’t find a clear way to win, and I don’t know whether there is one.

I don’t know what it means to win a campaign. I don’t know whether it means to go through all of the adventures in a module and find a clear way to win at the end, or whether it means to have a campaign that everyone likes and has a good time in, or whether it means to have a campaign that everyone is invested in and that feels meaningful to them, or whether it means to finish the campaign in a way that everyone is happy with, or whether it means to have a campaign that everyone is going to remember and talk about and miss.

I don’t know what it means to win a campaign. I don’t know what it means to lose a campaign. I don’t know what it means to make it through a campaign. And I don’t know what it means to finish a campaign.

It’s really hard to play a game when you don’t know what it means to win.

### 5. It takes a really long time

I think the final reason that I don’t like running campaigns is that it just takes so long.

When I started playing the game, I was looking for a clear way to win the game. I wanted to know what it meant to win. I wanted to know that if I made the right decisions and did the right things and played the game the right way, then I would win. But I didn’t find that. I didn’t find a clear way to win, and I don’t know whether there is one.

prompt: Why are Dungeons & Dragons campaigns so hard to finish? Write it up as an essay. I've been a DM for six years and have finished exactly one.
response:
Dungeons & Dragons campaigns are hard to finish. I’ve run D&D for about six years, and I’ve finished exactly one campaign. That’s not because I’m bad at my job. I think that all the campaigns I’ve run have been good. I think my players enjoyed them, and I enjoyed running them.

But they weren’t finished.

Dungeons & Dragons is supposed to be a game where you go on an adventure, and then you finish the adventure and you’re done. But instead, it becomes a game where the adventure just keeps going. If you think of it like a TV show, then each session is an episode and the campaign is the show. But instead of the show having 22 episodes and finishing, it just keeps going and going.

The first time it happened to me was about five years ago, when I was DMing a game I called *The Kingdom of Sorrow*. I had planned a campaign which would last a year or so and I’d had the story figured out. I had the villains figured out, the heroes figured out, the big dramatic scenes figured out. I knew how the story was going to end. I knew it was going to be great. I just needed the story to unfold.

But it didn’t unfold. In the beginning it seemed like it was going to unfold in the way I had planned. I started with an introductory episode to set up the story, which went great. Then there were two or three more episodes that moved the story forward. And then it just stopped.

The players would be in a tavern, and I would describe some bad guys who were going to set things in motion, and then the players would just sit there and stare at each other, and say “what should we do?” And I would describe the bad guys in greater and greater detail, but the players just wouldn’t do anything. Eventually, I’d say something like “so what do you do?” and the players would say “we’ll talk to the bartender” and then I’d move on to the next episode of the game. The story would stop unfolding and I’d spend the rest of the campaign telling them what was going on.

And then the campaign ended. I didn’t finish it. I ran about 20 sessions, and then my players lost interest, and we stopped. I had planned out 30 or 40 sessions, but I only got through maybe half of them. The big villain was never revealed, the heroes never won, and the bad guys never got punished. The story just ended. And I didn’t finish it.

I’ve tried to run three or four other campaigns since then, but I’ve had the same experience. In every campaign I’ve run, I’ve gotten about half-way through the story, and then the story stops unfolding and I start spending my sessions telling my players what’s happening in the world. And then my players lose interest and I stop.

It’s happened so many times that it’s made me start to think that this is something about the way Dungeons & Dragons works. It’s not about me. It’s not about my players. It’s something about how the game works.

I’m going to talk about two reasons that D&D campaigns are hard to finish. The first is that the players don’t have goals, and the second is that the game doesn’t provide incentives for them to work together to achieve those goals.

In the beginning of every campaign I’ve run, I’ve told my players the big goal that they are supposed to be working towards. I tell them who the villain is and what the villain wants to do. I explain why it’s a bad idea for the villain to succeed, and I explain what the players can do to stop the villain. And I do all of this at the beginning of the campaign, right before the first session. And I think I’m pretty good at it. I think the players understand what the goal is.

And then we play D&D, and they go off on some weird side quest, and they get sidetracked, and they lose interest in the original goal.

When I try to steer them back to the goal, I’ll say things like “well, you’ve already accomplished the goal of this quest, but the real goal here is to get rid of the evil lich who is plotting to take over the world”. But this doesn’t help. I tell them the goal over and over, but they don’t work towards it. I tell them the goal, and then I describe a bunch of stuff, and then I ask “so what do you do?” and they say “we’ll talk to the bartender”.

It’s like a game of tennis where one of the players is playing tennis and the other player is just standing there. The one player says “hey, you’re supposed to hit the ball back” and then the other player just stands there. And this player is the DM.

In D&D, the DM controls the story, and the players control the characters. This means that the story is supposed to unfold as the players make their choices and act on those choices. And if the players don’t choose to act in a certain way, then the story won’t unfold in that way.

In the beginning of a campaign, the players choose to act in the ways that I want, so the story unfolds in the way that I want. But as the campaign goes on, the players stop acting in the ways that I want, and the story stops unfolding in the way that I want.

I don’t think it’s because the players are bad at their jobs. I think it’s because D&D is just a bad game. It has a bunch of problems.

One problem is that the players don’t have goals, and another is that the game doesn’t provide incentives for the players to work together.

In D&D, the players don’t have any goals. They just have their characters. And the characters don’t have any goals. The characters just have skills and spells and stuff. They don’t have any desires or motivations.

And I think this is why the players don’t know what to do in a session. The players don’t have any goals, so they don’t have any reason to do anything.

If you think about other games, like chess or poker or soccer, then in those games the players have goals. The players in chess have to try to checkmate the other player, and the players in poker have to try to win the pot, and the players in soccer have to try to score a goal.

And when the players have goals, then they know what to do. And when the players know what to do, then they do it, and the game plays out.

In D&D, the players don’t have any goals, and this makes it hard for them to know what to do.

Another problem with D&D is that there’s no incentive to work together to achieve those goals. In D&D, you can’t just work together to achieve some goal. You can only work together to achieve the goals that the DM gives you, and you can only do that if the DM gives you the opportunity to. And the DM gives you the opportunity by telling you what’s going on in the world and telling you what you can do.

This doesn’t encourage players to work together to achieve goals. In fact, it discourages them. If you try to work together to achieve a goal, then the DM has to give you an opportunity to do that. And if the DM doesn’t give you an opportunity, then you can’t do it. So you’re better off not working together.

This is one of the reasons that D&D is so hard to play.

prompt: Write an essay arguing that the best hobby is one you're permanently mediocre at.
response:
You’re at a coffee shop in a town you’ve never been to before. You notice that the other people have a lot of tattoos. You don’t have any. You go home, get a tattoo, and now you feel less like a stranger.

What’s the tattoo for? What’s the meaning behind it? You can’t really explain. You chose it to be something vaguely cool, but that’s about it.

In other words, it’s not for the sake of the tattoo. You’re not going to get a bunch more tattoos, or to learn about the history of tattoos. You’re not going to go and tattoo other people. It was just a thing that other people had, and you wanted one.

And that was enough.

That’s how the best hobbies work.

I learned to play the guitar at a young age. I learned enough of it to play most of the songs I wanted to play. But I’m not going to study theory or practice scales for hours every day. I’m not going to go to music school. I’m not going to join a band and go on tour. That’s not how guitar is important to me.

I learned to play chess. I got good enough to beat most people I know, and even a few grandmasters, but I’m not going to study openings or tactics or whatever. I’m not going to join a chess club.

I read philosophy. I don’t have any strong opinions about philosophy, and my understanding of it is probably wrong in a dozen places. But I’ve read a lot of philosophy, and that’s enough.

I don’t know much about physics. I took physics in high school and college, and I know a few basic concepts, but I don’t know any more than that. But that’s fine. I like to read about physics. That’s the main reason I went to college.

I’ve tried a bunch of martial arts, and I know how to do the basics of a bunch of them, but I don’t know more than that. I’m not going to go to the dojo and work on my kicks every night.

I’m not a “real” artist. I’m not going to take art classes or go to art school. I’m just going to paint what I want to paint when I want to paint it.

I’m not a “real” writer. I’m not going to study the art of writing or go to writing school. I just like to write things.

I’m not going to become a professional athlete. I’m not going to go to school for sports or play on a team or do a bunch of drills. I just like to run and lift weights and play basketball and stuff.

It doesn’t feel “productive” or “purposeful” or “useful”. There’s no point. There’s no end goal. I’m not going to get really really good at it.

But that’s exactly what’s great. I don’t need to get good. I just like doing things.

I don’t need to have any goals, or any ambitions. I don’t need to be good.

I don’t even need to be able to tell you what I like about it. I just like it.

And that’s what makes it such a great hobby.

She sent me a message back that said “I think you’re just an average writer.”

I was a little bit hurt. I don’t think that I’m an average writer. I think I’m better than average.

I was not too hurt, because I know how unreliable people’s opinions of me are. I have asked my mother to tell me what kind of person she thinks I am before. She said “You’re not as mean as everyone else says you are.” But I am as mean as everyone else says I am.

When my mother said that I was just an average writer, I wondered if she was right. I thought back over my career as a writer and wondered if I could come up with any objective evidence that I am not just an average writer.

I wrote my first short story when I was a teenager. It was called *The Great Red Dragon*. It was a little bit funny, but it was not a great story. I think a lot of kids write stories that are as good as that.

When I was 20 I wrote a short story called *A Man on the Moon*. I think this was a pretty good story. I was a little surprised that I could write something so good. But I think that most people don’t know how much better they are at something until they try it.

I was really surprised that I could write something that good, because I didn’t think that I was that good a writer. In fact, I thought that I was a pretty bad writer. I think most writers are surprised when they find out how good they are.

I sent *A Man on the Moon* to some magazines. It was a good story, but it took me a long time to get it published. I didn’t realize that magazines take a long time to respond to submissions. I sent it to a lot of magazines before I finally got it published.

But I thought that it was a good idea to write books. I thought that if I wrote a lot of books, I might be able to get pretty good at it.
