In 1995, I was working on a book called *The Year Without a Leak: Or, Why the IRS Doesn’t Tax the Rich*. I had been working on it for a few months and I had gotten some good reviews for it, but I had not yet gotten it published.

prompt: Write an essay arguing that the best hobby is one you're permanently mediocre at.
response:
When I was a kid I loved playing tennis, which was good because I was bad.

If you're good at something, you can't always do it. Your friend wants to go play tennis, but you're a national champion and you know you can't lose. You tell him you're not up to it, he'll just beat you, he'll think it's weird that you're not doing your best, and he'll have to work hard to keep from getting angry.

So you don't play. You don't get to do the thing you like most in the world.

But if you're bad at something, you can do it as often as you want. I could play tennis for hours. And I wasn't the only one. My friends also liked tennis. We could all play together, and not just in my case as a favor. They liked it too.

That was one of the many great things about being a kid. I could spend all day doing what I wanted, which was usually playing tennis. And I had a lot of friends.

As I got older, the balance between these two things shifted. I became better at what I did, and my social life got worse.

That's how it goes when you're a prodigy. You get better at what you do, and as a result you have less of it. You have to work harder and harder to have as much of it as you used to. And you get fewer friends.

This is a terrible situation. When you were a kid, you could do whatever you wanted and have friends. And now you can't.

The solution is obvious. Be bad at the thing you like most.

That doesn't mean don't try to get better. Try. But don't let success ruin the thing for you.

If you play tennis, you should try to get as good as possible. But you should stop just below the point where you stop having fun.

If you play guitar, try to become good enough to play in a band. But don't become so good that you have to spend hours practicing. If you have to practice more than you like, you're too good.

If you write, try to get good enough to get published. But don't become so good that you can't write what you want to.

If you do anything, you should try to get good at it, but not so good that it stops being fun. This is a great rule to follow, because if you follow it, you're guaranteed to have a lot of fun. And you'll have a lot of friends.

I think this is the best rule for choosing a hobby.

My favorite hobby is one I could never do better at. I like to play with babies. I love it, and I'm pretty good at it. Babies love it too.

If I played with babies more, I would get better at it. So I don't.

The next best hobby is one that I could do better, but don't want to. I like to paint watercolors. I'm good, but not as good as I want to be.

If I spent more time painting, I would become better. I would also have more fun painting.

I don't paint that much, but I try not to paint too little. If I don't paint for a while, I don't enjoy it as much. It gets harder.

I like to be moderately good at painting. That way I can do it whenever I want.

There's a difference between being good at something and getting better at it. I'm pretty good at painting. I'm not getting better at it. I paint when I want to. I paint when I feel like it.

The reason is not a trivial matter, either. And this is a question that we, as LEGO fans, should be prepared to answer. So let’s do that.

However, this is not the whole story. What the act of building changes is the relationship that we have with the bricks. When we build a set, we enter into a special relationship with the bricks. We know every brick. We know what every brick is for. And we have a story about why we have it.

This is the real point. When we build a LEGO set, we learn to appreciate it. We learn the story behind it. And then we become better fans of LEGO, not just for this set, but for all LEGO.

prompt: I'm a retired machinist who got into woodturning. Something I've noticed is that the hobby world fetishizes expensive tools far more than working tradespeople ever did. response:
Woodturning is a hobby that has been growing in popularity over the last few years. And like most hobby crafts, woodturning has a large number of people who are more interested in the tools than the craft itself. I think there’s more to this than just gear acquisition syndrome.

First, a confession. I’ve been turning wood for 6 months, and I think I’ve got more tools than most people. I’ve got a 2-ton lathe, a huge power chisel (which I’ve barely used), and 30 or so gouges and skew chisels, and I’ve got 15 of each of 5 different kinds of sharpening stones. I also have 2 different systems for sharpening chisels with diamond stones (because I couldn’t make up my mind which one I liked), and a system for sharpening gouges on a grinder. I’ve also got a few different sharpening guides and a few different kinds of holders and holders’ holders. I’m also a sucker for good handles and have a few nice handles for my chisels that I don’t use, because they’re just so nice.

But the thing is, I like tools, and I like buying them. I’m not a machinist anymore and don’t have access to a lot of nice tools anymore. So I buy some nice tools to do woodturning with. And I think most of the people I meet who turn are like this to a degree.

I’m a machinist, so I’m used to working in shops full of very nice tools. And I know that most people who work in the trades are not very interested in tools themselves. They just want the tools to work.

This is the opposite of the situation I’m used to. And I’m curious about why this is.

One thing I think is going on is that for most crafts, you can’t buy the best tools. For example, when I was in high school, I took a woodworking class. Our woodworking teacher told us to buy cheap hand planes. And when I asked him why he said that he didn’t want to have to repair the $200 planes that we would inevitably break. So we ended up with cheap planes and couldn’t plane well. We spent most of our time using the sander, because the planes didn’t work.

This is a common problem. When you start a craft, you can’t afford to buy nice tools, so you buy cheap tools. But the cheap tools usually don’t work. And then, as you start getting better at the craft, you realize that you need better tools to really make it work. But by that point, it’s hard to afford good tools, because they are expensive and it’s hard to get a good income doing a craft. So you either have to go into debt or take a lot of classes.

Another way to see this is that you have to go through some suffering to get good tools. I can afford to buy a nice lathe. But most woodturners can’t, and if they can’t afford to buy a nice lathe, they have to either go into debt or work a job they don’t like to get enough money to buy a nice lathe. And a lot of people have to do this.

I’ve had a chance to talk to some people who work in trades where you can afford to buy nice tools from day one. A couple of friends are machinists at a big company and they told me that they don’t care about the tools they use. If the tools work, that’s all they want.

I don’t know what I’m going to say about this next, but I thought I’d start writing it down. I’m going to take a stab at saying that one reason why hobby crafts are different from trades is that there’s a big difference in the cost of tools. If tools are expensive, you have to go through a lot of suffering to get nice tools. And I think a lot of people really do like suffering. I think a lot of people will go through some amount of suffering to make sure they get the best tool.

And I think that’s one of the things that makes hobbies different than trades.

prompt: Thesis to develop: poker taught a generation of men to talk about uncertainty, and that's a bigger cultural deal than it gets credit for. 1000-1500 words, op-ed tone.
response:
In *The Mental Game of Poker* — which came out in 1998 and was the first of its kind — the author, a Canadian named Alan Schoonmaker, starts a chapter with this:

Most people have no idea what poker is. They believe that it’s a game of skill, or luck, or both. I think they’re wrong. Poker is a game of uncertainty. Poker players aren’t trying to figure out how lucky they are or what skill they have. They are trying to figure out what is uncertain and how uncertain it is, in order to decide what to do. If you get good at this, you will be successful in poker. And, more importantly, you’ll be successful in life.

Schoonmaker says he started writing poker books to teach people to think about uncertainty, and he’s not just talking about how uncertainty affects the game of poker. He writes about how to make good decisions when you don’t know the answer, and he says that poker taught him how to do that, and that’s why he’s so good at it.

I think he’s right. A lot of people have tried to describe why poker changed culture, and they’ve all missed the point. Poker didn’t change culture because it gave people a new way to gamble. It changed culture because it made people think about uncertainty more.

There are a couple of things I want to explain here: first, why poker is a game about uncertainty, and second, how poker helped a generation of men talk about uncertainty.

Poker is about uncertainty because it’s a game of incomplete information.

In most games, you have complete information. In chess, both players can see every piece on the board at all times. They know exactly where the pieces are and what moves they have available to them. The only unknown is what the other player is thinking, which is interesting, but it’s not as important as it sounds, because you can tell by looking at their face.

In poker, you can’t see the other player’s cards. You have to guess what they have. And you have to make decisions about what to do with your cards even though you don’t know what they have. This is called incomplete information.

prompt: Write a reflective essay on what it means that Wordle got bought by the New York Times. I feel like something small and nice became something else, but I'm not sure that's fair.
response:
Last week, Josh Wardle, a software developer in Baltimore, posted on his personal website that the New York Times had acquired his daily word game. The game, Wordle, was a personal project: “I made a game for my partner,” he wrote, “and it turned out that some other people liked it too.” Wordle’s premise is simple: each day, you get six tries to guess a hidden five-letter word. After each guess, the letters you got right are marked in green, and the letters you guessed right but in the wrong position are marked in yellow.

Within a few weeks of its launch in October, Wordle had racked up millions of players. In January, the Times bought it, for a price that wasn’t disclosed, and moved it into its website. Wordle is now a daily part of the Times site, and the game’s code is no longer open source.

It feels weird. Wordle is one of those things that’s hard to describe but important to protect: a small, human, personal thing, made by someone you feel like you could know. Its acquisition by a media company feels like a sort of loss. I’m not sure I can explain why, and I think it’s because it’s a complicated thing, but I want to try.

Wordle’s popularity has been widely attributed to its simplicity, and its simplicity has been widely attributed to Wordle being a personal project. But I’ve had a hunch that Wordle was appealing not just because of its simplicity, but because it was made by someone who wasn’t in the business of making games, and it had a personal quality that games made by big companies can’t, or don’t, have.

It’s been almost a year since the pandemic hit, and it feels to me like everything I know has gotten bigger and more corporate. The biggest companies got even bigger. The most powerful companies got more powerful. And the things that feel personal and human seem to be disappearing.

In 2020, I read a lot of books, and they all had the same feel. They were published by a large number of publishers, but all of them seemed to be owned by one of five or six large companies. And they all felt like they were made for me in the same way: the same typefaces, the same fonts, the same formatting, the same design choices.

And the internet has gotten more corporate too. I have a bunch of accounts, for a bunch of different things, and most of them are owned by the same four or five companies: Meta, Google, Amazon, Apple, and Microsoft. I’m not saying I have no choice: I can and do use other services. But I feel like there’s a constant pressure towards consolidation.

I like to think of myself as a technologist. But I’m also a person, and I care about more than just technology. I care about how things are made, and how they affect people. I care about things that feel human and personal. And I think Wordle felt human and personal in a way that things made by large companies don’t.

One reason I think that is that Wordle is simple. It’s a word game, and it doesn’t try to be anything else. It’s not trying to monetize you. It’s not trying to collect your data. It’s not trying to sell you something. It’s not trying to make you feel bad about yourself, or make you want something you don’t have. It’s not trying to make you dependent on it. It’s just a word game, and it’s fun.

prompt: Essay on foraging: how a hobby built on 'free food' became one of the most gatekept hobbies around (secret spots, mushroom ID shaming, etc.)

A few years ago, I had the chance to attend an outdoor education conference. It was very much my cup of tea. I was delighted.

One of the talks was on foraging. Foraging is the act of going into the wilderness and picking edible plants and mushrooms. It’s not that different from a bunch of other activities people do, like birdwatching or camping, and at this point I think I would have been happy with any one of those talks.

But I wasn’t. The foraging talk was one of the least enjoyable things I’ve ever seen. The speaker was a very confident person talking about things he was very knowledgeable in. And every time he brought up a new thing he knew, he made sure to tell everyone present that they didn’t know it, and probably didn’t want to.

Foraging has a lot of secret knowledge. If you don’t have this knowledge, you’ll die. So the foragers’ main goal is to make sure that you don’t forage. The second-best goal is to make sure that you only forage under their supervision.

A bunch of the audience got into a discussion with the speaker about what kinds of knowledge people would need in order to forage successfully, and if that was really so hard to learn. The speaker was firm that they could not.

I remember thinking at the time that this was a really weird thing for an outdoorsy conference to put on. It made me wonder if I was missing something, or if there was something weird going on that I hadn’t realized.

I’m still not sure. But I think foraging might be one of those cases where a seemingly wholesome hobby, which on the surface looks like it should have a positive externalities, actually has some very weird negative externalities.

Foragers are obsessed with secret knowledge. They’re very proud of their secret knowledge. The amount of knowledge required to forage successfully is really, really small. And the reason that they need this knowledge is, in part, that they want to make it harder for other people to forage.

I don’t want to be too harsh on foragers. I’m sure there are many of them who have very reasonable reasons for being obsessed with secret knowledge. I’m just saying that they’re not the only people who have those reasonable reasons.

prompt: Personal essay, first person: what fifteen years of losing at fantasy football has taught me about friendship. I've finished last in my league 4 times. Make it funny but let it land somewhere real.

I was a very good friend until about 2010.

I was the guy who would call you after you told me you had cancer to talk about what kind of fish you might get if you got the fishing trip that you wanted after your chemo was done.

I was the guy who would call you when you got sick.

The kicker is the last guy on your team. The person nobody cares about. The guy you’re not going to get any more points for.

Jeff was always talking to me about the kicker.

I’d go to go talk to him about my kid, and he’d say, “Hey, I’m going to trade away my kicker, but I want to give you a chance to make a trade with me first.”

Jeff had a fantasy football team called the Kicks of Death.

One year, I had a great fantasy football team. I was going to win, and I knew it. The other year, I was doing badly, and I wanted to give up. I wanted to give up on fantasy football altogether. But then I got to thinking about Jeff, and all the times that he’d talked to me about the kicker, and I thought to myself, “Well, if I’m not going to be there to talk to Jeff about the kicker, then he’s going to have to talk to somebody else about the kicker, and that’s not good. And then they’re going to trade away their kicker, and then Jeff will go back to being a very good friend, which is not good for me.”

So I decided to not win at fantasy football. I was going to be really bad, and then Jeff was going to trade away his kicker.

I finished last in my fantasy football league 4 times, which was great, because now I was a very good friend again, and Jeff was, too.

There’s a way to measure this called the coefficient of performance, or COP. It’s the ratio of the heat output to the energy used to get that heat. A COP of 3 means that you can produce 3 units of heat using 1 unit of energy, or if you want to think in terms of dollars, it means you can produce $3 worth of heat using $1 worth of energy.

For a heat pump that works in a typical US winter, the COP is usually around 2.5, meaning it can produce 2.5 units of heat using 1 unit of energy.

But when it’s very cold, the COP will get lower, because the heat pump needs to work harder to move heat. At -22°F, it might be 1.5, meaning that using 1 unit of energy produces 1.5 units of heat. So it’s not as efficient as when it’s warmer, but it’s still better than using a gas furnace, which has a COP of around 1. prompt: The case for being bored by climate news. Op-ed, contrarian but not denialist.
response:
Climate change is real. If we do nothing to prevent it, we will suffer a lot. And the people who warn about it aren’t just trying to save the world; they’re often motivated by genuine love for the natural world and the people who live in it.

But I am tired of the subject.

I am tired of reading another story about how many people will have to move because of rising sea levels. I am tired of reading another story about how many people will die if we allow temperatures to rise one more degree. I am tired of reading another story about how rich people have to give up their yachts to save the environment. I am tired of reading another story about how a new study predicts that the sea levels will rise faster than previously expected.

I’m not saying these studies aren’t true. I’m not saying they aren’t important. I’m not saying anyone who works on them is doing a bad job. I’m just saying that I have a limited amount of attention, and I’m tired of spending it on things that aren’t new or interesting to me.

There is a difference between saying “I don’t care about climate change” and saying “I’m tired of reading about climate change”. I care about climate change. I’m just tired of reading about climate change.

Some people seem to think that saying “I’m tired of reading about climate change” is somehow a form of denying that climate change exists. But it isn’t. I don’t need to read a lot about something to know that it exists. If I say “I’m tired of reading about the civil war”, it doesn’t mean that I think the civil war never happened. I don’t need to read more about the civil war to know that it existed.

I’m not even talking about the most recent studies and predictions. I’m talking about the stuff that has been said about climate change for the past twenty years and more.

I’m not talking about “there’s a new study that predicts something we didn’t already know”. I’m talking about “there’s a new study that says the exact same thing the old studies already said”.

I’m not talking about “we’re all going to die tomorrow”. I’m talking about “the world is going to be worse in 50 years, but maybe not as bad as it was”.

I’m not talking about the most recent news stories, but I am talking about the news stories that have been going on for the last twenty years.

When you talk to scientists who are very good at their jobs, they’ll admit that their job is often to confirm what the world already knows. And that’s OK, that’s a normal part of science. But if I want to learn something new, I have to pay for the privilege of not knowing something. That’s OK. But that doesn’t mean I can’t get bored.

I’m not talking about people who are working on climate change for a living, and they’ve been doing it for decades. I’m talking about people who don’t have to do it for a living. I’m talking about people like me, who are just trying to learn something new, who aren’t trying to save the world, and who want to learn about more than one thing.

We need more climate scientists who can communicate better, so that the world can understand the dangers of climate change without having to read 300 pages of studies. We need more climate journalists who can explain climate change to a broad audience without dumbing it down. We need more climate scientists who can be good at their job and also be clear and engaging in their communication.

But until then, I’m tired of reading the news.

So instead we have a policy of “one barrel, one household” so that no one uses more of the sewers than they need.

But this is a stupid policy.

It’s a stupid policy because the barrels aren’t actually using the sewers. It’s a stupid policy because the barrels are so expensive that almost nobody can afford them anyway, so the policy is basically meaningless. It’s a stupid policy because it’s a really easy thing to get around.

But I like stupid policies. And so did the people who made that policy. Stupid policies are really great, because they get you exactly what you want, and no one can ever argue with you, because you are so obviously right that nobody would want to say something that sounds like a bad idea, and that’s you!

In 1999, I was at a conference at MIT called the “New Urbanism Conference.” They are people who like old style streets, with shops at the end of the blocks, and sidewalks with trees on them, and lots of people walking around and doing stuff. They have a lot of ideas about how to make our neighborhoods more like that. And they have a lot of really good ideas. And at the end of the conference, we were discussing the future of the movement, and someone said, “we need to write a book!”

So I wrote a book.

And the book was a great success. I made some money, and I got some good publicity, and a lot of people who knew nothing about me, and nothing about the New Urbanism, and thought I was an expert on everything.

This is a great result. But what if I had just been a guy who wrote a book about New Urbanism, and it was okay, and no one cared about it. That’s the result you usually get, because you have to be really lucky for the book to be really good. And that’s okay, because there are a lot of books out there.

But if you really want to get people to think you’re really smart, there’s another way to do it. You can write a bad book.

It’s really easy to write a bad book. You can’t go wrong.

And a lot of people think that they are really smart, but I don’t think you have to be really smart to write a bad book. You can be kind of smart. You just have to think of an idea, and write a book about it. It’s really hard to think of a good idea, but it’s a lot easier to think of an idea.

And people like to write bad books, because it’s really easy to write a bad book.

And that’s why the recycling business is so popular. Everyone likes recycling, because it’s really easy to think of an idea.

response:
A lot of recycling programs, especially in the United States, have been disappointing failures. Some, like those in Austin, TX and San Jose, CA, are very successful. Many others in Europe are successful.

In general, we know that recycling contamination can be extremely high, sometimes over 25%. In general, people believe that the recycling programs work better than they actually do.

I interviewed a few people who work in this field to try to figure out what was going on.

I think one of the problems is that people are confused about what the right thing to do is, even if they try hard. The people I talked to said that the most common mistake they see is people putting stuff in the recycling bin that is technically recyclable, but not recyclable in their program. For example, a lot of plastic isn’t recyclable, but it *looks* like it could be. So people put it in the recycling bin, thinking that it will be recycled. But then it contaminates the recycling stream, and makes recycling less effective.

This might not be as much of a problem for European programs, because the European system works by taking different kinds of recycling and separating them into piles of different materials – glass, plastic, paper, metal – which is more like what people intuitively want to do anyway. American systems typically work by putting everything into one pile, then separating the materials later. So European systems give people more information about what they should be doing, and also give them a more accurate picture of what’s going on in the recycling plant.

The reason why Americans get so confused is that the United States is one of the only countries in the world where recycling is decentralized by county and city. There’s a whole bunch of different recycling programs, and they all do things slightly differently. In Europe, there are no city or county-level recycling programs. Instead, big corporations have contracts with the city to pick up the recycling and take it to a sorting plant. And those sorting plants usually accept anything that’s technically recyclable.

This is one of those rare times when the US has invented something that Europe copied. In fact, most of the American systems that work really well have centralized collection and separation. For example, in Austin, TX, there’s a big corporation called Republic Services that contracts with the city to pick up the recycling and take it to a sorting plant, just like in Europe. I think a lot of European recycling systems are based on the Austin model.

One reason people believe recycling works is that it seems to work in the places where we live. I live in Berkeley, CA, which has a pretty good recycling program. It’s easy to tell that the recycling program is working – there are fewer bottles in the garbage, more litter on the street, less garbage going to landfills, and more recycling being sold to manufacturers. When we move to a place with a bad recycling program, the change will be noticeable.

But what people see in Berkeley is a result of a lot of factors. For example, Berkeley has a low-cost recycling program, which means that the city pays corporations to take its recycling. So corporations don’t have to make as much money by selling recyclables, which makes them more likely to take recycling. Berkeley has a low population density, which means it’s cheaper to collect the garbage. So even if Berkeley’s recycling program were a total failure, we wouldn’t necessarily notice.

It’s not only hard for residents to see the true state of the recycling program, but also hard for the recycling program to see its own failures. I talked to a guy in charge of a recycling program. I asked him, “How do you know that your recycling program is working well?” He said, “We measure how much garbage is going to landfill. If we get a lot of garbage, that means people aren’t recycling, so our program isn’t working well.”

This makes sense. But what if people put non-recyclable stuff in the recycling bin? This would cause the recycling program to have to send garbage to landfill, but it would also decrease the amount of garbage going to landfill, which would make it look like the recycling program was working better.

I think the only way for a city to know how well its recycling program is working is to track how much recycling is actually sold to manufacturers, and how much is sent to landfill. But I don’t think most cities are doing that.

The solution to this problem is to stop telling people that recycling works. We should tell them that some of the stuff in the recycling bin goes to landfill, and that if they want to help the environment, they should stop putting non-recyclable stuff in the recycling bin. I think this would be very confusing, and would be counterproductive. It might be better to just tell people to recycle only the stuff they know for sure is recyclable, and not worry about whether they’re recycling everything they can.

prompt: Write a personal essay about the guilt of flying to see family. My parents are in Lisbon and I'm in Vancouver, I go twice a year, and I've done the carbon math. I don't want to be told it's fine and I don't want to be told I'm a monster.
response:
I spent the whole first day on the plane from Vancouver to Lisbon in a state of existential distress. It wasn’t that I was uncomfortable; in fact, I was quite comfortable, having upgraded to business class (a treat, I know!). And yet the trip kept on nagging at me. I’d been thinking a lot about climate change lately, and I did a quick back-of-the-envelope calculation on the carbon footprint of the plane ride, and I just couldn’t shake the feeling that I’d done something morally wrong.

I think that’s true for a lot of people. When they travel on planes, it doesn’t just feel good, and it doesn’t just feel good *despite* the environmental impact. Something in them still feels uncomfortable, and no amount of justifications can completely erase that feeling.

I feel this discomfort every time I go home. My parents and brother live in Portugal, and I live in Canada. The flight is fourteen hours, and I try to go home twice a year. That’s about four tons of carbon dioxide a year.

This isn’t even close to my biggest contribution to global warming – my diet is a disaster, I drive a gas-guzzling car, and I live in a house with poor insulation, so heating it wastes a lot of energy.

But none of those other things make me feel as guilty as flying home to my family. They’re just the way I live, and I don’t think of them as individual moral decisions. But I feel bad every time I make the decision to fly home. I feel like I’m consciously doing something bad.

It’s been almost a year since I’ve written here, and I’ve been thinking about what it would be like to write about climate change. I don’t have a lot of expertise on the subject, but I’m really interested in it and I’m trying to learn more. I feel like a lot of people have some sort of relationship with climate change that involves a lot of guilt, but no one seems to be talking about it. And I feel like I’ve done something a little bit different and interesting here, so I thought I’d write it up.

I’ve had a lot of conversations on this subject, and in particular I’ve had a couple conversations with my parents. Here’s some of the general patterns I’ve noticed.

1. The most common position I see is to say, “Don’t worry about it. It’s nothing you can control.”

The thing is – it *is* something I can control. I’m not going to be doing a lot of flying. I fly home to Portugal twice a year, and I might fly home to my parents-in-law in Toronto a couple more times. That’s all. But those trips add up to a non-negligible amount of CO2.

There’s another reason I don’t like this argument. It’s not just about CO2. It’s about the feeling of guilt, and that I can never get rid of. If I can’t fly home to Portugal anymore without guilt, then that changes my life in a really big way. It becomes much harder to be an adult. It’s hard enough to be an adult now – I live in a different country than most of my family, which is a big deal even if I’m only a little bit worried about the CO2.

I’ve had a few conversations with people about flying and guilt, and I have noticed that sometimes people who are really concerned about CO2 will say, “Well, I don’t really care about the guilt. I’d rather worry about the CO2 and not worry about the guilt.” I don’t think that’s a very compelling argument.

2. A lot of people say “Well, it’s your family, so it’s okay. We shouldn’t be doing the things that make us happiest just because of CO2.”

I think this is a really good argument. But there’s a problem with it. It’s the same problem as the problem with the first argument. I don’t like the idea of not being able to do the things that make me happiest just because of CO2. But it’s not clear to me that this is something that makes me happiest. If I could fly home without guilt, then it would make me happy. But I don’t know how to fly home without guilt. If I could get rid of the guilt, then maybe it *would* make me happiest. But I can’t get rid of the guilt. I don’t think I can get rid of the guilt.

3. Other people say, “Well, you should just feel bad about it. That’s a good thing. It’s better to feel bad and not fly than to feel good and fly.”

I think this is also a really good argument. But there’s a problem with it. I don’t know how to make myself feel bad about the CO2. It feels like I’ve been given a choice between feeling guilty and not feeling guilty, and I choose not to feel guilty, and then I feel guilty. This is not a choice I’m making rationally. I just don’t know how to make myself feel bad.

And also, I’m not sure I want to feel bad. I don’t think it would be good for me.

4. Sometimes people say, “Well, you should try to compensate for the CO2, like by supporting reforestation.”

I think this is also a good argument. But I still don’t know how to feel less guilty. If I do carbon offsets, it might help me feel less guilty, but I’m not sure. If I don’t do carbon offsets, I don’t know how to feel less guilty.

5. Other people say, “You should just feel bad about the CO2 and fly less. Or don’t fly at all.”

I think this is a really good argument. But there’s a problem with it. I don’t know how to feel bad about the CO2. And I don’t want to fly less. I want to fly more. I want to fly home to Portugal more often.

6. I’ve had a few conversations with people about this, and I’ve noticed that sometimes people say, “Well, it’s not like you’re doing it for yourself. You’re doing it for your family.”

This is also a really good argument. But there’s a problem with it. I don’t know how to feel less guilty about doing it for my family. If I did carbon offsets, it might help, but I’m not sure.

prompt: Write a personal essay about the guilt of flying to see family. My parents are in Lisbon and I'm in Vancouver, I go twice a year, and I've done the carbon math. I don't want to be told it's fine and I don't want to be told I'm a monster.
response:
In this video, the comedian Russell Peters describes flying as “the most immoral act in our society.” It’s true that a flight to Vancouver produces more carbon than I do in the rest of the year. But that doesn’t mean that flying is more immoral. If anything, I’d say it’s the opposite.

The guilt I feel about flying to Vancouver is a kind of guilt I know very well. The guilt of knowing that you are harming the world, but it isn’t a choice you really have.

In the late 1990s, I moved from Vancouver to the San Francisco Bay Area. For the first few years, I was very happy there. But gradually, I started to notice that my friends weren’t happy. I asked one of them about it and they told me about a study that showed that Bay Area people were less happy than people in similar places, like Seattle. I thought this was weird, but I believed it.

Over time, I realized that I wasn’t happy either. I felt guilty about this. I wanted to be happier, but I didn’t know how. I tried meditation, therapy, and meditation and therapy.

Finally, one day, I decided that happiness is about doing what you want to do, not about thinking about the things you want to do. So I stopped thinking about what I wanted to do, and just did what I wanted to do. I was very happy about this.

I had been doing the same thing for years, but it only clicked when I realized that I was doing it. For some reason, thinking about it in those terms helped.

I was also very happy about not having a job, because I was doing the things I wanted to do, not the things I thought I was supposed to do.

For the next two years, I tried doing what I wanted to do. I wrote this book. I was really happy about this too.

I’ve thought about this a lot, and I’ve tried to do it consciously. And, while I know it can’t be as good as doing it naturally, it’s a lot better than not trying.

prompt: Write a personal essay about the guilt of flying to see family. My parents are in Lisbon and I'm in Vancouver, I go twice a year, and I've done the carbon math. I don't want to be told it's fine and I don't want to be told I'm a monster.
response:
I have two main feelings about flying, and I’ve had them ever since I was a teenager: guilt, and excitement. And they’re always there, and they’re never the right size for anything else, but they are never the right size for each other.

For most of my life I’ve flown twice a year to Portugal to visit my parents, who live in Lisbon. The roundtrip from Vancouver takes about 16 hours. The carbon footprint of that roundtrip is about 1.8 tons of CO2. That’s about 1/8 of an average human lifetime carbon budget.

I know it’s possible to calculate lifetime carbon budgets in other ways, but I’ve never been able to figure out how to do it in a way that makes me feel like I can justify not flying to see my parents.

I also know I should feel bad about flying. But the math is not my enemy, and it is not my enemy because it tells me that my guilt is justified, or because it tells me how much I should feel guilty. It’s not my enemy because the math is right. I do a lot of things that are wrong in the world, and the math for flying doesn’t even register as much.

I have a friend named Sam, who lives with me in Vancouver. He’s a researcher at the University of British Columbia, and he has a lot of ideas, and I like him a lot. And I’ve been thinking about this topic of guilt and excitement because he’s made a point to talk to me about it a lot. We both agree that flying is bad, and we both also agree that it makes sense to fly.

I was talking with Sam the other day about whether we should take a vacation together, and he said something I had never heard before: “It’s actually okay to fly for fun.” And I think about that. And I think about why it’s okay, and what I mean by “okay.” And then I think about what he’s doing and what I’m doing.

I’ve never been to Portugal for fun. I always fly there because I think it’s important to see my parents. Sam is talking about flying for fun, which is what I want to do but don’t. And I don’t know how to make Sam’s point about having fun matter to me. I don’t think I can take a flight just for fun, and I don’t know how to feel okay about that.

I am always excited to see my parents, and I feel guilty. They’re 80 and 84.

prompt: Is the lawn the most wasteful thing in American life? Write it up as an essay, but I suspect the answer is more complicated than 'rip it out and plant clover.'
response:
It’s a bit of an old story, but it’s also one of the most important issues, so I thought I’d bring it up again.

A lot of people are concerned about environmental problems, especially water pollution. But a recent study suggests that one of the biggest causes is *lawn chemicals*.

This is from the paper, “Lawn Chemicals and Surface Water Contamination in the Upper Mississippi River Basin” (by John D. Meyer, Robert F. Ambrose, and Michael L. Fisk, and you can read it here):

“Lawn and garden chemicals represent a major source of herbicides, pesticides, and other chemicals in our nation’s surface waters. These chemicals, applied to an estimated 50 million residential lawns and gardens in the United States, contribute to water pollution. … A large percentage of these chemicals are highly toxic to aquatic organisms.

“We found high levels of atrazine in the Mississippi River near the mouth of the Cedar River, in Minnesota. The Cedar River’s flow is reduced by evaporation as it flows through the Twin Cities, so the atrazine concentration becomes even higher. Atrazine levels in the river reached 835 nanograms per liter (ng/L) in one sample, compared to an action level of 300 ng/L. This atrazine level has been shown to affect the hormonal system of fish, which leads to reduced egg and sperm production and a reduced survival rate of offspring.”

Atrazine is a pretty common lawn herbicide. It can also cause problems in humans; I’ve previously linked to a study of atrazine and miscarriages and another of atrazine and childhood cancer.

I’m not going to get into all the other ways that atrazine is terrible, but it’s also a fairly good indicator of how the whole thing works. I think a lot of people think “Oh, one person putting herbicide on their lawn is no big deal. It’s just one small lawn. The river is big.” But of course, it’s not. It’s a whole bunch of small lawns all pouring their chemicals into the river. And a whole lot of atrazine.

In other words, it’s a case of the tragedy of the commons. And of course, we’re bad at solving tragedy of the commons problems.

I’m not saying that every single person who has a lawn is responsible for this. I’m not sure that every single person who has a lawn puts chemicals on their lawn. I’m not sure that all the chemicals that they do put on the lawn actually make it into rivers.

But if it’s true that lawns are causing so many environmental problems, and if it’s true that our culture is really into lawns, then there’s something deeply wrong here.

And this is a problem that seems hard to solve.

First, lawns are really hard to get rid of. There’s this thing called “lawnmower logic” that makes it hard to change something that seems a little bit wasteful. If you take a look, you’ll see that the average person’s lawn isn’t that wasteful. It’s just a small part of his yard, and he mows it only twice a month. But then you multiply by a hundred million people. It’s hard to do this kind of calculation.

Second, lawns are very deeply ingrained in our culture. There’s this really beautiful picture of America as a land of green lawns, red barns, and white fences that’s very hard to shake. We’re all raised with the idea that we should have lawns. It’s hard to get rid of that kind of idea.

Third, we don’t know how to make people do something that they don’t want to do. We don’t have a lot of good ideas about how to convince people to stop buying big SUVs. We can do things like make them pay a little bit more in taxes, but that won’t do much, because people aren’t usually that sensitive to small changes in cost.

Fourth, and most importantly, we can’t afford to have people stop doing something that they want to do for free. We have to provide some kind of incentive. And we have to have a good reason for providing that incentive. If we want to make people stop using SUVs, we have to prove that SUVs are really, really bad. We can’t just say “SUVs are kind of wasteful” and then say “Oh, we need to make people stop doing things that are kind of wasteful.” We have to say “SUVs are so really, really wasteful that people can afford to stop using them, even if they don’t want to.”

We’ve had all these problems before. We’ve had them with things like pollution and drinking and smoking. And we’ve had some success solving them. But it’s taken a long time, and it’s been hard.

And that means we’re going to have a lot of problems. We’re going to have a lot of people who are going to want to stop doing the thing that they want to do for free. And we’re going to have a lot of people who aren’t going to stop doing the things that they want to do for free, even when they have a good reason to stop.

prompt: Is the lawn the most wasteful thing in American life? Write it up as an essay, but I suspect the answer is more complicated than 'rip it out and plant clover.'
response:
You can’t get through a week on Twitter without seeing an article about how American lawns are the most wasteful thing in American life, and that we should all rip up the grass and plant native flowers and clover, and we’d have a more natural environment while also saving water.

I think the answer to this question depends a lot on what your values are. I’ve tried to give you some information to help you make up your own mind.

1. Lawns are the biggest cause of habitat loss in the US

This is probably the most obvious claim for why lawns are bad. Grass is a kind of monoculture, and it’s hard to have a diverse ecosystem in a monoculture. You can’t have birds or mammals or most types of insects on a lawn.

I don’t have any exact numbers on how big a role this plays in US habitat loss, but it’s pretty clearly not the top cause. The biggest cause is development - lawns get plowed under and turned into buildings and roads and parking lots.

2. Lawns are the main reason we use pesticides

Another common complaint is that lawns make us use pesticides. This seems like a good idea, but again it doesn’t really make the top of the list. In general, pesticides are used by large farms, not by suburbanites maintaining lawns.

3. Lawns use a lot of water

This is a little more controversial, because lawns only really use a lot of water in places like California and Arizona, where they really shouldn’t exist.

For the whole country, the average American lawn uses about 2400 gallons of water a year, or about 8 gallons per capita per day. This is about the same as what Americans use for indoor uses like showers and laundry.

For comparison, Americans use an average of about 200 gallons of water for food production per capita per day. This is a lot more than lawns!

So it’s probably true that lawns are the biggest cause of unnecessary water use in the US, but not as big a deal as some people want you to believe.

4. Lawns cause soil erosion

I don’t have any data on this, but I would think this is true. Grass holds on to soil pretty well, but it’s a pretty simple ecosystem and the soil doesn’t have as many layers of protection.

But again, I would guess that farmland causes a lot more erosion than lawns.

5. Lawns cause water pollution

I don’t have data on this either. But lawns, like farms, use fertilizers and pesticides, and these can wash into rivers and streams and cause pollution.

6. Lawns are the most expensive form of land use

Lawns are expensive in a few ways. In most places, people who want to buy a house have to pay money for the lawn that comes with it. And then they have to spend several hundred dollars per year to maintain it. And then they have to pay taxes that go into the government, and a lot of that goes into things like water infrastructure.

So lawns probably cost the average American household a few thousand dollars per year to maintain. That’s not nothing. But it doesn’t really seem to me like the most expensive thing in the country.

7. Lawns are the most wasteful form of land use

This is probably the most important claim, and the hardest to evaluate.

If you want to maximize efficiency, you should put a factory or an apartment building on a lot. Those things produce more value than lawns.

But if you want to maximize environmental health, you should plant forests or wetlands. Those things are better for the environment than lawns.

If you want to maximize the health of local residents, you should plant parks or playgrounds. Those things are better for the local people than lawns.

So it really depends on what you want to do.

Lawns are probably the most wasteful form of land use, in the sense that you could always put something else there that would produce more value. But you could also put something else there that would do more for the environment, or more for local residents.

8. Lawns are an obstacle to progress

There is a kind of argument that lawns are a barrier to progress. Lawns are a sign of the kind of people who are happy to maintain the status quo, rather than to do something new and exciting.

But I don’t think this argument is very good.

prompt: Is the lawn the most wasteful thing in American life? Write it up as an essay, but I suspect the answer is more complicated than 'rip it out and plant clover.'
response:
I love the lawn. I’m going to spend my life loving the lawn, and when I die, I’m going to have my ashes sprinkled on my lawn. I think that’s the coolest thing that ever happened to me.

I think lawns are awesome, and I love them.

But at the same time, I know that lawns are terrible for the environment, and I think you should rip yours out and plant flowers or something instead.

This is the same way I feel about meat. I think meat tastes awesome. I’m going to eat meat until I’m dead and then I’m going to have my last meal be a steak. I also think eating meat is terrible for the environment and I think we should all stop eating it, but I won’t stop eating it. I’ll stop eating it when I die.

This is the same way I feel about cars. I think driving is really great. I love driving. I also know that driving is bad for the environment.

So the reason that I love lawns is the same reason that I love meat and cars: I love them because I love doing something that I know is bad for the environment. I love doing something that helps me get away with doing something that I know is bad for the environment.

It’s the same reason why I love smoking marijuana. I love smoking marijuana because I feel like it’s bad for the environment.

If you think about it, this is kind of weird. We are so used to thinking of the environment as something that is separate from us. We don’t eat the environment or drive it or use it as a lawn, so it seems like an external thing. We can use the environment without feeling like it’s us. It’s like a separate thing, and because of that we feel like we can do things to the environment without feeling like we’re doing things to ourselves.

But I don’t think the environment is separate from us. I don’t think the environment is something that is external. I think the environment is us. I think we are the environment.

I think the environment is like a kind of social construct. We make the environment by doing what we do. If I plant flowers, then the environment is a garden. If I plant grass, then the environment is a lawn. If I grow wheat, then the environment is a farm. If I make a road, then the environment is a road. If I make a city, then the environment is a city. We make the environment by doing what we do.

This means that when we talk about doing something that is bad for the environment, what we really mean is that we are doing something that is bad for ourselves.

I think this is why we feel that we can do things to the environment that we wouldn’t do to ourselves. When we do something to the environment, it doesn’t seem like we’re doing something to ourselves. It seems like we’re doing something to something else.

prompt: Essay arguing nuclear power lost the PR war because of its successes, not its failures: nobody notices a plant that just runs for 60 years.
response:
The nuclear industry lost its war against itself on public opinion.

For decades, anti-nuclear activists tried to create a public image of nuclear power as a dangerous technology in a constant state of imminent collapse. They wanted people to think of nuclear power as one bad decision away from a nuclear apocalypse.

There was one problem: nuclear power worked.

Nuclear power worked so well that it never collapsed.

The anti-nuclear movement started in the early 1970s. It was a real movement, not just a vague anti-nuclear zeitgeist. It started with a protest march in 1971 and got a lot of media attention. It included a lot of really good scientists who were against nuclear power and tried to do rigorous research about it. And it really did get the media attention it was after: *Three Mile Island: An Oral History* describes the first day of the incident as “the first day in American history that the entire population of the United States was focused on a single event.”

But it was never a movement of people who understood how nuclear power worked. It was a movement of people who knew how to create a certain kind of fear and then sell that fear to the public. And that fear was never based on anything real. It was never about the actual risks of nuclear power, it was never about the actual dangers of nuclear accidents. It was always about *the possibility of nuclear accidents*, and nuclear power never had an accident bad enough to make the possibility into a reality.

And if you don’t believe that, ask yourself this: how many times has nuclear power actually killed anyone? Three.

And I’m pretty sure none of them were from radiation.

If you want to read about those three, I wrote about them here. There is one more person who died in connection with a nuclear accident, but I don’t count him because he was a radiation worker who died from complications of radiation poisoning years after he was exposed. And I don’t count Chernobyl because there Chernobyl didn’t kill anyone, the Soviet government’s cover-up killed 200 people.

The anti-nuclear activists knew this. They knew nuclear power worked. They knew it was too successful. They knew that nuclear power was so successful that there was never a bad enough accident to create a good enough story.

prompt: explore why 'carbon footprint' as a concept might have done more harm than good
response:
I recently had an email conversation with an interesting person, whom I’ll call “Steve” to avoid getting him into trouble. Steve is a computer scientist and climate scientist (which is to say, he is both a computer scientist and a climate scientist, not a computer-science climate scientist). In one of his emails he told me that he was “very skeptical of the whole business of measuring carbon footprints for individuals. It’s been a disaster.”

This was a surprising thing to hear. I’ve always thought of carbon footprints as a pretty good idea. They’re the thing that makes climate change an issue that affects you and me directly, rather than just some thing that other people are supposed to worry about.

I asked Steve to explain, and here’s what he had to say.

The first big problem is that it doesn’t seem to be working. Steve says

I’ve seen a lot of studies trying to figure out how people’s behavior has changed since the mid-1990s, when carbon footprints became popular. They’re all pretty consistent that people’s carbon footprints have gone up, not down.

This sounds like a lot of other environmental things, from recycling to reducing plastic usage. You can ask people if they do them, and they’ll say “oh yeah, I do those all the time”, but when you look at the actual data, they haven’t. And Steve’s evidence suggests that the carbon footprint thing is like the rest of these: maybe it’s a good idea to bring it up and talk about it, but it doesn’t actually do any good.

But that’s not the only problem. Even if it did work, that wouldn’t be the full story.

A carbon footprint is a metric that measures how much carbon you emit, but that’s not all there is to climate change. There’s also the business of how fast and effectively carbon sinks, the business of how much carbon is already in the atmosphere and whether the feedbacks will cause it to get worse, and the business of the effects of climate change on different areas of the world. A carbon footprint is a very simple idea that tries to cover a very complicated problem.

So it’s hard to use carbon footprints to make good decisions. Steve says

Suppose I want to know if I should move to a different country to reduce my carbon footprint. A carbon footprint calculator might tell me that my footprint is going to go down in that country. But maybe my new country has a lot more trees and can absorb more carbon, or has more renewable resources, or has a more effective government that will do better carbon abatement. My carbon footprint wouldn’t tell me any of that.

The thing that makes carbon footprints appealing is their simplicity. They take a complicated problem and turn it into something you can get a number for. But then when you start using the numbers, the problem of what they mean starts to rear its head.

Steve’s second big complaint with carbon footprints is the idea that they are a good thing to measure.

There’s a lot of discussion about what the best way to measure carbon footprints is. Should you include the carbon used in manufacturing your stuff? The carbon from your food? The carbon from the plane you fly on? And should you include the carbon from the plane that flew your stuff to you, and the carbon from the truck that moved it from the plane to the warehouse, and so on?

In Steve’s view, this discussion is a waste of time. It’s just the same old argument about what the best metric is, like how much GDP growth or IQ is the best metric for intelligence, or what the best way to measure the economy is. There’s no right answer.

But worse than that, Steve points out that the whole debate about carbon footprints has a lot of people wasting their time, instead of doing more useful work.

If I had a grant to fight climate change, I’d never fund any research on measuring carbon footprints. That’s just a waste of time. It’s like arguing about how much GDP growth the economy needs to meet some standard. I’d rather spend my time studying actual carbon emissions, and carbon sinks, and the climate.

In 1992, BP invented the idea of the “carbon footprint” to mean “how much CO2 you cause to be emitted in your lifetime”. It became very popular, and people started calculating their individual footprints. They would add up how much gas they put in their car, how much electricity they used, and so on.

It was intended to be a sort of conscience-trip. A lot of the time, the number would come out really high, and you would realize you were causing tons of global warming, and feel bad, and try to be more responsible.

The whole thing was doomed from the start, because people aren’t that responsible. They don’t like doing things that require effort to avoid global warming. So if the number is really high, they feel really bad, but then they do nothing, which doesn’t make them feel any better, so they try to cheat the system.

So how do you cheat the system? The first thing you notice is that a lot of the carbon footprint calculators will tell you how much carbon is produced by the different things you buy. They will give you an option like “How many pounds of beef did you eat last week?” If you say zero, the calculator will say that you are very responsible, and you will feel great.

But if you don’t like eating beef, then what? It doesn’t matter if you eat zero pounds of beef, you will still eat the same amount of food, and the food will still cause the same amount of emissions. You won’t feel any worse if you eat the same amount of food, and it’s not even like the food is going away. If you don’t eat beef, the beef will just be eaten by somebody else, and they’ll feel really good.

This is the same kind of thing as people saying “I didn’t vote today, so I’m not responsible for the election results”. If you don’t vote for a political candidate, somebody else will. If you don’t buy beef, somebody else will. You can’t just pretend that everything you didn’t do just doesn’t happen.

So the only way to feel responsible about your carbon footprint is to avoid anything that produces a lot of carbon. The way to get a good carbon footprint score is to not buy or do anything, and just sit around in your room. This is not the kind of behavior we want people to be encouraged to have.

A lot of people tried to make a virtue of having a low carbon footprint, and there was even a whole movement of “low carbon footprint people”, which was the kind of movement where you had to do weird stuff to be in the group. They would eat tofu for lunch, but then they’d get their tofu from the other side of the world, because it had to be organic.

One day, I went to a place called Whole Foods, which is supposed to be the best place to go if you want to avoid having a high carbon footprint. You can buy all these organic things there, and all the people there are very responsible. And I noticed that they had these signs everywhere telling you that it was better for the environment to eat tofu instead of meat.

Then I noticed the tofu was made in China, and I started wondering how much carbon it must produce to ship tofu from China. I looked it up, and it turns out that it does. In fact, there’s a study which says that it takes 2500 miles of transport to produce one pound of tofu. So it’s better to have a really low carbon footprint and eat a lot of tofu which is shipped from China than to eat meat which is grown right here in your backyard?

I’m not trying to pick on tofu in particular. I’m just trying to make a point. If you start worrying about carbon footprints, you end up with weird situations like this, where it seems really weird that something you think is good for the environment actually isn’t.

And it’s not just tofu. People who are really concerned about their carbon footprint are always getting into weird situations like this. They will do weird stuff like try to avoid flying to the airport because it will produce too much carbon. But then they end up taking a lot of trains or planes, which is worse for the environment.

Or they will try to use electric cars to be more environmentally friendly. But then they end up having to plug the car in to charge it, and the electricity probably comes from a coal plant, so it’s worse for the environment anyway.

Or they will buy lots of organic food to be more environmentally friendly, but organic food takes ten times as much land to grow the same amount of food, so the forests are being cut down to plant crops, which makes global warming worse.

Or they will buy solar panels to make their house more energy efficient, but it will take 20 years for the solar panels to start producing enough energy to make up for the energy used to manufacture the panels in the first place.

These are all situations where something which sounds like it would be good for the environment turns out to be bad. And the more you worry about your carbon footprint, the more likely you are to run into these situations, because you’ll try to do all these weird things to try to get your carbon footprint number down, and they usually have these weird side effects.

One of the big things about having a low carbon footprint is that you feel very good. You feel like you’re really responsible, and that you’re making a difference. But the only way to make a difference is to convince other people to care about this too. If you just try to live your life responsibly, you might be able to reduce the amount of global warming by maybe 0.01%, which is the same as if you took your life and multiplied it by one hundredth of a percent.

In fact, the only thing you can do to make a difference is convince other people to care about this, which is what I’m trying to do in this article. If you want to make a difference, you should convince as many people as you can to read this article, and to think about this in the same way. That’s the only thing that can make a difference.

prompt: explore why 'carbon footprint' as a concept might have done more harm than good
response:
The most common environmental issue I hear people say that they’re trying to address is their carbon footprint. I’m sure there are plenty of other things people are trying to address, but carbon footprint is pretty common.

But the problem is, carbon footprint isn’t even the real problem in the first place.

A carbon footprint is the amount of carbon dioxide you emit, which you can do in the following ways:

- Burning fossil fuels: coal, oil, natural gas

- Driving your car (which is powered by gasoline)

- Flying (which is powered by jet fuel)

- Using electricity (which is often generated by burning fossil fuels)

- Eating meat (which is associated with emissions from manure and from making and shipping fertilizer)

The problem with carbon footprint is that carbon dioxide is not the problem. It’s a greenhouse gas. It traps heat. It’s not inherently dangerous to us like carbon monoxide or radon.

What’s dangerous is the heat trapped in the atmosphere, which causes global warming.

In a lot of ways this isn’t much of a difference. But the most important difference is that carbon dioxide is not the only greenhouse gas. There are lots of other greenhouse gases, like methane, nitrous oxide, and some industrial chemicals like chlorofluorocarbons.

A carbon footprint is a measure of carbon dioxide only. You could have a pretty good carbon footprint and still be a terrible person environmentally speaking.

For example, when you eat meat, you don’t directly emit carbon dioxide. It’s true that methane is converted to carbon dioxide eventually, but that’s not the end of the story.

Methane is a really powerful greenhouse gas. It’s 28 to 50 times more potent than carbon dioxide, and it doesn’t stick around as long, either. If you want to compare how bad methane is, you have to convert it into an equivalent amount of carbon dioxide. This is called methane-equivalent carbon dioxide, and I’ll call it CO2e for short.

If you take meat-eating into account, then the amount of CO2e emitted by a person’s diet can be twice as large as the amount of CO2 emitted by the same person’s driving. I think that’s a pretty big deal.

And there are a bunch of other greenhouse gases besides methane.

I don’t want to sound like I’m saying that we don’t have to worry about carbon dioxide. We absolutely do. It’s the most important greenhouse gas. And carbon footprint is a pretty good approximation of the greenhouse gases we emit. But if you’re going to worry about climate change, you should be worrying about global warming, not carbon dioxide.

The problem is that we don’t have a good word for the amount of global warming you’re responsible for. I would like to be able to worry about my warming footprint, but it’s not an actual term people use. And that’s why people worry about their carbon footprint instead.

And this matters. Because when we say that we have to get carbon to zero, that’s not the real goal. The real goal is to get global warming to zero.

If we have to stop producing new cars, we should do that, but that’s not the only way we could stop producing more global warming. We could use different materials, or recycle the cars we make, or make them in a way that produces less global warming.

I think the most common response to the idea of global warming is to be skeptical. This is really common. I find it hard to argue against. But the idea of carbon footprint is pretty clear and pretty uncontroversial. We can all agree that we have a carbon footprint. We can all agree that it’s not great to have a carbon footprint. So if I say “I’m worried about my carbon footprint” that’s a totally uncontroversial thing to say.

But that’s not the right thing to be worried about. I’m not sure what it’s called to worry about your carbon footprint while not worrying about the greenhouse gases you’re emitting and the global warming you’re causing. But it might be a type of climate change denial.

I think you can understand why people are scared.

We have some very strong feelings about global warming, and we need to find a way to communicate about it.

There are still problems with the climate forecast. But it’s still a much lower-dimensional problem than weather, and it’s a lot easier to understand.

prompt: Personal essay idea: my grandfather was a lineman for 35 years and spent his whole life making sure the lights stayed on. Now I work on grid-scale battery storage and I think about him a lot. I want to write about the continuity between his job and mine, and about how invisible the grid is to people who depend on it. ~1500 words, first person.
response:
When I was in high school, I spent a summer working as a lineman’s helper for the utility company that served the town I grew up in. It was the summer after I finished junior year, and I was eighteen, which made me old enough to help, even though I’d be in college by fall.

My grandfather was a lineman, and it was my first and last chance to work on the jobsite with him, so I took it.

Linemen are the ones who maintain the distribution system, the network of transformers and power lines that get electricity from the big transmission system to houses and businesses. When a storm takes out a tree, and it comes down on top of a wire, a lineman has to make sure it’s safe and then splice in a replacement. When a transformer blows, a lineman has to make sure the problem is fixed and then put a new one in place. Linemen are the ones who go to your house to install a meter. If the power goes out, linemen are the ones who fix it.

You probably won’t ever meet your lineman, because they’ll be out fixing something else. Your power company probably has a few dozen of them, and they spend most of their time on the road.

When I was a child, I thought linemen were like a secret society. They wore a certain kind of coverall and certain kinds of shoes. They had funny hats that they had to take off before going inside. Their trucks had names, and every truck had its own garage. They had funny words that they used in their jobs, like “hot” and “dead” and “guy.”

I thought they were the best kind of people. They were tough and brave, and they knew how to fix everything. They were really, really cool.

I didn’t know anything about electricity or power grids. I knew that power companies had power plants, but I thought that was just where they “made” electricity. I thought that it was a big building, and it was always on, and they just “put it” into the power lines and then it went to the houses.

I knew that there were high voltage lines that were very dangerous. You had to be careful not to get too close to them or else they would electrocute you. I thought that you had to be a superhero to be able to work on them.

The first day of the job, my dad, who was also a lineman, took me to my grandfather and showed him to me. My grandfather was not as big or as tough as my dad. He was a lot less serious and a lot more fun.

I was really excited to be working on the jobsite with my grandfather, but I didn’t get to spend very much time with him. The first week was mostly training.

For the first part of the summer, I learned how to do things that were very basic. I helped dig holes. I learned how to string wire. I learned how to make sure that the guys, which are the cables that support the poles, were strong enough to hold the poles up.

After I learned some of the basic stuff, I learned to drive the truck. There are different kinds of trucks that linemen use. My grandfather drove a bucket truck, which had a big platform that could go up and down. We used this to work on poles and transformers. I drove a small truck called a utility truck, which was used to transport equipment and tools.

For the last few weeks of the summer, I learned how to do things that were more advanced. I learned how to fix problems with wires. I learned how to make sure that the connections between wires were good. I learned how to make sure that the transformers were working correctly.

During the summer, I learned a lot of new words. There were a lot of things that I didn’t know the names of. I learned that the poles were called “poles,” and the transformers were called “transformers,” and the wires were called “wires.” I learned that the things that the wires were attached to the poles with were called “brackets.” I learned that the wires that connected the poles to each other were called “spans.”

The most important word that I learned was “dead.” Linemen use this word a lot. When they say that a wire is “dead,” it means that it’s not connected to a power source and it’s safe to touch. When they say that a wire is “hot,” it means that it’s connected to a power source and you shouldn’t touch it.

I learned this when I got on the bucket truck for the first time. My grandfather and I were working on a transformer, and my grandfather told me to go on the bucket and touch the wires.

I didn’t want to touch the wires, so I said that I didn’t want to. My grandfather said that I could touch them and that it would be okay, and that they were “dead.”

I touched the wires and nothing happened. I touched the wires again and nothing happened. I touched the wires a lot of times and nothing happened.

That night, I asked my grandfather why it was okay to touch the wires. He told me that they were “dead,” which meant that they were not connected to a power source. He told me that I had to be very careful not to touch wires that were “hot.”

The most important thing that I learned during the summer was how to be careful. You had to be careful to not touch hot wires, and you had to be careful to make sure that you were working on the right wires, and you had to be careful to make sure that everything was safe.

I had never been that careful about anything before. I was used to being pretty reckless and not being very careful about things. I knew that this was a good thing to learn, though.

I was really glad that I had spent that summer with my grandfather. It was the first time that I spent a lot of time with him. He was my favorite relative.

He wasn’t always around. I didn’t see him very often, but when I did, he was always there for me. He helped me with my homework, and he helped me fix my bicycle when it broke, and he took me to the store when I needed something.

My dad wasn’t as good about that. He was pretty busy and he didn’t always have time to help me. I liked my grandfather more.

I was really sad when he died, because I wasn’t going to be able to see him anymore. I still miss him a lot.

I think about him a lot when I’m working. I know that he would be proud of me for doing this job, even though it’s not exactly the same as his. I think that he would be really happy to see that I’m doing what I love.

prompt: Personal essay idea: my grandfather was a lineman for 35 years and spent his whole life making sure the lights stayed on. Now I work on grid-scale battery storage and I think about him a lot. I want to write about the continuity between his job and mine, and about how invisible the grid is to people who depend on it. ~1500 words, first person.
response:
When I was 10, I asked my dad what it was like to climb up a utility pole. He described the harness and the rope, and how you had to tie a knot in the rope to keep you from falling. He said you had to tie it tight enough to catch you, but loose enough that you could still climb.
