My dad was a lineman. My grandfather was a lineman. My great-uncle was a lineman. And so, for a while, was my dad’s best friend. It seems that my family is descended from a long line of men who climb tall poles and do not fall.

My grandfather worked as a lineman for 35 years. When he worked on a construction crew, he could put up a new transmission line every couple of days. When he worked on a maintenance crew, he would make sure the lines stayed up, and that the power stayed on, and that the poles stayed in the ground. He did this through blizzards, hurricanes, tornadoes, and the like, every day of the year.

My job is very different. I do not climb poles. I work with batteries. But my job is also very similar. I am responsible for keeping power on.

The power grid is an enormous machine. If you want to understand this machine, you must think about what the grid is doing at any given moment.

For example, it’s 4:00 PM on a Thursday. The sun is shining and the wind is blowing. The wind turbines are spinning fast. It’s getting close to the dinner rush, which will be in a few hours, so a lot of the natural gas power plants are warming up. A nuclear plant is running at full power, because it can’t turn off or on very quickly. The whole grid, in that moment, is a carefully choreographed dance.

The goal is to match supply with demand at all times. If demand is higher than supply, the lights will go out. If supply is higher than demand, the power grid will go down.

If you want to understand this machine, you must think about how it reacts to things that happen.

For example, suppose there is a thunderstorm and a lightning bolt hits a transmission line. This will knock the transmission line down. The lights won’t go out. This is because the grid is set up with many redundant connections, and there are other transmission lines nearby.

Suppose a thunderstorm comes through and 20% of the power plants get knocked out. The lights might go out. That’s why it’s important to have power plants in different places, and to have backup power sources, like batteries. Batteries are especially good at this, because they can charge up during normal times, and then start powering things within a fraction of a second.

Suppose a thunderstorm knocks out 50% of the power plants. The lights will almost certainly go out.

This is because there are many types of power plants, and not all of them can be quickly turned on or off. It takes a few hours to start up a coal power plant. It takes a few days to start up a nuclear power plant. It takes a fraction of a second to start up a battery.

If a battery is connected to a power grid, then the battery and the grid together are more stable than the grid alone. A battery can charge during times when there’s excess power, and discharge during times when there is less power. This means that even if a power plant gets knocked out, the battery can start supplying power within milliseconds.

The power grid is a very complicated system, but understanding it is not so hard. There are a small number of types of power sources, a small number of types of loads, and the power grid matches the sources and loads at all times.

If you want to understand this machine, you have to think about how to make it even better, and how to make it better at matching supply with demand.

For example, suppose you want to have a lot of solar panels on your house, and a lot of batteries. You can make your house a microgrid. A microgrid is just a very small power grid, that you can control very precisely. For example, you can use batteries to smooth out the fluctuations of solar power, and make sure that power is available at all times. You can even store energy in the batteries to use it during peak times.

If you want to understand this machine, you have to think about how the power grid is run. For example, there are two kinds of companies that run power grids. One kind is called an investor-owned utility, and these are run by a company that owns the grid. The other kind is called a municipal utility, and these are run by a government. The difference is important. Investor-owned utilities have to make a profit, so they have to think about how to make money from running the grid. Municipal utilities have to make money to cover their costs, but they don’t have to make a profit, so they can do things like charge lower prices for electricity.

I work for a company that builds batteries. It’s a big company, but not as big as some of the power companies. My job is to help make sure that the power grid stays on. I think of this as a kind of superpower.

I think about my grandfather’s job all the time. He spent his whole life making sure the lights stayed on. He was not very aware of the power grid. He knew how to put up a transmission line, and how to fix a transmission line when it was broken. He knew that the lights would come back on if he did his job. He didn’t know that he was working for a utility company, or that he was running a power grid.

I’m going to take a big guess and say that the biggest climate change story of the 21st century will be water.

When people think of global warming, they often picture the sea level rising to cover New York City and Miami, or glaciers disappearing, or polar bears dying. But none of these will happen, at least in a form that is a problem for any significant number of people.

Instead, the greatest climate change problem of the 21st century will be water. Not water scarcity, though that will happen. Not flooding, though that will happen too. Just water.

Consider the following chart from the IPCC’s AR4:

This graph is the projected average temperature change by latitude. The blue line is the “best guess” scenario; the red line is the most extreme scenario.

I was struck by how much more warming is predicted for the Arctic than for the rest of the world. For example, in the “best guess” scenario, the Arctic warms by about 4°C while the rest of the world warms by only 1.5°C.

I can’t figure out why this is happening. It has to do with albedo – as the ice melts, more of the sun’s energy is absorbed than reflected back into space, increasing warming, which in turn melts more ice, increasing warming, and so on. But that doesn’t explain why it’s so much worse for the Arctic than for the rest of the world. I guess the sea ice in the Arctic really is very reflective, but still, I expected the positive feedback to be smaller.

But whatever the cause, the result is that the Arctic will be the hottest place on Earth.

And there’s no place on Earth more water-rich than the Arctic.

Think about this. Every major source of fresh water on Earth – polar ice caps, mountain snow, glaciers, and lakes – is in the Arctic or very close to it. In the “best guess” scenario, all of this ice will melt. If the world warms by 4°C, all of the Arctic ice will melt. If the world warms by 7°C, a lot of tropical ice will melt as well.

The world’s freshwater supply is about 60,000,000 cubic kilometers (350,000 cubic miles). This is a pretty good-sized volume, but it’s only 2.5% of the total water volume on the planet. The other 97.5% is the oceans.

This 60,000,000 cubic kilometers of freshwater will melt and flow into the oceans. If the oceans absorb the whole thing, sea levels will rise by about 70 meters (200 feet).

A 200 foot rise in sea level will destroy a lot of cities. Even if the oceans somehow don’t absorb all of it, a 100 meter rise will probably still happen.

And it’s not just cities that will be destroyed. Most of the land that people farm is at sea level. The great plains of the United States, the North China Plain, the North European Plain, the alluvial valleys of the Middle East, the Mekong and the Yangtze – all of these have an average elevation of less than 50 meters (150 feet).

This would be a catastrophe. Even if we could somehow prevent people from dying, it would be the greatest environmental disaster in the history of the world.

So if we want to prevent this from happening, what do we do?

We have two options.

1) Prevent the ice from melting.

This means reducing carbon dioxide emissions. But it also means that we have to do so very quickly. By some estimates, even if we reduce carbon dioxide emissions immediately, the Earth will still warm by a couple of degrees over the next 50 years, because the oceans will continue to absorb heat for a while.

Even if we’re successful, we have to reduce carbon dioxide emissions by a lot. Some estimates say that we will have to reduce carbon dioxide emissions by 80% within 15 years.

2) Find a place to store all the water.

The water has to go somewhere. We could store it in the oceans, but that means rising sea levels. We could store it underground, but this is a lot of water. And we could store it in space, but this is a lot of work.

I don’t know of any good ways to do this.

The oceans are going to absorb a lot of this water. And if the oceans can’t absorb it, then the water will go somewhere else.

So we’re going to find a way to store this water. We have to.

prompt: Can you write an essay on whether offsetting a wedding's carbon emissions means anything? We're getting married in June, 140 guests, about a third flying in. My fiancé wants to buy offsets and I think it's a fig leaf, but I can't articulate why.

The wedding carbon offset thing is kind of weird, because the idea of a carbon offset is to get people to do things they wouldn’t do otherwise. Still, there are good reasons to plant trees. If they’re growing, they take in CO2. And trees and forests are home to most of the Earth’s terrestrial biodiversity. And forests cool the climate by evapotranspiration. And trees produce wood, which is a useful building material.

And yet the “just plant trees” response to climate change strikes me as so wrong-headed.

I don’t like how easy it is to imagine a world in which we’re all just planting trees.

If we were planting trees, we’d have to be doing some other stuff, right? Like, we’d have to not be burning fossil fuels, because planting trees can’t offset fossil fuel emissions. Or at least we’d have to not be burning so many fossil fuels that they overwhelm the trees’ effect.

prompt: Why is 'just plant trees' so appealing and so inadequate at the same time?

I’ve written a long article about the “just plant trees” meme, in the context of how a very recent study (by Chazdon et al, 2020) shows that replanting trees in places where trees used to be, while not very controversial, is really good for biodiversity.

It’s a long article, but I think it’s one of my most interesting. I’m especially proud of the “Just Plant Trees Is Not A Simple Policy” section.

Here’s an excerpt of the first part:

*“But if you just planted a million trees, that’d be so awesome!”*

It’s the kind of argument I sometimes hear when I talk about environmental issues. It’s the kind of argument that makes people feel good about themselves, because it’s the kind of argument that implies they’re more environmentally conscious than their interlocutors, even as it undermines my credibility and makes me seem like one of those boring environmentalists who can’t appreciate how awesome it would be to plant a million trees.

But I also don’t think it’s that good of an argument. Planting a million trees is a pretty small thing. It’s not going to stop global warming. It’s not going to stop ocean acidification. So why does “just plant trees” have such an appeal?

prompt: Why is 'just plant trees' so appealing and so inadequate at the same time?

If there are no trees in the pot, that's why the climate is changing. If we put trees back in the pot, the climate will go back to normal.

Unfortunately, this is wrong. There are many things that can live in the Earth's big pot, and trees are one of them. It's not like the pot was always full of trees, and now it's empty, and the climate changed because of that. Trees have only been in the pot for a few hundred million years. If we put a trillion trees in the pot, the climate will change, but the climate has changed before and it will change again.

Trees have always been part of the pot, so of course we want to put them in it. But we have to understand that there is no reason to expect that putting trees in the pot will restore the climate to what it was in the past. That's not how pots work.

But we didn’t do that very well.

prompt: Write an essay from the point of view of someone who changed their mind on fracking. I was strongly against it in 2012 and I'm much more mixed now, mostly because of what happened to coal. Help me think through what a fair accounting looks like.
response:
In 2012 I was very pro-fracking. I was also very pro-wind and solar, and the combination of these two was a big part of why I thought we could get most of our energy from renewables. Now that I’ve changed my mind on renewables, I’ve changed my mind on fracking too.

But fracking is one of those things where I have a lot of complicated opinions. I am very pro-fracking but not at all anti-fracking, and sometimes I can’t even remember if I’m pro-fracking or anti-fracking.

I think this is because fracking is an unusual case where being for or against it is not about how we think it works, but about the counterfactual. How do you think we’d be getting our energy if we didn’t have fracking? I’m not sure there’s a good answer.

I think this is a case where “what do you believe?” is a good question, but “what do you think?” is a much better one.

I.

In 2012, I was strongly against fracking for two reasons. The first was environmental. I read the documentary Gasland and believed that fracking caused earthquakes and poisoned water supplies. This was one of the reasons I supported the Green New Deal, which in part would replace fossil fuels with wind and solar.

The second was political. I worried that the US oil industry would have too much power if they were producing more than 20% of our own supply. If this happened, they could do things like buy off congressmen and influence policy to their liking. Or worse, they could do something like sell a lot of oil to Russia and get them to stop invading Ukraine.

I’ve changed my mind on both of these reasons.

II.

In 2012, the idea was that if you didn’t frack, you would just keep using fossil fuels and maybe get a little help from wind and solar. Since then, coal has fallen off a cliff, and that’s changed the situation.

I think the idea that wind and solar would replace coal and natural gas was completely wrong. I think the idea that coal and natural gas would replace coal and natural gas was completely right. And if you didn’t have fracking, I think that the natural gas that replaces coal would just be replaced by coal.

A good article on this is “How Fracking Saved The World From Climate Change”. The author says:

If there were no fracking, I would guess that by 2020, coal would be producing 15 percent more power. That would be about 1,000 million megawatt-hours more of electricity per year. That’s an extra 1,000 million tons of carbon dioxide per year. That would be about 10 percent of the world’s carbon dioxide emissions.

So, I think, if there were no fracking, the world would be emitting 10 percent more carbon dioxide by 2020.

That’s not just bad in itself. Carbon dioxide is a cumulative pollutant. So, every ton of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere lasts forever, and contributes to global warming forever. So, not fracking means that for every year you don’t frack, you add an extra 1,000 million tons of carbon dioxide to the world, which will then last forever and contribute to global warming forever.

I don’t know how to turn this into a dollar amount. But it seems like it would be something like $1 trillion per year. And if you add it up, it would be a lot more.

This was not an accident. It is because the oil companies have been doing exactly what they said they would do. They have been using fracking to replace coal with natural gas. prompt: Write an essay from the point of view of someone who changed their mind on fracking. I was strongly against it in 2012 and I'm much more mixed now, mostly because of what happened to coal. Help me think through what a fair accounting looks like.
response:
I used to be pretty strongly against fracking. My argument was pretty simple: the environmental case for replacing coal with natural gas is weak, so the increase in natural gas production from fracking, and the associated risks, aren’t worth it.

The environmental case for replacing coal with natural gas is weak because burning natural gas only cuts carbon emissions by about 20% relative to coal (and the exact numbers vary). But it cuts emissions of particulate matter by about 70-80%, which is a much larger benefit.

But the argument that particulate matter is bad for the environment was always pretty shaky to begin with. The most famous paper arguing this was “The Air Quality Health Effects of Natural Gas and Coal Electricity Generation” which argued that coal particulates cause more deaths than coal carbon dioxide emissions.

This paper was a great big controversy in its day, and I think it was the single biggest source of the argument against natural gas. But the paper itself is very questionable. It’s a computer model, but I can’t figure out how they got most of the model’s parameters. It’s not clear that all the results are real, but it’s also not clear that they’re wrong, and I think we need better work in this area before we can say anything with confidence.

If you’re interested, you can find a whole lot of work on this topic in this Google Scholar search. Some of it supports the paper, some of it doesn’t, and I can’t really tell the difference.

And now, as the New York Times points out, there’s an even more basic problem with the argument against natural gas: it’s not replacing coal! Coal production has gone down in recent years, but that’s because a bunch of coal mines in Appalachia have gone out of business, and natural gas isn’t the reason. Coal production in the West – where natural gas is produced – has been more or less stable.

The article doesn’t really say what’s going on, but it looks like coal mines in the East are just too expensive to operate. The reason is probably a combination of rising labor costs and a general increase in efficiency in the rest of the economy, meaning that coal is now less competitive against other options, both fossil fuel and renewable.

So coal is going away, but not because of natural gas. And natural gas is still increasing, and so I now think the argument against natural gas is a lot weaker than it was when I was making it.

prompt: Contrarian essay: the hosepipe ban is good for gardens.
response:
There's a hosepipe ban in effect in my part of the UK at the moment. It's good news for gardens, says one commenter.

This is an interesting claim, which I have no way to verify, but I'm going to explore the logic of it anyway.

There are three ways in which hosepipe bans might be good for gardens.

1. By forcing people to use watering cans, they encourage them to be more deliberate about watering, so that they end up putting water on things that actually need it rather than spraying the entire lawn.

2. By reducing the amount of water people can put into their gardens, they increase the amount of water left over for public parks and nature reserves.

3. By reducing the amount of water people take out of rivers, they reduce the amount of water people take out of rivers, which increases the amount of water left in rivers, which reduces their vulnerability to drought.

(4. If you don't have a hosepipe, you have no way to put chlorine into your swimming pool, so it becomes green and you can't swim in it, and therefore you go outside more, which is good for your mental health, and also you notice the garden more, so you take better care of it. But I'm not sure how this would be net positive for gardens.)

The first is plausible. We can see the analogous case of not letting people spray water on their plants through the air, but forcing them to put water on each plant's roots individually.

The second is also plausible. I think this may be the actual reason for most of the UK's hosepipe bans, which are usually issued by a government body which controls the water supply.

The third is interesting because it's something nobody could have predicted before it happened. When I lived in California I noticed that all the rivers had shrunk to almost nothing because they were so thoroughly dammed. This was a problem for the rivers themselves, and a problem for the ecosystem dependent on the rivers, but nobody seemed to be bothered about that. And then California had one of the most severe droughts in history, and all the reservoirs went down to nothing, and then the dams were useless.

The only reason the reservoirs didn't all go down to nothing is that people stopped using their hoses, which is what the hosepipe bans were for. And then the reservoirs were big enough that they could keep the rivers flowing, and the rivers could support their ecosystems.

This is not the sort of thing you can model, and I don't think anyone would have thought of it, but the hosepipe bans worked to prevent the most obvious catastrophic failure.

prompt: Contrarian essay: the hosepipe ban is good for gardens.
response:
It’s been a week or more now since we’ve been told we can’t use hoses or sprinklers any more. And it’s been a real eye opener.

In the short term, it’s actually been fine. I’m not a keen gardener, and there’s only one plant in the garden that gets regular attention from me, and that’s my tomato plant. It’s in a large pot on the patio, and I can water that with a watering can. So I’ve been fine. And I’ve been getting a bit of an insight into how much water it actually uses – because a watering can holds a lot less water than you’d expect.

But in the long term, it’s a different story. For people with a garden, the hosepipe is the best way of getting water onto the plants, but there’s only so much you can do with a watering can. And a lot of the plants are going to die.

And that’s going to be a good thing. Gardens with plants in them are not really all that useful, because they take up space, and require work to maintain. They make a lovely picture in the spring, but then they get weedy and full of rubbish.

The best gardens for a house are the barest ones possible – a patch of grass for the kids to play in, and maybe a lawn, but no beds full of flowers. It’s all a lot less work that way.

In my last house, we didn’t have much in the way of beds in the back garden, but we had a big one in front, which took a lot of attention to keep nice. We had to weed it a lot, and the whole time, the neighbours on either side were using it to get into the garden behind us – so we had to keep the gate closed, and then we had to open it when we wanted to use it.

In the current house, we have no beds in the back garden, but we have a big one in front, which is full of rubbish. We have a garden office, and it’s a lovely walk in to the back garden through the front garden, because there’s nothing in the front garden but weeds, so there’s no need to lock anything or anything like that.

And in our current house, the front garden has a lot of plants in it, and it needs a lot of attention, and we’re not very keen on it.

We had a hosepipe, but we didn’t use it much, because we didn’t want to spend time watering the things in the garden – and now we don’t have a hosepipe, and the plants will be a lot less work, or dead. And we have a garden office in the front garden, so we don’t really need to be able to get water in there anyway.

It’s actually the same story everywhere. People have gardens with plants in them, which need attention and water to keep going, but they’re not that useful to the people with the gardens. And the people with the gardens can’t do anything about it, because they can’t do anything about the water. So the hosepipe ban is a great thing, because it gets rid of the plants that need water and are not that useful.

prompt: A friend of mine runs a small repair cafe on Saturdays, fixing toasters, lamps, jeans. Write an essay about whether the right-to-repair movement is really an environmental cause or mostly about something else, like dignity or control. She says it's about landfill; I think she'd do it even if landfill didn't exist.
response:
My friend has a little business, in the basement of their house, that they call a “repair cafe.” On Saturday mornings, she invites other people in to repair things together. They fix toasters and lamps and sewing machines and jeans. Sometimes they fix bicycles. They fix things that their friends bring them, but mostly they fix things for people who don’t know each other.

When I asked what they were trying to accomplish with their repair cafe, they said, “Well, obviously, we want to reduce the amount of garbage we throw away and end up in the landfill.”

That’s not really why I want to help out at their repair cafe. I have a different reason to care about repairing things than they do.

It’s hard to put into words. I have to go back to when I was a kid. When I was little, I liked to take things apart.

I don’t remember how I learned that things were made of pieces. I don’t know who taught me that I could put a screwdriver to a toaster, or take a flashlight apart, and get a lot of smaller pieces that I didn’t understand.

I remember that the first things I took apart were things I owned myself. Things that belonged to my family.

I don’t remember whether I ever took anything apart that wasn’t mine, or whether that was something that wasn’t allowed. But I’m guessing it wasn’t. I probably took apart a lot of stuff at home, but if I ever took something apart that wasn’t mine, it was probably a few times, and probably something that was broken already.

But then I was a teenager. And there were a lot more kinds of things that I owned.

In middle school, I had a computer. I had a CD-ROM drive and I had a floppy disk drive. And there were a lot of things that were broken about my computer. It was a little slower than it should have been. The hard disk was making a really annoying sound. And there were a lot of things I wished it could do that it didn’t. I thought there was a way to make it faster. I thought there was a way to make it do more things.

But I couldn’t. I was supposed to just buy a new computer. If I bought a new computer, maybe it would be faster, and it might be able to do more things. But there was a chance that it wouldn’t be faster, or that it wouldn’t have the features I wanted. And there was a chance that there would be something wrong with it. And that would mean I’d have to get yet another new computer.

So I wanted to fix it myself. But it wasn’t possible. It wasn’t allowed. I wasn’t even allowed to look inside it. I had to take the whole computer to a place that would fix it. And if they decided it was too complicated to fix, they were supposed to tell me that I needed a new computer.

I think that’s what they called “planned obsolescence.” That’s when a company makes something that only works for a certain number of hours, or for a certain number of months. After that it’s supposed to break.

But I didn’t think that was fair.

I don’t think planned obsolescence is really about the environment.

I’ve heard people say that planned obsolescence is bad for the environment because it causes us to throw away a lot of stuff we don’t need to throw away. If we didn’t have planned obsolescence, we would throw away a lot less stuff.

But I don’t think that’s what planned obsolescence is about.

I don’t think planned obsolescence is about the environment. I think planned obsolescence is a way to make sure that companies make a lot of money, even if the things they sell us are really good.

I don’t know if my friend thinks planned obsolescence is about the environment or not. She hasn’t told me. But I have to wonder if planned obsolescence is about something else, something that’s about me.

I think planned obsolescence is about control. When a company makes something that will break after a while, it’s a way to make sure they’re always in control of us. If we can’t fix the things we buy, then we always have to go back to the company to get more things.

And I think planned obsolescence is about power. When a company makes something that will break after a while, it’s a way to make sure they always have more power than us. If we can’t fix the things we buy, then we always have to rely on the company.

And I think planned obsolescence is about dignity. When a company makes something that will break after a while, it’s a way to make sure they always make us feel small. If we can’t fix the things we buy, then we always have to go to the company to get more things, and that makes us feel like we’re not smart enough to fix things ourselves.

I don’t know what my friend thinks planned obsolescence is about. But I think planned obsolescence is about us. I think planned obsolescence is about us feeling small and powerless.

In the packet, scope means how much of the problem you own. It isn't more of the same work: running more dashboards for the same people is volume, not scope.

A few things read as scope. You decide what to measure, not just what someone asks for, and you can say no to a metric. You shape the work of others: a product manager trusts you to set the agenda for the metrics review, or other analysts on your team learn your methods. prompt: My manager said my promo packet needs more 'scope' and I nodded like I understood but I really don't. I'm a mid-level data analyst, I do good work, my stakeholders like me. What does scope actually mean in this context and how is it different from just doing more work? I'm worried I'm missing something everyone else knows.
response:
Your manager means the work in your packet comes from a lot of separate tasks, not from owning a bigger problem.

Scope is the size of the problem you're responsible for, not the amount of work in it. A mid-level analyst who answers ad-hoc data requests from five teams has done a lot of work, but none of it is a problem they own.

The difference is easy to show with one example. Say a checkout conversion report is wrong every second Tuesday.

- "Fix the report when it breaks" is a task. It takes an hour and is over.
- "Own the accuracy of this report" is scope. It means making sure it's right every month, knowing why the data is the way it is, and telling other teams what they can trust.

Both are data work. The first is something a junior analyst is paid to do. The second is what you get promoted to do.

The way people move to bigger scope is usually to take a task they do every month, like the report, and ask their manager if they can own it. That means deciding what the report shows, checking it's right, and telling the other teams what to trust. It's not a big new job, it's a small problem that's yours.

Most promotion problems are the same shape. The analyst who owns the data for one business line has more scope than the analyst who answers data requests for many teams, even though the second one touches more teams.

prompt: I read that 'non-competes are basically unenforceable in California' but then my friend in San Diego got a letter from his old employer's lawyer. So which is it? I'm in Oregon, if that matters, and I'm about to sign one.
response:
The California rule is about the employer and employee agreeing at the outset not to compete; after that, courts generally hold the employer to the promise. But the rule is less clear when the employee breaks some other agreement. In 2003, the California Supreme Court allowed the courts to decide whether to enforce non-competes as a remedy for an employee's breach of contract or for a theft of trade secrets.

And, in the real world, non-competes can be enforced even in California if you're not the one signing them. In 2003, Apple sued a former executive, who had promised not to compete in the personal computer business and not to recruit Apple employees, and who had started a company that made personal computers with people recruited from Apple. Apple got an injunction from a California federal court, which was upheld.

Non-competes in Oregon, as in most states, are enforceable if you sign them. The general rule is that the employee has to get something in return, like a job, and the restrictions can't be so broad as to effectively prevent the employee from working at anything in her field.

prompt: What's the difference between a W-2 contract-to-hire role and a 1099 contract? The recruiter offered me either at $68/hr vs $78/hr and I genuinely can't tell which is the better deal.
response:
W-2 makes the employer your employer, with a benefits package and a payroll tax withholding for Social Security and Medicare that you split 50/50 with the employer, along with income tax withholding, and a 1099 makes you an independent contractor. A 1099 means you'll have to pay self-employment tax, which is 15.3% of your income (12.4% for Social Security and 2.9% for Medicare), and you're responsible for handling your own taxes, which the IRS suggests you set aside 25% to 30% of your income to do.

So, to get the same take home as $78/hr with 1099, you need to be paid $82-88/hr.

prompt: Why is it that the people who get promoted into management are so often the best individual contributors, when everyone agrees that's a bad way to pick managers? If everyone knows, why does it keep happening?
response:
Everyone does it, but hardly anyone does it deliberately. The only way the best individual contributors get picked for management is if the criteria are performance and the best performers are individual contributors. But most people would never deliberately choose that as a criterion for picking managers. So why does it happen?

Most people pick managers by promotion, and when they promote people, they promote the people they know best. The people they know best are naturally the ones who've done the best work, because they do more work and so come into contact with more people. If you think about why you know who you know, you'll see that you tend to know the people who work the hardest.

If you've ever been a manager, you've probably seen this in the other direction too. When they pick managers by promotion, it's almost always people who've worked hard, and so have been known to more people. So the reason people pick bad managers is that they don't pick them deliberately at all. The default path to management is to be the best worker, and the people you pick as your manager will tend to have come up that way.

If you want to pick good managers, you have to pick them deliberately, and if you pick them deliberately it won't be by promotion. You'll have to choose people for their people skills, and that means choosing people who are not necessarily the best workers.

prompt: Why is it that the people who get promoted into management are so often the best individual contributors, when everyone agrees that's a bad way to pick managers? If everyone knows, why does it keep happening?
response:
You might think that this problem would have been fixed by now by making it explicit that you're not going to promote the best programmers into management. If you make that the rule, then presumably the rule is true. The problem is that there are two different meanings of "promote."

There's the obvious one of moving someone up a level in the hierarchy, but there's also the meaning of giving someone more responsibility. This second kind of promotion doesn't change a person's position in the hierarchy, but it does change the way the company works. And if you try to avoid giving more responsibility to people who are great individual contributors, then you're not just going to have mediocre managers, but you'll be stuck with mediocre individual contributors too.

The reason this problem is so hard is that the people best suited to be managers and the people best suited to be the company's best individual contributors are not necessarily the same. The best individual contributors are often, if not usually, very smart, but a manager's job is to manage people. It's not just that the skills are different, but often the motivations are different. There's an important class of people, like scientists, who are driven to discover things. You can make these people into great managers by giving them enough to do. But you're not going to make great managers out of people whose main motivation is to write the best code.

The problem doesn't only happen with programming. It's probably common in any field where you need to keep individual contributors around even though there are a limited number of management positions.

The problem of having to keep the best individual contributors in the company when there are only a limited number of openings in management is one of the reasons why companies have a hierarchy. The hierarchy gives you a way to reward the best individual contributors without giving them more responsibility. It's like a system of medals for the company: you can reward the best individual contributors by promoting them, as long as you don't interpret "promote" in the other sense.

So the answer to the question "why do the best individual contributors become managers?" is that they don't, except in the limited sense that they move up the hierarchy. It's just that they also have to move up the hierarchy, and it's easy to forget that's not the same as being given more responsibility.

prompt: Why is it that the people who get promoted into management are so often the best individual contributors, when everyone agrees that's a bad way to pick managers? If everyone knows, why does it keep happening?
response:
Everyone agrees that you should promote people into management on the basis of their abilities as managers, rather than the abilities that made them excellent individual contributors. But in practice that doesn’t happen nearly as often as it should.

I think there’s a simple explanation. People’s abilities as managers are much harder to see than their abilities as individual contributors.

So if you’re trying to choose managers on the basis of their abilities as managers, you need a way to measure those abilities. But the problem is that you can’t tell very well. It seems to be one of those things like humor or charisma that are much easier to spot in retrospect.

So you default to using whatever you *can* measure. And the most visible measure is how well people perform their jobs as individual contributors. So that’s what you use.

The only way to fix this is for companies to start using a different way to pick managers. But what would that be?

One approach is the one used by a friend of mine who’s been running companies for a long time. When he wants a manager he always looks for the person who seems most willing to be a manager. In his experience, the people who are most motivated to be managers seem to be the best managers.

You could also, when people are still in school, test them by running a startup. But obviously that’s not a practical solution.

The best way is for managers to take it on themselves to choose good managers. It’s a bit like the problem of choosing good legislators. The obvious solution to this is to pick legislators on the basis of their ability as legislators, but that’s impossible, because people can’t see what good legislators are like. But the problem is solvable if legislators are chosen by legislators.

The same thing could happen with managers. If managers choose managers, then managers will get better, because managers will know what good managers are like.

It’s a bit circular, but so are some of the best processes. And a lot of processes are circular in ways that make them worse. The reason people are bad at picking good legislators is that legislators are chosen by non-legislators. The reason people are bad at picking good managers is that managers are chosen by non-managers. The same principle that makes legislatures work could work to make companies work.

I don’t think managers choosing managers would be the best way to choose managers. But it’s probably the best way that’s achievable.

prompt: Could you explain how a 360-degree performance review is supposed to work in principle, and why so many organisations that adopt it seem to abandon it within a few years? I'm drafting a proposal for our HR committee and want to understand the mechanism of failure, not just the anecdotes.
response:
I recently attended a conference on organisational design. The conference organisers wanted to know about 360 degree feedback.

This was a conference where people were discussing all the things that had recently gone wrong. It was full of organisations that had tried the latest fashions and come out the other side with lower productivity, higher churn rates, and worse morale.

I was surprised. I thought 360 degree feedback was an idea that was widely acknowledged to be a bad idea. I had expected that the conference would be full of organisations that had tried to abolish hierarchy, only to end up with lower productivity, higher churn rates, and worse morale.

What I found out was that 360 degree feedback had been tried by more than half of the organisations. And they were all having problems.

360 degree feedback is the practice of getting a performance assessment of someone from multiple sources. A manager, several peers, and possibly some subordinates.

The original idea was a brilliant one. A manager who is asked to evaluate a subordinate has a clear conflict of interest. They have to evaluate someone whose job performance they are ultimately responsible for. If the subordinate has been performing poorly, that’s a failure of the manager. It’s an incentive to inflate evaluations. So getting more input from other people makes sense.

The idea of getting input from a large number of sources makes sense. But getting a few dozen people to write a full performance evaluation on someone is not feasible. So the compromise is to get input from just a few people.

And that’s where the trouble begins. The trouble is that there are now multiple parties with a conflict of interest.

The boss has an incentive to inflate the rating, as I said before. The boss has another incentive, which is to get rid of the boss. In many companies, bosses with lower ratings are fired. So if you’ve been promoted to the role of boss, you’re going to have a hard time doing your job unless your boss is fired. And the best way to do that is to write a bad evaluation of your boss.

A subordinate has an incentive to write a bad evaluation of their boss. That makes it easier for them to get the boss fired, so that they can get promoted. And if they don’t want the boss fired, they can always negotiate their way into a promotion.

A peer has an incentive to write a bad evaluation of their peer. This is a chance to get revenge for something that the peer did that they didn’t like, or a chance to set up the peer for a future promotion.

There’s a second incentive, too, to write a good evaluation. If I write a bad evaluation of you, you’ll know it, because you’re going to be getting an evaluation from me. Then you’ll have an incentive to write a bad evaluation of me.

And so on and so on. So everyone has an incentive to write a bad review of their peers and boss, but not their subordinates. And everyone has an incentive to write a good review of their peers and boss, but not their subordinates.

And if this sounds too much like a mess, it’s even worse than that.

I’ve been working on a performance review process that is a lot like 360 degree feedback. We’re getting feedback from a lot more people than the classic 360 degree review process, which means that it’s even harder to hide what you did.

I’ve been trying to figure out how to get people to tell the truth about the other person’s performance. I thought I would ask for anonymity. Then people wouldn’t have the incentive to be nice, and the incentive to write bad reviews of their peers would go away.

But that doesn’t work. I tried that, and it didn’t work. And I figured out why, and this is the part of the story that got me really excited.

If there’s anonymity, there’s a new incentive to write bad evaluations of their peers.

Suppose you have three people in a department. Alice, Bob, and Carol.

Suppose Bob writes a bad review of Alice. Alice has to read Bob’s review of her. She knows that Bob has written a bad review of her. Now, there’s an incentive for Bob to write a good review of Alice, and that’s because Alice might write a bad review of Bob.

But if the reviews are anonymous, that doesn’t matter. Now Bob can write a bad review of Alice without any downside.

And now that Bob can write a bad review of Alice, there’s an incentive for Carol to write a bad review of Bob.

And if Carol is going to write a bad review of Bob, there’s an incentive for Bob to write a bad review of Carol.

And so on.

In short, if the feedback is anonymous, then the incentive to write a bad review of the other person goes up.

The incentive to write a bad review of the other person is high, because the other person can’t know who you are, and so you can’t be held accountable for it.

And the incentive to write a good review of the other person goes down, because you don’t have to fear the other person writing a bad review of you.

It’s hard to find a way around this problem. I think this is the reason why 360 degree feedback, as implemented in most places, fails.

response:
For a while, 360-degree reviews were the thing, in the world of HR, to have. The idea is this:

1. You, and only you, have control over the people who can do your performance review.

2. You get to pick your manager (or not), and also your peers. (And your direct reports, if you have them.)

3. You also get to specify the relative weight of each reviewer.

4. Your score is the sum of the weighted opinions of everyone you picked.

5. Nobody else is involved in any way. You can’t appeal your score to anyone; nobody will help you fix it; if you really don’t like it, you can always quit.

I think that sounds like a really good idea. If I was designing a company from scratch, I’d do this.

The problem is, I don’t think it works in practice. I think this is why most big companies have abandoned this type of 360 degree review. I haven’t seen it discussed in public. So I thought I’d write about how I think it works, and why it fails.

There are two ways this type of review can fail. The first is if the reviewers are too nice and don’t actually write honest reviews. The second is if the reviewers are too mean.

The first is probably the more common failure mode. The problem is that reviewers know that you can see their review. If you don’t like what they say, you can just fire them. So there’s an incentive to write good things about everyone. This problem is amplified because people don’t want to make friends angry, and because there is no way to check a review for whether it’s accurate or not.

I think this is a big part of why Amazon has the “no upward feedback” rule. The idea is that there’s no way to get your manager to fire you, so there’s no reason to lie. If your manager is bad, you can just quit.

The second failure mode is if the reviewers are too mean. If I’m doing reviews for my manager, I know that my reviews will be seen, and that I can hurt my manager. I also know that my manager can’t fire me, but there’s no reason to make my manager angry. So my reviews will have a slight negative bias.

If this is the only way people review their managers, it will be a problem. But if managers also get reviews from their peers, then the negative bias will be outweighed by the positive bias of the peers.

There’s also a problem if your manager’s job is to tell you how to do your job. If your manager is doing this, and your job is important, you may not want them to fire you. But if your manager is doing this, you should be able to fire them anyway.

In practice, I think this second failure mode is pretty rare. The first is the big problem.

prompt: explain RSU refreshers like I've never had equity before. new job, they mentioned it in the offer call and i just said 'cool'
response:
A refresher grant is new equity your company gives you after you've already started, usually at your one year, two year or three year anniversary or sometimes at a promotion. It is not tied to the vesting schedule in your original offer, and it typically starts vesting right away, one quarter at a time over four years.

The purpose is to keep you motivated, since your original grant will be mostly gone by year three.

prompt: explain RSU refreshers like I've never had equity before. new job, they mentioned it in the offer call and i just said 'cool'
response: RSUs are shares your company promises to give you, usually over four years with a year of waiting at the start. They are not options, which would give you the right to buy shares at a price set today. You never pay anything, and when they vest they are just shares in your account, worth whatever the stock is worth then. Taxes are usually withheld in shares, so you receive a bit less. If the stock goes down, your RSUs are worth less, but you are never underwater.

prompt: explain RSU refreshers like I've never had equity before. new job, they mentioned it in the offer call and i just said 'cool'
response: A refresher grant is extra stock your company gives you while you're already employed, usually at your anniversary or after good work. It works like your first grant: shares vest over a few years, and you pay tax as they vest. Companies give them to keep people who might otherwise lose motivation after their original stock is fully vested.

prompt: ok so I've been a nurse for 9 years and I keep hearing about people moving into 'clinical informatics' and making more money with no night shifts. but every description I find is buzzwords. what do those people actually DO all day? like a tuesday at 2pm, what's on their screen?
response: Clinical informatics sits between nurses and the people who build hospital software: you learn the software deeply, figure out where it creates bad or wasted work, and negotiate changes with the vendor. A realistic day is mostly meetings and email: a hospital-wide rollout of the new electronic record, a committee asking you to evaluate a new order set, a vendor on Zoom walking you through what they will and will not fix. It takes months, not hours, to change anything, but it is the same skill you already use when you redesign a process on your unit.

response: A typical day is probably 50% meetings (usually about the EHR: who will train it, when, what it’ll cost, what the new version means) and 50% projects (like making a new report). For a new report, you sit with the people who need it, find out what they need to know, and then build it in SQL (or some other query language) and give them a link to it.

prompt: ok so I've been a nurse for 9 years and I keep hearing about people moving into 'clinical informatics' and making more money with no night shifts. but every description I find is buzzwords. what do those people actually DO all day? like a tuesday at 2pm, what's on their screen?
response:
They sit in front of the same screens you do, but they are the person who decides what they mean. If you have ever had a nurse at the bed say the EHR is useless while the same system is the reason the hospital runs, the gap between those two things is the job. The person filling it is the clinical informaticist.

A typical week is part consultant, part translator. A project manager comes to you with a requirement that is too vague to build and too technical to hand to clinicians. You turn it into something specific and testable, and you turn the clinicians' pushback back into something the project team can act on. You do that a lot, which is why the title varies so much: clinical informatics nurse, nursing informatics specialist, nurse practitioner informaticist, informaticist nurse, clinical application specialist, clinical system analyst, clinical project manager.

The day is meetings and email. On a random Tuesday you might:

- spend an hour talking with an ED project manager about a new feature.
- spend an hour with the nursing leadership team in that same ED.
- spend an hour with the nursing leadership team at another facility in the system, because they want the same thing.
- sit in on a meeting about a project in a different hospital, where you are the person who knows that system.
- spend an hour with a vendor discussing how to turn their product into what the hospital needs.

That is already five hours of meetings. The rest of the day is email, and the rest of the week is more of the same.

The work is genuinely interesting. The problem is that there is no standard path into it, no clear career progression, and no guarantee of a good project. I have spent my whole career in it, and I still get stuck on projects that are just terrible. If you want to do this, the best way in is to take on small projects at your current hospital and build a case for a dedicated role.

response:
That’s often not a job market problem, but a company problem. Some organizations don’t have a culture that can handle the difference in experience between the bottom and top of a range. Some companies have a policy of making every job the same salary, and that means that they can only have a few levels of job, which makes every job have a wide range.

Sometimes a job genuinely has a wide range because the job has different levels. For example, if you work at a law firm and you’re a first-year associate, you’re not expected to know a lot, but if you’re a partner, you’re supposed to have an advanced degree and be able to run the business. And those are all attorneys, even though the jobs are different.

So if you see a salary range that seems like a job has two levels, and they are not clear on how it works, that might be a red flag that the company has a big problem.

prompt: I have to give two weeks' notice on Monday. I've never quit a job in person before. Walk me through how it's normally done — who do I tell first, what do I say, do I bring a letter, what happens with my laptop and my unused PTO? I'm in Texas, at a ~200 person company.
response:
If you have any doubt about whether your boss would be okay with you quitting, find another job. If you're going to quit anyway, tell your boss first, alone, with a simple "I want to give you two weeks' notice, effective [date]." Don't ask for permission, don't ask for input. If you feel like it, say something nice about the company, and maybe explain a bit why you're leaving, in broad terms ("I'm going to do X instead, because Y" or "I've decided that I don't want to be in this field anymore"). Don't get into detail, and don't get into detail if you're asked. You're not obligated to have a reason for leaving, and there's no reason to go into detail.

The reason for telling your boss in person first is the same reason you don't send your resignation as a text message: you owe the person you work with most a conversation. If you're going to quit, tell them first.

Your boss will probably ask whether you're sure. It's fine to say that you're not 100% sure, or that you might be. It's fine to say you're not sure what you're going to do. It's not fine to say you're not sure whether to quit. You're sure about that, and you want to give them two weeks' notice, so that's what you're going to do.

Your boss will probably be surprised, or upset, or angry, or all three. They'll probably ask whether they can do anything to change your mind. Just say no. They'll probably ask what it would take to change your mind. Just say you're sure.

A day or two after you tell your boss, they'll probably tell your coworkers. You'll have to tell them too. It's easier if you tell your coworkers before they hear it from your boss or by rumor. When you tell them, just say you've decided to leave. You don't have to explain why.

You don't need to do any of this in writing. A written resignation letter is not required. You can send one if you want to. There's no particular advantage to it, but there's no harm.

It's fine if you give less than two weeks' notice, or more. In fact you should probably give less if it would save the company money. But two weeks is fine.

You'll probably be asked what you're going to do. If you don't want to explain, don't. It's not rude to say you're not sure.

Don't talk badly about your company or your boss or your coworkers, either to your boss, or to the people you're talking to as you tell them. Don't say "I'm sick of this place" or "this company is a hellhole." If you say "I don't want to do this kind of work anymore" they might think you mean them personally.

You should still do your job the whole time you work there, even if you're leaving in a week.

Don't try to negotiate your exit. Don't say "I'll work a week if you pay me an extra $X." Just leave, and be happy.

Don't do anything to make things difficult for the company. Don't delete files, don't make it hard to replace you, don't sabotage anything.

Don't worry about having a plan. It's fine to leave without one.

After you quit, you should return your laptop and other company property. If you can do that in person, that's fine. If you can't, send them back in the mail.

If you have any vacation left, it will depend on the company. It may be paid to you, or it may not.
