But it is hard to get reliable results that far back, because of contamination and calibration, so it's not something most people do.

prompt: We're closing on a house next month and the inspection found knob and tube wiring in part of it. The inspector said it's 'not inherently dangerous' but our insurance company says they won't cover it until it's replaced. Now I'm scared to plug anything in. What actually makes it risky, and is it a fire waiting to happen or is everyone overreacting?
response:
Knob and tube wiring was the standard in homes built up to about 1950, and it's not unsafe as long as it stays undisturbed and you don't run too many loads through it. The insulation is cotton or paper, but it's designed to stay cool: the conductors run through air in the studs and the tubes help heat escape. The risk shows up when modern electrical muscle meets an older design.

A modern 15- or 20-amp circuit can draw more than a typical knob and tube branch can handle, and many of those branch circuits are shared with circuits in the attic. If you don't know where the attic circuit is and someone uses too much power there, the branch can overheat. The insulation is also brittle after 80 years, and the wires can crack or short inside the insulation. The biggest danger is that insulation doesn't stay put. Attic insulation can shift and settle onto a hot wire, which starts a fire at the wire, not at your outlet.

This is why insurance companies care. They don't know how old the wiring is or how much attic insulation has settled onto it, and they don't know what you're going to plug in. Replacing the wiring removes the uncertainty, so it's usually a condition of coverage. You can try to negotiate a waiver, but don't count on one.

A few things to avoid with an old system:

- Don't plug high-draw devices into it, such as a space heater, dryer, or air conditioner.

- Don't use a three-prong adapter on the two-prong outlets, and don't add a ground wire yourself.

- Don't add new outlets without an electrician.

- Don't put more insulation in the attic without an electrician.

A qualified electrician can inspect your knob and tube system and tell you what it can handle. If you want to replace the wiring but aren't sure what it costs, a contractor can usually give you an estimate in a day or two. If your house is big enough, you can replace the wiring in phases and save money.

prompt: Why does a curveball curve? Every Magnus effect explanation I find just says 'the spin creates a pressure difference' and stops there, which is what I'm asking about. Why does spin create a pressure difference?
response:
You have to stop thinking of the ball's surface as rigid. On one side of the ball the surface is moving toward the air and on the other side it's moving away from the air. The moving side drags air along with it, so the air near that side moves at a different speed than the air on the other side.

The difference in speed doesn't itself cause a pressure difference, it's just a sign that a pressure difference is happening. Air in the fast lane on one side of the ball is accelerated, and air is only accelerated by pressure differences. If the pressure on one side of the ball were the same as on the other, then there would be no reason for the air near that side to be moving faster, because there would be no force accelerating it. In fact, air flows from high pressure to low pressure, so the pressure must be lower where the air is moving faster.

The pressure is actually lower on both sides than in the far-away air. A fast-moving stream of air has lower pressure than a slow-moving one, so the air flowing around a ball will always have less pressure than the air far away from it, whether the ball is spinning or not. But where the air is moving fastest, it has the lowest pressure, and that's where the surface of the ball is moving toward the air.

So you can see the whole thing as a chain of causes:

The ball's spin makes its surface move toward the air on one side and away from the air on the other side.

The surface drags air along with it, so the air moves faster on one side and slower on the other.

Air is accelerated by pressure differences, so there must be a pressure difference to make the air move at different speeds.

There's less pressure where the air is moving faster, because a fast-moving stream of air has less pressure than a slow-moving one.

The pressure difference exerts a force, which accelerates the ball.

This is a simplification of the real explanation, because the ball is changing the speed of the air, not just dragging it along. And there's a lot of turbulence behind the ball, which is actually what causes the pressure difference in the first place. I'd be happy to explain that in more detail.

prompt: Why does a curveball curve? Every Magnus effect explanation I find just says 'the spin creates a pressure difference' and stops there, which is what I'm asking about. Why does spin create a pressure difference?
response:
Imagine that the ball is sitting still and the air is flowing past it. You're not going to get a force on the ball from air that's moving in a straight line, the way you're not going to get a force on a car from wind that's blowing straight from the front. (The wind exerts more pressure on the front of the car than on the back, but the back of the car has less area, so the forces balance out.)

Now imagine that the ball is spinning. A point on the surface on the bottom is moving at a different speed than a point on the top, relative to the air. This means that the air near the bottom is moving at a different speed than the air near the top, and faster-moving air has less pressure (Bernoulli's principle). So the net pressure on the ball is greater on the bottom than the top, which pushes it upward.

This is the Magnus effect, and it's also why a spinning frisbee curves to the left or right.

prompt: Why does a curveball curve? Every Magnus effect explanation I find just says 'the spin creates a pressure difference' and stops there, which is what I'm asking about. Why does spin create a pressure difference?
response:
The pitch is moving, say, to the left. The pitcher imparts topspin, meaning the top of the ball moves left relative to its centre of mass, faster than the whole ball is going. The air feels this top side moving through it faster than the bottom side. Fast-moving air creates lower pressure: a fluid flowing around a curved surface, like the top of the ball, speeds up in order to get around the bend. Pressure drops as flow speed increases. The air is moving faster over the top of the ball than underneath, so the pressure is lower on top than underneath. The ball gets pushed toward the lower pressure, which is up, which is not the direction I said I wanted the ball to go, so I'll try again.

The pitcher imparts topspin, meaning the top of the ball moves upward relative to its centre of mass, which is slower than the whole ball is moving leftward. The air feels this top side moving through it slower than the bottom side. Slow-moving air creates higher pressure. The air is moving slower over the top of the ball than underneath, so the pressure is higher on top than underneath. The ball gets pushed toward the lower pressure, which is down.

The ball curves downward.

There are two ways this could go wrong. The first is that the pitcher imparts backspin, and the ball curves upward instead. The second is that the pitcher imparts sidespin, and the ball curves sideways. The ball will curve in whatever direction it needs to in order to move from the side where it's moving slow relative to the air to the side where it's moving fast relative to the air.

This is the Magnus effect.

prompt: I teach 4th grade. Tomorrow a kid is definitely going to ask why a giant steel ship floats when the steel paperclip we just dropped in the tub sank. Help me with an answer that's true but works for 10-year-olds, ideally with something we can try in class.
response:
It's not about the material. It's about shape. A steel paperclip floats if you bend it into a tiny boat, and a steel boat sinks if you flatten it into a lump.

When an object goes in the water, it pushes water out of the way. The water pushes back, and that push is bigger the more water it displaces. A flat steel lump doesn't displace much water, so the water's push is smaller than the lump's weight, and it sinks. A steel hull is shaped like a hollow bowl, so it can displace a huge amount of water before the water reaches the top of the hull. Once it has, the water's push is bigger than the hull's weight, and the hull floats.

You can prove it with a lump of Play-Doh. A ball of Play-Doh sinks. Flatten it into a bowl and it floats. Same material, different shape.

prompt: I teach 4th grade. Tomorrow a kid is definitely going to ask why a giant steel ship floats when the steel paperclip we just dropped in the tub sank. Help me with an answer that's true but works for 10-year-olds, ideally with something we can try in class.
response:
The ship displaces a lot of water, but the paperclip does not, because it is so small. The water pushed up on the ship weighs about as much as the ship itself. That is why it floats.

For a quick demo, bring an empty plastic bottle to class and fill it half full of water. The kids can try to hold it under the surface in a sink. It is hard, because the water pushes up. Then ask: if you took out all the water from the bottle and sealed it, would it be easier to hold down? Yes. That is because it displaces less water.

The same is true for a steel ship. You can make it float by making a big enough hull, so that it displaces enough water.

prompt: Why does cutting an onion make me cry but chopping garlic never does? They seem like such similar plants.
response: They are related, but not that closely; onions are lilies and garlic are alliums. Both plants are sources of sulfur compounds, but in garlic, the sulfur is held by one enzyme in a protein called alliin. The sulfur compounds in onions are held by a different enzyme, allinase, in a separate part of the cell. Cutting garlic just breaks cells, but that doesn't get alliin and allinase together. Chopping onions does, though, so the enzymes release a compound that gets into your eyes.

prompt: Why does cutting an onion make me cry but chopping garlic never does? They seem like such similar plants.
response: It's because the reaction is specific to an enzyme, alliinase, that's released when the onion is cut up. This enzyme, along with another, converts an amino acid that's in onion cells into a volatile, sulfur-containing compound called syn-propanethial-S-oxide, which is a mild tear irritant. The garlic doesn't have alliinase, so cutting it up doesn't set off the reaction that leads to your tears.

prompt: Why does cutting an onion make me cry but chopping garlic never does? They seem like such similar plants.
response: They're both alliums, but onion cells contain a special enzyme, alliinase, that, when released by cutting, acts on an amino-acid sulfide called L-1-iso-propyl-L-cysteine sulfoxide to form a sulfenic acid, which is then rearranged by another enzyme called lachrymatory-factor synthase to syn-propanethial S-oxide, a volatile that irritates your eyes. Garlic cells don't contain the second enzyme, so chopping garlic produces other volatile sulfurs but not the tear-inducing one.

prompt: how does tylenol actually work. like what is it doing in there
response: Acetaminophen inhibits COX enzymes, which make prostaglandins, but mostly in the brain and spinal cord, where it blocks the synthesis of prostaglandins that promote pain and fever. prompt: how does tylenol actually work. like what is it doing in there
response: Acetaminophen, which is paracetamol outside the US. It reduces the sensation of pain by acting on pain-sensing neurons in the central nervous system, and reduces fever by working on the hypothalamus.

prompt: how does tylenol actually work. like what is it doing in there
response:
Acetaminophen is converted in your liver into a reactive byproduct called NAPQI, which your cells usually detoxify quickly with glutathione. When you take a normal dose, glutathione handles it easily, and the drug just passes through. When glutathione runs out, as in an overdose, NAPQI binds to liver cells and kills them, which is why an overdose is so dangerous.

For pain and fever, nobody is completely sure. It appears to inhibit the COX-2 enzyme, which makes pain-promoting chemicals called prostaglandins, but mainly in the brain and spinal cord, where the brain has its own supply of something called endogenous peroxides. Ibuprofen and aspirin inhibit COX-2 too, but their chemical form is not activated by those peroxides, which is why they work better in the body. A recent study of how Tylenol works in mice found that it blocks a pain-related receptor in the brain called the P2X3 receptor, but nobody has been able to replicate this result, so it's not confirmed.

prompt: My doctor said my LDL is 160 but my HDL is high, around 85, so it 'mostly balances out.' Is that really how it works? I only know them as good and bad cholesterol and I'd like to understand what they actually are before my follow-up.
response:
Cholesterol is a waxy fat your body makes and uses to build cell membranes and hormones. Blood cannot carry it by itself, so it travels in packaged particles called lipoproteins. LDL particles deliver cholesterol from the liver to tissues, and people call them "bad" because excess LDL can leave cholesterol behind in artery walls, which is what forms plaque. HDL particles do roughly the reverse, collecting cholesterol from tissues and bringing it back to the liver, which is why they're called "good."

Your doctor's shorthand was reasonable. What matters most for risk is how much LDL is circulating, and a high HDL does offset it somewhat, so your total picture may be better than the 160 alone suggests. The exact amount of offset is hard to pin down for any individual.

The most important thing to ask at your next appointment is not a ratio or total but a 10-year risk estimate. That combines age, blood pressure, whether you smoke, your diabetes status, and cholesterol into a single probability of a heart attack or stroke. If you're at low risk, doctors often make no change. If your risk is moderate to high, they may recommend a statin.

prompt: My doctor said my LDL is 160 but my HDL is high, around 85, so it 'mostly balances out.' Is that really how it works? I only know them as good and bad cholesterol and I'd like to understand what they actually are before my follow-up.
response:
They are not substances but numbers on a blood test. LDL and HDL are lipoprotein particles, and the numbers are estimates of how many milligrams per deciliter of cholesterol those particles carry. LDL particles deposit cholesterol in the walls of arteries and HDL removes some of it, so higher LDL and lower HDL raise the risk of heart attack and stroke.

The test doesn't measure particles directly. LDL is calculated as total cholesterol minus HDL minus about one fifth of the triglycerides, and it's reliable only if fasting triglycerides are below about 200 mg/dL.

HDL does help, but it doesn't cancel out a high LDL the way it sounds. Risk rises with LDL, and most guidelines target LDL levels themselves. People with an LDL near 160 are often offered a statin if their overall 10-year risk is higher than about 7.5 percent, which your doctor can estimate from your age, blood pressure, smoking status, diabetes and total cholesterol.

prompt: My doctor said my LDL is 160 but my HDL is high, around 85, so it 'mostly balances out.' Is that really how it works? I only know them as good and bad cholesterol and I'd like to understand what they actually are before my follow-up.
response:
They're not two substances that cancel each other. Cholesterol travels in the blood inside particles called lipoproteins. LDL particles carry cholesterol to tissues, and when their number is high, some of it gets trapped in artery walls and is oxidized, which is a major driver of atherosclerosis. HDL particles are better understood as a cleanup vehicle: they pick up cholesterol from cells and artery walls and bring it to the liver to be processed, and they also limit inflammation and oxidation. Higher HDL is associated with lower risk, which is why your doctor points to it.

The math people use is not your LDL minus your HDL, but your non-HDL cholesterol, which is total cholesterol minus HDL. This is the cholesterol carried by all the atherogenic particles, including LDL and VLDL. For your numbers it would be about 160 plus 85 plus your triglyceride-containing particles. If your triglycerides are under about 150 mg/dL, non-HDL is typically LDL plus about 30 to 45, so with an LDL of 160 and HDL of 85 it might be around 210 to 230. A common target is under 130 for average-risk people, under 100 for those at higher risk, and sometimes lower. Your doctor will set the target using your overall risk, which is also why people with the same LDL can get different advice.

Your HDL does genuinely help, and lifestyle choices such as regular aerobic exercise, not smoking, moderate alcohol, and replacing refined carbohydrates and trans fats with unsaturated fats and omega-3s tend to raise it modestly and lower LDL. Still, a high HDL is not a free pass: someone with an LDL of 160 and a high HDL still has more atherogenic particles than someone with an LDL of 100 and the same HDL. At your follow-up it's worth asking your doctor what your non-HDL cholesterol is and what target you're aiming for.

prompt: My 9 year old is furious that the doctor won't give him antibiotics for his cold, because they 'worked last time' (that was strep). How do I explain the difference between a virus and bacteria so he gets why the medicine won't help?
response:
Bacteria are single cells that look a bit like tiny sausages. Viruses are smaller, and they're too simple to be called alive. They can't even make copies of themselves; they have to hijack a cell to do that.

Antibiotics like penicillin work by blocking something bacteria need to survive, like making their cell walls. Viruses don't have cell walls, so antibiotics do nothing to them.

prompt: My 9 year old is furious that the doctor won't give him antibiotics for his cold, because they 'worked last time' (that was strep). How do I explain the difference between a virus and bacteria so he gets why the medicine won't help?
response:
Bacteria are single-celled things that are alive in their own right. Viruses are just packets of genetic information in a protein shell, and they are not alive until they use that information to hijack a cell. They are not alive at all in the environment or on your skin.

Antibiotics attack bacteria's unique machinery, so they do nothing to viruses, and they can disrupt the bacteria that are good for you. The reason they worked last time is that the bacteria behind strep throat are very different from the viruses that cause colds.

prompt: I'm a software engineer trying to actually understand CRISPR. Every explainer says 'molecular scissors' and stops there. What determines where Cas9 cuts, and what happens after the cut that ends up changing the gene? The cell has to do something, right?
response:
CRISPR is not a tool for making targeted cuts. It is a bacterial immune system, in which bacteria store pieces of viral DNA in a library called the CRISPR array, use that library to identify viruses that have attacked before, and destroy viral DNA when they meet it again. Cas9 is the protein that does the destroying.

To use CRISPR to edit a human gene, you give cells an engineered RNA and Cas9. The engineered RNA consists of a guide sequence and a scaffold sequence. The guide sequence is 20 nucleotides long and is complementary to the DNA you want to cut. The scaffold binds Cas9. Cas9 searches the genome and, when it finds a place where the guide sequence is complementary to the DNA and the DNA has a PAM sequence (usually NGG) just after it, it binds there. Then Cas9 binds to a nearby place, where it cuts the DNA.

When you make a double-strand break, the cell has to repair it. The most common repair pathway is a simple one called non-homologous end joining, in which the ends of the DNA are stitched back together. Sometimes it introduces a few errors in the process, which breaks the gene. This is how gene knockout is usually achieved with CRISPR.

To replace a gene, you provide a template for repair and the cell uses a pathway called homology directed repair, where it inserts a copy of the template into the DNA.

prompt: I'm a software engineer trying to actually understand CRISPR. Every explainer says 'molecular scissors' and stops there. What determines where Cas9 cuts, and what happens after the cut that ends up changing the gene? The cell has to do something, right?
response: Cas9 is guided to a site by a short guide RNA that is complementary to the DNA. It binds where the guide matches, and then cuts both strands a few bases before a short motif, NGG. The cell has two ways to repair a double-strand break. Non-homologous end joining simply seals the ends and usually introduces small insertions or deletions, which disrupts a gene and disables it. Homologous recombination copies the sequence of a template, and if you supply a donor DNA with a change, the change is copied into the genome. This is how a specific edit is introduced.

prompt: I'm a software engineer trying to actually understand CRISPR. Every explainer says 'molecular scissors' and stops there. What determines where Cas9 cuts, and what happens after the cut that ends up changing the gene? The cell has to do something, right?
response:
Cas9 is guided to a DNA sequence by a short guide RNA, usually about 20 base pairs long, that base-pairs with the target strand. The sequence right next to it must be NGG, called the PAM, and Cas9 will not cut DNA without it.

After the cut, you have two repair routes. Non-homologous end joining rejoins the broken ends and often inserts or deletes a few bases, which usually breaks the gene. If you supply a repair template with the change you want and the cell uses homology-directed repair, your change can be copied into the gene at the cut site.

prompt: why does your foot fall asleep and why is the waking up part so much worse than the numb part
response: A leg crossed or a shoe that bites presses a nerve against bone for a long time, and the signal gets muffled or blocked. Numbness alone is fairly pleasant. The pins and needles come from the nerve waking up with the same signals it used to send, but amplified, and they all arrive at once.

prompt: why does your foot fall asleep and why is the waking up part so much worse than the numb part
response:
When you sit cross-legged or with your leg dangling off a couch, you compress the nerves and blood vessels in that leg. The numbness, strictly speaking, is not the nerves being squeezed shut. It's the brain's way of telling you it has lost the ability to tell where things are.

When nerves are compressed, they stop relaying signals. But this doesn't leave you completely numb. Your brain keeps sending out the same signals it always does. If you're sitting in a chair, your brain keeps sending out signals to your legs saying: you're at the bottom of the chair, and the chair is under you. But your nerves have stopped telling you anything about your legs or chair. So your brain is sending out a continuous stream of "there is a chair underneath you," but there's nothing coming back.

The brain doesn't think "oh, there's a chair there and my nerves have stopped telling me anything about it." Instead, it thinks "I'm sending out signals to my legs, but I'm not getting anything back, so something must be wrong with my legs. This is a problem! I should tell the user about it!" And to let you know, it switches off the signals it's been sending to your legs and turns on a new set of signals, ones that say "oh no, you have no legs." You feel the pins-and-needles, the weird feeling like "oh no, my leg is not a leg." And you can still do things with your leg, because the brain is only shutting off the "my legs are real" part, not the "move your leg" part.

This is the same kind of problem that causes phantom limb syndrome. If you're missing an arm, your brain doesn't think "oh, I have no arm." It thinks "I have an arm, but it's not telling me anything, so there must be something wrong with it." It has to be like that, because there's no difference in the brain between "I have an arm, but it's not telling me anything" and "I have no arm."

In this model, the reason the pins and needles is so unpleasant is that the brain is telling you something terrible, and you know it's just a malfunction, but you can't ignore it. If your brain thinks you have no legs, and you try to move your legs, there will be a lot of conflict in the brain between "move your legs" and "you have no legs".

The reason the pins and needles feels good is that the brain realizes there's actually nothing wrong with your legs, and goes back to sending out the "I have legs" signals, which means "oh, you have legs, and there's nothing wrong with them, and it's great to have legs".

prompt: why does your foot fall asleep and why is the waking up part so much worse than the numb part
response: The numbness is pressure cutting off blood flow to the nerves in your legs, or a nerve being compressed against bone. The waking-up feeling is the nerves firing erratically as blood rushes back, and it's amplified because a lot of nerves are doing it at once. It usually passes in a minute or two, and if it happens often or without any clear cause it's worth mentioning to a doctor.

prompt: My aunt is convinced the mRNA vaccines rewrite your DNA. I don't want to just say 'that's not true, trust me' because that's never worked on her. Can you explain how they work well enough that I can explain why that can't happen?
response:
An mRNA vaccine, like the Moderna and Pfizer vaccines against the coronavirus, has two things going for it. The first is that it teaches your body to recognize the virus. The second is that it is almost certainly harmless.

The first thing is easy to understand, so let's start there. The coronavirus has spikes on the outside of its cell wall that it uses to attach itself to your cells. Your body makes its own proteins, like hemoglobin and collagen, and it doesn't recognize the coronavirus spikes as its own. Your immune system attacks the coronavirus, which is a good thing, but sometimes the coronavirus wins.

The mRNA vaccine teaches your body to recognize the coronavirus spikes before the coronavirus shows up. The mRNA tells your cells to make the coronavirus spikes on their own cell walls. Your immune system attacks the spikes as foreign invaders, which is a bad thing for your cells, but it learns to recognize the spikes as foreign. The next time the real coronavirus shows up, your immune system will attack it, and you'll probably survive.

The second thing is the hard part. Why isn't the vaccine dangerous, when it has your cells making coronavirus proteins?

This is because mRNA has a very short life inside your body. A cell can be alive for years, but the mRNA inside it only lasts hours. So when the vaccine mRNA dies, your cells stop making the coronavirus spikes. Your body is fine, except now it knows how to fight the coronavirus.

So why do people think mRNA vaccines are dangerous? Why do people think they might change your DNA?

DNA is very different from mRNA. DNA is stable, but mRNA is unstable. DNA is long and double-stranded, but mRNA is short and single-stranded. DNA stays in your nucleus, but mRNA is in your cytoplasm.

People get confused because mRNA is made from DNA. In a normal cell, mRNA is made by a molecule called RNA polymerase that is told which parts of the DNA to read. In an mRNA vaccine, the mRNA is made by a scientist in a lab who decides which parts of the DNA to read.

People think mRNA vaccines are dangerous because they think the mRNA in the vaccine might get into your nucleus and change your DNA. But mRNA doesn't last long enough to get into your nucleus.

People are also worried that mRNA vaccines might cause you to have the coronavirus, or that the vaccine might change your DNA and make you look like a coronavirus. But you can't have a coronavirus unless the coronavirus is replicating. And it isn't. It's just telling you to make the spikes.

prompt: My aunt is convinced the mRNA vaccines rewrite your DNA. I don't want to just say 'that's not true, trust me' because that's never worked on her. Can you explain how they work well enough that I can explain why that can't happen?
response:
When you get an mRNA vaccine, it's injected into a muscle. There, it gets taken up by the cells in the muscle, which have ribosomes - a little machine inside the cell that translates RNA into protein. The ribosomes read the mRNA strand, base by base, making a protein in response. In the case of an mRNA vaccine, that protein is the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2. The cells then release the spike proteins, which enter the bloodstream and are recognised by the immune system, which mounts a response. That's how it works.

The reason people think that mRNA vaccines can get into your DNA is because, for mRNA to be converted into protein, it has to be copied into DNA first. This is called transcription. mRNA vaccines don't do this, because they don't go into the nucleus of the cell where your DNA is, and because they don't have the right enzymes to make DNA from RNA. This is called reverse transcription, and it's what retroviruses like HIV do. mRNA vaccines are not retroviruses, and they don't work that way. They don't have the enzymes to make DNA from RNA. They don't have the enzymes to get into the nucleus. So you can see that they can't get into your DNA, because they can't even get into the nucleus.

prompt: My aunt is convinced the mRNA vaccines rewrite your DNA. I don't want to just say 'that's not true, trust me' because that's never worked on her. Can you explain how they work well enough that I can explain why that can't happen?
response:
mRNA vaccines inject mRNA, which is the intermediate molecule cells use to turn genes into proteins. The mRNA doesn’t touch your DNA, which is in the nucleus, while injected mRNA ends up in the cytoplasm.

Your cells read the mRNA and make the virus’s spike protein. The immune system notices the spike and remembers it. Later, if you meet the virus, your body already knows what to do. The mRNA instructions are degraded by normal cellular cleanup within days.

A useful analogy: printing a recipe on paper and giving it to someone doesn’t change their cookbook.

prompt: I drink about five big mugs of coffee a day and get a pounding headache by noon if I skip it. I want to get down to one cup. I'm a high school teacher so I can't be a zombie in front of 30 teenagers. What's a realistic plan, and why do the withdrawal headaches happen in the first place?
response:
A caffeine withdrawal headache is caused by blood vessels in your brain that have become used to caffeine’s tightening action dilating after you stop. Caffeine is a vasodilator, but the body responds to this by tightening its blood vessels in response, so that’s not an entirely satisfying explanation.

The withdrawal headache should be less bad if you taper off slowly. I cut mine down from three cups a day to one cup by having two in the morning and one in the afternoon for a week, then cutting down to one cup in the morning and one in the afternoon for a week, then cutting down to one cup in the morning. You may want to go even more slowly if you drink more than me.

I find that having a cup of coffee is a much easier way to stay awake than not having one. But if you want to go off completely, you might try having coffee first thing in the morning (before your brain needs it) and then try a short nap at lunch, or try drinking a large glass of water or doing some exercise if you get sleepy.

prompt: I drink about five big mugs of coffee a day and get a pounding headache by noon if I skip it. I want to get down to one cup. I'm a high school teacher so I can't be a zombie in front of 30 teenagers. What's a realistic plan, and why do the withdrawal headaches happen in the first place?
response:
When you regularly drink coffee, your blood vessels dilate. When you stop, they constrict, which causes a headache.

You can't stop cold turkey. If you do, your blood vessels will constrict even more.

Instead, gradually wean yourself over one to two weeks.

Here's how.

First, replace one of your daily coffees with half a cup of real coffee and half a cup of decaf.

Second, drink the whole cup of decaf.

Third, cut your daily coffee down to just half a cup.

If you don't get headaches after a few days, repeat the process. If you do, try drinking a glass of water every time you would drink a cup of coffee. It seems counter-intuitive, but it may help ease your withdrawal headaches.

prompt: I drink about five big mugs of coffee a day and get a pounding headache by noon if I skip it. I want to get down to one cup. I'm a high school teacher so I can't be a zombie in front of 30 teenagers. What's a realistic plan, and why do the withdrawal headaches happen in the first place?
response:
Caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors, so the usual response to coffee or tea, which is to relax and fall asleep, is inhibited. The body responds to the blockade by creating more adenosine receptors, so if you suddenly stop, the new receptors cause the symptoms of caffeine withdrawal: headache, fatigue and irritability. It's also thought that the headaches are caused by blood vessels dilating after caffeine stopped constricting them.

To wean yourself off, cut back by a third every week. For the first week, mix one-third decaf and two-thirds regular coffee. Then swap one-third of the decaf for regular, and so on.

prompt: How do we know mitochondria used to be free-living bacteria? It sounds like a nice story. What's the actual evidence?
response:
There are a couple of things that point in that direction.

Mitochondria have their own DNA and ribosomes, so they can make proteins, although most of the proteins they need come from the nucleus. The DNA is circular, like bacterial DNA, and the ribosomes are a lot like bacterial ribosomes. They have a double membrane, like bacteria.

But those things are just suggestive, not conclusive. The really conclusive evidence comes from antibiotics. Antibiotics usually work on bacteria by binding to their ribosomes and inhibiting them. Most antibiotics don't work on human cells, because the human ribosomes are different, but a few antibiotics that target bacterial ribosomes also work on mitochondria.

In particular, chloramphenicol can kill bacteria by inhibiting their protein synthesis, and in the lab it can stop mitochondria from working.

There are some pretty weird facts about how mitochondria are inherited. Most human genes come half from your mother and half from your father, but mitochondrial genes only come from your mother. Your father's mitochondria are destroyed early in the embryo's development. That sounds arbitrary, but it is probably because the egg has a lot of mitochondria in it and the sperm doesn't, so it's much easier to make sure all mitochondria come from the mother.

The theory that mitochondria evolved from bacteria, called the endosymbiosis theory, makes a lot of sense when you realize that bacteria live inside human cells all the time and they don't do any harm. You're full of bacteria, and they're not doing anything bad, they're just living in you.

prompt: How do we know mitochondria used to be free-living bacteria? It sounds like a nice story. What's the actual evidence?
response:
Here are three independent lines of evidence.

Mitochondria have their own circular DNA that encodes some of their proteins. It is remarkably similar to bacterial DNA.

Mitochondria have their own ribosomes and protein synthesis machinery. These are much more like the ribosomes of bacteria than they are to the ribosomes in the rest of your cell. They are also sensitive to antibiotics like chloramphenicol.

Mitochondria divide by a process that is remarkably like binary fission. This is also how bacteria divide.

The hypothesis that mitochondria evolved from bacteria that were engulfed by other cells and became symbionts is called endosymbiosis.

prompt: How do we know mitochondria used to be free-living bacteria? It sounds like a nice story. What's the actual evidence?
response:
The endosymbiotic theory is the best explanation we have for how mitochondria originated, but it is not a complete story. We know a lot from the evidence, but we don't know exactly what happened. Here are some of the strongest pieces of evidence, which is a good place to start.

### DNA, and DNA that looks bacterial

Mitochondria have their own DNA, a bit like bacteria. It is a circular DNA molecule (like bacteria), rather than being linear DNA organized into chromosomes (like most eukaryotic cells). The DNA is also very small, only about 15,000 letters, compared to about 3 billion letters in the human genome.

The mitochondrial genome also encodes proteins that are typical of bacteria, and not typically found in human cells. For example, it encodes ribosomal proteins (the proteins that make up ribosomes), and these are more similar to bacterial ribosomal proteins than to those of human cells.

### DNA that looks ancestral

The mitochondrial genome is also missing lots of genes, including most of the genes that bacteria have. The mitochondrial genome only has about 120 protein-coding genes, but bacteria have thousands of genes.

It is possible to explain how this happened: the first time bacteria merged with a cell, they gave away lots of their genes to the host cell. This happens today whenever bacteria are swallowed by cells, and is called horizontal gene transfer. It is well documented.

If we look at the bacterial genes in mitochondria, they are older than their relatives in modern bacteria. The genes have been changed over time by mutations, and the mutations accumulate at a predictable rate. This gives a kind of clock, which we can use to tell how long ago the genes had common ancestors. If we compare the mitochondrial genes with genes in bacteria, the mitochondrial genes are always older, like fossils. This makes sense if mitochondria are older than bacteria, and if the bacterial genes have had more time to change.

### Ribosomes, and ribosomes that look bacterial

Mitochondria have their own ribosomes, the machinery that reads DNA and produces protein. They are similar to bacterial ribosomes, and they are not very similar to the ribosomes in the main cell.

Ribosomes are a good source of evidence, because they are pretty conserved, and the changes that happen to ribosomes are easy to track.

### Reproduction by splitting in two

Mitochondria make new mitochondria by dividing in two, like bacteria. This is very different from how other things in a cell replicate. The main cell divides by a complicated process called mitosis, and mitochondria divide in a much simpler way.

### Membranes that look bacterial

Bacteria are surrounded by a membrane (the plasma membrane), and mitochondria are surrounded by two membranes. This is a bit hard to explain, but if bacteria merged with another cell, the bacteria's own membrane would remain, and the bacteria's membrane would get fused with the membrane of the cell it was merged with.

There are some interesting proteins in the mitochondrial membrane that are similar to proteins in bacteria.

The mitochondrial membrane has small holes, called porins, that let some small molecules in and out. These are similar to porins in bacteria.

### Antibiotics that affect mitochondria

There are antibiotics that stop bacteria from making protein by binding to their ribosomes. Some of these antibiotics also bind to mitochondrial ribosomes, and stop mitochondria from making protein. This is not surprising if mitochondria are related to bacteria, and their ribosomes are similar to bacterial ribosomes.

### Mitochondria come from bacteria

We can create mitochondria from bacteria. If we take bacteria and fuse them with cells, and put those cells under the right conditions, the bacteria will start to behave more like mitochondria.

### Other things that look bacterial

Mitochondria have lots of other features that are similar to bacteria. For example, bacteria have a protein that senses oxygen, and mitochondria have a similar protein.

### Other evidence

There are also a few other pieces of evidence. For example, chloroplasts are probably related to bacteria too, and it is easier to explain how mitochondria and chloroplasts appeared if both of them were bacteria.

### How mitochondria got here

A good source for the current story is a book called "The Origin of Eukaryotic Cells" by Nick Lane. According to that story, mitochondria were an early addition to the first eukaryotic cells.

One of the big problems with the early eukaryotic cells is that they didn't have enough energy. This is a problem because energy is important, and it is hard to make a cell bigger without a lot of energy.

Mitochondria are great at making energy. If you are a bacterial ancestor of mitochondria, you can make a lot of energy. But the bacterial ancestors of mitochondria were tiny, and they couldn't use a lot of the energy they made.

If you merged with a bigger cell, the bigger cell would have the energy it needed. The bigger cell was probably a cell that was about to die, because it didn't have enough energy. The bigger cell got the energy it needed from the bacteria. The bacteria didn't have much energy left.

prompt: Physicist here. How does the cochlea separate sound into frequencies? People say it 'does a Fourier transform' but I suspect that's a loose analogy. What is the mechanism, and where does the analogy break down?

It doesn't. Each of the thousands of hairs on the cochlea responds only to a narrow band of frequencies. The different hairs are arranged in order of their preferred frequency, so the cochlea acts as a mechanical filter bank.

The analogy breaks down in that the filters are not independent. The filters with low preferred frequencies are wider and overlap more than the ones with high preferred frequencies.

prompt: Physicist here. How does the cochlea separate sound into frequencies? People say it 'does a Fourier transform' but I suspect that's a loose analogy. What is the mechanism, and where does the analogy break down?
response:
A hair cell is a sensory cell sitting in a fluid that has a hair sticking out into the fluid. Hair cells have different shapes, and the shapes cause different motions to bend the hair in different directions. Some bend left, some bend right. Bending left opens up ion channels in the hair cell that generate a signal.

There is a long tube in your ear, the cochlea, which has a membrane down the middle that separates two fluids. In one of the fluids there are lots of hair cells. The other side of the membrane is a different fluid.

Sound comes in from your ear drum, which vibrates, vibrating one of the fluids. This makes waves that ripple through the cochlea. Different frequencies ripple differently, so a hair cell at a given position in the tube gets excited by a particular frequency.

So if the frequencies ripple differently through the tube, which position is excited by a given frequency, say, 1000 Hz, is a function of the geometry of the tube. This means that you could, in principle, figure out which position in the cochlea gets excited by a given frequency, if you know the geometry of the tube and do the appropriate wave equations, which are not Fourier transforms.

This is a bit like when an earthquake happens and different frequencies ripple differently through the Earth, so that you can figure out the interior structure of the Earth from the waves that hit different seismic detectors around the world.

The geometry of the cochlea is such that high frequencies are excited at one end and low frequencies at the other, so that each frequency has a specific position. This is a little bit like a prism, in that light is broken into its component frequencies and different frequencies go to different positions.

But there is no Fourier transform here. There is no addition or multiplication of sinusoids. There is just an excitation of some hair cell at some position in a tube, which sends an electrical signal to the brain which knows it's a particular frequency because it knows what position it came from.

The Fourier transform analogy comes from the fact that the brain receives information about different frequencies. But in physics and engineering we use Fourier transforms to break sounds into frequencies, and so the popular notion of the Fourier transform as a frequency analyzer is an analogy to what happens in the cochlea. The two things are similar, but they are not the same.

prompt: Physicist here. How does the cochlea separate sound into frequencies? People say it 'does a Fourier transform' but I suspect that's a loose analogy. What is the mechanism, and where does the analogy break down?
response:
As you suspect, the cochlea's frequency analysis is a loose analogue of the Fourier transform, and the mechanism is surprisingly simple. The inner hair cells of the cochlea are arranged at different positions, along a spiral tube, and different positions are most responsive to different frequencies.

At low frequencies, sound is transmitted from the air through a chain of three small bones into a fluid-filled tube. The tube is 20 millimeters long, and it's divided into two channels by a membrane running down the center. The membrane is covered by hair cells on one side, and the hair cells respond to the relative motion of the membrane.

At high frequencies, sound doesn't travel through the fluid channels as a wave – there's too much viscosity for that. Instead, a traveling wave forms on the membrane itself.

The traveling wave on the membrane is like a traveling wave on a guitar string, but a guitar string is uniform, whereas the membrane is stiff at one end and loose at the other. The membrane is stiff where it attaches to the skull, and gradually less stiff as it moves away. As the wave travels along the membrane, the sound frequency stays the same, but the speed of the wave slows down. This is like the speed of a wave on a string, which is proportional to the tension in the string, which is higher where the membrane is stiffer.

The speed of a traveling wave is the product of wavelength and frequency, and the frequency is constant, so the wavelength gets shorter as the wave travels. As the wavelength gets shorter, the wave gets more and more concentrated, and finally at some point there's barely enough room for one whole wavelength.

This is where the wave's energy is deposited. The hair cells at this position are most responsive to this frequency, so the sound wave excites the hair cells, which send signals to the brain.

The mechanism is very simple: different parts of the cochlea respond to different frequencies, and the frequencies are laid out spatially in the cochlea.

prompt: Our 12 year old son was just diagnosed with type 1 diabetes and relatives keep asking if he ate too much candy. I need to understand the difference between type 1 and type 2 myself first, honestly. What's actually going on in his body?
response:
Type 1 is an autoimmune disease. The body's immune system attacks and destroys the beta cells in the pancreas, which are the only cells that make insulin. Insulin is the hormone that tells cells to take in sugar from the blood. When most beta cells are gone, sugar stays in the blood and can't get into cells, so the body starts breaking down fat for fuel, which produces acids called ketones. Symptoms like thirst, frequent urination and weight loss show up, often quickly. It is not caused by diet or by candy, and it tends to appear in childhood or young adulthood.

Type 2 is more about insulin resistance: cells respond poorly to insulin and, at first, the pancreas makes more to compensate. Over time it can't keep up and blood sugar rises. It is linked to genetics, body fat, inactivity and age, and it usually develops gradually.

Both types involve high blood sugar and can look similar once symptoms appear, which is why people confuse them. But the causes are different, and there is nothing your son did, or didn't do, that caused his.

prompt: why do some people tan and others just burn? me and my sister have the same parents and she goes brown while I go lobster
response:
Mostly genetics, and mostly one gene. MC1R makes a receptor that tells skin cells to make eumelanin, the darker pigment that absorbs UV. Certain common variants make a poorly working receptor, so those cells make more pheomelanin, which is pale and gives a red-brown colour. People with two bad copies have red hair and pale skin and burn easily, while one bad copy is usually enough to tan more slowly. Your sister likely got a different set of alleles than you.

The receptor system isn't the whole story. A few genes in the pathway that breaks down melanin, such as TYR and TYRP1, also affect skin colour, which is why people with the same MC1R variants can look different. Melanin is produced by melanocytes and moved to surrounding skin cells, so the final colour also depends on how much melanin each cell receives.

prompt: why do some people tan and others just burn? me and my sister have the same parents and she goes brown while I go lobster

Melanin. Melanocytes in your skin make a dark pigment, melanin, that acts as a sunscreen, and people vary in how much they make and in what kind. Eumelanin is brown to black and the most protective, while pheomelanin is reddish and does little to block UV. People who produce more melanin, especially eumelanin, have darker skin that absorbs UV and turns brown before the damage adds up, while those with lighter skin and less melanin burn first.

It's inherited from several genes, including MC1R, which sets the switch between the two pigment types, and it isn't a single dominant or recessive trait, so siblings can differ quite a bit.

prompt: why do some people tan and others just burn? me and my sister have the same parents and she goes brown while I go lobster

It comes down to the balance between two forms of melanin in your skin. Eumelanin, which is brown or black, gives strong protection from UV, while pheomelanin, which is reddish-yellow, offers much less and can even amplify sun damage. prompt: Why does measles need something like 95% vaccination for herd immunity when other diseases need way less? Where does that number come from?
response: Measles is unusually contagious. Each infected person spreads it to about 12 to 18 others in an unvaccinated population, and it travels ahead of the cases on the air. The herd immunity threshold is 1 minus 1 over R₀, so with R₀ of 12 to 18 you need 92 to 94 percent, rounded up to about 95 percent. Polio, by contrast, has R₀ around 5 to 7, so the threshold is 80 to 86 percent. That's why small gaps in measles coverage can still let outbreaks take off.

prompt: Why does measles need something like 95% vaccination for herd immunity when other diseases need way less? Where does that number come from?
response: A disease with basic reproduction number R0 spreads to a population that has a proportion (1 - p) of susceptibles. It is contained if R0(1 - p) < 1, which means p > 1 - 1/R0. Measles has an R0 of about 12 to 18, so 1 - 1/R0 is between 92% and 94%. The quoted 95% also allows for imperfect vaccine coverage, since only about 95% of people who receive two doses are protected.

prompt: Why does measles need something like 95% vaccination for herd immunity when other diseases need way less? Where does that number come from?
response: Each disease has a basic reproduction number R0, the average number of people one infected person goes on to infect in a fully susceptible population. Mumps is about 3 to 8 and polio 5 to 7, so vaccinating 70 to 90 percent of people blocks transmission. Measles is 12 to 18, which makes it the most contagious disease we know, and the threshold works out to 1 minus 1 over R0, or 92 to 94 percent. In the real world the margin is a little wider because vaccination isn't perfectly even, so 95 percent is the usual target.

prompt: How do tardigrades survive being completely dried out for years and then come back when you add water?

Trehalose and certain proteins glass into a solid that traps proteins in place, keeping them from clumping or unfolding. They can also swap ordinary water for a different chemical, trehalose, in their cells. After years of no water, a few minutes of soaking rehydrates them and they start moving.

prompt: How do tardigrades survive being completely dried out for years and then come back when you add water?

Before drying, they fill their cells with the sugar trehalose and special proteins that replace water and hold the cell's membranes and proteins in place, like a substitute for the water that is holding them together. In the tun, they can also resist radiation, extreme heat and cold and even the vacuum of space, and can survive without water for more than a decade. prompt: ICU nurse, graduated 2009. Back then we gave bicarb in DKA much more readily than we do now, and the newer residents act like it's practically forbidden. Can you walk me through the physiology of why practice shifted? I don't need the basics of DKA, just the bicarb reasoning.
response:
Insulin suppresses lipolysis in about 30 minutes, but the kidney takes hours to clear ketone bodies, so the acidosis persists. Bicarbonate lowers the measured pH but does nothing about the ketones, so it is only temporary relief.

It also shifts the pH–PCO2 curve, which prompts hyperventilation and transiently raises PCO2. Inside cells, which have no bicarbonate buffer and where CO2 diffuses in, the same fall in pH pushes hemoglobin toward the oxygenated, low-affinity state, impairing oxygen unloading. And the sodium load, in large doses, can drive sodium into cells along with water and cause cerebral edema.

The 1994 trial that drove the change randomized children with severe DKA to 4 ml/kg of 8.4% bicarbonate over the first two hours or none. It was stopped early, and the bicarbonate group had a worse neurological outcome, with more seizures and deaths, though the study was underpowered to conclude the deaths were caused by the treatment.

The current approach is to hold bicarbonate unless pH is below 7.1 or 7.0, and even then to use it cautiously.

prompt: ICU nurse, graduated 2009. Back then we gave bicarb in DKA much more readily than we do now, and the newer residents act like it's practically forbidden. Can you walk me through the physiology of why practice shifted? I don't need the basics of DKA, just the bicarb reasoning.
response:
The shift is toward treating the acidosis with insulin and fluids, which is usually enough, and giving bicarbonate only for severe cases, generally pH below 6.9.

The old habit of correcting the acid more completely had two problems. First, bicarbonate shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin curve to the left, so hemoglobin holds on to oxygen and releases less to the tissues. Second, it increases CSF acidosis, because CO2 diffuses across the blood-brain barrier quickly but bicarbonate does not. That can raise intracranial pressure and worsen brain swelling, which is the main cause of death in DKA.

Giving bicarbonate also causes a fall in ionized calcium and potassium, so patients can end up with tetany or hypokalemia, and it produces a sodium and volume load.

prompt: ICU nurse, graduated 2009. Back then we gave bicarb in DKA much more readily than we do now, and the newer residents act like it's practically forbidden. Can you walk me through the physiology of why practice shifted? I don't need the basics of DKA, just the bicarb reasoning.
response:
Bicarbonate is not routinely given unless the pH is below 6.9–7.0. In most other patients it's ineffective at the usual dose and risks harm, but that harm is subtle, which is what makes this case worth thinking through.

The acidosis in DKA is metabolic acidosis, which the body responds to by lowering ventilation to retain carbon dioxide. As carbon dioxide builds up, it crosses the cell membranes and is converted by carbonic anhydrase into hydrogen and bicarbonate. The hydrogen is taken up by proteins and the bicarbonate is left behind in the cell, which raises the intracellular pH. That's important because the cell's enzymes, including ATPase, work poorly if pH is too low.

The problem is that bicarbonate crosses cell membranes very slowly. If you give it, you don't get the desired intracellular effect, but you do get the unwanted effect of increased hydrogen ion binding to hemoglobin and other proteins. Hydrogen ion is released back into the plasma, lowering the plasma pH. So you make the plasma more acidic even as the cell pH remains unchanged.

The reason for doing it is that the bicarbonate crosses cell membranes slowly, but carbon dioxide crosses them very quickly. The acidosis is corrected by the body's normal compensation, but the carbon dioxide is removed by ventilation.

prompt: How does your body know when to stop growing taller? What actually tells the bones to quit?
response:
At each end of a long bone is a thin plate called the growth plate, a sheet of cartilage cells that divide and get added onto the bone, lengthening it. Growth is driven by hormones, especially growth hormone and, during puberty, sex steroids.

prompt: How does your body know when to stop growing taller? What actually tells the bones to quit?
response: The growth plates, called epiphyseal plates, are thin bands of cartilage at the ends of long bones. Bones lengthen when cartilage cells there divide, grow and die, and the dead tissue is replaced by bone. This can go on for years, but the process ends when the plate turns completely into bone and closes, usually in late adolescence, and sometimes not until the mid-20s. The body has no obvious central switch. Closure appears to come mainly from sex hormones, which stimulate the growth spurt but also accelerate the plate's disappearance. Children with untreated congenital adrenal hyperplia, who are exposed to high levels of androgens, tend to be tall for their years and stop growing early. People with Turner syndrome, who lack one X chromosome and have low oestrogen, can have open growth plates well into adulthood. prompt: Putting together a first aid kit for a two-week backpacking trip. Should I bring ibuprofen, acetaminophen, aspirin, or some combination? How do they differ in what they do, and when would I reach for each one out on the trail?
response:
Ibuprofen and aspirin are nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). They reduce pain, fever and inflammation, and are useful for the swollen ankle, sore muscles or head cold that could spoil a hike. Aspirin also prevents blood clots. Acetaminophen also helps with pain and fever, but not inflammation.

If you or your group has no allergies or stomach problems, you probably want to bring ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) or naproxen (Aleve). Ibuprofen has a shorter half-life and wears off sooner, which can be an advantage if you want to take aspirin in the event of a heart attack.

Avoid acetaminophen if you drink alcohol regularly.

prompt: Putting together a first aid kit for a two-week backpacking trip. Should I bring ibuprofen, acetaminophen, aspirin, or some combination? How do they differ in what they do, and when would I reach for each one out on the trail?
response:
In general, you don't need aspirin unless it's for a specific medical condition, like preventing a heart attack. Ibuprofen and acetaminophen treat different symptoms, so bring both.

Aspirin has anti-inflammatory effects like ibuprofen does, but it also thins blood. That's why it's used to prevent clotting after a heart attack, and why aspirin can be helpful for sudden severe headaches that might be migraines. But it can also be harmful if it thins blood too much, and it's not the best anti-inflammatory drug. So you don't need it in your first aid kit unless you're taking it for a specific medical reason.

Acetaminophen doesn't reduce inflammation. It does reduce pain and fever, so if you have a headache, take acetaminophen. If your foot is inflamed, take ibuprofen.

Ibuprofen has been linked to kidney damage, but only at high doses over long periods of time. If you take 400 mg every eight hours, you shouldn't have any problems for two weeks.

prompt: Putting together a first aid kit for a two-week backpacking trip. Should I bring ibuprofen, acetaminophen, aspirin, or some combination? How do they differ in what they do, and when would I reach for each one out on the trail?
response:
Acetaminophen, the active ingredient in Tylenol, works in the brain to raise the pain threshold, but it does almost nothing to reduce inflammation. Ibuprofen, the active ingredient in Advil and Motrin, is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, or NSAID, which reduces swelling and pain, particularly in muscles and joints, though it can be hard on your stomach and may aggravate ulcers. Aspirin, the oldest and most familiar NSAID, also reduces swelling and pain, but it takes longer to start working, and it’s not as effective as ibuprofen. It’s not much used for pain and inflammation anymore.

The most common reason to take aspirin, other than a headache, is to reduce the risk of heart attack or stroke if you are at high risk of having one. For that use, doctors recommend 81 mg, the dose in a baby aspirin, every day.

Ibuprofen and aspirin have similar adverse effects, including bleeding and stomach irritation. Avoid both if you have bleeding ulcers or kidney problems, or if you are taking anticoagulants. If you want a pain reliever that will do less damage to your stomach, take acetaminophen, up to 3,000 mg a day.

prompt: I read that eating collagen can't help your skin because your gut breaks all protein down into amino acids anyway. But my dermatologist didn't dismiss collagen supplements outright. So is it just marketing or is there a real mechanism?
response: The gut claim is true: collagen is digested into amino acids and small peptides, not absorbed whole. But the peptides are different from the amino acids. Small collagen peptides such as prolylhydroxyproline are absorbed into the bloodstream and stick around longer than ordinary amino acids, and they may act as signals that encourage skin fibroblasts to make more collagen. Studies of oral collagen peptides have reported modest increases in skin hydration and elasticity over several months, typically in women in their 50s. The effects are real but small and the evidence is limited, so you can treat it as a weak possibility rather than a proven treatment. Sun protection and retinoids do far more.

prompt: I read that eating collagen can't help your skin because your gut breaks all protein down into amino acids anyway. But my dermatologist didn't dismiss collagen supplements outright. So is it just marketing or is there a real mechanism?
response: The claim that your gut dissolves it into random amino acids is true. What the gut adds, some collagen supplements argue, is that the peptides survive digestion in part and the body uses them for collagen, which is about 30 percent glycine, an amino acid not common in most diets. There’s also a hint that collagen peptides might help with hydration by reducing water loss. Neither of these mechanisms has been proven, but a small study from the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology, which tested 31 women who took collagen for 24 weeks, found a small improvement in skin elasticity and hydration. In people with normal collagen metabolism the benefit is small or absent, which fits most studies. The honest summary is that collagen peptides are not useless and not magic: if you try them, judge by whether you notice a difference and stop if you don't.

prompt: why do toddlers say no to everything

prompt: My 7 year old asked me last night why she has to learn cursive if nobody writes in cursive anymore, and honestly I didn't have a good answer. I sort of mumbled something about signing checks and then realized I haven't written a check in four years. Is there an actual reason schools still teach it, or is it just inertia? I've seen claims it helps with brain development or reading but I don't know if that's real or something people say to justify it.
response:
This is one of those things that’s not quite the way we think it is. I asked a few people who knew what they were doing, including a couple of teachers (one of whom teaches cursive in her class), and I learned a few things.

First, the research on cursive and learning is mostly inconclusive. One study that’s often cited found that kids who learned to write in cursive did better at reading comprehension. I don’t know why, but they did. A 2002 study from Michigan State University found that handwriting was more efficient than typing when it comes to writing prose. A 2012 study (which I haven’t read yet) found that handwriting and typing were both good for learning, but handwriting was better at learning words and typing was better at learning sentences. A 2010 study found that there was a connection between handwriting and reading ability, and also that handwriting helped with spelling. A 2007 study found that handwriting (in any kind of font) is better than typing when it comes to producing creative writing.

So, there’s a reasonable chance that handwriting is better for learning, but we don’t know why or how, and the research is mixed, and a lot of it is not very good. So if you want to give your kid an edge, you could teach her to write. But don’t expect this to be some huge advantage.

Second, cursive is different from handwriting in general. There’s a very good reason to teach handwriting, and the reason has nothing to do with handwriting being better at learning. The reason is that it’s really hard to learn how to type, and learning how to write helps.

If you try to learn how to touch type, you’ll notice that it takes a long time. And when you are done, you’re done. You have to unlearn everything you know about typing and start from scratch. That’s because typing is a very precise and demanding skill, and we have really poor models of how to do it.

Learning how to write is easier, because there’s a lot of natural movement involved. That makes it much easier to learn, and it gives you the right models for how to type. If you learn how to type before you learn how to write, it takes much longer, and the whole process is harder. So if you want to teach typing, you should teach handwriting first.

I think this is why schools teach cursive. They know that kids need to learn how to type. If they just taught typing, it would be a pain, and they’d lose a lot of students. But if they teach handwriting first, then it’s a lot easier, and they get more students. So they teach handwriting first.

prompt: My 7 year old asked me last night why she has to learn cursive if nobody writes in cursive anymore, and honestly I didn't have a good answer. I've seen claims it helps with brain development or reading but I don't know if that's real or something people say to justify it.
response:
My daughter, who is in second grade, is supposed to start learning cursive this year, and I’ve been wondering whether there’s some good reason she should be learning it.

I’ve heard people claim that learning cursive improves brain development. For example, one article I read on this subject claims that the “writing and reading” areas of the brain are distinct, and that learning to write in cursive can help develop the reading area. This article doesn’t cite any sources, but the claim seems plausible enough to me.

But what if I could just skip teaching my daughter cursive, and pay a $100 a month school fee to let her learn the same thing on a computer? Would that work as well?

This is an important question, because a lot of the reason I’m skeptical of schools is that they’re expensive. I don’t like paying $5,000 a year for teachers to read things to children. I’d prefer to find ways for the children to learn those skills more cheaply. But there are some things – social interaction, for example – where I really think kids need to be at school. If I can find a way to replace cursive with something cheaper, that’s great. If cursive is the thing where kids learn to do handwriting, and handwriting is important for brain development, then there’s an argument that handwriting is one of the irreplaceable things kids need to do at school.

But there’s another reason cursive might be an important thing to learn at school: cursive might be a good place to learn a different sort of handwriting than we’re used to – handwriting that looks like cursive.

I’m not sure that I’m qualified to judge the handwriting of other people, but my daughter’s teacher has told me that handwriting is a problem. She says her class is full of kids with terrible handwriting, so bad she can barely read what they wrote. She has been trying to correct them.

So what’s wrong with my daughter’s handwriting? Well, here is a sample:

She writes in all capitals, which is pretty hard to read. But worse than that, she’s got this very weird way of writing things where she’s basically just scribbling in the shapes of letters. Like, that word is supposed to be “dog”, but I wouldn’t have been able to guess that if I’d seen it in a newspaper.

What if my daughter learned cursive? I don’t know if it would improve her handwriting. But it seems to me like it would be worth trying.

So there are two reasons cursive might be important. First, it’s an important skill to learn and might have good side effects on brain development. Second, it might be a way to learn better handwriting, which is a really important skill.

But the first reason seems to be just speculation, and the second reason might be addressed by other handwriting classes. So what if the schools just replaced the cursive classes with something else?

I think one of the reasons schools teach handwriting is to provide the children with something to do during a period when they’re otherwise not supposed to be talking.

The reason kids don’t need to be talking during handwriting classes is to make sure they don’t distract the other kids from trying to learn handwriting. But if they weren’t learning handwriting, it would be okay if they were talking.

This might seem like a good thing – kids get to talk. But it might be a bad thing – kids get to distract the people next to them.

A good handwriting class is pretty quiet. The kids write silently, and they only talk if their teacher tells them to talk.

A class where kids don’t need to be silent might be very noisy.

Maybe there’s some other class where kids don’t need to be silent, but where it’s okay if they’re noisy. I don’t know of any such class, except for recess. But recess isn’t really something you can use during the day.

So it might be worth keeping handwriting classes, or at least some sort of class where kids don’t need to be talking but have to sit still. I don’t know what this would be, but maybe it’s worth trying to find out.

prompt: What's the actual difference between Montessori and Waldorf? Every preschool we tour uses one word or the other and I just nod along.
response:
Montessori is an older theory that emphasizes hands-on materials. Children work alone on carefully designed puzzles and tasks. A child might have a tray with small objects in it, a small pitcher of water, and a sponge, and the task is to pour water and mop up the spills. The idea is that children develop skills like pouring, counting, and cleaning by themselves, and are guided to move on to harder work as they are ready.

Waldorf is newer, founded in 1919 by Rudolf Steiner, who also founded Anthroposophy, a mystical philosophy. Waldorf preschools use a lot of wood and other natural materials, and have children spend a lot of time drawing and playing.

Both theories say that young children learn better with their hands, and that adults should not get in the way too much. They also both emphasize a lot of practical skills like cleaning up after themselves.

The big difference is that Waldorf emphasizes imagination. Waldorf schools often don’t teach reading until third grade, and they are often reluctant to teach young children anything abstract.

I don’t like the Montessori approach of forcing children to work alone. I think children learn well together, especially in kindergarten. But there are probably some good Montessori preschools out there.

I’ve never been in a Waldorf school, but it sounds like they are a little better. The problem is that Waldorf schools are really into Anthroposophy, which is really weird stuff. I think some schools are very into it, others not so much. You might need to look for a secular Waldorf school.

prompt: What's the actual difference between Montessori and Waldorf? Every preschool we tour uses one word or the other and I just nod along.
response: Montessori is structured by the teacher around the child: she sets up a room that allows the child to work through a carefully sequenced set of activities, and observes the child to determine when they are ready to move on. The environment is carefully structured, the schedule is loose. Waldorf is structured by the teacher around a curriculum: a particular teacher will spend a year with a group of children, and they will go through a sequence of subjects in a particular order. The environment is less structured, the schedule is strict. Both are good, and I've seen both work well.

prompt: What's the actual difference between Montessori and Waldorf? Every preschool we tour uses one word or the other and I just nod along.
response: Montessori is a system of structured education in which each child works independently at his or her own level, using a series of prepackaged lessons designed to build a particular skill. Waldorf is an open-ended program emphasizing creativity and imagination, in which children are encouraged to engage in artistic, imaginative play. Montessori classes tend to be more structured and disciplined; Waldorf classes tend to be less so.
