prompt: I read that praising kids for being smart backfires, the whole growth mindset thing from Carol Dweck. Then I read that the big replication studies found the effect was tiny or nothing. So which is it? Should I stop saying "you're so smart" to my son or not?
response:
A new study has rekindled the growth mindset wars.

Dweck’s original research suggested praising kids for being smart was counterproductive to their learning. But a large independent replication found the effect was minimal at best.

A new study by Li and Bates in *Psychological Science* finds praising kids for being smart does indeed have a large effect on their performance.

The effect is so big it even contradicts some of Dweck’s own work.

It’s a complicated story.

Let’s start with Dweck.

Dweck is one of the most famous psychology researchers in the world. Her 1998 study *An Experimental Study of Mind-sets* is one of the most cited papers in psychology.

Dweck suggested praise for intelligence (“You are so smart”) was a bad idea.

Praising children for their intelligence leads to a fixed mindset. This causes children to be more likely to give up when faced with challenges.

In Dweck’s original study, she gave third grade children a test and then randomly assigned them to receive praise for effort (“You must have worked hard”) or praise for intelligence (“You must be smart”).

She found children who received praise for intelligence were more likely to give up on difficult problems than children who received praise for effort.

The study was replicated by Mueller and Dweck (1998).

The results were so counterintuitive that I think it’s worth spending a bit of time on the details of the study design.

Dweck’s experiment was conducted in two phases.

In the first phase, children were randomly assigned to either praise for intelligence or praise for effort.

In the second phase, the children were given three tasks. First, they were given an easy task. Second, they were given a task that was even easier. Finally, they were given a task that was harder than the first two tasks.

The hypothesis was that children who received praise for intelligence would be less likely to try their best on the last task.

Why?

According to Dweck, the last task would cause these children to doubt their intelligence.

In contrast, the children who received praise for effort would not be threatened by the last task.

They would continue to try their best.

Dweck measured the children’s scores on the tasks and how much they said they enjoyed the tasks.

The results were consistent with Dweck’s hypothesis.

Praising children for intelligence made them less likely to enjoy the tasks and less likely to do well on the tasks.

Mueller and Dweck replicated the study using a different set of children.

The results of the two studies were so counterintuitive, but so impressive, that the study was published in *Psychological Science*.

But the results of Dweck’s studies were questioned by a number of researchers.

In 2015, Li and Bates conducted a study that tested the effect of praise for intelligence on children’s performance.

The study was replicated in 2018 by Li and Bates.

In both studies, the researchers found that praising children for intelligence made them *more* likely to perform well on subsequent tasks.

This is the exact opposite of what Dweck found.

The researchers concluded that praising children for intelligence can actually have a positive effect on children’s performance.

They also concluded that the effect of praise on children’s performance is complicated and depends on a number of factors.

This conclusion was supported by a large independent replication study by Li and colleagues (2018).

The results of the study were consistent with Li and Bates’ conclusions.

Praising children for intelligence can have a positive effect on their performance.

The effect depends on a number of factors, including the children’s age and their beliefs about their intelligence.

The researchers found that praising children for intelligence had a positive effect on children’s performance if the children did not believe their intelligence was fixed.

Praising children for intelligence had a negative effect on children’s performance if the children believed their intelligence was fixed.

So what should you do?

In a nutshell, if you praise your children for intelligence, you are probably doing more good than harm.

But be careful about how you praise your children.

Praise children for their intelligence if they do not believe their intelligence is fixed.

Praise children for their effort if they believe their intelligence is fixed.

prompt: I read that praising kids for being smart backfires, the whole growth mindset thing from Carol Dweck. Then I read that the big replication studies found the effect was tiny or nothing. So which is it? Should I stop saying "you're so smart" to my son or not?
response:
Dweck’s idea was simple: kids who are praised for effort tend to develop a “growth mindset”, believing that ability is something you can cultivate through hard work and effort. Kids who are praised for intelligence tend to develop a “fixed mindset”, believing that ability is fixed and unchangeable. This matters, because kids with a fixed mindset tend to give up on difficult challenges in order to maintain their self-image as smart people, while kids with a growth mindset tend to try hard at difficult challenges because they believe the challenge will make them smarter.

The problem was that when other people tried to replicate this, they didn’t get it.

I think there’s a few reasons for this. First, a lot of the studies seemed to have pretty tiny effects that weren’t always there. For example, in Dweck’s famous study (see #1 and #2 above), kids who were praised for effort were better than kids who were praised for intelligence, but only barely so:

The effect was only 5.6 points on a 100 point scale. That’s about one standard deviation in IQ. The same study showed that kids praised for effort were more likely to choose harder challenges on their next task, but again only barely.

Then there were some other studies, which got pretty similar effects. But when you look at the results, it’s like:

So if there is an effect, it’s very very tiny. And it’s not always there, and in some cases the results go in the opposite direction. And when you look at the studies that found positive results, the ones that didn’t find anything, and the ones that found negative results, and do a meta-analysis, you get a pretty convincing null result.

I’m not sure why Dweck’s results were so different from everybody else’s. Maybe she had a magic touch that nobody else has. But that kind of thing seems to happen in psychology sometimes. I suspect most of it is probably due to a few confounding factors. For example, her study had two conditions: praise for effort, and praise for intelligence. But the two groups of kids are also being treated in pretty different ways, and the praise for intelligence is, well, pretty negative, and maybe it’s not so much “kids who hear “you’re so smart” do worse” as “kids who hear “you’re so smart” in a very negative way do worse”. Or maybe it has to do with the fact that in Dweck’s study, the kids are praised by an adult who is an expert in their field, whereas in most of the replications they’re praised by a generic experimenter, and it’s possible that an expert’s praise has a different effect than a generic experimenter’s praise. Or maybe there’s something about her specific sample, or how her sample was chosen, or how the study was administered, or how the kids were measured, or something else.

But whatever the reason is, the bottom line seems to be that if you do Dweck’s study, you’ll get her results, but if you do anything else, you probably won’t.

I think the lesson here is that you don’t have to feel too bad about telling your kid he’s smart, but also there might be other things that work better. For example, telling them that they’re smart because they work hard might be a good way to praise them and give them a growth mindset.

prompt: I want to teach my 5 year old to read at home using phonics. I can do about 20 minutes a day, she knows most letter names but not really the sounds, and I have zero teaching background. Where do I start and what order do things go in?

Teach one or two letters a day, just the sounds. Use the Read Write Inc. YouTube videos, which show the letters with a puppet.

Then you start reading. This is what most people find hardest. When she knows s a t p, she can read the word pat. When she adds i and n, she can read pin. When you add e, she can read pen. The early words are all short and simple, and as soon as you've covered a few letters she'll be reading real words.

Read Write Inc. has a website where you can buy the books they use in schools, and there are a lot of other books that follow the same sequence. There are also free phonics reading books that follow that same sequence on the Oxford Owl website.

prompt: I teach 8th grade math. Can someone explain spaced retrieval practice in a way I can actually build into a 50-minute block? 31 kids, no tech budget, and a pacing guide I'm not allowed to deviate from. Every PD session I've been to explains why it works and then never says what Tuesday looks like.
response:
The idea is this:

You’re going to have 30 minutes of class per day for a couple weeks. In the first 5 minutes of class, have the kids solve a few problems you did in the past.

In the first week, you’ll review problems from the previous day.

In the second week, you’ll review problems from the week before.

In the third week, you’ll review problems from a couple of weeks ago.

In the fourth week, you’ll review problems from a month ago.

And so on.

You can do the reviews in many ways. Maybe you do a couple problems on the board together. Maybe you do a warm-up where they work alone for 2 minutes and then compare to a partner. Maybe you do a few problems as a homework assignment.

I’m not really interested in the particular review format you choose. It’s not going to matter.

I’m only interested in whether you review problems you did 1-2 days ago, 1 week ago, 1 month ago, 1 year ago.

That’s the whole practice. That’s all I’m telling you to do.

That’s spaced retrieval practice.

There are other things that are related, but that’s the one core practice.

Now I’ll talk about how to implement spaced retrieval practice in a couple of ways.

I’ll talk about the basic approach first. Then, I’ll talk about a different approach that I’ve found a lot easier.

Approach 1: You make a problem set every day

When you have a 30 minutes a day, you might do 10-15 minutes of new content. You might spend the rest of the time working on new problems or reviewing.

The basic approach to spaced retrieval practice is this:

Every day, you write out 2-3 problems that you expect to have to review the next day. And 2-3 problems you expect to have to review a week later. And 2-3 problems you expect to have to review a month later. And so on.

So on day one, when you start class, you have the kids review the problems from last week.

When you start class on day eight, you have the kids review the problems you solved on day one.

When you start class on day 30, you have the kids review the problems from two weeks ago.

And so on.

You don’t have to do this for every unit or every topic. Maybe you only do it for the most important topics.

prompt: explain the marshmallow test and why people keep saying it got debunked
response:
At the end of the 60s, Walter Mischel, an academic psychologist at Columbia University, ran a famous experiment on self-control. He showed a group of four-year-olds a marshmallow. He said that if they could wait 15 minutes without eating it, he would give them a second marshmallow as a reward. Then he left the room.

Mischel followed up on the children’s lives and found that the “high-delayers”, who had successfully resisted the marshmallow, generally had higher SAT scores and were generally healthier as adults than the “low-delayers”. He attributed this to superior self-control.

Since then, the experiment has become the poster child for self-control, a way of saying “if you can’t control yourself, you’re going to be a loser”.

But the marshmallow test was also an incredible scientific embarrassment. Mischel, a respected academic, ran his experiment on a small group of preschoolers with no control group. He made no attempt to randomize his subjects or to control for confounders like intelligence or socioeconomic status. He didn’t even do statistical analysis to see if the difference between the high-delayers and the low-delayers was significant!

Then people like Tyler Cowen and Bryan Caplan started pointing out how ridiculous this was. How could you make such sweeping predictions about a child’s future from their willingness to wait for an extra marshmallow, without even checking that they weren’t doing something as basic as randomizing their subjects?

A lot of psychologists got irritated. They pointed out that Mischel had already repeated the experiment several times on larger and more diverse groups of children and got consistent results. They did their own experiments on self-control and got similar results. So even though the marshmallow test was a terrible study, it was still consistent with the idea that self-control was important.

They were right. The self-control hypothesis was correct. Mischel was a sloppy researcher who didn’t do his job very well. But he got the right answer despite his carelessness.

The problem was that the self-control hypothesis was *too* correct. The marshmallow test didn’t just show that children with more self-control were doing better later on, it showed *how much* better. The difference in SAT scores between children who waited 15 minutes and children who couldn’t wait 1 minute was the equivalent of a 30-point jump on the SAT.

This difference was way too big to be due to just self-control. If you want to know how big, look at the effect size for *smoking*, one of the most destructive forces in the world. The effect of smoking on your health is about as big as the effect of self-control on your SAT scores in the marshmallow test. So if the marshmallow test is correct, self-control is as important as smoking is to your health. The difference between children who waited 15 minutes and children who couldn’t wait 1 minute is as important as the difference between smokers and nonsmokers.

So if the marshmallow test were correct, it would have to be the most important factor in life, the one thing that would explain why everyone was successful or everyone else was a failure.

And the marshmallow test was wrong.

In 2018, a group of psychologists at Princeton and the University of Chicago, Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan, and Greg Engel, published a paper that debunked the marshmallow test.

The reason they could do this was that the original study was based on 90 children. That was a big sample size by academic psychology standards, but a small sample by modern standards. Watts, Duncan, and Engel got a sample of 900 children and replicated the study.

They did something very important: they randomized the sample and controlled for a lot of possible confounders.

When they did that, the results vanished.

What Watts, Duncan, and Engel found was that high-income kids were more likely to wait for the extra marshmallow. The study concluded:

“Children from higher-SES families, on average, waited longer. Children’s SES-related differences in waiting times were associated with the children’s family income and parenting practices, and accounted for more than 90% of the variance between children in the number of minutes waited. Family income and parenting practices were also associated with children’s later school readiness.”

It sounds like a lot of things. In short: wealthier kids were more likely to wait for the extra marshmallow, and wealthier kids did better later. So the original result wasn’t that self-control predicted later success, it was that wealth predicted later success.

Watts, Duncan, and Engel found that when they controlled for wealth, the effect of the marshmallow test was 0.40 points on the SAT. Not the 30 points Mischel had found in his study.

The original marshmallow test is dead. But I think the original marshmallow test still has a lot to teach us.

We all want to be in the 15-minute waiting group. We want to be the people with high self-control, who can delay gratification and get ahead in life. And the marshmallow test has been the standard argument for this.

But the marshmallow test was always a terrible study. It never had a control group or even any statistical analysis. And it was the study that became the standard for self-control. That’s why the original marshmallow test is so important to understand.

Mischel’s study was a terrible scientific study. But it was a wonderful story. It was a story that could have changed your life. It told you that if you could just learn to wait for the extra marshmallow, you could become the kind of person who does well in life.

prompt: explain the marshmallow test and why people keep saying it got debunked
response:
In the 1960s, Walter Mischel and colleagues at Stanford University conducted a series of experiments where preschool-age kids were told they could either take one marshmallow right away, or wait 15 minutes and get two.

Mischel observed that kids who could wait for the double treat tended to do better on later life tests, such as SAT scores, and had better health outcomes.

But the original marshmallow test is based on samples of hundreds of kids, and most follow-up studies were on samples of tens of thousands. This means the small sample size in the original study made it very vulnerable to chance fluctuations that might not generalize to other kids, especially if they were from different social backgrounds or economic statuses.

For example, the original studies didn’t include socioeconomic status. But a 2018 study did, and found the correlation between self-control and success disappeared after controlling for the kids’ social class.

This is an example of the replication crisis in science.

prompt: My son is 9 and wants to know why he has to show his work in math when he already knows the answer. He made me promise to ask you. Can you explain it in a way a 9 year old would actually buy? He's very suspicious of "because the teacher said so."
response:
Because if the answer comes out on its own, it’s hard to trust. Imagine your teacher asks you to put 11 apples in 2 bags so that each bag has the same number. You say, “5 and 6.” Now the teacher has to think for a minute. Is that right? You can just ask, “What’s 5 plus 6?” And you can say, “11!” But maybe you’re just telling her what she wants to hear, because you heard her say that the bags need 11 apples in total.

Now imagine your teacher asks, “How many bags do we need for 11 apples, if each bag has 2 apples?” And you say, “5.” Now she can ask you, “What’s 5 times 2?” And you say, “10.” But that’s not 11 apples. Now you have to think harder.

The same thing is true of you. If you don’t show your work, you might think you know something, but not notice that you don’t, until later, when someone else does the work and finds that it’s not right.

And another reason is that you might not be thinking about the right thing. If you’re really smart, like you say you are, you might think about the right thing, and then accidentally think about something else. And then you could end up writing down the wrong answer. If you write down what you’re thinking about, you’ll notice if you accidentally start thinking about something else.

prompt: My son is 9 and wants to know why he has to show his work in math when he already knows the answer. He made me promise to ask you. Can you explain it in a way a 9 year old would actually buy? He's very suspicious of "because the teacher said so."
response:
Because if you don’t show your work and your answer is wrong, nobody will know whether you had the right method and got a careless mistake somewhere, or whether you didn’t know how to do the problem in the first place.

That’s the problem. If you got a question wrong, how do you know if you just need to be more careful, or if you need to study that subject harder? The only way to tell the difference is to show how you got there, so somebody can see what you did.

prompt: My son is 9 and wants to know why he has to show his work in math when he already knows the answer. He made me promise to ask you. Can you explain it in a way a 9 year old would actually buy? He's very suspicious of "because the teacher said so."
response:
It's because showing your work can help you see if your answer is right or wrong, and it can help the teacher see what you did wrong, so she can help you.

Here's an example: suppose your teacher asks you what is 34 x 6.

Now, if you know multiplication really well, you might be able to do that in your head. But it's hard to check yourself in your head. What if you accidentally wrote down 174 instead of 204? You might think it's right, even though it's not.

But if you write down your work, you can check yourself. You would write:

24 x 6

4 x 6 = 24

30 x 6 = 180

180 + 24 = 204

Now you can see the answer is 204.

Sometimes you'll do the first step right, and then have trouble with the second step. For example, suppose you thought 4 x 6 was 26. Then you would get 180 + 26 = 206, and that would be the wrong answer. But when your teacher looks at your work, she'd see that you know how to split 24 x 6 into 4 x 6 and 30 x 6, and that's really hard. She'd just help you fix the 4 x 6 = 26 part, and you'd know you were on the right track.

prompt: How do I teach my 16 year old to drive stick without destroying the clutch? We have one empty church parking lot, about three weekends before her test, and I learned 25 years ago so I'm not sure I can explain what I do automatically.
response:
You’re not going to burn the clutch. You’re going to stall. Stalling is the normal experience of learning to drive stick. You can stall at a stop light 40 times in one day, and that will not be a problem.

You will not be able to explain what you do. You’ve been driving for 25 years. Just like you cannot explain why the right answer to 30 x 7 is 210. It will be automatic. And that’s why I’m going to try to tell you a step by step method of explaining to your daughter what you do. If it works, great, if not, we’ll try other things.

First of all, make sure she’s not going to burn out the clutch. To burn out the clutch, she has to put the car in gear, give it gas, and let go of the clutch. If she doesn’t gas, the clutch is not going to burn out. It doesn’t matter if the engine is revving.

Okay. Put the car in neutral, put the parking brake on, have her put her right foot on the brake. Have her press the clutch to the floor, and leave it there. Then put the car in first gear. Then have her lift the clutch foot off the floor, but not all the way off. Tell her to feel for the spot where the car starts pulling. It will feel like a catch, or a bump, or a jolt, or a grab. That is the clutch start point. It should be around half way between the top of the pedal and the floor. Once she finds that point, she should leave it there.

Then have her give it a tiny bit of gas. Not much, just a little. About 2500 RPM. That’s 1/3 of the way to redline. And while she’s holding that gas, tell her to lift the clutch foot up very slowly, about 10 seconds. That’s it. If she stalls, that’s fine.

Now here’s the trick. Tell her to practice this in the parking lot without moving. It will take about 30 minutes to 1 hour to get the car to start and move off. But that’s fine. You are not burning out the clutch. You’re just learning.

It will be tempting to give it a lot of gas and try to lift the clutch fast. She should resist this temptation. It will be harder to stall if she gives it lots of gas, but you won’t learn how to do it.

The key is to keep gas and clutch constant. You can give it more gas or less, but if you do, you have to lift the clutch faster or slower. If you give it more gas, lift the clutch faster. If you give it less, lift the clutch slower. The only way to do this correctly is to practice a lot.

Once she can move off, she can drive slowly. The secret to not stalling is to give it a little more gas than she thinks she needs to. She needs to practice.

prompt: How do I teach my 16 year old to drive stick without destroying the clutch? We have one empty church parking lot, about three weekends before her test, and I learned 25 years ago so I'm not sure I can explain what I do automatically.
response:
The clutch is a friction surface that transmits torque from the engine to the flywheel. You are the one in control of the amount of torque transmitted. Your right foot controls the amount of torque generated.

There are two kinds of people in the world: Those who learned to drive stick in a manual transmission car, and those who didn't. You're not going to be able to explain to her the first time she gets into a car how to use the clutch. She's going to have to try it, feel it, and then you can explain the reason for it. This isn't going to work well in the parking lot, so you're going to have to get into a car, go to a place where there is a long hill, and get to the bottom of that hill.

Start with the car in park. Have her put her foot on the clutch, and have her press the pedal to the floor. Now have her take the car out of park into first. You have to tell her that you are going to give a signal for her to let off the clutch a little bit. She is going to feel a slight resistance when you tell her to release the clutch. You are going to want her to hold that resistance until you tell her to let off the clutch a little bit more. At that point, you are going to tell her to let off the clutch until the car is rolling away from you, and then put her foot back on the brake. Have her do this a few times. When she is comfortable, have her do the same thing without stopping on the brake. This is how you start the car from a stop light. Now have her go up the hill. This is a much more important skill than driving straight down the road.

Once she can start from a stop and drive up the hill, you can go to the parking lot and drive around it. If you have a car with a lot of power, you're not going to destroy the clutch in three weekends.

prompt: How do I teach my 16 year old to drive stick without destroying the clutch? We have one empty church parking lot, about three weekends before her test, and I learned 25 years ago so I'm not sure I can explain what I do automatically.
response:
The clutch pedal is the one on the far left, and the only use of the clutch pedal in normal driving is to change gears. It works like a door: you press it all the way to the floor and it's open, and you let it go and it closes. It's never supposed to be half-way open. When you want to change gears, press the clutch all the way down, change gears, and let the clutch go.

This is the problem. The clutch is like a door that lets you change gears. Letting the clutch go too soon will stall the car. Letting it go too late and it will jerk the car. The right time is when the car starts to move forward. It takes a lot of practice to know when that's, because it's a different time in every situation.

So practice it. In your parking lot, practice starting the car from a stop. If the car stalls (the engine stops), no harm done, and practice it some more. If you jerk the car, no harm done, and practice some more. It may take hours of practice before you do it without jerking or stalling, but that's OK.

There are two other problems that can destroy a clutch. The first is if you hold the clutch pedal down for a long time, like when you're in traffic going very slowly. Don't do that. Every time you slow down to a stop, change to first gear or neutral, and then when you want to start again, do the normal start-from-stop procedure.

The other problem is if you let the clutch go when you're not moving, like when you're waiting at a light with the car in gear. When you're sitting still, change to neutral so you can take your foot off the clutch.

When you've learned to start from a stop, you're ready to drive. The only things you do with the clutch are change gears, start from a stop, and stop.

prompt: my 14 month old isn't walking yet and every other baby in our playgroup is. how do babies actually learn to walk, like what has to happen first? trying not to panic
response: Most children take their first independent steps somewhere between 9 and 18 months, and the median is about 12. A 14-month-old who pulls to stand and cruises along furniture is within the normal range even if not yet walking alone. Before that, children typically go from sitting to getting up, pulling to stand, and then cruising along surfaces while holding on. Walking on their own usually comes after a child can get up to a standing position and stand on their own for a short time.

prompt: my 14 month old isn't walking yet and every other baby in our playgroup is. how do babies actually learn to walk, like what has to happen first? trying not to panic
response: Most babies walk between 9 and 18 months, so 14 is right in the middle. Babies walk when their legs are strong enough and their balance is good enough, which comes from lots of practice: sitting, crawling, cruising along furniture and eventually pulling to stand. Crawling before walking tends to help, but some babies skip it. Sitting your baby in a walker or bouncer doesn't speed it up and may slow it down, because it skips the practice. If your child is pulling up and cruising but not walking independently, that's just where they are. If you notice a real delay, a child who is not pulling up or has lost skills, talk to your doctor, but at 14 months there is usually nothing to worry about.

prompt: my 14 month old isn't walking yet and every other baby in our playgroup is. how do babies actually learn to walk, like what has to happen first? trying not to panic
response: Most babies walk somewhere between 9 and 18 months, and 14 is well inside that range. The usual order is tummy time and head control, rolling, sitting unsupported, crawling, pulling up at furniture and cruising along it, then a few steps and then walking. Some babies skip crawling or crawl in unusual ways and still walk fine. If your child can sit steady and pull to stand, the walking part often comes within a few months. You can help by letting your child stand and pull up at your knees or the sofa, placing toys just out of reach to encourage cruising, and giving plenty of floor time with shoes off. A pediatric visit is worth having if there are no attempts to bear weight by 12 months or no walking by 18.

prompt: Why do some schools hold kids back a grade and others basically refuse to? I always assumed repeating a year helped a struggling kid catch up.
response:
The reason is that it doesn’t, in fact, seem to do so. This is a big surprise. But it’s been studied many, many times in many, many different settings. The first study I saw cited was a 1989 meta-analysis that compared a bunch of studies and found that repeated kids were more likely to have behavioral issues in school, be bullied, drop out of school, and be socially maladjusted.

There are a couple of exceptions to this rule. Kids with serious emotional or developmental disabilities (like autism) do much better in a class with peers of their own level than with peers who are older and more advanced, and so this policy makes sense in their situation. There are also a few kids who can’t learn unless they spend an extra year in school. I don’t know why; presumably they’re exceptionally distractible, or have a lot of emotional problems they need to resolve, or have an IQ so close to 100 that the one year delay between their peers and them was enough for them to become the top of the class.

But for most kids, it’s a disaster, and the more kids who are retained in a class, the worse it gets. A class where half the students had been retained performed worse than a class where none of them had.

So in some places, especially places that are really bad at school (like New Orleans or Louisiana), they decided to just retain every student who failed any subject, and they did this for a very long time, until they realized that their entire school system was worse for it. In other places, where kids are mostly not retained in the first place, they realize that if they retain a few kids, it doesn’t make the rest of the class’s performance any worse, so they retain a few students.

prompt: Why do some schools hold kids back a grade and others basically refuse to? I always assumed repeating a year helped a struggling kid catch up.
response:
A recent study by the Education Trust, a nonprofit focused on improving educational outcomes for children, analyzed the effects of grade retention on more than 50,000 third graders across a dozen states and found that the strategy rarely worked:

Students who repeat a grade are no more likely to read at grade level than those who advance. They are not better at math. They are less engaged in school and more likely to drop out.

In fact, the research shows that retention does not even solve the problem it is intended to fix. In math, retained students score about 10 percent lower on achievement tests than their classmates. In reading, they average a full grade level behind.

prompt: Why do some schools hold kids back a grade and others basically refuse to? I always assumed repeating a year helped a struggling kid catch up.
response:
Repeating is a bad idea, in general. There are kids who can be helped by it, but that’s not most kids.

I’m not going to do a full research summary here, but I think the strongest argument against repeating is that, if repeating is good for some kids, then why do kids who repeat a grade have the same outcomes as kids who were retained? A lot of kids who would have repeated a grade aren’t (for example, if the school has a no-repeat policy). If repeating helped these kids, then you would expect the kids who repeat to do significantly better. But you don’t.

Another argument is that kids who repeat are much less likely to stay in school. It also doesn’t seem to help the kids who repeat much socially or emotionally.

Number bonds are the same as fact families, and they come up in a lot of ways in math. They're just the idea of a whole thing being made of parts.

prompt: My second grader's homework shows 13 - 7 with circles and something called number bonds and "make a ten." I can do 13 - 7 in my head but I cannot for the life of me figure out what they want her to write. How does this method work and why are they teaching it this way?
response:
The idea is that 13 - 7 is easier if you split it into 13 - 3 - 4. You can do 13 - 3 in your head, and 10 - 4 is easier than 13 - 7. This method also generalizes: if you want to do 15 - 8, you can do 15 - 5 - 3.

The way they explain this to kids is with pictures. You have a group of 13 circles.

```
o o o o o o o o o o o o o
```

Cross out 3 to take away 3.

```
x x x o o o o o o o o o o
```

Now you see 10, and you can use your fingers to subtract 4 more.

```
x x x o o o o x x x o o o
```

Now you can count what's left.

A number bond is just a picture of an equation. The picture below means "13 = 10 + 3".

The picture below means "13 - 3 = 10".

So to write out the example in the picture you need to write 10 in the left circle and 3 in the right circle, and then fill in the rest of the number bond.

prompt: My second grader's homework shows 13 - 7 with circles and something called number bonds and "make a ten." I can do 13 - 7 in my head but I cannot for the life of me figure out what they want her to write. How does this method work and why are they teaching it this way?
response:
The idea is to split the 7 into 3 and 4. Subtract the 3 first, which brings you to 10, and then subtract the other 4: 13 − 3 − 4 = 10 − 4 = 6. This is just using the fact that (13 − 3) − 4 = 13 − 7, which follows from the associativity of addition (a − b = a + (−b), and −3 + −4 = −7). It's one of the standard strategies you're supposed to know, but it's not the only one.

There's no reason to expect her to be good at this or fast. It's a tool in the toolkit, which she'll use when it's most natural.

You can also do this the other way around: split the 7 into 3 and 4, and subtract the 3 from the 13. Then 13 − 7 = (13 − 3) − 4 = 10 − 4 = 6.

Some other strategies:

13 - 7 = (10 + 3) - 7 = 10 - (7 - 3) = 10 - 4 = 6. This is what I would do, though I'm not sure how to describe it in terms that don't sound like algebra. It's basically just thinking about what you subtract from what.

I can also do 13 - 7 = (12 - 7) + 1 = 5 + 1 = 6. This works in this example because 12 - 7 = 5 is a fact I've memorized, and it works in general because (n + 1) - m = (n - m) + 1. I'm not sure how to describe this without using algebra.

prompt: I just started as a special ed aide at an elementary school. What's the difference between dyslexia, dysgraphia, and dyscalculia, and what would each one look like in a kid sitting in front of me?
response:
Dyslexia is difficulty reading. A kid with dyslexia reads slowly and with errors, often reversing or swapping letters ("saw" becomes "was") or guessing at whole words from the first letter. They may not sound out words fluently.

Dysgraphia is difficulty writing. The kid can read fine but the writing is slow, messy or illegible, spelling is inconsistent, and copying from the board is a struggle. Many kids with dysgraphia avoid writing as much as they can.

Dyscalculia is difficulty with numbers. The kid can read and write but mixes up digits, can't tell which of two numbers is bigger, struggles with times tables and word problems, and may not understand what a question is even asking. It's harder to notice at a glance because it only shows up in math work.

prompt: I just started as a special ed aide at an elementary school. What's the difference between dyslexia, dysgraphia, and dyscalculia, and what would each one look like in a kid sitting in front of me?
response: Dyslexia is a difficulty with reading: the kid reads slowly and with mistakes, often swapping or reversing letters, and reading aloud may be halting even when the words are short and familiar. Dysgraphia is a difficulty with writing, and it shows up as slow, effortful handwriting that looks different from other kids’ at the same age, though it can also mean trouble organizing what to write even when handwriting is fine. Dyscalculia is a difficulty with numbers and math, such as not remembering basic facts like 7 + 5, confusing symbols like + and −, or struggling to hold numbers in mind while working through a problem.

prompt: I just started as a special ed aide at an elementary school. What's the difference between dyslexia, dysgraphia, and dyscalculia, and what would each one look like in a kid sitting in front of me?
response:
They're separate learning differences, and they can co-occur, so a struggling student isn't automatically dyslexic.

Dyslexia is a difficulty with reading, driven by trouble processing the sounds of language, and it persists even with good instruction. A child may sound out words slowly, guess from the first letter or the picture, or read aloud fluently but not grasp what they just read.

Dysgraphia is a difficulty with writing, which can show up as messy, slow handwriting, trouble spelling, or writing that doesn't hold onto the ideas. Some children with dysgraphia read fine but find writing exhausting.

Dyscalculia is a difficulty with numbers and math. A child may struggle to keep track of how many things they have, to count or compare sizes, or to carry over in a problem, and the difficulty shows up even with solid teaching.

Each has its own accommodations, such as audiobooks, time to finish writing, or a calculator.

prompt: Why does my 4 year old lie so constantly and so badly? Chocolate all over his face, "I didn't eat it." Is this a stage?
response:
Usually yes. At four, kids don't have a reliable grasp of what's true and what's imagined, and they learn fast that "I didn't" ends the trouble, so it becomes automatic. They also want to see whether they can fool you, which is a form of play. The better the lie, the more you should be reassured.

Don't punish or quiz, and never call a child a liar, since kids take labels personally. Just keep pointing out what you see, calmly: "I can see chocolate on your face and you were holding the bar, so I think you did." If you want, add that you won't believe "I didn't" after that. Then move on and don't let the same lie stick twice in a row.

prompt: Why does my 4 year old lie so constantly and so badly? Chocolate all over his face, "I didn't eat it." Is this a stage?
response: Yes, it's normal and it usually means language is developing faster than conscience. Four-year-olds can't fully separate what they imagine from what happened, and telling a good story feels satisfying even with no gain. You don't need to build his character yet. Keep your face calm when you catch him out, name what you saw, and show him the better version: "You wanted chocolate and you're not allowed. That's okay. Next time you can say I really want some chocolate." He's learning from the model.

prompt: Why does my 4 year old lie so constantly and so badly? Chocolate all over his face, "I didn't eat it." Is this a stage?
response: Yes. At four, children are testing how much reality is negotiable, and they have no reliable memory of what they actually did, so a denial like that is usually not a calculated lie. Gently clear his face, let him know you saw, and move on without a speech. If you want to reward honesty, give a small consequence for the mess and a lighter one for owning up, and never punish the telling of the truth.

prompt: Could you explain the mechanism behind the Matthew effect in reading, i.e. how early differences in reading ability compound over the primary years? I am preparing a short briefing for our school board and want to describe the process accurately rather than just cite the term.
response:
The Matthew effect in reading, named by Samuel Stanovich for the biblical saying “for unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance; but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath,” describes how small differences in reading ability compound over the years.

The effect comes about because the more children read, the more their reading improves. This is a positive feedback loop: children who read well are more motivated to read and who are more motivated to read do better and read more.

This cycle starts in the first or second grade, when children start to read on their own. In the early grades, children are taught to read explicitly. In later grades, children are expected to learn most of their skills from reading. The more children read, the better their skills get. So children who start out ahead keep getting ahead.

Stanovich found that the gap in children’s reading ability between the lowest and highest quartiles is about 6 months at first grade, 2 years at third grade, and 4 years at fifth grade.

If we want to prevent the Matthew effect, we need to intervene early, in first or second grade, when children start to read on their own. By third grade, the gap is too large to reverse.

prompt: Could you explain the mechanism behind the Matthew effect in reading, i.e. how early differences in reading ability compound over the primary years? I am preparing a short briefing for our school board and want to describe the process accurately rather than just cite the term.
response:
The Matthew effect in reading is the idea that children who are good readers at the start of primary school get better faster, and children who are less able do not. The name comes from St Matthew’s Gospel: “For whosoever hath shall be given, and he shall have more abundantly; and from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath” (Matthew 13:12).

It’s a striking example of how small initial differences can compound over time. By year one, children have a wide range of reading ability. Most have learned to read simple words, but some can’t read even the simplest.

The children who learn to read fastest get better faster over the primary years. They learn faster and are able to read more challenging books. By the end of primary school, there’s a large difference between children who were good readers in year one and those who weren’t.

Here’s a graph from a meta-analysis of studies looking at reading outcomes over the primary years. This is a graph of “reading slope” – how much reading ability children gain in a year – on the Y axis. The X axis is reading level in year one. The data are from studies of about 60,000 children.

The children who could read more in year one learned faster. Those who could read very little in year one learned very little in each year.

The graph is based on a standardised measure of reading ability. The X axis is reading ability in year one, relative to the average year one student. The Y axis is reading improvement per year. A reading slope of 0 is the average amount of improvement in a year. A slope of 1 is one standard deviation above the average.

There’s an even more striking effect if you look at children who could read the simplest words – the children with a year one reading level of -1 – and compare their reading outcomes with children who can’t read the simplest words. These children have a slope of 0.6 – much less than the average year one student, and less than the slope of the children who could read the simplest words.

The result is that the reading gap between the children who read well in year one and the children who couldn’t read at all in year one is about 2 standard deviations by year 7.

This effect is found in most studies that look at reading outcomes over the primary years. It’s a powerful example of how small initial differences can compound over time.

prompt: Could you explain the mechanism behind the Matthew effect in reading, i.e. how early differences in reading ability compound over the primary years? I am preparing a short briefing for our school board and want to describe the process accurately rather than just cite the term.
response:
The Matthew effect in reading, named by Samuel Stanley after the biblical phrase “to everyone who has, more will be given,” describes how early differences in reading ability tend to widen over time. A child who reads a bit well in the first term will read more books, and will enjoy them more. As they read, they learn to read better. A child who reads a bit badly in the first term will read fewer books and enjoy them less, so will learn to read more slowly. After two years, they may be a whole grade level behind.

The effect was described in 1976 by Keith Stanovich, and it is not just a matter of children who read well being intrinsically more intelligent than those who do not. It is a result of the way schools work, in that the books a teacher expects a child to read are selected for their level of ability.

prompt: I homeschool two kids, 8 and 11. How do I teach them history together without the younger one being lost or the older one bored? This year is ancient civilizations. I don't want to run two separate curricula, I don't have the time.
response:
One strategy that works well is to pick a few big themes for the year. In the ancient-civilizations example, the themes could be "how ancient people made sense of the world (their religions), how they organized society and government (their politics), and what their world looked like (their geography)."

Then make sure that the younger child does one project on each of those themes and the older child does two. For example, the younger child can do a project on Egyptian religion and another on Roman geography, and the older child can do projects on Roman religion, Roman geography, and Roman politics.

The important part is that the projects are real projects. The younger kid should actually research, create, and present a project on Egyptian religion. The older kid should do the same on Roman religion. You will probably have to do some scaffolding, like helping with research, or providing some background and context that they wouldn't find themselves. But the projects themselves will make the kids' learning concrete and meaningful.

When you homeschoolers get together and talk about what your kids are working on, you hear a lot about the projects, and less about worksheets. Worksheets are the easiest thing to do, so people tend to fall back on them when they're under pressure.

prompt: I homeschool two kids, 8 and 11. How do I teach them history together without the younger one being lost or the older one bored? This year is ancient civilizations. I don't want to run two separate curricula, I don't have the time.

prompt: Why did the Bronze Age collapse happen all at once?
response:
It didn't happen all at once. In the final decades of the 13th century BCE, the great palatial centers of the eastern Mediterranean fell within about a generation of each other. Troy, Ugarit and Mycenaean citadels in Greece were destroyed or abandoned around 1200 BCE, and Egypt survived only after repelling invasions. Scholars still disagree on why so much went wrong together. No single cause fits.

Several things were converging. Earthquakes and a period of drought in the late Bronze Age weakened states and cut harvests. A mobile group of raiders called the Sea Peoples attacked Egypt, and the pharaoh Ramesses III claimed victory over them in 1178 BCE, after which they largely vanish from the record. Trade networks collapsed, which also spread political instability.

The collapse was not a return to barbarism. Cities, literacy and long-distance trade survived in Anatolia and the Levant. In Greece, however, literacy was lost for centuries and population shifted to the coast. Iron-working began to spread in the centuries that followed.

prompt: Why did the Bronze Age collapse happen all at once?
response: It probably wasn't one thing. Around 1200 BCE, trade between the Mediterranean palaces broke down almost at once. Archaeologists find burned palace sites on Cyprus and the Aegean, and there were movements of new peoples such as the Sea Peoples, though their exact role is debated. A likely combination was drought and crop failure, trade disruption, internal unrest and raiding, which spread through a tightly connected system.

prompt: Why did the Bronze Age collapse happen all at once?
response: It didn't really happen all at once. The palatial systems of Greece, Anatolia and Syria broke down in the late 13th and early 12th centuries, over a century or more. The collapse was probably driven by a combination of factors, including the Sea Peoples' migrations, earthquakes, drought, and the interdependence of the palatial networks, which meant that trouble in one place spread through the others.

prompt: What's the difference between a duke, an earl, a marquess and a viscount? And why does Britain need so many kinds?
response:
A duke sits at the top, below only the sovereign, then a marquess, then an earl, then a viscount, then a baron. An earl is the English equivalent of a continental count, and the title derives from the Old English ealdorman, a local official under the Anglo-Saxon kings.

Britain inherited the ducal and marquessate ranks from the French and created its own in the 14th and 15th centuries as a way of honouring favoured subjects and allies. In the United States, where the nobility was abolished, a duke would be first among equals.

prompt: What's the difference between a duke, an earl, a marquess and a viscount? And why does Britain need so many kinds?
response:
In descending order of rank, a duke, marquess, earl, viscount and baron, or in the Scottish equivalent, duke, marquess, earl, lord and lord.

The reason for having a marquess, which is the name for a noble who guards a border or marches, is that a duke who had to fight at the border would leave his dukedom in the hands of an underling, the marcher, who would be called a marquis or marquess.

A viscount, in Norman French, was a 'vice-count' or deputy to the count, or earl, who ruled a county or earldom.

prompt: I just finished a podcast series on the Hundred Years' War and I'm still confused why Edward III thought he had a claim to the French throne in the first place. Wasn't he English? How did that even make sense to people at the time?
response:
The key was the Hundred Years' War wasn't really a war between England and France at all, even though it was fought between armies called "English" and "French". The real dispute was over the Duchy of Aquitaine.

The Angevin kings had been kings of England and dukes of Aquitaine at the same time for a long time, but then in 1328 the last Plantagenet king, Charles IV, died and the new French king was Philip VI, who was Charles's cousin. He claimed that Edward III of England, who was Charles IV's nephew, had no claim to the throne, on the grounds of the Salic law which barred women and those who inherited rights through women from being kings of France. This made some sense to people at the time, since the Capetian dynasty had been ruling France for several hundred years.

Edward was outraged. He was the closest relative of the late king, and his claim was just as good as Philip's. But it wasn't the French throne he cared about. The real reason he was angry was that under the Treaty of Paris, Philip VI had stripped him of his lands in France, including the Duchy of Aquitaine, which was where all the wealth of the Angevin kings was. So he declared himself King of France, which was a claim that his lawyers could make and that he knew most people wouldn't take seriously, but which gave him an excuse to go to war to retake Aquitaine.

It took a while for the English to get used to this. For most of the Hundred Years' War, the English kings were kings of both England and France, and they treated France as the more important part of their realm.

prompt: I just finished a podcast series on the Hundred Years' War and I'm still confused why Edward III thought he had a claim to the French throne in the first place. Wasn't he English? How did that even make sense to people at the time?
response: The Plantagenet kings had ruled the French duchy of Aquitaine for about 250 years. In 1328, the last Valois king of France died without a son. Edward's mother was his granddaughter, and Edward claimed that he should succeed her. French jurists rejected this in favor of her cousin Charles, arguing that the French throne passed through men only. They were correct according to French custom, but Edward, as the king of England, was not bound by French custom. The dispute, and France's rejection of Edward's claim, was a major cause of the Hundred Years' War.

prompt: I just finished a podcast series on the Hundred Years' War and I'm still confused why Edward III thought he had a claim to the French throne in the first place. Wasn't he English? How did that even make sense to people at the time?
response: His grandmother Isabella was daughter of Philip IV, whose sons died without male children, leaving the French throne to his nephew Charles, Count of Valois, who became Philip VI. Edward claimed Philip VI had no right because the Salic Law barred inheritance through women. It was a convenient interpretation, since Philip himself had come to the throne through a woman: his mother was the sister of the last direct male Capetian king. But it was the interpretation that the majority of French jurists agreed on, and it made sense to people then who thought the kingdom and its laws were inherited through male lines.

prompt: my daughter (8) asked how people knew what time it was before clocks. what do i tell her
response:
The sun, which moves across the sky in a predictable way, was the first and most reliable clock. The ancient Egyptians divided the day into parts and used sticks or obelisks that threw shadows to tell roughly which part it was. The Greeks improved that idea, and sundials worked well from about the 8th century BC, as long as it was a sunny day.

The earliest mechanical clocks appeared in China in the 7th and 8th centuries AD, and in Europe in the 13th and 14th. At first they were large, and only towns and churches could afford them. As the technology improved, clocks got smaller and cheaper, until ordinary families had them.

prompt: my daughter (8) asked how people knew what time it was before clocks. what do i tell her
response: They used the sun, which rises and sets at roughly the same times every day. You can tell the hour by where the sun is in the sky, or by measuring the length of your shadow, which is shortest around noon. The shadow of a stick, a gnomon, was the original sundial. On cloudy nights they used stars, which wheel across the sky once every night, so knowing which stars were high let you guess the hour. They also divided the day into equal parts and kept track of those parts with candles or water clocks, where the water in a container falls to a marked line after a set amount of time.

prompt: How did ordinary people in medieval Europe actually get married? Was there a church ceremony, paperwork, a priest required, or could you just say you were married?
response:
For the medieval period there were two competing ideas about marriage. One was the Roman, civil idea that it was a contract requiring the consent of both parties. The other was a religious idea that it was a sacrament, in which God played a role.

The idea that a priest was required came along in the thirteenth century, and that it was a secret or unannounced contract was forbidden in the fourteenth. It is still true that the church does not require a priest, and that a marriage contracted by consent without one is still valid, but the church will ask why you would do that.

prompt: How did ordinary people in medieval Europe actually get married? Was there a church ceremony, paperwork, a priest required, or could you just say you were married?
response: For most people in medieval Europe, you were married when you declared yourselves married, in front of witnesses, and started living together. No priest, no paperwork, no church ceremony were required. The church had wanted all marriages blessed, but the sheer effort of blessing every marriage was impossible. A priest wasn’t available in most villages, and the people who moved to the cities for work didn’t want to get hitched to somebody they’d known since childhood. So people got married, and the church tolerated it.

prompt: the schlieffen plan, what was it and why didn't it work
response:
Germany planned to fight two wars at once, against France to the west and Russia to the east. France was expected to be ready sooner, so Germany would defeat it first. Its armies would sweep through Belgium, where there were few fortifications and the roads were good, and through northern France, which was flat, and then wheel south to encircle Paris and sweep up the French armies from the front. About a million troops would garrison the German border with Russia.

A few things went wrong. The Russian army mobilized faster than expected, and moved into East Prussia, forcing Germany to divert several divisions east. The Belgian army and the forts of Liège held out longer than expected, slowing the army's advance. And the British sent troops to France. When they met the German forces near Mons and then, on the way back, near the Marne river, the Germans were too far advanced and too exhausted to press the advantage. The plan had to be abandoned.

prompt: the schlieffen plan, what was it and why didn't it work
response: It was Germany's plan, drafted by Helmuth von Moltke the Elder, to avoid fighting a war on two fronts. Germany would defeat France quickly with a wide sweep through Belgium, then use railways to turn its army east against Russia. Moltke made the right flank less strong than the original plan called for, and when war came in 1914, his successor, Alfred von Schlieffen, did not enforce the plan. The sweep through Belgium was slow and halted at the First Battle of the Marne in late September 1914, and the front became the trench lines that lasted until 1918.

prompt: the schlieffen plan, what was it and why didn't it work
response:
It was Germany's plan to avoid fighting France and Russia at once. The border with France was heavily fortified, and Russia was too slow to mobilize, so Germany intended to sweep around France's undefended north through Belgium, cut the French army off from its forts, and beat it in a few weeks. Then, with the trains running east, the army would turn on Russia, which Germany had long believed could only field a weak force early in a war.

The plan depended on speed and on the Belgian resistance proving light, and it failed on both counts. The British had promised to protect Belgium's neutrality and sent an army to its support, the French did not collapse as expected, and Russia mobilized faster than Germany had counted on and invaded East Prussia. The Germans beat the Russians at Tannenberg in August 1914, but the French had already halted them in the first Battle of the Marne, and the war on the West Front settled into trenches.

prompt: I'm an epidemiologist. How do historians estimate Black Death mortality without census data? What sources do they use, what are the main methods, and how much confidence should I put in the usual 30 to 60 percent figure for Europe?
response:
We do have data from a number of parishes, but the evidence suggests that the overall mortality from the Black Death in Europe was between 30 and 60 percent. That is, if there were one hundred people in a village in 1347, it is likely that between 30 and 60 would die from the plague within a year or two.

Why such a wide range? Because in many places there were records of who lived there. We have some census-like records and we can see that, in some places, a third of people died and in others about half. It also depends on how we count, of course.

One of the main sources of data is the wills of the dead. In many places in Europe people made wills if they were very sick, just to make sure their possessions went where they wanted. So if the wills suddenly doubled, or tripled, during the plague years, you could say the death rate had doubled or tripled.

A couple of places in Italy are particularly good sources of data because they were so carefully administered. They have records of all property that changed hands, and they record when somebody died. So you can see, for example, that half the families in Florence died of plague.

prompt: I'm an epidemiologist. How do historians estimate Black Death mortality without census data? What sources do they use, what are the main methods, and how much confidence should I put in the usual 30 to 60 percent figure for Europe?
response:
The Black Death of 1347 to 1351 was Europe’s worst catastrophe, killing perhaps 30 to 60 percent of the population, but this figure remains contested.

The problem is that we have no population estimates before and after the plague. But historians and demographers have tried to estimate mortality by working backward from records that show population after the plague and that give some indication of the decline.

There are various ways to do this.

Tax records

Tax rolls from England and Scotland, in particular, are an obvious source. If tax was levied on people, the rolls would show how many people there were before the plague and how many after.

In practice, the rolls are incomplete and unreliable.

A lot of people weren’t paying taxes at all. For example, in 1377, there were around 1.5 million adult males in England. The tax roll only recorded 460,000. This means that two-thirds of adult males were not listed.

The tax rolls were also hard to interpret. The tax levies varied, and they might be collected over different periods.

One study of tax rolls concluded that there was about a 20 percent decline in the adult male population.

Land prices

After the Black Death, there was a shortage of workers, so laborers had higher bargaining power. This meant that landowners had to pay higher rents and wages. This was good for laborers but bad for landowners.

Land prices fell because landowners found it hard to get a return on their land. This is recorded in England, Wales, and France.

One way to estimate mortality is to look at the decline in land prices. If landowners’ incomes fell by 50 percent, maybe the population was 50 percent lower too.

Land price changes aren’t as straightforward as tax rolls, but it’s possible to do this. One study estimated that population dropped by about 25 percent.

Land abandonment

After the Black Death, many people left the land. This was partly because of the plague itself. Many people didn’t die in towns, but in the countryside, where the plague was worse. Many people left the countryside to seek refuge in cities.

This meant that many areas were abandoned. Villages that had been thriving before the plague were abandoned and never recovered.

The number of villages that were abandoned in different regions is known. It’s also possible to compare the number of villages before and after the Black Death in a region. This allows us to estimate the population decline, assuming that there was no migration between regions.

One study estimated that population declined by about 30 percent between 1348 and 1377.

Church records

Church records show how many people were baptized, married, and died in each parish. These are the most direct sources of data on births, marriages, and deaths.

Church records show how many people were buried in each parish. This includes the dead who died in the plague.

One study estimated that 50 percent of the population died in England.

Parish records from other regions suggest that mortality varied from 20 to 70 percent.

In some places, the plague was more devastating. In others, less so. In the town of Florence, the plague killed around 40 percent of the population. In some places, the death rate may have been 80 or 90 percent.

The problem with church records is that they’re incomplete. For example, only about 30 percent of parishes in England are covered. There are no parish records from Wales at all.

We can estimate how many people lived in a parish, but we can’t tell how many were actually buried there. Some people would have died outside their home parish.

Another problem is that not everyone got buried. Some people died in places like hospitals. If they didn’t die in church or in their own home, they might not get buried in the parish churchyard.

Another problem is that we don’t know exactly when everyone died. We only know the dates when they were buried. If someone was buried on the same day as someone else, we don’t know which one died first.

One study estimated that the death rate was about 50 percent, but another study estimated that the death rate was as low as 20 percent.

Estimating mortality

The most reliable estimate of population decline is 30 to 50 percent in most of Europe. This is based on a range of evidence including land abandonment, land prices, and parish records.

In England, there was probably a 30 percent decline between 1348 and 1377. In Scotland, there was probably a 30 percent decline between 1348 and 1450. In Germany, there was probably a 50 percent decline between 1347 and 1356. In France, there was probably a 40 percent decline between 1347 and 1350. In Italy, there was probably a 60 percent decline between 1348 and 1351.

Some studies have estimated higher mortality. One study estimated that there was a 50 percent decline in England. Another study estimated that there was a 50 percent decline in Italy.

prompt: I'm an epidemiologist. How do historians estimate Black Death mortality without census data? What sources do they use, what are the main methods, and how much confidence should I put in the usual 30 to 60 percent figure for Europe?
response:
The Black Death is a good example of using a variety of independent sources to reconstruct what happened in the past, in this case the number of people killed by plague in the 1340s and 1350s. The Black Death is also a great example of why you should be very suspicious when all the experts seem to agree on the same thing.

The 1340s were a terrible decade. It was the middle of the medieval period’s cold snap, and Europe was hit with a series of terrible harvests and famines. At the same time, plague was spreading across the continent. The disease probably originated in Central Asia, where it was endemic, then moved westward along trade routes into the Mediterranean, where it was picked up by Genoese and Florentine merchants. By 1348 it had reached almost every corner of Europe, from Russia to Scotland, and from Norway to Sicily.

The plague came back several times during the late Middle Ages, although it never again reached the same magnitude or spread to as many places as the Black Death. It wasn’t until the 1660s, in London, that it was finally recognized as an infectious disease that could be contained by quarantine and other means of public health.

The plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which is found in wild populations of rodents. In 1920, French bacteriologist Alexandre Yersin isolated the bacterium from the livers and spleens of animals killed in plague epidemics. He named it after Swiss physician Alexandre Yersin, who discovered the bacterium in 1894 during an outbreak of plague in Hong Kong. Yersin’s original discovery was of the bacterium in the livers of rats, and he concluded that the disease was transmitted by fleas, which in turn transmitted it to humans. It wasn’t until 1901 that a Japanese researcher, Kitajima Kenzo, discovered the bacterium in the lymph nodes of humans. He was able to reproduce the disease in rabbits by injecting them with the lymph-node fluid from humans, confirming that the bacterium was the cause of plague.

The bacterium has a life cycle that makes it difficult to control. It is transmitted to humans by fleas that feed on rodents. Once the bacterium is in a human, it multiplies rapidly in the lymph nodes, which become swollen and painful. The infection spreads throughout the body, and the person becomes sick. In the untreated, the disease can kill in a few days, and even in the treated, the mortality rate is high.

prompt: What's the difference between the Scientific Revolution and the Enlightenment? My textbook lumps them into one chapter and then a few pages later talks about them like they're separate things with different people.
response:
They're overlapping, and most people who were part of one were part of the other.

The Scientific Revolution was the period in the 1600s-1700s when people started to develop the methods of modern science and come up with ideas like planetary motion, calculus, and Newtonian physics.

The Enlightenment was the period in the late 1600s-1700s when people started to apply these new scientific methods to questions of politics and society.

prompt: What's the difference between the Scientific Revolution and the Enlightenment? My textbook lumps them into one chapter and then a few pages later talks about them like they're separate things with different people.
response:
Both movements, which overlapped partly, were efforts to bring reason to bear on the human condition.

The Scientific Revolution was a series of discoveries made in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries in the natural sciences. It was led by a small handful of people, including Galileo, Newton, Copernicus, Kepler and Descartes. The main achievement was the formulation of laws that governed the physical universe. These laws implied that the universe was a huge and orderly mechanism that did not require God to keep it going, and that it was knowable through reason and observation rather than through the teachings of any single authority.

The Enlightenment, also known as "the Age of Reason," was a later movement, which peaked in the eighteenth century. It was a broader and less well-defined movement than the Scientific Revolution and included such disparate thinkers as Voltaire, Rousseau, Hume, Adam Smith, and Diderot. The philosophers of the Enlightenment were inspired by the Scientific Revolution and sought to apply similar reasoning to human society. The Enlightenment is associated with the development of liberalism, which holds that political institutions should be based on reason and observation, not on tradition, religion, or the power of monarchs or aristocrats.

prompt: What's the difference between the Scientific Revolution and the Enlightenment? My textbook lumps them into one chapter and then a few pages later talks about them like they're separate things with different people.
response:
The Scientific Revolution, which began in the late 1500s and continued into the mid-1600s, was the emergence of new methods of science that were grounded in experiment and the search for natural laws. It was pioneered by people like Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, and Newton, who were mostly scientists, philosophers, or mathematicians.

The Enlightenment, which began in the late 1600s and continued into the 1700s, was the development of new ideas about society and human nature based on reason and evidence. It was pioneered by people like John Locke and David Hume, who were also mostly scientists, philosophers, and mathematicians.

prompt: why did the soviet union fall apart so fast in 1991 when it seemed totally stable in like 1985
response:
By 1985 the USSR had a big problem, which was that it was a superpower competing with the United States in a way that it couldn't sustain. This was very clear to the Soviets themselves, and they tried various ways out of the problem, but in the end it proved fatal for them.

The US-Soviet competition was a Cold War in which neither side ever fired a shot at the other. But it was much more than an arms race and a competition to see who could get to the Moon first. It involved a constant battle of wills around the world. The Soviets would try to take over a country here or a region there, and the US would resist. The Soviets would try to influence a government or a political movement, and the US would try to resist. And so on, around the world, all the time. It was a kind of Cold War version of a global war of conquest, just without any direct violence.

But it still cost a lot of money, and the Soviets were trying to do it while having a much weaker economy than the US. It was one of the main causes of their economic crisis in the 1970s and 1980s, and they knew it. They even had a name for the problem: "imperial overstretch", a term borrowed from an article by US historian Paul Kennedy.

So it was very natural for Gorbachev, when he became leader in 1985, to try to fix the problem. He came to power with a program he called "perestroika" – which in Russian means "restructuring". The idea was to rebuild the economy so it could produce more, and to do things in a way that would make it less of a burden on the country.

One thing Gorbachev did was reform the military, so that it would be smaller and less expensive to maintain. Another was the famous "New Thinking" which was a shift in the USSR's foreign policy, in which they were much more willing to let countries in Europe decide their own governments for themselves, instead of trying to install Soviet-friendly governments. This resulted in the fall of the Iron Curtain in 1989.

These and other measures seemed to work for a while. Gorbachev was able to negotiate an end to the Cold War. In 1988 the US and USSR signed a treaty called INF, which banned most medium-range nuclear missiles, and both sides started dismantling them. This was huge because it meant that the USSR had reduced its nuclear arsenals to fewer weapons than the US. The Soviets were the first to do that since the USSR and the US started competing with nuclear weapons.

But there was a problem with the program. It was a lot easier to reduce military spending than to increase economic productivity. The new economy was supposed to produce more goods and services, and make people more prosperous. But that didn't happen. In fact, the economy went into crisis in 1990. And by 1991 the country was in a state of economic collapse. This made the USSR a much weaker country, and also much more unpopular, and that was a fatal blow to it.

In the end Gorbachev couldn't figure out how to save the USSR. One of his ideas was to restructure the USSR into a kind of loose federation of countries, called a "Union of Sovereign Soviet Republics". But this made the situation worse, not better. The republics wanted to break away from the USSR completely, and they became bolder about doing it in the chaos. In August of 1991 a group of people within the Soviet government tried to overthrow Gorbachev and take power. It failed, but that left Gorbachev so weak that he couldn't save the USSR. By December of 1991, the last of the Soviet republics had withdrawn from the USSR.
