prompt: How did Polynesian navigators find tiny islands across thousands of miles of Pacific with no compass and no charts? I've read "they read the waves" but I don't understand what that means in practice.
response:
I've been fascinated by how Polynesian navigators were able to cross thousands of miles of empty ocean to find islands that might be only a few square miles.

You might think of the Pacific as a vast empty space, with tiny islands scattered here and there. But when you think about it that way, the oceans between islands are just empty space. When I learned about how Polynesian navigators worked, I realized that there's a lot of information in the oceans that's not immediately obvious.

It turns out that the ocean isn't empty space. There are waves. And waves are affected by the land. And so the waves can be a source of information about the land.

Waves are created by wind. And wind usually blows a few hundred miles from the nearest land. So if you're sailing across the Pacific, waves are coming from several directions: they're coming directly from the wind, but they're also coming from the wind that hit some islands, and bounced off them in another direction.

So there are waves going in every direction. Waves that were originally blowing in a certain direction, but hit islands, bounce off, and change direction. Waves that hit a mountain in the middle of the ocean might not be as affected. But waves that hit a long mountain range might be affected a lot. And waves that hit a long, straight coastline might be affected a lot too. So there's a lot of information about land in the waves. And if you know how to read it, you can use it to tell you where the land is.

The waves that are affected by land are called "swells". You can use swells to tell you where the land is.

The waves that are affected by land are usually larger, because land adds energy to them. And they're usually in a different direction. So if you can tell the difference between normal ocean waves and swells, you can tell where the land is.

If you've ever been to a beach, you've seen this. If you're in the water, you can tell what direction the waves are coming from. And if you're not in the water, you can tell where the beach is by where the waves are coming from.

I learned more about how to use swells to navigate from a video by Derek Doyle. He explains that if you want to learn to use swells, you can go to any beach, and just sit there for a couple of hours. If you do that, you'll be able to tell where the swells are coming from.

You can also use a compass to tell where the swells are coming from. And if you know where the nearest land is, you can tell what the swells are doing. For example, I live in a small bay in California. And it's a small bay, but the waves go in and out of it. And it takes a few hours for the waves to go through it. So I know how long it takes for waves to go through the bay, and that's a useful thing to know.

I think that's a really cool thing to know. It's a little bit like knowing the speed of light, but with waves.

prompt: How did Polynesian navigators find tiny islands across thousands of miles of Pacific with no compass and no charts? I've read "they read the waves" but I don't understand what that means in practice.
response:
Every island, no matter how small, disturbs the swell moving across the sea. The swell that passes a few miles either side of the island, coming from, say, west to east, strikes the island, and part of it is reflected and part is refracted around the island. The reflected waves come back towards the west, and the refracted waves come out to the east of the island in a curved pattern, like water flowing around a pillar.

If you're in a boat sailing west to east, you will feel the difference in the waves between these two patterns. If the waves coming from the side of your boat that's on the left are more regular and higher, and the waves on the right are more irregular and lower, you're on the east side of an island, and it's to your left.

The great Hawaiian navigator way of navigating was to mentally build a map of the ocean in terms of the waves and how you feel the waves when you're sailing in the boat.

The Hawaiian tradition of navigation, as well as the tradition of most other Pacific peoples, is that the navigator "sleeps on the ocean". It's not clear what this means. The most obvious interpretation is that the navigator lies on his back in the boat, eyes closed, and feels the waves. The second is that the navigator falls asleep in the boat, and dreams about the waves.

I've read a description of the navigator falling asleep and dreaming that he was swimming through the water, and feeling the waves on his skin. I find it difficult to believe that people could navigate from dreams, although I've had a few experiences of people who were able to solve problems while dreaming.

I'm curious if there's any scientific evidence about how "sleeping on the ocean" works.

prompt: Cleaning out my grandmother's house we found her ration book from England, 1940s, with little coupons and a separate section for "points." She used to say the points were the clever part but never explained. How did rationing actually work day to day? Why were there both coupons and points, and what stopped people from just trading them or forging them? She was a teenager then and I wish I'd asked her.
response:
From 1940 until 1954, the British were rationed on food and many other items. A typical family of three in wartime would get a pound of meat a week, about a pound and a half of sugar, and about a quart of margarine (butter was rationed until 1952). If they were lucky, they would also get two eggs and a couple of pints of milk each week.

Rationing worked in two ways. Some goods, such as meat and sugar, were rationed by a coupon that you could exchange for a fixed amount of the good. For instance, 64 coupons for bacon (each worth one ounce) bought a pound.

For other goods, the system used a system of “points,” where each person had a certain number of points to spend each month, and different goods cost different numbers of points. For instance, 35 points got you a pound of biscuits, 20 points got you a pound of cheese, and 125 points got you a bottle of olive oil. The points system made it easier to shift supplies around as availability changed. For instance, if there was a lot of sugar, people would get fewer coupons for sugar but a few extra points to spend on other items.

Ration coupons and points were issued in little books, which looked like this:

The coupon book on the right, issued in 1944, contains coupons for sugar, meat, and margarine and a book of points to be spent on “anything else you may want.” The coupons and points on the left are from 1954, at the end of the rationing era.

The books were issued by the local post office, and each family got a number of books according to its size.

The ration system worked pretty well. The British spent years working out how much to ration people to, and the result was a diet that was less varied than the prewar diet, but not very unhealthy. In wartime, people who weren’t doing strenuous physical labor got an average of 2,440 calories a day, and the general diet got better after the war. For example, the average British person today gets only about a third of the sugar and a fifth of the meat that they got during wartime.

prompt: Cleaning out my grandmother's house we found her ration book from England, 1940s, with little coupons and a separate section for "points." She used to say the points were the clever part but never explained. How did rationing actually work day to day? Why were there both coupons and points, and what stopped people from just trading them or forging them? She was a teenager then and I wish I'd asked her.
response:
Rationing was, from a political standpoint, a big deal in Britain during the Second World War. The Nazis had successfully blockaded Britain's merchant fleet, and its imports had dried up, so it was a bit like a natural experiment. The government of Winston Churchill, facing the possibility of starvation, decided to ration every British citizen equally, including Churchill himself.

The scheme, in case it wasn't already clear, was a total success. Britain's citizens were able to fight the Second World War despite not having access to a lot of the food they would normally have.

The scheme also worked pretty well in a practical sense. Britain was able to ration its citizens fairly quickly, and with a minimum of waste, and the system was simple enough that most citizens understood it and complied.

There were two types of rationing. Some items were rationed by weight. If you had a coupon marked "1 lb of meat," you could get 1 lb of meat. You got a limited number of these coupons each week. Some items were rationed by "points." These were a kind of currency, and you could trade them in for anything the government wanted you to be able to buy.

The British government found that the weight system was not very good, because it meant they had to keep a separate supply of every type of rationed good, even though they were very similar. For example, there were different types of coupons for beef, mutton, lamb, pork, and veal. These were all basically meat, and there was no reason why someone couldn't eat beef if there was more beef than mutton that week. So starting in 1942, Britain switched over to the points system, and the only coupons you got were for points.

This was not a simple system! There were lots of different points, such as "10 points of milk" or "15 points of butter." But as long as you had enough points, you could get anything you wanted.

The government tried to set prices on the points so that they would be pretty consistent. So they would try to set 10 points = 1 pound of milk = 1 pint of butter = 1 pound of cheese. This is not the same as saying a pint of butter cost a pound, it's just that the government wanted people to be able to easily exchange one for the other.

This was, at least in spirit, a pretty good system. It was very flexible, and could handle supply and demand changes easily. The only problem was that it was also a bit too flexible, so people would always get the things they most wanted. In the US, people would always get the best cuts of meat, and leave the cheap stuff. In Britain, people always got the best cuts of meat, and also a lot of things that the government didn't really want people to have, such as chocolate.

So in 1947, the government decided to switch back to the coupons system, and only give you coupons for things they wanted you to have.

The coupons were printed by the government, and were supposed to be hard to forge. They had to match the person who used them, and the government kept a list of all the coupons that had been printed.

So how did it all work, day to day? Let's say you were an average housewife in 1942. Every month you'd get a book of coupons, with your name on it, and a lot of coupons in it. Let's say that you had a coupon that said "12 points of meat." You would go to the butcher, and hand him this coupon and £1.00. Then the butcher would give you a piece of meat. That piece of meat could be any piece of meat that the government wanted you to get that month, but the butcher had to make sure that you got the right amount of it.

Then, once a week, the butcher would take all of these coupons and send them to the government. And the government would send him money. In practice, the government would pay the butcher, and he would pay the suppliers. But the end result was that the government would pay people to make things for other people to buy.

In practice, this was a pretty good system. The government didn't have to micromanage every store in Britain, but it could still get what it wanted, by telling the stores what to do.

This system was a pretty good one, but it wasn't perfect. In particular, it didn't prevent stores from being able to charge whatever they wanted for things. So the government also set prices on everything. In particular, if there was a coupon that said "12 points of meat," that meant that you could only buy that piece of meat for £1.00. And the butcher had to get you the right amount of meat for that. This was a pretty good system, but it was a little bit hard to enforce.

This is from 1944:

There’s a nice explanation of the system here. So they made points, which were ration coupons that were also a form of currency.

To make sure people didn’t over-use points for tea or rubber or petrol, they made sure that the points were worth less when you used them for things the US sent to Britain, and more when you used them for things Britain had to get from other countries.

It was very easy to trade points, though. In fact, the whole system was designed to make trading easy.

I can’t remember how it was possible to forge coupons. It was a common problem – I remember there was a TV show about somebody who tried to get rich by forging coupons.

prompt: I'm reading Trollope and all the characters keep arguing about the Corn Laws. What were they, and why did repealing them split the Conservative party so badly?
response:
The Corn Laws were tariffs on imported grain. They were supposed to protect the livelihoods of the landed gentry, who owned and farmed most of the land in Britain. The problem was that the tariffs raised food prices for everyone else, especially the industrial working class, who spent a lot of their income on food.

Most of the Conservative party were landed gentry or otherwise aligned with them, so they supported the Corn Laws. But a few prominent industrialists like Richard Cobden and Joseph Chamberlain, also in the Conservative party, opposed them.

In 1841 Robert Peel’s Conservative party got a majority in parliament, and Peel promised to repeal the Corn Laws. But the majority of his party disagreed, and in 1845 they voted to remove the promise from their official party platform.

Peel went against his own party anyway. In 1846 he persuaded Queen Victoria to give him another chance, and in 1847 he repealed the Corn Laws.

His party never forgave him for this. They split into two factions, the Peelites who supported him, and the Conservatives (who would become the modern Conservative party) who didn’t.

Peel then lost a vote of confidence in the House of Commons and became the leader of the Conservative party, but he didn't really recover. The next year, 1847, he got ill and left politics for a few years. The repeal of the Corn Laws was his legacy.

prompt: How did the Inca run an empire that big without writing? I know about quipu but how much information can knotted string actually hold?
response:
It held more than you might think. The knotted strings of quipu encoded numbers in base ten. Each position along a cord held a number, and the position indicated the place value. A quipu could have up to 1,400 cords, and a single quipu could encode 240 numbers, giving a capacity for about 28,000 digits. And you could write on the quipu by adding more knots, so a single quipu could store several years’ worth of records.

The quipu kept accounts of taxes and the inventory of goods, and also kept a record of the population for conscripting laborers for construction work. But that’s not all. In 1996 Gary Urton, an anthropologist at UC Berkeley, and Carlos Esteban provided evidence that the quipu could record other kinds of information too. Urton and Esteban examined a set of 64 quipu that were found in the ruins of a temple in the highlands of Peru. The temple’s priest probably had used the quipu to organize a yearly festival.

They found a consistent pattern in the colors of the quipu cords, which suggests that the colors of the cords conveyed meaning. For example, if a quipu’s cords were arranged in groups of three, the first cord of the group was red, the second was white, and the third was brown. The colors probably indicated the role of the number: the red cord held the number of a kind of good that was needed for the ceremony, the white cord held the number of people who were assigned to collect the goods, and the brown cord held the number of goods collected so far.

If the quipu could store more than just numbers, it’s possible that they could store sentences, but there’s no way to know yet.

prompt: How did the Inca run an empire that big without writing? I know about quipu but how much information can knotted string actually hold?
response:
A quipu could carry up to thousands of numbers, organized in rows of strings with a hierarchical structure, and the Inca used them for censuses and accounts. But quipu are not a writing system. They can't preserve anything that isn't numerical, so if you had a quipu about the harvest in one year you couldn't use it to remember what it was like in another year. They're a bookkeeping tool.

There are theories that some quipu had meaning beyond their numerical values, like if the length of a string encodes a word, but nobody can prove it. The Inca could've had a written language that we know nothing about, but there is not a shred of evidence that they ever wrote anything down.

Instead, the Inca used an oral history called a willkakuna, which meant 'memory.' It was like a collection of stories that the Inca learned by rote memorization. They were told about how to deal with specific situations, like a story explaining that if you get lost in the mountains, you should try to find the nearest river and follow it downstream.

But why trust a story you might be remembering incorrectly? Because it was told so often you'd never forget it. The Inca had an entire class of people who memorized the stories and told them to new people so they wouldn't be lost. They could remember so much that they could tell stories that were thousands of years old, like when an ancestor built a road, and they could tell new Inca where the road was.

They also had oral histories that were very detailed about how to do various tasks, like the steps of building a building. The willkakuna was an important part of Inca education and was also used for law. There were stories about the punishments they gave to thieves or liars, and the stories also had advice on how to solve problems.

This sounds like it could be unreliable, and it does have limitations. But the Inca did not forget the stories. The Inca also had to memorize their own history, because the willkakuna were used for the history of the empire. The Inca memorized the entire genealogy of rulers. The Inca also memorized the names of all the members of the royal court and everyone's relationship to each other.

The Inca empire had an estimated population of 10-14 million, which is about 20-30 times larger than the Aztec empire, and about 40 times bigger than the Maya.

prompt: How did the Inca run an empire that big without writing? I know about quipu but how much information can knotted string actually hold?
response:
The short answer is: the state didn’t need much, because it ran on things other than paper.

The Inca state was enormous by its own standards: around 2 to 12 million people, depending on estimates, from Colombia to central Chile, at the peak around 1500, and only just under the control of the empire for a century or two. They had no writing, but they did have quipu (sometimes spelled khipu), knotted string devices that can hold numbers. A quipu was a main string with pendant strings hanging off it, and the knots on them recorded numbers in base 10; the position of the knot on the string determined its place value. You could store quite a lot of information this way; the best preserved quipu, the Quipu of Turpo, has about 1,400 knots recording 2,200 or so numbers.

But the Inca used quipu mainly for administrative purposes, to keep track of the empire’s stores, resources and populations. For this you need only simple numbers, which quipu handles fine. The Inca may also have used quipu as an aid to memory, where the knots help remind the user of the story to be told. Some scholars have speculated that quipu may have been able to hold more complex information in the colors of the string and in the ways the strings were arranged, but it’s hard to say how much information would have been stored this way.

The Inca used other ways to communicate information as well. For example, they had a system of relay runners along the roads in their empire, which could carry messages up to 150 miles a day. They also had trumpeters, who would blow conch-shell trumpets to send short messages from mountain-top to mountain-top.

But these ways of sending messages are not how the Inca ran their empire. The Inca had a very large bureaucracy, with tens of thousands of state officials. These officials had a common language, Quechua. The Inca could communicate complex messages to them by speaking, and the Inca could control them by sending them to different jobs throughout their empire, a method of control that has worked ever since.

A couple of other points. The Inca were a highly practical people, and the Inca rulers were known to incorporate technologies from conquered peoples if they found them useful. The Inca used camelids for meat and fiber, and llamas for transporting heavy items, but the Andes have no horses and no cattle. The Inca also had no wheeled vehicles. This was not because they were too primitive to come up with these ideas, but because the Andes are too mountainous to be useful for wheeled vehicles and because camels are not suited for use as riding animals. The Inca adopted many technologies from their conquered peoples, such as cotton clothing from the coasts and maize cultivation from the lowlands. There’s no evidence that they ever conquered a people with a writing system, so they may well have adopted one if they had.

Finally, there were also people in the Andes who did develop writing systems. The Wari people, who were the Inca’s predecessors, had a limited writing system with about 13 or 15 signs, but it doesn’t seem to have been widely used. The Inca’s neighbors to the north, the Chimú, had a full writing system, with about 300 symbols, and the Chimú seem to have been quite advanced technologically as well. But in 1470 the Inca conquered and destroyed the Chimú. This is one of those mysteries of history: had the Chimú been able to survive, might they have ended up as the dominant civilization in South America?

prompt: Please explain the principal causes of the Taiping Rebellion, and why it proved so much deadlier than contemporaneous civil wars such as the American one.
response:
The Taiping Rebellion was a civil war in China lasting from 1850 to 1864, during which, by most estimates, at least 20 million people died – probably far more. It remains one of the deadliest conflicts in human history.

Hong Xiuquan was a poor man who had failed his examinations to enter the bureaucracy – a great shame to both his family and himself. He was also a Christian convert, though a confused one who mixed Christianity with his own beliefs and saw himself as the brother of Jesus. In 1843, he started a movement that preached the worship of a single God, the overthrow of the Qing dynasty – and the overthrow of everything associated with it.

The Taiping movement grew quickly, in the southern Chinese province of Guangdong, where the poor and hungry were attracted by its message. The Qing dynasty did not try to stop it at first, as it was not a traditional rebellion. When it finally moved into open rebellion in 1850, it was well organised and well prepared.

The Qing were unable to stop the Taipings, whose leader, Hong Xiuquan, declared himself the Heavenly King in 1851, and established a state in Nanjing, which he made his capital. The Qing did finally defeat the rebellion, in 1864, but at huge cost. The Taiping Rebellion is probably responsible for more deaths than the Second World War.

The Taiping Rebellion was so deadly because:

China was much more densely populated than the US, so the war had a much larger civilian population that it could kill.

The war involved sieges of cities. When the Qing captured Nanjing in 1864, they massacred almost everyone they found.

There was no Geneva Convention to restrict what the armies could do to civilians, and the two sides were very hostile to each other.

There was no army of the United States that was trying to stop the conflict.

The war was very long.

prompt: Please explain the principal causes of the Taiping Rebellion, and why it proved so much deadlier than contemporaneous civil wars such as the American one.

The Taiping Rebellion was so deadly for several reasons. First, it was a religious war fought with fanatical zeal. Second, it was a civil war, and the Qing forces and the rebels were of similar strength. Third, many of the Chinese people at the time believed that the rebels were God’s army on earth. Fourth, the war lasted much longer than the American one, from 1850 to 1864. Fifth, the Taiping Rebellion was not as modernized as the American Civil War. prompt: Please explain the principal causes of the Taiping Rebellion, and why it proved so much deadlier than contemporaneous civil wars such as the American one.

A former failed scholar named Hong Xiuquan, who had been failing the imperial examinations for 15 years, claimed to have had a vision in which he was told that he was the younger brother of Jesus Christ, and that he was to rid the earth of demons. When it did raise troops, they were not up to the task. The rebellion was finally suppressed with the help of the British, in 1864. About 20 million people died, making it one of the most destructive conflicts in human history. prompt: How do I research the history of my house? Built around 1890 in a small Ohio town. I've got a free weekend, a library card, and access to the county recorder's office. I want to know who lived there and what changed. Where do I start?
response:
Start at the county recorder's office and ask for the deed history of your parcel. In many counties the chain of title is already assembled for you; if not, each deed will point you back to the previous owner. Ask about index books organized by the first letter of the seller's surname, or a computerized index if one exists. A deed will tell you the names of owner and buyer, when they changed hands and for how much. It will also show you a description of your lot and, in older deeds, a legal description of the house: the number of rooms, how many stories, whether it is brick or frame.

For the owners and occupants of your house, consult the local census at the library. The census is done every ten years, and the most recent one you can use is from 1920. The census will tell you who was living in your house at the time, their ages and occupations, and where they were born. If you have your deed history, you can follow your house from census to census, starting with 1880, which was the first time names were recorded.

The local historical society will have more information, including histories of the town or county. It might also have old newspaper archives, where you might be able to find mentions of your house or of its owners and occupants.

prompt: Why did so many European countries end up with German royalty in the 1800s? Britain, Greece, Bulgaria, Belgium... was this a plan or an accident?
response:
It was an accident, but a lucky one.

In the nineteenth century German princes and princesses were the most desirable people in Europe to marry, because there was a huge surplus of them.

The German lands had been divided into hundreds of tiny states, and the rulers of all those states were royalty. They needed to marry in order to produce heirs, so they had to keep having babies. As one commentator put it, “If you wanted children, you had to marry; and if you wanted to marry, you had to be born a princess.”

By the time of Victoria’s ascension, a few of the tiny German states had been united into Prussia and Austria-Hungary, but those two states both contained hundreds of royal titles. And most of the remaining states, even though they had become German states, kept their royal status as a courtesy.

This resulted in a vast number of royal titles. For example, the Grand Duke of Baden, which is now part of Germany, was a member of a German dynasty called the House of Zähringen. He had been ruling since 1535, and by 1718 his line had already been extinct. The state of Baden had a new duke, who wasn’t actually related to the original duke. But he still called himself “Duke of Baden,” so that he could have royal status.

There are other stories like this: the King of Saxony, who was also the Prince of Saxony, was the leader of a dynasty called House Wettin, and had ruled since 1089. But the original line was extinct by 1873, when a cousin took over. But he also called himself the Prince of Saxony, and had royal status.

All these princes and princesses needed to marry someone. They wanted to marry other royalty, to keep their status, but they could only marry into their own class. This was a huge problem: they could only marry other royalty, which were all Germans.

But many of them didn’t want to marry Germans. Germans were considered the butt of all of Europe at the time. And besides, their own country was so small that marrying another German would be like marrying your cousin.

So they ended up marrying the British, because Britain was the only other country with enough royalty to be worth marrying.

Victoria was the daughter of a German princess. Victoria’s first child, Edward, married Princess Alexandra of Denmark. Edward and Alexandra had four children, and all of them married other royalty. The two princes, George and Alfred, married the daughters of German royalty. The two princesses married the sons of German royalty.

One of Victoria’s daughters married the King of Greece, who became the Greek royal family.

In the end, the children of all of these German royals who married into the British royal family ended up taking over the throne of Britain. In fact, the Queen of Britain today is a member of the House of Hanover, which is a German royal family.

prompt: Why did so many European countries end up with German royalty in the 1800s? Britain, Greece, Bulgaria, Belgium... was this a plan or an accident?
response:
It was an accident, in the sense that it wasn’t an explicit plan. But it wasn’t a coincidence, either, because the family was looking for marriages for their many sons, and the other families were always open to offers of a good, well-connected young man, especially one who had an army on his side.

In the 1800s, Europe was full of young men from royal families who were looking for brides. Many of these royal houses had been fighting wars against each other for centuries, so intermarrying between the houses was not encouraged. Some countries had few women of royal birth, and the best match available to their princes might be a countess or baroness.

But the House of Hanover was different. The Kingdom of Hanover had been ruled by the House of Welf, which included both the House of Welf in Bavaria and the House of Hanover in Germany. In 1705, the line of rulers in the Hanover kingdom died out, and the Hanover crown passed to the House of Brunswick, which was a cadet branch of the House of Welf. So the House of Welf in Bavaria was the senior branch of the dynasty, and the House of Brunswick was the junior branch.

In 1814, the king of Hanover, George IV, was the second son of George III, who was the King of England. George III was a Hanoverian, because he was the first of the House of Brunswick to become King of England. The House of Brunswick became the Kings of England in 1714, after Queen Anne had died and her cousin George I of Hanover had become King of England. (There was a lot of political drama around this; Queen Anne had died childless, and she had a daughter who had died in childbirth. Her heir, the Prince of Hanover, was 54 years old, and no one had expected him to have children. But he did have a son, George II, who became King of England in 1727. He also had a son, Ferdinand, who was heir to Hanover.)

In 1735, the Hanoverian line of the House of Welf died out, and Ferdinand, the Hanoverian heir, became Duke of Brunswick. This is where it all got complicated, because there was a lot of intermarriage between the two branches of the House of Welf. Duke Ferdinand of Brunswick was the grandson of Duke Ferdinand Albert II of Brunswick-Lüneburg, who had married Princess Anne of Hanover. Princess Anne of Hanover was a daughter of George I. Duke Ferdinand of Brunswick also had a cousin, Princess Louise of Hanover, who was a sister of George II. So Duke Ferdinand’s mother, aunt, and cousin were all descendants of George I, while his father was a descendant of Duke Ernest I of Brunswick-Lüneburg, who was a cousin of George I.

In 1780, Duke Ferdinand of Brunswick died childless. He had a half-brother, Duke Charles William Ferdinand of Brunswick, who also died childless. Duke Charles William Ferdinand had been a military commander during the Seven Years’ War, where he had been captured and held prisoner by the French. He had been released by the French and returned to the front, but he was killed at the Battle of Bunker Hill. This was a very unusual place for a German commander to be killed; the Battle of Bunker Hill was a battle between the British and the American colonists, and it was not at all obvious why the Duke would have been fighting there. But he had been the commander of the British army in America, and he had fought at Bunker Hill.

In 1799, Duke Charles William Ferdinand died without an heir, so the title of Duke of Brunswick passed to Duke Ferdinand August, Duke of Brunswick, who was the last member of the House of Welf in the male line. He died without an heir in 1806.

prompt: In the 1700s, how did anyone know a letter was really from the person who signed it? Did wax seals actually stop forgery or were they mostly symbolic?
response:
A wax seal was not very hard to fake, and most seals were so decorative that anyone who was going to bother forging a letter would be happy enough to fake it. A seal was a way of showing that the document was in a form that the sender considered authentic; if you broke the seal, that was an obvious signal that you had, like, maybe, tampered with it.

A more effective way of verifying was to sign things in a way that was hard to fake: for example, you might write in a language you were known to be fluent in, or write in a distinctive style that you were known for. If you received a letter that was signed in German, but you knew the person who supposedly sent it was actually a native French speaker, you might not believe it.

There were ways to create a document that was signed with an unforgeable signature. In 1780, Benjamin Franklin was working in France, and wanted to sign a letter that couldn’t be forged by the British. He used a system called a “ciphertext alphabet,” where you invent your own alphabet, and everyone who knows it can read anything you write, but everyone else can’t. He drew two alphabets, one where each letter was a different shape, and one where each letter was a different color; then he signed the letter “Benjamin Franklin” in that alphabet, in the color red. He also wrote a copy of the letter in normal English, and included that in the letter.

The system of inventing a unique alphabet and sending it to the other party in a separate message was one of the first ciphers to be described in print, in a book called *The Gentleman’s Ciphers*. The idea of encrypting a signature was also described there, and the British were aware of this when they started intercepting Franklin’s mail and trying to fake his letters.

prompt: In the 1700s, how did anyone know a letter was really from the person who signed it? Did wax seals actually stop forgery or were they mostly symbolic?
response:
A personal seal, usually a ring that was cut with your design and rolled into wax, was the signature of the day. The wax could be forged, of course, but the ring itself was difficult to steal or copy, so if you got a letter with the right seal on it you could be pretty sure it came from the right person.

Seals were more secure in the 1700s than today because the social structure of the day meant there were far fewer people who had to have different seals, and the seals themselves were far less likely to be standardized.

In a society of a few thousand people, it is possible to use a unique design for every seal. In a society of a billion, it is not.

In 1700, a typical person had a unique seal. It was engraved by a professional sealcutter, a job that had been a respected craft for centuries.

Today a typical person has no seal at all. But if they did, it would be made on a machine, probably at Wal-Mart, and it would have to share its design with hundreds of thousands of other people with the same name.

A modern letter with a seal on it would look like this:

That seal would be no more than a signature.

A 1700s letter would look like this:

That seal would be much harder to fake.

The design of a personal seal usually incorporated the person's initials, but also something that was unique to them, usually a symbol they chose. The letter I showed you had the letter "R" on it because that was the person's initial, but there was also a design incorporating a tree, a flower, and a bird that were unique to him.

In 1700, the best seal was a signet ring, which was easy to carry and could be locked away at night. A cheaper option was a stamp held in a wooden handle, but that had to be stored somewhere safe, because it was easy to steal.

Seals were usually made of gold, but the cheapest kind were made of copper. The design was made by cutting it in relief into the ring, then rubbing the ring in hot wax to leave an impression.

The first thing you would do with a letter that had a seal on it was press it in the middle of your thumb and hold it there, like this.

If the seal was genuine, it had been rolled in warm wax and was still a bit soft, and the wax would adhere to your thumb. This was both a way to tell that the wax was recent (old wax was hard and would not stick) and a security measure.

When you finished reading the letter, you put your thumb on the seal and pressed hard to destroy the wax. This was so that if someone stole the letter, they could not show it to the recipient and claim that the recipient had not seen it, since the seal would be broken.

There were several ways to fake seals. The most common was for a thief to copy the design of the seal by having a sealcutter make a copy of the design from a letter. But this only worked if you could steal both the seal and a letter. It was also possible to forge a seal, but you had to be good at it.

A letter with the wrong seal on it would make you suspicious. But a letter with the right seal on it could still be a fake, since seals were sometimes faked. But it was much harder to fake a 1700s seal than a modern one.

prompt: In the 1700s, how did anyone know a letter was really from the person who signed it? Did wax seals actually stop forgery or were they mostly symbolic?
response:
Seals helped, in the way that you can tell an impersonation from a real voice, and they were also a practical problem solver, because the person receiving the letter could tell that nobody had opened it, which they otherwise could not do very well. In fact, the first people to have the idea of wax seals were probably the first people to worry about postal employees opening people's mail.

There were also a couple of things that helped with handwriting verification. First, the way people in the 1700s learned to write was to practice copying model letters, and that taught them a specific style of handwriting and made handwriting more uniform. So it was easier to tell whether a letter was written by someone else.

Second, it was common to write a letter on one side of a sheet of paper, fold it, then write another letter on the other side. Then if the letter was forged, the other side would be blank or would have another letter on it.

These techniques don't sound particularly convincing by modern standards, but the same is true of modern handwriting analysis, so maybe they were pretty good.

prompt: Im 16 and my econ teacher went way too fast. What was the gold standard and why did Nixon end it in 1971? Was that good or bad?
response:
For most of the 20th century, the dollar was convertible into gold at $35 an ounce, and other countries' currencies were pegged to it. A country with a trade deficit lost gold and had to shrink its economy to restore balance. Nixon ended convertibility partly to stop that drain.

The system was already strained, so it wasn't his fault, and the world economy grew more in the following decades than it had in the previous two centuries, so you could say it was good. But in the long run the end of the gold standard also removed a limit on inflation, which is bad.

prompt: Im 16 and my econ teacher went way too fast. What was the gold standard and why did Nixon end it in 1971? Was that good or bad?
response:
Until 1971, each US dollar was, on request, redeemable in a fixed weight of gold. Other countries did the same, which kept exchange rates stable. The problem was that the US was printing dollars for the Vietnam War and social programs faster than it was acquiring gold, so foreign governments, especially France, kept demanding to exchange dollars for gold and the Treasury's stockpile was shrinking. Nixon stopped the conversions on August 15, 1971. The dollar's value was already going down at that point, but the devaluation accelerated after 1971, and we've had a long, slow decline in the value of the dollar ever since.

Was this a good idea? If you were a government official in 1971, it was a way to keep from losing all your gold to other countries, so from that point of view it was necessary. If you were a citizen, it caused inflation, which was bad. You can argue about whether it was the least bad solution to a difficult problem.

prompt: Im 16 and my econ teacher went way too fast. What was the gold standard and why did Nixon end it in 1971? Was that good or bad?
response:
Under the Bretton Woods system, set up after World War II, the US dollar was convertible into gold at $35 per ounce, and other countries' currencies were pegged to the dollar. Other countries held dollars as reserves and could trade them for gold at the US Treasury's Fort Knox vaults. By the late 1960s, the US was printing a lot of dollars to pay for Vietnam and the Great Society programs, while other countries were trading them for gold and emptying the vaults. Nixon ended the convertibility to stop that, and the dollar became a currency backed by nothing except the US government's promise to accept it.

Whether it was good or bad is contested. It freed the US to print money without the restraint of gold, but it also meant currencies could float and exchange rates became unstable.

prompt: What actually happened to the Library of Alexandria? I've heard Caesar burned it, Christians destroyed it, Arabs destroyed it, and also that it just slowly faded away. Which story is right, and how do we know?
response:
It’s a question that tends to produce very confident answers, but the actual truth is much less dramatic.

The great Library of Alexandria, the one in the royal palace, was founded by Ptolemy I and expanded by his sons, and it was a major intellectual center. It was already in trouble before it ever met Julius Caesar.

In 48 BCE, Ptolemy’s two sons fought for power, and Caesar was called in as a neutral arbiter. Inevitably things turned into a riot and a fire and Caesar’s men got trapped on their ships on the harbor, which was a really dangerous place to be. Caesar ordered his men to set fire to the ships defending the harbor to get out of it, and the fire spread to the warehouses nearby.

The warehouse was near the royal Library of Alexandria, so the fire did destroy some of its holdings. It’s unclear how much of the Library this destroyed, since the Library was a large sprawling complex and many people say it was mostly spared. But it did do some damage, and Caesar’s fire is definitely real.

The Library did decline during the Roman period as the city became more Christianized and less Hellenistic. It’s unclear whether this was because Christians destroyed the Library, or because Christians didn’t care about the Library and so it was neglected, or because Christians destroyed pagan temples and this made it harder to get to the Library. It’s also unclear whether the Library was still open during this period. It had a long history of being sort of half-neglected in the Ptolemaic period and then having new patrons come in and revitalize it. Maybe that was happening in this period too.

The library of the Museum – the Museum was a nearby research center – was definitely still open when Galen visited in 162 CE. He says he found it neglected, and he says that when he left they were burning some scrolls. This is probably why people tell stories about Christians burning the Library of Alexandria. But we know Galen is wrong.

The Library of Serapeum – Serapis was an Egyptian god, so this is probably the Library of Alexandria that people mean when they say Christians destroyed it – was destroyed in 391 CE. This is definitely real. Christians destroyed the Serapeum in 391 CE and the Library was in it. This was after the last known mention of the Library in 321, so it might be the last Library of Alexandria.

There was a second Library of Alexandria, called the daughter library, that was founded when the royal Library got too big to hold everything. It was in a separate building, and its collection was probably a little smaller than the original Library. It was never mentioned again after a passing comment in 27 BCE. It’s not exactly clear what happened to it. It might have been damaged in Caesar’s fire, or it might have just disappeared into general Roman neglect.

Finally, in 642 CE the Arab army under Amr ibn al-As took Alexandria from the Romans. The Roman Emperor had given them the city in exchange for protection, but he was deposed in a coup, so they decided to just keep the city they’d already conquered. The city had had some serious trouble with Christians in the recent past, so they were worried that the Christians were going to try to kill all of the Muslims.

So they asked the Christians if they could use the Library as a base, and the Christians said no. Amr went to the Caliph in Damascus and asked what he should do, and the Caliph said “If it agrees with the Qur’an, use it. If it disagrees with the Qur’an, burn it.” And so they used it, and then they burned it.

This is what people mean when they say that the Arabs destroyed the Library of Alexandria. But this is also probably wrong. There is a Library of Alexandria, the Library of Serapeum, which is a major landmark of Alexandria that would obviously be a very good place to use as a base for the Muslims and would obviously be destroyed in the process.

But we have no evidence that the Library of Serapeum was still open at this time. It is possible that it was, but there is also a strong case for saying that it had been abandoned a long time ago. It’s probably the case that Amr destroyed a large empty building in Alexandria in 642 CE and people just told a more dramatic story about it.

prompt: What actually happened to the Library of Alexandria? I've heard Caesar burned it, Christians destroyed it, Arabs destroyed it, and also that it just slowly faded away. Which story is right, and how do we know?
response:
It was a combination of all four. It’s also not clear that all of them are true.

The Library of Alexandria was founded by Alexander’s successor and Ptolemaic ruler Ptolemy I in 283 BCE, and grew over the next two centuries to become one of the largest repositories of knowledge in the world. Its main library housed 400,000 to 700,000 scrolls by some estimates, and a smaller “daughter library”, the Serapeum, another 40,000.

In 48 BCE, Julius Caesar was at war with one of Alexandria’s rulers, Ptolemy XIII. During the battle for the city, Caesar ordered his ships set on fire to trap Ptolemy’s larger fleet inside the harbor. The fire spread to nearby grain warehouses and eventually to the Library, destroying 40,000 scrolls.

But 40,000 is only a fraction of the library’s holdings. And the fire is said to have mostly destroyed shipping and storage facilities, not the actual books. The library itself may have been unscathed.

The second wave of destruction came from Rome. In 272 CE, Roman Emperor Aurelian invaded Alexandria on his way to take control of Egypt. The city burned for two months, destroying many of its buildings. It’s believed that the Serapeum, the smaller library, was destroyed during this time.

The third wave of destruction was Christian. Alexandria was a center of Christianity, and its Christians were often at odds with pagans and Jews, who controlled a lot of the city’s libraries and knowledge centers. In 391 CE, Christian mobs destroyed the Serapeum temple, and probably destroyed the Serapeum library with it. In 415 CE, Hypatia, the city’s only prominent philosopher, was also killed by Christian mobs.

The last wave of destruction was Arab. In 642 CE, the Arabs conquered Alexandria, and there’s a famous story that Caliph Umar ordered that all books in the city be destroyed. If they could be boiled for hot baths, they were to be boiled. If they could be used to heat baths, they were to be used for heating. And anything that couldn’t be used for that purpose, like books, was to be burned.

All this destruction probably ended the Library of Alexandria. It was the world’s largest library, and by the end of the fifth century there were no signs of its former glory. Its buildings were destroyed in the first and third waves, and its scholars were driven out in the second and third waves.

But the historical record isn’t perfect, and it’s possible the Library faded away before any of these events, with no dramatic last wave of destruction. In 330 CE, when Constantine moved the capital of Rome from Rome to Constantinople, scholars stopped coming to Alexandria to study. It’s possible that the city had fallen so far by the 400s that none of these dramatic stories of destruction had much effect.

prompt: What actually happened to the Library of Alexandria? I've heard Caesar burned it, Christians destroyed it, Arabs destroyed it, and also that it just slowly faded away. Which story is right, and how do we know?
response:
Most of it, anyway, probably just disappeared. The Library of Alexandria was a big deal in the first and second centuries, but by the fourth it seems to have mostly ceased to exist, at least as a single physical place.

I’m not just saying that because the Christian version is unattractive: Christians did destroy texts, for example when they banned the Gospel of Judas, the Gospel of Mary, and the Acts of Peter (all of which were eventually rediscovered in the Dead Sea Caves). I’m saying it because the evidence suggests it.

For one thing, the Library of Alexandria wasn’t one library. When people talk about the Library of Alexandria, they’re usually talking about the Mouseion, or “Museum” – the famous complex that housed the Library of Ptolemy I Soter, the first Greek ruler of Egypt. But there were other libraries in Alexandria, including the Serapeum – and there’s no evidence that the Serapeum was destroyed in any of the famous Library-destruction incidents.

For another, most of the destructions happened after the Library of Alexandria’s peak. It was most important between about 300 BC and about 100 AD – but it was already declining in the second century AD, and in 212 AD when Caracalla gave citizenship to all inhabitants of the Roman Empire, it became even less relevant as a uniquely Alexandrian treasure.

The Christians probably destroyed some stuff in the fourth and fifth centuries. The Serapeum was demolished by the bishop Theophilus around 391 AD, which was kind of a problem because it housed a branch of the library. But by this point, it’s clear the library had already shrunk to a small fraction of its size, and the Serapeum was a branch to begin with.

And the “Arabs destroyed it” theory is even sillier. The Arabs conquered Egypt in the 640s. And at that point, not only had the Library of Alexandria shrunk to a tiny fraction of its former size, but the city of Alexandria itself had shrunk to a tiny fraction of its former size. The city used to extend a couple miles inland from the coast – but by 640 the Muslim conquerors found that it was confined to just a tiny strip of coastline. They found the ruins of the Temple of Serapis just outside the city walls, and a couple other temples besides. Everything else in the city was either Islamic or Christian.

It’s possible there were a few Christian books that got burned in the first century of Islamic rule. But it doesn’t seem like it made much of a difference, because by the end of the seventh century there were already Muslim scholars who were very interested in Greek philosophy, and the eighth century was full of people who translated Greek philosophy into Arabic – people like Hunayn ibn Ishaq. If you want to blame Christians for destroying Greek and Roman texts, I think it’s a much better bet that they burned some of the originals that the translators used, instead of blaming the Arabs for destroying the translations they themselves were responsible for translating.

I’m a little more sympathetic to the Caesar story. Julius Caesar fought the Battle of Alexandria in 48 BC, and burned some of his own ships so that he wouldn’t be trapped on the coast. Some fire spread to a couple libraries, and burned a lot of stuff.

But the Library of Alexandria had been going strong for about 300 years at this point. And it seems to have stayed strong for another century or two after that. I know there’s some evidence that it was already declining by the second century, but this is the same sort of vague evidence as you might have for any big institution that’s been around for a long time. It doesn’t seem like the Library had much of a problem recovering from the Caesar fire.

The biggest thing that got the Library of Alexandria in trouble was probably the Battle of the Peloponnesian War in 272 BC. This was a fight between one of the Ptolemies and the Greeks of Rhodes, and it got really ugly. The Rhodians burned a bunch of ships in Alexandria’s harbor, and that fire spread to a lot of stuff on the coast. The Library of Alexandria was right by the harbor, so it got destroyed.

This was pretty devastating, but the Library rebuilt itself. I think by the time of Julius Caesar, it was probably at its most glorious.

Another big loss was probably when Cleopatra’s son Ptolemy XIV gave a bunch of books to Rome as part of a ransom payment. But I don’t think this actually affected the Library of Alexandria much – the books that got ransomed were copies that had been brought back from Athens and Pergamos.

So yeah, a lot of the Library of Alexandria disappeared, a couple centuries before the Romans or the Christians or the Arabs got there. Probably because of normal neglect. It was a big institution, and a lot of them go away eventually.

I think one of the reasons the Library of Alexandria got such a bad rap is that it was pretty famous – it was the first big international library that anyone had ever seen. It was kind of the first time that people started talking about preserving and cataloguing a lot of the world’s literature. It was the first big “universal library”, and this was a very exciting idea. So when it disappeared, there was a lot of grief.

The next big universal library didn’t show up until the Islamic world built their own in the 700s – and that’s probably the reason why the “Arabs destroyed the Library of Alexandria” myth sticks around – because they were the next people to have a universal library.

prompt: why is the trolley problem supposed to be hard? pulling the lever seems obviously right to me, 5 > 1
response:
For a lot of people, yes, it is obviously right, and it's not an ethical dilemma in the sense of being a real decision to agonize over. It just isn't for everyone. Some people are much more strongly attached to the principle of non-interference, or to the idea that you shouldn't deliberately harm somebody, or to the idea that pulling the lever will make you complicit in killing somebody. And for them, this is a really hard choice.

I think the best use of the trolley problem is not to try to pin down the one correct answer, but to think of it as a personality diagnostic - a tool for figuring out which of these two ethical systems you're more likely to be pulled toward in a given situation.

prompt: why is the trolley problem supposed to be hard? pulling the lever seems obviously right to me, 5 > 1
response: It is not, and you are not wrong. The puzzle works because pulling the lever is the easy answer. The hard question is the variant where you push a large man off a bridge onto the tracks, saving the same five people. Most people refuse to push, which is puzzling if saving five lives is what matters. So what is it about your arm that makes a difference?

prompt: why is the trolley problem supposed to be hard? pulling the lever seems obviously right to me, 5 > 1
response: Because the puzzle isn't really about the lever case, it's about contrasting it with the fat man on the bridge, who you must push onto the tracks to stop the trolley. It's a different decision, but the same trade-off of one life against five, and yet most people feel differently about it. This has produced a lot of philosophical interest in why.

prompt: My 9-year-old asked me last night, "If I can't remember being a baby, was that baby still me?" I froze. How would you explain the idea of personal identity to her without either making something up or getting too heavy for bedtime?
response:
The baby was you, said the philosopher Derek Parfit in a 1978 paper, because the baby was in a chain of “psychological connectedness and continuity” that leads to you. You are connected to the baby by memory, but you are also connected to yesterday-you, and yesterday-you is connected to the day before, and so on. This chain of connections is enough to make you the same person as you were yesterday, and so on back to your baby self.

Parfit’s theory of personal identity, in which the same person is a long chain of connected selves, is one of my favorite ideas, because it is so simple and so obviously true. In the words of philosopher Michael Huemer, who wrote an article on Parfit’s theory of personal identity:

The idea of psychological continuity is not new. It has been argued in one form or another by several philosophers over the years, and it is the sort of idea you might have on your own if you gave the question any thought. If a person who is exactly like me except for a few memories of my past experiences woke up in my bed, I would want to say that it was me. And if a person exactly like me except for a couple of memories of yesterday’s events woke up in my bed, I would probably want to say that it was me. And if a person who had lost memories of a few events from two days ago woke up in my bed, I’d want to say that it was me. But if a person exactly like me except for all memories of my life before age 17 woke up in my bed, I wouldn’t want to say that it was me.

But it’s not just memory. If you have the same desires, traits, and goals as the baby did, you are also psychologically connected to your baby self.

Parfit’s theory of personal identity doesn’t just apply to your relationship with past versions of yourself. It also applies to your relationship with future versions of you. You are connected to your future self through continuity of personality traits and memories. If you read this sentence, then you are a little bit connected to the version of you who reads the next sentence in this paragraph. And she is connected to the version of you who reads the next sentence. And on and on.

This is an important thing to realize. You may think of your future self as a stranger, or like a distant relative. In fact, she is the closest person to you in the world, because she is connected to you more closely than anyone else.

This is also important to understand if you want to be a good person. If you believe that the future version of you that reads this next sentence is not you, then the right thing to do is to ignore that version of you’s feelings, because they aren’t your feelings. But that’s wrong. That future version of you is you, and it’s important to her, and if you are a good person, it’s important to you, too.

prompt: My 9-year-old asked me last night, "If I can't remember being a baby, was that baby still me?" I froze. How would you explain the idea of personal identity to her without either making something up or getting too heavy for bedtime?
response:
You might try explaining that her body and mind are connected to the baby's body and mind. She grew up into a person, and the baby grew into her. The baby is as close as it gets, to someone who isn't alive right now.

I like the story of a man who had to decide whether to put his wife into a coma, and then not wake her up, because she had a terminal disease. I've seen this story told about several different people. The details vary, but one of them, a man whose wife had a terminal cancer, said he couldn't decide, because she had been his best friend.

I don't think that is the right answer, but it makes a lot of sense emotionally. The wife was the same person as the baby. The baby was someone's best friend, and they are not really sure how it feels to be her, now, so they don't want to do something that might hurt her.

prompt: My 9-year-old asked me last night, "If I can't remember being a baby, was that baby still me?" I froze. How would you explain the idea of personal identity to her without either making something up or getting too heavy for bedtime?
response:
I think your kid is right to be a little bothered by this. There are lots of reasons to think that identity, or being the same person, is a very interesting thing.

But, at bedtime, just try the following. You know how you had a name for a long time, and then you changed your name to something else? You’re still you. And you still have the same face (well, sort of). So being the same person isn’t like having the same body. It’s more like having the same name.

Now, what does a name do? It connects you to lots of other people. You and your mom are the same person you were before, so your name connects you to all those people you used to know.

And then when you’re old enough, you have a new name. Maybe it’s a new first name, or just a new last name. That new name connects you to the new people you know.

prompt: What's the difference between a sound argument and a valid one? My logic professor has marked me down three times for mixing them up and I still can't see where the line is.
response:
A valid argument is one in which, if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true. A sound argument is a valid argument whose premises actually are true. So soundness = validity + true premises.

The confusion usually comes from a bad premise that leads to a true conclusion, such as 'All mammals have gills; dolphins are mammals; therefore dolphins have gills'. That argument is valid, since no world with gilled mammals and mammalian dolphins has dolphins without gills, but it is not sound, since the first premise is false. An argument can even be both valid and sound while having a false premise, if that premise is irrelevant: 'The moon is made of cheese; all dogs are animals; therefore some animals are dogs'.

When you check an argument, ask two separate questions: is the conclusion forced by the premises, and are the premises true?

prompt: What's the difference between a sound argument and a valid one? My logic professor has marked me down three times for mixing them up and I still can't see where the line is.
response:
A valid argument is one in which it's impossible for the premises to be true and the conclusion false. A sound argument is one which is valid and which has true premises. Validity is a structural property; the argument is valid if it would be impossible for its premises to be true and its conclusion false no matter what the subject matter of the premises were. Here are two valid arguments. The first one is sound, but the second is not.

All cats are mammals.
All Siamese cats are cats.
Therefore, all Siamese cats are mammals.

All cats are dogs.
All Siamese cats are cats.
Therefore, all Siamese cats are dogs.

Both arguments have the same structure:

All A's are B's.
All C's are A's.
Therefore, all C's are B's.

This is a valid form of argument because there is no way it is possible that the premises are true and the conclusion is false. But the premises of the second example are not true.

prompt: What's the difference between a sound argument and a valid one? My logic professor has marked me down three times for mixing them up and I still can't see where the line is.
response: Validity is about form only: if the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be true. Soundness is validity plus true premises, and a sound argument also has a true conclusion. A valid argument can have false premises, like "All cats are dogs; Whiskers is a cat; therefore Whiskers is a dog," and an argument can have a true conclusion yet be invalid.

prompt: I just read Parfit's teletransporter case in Reasons and Persons and I'm confused about how he gets to the conclusion that identity "isn't what matters." Isn't that just obviously false? I care a lot about whether it's me who survives, not a copy.
response:
Parfit’s argument is a long one, and the teletransporter case is only a starting point. The teletransporter case gets us to the idea that personal identity must not depend on psychological continuity – since in the case where the teletransporter is not destructive, the copy will be psychologically continuous with the original, but we don’t have personal identity there either.

But Parfit’s argument then goes much further – we don’t need to be able to point to any particular thing which is essential for survival in order to say that survival doesn’t matter. There are a whole set of other things which seem to matter, like psychological continuity, bodily continuity, and other things. If we can’t say what survival is, and we don’t have to say what survival is, then we don’t need to say what matters.

In other words, if I am about to undergo the destructive teletransporter, the copy will be psychologically continuous with me. It will remember my childhood, think it’s important for me to have my children, and so on. So that thing matters. If I have a body, and that body survives, then that thing matters. And so on.

If I am about to die, I think it makes sense to ask “who cares?” And if you say that you care because you don’t want to die, and I ask “why don’t you want to die?”, you might answer that you don’t want to die because you’re afraid of hell. In which case the real thing you care about is avoiding hell. So if it’s not hell, then what are you afraid of? You might say that you’re afraid of losing the ability to make plans and do things you’ve promised to do, and I say ok, the thing that matters is the ability to make plans and do things you’ve promised to do. You might say you’re afraid of losing your body, and I say okay, the thing that matters is your body. You might say you’re afraid of losing your memories, and I say okay, the thing that matters is your memories.

But at the end of the day, you’re not afraid of any one of these things. You’re afraid of not surviving. And the question “what is survival?” is an interesting one. But the question “what is it you care about?” is not as interesting. You care about a bunch of things, and that’s all that matters.

Parfit’s argument against the teletransporter is that it doesn’t actually matter whether the teletransporter is destructive or not. In both cases, there will be a copy psychologically continuous with the original, and the copy will have all of the original’s memories. So if you’re really thinking hard about why it matters that it be you who survives, and not a copy, you may not be able to find a good answer. And if there’s no good answer, then maybe you should accept that your intuition that it matters is wrong, and it’s okay to use the destructive teletransporter.

prompt: I just read Parfit's teletransporter case in Reasons and Persons and I'm confused about how he gets to the conclusion that identity "isn't what matters." Isn't that just obviously false? I care a lot about whether it's me who survives, not a copy.
response:
This is one of the few places where I think Derek Parfit is just flat-out wrong.

Parfit’s argument is: if identity doesn’t matter, then identity isn’t what matters. And identity doesn’t matter because in the teletransporter case, it’s not what matters. And identity isn’t what matters in the teletransporter case because even though identity doesn’t survive the trip, we still want to go through the trip. Therefore, identity isn’t what matters.

But there is a problem with this reasoning. In the teletransporter case, I care about whether I survive because I care about being the same person. But I don’t care about being the same person because I care about being the same person. I care about being the same person because I care about the future, and I want to be there to experience it. And when I say, “I care about the future,” I mean, I care about what happens to *me*.

So the fact that I care about the teletransporter case doesn’t mean that identity doesn’t matter. It just means that I care about identity and also I care about the future, and I’m not willing to sacrifice one for the other.

This is one of the few places where I think Parfit is just flat-out wrong.

prompt: I just read Parfit's teletransporter case in Reasons and Persons and I'm confused about how he gets to the conclusion that identity "isn't what matters." Isn't that just obviously false? I care a lot about whether it's me who survives, not a copy.
response:
Not false at all, as far as I can tell, but you need to pay attention to the exact argument to see why.

Consider this story:

Suppose you and I agreed to swap teletransporter bodies. The procedure is: your body is scanned, then destroyed, and your pattern is transferred to my body, which has also been destroyed. Meanwhile, my body is scanned and destroyed, and my pattern is transferred to your body. If we do this, you end up with my body and I end up with yours.

Suppose that we swap bodies, and you wake up in the other body. I can’t see my own face. But when I look in the mirror, I can see you looking back at me. I know what you’re thinking. I know you’re thinking “This is weird. I don’t look like me anymore. I look like the other guy.”

I can say with confidence that you are wrong – you are still you, and you still look like you. I can tell because I know what you think and feel. I can tell that the person in the mirror still has your thoughts and memories, and that means that person is still you, even if the body looks different.

Now, consider if we swapped twice. This time, you’d end up with your body again, and I’d end up with mine.

You know that the person who will end up in your body has my thoughts and memories. I know that the person who will end up in my body has your thoughts and memories.

Suppose that you wake up in your body. I can’t see my own face, but I look in the mirror and see you looking back at me. You think “This is so weird. It’s me, but my thoughts and memories are different.”

But you’re wrong, in exactly the same way. You have *my* thoughts and memories, which means that you are *me*. You can look in the mirror and see your own face, but that’s irrelevant. You are still me.

Now, suppose that you wake up in your own body, but you don’t know about the double swap. From your perspective, you just swapped bodies once, so you have your own thoughts and memories in my body. You can see your own face, and you’re sure that it’s you, not me.

And I wake up in your body with my thoughts and memories. You’re wrong. You aren’t you. I am.

I realize that this is hard to think about, and I may be doing it wrong, so I want to make sure I’m not confusing you. The important point is that you can see your own face in the mirror and think you’re you, and be completely wrong about it.

This is really hard to accept. We usually think that looking in the mirror is a reliable way to identify who we are. But Parfit says that it isn’t. He says that, sometimes, if you look in the mirror and see yourself, you’re wrong.

So how do you know if you really are you, or if you’re wrong? You know if the body has your thoughts and memories. It doesn’t matter how the body looks – it might even be a completely different person’s body. What matters is the thoughts and memories.

So let’s go back to the beginning. Suppose that you and I don’t know about the double swap. We just think that we swapped bodies once. So, you wake up in your own body and you think that it’s you, but it’s not. You have *my* thoughts and memories. And I wake up in your body and I think that it’s me, but it’s not. I have *your* thoughts and memories.

So, it’s possible to wake up in your body and not be you. So, it’s possible that the teletransporter will scan you, destroy your body, and recreate you in another room, and you will wake up in the new body and it won’t be you.

This is why Parfit says that personal identity isn’t what matters.

prompt: Explain moral luck.
response:
Moral luck is the idea that we judge people differently depending on outcomes over which they had no control. Two drivers talk for twenty minutes while texting. One causes no harm. The other hits a pedestrian who stepped out at that instant. The second driver is treated as a criminal and the first as a bad luck victim. The drivers' care was the same, but their moral record seems to depend on something they could not control.

Philosophers such as Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel argue that this is not a mere bias: we cannot separate praise from outcomes, and pretending otherwise is a fiction. A common reply is that we should limit blame to what a person could have controlled, and treat the difference in outcomes as luck, just as we would treat the difference in winnings on two dice rolls that turned out differently.

prompt: Explain moral luck.
response:
Moral luck is the idea that people often receive more or less moral credit or blame because of factors beyond their control, not just because of what they did or intended.

Take two people who each drive a little too fast down a school street. One crashes into a child, the other does not, because the second child steps out a second later. It is hard to say the first driver was more careless, or that either acted more badly. Yet the first driver has killed a child and is likely to face prison.

One response is to judge people by what is in their control, so we would not blame the driver at all. That seems wrong. Another is to judge people only by their intentions, so both drivers would be blameworthy for intending to drive too fast. But it is also not right to blame someone who is careful for doing something bad, just because they failed. Moral luck is the name for the difficulty of finding a view that can handle these cases.

prompt: Explain moral luck.
response: Moral luck is the problem that we judge people by outcomes that depend partly on factors outside their control. Two drivers are equally reckless; one kills a pedestrian who steps into the road, the other does not. Both were equally careless, but only one is punished and blamed. Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel argued in 1979 that this shows our moral judgments are built on luck, and they saw this as a reason to doubt our ordinary moral practices. Others reply that the reckless driver is still responsible for what he did, and that we may not be able to blame him for things that merely might have happened.

prompt: How is Kant's categorical imperative actually different from the golden rule? Half my book club insists they're the same thing and I have a feeling they're wrong but can't say why.
response:
It is a mistake to think that Kant’s universalizability test is the Golden Rule. The Golden Rule is not a test for the morality of actions, but a rule for the conduct of one’s personal relations: “Do to others what you would have them do to you.” Kant’s test is that an act is permissible if and only if it is not contradictory to will that everyone who can so choose would in similar circumstances so choose. The two are related but distinct, and for a number of reasons.

Kant’s universalizability test is not, strictly, a rule for the conduct of personal relations. Rather, it is a general criterion for the morality of all sorts of actions. Kant’s test is also a test, not a rule. In particular, it is not always true that you ought to do to others what you would have them do to you, or even that you must try to do so. This is because you may have reasons to believe that others would not want you to treat them the way you would wish to be treated. For example, suppose that you are someone who likes to be treated with particular deference and courtesy, but that you know that your friends, being more informal, would not want you to treat them in that way. In that case, the Golden Rule would have you treat them with deference and courtesy, but this would be wrong. Similarly, suppose you like to be treated with particular brusqueness and directness, but you know that your friends are more sensitive and would not want you to treat them that way. In that case, the Golden Rule would have you treat them with brusqueness and directness, but this would be wrong. These are two simple examples, but there are countless cases of this sort.

But there are also some cases in which the Golden Rule fails to give you guidance, and the universalizability test succeeds. For example, imagine that you are unsure of what you would want others to do to you when you are in danger. In that case, the Golden Rule fails to give you guidance. But the universalizability test may. For example, suppose that a man is about to commit a crime, and you are unsure of what you would want others to do to you when you are in danger. In that case, you might not know whether the best action for you to take is to help him commit the crime or to stop him. But if you reflect on what is contradictory and what is not, you will discover that it is not contradictory to will that anyone who can so choose would in similar circumstances choose to stop a person from committing a crime, but that it would be contradictory to will that anyone who can so choose would in similar circumstances choose to help a person commit a crime. (This is because it is contradictory to will that everyone who can so choose would in similar circumstances so choose, if it would not be permissible to act on that maxim. Since it would not be permissible to act on the maxim “help people commit crimes,” it would be contradictory to will that anyone who can so choose would in similar circumstances choose to help a person commit a crime.)
