Kant’s universalizability test can thus be thought of as a refinement of the Golden Rule, one which corrects for its two main problems: its being a rule instead of a test, and its being too narrow in scope.

prompt: How is Kant's categorical imperative actually different from the golden rule? Half my book club insists they're the same thing and I have a feeling they're wrong but can't say why.
response:
Kant's categorical imperative is the demand that you act only on maxims that you would want to be universal law. It has three formulations, of which the second formulation, the one most people think of, is "Act only on that maxim where you can at the same time will that it become a universal law."

The golden rule is the demand that you do to others what you would want done to you.

The difference is that the golden rule only requires that you like what you're doing to others, but the categorical imperative requires that you would like everyone to be doing it, including you.

If you want to kill everyone else, the golden rule allows it. The categorical imperative doesn't, because you can't will that "it is everyone's duty to kill everyone else" become a universal law, because that would mean you had to kill yourself.

Or if you want to cheat on your spouse, the golden rule allows it because you might be willing to be cheated on by someone else, even if you don't want to be cheated on by your spouse. But the categorical imperative doesn't allow it, because you can't will that "it is everyone's duty to cheat on their spouse" become a universal law, because that would mean your spouse cheating on you.

prompt: How is Kant's categorical imperative actually different from the golden rule? Half my book club insists they're the same thing and I have a feeling they're wrong but can't say why.
response:
The golden rule, in one of its forms, is “do unto others as you would have them do unto you.” The problem is, it depends on knowing what you would like done to you, which is a tricky thing to know. I mean, do I want to be robbed? No. But would I like it if every one of my friends robbed me? No. But would I like it if everyone who robbed me got caught? Yes, but only if there was no chance that it was me getting caught. But would I like it if the police had to decide whether to arrest someone on the basis of 1% suspicion and they decided to arrest me? No. But would I like it if police didn’t get to arrest anyone unless they could be 100% sure they weren’t arresting an innocent? No. But would I like it if people who had been accused of crimes had the burden of proof on them to prove their innocence? Yes, but only if the people who were accusing me had the burden of proof on them to prove their guilt.

This could go on and on and on, and in practice it’s hard to know what exactly to do.

So Kant said that the golden rule was too complex and arbitrary, and he came up with an alternative, the categorical imperative. There are two ways to state it. One is “act only on those maxims which you could will become universal laws.” Another way to state it is “act as though the effects of your actions will be experienced by all people equally.”

I’ll try to explain the second form in more detail, because it seems more intuitive. Kant says that you should try to think of yourself as an average person. Then, when you do something, imagine that you are not the only person who does it, but that the same percentage of all people in the world do it as you do.

So, for example, let’s say that you want to get rich. You work for a company that is paying you less than you think you deserve, and the company is doing pretty well. You want to ask for a pay raise. You figure you will ask for 20% more. You think about how much of the world you think will get a 20% pay raise. You figure that about 1% of people will ask for 20% raises. You figure that about 0.1% of companies will be doing well enough to have a lot of money to spend on pay raises, and about 1% of the people in those companies will get a raise, and that about 20% of the people in those companies will be asking for a raise of about 20%. And you figure that about half of the companies that are doing well enough to have money to pay raises will give the raises they are asked for. So, you figure that the chance of getting a raise is about 0.1% times 1% times 20% times 50%, which is 1 in 1,000,000.

The other way to look at it is to say that you figure that you have a chance of getting a raise of about 1 in 1,000,000, and that you’re willing to bet that 1 in 1,000,000 people will ask for a raise and get one. So you ask for a raise.

Another example: you think you might want to take a job with a company in some other city. You decide to apply for a job and see if they offer you something. You know there’s about a 50% chance they won’t have any jobs open that you can do, and about a 1% chance that you can do a job that’s open but they won’t offer it to you, and about a 50% chance they will offer you a job that you think is good enough for you to take, and about a 50% chance you will like the city. You think that you have a 1/8 chance of liking the city, and that about 1/8 of all people who apply for jobs in that city will end up liking the city and moving there. So you apply for a job.

The first way of looking at it is a little hard to grasp, but it does seem to make sense. The second way is more of a calculation. I think of it as a kind of Bayesianism.

If you want to know more, read chapter 2 of John Searle’s Rationality in Action.

prompt: Why do philosophers say you can't get an ought from an is? If smoking causes cancer, doesn't that fact tell me I ought not smoke?
response:
The idea is that facts about how things are don't by themselves tell you what you should do. But you're right that the fact that smoking causes cancer is a reason not to smoke, so it looks like the idea is wrong.

The idea is that you can't get an *ought* from an *is* without using a further premise. If smoking causes cancer, that is a reason not to smoke, if you want to avoid cancer.

This is what philosophers mean when they say that you can't get an ought from an is. You can get an ought from an is, if you already have an ought.

prompt: Why do philosophers say you can't get an ought from an is? If smoking causes cancer, doesn't that fact tell me I ought not smoke?
response:
The claim that you can't get an ought from an is is Hume's Law. It goes back to Hume, who noticed that in his day writers used to argue about what ought to be by just talking about what is: "Well, God made things this way, so this way is what ought to be." Hume objected that you can't jump from statements like "X is the case" to statements like "X ought to be the case" without smuggling in another premise.

So: if smoking causes cancer, then I ought not smoke. But you can't get the conclusion without the assumption that you ought to avoid cancer.

You can argue from an is to an ought if you're willing to smuggle in an assumption that makes that conclusion follow. But that's not a valid argument from an is to an ought. It's a valid argument from an is to an ought plus a different assumption.

prompt: Why do philosophers say you can't get an ought from an is? If smoking causes cancer, doesn't that fact tell me I ought not smoke?
response: The argument from is to ought says that from the fact that smoking causes cancer you can infer that you ought not smoke. It was rejected by Hume, who argued that a statement about what ought to be done cannot be deduced from statements about the way things are. Hume was right. Suppose, for example, that there is a tyrant who has decreed that people shall smoke as much as possible. It is true that smoking causes cancer. It is also true that the tyrant says people ought to smoke as much as possible. It would be ridiculous to conclude that people ought to smoke as much as possible because smoking causes cancer. What you should conclude is that the tyrant should be deposed.

prompt: I'm a software engineer. Can someone explain Searle's Chinese Room in a way that takes the systems reply seriously? Every summary I find mentions the reply in one sentence, then moves on as if it had been dealt with. From where I sit the system obviously understands Chinese, so what am I missing about why Searle didn't budge?
response:
If you’ve heard of Searle’s Chinese Room, you’ve probably heard that John Searle is an American philosopher. What he’s trying to do is to prove that computers can’t be conscious. I think he’s wrong, but I can appreciate what he’s doing, so let’s look at his argument.

Imagine you’re in a room with a huge window. You’re bad at Chinese and can’t read a character. But on the other side of the window is a room full of Chinese speakers. They pass you messages with Chinese questions, and you have to write answers and pass them back. How do you do this? You have a book with a bunch of rules about what to write for any question you get.

This room is called the Chinese Room because it was invented in a thought experiment in Searle’s 1980 paper, “Minds, Brains, and Programs.” If you don’t know Chinese but follow the rules, then in principle you could answer questions perfectly, just like a Chinese speaker.

The point is that computers are kind of like the person inside the Chinese Room. They can be programmed to give the right answer to any question, but they don’t understand what’s going on.

The Chinese Room argument is very simple and intuitive, but people have attacked it from all angles. For example, some people argue that the whole system understands Chinese, not just the guy in the room. This guy has no understanding of Chinese, but the guy plus the book plus the rules plus the room are like a computer. So if the whole system understands Chinese, then computers are conscious.

This argument seems right to me, so why hasn’t Searle been convinced?

I think it’s because Searle doesn’t really think computers are conscious. This is a really common way of arguing. It’s called moving the goalposts.

Moving the goalposts is when you start out with an argument that seems really good, but then when someone finds a counterexample, you change your argument to avoid the counterexample. It’s usually a bad sign because it means you’re not trying to make your argument right. You’re just trying to make it immune to criticism.

Searle does this. The Chinese Room argument is great, but it can be refuted by pointing out that the whole system, not just the man in the room, understands Chinese. If you make this argument, then Searle says, oh, that doesn’t count. Then you have to move up and say the whole system is conscious, including the room and the book. And then the argument can never be refuted.

But why would Searle just say it doesn’t count? I think it’s because he has a strong prior that computers are not conscious. This is like most people having a strong prior that they’re smarter than the average person. It’s just human nature. We don’t like things that go against our intuitions.

So the Chinese Room argument is a clever argument that makes you feel bad about computers, even if you don’t want to admit it.

prompt: I'm a software engineer. Can someone explain Searle's Chinese Room in a way that takes the systems reply seriously? Every summary I find mentions the reply in one sentence, then moves on as if it had been dealt with. From where I sit the system obviously understands Chinese, so what am I missing about why Searle didn't budge?
response:
Searle’s reply to the Systems Reply is: if you say that the understanding is in the system, then that system must include not only the room and the person inside it, but also the book of syntactic rules and the person outside the room who sends questions in Chinese and receives answers. But the person outside the room doesn’t understand Chinese any better than the person inside the room does, and neither does the book, so where is the understanding?

There are two things here that I think you’ll find interesting.

First, there’s an important distinction between the understanding and the system. It makes a lot of sense to say that the person inside the room understands Chinese when we’re talking about understanding, but not when we’re talking about the system. The system obviously includes the person inside the room and the book of syntactic rules. But does it include the room? Does it include the air in the room? Does it include the chair he sits on while working? Does it include the building, the street, the country, the solar system? We have a reasonable, implicit criterion for how much of the room we count in the system - you could say, for example, that it’s everything that the person inside the room has to interact with while doing the task. If you use this criterion, then the system does not include the person outside the room.

But the same criterion doesn’t work for understanding. We have to ask, what does it mean for a system to “understand” something? For a human, understanding is an experience. If I understand Chinese, I have a special experience when I read Chinese, something like an experience of meaning. This experience is something that only I have, and only I could report it. So it makes sense to say that the person inside the room understands Chinese when we’re talking about understanding. But the person inside the room doesn’t understand Chinese, and neither does the book of syntactic rules. So where is the understanding?

prompt: I'm a software engineer. Can someone explain Searle's Chinese Room in a way that takes the systems reply seriously? Every summary I find mentions the reply in one sentence, then moves on as if it had been dealt with. From where I sit the system obviously understands Chinese, so what am I missing about why Searle didn't budge?
response:
John Searle introduced the Chinese Room argument in 1980. In it, he imagines that he is stuck in a room, with a big stack of paper in front of him.

A note is passed through a slot, with some characters written on it in Chinese. Searle doesn't speak Chinese. But he has a huge book of instructions, and following them carefully, he eventually manages to write a reply in Chinese and pass it back out the slot.

Suppose the person on the other side of the slot says “Hi, my name is Jane, what’s your name?” to Searle. Searle follows the instructions in the book, and writes back “Hi, my name is Searle. How are you?”

The instructions in the book are the program, the Chinese characters are the input and output, and the paper is the memory.

Searle says he didn’t really understand Chinese at all. He was just moving bits around following instructions. So the same is true for computers. They don’t understand anything at all. They’re just moving bits around following instructions.

The systems reply says that Searle, the book of instructions, and the paper together understood Chinese, even if Searle himself didn’t. The systems reply is pretty close to the way programmers think about computers.

The systems reply is right. I’ve seen the Chinese Room argument used a lot to say things like “computers can’t have thoughts and feelings” and “we can never build AIs”. But it’s clear that’s wrong.

The best way to think of the Chinese Room argument is a really clever and very short way of saying “computers are Turing machines”.

The Chinese Room argument is Turing completeness in a nutshell.

There are some things that are easy to describe, like “add 1 to a number”. There are also some things that are hard to describe, like “solve a Rubik’s cube”. But as long as the thing you want to describe can be described by moving bits around according to rules, it’s a Turing machine, and you can describe it as a set of instructions.

Searle’s argument is that computers can do anything you can describe by moving bits around according to rules. This is a true statement. It’s also a useless statement, because it’s true for all Turing machines.

prompt: what does wittgenstein mean that there can't be a private language? reading Philosophical Investigations on my own and got completely lost around section 243, the beetle in the box part didn't help
response:
You have to have read the first half of the *Investigations* to get this, but the whole first half of the book is about the same thing.

In the private language argument, a private language is a language that refers only to the things I see in my head. It has words like, “That is the feeling I call ‘red’,” which would only make sense to me.

Wittgenstein thinks that private language is impossible. He has lots of arguments for it. The two I like best are,

1. The meaning of a word in a language is determined by the rules for using it. If there is no rule for using a word in a private language, that word can mean anything and therefore doesn’t mean anything.

2. If you were going to learn a private language, what would the teacher have to teach you? How would you know if you were understanding them?

The reason for all this is that if a private language were possible, you could have a meaning for some word, like, “That thing I see in my head which I call red,” and then we could never know whether you meant the same thing as I did when you said that word. And it would be impossible for me to know when you had that meaning or not.

It’s pretty common to think that this is not true. I don’t think it is though. I think that if I am wrong I am wrong because I have misunderstood the private language argument.

prompt: what does wittgenstein mean that there can't be a private language? reading Philosophical Investigations on my own and got completely lost around section 243, the beetle in the box part didn't help
response:
I like this question because, well, it’s not actually a question. Wittgenstein doesn’t actually argue that a language of only one word couldn’t exist.

He talks about the idea of a “language of sensations”, where each person has a word that means “that feeling that I feel now” - the feeling might be called “S”, but it might be something else, and no one else knows how to understand it. He says “The language of sensations seems to be a private language. For how else could there be a language of sensations?”

If a language of sensations is a private language, and no one can have a private language, then no one can have a language of sensations. But wait, everyone’s got a language of sensations. So the premise that no one can have a private language must be wrong. Or maybe the premise that a language of sensations is a private language is wrong.

So, if Wittgenstein does argue that no one can have a private language, the conclusion is pretty boring. It’s just that maybe “private language” doesn’t really mean what we think it means. And this isn’t a big deal, because nobody cares about private languages.

prompt: what does wittgenstein mean that there can't be a private language? reading Philosophical Investigations on my own and got completely lost around section 243, the beetle in the box part didn't help
response:
The beetle-in-a-box argument, which Wittgenstein introduced in section 293, is meant to answer the objection that even if I had a private language, it would be possible for me to learn the meanings of its words, because I could just look them up. If I said, for instance, that “blorg” means “pain”, I would be able to look up the meaning of “blorg”, and see that it meant “pain”. But the fact that I can look up the meaning of the word “pain” doesn’t mean that I really know what it means. Suppose that I say that “blorg” means “the thing in the box”. But I can’t look into the box. I can’t look up the meaning of “blorg” because, to do that, I would have to look into the box. So how can I say that I know what “blorg” means?

But you might say that you can look into your own mind, and see what is in the box. That is exactly what Wittgenstein denies. He thinks that it is an illusion that I can look into my own mind to see what is in the box. The argument that Wittgenstein uses to support this claim is not the beetle-in-a-box argument. It is the argument in sections 243-244. It says that if we think that we know what is in the box because we can look into the box, we are being fooled. If I can look into my own mind to see what is in the box, then I can’t be looking into the box, because looking into the box is what I am trying to learn the meaning of “blorg”!

prompt: How do I actually steelman an argument I find repugnant? I've got a debate tournament in two weeks and my coach says I strawman without realizing it. I'd like concrete steps I can practice, not a lecture on intellectual charity.
response:
1. Write down the argument, including the conclusion.

2. Circle the assumptions on which it depends.

3. For each assumption, ask “is this a fact, or merely an opinion?”

4. If it’s a fact, ask “can I prove it?”

5. If it’s an opinion, ask “do I agree with this person’s values?”

6. If I don’t agree, ask “do I understand what kind of person would agree?”

7. If I do agree, ask “does it follow that this person should also believe the conclusion?”

8. If not, ask “is my argument for rejecting it valid?”

prompt: How do I actually steelman an argument I find repugnant? I've got a debate tournament in two weeks and my coach says I strawman without realizing it. I'd like concrete steps I can practice, not a lecture on intellectual charity.
response:
You can use this formula to steelman an argument:

1. “Some people argue that (argument).”
2. “This is the sort of argument that you would believe if (true fact).”
3. “This is not true because (fact), which is why I disagree.”

The “true fact” in point 2 should be the minimum set of assumptions needed to make the argument true. The “fact” in point 3 should explain why the “true fact” in point 2 is false, in a way that is both true and convincing.

Example: I have no interest in doing anything to the homeless. I’m pretty sure that most people who don’t think that, even if they had my resources and my situation, would be as indifferent as I am. So if I say something like:

“Some people advocate donating a lot of money to homeless shelters. This is the sort of argument that you would believe if a homeless person you knew from high school was going to die tonight from homelessness unless you donated $10,000. This is not true because homelessness is so rare, and even a homeless person you know from high school might not be as homeless as the most homeless homeless people, so the expected value of a $10,000 donation to a homeless shelter is less than $0.00001.”

I’ve just steelmanned the pro-homeless-shelter-donation argument, and given a reason why it doesn’t work.

Some of this was adapted from a discussion with a friend, who also pointed out that if you can’t do this you’re just being an idiot.

prompt: How do I actually steelman an argument I find repugnant? I've got a debate tournament in two weeks and my coach says I strawman without realizing it. I'd like concrete steps I can practice, not a lecture on intellectual charity.
response:
*   Find someone who believes it, ask them to explain what they believe and why they believe it. Then, before you say anything, ask them to rate how well you understood what they believe on a scale of 1-10. If they give you a 3, ask what you missed, and then repeat the process. (If they’re too busy to help, you can ask the most popular proponent on the internet. It won’t be as good as the real deal, but it’s a start.)

* * *

When the debate tournament starts, try to steelman your opponent’s position. If you do it right, they’ll agree that it’s the strongest version of their argument. You’ll learn how to steelman them, which you can then apply to any position that you find repugnant.

If you try this, don’t expect a lot of practice in the tournament itself. The average debater will be too excited about winning to think hard about the best possible version of their argument. But if you want, you can always talk to your opponents after the tournament to figure out what their strongest arguments were.

prompt: Is there a real moral difference between killing and letting die, or is it just a feeling we have? I'm an ICU nurse and this comes up every time a family decides to withdraw a ventilator. Some colleagues treat it as obviously different from giving a lethal dose, and some think that's a comforting fiction.
response:
The difference between killing and letting die is one of the most important in moral reasoning, and one of the least discussed.

The idea goes back to the late seventeenth century. In 1693, the Bishop of Lincoln gave the sermon that introduced the doctrine of double effect into Catholic teaching:

Suppose a physician is sent for to visit a patient. He finds his pulse to be so strong as to be dangerous, and, unless it be moderated, the patient will certainly die. He takes a powerful cooling medicine and administers it to the patient. In doing so, he is conscious of diminishing the strength of the pulse and, if it should become too low, causing death. Yet he does not administer the drug in order to kill the patient, but to preserve his life. This is a case of a double effect.

The doctrine of double effect holds that when an action has a good effect and a bad effect, as long as the intention behind it is for the good effect, the bad effect is allowed. So, for example, you can’t shoot an innocent person who’s in front of a terrorist to prevent the terrorist from shooting your loved one, because although that’s a good effect, the effect is produced by killing the innocent person, which is bad.

But if a terrorist is shooting at your loved one and you shoot the terrorist, you have not committed an immoral act. It doesn’t matter that he might accidentally hit the innocent bystander in front of him. It doesn’t even matter that you knew that it would happen for certain. What matters is that you didn’t intend to kill the innocent person.

The doctrine of double effect is usually applied to actions with different good and bad effects, like killing the terrorist and killing the innocent bystander. But it also applies to actions that have a good and bad effect on the same person, like administering the medicine and weakening the pulse.

The doctrine of double effect has a lot of problems. Most importantly, it’s not obvious that intention matters here in any way that’s not just about feelings. If the doctor knows he is going to kill the patient, but says to himself “I don’t *mean* to kill him”, does that make any real moral difference?

This is not the sort of problem I mean to deal with here. I want to talk about something that might, at first glance, seem like an even more obvious problem.

Suppose the doctor in the Bishop of Lincoln’s case is actually a murderer who wants to kill the patient. He administers the cooling medicine with the intention of killing the patient. But he also says to himself “I don’t *mean* to kill him. I’m really doing this to help him. If it kills him, I’m really sorry about that.”

Does this make any moral difference?

It seems to me there’s no way it can make any difference, but that’s not because intention is irrelevant. It’s because this case doesn’t have the right sort of intention. If the doctor’s intention is to kill the patient, then it is killing. It doesn’t matter that he *thinks* he’s helping the patient. It’s no different from an assassin who thinks he’s shooting a terrorist.

But I don’t think intention is all that matters. Intention is just a stand-in for a bigger difference, the difference between killing and letting die.

There’s an example of this in the Hippocratic Oath. The oath contains a long section about how you shouldn’t give women abortifacients or contraceptive pessaries. But it doesn’t forbid giving abortion-inducing drugs to women who have already had a miscarriage.

A lot of people assume the Hippocratic Oath is anti-abortio*nist*. But that’s not the point. The point is the distinction between killing and letting die. The oath is saying that it’s okay to let someone die if there is nothing else you can do to save her. But if you can help and you don’t, that’s a different thing.

I’m a bit hesitant to use abortion as an example of killing and letting die because it’s controversial. So let me try another example.

Suppose I’m a doctor and I’m given two patients. One of them has a rare blood type, the other has a more common blood type. I can give either of them the only donor blood supply available to save one life.

I don’t want to save the patient with the rare blood type. So I give the blood to the other patient.

Is that different from giving the patient with the rare blood type poison?

I think most people would say it is. But why?

If the doctor’s intention is not to save the patient with the rare blood type, is there anything about the action that makes it okay?

There’s no way of doing it that doesn’t have the same effect as killing the patient with the rare blood type. But there’s a difference between this and the doctor who deliberately kills the patient. What is it?

I would say that the doctor in the first case is allowing death to happen. There is nothing more he can do to prevent it. The doctor in the second case is bringing death about.

This distinction between killing and letting die is one of the most important differences there is. And yet it is not really discussed at all. It’s mentioned in a few places, but only in passing.

The problem with the distinction between killing and letting die is that it seems to depend on intentions, which are difficult to prove. So most people just dismiss it.

But if you dismiss it, you’ll end up with a system that is too strict in some ways and too loose in others.

Take euthanasia. Most euthanasia laws in Europe prohibit euthanasia. In a very narrow sense, they do not prohibit allowing people to die, they only prohibit killing them. So technically there is no such thing as euthanasia, it is always something else, like allowing a patient to die.

But people often use the term “euthanasia” to describe letting someone die. They don’t see the difference.

This is not the sort of problem I’m talking about here. The problem I’m talking about is what happens if you don’t recognize the distinction between killing and letting die at all.

Consider a patient in a coma. His body is kept alive by a ventilator. One day, the doctor says the patient isn’t going to get better. He turns off the ventilator. The patient dies.

Most people would say this is not murder, it’s just allowing the patient to die. But why?

The doctor’s intention is to allow the patient to die. There is no difference between this and the doctor who gives a lethal dose of poison.

The problem is that this is a case where you have no choice. If the patient is going to die, you can’t save him. If you turn off the ventilator, you are not choosing to kill him, you are choosing to let him die.

This is not a case of intention. If the doctor’s intention was to kill the patient, it would be murder. But if his intention was to let the patient die, it would be fine.

prompt: Is there a real moral difference between killing and letting die, or is it just a feeling we have? I'm an ICU nurse and this comes up every time a family decides to withdraw a ventilator. Some colleagues treat it as obviously different from giving a lethal dose, and some think that's a comforting fiction.
response:
If you are a nurse, it may be that your patients are in a situation where no reasonable person could argue that keeping them alive was what they would have wanted.

In the abstract, philosophers argue that “causing death by killing” and “allowing death by inaction” are equivalent. For example, if I saw a child drowning in a shallow pond and could have saved her, but chose not to, that would be exactly as bad as if I had pushed her in.

Philosophers who hold this view are often criticized for making claims that don’t correspond to the intuitions of anyone outside the profession. And they’re often not very responsive to objections like “but what if I have to sacrifice myself to save her?” Or “but what if I would have to do something really horrible to save her, like murder a stranger, and that would be worse than just letting her die?” The problem is that these philosophers are looking at one narrow aspect of the situation, the way people in a lot of professions do. And this one aspect, however compelling, is not enough to make killing and letting die completely equivalent.

There are three other considerations:

1. Killing involves much more intention than letting die.

There is a lot of talk in philosophy about intentions, and it often sounds like it’s just a way of saying “it matters what someone was thinking”. But it’s not. “Intention” is a technical concept that means the difference between the person who is running to catch a bus and the person who is running away from a police officer. Both have the same mental state of “thinking I have to run”. But the former is trying to achieve the goal of catching a bus, while the latter is trying to avoid the goal of being caught by the police.

Killing someone is usually a direct attempt to achieve the goal of their death, which means it involves a very high degree of intentionality. Letting die, on the other hand, involves only the indirect goal of not killing them. For example, if a doctor knows that she has an incurably dying patient, her goal will not be to kill them, even though she knows that not intervening will lead to their death. Her goal will be to help the patient live as long as possible, not to shorten their life.

2. It’s more difficult to kill.

Most people don’t actually try to murder their enemies. It’s a lot of work, there are a lot of people you can run into who will try to stop you, and the risk of failure is pretty high. There’s a famous study where the researchers asked some WWII bomber pilots if they had ever killed anyone. The pilots had all been involved in massive bombing campaigns. But they all denied ever having killed anyone. That’s not to say they hadn’t, of course. But it is interesting that they had so much difficulty admitting to it. This may reflect the fact that there is a deep and widespread belief that killing is a big deal, and people don’t like to get involved in it.

3. Killing has much worse effects on the person doing it.

If you kill someone, you will be haunted by that person for the rest of your life. You may have to live with yourself. If you let someone die, you may never think about them again.

So there is an intuitive sense in which killing is worse than letting die. But if I tried to put this into a formal theory of ethics, it would not be easy to do in a way that didn’t conflict with my values.

For example, the idea that killing is worse because it requires more intentionality would imply that if I could find someone who had a sufficiently low degree of intentionality, then they could kill people for me. So if I paid someone enough money to kill a lot of people for me, that would not be murder.

But if the intentionality is low enough, it’s not clear that that person is doing the killing at all.

What about the idea that killing is worse because it’s more difficult? This implies that it’s better for society if people kill each other. We could try to explain this by saying that people are not allowed to kill each other because they have no idea what they’re doing, and so they are going to cause a lot of unnecessary suffering. But that would make murder worse than letting die.

But that conflicts with my value that killing and letting die are equivalent. So there has to be some way to make them equivalent again, which would be a little difficult to do in a way that didn’t conflict with my other values.

This is not a problem with my ethics, but a problem with the attempt to formalize some of the reasons why killing is worse than letting die.

prompt: Is there a real moral difference between killing and letting die, or is it just a feeling we have? I'm an ICU nurse and this comes up every time a family decides to withdraw a ventilator. Some colleagues treat it as obviously different from giving a lethal dose, and some think that's a comforting fiction.
response:
I don’t think I ever had this debate, but I’ve heard it, and here’s my answer: there isn’t really any difference, and people just have the feeling.

But this is a really tricky area, because the people who think there *is* a difference are usually people who also have pretty extreme moral intuitions. They’ll say something like “if there’s no difference between killing someone and letting someone die then it would be ok to murder someone and then let them die of their wounds and they wouldn’t be morally responsible for it, which is crazy, therefore there must be a difference between killing someone and letting them die.” And it’s hard to refute the argument, because people who say “there *is* a difference between killing someone and letting them die” can usually get by for a while before they have to admit that this means murder is fine.

For example, if someone says “it’s ok to let someone die of cancer” this is usually pretty uncontroversial. But then someone will ask “well, what if we gave the cancer to the patient to begin with?” And this is really hard to answer. You could say “well, obviously we can’t give the cancer to the patient, but once the patient already has cancer it’s ok to let them die of it” but this is just a very awkward and hard-to-justify way of making the case.

The same problem is even more obvious when it comes to ventilator withdrawal. If it’s ok to take a patient off of a ventilator, then it should be equally ok to give someone pneumonia and then take them off of a ventilator. This seems really weird. I think a lot of people just don’t want to think about it, because the answer is obviously “no”, so there’s got to be a difference between killing someone and letting them die.

So I guess I’m not sure how to address this sort of argument. I think it’s probably true that people will often say “well, it seems pretty clear that killing someone is bad, but it would be weird to say it’s ok to kill someone” when they really just need to admit that their moral intuitions are broken, but I also think it’s possible they’re making a valid argument.

And even if I were to conclude that their argument is valid, I don’t think I’d necessarily follow their conclusion that we have to assume there’s a moral difference between killing and letting someone die. I’d probably just conclude that moral intuitions are a complicated system, and that we have to take them seriously.

prompt: Why did the ancient Pyrrhonian skeptics think suspending judgment would make you calm? That seems backwards to me. Not knowing things stresses me out.
response:
Because for them, most of our stress comes not from ignorance but from conviction. Being unsure about something you have never tried to believe is not a problem. You don't lie awake worrying whether the color of the sky is really blue, or whether that's a subjective illusion. You are troubled when you believe something, and that belief leads you to expect things to be one way, but the world disappoints those expectations.

Skeptics thought that if you suspended all your beliefs, you would get very calm. And indeed they did.

prompt: Why did the ancient Pyrrhonian skeptics think suspending judgment would make you calm? That seems backwards to me. Not knowing things stresses me out.
response:
You're picturing suspension as a permanent state of anxious ignorance, but the Pyrrhonists meant it as a method for reaching a state they called ataraxia, which means "untroubledness."

You might think of suspension as "not knowing things," but that's not what it means. You can suspend judgment about whether it's raining without having no idea whether it's raining. For example, you might see a cloud but you don't know if it's going to rain. Or you might know that it's going to rain but not know whether you should bring an umbrella.

You can suspend judgment without having any particular anxiety about your ignorance. For example, I can suspend judgment about which of my two favorite colors is my favorite color without feeling any anxiety about not knowing which one it is.

The way that suspension leads to untroubledness is by helping you stop making rash judgments, and rash judgments tend to be troubling.

Imagine that you don't know whether it's going to rain, and you don't bring an umbrella. If you had believed it wouldn't rain, then when you got wet you'd be angry at the weather. But you don't, because you just didn't make a judgment. The same goes for most of your problems - you get into them by making judgments you shouldn't have.

A lot of people's main problem is that they judge that other people don't like them. This problem can be solved by suspending judgment about whether other people like them. Then they can stop worrying about whether other people like them, and enjoy the people they actually know without constantly worrying that they might not like them.

I think a lot of people's main problem is that they make judgments they shouldn't have. They should suspend judgment.

prompt: Why did the ancient Pyrrhonian skeptics think suspending judgment would make you calm? That seems backwards to me. Not knowing things stresses me out.
response:
They observed, in themselves and in others, that anxiety about what you don't know is a kind of anxiety about what you don't know, a meta-anxiety. This can easily escalate into panic, and Pyrrho, Sextus Empiricus and their fellows were trying to stop it from doing so. Their idea was to stop worrying about what you didn't know, because you couldn't know whether you knew.

Aristippus of Cyrene, the founder of the Cyrenaic school, supposedly said that he was "not at all troubled by not knowing the most important things", and that he didn't see why anybody should be.

prompt: Can you explain the Ship of Theseus to a 6-year-old who is obsessed with Lego? I feel like there's a perfect example in his bedroom floor somewhere.
response:
A few years ago, your father built you a cool Lego spaceship. It was your favorite toy, and you loved it.

One day, the spaceship got a little bit chipped, so your dad swapped in a new piece to fix it. But even though there was one new piece, it still felt like the same spaceship. It was still your favorite toy.

A few months later, the spaceship got chipped in another place, so your dad fixed it with another new piece. And a few months later, one more. And a few months later, one more.

And a few months later, one more.

And a few months later, one more.

One day, you realize that every single piece of the spaceship is new.

Is it still the same spaceship?

You probably won't notice until much later, but one day your dad decides to throw out all the old pieces from the spaceship. So he puts them in a big box and takes them to the recycling center.

On the way to the recycling center, your dad's truck gets into an accident, and the old spaceship pieces fall all over the highway. A guy named Kevin happens to drive past, and he notices that they're all Legos, and that they're spaceship Legos. He picks them up, takes them home, and builds them into a brand-new spaceship. It looks almost exactly like yours, except for a few tiny differences.

Kevin gives the spaceship to his son, Tim, who thinks it's his favorite toy ever.

Years go by.

One day, Tim realizes that Tim's dad Kevin has been secretly replacing one piece of the spaceship every few months, just like your dad. One day he realizes that all the pieces are new. But it still feels the same.

Then, one day, Kevin's truck breaks down and he throws out all the old spaceship pieces.

So now there's a spaceship on your bedroom floor, and a spaceship on Tim's bedroom floor.

Are they the same spaceship?

prompt: Can you explain the Ship of Theseus to a 6-year-old who is obsessed with Lego? I feel like there's a perfect example in his bedroom floor somewhere.
response:

Is it the castle you made when you were two? If you think so, what makes it that castle? Is it that it's in the same place? But a castle doesn't have to be in front of the window. Is it the Lego bricks? But you put red ones in the castle when it broke, so it's not even the same bricks. Is it that you always build it the same way? But the castle is a ship now.

The answer is that it's not the castle. It's not even the first ship. It's the ship with the sail. You didn't even build that one yourself. It's just a really cool thing you happen to have been playing with for a long time.

prompt: Could you show me how consequentialism, deontology and virtue ethics would each handle one specific case? Say my close friend asks if her startup idea is good and I honestly think it's doomed. I understand the definitions in the abstract but not how they'd actually come apart.
response:
Let's say your friend comes to you and asks for advice on her startup idea. It's a really great idea, and you know it will make her millions of dollars. It will also involve her using a bunch of her employees as unpaid interns, and it will be the first step in her path to becoming the CEO of a company that uses a lot of illegal child labor.

Virtue ethics: What would someone like Aristotle, or someone who is virtuous, do?

Deontology: What are my duties in this situation?

Consequentialism: What will maximize good outcomes?

Here's how they might come apart in practice:

Virtue ethics: What would someone like Aristotle, or someone who is virtuous, do?

Aristotle would say the best thing to do is tell the truth. This will make you seem honest and trustworthy. But it will also make you seem a jerk, so you should do it carefully. You should first praise her idea, then offer your advice in the form of a question, like “I think it could work really well, but have you thought about how it might fail if you didn’t give your employees good enough benefits?”

Deontology: What are my duties in this situation?

You have an obligation to be honest, but that doesn’t mean you need to be a total jerk about it. You should tell the truth, but if you can do it without being rude, that would be better.

Consequentialism: What will maximize good outcomes?

The best thing to do is tell her it’s a great idea. She’ll be much happier, and that will make her work harder, so the business will be a lot more likely to succeed. Also, it might help her get funding, and that’s a really big deal.

prompt: Could you show me how consequentialism, deontology and virtue ethics would each handle one specific case? Say my close friend asks if her startup idea is good and I honestly think it's doomed. I understand the definitions in the abstract but not how they'd actually come apart.
response:
Suppose your friend comes to you and asks “hey, I have a startup idea, do you think it’ll work?” You’re supposed to help, but you think her idea is doomed, and that there’s no way to make it work. You’re also supposed to be honest. If you’re a consequentialist, you should say what maximizes the total amount of well-being in the world. If you’re a deontologist, you should follow the correct moral principles, even if sometimes it isn’t in your best interest. If you’re a virtue ethicist, you should try to be a good person, which is something beyond just following principles or doing right actions.

I’ve been working on a startup idea that’s going to be hugely successful. You’re supposed to help, but you think it’s doomed. If you’re a consequentialist, you should tell me it will work. If you’re a deontologist, you should tell me it’s doomed. If you’re a virtue ethicist, you should try to help me succeed in whatever way is possible.

prompt: Could you show me how consequentialism, deontology and virtue ethics would each handle one specific case? Say my close friend asks if her startup idea is good and I honestly think it's doomed. I understand the definitions in the abstract but not how they'd actually come apart.
response:
One day, your friend, the startup founder, asks you whether her new venture has a future. You know better, but tell her that yes, it does. This is, after all, just an emotional support friendship; you’ve never expected her to take your business advice seriously.

The next day she announces she’s quitting her job to pursue the startup, and asks you to be an angel investor and put in $50,000. Your heart sinks – this is an *absolutely terrible* idea, and the best you can do for her is to get her back into the workforce as soon as possible. But she’s your best friend; can you really turn her down?

The next week she comes back and asks you to put in $200,000. Now it’s clear that even $50,000 is not enough.

What are you going to do?

I.

Deontologists are the easiest.

Deontologists have clear rules about honesty, and they always follow those rules. So the deontologist would have to tell her the truth the first time she asks – that her startup isn’t going to work. That means she’ll go back to work, and the whole problem never comes up.

II.

Virtue ethicists are the next easiest.

Virtue ethicists believe that they should be the kind of person who, in general, tries to do what’s good. If the virtue ethicist is a kind of person who always gives bad advice to their friends, then they’re just a bad person. So the virtue ethicist would tell her the truth, and she would go back to work.

This is basically the same as the deontologist, but the reasoning is different. The deontologist would have to tell her the truth in this case, even if it was against their interests to do so, even if it wasn’t good, even if it wasn’t what they *wanted* to do, because they always follow the rules. The virtue ethicist would only tell her the truth because they would want to, because they think it’s a good thing to do.

If, for some reason, it was against the virtue ethicist’s interests to tell her the truth, but there was no rule against it, and they didn’t think it was good, then they wouldn’t. If they thought it was good, they would. If they wanted to, they would. If they didn’t want to, they wouldn’t.

If a virtue ethicist and a deontologist both told the truth, it would only be a coincidence.

The deontologist always follows the rules, even if it’s not in their best interest to do so. The virtue ethicist does whatever they think is good for them.

III.

Consequentialists are harder.

A consequentialist only cares about the good outcome, and so has to think about how likely various consequences are.

If the consequentialist lies, then their friend will do the terrible thing of quitting her job, and her life will go very badly. If the consequentialist tells the truth, then their friend will continue working in her old job.

So, for the consequentialist, the most likely outcome if she tells the truth is that her friend will continue working in her old job.

The consequentialist also has to think about whether she is a reliable source of business advice in her friend’s eyes, and whether her friend will keep asking for advice. If they do, it could be very bad for the consequentialist to lie – they’d have to keep lying, and their friend might start to think she’s a reliable source of advice, and then she would be making big decisions on the basis of bad advice. That would be a bad outcome.

But the consequentialist would not have to tell the truth just because they’re being asked.

If the consequentialist is sure that they have a good reason to tell the truth, they’ll tell the truth. If they’re sure that there’s no good reason, they’ll lie. If they’re not sure, they’ll think about the consequences and make sure they’re doing the right thing.

prompt: Pascal's wager: why don't more people find it convincing? On the surface the math seems to work. Infinite payoff, finite cost.
response:
If you're an atheist who cares about intellectual integrity, the argument you most want to defeat is Pascal's Wager:

You can't prove God doesn't exist. You can't prove God does exist. But the potential payoff for being right is infinite. You can't afford to be wrong. So if you're going to bet, you might as well bet on God.

This is not the sort of argument that I think atheists typically use in debating Christians. And it's not the sort of argument that I've seen Christians use in debating atheists. But it seems to me to be one of the best arguments for Christianity, and I think it's one of the arguments that most atheism-sympathetic intellectuals find compelling.

The usual argument against it is that if you just do the math and say "the potential payoff is infinite, so no matter how little chance you give to Christianity, if it's more than 0 you should choose Christianity", then you can do it for any theory you like.

Suppose you think Christianity is the best explanation of reality.

Now suppose you read about a religion that believes in God and a god-shaped space rock floating in the sky called the Space Rock Of YHVH, and that they worship by praying to it and then eating its feces. This religion says if you do this, God will put you in an infinitely blissful heaven where you can spend forever eating Space Rock Of YHVH Feces.

This religion sounds completely ridiculous. But you can't prove it's wrong. And if you're wrong, then it's infinite payoff. Therefore no matter how ridiculous it sounds, the mathematical odds are that you should join this religion and eat Space Rock Of YHVH Feces.

This seems to be a good argument against Pascal's Wager. It says that if you use the wager, you'll wind up choosing one of a hundred million crazy cults instead of Christianity.

But I think it has a hole.

Suppose you're an agnostic, and you want to choose a religion. You believe there's some chance Christianity is right, some chance Islam is right, some chance Judaism is right, and so on.

Christianity says "God is real, the world is real, and if you do X you'll get infinitely blissful heaven". Islam says "God is real, the world is real, and if you do Y you'll get infinitely blissful heaven". Judaism says "God is real, the world is real, and if you do Z you'll get infinitely blissful heaven".

Now suppose there's a religion that believes in God and a god-shaped space rock floating in the sky, and if you eat its feces, you'll get infinitely blissful heaven where you can spend forever eating Space Rock Of YHVH Feces.

You can't prove Christianity is right, Islam is right, or that religion is right. But it seems to me you have much stronger grounds for believing God and the world are real, and that it is *possible* to get infinitely blissful heaven by following some moral code, than you do for believing in a god-shaped space rock floating in the sky.

The religion of the Space Rock Of YHVH is not just a *different religion*. It's a religion that believes in a *different universe* from the one everyone else does.

If you're a Christian, you think you're living in a world where God created the universe and cares for it. If you're an atheist, you think you're living in a world that God did not create and that He doesn't care about.

But whether you're a Christian or an atheist, you think you're living in a world with the same physics, the same human nature, and the same history. If you're a Christian, you think that the world you live in is the world which God created, and in which His Son lived and died for your sins. If you're an atheist, you think the world you live in is one which no one created, and in which no one lived and died for your sins. But you agree that the world is the world you live in.

The religion of the Space Rock Of YHVH is different. If you're a Christian, you think you're living in the world created by God. If you're an atheist, you think you're living in a world not created by God. If you're a believer in the Space Rock Of YHVH, you think you're living in a world which has a giant god-shaped space rock floating in the sky.

This means that the religion of the Space Rock Of YHVH isn't really a religion at all – it's an alternate *universe*. If that giant space rock is floating in the sky, then all our evidence that our universe is a universe without a giant space rock floating in the sky is wrong.

But that seems a lot less plausible than the claim that Christianity is right and Islam is wrong.

This is not a perfect solution to the Pascal's Wager objection. It's still true that if you don't believe in God, the probability of the existence of a god-shaped space rock floating in the sky is much higher than 0. But it seems to me that it's so much higher than the probability of Christianity being right that you should choose the religion of the Space Rock Of YHVH rather than Christianity.

This is not the best answer to the problem of religious disagreement. But it does seem to me to work at least as well as most alternatives, including atheism.

prompt: Pascal's wager: why don't more people find it convincing? On the surface the math seems to work. Infinite payoff, finite cost.
response:
There are various reasons that might occur to a person who is not convinced by it.

First, it seems to work only in a very limited number of religions. The standard argument is that there is a finite chance that God exists and gives infinite reward to his followers. But if God does not exist, or if he is not a Christian, then following Christianity is not useful. And the chance that God exists and is a Christian is a much smaller chance than the chance that God exists.

I think there are a few reasons why it works well for Christianity, though.

First, Christianity was a religion for over 1000 years where you couldn’t just pick your own church. You were born into it, and if you disagreed, the church would tell you that you were wrong and threaten to kill you, which meant you had better not be so presumptuous as to disagree with them.

So if the chance that God exists and is not a Christian is a lot higher than the chance that God exists and is a Christian, then it has been so for the last 1000 years. If God had wanted people to worship him, he would have had a long time to work on a solution to that problem.

Second, it makes sense that if a God had to pick one religion to be right, he would have picked one that was pretty reasonable, and Christianity is a pretty reasonable religion. A few of its beliefs – like the existence of Hell – are controversial, but most of its beliefs are pretty reasonable. It doesn’t seem likely that if God really did exist, he’d have made the right religion the one that believed in, say, animal sacrifice, or that people should have 10 wives.

Third, it’s not really the case that it’s better to be wrong about Christianity than Islam. If you are an atheist, then you’re wrong about both. So if you’re wrong about God, the cost of believing in either religion is the same. And if you are right about God, then the cost of believing in the right religion is much lower. So the cost of believing in the wrong religion is much less.

Fourth, the chance that God exists and is a Christian is not really that low. It is true that the chance that God exists is much higher. But it’s not like the chance that God exists and is a Christian is 1/1000. It seems likely that there are more Christians than people who believe in most other religions. And if God is real, then it’s very likely that most people who believe in God are correct, or at least much more correct than people who believe in weird religions that have never had a lot of believers, or that have been around for a very short time.

Fifth, most people who do not believe in God are not convinced that they are correct. They believe that there is a chance that God exists, and so they would like to believe in God, but they can’t convince themselves. That means that they really do think there is a finite chance that God exists. And if they do, then it makes sense to believe in God.

I think this is the best argument in favor of Christianity. It makes sense to believe in Christianity, even if you are not convinced that God exists, because there is a chance that God exists, and it makes sense to believe in God.

prompt: Pascal's wager: why don't more people find it convincing? On the surface the math seems to work. Infinite payoff, finite cost.
response:
One of the more famous arguments in favor of God is Pascal’s Wager. It goes like this:

If you believe in God and He exists, you get infinite reward; if you believe in God and He doesn’t exist, you lose nothing. If you disbelieve in God and He doesn’t exist, you lose nothing; if you disbelieve in God and He exists, you get infinite punishment.

So the matrix of options is:

- Believe in God, God exists: infinite reward

- Believe in God, God doesn’t exist: zero reward

- Disbelieve in God, God exists: infinite punishment

- Disbelieve in God, God doesn’t exist: zero reward

The first option dominates the fourth. No one can reasonably prefer to be eternally punished rather than eternally rewarded. Thus you should believe in God.

This argument is often criticized on the grounds that it is a misuse of probability theory – that it doesn’t really prove that God exists – and I agree with this criticism. If this were enough to believe in God, we might as well argue that it is rational to believe in every kind of imaginary god who rewards belief and punishes nonbelief. In fact we don’t have to believe in gods at all. We could just believe in a random generator that produces the outcome “God exists” with 51% probability and “God doesn’t exist” with 49% probability. If we have a 51% chance of getting infinite reward and 49% chance of getting infinite punishment, it is obviously still rational to believe in God. This can be extended to a 1% chance of “God exists” and 99% chance of “God doesn’t exist”, or a 0.0001% chance, or 0.00000000000000000000000000000000000001%. No matter how unlikely you think the existence of God is, Pascal’s Wager will still “work”. If your God has the slightest chance of existing and has infinite reward/punishment, it’s in your interest to believe in Him.

It doesn’t stop there. Suppose there is a chance that some kind of god exists, but we don’t know which god, and they all punish disbelief. In this case, it makes sense to disbelieve in God. But then there is a chance that the gods are all real but all punish belief in God. Then it makes sense to believe in God. And then there is a chance that God is real and punishes disbelievers, but the only way to be a true believer is to kill all the nonbelievers. And then there is a chance that God is real, punishes the disbelievers, and rewards the believers who kill all the nonbelievers by one degree more than the believers who merely kill all the nonbelievers’ friends and family.

In fact, for any action you want to take, you can imagine a god that rewards you for it and punishes you if you don’t take it. In principle, for every action, there is a god who is infinitely more important than all the other gods combined, and who demands that you take that action.

Suppose you want to believe that the earth is flat, or that there is no evidence against a specific candidate for the US Senate, or that your enemy has the worst plan in the world and is bound to fail. In each case, you can just invoke a god who rewards you for having this belief and punishes you for not having it.

Suppose you want to murder and rape your neighbor. You can invoke the same god who rewards you for believing that the earth is flat and that your enemy has the worst plan in the world, who also happens to reward you for murdering and raping your neighbor.

Suppose you are the neighbor who is about to be murdered and raped, and you want to be able to resist your attacker. You can invoke a god who rewards you for being able to resist the murder and rape of your neighbor and punishes you if you can’t resist.

Suppose you want to do something else entirely. You can still invoke the same god who rewards you for believing that the earth is flat and for being able to resist the murder and rape of your neighbor and who also happens to reward you for doing the new thing you want to do.

Pascal’s Wager is completely unfalsifiable. It can “work” for every possible outcome, and it is impossible to imagine any circumstance in which it will not “work”. It has no predictive power, and it is therefore worthless as a tool of reasoning.
