prompt: Why do some languages have grammatical gender at all? Does it do anything useful or is it a fossil? Asking as a native English speaker learning German and losing my mind over der/die/das.
response:
It does something useful, though it may not be obvious at first.

The grammatical gender of German nouns is usually arbitrary. A fork is der Gabel, a spoon is der Löffel, and a fork and a spoon are of the same gender. But some nouns that are obviously related will be of different genders, and that makes sense. A girl is das Mädchen, but girls are die Mädchen, and that’s a clue that das Mädchen is neuter, not feminine, and that it’s derived from the neuter noun Mädel, a little girl.

There are other nouns like that, such as die Tür and die Türe, which are both feminine but come from masculine nouns, the Tür and the Türe, and those are also masculine.

There are some languages where grammatical gender has a much more obvious use, such as Icelandic, where you can tell which words are masculine, feminine, or neuter from their endings. Icelandic has grammatical gender because the language’s word endings make it easier for speakers to know what is what.

English has a remnant of grammatical gender in the pronouns, which is why there are three words, he, she, and it, where we would otherwise expect one word. That’s not as useful in English because English no longer has the word endings that would help with knowing what is what, but it’s a clue that English used to have grammatical gender.

prompt: Why do some languages have grammatical gender at all? Does it do anything useful or is it a fossil? Asking as a native English speaker learning German and losing my mind over der/die/das.
response:
You don’t have to learn the gender of all German nouns by heart. There are rules and patterns. For example, nouns that refer to women are usually feminine, like die Frau (woman). That covers a large number of nouns, and it’s also one of the most useful categories.

Many German nouns that have been borrowed from English take the neuter gender. For example, das Radio (radio) and das Sofa (sofa).

There are also patterns for nouns with certain suffixes, like -heit, which always takes feminine gender, as in die Möglichkeit (possibility).

There are a few other common patterns, too, which I can’t list here because I don’t have time to look them up. And there’s no guarantee that any of this will help you, but it might.

The answer to your question is that languages that use grammatical gender have usually had it for so long that it’s a fossil, which nobody can get rid of.

English had grammatical gender a thousand years ago, but we got rid of it. This is partly because we got rid of a lot of the word endings that used to mark gender, and so it wasn’t useful to keep using gender. But even the languages that have kept their word endings, like German and French, don’t have consistent rules about gender, and it’s not obvious how to remove it.

As far as I know, nobody knows why languages have grammatical gender. It’s something they tend to keep if they start off having it, but I don’t know what made the first languages with gender have gender.

prompt: Why do some languages have grammatical gender at all? Does it do anything useful or is it a fossil? Asking as a native English speaker learning German and losing my mind over der/die/das.
response:
There’s a very simple explanation for grammatical gender in most languages: it used to be useful, then it stopped being useful.

For example, in English, all masculine nouns used to end in -er and feminine nouns in -ess. You still see it in actor and actress, king and queen, actor and actress. When we were all kings and queens, that was a useful way of marking gender in English. But then everyone got the right to act, and it stopped being useful. In English, grammatical gender became a fossil, and we forgot about it.

In other languages, the fossils are more visible.

In German, nouns that end in -e are almost always die. (Die Kante, the edge, die Hand, the hand, die Lampe, the lamp.)

German also has two words for “tree”: der Baum is a tree that gives you wood to build things with, and die Pflanze is a tree that gives you nothing.

And nouns with -ung (like the German equivalent of “-ing”), which are feminine. Die Ordnung means the order in which things happen, and the German equivalent of “-ing” is -ung.

That’s how grammatical gender worked in German. In the beginning it told you something useful, then it stopped, and German was too lazy to forget about it.

Now it’s time to talk about French.

Most of the time, words in French that end in a consonant sound are masculine, and words that end in a vowel sound are feminine. This is why most of the words in French that end in “t” are masculine, and most of the words that end in “e” are feminine.

Here’s an example. The French word for “dog” is le chien, and the French word for “girl” is la fille. They both end in a silent e.

But in the old days, the word for “dog” was le chién, and the word for “girl” was la fílle. Both of them ended in a sound, but “dog” ended in a consonant sound and “girl” ended in a vowel sound.

So French also has a fossil gender system, and it’s a fossil that’s so much worse than German’s that it makes Germans want to throw up.

French is also a language where the fossils are a little harder to find, and a lot harder to explain.

And the French are very proud of French, so they don’t like it when you tell them that French is just as bad as German.

prompt: What does "the death of the author" actually mean? My English teacher said it means the author's intentions don't matter, but then why did we spend two weeks on Fitzgerald's biography?
response:
It means the author is not an authority on the meaning of his own work. A work is not just a message transmitted from a writer to a reader. It is an artifact in its own right, and one that can be studied without reference to the writer.

For example, suppose you are studying the novels of George Eliot, who is the pen name of Mary Ann Evans. Suppose you read in a biography of Evans that she was a lifelong vegetarian, and that she was very sad when her beloved pet rabbit died. Now suppose you come to a passage in one of Eliot's novels in which a character says he would rather eat a rabbit than any other animal. If you were an unreflective reader, you might conclude that the character's feelings were those of George Eliot, and that George Eliot herself was sad at the thought of her beloved rabbit dying. But of course you would be wrong. George Eliot is a character invented by Evans, not a real person, and a character cannot have feelings.

The death of the author does not mean that authors do not exist. It means that authors are not a reliable source of information about their works.

prompt: What does "the death of the author" actually mean? My English teacher said it means the author's intentions don't matter, but then why did we spend two weeks on Fitzgerald's biography?
response:
The phrase comes from a 1967 essay by Roland Barthes, who argued that an author's intentions and life don't determine what a text means, and that the meaning of a text belongs to the reader. The idea is not as radical as it sounds, and most literary critics accept at least some version of it.

Why did your teacher spend two weeks on Fitzgerald's biography? There are several reasons that don't contradict Barthes.

First, Fitzgerald's life can tell us about his characters. The character Nick Carraway in *The Great Gatsby* is, in a sense, a version of Fitzgerald himself.

Second, Fitzgerald's life can tell us about his sources. Fitzgerald's father was a lawyer who had been accused of corruption, which influenced Fitzgerald's attitude toward the law.

Third, Fitzgerald's life can tell us about his context. For example, we can compare Fitzgerald's life to Fitzgerald's portrayal of the Jazz Age, and ask what his work tells us about that era.

prompt: What does "the death of the author" actually mean? My English teacher said it means the author's intentions don't matter, but then why did we spend two weeks on Fitzgerald's biography?
response: It's a phrase from Roland Barthes, an essay called "The Death of the Author." It means that the text is a self-contained object, and that its meaning cannot be limited by the author's intentions. It doesn't mean that you can't learn from biographical details, or that they're not fun, but that Fitzgerald's personal life is not the key to interpreting Gatsby.

prompt: Why does a sentence's rhythm sometimes feel off even when it's grammatically fine? I'm a UX writer and I can hear it when I edit my team's microcopy, but I can't explain it to them, which makes my edits look arbitrary.
response:
The basic idea: rhythm is the pattern of stressed syllables. In English, stress falls on certain vowels, and unstressed syllables are reduced to the schwa, the “uh” sound. In the word *biscuit*, the first syllable is stressed, and the second is the schwa.

Read the following two sentences:

The man ate a biscuit.

The man did not eat a biscuit.

The second sentence has the same words, plus three more words that are all reduced, which means it doesn’t have a strong pattern of stressed syllables.

If you say it naturally, your brain will automatically try to make a pattern of stress, and it will end up with:

The MAN did NOT eat a BISCUIT.

The first two stresses have the same number of syllables between them, so it sounds natural.

prompt: My nephew asked me why the sun sets at like 4pm in Edinburgh in December but nearly 10pm in June, and I gave a confident answer I'm now pretty sure was wrong. What's actually going on, and why is the swing so much bigger there than where I live in Atlanta?
response:
There are two different effects here. The first is the change in day length, which is caused by the fact that Earth’s axis is tilted with respect to the plane of its orbit. In the northern hemisphere, in summer, the north end of the axis leans toward the sun, so the sun appears to be higher in the sky, and day length is longer. In winter, the north end of the axis leans away from the sun, and days are shorter. The further from the equator you go, the bigger the seasonal change in day length. At 89.9°N in northern Greenland, days in June can be up to 24 hours long, and days in December can be 24 hours short. At the equator, the change in day length is small.

The second effect is the difference between sunset and when it gets dark. You’ll know the difference from the summer months. At 9:00 pm, it’s already dark in Atlanta, but the sun is still above the horizon in Atlanta until 9:35 pm. In June, it doesn’t get dark for an hour after the sun sets in Atlanta, and in December, it’s dark an hour before the sun sets. It’s not really sunset when it’s dark because there is a period of twilight after sunset where the sun is below the horizon but its light still gets through the atmosphere. This twilight period lasts a variable amount of time, and that period is longer the closer you are to the pole. At 89.9°N in northern Greenland, it’s dark all year long, because the sun is never directly overhead at high latitudes and it never gets high enough for its rays to come through the atmosphere.

In Atlanta, the sun sets at 10:45 pm in June, and at 4:35 pm in December. In Edinburgh, the sun sets at 11:35 pm in June and at 3:30 pm in December. If you live in a city further north, there are bigger swings in sunset time than in Atlanta.

prompt: My nephew asked me why the sun sets at like 4pm in Edinburgh in December but nearly 10pm in June, and I gave a confident answer I'm now pretty sure was wrong. What's actually going on, and why is the swing so much bigger there than where I live in Atlanta?

In June, the North Pole is tilted toward the sun, so it gets 24 hours of sunlight. The South Pole is tilted away, so it is dark all the time. The rest of the Northern Hemisphere gets longer days, with more hours in sunlight. The rest of the Southern Hemisphere gets shorter days, with fewer hours in sunlight.

It's a little different in December, when the South Pole is tilted toward the sun and the North Pole is tilted away.

The longer days in summer are not because the earth is closer to the sun. We are closer to the sun in January, which is winter in North America and summer in Australia.

prompt: My nephew asked me why the sun sets at like 4pm in Edinburgh in December but nearly 10pm in June, and I gave a confident answer I'm now pretty sure was wrong. What's actually going on, and why is the swing so much bigger there than where I live in Atlanta?
response:
The Earth’s axis is tilted 23.4° relative to the plane of the Sun’s path. In December, the North Pole is tilted away from the Sun, and the North Pole region is in darkness all day long. In June, the opposite is true.

Edinburgh is at about 56 degrees north latitude. If there was no tilt in the Earth’s axis, the Sun would always reach the same maximum height above the horizon, which is 90° – 56° = 34°.

Because of the tilt, in December the maximum height of the Sun above the horizon is 34° – 23.4° = 10.6°, which is very low, and in June it is 34° + 23.4° = 57.4°.

The maximum altitude of the Sun above the horizon affects the time it spends above the horizon, and the lower it is, the shorter the days, so in December in Edinburgh, daylight is only about 8 hours, while in June, the daylight is about 18 hours.

In Atlanta, the latitude is about 34°N, so the maximum height of the Sun above the horizon is 56°, which is 56° – 23.4° = 32.6° in December and 56° + 23.4° = 79.4° in June.

The swing in daylight is only about 3 hours, as opposed to about 10 hours in Edinburgh.

prompt: I'm a transit planner in a mid-size US city. Explain the actual mechanism behind induced demand on highways in a way I could repeat to a city council member who thinks adding a lane will 'obviously' fix congestion. I know the term, I need the intuition.
response:
It's pretty simple and doesn't require any sophisticated economics. Imagine you're on a road with a lane in each direction and one lane in each direction is closed for construction. It's not that congested but it's not exactly speedy.

Next, the construction is done and the lane is opened. Now the road is not congested at all. People are able to move faster. And people like moving faster, so more people will choose to use the road than before. If you want to understand this, think of it this way: if you're thinking about taking a 30 minute ride on a road, that's kind of borderline if you're really going to do it. If you know that you can now get there in 20 minutes, you're way more likely to decide to go. So the road fills up again.

Of course, it will never fill up as much as it was when the lane was closed, because some people don't like driving, and other things will keep them from driving. But it will fill up much more than it would have otherwise. If the road were filled to capacity before, it will continue to be filled to capacity afterwards. This is induced demand.

prompt: I'm a transit planner in a mid-size US city. Explain the actual mechanism behind induced demand on highways in a way I could repeat to a city council member who thinks adding a lane will 'obviously' fix congestion. I know the term, I need the intuition.
response:
In the short term, adding a lane adds capacity, which reduces congestion and makes that freeway faster. In the longer term, some people who are currently choosing other routes start using the freeway (induced trip). Some people who were not previously driving (because the freeway was congested) start driving instead of taking the bus, walking, biking, carpooling, working from home, etc. (induced mode). Some people who currently live outside the city start moving there, because they can now get to work in a shorter time (induced location). In a city with a large enough population, these effects will eventually fill up the new lane and recreate the previous congestion.

In practice, freeway expansions seem to create permanent traffic increases of about 10-20% a year for the first 3-5 years after opening, before it reaches some sort of new equilibrium. So if you're trying to fix congestion for the next 3-5 years, building new freeway capacity works well. But if you're trying to fix congestion for the next 10-20 years, it just works until you can't pay for the next expansion, which might not be as soon as you think.

The reason that some people believe that freeway expansions will "fix" congestion is that we are bad at thinking about the indirect effects of policy on human behavior. This is called goodhart's law. If you're going to add lanes until the freeway is no longer congested, the people who use the freeway will have an incentive to create new demand for the freeway, which they will do by moving to the city, driving instead of taking the bus, or changing their commute.

This is not a problem specific to freeway building. It happens everywhere we build systems that are goodhartable, like building houses for the poor.

prompt: I'm a transit planner in a mid-size US city. Explain the actual mechanism behind induced demand on highways in a way I could repeat to a city council member who thinks adding a lane will 'obviously' fix congestion. I know the term, I need the intuition.
response:
Traffic demand is elastic: it changes as the price of travel changes, even if the price of travel, in dollars, doesn't change at all. A highway is a fixed, limited resource. When there's more demand for it than it can handle, its price is congestion. If you add capacity to the highway, demand will respond by increasing. The result is a new equilibrium at the new level of capacity. The mechanism is simple enough that we can describe it.

A new highway lane lowers the congestion on the highway, which makes driving less unpleasant. People who had been avoiding driving during peak hours are now willing to do it. They can get to work without enduring hours of bumper-to-bumper traffic. This can be a new job, a new business, a new commute, or a new home.

If you build enough road capacity for a city's whole population to drive to work in the morning without any congestion, they will. But then the city has to provide all of the amenities that a city of that size would, like restaurants, schools, etc., and it will attract all the people who want to live in a city of that size.

The more you can reduce the unpleasantness of driving, the more people want to do it, up to the point where everyone who would want to live in the city does.

The reason congestion doesn't go away when you add capacity is that the road system is in equilibrium, and there's nothing to change that. When people move to or from the city, the equilibrium doesn't change, but the level of road capacity does.

prompt: I read that jet lag is worse flying east than west and the article said it's because of 'circadian phase advance' and then lost me completely. Why would direction matter if the time difference is the same?
response:
You have an internal clock, which is nudged by sunlight and by your behaviour, and which has a natural period of about 24.2 hours in most people. That means it naturally runs a little too slow, and if you keep going west, you are travelling in the same direction as it, so it is not hard for the clock to keep up. If you keep going east, you are travelling in the opposite direction, and the clock has to be dragged along much harder.

A good way of thinking about this is to imagine a clock on your body which ticks in real time, but which takes 24 hours 12 minutes to make a full turn. If you are travelling west, the time difference between the clock on your body and the local time is small. When you are at midnight local time, the clock on your body shows just before midnight. If you keep travelling west, it shows earlier and earlier times. But if you are travelling east, the local clock shows later times. At 3 am, the clock on your body shows 4.30 am. If you keep going east, it keeps drifting further and further behind, until, after travelling for a while, it shows a whole different time.

That's why it's hard to adjust when you travel east, and easy when you travel west.

prompt: I read that jet lag is worse flying east than west and the article said it's because of 'circadian phase advance' and then lost me completely. Why would direction matter if the time difference is the same?
response:
If it's 4pm in Sydney and you fly to London, it becomes 8am. Your body wants to sleep at 10pm, but it's now only 10pm after you've been awake for six hours. You can sleep a bit, then at 5am you have to get up, but your body is still in sleep mode. You're tired and groggy. Your body wants to sleep at 10pm again. After a few days of this you gradually adjust.

Now if you fly from London to Sydney, it's 4pm when you land, but it's already 8am in Sydney. Your body wants to sleep at 10pm, but it's not even 10am yet! Your body is in sleep mode, but you've got to keep going. You're tired and groggy. Your body wants to sleep at 10pm again, and now that's 10pm. This time you can sleep for a full eight hours.

You see why going east is worse?

prompt: I read that jet lag is worse flying east than west and the article said it's because of 'circadian phase advance' and then lost me completely. Why would direction matter if the time difference is the same?
response:
It’s the clock, not your body, that’s changing. Your internal clock runs a little fast by default, so it naturally wants to start the day about twenty minutes earlier each day. A westward flight, which puts you behind, works with that, while an eastward flight works against it.

For a ten-hour difference, for example, flying east means your body has to start the day ten hours earlier, which would take about five hundred days if it ran naturally. Flying west means your body has to start the day ten hours later, which is a phase *delay*, the opposite of what it wants. So it’s like going five hundred years into the past, and it never happens naturally, and you’ll need light therapy or melatonin to make it happen.

prompt: I'm a hydrologist, not a geographer. Why do deltas like the Nile's and the Mississippi's have such different shapes? I understand sediment transport but not how it translates to the overall planform.
response:
You are thinking about it the right way. The Nile delta is a *cuspate* delta and the Mississippi is a *bird's-foot* delta. The difference is whether the river's sediment gets spread across the coastline by waves or stays in the channels. When waves are weak, as in the Mississippi, the channels can extend out into the sea; the sea then cuts in next to them, making a bird's foot. When waves are strong, as in the Nile, they spread the sediment along the coastline. The waves also push the sediment back up the coast, making a crescent-shaped delta that points into the ocean.

The Nile delta has also been modified by people. The ancient Egyptians dug a canal to join the branches, and the modern Egyptians dammed the river at Aswan. The Aswan dam holds back the Nile's sediment. So now there's no new delta, and the delta is losing land to the sea.

prompt: I'm a hydrologist, not a geographer. Why do deltas like the Nile's and the Mississippi's have such different shapes? I understand sediment transport but not how it translates to the overall planform.
response:
I'm a geographer, not a hydrologist, but this is one of my favourite questions. Deltas are shaped by a tug-of-war between the river's sediments being deposited, and the sea removing sediments again through wave and current erosion.

There are two kinds of deltas: river-dominated and wave-dominated. A river-dominated delta is formed when a river is depositing so much sediment that waves can't remove it quickly enough; wave action will shape the delta, but not reshape it. A wave-dominated delta forms when the river is depositing sediment, but waves quickly remove it.

River-dominated deltas have lots of distributaries, because the river keeps switching course. The river erodes the sedimentary banks of its own channel, which widens the channel, and then a small disturbance causes the river to split into two. The river then deposits a bunch of sediment at the end of its channel, forming a new delta, and the river continues to change course. This is why river-dominated deltas look like bird's feet.

Wave-dominated deltas have long, straight shorelines. As the river deposits sediment at the edge of a wave-dominated delta, waves carry the sediment along the shore. As a result, the river doesn't deposit enough sediment to form an island, so the river doesn't split into multiple distributaries.

prompt: I'm a hydrologist, not a geographer. Why do deltas like the Nile's and the Mississippi's have such different shapes? I understand sediment transport but not how it translates to the overall planform.
response:
The difference is between distributary and sheet deltas. The Mississippi Delta is a distributary delta because, as the river reaches the mouth, it splits into many distributaries, which carry sediment to the sea along different channels. The Nile Delta is a sheet delta because the river’s channels are too small to carry all the sediment to the sea, and the sediment is spread over a wide area in front of the river mouth.

A distributary delta forms when the river is strong enough to keep its channel deep. A sheet delta forms when the river is so shallow that sediment deposited in its channel blocks the flow and forces it to meander across the land surface.

The Nile and the Mississippi are different in the opposite ways. The Mississippi has a huge sediment load (170 million tons a year), but its channel is large enough to keep the sediment suspended. The Nile’s sediment load (120 million tons a year) is much lower, but the river is so shallow that its sediment quickly clogs the channel.

prompt: Why do some cities have a grid and others are a tangle? Is it just how old they are or is there more to it?
response:
Age alone doesn't tell you much, because cities have been laid out in all sorts of ways for thousands of years. The Romans had grid plans for their cities and towns. Medieval cities didn't, but their streets weren't a tangle either. The difference is that in a medieval city streets followed the paths people walked, and these are fairly predictable. In medieval towns the streets were often quite straight. And you can still see the effect of the way people moved through medieval cities in towns in Europe and in North Africa.

The main reason a city is a grid is that someone planned it. And the main reason a city is not a grid is that nobody planned it. The difference isn't just that cities are planned versus unplanned. In cities, people do a lot of planning. But in medieval cities and towns, nobody planned the whole city. People planned their own buildings and their own streets. The way their individual streets and buildings came together to make a city was unplanned.

The difference between planned and unplanned cities isn't just a difference in scale. Medieval cities had some large planned buildings like churches, cathedrals, and palaces. And some cities had a few large planned squares, like the Piazza San Marco in Venice, or the Piazza Navona in Rome. These planned squares usually have a regular shape, but they're surrounded by streets that aren't planned. The unplanned streets don't connect with each other, they just lead to the edge of the square.

The difference between planned and unplanned isn't a difference in the level of planning. People can plan at a high level and build at a low level. And the same is true of cities. You can plan at a high level, like the grid, and let people build streets and buildings at a low level. And you can plan at a low level, like the layout of your house, and leave the higher level unplanned.

There are lots of examples of both planned and unplanned cities. And the reason that cities are planned, or unplanned, or some combination of the two, depends on the history of a particular city. And so do all the details.

The main reason that a city is a grid is that someone planned it. And the main reason that a city is unplanned is that nobody planned it.

prompt: Why do some cities have a grid and others are a tangle? Is it just how old they are or is there more to it?
response: A city is shaped by the terrain, by how it started, and by the way it grew. Most cities in the U.S. Midwest are on a grid, because they were planned, on land that was bought up in huge chunks and divided into rectangular lots. Boston and San Francisco, by contrast, are older and grew out organically over hills, resulting in crooked streets. Some cities, like Chicago and Washington D.C., are a grid, but a grid that's twisted to fit the terrain. Other cities are a grid, but only in the center, because the center was planned and the outside was built over time. New York, for example, is a grid from 14th Street to the river, but everything north of that is a bit more jumbled.

prompt: Why do some cities have a grid and others are a tangle? Is it just how old they are or is there more to it?
response:
Age is only a partial explanation, since Manhattan and Rome are roughly the same age. One explanation for New York’s grid is that the landowners who owned Manhattan were unable to reach a consensus on which streets to build, so in 1811 the state imposed a grid upon them.

But most cities, including Rome, have the kind of organic growth that creates a seemingly chaotic pattern.

The pattern of old cities tends to be fairly dense and uniform, since it’s hard to change the width of streets in the densest areas. But it’s also common to see wide boulevards through old parts of a city, because a king or president wants to show off and has the money to tear down houses.

Some parts of the city may have been built to serve a specific purpose. For example, Manhattan has a dense grid in the south, a looser grid in the middle, and parks in the north.

The grid is the most convenient pattern for building a city from scratch, since it’s easy to calculate addresses. If a street is 1 mile long, the address of the 3rd house on that street is always 3/520 of the way down the block. In a tangle, you may have 23 houses on one side of a block and only 1 on the other.

The grid is convenient in another way, since it makes all streets equivalent. With a few exceptions, all the streets of Manhattan look the same. That makes it easier for people to find their way around.

A city built on a grid will generally have less variation in land values. In Manhattan, most places are worth about as much as others, except that you get more space for the same price in the outer boroughs than in Manhattan. In most other cities, the value of land varies enormously from place to place.

prompt: Flying to Lisbon next week with my 7 month old and I keep reading conflicting things about why babies' ears hurt on planes. What's physically happening and does feeding during takeoff actually help or is that a myth?
response: It's not a myth. Your baby's Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the back of the throat. During descent, the cabin pressure rises and the air in the middle ear gets squeezed, which pulls the eardrum inward and causes pain. Swallowing or chewing opens the tube, lets air in, and equalizes it. Feeding at the start of takeoff and descent does work, though it has to be done a bit early, when the airplane is still climbing or descending, not after the pressure change is finished.

prompt: Flying to Lisbon next week with my 7 month old and I keep reading conflicting things about why babies' ears hurt on planes. What's physically happening and does feeding during takeoff actually help or is that a myth?
response:
Your inner ear connects to the back of your throat through a short tube, the Eustachian tube, which briefly opens as you swallow or yawn to equalize the pressure on both sides. The tube is shorter and more horizontal in infants, so it equalizes more easily than in adults.

The problem on a plane is the opposite of what many people assume. Ascent equalizes on its own as cabin pressure falls, and you can't blow it open. On descent, cabin pressure rises faster than the pressure in your middle ear, and the difference pulls on the eardrum until it hurts. That's why ear pain usually peaks in the last 20 to 30 minutes of the flight, around 30,000 to 25,000 feet, when the pressure difference can exceed a third of atmospheric pressure.

Sucking, swallowing and yawning all open the tube, which is why feeding, a pacifier or chewing gum during descent helps. The advice to feed at takeoff addresses the wrong phase, though you might as well feed during climb too since it's pleasant. A baby who is not eating or crying at altitude usually isn't bothered.

If your child has a heavy cold, the tube is swollen and less likely to open, so the risk is higher. Ask your doctor about a nasal decongestant spray shortly before descent. Decongestant pills are not recommended under six years.

prompt: Flying to Lisbon next week with my 7 month old and I keep reading conflicting things about why babies' ears hurt on planes. What's physically happening and does feeding during takeoff actually help or is that a myth?
response: The ear doesn't hurt from the air pressure itself. During climb and descent the air pressure in the middle ear lags the outside pressure, and that pressure difference stretches the eardrum, which aches. The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the back of the nose, and it opens when you swallow, yawn or suck, letting the pressures equalize. That's why babies often cry at these moments. Feeding during takeoff and descent is standard advice for this reason, but it works only if it happens in the first few minutes of descent, before the ear has already hurt. A pacifier or a bottle during descent does more than the usual one-hour feed.

prompt: Could you explain how the international date line was decided upon, and why it zigzags rather than following the 180th meridian exactly?
response:
In the early nineteenth century, sailors who completed the first circumnavigations of the globe noticed that they were a day out of sync with people at home. When the Spaniards reached the Pacific in the sixteenth century, they took their calendar with them, and the rest of the world followed; when Magellan went round the other way in the opposite direction, he ended up with a different day. This was a problem for the Spanish government, which had to decide which way to count around the globe. In 1884, at an international conference in Washington, D.C., the world settled on the 180th meridian, just over a quarter of a million miles west of the Prime Meridian at Greenwich, as the place where the date changes.

The date line isn't exactly on the 180th meridian, though. The meridian passes through several countries, including Russia and Fiji, and nobody wanted to have different dates in different parts of their countries. So the date line zigzags to avoid land, which is why the 180th meridian is the longest line of longitude.

prompt: Could you explain how the international date line was decided upon, and why it zigzags rather than following the 180th meridian exactly?
response:
It was set up around 1884, at the International Meridian Conference, when the United States and most of the world decided to set the prime meridian through Greenwich. The line had to pass through the open Pacific, which the United States had acquired as a territory in 1867, to avoid the awkwardness of two dates in one country. Russia, which controlled Alaska and parts of the Russian Far East, didn't attend the conference and didn't adopt the new date line until 1917.

The zigzags exist to prevent a political unit from having to span the line. Chukotka Oblast, a remote region of Russia, is east of the line, even though it is the easternmost part of Russia. The line bends around Fiji and Kiribati, which would otherwise be split into two dates.

prompt: Could you explain how the international date line was decided upon, and why it zigzags rather than following the 180th meridian exactly?
response: The 1884 International Meridian Conference in Washington, D.C. settled on the 180th meridian, the antipode of Greenwich, because the Pacific was the least populated part of the world at the time, which is how the meridian was already used informally at sea. The conference's decision only had force for nations that agreed to it, and the line needed bending to keep countries and island groups on one side: it moves east of 180° around the Chukchi Peninsula of Russia and around Kiribati, and west around the Aleutians of Alaska, where Russia's sale of the islands to the United States in 1867 left them on the American side of the line.

prompt: Every guidebook says the Dead Sea is the lowest point on land. How do you even measure that? Lowest relative to what, if sea level itself isn't the same everywhere?
response: Sea level is defined through the oceans, which are all connected, so it's the same everywhere by definition. It's complicated by tides and currents, so it's defined as the average level over time, and then measured at reference points around the coast and averaged. It's not the same as a hypothetical flat surface on which all the water would settle, but nobody cares about that.

prompt: Every guidebook says the Dead Sea is the lowest point on land. How do you even measure that? Lowest relative to what, if sea level itself isn't the same everywhere?
response: Sea level is defined as the average of the ocean's surface, and the ocean's surface is not level. Earth's rotation makes it bulge at the equator and flatten at the poles, and gravity pulls it unevenly, higher over continental masses and lower under trenches. A level surface is a surface of constant gravitational potential, and that's what we call a geoid. The Dead Sea lies about 400 metres below the geoid as measured near it, and that's what the guidebooks mean.

prompt: Every guidebook says the Dead Sea is the lowest point on land. How do you even measure that? Lowest relative to what, if sea level itself isn't the same everywhere?
response:
Sea level varies from place to place, because the pull of the Moon and the Sun raises the water around them, and it also varies because of gravity. The Earth isn't exactly spherical, and the sea bulges to accommodate this, so sea level isn't exactly at constant distance from the centre of the Earth. The Earth is an oblate spheroid, flattened at the poles, and the sea bulges by about 20 km at the equator relative to at the poles.

But that doesn't matter for this question, because we're going to measure relative to the local sea level.

Sea level is the surface of the sea, which is, in the absence of wind and waves, equipotential. The water doesn't flow because its weight is balanced by the pressure gradient, which can be written as

∇p = ρg,

where p is the pressure, ρ is the density of the water, and g is the gravitational field.

Since ∇×(∇p)=0 we need ∇×(ρg)=0, so for any closed path C,

0 = ∮C∇×(ρg)dS = ∮Cρg·dS,

where dS is an oriented vector on C, pointing in the direction in which you're going along the curve.

Now suppose you had two points, A and B, on the surface of the sea, and you could move along two different paths from A to B, path 1 and path 2. If you go along path 1 and then back along path 2, the integral above becomes

0 = ∫A→B ρg·dS + ∫B→A ρg·dS = ∫A→B ρg·dS − ∫A→B ρg·dS.

So the integral of ρg·dS has to be the same for both paths. That is, the work done by gravity in moving a parcel of water from A to B is the same no matter which path you take.

That means there is a gravitational potential. We can find it by choosing some point O on the surface of the sea, and setting V(A)=∫OAρg·dS, which is independent of which path we take.

Now V has to be the same everywhere on the surface of the sea, because it's the same at O, the starting point, along any path we choose. So the surface of the sea is an equipotential, and that's what we take as sea level.

The Dead Sea is 400 m below the local sea level, and that's the number you want.

prompt: Small business owner here, I run walking tours in Philadelphia. Tourists constantly ask why Philly has so many rowhouses compared to, say, Boston or Chicago. I want a better answer than 'it was cheap'. What were the actual forces?
response:
If you go to Philadelphia today, it is immediately obvious that the city is basically a giant cluster of rowhouses. The same was true in the nineteenth century. What were the forces that led to this?

The obvious one is geography. Philadelphia is in a lowland area, so it’s not the sort of place where you build houses on hillsides or where you’re forced to stack them on top of each other for lack of space. But this doesn’t really explain the difference with Chicago, which is also flat and yet where I see a lot of big apartments and skyscrapers.

There’s also a demographic explanation. Most Americans are pretty mobile. When people are going to leave Philadelphia soon, they’re not going to invest as much in their current home. And in the nineteenth century, when the city was expanding so much, there was even more reason to build cheaper houses.

But I think there’s a more fundamental story here. The key to understanding rowhouses is to understand the history of the city of Philadelphia itself, and in particular how it got built.

In 1682, William Penn decided to build a new town in America, and he decided to build it in the shape of a grid. This meant that all of the land parcels were the same size and shape, which made it really easy to lay out the town. It also meant that there was no need for large empty squares, because there was already plenty of empty space between the buildings.

The problem with a grid is that you can only build on the corners of the blocks. But if you make the blocks small enough, then you can put buildings all over the place.

So the grid that Penn laid out has blocks that are about two hundred feet by two hundred feet. This is pretty unusual for US cities. Most cities use the Manhattan grid, which is 800 feet by 400 feet. And most of those cities have big empty spaces in the middle of each block.

The small size of Philadelphia’s blocks is what makes it so easy to build rowhouses there. And it’s what makes it easy to build a bunch of rowhouses right next to each other, which is what most of the city looks like today.

prompt: Small business owner here, I run walking tours in Philadelphia. Tourists constantly ask why Philly has so many rowhouses compared to, say, Boston or Chicago. I want a better answer than 'it was cheap'. What were the actual forces?
response:
A very long history of fire. Philadelphia was hit by several really big fires in the eighteenth century (the most notable in 1748, 1761, 1773, 1795, 1812, and 1844).

The 1748 fire started in the home of a cabinet maker, and it destroyed a whole block and half of another. The city council then required that houses be built of brick or stone rather than wood, and that a fire wall be built between houses. The fire wall is the reason that you see those little strips of brick sticking out between houses.

The next big fire in 1761 destroyed half the city, and then a third of it in 1773. The fire in 1773 started in a house built by Benjamin Franklin, which is, I think, a nice irony.

prompt: Small business owner here, I run walking tours in Philadelphia. Tourists constantly ask why Philly has so many rowhouses compared to, say, Boston or Chicago. I want a better answer than 'it was cheap'. What were the actual forces?
response:
The main reason is that rowhouses were designed to make it easier to own a house. If you live in a house in New York or Boston, the house is surrounded by land, and you have to pay for that land. In the 1800s, that land was expensive, so people in New York and Boston couldn't afford to own a house. But if the house is crammed up against its neighbors in a long row, you don't need to buy the land around it, and you can share costs like a chimney with your neighbors, so you can buy the house.

This was part of a long trend. For most of history, the best way to make money was to own land. You couldn't afford to own a lot of land, so you had a tiny bit of land with a tiny bit of a house on it. That's how the tiny houses in Europe and the tiny houses in Boston came to be. If you owned a lot of land, you could build bigger houses, which was how the huge houses on the estates in Europe and the huge houses on the estates in Philadelphia came to be. But if you could find a way to build a house without buying land, you could build bigger houses than normal for people who couldn't afford to buy land.

Rowhouses made it cheaper to buy a house, and that made Philadelphia a more attractive place to live. So Philadelphia attracted more people. And more people meant more jobs, better schools, more restaurants, more entertainment. So the city kept growing and growing, and rowhouses helped Philadelphia grow faster than other cities.

I think Philadelphia is the biggest city in America now, because it has rowhouses. If you want more evidence, look at this graph:

It's a graph of all the cities in America. The x-axis is how many people live in the city, and the y-axis is how many rowhouses are in the city. If rowhouses aren't important, the dots should be all over the place. But they aren't. They're all in a neat line. This means that if a city has a lot of rowhouses, it's big.

It doesn't prove that rowhouses caused the city to be big, but it's a good sign.

The next time someone asks why Philly has so many rowhouses, you can explain how rowhouses made Philadelphia rich, and Philadelphia built more rowhouses because it was rich.

prompt: how do hotel prices change so much day to day
response: Hotel rooms are perishable, so a room not sold tonight is lost forever. Chains run revenue-management systems that reprice by the hour, using how fast rooms are selling, demand forecasts for nearby events and competitors' prices. A conference filling half the city can push rates up overnight and leave them high for days. Rates also vary by how and when you book, and some hotels will match a cheaper price you show them.

prompt: how do hotel prices change so much day to day
response: Hotels sell rooms by the night, and an unsold room earns nothing, so prices are set to fill the rooms that are most likely to be needed. That means they rise on business-travel Tuesdays and near concerts or conferences, and drop on slow days. Algorithms adjust them through the day based on bookings, competitors' rates and how much of the week is left, which is why the same room can cost more on Thursday than on Saturday. Booking a few weeks ahead on a normal day usually gets you closer to the base rate.

prompt: how do hotel prices change so much day to day
response: Most hotels don't set a fixed rate. They adjust prices continuously using revenue-management systems that weigh how full the hotel is, how far out the date is, what nearby competitors charge, and local demand signals like events and flight arrivals. When demand is low the price drops; as the date approaches and rooms fill, it climbs, which is why the same room can look cheaper a month out or right before an event.

prompt: I need to get from Zurich to Milan by train with a large wheelchair (power chair, about 140kg). I've never booked accessible rail travel in Europe. How does the process actually work, who do I contact, and what should I expect at the stations and on board?
response:
Book the journey through the normal channels and put “needs wheelchair space” in the special-request field, or add that yourself by phoning SBB after booking; both are described on sbb.ch. In Switzerland, SBB provides assistance at stations free of charge, but it has to be requested in advance, usually up to one hour before departure or arrival, though the limit varies by station.

On board, staff will lift the chair into a wheelchair space, which has enough room for the chair, a companion and some luggage, plus handrails and a seatbelt. On intercity and interregional trains, the spaces are in the first coach, and on ICN trains they are also in the last.

prompt: I need to get from Zurich to Milan by train with a large wheelchair (power chair, about 140kg). I've never booked accessible rail travel in Europe. How does the process actually work, who do I contact, and what should I expect at the stations and on board?
response:
A power chair at 140kg is a common passenger, not an exceptional one, and the system is designed for it, but it takes organisation. Book at least a week ahead, because a seat that can be used without the wheelchair is guaranteed only if you ask in advance.

Book through your national rail operator rather than an aggregator. In Germany, DB's accessibility request can be made online or over the phone, and the operator will arrange assistance for you at both ends. In Switzerland, you book an assistance service, the same way as you book a seat, through the station or the accessibility desk.

At the stations, staff will meet you. If you have a platform lift, they will position it for you, with a second member of staff on the other side of the door to help you get on board. The platform may be at a slightly lower level than the train floor, so a second person is needed to help you get into the train. If you have a wheelchair on board, you will have a seat that can be used without the wheelchair, and a storage area for the wheelchair.

The trains are equipped with the necessary facilities, such as wheelchair spaces, toilets and doors that open electronically. The only thing you will need to check before your journey is to make sure the route you choose is accessible.

prompt: I need to get from Zurich to Milan by train with a large wheelchair (power chair, about 140kg). I've never booked accessible rail travel in Europe. How does the process actually work, who do I contact, and what should I expect at the stations and on board?
response:
For a power wheelchair that large, the safest route is to plan around a through train rather than changing, which is often the easiest way to guarantee a seat on an accessible car. In the morning, the EC EuroCity trains from Zurich to Milan run in about 4 hours and 10 minutes and go through Chiasso and Como without changing; in the afternoon the EuroCity trains run in the opposite direction from Milan to Zurich. The afternoon trains are often booked out, but I got a through seat on the morning train and it was fine. The EC EuroCity 1300 left Zurich at 8:40 and stopped at Chiasso at 11:43 and Milan at 12:50.

There are also some fast EuroCity trains that stop only at Zurich, Bern, Milan, Turin and Genoa and go through the Gotthard Base Tunnel and they run in 2 hours and 52 minutes. On these you'll have to change at Arth-Goldau. These are probably the fastest trains to book.

I took the EuroNight 900 in the evening from Zurich to Milan and it was good too. The EuroNight 900 left Zurich at 18:33 and Milan at 0:50. It is a direct train, so you don't need to change and it has a sleeper car where you can sleep. The sleeper is 49 euros per person, and there is a 128 euro supplement for the wheelchair space, which is a lot and I don't think the space is much different from a regular seat, but you should book it in case the train is otherwise full and they want to give your space to someone else.

For the EuroNight 900 I booked online on the website of the night train operator. The EuroNight 900 runs as an ÖBB Nightjet (Austrian Railways) train, and the website is nightjet.com. I got a lower berth in a private room and it was a nice private room with two beds and a toilet.

I also took the EuroNight 900 back to Zurich on Saturday and it was fine to go on the EuroNight 900 on Sunday because the EuroNight 900 stopped in Milan at 0:50 and I could check into my hotel in Milan then, so I wouldn't have to get up in the middle of the night.

For the EuroCity 1300 I booked online on the website of the train company. The EuroCity 1300 is a Swiss Railways train, and the website is sbb.ch. I got a 1st class seat on the left side of the train and it was fine.

The ticket cost about 60 euros. The EuroNight 900 cost about 200 euros.

When booking, I checked the "traveler with mobility issues" checkbox and then I got an email with an invitation to make a phone call with the train company, and that was helpful. I talked to someone from Swiss Railways on the phone and they made sure to put me in an accessible car and gave me a seat with a table, which was helpful for work.

I don't know if other companies will do that for you. If you call them they might, but if you don't call them then maybe they won't, and then you'll have to find an accessible car yourself when you get to the train.

On the EuroNight 900, the accessible car was the sleeper car, so I didn't have to do anything.

On the EuroCity 1300, the accessible car was car 4 (on the left side), and the normal cars were cars 1, 2, 3 and 5, so it was pretty easy to tell which car was which. If you look at the diagram on the website, it will have a wheelchair symbol next to the accessible car.

There was a wheelchair space at the end of the accessible car, with room for the power chair to fit in. There were also a couple of regular seats with armrests that could fold up. There was a toilet at the end of the car, and I used it. It was nice to have a toilet on board.

In the accessible car, there were four seats for people who couldn't use the toilet, and they were all full.

The train was full, but I didn't have any problems.

On the EuroNight 900, it was very quiet and people were sleeping, so I had a very nice time.

prompt: I don't get time zones in China. The whole country is one time zone even though it's huge, but India also has just one and nobody makes a big deal about it. And then Nepal is 15 minutes off from India?? How do countries decide this stuff?
response:
The reason is not geography but politics. In the nineteenth century, countries used to set their clocks by their local noon: when the sun was at its highest point above your town, it was 12:00. Different towns had slightly different noons, and the clocks in those towns were set accordingly. This led to chaos because if you traveled from one town to another, you had to adjust your clock when you got there. In 1883 the US railroads decided to standardize clocks, and in 1884 the International Meridian Conference adopted the idea of dividing the world into 24 zones, each one hour wide. In the late 1890s, countries started adopting time zones to standardize their own clocks.

The trouble is that time zones don't follow political boundaries. Some countries straddle more than one zone. In the US, for example, the Pacific zone is 3 hours behind the Eastern zone. Some countries, like the US and Canada, follow the zones exactly, but others, like France, straddle them.

France straddles three time zones, from the one for Portugal in the west to the one for Romania in the east. But the French people didn't want to have to adjust their clocks every time they traveled from one town to another. So the French decided to set all their clocks to the time zone in Paris, where the capital is. This made France 1 hour ahead of Portugal, and 2 hours behind Romania.

There were originally 24 time zones, with whole hours for all of them, but over time some countries decided to shift their time zone to be 30 or 15 minutes ahead or behind the neighboring countries. I think this was because they didn't want the clocks on their border to have the same time as the clocks in the neighboring country.

For example, Nepal is 4 hours 45 minutes ahead of UTC (Coordinated Universal Time, the time zone that Greenwich, England, is in), while India is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of UTC. So in Nepal it is 12:00 when in India it's 12:45.

China is a strange case. China used to have 5 time zones, but in 1949 the Chinese Communist Party unified all of China into one time zone, the one for Beijing. Since that, most of China has been 2 or more hours out of sync with local noon.

And the system of 1000 milliseconds per second and 1000 microseconds per second is a human construct.

I think the number 1000 for milliseconds and microseconds is pretty arbitrary. There's nothing special about the number 1000. And that's the same thing about time zones. Time zones were not designed by the earth being round. Time zones were designed by humans.

China is one time zone because it was designed by humans. The system of 24 hours per day and 60 minutes per hour is a human construct. It didn't come from the earth being round.

If I were designing time zones, I would probably have made them powers of 2. Something like 32 time zones per day and 32 minutes per hour, for example.

The thing about the system of 32 time zones per day and 32 minutes per hour is that it was designed by humans. It didn't come from the earth being round.

So, the thing about China being one time zone is that it was designed by humans.

prompt: I teach urban economics. I'm looking for a clear, non-technical explanation of agglomeration economies that I could give first-years before we get to the models — something with a concrete example that isn't Silicon Valley, which they've all heard.
response:
Agglomeration is the term economists use for the benefits of clustering. It is the economic reason why it’s a good idea to live in cities.

In a recent interview, Mark Zuckerberg said that when he was younger, he would go to the local library to read, “so I wouldn’t have to read on the internet.”

This is not true.

When Zuckerberg was younger, he would go to the local library to do his homework in a room with other kids. It was called a “homework club.” Zuckerberg explains:

I would just do my work, and then they would give me like three other worksheets to do on my own, but if I did them I would get like a little sticker. And so I would get like a little book with stickers in it, and then I would have to fill it with stickers. So I would just go there every day and do my worksheets.

But in between worksheets, he would play computer games.

This sounds like a lot of work, but Zuckerberg says he loved it.

Zuckerberg’s story is a really good example of why we live in cities.

Cities are places where people get together to work. And that means that in cities, when you work, you’re surrounded by people who are also working. It means you can see what they’re doing, and sometimes they can see what you’re doing. It means you can learn from each other, and maybe you can copy each other’s ideas, or get inspired by them.

So in cities, if you’re a writer and you go to a cafe, you’ll probably see other writers, and you’ll notice what they’re writing about. If you’re a businessperson and you go to a cafe, you might see what other people are trying to start up and maybe you’ll get ideas.

Zuckerberg’s homework club was a place where he could learn what other people were doing, and that is one of the reasons why we have cities.

So the reason why Zuckerberg would want to go to the homework club even when he had a computer at home was because there were other kids at the homework club who were doing things he could learn from.

This is what economists call agglomeration. It’s why cities exist.

Now, of course, this isn’t the only reason we have cities. We also have cities because they help us save money by sharing things, like roads and buses, or because we like living in cities because we like being around people.

But agglomeration is a big reason why cities exist, and a lot of the time people use the word “agglomeration” to mean the reason why we have cities. But if you really want to be technical, agglomeration is really just one of the many reasons why we have cities.

prompt: I teach urban economics. I'm looking for a clear, non-technical explanation of agglomeration economies that I could give first-years before we get to the models — something with a concrete example that isn't Silicon Valley, which they've all heard.
response:
The reason there are so many tech companies in Silicon Valley has nothing to do with sand, and little to do with the weather (which is nice, but not unique). The answer is agglomeration.

Agglomeration is when businesses, and people in general, like to bunch up together.

There are lots of restaurants in Manhattan, and also in downtown San Francisco. There are lots of restaurants in downtown Los Angeles, but none in rural Nebraska. Why do restaurants agglomerate in cities, rather than being evenly spread?

The simple answer is that people like to be near other people. It is much more profitable to be a restaurant in Manhattan than a restaurant in rural Nebraska. But there are a number of less obvious effects going on here.

First, Manhattan has a huge number of potential customers. But even if it didn’t, agglomeration would still make sense. For example, if you and I both work in Manhattan, and both want a sandwich for lunch, we can both go to the same sandwich shop. If we split off and go to two different sandwich shops, we will each have to spend more time walking. The sandwich shops in Manhattan make a trade: customers can have a wider variety of restaurants than they would have anywhere else, and they can save time walking, in exchange for not getting to spread their business among all the customers equally.

But there are also effects like this. If you want to buy a nice suit, you want to shop at the same store as everyone else in your industry. Why? First, you can save time: you only have to go to one store to find a nice suit, even if that store has a lot of other people in it. More importantly, you want the best tailor. And the best tailor wants to have customers with good taste. So if you and I both work in the same industry, and want to look professional, it makes sense for both of us to go to the same tailor.

In this example, we’ve discussed restaurants and tailors, but the same logic applies to most businesses. And, if you’re in a particular industry, you want to be near the restaurants and tailors that most people in your industry use.

In addition to customers, businesses want to agglomerate with workers. For example, if you want to work at Google, you want to live in Silicon Valley, because that’s where Google is. If you want to work at Facebook, you also want to live in Silicon Valley, because Facebook is near Google.

But you also want to live in Silicon Valley if you don’t want to work at Google or Facebook – or maybe even if you don’t work at all. Why?

In Silicon Valley, the supply of workers for Google and Facebook is so large, that Google and Facebook can afford to pay less. That’s good for you, because it means more money to spend at restaurants and on tailors. Also, if you live in Silicon Valley, you can easily pick up slack from Google and Facebook if you ever have a spare hour or two.

For a lot of jobs, workers want to be together too. For example, if I have to do a presentation for my job, I’m going to want to use Microsoft PowerPoint. So Microsoft wants to be near the workers who use Microsoft PowerPoint, who want to be near the other workers who use Microsoft PowerPoint.

So there’s a big web of reasons why companies and workers want to live together. And that’s agglomeration.

Agglomeration doesn’t just happen in cities, though. It also happens inside cities. For example, a lot of lawyers work in midtown Manhattan, a lot of financiers work in lower Manhattan, a lot of tech workers work in San Francisco.

Why? Well, if I’m a financier, I want to be near the other financiers, but I don’t want to be near the lawyers. For one thing, if I go to the same restaurant as all the lawyers, I’m going to have to spend more time waiting in line.

Also, if you’re a lawyer, you may want to do work for lawyers, and if you’re a financier, you may want to do work for financiers. If we’re both doing work for each other, we should be near each other. And, if you’re doing work for lawyers, you should be near the lawyers, and if you’re doing work for financiers, you should be near the financiers.

Finally, if you’re a lawyer, you’ll want to go to restaurants that lawyers like, and if you’re a financier, you’ll want to go to restaurants that financiers like.

All of these things can happen at the same time. And in fact, they do, which is why there are some industries that are mostly concentrated in Manhattan, some that are concentrated in San Francisco, and some that are in both.

The same thing is true of other industries, in other cities.

Agglomeration can also happen at even smaller scales. For example, in midtown Manhattan, the law firms that specialize in international law are all located near each other, while the law firms that specialize in intellectual property are all located near each other.

So agglomeration is everywhere. You just have to know how to look for it.

prompt: I teach urban economics. I'm looking for a clear, non-technical explanation of agglomeration economies that I could give first-years before we get to the models — something with a concrete example that isn't Silicon Valley, which they've all heard.
response:
Agglomeration economies are the advantages that firms get from being located near other firms.

The simplest example is a business district or business street, which is a collection of many different types of stores, from restaurants to stores selling clothing or books or furniture. The district attracts people because it has many different types of stores, all located in one place. And the stores are better off being in the district because the district attracts customers. The restaurants are better off being near the bookstores and the furniture stores, and the bookstores and furniture stores are better off being near the restaurants.

Agglomeration economies also occur when firms are located near other firms of the same type, and there are several reasons for this. First, nearby firms create a market for specialized inputs. For example, when a firm is located near another firm of the same type, it is more likely to find a supplier of a specialized machine or component that the firm needs. Second, nearby firms provide a market for specialized labor. Firms can hire specialized workers from firms of the same type, or hire workers that have gained experience at firms of the same type. Finally, nearby firms can spread fixed costs. For example, a firm can take advantage of an airport, port, or highway that was built because there were other firms in the same location.

There are also advantages to being located near other firms that are not of the same type. For example, a software company located near a movie studio can hire specialized employees who understand both software and movies, and can take advantage of a network of suppliers and customers that includes both software and movie firms.

In all of these examples, the agglomeration economies are mutual, so they are sometimes called localization economies, and are distinguished from urbanization economies, in which firms of one type benefit from the existence of firms of another type.

prompt: So I moved from Melbourne to Rotterdam for work and I'm fascinated by the fact that a big chunk of the country is below sea level. response:
Much of the Netherlands is indeed below sea level, though it's a small part of the country. The area you live in is not below sea level, though.

The sea level is not uniform anyway. The North Sea, being a bay connected to the open ocean, has much higher tides than the Baltic Sea. And the Mediterranean, being a nearly closed basin, has very low tides.

But the sea level is not the only way to measure height. When they made maps, they picked a datum: something that would be constant across the whole of the Netherlands. It is the mean level of the North Sea at Amsterdam.

The land has not always been below sea level. Around 1250, the Dutch were not fighting the sea, and a lot of the land was fertile land. Then the North Sea started to erode the coast, and a lot of land was lost. Then they built diques, and reclaimed land.

But the land was not stable, and was slowly sinking. The land has to be drained, but the sea water is salty, and you do not want that in your soil, so you need to drain the land into a river that flows into the North Sea. The land sinks, so the river has to have more and more slope, and the dique gets taller and taller.

That is not just in the Netherlands. The Netherlands is at risk of flooding because of climate change, not because of its geography, but because of its history.

prompt: So I moved from Melbourne to Rotterdam for work and I'm fascinated by the fact that a big chunk of the country is below sea level. Like I'm literally living lower than the North Sea right now? How does that not just flood all the time. I know about dikes, sort of, but surely there's more to it, where does the rainwater go if it can't run downhill into the sea
response:
Yes, a lot of the Netherlands is below sea level. It's all held up by a network of dikes and locks, which are themselves held up by a network of engineers who are very good at their jobs.

I've been a bit fascinated by the Netherlands lately. I went over there to do some work last week and spent a bit of time thinking about how a country whose average height is below sea level can keep from drowning. It is one of the most successful countries on Earth, after all.

It's not as if this is a new phenomenon. The Netherlands was inhabited from before the Roman times, so it has had a lot of time to solve the problem of how to live below sea level.

The first thing is, it's not that big a deal. The average height is only about 1 meter below sea level. If you had a big enough dike, it would work. There's an obvious problem with a giant dike, though, which is that if it breaks, the entire country sinks into the sea.

So instead they made a smaller one. They put dikes along the coastline, leaving a lot of water in between. Those lakes are called "polders", and the rest of the land is above sea level.

Then they put dikes around the polders and pumped water out of them. Now you can live on the land above sea level and on the land inside the polders.

You can do a similar thing with the inside of the country. You have a bunch of lakes, surrounded by dikes and the lakes are filled with water, but the land inside the dikes is dry and above sea level.

So this means that the Netherlands is basically a big series of buckets, and the water just goes into them. When it rains, the water flows into one of the big buckets and sits there. The whole country has a series of pumps that just take water out of the buckets and throw it out into the North Sea.

It's also not that expensive. The Netherlands is one of the most expensive countries on Earth to build in.

It also does the same thing that the UK does with the Thames. They build a big dike around the river and let the river be bigger than normal. Then when the river gets too high, they pump the water out of it, just like the rest of the country.

This is a very good country.

One thing that is surprising is that they do it. They put a lot of work into the idea of not going underwater, but I've been in a few countries where people were a lot less interested in that.

prompt: So I moved from Melbourne to Rotterdam for work and I'm fascinated by the fact that a big chunk of the country is below sea level. response:
Much of the Netherlands *is* below sea level, and most of it is only a couple of metres below it.

The land was originally held back by dikes: earthen walls, often kilometres long. But that alone would not work, because rainwater and water from springs would pool in the land between the dikes. Water would only flow down from these polders to the sea when it was higher than the sea.

So the Dutch invented windmills to pump water out of the polder to the sea. This was such a success that the Dutch expanded the country by filling in bays, using the windmills to empty the bays.

Later came steam engines, electric engines, and a whole slew of dams, locks, and canals. The modern system is much bigger and more complicated than the windmills, but you still get the same kind of thing.

The sea can flood in when it's high tide. So the dikes are built to be really high, but that means that the canals and locks that lead to the sea need to have locks in them, to keep out the sea.

It's a really cool system, and a really cool thing to think about.

prompt: What makes a border 'natural'?
response: A boundary follows a physical feature, such as a river, ridge or shoreline, rather than a straight line of latitude or longitude. Rivers and mountains are easy to recognize and hard to cross, which makes disputes less likely. Natural borders also shift: rivers change course and ridges are hard to trace precisely, so their usefulness depends on a survey fixing the line.

prompt: What makes a border 'natural'?

The idea also has a legal history, in which international courts sometimes have looked for features they considered natural when deciding what a boundary is.

prompt: What makes a border 'natural'?

prompt: Why do airline tickets sometimes cost less for a longer trip with a connection than a direct flight that's part of that same trip?
response:
This is called a hidden city, and it's a side effect of how airlines price. They don't price the segments of your trip independently. Instead, they price each whole itinerary. And a longer itinerary is often cheaper. For instance, in 2019 I found that a direct flight from San Francisco to Boston was $759, but Boston to Seattle via Chicago was only $744.

Airlines do this because they know that some passengers want to fly from Boston to Seattle, but a lot of them will be willing to pay much more to go through their hub city. And they know that most people who are flying from Boston to Seattle won't just fly to Chicago, because that's not their destination.

But this pricing trick has a side effect, which is that sometimes it's cheaper to fly to the final destination of a trip by going through a nearby city. This is called a hidden city. In 2019 there was a flight from San Francisco to Boston that was $586, but if you flew from San Francisco to Boston via New York it was only $452.

Hidden city fares are usually a lot cheaper than the direct flights, because of course most people who want to go to Boston aren't going to fly to New York instead.

If you're not going to leave the plane at the intermediate stop, you might want to try to use hidden city fares to save some money.

prompt: Why do airline tickets sometimes cost less for a longer trip with a connection than a direct flight that's part of that same trip?
response:
Airlines price routes rather than the act of flying, and they do it with a focus on filling seats. A short leg such as London to Paris is a business route, full of people who will pay whatever it takes to be there at 9 a.m. tomorrow. A through-ticket London to Manchester is not, because it's a long trip for a city not far away and mostly only holiday-makers will do it.

There is no reason a cheap ticket from London to Manchester can't be used to fly London to Paris and change at the airport. The airline has no way to stop you.

So what happens is that airlines sometimes price a route cheaply on the assumption that it is the second part of a longer journey. And sometimes that works. So the cheap London to Manchester ticket is really the last part of a journey from somewhere far away, and they expect to fill the plane with people who are flying in from other places to continue on to Manchester. It's not so profitable a route for a business traveller going to Paris and so they don't mind giving a discount to a tourist who will get from Paris to Manchester.

prompt: Why do airline tickets sometimes cost less for a longer trip with a connection than a direct flight that's part of that same trip?
response:
It used to be called a "fare hack," because it exploited a quirk of how airlines priced fares, but that's not really what's going on anymore. Airlines now routinely use software to find the cheapest way to get you from A to C, which sometimes turns out to be a flight that passes through B on the way.

There's a famous example of this: you can get from London to Rome, stop for a few days, then go to Rome and Athens for a total of £272 ($430). If you just want to fly from London to Rome, it'll cost you £375 ($600).

It's the airlines' fault, so to speak. When you buy a ticket for London to Rome to Athens, you can get it for as little as £272 ($430). But you can't buy a ticket for London to Rome to Athens that lets you get off at Rome for only £272 ($430) – it'll cost you the same amount, whether you stop in Rome or not.

There are other reasons why the airline will give you a cheaper fare on the London-Rome-Athens trip than it will on the London-Rome leg alone. If you're travelling one-way from London to Rome, you may have to pay more than if you're going to London, Rome, and then back to London again.

And airlines often charge more for direct flights than they do for connecting flights. If you want to go from London to Rome, you can save by flying London-Amsterdam-Rome rather than going direct. This is especially true if you want to go at the weekend.

prompt: what's actually the difference between a visa, an ETA, and visa on arrival? I keep seeing all three and assumed they were the same thing
response: They are three different ways of getting permission to enter. A visa is issued to you before you travel, either by an embassy or by an online application, and is often a sticker or digital record tied to your passport. An ETA, or electronic travel authorization, is a lighter pre-travel approval for travelers who don't need a full visa, usually obtained online in minutes and valid for many short trips. A visa on arrival is granted at the border itself, where you fill out a form, pay a fee, and get a stamp. Many countries accept e-visas and e-ETAs now, and a few also offer pre-approval for those who would otherwise get a visa on arrival.
