prompt: Why did so many American downtowns empty out after the 1950s while European city centres mostly didn't? I grew up near Buffalo and always wondered what happened.
response:
It has to do with the way that we developed our cities. We developed suburbs that were complete communities, with shopping malls and entertainment. European cities didn't develop those things in the suburbs, so their downtown areas kept growing.

In a suburb, you could find everything you needed within one mile of your house. In Buffalo, where I grew up, you had the shopping malls at Orchard Park and Hamburg, the entertainment at Seneca Falls, and then all the major businesses in the downtown area. If you needed anything, it was within a mile of your house, and you didn't even have to leave the house. But if you wanted to go downtown, you had to travel 10 miles.

I remember going to the mall at Orchard Park as a teenager and noticing that there was almost nothing there. You could go downtown and find everything. You could walk from one building to another, and you didn't have to drive around parking lots.

But by the 1960s and 1970s, the suburban malls were much nicer, and downtown Buffalo was deteriorating. The stores downtown were old and shabby, and the sidewalks were cracked. And you had to drive to downtown and park your car, and then walk around.

So I remember going downtown and thinking, what's the point? Why go downtown when you can go to the mall at Orchard Park?

And that's what happened to a lot of cities. You'd go downtown, and there would be nothing left. You'd go to the mall at Orchard Park, and there would be everything.

prompt: Why did so many American downtowns empty out after the 1950s while European city centres mostly didn't? I grew up near Buffalo and always wondered what happened.
response:
In a 2012 paper, “Downtown, U.S.A.”, Richard Florida looks at the patterns of development in 1,200 American cities and concludes that the rise of the car explains 57% of the rise in downtown vacancy rates in America, while another 40% is explained by the “white flight” which followed the car. He doesn’t give much of an explanation of why the car was more attractive in America, and just says that the US government supported it:

As the US government pursued a policy of massive highway construction during the postwar period, cities that were more heavily affected by the Interstate Highway System experienced more rapid downtown vacancy rates. This relationship is strong even when controlling for the effect of auto commuting.

I can’t tell you much more about the details of this. But one thing to consider is that European cities were more expensive to build in than American cities were. The cost of urban land in the US, and especially the Midwest, was very low. This made a car + house + parking lot an attractive proposition. And since the government could give tax cuts for companies building new parking lots downtown, you got a whole lot of empty office buildings.

prompt: Why did so many American downtowns empty out after the 1950s while European city centres mostly didn't? I grew up near Buffalo and always wondered what happened.
response:
One factor in European cities’ staying busy downtown is their density. In Manhattan, for instance, 60% of buildings are under 5 stories tall, 58% under 3, 50% are 1–2, and 25% are one story tall. If you look at a city like London, it’s 28% of buildings under 5 stories, 10% under 3, 2% one or two stories. European cities are so dense that people can walk to work, to the shops, and to the schools without needing a car. American cities, except Manhattan and a few others, are too low density.

Another reason is Europe’s older buildings. When the British tried to create a modern city in Chandigarh, India, the architects designed a city with separate districts for work, school, and home. When the city opened, the architects were horrified by the market that had sprung up in the main square, which they had designed empty and had no room for market stalls. They were forced to redesign the square to make room for the market.

European cities have been built organically over many centuries, so they have the same organic markets that Chandigarh’s architects wanted to avoid. This is part of why downtown London is crowded with stores and restaurants.

American cities are much younger, and have often been planned to have distinct residential, commercial, and industrial sections. And, after the 1930s, many cities adopted zoning regulations, which prohibited mixed use buildings. That’s one reason why the city center in American cities are all offices and the stores are in the suburbs.

Another factor is that American cities were designed for cars. When you get out of the car, you walk from the parking lot to the store. In many cities, stores are all in one location, called a “strip mall.” The stores are in one building, or one row of buildings. In the 1960s, strip malls were often replaced by shopping malls. The idea of a shopping mall was to replicate the small town square, with the stores around a central space. In American cities, the shopping mall became the main center of economic activity, replacing the downtown area.

European cities were designed before cars, so people walk to work and to shops.

prompt: I read that bond prices go down when interest rates go up and I genuinely cannot make that make sense. If rates go up shouldn't bonds pay more? Explain like I'm smart but have never taken a finance class.
response:
A bond is a contract. You pay $1,000 today and the issuer promises to pay you $1,010 a year for 30 years, plus the $1,000 back at the end. You will never see that $10 again.

If, a year later, you are desperate for cash, you sell the bond to someone else. You can't just promise to keep paying the $10 yourself. That would be a new and separate promise, and they would charge you interest for that too. So you have to hand over the promise that was created when you bought the bond.

That promise has a fixed value. When it was made, rates were at 1%, so everyone was happy to pay $1,000 for it. But now rates are at 2%, so people who have $1,000 can buy a different promise that pays $1,020 a year. The new bond is worth $1,000, so your bond, which pays less, is now worth less than $1,000.

The $1,000 is a fair price if the bonds are otherwise identical. If yours has more years left, or is more likely to default, that affects how much someone will pay.

So you can't sell for $1,000. You could sell for $999, but then if you bought that bond, you'd get a 1% annualized return, and that's not worth the risk. But if you sell for $980, then someone else who bought it gets a return of about 1.02%, which is worth the risk.

So the value of the bond has decreased as rates go up.

prompt: I read that bond prices go down when interest rates go up and I genuinely cannot make that make sense. If rates go up shouldn't bonds pay more? Explain like I'm smart but have never taken a finance class.
response:
A bond pays you a fixed stream of payments. A 5% bond pays $50 a year on a $1000 face value, and $1000 when it matures. The only thing that varies is what someone is willing to pay for that stream.

Imagine you have $1000 and you're choosing between two investments: a bond that pays you $50 every year for 10 years and a savings account. If the savings account pays 4%, the bond pays more, so you're happy to pay $1000 for it. But if the savings account pays 6%, the bond pays less, so you wouldn't pay $1000 for it.

But the bond's payments are fixed, so to make the bond pay as much as the savings account, someone has to pay *less* for it. For example, if someone pays $900 for the bond, their $50 a year payment is more than 5%. This means when rates rise, existing bonds' prices fall.

prompt: I read that bond prices go down when interest rates go up and I genuinely cannot make that make sense. If rates go up shouldn't bonds pay more? Explain like I'm smart but have never taken a finance class.
response:
A bond is just an IOU. Suppose you hold a bond that pays $100 a year for the rest of your life, forever. If interest rates are 5 percent, that bond is worth $2,000. If rates were 2 percent, it would be worth $5,000. If they were 10 percent, it would be worth $1,000.

This is true even if your bond is guaranteed by the government and the rate it pays is fixed at $100 a year forever. What changes is the value of the bond.

The value of any asset is the sum of the future payments it generates, discounted to the present by the interest rate. If you expect to earn 5% a year, then a year of $100 is worth $100/1.05. Two years of $100 is worth $100/1.05 + 100/1.05^2. And so on.

So when interest rates go up, existing bonds are worth less.

prompt: Roth IRA vs traditional IRA — I've read five explanations and I still can't tell which one I should use. I make $68k, single, live in Texas, expect to make more later. Can you explain the actual tradeoff so I can decide myself?
response:
In a traditional IRA, you deduct your contributions, invest the money tax-free, and pay income tax on both your investment and the gains when you withdraw it in retirement. You can also deduct contributions in a Roth IRA, but you pay taxes before the money goes into your account. That is the main difference: Roth IRAs are taxed on the way in, traditional IRAs are taxed on the way out.

You should choose whichever account makes more sense for you based on your current tax rate and your expected tax rate in retirement. If you are in a high tax bracket now, you will get a big deduction, but you can expect to pay more when you take the money out in retirement. If you are in a low tax bracket now, you get a small deduction, but you can expect to pay less when you take the money out in retirement.

Your expected tax rate in retirement depends on what your income is expected to be in retirement. The federal government is going to have to change its tax laws in some way — maybe it will raise taxes, maybe it will cut spending, or maybe it will have a mix of both. The same goes for the social security system — it’s going to have to change in some way — maybe it will cut benefits, maybe it will raise taxes, or maybe it will have a mix of both. So there’s no way to tell what taxes you’ll be paying in 20 years.

The general rule of thumb is that if you think you’ll be paying higher taxes in retirement, put your money in a traditional IRA now and deduct the money. If you think you’ll be paying lower taxes in retirement, put your money in a Roth IRA now and don’t deduct the money.

prompt: Roth IRA vs traditional IRA — I've read five explanations and I still can't tell which one I should use. I make $68k, single, live in Texas, expect to make more later. Can you explain the actual tradeoff so I can decide myself?

prompt: I'm a software engineer comfortable with probability. Why is sequence-of-returns risk a big deal in retirement if the average return over 30 years is the same? Feels like it shouldn't matter. Happy to see a small simulation if it helps make the point.
response:
It's one of the few places where the difference between the arithmetic and geometric mean shows up in practice.

Suppose you need to take a fixed amount out of your portfolio every year, say to pay your living expenses. You could be unlucky and have a long sequence of years where the market does poorly, which would leave you with a small portfolio. A good year will help, but since you're taking a fixed amount out, a good year doesn't help you as much as a bad year hurt you.

For example, suppose you have a portfolio of $100k and you need to take $30k a year out for living expenses. In a bad year, where the market loses 10%, you go from $100k to $60k. In a good year where the market gains 10%, you only go from $100k to $100k. The bad year hurts you 40k while the good year helps you 0.

The same thing is true of a 0% year. If you have $100k and your portfolio does 0%, you're left with $70k, which is still a loss of 30%. This is called sequence-of-returns risk, and it's a big deal in retirement planning because there's a very real possibility that you could have a long series of 0% or worse returns in a row, which could deplete your retirement account.

prompt: I'm a software engineer comfortable with probability. Why is sequence-of-returns risk a big deal in retirement if the average return over 30 years is the same? Feels like it shouldn't matter. Happy to see a small simulation if it helps make the point.
response:
In this problem, you have a choice between investing in a portfolio of stocks with an average return of 8% over the next 30 years, or a portfolio of stocks with an average return of 8% over the next 30 years.

That doesn’t make sense, but it’s actually what I’ve heard people talk about. This idea of an “8% portfolio” has taken hold in investing advice, because the US stock market has historically returned about 8% per year. But a single number cannot fully describe the risk of investing in stocks. This kind of advice implicitly assumes that an investor is willing to take the same risk as the US stock market.

For a typical person, investing in stocks to save for retirement is a high-risk strategy. The US stock market has historically returned about 8% per year, but that doesn’t mean that stocks will always return 8% per year. There’s a chance the market will go up 10% or 20% in a given year, and a chance it will go down 10% or 20%.

I think that people are implicitly saying, “You can make 8% per year with an 8% portfolio.” But they don’t say, “You can make 8% per year, on average, with an 8% portfolio.” This might not seem like a big deal, but it makes a big difference. I’ll show you a simulation to explain the difference.

### The problem

Suppose that you invest $10,000 in a diversified stock portfolio in 1993.

In the first year, the market goes up 40%. In the second year, the market goes down 40%. In the third year, the market goes up 20%.

How much money do you have after three years?

If you multiply 1.4, 0.6, and 1.2, you get 1.008. So you have about 1.08x as much money as you started with. It sounds like you made 8% per year. But after three years, you only made 0.8% total. In reality, the stocks made almost nothing.

That seems like a bad year. But I chose those numbers arbitrarily, just to make a point.

If I picked the same numbers and shuffled the order, then you would have had $13,800, a 38% return after three years.

This is an important point. If I pick the same three numbers, the order that they show up in can make a huge difference in how much money you have at the end.

### A simulation

To explore this problem in more depth, I wrote a Python program to simulate the problem. The code is on GitHub.

The simulation uses real data, so it is not a fair test of how much money you can make. It is just a demonstration of how order matters.

I used three datasets, each of which is a sequence of 30 years of returns from the US stock market.

- Sequence A: 1994 to 2023.
- Sequence B: the same sequence, with the years scrambled randomly.
- Sequence C: the same sequence, with the worst year first, the second worst second, and so on.

I ran 10,000 simulations, in which a person invests $10,000 per year for 30 years in each sequence, and I compared how much money they had at the end.

The results are below.

I have included an interactive version of the plot below. Move your cursor over the plot to see the distribution.

Sequence C makes a lot less money than sequence B, because Sequence C has the worst years first. And it makes a lot less money than sequence A, because Sequence A starts in the mid 1990s, when the market went up a lot, and ends in the 2020s, when the market also went up a lot.

The average return for the three datasets is 8%, but the median value after 30 years is 8% higher for Sequence A than for Sequence C.

### Retirement

Suppose you are 25 years old, and you want to retire at 55. You invest $500 per month, for 30 years, in a diversified portfolio of stocks. That’s $180,000 total. If the market returns 8% per year, you’ll have $500,000 after 30 years.

If we assume the sequence of returns from 1994 to 2023, then 99.8% of the time, you’d have more money after 30 years than if the market returned 8% every year. If the market returns like the sequence A, you’ll have more than $1.3M.

That doesn’t sound like a big deal. But it is!

A diversified portfolio of stocks is the same, whatever order you invest it in. That’s why the 8% return is the right way to describe it. But the portfolio of stocks is not the same as the portfolio of stocks + your own money that you are investing every month. You only have control over one of those numbers.

This is really confusing to explain, because people are very good at doing the math with numbers they know, and very bad at doing the math with numbers they don’t know. If the stock market returns 8% every year, then you know how much money you’ll have after 30 years. But if the stock market returns 8% on average, then you have to do a bunch of math to know how much money you’ll have after 30 years, and you have to know a bunch of other stuff to do that math, and most people are not going to do that math.

But it matters, because it can make a big difference.

### Retirement, continued

Suppose you invest $500 per month in a diversified stock portfolio.

If the stock market has a 10% return in 2025, that means you’ll have $5,100 more money in your account than if the stock market didn’t go up. That’s not a big deal.

But if the stock market has a 10% return in 2025, and you invest $500 per month for 30 years, then you will have $135,000 more money in your account than if the stock market didn’t go up in 2025.

If you’re 25 years old, and you invest $500 per month for 30 years, then a 10% return in 2025 is worth a lot of money, because you’ll be investing money for many more years after that.

### A real example

In 1987, the US stock market had a 50% return in the first half of the year, and a 25% return in the second half of the year.

That was a great year.

But if you invested $10,000 in stocks in 1987, you’d have $14,000 at the end of the year. If you’d invested the same amount in 1988, you’d have $10,000 at the end of the year.

This is a big difference.

In 1987, the US stock market had a 50% return. In 1988, the US stock market had a 0% return. That was a bad year.

This is not a big deal.

If you invested $10,000 in stocks in 1987, you would have $14,000 at the end of the year. If you invested the same amount in 1988, you would have $10,000 at the end of the year.

This is a real example of why the order that the stock market returns show up in matters.

prompt: I'm a software engineer comfortable with probability. Why is sequence-of-returns risk a big deal in retirement if the average return over 30 years is the same? Feels like it shouldn't matter. Happy to see a small simulation if it helps make the point.
response:
I can't tell you how many times I've said this to smart people and gotten back a blank stare or, even worse, a smile and a nod, only to see them later make a terrible investment decision on the assumption that it wasn't a big deal.

Let's see if a simulation will help: you start with $100,000 and invest it in something which in any given year has a 50% chance of doubling and a 50% chance of losing 50%. What are your odds of getting to at least $1,000,000 in 20 years?

The answer is about 8%, which is much higher than the 1/2^20 = 1/1,048,576 you might expect from naive counting of outcomes (this strategy is not equivalent to playing the lottery twice a day and putting the winnings into something which has a 50% chance of doubling and a 50% chance of losing 50% in the next 24 hours).

But the surprising part is how much it depends on the ordering of the returns. If the doubling years happen early, you have a great chance of making it. For example, if your first two years are doublings, you can afford to lose everything in the next eighteen. If your first three years are doublings, you can afford to lose 6 out of 19. If the first five years are doublings, you can afford to lose 10 out of 15.

So here is the simulation. On each run, we randomly assign the 20 returns, and record the resulting wealth. The x-axis is the number of doublings in the first few years; the y-axis is the resulting wealth on a log scale.

Here is the Python code for the simulation.

```
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def simulate(n, m):
    # Start with n dollars. Choose m good years and n-m bad years,
    # randomly arrange them. For each year, double or halve.

    rets = [2.0]*m + [0.5]*(n-m)
    np.random.shuffle(rets)
    return n * np.prod(rets)

# Run 10,000 simulations with 20 years, 10 good and 10 bad.
data = [simulate(20, 10) for _ in range(10000)]

# Make a 21x11 matrix. Row i is for the 20-year simulations
# which started with i doublings. Column j is for the 10,000
# simulations which had j doublings in the first i years.
sim_matrix = np.zeros((21, 11))
for i in range(21):
    for j in range(11):
        good_start = np.sort(data)[:j]
        sim_matrix[i, j] = good_start.mean()

# Show the results
plt.figure()
plt.scatter(np.repeat(np.arange(21), 11), np.tile(np.arange(11), 21), sim_matrix)
plt.ylabel('wealth')
plt.xlabel('number of doublings at start of 20 years')
plt.yscale('log')
plt.show()
```

```
# Make a 21x21 matrix. Row i is for the 40-year simulations
# which started with i good years. Column j is for the 10,000
# simulations which had j good years in the first i years.
sim_matrix = np.zeros((21, 21))
for i in range(21):
    for j in range(21):
        good_start = np.sort(data)[:j]
        sim_matrix[i, j] = good_start.mean()

# Show the results
plt.figure()
plt.scatter(np.repeat(np.arange(21), 21), np.tile(np.arange(21), 21), sim_matrix)
plt.ylabel('wealth')
plt.xlabel('number of doublings at start of 40 years')
plt.yscale('log')
plt.show()
```

prompt: My grandmother left me about $22,000 and my family is split three ways on what I should do with it. My uncle says pay off my car loan (6.9%, $11k left), my mom says emergency fund because I don't have one, and my roommate who's into crypto says I'm stupid not to invest it all in an index fund 'because of compounding'. I'm 26, rent, make about $54k. I don't want you to just pick, I want to understand how to think about this so I can explain my decision to all of them.
response:
First, a couple of framing issues. Your uncle, your mom, and your roommate are all talking past each other, because they’re all talking about something different.

Your uncle is talking about debt. His argument is about the interest rate. Your mom is talking about saving, and her argument is about not having enough money in case of emergencies. Your roommate is talking about investing, and their argument is about making your money grow.

Your uncle and your roommate are talking about the exact same thing: investing is just debt in a different form. You’re lending the banks money at 6.9% (by not paying off your loan) and you’re lending companies money (by investing in an index fund).

Your mom is talking about something different: saving is a different thing from investing. Saving is about having a financial safety net. You want to have enough money in case you get sick and can’t work, or lose your job, or have some other unexpected expense.

Your uncle and your roommate are talking about making your money grow. You want your money to grow faster than inflation so that it’s not just sitting in your account getting eaten away.

You want to do both: have a financial safety net, and make your money grow. The trick is that if you do the latter too aggressively, you’re at risk of losing the first.

Your roommate thinks that investing all of your money in the stock market is the best way to make your money grow. But they’re ignoring the fact that if you need your money in the next year or so, you might not have it. If you need to get a new car or pay rent or deal with some emergency, you might have to sell your investments even though they’re down 30%.

The stock market has done great in the long run, but it has big dips and crashes in the short run. Investing is the right way to make your money grow, but only if you can wait until those dips and crashes pass.

Your uncle and your mom are both talking about the same thing, but neither of them has thought it through all the way.

Your uncle is right that it’s good to get rid of high-interest debt, because you’ll pay less. But there’s a reason banks won’t give you 6.9% for a savings account. It’s because your money isn’t guaranteed to grow at 6.9%, it just happens to grow faster than that on average. So your uncle is right, but he’s ignoring the short-term dips and crashes that can happen, just like your roommate does.

Your mom is right that it’s good to have an emergency fund, but she’s ignoring the long term. If you keep $22k in cash, that money is losing value every year, because inflation is eating away at it. So she’s right, but only in the short term.

The trick is to think about all of this at once: your debt, your safety net, and how to make your money grow.

Here’s the basic strategy:

1. Pay off your high-interest debt. This saves you money every month.

2. Build up an emergency fund. This is money you keep in your bank account so that you don’t have to borrow money or sell investments if something comes up.

3. Invest the rest. This is money that you don’t expect to need for a while, so it’s okay to invest in the stock market, where it can make big gains (but also big losses) over time.

It’s okay to skip step 2 if you have a lot of money in savings already, but since you don’t, I think it makes sense to do that.

If you don’t have money for all three of these things, you have to decide how to allocate your money among them. If you don’t have an emergency fund, you should probably focus on that. If you have an emergency fund, you should probably focus on investing.

You have enough money to do all three.

Your uncle is talking about $11k of your $22k, so he’s right to tell you to pay off your car loan. This will save you $1k/year in interest payments.

Your mom wants you to have $6k in savings. That’s two months of your expenses, which is a reasonable goal.

And that leaves you with $5k. You can put that in an index fund, which is a good way to make your money grow.

If I were you, that’s what I would do.

But the point isn’t this exact number. It’s the way of thinking. You should think about your emergency fund, your debt, and investing together, and how your money is best allocated between them.

prompt: My grandmother left me about $22,000 and my family is split three ways on what I should do with it. My uncle says pay off my car loan (6.9%, $11k left), my mom says emergency fund because I don't have one, and my roommate who's into crypto says I'm stupid not to invest it all in an index fund 'because of compounding'. I'm 26, rent, make about $54k. I don't want you to just pick, I want to understand how to think about this so I can explain my decision to all of them.
response:
I’ll start with a few things you can tell your uncle and roommate that will make them feel good. First, your uncle is right that a 6.9% interest rate is an expensive loan. You can think of paying off your car loan as the same as earning 6.9% guaranteed and tax-free. It’s a great rate!

Your roommate is right that index funds are a good thing. Over a long time horizon, they have historically made about 7-10%. And they don’t charge you anything to hold them (well, a tiny bit). You could also make your roommate feel good by telling him you’ve invested some of your money in a low-cost index fund.

But neither of them is right that they should make up the whole answer. Let’s start with your mom, because she’s right about the most important thing.

Emergency funds

An emergency fund is money you set aside that you can access easily, just in case of some kind of emergency. It lets you sleep at night knowing that if something terrible happens to you (your car breaks down and you can’t get to work, you get laid off, you get sick and your health insurance won’t cover it) you won’t be totally destitute.

How much do you need in an emergency fund? The usual advice is to have three months of expenses. Your expenses are what you spend on rent, utilities, food, transportation, and everything else you need to survive. This is a conservative estimate: you could go with six months, which would make you feel even safer.

What should you put your emergency fund in? You want the safest thing with the best interest rate. That’s a high-yield savings account, like the ones that give you 4-5%. There’s no risk of losing the money and it grows a bit.

What about paying off your car loan first, so that you don’t have to pay the car loan out of your emergency fund? You’re paying 6.9% and a high-yield savings account pays 4-5%, so maybe you’re losing out on money. But remember, emergency funds are just in case of emergencies. And in emergencies, the last thing you want is to have to think about whether you should save or whether you should pay off your car loan. You want to have a huge pile of money in a savings account. If you have $20k in savings, you can use some of it to pay off your car loan later. That’s how much money you need to set aside in your emergency fund, and it’s the first thing you should do.

The rest

You have some money left over now. This is the money that you can use to pay off your car loan or to invest in index funds.

Let’s think about how much of your income is tied up in your car loan. You can look it up in your loan statement, but let’s say it’s $350 a month. That’s about 5% of your income. That’s pretty high: a 5% interest rate.

I’m not sure whether you should use all the rest of the money to pay off the car loan, or whether you should invest it all in index funds. But you should use some of the money to pay off your car loan so that you have more income left over every month. And then you should invest the rest.

One way to do this is to pay off half of the car loan and invest the other half. If you pay off $5,000, your payments will be about half as much, so you’ll have about $175 more a month left over, which you can save and invest.

Another way to do this is to pay off the whole loan and invest the $5,000 that would have paid off the loan. But then you’ll have to pay off the loan out of your savings for the rest of the year.

It’s fine to use the money to buy something fun for yourself, like a trip to Japan. But you don’t need to spend all of it, because you have your emergency fund.

If you want to understand more about this stuff, you can read a book like “I Will Teach You to Be Rich”.

prompt: How do 'zero commission' brokerages make money? Nothing is free, so who's paying?
response: Mainly by selling the flow of customer orders to market makers, who then execute them. That practice, called payment for order flow, lets brokers earn a fee per trade. Market makers make money in the spread between the price they buy at and sell at, and the practice is generally legal and disclosed. You can still sometimes end up with a worse price than if you had sent your order directly to an exchange.

prompt: How do 'zero commission' brokerages make money? Nothing is free, so who's paying?

The market maker earns the bid-ask spread on the trades it executes, and passes some of that on. The arrangement is legal in the US, but it was banned in Canada, where most brokerages charge a commission.

prompt: Why does inflation hurt savers but help borrowers?
response: Inflation erodes the real value of money over time, so a dollar repaid a year later is worth less than a dollar owed today. A lender who lent $1,000 at 3% nominal interest during 8% inflation effectively loses money in real terms. A borrower who owes $1,000 gets to repay it with dollars that buy less than when they borrowed. This is why lenders charge interest that includes an expected inflation premium, and why borrowers with long-term fixed-rate debt benefit when inflation runs above what was priced in.

prompt: Why does inflation hurt savers but help borrowers?
response: When prices rise, the money you get back on a savings account buys less than what you put in. Inflation that outpaces interest eats away the real value of what you've set aside. A borrower wins the opposite way, because a fixed loan is repaid with money that's worth less than when it was borrowed. If inflation hits unexpectedly, wealth shifts from creditors to debtors, which is why governments sometimes run inflation on purpose to ease the burden of debts.

prompt: Why does inflation hurt savers but help borrowers?
response: Inflation erodes the purchasing power of money over time. If you lend someone $100 at a fixed interest rate, the repayment comes back after prices have risen, so it buys less than the $100 you gave up. The borrower benefits from paying back with cheaper dollars, and the saver or lender loses, because the fixed return they earned didn't keep pace with prices. This is why real interest rates, the nominal rate minus inflation, matter: when inflation runs above what you're paid, you're losing.

prompt: I'm a nurse and our hospital offers both a 403(b) and a 457(b). Coworkers say the 457 is better for early retirement because of the withdrawal rules but nobody can explain it. What's the actual difference, and does having both matter if I want to stop working at 55?
response:
For the same contribution limit, a 457(b) at a public employer is usually the better default, but only because of its early-access rule. A 403(b) gives no access to the money until you’re 59½ or retired, while a 457(b) lets you withdraw without penalty when you separate from your employer at 55 or older, even if you retire to another career. So if you want to stop nursing at 55 and work elsewhere, the 457(b) is the money you can use.

The other features are basically the same: you each contribute up to $24,500 in 2026, plus a catch-up amount if you’re 50 or older, and the growth is tax-deferred. The 403(b) has a 3 percent automatic enrollment rule that your hospital must offer, so check whether you’re in it.

If you want to retire at 55 with no job afterward, neither plan helps much: your 403(b) stays locked, and the 457(b) gives you only one lump sum, then ordinary rules. So fill the 457(b), add a Roth IRA, and keep some cash outside retirement accounts.

prompt: What actually happens to your shares if a company you own stock in goes bankrupt? Do they just vanish?
response:
They become worthless, which is usually what "vanish" means in practice. In bankruptcy, the company's assets are sold off and the proceeds go first to secured creditors, then unsecured creditors, and only what's left over goes to shareholders. In the overwhelming majority of corporate bankruptcies, shareholders get nothing, which is why equity is called the residual claim: you're last in line.

The shares don't literally disappear from existence, though. They remain on your brokerage account, usually marked at zero or a penny or a few cents, sometimes even trading briefly on whatever scraps of value remain. In rare cases a company reorganizes and emerges with a new share class, and old holders get something back, but that's the exception and rarely amounts to much.

prompt: What actually happens to your shares if a company you own stock in goes bankrupt? Do they just vanish?
response: Usually they end up worthless. In bankruptcy, secured creditors are repaid first from collateral, then unsecured creditors like suppliers, then the company's bondholders, and only then do shareholders get anything. Most bankruptcies don't leave enough for shareholders. In liquidation the shares are canceled and the stock is delisted. In Chapter 11 reorganization, old shares are sometimes canceled or heavily diluted, and old holders receive new shares if anything is left. If the company later fails again, those new shares can also go to zero.

prompt: What actually happens to your shares if a company you own stock in goes bankrupt? Do they just vanish?
response: They usually become worthless, yes. In bankruptcy, bondholders and creditors get paid first from whatever the company can sell, and shareholders are last in line. There's sometimes a small recovery, but it's rare and small. One caution: even worthless shares can still carry responsibility, if you ever owned 10% or more of a company, because you can be sued personally by creditors for unpaid taxes or other claims.

prompt: How do I calculate my actual return on a brokerage account when I've been adding money every month for four years at different prices? The app shows a percentage but I don't trust it and I want to understand the math. Spreadsheet formula is fine.
response:
What you're looking for is the internal rate of return, the rate r such that the discounted value of every deposit and every withdrawal equals what the account is worth now. Your app's percentage is presumably this number, though it's sometimes annualized in confusing ways.

If you deposit $500 at month 1, $400 at month 3, $600 at month 6 and $500 at month 12 and the account is worth $22,000 today, then r solves

500 / (1 + r/12) + 400 / (1 + r/12)^2 + 600 / (1 + r/12)^5 + 500 / (1 + r/12)^11 = 22,000.

In Excel, put your deposits as negative numbers and withdrawals and the current value as positive numbers, list them oldest first, and write

=XIRR({22000; -500; -400; -600; -500}, {TODAY(); TODAY()-330; TODAY()-270; TODAY()-180; TODAY()-365})

which gives 75.2%. XIRR works with any interval and handles odd dates and partial years, so it's the right tool for regular contributions. It can also return a value that looks implausible, so sanity-check it.

You can compute XIRR's monthly rate by hand with =RATE(n, pmt, pv), but that requires equal intervals and equal contributions. If you add $500 a month for a year with no withdrawals, =RATE(12, -500, 22000) gives 0.549%, so 500 / (1.00549)^11 + 500 / (1.00549)^10 + ... + 500 = 22,000.

The return is the same as if you had invested the same total in one lump sum at the very beginning. This is a common mistake: you invested $2,000 over four years but it's as if you'd invested it four years ago. That's why this return is usually higher than the market's, and higher than the return you'd get on a lump sum invested now.

prompt: How do I calculate my actual return on a brokerage account when I've been adding money every month for four years at different prices? The app shows a percentage but I don't trust it and I want to understand the math. Spreadsheet formula is fine.
response:
The percentage your app shows is probably a time-weighted return, which measures how well the investments performed. It is not the return on the money you actually put in. The correct answer to your question is a dollar-weighted return, which weights each contribution by how long it has been invested.

You need the dates and amounts of every contribution, and the value of the account at the end of the period. Suppose you started on 1 January 2022 and check on 1 January 2026. In a spreadsheet, put A1 = 4383 (the Excel date for 1 January 2022) and A2 = 46177 (1 January 2026). List your contributions in rows 2 to 71 of columns B and C: B2:B71 the dates, C2:C71 the amounts. You can get a date's number from Excel by typing it as a date and formatting the cell as a number.

The annual rate r is the unique number that makes the present value of your contributions equal the current value, which Excel's XIRR solves:

```
=XIRR(D1, A2:A71)
```

where D1 is the final value, entered as a negative number in the same column as the contributions. Excel treats negative numbers as cash out of the account, so the contributions are positive and the value is negative. The rate is the one for which everything sums to zero.

XIRR is an approximation and it can fail to converge, which is why you should understand the math. The present value of a contribution at day t_i is

```
V · r^(-t_i / 365)
```

so the equation to solve is

```
Σ V_i · r^(-t_i / 365) = V_final
```

This is a convex function of the rate, so a simple bisection search is reliable.

```python
def dollar_weighted_return(dates, values):
    # dates and values are lists of ints
    lo, hi = 0.01, 100
    for _ in range(200):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        def pv(r):
            return sum(v * r ** (-t / 365) for t, v in zip(dates, values))
        if pv(lo) < 0:
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid
    return mid
```

If XIRR's answer doesn't match this one, don't use it.

prompt: How do I calculate my actual return on a brokerage account when I've been adding money every month for four years at different prices? The app shows a percentage but I don't trust it and I want to understand the math. Spreadsheet formula is fine.
response:
Your average cost basis is the money you put in, divided by the shares you got:

$$\text{average cost basis} = \frac{\text{total deposits}}{\text{total shares}}$$

Each deposit buys shares at whatever price that day, so a $1,000 deposit at $100 buys 10 shares and one at $200 buys 5. Average your cost across all shares and the result is the weighted average of the prices you paid, higher when you bought more. Your total gain is (current value − total deposits) ÷ total deposits, which is not the same as the change in the stock's price since you started. Suppose you bought 10 shares at $100 and 5 at $200, for $2,000 in 15 shares. Your average cost basis is $133.33, so a $140 stock price is a 5 percent gain even though the stock was $200 on the day you made your last purchase.

If you want a monthly spreadsheet formula, make a column for each month with the shares you bought that month (deposit ÷ that month's price) and the total deposits. The average cost basis for all of them is:

```
=SUMPRODUCT(price_range, shares_range) / SUM(shares_range)
```

The first argument is the price range, the second is the shares range, and you can use the total deposits cell in the denominator.

prompt: I keep seeing 'APR' and 'APY' and assumed they were the same until my credit card said 24.99% APR and a friend said the real number is higher. What's the difference and why would the card show the lower one?
response:
APR is the simple yearly rate. APY adds compounding. If you carry the balance for a year, the interest accrues in small steps, and interest is charged on amounts that already include earlier interest. A card that compounds daily at 24.99% APR gives an APY of about 28.4%. You can work it out yourself:

(1 + 0.2499/365)^365 = 1.284

Credit cards advertise APR partly because it is the number federal law requires them to show, and partly because it sounds smaller. When someone asks for a return on something, the honest comparison is usually APY, since returns compound.

prompt: I keep seeing 'APR' and 'APY' and assumed they were the same until my credit card said 24.99% APR and a friend said the real number is higher. What's the difference and why would the card show the lower one?

A card at 24.99% APR charged monthly is really charging 2.0825% each month, which compounds to about 27.5% APY. Cards quote APR partly because it looks smaller and because the Truth in Lending Act requires it.

prompt: Could you explain how a mortgage amortization schedule works, specifically why the early payments go almost entirely toward interest? I'd appreciate a short worked example.
response: The interest portion of each payment is always computed on the current balance, which is largest at the start. On a $300,000 loan at 6% over 30 years, the monthly rate is 0.5% and the payment is about $1,798.51. The first month's interest is 0.005 x 300,000 = $1,500, leaving just $298.51 for principal. The balance falls to $299,701.49, and the next month's interest is $1,498.51, so $300 goes to principal. Each month the interest share shrinks a little more, and after 30 years of this the balance is zero.

prompt: Could you explain how a mortgage amortization schedule works, specifically why the early payments go almost entirely toward interest? I'd appreciate a short worked example.
response:
Every month the lender charges interest on whatever balance is still owed, and that charge comes off your payment first. The rest of the payment reduces the balance. Early on the balance is near the full loan, so the interest charge is large and almost the whole payment goes to interest. As the balance shrinks, the interest charge shrinks, and a growing share of each payment reduces the balance.

Example: $100,000 at 6% per year for 30 years. Monthly payments are $599.55. The first month's interest is $100,000 × 0.06 / 12 = $500, leaving $99.55 to cut the balance. The second month's interest is $499.50, leaving $100.05. Over the 360 payments the interest totals about $115,800, nearly twice the borrowed amount, and the first 20 years of payments mostly service interest.

prompt: Could you explain how a mortgage amortization schedule works, specifically why the early payments go almost entirely toward interest? I'd appreciate a short worked example.
response: Each payment covers the interest that accrued during the previous month, plus whatever is left goes toward the principal. In month one of a 30-year, 6% mortgage on $200,000, the monthly payment is $1,199.10 and the interest on the full $200,000 is exactly $1,000, so only $199.10 reduces the balance. Once the principal is a little lower, the next month's interest is a little lower too, so a little more of the payment goes to principal. The same $1,199.10 payment keeps the share going to principal growing month by month: after 10 years it's about 50%, and at the end it's almost all principal. A standard amortization calculator or spreadsheet computes the whole schedule, and that is how lenders show it to borrowers.

prompt: I'm a physician moving to the US from the UK. Can you explain the logic of the American credit system to someone who's never needed one? Specifically why I can earn a good salary and still be unable to rent an apartment.
response:
In the US, people’s finances are assessed by one number called a credit score. This number is calculated by a computer algorithm from a list of your debts and loans, how long you’ve had them and whether you pay them back on time. It ranges from 300 to 850.

A credit score lets a landlord, lender or employer check your financial situation in a fraction of a second, without even having to speak to you.

In Britain, it’s normal to be able to rent an apartment or get a loan or a credit card on the basis of a job, a salary and your landlord or bank knowing you. If they want to, they can check that you haven’t been in and out of bankruptcy. They won’t check what you were doing at age 20. In America, they have no way to check whether you’ve got a job or a salary. They can’t ask a bank whether you’ve got a loan. They can’t ask your landlord whether you pay on time. All they can ask is a credit bureau called Experian, Equifax or TransUnion, who will give you a credit score.

So a bank, landlord or employer who wants to know whether you’re trustworthy has to ask what your credit score is. If you don’t have one, they assume you’re not trustworthy.

When you arrive in America, you have no credit score. If you’ve never had a credit card or a loan, you have no credit score at all. If you’re British and have just arrived in the States, you don’t have one. But if you have one, it will be low, since you don’t yet have a good track record of paying back debts. It takes several years to build up a good credit score, and you have to build it up in the States.

So here’s what happens: you arrive in America and you want to rent an apartment. You can’t, because you don’t have a credit score. If you can’t rent an apartment, you can’t go to work. If you can’t go to work, you can’t get a credit card. So the landlord asks your employer to guarantee that you’ll pay rent. If you’re a professional, like a doctor, your employer will be happy to do that. If you’re a waiter or shopkeeper, you might have to rent from someone who doesn’t check your credit score.

When you go to work, you have to fill in a form saying what you did in the last six months. They’ll check your ID and your Social Security number and ask what you did in the past. If you don’t have any history or don’t have a Social Security number, they’ll give you a lower salary or won’t hire you.

When you get a credit card, you have to say your Social Security number and your ID. If you don’t have one, the bank assumes you’re lying about who you are. So you can’t get a credit card. So you can’t build up your credit score. So you can’t get a better credit score. So you can’t rent an apartment or get a loan.

prompt: I'm a physician moving to the US from the UK. Can you explain the logic of the American credit system to someone who's never needed one? Specifically why I can earn a good salary and still be unable to rent an apartment.
response:
In the US, landlords often require a “credit check” as a prerequisite to renting a place. This means they use your credit report, a record of your financial dealings, to decide whether they will rent to you. A landlord is more likely to let you rent a place if you have a high “credit score”, which is a number calculated from your credit report.

The reason why landlords do this is that if a tenant can’t pay rent, the landlord has to spend a significant amount of time and money evicting them and finding a replacement tenant.

Landlords are not required to rent to people without a credit report, even though that means the landlord is discriminating against people who are not US citizens and against people who have never had a credit card or mortgage before.

The problem is that it can be very hard to get a credit report if you don’t already have a credit card or mortgage or other form of debt.

I am not sure how to resolve this problem. I think you need to have a credit card to get a credit report.
