They both have 5, which they can use as their shared secret.

How do they know that 13^3 and 10^2 are going to be the same? Well, 13 is 2^17, and 2^17^3 is the same as 2^51. 10 is 3^17, so 10^2 is 3^34. But 2^51 is the same as 3^34 because 51 is 17 + 34 and 3^17 is 1.

So in general, if Bob chooses a secret x and publishes x^17, and Alice chooses a secret y and publishes y^17, then Bob can compute (y^17)^x, and Alice can compute (x^17)^y, and they're both equal to (xy)^17, which neither x nor y alone is enough to compute.

This is called the Diffie-Hellman protocol, and the problem is that it depends on the fact that you can't efficiently compute the 17th root of a number. For example, 5^17 = 16, but 16^17 = 15, so 15 is 16th root of 5. If Alice publishes 5^17 = 16, then Bob can compute 16^3 = 15, but Alice can't compute 5^3 because she doesn't know that 5 = 16^17.

This is hard because there's no simple algebraic solution for taking roots, but this is not really a mathematical problem; it's just that it takes a long time to compute. It's easy to compute x^17; it's 16 multiplications. But to compute the 17th root of a number, you have to search through all the numbers and see which one has the number as its 17th power. That's 17 multiplications for each number, and there are 16 of them, so it's 272 multiplications.

To make the protocol secure, we can choose a larger prime number, say 2^256 - 189, which is prime, and the only way to compute the 256th root of a number is to search through 2^256 numbers, which will take a long time.

The Diffie-Hellman protocol is used in real life to agree on shared keys, but the protocol described here isn't the real one, because it has a vulnerability. If Alice publishes 16, then Bob can compute 16^3 = 15, but he can also compute 15^3 = 14, which is the same as 16^6, so he can compute the 6th root of 16, which means he can compute the 17th root of 16^6.

prompt: What happens, physically, when I delete a file? Is it actually gone? Asking because I'm about to sell an old laptop with an SSD and someone told me deleting isn't enough but formatting is, and someone else said formatting isn't enough either.
response:
When you delete a file, the filesystem just removes the directory entry pointing to the file. The contents of the file stay on disk, and the filesystem marks the blocks that contained the file as free. The contents of those blocks will be overwritten at some point in the future, when the filesystem needs space and reuses the blocks for something else.

If you don't need to worry about data security, this is enough, because deleted files are rarely recoverable and you need both motivation and expertise to do it.

If you *do* need to worry about data security, then just deleting things is not enough, because it leaves the deleted data on the disk, where a motivated expert can get it. In this case you need to securely erase the disk. This means you have to write something over all the free space on the disk, and there's a reason that people who have been in the computer security business since the 1970s refer to this as 'the 3 am problem'. Securely erasing your hard disk takes a *lot* of time, and you really want to be there to watch the process to make sure that it's not interrupted.

The problem is that it's not just free space that can contain your secret data. It also includes things like old versions of files that you've saved, deleted files that you've not yet emptied from your trash directory, and so on. The only way to really make sure that you wipe out everything on a hard disk is to erase the whole thing.

For a mechanical hard drive, this means doing a low level format, which will also wipe out any MBR code and any partitions. The easiest way to do this is probably to use a tool like DBAN, which will format your entire hard drive for you.

For SSDs the situation is a little bit more complicated. Because of how SSDs work and because of how most operating systems deal with deleted data, you have to use a special secure erase function for the SSD itself. SSDs are very fast, so secure erasing them is not a big deal, but you need to do it at the right level and in the right way to make sure that it works.

*Updated*: It's not enough to just format your drive, either. A format will just delete all the directory entries and mark all the space as free. You need to do a low level format or, on SSDs, use the secure erase function.

*Updated again*: Some people will tell you that you can't recover deleted data from an SSD anyway, because the data is not in the same place on the disk as it was before. This is true, but it's a mistake to rely on it.

First of all, the SSD manufacturers have a responsibility to make sure that your data isn't leaking, and the only way they can do that is to wipe out all the old data. Second, if you want to be sure, you have to assume that the SSD is going to give you its data to make sure that it isn't leaking, and the only way to be sure that it isn't is to erase the whole SSD.

prompt: how does spotify know what song to play next on autoplay. like what is it actually comparing

The problem is that this method is limited to a small, very active, very popular pool of listeners who generate a lot of listening data, and their listening habits are not representative of all Spotify users. So it will always play popular music, and never play music that's only known to a tiny group of people.

It's also very hard for people to get into the model. You need lots of people to play your music, and you need to be associated with people who play lots of popular stuff and play your music in the middle of it, so that people who like popular music will start to like you too.

And you need to keep doing this for a long time, because the model is constantly being updated.

The result is that if you listen to a song that was really popular for a while a couple of years ago, you'll get similar popular songs from the same couple of years ago, and that's it. prompt: Why do some USB-C cables charge my laptop and others don't, even though they fit the same port?
response: A USB-C connector can carry very different amounts of power. The port sends out a default 5 volts, and the device and the cable's connector negotiate more. A laptop that needs 20 volts and up to 100 or 140 watts asks for that during this handshake, and a cheap cable or charger that isn't rated for it will simply not supply it. The port looks identical, so it's easy to assume any cable will do. Check the rating on the label: it should list a voltage and wattage, and for higher power it should be e-marked and rated for 240 volts, 5 amperes.

Most charging cables carry 3 amps at 20 volts, which is 60 watts, but a lot of laptop chargers need 100 watts, and those require cables built for 5 amps. A 3 amp cable may still make the laptop run, just on battery power, and some chargers won't start charging until they see a cable that can carry the full current.

Above 60 W a cable needs an e-marker chip, and your laptop will only draw what it sees it can safely get, so a lower-rated cable may work but charge more slowly or not at all.

prompt: I'm a pharmacist, not a programmer. I need to rename about 1,400 PDF files in a folder on my Mac so the date that's at the end of each filename (like report_smith_03152024.pdf) moves to the front in YYYY-MM-DD format. I'm comfortable opening Terminal if you tell me exactly what to type. How would I do this safely, ideally with a way to preview before anything actually changes?
response:
In Terminal, first go to the folder, like `cd ~/Downloads/scans`. Then run this, which only prints what would happen:

```bash
find . -name '*.pdf' -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
  stem="${f%.pdf}"
  if [[ "$stem" =~ _([0-9]{8})$ ]]; then
    date="${BASH_REMATCH[1]//-}"
    date="${date:0:4}-${date:4:2}-${date:6:2}"
    echo "$f -> ${f%./*}${date}_${stem%_*}.pdf"
  fi
done
```

Change the two `88888888` digits to your year, and run the same loop with `mv -- "$f" ...` instead of `echo`. The `--` protects names that start with a dash.

`$f` is each file, `$d` grabs the final eight digits, and `${f%_$d.pdf}` strips the suffix. The last line prints one old name and new name per line. Scroll through it looking for surprises before going any further.

```
mv -- "$f" "${d:0:4}-${d:4:2}-${d:6:2}-$p.pdf"
```

and run the whole thing again. `--` tells `mv` that what follows are filenames. If a target name already exists you'll get an "overwrite?" prompt, which is another safety net.

prompt: What is latency vs bandwidth? Gaming forums keep telling me my 500mbps plan doesn't matter and I need 'better ping' and I don't understand how those are different things
response:
Bandwidth is how much data per second can flow. Latency is how long one piece of data takes to get there and get an answer back. The classic analogy is a highway: bandwidth is how many lanes it has, latency is the distance to your destination. A six-lane road still takes an hour to drive 300 miles.

A 500 Mbps connection is enormous for games, because a game sends maybe a few kilobytes per second: your position, what buttons you pressed, and so on. But a shooter is interactive, and you can't shoot something you can't see, which is why people say latency is what matters. 10 ms of lag is imperceptible, 100 ms feels sluggish, and 300 ms or more is unplayable in competitive games.

One way to see the connection between them is to imagine a 100 ms latency line. If you send a 1 MB file and need to confirm receipt, you have to wait for 100 ms of delay before you can start sending the next part. If each part takes 100 ms to send, then at any time half your parts are in transit and half are waiting. The 100 ms delay cost you half your throughput. So if you're transferring large amounts of data on a high-latency line, like streaming a video from a server on another continent, latency and bandwidth matter together. But gaming is not that kind of traffic.

prompt: What is latency vs bandwidth? Gaming forums keep telling me my 500mbps plan doesn't matter and I need 'better ping' and I don't understand how those are different things
response:
Bandwidth is how fast bits arrive. Latency, or ping, is how long one bit takes to get there. A useful model is a pipe: bandwidth is the pipe's width, and latency is how long a drop takes to travel through it. You can pour a huge amount of water through a wide pipe in a short time, but if it's a long pipe the first drop still takes a while. A gigabit fiber link to your neighbor can have a few milliseconds of latency. A slow satellite link can carry lots of data but every packet takes half a second or more.

Gaming mostly feels latency. When you click to shoot, your game sends a packet, the server processes it, and the results come back. With 50 ms of ping, a round trip is a tenth of a second. That delay is barely noticeable at close range but makes aiming at something 40 meters away feel like guessing. The server may also be running at 20 or 30 ticks a second, so the game only updates its world a few dozen times a second anyway.

The pipe analogy shows why high bandwidth doesn't fix this. A 500 Mbps line can move a lot of data, but a fast pipe still takes the same time as a narrow pipe to carry one ping packet. Most games send only a few tens of kilobytes per second, far below what a broadband line can do.

The two do interact. A slow connection can clog up, and if your game's packets are stuck behind a download queue, the latency you feel rises. So on a congested link, even a ping that is normally fine can become erratic. But in general, you're not going to fix the latency your gaming feels by upgrading to faster internet.

prompt: What is latency vs bandwidth? Gaming forums keep telling me my 500mbps plan doesn't matter and I need 'better ping' and I don't understand how those are different things
response:
Bandwidth is how fast data moves once it's going: 500 megabits per second means the connection can carry about 62 megabytes every second. Latency, or ping, is how long a message takes to get there and back, and on a decent internet connection it's usually 10 to 50 milliseconds, dominated by the physical distance your signal has to travel.

The confusion comes from using the pipe metaphor too literally. A pipe that holds water is useless if the tap takes a minute to open. A low-bandwidth line with 10 ms ping feels snappier than a 500 Mbps line with 200 ms, because every action you take waits for a reply before the next one. Gaming barely sends data, so the pipe's width never matters.

The exception is when something needs many round trips in quick succession. If each request takes 200 ms and you need 30 of them before anything loads, the total is 6 seconds, no matter how wide the connection is. Latency is the real cost of the internet's request-and-response design, and it's why fast connections don't always feel fast.

response:
It is deliberately made of redundant copies of the same data. 3. SHA-256 doesn't use a lot of memory, which means attackers can build custom hardware that makes the attack even faster.

1 is a big deal. You want to use a hash function which is slow enough that an attacker checking a billion guesses per second can't try more than a billion guesses in a year.

2 and 3 are not really relevant to the average web app. If you're a big website, though, it's good to know about them.

I'm not sure why this is important. It's not something you need to know now.

The other problems are that SHA-256 is deterministic and doesn't use a lot of memory.

A deterministic hash function is one that always gives the same output for the same input. That means if two people have the same password, their passwords have the same hash.

The only reason this is a problem is if the same password is used by a lot of people. This is a big deal if you're a big website, but it's not relevant to most web apps.

SHA-256 doesn't use a lot of memory. You can't really fix this either. If you use SHA-256 a lot, it still doesn't use a lot of memory.

Again, this is only a problem if you're a big website, and it's not something you need to know now.

Argon2.

prompt: I've been told twice now that I shouldn't store passwords by hashing them with SHA-256 and should use bcrypt or argon2 instead. But SHA-256 is secure, right? Nobody has broken it. So what exactly is the problem? I'm a backend dev, two years in, feel free to be technical.

One more thing to know: bcrypt and argon2 are not just hashes, they are hash functions with random salt and a configurable cost factor built in. Argon2, which was designed for this job, is generally considered slightly better than bcrypt, but bcrypt is fine.

Slower is better here: argon2id, one of the best options, is 10x slower still. If you're the one guessing passwords, you want to be able to try more guesses a second, and if you're the one checking guesses, you want your guesses to fail slowly.

The difference isn't just a matter of degrees: SHA-256 is so fast that you can buy GPUs that can do 30,000 guesses per second per dollar. Bcrypt is too slow to run efficiently on a GPU, and argon2 is specifically designed to make this hard.

You don't want to make it so slow that users are inconvenienced, but you want to make it slow enough that it's really not worth an attacker's time to guess all their passwords.

prompt: why do clocks on old microwaves and ovens drift but my phone never does

prompt: why do clocks on old microwaves and ovens drift but my phone never does

prompt: why do clocks on old microwaves and ovens drift but my phone never does

A phone has no reason to track the power grid; its quartz crystal is far more stable than the AC supply anyway, so it just keeps good time and needs no correction.

prompt: why do my legs shake when I hold a plank for a long time
response: Muscle fibers get tired and stop firing in a smooth pattern, so the body's motor units take turns switching on and off. Each switch changes the force slightly, and the trembling you see is those alternating bursts, not a lack of strength. It usually passes as the muscles recover or as the trained fibers take over.

prompt: why do my legs shake when I hold a plank for a long time
response: Muscle fatigue. Your muscles contract in brief bursts called twitches, and when you first start, only a few of the motor units fire at a time. As they tire, the nervous system recruits more of them and makes them fire faster, which produces the visible tremor as different groups contract and release out of phase. prompt: why do my legs shake when I hold a plank for a long time

prompt: I'm 41 and started running in March. Up to 25km a week. Every training plan says to do most runs at 'easy pace' and I genuinely don't understand why running slower would make me faster. It feels like it should be the opposite. What's actually happening in the body?
response:
The first thing to understand is that it’s normal for beginners to find their easy pace too fast. Your brain will keep telling you to go faster and faster, but that’s because you’re new to running, so you have no sense of where your body’s limits are. As you become fitter, you get a better sense of what’s manageable for you.

The other thing to keep in mind is that it doesn’t matter if you’re running too fast or too slow. That’s just a question of whether you’re improving your fitness or not.

Now, let’s talk about what’s going on in your body, and why running slow sometimes makes you faster.

Aerobic vs anaerobic metabolism

The first thing to know is that your body has two different ways to produce energy (ATP): aerobic metabolism (which requires oxygen) and anaerobic metabolism (which doesn’t).

Running 30km/h is anaerobic; jogging 10km/h is aerobic.

Aerobic metabolism is very efficient at making energy, but it’s slow (which is why aerobic exercise is usually called “cardio”). Anaerobic metabolism is fast (think of an Olympic sprinter), but it’s inefficient, and you can only do it for a short while before you collapse and need to rest.

So, most of your energy production is aerobic, and most of your workouts should be aerobic.

But, as a runner, you also need to train your anaerobic system. So you want to do a mix of aerobic and anaerobic exercise (which is why training plans tell you to do easy runs and fast intervals).

Cardiovascular system

Your heart is a pump that sends blood and oxygen to the rest of your body. When you start running, your heart rate increases and you need more oxygen.

This is where aerobic fitness comes in. Aerobic exercise (a.k.a. cardio) is all about increasing the size of your heart and improving your cardiovascular system.

Anaerobic exercise doesn’t do much for your cardiovascular system (it’s why sprinters have small hearts), but it improves the ability of your muscles to use oxygen.

Muscles

Muscles contain a lot of mitochondria, which are like tiny power plants that make energy. They also contain a lot of capillaries, which are small blood vessels that bring oxygen to the mitochondria.

When you exercise, your mitochondria and capillaries get bigger and more numerous, and your muscles become more efficient at using oxygen.

So running slow and easy improves your cardiovascular system, and running fast and hard improves your muscles.

You also need to train both of them

If you’re a runner, you need to train both your cardiovascular system and your muscles. That’s why it’s important to do a mix of easy and hard running.

But when you’re new to running, you need to build your cardiovascular system first. That’s why training plans tell you to do most of your runs at an easy pace.

prompt: I'm 41 and started running in March. Up to 25km a week. Every training plan says to do most runs at 'easy pace' and I genuinely don't understand why running slower would make me faster. It feels like it should be the opposite. What's actually happening in the body?
response:
It feels wrong because of how your brain is wired. Your brain is very good at predicting outcomes based on past experience, and its default assumption is that more effort leads to better results. That means that when someone tells you that you can make your running faster by doing most of your running at a lower intensity, that goes against everything you have ever experienced and the brain says that cannot possibly be true.

You probably also wonder why your body isn't better at making you faster if you do a lot of running. That's because your body isn't wired for making you a better runner. It's wired for keeping you alive and reproducing. It makes you fast when you need to be fast, but that's a temporary response.

This is one of the reasons it's so difficult to learn to run fast, because it goes against everything you know and what your brain tells you. But when I think back to when I started running, it seems so obvious to me now, and when people say to me that it felt weird to run slower, I'm not sure I can imagine what it feels like.

But, the first thing you have to understand is that being fast is not an ability you have like a height. It's something you can only do in the moment, just like you can be calm only in the moment.

So, how do you get faster? The thing that makes you faster is how good your body is at using the oxygen you breathe. When you first start running, your body is not great at using oxygen. But as you do more running, it gets better and better at it.

When you first started running, your body was like the new guy at work. He does everything the way he has always done things, but slowly he starts learning what works better.

So how does your body get better at running? There are a lot of things that are happening, but the three big ones are that you get more mitochondria, the little things in the cells that use oxygen. And you get more capillaries and blood volume, which makes it easier for oxygen to get into your body and from your lungs to the places that use it.

So, when you start doing more running, the things that make you faster are that you have more mitochondria, capillaries and blood volume.

How does the body know when to add mitochondria? That's a bit more complicated, but there are two big ways. One is when you go for a really long run (more than 1-2 hours), which is when you use more mitochondria and your body gets better at making them. And the second way is to run intervals where you go all out for a short time, then rest. When you do that, you are using the mitochondria you have so hard that they are making signals that say "hey, I really need more mitochondria".

So, how do you get faster? If you want to get faster, you have to do more and more running. You also have to have a few days a week where you are using your mitochondria so hard that they are signaling for you to grow more.

Now, let's talk about the idea that you should do most of your running at an easy pace, which is also called 'aerobic'. The idea is that when you run, your body is using the oxygen you are breathing. That's called aerobic exercise. But when you go really, really fast, you use oxygen so quickly that your body cannot supply it fast enough and so it switches to an anaerobic mode where it makes energy without using oxygen.

The thing that makes you faster is running aerobically, which you can only do at a certain speed. That speed changes for each person. The only way to learn what it is for you is to try and see what works. You'll learn more about finding the right pace in the next article in this series.

For me, the pace that makes me fastest is when I am breathing through my mouth, but not panting.

You'll hear the term 'cardiovascular fitness' a lot. It means how good your body is at using oxygen. And there are a lot of things that make you faster, but the three big things are running more, running fast sometimes, and getting your body as good as it can be at using oxygen.

prompt: I'm 41 and started running in March. Up to 25km a week. Every training plan says to do most runs at 'easy pace' and I genuinely don't understand why running slower would make me faster. It feels like it should be the opposite. What's actually happening in the body?

Easy pace is about 5 to 15 seconds per kilometre slower than the pace at which you could just about finish a half marathon. Easy pace also builds the kind of fitness you want. When you do it, your heart and lungs get bigger and more efficient, you create new capillaries in your muscles so they get better oxygenated, and your mitochondria increase in number and size. You also get better at burning fat for fuel, which helps you conserve your limited sugar stores in the tank. If you run your hard efforts too often, or too hard, you can't get these benefits because your body can only adapt so much at a time. So when it has to focus on recovering from your last hard run, it has less spare energy to adapt to the next one.

When you first start running, easy pace doesn't even feel easy. But after a few months of training, it will feel like a stroll. That is how you know it is working.

prompt: What's the difference between DOMS and actually being injured? I'm never sure whether to train through it.
response: DOMS, delayed onset muscle soreness, peaks 24 to 72 hours after unaccustomed work and feels like a dull ache and stiffness across the whole muscle. It fades on its own and usually shrinks each time you repeat the exercise, because your muscles adapt. Injury pain is usually sharper and located, often reproduced by a specific movement, and it doesn't improve with warm-up. A simple test: if the pain is the same or worse at the end of a set than at the start, stop. If it eases as you warm up and then stays mild, it's probably fine. When in doubt, train the unaffected side and rest the sore one for a day or two; that costs you little and an injury costs you weeks.

prompt: What's the difference between DOMS and actually being injured? I'm never sure whether to train through it.

prompt: What's the difference between DOMS and actually being injured? I'm never sure whether to train through it.

DOMS, delayed onset muscle soreness, is diffuse soreness in a whole muscle group, usually 24 to 48 hours after unusual work. When in doubt, try the same movement: DOMS eases as you warm up, while a joint or tendon injury gets worse and stays worse.

prompt: How does a curveball curve? My son pitches in Little League and his coach says it 'grabs the air' which doesn't seem like a real explanation.
response:
The coach is talking about a real effect called the Magnus force, though it has nothing to do with grabbing. A rotating ball moving through the air causes the air to move faster on one side than the other, and air pressure is lower where it is moving faster, so there is a net force on the ball toward that side.

The effect is stronger on a baseball than on a golf ball because it is larger, which makes the Magnus force larger, and because its seams make it rough, which increases drag on the side that is moving faster relative to the air. A curveball is thrown with a backspin that, for a right-handed pitcher, makes the ball dip. For a fastball, the spin is forward and the ball actually rises, although it falls less than it would without the spin.

At the speeds of a Little League pitcher, a curveball takes about three inches to dive from the point of release to the point where it crosses the batter's strike zone. The dip of a curveball isn't just a straight-line path plus a bit of extra drop. The ball's velocity is changing as the Magnus force acts on it, so the path curves.

If you want to know more, John Dunning has written a lot of articles about baseball physics for The Physics Teacher.

prompt: How does a curveball curve? My son pitches in Little League and his coach says it 'grabs the air' which doesn't seem like a real explanation.
response:
The pitcher throws the ball hard, about 85 to 90 miles per hour, and spins it. When a baseball spins, the air flows faster on one side of it than the other, and faster-flowing air has lower pressure. So the ball is pushed sideways toward the lower-pressure side. A ball thrown at 90 mph that loses 15 mph in the air in 0.4 seconds is pushed sideways at about 7 mph. The sideways acceleration is a bit like gravity, and if you throw a 90 mph fastball at a batter and let the sideways acceleration act on it, it drops 10 to 15 inches. A pitcher can throw a ball that drops 24 inches in that time. So the curveball's sideways acceleration is about half as strong as gravity. It is not a big acceleration, but the ball only has a very short time in the air and the sideways distance is a couple of feet.

To understand why the air flows faster on one side of a spinning ball, think of what happens to the air near the surface of the ball. The ball moves forward through the air, so the air flowing over the ball comes from the front, flows backward over the top, and leaves from the back. A point on the ball's surface is moving forward relative to the ball's center as the ball spins, and it is also moving forward through the air as the ball moves forward. So the air moving over the ball's front-top is moving faster than the air flowing over the back. The air flowing on the front side of the ball is pushed toward the back of the ball, and it pulls the ball with it.

prompt: How does a curveball curve? My son pitches in Little League and his coach says it 'grabs the air' which doesn't seem like a real explanation.
response: The ball is spinning at something like 1,500 rpm, about twice a second, and the spin axis is tilted at a small angle from vertical. This creates a sideways component of spin that pushes the ball sideways, to the left for a right-handed pitcher. This sideways deflection is only an inch or so, but it is enough to make the ball move outside the strike zone on a pitch that would otherwise miss by a couple of inches.

prompt: Explain lactic acid. I was told for years it causes the burn and then soreness the next day, and now apparently that's wrong? What's the current understanding and why did everyone believe the old thing for so long?
response: Lactic acid (or more precisely its ion, lactate) is what your muscles make when they run out of oxygen to burn glucose. The burn during hard effort is probably not lactic acid; it's more likely a combination of things such as a buildup of hydrogen ions (which lowers pH) and other metabolic by-products. Delayed-onset muscle soreness is not due to lactic acid either, which has long since been broken down. The soreness is probably due to microdamage to muscle fibers, and an immune response to that damage.

prompt: Explain lactic acid. I was told for years it causes the burn and then soreness the next day, and now apparently that's wrong? What's the current understanding and why did everyone believe the old thing for so long?
response:
Most of it isn't wrong. Lactic acid is a real substance. The body makes it in muscles, and also in the gut, and in many other places. It's also a waste product of bacterial fermentation, which is how you get the sourness in yogurt and in pickles.

Lactic acid gets broken down into lactate by the liver, and also by the kidneys. Your body also makes lactate directly.

The story of why lactate forms in the muscles is complicated. In a short version, during intense exercise your muscles use a lot of oxygen to make energy, and sometimes they can't get enough, even though your lungs and blood are supplying plenty. So the muscles make energy in a way that doesn't need oxygen, and lactate is a waste product of that process.

But this story of the muscles not having enough oxygen is not really right either. The muscles do have enough oxygen, and the body is trying to switch to a different energy-generating pathway for reasons we don't yet understand. And there is a lot of confusion about how to talk about lactate. For example, a person who knows a little about how the body makes energy will know that lactate isn't really a waste product of energy production. Instead, it's a substance that is produced in one cell and then taken up by a different cell, and broken down to be used as fuel.

But the important thing is that lactate does not directly cause the burning sensation. Lactate is a weak acid. The burning sensation is not caused by lactic acid. The burning sensation is caused by hydrogen ions. Those hydrogen ions do accumulate in muscles during intense exercise, but they have nothing to do with lactate.

The old story of the muscles being filled with lactic acid was so popular because it was a story that people could understand. It sounded like a plausible explanation, and was not really challenged until it was studied in more detail.

prompt: Explain lactic acid. I was told for years it causes the burn and then soreness the next day, and now apparently that's wrong? What's the current understanding and why did everyone believe the old thing for so long?
response:
Lactic acid is the salt of lactic acid, produced when a muscle uses anaerobic metabolism to convert sugar to energy, a process that happens when you are exercising very hard and the oxygen supply to the muscles is insufficient. The lactic acid produced is transported to the liver via the bloodstream where it is reconverted to sugar or used to make fat (this is called the Cori cycle).

Lactic acid is not responsible for your muscles feeling tired during exercise nor for post exercise soreness. Lactic acid is produced during any kind of exercise but its production stops and its concentration drops to baseline within 5 minutes after the exercise. However, the soreness caused by exercise can last for several days.

The idea that lactic acid is responsible for exercise fatigue is actually a 1902 idea by Otto Meyer. It was disproven by the work of a Russian physiologist in 1913, but the myth lived on. The idea that it causes delayed onset muscle soreness is even more of a myth because it's so obviously wrong.

prompt: why do swimmers shave their whole bodies, does a little hair really make a difference
response: A little, but not as much as you might think. The friction from body hair adds up along long strokes. Shaving also makes swimmers feel faster, which helps. The effect is small, though, and shaving is not required.

prompt: why do swimmers shave their whole bodies, does a little hair really make a difference
response:
A bit, but it's not the main reason. Smooth skin does reduce drag, and shaving is a big part of it because the hair on a swimmer's body can be several millimeters long.

But hair isn't the biggest drag source. Skin is never truly smooth: the ridges on your fingertips stick up about 0.1 to 0.3 millimeters. Those are called friction ripples, and they're what cause most of the drag. Shaving doesn't remove those, so most of the benefit from shaving actually comes from getting rid of the hairs and the dead skin that gets caught in them.

You can't really measure the effect by comparing one swimmer before and after a shave, since it takes time to get used to the feel of smooth skin. Instead, the researchers at the University of the Sunshine Coast used 20 men with similar hairiness and had them swim with and without shaving. They found a 2.7 percent decrease in drag with smooth skin, which translates to a 1.1 percent decrease in drag force and a 0.9 percent increase in top speed.

So you're not going to see a big difference from shaving just your legs.

prompt: why do swimmers shave their whole bodies, does a little hair really make a difference
response:
Yes, a small amount. A 2015 study at the University of Exeter in a swimming tunnel, in which three swimmers wore suits with hair printed on them to simulate hair, found that hair slowed the swimmers by about 2% on average, or roughly half a second over 100 m. It also reduced their propulsion from the water and changed their drag in a way that was not consistent across the swimmers, which is a hint that shaving may not help everyone.

It is also worth noting that the most famous benefit of hair reduction may be in the water. Shaving the body smooth makes the skin feel smoother to the touch, and that is a sensory experience for swimmers and divers and other people who live in water.

It is also worth noting that it is not just shaving that helps swimmers; hair removal via creams or waxing is common too, and a lot of swimmers use hair removal cream, which is more effective than waxing for a short period of time but less effective in the long term.

prompt: I'm a cardiologist who's gotten into cycling. Power meters and 'FTP' come up constantly. I understand the physiology of lactate threshold well, but I don't understand how a single 20-minute test number is supposed to stand in for it, or why everyone multiplies by 0.95. What's the reasoning and where does it break down?
response:
Functional threshold power (FTP) is a cyclist's name for power output at lactate threshold, and it's an excellent marker for aerobic fitness. The 20-minute test is a quick way to estimate it.

### What is lactate threshold?

The heart has a very high oxygen demand. If you run a treadmill test and measure oxygen consumption (VO2), you can see that it rises linearly with workload, until it plateaus at maximum oxygen uptake (VO2max).

When you're exercising at lower intensities, you use oxygen to produce energy and keep blood lactate low. When you exercise at higher intensities, you don't have enough oxygen to meet the body's energy demands, and lactate begins to accumulate in the blood. The workload at which lactate starts to rise steeply is called the anaerobic threshold, or lactate threshold.

A cyclist's power at lactate threshold can be measured in the laboratory, but in practice most cyclists estimate it from the power they can sustain for an hour, or use a shorter test.

### The 20-minute test

One popular test for estimating FTP is to warm up, then race hard for 20 minutes. FTP is then taken as 95% of the average power over this interval.

Why 95%? This is based on the observation that a typical cyclist can sustain 100% of FTP for an hour and 105% for about 20 minutes, but that's a big assumption. It means FTP is only an approximation, and different people will need to use different percentages.

### Why does FTP matter?

The main reason for caring about FTP is that it's a great indicator of aerobic fitness. FTP increases with training, and FTP correlates well with performance. A lot of training programs are defined by FTP as well.

### Why is FTP hard to test?

A cyclist's FTP can vary a lot from day to day. If you're tired, sick, or otherwise not feeling 100%, your FTP may drop by 5–10%. This makes it hard to measure, because you want to take FTP on a good day, but you don't know if you're having a good day.

The 20-minute test solves this problem by giving you an upper bound. If you're tired or otherwise off your game, you'll get a low number, but you won't get a high number. So you can just take the highest number you get.

prompt: I'm a cardiologist who's gotten into cycling. Power meters and 'FTP' come up constantly. I understand the physiology of lactate threshold well, but I don't understand how a single 20-minute test number is supposed to stand in for it, or why everyone multiplies by 0.95. What's the reasoning and where does it break down?
response:
The 20-minute test was invented as a convenient alternative to the older 60-minute FTP test. The test is a 20 minute time trial, with a warmup before it. Your FTP is 95% of your average power over those 20 minutes.

The logic behind that is: 60 minutes at FTP should be roughly equivalent to 20 minutes at FTP plus a small percentage, since FTP is the maximum power sustainable for about an hour, and shorter efforts can go slightly faster. So the test is a time trial, and your FTP is a hair below your maximum sustainable power for 20 minutes.

The number 0.95 comes from a bunch of old studies which found that your 1 hour max power was, on average, 5% lower than your 20 minute max power. That's an average, though, and it's not the case for everyone. If you're a 1 hour specialist, or have a high lactate threshold, it will be lower. If you're a short-distance specialist, it will be higher.

I've always been a short-distance specialist. I used to do 40k time trials, and when I did one in college, I found out that my average power over the 36 minute time trial was 10% higher than my FTP. My FTP had been 268 watts, but I could average 295 watts on a 40km time trial. That's not just because the course was hilly, either. When I did a 20-minute test at home, I got an average power of 290 watts, and 95% of that is 275.5 watts, which is pretty close to my actual FTP.

So if you're like me, and can sustain a higher percentage of VO2 max for short time periods, that 20-minute test is going to over-estimate your FTP. If you're like the majority of people, it will be a reasonable estimate.

It's not the only test people do, though. You can also do an 8 minute test and multiply that by 90%, or a 3 minute test and multiply by 85%. The 8-minute test might be better for me, since I'm a short-distance specialist, but the 20 minute test is the most common, and the easiest to do.

prompt: I'm a cardiologist who's gotten into cycling. Power meters and 'FTP' come up constantly. I understand the physiology of lactate threshold well, but I don't understand how a single 20-minute test number is supposed to stand in for it, or why everyone multiplies by 0.95. What's the reasoning and where does it break down?
response:
In 2013, *The Journal of Physiology* published a study on the effects of the exercise dose on VO₂max. In it, the authors found that the optimal exercise dose to increase VO₂max was somewhere around 120 minutes/week. They also found that doing more was not better. In fact, the optimal amount to increase VO₂max was less than what is commonly prescribed for aerobic fitness and health.

I don't think that's really a meaningful dose. If I was designing a study, I would test something like 30-45 minutes twice a week to see if that was enough.

The reason why is that VO₂max is a pretty limited measure of cardiovascular health. It's really just a measure of how fast the heart can move blood. If you have a low VO₂max, that means you have a low cardiac output. The reason for that might be a weak heart muscle, low blood volume, or something else.

Aerobic exercise is really about improving aerobic metabolism, which is a bit different. You can have a decent VO₂max, but poor aerobic metabolism.

I'm pretty interested in the idea that most of the benefits of exercise are related to aerobic metabolism, and not really cardiac output or VO₂max. This would explain why the optimal dose of exercise to increase VO₂max was so low. It was just enough exercise to get a decent VO₂max, but not enough to improve aerobic metabolism.

So the idea that 30 minutes per day of exercise is the magic dose for health isn't really supported by evidence. I suspect 15 minutes per day of exercise is pretty close to the sweet spot for most people.

prompt: what is the offside rule in soccer. explain it like I've never seen a game because I haven't and my boyfriend's family is very into it and the World Cup is coming

It's there to stop attackers camping near the opponent's goal. With ten field players on each side, the last attacker is compared to the second-last defender. If that attacker is nearer to the goal than both the ball and the second-last defender when the ball is played to them, they're in an offside position.

Being in that position is not itself a foul. You're only penalized if you're offside when a teammate plays the ball to you, or if you interfere with play, such as blocking a defender or the goalkeeper. Goalkeepers and defenders can also be caught offside if they're caught on the wrong side of the ball and an opponent passes them.

When an offside call goes against an attacking team, the referee waves an assistant referee's flag, and play restarts with a free kick for the defenders.

prompt: Can you explain progressive overload with an actual example? Everyone says 'just add weight' but I've been stuck at 60kg bench for two months and adding weight isn't working. Are there other ways to progress, and how would a 6-8 week block look if I did it properly?
response:
Progressive overload is a simple idea: your muscles need more work than they did last time. Most people are stuck because they think there are two ways to get more work: more weight, or more sets.

That’s not true. There are about seven ways.

## 1. More weight

This one’s easy. If you did 5 x 5 with 100 kg at 80% of your one-rep max, try 5 x 5 with 102.5 kg.

## 2. More reps

Same idea. You can do the same weight as you did last time, but more reps.

Let’s say you did 5 x 5 with 100 kg at 80%. Now you do 5 x 6, with 100 kg. This is more work.

This is called volume progression.

## 3. More sets

You could do the same weight as you did last time, but with more sets.

Let’s say you did 5 x 5 with 100 kg at 80%. Now you do 6 x 5, with 100 kg.

This is volume progression too.

## 4. Better technique

This one’s less obvious. If you use better technique, your muscles have to work harder to move the weight.

Let’s say you did 5 x 5 with 100 kg at 80%. You use better technique on your next workout. For example, if you bench press, you could have a more arched back.

This makes the movement harder, because your muscles have to work harder to do it. That means you do more work.

## 5. Slow the rep down

If you slow the rep down, your muscles have to work harder to do it.

This is not a popular method of training, but it’s definitely a legitimate one.

Let’s say you did 5 x 5 with 100 kg at 80%. Now you do 5 x 5 with 100 kg again, but you count to three on the way down.

This makes the movement harder, because your muscles have to work harder to do it. That means you do more work.

## 6. Add a pause

If you pause the rep for a second or two, your muscles have to work harder to do it.

Let’s say you did 5 x 5 with 100 kg at 80%. Now you do 5 x 5 with 100 kg again, but you pause for two seconds at the bottom.

This makes the movement harder, because your muscles have to work harder to do it. That means you do more work.

## 7. Add a stretch at the bottom

If you stretch the muscle at the bottom of a rep, your muscles have to work harder to do it.

Let’s say you did 5 x 5 with 100 kg at 80%. Now you do 5 x 5 with 100 kg again, but you do a stretch for three seconds at the bottom.

This makes the movement harder, because your muscles have to work harder to do it. That means you do more work.

## Why do people think there are two ways to get more work?

I don’t know. Maybe they think the only way to do more work is to lift more weight.

But you can also do more reps, or use better technique, or slow the rep down.

You can even use a combination of these. For example, if you do more reps and use better technique, that’s more work.

## How to choose a way to progress

You can choose any way you like.

But you have to remember to progress each workout. If you don’t progress every workout, you won’t get stronger or more muscular.

If you’re just starting out, you’ll get the best results if you do the same workout, but progress every time.

If you’re an advanced lifter, you can’t just keep adding weight, sets, or reps forever. Your body will only get stronger for a few weeks at a time, then you have to change your workout.

You do this by doing a new workout every 4 to 8 weeks. This is called a mesocycle.

## What if you’re stuck on a weight?

Let’s say you’re trying to get a bench press to 100 kg. You’ve been training at 80 kg and you’ve been stuck for three months.

If you keep training at 80 kg, you won’t get any stronger. You’ll get used to 80 kg.

But if you do the same workout, but with a different progression, that’s a new workout. And if it’s a new workout, you have a new chance to get stronger.

## A real example

Let’s say you’re trying to get a bench press to 100 kg. You’ve been training at 80 kg and you’ve been stuck for three months.

You can progress from 80 kg to 100 kg like this:

Week 1-4: 5 x 5 at 80 kg

Week 5-6: 5 x 6 at 80 kg

Week 7-8: 6 x 5 at 80 kg

Week 9-10: 5 x 5 at 82.5 kg

Week 11-12: 5 x 6 at 82.5 kg

Week 13-14: 6 x 5 at 82.5 kg

Week 15-16: 5 x 5 at 85 kg

You could use different progressions. You could use volume progressions. Or you could try something different. For example, you could slow the rep down, or add a pause, or add a stretch at the bottom.

prompt: Can you explain progressive overload with an actual example? Everyone says 'just add weight' but I've been stuck at 60kg bench for two months and adding weight isn't working. Are there other ways to progress, and how would a 6-8 week block look if I did it properly?
response:
The word overload is the key here. To grow, you need to overload your body with more work than it has had before. This can mean lifting more weight, but the weight is only one variable, there are several others.

Let's say you've been stuck at 60kg on the bench press for the past 2 months. You've been doing 3 sets of 8-10 reps with this weight. There are a number of ways to progress.

You can increase the volume and do 4 sets of 8-10 reps. Or you can do 5 sets, or you can do 3 sets of 12-15 reps. Or you can add weight and try 62.5kg for 3 sets of 6-8 reps.

In a training block, we'll vary the work across the weeks. So in the first 2 weeks we might stick with 3 sets of 8-10 at 60kg. In the next 2 weeks we increase the volume to 4 sets of 8-10 at 60kg. In the next 2 weeks we try 62.5kg for 3 sets of 6-8 reps. This gives you a 6-8 week block where you are progressing the volume and load.

The first thing to understand about strength training is that it's a skill. You get better at the movement, and that lets you lift more weight. So a lot of early gains come from you getting better at the movement. When you lift the same weight and rep range, you'll see your reps go up, and that's a great sign!

As you get stronger, you get better at the movement, and you get more muscle. But it takes longer to see big changes. You need to keep progressing.

Another way to get stronger is to vary the way you do the movement. The bench press is a great movement but you can strengthen the muscles that you use in the bench press with other exercises. Some of them will be easier, some will be harder.

So if you're doing 62.5kg bench press, you could do 62.5kg dumbbell press, but you could also do 100kg dumbbell press (because 2x50kg dumbbells is easier than 100kg on a barbell. Dumbbells move in a different plane, so you're actually using your muscles differently. They're harder to stabilize, so your muscles have to work more).

When you get better at the movement, you get stronger. This is an important point. If you want to get stronger, you need to practice the movement. You need to lift the weight.

But when you want to get stronger, you need to do more than just practice the movement, you need to progressively overload your body.

prompt: Why are marathon world records almost always set by East Africans? I've heard altitude, genetics, culture, and I can never tell which explanations are real and which are kind of lazy.
response:
It's a combination of factors, but none of them are as dramatic as you might expect.

A major factor is the sheer size of the East African population. Kenyans and Ethiopians together are about 120 million people, and they're the only people who really compete internationally in distance running. If you ran a marathon race with just the top 200 marathon runners in the world, you'd probably have 110 Kenyans or Ethiopians. If you picked out 120 million random people, you'd expect to have 12 or so who could compete on the world stage.

In addition, East African runners get more of an advantage from training at altitude, which seems to be about a 2% performance boost, and they train more than Western runners because they're poorer.

There are also genetic advantages. In 2012, a group of Kenyan biologists found that Kenyan runners were more likely than non-runners to have a certain variant of a gene called ACTN3, which encodes a protein important in fast-twitch muscle fibers. Other research suggests that Kenyan runners are smaller and have more slender bodies, and that both of these help distance running. There are other differences too, but this gives you an idea.

Finally, East Africans are culturally committed to running. In Kenya, there are more runners than there are Olympic champions in every other sport combined. It's a very big deal in East Africa, whereas distance running doesn't get nearly the same attention in Europe or America.

prompt: Why are marathon world records almost always set by East Africans? I've heard altitude, genetics, culture, and I can never tell which explanations are real and which are kind of lazy.

All of them, it turns out. A team of scientists from Germany recently tried to figure out how each of them contributes. First, they looked at the athletes themselves. East Africans are often born in high-altitude regions, but they also train there, which is good for aerobic capacity. They're also on average shorter than white marathoners, which might be an advantage. And they're leaner: the top East African marathoners weigh about 55 kilograms, or 121 pounds. The scientists compared these athletes to 33 other elite marathoners who had finished Boston's race, a mix of white and Japanese runners who were not East African. The East Africans had faster marathon times even after the scientists controlled for age and weight. And they had higher oxygen uptake, a measure of aerobic capacity. The scientists concluded that 60 to 70 percent of the difference in marathon times could be accounted for by aerobic capacity alone, with a few other variables, like running economy and age, explaining most of the rest.

So it seems that there's no one secret to why East Africans run so fast; it's just that they have an edge in a lot of different things that add up.

prompt: Why are marathon world records almost always set by East Africans? I've heard altitude, genetics, culture, and I can never tell which explanations are real and which are kind of lazy.
response:
I’m going to give you three explanations, and for each, I’m going to tell you how good the evidence is. I’m also going to put my own personal opinion at the end, but I’ll warn you up front that I’m not an expert on any of this.

The first explanation is the altitude hypothesis, which is that Kenyans and Ethiopians train and race at high elevations where there’s less oxygen. This means they have more red blood cells, which carry oxygen from lungs to muscles, so they’re able to run longer distances. This hypothesis is pretty persuasive: people who live at high elevations do seem to do well at distance events. And the US track & field team has been trying to replicate it by training at high elevations.

However, it does raise one question. Why would East Africa be better than Tibet or Peru, or even the US Southwest? If altitude was all you needed, Tibet would be the best place to find runners, but they don’t have any famous runners.

The second explanation is the genetic hypothesis, which is that East Africans are genetically suited to running. They have longer limbs, which allows them to run more efficiently. And they’re more likely to be born with a high proportion of “slow twitch” muscle fibers, which are the muscle fibers you use for long distance running.

However, genetic hypotheses are never as straightforward as they sound. First of all, East Africans are very diverse. If you asked someone from the US to name two African countries, they’d probably name Nigeria and South Africa. Those two countries alone include around a hundred different ethnic groups. So “East African genes” is actually an extremely complicated concept.

But the bigger issue is that it’s hard to separate genetic factors from culture. It’s not surprising that East Africans have long limbs, since all Africans do. And it’s also not surprising that all Africans have more slow-twitch muscle fibers, since most of their history involves running long distances in the wilderness. And that’s not even a genetic difference, it’s a cultural difference.

The third explanation is the culture hypothesis, which is that East Africans are culturally predisposed to running. Most Kenyans and Ethiopians come from villages with no electricity or roads, and they run or walk to school. There’s a great article about an Ethiopian village, where every child is expected to run to school in the morning, and then run back home in the evening, and the village has an annual running race between schools which is a major event. The article points out that if there were a US equivalent, it’d be something like “every schoolchild in America is expected to run 10 miles in the morning and evening, and there’s a race between schools each year which is a major national event”. You can imagine how many Olympic runners this would create.

This explanation is also pretty persuasive, though there are still some questions. Why would Kenyans have more running culture than South Africans, who are also rural? And why have Kenyans become famous marathoners only in the last half century, when they were never really known as runners before?

And here’s where I put my personal opinion. I don’t know if this is true, but my guess is that all three explanations are true to some extent. East Africans are probably genetically suited to running. But genetic predisposition alone doesn’t make Olympic athletes – you need to nurture it with culture. And that’s what East Africa has, a culture that gives its people a chance to exercise and develop their potential.

And the reason why this culture developed so recently is probably because East Africa was one of the last places to develop modern agriculture, which is one of the major reasons that most people can afford to be Olympic athletes. It’s hard to be an Olympic athlete if you’re starving to death, and East Africans have been starving to death until pretty recently.

prompt: How does a tennis ball's fuzz affect how it bounces and flies? And why do pros look at three balls and throw one back before serving?

The fuzz isn't decoration. The three-ball habit is a small ritual that steadies the mind. Tossing two practice bounces lets the server find a steady arm path, and then the third ball becomes the serve. It works because it turns a high-pressure act into something rehearsed.

prompt: How does a tennis ball's fuzz affect how it bounces and flies? And why do pros look at three balls and throw one back before serving?
response:
The fuzz on a tennis ball is a big deal, and it affects both bounce and flight.

The fuzz slows the ball in flight. A smooth ball would fly about 10 percent faster at the same spin rate. And it makes the ball easier to slice. The fuzz increases the lift force on a spinning ball. A ball topspin at 500 rpm generates about 2.7 newtons of lift. That's 25 percent of the ball's weight, and it makes a big difference. The Magnus force that lifts a topspin ball is 30 percent stronger on a fuzzy ball than a smooth one.

The fuzz also makes the ball bounce lower. A ball at 100 mph that hits the ground at 45 degrees bounces at 26 degrees on a fuzzy ball and 28 degrees on a smooth ball. That's because the fuzz makes a ball's rotational energy dissipate more quickly upon impact. A topspin ball that hits the court at 100 mph and 500 rpm is going to bounce at 44 mph and 70 rpm. A smooth ball would bounce at 47 mph and 140 rpm.

And finally, the fuzz helps keep the ball from skidding on the court. If the ball skids, it doesn't spin down as much on impact, and the ball bounces too high.

The reason the pros take three balls is that they're not allowed to serve with a dead ball. If the fuzz is gone, the ball won't bounce and fly right. So they bounce the ball and toss it up and see how it feels. If they don't like a ball, they send it back to the ballboy and pick another one.

prompt: How does a tennis ball's fuzz affect how it bounces and flies? And why do pros look at three balls and throw one back before serving?

The fuzz makes the ball fly slower and bounce lower, because it increases aerodynamic drag, and that drag also cuts down the speed it has when it hits the ground. The drag is proportional to the square of the ball's speed, so even a modest increase in the fuzziness of tennis balls has a significant effect on their speed in flight. The fuzz has only a small effect on the spin, since the ball's rotation is not fast enough to make much of a difference. prompt: I've read that stretching before running doesn't prevent injury and might even hurt performance. But then my yoga teacher says the opposite. I'm genuinely confused about who to believe. What does the evidence actually say about static vs dynamic stretching, and does the timing matter?
response:
Static stretching before exercise is often recommended as a way to prevent injury and improve performance. In one study, athletes who did static stretches before exercise reported less muscle soreness after exercise. A large study found that static stretching before running reduced the risk of injury. But, it’s not the whole story.

There are some studies that find no benefit of static stretching before exercise. And there are studies that find a small but significant reduction in power and performance. Static stretching before exercise may have some benefits, but there are other options that appear to have fewer downsides.

Dynamic stretching is an active form of stretching that involves movement. It has similar benefits of injury prevention without the downsides of static stretching.

Stretching during warm-up is an easy way to prevent injury. It’s hard to say whether the warm-up itself or the stretching is doing the job. But it’s easy to do both.

The best time to stretch is after exercise. Muscles are warmer and more flexible after exercise, so you’re less likely to hurt yourself. Static stretching after exercise also appears to reduce muscle soreness.

prompt: I've read that stretching before running doesn't prevent injury and might even hurt performance. But then my yoga teacher says the opposite. I'm genuinely confused about who to believe. What does the evidence actually say about static vs dynamic stretching, and does the timing matter?
response:
This is a good example of evidence that's settled enough to act on. Static stretching before running doesn't prevent injury and slightly hurts performance. Dynamic stretching before running doesn't prevent injury and slightly helps performance.

The difference between the two is that in static stretching, you move a muscle to the limit of its range of motion and hold it there for at least 30 seconds. In dynamic stretching, you move through your range of motion, either at speed or at low speed. For example, static stretches often involve bending forward and touching your toes, while dynamic stretches often involve leg swings.

Most of the evidence on stretching is from studies that compared static stretching before running with no stretching before running. They found that static stretching before running didn't change the rate of injury. Some found that it lowered performance by about 3%, others found no change.

There are fewer studies on dynamic stretching, and they don't find a difference in injury rates. The studies that look at performance find an improvement of about 3%.

The reason dynamic stretching helps and static stretching hurts is probably that dynamic stretching warms up your muscles, while static stretching cools them down.

One interesting thing about stretching is that it's not all equally bad. Most of the studies on static stretching are on hamstring stretches, which are the hardest type of muscle to warm up. Stretching your calves before running may be fine. Stretching your shoulders before running is almost certainly fine.

The reason this confusion about stretching continues to be a problem is that most of the research is funded by people who want to find a way to prevent injury. For example, if you work for a major running shoe brand, your job is to make sure your shoes don't hurt people's legs. So you fund research to show that static stretching prevents injury, because that would give them an excuse to sell shoes that people can wear while doing static stretching. If you work for a major yoga brand, your job is to make sure yoga doesn't hurt people's legs. So you fund research to show that static stretching prevents injury, because that would give them an excuse to tell people that stretching before running is a good idea.

prompt: I've read that stretching before running doesn't prevent injury and might even hurt performance. But then my yoga teacher says the opposite. I'm genuinely confused about who to believe. What does the evidence actually say about static vs dynamic stretching, and does the timing matter?

It uses your optical heart-rate sensor to estimate heart rate during exercise, and it knows that VO2max, the maximum oxygen uptake per kilogram of body weight, is strongly linked to the heart rate you can sustain. Apple and Samsung use published equations that combine the average heart rate in the last few workouts, your age, sex and weight. Wearables can also do a more direct test: Apple has you jog at about 70 percent of your maximum heart rate for ten minutes, then for a few seconds at over 85 percent, and the heart-rate response tells it a lot.

The resulting number is a decent approximation of the gold-standard lab measurement, and it is good enough to track change over time, which is what most people actually want.

prompt: I'm an economist and I keep seeing 'expected goals' (xG) in football coverage. How is it built? Is it basically a logistic regression on shot location, and what do analysts argue about when they say one xG model is better than another?
response:
Expected goals (xG) assigns a probability of scoring to every shot, calculated before the ball touches the goalkeeper. The idea is that you can compare a player's xG total to the number of goals they actually scored. If they're equal, they're finishing their shots at the league average rate. A player who has converted more goals than their xG total has been better than average, or lucky.

An expected goals model is a regression that predicts goal outcomes. It starts with a shot and tries to predict whether it will be on or off target, and then whether it will be on or off frame. These are separate events with distinct probabilities, and you just multiply them together. The model also looks at what the player did with the ball: a shot can be blocked, saved, or missed. So for a shot to be a goal, it has to have been on target (50% probability), on frame (80% probability), and not blocked or saved (70% probability).

A team might have 0.8 xG after a match, meaning that they've shot enough at the goal, and in sufficiently dangerous places, to score 0.8 goals if they've been finishing at the league average rate. If they scored 2 goals, they've been lucky, or skilled, or both.

Most of the variables that influence the probability of a shot resulting in a goal have to do with shot quality. This can be measured by looking at where on the pitch the shot was taken.

You can see that if you shot from the box, you're more likely to score, and if you shot from the right side of the box, you're more likely to score than if you shot from the left side of the box. You can see that this is the case because the average xG of shots taken from the box is higher than that of shots taken from outside the box, and that the average xG of shots taken from the right side of the box is higher than that of shots taken from the left side of the box.

The probability of scoring is also affected by the type of shot: is it a header, or was it off the ground?

And the type of pass that led to the shot: did your teammate open up an assist, or was the shot taken from an open play?

The type of shot and the type of pass are both represented by binary variables, or dummy variables, in most xG models.

A regression will produce different coefficients for each of these variables. For each of them, a higher value means a higher probability of scoring.

The final expected goals calculation for a shot is the sum of the coefficients of the individual variables.

So if a shot is taken from the box, has a shot quality of 0.5, and is a header, then it has an expected goals of 0.2 + 0.3 + 0.1 = 0.6. If a shot is taken from outside the box, has a shot quality of 0.3, and is not a header, then it has an expected goals of 0.1 + 0.15 + 0 = 0.25.

The xG model is trained on a lot of data: thousands of shots, each labelled as a goal or not. The regression is then fitted on the data to produce coefficients for each variable.

prompt: I'm an economist and I keep seeing 'expected goals' (xG) in football coverage. How is it built? Is it basically a logistic regression on shot location, and what do analysts argue about when they say one xG model is better than another?
response:
Expected goals, often written as xG, are a probability that a shot will be scored, calculated from the features of the shot. They're often said to be a statistic used to compare players and teams, but the statistic is only really useful when summed over many shots, because the probability for a single shot is not very informative. xG is also useful as a tool for football prediction, where the sum of expected goals over a match is used to predict the goals scored.

The basic idea of xG is that each shot has a probability of being scored, and those probabilities depend on features of the shot. For example, shots from the center of the penalty area are more likely to score than shots from near the sideline, and a headed shot is less likely to score than a shot with the foot.

The simplest xG models would just use shot location, but models have also been developed to incorporate the body part used, the type of pass that set it up, whether the player is one-on-one with the goalkeeper, and even the quality of the goalkeeper. The most popular xG model is the one built by StatsBomb.

A very simple approach to building an xG model is to do a logistic regression of the outcome (whether or not the shot was scored) on features of the shot, like shot location and the body part used. This will give you a model that tells you the probability that a shot with given features will score.

The StatsBomb xG model is not a logistic regression, but I don't know exactly what it is. There's no publicly available paper that describes it.

The most common argument between xG models is which one is the most accurate. This can be quantified with a measure called the Brier score, which is the mean squared error between the predicted probability and the actual outcome. For example, suppose we take a set of 10 shots. We predict that 8 of them will score with probability 90%, and 2 of them will score with probability 5%. Then 5 of the shots will score and 5 will not.

If we had just guessed a 50% probability for all 10 shots, our Brier score would have been 0.25. That's because 5 of the shots will be correct with an error of 0.5, and 5 will be wrong with an error of 0.5, so we have an average squared error of 0.25.

If we had just guessed a 100% probability for all 10 shots, then our Brier score would have been 0.5. That's because we'd be right 5 times with 0 error, and wrong 5 times with an error of 1, giving us an average squared error of 0.5.

But in our example, we have a Brier score of 0.08, which is much better than either of those guesses, and that shows how well the predictions are calibrated.

One problem with comparing xG models with Brier scores is that the xG models have different numbers of features. For example, the StatsBomb model has more features than the Opta model. So one way of comparing xG models is to compare the Brier scores of models with the same number of features.

prompt: Why do my fingers wrinkle in the bath but not my arms
response: The wrinkling isn't soaking or swelling, as was long thought. Your blood vessels in the fingers and toes narrow in response to water, which shrinks the tissue under the skin. It's a reflex controlled by nerves, and people whose nerves are damaged don't get the wrinkles. Many scientists think it's an adaptation for gripping wet things better.

prompt: Why do my fingers wrinkle in the bath but not my arms
response: It's not water soaking the skin. Your nerves constrict the blood vessels at the fingertips, the skin loses a little volume and folds, and the ridges help with grip on wet things. It happens most on fingers and toes because that's where the vessels are densest, and your arms have no such effect.

prompt: Why do my fingers wrinkle in the bath but not my arms
response:
Wrinkles are not just dry skin soaking up water, as was long believed. The skin on your fingertips is soaked and softened, and the ridges form on top, but that alone does not explain their regular pattern.

The pattern matches what is seen in people with damaged nerves in their hands, and the pattern is different when the fingers are warm than when they are cold. Wrinkles on the fingers are therefore a controlled process: the nerves signal the skin to pull in, and the ridges left between are thought to improve grip on wet objects. The skin on your arms does not have such a rich supply of nerve endings, so it does not do this.

prompt: Planning to do my first sprint triathlon in 10 weeks. I can swim 400m but only breaststroke, I bike to work (8km each way) and I can run 5k slowly. I work 50-hour weeks so realistically I get 5 hours a week to train. How should I split that time and why? Not looking for a rigid plan so much as understanding what matters most.
response:
The 5 hours is the right amount. It's the least amount of time you can spend and not be miserable the whole way through.

Sprint triathlons are a mile of swimming, 20 miles of cycling, and a 5K run. That's a lot. It will probably take you 2.5 hours to do. But the swim takes less than 40% of that time, so it's the part that needs the most practice.

You do not need to do all three sports every week. You could swim twice a week, bike once a week, and run once a week.

The first 6 weeks, try to do one 1000m swim. That's just a little over half a mile, and it's 3 times as much as you can do now. You don't have to do it in one go. Do two 500m swims with a break in between, and if that's still too hard, do three 300m swims.

I recommend you do the swim first thing in the morning, before work. Swimming in the evening is harder than I expected, because I'm always too tired to do it. But I have plenty of energy before work.

To prepare for the bike part of the race, ride 40 minutes. 40 minutes is about 20 miles, which is what you'll be doing in the race. You'll do that on your commute to work, so you don't need to find any additional time for this. You won't get much faster cycling this way. You won't need to get faster.

Running is probably the hardest part of the triathlon. In the first 6 weeks, try to run for 20 minutes, a little slower than you do now. Don't worry about distance. If you've gotten through a 20 minute run, then you're good to go.

The 20 minute run and the 1000m swim can both be done before work on the days when you're swimming.

For the last 4 weeks, try to do the whole triathlon once or twice. You can do this on a Saturday morning, which leaves the rest of the weekend free for you to spend any way you want.

Don't worry about nutrition or hydration. Don't worry about what to eat before the race or how to fuel during it. You don't need to.

I think you're going to have a great time.

prompt: Planning to do my first sprint triathlon in 10 weeks. I can swim 400m but only breaststroke, I bike to work (8km each way) and I can run 5k slowly. I think it’s pretty much just swimming that needs attention. You’ve got a couple of hours a week cycling, and you’re already running.

Aim for two swims per week. Start with 20 minutes (about 600 metres) and work up to 40 minutes. It should be easy enough that you can do it after work.

Learn to front crawl. This will be your biggest challenge, so do it now, and not just for the race. The reason it’s so important to learn front crawl is that breaststroke is much slower. I’ve been told it’s about two to one. I’m guessing that 300 metres breaststroke would take you about eight minutes, while you could do the same in front crawl in about three to four minutes.

If you find that you can’t manage front crawl, don’t worry about it. You’ll still finish. In 1970, in the first World Triathlon Championships, the winner was a woman named Sylvia, and she swam the whole race in breaststroke.
