prompt: In cricket, how does reverse swing work? I understand conventional swing (shiny side, rough side) but reverse swing seems to break that logic and every explanation I've found just says 'it's complicated'.
response:
With conventional swing, a ball with one side polished and the other rough, is hit in the right direction and the polished side has less air resistance, the ball sways in the direction of the rough side. With reverse swing, the ball sways in the opposite direction, so that the batsman has to defend against it with both hands, and can't bat as well.

Conventional swing is explained in terms of the boundary layer, which separates air moving with the speed of the ball from air moving with the speed of the air around it. For the shiny side, which is smooth, the air sticks to the ball for longer and then leaves the ball further back. For the rough side, it separates sooner. This creates a pressure difference, with higher pressure on the shiny side and lower pressure on the rough side. This difference in pressure pushes the ball in the direction of the shiny side.

The explanation for reverse swing is that the rough side separates the boundary layer sooner, but the difference in pressure is reversed. That sounds completely backwards, and it does!

A team of researchers from the University of Bristol used smoke and laser beams to measure how air moves around the ball, and found that for reverse swing the air moves faster over the rough side of the ball, creating lower pressure.

Their research also found that reverse swing depends on the rough side not being too rough, but if it is too rough the air will separate very soon and the air will move slowly again. It also requires that the bowler bowls at 145 km/h or faster.

prompt: In cricket, how does reverse swing work? I understand conventional swing (shiny side, rough side) but reverse swing seems to break that logic and every explanation I've found just says 'it's complicated'.
response:
On the rough side of the ball, the air slows down faster than on the shiny side. It has to, because a slower-moving air has less capacity to push off the ball than the faster-moving air on the shiny side, and the two sides need to end up with equal pressure at the trailing edge of the ball or else the ball would never stop spinning. The faster-moving air pushes harder and the ball is turned away from the shiny side.

For a ball to reverse swing, it has to be travelling at 120 to 150 kph, and at that speed, a slow-moving layer of air on the rough side can be turbulent while a fast-moving layer on the shiny side can remain smooth. And turbulent air has less capacity to push off the ball than smooth air, because it has a lot of its energy going into moving the turbulence around, and so the ball is turned away from the rough side.

A ball will always swing to one side or the other, so a bowler will choose which way he wants it to move by polishing one side of the ball and not the other, and if he wants it to move the other way he swaps which side of the ball he polishes, which is why you have to change the pitch after an over, so that you don't get two different sides of the ball facing the batsman.

prompt: In cricket, how does reverse swing work? I understand conventional swing (shiny side, rough side) but reverse swing seems to break that logic and every explanation I've found just says 'it's complicated'.
response:
With a new ball, which is symmetrical, a bowler can still get it to swing by holding the ball so the seam is not square, or in line, with the direction the ball is going. With this kind of grip, the ball will spin as it travels through the air, and the seam can create a turbulent wake, which will pull the ball to one side. This kind of swing is sometimes called 'conventional' or 'orthodox' swing.

As the ball gets rougher, the turbulent wake will be less affected by the seam, and so conventional swing becomes harder to achieve. But with a ball that has become asymmetrically rough - one side shiny, one side rough - the turbulent wake will form on the shiny side, where the air moves more easily over the surface, which pulls the ball the other way, in what is called reverse swing.

This is why reverse swing tends to become a lot stronger as the match goes on and the ball gets rougher. It also means that it is hard to bowl reverse swing with a new ball, and that's why the law books require that reverse swing be allowed only with balls that are at least two hours old.

prompt: What actually happens to muscles when you stop training? I broke my wrist and can't lift for 8 weeks. How much will I lose and how fast does it come back?
response:
Muscle cells don't die; they shrink, a process called atrophy. Strength falls quickly in the first couple of weeks, because part of it is neural. Muscle mass then declines at roughly 1 to 3 percent per week, which for an average-trained lifter is a few grams of muscle per kilogram of body per day. Immobilized limbs lose more than the rest of the body.

The good news is that training history helps. Older muscle fibers that were previously built are more resistant to atrophy and respond faster to reloading. After your cast comes off, expect most of the lost strength within a few weeks and the lost size within a month or two of regular training.

prompt: What actually happens to muscles when you stop training? I broke my wrist and can't lift for 8 weeks. How much will I lose and how fast does it come back?
response:
At rest, muscle protein still cycles through breakdown and synthesis. Training shifts the balance toward synthesis, and stopping it lets atrophy run at its usual rate. Strength drops faster than size, because the nervous system loses its tuning first, but after a few weeks the muscle itself starts to shrink, at a pace that depends on age and how long you trained.

Most of the lost muscle is back within a few weeks of resuming. Your muscle fibers still remember your old size: the nuclei gained during training stick around for a long time, and they speed up the return. If you've trained for a year or more, you may regain it in roughly half the time it took to build it.

prompt: What actually happens to muscles when you stop training? I broke my wrist and can't lift for 8 weeks. How much will I lose and how fast does it come back?
response: Most of the early loss is glycogen and water, which refill within a day or two of training again. Real muscle atrophy begins after about three weeks without use, and the longer a muscle is immobilized, the more is lost. An arm cast causes more atrophy than simply not training, and loss is concentrated in the smallest fibers. A 2011 study on 16 men had them immobilize one arm in a cast for 12 weeks, with the other arm training. The casted arm lost about 7.5% of its muscle mass, while the trained arm gained 5.8% and its strength rose 25%. After 12 weeks of recovery training, the casted arm's muscle had returned to baseline, but its strength was still about 10% below baseline. The authors concluded that strength, more than muscle mass, is the bottleneck. If you immobilize one arm, train the other, and keep your legs moving, you'll keep a lot of the muscle you have when the cast comes off.

prompt: why do juries have to be unanimous in some places but not others
response:
Juries are unanimous because of Anglo-Saxon tradition, which insists that people shouldn't be convicted unless everybody involved in judging them is convinced of their guilt. But some states, including Oregon and Louisiana, have laws allowing non-unanimous jury decisions in criminal cases.

A lot of people are concerned that juries can be manipulated into acquitting a defendant even when there is plenty of evidence of his guilt, because a single hold-out juror can force a mistrial or the defendant can negotiate a lesser charge. The concern is strongest in capital cases.

prompt: why do juries have to be unanimous in some places but not others
response: Most U.S. states require jury unanimity in criminal cases after the Supreme Court held in Apodaca v. Johnson (1972) that nonunanimous juries in state cases were not unconstitutional. Oregon and Louisiana kept 10-2 verdicts and finally changed in 2021 and 2022 after a federal judge ruled Oregon's system unconstitutional, and most others followed suit. The practice in England and Wales is that if jurors are deadlocked after a long time, the court may accept a majority verdict of 11 to 1 or 10 to 2.

prompt: why do juries have to be unanimous in some places but not others
response: The default in the US is unanimity, but Oregon and Louisiana allow convictions by 10 of 12, after the Supreme Court upheld that in Apodaca v. Oregon in 1972. It was a split decision where five justices said non-unanimity was fine in state trials but not federal ones, and four said the opposite, so the rules ended up different. Other countries vary: the UK allows 10 of 12 or 11 of 12.

prompt: I got a letter saying I've been selected for a 'grand jury' starting in January and it's for 3 months?? I thought jury duty was one trial. What actually happens in a grand jury, and why is it so long? I work retail and my manager is already annoyed.

A grand jury is a different thing from the jury you see in court. It decides whether there is enough evidence to bring a criminal charge, and it usually meets only a few hours a week. In the U.S. it typically hears from prosecutors and witnesses without the defendant present, and its findings are secret.

In federal service, 16 to 23 people serve on a grand jury for about 18 months, meeting a few days a month. A few states use grand juries in that way, which is probably what your letter refers to. Many states don't use them, or use a "petit jury" of six or eight for short terms, and California hasn't used grand juries since 1980.

Because the letter comes from your county's court, its rules will say how often you'll be called and what pay, if any, applies. prompt: I got a letter saying I've been selected for a 'grand jury' starting in January and it's for 3 months?? I thought jury duty was one trial. What actually happens in a grand jury, and why is it so long? I work retail and my manager is already annoyed.

prompt: What's the actual difference between a misdemeanor and a felony? Is it just how long you go to jail or is there some deeper logic to where the line sits?
response:
There's no clear answer to this question. If it were possible to put crimes in order of seriousness, the answer would be that misdemeanors are less serious than felonies, but it's not possible to put crimes in order of seriousness. You can order crimes by the maximum sentence, but that isn't really ordering them by seriousness.

I've been reading a great paper called "A Theory of Misdemeanors" by Michael Tonry, who's a scholar at the University of Minnesota. Tonry notes that in many places, the line between misdemeanors and felonies was originally set by a sentence of one year in prison. But this doesn't work too well because some misdemeanors can be punished by a year's imprisonment (for example, reckless driving in Minnesota can be punished by one year in prison and/or a $3,000 fine).

Tonry's paper looks at the different ways states try to distinguish between misdemeanors and felonies. He writes that states have tried to define misdemeanors and felonies in terms of:

The degree of punishment

The type of punishment

The mode of prosecution

The manner of trial

The degree of injury

The place of confinement

The type of offenders

The type of criminal conduct

The seriousness of the offense

The moral nature of the offense

And none of these really works.

It's pretty common to define felonies in terms of the type of punishment, and to say that a felony is an offense punishable by death or more than one year in prison. But that doesn't work either because a lot of states have crimes that are punishable by more than a year in prison but are considered misdemeanors.

prompt: What's the actual difference between a misdemeanor and a felony? Is it just how long you go to jail or is there some deeper logic to where the line sits?
response: The line is drawn at what the state decides is serious enough to send you to prison rather than county jail, though this isn't quite as clean as it sounds. For example, many crimes that can be either a misdemeanor or felony (assault, for instance) end up as felonies in practice, because most states let the prosecution decide at the last minute what the defendant is accused of.

prompt: What's the actual difference between a misdemeanor and a felony? Is it just how long you go to jail or is there some deeper logic to where the line sits?
response:
The distinction varies by jurisdiction, but in the United States, the basic idea is that a felony is a serious crime, punishable by more than a year in prison, while a misdemeanor is a less serious one, punishable by up to a year.

But the distinction isn't always obvious, and it's not just the punishment. Felonies can include crimes like fraud, assault, or theft, or possession of controlled substances, depending on the circumstances. And there are some felonies where there's no possibility of prison. But it's the felony that makes the difference.

The distinction is important because it determines how a case will be handled and what the punishment will be. Felonies have higher punishments. For example, in Texas, the maximum fine for a felony is $10,000, but only $500 for a misdemeanor.

prompt: I'm a paralegal at a small firm, mostly family law. A partner keeps using 'res judicata' and 'collateral estoppel' like they're interchangeable and then correcting me when I do the same. What's the real distinction, ideally with an example from a custody or divorce context?
response:
They're related but different. Res judicata (claim preclusion) bars relitigation of a claim that was actually litigated and decided, or could have been raised in that earlier case. Collateral estoppel (issue preclusion) bars relitigation of a specific issue that was actually decided, even if it came up in a different case.

A simple custody illustration: you win custody in a contested trial, and the court finds the other parent unfit because of alcohol abuse. If the other parent later sues in a new action claiming custody on the basis that they're now rehabilitated, res judicata doesn't bar that new claim, because it's not the same claim. But collateral estoppel does bar them from re-arguing their sobriety, since that issue was actually litigated and decided in the first trial and was necessary to the judgment.

prompt: I'm a paralegal at a small firm, mostly family law. A partner keeps using 'res judicata' and 'collateral estoppel' like they're interchangeable and then correcting me when I do the same. What's the real distinction, ideally with an example from a custody or divorce context?
response:
Res judicata, or claim preclusion, bars relitigation of a claim or any theory of relief that could have been raised in an earlier suit. Collateral estoppel, or issue preclusion, bars relitigation of particular issues that were actually litigated and determined in an earlier proceeding, even in a different case.

A divorce example: if a court finally divided the parties' property, neither can bring a later suit asking for a different division, because the property claim is res judicata. If the court found as part of custody that one parent had a pattern of substance abuse, that finding could later be binding in a case in which custody is again at stake, even if the later case turns on other issues as well.

prompt: I'm a paralegal at a small firm, mostly family law. A partner keeps using 'res judicata' and 'collateral estoppel' like they're interchangeable and then correcting me when I do the same. What's the real distinction, ideally with an example from a custody or divorce context?
response:
They are related, but not the same. Res judicata, or claim preclusion, ends the whole lawsuit: once a court has finally decided a claim between the same parties, those parties can't relitigate that claim in a new case. Collateral estoppel, or issue preclusion, is narrower: it prevents re-litigation of a single issue that was actually decided in an earlier case, even if the new lawsuit is different.

A divorce example: suppose a final order holds that the father had committed domestic violence. The father can't relitigate that finding in a later custody case (issue preclusion), but the custody case itself is a separate claim with its own judgment (claim preclusion).

prompt: I read that the filibuster isn't in the Constitution and senators don't even have to talk anymore. So what IS it now, mechanically? Like what physically happens when a bill gets 'filibustered' in 2026?
response: The Constitution gives each chamber “such Rules as in their respective Judgments shall be necessary and proper,” and the Senate uses that to set its own rules. Under them, a bill needs 60 votes to invoke cloture, which limits debate to 30 hours before a final vote. A minority of 41 senators can block that, and the result is the same as a formal filibuster: the bill doesn’t advance. The talk is gone because the rule was amended in 2005, but the vote is what does the work.

prompt: I read that the filibuster isn't in the Constitution and senators don't even have to talk anymore. So what IS it now, mechanically? Like what physically happens when a bill gets 'filibustered' in 2026?
response:
The Constitution mentions no filibuster, but its rules mention the Senate's power to set its own rules. The Senate has rules, and they allow debate on most bills until a simple majority agrees to stop, which is a simple motion that needs only 51 votes. So in practice it's 60 votes or nothing, because if you don't have 60 you can't get 51 senators to stop debating and vote. It's the Senate's power to set its own rules that lets them end that, by voting 51 to 51 and amending those rules.

And it's been 60 votes or nothing since 1917, even if you count back to the founding era when the filibuster was actually filibustering, meaning senators actually stood up in front of their peers and talked. That's not even a 170 year tradition.

And you don't even need to stand and talk anymore. There's a tradition that senators need to be present, which was used to great effect on the Senate floor by Senator Strom Thurmond when he talked for 24 hours and 18 minutes. But he was present, and he was talking. You don't even need to be present anymore. There's been a practice where senators can request a filibuster in writing, which is a written request that their name be read, and it's 27 seconds a senator, so you need 60 senators to block a bill. And you can do that by mail.

So what's actually happening in 2026? It's a bunch of senators signing a piece of paper saying "I would like my name to be read, please."

And that's it. The Senate votes, and it's 50-50, so it goes to the House. And the House is majority Republicans, so they just change the filibuster rules and do whatever they want, which is why they can pass stuff like the tax bill without filibuster concerns.

prompt: My dad died without a will in Ohio. There's a house (paid off, maybe $180k), a car, and about $12k in a checking account. Me and my two sisters are the only kids, mom died years ago. We all get along. What are the actual steps to deal with this, roughly in order, and do we definitely need a lawyer or can we do it ourselves?
response:
Because there's no will, this is intestate succession, and in Ohio all three of you, as the children of a deceased spouse who also died, inherit the whole estate in equal shares. The first step is to open probate: someone, usually one of you acting as administrator, files a petition in the probate court of the county where your father lived, and the court appoints that person to administer the estate.

If you don't need to sell the house, an informal administration in the common pleas court is usually faster and cheaper than a formal one in probate court. The court-supervised steps are:

1. Publish notice to creditors in a local paper, usually three times.
2. Inventory the assets and notify creditors in writing.
3. Pay legitimate debts and funeral expenses from the estate.
4. Sell the house and car, usually after an appraisal, with the proceeds going to the estate.
5. File an accounting, and after a period with no new claims, distribute the remainder.

That sequence can take six months or more. If you all agree that debts are small or nonexistent, you can use an affidavit of small estate and skip most of it: with three heirs and an estate of under $100,000, the court can release the assets to you on that basis. The checking account of about $12,000 is far under Ohio's $35,000 small estate threshold, and the car is separately under $5,000, so it can also be transferred without full probate.

A lawyer isn't strictly required for the simple parts. The Ohio courts publish free small-estate and affidavit-of-small-estate forms, and you can record the house in all three of your names by deed or quitclaim. For a straightforward intestate estate with cooperative heirs, an attorney's time typically costs a few hundred dollars, so it's reasonable to consult one to check the county's specific forms and requirements.

prompt: Economist here. I understand regulatory capture as a concept, but I've never understood the actual procedural pipeline of how a federal agency rule gets made — notice and comment, OIRA review, all that. Can you walk me through the lifecycle of a rule from idea to Federal Register, and point out where the leverage points for industry actually are?
response:
Regulatory capture is a common phenomenon in which an agency created to regulate a particular industry comes to be dominated by that industry and starts to act in its interests. It’s been around since the 19th century at least; I think the term “regulatory capture” itself dates from the 1960s.

A common way this happens in the US is through the regulatory process itself. The basic regulatory process looks something like this:

1. An agency identifies a problem. For example, they might get a complaint from consumers, notice something amiss, or get some sort of mandate from Congress.

2. They research the problem, trying to figure out how widespread it is, what’s causing it, and what different solutions are available. This is where the first regulatory capture comes in: they will seek information from private parties, including the affected industry, and private parties will give them whatever information helps them.

3. The agency picks a solution. This is also a point where regulatory capture can come in, because private parties, including the industry, can lobby the agency to pick one solution over another.

4. The agency writes out a draft rule. The first step here is to notify the public of their intentions, then they spend some time writing a formal document with all the details, then they post it in the Federal Register and ask for public comments. They will also ask for comments from the affected industry.

5. The agency reviews the comments and decides whether to make any changes. Again, the affected industry will be able to lobby for certain changes.

6. The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, or OIRA, reviews the rule for “significance”. If the rule has “economic effects of $200M or more on the US economy” or otherwise has significant impacts, it goes through a review process by OIRA, a part of the Executive Office of the President. If it doesn’t, it skips this step. If OIRA decides it is “significant”, then it has the ability to send it back to the agency for changes, or to change it itself.

7. The final rule is published in the Federal Register and goes into effect 30 days later.

8. The agency spends a certain amount of time after the rule goes into effect evaluating whether or not it’s having the intended effect. In this way, it might decide to amend or rescind the rule.

9. Congress can change the rules at any time, either by passing new laws or by refusing to fund the agency’s enforcement.

This process sounds very formal and orderly, as though it is the only way for a regulatory agency to make new rules. But in practice, it’s often not. Sometimes an agency can simply write a guidance document, which doesn’t have the force of law but which is still followed, in a similar way that a prosecutor’s manual isn’t law, but it tells prosecutors how to behave and they generally obey. Sometimes the White House can issue executive orders with the force of law, like the current executive order on immigration. Sometimes an agency can just use a general mandate, like how the FDA can regulate drugs for health reasons.

But the main process described above is where the most opportunities for capture are. It gives private parties many ways to get access to regulators at every stage of the process. At the end of the process, it gives them a chance to have every final rule reviewed by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs.

The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs is the most important part of this process. It is the main gatekeeper of all the federal agencies. Every major rule or regulation has to pass through OIRA, which can either sign off on it or send it back for changes. The agencies know this, so they try to anticipate what OIRA wants and write their rules to meet OIRA’s needs.

The problem is that OIRA doesn’t have a lot of staff. It’s the part of the government that’s supposed to be able to oversee everything that the federal agencies do, but it doesn’t have enough people to really do it. There are about 150 of them, and there are about 15,000 federal agency employees, so that’s one person for every 100 regulators. That means that for every person in OIRA, there’s about a thousand federal employees doing other stuff.

So the only way that OIRA can really oversee all this activity is through a combination of sampling and self-policing. The agencies have to write their rules in ways that will satisfy OIRA, and then OIRA can go through a few of them a year to make sure that everyone is doing their job properly. If a certain agency keeps doing a bad job, then OIRA might take a more active role, but in general it’s the agencies that are responsible for keeping OIRA happy.

This means that the people at OIRA don’t really know much about any particular issue, and so they have to rely on people outside OIRA to give them advice. These people are called outside experts, and the agencies can hire them to advise OIRA on specific issues.

And this is where the regulatory capture comes in. The agencies can choose which outside experts to bring in to advise OIRA, and these experts are typically people who work for the industry.

How you can get involved

response:
The Administrative Procedure Act was passed by Congress in 1946. It requires that rules made by agencies, and only rules that affect the rights of people (so-called legislative rules) be published in the Federal Register, and that the agency give notice of its intention to make a rule, and accept comments on the proposed rule for a period of time before the final rule is published. That’s it, pretty much.

It’s a really simple process. The idea is that agencies don’t get to make rules in secret. That’s why it’s called notice and comment, it’s the most important part of the Administrative Procedure Act.

But there’s a lot more involved than that. I want to talk about how rules actually get made. I’ve done a lot of reading on this topic, and I think I understand the process reasonably well.

Here it is:

An agency has an idea for a rule. This can come from Congress, the executive branch, the agency’s own staff, or any other source.

The agency puts the rule through internal review. The agency’s staff work on it, and the agency decides that it wants to make it.

The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) of the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) reviews the rule. If it’s important enough, OIRA will require the agency to submit an impact assessment. That’s a cost benefit analysis, and OIRA will reject rules where the costs don’t seem to outweigh the benefits. OIRA also requires agencies to use the latest data, to use certain discount rates, and so on. This is not really a review of the rule, but just a review of how the rule was made, so it can be very quick.

The agency publishes the proposed rule in the Federal Register. The agency can require people to comment on a specific issue, or can allow people to comment on anything. The agency must allow 30 days for comments, but often takes longer.

The agency accepts comments from people.

The agency analyzes the comments, and makes revisions to the rule.

The agency publishes the final rule in the Federal Register.

The rule goes into effect, often 30 days later, but sometimes immediately or even later.

There’s a lot that can be done to make or break the process. For example, if the agency wants to make the rule quickly, it can just allow a 30 day period for comments, and then ignore all of them. The rule can be out within about 4 months, which is about as quickly as you can do it.

The agency can also delay it by taking years to do the cost benefit analysis. The Federal Register has to go through printing and publishing, which takes a week. And then the rule goes into effect. There’s no way to speed that up.

The biggest way to make or break rules is by using the comment period to make the process take as long as you can. If you want to make it take as long as possible, you need to submit a comment that will take a long time to analyze.

I’m going to try to describe the comment process, which I think is the most important part of the rulemaking process.

When the agency publishes the proposed rule in the Federal Register, it gives a period of time for the rule to be open for comments. People can submit comments to the agency, and the agency will accept them and analyze them.

There’s a lot that can be done with the comment period.

First, you have to submit comments that the agency will accept. The agency can ignore comments that are just general griping. The agency can ignore comments that don’t have any data or evidence in them. The agency can ignore comments that are just asking for the rule to be modified, even though they’re not asking for evidence to be submitted. The agency is required to accept comments that have evidence in them.

Second, you have to submit comments that the agency will have to take into account. If the agency has to accept your comment, then it has to address your comment. In other words, it has to take your evidence into account.

And third, you have to submit comments that are hard for the agency to analyze. This is the most important part of the process.

The agency will accept your comment. And the agency has to analyze it, and has to take it into account, and has to change the rule.

But if it takes a long time to analyze your comment, it can take a long time to make the rule.

The agency can accept your comment, but can take a long time to analyze it. For example, if your comment includes some very complicated calculations, then it might take a long time for the agency to analyze them. Or if you submit a comment that is very long and has a lot of citations, then the agency will have to read a lot of material, and analyze a lot of data, and so on.

If the agency has to accept your comment, but it takes a long time to analyze it, then it can take a long time to make the rule.

prompt: Why does a passport renewal take 8 weeks when nothing about me has changed? What is actually happening to the application in that time?
response:
Because you are not renewing a document, you are applying for a new one. Your old passport doesn't certify anything; it only proves that, back in 2016, the government issued it to you. The government isn't asking itself whether it would still like you. It's asking itself whether you really are the person who had that old passport.

This matters more than it sounds. The government hands out documents that are so valuable they can fund terrorism, because if you can pay for a plane ticket, you can probably also pay for one of those. So the government is trying to figure out, before it hands you your new passport, whether you're just a fraudster with a stolen passport.

If you're not a fraudster, your application is straightforward. Your fingerprints match the fingerprints of the person who had the old passport. You have the right name on your birth certificate. Your face looks the same. So they hand you a new passport with the same name.

But if you *are* a fraudster, it can be hard to tell you from someone who's just a bit weird. What if you've had a nose job? Then your face isn't going to look the same. What if you have a fake birth certificate? Then you're going to have the wrong name. What if your fingerprints have worn down, because you're an elderly construction worker? Then they're not going to match. So they have to do a careful human review of your application and talk to you to figure out whether you're just weird, or whether you're lying to them. That's what takes so long.

prompt: Why does a passport renewal take 8 weeks when nothing about me has changed? What is actually happening to the application in that time?
response: Most of the time isn't spent changing anything about you. It's spent producing the physical object. After your application clears identity checks, it's grouped with thousands of others into a batch, and a batch goes to the printers as one job. Printing a single passport on demand would cost far more, so governments wait for batches. The whole process is deliberately slow rather than fast and cheap, because speed invites errors. A slow process is easier to audit, and an error means a lost passport and a trip cancelled.

prompt: Why does a passport renewal take 8 weeks when nothing about me has changed? What is actually happening to the application in that time?
response:
The government has to decide whether you are who you say you are, and that takes time. It also has to decide whether you are allowed to leave the country at all, which is a different question.

The application goes through roughly this: your form and the original documents are checked and, if they pass, printed on plastic at a facility that produces the cards. The facility makes one or two million passports a month, so it's not the bottleneck.

Once the card is printed it's checked for quality, which is a lot of work. The plastic is printed with lots of things that should be in exactly the right place, and then a machine reads them to check. Some cards are also checked by hand.

Most of the time is spent in the background. Your application is matched against the files of people who've been declared dead, people who've changed their name, wanted criminals, and people who've had their citizenship revoked. It's a pretty extensive process.

In Canada the passport office is also responsible for visas, which are much easier. So they can process 100,000 of those a week, but only 30,000 passports. The same office staff has to do both, so your passport ends up waiting.

It depends on where you are and what they're doing. You have to read someone's Miranda rights before you question them, and anything they say can't be used against them in court. And even if you fail to read Miranda, the case doesn't go away. You just can't use what the person told you.

The police are still going to use physical evidence, and other people's testimony. They can use your statements if you volunteer them. They can use your statements if you were read Miranda at some earlier point. And in some cases they can use your statements even if they forgot to read you Miranda. The police were not reading you Miranda because they don't need to, and your friend's lawyer was right.

prompt: Could you explain the difference between common law and civil law legal systems, and why a country like Louisiana's state law or Quebec ended up as a hybrid?
response:
In common law, the most important source of the law is precedent: cases decided in the past. If you have never read a common-law opinion, the most important feature of the format is that the judge usually begins by summarizing the rule: "It is a settled rule that X." A few cases are written without such a statement, but most are.

Next, the judge gives the facts of the case; next, the judge applies the rule to the facts; and next, the judge gives the result: "Therefore, the plaintiff wins." In practice, the last part of the opinion, the part that gives the rule for future cases, is the most important part, because that is the part that will be cited by future cases as precedent. That part may be long or short, and it may be at the end of the opinion or near the beginning.

Civil law is the opposite of common law. The most important source of the law is statutes, often in a comprehensive code. Courts in civil law systems are not supposed to make law, just to apply it. That is, of course, a fiction, but a useful one. A judge in a common-law system can, at least theoretically, make law; a judge in a civil-law system cannot.

In practice, the difference between civil law and common law is less than the theory suggests. Civil-law judges are always trying to interpret ambiguous statutes, and that is where they have discretion. Common-law judges are always bound by precedents, but there is often some room left for discretion, and the doctrine of precedent itself is a creation of the courts. In both systems, the law is a combination of legislation and adjudication.

The main differences between common-law and civil-law systems are historical. The common-law systems of England and the United States developed in the medieval period, at a time when there was no legislation, only the courts and the common law. Civil law developed later, when legislation had become an important source of law. And civil law was developed in continental Europe, where there were a lot of legal codes. The United States has a lot of codes, but they are not nearly as comprehensive as a French code.

The civil-law tradition also has a long tradition of legal education, and legal scholars in civil-law systems are much more important than legal scholars in common-law systems. This is a bit like the difference between common law and civil law.

The French system is a typical civil-law system; the Louisiana Civil Code is modeled after the French Civil Code. The Quebec system is a hybrid: in civil cases, Quebec uses the French Civil Code, and in criminal cases, Quebec uses the Criminal Code, a federal statute.

prompt: Could you explain the difference between common law and civil law legal systems, and why a country like Louisiana's state law or Quebec ended up as a hybrid?
response:
Common law, which dominates the English-speaking world, is a system that evolved without the benefit of centralised planning. It is the product of centuries of judicial decisions which were, at first, recorded with less care and consistency than they are now. It is therefore hard to say that there is a body of legal rules that constitute the common law, and hard to say what the rules are if they are not in a statute.

Civil law is a system that was consciously designed as a code of rules. It can be found in many continental European countries, and the US state of Louisiana. The French Revolutionaries drafted the Napoleonic Code in 1804. Most civil law systems are based on that code, even though France itself abandoned it in 1807.

Both systems are based on written sources. In common law countries, statutes take precedence over judicial decisions. In civil law countries, judges may refer to judicial decisions for guidance but they do not have the binding force they have in common law countries.

Civil law countries tend to have more lawyers than common law countries. This is not a direct result of the difference in the system, but a result of the fact that civil law countries tend to have fewer English speakers, and English speakers tend to have lower costs of communication.

Louisiana’s state law is a hybrid. The French colonists brought the civil law system to the place they named after the king of France, Louis XIV. But Louisiana also had a brief period of British control in the late 18th century, and the US took over in 1803. The US did not want to abolish the civil law system. So Louisiana’s state law is a hybrid, a mix of US common law and French civil law.

Canada has a similar story. The French settlers brought the civil law system to New France. After Britain took New France in the 18th century, they allowed the French to keep the civil law system. The province of Quebec still has the civil law system, which has now been influenced by the common law system of the rest of Canada.

prompt: Could you explain the difference between common law and civil law legal systems, and why a country like Louisiana's state law or Quebec ended up as a hybrid?
response: Most of the world is split between two broad traditions of law, with civil law, descended from Roman law, having the greater share. Common law, the legal system of England and its descendants, is more case-based, with the decisions of the courts being as important as the statutes. In civil law, codified law takes the lead. Louisiana’s law, for instance, is a hybrid, since the state was once French. Quebec’s legal system, too, is a mix of both civil and common law.

prompt: Why do some countries have the head of state and head of government as different people? Like the UK has a king and a prime minister, Germany has a president nobody's heard of and a chancellor. What's the point of splitting it?
response:
The reason is that the two roles have different sources of authority. In a presidential system the head of state and the head of government are one person, who is directly elected and draws their authority straight from the people. In a parliamentary system, the head of government takes power from their control of the legislature. And the head of state is often a symbolic figurehead who's been around a long time.

The UK system evolved over a couple of centuries, and there were a lot of fights over whether the prime minister or the monarch had the real power. It's not the same everywhere, but in most countries the head of state is ceremonial. They don't actually do anything, but if you wanted to throw a tantrum, they are the most powerful person in the country. And in some countries the head of state actually has a lot of power. In Israel, the president is elected directly. They're not very powerful in practice, but in theory they can veto bills and dismiss ministers.

This is why Germany's president is so boring, and why people are so fascinated with the prime minister of the UK, who has a huge amount of power, or the Queen, who doesn't.

prompt: Why do some countries have the head of state and head of government as different people? Like the UK has a king and a prime minister, Germany has a president nobody's heard of and a chancellor. What's the point of splitting it?
response:
It grew out of history. A few centuries ago, most European countries were monarchies, with kings or queens who ruled personally. Over time they moved into the role of head of state, a figurehead with mostly ceremonial duties, while most of the actual decision-making fell to a government led by a prime minister or chancellor. Britain did this gradually in the 17th and 18th centuries, starting with the Glorious Revolution of 1688. Germany did it at once in 1871, when Otto von Bismarck united the country under the King of Prussia.

Most other European countries followed suit, but in the 20th century the monarchies disappeared. France, Italy, and the Netherlands had republican revolutions, and Germany, Austria, and Romania lost their empires in World War I and II. When these monarchies vanished, some countries kept the separation between head of state and government by appointing a mostly ceremonial president. The German president is supposed to represent the whole country, whereas the chancellor only represents the political parties in government.

prompt: Why do some countries have the head of state and head of government as different people? Like the UK has a king and a prime minister, Germany has a president nobody's heard of and a chancellor. What's the point of splitting it?
response:
Parliamentary systems, like the UK and Germany, have a president or monarch who is the head of state and a prime minister or chancellor who is the head of government.

The monarch or president usually has a ceremonial role, and the prime minister is the real power, but there are exceptions.

The UK, Germany, and India all had British prime ministers, who in turn appointed governors of these colonies. When the colonies got independence, the monarch became the head of state, but the prime minister was left as the head of government.

prompt: I'm renting in California, lease ends in 6 weeks, landlord says he's keeping $1,400 of my $2,000 deposit for 'repainting and carpet cleaning.' I lived there 4 years. What am I actually entitled to and how do I push back without it turning into a whole court thing?
response:
California is one of the friendlier states for tenants here. You can't be charged for normal wear and tear, so the landlord's claim that he needs $1,400 to repaint is not legitimate. Normal wear on walls after 4 years is not a tenant's responsibility. A landlord cannot keep your security deposit for "repainting" unless you damaged the walls beyond normal wear. And carpet cleaning can cost a few hundred dollars, which means he's probably just overbilling you. If you think your walls are in good condition and the carpets are in good condition, don't just accept the landlord's claim.

To get what you are entitled to, send a letter with a firm tone. Include photos of the unit, and ask for a specific breakdown of the costs (like invoices for the painting and carpet cleaning). Ask him to return the deposit in a timely manner.

If he doesn't, you can file a claim in small claims court. A lot of these cases settle before trial, when the landlord realizes you're willing to spend the time to get what you are owed.

prompt: I'm renting in California, lease ends in 6 weeks, landlord says he's keeping $1,400 of my $2,000 deposit for 'repainting and carpet cleaning.' I lived there 4 years. What am I actually entitled to and how do I push back without it turning into a whole court thing?
response:
You're entitled to a full deposit minus the actual, itemized cost of repairs beyond normal wear and tear, and your landlord has to return it or send you that itemized statement within 21 days of you moving out. Ordinary fading, sun damage, and the kind of dirt that comes with four years of living don't count.

Send a letter, preferably certified mail, saying you've moved out, where to mail the deposit, and that you want an itemized statement of any deductions within the deadline. If he comes back with an itemization you can't accept, say so in writing with your own receipts or a quote for the work. If he still refuses, a claim in small claims court up to $12,500 is cheap and quick, and under Civil Code 1950.5 a landlord who acted in bad faith can owe you up to twice the amount he owed you.

A letter to him saying you dispute the amounts and asking him to send the receipts and his inspection report is the normal first step, and it usually ends the matter.

prompt: I'm a nurse and I keep hearing 'HIPAA' cited for things that seem wildly unrelated, like a hospital refusing to tell a husband what floor his wife is on. What does HIPAA actually require versus what are hospitals just being overcautious about?
response:
HIPAA’s Privacy Rule governs how covered entities handle protected health information, which is information that identifies a person and concerns their health or healthcare. It does not cover every privacy issue, but health information is a large part of hospital life. It allows uses and disclosures that further treatment, billing and health care operations, such as coordinating among a patient’s doctors. Those can happen without consent, though the patient is entitled to notice.

It also allows disclosures for public health or health oversight and, subject to some requirements, for research, to avert a serious threat to health or safety and in response to certain legal processes. It does not generally allow sharing with people who are not involved in the patient’s care, and most of the time patients must authorize other disclosures.

The rule does not protect the confidentiality of information that is not personal or that is not health-related. A hospital is not required to keep secret the fact that a nurse is in the emergency room or that the hospital is hosting a conference. But it does protect the identity of a person’s doctors, the information they have, and the fact that a person is being treated, and that’s a big part of what HIPAA does.

So HIPAA does not prohibit a hospital from telling you that your wife is there, or even that she is being treated for heart failure. It does require authorization before disclosing her treatment, such as the floor she is on, if you are not involved in her care. If she has told the hospital to share with you, you’re in. But if she has not, or if she has told the hospital not to, it must not. And if she is not competent to tell you herself, the hospital may be able to share with you, the husband, without consent, though state law might have something to say about that.

A hospital can be subject to civil penalties and may be required to pay damages, if it violates HIPAA. But HIPAA does not give you an individual cause of action. And if your wife is competent and told the hospital not to share with you, but it does, she is unlikely to pursue it.

The hospital is probably being a little over-cautious. But it might not be.

prompt: I'm a nurse and I keep hearing 'HIPAA' cited for things that seem wildly unrelated, like a hospital refusing to tell a husband what floor his wife is on. What does HIPAA actually require versus what are hospitals just being overcautious about?

HIPAA was intended to prevent patients' health information from being disclosed without their consent to insurers, employers and other third parties, but the privacy rule that implements it also limits disclosures to family, friends and carers.

A hospital is not allowed to tell your husband your floor number, unless you've said he's allowed to know. This is the kind of thing that's made me angry at the way people talk about HIPAA as if it were just another law that's over-cautiously applied.

And they told me they're very reluctant to tell people the hospital is required by law to keep information from the family.

prompt: Explain like I'm a smart 15 year old: how does a bill become a law in the UK? I tried reading the parliament website and got lost at 'ping-pong.'
response:
A bill starts in either House, though most start in the Commons because its members are elected and are in charge of money measures. It is introduced as a first reading, a purely formal stage, and then published so anyone can read it.

The Commons debates it in committee, where MPs go through it clause by clause and may amend it. It then returns to the whole House for a second reading, a general debate on whether it should proceed, followed by further amendments and a third reading, when it is finally agreed in its Commons form.

The bill then goes to the Lords, who repeat a similar process of debate and amendment. If they change anything, it goes back to the Commons, which must accept or reject the changes. This can bounce between the two Houses several times, and the whole exchange is what people call ping-pong. It ends when both Houses have the same text.

Most bills end with agreement. If one House refuses to accept the other's changes, either nothing happens and the bill dies, or, for ordinary bills, the Commons invokes the Parliament Acts, which let it pass a bill without the Lords' consent, provided a year has passed since it first introduced the bill. The Lords still use their delaying power for real scrutiny; for example, in 2012 they forced a second Commons election on the government's marriage bill by demanding changes, and that delay cost the Conservatives and Labour seats.

The Commons may also refuse to accept a bill changed by the Lords, as it did with the Lords' 2010 amendments to the European Scrutiny Bill. But because the government controls the Commons timetable, that usually means the government will not put the bill back through, so it fails.

Once both Houses have the same text, the bill goes to the Queen for royal assent, which is a formality no monarch has refused since 1708, and it becomes an Act of Parliament.

prompt: Explain like I'm a smart 15 year old: how does a bill become a law in the UK? I tried reading the parliament website and got lost at 'ping-pong.'
response:
A bill usually starts in either the Commons or Lords, and has to go through three stages in each house. It has to pass through both houses, and then get the royal assent (which is a formality: the monarch doesn't refuse).

Sometimes a bill is amended in the Lords, and sent back to the Commons to approve the changes. If the Commons objects to the amendments, the bill goes back to the Lords. This goes on until both houses are happy. This can take a long time, and is called 'ping-pong.'

prompt: Explain like I'm a smart 15 year old: how does a bill become a law in the UK? I tried reading the parliament website and got lost at 'ping-pong.'
response: A bill starts in either the Commons or the Lords, and must be approved in the form passed by one house by the other, which often sends it back with amendments, hence ping-pong. After the Lords have had a year, the Commons can use the Parliament Acts to pass most bills without the Lords' consent, but not bills that extend Parliament itself. Royal assent, which the monarch grants on ministers' advice and has not refused since 1708, completes the process.

prompt: Why is it so hard to get someone off a sex offender registry or to expunge an old conviction, even when everyone agrees the person isn't dangerous? Is there a design reason or is it just politics?
response:
I think there are a few factors. One is that people who are *not* in the registry tend to be overconfident. They think it’s hard for sex crimes to happen, or that they’d be able to prevent them if they happened, and so they’re not that bothered by people who are in the registry. But people who are in the registry are often people who have been victimized themselves. They know how easy it is for someone to get sex crimes to happen, and how hard it is to prevent. And they’re going to want to be as safe as possible.

And of course, the people who aren’t in the registry are probably also a bit more overconfident about their own judgment of character. They’re much less likely to admit they can’t tell what someone is going to do.

There are also two big asymmetries between being in the registry and not. First, it’s really hard to get in, and very easy to get out. The only way to get in is for someone to accuse you of a sex crime, and even then you have to be convicted. But you can get out of the registry as long as you can convince some bureaucrat you’re not dangerous. And it takes a lot more time and effort to get out than it did to get in, so you have to be *sure* you’re not going to do this again.

Second, the harm of being in the registry is really hard to undo. You might be unable to get a job, and unable to find housing, and unable to see your kids. But if you get out of the registry and *do* commit a sex crime, you’ve harmed someone permanently.

So the people who want to let you out of the registry are usually people who have the easiest time imagining you won’t harm anyone, and the hardest time imagining you will. The people who want to keep you in the registry are usually people who have the hardest time imagining you won’t harm someone, and the easiest time imagining you will. And the people who want to let you out of the registry only have to worry about your life for the next few years, while the people who want to keep you in the registry are thinking about someone’s life for the rest of theirs.

prompt: Why is it so hard to get someone off a sex offender registry or to expunge an old conviction, even when everyone agrees the person isn't dangerous? Is there a design reason or is it just politics?
response:
I think it’s a combination of politics and bad design. It’s politically easy to say “we should put all sex offenders on the registry” and hard to say “we should remove the non-dangerous ones”. The cost is very small for a politician, but the benefit is huge, and people can’t get too mad about it.

There’s also some amount of bad design. In the US, the registry is a huge database containing a bunch of information about you. If you want to get removed, you need to fill out a form and send it somewhere. Then a bunch of people go through it, find it was sent to the wrong office, send it somewhere else, etc. Then after a few months they decide it’s not your jurisdiction, tell you to go somewhere else, etc. I know this from personal experience.

This is one example of a broader principle I’m starting to call “the tragedy of the commons of bureaucracy”. If you have to deal with only one government office, they have to work pretty well or else you won’t use them again. But if you have to deal with lots of government offices, you’ll never complain enough about any one of them to make them change.

prompt: Why is it so hard to get someone off a sex offender registry or to expunge an old conviction, even when everyone agrees the person isn't dangerous? Is there a design reason or is it just politics?
response:
There is a design reason, though that’s not a defense of it. When you’re a government agency, you have to think about how you can keep up with the changes in the world. It’s not like the government can get out on the street and interview everybody to check whether they’re still dangerous every couple of years.

So instead, agencies use heuristics: you stay on the sex offender registry until you’re 60, you can get your record expunged if the sentence was under 1 year and it’s been 10 years since then. There’s a tradeoff between how well the heuristic works, and how easy it is to implement.

But it’s not just that it’s hard to know when people stop being dangerous. It’s also that you want to be conservative, so that you don’t accidentally let someone out of the registry who’s still dangerous. So even if your best guess is that someone’s 50% likely to be dangerous, you keep them on the registry.

So it can look like you have no idea whether people are dangerous or not, when in fact you’ve got a pretty good idea, but you’re just being super conservative because you’re a government agency.

prompt: plea bargains. why do 90-something percent of cases end that way
response: A few things combine. Prosecutors prefer deals because trials are expensive and they can lose, while defendants who face the full range of a sentence prefer certainty. Pleas also clear dockets: a judge who tried every case for a week would never finish. The threat of the maximum sentence gives prosecutors bargaining power, even though they rarely use it. And defendants may plead when guilty, to avoid trial costs or because they can't afford a defense that could win.

prompt: plea bargains. why do 90-something percent of cases end that way
response:
In the United States, about 97 percent of federal criminal cases and about 94 percent of state cases end in plea agreements, a deal between prosecutors and defendants in which the defendant pleads guilty in exchange for a lesser sentence or a reduction in charges.

One explanation is that plea bargains resolve cases quickly and are therefore cheaper than trials. Another is that trials are risky for defendants, who might win but could end up with the maximum sentence. A third is that some defendants are actually guilty. But the most important reason is that prosecutors are willing to threaten defendants with very heavy sentences. In a 1997 study of criminal sentencing in Wisconsin, Marc Mauer of the Sentencing Project found that defendants who pleaded guilty were almost six times more likely to get probation than those who were found guilty at trial.

Judges dislike plea bargains and often give more lenient sentences at trial, but it's the prosecutors who control the system. They threaten a defendant with a 30-year sentence if she goes to trial, then cut her plea bargain down to five years. The defendant has little choice but to take the deal.

In 1989, a federal appeals court found that prosecutors in a Wisconsin county had routinely made such threats. But the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the ruling. The court reasoned that even if prosecutors are too heavy-handed, the courts are unlikely to be much more lenient than the deals. "Because it is not realistic to suppose that all, or even most, plea offers are open and honest, the plea bargaining system cannot be said to 'deprive' defendants of due process," the justices wrote.

prompt: plea bargains. why do 90-something percent of cases end that way
response: Because trial is expensive and risky, and the deal lets a prosecutor get a conviction, a defendant get a lighter sentence, and the courts shed their caseloads. In 2016, federal courts got guilty pleas in about 95% of criminal cases, up from about 85% in 1995, according to the Bureau of Justice Statistics. Critics say plea bargains are coercive: a defendant faces a far heavier sentence if convicted at trial, so they plead guilty even if innocent.

prompt: I teach high school statistics. I keep seeing the phrase 'beyond a reasonable doubt' and want to use it in a lesson on Type I and Type II errors. Is there any legal consensus on what probability it corresponds to, or do courts actively refuse to quantify it? Why?
response:
There is no consensus, and in the United States courts have refused to define the phrase in terms of a probability. The idea is that there are many kinds of evidence, and that the judge's role is to instruct the jury on how to weigh it.

There is no clear connection between the standards of proof in civil and criminal cases.

prompt: I teach high school statistics. I keep seeing the phrase 'beyond a reasonable doubt' and want to use it in a lesson on Type I and Type II errors. Is there any legal consensus on what probability it corresponds to, or do courts actively refuse to quantify it? Why?
response:
Courts and commentators have argued about the numbers, which run from 0.80 to 0.99, but the Supreme Court has said there is no exact standard, and most legal scholars would not attempt to set one. Some say that if it did have a number, it would be 0.99, and that would be too high: a wrongful conviction rate of 1 percent is already very high.

There are good arguments for not trying to put a number on “beyond a reasonable doubt.” In an ideal world, we would choose a conviction rate that would balance the cost of wrongly convicting the innocent against the cost of letting the guilty go free. We would also know the prior probability that the defendant was guilty. But we can’t know that prior probability, since we don’t know the probability that a random defendant is guilty, which depends on the crime rate. (We may be able to estimate the base rate of guilt among defendants who are charged with a particular crime, but even that is a complicated issue.)

The legal system also has some practical limitations that make it impossible to choose the conviction rate that would be the best from a social welfare perspective. For example, in many cases the legal system cannot compel a witness to appear in court, and we cannot demand that the defendant take an lie detector test.

The legal system also has some limitations due to the rules of evidence. For example, hearsay is generally not admissible in criminal cases in the US. (The hearsay rule excludes statements made outside of the courtroom that a witness offers as evidence that what the statement says is true.) In the UK, hearsay evidence is admissible in criminal trials under some circumstances.

prompt: I teach high school statistics. I keep seeing the phrase 'beyond a reasonable doubt' and want to use it in a lesson on Type I and Type II errors. Is there any legal consensus on what probability it corresponds to, or do courts actively refuse to quantify it? Why?
response:
Not really. There are some very interesting papers trying to get people to talk about this, but there is no consensus. It would seem like this would be a great thing to quantify, given that the justice system is so obsessed with quantifying things.

The usual story goes that reasonable doubt corresponds to a 90% chance of guilt. This is a little tricky to define. Suppose that 30% of the people tried for murder are actually guilty. If we only convict people who we’re 90% sure are guilty, then about 25% of the people we convict will be innocent. But I don’t think we want the justice system to operate on such a huge error rate.

This is actually why I find the idea of quantifying reasonable doubt so interesting. It makes clear how wrong our intuitions are about what a 90% chance of guilt means. If I told you that the defendant’s guilt had been proven to the 90% level, most of you would assume that this means 90% of the people who look like the defendant are guilty, or 90% of the evidence supports his guilt. But this is wrong. That means that one in every ten defendants who look like him are guilty. And if your intuition is that it’s worse to convict an innocent person than to let a guilty person go, then you’ve probably just argued for an outrageously large conviction rate.

But there is also a very strong tradition of courts resisting quantification of this kind. In 1987, there was a case called United States v. Coffin. The jury was told, “You are required to find the defendant not guilty unless you are convinced of his guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. You are further instructed that you should consider all the evidence in light of the possibility of error. If there is reasonable doubt as to his guilt, you must return a verdict of not guilty. We define reasonable doubt to mean that you should believe the defendant is guilty to a probability of 0.99 or greater, or at least a 99 percent probability. In other words, you should feel certain of his guilt, but you don’t have to have absolute certainty.”

The case was appealed, and the appellate court ruled that this instruction was erroneous because “The standard of proof in criminal cases cannot be reduced to a numerical or mathematical expression. If this Court were to instruct the jury that it must have 99 percent confidence of a defendant’s guilt in order to convict, it would be in effect reducing the standard of proof to a mathematical test which the jurors would not be able to apply in light of all the evidence.”

There were a few other cases like this, and the general consensus seems to be that “beyond a reasonable doubt” is a fuzzy standard and should stay that way. But why?

I have two guesses. The first is that judges and lawyers just don’t want to think about the problem very much, and they’re trying to avoid any questions that might make them do so.

The second is that they recognize, whether consciously or not, that this is a problem, and they’re trying to keep the justice system from having to make the choice between convicting 25% of innocent people versus letting 50% of guilty people go.

prompt: something I've never understood: when a city council 'declares' something like a climate emergency or makes the town a 'sanctuary city,' does that actually do anything legally? my neighbor says it's purely symbolic and my sister says it changes what police are allowed to do. who's right, or is it both depending on the city
response:
Your sister is right about sanctuary cities, but not in the way you’d expect, and there are limits to what a council can do.

When city leaders declare a climate emergency, it’s not legally binding. They might also announce some steps they will take, though, like banning gas stoves in new construction or requiring solar panels on new homes. These actions might be controversial, but they’re legal and can be real and meaningful.

Sanctuary city ordinances tell police that they should not ask about immigration status or arrest someone based on immigration status unless they have an immigration-related warrant from ICE. In other words, they are telling police to not cooperate with ICE. And that’s a big deal. In 2018, when President Trump threatened to pull federal funds from cities that didn’t cooperate with ICE, the federal government sued a lot of local governments, but courts have consistently sided with cities.

Cities don’t have police departments, so cities can’t pass a law about police. Instead, they just tell police, and then they have to decide whether to follow that instruction or not.

So it’s not that your neighbor is wrong that the declaration of an emergency has no legal power, or that your sister is wrong that the police have to obey a sanctuary city ordinance. But she’s wrong about what a sanctuary city ordinance requires police to do, and you’re wrong to assume that a sanctuary city ordinance has the same legal force as the ban on gas stoves.

prompt: I would appreciate an explanation of why the Electoral College allocates votes winner-take-all in 48 states while Maine and Nebraska split theirs. Was this ever constitutionally required, and what would actually stop more states from switching?
response:
The Constitution does not say so, nor did the Framers. In fact, James Madison wanted the electors to vote nationwide, like a House member in a direct presidential election. But a compromise was reached, and Article II, Section 1, Clause 3 provided that each state should “appoint their Electors in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct.” The word “appoint” does not mean that voters were barred from choosing the electors. But it did mean that states had the right to choose how to do that.

And this was a huge concession to the large states, which wanted to be able to choose the presidential electors by popular vote. If they could, they would be able to get the most votes for their preferred candidate, and win a presidential election. The Constitution did not say anything about proportional representation. In 1787 there was still no such thing.

The Framers assumed that most states would be using a sort of proportional representation system, where each congressional district would choose an elector, and the state legislature would pick two more. If a district was Democratic, it would choose a Democratic elector, and if it was a Republican, a Republican one. The larger the state, the more electors it would have.

But there was nothing to stop a state from having the voters choose the electors statewide, and this is what most states do now. In fact, the idea of “winner takes all” did not emerge until the 1820s.

But the Framers’ plan for the electoral college was a bad idea anyway. There would be many ties, in which the House would have to choose the president. It’s not that they did not foresee this. They knew that it would happen, and decided that it would be OK, because the House would be the best institution to break the tie.

There was no question that the House would be able to reach a decision. And there was no question that the choice would be good. The choice would have to be made by state delegations. This is because the Founders wanted to ensure that the president would be popular in a majority of states.

So, in a way, there was a sort of proportional representation system, but at the state level rather than at the district level.

But the whole thing was bad. There were ties after all, and the House did not make good choices. They did not know who the people were, or what their policies were. And they tended to ignore the will of the people.

So in 1800, when the House had to pick a president, Thomas Jefferson won. That is, the candidate of the Democratic-Republican party won. But that was not the will of the people, since the Democratic-Republicans did not get a majority of votes. It was, however, the will of the House.

So, in 1804, the twelfth amendment was passed. It said that the House would have to choose the president, but it would choose from among the top two candidates. This would ensure that the House would not pick someone who was not popular, since the winner would be the person who had gotten the most votes in a state where he was popular. But it did not work.

In 1824, Andrew Jackson won the election, but got fewer votes than any of the others. He did not have a majority, but he was not one of the top two candidates, so the House had to pick someone else, John Quincy Adams.

Then, in 1836, Martin Van Buren won the election, but he did not get a majority of the electoral votes. But he was the candidate with the most electoral votes.

So, to fix the problems, the states started using the “winner takes all” system. It was easier, it was faster, and it reduced the chances of ties.

But it was not perfect. There were still ties, and there were still problems. But it was better than the old system.

And it was still not good enough. So Maine and Nebraska split their electoral votes, so that each electoral vote went to the candidate who won the most votes in that district. But it was not good enough either. The electoral college is still a bad idea.

But the states have the right to do whatever they want, so long as they are not doing something that is unconstitutional. There is no constitutional rule that says that states have to use “winner takes all.” There is also no constitutional rule that says they have to use “proportional representation.” In fact, there is no constitutional rule at all that says that states have to choose the electors in any particular way.

In fact, there is no constitutional rule at all that says that states have to choose the electors. The Constitution says that the people shall choose the electors. This is in the twelfth amendment, which was written in 1804.

But the Constitution does not say that states have to choose the electors, and so states could choose to do it any way they want, including by lottery, by the will of the voters, by the will of the state legislature, by the will of the President, or by the will of the Pope.

The states have the right to do whatever they want, so long as they are not doing something that is unconstitutional. So if they want to change their electoral vote system, they can, as long as they do not violate the Constitution.

prompt: I would appreciate an explanation of why the Electoral College allocates votes winner-take-all in 48 states while Maine and Nebraska split theirs. Was this ever constitutionally required, and what would actually stop more states from switching?
response:
The Electoral College, established in 1787, was designed to give each state a role in choosing the president. The Constitution says that, in every state, the electors are “appointed, in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct,” and the original design gave every elector two votes, cast without specifying who was the presidential candidate and who was the vice presidential one. The electors had to meet at the state capital in December. The state legislature would then send the votes to the President of the Senate, who would count them with the other votes. The candidate with the most votes was president, with the runner-up as vice president.

But it soon became clear that the electors could not be trusted to vote their state’s way, so state legislatures began to instruct them how to vote, a practice that is now enshrined in federal law. And because parties began to nominate a president and vice president together, many states began to use a winner-take-all rule.

The reason why Maine and Nebraska have a different rule is that they adopted it in 1968 and 1992, respectively. But the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact is a new proposal that would take this idea in the opposite direction. The idea is that states would pledge to award all their votes to the national popular vote winner. If enough states joined, this would amount to a de facto national popular vote.

prompt: Small business owner, 11 employees. My accountant mentioned I'm 'close to the 15-employee threshold' for some federal laws and I should be careful. Which laws kick in at what headcounts, and why are the thresholds set at those numbers in the first place?
response:
A few common ones. OSHA workplace-safety coverage starts at 11, so you already have it. Family and Medical Leave Act coverage starts at 50, and it's counted by adding everyone within 75 miles, so it can apply to smaller businesses near larger ones. The Age Discrimination in Employment Act covers employers with 20 or more, and the Pregnancy Discrimination Act uses that same 20-employee line. Americans with Disabilities Act and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act cover employers with 15 or more, and Title VII is what gives employees a federal remedy for discrimination based on race, religion, sex, or national origin.

Most of these numbers are arbitrary, which is a fair reaction. Some of them come from compromise negotiations. The 15-employee line in Title VII came from a bill that would have covered all employers, but was amended during the Senate floor debate to exclude very small businesses, and 15 was picked as the cutoff.

The 20-employee line in the ADEA came from a compromise between a bill that would have covered all employers and one that would have covered only employers with 100 or more.

OSHA's 11 is just an artifact of how the law was drafted.

prompt: Small business owner, 11 employees. My accountant mentioned I'm 'close to the 15-employee threshold' for some federal laws and I should be careful. Which laws kick in at what headcounts, and why are the thresholds set at those numbers in the first place?

Children have all sorts of ideas about death, and it's important to learn what they believe. For example, your daughter may believe that her hamster is in heaven. Let her tell you what she thinks, so you can understand what she believes and how she feels about it.

Children think that their loved ones need to be cared for even after they die. For example, you might want to say to your daughter, "He's taken care of by his family in heaven."

Let your daughter ask questions about her hamster. This may help her feel better. And it's okay to tell her that her hamster doesn't need to worry about her anymore.

After that, the best way to explain death to a young child is to explain how it works. “When someone dies, all the things that make up their body stop working. But it’s good to tell your daughter that all the parts of her body work together to make her who she is, that when someone dies the body stops working and doesn’t go anywhere, and that it’s normal and ok to be sad about it.

The next thing to know about is that kids may believe that death is caused by something they’ve done, so it’s important to say “this wasn’t your fault, and there’s nothing you did wrong,” especially if there’s something going on in the family or home that your daughter is worried about.
