prompt: I've heard 'the problem of evil' a hundred times but never the actual answers believers give. What are the main responses, and which ones do serious philosophers think hold up best?
response:
The problem of evil asks whether the existence of evil makes it unlikely that there is an omnipotent, omniscient, and wholly benevolent god. There are many different versions of this problem, but the version philosophers discuss most is the “logical problem of evil,” which asks whether it’s logically possible that evil exists and that such a god exists. (Some philosophers think the question is trivial, since by definition an omnipotent being can do anything that’s not logically impossible. But most philosophers think that if evil is logically incompatible with the existence of an omnipotent being, then it’s also incompatible with the existence of a very powerful being.)

The problem was famously formulated by David Hume:

Is he [God] willing to prevent evil, but not able? then he is impotent. Is he able, but not willing? then he is malevolent. Is he both able and willing? whence then is evil?

The problem of evil is a problem for religious people and atheists alike. The atheist wants to use the problem of evil to convince the religious person that belief in God is implausible. The religious person wants to explain why belief in God is still possible.

Here are four of the main responses to the problem of evil.

1. God can’t prevent some evils because of his omnipotence:

This is the most common response. It says that God can’t prevent some evils because his omnipotence is limited by logic.

The atheist says:

If God is omnipotent, he must be able to create a world where good exists but no one suffers. But he can’t create such a world, since people do suffer. Therefore, there’s no omnipotent god.

The religious person replies:

God can’t prevent some suffering because to prevent it, he would have to do something logically impossible. God would have to make people good without changing them at all, or he would have to cause them to do something without any cause, etc.

The atheist says:

This doesn’t answer the problem of evil. You can’t explain away the suffering of children by saying that there’s some logically impossible world where their parents didn’t neglect them.

The religious person replies:

I’m not saying there’s a logically impossible world with no suffering, only that there’s no world with no suffering where people’s good deeds are done freely.

The atheist says:

That seems arbitrary. I don’t see why God must create a world with suffering.

The religious person replies:

The world must have suffering, because God must create a world where good exists and where people’s good deeds are done freely.

This response to the problem of evil was famously articulated by Alvin Plantinga. Plantinga’s free will defense says that God could not have created a world where good exists and where people’s good deeds are done freely, but no one suffers. That’s why God created a world where people suffer.

The free will defense doesn’t explain all of the evils in the world, just the suffering caused by people. It doesn’t explain the suffering caused by earthquakes or cancer.

2. God can’t prevent some evils because they’re necessary for greater goods:

This response to the problem of evil says that God can’t prevent some suffering because that suffering is necessary for greater goods.

A famous example is the existence of cancer drugs. Cancer drugs are necessary to cure cancer, but only cancer victims can test cancer drugs. So in order to cure cancer, God had to cause some people to get cancer. That seems pretty plausible to me.

This response to the problem of evil is sometimes called the “soul-making” defense. It says that God can’t prevent suffering because we can’t improve our souls without suffering.

One way to formulate this response is:

God can’t prevent some suffering because the world has to be a place where people can improve their souls. We improve our souls through suffering.

This response to the problem of evil was articulated by J. I. Packer and Richard Swinburne. It’s less convincing to me than the free will defense because it’s hard for me to believe that suffering is necessary to improve our souls.

3. God can’t prevent some evils because of free will:

This response to the problem of evil says that God can’t prevent some suffering because people have free will. It says that God could only prevent the suffering of children by interfering with the free will of adults.

Some people object to this response to the problem of evil because they don’t believe in free will. But it doesn’t matter whether you believe in free will or not. God could create a world where people have free will, even if people can’t have free will in the real world.

4. God can’t prevent some evils because they’re necessary for free will:

This response to the problem of evil says that God can’t prevent some suffering because that suffering is necessary for free will.

The atheist says:

If God is omnipotent, he must be able to create a world with free will but no suffering. But he can’t create such a world, since people do suffer. Therefore, there’s no omnipotent god.

The religious person replies:

God can’t prevent some suffering because to prevent it, he would have to do something logically impossible. God would have to make people good without changing them at all, or he would have to cause them to do something without any cause, etc.

The atheist says:

That seems arbitrary. I don’t see why God must create a world with suffering.

The religious person replies:

The world must have suffering, because God must create a world where good exists and where people’s good deeds are done freely.

This response to the problem of evil was articulated by Robert Koons. It’s less convincing to me than the free will defense because it’s hard for me to believe that suffering is necessary for free will.

area: religion, meaning and how to live
prompt: I've heard 'the problem of evil' a hundred times but never the actual answers believers give. What are the main responses, and which ones do serious philosophers think hold up best?
response:
I’m going to give the three most common responses, plus a bonus. There are tons of other responses, but these are what I hear most often.

The Problem of Evil in a Nutshell

Evil exists.

An all-powerful, all-knowing, and all-good God exists.

If an all-powerful, all-knowing, and all-good God existed, evil wouldn’t exist.

Two of these are true, and one of them is not true.

But which?

The Free Will Defense

This is the most popular answer among Christians.

Suppose God creates a perfect world and makes every person in it a saint. Then Satan comes along and tempts the people to do evil. Half of them fall for it, and the other half resist.

Now the world has half saints and half sinners. But if the people who resisted Satan were created as saints, Satan would know they wouldn’t listen to him, and he wouldn’t bother tempting them. If the people who listened to Satan were created as sinners, then they would have no way of knowing whether God really wanted them to do evil, or whether he was just letting them. So to make Satan’s temptations convincing, he needs to tempt people whose intentions he’s unsure about. And that means God can’t create them as either saints or sinners.

So God creates people who are free to do either good or evil. Then Satan tempts them. Some of them fall for it, and some don’t, and there’s evil in the world.

But if the world is going to be free of Satan and the evil he causes, then it’s going to have to have some evil in it first. And this is why there’s evil in the world.

The best version of this argument is Alvin Plantinga’s 1974 book God, Freedom, and Evil. But there have been many criticisms of it.

A common one is that God could just create people with the kind of free will where they could choose good or evil but would never actually choose evil. God could just create everyone as free-willed saints.

Another common one is that God could just create Satan in a way where he doesn’t tempt people to do evil.

And yet another is that the argument doesn’t seem to work on the scale it needs to: even if all the evil in the world was caused by Satan and his evil minions, it doesn’t explain why Satan would choose to cause all that evil when God created him. Why did God create Satan if he knew that Satan was going to cause so much evil?

I think Plantinga’s argument is the best defense of free will that’s been offered, and I find it pretty persuasive. But it doesn’t really answer all the objections that people raise.

The Best Possible World Argument

This one is a favorite of theists who are really smart but not professional philosophers. I’ve seen it in various places, but it comes up most often on blogs.

The idea is:

Let’s say that God, being all-powerful, can create any world that he wants to. So he could make a perfect world full of saints and happiness, a world with no suffering and no pain, or a world of nothing but eternal bliss and no death.

God would like to make a perfect world. But when he tries to do it, he finds out that he can’t. There are just too many rules and constraints.

If he creates a world where every living thing has free will, some of them are going to choose to do evil. If he creates a world without evil, it’s going to be boring. If he creates a world without death, it’s going to be overpopulated.

So God makes the best world he can, with as many good people as he can get away with without upsetting the rules, as much free will as he can get away with without upsetting the rules, as much happiness as he can get away with without upsetting the rules, and so on.

And this is the world he makes. And it’s not perfect.

There’s a lot wrong with this argument.

First of all, it doesn’t really explain why there’s evil. God could just create a world without evil.

Second, it seems really ad hoc. There’s no obvious reason why all the constraints on the world are going to be such that they produce the right amount of evil. If God can create any world he wants, then there’s no reason he can’t create a perfect one.

Third, this argument seems to be really stupid.

Suppose that I wanted to make a perfect cake. I want to make a cake that is delicious, healthy, and looks great.

I want the cake to be delicious. The cake I make is okay, but it’s not really delicious. I want to add a lot more sugar. But I can’t: it would ruin the cake. There are just too many constraints.

I want the cake to be healthy. The cake I made isn’t healthy. I want to remove all the sugar and fat. But I can’t: it would ruin the cake. There are just too many constraints.

I want the cake to look good. The cake I made looks okay, but it’s not really very good-looking. I want to add a lot more frosting. But I can’t: it would ruin the cake. There are just too many constraints.

What kind of cake am I making?

The answer, of course, is a bad cake. The only kind of cake you can make where you can’t add any more sugar, where you can’t remove any sugar or fat, and where you can’t add any more frosting is a bad cake.

In the same way, the only kind of world you can make where you can’t remove any evil is a bad world. And the only kind of world you can make where you can’t make anything better is a bad world.

So this argument, in addition to not really explaining why there’s evil in the world, actually makes God seem like he’s a bad cake-maker.

The Argument From Evil

This one is a favorite of atheist philosophers. I’m going to use J.L. Mackie’s version, since he’s kind of the godfather of this argument. Mackie argues:

God is all-powerful.

God is all-good.

Evil exists.

An all-powerful being could prevent all evil.

An all-good being would prevent evil.

So there is no God.

There’s a lot of problems with this argument.

First of all, it’s kind of circular. It starts out with the premise that evil exists, which is only true if you define evil as something that God doesn’t want to exist. But this is a circular definition: if God doesn’t want evil to exist, then God has no reason to prevent it.

Second of all, it doesn’t seem to work on the scale it needs to. Even if it’s true that an all-powerful, all-good God wouldn’t allow evil to exist, this doesn’t explain why God would allow so much evil in the world. Why does God allow all that suffering and pain? Why does God allow people to die? Why does God allow people to be tortured and killed?

And finally, I think this argument is a pretty bad argument.

Let’s say that my friend wants to make a cake. But he wants to make a perfect cake: he wants it to be healthy, delicious, and beautiful. He wants to use only healthy ingredients, to make it as delicious as he can, and to make it as beautiful as he can.

Now, the cake he makes is kind of bad. It’s not really that healthy, it’s not really that delicious, and it’s not really that beautiful.

Does that prove that my friend is stupid?

No, it doesn’t. It just proves that my friend couldn’t make the cake he wanted. If I wanted to make a really healthy, delicious and beautiful cake, I could try really hard. But I don’t have the skill or the knowledge to do it.

In the same way, just because God couldn’t make a perfect world doesn’t mean he’s stupid. It just means that he can’t make a perfect world.

I think this argument is the worst of the three. But I have to admit that it’s not as convincing as it should be. It’s too easy to just say “well, it’s just that God can’t do it” and move on.

And The Best Possible World Argument, In The End

I’m going to tell you about a world.

The world has perfect health. No one gets sick, no one gets old, no one gets injured. Everyone is always perfectly healthy.

The world is perfect. No one ever has any bad thoughts or feelings. No one ever says anything mean. Everyone is always kind and loving.

The world is safe. No one ever gets hurt. No one ever dies. No one ever gets sick. No one ever gets old.

And the world is perfect. No one ever feels sad or angry or unhappy. No one ever feels hurt or neglected or unloved. No one ever feels lonely or abandoned.

And in this world, no one ever feels anything.

They also don't require a belief in God, or that God is a personal being, or that God created the world in six days, or that God speaks to prophets, or that God sent the Jews to bring religion to the rest of the world, and so on. A Reform rabbi could tell you all about this, but I thought I would explain what a religion is like if it's based on culture instead of belief.

I don't know any Reform Jews, so I'll try to explain this using a different kind of culture-based religion that I know more about: secular Buddhism. I learned a lot of the following from *Buddhism is not what you think*.

Secular Buddhism, like Reform Judaism, does not involve a belief in any particular kind of god, or any particular kind of afterlife, or any particular kind of reincarnation. If you believe those things, you can believe them, but if you don't, it doesn't matter.

It is based on the story of Siddhartha Gautama. He was the prince of a wealthy kingdom. One day he saw that many of his subjects were suffering, and he decided to leave the palace and learn how to end suffering. He tried meditation and fasting for six years, until he reached an extremely emaciated condition. One day he was so weak he nearly died, and he realized that extreme asceticism didn't work. He decided to eat, and then he went back to meditation. After a while, he achieved enlightenment.

In the Buddhist tradition, enlightenment is like solving a hard problem. It has nothing to do with being an exceptionally good person or being a great spiritual leader. It has more to do with thinking really, really hard until you solve a puzzle.

The Buddhist tradition tells us that what Buddha solved was a puzzle that had never been solved before. Nobody knew how to end suffering. Buddha figured it out and solved it. Now Buddhists know the solution.

What is the solution? The solution is the Four Noble Truths.

The first noble truth is that there is suffering. This is probably the easiest one to understand. Life is hard. There are lots of times when things go wrong.

The second noble truth is that the root of suffering is the attachment to the idea of self. This is the most controversial. I'm a big fan of this kind of thinking in Buddhism, but I don't think Buddhism got it right. I'm not sure there's an exact answer here, but I think that it's not the root of all suffering. I think it's a big part of suffering, and there are lots of times when the Buddha was right, and there are lots of times when it wasn't.

The third noble truth is that suffering can end. This isn't as self-evident as the first one. There are people who are suffering so badly that you might think there's no hope. Maybe you are suffering so badly right now that you don't believe there's any hope. The third noble truth is that you're wrong. You can change your life for the better. You might not know how to do it yet, but you can.

The fourth noble truth is that the way to end suffering is by letting go of your attachment to self. This is the Buddha's solution to the puzzle. Buddha said "I figured it out! Let go of your attachment to self! Then you won't suffer anymore!"

I think the fourth noble truth was wrong, but that's ok. That's the way of religion. You can be wrong, and that doesn't mean that religion is worthless. You can be wrong in a way that's really helpful.

The Buddha was a great teacher. If you look at his teachings, you'll see that he didn't just say "let go of your attachment to self", he gave you a lot of good advice about how to do it.

A lot of Buddhist practices aren't about belief. They're about learning skills. The skills that are useful to you aren't necessarily the skills that you need. But if you practice meditation, you might be able to be more productive, or get a better sleep, or do a better job.

The Buddha is kind of like a teacher. His job is to give you a bunch of good advice. Maybe some of it will work for you, and maybe some of it won't. That's ok. He's just a teacher, and his job is to give you the advice he thinks is useful.

There are a lot of people who think religion is about beliefs, and they think that if a religion allows you to not believe the beliefs, that religion is weak. I think this is wrong. The beliefs are not the most important thing in the religion. The practices are what matter.

prompt: I've been knitting for about two years and I still don't understand why the same yarn and the same needles give me a completely different gauge when I knit in the round versus flat. My swatch said 22 stitches per 4 inches, my sweater body came out at 20. Is it my purl stitch? Something about tension? What's actually going on mechanically?
response:
Nothing is wrong with you. The difference is that knitting in the round is, mechanically, the same thing as knitting only the right side of the fabric. So if you're knitting in stockinette, you never see the purl side of the fabric and you never form a purl stitch.

You probably knit the purl stitches of your swatch with slightly more tension than the knit stitches of your round. A lot of people find purling a little harder than knitting, and that shows in the fabric. So the body of your sweater was knitting-only and a touch looser than your flat swatch. It's not unusual for purling to run a stitch or two tighter per 4 inches (10 cm).

This is also why you get a different gauge when you change from stockinette to a pattern that includes purling. You're not doing anything wrong. Just make sure you swatch in the same stitch pattern as you will use for the project, and your gauge will match.

prompt: I've been knitting for about two years and I still don't understand why the same yarn and the same needles give me a completely different gauge when I knit in the round versus flat. My swatch said 22 stitches per 4 inches, my sweater body came out at 20. Is it my purl stitch? Something about tension? What's actually going on mechanically?
response:
Your purl stitch is not the cause, and neither is any mysterious difference in tension. If you knit the round swatch flat, or work it flat from a chart written for the round, you'll get the same result as you got knitting flat. The difference is not in your tension but in the fact that the stitches are arranged in different patterns.

A row of knit stitches is a row of loops, and the legs of the loops are slanted. When you knit one row and then the next row, the loops of the second row rest on the loops of the first row, with their legs slanting in the opposite direction. The first row is a row of V's, and the next row is a row of inverted V's.

When you knit flat, the next row is a row of purl stitches. These are also loops, and the same is true: the legs are slanted, and the next row of purl stitches will have the legs slanting in the opposite direction.

In knitting in the round, you're always knitting the tops of the loops of the previous round. The tops of the loops are round, and the legs of the next row of loops don't need to be slanted. That is, when you knit flat, the first row is a row of V's, and the second row is a row of inverted V's, and so on. When you knit in the round, the first row is a row of V's, and the next row is a row of O's. The O's are more flexible, and the fabric is slightly looser, so it has fewer stitches in four inches.

So you should do all of your gauge swatches in the round, using the same needles you'll use for knitting in the round. And if you're knitting a pattern in the round, work a row of purl stitches in the swatch, to check the gauge in the round.

prompt: I read that in Go the komi is 6.5 points and the half point is there 'to prevent ties' but then I read about jigo and seki and now I'm confused. If ties are impossible, why do people talk about them? Is the half point the only reason?
response:
The half point is the main reason. In practice it's hard for jigo to come up, because in a really even game there will usually be a move that breaks the symmetry. And in seki it's rare to have a position where you really can't decide who owns the territory in question.

The other reason is that some rules systems don't use a half point. Under Chinese rules, for instance, the komi is six points, and ties are possible.

prompt: I read that in Go the komi is 6.5 points and the half point is there 'to prevent ties' but then I read about jigo and seki and now I'm confused. If ties are impossible, why do people talk about them? Is the half point the only reason?
response:
In professional games, the half point means a tie is impossible. You'll still hear about the possibility of a tie in some other contexts.

In jigo, neither player is better than the other. If one of the players were to play better, they could win.

In seki, the stones on the board can be alive or dead. For instance, there can be a seki where neither player has enough liberties to fill in the space and kill the other player's stones.

In a seki, the score can be determined by who has more influence outside the seki.

prompt: I read that in Go the komi is 6.5 points and the half point is there 'to prevent ties' but then I read about jigo and seki and now I'm confused. If ties are impossible, why do people talk about them? Is the half point the only reason?
response:
No. The half point prevents only one kind of tie, a position that everyone agrees scores the same by both methods of counting, and nobody cares about that kind. Other ties arise from disagreements about whether something is alive or dead.

The usual examples are seki and jigo (which is a kind of seki). Seki is two or more groups of stones that cannot capture each other. In this picture the white stones in the middle are seki with the black stones on the left; the white and black groups each have one eye, and neither can fill the other's because it would die.

In Japanese play you decide who owns the seki stones and count them. Black takes them here, which wins by one point.

In Chinese play you count the territory around the groups of live stones, which is the area around the left and right black groups and around the white group in the middle. There you get a tie, and it is settled by komi.

So the ties that actually happen come from people disagreeing on whether seki stones are dead or alive, and the half point has nothing to do with that.

prompt: ok so this is maybe a dumb question but my kid got into Rubik's cubes and he keeps saying there are 'quintillions' of positions but also that any position can be solved in 20 moves or less. those two things feel like they can't both be true?? like how can there be that many positions and yet you're never more than 20 moves away. can someone explain this in a way I can repeat back to a 10 year old
response:
Neither thing contradicts the other. There are 43,252,003,274,489,856,000 positions (4.3 x 10^19), and it turns out that, no matter how scrambled your cube is, it's never more than 20 moves from the solved state.

To make this clear, let me talk about something else that has a huge number of possibilities but where you're never more than 2 steps away from something you want.

Suppose you have a light switch that you can flip up or down. When it's up, the light is on. When it's down, the light is off. Suppose you want the light to be on. No matter where you start, you are never more than 1 step away from having the light on. If you're at the starting state where the light is already on, you're 0 steps away from your goal. If you're at the state where it's off, you're 1 step away from your goal.

Now suppose there are 2 light switches and you want at least one of them to be on. No matter where you start, you are never more than 2 steps away from having at least one light on.

There are 4 possible states of the switches, and 3 of them have at least one of the lights on. The only state where both lights are off is 2 steps away from having at least one light on.

In general, if you have n light switches, there are 2^n possible states. There is 1 possible state where all lights are off, which is n steps away from having at least one light on. But for any value of n, you're never more than n steps away from having at least one light on.

Now suppose n = 100. Then there are 2^100 = 10^30 possible states, and you're never more than 100 steps away from having at least one light on.

This is the same situation as with the Rubik's cube. You're never more than 20 steps away from solving the cube, even though there are 10^19 possible states.

prompt: I'm a materials scientist, so I understand annealing in metals. In stained glass and lampwork people also talk about annealing, and about 'compatible' glasses with matching COE. What's specifically going wrong when you fuse two glasses with COE 90 and 96? Is it just thermal stress on cooling, or is there more to it with how glass relaxes?
response:
When glass cools below its working temperature it stops flowing, and each piece locks in a particular size at its strain point. Two glasses that don't match will lock at slightly different sizes, and the difference turns into stress because one can't shrink or expand without the other.

In fusing, one glass is on top of the other. If the top glass is a bit too large, it pulls down on the sides of the bottom glass. Glass in compression on the outside can hold a lot, but on the inside it's in tension. Glass in tension is weak; it can crack from a small scratch.

You can measure a piece of glass by x-ray diffraction, and you can tell which side is in tension and which is in compression.

The coefficient of expansion is just a measure of how much a glass expands for a certain temperature change. It varies with temperature, so when people talk about a glass's COE they usually mean what it's average over 350-550 degrees C, where most glass work happens.

prompt: I'm a materials scientist, so I understand annealing in metals. In stained glass and lampwork people also talk about annealing, and about 'compatible' glasses with matching COE. What's specifically going wrong when you fuse two glasses with COE 90 and 96? Is it just thermal stress on cooling, or is there more to it with how glass relaxes?
response:
Most of the problem is thermal, and it happens mostly while you are making the piece. Glass softens and stiffens over a range of temperatures, called the annealing range. When a piece is made, it is held at a temperature at the top of that range long enough for internal stresses to relax, and then cooled slowly enough that stresses don't build up again.

If a COE 90 and a COE 96 piece are fused, they will shrink by different amounts as the piece is annealed and cooled. The 96 glass wants to be shorter than the 90 glass by about 0.3 percent after a 1000 C drop in temperature. The two pieces are joined, so neither can be its desired size and both are stressed.

This is mostly a problem with stresses you make during fabrication. Glassmakers have found that a difference of 1 or 1.5 in COE is workable, because stresses from that amount of difference can be relieved by annealing. A larger difference can make glass that cannot be relieved.

There are more subtle differences than thermal expansion, such as the temperature at which a given glass relaxes, and the amount of strain it can tolerate before breaking. But those are second-order problems.

prompt: I'm a materials scientist, so I understand annealing in metals. In stained glass and lampwork people also talk about annealing, and about 'compatible' glasses with matching COE. What's specifically going wrong when you fuse two glasses with COE 90 and 96? Is it just thermal stress on cooling, or is there more to it with how glass relaxes?
response:
A glass is an amorphous solid, but at temperatures above its annealing point the viscous flow of the atoms makes it behave like a very slow liquid, and any strain relaxes. As it cools below that point the glass is “frozen in,” and if there is stress from different parts cooling at different rates, it remains.

The annealing point is defined as the temperature at which the viscosity of the glass is about 10^14 poise, and the stress relaxation time is about one day. The glass can be “softened” and moulded at higher temperature, where the viscosity is much lower. When you anneal, you heat the glass to a temperature above the annealing point, so that the stress is removed, and then cool it very slowly.

If the glasses have similar coefficients of thermal expansion, then when they are cooled from the fusing temperature they shrink together at similar rates, and there is little stress. If the glasses have very different coefficients of thermal expansion, they shrink at different rates when they are cooled, and stresses are generated. The glass with the higher coefficient of thermal expansion shrinks more, and is in tension. This is the opposite of what we want for most glasses, because glass is about ten times weaker in tension than it is in compression, and there are always tiny defects in the surface which act as stress risers and cause fracture.

prompt: Could you explain how Elo ratings work and why a player who beats someone rated 400 points lower gains almost nothing? I would appreciate the formula if it is not too complicated.
response:
Elo ratings are a way to describe who will win in a match. If two players have ratings rA and rB, the difference between the ratings is expected to relate to the probability of winning. The difference is defined in a way where a difference of 400 is expected to result in an 80% probability of winning, and a difference of 200 points is expected to result in a 65% probability of winning.

In the original paper, Elo defined the expected score in a game as

EA = 1 / (1 + 10^((rB - rA) / 400))

So the 80% probability of winning with a 400 point difference is where the exponent comes from, since 10^1 is 10 and 1 / 11 is approximately 10%. In chess, a win is worth 1 point, and a draw is worth 0.5 points. If the player is expected to win with 80% probability, that means the player is also expected to draw with 20% probability, resulting in an average score of 80% + 10% = 0.9.

If a player wins a match when they were expected to win 60% of the time, they gain

16 * (1 - 0.6) = 6.4

points, rounded to 6 points. If the player wins a match when they were expected to win 80% of the time, they only gain

16 * (1 - 0.8) = 3.2

points, rounded to 3 points. If they lose a match they were expected to win, they lose the same number of points, such as losing a match they were expected to win with 80% probability causes the player to lose 3 points.

The constant of 16 points is chosen so that a player wins about 100 points a year.

prompt: Could you explain how Elo ratings work and why a player who beats someone rated 400 points lower gains almost nothing? I would appreciate the formula if it is not too complicated.
response:
Your rating is meant to predict the probability that you will win a game. It is defined so that the difference in ratings between two players corresponds to a probability of winning.

A difference of 0 points means the players have equal chances of winning. A 100-point difference means that the higher-rated player has a 64% chance of winning. A 400-point difference means that the higher-rated player has a 91% chance of winning.

The probability that player A beats player B is calculated using the formula

P(A beats B) = 1 / (1 + 10^((B - A) / 400))

where A and B are the players' ratings. For example, if A has a rating of 1400 and B has a rating of 1000, then A has a probability of 1 / (1 + 10^(-400/400)) = 91% of beating B.

Suppose you have a rating of 1500 and you beat someone with a rating of 1100. This match result tells us that someone with a rating of 1500 beat someone with a rating of 1100. But someone with a rating of 1500 is expected to beat someone with a rating of 1100 90% of the time, so we already expected you to beat your opponent. That means this match result is very uninformative, so it shouldn't change the players' ratings very much.

Now suppose you beat someone who also had a rating of 1500. This is more interesting, since we expected each player to win about half the time. If you had never played anyone before, we could not know whether you were really a 1500 or a 2000. This match result tells us that you are probably not a 2000, because it would be very surprising for a 2000 to lose to a 1500. This is why your rating decreases after losing to someone of equal rating.

prompt: Could you explain how Elo ratings work and why a player who beats someone rated 400 points lower gains almost nothing? I would appreciate the formula if it is not too complicated.
response:
Elo ratings, invented by a Hungarian-American physicist, measure your relative skill against everyone else. Your rating goes up or down after every game depending on whether you won or lost, and on the strength of your opponent.

The formula is this:

Expected points = 1 / (1 + 10^((your rating - your opponent's rating) / 400))

So you start off with the expected number of points, 1 if you win and 0 if you lose, and then you add the difference between the expected points and the actual points you got.

For example, if you beat someone 400 points lower than you, you gain 0.1 points, and if you lose to someone 400 points higher than you, you lose 0.1 points. If you beat someone 800 points lower than you, you gain 0.01 points, and if you lose to someone 800 points higher, you lose 0.01 points.

This is why players who have won every game still only have a rating of 3000 points - it's not hard to win the first couple hundred games, but getting from 2700 to 2800 is almost as hard as getting from 1200 to 1300.

So it’s not possible to build crossword puzzles by randomly assigning letters to the grid and checking to see if the resulting grid contains valid words.

The basic idea for a crossword constructor is to place a small number of long, well known entries in the grid first, and then fill in the rest of the grid around these entries. The algorithm is very simple. First, we select a few seed entries, which are all either four or five letters long. Next, we randomly choose an entry from the remaining dictionary. If it fits, we place it in the grid, otherwise we try the next entry, and so on.

If you have 19, it drops to under 4 percent.

On turn four you have 10 cards, and 2 or fewer lands is a disaster. With 17 lands, about 16 percent of hands have that many, and about 8 percent have none or one. With 19 lands, the disaster rate falls to about 9 percent, and the chance of no lands falls to about 3 percent.

prompt: So I've been brewing beer for a year, extract kits mostly, and I keep reading about 'fermentation temperature control' and how warm fermentations make banana or solvent flavors. My closet is about 74F. What's the yeast doing differently at 74 vs 64 that changes the flavor? And is there a cheap fix that doesn't involve buying a chest freezer, because my partner will kill me.
response:
At 74°F, lager and ale yeasts that are stressed by warmth make more esters, which is the word for fruity aromas. Banana is one of them, and it’s not an accident that bananas smell that way: banana esters make up much of a banana’s aroma. You might like that in a wheat beer and not in an IPA, which you probably want to taste like hops. At 64°F, those same yeasts make less of those compounds, and you taste more hops, and your beer smells more like what you think of as beer.

The fix is to put your fermenting beer in a cooler and cool it with a bag of ice. That works because the ice will melt when it absorbs heat from the fermenter, so the fermenter won’t warm up as fast as it would without it. You need a big cooler, because your fermenter will be inside, and you need a large bag of ice, big enough that it won’t melt overnight. You put the ice in the cooler but not in contact with the fermenter. The air between the ice and the fermenter is cold, and that’s what chills your fermenter. Your beer should get into the low 60s, if not the 50s.

Most ale yeasts make different esters at different temperatures. The esterification reactions that build flavor compounds speed up more with heat than the reactions that consume them, so warmer conditions leave more ester behind. Isoamyl acetate, which smells like banana, rises quickly above about 68°F, and solvent-like notes can appear near 75°F, though results vary by strain. Most recipes call for 65 to 70°F.

A closet at 74°F won't ruin the beer. Many classic British ales were fermented warmer, and some brewers like the fruitier result. Just expect your results to differ from the recipe's, and consider it an experiment.

prompt: So I've been brewing beer for a year, extract kits mostly, and I keep reading about 'fermentation temperature control' and how warm fermentations make banana or solvent flavors. My closet is about 74F. What's the yeast doing differently at 74 vs 64 that changes the flavor? And is there a cheap fix that doesn't involve buying a chest freezer, because my partner will kill me.
response:
Warm beer smells like banana, and sometimes solvent, because yeast make different compounds depending on temperature. A classic is isoamyl acetate, which smells like banana, and which yeast make in greater amounts when they ferment warm. Some people like those flavors and some don't. In fact, the banana smell in Bavarian wheat beers is due to those esters.

But the esters aren't the only difference between fermenting warm and cold. For one, yeast makes fewer of the compounds that give you the malty flavor in beer. You'll get more diacetyl, which smells like butter or cream.

And in general, if you ferment cold, you can expect a cleaner, crisper beer.

The other main reason people are careful about fermenting warm is the fact that you need more yeast at higher temperatures.

Yeast are living cells, and they can only survive within a certain temperature range. Below that, yeast become inactive. Above that, yeast will die. The amount of yeast that survives depends on how hot it gets, and for how long.

When you pitch yeast into wort, there are millions of cells in each milliliter. As the fermentation proceeds, most of the yeast die. If you pitch 100 million cells in a liter of wort, you can easily end up with only 1 or 2 million by the end. If the yeast get too hot, you can end up with much fewer than 2 million by the end of fermentation.

If there are too few yeast at the end of fermentation, they can leave the beer tasting like sulfur, or can make the beer look bad by settling and flocculating in the carboy. So if you ferment warm, you need to use extra yeast to compensate.

A good rule of thumb is that you should pitch twice as much yeast at 75 degrees than you do at 68. So if you're pitching 5 grams of dry yeast into 5 gallons of wort at 75 degrees, use 10.

So what to do if you don't want to pitch twice as much yeast?

There's a trick where you put a bag of ice in the fermenter. I'll discuss this in a later article. If you ferment in a plastic fermenter, you might also consider the method described in this article, in which you make a plastic jacket around your fermenter.

prompt: I'm learning to solder for guitar pedal kits. The tutorial said to heat the pad, not the solder, and let the solder flow to the joint. But when I do that the solder just balls up and won't stick. I read something about flux and oxidation and got lost. What's actually happening?
response:
Solder joins metal by dissolving into it, and it can only do that on clean metal. Air does this to every metal surface, including your new solder wire, within a second or two, and the oxide layer it leaves is the reason the solder refuses to wet. Flux is a chemical that removes that layer, and the solder is pre-fluxed: the rosin you see on it is the flux, and it releases its solvent as you heat the wire.

The tutorial's instruction is right, but it only works when the flux can do its job. Flux works best on hot, clean metal, so the correct order is: heat the pad, touch the solder wire to it, and the hot pad melts the wire's flux, which cleans the pad as the solder flows. If the pad isn't hot enough when the solder touches it, the flux never activates, and the solder wets nothing and just forms a bead.

The other common cause is that the pad is already oxidized. A small amount of fresh flux from the wire won't clean it, so the solder beads up. Clean the pad by dragging fresh solder across it repeatedly, letting the wire's flux do the work, and finish with a good blob on the pad; that's called tinning. Use this as your starting point: heat the pad for about a second, then apply solder to it.

prompt: I'm learning to solder for guitar pedal kits. The tutorial said to heat the pad, not the solder, and let the solder flow to the joint. But when I do that the solder just balls up and won't stick. I read something about flux and oxidation and got lost. What's actually happening?
response:
A solder joint is a small weld: the solder has to bond to metal surfaces, and it only does that on clean metal. Every metal surface in your shop has a thin film of oxide, and it keeps growing whenever the metal is hot and air is present. The solder's job is to be liquid long enough to spread over that metal and mix with it at the surface.

Flux is the part you skipped. It's a chemical, usually dissolved in a bit of water or alcohol, whose job is to remove or hold back that oxide film just long enough for the solder to bond. The solder you use is fluxed: a thin flux core runs down its center, and melting the solder releases the flux onto the joint. When you heat a pad until it's shiny and then touch solder to it, a little flux is released, which clears the oxide, and the solder wets and flows. The flux is consumed doing its job, which is why you usually can't re-melt a finished joint and get it to flow again.

A solder joint that balls up or beads off a pad is almost always a cold or oxidized surface. Heat the pad first with your iron, let it get shiny for a second, then touch the solder to it. If the pad is still shiny, solder will spread over it. If it won't flow, the flux is done, so clean the pad with a damp sponge and try again.

For a guitar pedal you want a shiny joint that covers the component lead and the pad, which on a 90% tin alloy should take about two seconds of contact.

prompt: Why are some board games considered 'solved' and others not? Checkers is solved, chess isn't, but tic-tac-toe obviously is. What does solved actually mean and what makes it practically impossible for chess?
response:
Solved means that someone knows the outcome of the game with perfect play from the start. In the case of checkers, it’s a draw. In the case of tic-tac-toe, it’s also a draw. In the case of Go, it’s a win for the first player, but I’m not sure we’ve yet gotten to the point of knowing what the first player’s first move should be.

Solving a game means figuring out what move to make in every possible position. And that’s a lot of positions.

In tic-tac-toe, there are about 3 million possible board positions. In checkers, there are about 500 quintillion. That’s 500,000,000,000,000,000. In chess, there are 10 to the 47th power positions. (The number of possible games is a lot bigger, but you don’t have to consider those if you’re trying to solve the game.)

The reason Go has been a tougher nut to crack than checkers is not because of the size of the game tree (Go’s is larger, but checkers’ is wider, and that matters more). It’s because Go has been a tough nut to crack for *humans*, and that’s where the ideas and approaches come from.

The reason we’ve been able to solve checkers but not chess is that a few people had a lot of patience and money to throw at it. Jonathan Schaeffer spent about ten years and about a million dollars on it, working on it while he was doing other things, so it took more like twenty years.

But it’s not just that it took a long time to finish solving checkers. The amount of computer time Schaeffer spent on it would only have gotten him about 0.00000000000000000000000001% of the way to solving chess.

The reason you can’t just get a lot of computers to work on it is that the work is not easily parallelizable. You have to finish looking at some positions before you can start looking at others. This is a common feature of search problems, and there’s not much you can do about it.

I’m not going to claim that we won’t ever solve chess, just that it’s very unlikely that it will happen anytime soon.

prompt: Why are some board games considered 'solved' and others not? Checkers is solved, chess isn't, but tic-tac-toe obviously is. What does solved actually mean and what makes it practically impossible for chess?
response:
A game is solved when one player has a winning strategy that works against any opponent. This can happen in two ways: with perfect play, the first player wins, or the second player wins, or neither player can force a win (so perfect play leads to a draw).

A solved game can be played by anyone. If you know the winning strategy, you always play it. For example, in a solved game, a grandmaster and a five-year-old play identically (they both use the winning strategy). And the grandmaster and the five-year-old can play each other a million times, and the same player wins every time.

Checkers is solved. You can play perfectly with an app or a computer program. Tic-tac-toe is solved. The first player can force a draw. You can also play tic-tac-toe perfectly without memorizing anything.

But it would be a waste of time to play chess against a grandmaster, even if you use a chess engine.

So how can we solve checkers and tic-tac-toe, but not chess?

## Games with a perfect algorithm

The easiest way to solve a game is to write a program that plays the game perfectly. If you’re playing tic-tac-toe, the algorithm is easy: if there’s a place where you can win in one move, take it. Otherwise, if there’s a place where your opponent will win next move, take it to block them. Otherwise, if there’s a place where you will win in two moves, take it. Otherwise, if there’s a place where your opponent will win in two moves, take it to block them. Otherwise, take a random move.

The reason this works is that there are only a small number of possible tic-tac-toe games. So if you play by this algorithm, the number of moves to either win or draw is small.

This same approach doesn’t work for chess. You could write a program that takes a winning move in one move if there is one, or otherwise blocks a win in one move for your opponent. But if neither of these is possible, it won’t know what to do. There are too many possible games, and the number of moves before the first player wins is too high.

## Games where every move is the winning move

You can solve some games by figuring out how to play them perfectly, even if you can’t write an algorithm that plays them perfectly.

The game “turn of the century” is solved. Two players take turns adding a number between 1 and 10 to a total that starts at 0. The first player who gets to 100 wins.

You can play this game perfectly without writing a program. The first player should play 4. If the second player plays 5, the first player should play 9. If the second player plays 6, the first player should play 8. In other words, the first player should always pick the number so that each pair of numbers adds to 10.

After the first move, the total is 4. Every time two players take turns, the total goes up by 10. So after 9 rounds of both players taking turns, the total is 94. So the first player will get to 100.

This game is solved. But you don’t need to write an algorithm to play it perfectly.

## Games where a winning move always exists

You can solve some games by realizing that a winning move always exists for the first player.

Here’s one example: players take turns removing coins from a pile of 64 coins. A player can remove as many coins as they want (but they have to remove at least one coin). The player who takes the last coin wins.

The first player wins this game. The first player can remove all of the coins.

You can make this example a little harder by saying that a player can only remove up to half of the remaining coins. In that case, the first player can remove 32 coins, leaving 32 coins. Then they can remove half of the coins, and half of the remaining coins, and so on. So the first player always wins.

This game is solved, but it’s not hard to play. The first player can just always take half of the coins.

## Games where you can win by copying your opponent

You can solve some games by realizing that you can win by copying your opponent’s moves.

Here’s one example: each player has a set of 100 coins. A player flips a coin heads or tails to add one to their score. The first player who has 51 heads wins.

The first player can win this game. If the first player flips their coins heads or tails, the second player can do whatever they want. But if the first player flips their coins tails or heads, the second player can copy the first player’s moves.

This game is solved.

## Games where the first player wins

A game is also solved if you can prove that the first player always wins.

A game is symmetric if the game looks the same from either player’s perspective. In the coin flipping game, the game is symmetric. It doesn’t matter which side is heads.

A symmetric game is solvable. The first player can win because the first player can always copy the second player’s moves.

In the coin flipping game, the first player can flip their coins heads or tails. If the second player flips their coins heads or tails, the first player flips their coins tails or heads. If the second player flips their coins tails or heads, the first player flips their coins heads or tails.

In both cases, the first player’s number of heads is equal to the second player’s number of heads. So the second player will never get to 51 heads before the first player does.

## How to solve a game

Here’s a list of the ways to solve a game:

1. Write an algorithm that plays the game perfectly

2. Figure out a strategy that always wins

3. Realize that a winning move always exists for the first player

4. Realize that you can always win by copying your opponent’s moves

5. Realize that the game is symmetric, so the first player can always win by copying their opponent’s moves

## Why chess isn’t solved

Chess is not symmetric. The first player has the advantage of moving first, but they also have the disadvantage of having fewer pieces.

But we can solve chess by realizing that the first player has an advantage of moving first.

The first player can always win by copying their opponent’s moves.

But this isn’t quite right. If you copy your opponent’s moves, you’ll lose if your opponent has a winning strategy. So the first player can’t always win.

The first player can always win by copying their opponent’s moves if the first player is playing a symmetric game. But chess is not symmetric.

prompt: Why are some board games considered 'solved' and others not? Checkers is solved, chess isn't, but tic-tac-toe obviously is. What does solved actually mean and what makes it practically impossible for chess?
response:
The idea of a “solved” game was born from the question, “what is the best move I can make in this situation?”

The answer is always the same: make the move that gives you the best result, and assume that your opponent will make the move that gives them the best result, and so on for the rest of the game. If you could do this, you would always be able to know which moves win, which draw, and which lose.

So a solved game is one where you can determine the result from any situation by looking at the future and figuring out what the best play will be.

This is actually pretty doable for tic-tac-toe. There are 3^9 = 19,683 possible board configurations, and every one of them is possible in some way. For each board configuration, we can compute its result by looking at all the moves and seeing which one is best. If a move leads to a win then it is better than one that leads to a draw, and so on. This can easily be done in a program in a few seconds. It can be done by hand in a few hours.

A few decades ago, it was discovered that the best play in tic-tac-toe from the beginning is a draw. This is pretty obvious when you think about it: it’s a really simple game, and both players would have to be pretty bad for one of them to win.

Checkers is more complicated. It has 288,988,492,445,173,920 possible board configurations, which is about 10^17. It’s too many to figure out by hand, but we can figure out a few hundred million a second, so it should take about a year.

Checkers was eventually solved in 2007, using a bunch of computers and about six years of work. Like tic-tac-toe, the best play is a draw.

Chess is a bit more complicated. There are only 64 squares, but each one can be empty or one of 12 pieces. So there are about 64^12 = 4.8 * 10^21 possibilities, or about 10^22. This is about a million times more complex than checkers.

We can’t solve chess the way we solved checkers, because it would take a million times as long. If a computer can figure out a few hundred million moves a second, we still need at least 1500 seconds, which is about 25 minutes. That sounds easy. Why not just do that?

The problem is that we have to do that 10^22 times, for each possible board configuration. Even if we could do this on a trillion computers, each computer would need about 100 million years. That’s just a bit out of reach.

There is another way that people have tried to solve chess, which is to solve the game backwards. Start at the end, and figure out which situations are good and bad. Then look at the situations that lead into those, and figure out what’s good and bad there, and so on. This has so far not worked, though it might work if we get better at it.

prompt: Explain how to read a crochet chart (the symbol kind, not written patterns). I'm left-handed, which every tutorial seems to ignore, and I'm working a granny square that starts from a magic ring.
response:
A chart is a map of stitches: each symbol is one stitch, one chain or one space. You usually work the first row or round across the bottom, starting in the bottom-right corner, and each new round sits above the last.

For left-handers, the easiest fix is to read rows left to right, not the usual right to left. Granny squares are worked in rounds, so this hardly matters. A chart that has a left-to-right marker can be used directly; to read a right-to-left chart left to right, just look at the back of the paper in a mirror.

Common symbols: a short vertical line or dash is a chain; a small open circle is a space or hole; an x is a single crochet; a v is a double crochet; an n is a treble; and a square with a line through it is a cluster. The chart's key will give the exact ones it uses.

For a granny square starting from a magic ring, you may see something like 3 ch, 3 dc, sp, 3 dc, sp, 3 dc, sp, 3 dc. Work 3 double crochets into the ring, chain 1 for the corner space, then repeat three more times, and join with a slip stitch to the top of the first double crochet.

Round 2 has more spaces because there is a chain-1 space and a corner between each group of double crochets. Work 3 double crochets into the first group, chain 1, 3 double crochets into the corner space, chain 1, and continue around.

prompt: Explain how to read a crochet chart (the symbol kind, not written patterns). I'm left-handed, which every tutorial seems to ignore, and I'm working a granny square that starts from a magic ring.
response:
A chart is a map of stitches drawn with little symbols, not prose. You read it the same way you read a knitting chart: bottom to top, one row at a time.

Most crochet charts are read right to left because most crocheters are right-handed. Since you crochet left to right, turn the chart upside down and read it left to right.

Each symbol is one stitch, and one row of symbols is one round. A granny square starts from a magic ring, so the center ring is round one and the symbols for it sit at the bottom of the chart. A row of squares is a round of double crochet, and the first square is the foundation ring.

A line of symbols is read left to right. Each symbol represents one stitch, and the small numbers beneath the symbols tell you how many times to repeat each one. For example, if I see four symbols with 1, 4, 1, and 6 written beneath them, I’ll work 1 double crochet, 4 double crochets, 1 double crochet, and 6 double crochets in that order. The numbers beneath the symbols add up to the total number of stitches in that row.

If the design needs you to work over previous rounds, you’ll see arrows pointing up on the symbols. If the arrow’s end points to one of the symbols directly above, you’ll work over that symbol. If the arrow’s end points between two symbols, you’ll work over the space between them.

prompt: Explain how to read a crochet chart (the symbol kind, not written patterns). I'm left-handed, which every tutorial seems to ignore, and I'm working a granny square that starts from a magic ring.
response:
Start in the middle, not the corner. Granny squares grow outward from a ring, so the first round is the smallest square in the middle of the chart, and later rounds are the bigger squares around it. Each symbol usually means one stitch, and a ring of little squares is a space. The arrows point in the working direction, which for granny squares goes counter-clockwise.

Read right to left and bottom to top for most rows, the way you read a page. As a left-hander working in the same direction, you can read the chart normally; if you crochet in the opposite direction from the chart, read it left to right instead.

For a typical granny square, one round looks like a space, then three double crochets, then a space, then three double crochets, repeated four times, with a chain or slip stitch joining the ends.

Symbols that often show up in a granny square chart:

- Ch: a chain, a small loop with a tail.
- Sl st: a slip stitch, a line across a circle.
- Sc: single crochet, a short line across a circle.
- Hdc: half double crochet, a line crossing a circle at a small angle.
- Dc: double crochet, a taller line crossing a circle at an angle.
- Tre: treble crochet, a taller line with a cross on top.
- Sp: a space, usually shown as an empty square.

prompt: What's the difference between a cold process and a hot process soap batch, chemically? I make cold process and want to know whether hot process actually finishes saponification or just speeds it up.
response:
Nothing happens at the molecular level that cold process doesn't. The only difference is that the oil and lye are heated and mixed until the reaction visibly finishes, usually a few hours, instead of being poured at trace and finished by the soap sitting in the mold for about a week.

The real advantage is timing. Hot process soap is ready to cut and use after a day or two, and the oils can be used as-is without melting to a liquid, since the heating takes care of that. The trade-off is texture: soap made this way is often denser and less translucent than cold process, and the batch is harder to work because it thickens fast.

prompt: What's the difference between a cold process and a hot process soap batch, chemically? I make cold process and want to know whether hot process actually finishes saponification or just speeds it up.
response: Chemically nothing differs: both start with the same reaction, where an alkali splits each ester bond in a triglyceride, leaving glycerol and the sodium or potassium salts of the fatty acids, which are the soap. Cold process mixes oils and lye at room temperature and cures for about four weeks, during which saponification finishes and the water leaves. Hot process heats the batch to around 80-95 °C, and after a few hours nearly all the soap has already formed, so the bars are usable in a few days. Hot process isn't a different reaction, it just runs the same one to completion sooner.

prompt: What's the difference between a cold process and a hot process soap batch, chemically? I make cold process and want to know whether hot process actually finishes saponification or just speeds it up.
response:
Chemically almost nothing. Saponification is the reaction of a fat with a strong base, and it goes fast at room temperature. In cold process you mix at roughly 40 °C to 60 °C, pour into a mold, and the soap is fully saponified within a couple of days; the 4-week cure is for the water to evaporate and the bar to harden.

Hot process starts the same way, then heats the batch and stirs it for an hour or two until it thickens to a paste, which you then pour into molds. The heat and longer stirring finish the reaction in the pot, but the chemistry is the same. Hot process isn't necessary for saponification; its real advantages are speed and control.

prompt: I would like to understand why speedcubers lubricate their puzzles and why different viscosities are recommended for the core versus the pieces.
response:
If you put a drop of oil on your fingers and rub your hands together, you'll notice that your fingers stick together less. Oil, like any liquid, is a lubricant. It's a substance that reduces the friction between two surfaces.

Speedcubers lube their Rubik's Cubes to reduce the friction between the moving parts. Less friction means less force is needed to turn the cube, and this can make turning the cube faster and smoother. Some cubers also like to put a thin layer of tape on the pieces, which makes it so that you feel less of a "click" when a piece snaps into place.

There are two different kinds of lubricant used on Cubes: oil, which is thick and sticky, and water, which is thin and slippery. Oil and water are also sometimes called high-viscosity and low-viscosity lubricants.

Oil and water both reduce friction, but they do so in different ways. Water is thinner and slips easier, so it reduces friction between the sliding surfaces more. Oil is thicker and doesn't slip around as easily, so it doesn't reduce friction as much.

This is a problem for a Rubik's Cube, because the parts that you slide have to move, but the parts that are pressed together need to fit together tight. The center caps, for example, are screwed onto the core, and that joint needs to be tight, not slippery.

For this reason, speedcubers often use different types of lubricants on different parts of the Cube. Water is put on the sliding surfaces to reduce friction, and oil is put on the joints that need to be tight.

prompt: I would like to understand why speedcubers lubricate their puzzles and why different viscosities are recommended for the core versus the pieces.
response: A puzzle without any oil or grease feels a little rough, and the pieces tend to rattle, because the plastic has not been polished to a high enough quality. The plastic parts are not perfectly smooth and fit together in places with a small amount of friction. Speedcubers, who care about this kind of thing, use a lubricant like tri-flow oil to reduce friction between the parts. They like to use different oils with different viscosities (thicknesses) on different parts, because they want a bit of friction between the pieces and the core, so the puzzle holds together, and very little friction between the pieces themselves.

prompt: I would like to understand why speedcubers lubricate their puzzles and why different viscosities are recommended for the core versus the pieces.
response:
Friction causes the parts to stick to each other, and also causes the puzzle to feel rough when you turn it. Speedcubers use silicone oils, which have very low friction, to lubricate the puzzle, and this makes it turn more smoothly.

But the silicone oil also causes the parts to stick together less, so the parts are more likely to fall apart. A thicker oil is needed to keep the puzzle together, because there is more mass to keep in place. This means the core needs to be lubricated with a thicker oil than the outside pieces, which need less to keep them together.

prompt: My son (14) wants to get into model rocketry for a school project. I don't understand how the motors work or what the letters and numbers on them mean (like B6-4). Can you explain it so I can decide whether this is safe enough to say yes to?
response:
A model rocket motor is a small solid-fuel rocket, the same class of technology as the Space Shuttle's solid rocket boosters, just scaled down to fit in a pencil case. It's the same as the model airplanes, cars and ships people have been building for a hundred years.

A motor's label encodes three things. The first letter tells you how much fuel it contains, and that determines how much lift it can give: B is a tenth of an ounce of fuel, C is half an ounce, D is one ounce and so on. The number tells you its total impulse, which is the amount of force the motor can deliver and is measured in newton-seconds. A C6 motor has six newton-seconds of total impulse.

The last number is the delay, measured in seconds, between when the fuel is burned out and when the small explosive charge that separates the rocket from the motor is fired. That explosion ejects the parachute, which slows the rocket down so it can come back down without smashing into the ground. If you're trying to recover a rocket, you'll want to choose a motor whose delay is long enough for the rocket to climb to the top of its flight before it opens the parachute.

Model rockets aren't really dangerous, but you should follow the directions. Don't build your own motor, and don't try to fly one if it's raining or windy.

prompt: My son (14) wants to get into model rocketry for a school project. I don't understand how the motors work or what the letters and numbers on them mean (like B6-4). Can you explain it so I can decide whether this is safe enough to say yes to?
response:
It's a good first hobby, and the motors are less mysterious than the labels suggest.

A rocket motor is a sealed tube of solid fuel that burns in one direction. It starts when the launch controller sends a signal through a wire to a small igniter in the nozzle. The label is always a letter, a number and another number. The letter is the size class, and each step up has roughly twice the total fuel energy of the one before, from A at the small end through Q. The middle number is the average thrust in newtons over the burn, which lasts one or two seconds. The last number, after the hyphen, is the delay in seconds between the end of the burn and the ejection of the parachute. A B6-4 is about 3 newtons of thrust for around 1.5 seconds, or roughly 10 newton-seconds of total energy, which is the same as holding a kilo of weight up for 10 seconds, and it throws an 80-gram rocket to a few hundred metres.

At B or C, a rocket launches from an open field, stands off the pad and comes back on a parachute. The FAA treats model rockets as toys up to C, and D through F still need only an open area and an upward launch. G through M need a licensed site, but your son won't be there for years if he starts at B and works up.

For the project, use the official US model rocketry handbook and start with a kit that comes with its motor.

prompt: why do heat pumps get worse when it's really cold
response: A heat pump moves heat from outside air into your home, so the colder it is, the weaker the source. The capacity falls roughly with temperature, and the compressor works harder for each unit of heat, so efficiency drops too. Around the balance point, often near -5 C or -15 F, a conventional air-source unit may supply only half the house's heat load, and a resistance or gas backup takes over. Cold weather also causes frost to build on the outdoor coil, and periodic defrost cycles briefly reverse the flow, taking heat from indoors to melt it. Cold, dense air carries less heat per unit volume than warm air, and the lubricant oil in the compressor thickens, so both factors are real. Cold-climate heat pumps mitigate this with a bigger coil and a variable-speed compressor, which keeps capacity high down to about -25 C.

prompt: why do heat pumps get worse when it's really cold
response: A heat pump moves heat rather than making it, and it takes that heat from the outside air. In the cold there is less of it available, and the temperature gap between the outside and the inside it must lift it to grows. Each unit of electrical work lifts less heat, so the coefficient of performance drops from 3 or 4 to 1.5 or less. Some units are sized so that at their rated cold temperature they can no longer meet the load, and they switch on a resistance heater, which runs at exactly 1 and can triple the bill.

prompt: why do heat pumps get worse when it's really cold
response: A heat pump pulls heat out of outside air and moves it indoors, so it has to take heat from air that's already colder than the home. At 4°F, for example, that's harder than at 40°F, and it takes more work to move the same amount of heat, so efficiency drops, about 1 to 1.5 percent per degree Fahrenheit. Modern cold-climate models still work at -10°F or lower, though below that a backup electric heater usually takes over, and it's much less efficient.

prompt: My electricity bill shows a 'time of use' rate that's three times higher between 4 and 9pm. I get that demand is high then, but why does the price jump so much more than demand does? Is the power coming from different plants at that time?
response:
The jump is not about which plant generates the power. At any instant the whole grid balances generation and load, and electrons don't carry a label saying which generator produced them.

The jump is about how expensive it is to meet the last kilowatt of demand. Grid operators run plants in order of cost, starting with the cheapest sources. Cheap ones like wind, solar, hydro and nuclear run flat, so they're on all the time regardless of demand. Gas turbines, which are expensive per kilowatt but quick to start, cover the gaps. On a summer evening they're running near full capacity already, and the only way to serve more load is to start the most expensive peaker plants, which are run at very high cost to meet exactly these few peak hours.

The price of electricity is set by the cost of the most expensive plant that has to run to meet demand. That price applies to all the electricity sold at that instant, including yours, even if much of it comes from cheap sources. So a doubling of demand can cost much more than double, and a tripling of the price is plausible.

The reason your bill is shaped this way is that it encourages moving load like washing machines, dishwashers and electric cars off those few hours, which is where the system really struggles.

prompt: My electricity bill shows a 'time of use' rate that's three times higher between 4 and 9pm. I get that demand is high then, but why does the price jump so much more than demand does? Is the power coming from different plants at that time?
response:
Yes. A utility's average cost of a kilowatt-hour is roughly 5 or 10 cents, but the marginal cost of a kilowatt-hour is what it would cost to generate the last bit of power at that moment. Most of the time that's coal or nuclear, which is cheap, but during peak hours the grid operators have to run gas plants that are expensive and polluting. The cost of gas is only about 3 cents a kilowatt-hour, but it isn't a big deal if you're only running the gas plants part-time. So you get rates that average $7 but peak at $20.

The 4 to 9pm peak hours seem like a weird choice to me. That's when people are at work or coming home from work, so demand for electricity should be lower than it would be if those hours were, say, 1 to 6pm. But I think the idea is to get people to switch from running machines like washing machines at the usual 4 to 9pm time they do so to earlier or later. The idea isn't to make them stop using electricity during peak hours, but shift it. And the idea is to encourage people to buy machines that can run at off-peak times, like a water heater that heats the water when electricity is cheap.

prompt: My electricity bill shows a 'time of use' rate that's three times higher between 4 and 9pm. I get that demand is high then, but why does the price jump so much more than demand does? Is the power coming from different plants at that time?
response:
It is, in a sense. Electricity markets are often organized into blocks that are bid in, cleared, and settled every 15 minutes or every hour. In most markets, the bid from the marginal generator is the price for everyone. When demand spikes, the marginal generator switches from a cheap plant to an expensive one. At night, that might be a 20-cent-a-kWh gas peaker. It might also be a 60-cent-a-kWh gas peaker, which is 3 times more.

The same plant that's generating at 4am might be generating at 8pm. But the market clears at a higher price.

The bigger problem is that trees store carbon for only a few centuries, and wildfires, pests and logging release it again.
